## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, entire, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, very carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the most extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of the individual pages and indicating the subject treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal but possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with innumerable indexes, but especially with two immense and general ones: one, namely, of subjects, through consulting which one may see at a glance whatsoever not merely this or that Father, but each and every one of the Fathers without exception, has written on any subject whatever; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented upon the individual verses of each book of Scripture, from the first of Genesis to the last of Revelation. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the entire course of the work, the low price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works pertaining to all ages, places, languages, and forms.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology, after the likeness of the Church itself, consists of and is divided into two parts, one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The former, entirely printed, is immense in 219 volumes and sells for 1,100 francs. The Greek is subdivided and has been published in two typographical editions. The former contains the Greek text together with a parallel Latin translation and will perhaps exceed one hundred volumes. The latter presents this translation alone and will therefore be contained within about fifty volumes. Each Greek-Latin volume costs only eight francs; each purely Latin volume, five francs. Yet in either case, that is, in order to enjoy this benefit, the purchaser must take the complete collection, whether Eastern or Western; otherwise the size and difficulties of the individual volumes will result in differing prices.**

**Volume CCXVII of the Patrology, and, apart from the indexes, the final volume of the entire Latin Patrology.**

**Innocent III, Roman Pontiff.**

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, at the street called d’Amboise, near the Paris gate commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1855.

## Thirteenth Century

# Complete Works of Innocent III, Roman Pontiff

Distributed in four volumes. The first three contain Baluze’s recension of the Registers, with the addition of the books of unpublished letters, formerly sought in vain by Baluze from the Vatican Library and brought to light by La Porte du Theil and Bréquigny. The fourth volume contains letters circulating outside the Register, and finally the sermons and various minor works of the pontiff, both those long ago published and those more recently printed by the most eminent Cardinal Mai, Dom Luigi Tosti, etc., etc. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

**Volume Four. The four volumes cost 30 French francs.**

## [The Complete Works of Innocent III]

[Col. 0003]

# A Notice of the Greatest Importance to All the Catholic Clergy

Since in this highly arduous edition of more than 217 large-format volumes it could not but happen that we might sometimes have erred in printing, perhaps even in doctrine, certainly without our knowledge—for this is not the labor of a single day, but of many years—it is our duty to inform the clergy and learned men, as we hope they will not find unwelcome, that the text of this Collection, which is available in its entirety by means of stereotype plates, has long been reworked by us with repeated care and subjected to the test of a most exact revision. Thus we have removed the notice on Pope Leo I taken from Schoenemann, as well as certain judgments about Augustine made by persons of unsound opinion; and we shall carefully correct, or altogether suppress, other matters that require amendment. Thus future editions will appear purged and, insofar as possible, corrected. Meanwhile, to those who already possess our *Patrology*, as soon as any fault becomes known to us, we shall arrange to send a corrective sheet, with all expense of postage borne by ourselves.

Everyone knows what expense must arise from the laborious care involved in repeated, universal, and minutely detailed revision or purgation of books so numerous and so vast. Nevertheless, we count both anxieties and costs as very small matters, provided that the most exact correction of the texts, and above all the truth of orthodox doctrine, may be preserved intact.

The more important a work is, the more securely and without stumbling we ought to proceed through it. And what can be compared with the whole of Catholic tradition in printed and widely disseminated books?

May the irreproachable cleanliness of every page shine forth under the twofold aspect of typography and theology. This is our wish. Therefore we earnestly and publicly urge readers: if anyone should be offended by a blemish in the text or by a word contrary to sound faith, let him kindly report it to us without delay. It is our settled intention and firm will to count as nothing whatever loss of sleep or painstaking labor, if only we can make our most beloved *Patrology* wholly irreproachable in respect both of the clearness of all its texts and of the integrity of orthodox doctrine.

Yet, as we hope, little remains to be reformed. We may cite two suitable witnesses from the most learned Bollandist family, who declared in a letter sent to us from Brussels that, in examining our volumes, they had encountered nothing, or only minor matters, requiring censure. To their testimony may be added that of the superior general of a congregation pre-eminent in educating young men in theology, a man conspicuous alike for eminent learning, prudence, and gravity of character, who did not hesitate to call the *Patrology* “an immortal monument erected by us to ecclesiastical learning.”

For the reader’s satisfaction and edification, we are pleased to make known that the Doctors, Fathers, and Ecclesiastical Writers reprinted in the 217 volumes of the Latin *Patrology* number no fewer than 1,600 authors.

# Supplement to the Registers of Innocent III, Roman Pontiff

## I. To the Provost

[Note: [Col. 0009B]

He was probably Rheinard II, concerning whom the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 823, provide the following brief information:

“X. Rheinard II, in 1190, in a charter of Conrad II, bishop of Strasbourg (*Hist. Als.*, proofs, p. 29), concerning the collegiate church of Lauterbach.”

His successor, Albert, is not mentioned before 1202. See the note to Letter VIII of Book Eight.]

To the Dean

[Note: [Col. 0009B]

Concerning the deans of the Cathedral Church of Strasbourg around the period with which we are dealing, very little is found in the authors cited above, ibid., col. 827:

“VI. Frivo, or Frico, 1178 and 1183. See Bishop Henry’s charter for the foundation of the Priory of Rubiacum.

“VII. Wernard, 1218, in Bishop Henry’s charter concerning the church of St. Arbogast.”]

and canons of the Cathedral Church of Strasbourg.—He confirms to them the prebend resigned by F., provost of St. Thomas. (1198; Lateran, March 2.)

[BRÉQUIGNY and LA PORTE DU THEIL, Appendix to the Registers of Innocent, vol. III, p. 1065. From a copy carefully collated by M. Grandidier with the original preserved in the archives of the Cathedral Church of Strasbourg.]

[Col. 0009A]

When parties agree together concerning a dispute that has arisen, or one of them renounces the dispute, the judge’s only necessary office is to cause what has been done by the parties to be observed inviolably, lest anyone be permitted thereafter to proceed contrary to a settlement or relinquishment made of his own accord. Certainly, when our beloved sons Arnold,

[Col. 0009B]

your messenger and fellow canon, and F., provost of St. Thomas,

[Note: [Col. 0009C] His name was Frederick, as M. Grandidier informed us from documentary evidence.]

had come before us, they disputed in our presence and in the hearing of our brethren concerning a prebend with which the same provost had been invested through our beloved son P., cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia,

[Note: [Col. 0009C]

Peter, a nobleman of Piacenza, was made cardinal deacon of the title of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano by Pope Lucius III on Ash Wednesday in the year of restored salvation 1185, in the third creation according to Ciaconius, but in 1184, in the second, according to Panvinio, Aubery, and others. He was afterward named cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia by Pope Clement III. Under Pope Celestine III he served as legate in Sicily, and under Pope Innocent III likewise fulfilled a third legation in Germany. He died under Innocent. Floravantes Martinellus declares him to have belonged to the Diana family, on the authority of Umberto Locati’s *Chronicle of Piacenza*. Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1120.]

then legate of the Apostolic See. When we,

[Col. 0010A]

having heard the arguments advanced on either side, wished, by the common counsel of our brethren, to formulate and pronounce judgment, the said provost approached us humbly and devoutly and voluntarily resigned into our hands whatever right he might have in that prebend. Therefore, desiring henceforth to provide for the peace and tranquility of your church, we have accepted his resignation, imposed perpetual silence upon him concerning that prebend, and, by authority of these presents, have released you and your church from his claim regarding it. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Nones of March [March 2], in the first year of our pontificate.

## II. To Matthew, Abbot of St. Nicholas of the Meadows at Ribemont, Diocese of Laon

[Note: [Col. 0010B]

Matthew I, an abbot of proven integrity, shone in the splendor of his virtues from at least 1197 until 1225. He was so highly esteemed by the countess of Blois, lady of Ribemont, Soissons, etc., that in 1225 she entrusted her treasures, gold, and necklaces to him for safekeeping.

He obtained from Pope Celestine III a catalogue of the possessions in 1197; another fifteen months later from Pope Innocent III—this is the very one here published; and a third from Pope Honorius III in 1224. Taken from the midst of his community’s immense grief, he was buried beneath a stone in the chapel of Blessed Mary, where the sacristy now stands. When his tomb was opened and moved before the choir door, it revealed the bones and very large skull of a tall man; indeed, the bones of his thighs measured twenty-two inches.]

—They are received under the protection of St. Peter, and their possessions are enumerated. (1198; Lateran, March 18.)

[We publish this bull from a copy transcribed from folio 9 verso of the cartulary of the monastery of St. Nicholas of the Meadows and deposited in our collection by M. Grenier. He also added this note: “This bull confirms the stability of the religious who had made profession in the abbey of St. Nicholas in that monastery, unless it be in order to embrace a stricter state; presentation to benefices; permission to grant burial to those who desire it, provided that they are neither excommunicated nor interdicted; election of an abbot by the community, his blessing and installation, without requiring either a palfrey or a silk cope, since such an exaction amounts to simony.” BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0011A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MATTHEW, abbot of St. Nicholas of the Meadows, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness should either turn them back from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion.

[Col. 0011B]

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; and, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Adrian, Alexander, Urban, and Celestine, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St. Nicholas of the Meadows, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods this monastery justly and canonically possesses at present, or may hereafter acquire, through the grants of pontiffs, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help,

[Col. 0011C]

shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to express the following by their proper names.

Namely, the place itself, free from every advocacy claimed by the successors of the noble man Anselm of blessed memory, the founder of the place,

[Note: [Col. 0011C]

Anselm, second of that name, son of Anselm, count of Ribemont, of most noble royal stock descended from the princes of Vermandois. Having first founded the monastery of Anchin, and having restored to Saint-Vincent the estates and rights which he had seized by force, he founded this monastery of the Meadows near his paternal domain in 1083. The charter of foundation is found in the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 189, Instrument III. In the following year he procured its confirmation by the authority of King Philip, then staying at Ribemont. See ibid., Instrument IV.]

with all its appurtenances, in the liberty which the same Anselm granted to that place from motives of devotion; the whole village adjoining it,

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Called Luciacus, in French Lucy. See the document cited above.]

with oven and mill, pasture, woods, water, fishing, meadows, ban and jurisdiction; the church of St. Germanus of Ribemont, with the adjoining treasury and school,

[Col. 0012A]

the parish of St. Peter, with its other appurtenances; the altar of Fontaines,

[Note: [Col. 0011D] In French, Fontaine-Notre-Dame.]

with three parts of the greater tithe of the same village, the entire lesser tithe, and all revenues and offerings of that place, except those offered to the priest in the celebration of his Mass; the altars of Bohain;

[Note: [Col. 0011D] In French, Bohain.]

the altars of Réteuil;

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Réteuil.]

the altars of Villers,

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Alternatively, *de Villari sicco*; in French, Villers-le-Sec.]

with all their appurtenances, which Simon of blessed memory,

[Note: [Col. 0011D]

Simon I of Vermandois, of royal descent, son of Hugh the Great, count of Vermandois and son of King Henry I, was elected or consecrated bishop of Noyon around the year

[Col. 0012C]

1123 and presided until 1143. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1000.]

formerly bishop of Noyon, gave to your church,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] In 1130 Simon gave the altar of Mont Benchien to the church of Bohain. Ibid., col. 1001.]

and which his successor Baldwin

[Note: [Col. 0012D]

In 1148, as may be read in Sigebert’s *Chronicle*: “Simon, the glorious pontiff of Noyon, ended his days at Seleucia; Baldwin of Boulogne succeeded him.” He was abbot: first, of Cugny in the diocese of Noyon; second, of Châtillon in the diocese of Langres. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of May [May 4], 1167. Ibid.]

afterward confirmed by his own charter; the land called Tassigny,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] In French, Tasigni; a place later united with Luciacus, French Lucy.]

with pasture, woods, water, fishing, meadows, ban and jurisdiction; the altar of Tenelle,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Tenelle.]

with its endowment; the village called Montigny,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Montigny-en-Arrouaise.]

except for the sixteenth

[Col. 0012B]

part of the common allod and half of Fulcheric’s land; the altar of that village, with the whole tithe, lesser as well as greater; at the village called Fieulaines,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Fieulaines.]

the whole greater and lesser tithe, with the land of Merallu, eleven *modii* of grain, one *modius* of peas, and three solidi of currency, which you receive yearly from the church of St. Foillan at the feast of St. Remigius; in the church of Clairfontaine, six *modii* of grain and one sextary; at the village called Dercis,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Dercis, in the diocese of Laon.]

the altar with two parts of the greater tithe and the whole lesser tithe; in the village called Leheries,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Leheries, in Thiérache.]

the entire land of a certain knight Christian; the land called Oger’s Meadow; one fourth of the same village; the land of Militricis,

[Col. 0012C]

which you hold from Rainier of Saints; at the village called Torsy,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Torsy, in the parish of Ribemont.]

the altar with its entire greater and lesser tithe; the land of the knight Ralph; the land of Gilbert Rasi; the land of St. Peter of Hunoncourt; and all the *guionage* which Ingeram of blessed memory, father of the late Ralph of Coucy, gave you, free and unencumbered; the altar of Chevresis,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Chevresis.]

with its endowment and one fourth of the same village, together with the entire greater and lesser tithe of that estate; in the village called Régicourt,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Régicourt.]

the land which Guido Cato gave you, with water, fishing, and pasture, by permission of his lord Guido

[Col. 0013A]

of Supy; the mill-site which Philip gave you, by permission of his lord Bliard; at the village called Andigny,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Andigny, a village near Guise.]

six *modii* of grain which the church of St. Martin of Laon owes you yearly and must transport at its own expense to your storehouse; in the village called Remies,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Remies.]

fifteen solidi of good coin, which the church of Blessed Mary of Laon owes you yearly at the feast of All Saints; the village called Monceaux,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Monceaux-le-Vieux.]

which Anselm, former lord of Ribemont, gave you, with ban, oven, and jurisdiction, and half the mill and half the fishpond; the land of Bardonroy, half of whose land-rent you freely receive, while Rainier of Guise receives the other half,

[Col. 0013B]

and from Rainier’s share you pay the church of St. Vincent of Laon three *modii* of grain yearly; in Flanders, at the village called Lo, one sheepfold and more; at Lecca, half a sheepfold; at Chevenses, five *modii* of grain, paid by Ralph of Hussel; the altar of Parpes,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Parpes-la-Ville, in the diocese of Laon, near Ribemont.]

with its appurtenances; the land which Walter, knight of Aines, gave you; one fourth of the land of Vargicourt,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Vargicourt, about which nothing is known today.]

near Ribemont; likewise, in Flanders, at the village called Lecca, the land of Morostralis and the tithe of seven *lots*; at Fressenat, half a mark and half a *fertón*; at Wallas, eleven solidi; and half the village called Puisieux,

[Col. 0013C]

both woodland and arable land, which Alberic Waler, Fredebert of Saints, and his son Gerard bestowed upon you.

Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands. You may also receive into conversion clergy or laypersons who are free and released from obligations, fleeing from the secular world, and retain them without any contradiction. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without the leave of his abbot, except for the purpose of entering a stricter religious order; and no one may presume to retain those departing without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict is laid upon the land, you may,

[Col. 0013D]

with doors closed, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells, celebrate divine offices in a low voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may elect your own priests; if they are suitable, the diocesan bishop to whom you present them shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they owe accountability to him in spiritual matters and to you

[Col. 0014A]

in temporal matters. Moreover, by apostolic authority, we strictly forbid anyone to pronounce upon you or your church a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause, or to impose upon you or your people new or unlawful exactions. We further decree that the cemetery of that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving, however, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of subreption or violence,

[Col. 0014B]

except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St. Benedict, shall provide to be elected. Moreover, under pain of excommunication, we strictly forbid anyone to dare demand or presume to extort from your abbot-elect for the time being, on account of his blessing or of conducting or installing him in his seat, under pretext of any custom, a palfrey, a silk cope, or anything else, since such a demand reeks of the depravity of simony. In addition, we decree by this present ordinance that the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to your monastery by kings, princes, and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, and the ancient and reasonable customs observed hitherto, shall remain whole and inviolate.

We therefore decree, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian,

## III. To the … Bishop of Soissons

[Note: [Col. 0015D] See the note to Letter XI of Book Three.]

and the … Abbot

[Note: [Col. 0015D] Robert IV governed the monastery of St. Germanus of the Meadows from 1192 until at least 1204. See new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 46.]

of St. Germanus of the Meadows at Paris.—That they are to protect and defend the abbot and convent of St. Denis against the bishop of Auxerre and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as lay. (1198; Rome, St. Peter’s, April 29.)

[Ibid., p. 1066, from the archives of the monastery of St. Denis.]

The beloved son … the Abbot

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

We have already dealt with the abbot of St. Denis in the notes to Letter XLV of Book Three. Yet this letter must certainly be compared with another, Book I, no. 179, dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [May 21], in which the pope confirms Hugh, then elect, as abbot. How the pope could here call him abbot before his confirmation is not easily understood.]

and convent of St. Denis submitted a petition to us, stating that our venerable brother … bishop of Auxerre,

[Note: [Col. 0016D] See the note to Letter XX of Book Three.]

and the beloved son … abbot of Lagny,

[Note: [Col. 0016D] See the note to Letter CXXXVII of Book Five.]

the noble man Theobald, count of Troyes, M. of Montmorency,

[Col. 0015C]

the mayor of Étampes, and others, secular as well as ecclesiastical persons of the province of Sens, are gravely troublesome and injurious to them and their church concerning possessions, villages, tithes, lands, woods, their men, and many other matters. They also invade the rights and possessions of their people and presume violently to usurp them. Therefore by apostolic letters we command your discretion, after summoning the parties and hearing the arguments put forward on both sides, to decide what is just, without appeal, and to cause what you judge to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. Should witnesses whom they call to establish their case withdraw through favor, hatred, or fear, so as not to bear testimony

[Col. 0015D]

to the truth, you shall compel them by ecclesiastical discipline, without appeal. If both of you cannot be present in carrying this out, you, bishop, shall nevertheless execute it.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of May [April 29], in the first year of our pontificate.

## IV. To Florentius, Abbot, and the Brethren of the Monastery of the Field of Blessed Mary

—He confirms their possessions and privileges. (1198; Rome, St. Peter’s, May 4.)

[ERHARD, *Regesta historiae Westfaliae*, Münster, 1847, quarto; *Codex diplomaticus*, p. 253. From a copy in the archive of Marienfeld, collated with the original, of which only fragments survive.]

[Col. 0016A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FLORENTIUS, abbot of the Monastery of the Field of Blessed Mary, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0016B]

It is fitting that those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness should either turn them back from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery in the Field of Blessed Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God, the Rule of St. Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help,

[Col. 0016C]

shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to express the following by their proper names.

The site itself on which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the estate at Hoswinkele, Honhart, Bleskenvorth, Brinchus, Brochus, Mattenhem, Middelseten, Rehey, Bellethe, Osthus, Menlage, Provestinhus, Niehof, Erthburg, Lutterhus, Meppeteslo, Tetinctorpe, Sletbruge, Bucheslo, Heminchus, Widenbrugge, Lindincsele, Culinthorpe, Bulte, Honlo; the mill at Sletbrugge; [Col. 0016D] Ripen, Givetenhorst, Herlage, Bokey, Pilichem; the tithe at Tetthen; the tithe at Berse; Honlo; properties in Frisia; Bilevelde. Likewise Tetinctorpe, Spechishart, Hemmincsile, Watherhus, Garthus, Caldehof, Alrebike, Berehornyn, Sculenburch, Oynchusen, Werse, Sunninchusen, Ostenuelde, Bechin, Stapellage [Col. 0017A] with all appurtenances; Vnkinthorpe with all appurtenances; Silehurst, Othelinchusen, Popinclisen, Catislare, Bobinthorpe, Bovinchusen, Bulthen; the mill at Bulthe; Bellete, Berehorn, Hohurst, Pichenhurst; likewise Catislare, Catinstort, Osthus, Vectorp, Herthe, Berchsethe, Veslero, Wchlo, Wrthen, Dagehusen; Bertram’s house near Telget; a holding at Jesechin; the holding of Albert of Susat; Spurcha; and the other things which Hermann, formerly bishop of Münster, of happy memory; Widekind, advocate of Rethe, and his mother Luttrudis; Bernard of Lippa; and Widekind of Waldeke with his brothers—the founders of your monastery—have justly and reasonably conferred upon you for the remedy of their souls, together with vineyards, lands, woods and thickets, [Col. 0017B] in woodland and plain, roads, trackless places, and paths, meadows, pastures, marshes, hunting-rights, waters, fisheries, ponds, fishponds, mills, vineyards, peat-bogs, mountains, hills, valleys, and other things.

Moreover, from the produce of your labours, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, or from your gardens, thickets, and fisheries, or from the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and released from secular life, who flee the world, and retain them without any opposition.

[Col. 0017C]

Furthermore, we forbid that any one of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, may lawfully leave that place without the permission of his abbot. No one may dare retain one who departs without security furnished by letters of the community. If anyone should presume to retain him, you may pronounce regular discipline against such persons, whether monks or conversi. We strictly prohibit anyone from personally receiving, or in any manner alienating, lands or any benefice of your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we decree them void. We further prohibit any monk or conversus bound by profession in your house, without consent of the abbot or the better part of your chapter, from acting as surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone [Col. 0017D] beyond the amount established by the prudent determination of your chapter, unless for the manifest benefit of your house. Should anyone nevertheless presume to do so, the convent shall not be obliged in any respect to answer for it.

Furthermore, in your own causes, whether involving a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brethren, lest through lack of witnesses your right should suffer loss in any respect. Moreover, by apostolic authority, we prohibit any bishop or other person from compelling you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit your property or possessions to secular judgment; nor may anyone presume to come to your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, hear cases, or convene public assemblies, [Col. 0018A] or impede the regular election of your abbot, or interfere in any manner, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in instituting or removing the person who at the time holds that office.

But if the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when duly requested with fitting humility and devotion, refuses to bless the appointed abbot and to confer upon you the other things belonging to episcopal office, that abbot may, provided that he is a priest, bless his own novices, exercise the other functions pertaining to his office, and receive from another bishop all things which have been improperly denied him by your own bishop. We add that, in receiving professions presented by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, the bishops shall be satisfied [Col. 0018B] with the form and wording established from the origin of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must make profession with their Order preserved, and must not be compelled to make any profession contrary to their Order’s statutes.

For consecrations of altars or churches, for holy oil, or for any other ecclesiastical sacrament, no one may dare extort anything from you under pretext of custom or in any other way; rather, the diocesan bishop shall supply all these things to you without charge. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer, provided that he possesses the favour and communion of the Apostolic See; relying upon our authority, he shall supply what is requested. Should the see of the diocesan bishop happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical [Col. 0018C] sacraments from neighbouring bishops, provided that no prejudice thereby be created in future against your own bishops.

Because you do not always have access to your own bishops, if a bishop in communion with the Roman See, as stated above, and fully known to you, should happen to pass through your territory, you may, by authority of the Apostolic See, receive from him blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks. But if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce in your monastery, or against persons established there, a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict—even against your hired labourers because you have not paid tithes [Col. 0018D], or on account of anything granted to you by apostolic favour; or against your benefactors because they have charitably provided you with benefits or services, or helped you labour on days when you work and others keep holiday—we decree that sentence void, as having been issued against grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall any letters have force which are shown to have been obtained while concealing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges.

Moreover, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide hereafter for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, [Col. 0019A] shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to use violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the privilege of this document, all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain things removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be kept whole, for every use benefiting those for whose governance and support they were granted, [Col. 0019B] saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to the Lord’s vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0019C] O LORD, SHOW ME A SIGN FOR GOOD.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop-cardinal of Ostia and Velletri.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s . . . , [lacuna] acting in place of the chancellor, on the fourth Nones of May [4 May], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198, in the pontificate . . . .

### V. To the abbot and brethren of Cluny.—Confirmation concerning the estate of Mercurey.  
*(A.D. 1198; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 4 May.)*

*[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, 1497.]*

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Cluny: greeting [Col. 0019D] and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and protect by the patronage of this document, for you and, through you, for your church, the grange at Mercurey which our beloved son, the nobleman Theobald, count [Col. 0020A] of Troyes, has charitably granted you with all its appurtenances, just as you possess it lawfully and without dispute. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this charter of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 4 Non. May [4 May], in the first year of our pontificate.

### VI. To the master and brethren of the House of God at Provins.—He confirms to them possession of a prebend in the church of Saint Quiriacus.  
*(A.D. 1198; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 11 May.)*

*[From a copy transcribed from the archive of the Hospital of Provins and preserved in our charter repository, with this note: “Collated with the original, on parchment eight inches and four lines wide by seven inches high, excluding the lower fold, by me the undersigned; at Provins, 3 January 1785. S. D. Balthelemi.” “The lead seal, attached with red and yellow silk threads, bears, on one side, in initial letters: INNOCENTIUS PP. III; on the other, the heads of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, with these letters above: S. P. A. S. P. E.” BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]*

[Col. 0020B]

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and bring to effect, by the result that follows, wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. [Col. 0020C] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, readily assenting to your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority and protect by the patronage of this document the prebend which you hold in the church of Saint Quiriacus, with the small portions of bread, wine, and money, and everything belonging to it, just as you possess it lawfully and peaceably. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this charter of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth Ides of May [11 May], in the first year of [Col. 0020D] our pontificate.

### VII. To Ranulf

[Note: [Col. 0019D]

The authors of the *new Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 444, state from documents that Peter V, the predecessor of Ranulf, abbot of Aurillac, remained in office until 1195. They seem not to have known in what year Ranulf himself began his rule, since they report only these few things about him:

“XXII. Ranulf is said to have died in 1203; I do not deny this at all. Certainly Gerald, his successor, was already presiding in 1204. But that Ranulf presided for twenty-two years is shown false by the foregoing statements concerning Peter V. He is said to lie in the Chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene.”

That Ranulf had already held the abbatial staff from the year 1198 is established by this letter of our Pope Innocent III.]

, abbot of the monastery of Aurillac, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.—He confirms to them their goods and possessions.  
*(A.D. 1198; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 13 May.)*

*[Ibid. From a copy preserved in the charter repository established by royal command for collecting documents concerning French affairs. The degree of confidence due to this copy is shown by the notes appended at the end, written in the vernacular language.]*

[Col. 0021A]

Although by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See we are debtors to all the children of holy Church, it is fitting that we apply a more earnest zeal of charity to those places and persons which adhere more specially to the Roman Church, and cherish them in the bosom of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; following in the footsteps of Pope Innocent, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of the Prince of the Apostles himself the aforesaid monastery of Aurillac, in which you are devoted to divine service, which Saint [Col. 0021B] Gerald, confessor of Christ, is known to have built in the honour and name of the Prince of the Apostles and offered to the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0021D] See the authors of the *new Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 438.]; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now lawfully and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of popes, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among them we have judged it proper to specify the following by name:

Kariacum, Soliacum, Varinium, Asperim Salientem, Espaniacum; the abbey of Mauzzien; the abbey [Col. 0021C] of Buxa, with all their appurtenances; Pauliacum; the place of Saint Peter of the Bank; the church of Polignac; the churches of Saint Pantaleon and Saint Paul of Toron Castle; the church of Valairac; the church of Calcis; the church of Saint Mary of Glenic, with the chapel of Serveria, which is known to belong to it by parochial right; the church of Saint Nazarius of Busmangis; the chapel of Saint Mary of Galasangis; the church of Saint Projectus of Romegos; the church of Saint Marcellinus of Ebreduno; the church of Saint Matthew of Saleru; the church of Fonte Gaiferio; the church of Saint Marcellinus of Valleveneria; Dalmariacum; the church of Saint Peter of Mota; the churches of Saint Mary, Saint [Col. 0021D] Andrew, and Saint John of Buichanna; the church of Saint John of Castello Fano; the church of Saint Peter of Cavanhaco; the church of Saint Mary of Beurcirias; the church of Saint Martin of Lechas; and the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Christopher of Angusta, with all their appurtenances.

[Col. 0022A]

They shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders, as well as of clerics belonging to the same monastery, from the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated, provided these bishops have been canonically ordained, possess the communion and favour of the Apostolic See, and are willing to provide these things freely and without improper payment. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. Furthermore, we decree that the monastery itself, its abbots, the governors of its places, and its monks shall be secure from every imposition of secular service and free from every burden of worldly oppression; diligent and peaceful in observing holy religion, they shall be subject in no respect or circumstance to anyone else—not to bishop or prince—but only to the Roman and Apostolic See, whose right they are.

[Col. 0022B]

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of subreption or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, determine should be elected. The person elected shall receive the gift of blessing from the Roman pontiff.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain things removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be kept unimpaired and whole, for every use benefiting those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token of this liberty received [Col. 0022C] from the Roman Church, they shall pay to us and our successors each year ten solidi of the old Poitevin currency. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, [Col. 0022D] so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

Thus signed below:

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Otomanus [Note: [Col. 0021D] “Otomanus.” Thus it is expressly read in the copy communicated to us by M. Vachez de Bourg-Lange. [Col. 0022D] (See the notes written in the vernacular.) But Octavianus should unquestionably be read. For the bishop of Ostia and Velletri at that time was Octavianus, whom we have already discussed in the notes to Letter XI of Book III.], bishop of Ostia and Velletri.

And in the same bull, in a certain circle and around the circumference of the circle, these words appear: “O Lord, show me a sign for good.”

And in the centre of the circle, below a square cross: Saint [Col. 0023A] Peter. Saint Paul. Pope Innocent III.

And in the first part of the bull, farther below:

I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0023A]

Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary. Here a new cardinal of the Holy Roman Church appears, if the copy of M. Vacher de Bourg-Lange deserves credence. [Col. 0023B] For no Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary, appears in Ciaconius or Oldoinus. Yet we fear that an error was made in transcribing the copy. What the title of Saint Mary is, we confess ourselves wholly ignorant. From Ciaconius, Panvinio, Aubery, and others, we know the title of Saint Mary in Trastevere, belonging to a priest-cardinal; and the titles of Saint Mary in Portico, Saint Mary in Aquiro, Saint Mary in Cosmedin, and finally Saint Mary in Via Lata, belonging to deacon-cardinals. But we nowhere read of the title of Saint Mary, stated simply. Indeed, we do not know whether there ever existed at Rome a church of the Blessed Mary called without any distinguishing epithet. Certainly, although we know of about seventy-nine churches or chapels dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God, none bears simply the name of Blessed Mary; all are distinguished by some epithet.

Indeed, Guido—of whom we wrote in the note to Letter [Col. 0023C] XXVIII of Book III—cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary in Trastevere; Nicholas—of whom we write below in note 61—cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin; and another Peter—of whom we wrote in the note to Letter XX of Book III—cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata, are found subscribed here. That the cardinal-deacons of the titles of Saint Mary in Portico and Saint Mary in Aquiro are not also found subscribed here presents no difficulty, since in documents of this kind not all cardinals whom history records as living, and even residing at Rome, at the time the documents were issued are ever found subscribed. Why should this be so, when authorities report that at the beginning of the pontificate of Innocent III presently under discussion they had discharged the office of legate, whether in Cisalpine Gaul or in Umbria? There remains, then, that Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary stated simply—of both his cardinalate and title the authorities preserve profound silence. [Col. 0023D] What then? Should “of the title of Saint Cecilia” be read? For we know that Peter—of whom we wrote in the note to Letter XXII of Book III—cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, was present at the election of Pope Innocent III. And indeed we shall shortly see Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, subscribed first among the order of priest-cardinals at the end of another diploma of the same sort, issued by Innocent III in the same year. In it we read nearly the same cardinals subscribed in nearly the same order as in the letter or bull now under discussion; there the name of Peter, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Cecilia, occupies the place of the name of Peter, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary, stated simply.] .

I, Philip, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscania [Note: [Col. 0023D] Philip, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscania. Here too the copyist erred. John, not Philip, should unquestionably be read. [Col. 0024A] From authorities and documents we have ascertained that the bishop who at that time held jointly the mitres of Viterbo and Tuscania [Col. 0024B] was named John, not Philip. See what we have noted on Letter CXVII of Book VI.]. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus [Note: [Col. 0024B] See the note to Letter XXVIII of Book III.]. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0024B]

“Equitius” must be supplied. We have already discussed Hugh, otherwise Hugutio, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Silvester and Martin *in Equitio*, in the note to Letter XLI of Book III. Concerning the title *Equitii*, attached to the church of Saints Silvester and Martin, the *Liber Pontificalis*, vol. I, p. 78, says:

“This man [Pope Saint Silvester] built in the city of Rome a church on the estate of one of his priests, surnamed Equitius; he established that title beside the Baths of Domitian, and it is called the title of Equitius to this day.”

Vignolius, however, in his notes in the same place:

“Panvinio identifies this title, Equitius, with the title or church of Saints Silvester and Martin in Montibus, which Pope Symmachus, as is said in his life, built from its foundations.”]

.

And farther below:

[Col. 0024A] I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill [Note: [Col. 0024C] See the note to Letter LXXXIII of Book V.].

And on the other side of the said bull was written:

I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. 0024C] Master Gratian, a Pisan, pro-chancellor and subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, was sent as legate to England by Pope Alexander III. According to Baronius, when King Henry II of England uttered many threats, Gratian answered him very severely and resisted him steadfastly. Therefore Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, gave him high praise as he returned to Rome from England, as an example to those who undertake before kings the handling of matters of this kind on behalf of the Apostolic See. Alexander made Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, after he had excellently discharged the English legation, and sent him again as legate to Normandy in order to subject the kingdom and king of England to interdict because of the murder of Saint Thomas of Canterbury. Having been made cardinal, he was the constant companion, in their travels, both of Alexander and of his successors, the Roman pontiffs; and he subscribed to a diploma granted by Alexander [Col. 0024D] to the monastery of Saint Mary of Organo and to many letters of different Roman pontiffs. He lived until the time of Innocent III and, after Celestine III, sought the supreme pontificate for himself. The registers of Innocent III and Honorius III mention him. Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1096.]. I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian [Note: [Col. 0024D] See the note to Letter LXXXIII of Book V.]. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Gregory at the Golden Veil [Note: [Col. 0024D] See the note to Letter LX of Book VII.]. I, Nicholas, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin [Note: [Col. 0024D] Nicholas Bobo, a Roman and, according to Panvinio, nephew of Celestine III, was made cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin by that pope and was present when the same Roman pontiff enrolled John Gualbert, founder of the monks of Vallombrosa, among the company of saints. He confirmed letters of Celestine himself, given on 3 March 1191 to Bentivolo, bishop of Gubbio; in 1192 to Mary, abbess of the Florentine monastery of Saint Peter Major, and to the abbot of Saint Mary in Flumine; and in 1196 to the church of Saint Peter of Modena. [Col. 0025D] He also subscribed letters of Innocent III written in 1199 to the Lateran Church. He died under the same Innocent. Oldoinus on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1166.]. [Col. 0025A] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo [Note: [Col. 0025D] See the note to Letter XXIX of Book V.]. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata [Note: [Col. 0025D] See the note to Letter XX of Book III.].

And below, in sequence, was written:

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting in place of the chancellor, on the third Ides of May [13 May], in the first indiction, in the year 1098 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

To all those who shall see these present letters: Guillaume de la Salle, Doctor of Decretals and Licentiate in Laws, Lieutenant-General of the noble and powerful lord, Sir Josselin du Boys, knight, [Col. 0025B] lord of Chabanet, counsellor and chamberlain of the King our lord, and his bailli of the Mountains of Auvergne, greeting. Be it known that today, on the date of these presents, we have seen, held, and read word for word, and caused to be seen and examined by the undersigned and signed notaries, certain letters patent in the form of apostolic bulls, sealed with lead and attached by yellow and red silk laces or cords in the manner of the Roman court, sound and entire in seal and writing. Their tenor is as follows:

“To RANNULF, abbot of the Aurelian monastery, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

‘Although to all the children of holy Church . . . ,’ etc.”

[Col. 0025C] Done and given in judgment in the court of the said bailliage sitting at Aurillac, in the form of a *vidimus*, and granted by us, lieutenant of the aforesaid lord, commissioner in this matter, to the most reverend father in God, Sir Cesare Borgia [Note: [Col. 0025D] A passage most worthy of notice. It concerns that famous son of Pope Alexander VI, Cesare Borgia, surnamed Valentino. From Ciaconius and others, we know that Cesare, elected archbishop of Valencia and cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary Nova, was created by Pope Alexander VI on Friday, 21 August 1493, in the second creation. But [Col. 0026D] that he held the abbey of Aurillac, in whatever manner or under whatever title, is not so well known. Certainly, in the series of abbots of Aurillac supplied by the authors of the *new Gallia Christiana*, the name of this cardinal does not appear at all. Indeed, that series seems somewhat confused in its chronological notices around the period now in question. It does not accord with the purpose of our undertaking to linger further in reconciling difficulties of this kind; see *Gallia Christiana nova*, II, 445.], cardinal of Saint Mary Nova, commendatory abbot of the Abbey of Aurillac, who so requests through Master Guillaume Couhfe, his procurator, against Brother Hugues de Malesses; and, because of the latter’s default and contumacy, to avail and serve the said de Borgia according to the contents of the royal letters of our commission, on 27 January 1494. On the following 3 February, Master Étienne Maubert, [Col. 0025D] in the name and as duly authorized procurator of the said de Malesses, appeared in judgment before us, the aforesaid lieutenant and commissioner, requesting to be heard, to see the original, and to be present at the collation. Notwithstanding the said proceeding, after hearing the parties in his presence, this present [Col. 0026A] *vidimus* has again been granted to the said petitioner as above.

(Thus signed.) G. DE LA SALLE, the aforesaid lieutenant and commissioner.

The collation was made by us, the aforesaid lieutenant and commissioner, together with the undersigned notaries, in the presence of Master Étienne Maubert, procurator of the said de Malesses, and granted to the said petitioner, to avail him against the said de Malesses according to the contents of the said letters contained in our commission.

(Thus signed.) P. CLERICI, present at this.

P. DE PODIO, present at this.

Collated by us, Jean-Charles Vacher de Bourg-l’Ange, lord of Bourg-l’Ange, advocate at the Parlement, charged with the orders of the [Col. 0026B] Keeper of the Seals of France, with the original held in the archives of the Abbey of Aurillac, on a parchment thirteen and a half inches long by twenty and a half inches wide. No fragment of the seal remains; only the tongue cut in the parchment, to which it had been attached. At Aurillac, 12 November 1786.

Signed, J. C. VACHER DE BOURG-L’ANGE.

### VIII. To Robert

[Note: [Col. 0026D] See the note to Letter 3, above.]

, abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris, and his brethren.—He receives them under protection and confirms their goods and possessions. Furthermore, by apostolic authority he confirms the agreement concluded between them and Guy, archbishop of Sens. The instrument of the agreement is included.  
*(A.D. 1198; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 14 May.)*

*[Ibid., p. 1070, from a copy carefully transcribed by M. Poirier from the autograph preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Denis.]*

[Col. 0026C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

From the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See we have been placed, though unworthy, by the Lord’s disposition, in order that we may willingly admit just petitions and endeavour to grant them a beneficial effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the authority of this present document, the monastery [Col. 0026D] of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, in which you are devoted to divine service, and which properly belongs to the right of blessed Peter, following the example of the Roman pontiffs Paschal, Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Anastasius, Alexander, Lucius, [Col. 0027A] Urban, Clement, and Celestine, our predecessors of happy memory. We decree first that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. By the text of this present privilege [Col. 0027B] we confirm in perpetuity for you and your successors that whatever liberty or dignity has been conferred upon your monastery by the privilege of Saint Germanus and by the charters of Childebert, Clothar, and other kings of the Franks shall remain unimpaired to it.

Furthermore, wishing to adorn you, beloved son Robert, abbot, and the monastery with the privilege of honour and favour, after the example of our said predecessors Alexander and Celestine, we have deemed it right, out of the customary benevolence of the Apostolic See, to grant to you, and through you to your successors, the use of the mitre, ring, and sandals. We command that chrism, holy oil, altar consecrations, ordinations, and whatever things are denied to you and your successors [Note: [Col. 0027D] Thus in the copy; something, however, is missing.]. We prohibit holy masses, ordinations, and stations from being performed in the same monastery by any bishop or cleric of the Church of Paris against the will of the abbot or community; nor may they exercise any authority there. Nor do we grant them power to prohibit them from divine offices, excommunicate them, summon to synod, or take action against the abbot, monks, priests, or clerics of the churches of that place.

We further add that in the parish churches which you hold outside the borough of Saint Germanus, priests shall be chosen by you and presented to the bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they shall answer to him concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters belonging to the monastery [Col. 0027D]. Should they perhaps refuse to do so, you shall have, by apostolic authority, free power to withdraw from them the temporalities which they hold from you [Col. 0028A].

By apostolic authority we also decree and grant you, out of the customary clemency and benevolence of the Apostolic See, that henceforth you need not be subject or subordinate to any legation, unless someone has been specially delegated from the side of the Roman pontiff. Nor may anyone, under pretext of a legation granted him by the Apostolic See, burden you, your successors, your monastery, or the churches within the borough of Saint Germanus with any sentence of interdict or excommunication, or exercise any jurisdiction over you or the said churches, unless this has been specially entrusted to him by the Roman pontiff.

Moreover, the settlement reasonably concluded between [Col. 0028B] your monastery and Guy, archbishop of Sens, of good memory [Note: [Col. 0027D] Guy, born of Milo, lord of Nuceries in Burgundy, had as his mother Mary of Châtillon-sur-Marne, according to the Sammarthani. His nephews were Hugh, bishop of Auxerre—on whom see the note to Epistle XX of Book III—and Angalon, lord of Silliniac. Eminently trained in the best studies and distinguished by his knowledge of both secular and ecclesiastical affairs, he undertook the governance of the archbishopric in 1176, having been provost of Antwerp and Auxerre and archdeacon of Sens. He died in 1193, on 21 December, and was buried in the Greater Church of Sens behind the high altar. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, col. 53.], concerning the procurations which he demanded from you in certain villages, as prudently and honestly made and received, observed until now, and fully contained in the instrument drawn up thereupon, we ratify and confirm by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0028D] Thus in the copy.]. For fuller evidence of this settlement, we have deemed it proper to insert word for word into this privilege that document, whose text is as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0028D] This instrument is printed among the proofs of the *History of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, part I, p. 50, no. LXXIII, where it is followed by another instrument of the same kind, namely the confirmation of this settlement issued by the Chapter of Sens in the same year.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: Guy, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, sends greeting in the Lord to all to whom these present letters shall come [Col. 0028C]. We wish it to be known to all, present and future alike, that the dispute which existed between us and Falco [Note: [Col. 0028D] Falco—or rather Fulco—is found, having formerly been prior, as abbot of Saint Germanus in instruments from as early as 1181. He died, according to the necrology of Saint Germanus, on 2 May 1192. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VII, col. 445.], abbot of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, and that church, concerning the procurations which we demanded from them at Émains, Ballereau, and Saint-Germain near Montereau, was settled in the presence of Philip, king of the Franks, in the following manner.

We have permanently released the abbot and Church of Saint Germanus from the procurations demanded from them in the aforesaid places, on the condition that the abbot and his successors shall pay to us, our successors, or our designated messengers, for those procurations, eight Parisian pounds every year at Émains on the octave of Easter. If we or our successors do not go once a year to Émains, Ballereau, or the village called Saint-Germain [Col. 0028D], [Col. 0029A] the abbot and his successors, or whoever holds the house, shall receive us and our successors; and we and our successors shall live there for one night at our own expense. The holder of the house shall not be obliged to give anything to us or our successors beyond lodging, unless he wishes to do so as a favour. If we or our successors have once been received in one of the said places, the monks shall not be obliged to receive us or our successors in any of the three during that same year.

We have also caused the said church and abbot to be released from one half of the wool-tithe owed by the priests established in the churches of Saint Germanus throughout the archbishopric of Sens, namely at Émains, Ballereau, and the village called Saint-Germain [Col. 0029B] near Montereau; the priests of those churches shall have the other half of that tithe. The messengers of the abbot of Saint Germanus shall make a pledge of fidelity to the priests who shall be in the said churches, and the priests, through their own messengers, to the messengers of the abbot, concerning the joint and faithful collection and division among themselves of the said tithe. Lest this may be erased by anyone’s forgetfulness or maliciously distorted, we have caused it to be confirmed by our seal, in the presence of the officers of our church: Galon, dean [Note: [Col. 0029D] *Galone*: thus it is expressly read in the copy communicated to us by M. Poirier. Yet it should undoubtedly be read *Salone*; so also in the proofs of the *History of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés* and in many other instruments. The authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 110, recognize Salone as dean of Sens from at least 1187 until at least 1196.], Manasses, archdeacon, William, treasurer, and Geoffrey, precentor.

Witnesses to this matter are Stephen, abbot of Saint Geneviève [Note: [Col. 0029D] Stephen, an Orléanais by birth, surnamed of Tournai from Tournai, of which he later became bishop, was abbot of Saint Geneviève from as early as 1175 and governed that monastery until 1192. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VII, col. 770.], and its canons Hugh and Amalric; Milo, abbot of Saint Remigius of Sens [Note: [Col. 0030D] The authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 121, state that Milo is found in instruments as abbot of Saint Remigius of Sens from as early as 1188 until at least 1192.]; Master Ansellus of the Chancery; and Ogerius of Avons. Done [Col. 0029C] at Fontainebleau, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1191.

Next, we prohibit anyone—except the Roman pontiff, a legate sent from his side without a special mandate of the Apostolic See, or the abbot, to whom their care and custody belongs—from excommunicating or placing under interdict the monks of your monastery wherever they reside by command of the abbot. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any craft of deception or force, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, shall have provided to be elected in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. The person elected shall receive the blessing either from the Roman pontiff or from whichever Catholic bishop he prefers [Col. 0029D].

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals [Col. 0030A]. By apostolic authority we further grant you that within the parishes of churches belonging to the aforesaid monastery, no one may dare to build an oratory, chapel, or church, or establish a cemetery, without the consent of the diocesan bishop and ourselves, unless they are perhaps Templars or Hospitallers, to whom this is known to have been granted by privileges of the Apostolic See.

Desiring also, by pontifical provision, to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we decree by the present privilege that if anyone transfers lands lawfully belonging to you, in which you have a share, or fields, by gift, sale, or any other title of alienation, to another church or religious house, other churches or religious houses may not retain them without our consent beyond a year and a day [Col. 0030B]; but, according to the custom of the churches of Gaul, they shall grant them, for a price or gift, to persons who will pay in full your rights to you and your monastery.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, to benefit in every respect the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being reserved. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance [Col. 0030C]. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri [Note: [Col. 0030D] See the note to Epistle X of Book III.]. I, Peter, bishop of Porto [Note: [Col. 0030D] See the note to Epistle LXIX of Book V.]. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia [Note: [Col. 0030D] See the note to Epistle XXXII of Book III.]. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0030D] See the note to Epistle CXVII of Book VI.]. [Col. 0031A] I, Guy, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus [Note: [Col. 0031C] See the note to Epistle XXVIII of Book III.]. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Aegidius [Note: [Col. 0031C] *Egidii*: thus the copy communicated by M. Poirier reads; but it should be read *Equitii*. See the note to the third epistle of this Appendix.]. I, John, cardinal priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill [Note: [Col. 0031C] See Epistle LXXIII of Book V.]. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. 0031C] See note 58 above.]. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian [Note: [Col. 0031C] See the note to Epistle LXXXIII of Book V.]. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Gregory at the Golden Veil [Note: [Col. 0031C] See the note to Epistle LX of Book VII.]. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin [Note: [Col. 0031C] See note 61 above.]. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo [Col. 0031B] [Note: [Col. 0031D] See the note to Epistle XXIX of Book V.]. I, Vobo [Note: [Col. 0031D] *Vobo*: thus the copy communicated by M. Poirier reads; elsewhere, *Bobo*. Bobo, a Roman, formerly a canon of Saint Peter’s and cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore, was appointed cardinal by Pope Celestine III in the second creation of cardinals according to Ciaconius, or in the fourth according to Panvinio. Some write that this Bobo was a relative of Celestine and belonged to the Ursini family. He died under Pope Innocent III. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. I, col. 1164.], cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata [Note: [Col. 0031D] See the note to Epistle XX of Book III.].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Rainald, notary of our lord the pope, acting as chancellor, on 14 May, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord 1198, in the first year of the pontificate of Innocent.

## IX. To the Abbot of Prémontré [Note: [Col. 0031D] Peter I, abbot of Saint-Just, an outstanding example of learning, piety, and humility, was, at the desire of the Premonstratensians and almost by force, torn from his monastery and reluctantly allowed himself to be elevated to the chief seat of the Order on 4 June 1196. He resigned on 14 October 1201. What is especially praiseworthy in so great a man is that, while prelates of other orders were asking Pope Innocent III for privileges, he asked the supreme pontiff only that neither he nor his fellow abbots might be permitted to use the mitre, gloves, or other pontifical ornaments, lest through their use they should seem exalted. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VI, col. 646.]; H., archdeacon, and Master R., canon of Laon.—He entrusts to them for adjudication the case between the abbot and monks of Saint Nicholas of Ribemont and W., deacon, concerning the Church of Villers-le-Sec [Note: [Col. 0032C]

M. Grenier appended this note to the copy; it is worth reproducing here:

> “Rescript of Pope Innocent III to the abbot of Prémontré, the archdeacon of Laon, and Master Robert, [Col. 0032D] canon of the same church, for settling a major dispute between the religious of Saint-Nicholas of Ribemont and a deacon who had caused the chapel of Villers-le-Sec to be established as a parish church, and had procured it for himself on a false representation and without the patron’s participation.
>
> “This document is very interesting for the manner of proceeding in the ecclesiastical forum in the twelfth century.”]

(1198. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 16 May.)

[From the parchment cartulary of the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Ribemont, fol. 47v. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0031C]

When there came into our presence our beloved sons Stephen, monk, and Jesse, priest, messengers of our beloved sons, the . . . abbot and [Note: [Col. 0032D] See above, Epistle 2, note.] monks of Saint Nicholas of Ribemont, and W., deacon, who asserted that he had been instituted in the church of Villers-le-Sec by delegated judges acting with apostolic authority, and both sides urgently sought a hearing, we assigned our beloved sons Robert and Hugolinus, our subdeacons and chaplains, as auditors. Before them the party of the said abbot alleged that, when John, a clerk and brother of W., had approached the Apostolic See, he falsely represented that the chapel of Villers-le-Sec had sufficient revenues to support a priest; that it lay far from the mother church; and that the priest of Ribemont could not adequately serve both the parish church and that chapel. Because of his absence, many had died intestate. Thus, by this false representation, he procured letters from our predecessor Pope C. of happy memory to our venerable brother the . . . archbishop [Note: [Col. 0032D] Michael of Corbeil, who held the see of Sens from 1194 until 1199, when he died on 28 November. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, col. 55.] and our beloved son the . . . dean of Sens [Note: [Col. 0032D] After Salomon, dean of Sens, who is said to have died in 1196, Hugh—first archdeacon of Sens and dean of Braye, then dean of Sens—is mentioned in instruments until 1204. Ibid., col. 110.]. The tenor of these letters was that, appeal being set aside, they should not delay instituting a priest there.

Although the abbot was cited by the authority of those letters, in which he was nowhere mentioned at all, he appeared before them. Since he could not obtain a copy of the letters, he maintained that he ought not to be summoned before judges outside the province and remote from him except upon a cause known and explicitly stated. He offered himself ready to prove that those letters, which he did not believe had issued with the knowledge of the supreme pontiff, ought to lack legal force. He also alleged that there was no mention that he, the abbot, had the right of patronage in that church; that the letters had been obtained with the truth concealed; and that, if a priest seemed necessary there, he ought nevertheless not to be instituted without the counsel of the abbot himself, or of the diocesan or metropolitan, or even—what was of greater consequence—without the command of the supreme pontiff [Col. 0032C].

When the judges nevertheless wished to proceed in the case, the abbot, perceiving a burden threatened against him, appealed to the Apostolic See. Once this appeal had been made, the parties, with the judges’ consent, agreed to arbitration. While the arbitration was pending, the aforesaid archbishop, without summoning the abbot, instituted the said W. in the chapel as he pleased, though W. was less suitable. On learning this, and being unable to approach those judges because of the great distance, the abbot renewed his earlier appeal before our venerable brethren, the . . . archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0033D] See the note to Epistle XIV of Book III.], cardinal of Saint Sabina, and the . . . bishop of Laon [Note: [Col. 0033D] Roger I of Rozoy, elected in 1174 and consecrated in 1175, governed the Church of Laon until 1107. See *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IX, col. 534.], and notified the said archbishop of Sens that he had so appealed [Col. 0033B].

The said clerk, relying on the judges’ action, though it was less than canonical, forcibly occupied the chapel. When the abbot wished reasonably to exercise his right, the clerk, with certain accomplices, expelled him in a shameful and irreverent manner, presuming to lay violent hands upon him. For this reason the abbot’s party sought from us that what had been done should be annulled and that the clerk should be compelled to make satisfaction for so grave an offence.

Against the rescript issued to the aforesaid judges concerning the institution of a proper priest in the chapel already mentioned, the following objection was raised: namely, that it ought to have no force, and that whatever followed from it should be deemed void and useless. For it made no mention of the abbot, who, by reason of a right possessed from antiquity and confirmed to him and his church by apostolic privilege, ought to institute the priest in the church of which the said chapel was a dependency [Note: [Col. 0034D] Compare the enumeration of the property and possessions of the monastery of Saint Nicholas of the Meadows at Ribemont, in Epistle 2 cited above.]. Nor had he been invited to this by any of his prelates; he was ready to produce sufficient witnesses there to prove it.
