Since this was not permitted to him, although appeal had been prohibited in the letters, he was lawfully entitled to appeal.

After supporting this by many other allegations and arguments, the same party maintained that the rescript was suspect because it did not accord with the style of the Roman Church; because, in the copy shown to him, the chapters said to follow continuously did not appear connected with the other chapters; and especially because, although the opposing party had promised to furnish him a copy, it had nevertheless taken no care to produce it in court or even show it once [Col. 0033D]. The abbot’s party further argued on many grounds that the rescript was invalid because it had been obtained by false representations: the revenues of that church could not suffice even for a priest’s sustenance; the chapel possessed no revenues; and the mother church was not shown to be very wealthy.

The party of the said Deacon W., on the contrary, alleged that only one priest ministered in two churches far separated from one another: Saint Peter’s, Ribemont, and Saint Mary’s of Villers, which had from ancient times a baptismal font and cemetery. Because the churches were distant, and because the castle in which the said priest resided was often found shut, especially as he could not go out at night, parishioners of Villers were compelled to die without receiving the divine sacraments [Col. 0034A]. To avert this danger, our aforesaid predecessor Pope C., upon the complaint of the parishioners of Villers, sent letters to the said judges. They were to institute a priest in the Church of Villers by apostolic authority if they found that it had tithes and revenues sufficient to support one priest, and that the priest of Ribemont was so far removed from the Church of Villers that he could not appropriately serve both churches, whereby, as was said, many had died intestate. They were also to assign him from the tithes and revenues belonging to that church enough for suitable support, while making the priest of the Church of Ribemont content to remain with that church, which was very wealthy [Col. 0034B].

The judges, devoutly and humbly carrying out the apostolic command, summoned before them those whom they saw were to be called according to the terms of the apostolic mandate. After a careful inquiry through suitable witnesses, they found the foregoing established. Having used the counsel of good and prudent men, they conferred the aforesaid Church of Villers upon the said deacon by apostolic authority, assigning to him a moderate share in accordance with the apostolic form: namely, one third of the greater and lesser tithe belonging to the Church of Villers, and all offerings throughout the year, except offerings at the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord and the Assumption of blessed Mary. Of these the deacon was to receive one third, while our beloved sons, the . . . abbot and monks of Saint Nicholas of the Meadows, were to receive the other two portions. Thus the deacon possessed the church granted to him by apostolic authority [Col. 0034C–D].

Afterwards, because the abbot was unlawfully disturbing his possession and committing violence against him in the same church—indeed, had laid violent hands upon him—and had caused him to be held almost as a prisoner for four days by secular force, forbidding food to be given him so that, tormented by hunger, he might at last renounce his right (from which confinement he was scarcely at length able to be freed through our venerable brother the . . . bishop of Laon); because the guards watched him lest he should be able to leave by the church door; and because the abbot had caused him to be despoiled of his movable goods by secular force [Col. 0035A]: after all this had been established before the aforesaid judges by suitable witnesses, the abbot was suspended by them under apostolic authority, as we have found contained in the judges’ authentic instrument.

Although the abbot, because he was bound by excommunication for laying hands on the deacon, had no power to appear in court either personally or through another, and although he had violently caused the deacon and his parishioners to be despoiled of their goods, the said deacon maintained that he was not bound to answer the opposing party unless the abbot first made full restitution. Nevertheless, subject to those exceptions and without entering into the merits, he tried by many arguments to show that the allegations of the opposing party were empty and vain. He asserted that the parishioners had proved before the judges through suitable witnesses that the said letters had been obtained upon a true representation [Col. 0035B].

He further firmly asserted that, upon the complaint of the parishioners of Villers, the said bishop had been warned that a priest ought to be instituted in the Church of Villers to celebrate divine offices there as required. After the letters had been obtained, the aforesaid judges repeatedly warned both the abbot himself and his predecessor, either personally or through their messengers; and it was adequately demonstrated by many arguments before the said auditors that the rescript had been included in the letters of citation, although the opposing party, as it alleged, could not obtain a copy. Since, as he said, the abbot had often been warned and had refused to consent, this institution could be made by delegated judges with apostolic authority without their consent [Col. 0035C].

When the auditors faithfully reported to us what had been set before them, we could not fully ascertain the truth of all the foregoing, because proofs were lacking for many of the assertions advanced by either party. Therefore, with the common consent of the parties, we have deemed it proper to commit the same case to you. Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, having summoned the parties, you shall investigate more carefully the truth concerning all these matters and any other matters they deem relevant to the case; and, setting aside appeal, you shall decree what you find canonically to be decreed [Col. 0035D], and cause it to be firmly observed by the parties through ecclesiastical censure. You shall annul whatever, after the investiture of the aforesaid deacon made by the said judges under apostolic authority, you discover has been unlawfully attempted against him.

Nevertheless, before entering upon the case, after first receiving from the said abbot sufficient security that he will obey the law, you shall grant him the benefit of absolution. No letters shall stand in the way, if any are found to have been procured from the Apostolic See without the parties’ consent. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, two of you shall nevertheless execute it [Col. 0036A].

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on 16 May, in the first year of our pontificate.

## X. To the Abbot [Note: [Col. 0035D] The following note was appended to the copy of Abbot Grandidier: “ATBOLD was then abbot of the Benedictine abbey of Gengenbach, still existing in the Ortenau and in the diocese of Strasbourg.” But the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* mention Gerbold as abbot of Gengenbach at about the period under discussion, vol. V, col. 871.] and convent of the monastery at Gengenbach, diocese of Strasbourg.—Confirmation of privileges. (1198, 3 July.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Gengenbach and communicated by Abbot Grandidier, of happy memory. Ibid.]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of the monastery at [Col. 0036B] Gengenbach, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Strasbourg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant kindly favour to the honourable prayers of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, readily assenting to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority for you, and through you for the same monastery, and strengthen by the protection of this present document, all liberties and immunities granted or bestowed upon you and your monastery by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, whether through privileges or other indulgences; likewise, the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you and your monastery by kings, princes, and other faithful Christians, as you justly and peacefully possess them [Col. 0036C]. Let no one therefore, etc.

Given on 3 July, in the first year of our pontificate.

## XI. To the King of the Danes.—That he should arm himself against the tyranny of Sverrir. (1198. At the town of Castello, 6 October.)

[Liljegren, *Diplomatorium Suecicum*, Stockholm, 1829, quarto, I, 130.]

INNOCENT, bishop, to the illustrious king of the Danes, etc.

[Col. 0036D] We believe that, because of the sins deserved by both clergy and people of Norway, the Lord has permitted the detestable cruelty and violence of the tyrant Sverrir to prevail so greatly against you and the whole kingdom of Norway. As we have learned, he has seized the kingdom neither by the election of princes nor by right of blood; and, though he once held ecclesiastical office, as is said, he rages against ecclesiastical men, oppresses churches, persecutes clerics, afflicts the poor, and is savage against the powerful. It is thought to have occurred by divine judgment that he who, even by his own assertion, was illegitimately born and should not have been advanced to holy orders, having been admitted to them contrary to canonical enactments, should rage all the more violently against those who did not observe the canons in his ordination [Col. 0037A].

We marvel, however—not at God, who has until now endured his tyranny for your correction, nor at Sverrir himself, whose spirit, hardened in evil and accustomed to iniquity, cannot unlearn it—but at those who still follow an apostate, sacrilegious, and impious man with the daring of sacrilegious rashness, and offer aid and favour to one whose tyranny they ought rather to pursue with all their strength. Although frequent commands have issued from the Apostolic See to subdue his cunning, his perversity has not yet been so restrained that he does not still rule in a part of Norway, with some people following him to the destruction of their souls, and there outdo the fury of the north [Col. 0037B].

To deceive you and all the people of Norway further, and to show that the kingdom had been confirmed to him by apostolic authority, he did not fear to forge a bull of our predecessor Pope Celestine, of happy memory, with which he sealed various letters. But He to whom all things are manifest exposed his falsity. Therefore, lest his perversity rage against the innocent, we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Royal Serenity in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters, to prepare yourself for defending the churches, preserving clerics in their liberty, freeing the poor and powerful from the hand of that persecutor, and indeed overthrowing that monster, which spares only those whom it cannot harm [Col. 0037C]. Thus may you deserve especially to obtain from God an eternal reward and from us special favour. Aid those who pursue so great an iniquity; resist his followers; so that that member of the devil may not again rage in the kingdom of Norway or raise further persecution in the churches.

Given at the town of Castello, on 6 October.

## XII. To Peter, Bishop of Aarhus.—He confirms the first six prebends of the Church of Aarhus. (1198, Lateran, 13 November.)

[Langebeck, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, VI, 388.]

[Col. 0037D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, bishop of Aarhus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The duty of our office and rightly ordered charity require that acts laudably performed by our brethren and fellow bishops should, under the safeguard of our authority, obtain unshaken stability and grant greater confidence for action in the future. As has been reported to us on your behalf, venerable brother in Christ, from your patrimonial goods and other property which you have lawfully acquired, and from that which the church entrusted to you had previously possessed, you have prudently arranged for six prebends to be assigned to canons who are to serve that church. We therefore commend this enactment [Col. 0038A] with fitting praise in the Lord, and, in order that it may remain firm more securely for all future time, just as it was circumspectly and prudently made and is set forth more expressly in the authentic document of our venerable brother Asger, Archbishop of Lund, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present page. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or, with rash boldness, to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November, in the first year of our pontificate.

XIII. To the abbot of the monastery of Nonantola in the diocese of Modena.—He grants him leave to absolve certain excommunicated persons. (1198, Lateran, December 9.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of the Abbey of Nonantola*, II, 348. From the autograph in the archive of Nonantola.]

[Col. 0038B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son . . . abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Modena, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your petition presented to us stated that certain monks and lay brothers of your monastery had incurred the bond of excommunication for violently laying hands upon one another, and indeed for retaining private property; others also for withholding obedience from you and [Col. 0038C] your predecessors, or for the offence of conspiracy. Some of these monks, while thus bound, celebrated the divine offices and received orders. You therefore humbly requested us to provide for their salvation in these matters. Having full confidence in the Lord in your prudence, we grant to your discretion by the authority of these presents that, on this occasion, you may absolve these excommunicated persons from sentences of excommunication of this kind in our stead, according to the form of the Church, imposing upon them what ought by law to be imposed; provided that you send to the Apostolic See for absolution those who laid hands violently, whose offence has been grave and enormous.

With those, however, who, forgetful of the facts or ignorant of the law, received orders and celebrated the divine offices without having obtained the benefit of absolution, after a suitable penance proportionate to their fault has been imposed and completed, you may, by virtue of the mercy which triumphs over judgment, dispense as you judge expedient for their salvation. But if the aforesaid excommunicated persons knowingly, though not in contempt of the keys, presumed to do such things, suspend them from exercising their orders for two years and impose a salutary penance upon them; thereafter, if they are of good conduct and life, admit them to the grace of dispensation. Any private property possessed by the said monks or lay brothers you shall cause to be surrendered into your hands and converted to the use of the said monastery.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the first year of our pontificate.

XIV. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem.—That the prior and canons of the Holy Sepulchre may have free authority to regulate the houses and priories of their obediences. (1199, Lateran, January 5.)

[Eugène de ROZIÈRE, *Cartulary of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem*, published from Vatican manuscripts. Paris, National Printing House, 1849, quarto, p. 271.]

[Col. 0039A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the Patriarch of Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the Lord’s Sepulchre, by indulgence of the Apostolic See and with the assent of your predecessors, have hitherto had free administration of their affairs, both houses and priories, and since we, following in the footsteps of those same predecessors of ours, have considered this to be confirmed to them, we must by no means endure that anyone should rashly act against our concession. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that you should in no way wish to hinder the aforesaid prior and brethren concerning the administration already mentioned, but rather permit them to use the apostolic concession, insofar as law permits; nor should you rashly oppose them, contrary to our indulgence, in appointing canons whom they have found useful and suitable for their church, since in this matter we wish your right to be preserved wholly unimpaired.

[Col. 0039C] Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

XV. To the abbot, Provost E., and Canon C. of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg.—That they protect the rights of the parish priest at Riekofen against the monastery of Walderbach. (1199, Lateran, March 5.)

[RIED, *Diplomatic Codex of Regensburg*, Regensburg, 1816, quarto, p. 281, from the original.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . the abbot of Saint Emmeram, Provost E., and Canon C. of Regensburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of our beloved son Wernard, parish priest of Lentechoven (today Riekofen), it has been disclosed to our apostolic office that the abbot and brethren of Walerbach [Col. 0039D] in the diocese of Regensburg improperly withhold from him one manor, called in those parts the endowment of his chapel of Tagmerengen (Taimering), and presume unjustly to retain it. When the parish priest at one time brought his case before the beloved sons, the chapter of Regensburg, the said abbot had recourse [Col. 0040A] to an appeal, which, as is stated, he did not pursue; and so the parish priest has not yet been able to obtain his right. Accordingly, appealing to the Apostolic See for the octave of Epiphany, now past, he restricted the term of the challenge lodged by the abbot. The same abbot is also said to be injurious and troublesome to the said parish priest concerning the tithes of the aforesaid village.

Desiring, however, that each person’s rights be preserved unimpaired, and since the foregoing has not been established before us, we have considered it proper to commit this case to you. By apostolic letters we command that, after summoning before you those who are to be summoned and more diligently investigating the truth concerning the foregoing, you determine what is canonical, removing the impediment of appeal; and that you cause what you determine [Col. 0040B] to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice. If all of you cannot be present for carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

Lead seal. INNOCENT, POPE III.

XVI. To Gerbodon [Note: [Col. 0039D] See Letter XII below, note], abbot, and the convent of Saint Wulmar, in the diocese of Boulogne.—He confirms the judgment rendered in their favour by the Bishop of Thérouanne and co-judges in the case between them and the Abbot of Cluny concerning liberty to elect abbots. (1199, Lateran, March 21.)

[Copied from the archive of the monastery of Saint Wulmar, no. 24. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0040C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERBODON, abbot, and the convent of Saint Wulmar, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honorable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the care of our office. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with favorable assent in your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the protection of this present writing, the judgment of our venerable brother . . . the Bishop of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0039D] See Letter CLXXXII of Book Nine], and of the beloved [Col. 0040D] sons . . . the abbots of Saint-Vaast [Note: [Col. 0039D] Henry III, formerly chamberlain, already advanced in years, was chosen abbot of Saint-Vaast in 1194. Because of old age he resigned his charge in 1209. See *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 385. Simon I, a monk of the monastery of Saint-Vaast, succeeded the deceased Abbot Alexander no later than 1175; according to Locrius, he died in 1202 or 1201. Ibid., col. 412.] and Anchin, against the Abbot of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0040D] He was still Hugh IV (of Clermont), son of Raynald, Count of Clermont in the Beauvaisis, and of Clemence de Barro, and kinsman of Raynald, Bishop of Chartres. First abbot of Saint-Germer-de-Fly, then of Saint-Lucian at Beauvais, and finally, from 1183, Abbot of Cluny, he did not die before 6 April of this year, 1199. See *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1143.], concerning liberty to elect abbots in your monastery. It was lawfully proved before the aforesaid judges that the brethren of your monastery had continuously enjoyed that liberty for forty years. Since the judgment was reasonably given and not suspended by a lawful appeal, we hold it valid and [Col. 0041A] confirm it by apostolic authority.

We decree therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of our pontificate.

XVII. To Gerbodon [Note: [Col. 0041D] “XI. Gerbodo, or Grebindus, or Grebinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Wulmar, now in the diocese of Boulogne. Though unnamed, as they relate, Pope Celestine III granted him confirmation of its goods and churches in 1193. He is recorded as a witness in 1192 in Countess Ida’s letters for Saint-Bertin. He appears in 1196 in the Chronicle of Andrés. In 1199, with Lambert, Bishop of Thérouanne, approving, he sold certain estates to the monastery of Clairmarais. He is still found in 1210 in the Cartulary of Saint-Josse.” *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1596], abbot of Saint Wulmar, and his brethren, present and future.—He receives them under the protection of Blessed Peter and enumerates the possessions belonging to them. (1199, Lateran, April 5.)

[BRÉQUIGNY and LA PORTE DUTHEIL, *Regesta of Innocent III*, vol. III, appendix, p. 1075; from a copy made by D. Vacher de Bourg-Lange from the autograph. See at the end of the bull itself.]

[Col. 0041B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERBODON, abbot of the monastery of Saint Wulmar, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Whenever a request is made to us that is recognized as consonant with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and afford appropriate support to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of Pope Celestine, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Wulmar, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. [Col. 0041C] First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order recognized as instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of popes, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly the following:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the village of Saint Wulmar, with its market, toll, and all jurisdictions and appurtenances of that village, internal and external, from the village itself to the fief of Witra, which is held from the Count, and to the fief of the village of Dudelli, and the fief of Dales, and to the fief of Tingri, and the fief of Werlinghetun, and to the stream of Cresbere and the river Elnac; the parish church of that village, with all its tithes and other appurtenances; the land, with the wood, held from the fief of Robert Rabel, from the foot of the hill to the fief of Lambert de Cors [Col. 0042A] and Baldwin de Milestrec, which you hold from him at an annual rent of ten shillings; the village of Hesding, with its church and all its other appurtenances; the village of Old Monastery, with its church and all its other appurtenances; the village of Saint Martin, with its church and all its other appurtenances; the village of Great Village, with its church and all its other appurtenances; the village of Colonia, with its church and all its other appurtenances—namely cultivated lands, and all . . . fisheries, marshes, and fens—at Niuniel, half a boat-right and a fishery; Cundeta; Richenacre; Berchem; Estruem; Fohem; Berneulas; Evelinghehem; at Stapes, thirty holdings; and in the aforesaid villages and hamlets, all comital rights and jurisdiction; the altar-right of Frene, and [Col. 0042B] two ploughlands of land and more, and the tenants whom you have in that village, with all jurisdiction and annual rents that they owe you, and in that same village the tithe from the mound; the altar-right of Tingri, with all tithes, and in that parish the tithe of increase; the altar-right of Laires, with the whole tithe; the altar-right of Quarti, with the whole tithe; the altar-right of Verlinghetun, with the whole tithe; the altar-right of Wilra; the altar-right of Saint Gertrude; the altar-right of Boninghes; the altar-rights of Auci and Servin; in the parish of Kestreke, the entire tithe of the Count’s sharecroppers; and in the same parish, the tithe of William the Chamberlain, the tithe of Businghehem, one third of the tithe of Helbesessem, the tithe of Dales, the tithe of Sckieses, the tithe of Berneulas, the tithe of Richer’s clearing, [Col. 0042C] the tithe of Wenegheval, the tithe of Saint Gertrude, one third of the tithe of Verna, the tithe of Welwinge, the tithe of Alinghetum; at Berebet, the tithe from the lands of Baldwin Bibuef and Simon Bustel, the tithe of Bossin; at Denebrac, the tithe of the Castellan of Faukenberge, and in that same village the tithe from Lambin’s land; in the parish of Reclinghehem, one ploughland of cultivated land; at Capella, the allods of Oilard of Businghehem; at Wichinghehem, the allods of Girold of Buccoll, Girold of Casroi, and Hugh of Chestreka; at Ledingheham, a certain part of the allods of that village; at Lustinghehem, the allods of Roger de Kaeu and of Gilla his sister, and, by their gift, two parts of a mill; in the parish of New Castle, the allods of Robert Cringeth and Walter Crolle; at Paningherum, the allods of Faram; at Huppem, half a ploughland of land; at Hecout, the allods of Hugh of Collesberc and Hugh of Kestrehe; at Hessinghehem, two ploughlands of land; at Hokinghehem, one ploughland of land; at Hermarenghes, the allods of Hugh of Seles and his sisters, and of Peter, Hugh, and their sister; at Yseche, the allods of Arnulf of Longavilla; at Ferchenes, the allods of Atron, his son John, and their kinsman Baldwin; [Col. 0043A] at Hellenboun, the allods of Rainer Caval; at Hellinghehem, six *polchini* of grain; at Marchines, two *polchini* of grain; at Boulogne, seven and a half shillings; at Camir, five shillings; at Badingherun, five shillings; at Malchesbere, five shillings; at Alles, five shillings; at Jorni, six shillings; at Bovelinghehem, five shillings; at Seninghehem, five shillings; the priory of Baileleth with all its appurtenances; in England, the altar-right of Fobinghes and the tithe of Ruiwale.

Moreover, no one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared land, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

[Col. 0043B] You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and absolved from secular obligations, who flee from the world, and retain them without any objection. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave that house without the permission of his abbot, except for the purpose of entering a stricter religious order. No one may dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, provided that they answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We also establish [Col. 0043C] that within the bounds of your parishes no one shall presume to build a church or *[lacuna]* without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, without prejudice, however, to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. By apostolic authority we . . . . [lacuna] that no one may pronounce against you or your church a sentence of excommunication or interdict without a manifest and reasonable cause, or impose new and unlawful exactions upon you or your people. We prohibit by apostolic authority the diocesan bishop from making *stationes* [visitations?] . . . . . . . [lacuna] in your monastery.

For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, the ordinations of your monks or clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, *[lacuna]* blessing or conducting [them] to [Col. 0043D] the see, or for any ecclesiastical sacraments, no one shall dare, under pretext of custom or in any other manner, to demand from you a palfrey, a silk cloak, wine, or anything else. We likewise decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving nevertheless the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that house, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of deception or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, provide to be elected. Moreover, we hold valid the liberties and immunities, as well as the ancient and reasonable customs, granted to your monastery and hitherto observed, and decree that they remain unimpaired in future times.

We decree therefore [Col. 0044B] that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and be of every benefit to the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you have bound yourselves to pay us and our successors one bezant yearly.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and Lord, our redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that house may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0044D] I, Octavian, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri [Note: [Col. 0043D] See Letter X of Book Three, note]. I, Peter, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina [Note: [Col. 0043D] See Letter LXIX of Book Five, note]. I, John, Bishop of Albano [Note: [Col. 0043D] John, Bishop of Albano. This is undoubtedly the same man who subscribes as Philip to Bull VII of this Appendix, but as John, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Clement and likewise Bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany, to Bull VIII of the same Appendix; we have discussed him in the notes both to those bulls and to Letter CXVII of Book Six. Historians unanimously report that in this very year in which this bull of Pope Innocent III is said to have been issued—namely, the year of the Incarnation 1199 and the second of Innocent’s pontificate—John was made Bishop of Albano from cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Clement and simultaneously Bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany. It should, however, be noted that Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 19, states that John was transferred to the see of Albano in 1199, but at Pentecost. Yet our present letter of Innocent proves that John had already acquired the episcopal insignia of Albano before April.].

[Col. 0045A] I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles [Note: [Col. 0045C] See Letter CXLV of Book Nine, note]. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia [Note: [Col. 0045C] See Letter XXXII of Book Three, note]. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor [Note: [Col. 0045C] See Letter LXXIV of Book Five, note]. I, Guy, cardinal priest of Santa Maria in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title . . . . [Note: [Col. 0045C] “Equitius” must be supplied. See the notes to Letter VII [Col. 0045D] of this Appendix, note]. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter LXXIII of Book Five]. I, Soffredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter VI of Book Five, note]. I, Bernard, cardinal [Col. 0045B] priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter LXXIII of Book Five, note]. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter XV of Book Three, note]. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter VII of this Appendix, note]. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter LXXXIII of Book Five, note]. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Aquiro [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter XXIX of Book Eight, note]. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter LX of Book Seven, note]. I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter VII of this Appendix, note]. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo [Col. 0045C] [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter XXIX of Book Five, note]. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore [Note: [Col. 0045D] See Letter VIII of this Appendix, note]. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea [Note: [Col. 0045D] Cencius Sabellus, a Roman according to Panvinio, was a regular canon of the Lateran or, according to Ciaconius, a canon of Santa Maria Maggiore. Pope Celestine III, in his second creation of cardinals according to Pavinio, but in the fourth according to Panvinio, made him cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orphea—for this, not “in Orthea,” is the correct reading—otherwise [known as] in Silice, chamberlain and vice-chancellor of the Holy Roman Church. Later Innocent III made him cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius; finally, after Innocent’s death, he was elected Roman pontiff and was called Honorius III.]. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace [Note: [Col. 0046D] See Letter LXX of Book Five, note]. I, Girard, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano [Note: [Col. 0046D] See Letter CCXXII of Book Nine, note].

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary of the lord pope, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the Nones of April, [Col. 0046A] in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1199, and in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Innocent III.

At the foot of the bull transcribed above, attached by cords of yellow and red silk, is the lead seal, bearing on one side the likenesses of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, with the letters S. PA. S. PE.; and on the other, an impression like that which follows:

INNOCENT, POPE III.

Collated by us, Jean-Charles Vacher de Bourg-l’Ange, lord of Bourg-l’Ange, advocate at the Parlement, charged with the orders of My Lord the Keeper of the Seals of France, in conformity with the original kept in the archives of the Abbey of Aurillac: on a parchment twenty-nine and a half inches long by twenty-two inches wide, pierced by two holes at the places [Col. 0046B] marked with asterisks, the first of them indicating an erased word which could not be read. At Aurillac, 12 November 1786. Signed J.-C. VACHER DE BOURG-L’ANGE.

XVIII. To John [Note: [Col. 0046D] John III of Ypres—concerning whom we have also written in the note to Letter XLV of Book Eight—“a monk of Lobbes, elected with the consent—indeed, the advice—of Simon, his predecessor, received benediction from Desiderius, Bishop of Thérouanne, on 11 July 1187. Two years later he obtained from Pope Clement III confirmation of all his goods; from Celestine in 1198 [read 1197]; and from Pope Innocent III in the same year or the following.” *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 500. The confirmation obtained from Innocent III is without doubt the same as our letter. John died in 1230.], abbot of Saint-Bertin, and his brethren, present and future, forever.—Confirmation of privileges. (1199, Lateran, April 9.)

[This letter, or rather bull, carefully copied from an old cartulary of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, was placed in our charter archive by D. Ch. de Witte with this note: “It is thus copied from an old Cartulary, vol. XXI, fol. 66v, in the year 1785.” It is read complete, word for word, in Book XII of the Registers of Innocent; but how it came to be inserted there we do not know [Note: [Col. 0046D] We have restored this letter from chronological notes to Book II; it is now number 38 bis in the book cited. PATROLOGIA EDITION.], since it plainly belongs to the second year of the pontificate. The names of the subscribing cardinals are lacking in Baluze; we have thought it worthwhile to add them here, because information of this kind often provides no small benefit toward a fuller understanding of history and toward establishing the chronological sequence of events. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0046C]

Established by the Lord in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, as [we] imitate our predecessors, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian [Note: [Col. 0046D] On the cardinals subscribing here, see above, at Letter II of this Appendix], Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. [Col. 0047A] I, Peter, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Pandulf [Note: [Col. 0047D] On Pandulf, who is not found subscribing the Letter II cited above, see Letter CXLV of Book Nine, note], by the permission of God alone cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, Bishop of Viterbo and Tuscany. I, Guy [Note: [Col. 0047D] The same applies to Guy; but see Letter XXVIII of Book Three, note], cardinal priest of Santa Maria in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0047B] I, Gerard [Note: [Col. 0048D] The same applies to Gerard, but see Letter LXXXIII of Book Five, note], cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Aquiro. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Horthea.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, notary of the lord pope, acting as chancellor, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198 [Note: [Col. 0048D] Thus in the copy placed in our charter archive by D. Ch. de Witte. But from the synchronisms it is beyond all doubt that 1199 must be read], and in the second year of the pontificate of the Lord Pope Innocent III.

XIX. To Elias, abbot, and the brethren of Saint Mary of Reigny.—Confirmation of privileges. (1199, Lateran, May 5.)

[*New Gallia Christiana*, XII, document 143.]

[Col. 0047C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ELIAS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Reigny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be at hand for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an attack of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religious profession. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of Reigny, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we establish that the monastic order recognized as instituted in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods [Col. 0048A] the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by grant of popes, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly the following:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with vineyards, lands, and all its appurtenances; the grange which is beside the abbey, with its appurtenances; the grange of Essars, with its appurtenances; the grange of Fontismo, with its appurtenances; the grange of Ulduno, with its appurtenances; the house of Campo-Leniae, with its appurtenances; the grange of Cherbonere, with its appurtenances; the grange of [Col. 0048B] Lescheriis, with all its appurtenances; the storehouse of Clamecin, with its appurtenances; the grange of Bellovidere, with all its appurtenances; the lands and meadows of Vaureta, with their appurtenances; the grange of Cosath, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Chatz, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Treclin, with its mill and all its other appurtenances; the storehouse of Vallibus, with all its appurtenances; and the storehouse of Chablie, with all its appurtenances.

Indeed, of the produce of your labours which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens, shrublands, fisheries, or the raising of your animals, let no one presume to demand or [Col. 0048C] extort tithes from you. You may also receive as converts clerics or laymen who are free and unbound, fleeing from the secular world, and retain them without any opposition.

Moreover, we forbid any of your brothers, after making profession in your monastery, to leave that place without his abbot’s permission; and let no one dare retain one who departs without letters of authorization from the community. Should anyone nevertheless presume to retain him, you may pronounce the regular sentence against such persons, whether monks or conversi. We more strictly forbid anyone to give personally, or otherwise alienate, lands or any benefice granted to your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. If any [Col. 0048D] grants or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we decree them void.

Furthermore, we prohibit any monk or conversus bound by profession to your house, without the consent and permission of your abbot and of the greater part of your chapter, from standing surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone beyond the sum fixed by the prudence of your chapter, unless for the manifest benefit of your house. Should he presume to do so, the convent shall not be bound in any manner [Col. 0049A] to answer for such matters.

Moreover, in your own causes, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may employ the testimony of your brothers, lest through lack of witnesses your right should in any respect be lost. We further forbid by apostolic authority that any bishop or any other person whatsoever compel you to attend synods or judicial assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions; nor may anyone presume to come to your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, hear causes, or convene public assemblies; nor may anyone impede the regular election of your abbot, or in any way interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in installing or removing whoever may at the time hold that office.

But if the bishop in whose parish [Col. 0049B] your house has been founded, when duly requested with fitting humility and devotion, refuses to bless the abbot-elect and to confer upon you the other things pertaining to the episcopal office, that abbot may, provided he is a priest, bless his own novices and perform the other functions belonging to his office; and you may receive from another bishop all that has been improperly refused you by your own bishop. We add that, in receiving professions tendered by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops are to be content with the form and wording instituted from the origin of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must make profession with their Order preserved, and may not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order.

For the consecration of altars [Col. 0049C] or churches, for chrism, or for any ecclesiastical sacrament, no one may presume to extort anything from you, whether under the pretext of custom or in any other way; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things for you without charge. Otherwise, you may approach any bishop you choose who enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and who, relying on our authority, shall provide what is requested. If the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighbouring bishops, provided that no prejudice to your own bishops is thereby created in future.

Since, indeed, you do not always have your own bishops available, if it should happen that a bishop enjoying, as we have said, the favour of the Roman See and communion with the Apostolic See—and of whom you have full knowledge—passes through your district, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks. But if bishops or other governors of churches pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict against your monastery or persons established therein, or even against your hired labourers because you do not pay tithes, or upon any pretext concerning matters granted you by apostolic favour; or if they pronounce such a sentence against your benefactors because they have charitably bestowed benefits or services upon you, or assisted you [Col. 0050A] in labour on those days on which you work while others rest, we deem that sentence to be annulled as pronounced against the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall any letters have validity which are shown to have been obtained while suppressing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges.

Wishing also to provide henceforth with paternal concern for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your estates or granges to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare to use violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, [Col. 0050B] as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons; and we strengthen them by the privilege of this present writing.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but let all things be preserved entire, wholly serving the purposes of those for whose governance and support they were granted, with the authority of the Apostolic See reserved. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt rashly to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to divine vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. [Col. 0050D] I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of Saints Pudentiana and Pastor. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Callixtus at Saint Mary in Trastevere. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin . . . . . I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 0051A] I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Geoffrey, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Saint Eudoxia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquino. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 0051B] I, Nicholas, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Oukea. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Rainald, notary and chancellor of the lord pope, . . . . . . . . . residing [perhaps at Verona] on the third day before the Nones of May, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Innocent III.

## XX. To the abbot and convent of Saint-Germain-des-Prés

[Note: See Letter III of the Appendix to this work, note.]

—He confirms to them the possessions which the noblewoman Philippa had granted to their monastery. (1199; Lateran, 15 May.)

[We publish this bull from a copy carefully transcribed by ourselves from the original kept in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which Dom Poirier shared with us. From this original hangs the seal or bull of the pontiff, very well preserved, on a red and yellow silk cord. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0051C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . . . the abbot and convent of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When that which is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the diligence of our office, to its due [Col. 0051D] effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, the possessions which a noblewoman named Philippa granted to your monastery by deliberate decision, just as you possess them justly and peaceably and as is more fully set forth in the authentic instrument made concerning them; and we strengthen them by the protection of this present writing. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of May, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXI. To the abbot and convent of the monastery of Altimont

[Note: Concerning the abbots of the monastery of Altimont around the period with which we are dealing, the following few remarks occur in the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 117:

“XVIII. Robert, in the year 1185, conveyed to the Church of Ninives all the right which he possessed in the parish of Xaintes; he also occurs in the following year.

“XIX. Radulf, in 1202 and 1209. Also recorded in 1212, etc.”]

—He confirms to them possession of the chapel of Grantreing. (1199; Lateran, 5 June.)

[From the cartulary of the monastery of Altimont. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0052B]

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to completion, by a corresponding result, wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, willingly concurring in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, the chapel of Grantreing [Note: [Col. 0051D]

Alternatively, “of Grandi-Renium,” as noted in the copy. “The village of Grantreing, *Grandi-Renium*, lies two and a half leagues from Maubeuge, on the road leading to Binch, in Austrian Brabant.”

[Col. 0052D] Is it the same as Reneh? Certainly, the right in the churches of Reng and Chiweneis had formerly been conveyed by the Chapter of Aachen to the brothers of Altimont. See Miraeus, vol. I, p. 544, ch. LVII. Those churches had been granted to the Chapter of Aachen by Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, in 1122. See ibid., p. 523, where J. F. Foppens noted: “Rench and Chivenis, otherwise Kuivei, are villages of Hainaut, whose altars or estates the canons of Blessed Mary of Aachen granted to the monks of Altimont, near the town of Maubeuge in Hainaut.”], just as you possess it justly and peaceably, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Therefore, let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone [Col. 0052C] presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of June, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXII. To John, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris

[Note: See Letter XLV of Book Three, note.]

—He grants him the use of the mitre. (1199; Lateran, 10 June.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from the original kept in the archives of the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève, which Dom Abbot Mongez, member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, shared with us. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0052D] son JOHN, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The special prerogative of affection and favour which we held, when we occupied a lesser office, and unceasingly hold, toward the church entrusted to you and toward your own person, admonishes and urges us to attend more carefully to your honour and advantage and to do those things which concern alike the benefit and advancement of that church and of yourself. Since the performance of works is a proof of affection, as a sign of the favour which you formerly found in our eyes, we have judged that your devotion should personally be adorned with the ornament and use of the mitre, for the honour of your church; and we intend and desire, God willing, to do greater things for you hereafter. Therefore, as a prudent and honourable man, use these things with such reverence that no abuse may be noted in you.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the second year of [Col. 0053B] our pontificate.

Seal.

## XXIII. To the dean and chapter of Saint Mary and Saint Theobald at Metz

—They are received under the protection of Saint Peter, and the church of Holy Cross and the chapel of Saint Ferrucius are specifically confirmed to them. (1199; Lateran, 30 July.)

[From the archives of the collegiate church of Saint Theobald at Metz. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Saint Mary and Saint Theobald at Metz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0053C] The most holy Roman Church is accustomed, in accordance with the duty of its customary piety, to cherish more warmly its devoted and humble sons and, like a loving mother, to protect them by the defence of her protection so that they may not be harassed by the vexations of wicked men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, willingly concurring in your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves your church and persons, together with all the goods which you now reasonably possess or may hereafter, by lawful means and by the Lord’s favour, acquire. In particular, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, the church of Holy Cross and the chapel of Saint Ferrucius, with all their appurtenances, just as you possess them justly and peaceably; and [Col. 0053D] we strengthen them by the protection of this present writing. Therefore, no person whatsoever may lawfully infringe this page of our protection and confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXIV. He confirms to the lepers of Saint Lazarus at Meaux one prebend in the church of Saint Stephen at Meaux

(1199; Lateran, 18 August.)

[DUPLESSIS, *History of Meaux*, II, 84.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0054A] sons, the lepers of Saint Lazarus at Meaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[lacuna]

. . . The prebend which you hold in the church of Saint Stephen at Meaux, with its appurtenances, just as you possess it justly and reasonably, . . . we confirm by apostolic authority, etc. . . .

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXV. To all Christ’s faithful established in Saxony and Westphalia

—That they may gird themselves manfully for the Christian faith. (1199; Lateran, 5 October.)

[LILEJEGREN, *Diplomatarium Suecanum*, I, 113.]

[Col. 0054B] INNOCENT, bishop . . . . . to all Christ’s faithful established in Saxony and Westphalia: greeting, etc.

Just as the ruling of ecclesiastical teaching does not permit unwilling persons to be compelled to believe, so the Apostolic See, which is the universal mother of all, grants the defence of its protection to those who believe freely, and by wholesome admonitions exhorts the faithful to defend them, lest, if the aid of defence is denied to recent converts, they either return to their former errors or at least regret having believed.

For we have learned that, when M., bishop of Livonia of blessed memory, entered the province of Livonia and cast the nets of his preaching in the word of the Lord for a catch, [Col. 0054C] among barbarian peoples who render to brute animals, leafy trees, clear waters, green plants, and unclean spirits the honour due to God, he advanced so far, by the Lord’s grant, that he led many persons recalled from their errors to knowledge of the truth and instructed with saving doctrines those reborn through the sacred water of baptism.

But the enemy, who prowls about like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, envying alike their conversion and salvation, stirred up by wicked suggestions the persecution of the neighbouring pagans against them. These pagans desire to wipe them from the earth and abolish from those regions the memory of the Christian name. Therefore, lest negligence be imputed to us if those who have already believed are forced to turn back, and lest anyone presume [Col. 0054D] to receive our faith if those who have already received it remain undefended against pagan attacks, we carefully admonish and exhort all of you, enjoining this upon you for the remission of sins: unless the pagans settled about the Church of Livonia are willing to make a truce with the Christians and observe the truce they have made, rise powerfully and manfully, in the name of the God of hosts, in defence of the Christians who are in those regions.

Moreover, by authority of this letter we grant to all from your regions who have vowed to visit the thresholds of the saints that, in exchange for the vow they have made, they may proceed to those regions in defence of the Church of Livonia, out of reverence for the Christian name. We receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves all who, fired with divine zeal, resolve to go in defence of the Church of Livonia and of the Christians [Col. 0055A] established in those regions, and we bestow on them the benefit of apostolic protection.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of October.

## XXVI. To Odo, bishop of Paris, and his successors

[Note: See the note to Letter X of Book Three.]

—Concerning the confirmation of goods and privileges. (1199; Lateran, 11 November.)

[From the cartulary of the bishop of Paris, manuscript in the Royal Library, no. 5185, p. 67. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

The more famous the noble and glorious Church of Paris is by reason of being the see of the king of the Franks, and the more devoted you show yourself, venerable brother Bishop Odo, by manifest proofs in love and reverence for Saint Peter and the holy Roman [Col. 0055B] Church, the more willingly do we grant the requested support in matters known to concern the honour and advantage of both. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Odo, favourably assenting to your reasonable petitions, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory—Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Alexander, Clement, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs—we strengthen by the privilege of apostolic protection for you and your successors, and through you for the Church of Paris, whatever the Church of Paris now justly and canonically possesses or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the liberality of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, God being favourable, acquire. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

[Col. 0055C] Namely, the church of Saint Marcellus; the church of Saint Cloud, with its estate and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Germanus of Auxerre; the church of Saint Eligius; likewise the church of Campellis, with its prebends and its three parishes—namely, Saint Medericus, Capella, and Kerris—belonging to that church, while preserving the annual payment to the Church of Sens of a rent of two solidi in the currency current in that region. The aforesaid churches are known to belong by right and ownership to the Church of Paris and its bishop; likewise, episcopal [Col. 0055D] jurisdiction in the following abbeys and their parishes, and over all their parishioners: namely, the abbey of Latiniacum; the abbey of Fossatum; the abbey of Saint Maglorius; the abbey of Saint Victor; the abbey of the Valley of Saint Mary; the abbey of Sarucia; the abbey of Heriyallis; the abbey of Hermeriae; the abbey of Mont-Estivus; the abbey of the nuns of Montmartre; the abbey of Edera; the abbey of Kala; the abbey of Gif; the abbey of regular canons of Livriacum; the abbey of Vallis Profunda; and, in addition, the church of Argenteuil.

Wishing also to provide for the peace and tranquillity of the Church of Paris, we forbid henceforth the imposition or collection by anyone of the exaction and tallage which [Col. 0056A] Louis, formerly illustrious king of the Franks of renowned memory, levied in the lands of that bishopric after the death of your predecessor Stephen, bishop of Paris of blessed memory. Rather, just as it was remitted in perpetuity and confirmed in writing by that king to your predecessor Theobald, bishop of Paris of blessed memory, and to his successors, we confirm it by this page of the present writing.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you the agreement and conventions made between your predecessor Stephen, formerly bishop of the aforesaid church, and the aforesaid Louis, king of the Franks of blessed memory, concerning the place situated in the suburbs of Paris called Campellus: namely, that a third part of the entire revenue arising from the ditch of that land—whether through rent, purchases, sales, profits, or any other means—shall be paid to you and your successors without any diminution, while the other two parts shall be rendered to the royal fisc. Whoever is the king’s provost in this matter shall swear fealty to you and your successors, and your provost shall swear it to the king and his heirs; and neither shall receive or dispose of anything from the land without the other.

We also establish that, if any canon of the Church of Paris is promoted to the honour of a bishopric, his prebend shall freely revert to the Church of Paris. We further forbid by apostolic authority anyone whatsoever to seize the furnishings of a deceased bishop of Paris; rather, they shall remain intact for the use of the church [Col. 0056C] and his successor, as was granted and confirmed in writing by the aforesaid Louis, formerly illustrious king of the Franks.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb you or your successors concerning this our confirmation, take away the possessions of the Church of Paris, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations whatsoever; but let all things be preserved entire, wholly serving the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, with the authority of the Apostolic See reserved in all things. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place and church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Raynald, archbishop of Acheruntia, acting as chancellor, on the third day before the Ides of November, in the second indiction, in the year 1199 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Innocent III.

## XXVII. To the abbot and convent of Saint Maximin of Micy

[Note: We cannot determine with certainty who at that time was abbot of Micy. In the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1534, Lancelin—also Jancelin, also Laurence—is mentioned in documents from 1183 down to the year [Col. 0058D] 1198. Soon afterward, but not before 1206, Humbert is mentioned, at least as late as 1212.]

—Possession of the church of Saint Mary of Burgo is confirmed to them. (1199; Lateran, 30 December.)

[From the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Maximin of Micy, fol. 22 verso, ch. 83. The copy contains the following note written in French: “This bull, which confirms to the Abbey of Saint-Mesmin the priory of Notre-Dame du Bourg, must be of Pope Innocent III and dated 29 December 1199. For this priory was founded about the year 1060, and from that time until 1270, when the cartulary of this house was written through the care of Abbot Adam, Innocent III is the only pope found at Rome in the second year of his pontificate, as is verified by the *History of the Popes*.” BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0057B]

It is fitting that we give ready consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to fulfilment, with the corresponding effect, wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your church the church of Blessed Mary of Burgo Monachorum, with all its appurtenances, just as you possess it justly and peaceably; and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Therefore, let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or [Col. 0057C] rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

## XXVIII. To the brothers of the Hospital of Jerusalem

—They are no longer to presume to celebrate in lands placed under interdict by the Church. (1200; Lateran, 21 January.)

[VARIN, *Archives of Reims*, II, 435, Cartulary G of the chapter, fol. 68.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0057D] sons, the master [and] brothers of the Hospital of Jerusalem: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we ought to extend the gaze of our consideration to all ecclesiastical men, we especially desire and ought to assist our beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Reims, in proportion as they more devotedly observe clerical propriety and more freely protect ecclesiastical liberty. You should know that the Church of Reims has stated before us that, while it places under interdict the lands of the noblemen N. of Ruminiacum and R. of Rosetum, you, abusing indulgences of the Apostolic See, presume [Col. 0058A] to celebrate divine offices in those lands and confer ecclesiastical sacraments upon those under interdict.

Since, however, we do not wish you to be deprived of your privileges, neither do we wish the rights of the Church of Reims—which holds a great place in the Gallican Church—or of other churches to be injured through you. We therefore command and strictly enjoin your discretion that in the aforesaid lands, and in others so long as they are subject to interdict, you presume nothing further than what has been granted you by the privileges or indulgences of the Church of Reims.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the third year of our pontificate.

## XXIX. To N. . . .

—That he shall cause the sentence of interdict pronounced against Philip, king of France, to be inviolably observed. (1199; Lateran, 11 March.)

[Col. 0058B]

“How much our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the Franks,” etc. It exists among the Registers of Innocent. See *Patrologia*, vol. CCXIV, col. 1014.

## XXX. To the chapter of Langres

—Concerning the provisional maintenance of the bishop of Langres upon his resignation of the bishopric. (1200; Lateran, 14 March.)

[From instruments reported in the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 195, ch. LXXXVI.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Langres: greeting and apostolic [Col. 0058C] blessing.

Since our venerable brother, your former bishop [Note: [Col. 0058D] He was probably Garnerius de Rochefort; see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 591.], resigned that bishopric into our hands, and we provided for his maintenance out of certain possessions of that church, we wish so to guard the Church itself against loss that it may suffer no injury in future concerning those matters known to have been done by our provision and command. Therefore, desiring to provide for you and your church with diligent care, we strictly forbid by the present authority the aforesaid bishop to presume, by any rashness, to enfeoff, alienate, or otherwise dispose of, or place under anyone’s tribute, any of those things [Col. 0058D] which we assigned to him for his maintenance. If he should attempt to act contrary to our prohibition, we decree his act void and of no effect.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the third year of our pontificate.

## XXXI. To R., abbot, and the convent of Saint Michael

[Note: Very little is found among the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* concerning this abbot of Saint Michael in the diocese of Verdun, vol. XIII, col. 1278:

“XXVII. Robert I, 1199 (indeed 1200), obtains a bull from Innocent III.”]

—He confirms to them certain possessions. (1200; Lateran, 26 March.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed by Dom Michel Calloz, subprior of Saint Airy in the diocese of Verdun, from the original preserved in the archives of the Abbey of the monastery of Saint Michael, bundle B. 7. See the end of the bull. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0059A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons R., abbot, and the convent of Saint Michael: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to completion, by a corresponding result, wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, willingly concurring in your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the testimony or protection of this present writing: the estate of Condeio, with its church, tithes, and altar, which you possess by the gift of Peter and Odo, bishops of Toul of blessed memory; [Col. 0059B] the hospital of Saint Denis at Bar, with its church and appurtenances; likewise the freehold of Gemelli Court and of Troium, which you purchased from the two knightly brothers Pontius and Hugh, with the approval and consent of their heirs; the fifteen pounds of Provins currency which Henry, former count of Bar, granted you to receive annually in the town of Bar; and those things which you now justly and canonically possess or may hereafter, by lawful means and the Lord’s bounty, acquire. Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our protection or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation [Col. 0059C] of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the third year of our pontificate.

I, the undersigned, Subprior of the Abbey of St. Airy of Verdun, certify that I have made the present copy from the original itself, and that it conforms to it entirely. Done at the Abbey of Saint-Michel, at Saint-Mihiel, 10 April 1788. Signed: D. Michel COLLOZ.

The original is written on a parchment measuring eight inches and five lines in width by six inches and one line in height, excluding the fold, which contains eleven lines; it is furnished with an ordinary lead seal, attached and suspended by a cord of yellow and green silk.

### XXXII. To Thiemon, bishop of Bamberg.—On the canonization of St Cunegunda.  
*(1200. Lateran, 3 April.)*

[We give fragments only. The complete text exists in *Patrologia*, vol. CXL, col. 219, after the *Life of St Henry the Emperor*.]

[Col. 0059D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEUMONI [Note: [Col. 0059D] Thiemo succeeded Poppo or Potto in 1192 and left the see in 1201.], bishop, and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Bamberg, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

Since, according to evangelical truth, no one, etc.

[Col. 0060A] Among these is Cunegunda of blessed memory, august empress of the Romans: while she once lived in the world, she was eminent in great merits; now, living in heaven, she shines forth through many miracles, so that her holiness may be proved by certain signs, etc.

Indeed, when the merits and miracles of the aforesaid empress had, through your report, come to the hearing of Pope Celestine of blessed memory, my predecessor, he entrusted their investigation, so that he might acquire more certain knowledge of them, by apostolic letters to our venerable brothers the bishops of Augsburg and Eichstätt and the bishop of Würzburg of blessed memory, and to our beloved sons the abbots of Ebrach, Langheim, and Heilsbronn [Note: [Col. 0060D] Ebrach, commonly so called, is a most distinguished Cistercian monastery in Franconia, situated in the diocese of Würzburg. Langheim is of the same order, but in the diocese of Bamberg itself. It was founded by Blessed Otto, bishop of Bamberg, as was also the following monastery, Heilsbronn, likewise of the Cistercian order.]. After his death, however, the miracles began to become so manifest and to multiply [Col. 0060B], etc., that we enrolled that blessed virgin Cunegunda in the catalogue of the saints and decreed that her memorial should be celebrated among the saints. Therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 3 April, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXIII. To the parish priests and all the clergy of the diocese of Castello.—That the name of John, patriarch of Grado, should be pronounced before that of the doge of Venice in the blessing of the candle, according to the ancient custom and the dignity of the patriarch of Grado.  
*(1200. Lateran, 21 April.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 1133.]

[Col. 0060C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the parish priests and all the clergy of the diocese of Castello, greetings and the apostolic blessing.
