At the complaint of our venerable brother the patriarch of Grado, who protested that he was being burdened in this matter by your bishop—because, contrary to an ancient custom which he himself had until then observed, the bishop was unwilling in the blessing of the candle to place the patriarch’s name before the doge’s name—we recall having sent him apostolic letters, ordering him, by following the example of his mother Church of Grado and of his fellow bishops, not to deny the patriarch the honour due to him. Therefore, by these apostolic letters, we command your whole body [Col. 0060D] that you yourselves, as you have hitherto been accustomed and as is observed in the other churches of the patriarchate of Grado, pronounce the patriarch’s name in the ancient manner, lest you appear to set a man before God, whose minister that patriarch is. Take diligent care not to raise any further question concerning the matters set out above; otherwise, however much we may wish, insofar as we can with God, to show deference to the aforesaid doge, whom we sincerely love in the Lord with charity, the consequences would teach you how grave it is [Col. 0061A] to refuse obedience to the commands of one’s superiors.

Given at the Lateran, 21 April, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXIII bis. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0061D]

Concerning the abbots of the monastery of Der, at the period with which we are dealing, these few notices occur in the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 920:

“XXIX. Evrard is found in 1197.

XXX. Nicholas, of whom there is only the bare name.

XXXI. Rainaud II settled a dispute with Clairvaux in 1230.”]

and convent of Der.—Confirmation of churches and rights in the diocese of Troyes.  
*(1200. Lateran, 26 April.)*

[From Cartulary II of the Monastery of Der, p. 6. BRÉQ., ibid.]

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and that we bring to fulfilment, through the resulting effect, prayers that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favourable assent to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to the same monastery, and fortify by the protection of the present writing, all churches, with their liberties, jurisdictions [Col. 0061B] and appurtenances, revenues, lands, dues, and rights which the monastery of Der has acquired in the diocese of Troyes through the grants of popes and the benefactions of other faithful persons, just as it possesses them all justly and peacefully and as they are contained in the instrument drawn up on this matter by Manasses [Note: [Col. 0061D] Manasses II, born of the lords of Pougy in the diocese of Troyes, kinsman of Manasses, bishop of Langres, educated from his earliest youth in the Church of Troyes, was raised from its archdeaconry to episcopal rank in 1181 and died about 1190. *Gallia Christiana*, ibid., vol. XII, col. 502.], bishop of Troyes, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0061D] This instrument must doubtless be understood as the one referred to in the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 290, where they speak of Witer, twenty-seventh abbot of the monastery of Der: “In the year 1185 William, archbishop of Reims, confirmed everything which the monks of Der possessed in the archbishopric of Reims, and Manasses, bishop of Troyes, what they possessed in the bishopric of Troyes.”].

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no one to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, [Col. 0061C] His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 26 April, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXIII ter. To the same.—Privilege concerning Gigny and the churches in the diocese of Châlons.  
*(1200. Lateran, 26 April.)*

[From Cartulary II of the monastery of Der, p. 91. BRÉQ., ibid.]

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that, through the solicitude of our office, it be brought to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by your just prayers, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your same monastery, and fortify by the protection of the present writing, all churches, with their liberties, jurisdictions and appurtenances, revenues, [Col. 0061D] lands, dues, and rights which the monastery of Der has acquired in the diocese of Châlons through the grants of popes and the benefactions of other faithful persons; likewise the church of Gigny, bestowed upon your same monastery from motives of piety [Col. 0062A]. We confirm these things just as the monastery possesses them all justly and peacefully, and as they are contained in instruments carefully drawn up concerning them by the bishops of Châlons and by our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Santa Sabina [Note: [Col. 0062D] On William, archbishop of Reims, see the note to Letter XIV of Book III. Compare also Letter XXX above.].

Let it therefore be lawful for absolutely no one to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 26 April, in the third year [Col. 0062B] of our pontificate.

### XXXIV. To all archbishops, bishops, abbots, etc.—That they are to protect and defend the privileges granted to the abbot and convent of Foigny.  
*(1200. Lateran, 26 May.)*

[From a copy carefully transcribed by Dom Jeannin, monk of Saint-Michel in the diocese of Verdun, from the original preserved in the archives of Foigny Abbey in the diocese of Laon. See the end of the letter. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops [Col. 0062C], and to his beloved sons the abbots, priors, archdeacons, deans, priests, and other prelates of churches to whom these letters shall come, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

We have heard—and, hearing it, have been astonished—that although it has been granted by our fathers and predecessors, and afterwards allowed and confirmed by ourselves, to our beloved sons, . . . . . . the abbot [Note: [Col. 0062D] Gilbert, formerly abbot of Bohéries and made abbot of Foigny, is known from instruments from at least 1187 until at least 1211. *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IX, col. 630.] and convent of Foigny, as to all brethren of the Cistercian order, that they should be bound to pay tithes to no one from the produce which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, certain persons nevertheless presume, contrary to the indulgence of the Apostolic See, to demand and extort tithes from them. By a corrupt and perverse interpretation of the clause in the apostolic privileges, they assert [Col. 0062D] that the phrase “from labours” is to be understood as referring to newly cleared lands.

Since it is manifest to all who think rightly that such an interpretation is perverse and contrary to sound understanding—because, according to that clause, they are altogether free and exempt from the payment of tithes both from those lands which they have brought or bring under cultivation, and from cultivated lands which they till by their own hands or at their own expense—lest anyone have grounds for maligning them or in any way vexing them contrary to justice, we command you by apostolic letters, ordering you to ensure that you prohibit all your parishioners by apostolic authority from presuming in any way to demand or extort tithes from the aforesaid brethren, whether from their labours, from other lands which they cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense, or from the produce of their animals. For if, in saying “from labours,” we had intended to refer only to [Col. 0063B] newly cleared lands, we would have said “from newly cleared lands,” as we do in the privileges of certain others.

Since it is neither fitting nor honourable for the ordinances of the Apostolic See—which ought to retain inviolable force—to be violated, we order and firmly command you that, if any canons, clerics, monks, or laymen, contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, burden the aforesaid brethren by demanding tithes, you shall strike the laymen with a sentence of excommunication; and, without contradiction, delay, or appeal, suspend canons, clerics, or monks from office. You shall ensure that both the sentence of excommunication and the sentence of suspension are inviolably observed until due satisfaction has been made. Furthermore, by the authority of the present letters, we command you [Col. 0063C] that if anyone lays violent hands upon the aforesaid brethren, you shall publicly declare him excommunicated, with lighted candles, and ensure that he is carefully avoided by all as excommunicated until he makes appropriate satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren and presents himself before the Apostolic See with letters from the diocesan bishop containing the true facts of the case.

Given at the Lateran, 26 May, in the third year of our pontificate.

I, the undersigned, delegate of the Lord Keeper of the Seals for the investigation and transcription of the historical monuments of Thiérache and part of the Laon region, certify that the present copy conforms to the original. This 18 April 1788. Signed: D. R. N. JEANNIN, monk of Saint-Michel.

### XXXV. To the monks of Saint-Denis.—That, while the land of Philip, king of the French, lies under interdict, they may celebrate divine offices “in a low voice, with closed doors.”  
*(1200. Lateran, 22 June.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis in France*, Paris, 1625, quarto, p. 536.]

[Col. 0063D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the convent of Saint-Denis, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

A request has been made to us on behalf of your monastery that, since you devoutly and humbly observe the interdict now imposed upon the land of our most illustrious son in Christ, Philip, the illustrious king of the French, [Col. 0064A] and since it appears rather dangerous for so great a community to cease altogether from the celebration of divine worship, we might grant you permission to celebrate divine offices in a low voice and with closed doors. Therefore, assenting to your petition in this matter from the customary kindness of the Apostolic See, we grant by the authority of these present letters to your devotion that two or three of you together in your monastery may read the canonical hours, rather than sing the divine offices, behind closed doors, with the interdicted excluded and in a voice so low that you cannot be heard outside.

Let it therefore be lawful for absolutely no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 22 June, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXVI. To the convent of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.—He grants them that, during the interdict, two or three of them may read the canonical hours together.  
*(1200. Lateran, 22 June.)*

[We carefully transcribed this bull from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The pope’s seal or bull, very well preserved, hangs from a red and yellow cotton thread. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0064B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the convent of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

A request has been made to us on behalf of your monastery that, since you devoutly and humbly observe the interdict now imposed upon the land of our dearest son in Christ, Ph[ilip], the illustrious king of the French, [Col. 0064C] and since it appears rather dangerous for so great a community to cease altogether from the celebration of divine worship, we might grant you permission to celebrate divine offices in a low voice and with closed doors. Therefore, assenting to your petition in this matter from the customary kindness of the Apostolic See, we grant by the authority of these present letters to your devotion that two or three of you together in your monastery may read the canonical hours, rather than sing the divine offices, behind closed doors, with the interdicted excluded and in a voice so low that you cannot be heard outside.

Let it be lawful for absolutely no one to infringe this page of our concession or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 0064D] the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 22 June, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXVII. To the archbishops and bishops established throughout the kingdom of England.—He grants various privileges.  
*(1200. Lateran, 3 August.)*

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., ed. 1816, I, 81.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops established throughout the kingdom of England, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

Your devotion deserves that the Apostolic See should protect you [Col. 0065A] by timely favour and distinguish you by the special privilege of grace. Therefore, moved by your petitions and wishing your rights to be kept unimpaired, we grant by the authority of these present letters to your whole body that, when ecclesiastical benefices belonging to your collation fall vacant, you may freely confer them, as pertains to you, without the hindrance of any opposition, upon suitable persons who are willing and able to serve usefully in them.

Let it therefore be lawful for no one to infringe this page of our concession or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

[Col. 0065B] Given at the Lateran, 3 August, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXVIII. To the noblewoman Gela [Note: [Col. 0066D] On Gela or Ghela, foundress of the convent here in question, see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 295.].—He confirms the foundation of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Sparmalia at Honkeuliet [Note: [Col. 0065D] On this monastery, belonging to the diocese of Bruges, see *Gallia Christiana*, cited place.].  
*(1200. Lateran, 4 August.)*

[Extracts from instruments reported in vol. V of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 360, chapter 14.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman GELA, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to fulfilment, through the resulting effect, prayers which do not depart from the path of reason. [Col. 0065C] Therefore, beloved daughter in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the chapel which, in honour of blessed Peter and with the consent of our venerable brother, the bishop of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0065D] See the note to Letter XLI of Book III.], in whose diocese it is situated, you have newly founded at your own expense, and in which you propose, having abandoned the error of worldly vanity, to serve the Lord under the religious habit. We receive it with all the goods which that chapel now rightfully possesses or may hereafter acquire by just means, God being propitious.

Let it be lawful for absolutely no one to infringe this page of our protection or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, [Col. 0065D] His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 4 August, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXIX. To the dean and chapter of Reims.—That the canons of Reims should adhere to common table fellowship.  
*(1200. Lateran, 7 December.)*

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 435.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Reims, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0066A] Although, as the charity of some grows cold and the evil of the day increases, nearly all have gradually and successively fallen away from the perfection of those of whom it is read that in the primitive Church they had one heart and one soul; and although the frailty of our time does not admit the ardour of such great charity, and, burdened by the loads of our sins, we may neither wish nor be able to imitate in all things the resolve of so great a perfection, yet we ought at least, from afar and insofar as we can, as it were to venerate their footprints. We should preserve in humility even that which has descended to us from them by the inviolable observance of our predecessors, as though by hereditary succession.

For just as Scripture forbids us to transgress the boundaries established by our fathers, so we are bound, insofar as we can, to follow their foremost resolve in the love of sacred religion and in the pattern of ecclesiastical propriety, and reverently and inviolably to preserve their praiseworthy customs and traditions—lest, if we act otherwise, which God forbid, we appear to have degenerated from our fathers and to have succeeded them not in their purpose and good desire but in place alone. Although this ought generally to be considered carefully and attentively by all, individually and collectively, those who hold the greater place in the Church of God, and whose conduct and acts are taken by others as examples, ought to weigh it with so much the more careful diligence and subtle reflection, as it would be more shameful for a lamp to smoke upon a lampstand than beneath a bushel, and for a worthless eye [Col. 0066C] to disfigure and darken the body than for some hidden and deformed member to do so.

Indeed, among almost all the provinces of the world, the province of France is powerful both through the endowment of learning and through the fragrance of virtues and the gravity of manners; and within it the Church of Reims shines with metropolitan dignity. Thus it is fitting that we preserve a more ample propriety both in words and deeds, in proportion as a more exalted position would afford your dishonesty a less secure hiding-place, and as your fall from the purpose of your predecessors would be more disgraceful—since a blemish is more conspicuous upon a shining body and a person is mutilated more grotesquely in the face.

We have learned that the following custom was anciently observed in that Church: all [Col. 0066D] the canons had a single refectory and a common table. Although not all ate there every day, some of the canons ate there on every day. All together applied themselves so diligently to works of piety and bestowed such care of hospitality upon the poor and sick that they not only supplied necessities to them through others, but at appointed times the dean and canons personally went to a hospital assigned for this work, washed and dried the hands and feet of the poor, and even kissed them as an example of humility; they gave each person his food allowance [Col. 0067A] and afterwards returned to the church in procession.

It is also said that such severity was observed in restraining and punishing offences that, even if a canon were falsely accused of some minor fault, he would not presume to excuse himself before, kneeling before the dean and chapter and kissing the ground, he had humbly sought pardon. Although these practices are still observed fairly honourably in that Church, you show no small negligence in attending the common table, since neither all of you nor every day are served in the common refectory. Thus, through your negligence, what was accustomed to be continuous in the times of your predecessors has become interrupted.

[Col. 0067B] Therefore, receiving gratefully and favourably what has generally been reported to our apostolic office concerning you, we admonish and exhort your discretion in the Lord, and command you by apostolic letters: applying yourselves to pious works, adhere to the footsteps of your predecessors; attend the common table regularly as of old; be diligent in rendering the service of hospitality to the poor; and be zealous in correcting offences.

You also, son Dean, are to exercise the rigour of ecclesiastical discipline over wrongdoers in such a manner that another’s offence, if it remains uncorrected, may not reasonably be imputed to your negligence; and if you neglect to disturb the perverse persons whom you can and ought, by virtue of the office of dean entrusted to you, to restrain, you will be convicted of fostering them in their perversity. Know moreover that we have kindly received our beloved son Ja . . . . , your canon, whom you took care to commend to us in your letters; he resides commendably and honourably at the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, 7 December, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XXXIX bis. To the archbishops of Armagh and Tuam [Note: [Col. 0067D] Compare Letter XLII of Book III.], and to all bishops, abbots, priors, and canons professing the Order of Arrouaise in Ireland.—That, according to the statutes of the Order of Arrouaise, at least one or two of them should not fail to attend the annual chapter of that place.  
*(1200. Lateran, 9 December.)*

[We publish this letter, or rather bull, from a copy transcribed from the archives of Arrouaise Abbey and deposited in our collection by Dom Quinsert. He appended to the copy the following French note, which we have judged worth reproducing here:

“This bull, very legible and complete, is of Innocent III, dated the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the third year of his pontificate. The lead seal, on one side of which are seen the customary effigies of St Peter and St Paul and on the other the name of Innocent III, *Innocentius Papa III*, is attached to the bull by a double tail of string. It is addressed to the archbishops and bishops of Ireland, in whose dioceses there were houses of regular canons belonging to the congregation of Arrouaise. It will not be useless to report here a passage from a manuscript written in the hand of Walter, abbot of Arrouaise, in the year 1179. ‘In the time of Gervase,’ he says, ‘who was abbot in the year 1121, Malachy of holy memory, archbishop of the Irish, passing by way of our house, inspected and approved our customs, took copies of our books and uses of the Church to his Ireland, and ordered almost all the clerics established in episcopal sees and in many other places throughout Ireland to adopt and observe our order and habit, and especially the divine office in the Church,’ etc.”

Thus far Dom Quinsert in his note. What is said of Gervase, the first abbot of Arrouaise, by the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 434, agrees very well with it:

“IV. Gervase, a native of Boulogne, otherwise called Bolonia, the first abbot—for formerly provosts governed the monastery of Arrouaise—was consecrated by Robert, bishop of Arras, in 1121. He built monasteries in various places and sent out the members of his own monastery to plant the Arrouaisian religious life; some canons of other orders, renouncing their own order, eagerly desired to embrace it.” BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0068B]

You ought to strive with your whole purpose for the observance of the religious life which you have freely professed, and diligently direct your minds to its increase, so that you may appear to advance from virtue to virtue and continually offer God service pleasing to Him. Therefore, since it has been prudently established for the strengthening and preservation of the Order of Arrouaise that [Col. 0068C] the brethren ought to assemble at the annual chapter of that place [Note: [Col. 0067D] On this statute compare the bull of Pope Alexander III addressed to WALTER, ABBOT OF ARROUAISE, and his brethren, given at VITERBO, 28 July, which is printed in the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, ibid., col. 436.], we ask and exhort your devotion in the Lord, commanding you by apostolic letters, that at least one or two of you should not defer attending the chapter at Arrouaise on the feast of St Matthew, apostle and evangelist, so that they may report the statutes of the general chapter to their fellow brethren who were not present and, in the Lord, carry out other measures pertaining to the advancement of the order.

Given at the Lateran, 9 December, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XL. Form in which the lord pope gives advice concerning the carrying out of a divorce.  
*(1200.)*

(BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, folio edition, III, 21.)

[Col. 0068D]

The lord pope advises that both grounds should be alleged, namely the ground of affinity and that of sorcery. Hence, if the queen should be unwilling to produce witnesses in the case concerning affinity, that will please the lord pope. But if she wishes to produce witnesses, he will not be able to refuse her. Nor should the lord king fear on this account, because the pope will have those witnesses received through his procurator. Nor should the king plead delay [Col. 0069A], because there is now a greater delay because of fear.

In the case of sorcery, the lord pope makes this concession to the lord king: if the king causes an oath to be sworn upon his soul that he attempted to have intercourse with the queen and did not have intercourse, and that he does not principally hate her for another reason, the king will be believed if the queen does not swear that intercourse took place. The lord pope believes that she can easily be induced not to swear. Therefore, if the king fears that a sentence may be issued against him on the aforesaid grounds, the issuing of sentence can be deferred. The king will then remain at the point at which he now stands.

There is one matter in which the lord pope could not spare the lord king: namely, he would have to try again to have intercourse with her, because sorceries of this kind are removed by prayers.

### XLI. To the canons of Holy Trinity, London.—He receives them and their possessions under his protection.  
*(1201. Lateran, 12 January.)*

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 82, from the original in the treasury of the Receipt of the Exchequer.]

[Col. 0069B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and canons of Holy Trinity, London, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious vows and to grant kindly favour to the honourable petitions of supplicants. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your church with all the goods, both ecclesiastical and temporal, which it now rightfully possesses or may in future [Col. 0069C] acquire, through the grant of popes, the benefaction of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour.

We especially confirm to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of the present writing, the churches of Lesnes, Braching, Toreham, Welcumstrove, Bromfeld and Alfiswic, Nutele, St Botolph outside the gate called Aldgate, All Saints above the walls of the city of London, St Michael in the street called Aldgate, and Bixle, with all their appurtenances, just as you possess them rightfully and peaceably.

By the authority of the present letters, we forbid anyone to dare pronounce a sentence of excommunication against you [Col. 0069D] or your vicars without manifest and reasonable cause. When there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, without ringing bells and in a low voice.

We decree that no person may lawfully infringe this page of our confirmation, protection, and prohibition, or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 12 January, in the third year of our pontificate.

### XLII. To Thaddeus, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Ferraria in the diocese of Teano.—He confirms their privileges.  
*(1201. Anagni, 23 January.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 563.]

[Col. 0070A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THADDEUS, abbot of the monastery of Ferraria, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those who choose the religious life should have apostolic protection, lest an assault of anyone’s rashness either recall them from their resolve or, God forbid, weaken the strength [Col. 0070B] of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the present writing, the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service.

We establish, moreover, that the monastic order, which is known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God, the Rule of St Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire through the grant of popes, the benefaction of kings [Col. 0070C] or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have judged it proper to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances, in the territory of Vagra, the strips of land from the small holding of Corneliano and of Palmento, and whatever you reasonably possess there. In the territory of Teano, the strips of land of Fraxo and Pedis Montis, and whatever else you have there. At Alife, the land which you hold in exchange from the notary Benedict, and the mill which you hold in the same land—the land, bounded in the territory of the castle of Sant’Angelo de Rave Canina [Col. 0070D], is called Perdita; and the land called Gironis, which Robert of Fossaceca, knight, gave you; and whatever else you have there. The holdings with the right of the mill which John of Miminiano gave you at Alife, and whatever else you reasonably possess there. In the city of Sessa, the entire estate of possessions which Tallacauzzus, lord of Caiano, gave you: Oliveta; a house; and a share in the milling of all the olives of the upland district of the castle of Miniano, together with liberty to mill your olives there; and whatever else you justly have there. In the territory of Calvi, Silavimata, which you hold beside the River Volturno, in the place called St Stephen; and the lands which you hold beside the rivers in Gen. and Appia, in the place called the Strip of Silice. At Capua [Col. 0071A], the houses and possessions which John of Ricc., John Concarrus, Marcus of Raino, Sibilia, wife of Brother John, Peter of Alife, and Judge Alexander gave you. At Telese, and at V . . ., the estates which the count of Caserta bestowed upon you, one of which belonged to John Bassus and the other to John Forte. At Isernia, the mill which Roger, count of Molise, gave you; half of two mills, which Peter of Bruto there bestowed upon you, with a vineyard in the place called . . . At Monte Rodon, that which Landulf of Sino gave you in . . . The land which Mattia, wife of the late Robert Licinii, bestowed upon you, and the mill with its fulling-mill which you have there. Lands with a mill and olives which you have at Pantanis Indracon. The lands which Henry [Col. 0071B] of Montefusculo gave you at Albiniano; the land which Maria of Albiniano bestowed upon you; and the estates which Benedict Calatia gave you there. Moreover, the liberties which you possess throughout the kingdom concerning Plateaticum, passage-toll, and herbage-dues.

Further, of the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens, shrub-plots, or your fisheries, or from the rearing of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and fleeing the world, and retain them without any contradiction. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in [Col. 0071C] your monastery, from leaving that place without the permission of his abbot; and let no one dare retain one who leaves without the guarantee of your common letters. If anyone should nevertheless presume to retain him, you may pronounce regular discipline against those monks or conversi. We strictly forbid anyone to give personally, or alienate in any other manner, lands or any benefice bestowed upon your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than has been stated, we decree them void.

Furthermore, we prohibit any monk or conversus bound by profession in your house, even with the consent and [Col. 0071D] permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, from standing surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone beyond the amount fixed by the prudent decision of your chapter, unless this is for the manifest benefit of your house. If he presumes to do so, the convent shall not in any way be bound to answer for it. Moreover, in your own causes, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brethren, lest through lack of witnesses your right should be lost in any respect.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop or any other person whatever to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own property or [Col. 0072A] possessions; or to presume to enter your houses for the purpose of celebrating ordinations, hearing cases, or convening public assemblies; or to impede the regular election of your abbot, or in any way to interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in appointing or removing the one who is abbot at the time.

If the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when humbly and fittingly requested, refuses to bless the substituted abbot and to confer upon you the other things belonging to the episcopal office, it shall be lawful for that abbot, provided that he is a priest, to bless his own novices and exercise the other functions belonging to his office; and for you to receive from another bishop all that has been improperly denied by your own [Col. 0072B] bishop. We add, however, that in receiving professions offered by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops shall be content with the form and wording instituted from the origin of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must profess with their Order preserved intact, and are not to be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order.

For consecrations of altars or churches, holy oil, or any ecclesiastical sacrament whatever, no one may presume, under pretext of custom or otherwise, to extort anything from you; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things freely. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0072C] and he, relying on our authority, shall supply what is requested. If the see of the diocesan bishop is vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighbouring bishops, provided that no prejudice thereby arises in the future against your own bishops.

Since, indeed, you sometimes do not have access to your own bishops, if a bishop who is in communion with the Roman See, as we have said, and of whom you have full knowledge, should happen to pass through your district, you may receive from him . . . the consecration of altars and the ordination of monks by authority of the Apostolic See.

But if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce against your monasteries or persons established therein a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict; or pronounce such a sentence even against your hired labourers because you do not pay tithes, or on account of any matter granted you by apostolic favour; or against your benefactors because out of charity they have conferred benefits or services upon you, or have helped with labour on days when you work and others keep holiday—we decree that sentence void, as pronounced against the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall those letters have force which are shown to have been obtained while suppressing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges. Desiring also with paternal concern to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity [Col. 0073A], by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone within the enclosures of your establishments or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to use violence.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, all the liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, [Col. 0073B] or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly presumes rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself to stand guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

**“Lord, make with me a sign for good.”**

St Peter. St Paul.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, William, archbishop of Reims, cardinal priest of St Sabina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of St Pudentiana, of the Shepherd. [Col. 0073D] I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of St Callistus of St Mary across the Tiber. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St Martin of Equitius. I, Cencio, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Geoffrey, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca. I, Cencius, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of St Pammachius. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus. [Col. 0074A] I, Benedict, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Peter of Berri, cardinal deacon of St Adrian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St Eustace. I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.

[Col. 0074B] Given at Anagni, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 10 Kalends of January [23 December], fifth indiction; in the year 1201 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### XLIII. To the brethren of St Remigius of Reims.—Confirmation concerning the fishery of Courmonsteruel, and twenty pounds of wax and twenty measures of wine remitted to them by the archbishop.  
*(1201; Anagni, 11 February.)*

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, II, 444; Cartulary of Saint-Remi, fol. 4, no. XIX.]

INNOCENT, bishop, etc. . . . . . . the grants which the venerable . . . . . W., archbishop of Reims, made to you concerning twenty measures of wine and twenty [Col. 0074C] pounds of wax, in which your church was bound to him each year; the fishery in the Vidula beside the village of Courmosteriolo, granted to you by him; likewise the remission of the violence which fishermen continually inflicted upon you in the water of Folipene . . . . . and all things as are contained in the authentic documents of that same archbishop and of our most dear . . . . . King Philip . . . . . we confirm to you . . . . . etc.

Given at Anagni, on the third Ides of February [11 February], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### XLIV. To the . . . Bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0073D] See Letter VIII of Book Eight, note.].—That he should support Otto, emperor-elect.  
*(1201; Lateran, 1 March.)*

[From a copy carefully collated by the late Abbot Grandidier with the original preserved in the archives of the Church of Strasbourg. BRÉQ., ibid.—It survives, though less complete, in Innocent’s Register concerning the business of the Roman Empire, no. XLV. See *Patrologia*, vol. CCXVI, col. 1046.]

[Col. 0074D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Strasbourg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have long learned by certain experience that, although you may perhaps seem, constrained by a kind of necessity, to support the noble man Philip, duke of Swabia, yet inwardly you support our most dear son in Christ, the illustrious King Otto, elected emperor of the Romans and, God willing, to be crowned by us at a fitting time; for we understand that you adhered to him from the beginning and swore an oath of fidelity to him. Since, however, with necessity removed, that which necessity compelled ought likewise to cease, we command your brotherhood by these our apostolic letters, ordering you that, since we cannot support two men in obtaining the Empire, and since it is not so much the person that must be provided for in the Empire as the Empire in the person, and since the one found more suitable is considered more worthy for this purpose: because we wholly reject the person of the said duke with respect to obtaining the Empire, especially at this time, owing to the evident impediments which we set out in general letters; and because we receive the said Otto as king—you are not to delay publicly adhering to that king and vigorously and courageously supporting his party, notwithstanding any oath that you may perhaps have sworn to the duke by reason of the kingdom, since, now that he has been rejected, we have decreed that oath need not be kept. Otherwise, since, as we have said, you have sworn an oath of fidelity to Otto, if—what we do not believe, indeed do not even doubt—you henceforth become a violator of your own oath, we shall be compelled to proceed more severely against you.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of March [1 March], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### XLV. To the archbishop of Sens.—On behalf of Clarembald, chancellor of the Church of Meaux.  
*(1201; Lateran, 22 May.)*

[DUPLESSIS, *History of the Church of Meaux*, from the records of the Church of Meaux, II, 85.]

[Col. 0075C]

PETER, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, to all whom the present letters shall reach, greeting in the Lord. We wish it to come to the knowledge of posterity that we have received the pope’s letter in the following form:

> “INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the archbishop of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Our venerable brother, the bishop of Meaux, appearing in our presence, caused it to be explained before us that concerning the chancellorship of the Church of Meaux, which he granted to Master Clarembald, a learned man, as was said, and honourable, he had arranged that a beneficed ecclesiastical office should be established, to the honour of God [Col. 0075D] and of the Church of Meaux itself. Thus the said Master Clarembald and the other chancellors who succeed him shall henceforth be persons of the Church of Meaux, and after the other persons of that church shall hold the first place both among the clergy and in the chapter. Since the chancellorship has no revenues, lest the chancellor should be compelled, contrary to canonical prohibitions, to exact anything for governing the schools, the bishop has, by a pious and prudent resolution, proposed to assign it specified revenues out of his own income.
>
> “Since, therefore, the establishment in churches of honours and dignities, for more devoted service of divine worship, pertains to the advancement of churches, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when the said bishop has assigned suitable revenues for the chancellorship, relying on apostolic authority you shall establish—removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal—that the said chancellor and his successors shall henceforth hold a beneficed ecclesiastical office in the same church and have the first place after the other persons in choir and chapter, as stated above; striking down any opponents by ecclesiastical censure.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, 11 Kalends of June [22 May], in the fourth year of our pontificate.”

Accordingly, when we came to the Church of Meaux and the dean and chapter had assembled, the aforesaid bishop assigned to the chancellorship half of the entire [Col. 0076B] tithe of Quinciano, sixty solidi from the rent of the church of St Simeon of Vana, and forty solidi from the rent of the church of Seinz. And we, so that the aforesaid chancellor and his successors may henceforth hold a beneficed ecclesiastical office in the Church of Meaux and have the first place after the other persons in choir and chapter, with the concurring assent of the dean’s beneficed office and of the canons present, established this by the apostolic authority which we exercised, assigning status to him and his successors in choir and a place in chapter. Therefore, lest the memory of our excommunication grow obsolete through the passage of time, or anyone hereafter presume to raise a scruple of objection, we have reduced our acts to writing and authenticated them with the impression of our seal. Should any opponents appear, we strike them by the same authority with a sentence of excommunication, so that through fear of punishment all iniquity may be compelled to shut its mouth against this act.

Given at Meaux, in the year 1201 of the Incarnate Word, in the month of August.

### XLVI. To Odo, bishop of Paris, and the abbot of Lagny [Note: [Col. 0075D] See Letter 96 of Book X.] against the clerics of Rebais.  
*(1201; Lateran, 23 May.)*

[D. DUPLESSIS, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, 85, from the records of the Church of Meaux.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ODO, bishop of Paris, and his beloved son the abbot of Lagny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

At the complaint of our venerable brother, the bishop of Meaux, it has been reported to us that the clerics and laymen of Rebais refuse to obey him as their bishop. Therefore, lest their disobedience, if left uncorrected, give them an incentive to offend, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, removing the evasion of appeal, you compel the aforesaid clerics by ecclesiastical coercion, justice mediating, to render due satisfaction to the said bishop concerning this matter and henceforth to give their bishop the obedience and honour which they owe him [Col. 0077A], etc. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of June [23 May], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### XLVII. To Peter, archbishop of Sens, and the abbot of St Columba.—On the appointment of rural deans in the Church of Meaux.  
*(1201; Lateran, 23 May.)*

[DUPLESSIS, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, 86, from the cartulary of Meaux.]

PETER, by the grace of God archbishop and abbot of St Columba of Sens, to all whom the present letters shall reach, greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to come to everyone’s knowledge that we have received [Col. 0077B] the lord pope’s letter in the following form:

> “INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop and beloved son the abbot of St Columba of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “The complaint set forth to us by our venerable brother, the bishop of Meaux, disclosed that, whereas it pertains to him to appoint and remove rural deans in the diocese of Meaux, as has been maintained in the times of our predecessors, the archdeacons of the Church of Meaux oppose him on this point. They assert that he ought not appoint anyone dean without consulting them; and they do not fear, to his serious prejudice, to claim for themselves the subsidies which the rectors of churches in their diocese are bound to furnish to them, leaving him only two parts of the harvest. The same archdeacons also do not hesitate, contrary to his will and prohibition, to extort money from the priests of the diocese of Meaux through unlawful exactions.
>
> “Moreover, he set forth his complaint concerning the dean of Meaux: when he assigns vacant prebends to suitable persons and sends them to the dean and chapter so that they may receive them as brethren and canons, and the dean may corporally invest them with the prebends, as the custom of the Church requires, the dean frequently delays and hinders their reception, absents himself on that pretext, or maliciously alleges some frivolous grounds. Therefore, so that those things attempted in the Church of Meaux apart from the rule of right may be restored to their due state by the office of our solicitude, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, coming to that Church of Meaux, you diligently investigate the truth concerning these matters and whatever else is proposed to you in this connection; and, having the Lord before your eyes, correct by apostolic authority, according to God and justice and with the obstacle of appeal removed, whatever you find there needing correction, causing what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, etc. . . . Should both of you not be able, etc.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June [23 May], in the fourth year of our pontificate.”

Accordingly, having come to the Church of Meaux, summoned the parties, and placed them before us, we made the following settlement with the consent of the bishop and archdeacons for the sake of peace: the bishop of Meaux may choose, appoint, and replace rural deans without consulting the archdeacons, provided always that the fidelity which they customarily swear to preserve the rights of the archdeacons is retained. The archdeacons also amicably agreed that, from the revenues of churches, both from harvest and other emoluments, until persons are appointed by the bishop, the bishop shall receive two parts and the archdeacons the third; and that the affairs of vacant churches shall be administered through the rural deans. Concerning the conferral of parish churches, the archdeacons acknowledged that they had never troubled the bishop and never would trouble or oppose him in his lifetime.

Since the bishop also complained that the dean, according to his own pleasure, delayed investing suitable persons to whom he had conferred vacant prebends, we accordingly settled this, with the consent of the parties: if the dean is present, he shall invest without delay the canon sent to him by the bishop; and in chapter he shall appoint in his place a canon who, if the dean is absent, will notify him and come to perform the investiture of the canon sent by the bishop. If the dean does not come within eight days, the canon appointed by the dean shall, by the dean’s authority, invest the person presented by the bishop.

If the canon whom the dean has chosen as his deputy, though present in any manner within eight days, does not perform the requested investiture, or happens to be absent, the first in rank among the priest-canons [Col. 0078C] who are present shall perform it in the dean’s name. At our counsel, the archdeacons withdrew from their demand for the third part which the bishop had made. The archdeacons themselves shall make no *demanda* in their archdeaconries unless the bishop gives consent. In order that this may remain ratified, we have caused the present writing to be strengthened by the protection of our seals.

Done at Meaux, in the year 1201 of the Incarnate Word.

### XLVIII. To Raymond, abbot of Nonantola.—He confirms his election.  
*(1201; Lateran, 20 June.)*

[Tiraboschi, *History of the Abbey of Nonantola*, II, 334; original from the Nonantola archives.]

[Col. 0078D] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAYMOND, abbot of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having formerly heard that the monastery of Nonantola had, through the negligence of its late abbot B., been diminished in temporal matters and dissolved in spiritual matters, we judged it right to entrust its provision and correction to our venerable brother, the . . . bishop of Ferrara, with the instruction that, if he found the abbot unfit, he should remove him from the office of abbot. Although he appeared repeatedly to make provision for the preservation of that monastery, he eventually understood that its condition could not be reformed for the better under that abbot; and, having found him unfit, he arranged to remove him from administration in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic mandate.

When, because of this, envoys of the said abbot came to the Apostolic See, we, wishing to provide rather for the Church than for the person, did not judge that what had been done by our delegate should be revoked, but instead held it ratified. We instructed the convent of Nonantola to set a suitable person over themselves as abbot by canonical election, on the advice of that bishop. Accordingly, assembling together at that bishop’s summons, they unanimously elected you as their abbot. When the envoys—the beloved son A., prior of the same monastery; our subdeacon G.; and the noble man James of Fontana, advocate of the monastery—came to our presence with letters from both that bishop and the convent and related the foregoing to us [Col. 0079B] in order, the beloved son W., monk of Nonantola, arrived, speaking both on his own behalf and on behalf of certain other monks. He alleged that they had elected the beloved son Ph., monk of Pomposa, as abbot, and objected against your election that the form of our mandate had not been observed in it. For, although we had instructed the bishop to go to the place, he did not go to the monastery but summoned the monks before him and caused an election of this kind to be held in his presence. He also objected that, although repeatedly requested, the bishop refused to show them our letters; and thirdly he added that simoniacal depravity had entered into the election.

The reply on the other side was that, after his deposition, the said abbot had ambitiously pressed—or rather, entrenched himself—upon the administration of the monastery; and that the bishop, fearing the power of his kinsmen and the multitude of vassals, and that the monks would not dare elect freely in the former abbot’s presence, summoned them not to an external place but to a priory of that same church. Moreover, as the said monk later acknowledged, the bishop had allowed the monks who asked to see the letters to do so; but when they asked that the letters be given to them for carriage to the monastery, understanding that they sought frivolous delays and occasions for malicious attack, he did not comply with their malice. The same monk, more carefully questioned, later confessed that he did not know that simoniacal depravity had entered into [Col. 0079D] your election; he believed only that its defect consisted in not having been held at the monastery of Nonantola according to custom. When his opponents objected, he also confessed again that, after your election as abbot, the said Ph. had been nominated by five men who had departed from the aforementioned bishop and by certain others who had remained with the said abbot in the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0080A].

We therefore, having understood what had been put forward on both sides, decree the nomination of the said Ph. void as frivolous; we confirm by apostolic authority the election made of you; and we grant you free leave to transfer from your church to the monastery of Nonantola. By apostolic letters we command you that, assuming its care, you strive to provide for it in such a way that, through the diligent effort of your solicitude, it may advance in spiritual observances and increase in temporal resources. We also will and command that, according to the form which we send under our bull to the said bishop, you take an oath in his hands concerning both the fidelity to be rendered to us and the Roman Church [Col. 0080B] and the preservation of the monastery’s rights.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of July [20 June], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### XLIX. To the dean [Note: [Col. 0079D] See the note on Letter XLI of Book Three.] and archdeacon of Amiens.—That they are to cause the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the burgesses of Saint-Omer, for their unjust detention of certain water and marshes lawfully belonging to the church of Saint-Bertin, to be observed inviolate until due satisfaction is made.  
*(1201; Segni, 11 July.)*

[From the Archive of Saint-Bertin, Papal chest, no. 52. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0080C]

The beloved sons, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0079D] See the note on Letter XVIII of this Appendix.] and convent of Saint-Bertin, have reported that our venerable brother, the . . . bishop [Note: [Col. 0079D] See the note on Letter XXV of Book Three.], and the beloved son, the . . . archdeacon of Arras, judges delegated by the Apostolic See in a dispute concerning certain water and marshes lawfully belonging to the church of Saint-Bertin, canonically pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the burgesses of the castle of Saint-Omer for contumacy; and that the burgesses neglect to observe it. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters to cause that same sentence, since it was reasonably pronounced, to be observed inviolate until due satisfaction has been made, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice [Col. 0080D].

Given at Segni, 5 Ides of July [11 July], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

### L. To the abbots of St Peter [Note: [Col. 0079D]

Who at that time was abbot of the Monastery of St Peter in the Black Forest is wholly unknown. See the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 1054, where only the following brief notices are found:

> “VII. Marquard died in 1183.
>
> “VIII. Berthold I survived until 1220.”]

, St Mary [Note: [Col. 0079D] It is not altogether clear which monastery’s abbot is meant here. In a note appended in French to his copy, Abbot Grandidier wrote: “This concerns the abbots of St Peter in the Black Forest, of the Order of St Benedict; of St Mary, of the Order of St Augustine; and of Tennenbach, of the Order of Cîteaux.” Yet we confess that we do not know what monastery of St Mary, of the Order of St Augustine, could have had an abbot to whom this letter of Innocent was addressed. Certainly, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vols. V and XIII, identify no monastery of St Mary of the Order of St Augustine either in the province of Mainz—to which the several monasteries discussed here appear to belong—or in the neighbouring province of Trier. They do discuss, in the province of Mainz, the monastery of Blessed Mary at St Urban, in the diocese of Constance, vol. V, col. 1086; its abbot at that time was Conrad I of Biethertan, known from documents from at least 1197 until his death in 1212. But that abbey belongs to the Cistercian Order, not at all to the Order of St Augustine [Col. 0081D].], and Tennenbach [Note: [Col. 0081D] Concerning the abbots of the monastery of Tennenbach, otherwise Portacoeli, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Constance, at about the period with which we are concerned, nothing certain is known from the incomplete succession of that monastery’s abbots in the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 1089.].—That they are to cause the sentence pronounced in favour of the monks of Cella Vilmari to be observed.  
*(1201; Segni, 4 September.)*

[From a copy carefully collated by the late Abbot Grandidier with the original preserved in the archives of the Abbey of St Peter in the Black Forest. BR., ibid.]

[Col. 0081A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of St Peter, St Mary, and Tennenbach: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Beloved sons, the poor monks of Cella-Vilmari, of the Cluniac Order [Note: [Col. 0081D] The monastery of Vilmarcel, in Breisgau and the diocese of Constance, of the Order of Cluny, was united in 1560 to the Abbey of St Peter. GRANDIDIER.], have informed us that, when our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0081D] See Letter VIII of Book Eight, note.], the bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0081D] Conrad, bishop of Strasbourg, obtained in 1200 from Berthold, count of Neuburg, the right of patronage and advocacy of the two monasteries—one of men at Vilmarcel, the other of women at Selden. GRANDIDIER.], had unjustly received from the gift of our beloved son, the nobleman B., count of Neuburg [Note: [Col. 0082C] Berthold, count of Neuburg. ID.], the right of patronage over the churches of Cella-Vilmari and Selden [Note: [Col. 0081D] The monastery of Selden, of the Order of Cluny, in the diocese of Constance, was united in 1595 to the Abbey of St Peter. ID.], which is known to belong to them [Col. 0081B], the said monks summoned that bishop before the beloved sons [Note: [Col. 0082C] M. must be supplied. For Mangold, otherwise Magnold, of Halweil, born of an illustrious family, then governed the monastery of St Blasius, which he greatly enriched from his paternal inheritance. In the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Celestine III, on 6 Ides of April [8 April], he obtained a privilege by which the hymn *Gloria in excelsis* and the Sequence could be sung on the feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St Blasius even after Septuagesima. He died in 1204, on 14 Kalends of May [18 April]. *Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. V, col. 1028.], M., abbot of St Blasius in the Black Forest, and B. [Note: [Col. 0082D]

Concerning the abbots of the monastery of Alpersbach, otherwise Alpirsbach or Albersbach, in the diocese of Constance, the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 1064, give very little:

> “II. Abbot Conrad, in the time of Werner, abbot of the Solitaries, or Einsiedeln, about 1130. Perhaps the same Conrad whom Trithemius states had been sent there from Hirsau as abbot.

“III. Berthold defended his proper jurisdiction in Dornheim against Volmar of Brandeck before Louis, Duke of Teck, in the year 1251.”

Since here the abbot of Alpirsbach is designated by the initial B., should he be considered identical with that Berthold whom documents prove to have still been alive in 1251?]

, of Alpirsbach, and M. [Note: This concerns the Abbey of Pairis (also Latinized as *Parisium*), of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Basel.], abbot of Pairis, judges delegated by the Apostolic See, met concerning the same matter. Having at last taken cognizance of the case, they pronounced a definitive sentence in favour of the monks themselves, imposing perpetual silence upon the aforesaid bishop concerning the right of patronage over those churches. But afterward the oft-mentioned bishop, asserting that he had been wronged by the aforesaid sentence, appealed by letters addressed to the same judges to our hearing in this matter. When the opposing party pursued that appeal at the appointed time, [Col. 0081C] the same bishop did not pursue it either personally or through a representative. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion diligently to investigate the ground of the appeal and, as justice shall require, to confirm or quash that sentence, [Col. 0082A] notwithstanding any objection or appeal; and nevertheless to condemn that bishop to the lawful costs of the opposing party, because he did not prosecute the appeal which he had lodged, no letters prejudicial to truth and justice having been obtained from the Apostolic See. If not all of you can be present for the execution of these matters, nevertheless let two of you execute them.

Given at Segni, 4 September, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

## LI. To Andrew, Archbishop of Lund.—He confirms the privileges of that Church.  
*(1201; Anagni, 23 November.)*

[Liljegren, *Diplom. Suecan.*, I, 141.]

[Col. 0082B] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANDREW, Archbishop of Lund, and to his successors canonically appointed, for perpetual remembrance.

Set, by the Lord’s disposition, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we properly discharge the duty entrusted to us when we confirm by our assent those institutions made by our predecessors which are known to have been established for the salvation of the faithful, and when we exercise exact diligence lest they be shaken by anyone’s rash attempt. For since God promised His Church, saying: “In place of your fathers, etc., sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth,” those seem rightly to have succeeded their fathers and profitably to bear the office laid upon them who rejoice not in power but in usefulness, and who exercise, in fear and trembling, the authority of the power entrusted to them for the salvation of those whom they must govern—always striving to conform themselves to their predecessors in good works, to preserve in themselves what was laudably done by them, and likewise to show others that it must be preserved. Therefore, moved by this consideration, and following the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory, we decree that what he, with the counsel and consent of his brethren, established concerning the completion of the kingdom of Sweden shall remain firm and inviolate for all time.

For he established that the Archbishop of Lund, whoever he may be at the time, should always hold primacy over that kingdom and should preside over it according to the arrangement which follows; for he will minister more frequently and more profitably to that land in matters pertaining to the salvation of the faithful insofar as, from proximity, he can more fully perceive their need and deficiency. He granted the pallium to your predecessor so that he might ordain an archbishop [Col. 0083B] in the kingdom of Sweden as soon as an opportunity arose, and that he should indeed confer the pallium upon that archbishop by apostolic authority, this order being observed: namely, that he who should there be established metropolitan through the Bishop of Lund, having received the grace of consecration through the hand of the Archbishop of Lund, should promise obedience by oath to him and to the Church of Lund, while preserving fidelity to the Roman Church.

He shall obtain the pallium in the following manner:

A messenger of the Church of Lund, together with a messenger of that Church, shall go to the Roman Church to obtain the pallium; and when they have obtained it from the Roman Pontiff, they shall bring it back to the Church of Lund. The Archbishop of Lund, receiving it, shall give it to the Archbishop of Sweden and shall promise by oath fidelity and obedience to the Roman Church. Moreover, the Archbishop of Lund shall for ever preside in the dignity of primacy over the metropolitan established there for the honour of God, the adornment of His house, and the salvation of the faithful; and that metropolitan shall take care humbly to render him obedience and reverence as to his primate.

This is known to have been fulfilled in Stephen of good memory, formerly Archbishop of Uppsala, who received, on account of old age, the grace of consecration under the aforesaid institution from your predecessor Eschil of pious memory, in the presence of Pope Alexander of blessed memory; and, under our predecessors Lucius, Clement, Celestine, and ourselves, according to the prescribed order, it was fulfilled in John and Peter of blessed memory and in our venerable brother Q., Archbishops of Uppsala, whom your predecessor Absalon of pious memory consecrated and upon whom, in place of those predecessors, he conferred the pallium. For this too, as it had been established by our aforementioned predecessor Adrian, was carried into effect under your predecessors Eschil and Absalon.

Following in this highly praiseworthy work the footsteps of Adrian and of our predecessors, the Roman Pontiffs Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Clement, and Celestine, all of blessed memory, we uphold it by our favour and that of our future brethren, and decree that it shall remain firm and inviolate for all time, without prejudice, of course, to the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0084A] Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he acknowledges his fault, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, John, Bishop of Albano.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the Holy Church.  
I, Jorot, pastor of St. Pudentiana and cardinal priest.  
I, Hugh, cardinal priest of St. Martin *in Equitio*.  
I, Linger, cardinal priest of St. Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, Sofredus, cardinal priest of St. Praxedes.  
I, John Sosprises, cardinal priest.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of St. Marcellus.  
I, Benedict, cardinal priest of St. Susanna.  
I, Gratus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Gerald, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 23 November, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1201 [Col. 0084D], and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## LII. To Andrew, Archbishop of Acerenza.—He confirms the privileges of the Church of Acerenza.  
*(1201; Anagni, 10 December.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VII, 36.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANDREW, Archbishop of Acerenza, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

By the office of the apostolate entrusted to us, we ought to love with sincere affection of charity our brethren and fellow bishops, both near and far, and to preserve for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their dignity and right. Therefore, venerable brother Archbishop, we graciously assent to your just requests and strengthen by the authority of this decree the Church of Acerenza, over which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside. We confirm to you and your successors whatsoever is known to belong to it by metropolitan right: namely, Venosa, Gravina, Tricarico, Potenza, and Tursi. Thus you and your lawful successors shall have authority canonically and by decretal law, as their archbishop, to confirm and consecrate bishops in them.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that Church now reasonably possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The Church of St. Angelo of Oblano, with all its appurtenances. Furthermore, in all towns, villages, monasteries, and churches situated within the boundaries of your diocese, we decree that the episcopal right shall belong to you and, through you, to the Church of Acerenza—excepting, of course, those things known to belong spiritually to the Roman Church. We also grant you the use of the pontifical pallium—that is, the fullness of office—by virtue of the dignity of the Apostolic See, as it is known to have been granted by our predecessors to your predecessors, so that you may use it on feast days and at the times and on the other occasions contained in the privileges of your church.

We exhort you, therefore, to show yourself so gentle toward those subject to you that they may be prompted to love rather than fear your uprightness. If their fault should perhaps require it, take care so to correct their transgressions that you in no way lay aside paternal affection from your heart. Be vigilant in guarding the flock entrusted to you, and keep careful watch, strict in zeal for discipline, so that the lurking wolf may neither disturb the Lord’s sheepfold nor prevail against the sheep through any occasion of deceit. Let the people entrusted to you recognize a different life in your speech; let the teaching of your brotherhood be for them a welcome stimulus to exhortation, and your life an example for imitation. Let the preaching word of your charity disclose what they ought to love and fear; let your efficacy obtain the fruit of such eternal recompense.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church of Acerenza, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things remain undiminished and entire, to the fullest benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should perhaps attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he corrects his fault by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Octavian, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri.  
I, John, Bishop of Albano.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia.  
I, Jordan, cardinal priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor.  
I, Guido, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus.  
I, Hugh, cardinal priest of St. Martin, of the title of Equitius.

I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Prisca.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Blasius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 10 December, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0086D] 1201, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

## LIII. To Odo, Bishop of Paris.—He settles a long-standing suit between Odo himself and the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris concerning possession of parochial jurisdiction in the parish of Mont, defining the rights of each party.  
*(1201; Anagni, 23 December.)*

[D. Félibien, *History of Paris*, V, 597.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ODO, Bishop of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Formerly, when a dispute had arisen between you, in the name of the Church of Paris, and our beloved son the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, on behalf of the abbey, concerning possession of parochial jurisdiction in the parish [Col. 0087A] of Mont, and when our venerable brother P., Archbishop of Sens, then a canon of Paris, acting as your procurator, and the said abbot in the name of his Church, came before the Apostolic See, we appointed as hearers our venerable brother J., Bishop of Albano, and our beloved son G., cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro, now cardinal priest of the title of St. Vitalis.

Before them your procurator alleged that the abbot was inflicting serious injury upon you concerning possession of parochial jurisdiction in the parish of Mont, since until your time the Bishop of Paris had exercised this authority over the parishioners of Mont and over the priest who ministered divine offices to them from time to time. Even if that priest were a regular canon, the bishop entrusted him with the care of the parish; and after receiving the cure from the bishop’s hand, the priest bound and loosed the parishioners at the bishop’s command. If anyone had been excommunicated or interdicted by the bishop, the priest did not admit him in any way to divine offices. Nor did he assume to himself the blessing of brides, the purification of women rising after childbirth, or public penances, except by the bishop’s special command. If that priest happened to be unable to minister to the people, the bishop notified the abbot and brethren of Sainte-Geneviève of his misconduct; after they had ascertained the truth, they removed the unworthy man and presented another to the bishop to receive the care of souls.
