When, therefore, you had most recently warned the abbot to take care to present to you his chaplains who were to serve the parishes, in order that they might receive the care of souls, he replied that he would do so and presented some. But when required to present the person who was to serve in the aforesaid parish of Mont, he said that he could not then be presented because of his absence. Since, though repeatedly warned, he did not take care to do this, you forbade the parishioners of Mont, under penalty of excommunication, either to hear divine offices in the church of Sainte-Geneviève or to receive any sacraments there except from that priest who had received the care of souls from the bishop. This sentence was publicly recited in the same church while the parish was present, and the parishioners of Mont had long observed it as they had been accustomed to do, until, when the canons of Sainte-Geneviève had assembled the people, it was publicly preached to them, by our venerable brother the Bishop of Tournai, formerly abbot of that church, upon the priest’s word and at the peril of his soul, that they could safely hear divine offices, since neither archbishop, bishop, nor archdeacon could pronounce upon them a sentence of excommunication or interdict. Thus induced by him, they received spiritual ministrations.

Your procurator therefore requested, as stated above, that you, despoiled of obedience from the aforesaid parish, should before all else be restored, as it were, to possession of parochial jurisdiction; that thereafter your adversaries should fully answer the matters which they thought ought to be alleged against you, since one despoiled ought not to answer his adversaries before restoration; and that the Bishop of Tournai and the aforesaid canons should be punished for the foregoing excesses, the cause afterward to be handled in due order before delegated judges. Before them the right of the Church of Paris would be more fully proved—something which could not then be done for want of evidence.

On the other hand, the aforesaid abbot alleged that you, now a new bishop, were inflicting a new injury upon him. He asserted that his church, together with the borough, had been free from the time of its first foundation and had never been subject in spiritual matters to anyone except the Roman Pontiff. He strove to establish this as a precaution by a rescript of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory, who, following the examples of his predecessors Alexander, Lucius, and Clement, Roman Pontiffs of pious memory, granted the aforesaid church, among other liberties, that no one might subject it, its canons, or the borough to interdict or excommunication except the Supreme Pontiff or a legate sent from his side. Contrary to that liberty, you had presumed to intrude a sickle into another’s harvest—something none of your predecessors had ever done—by demanding that a canon of that church, who administered spiritual things to the people of the borough, be presented to you so that he might receive from you the care of souls. Since you could not obtain this, after an appeal had been lodged and a journey undertaken to come to the Apostolic See, you bound with the bond of excommunication all those who heard the parochial Mass in the church of Sainte-Geneviève [Col. 0088C], together with those communicating with them. Moved by fear, the people, being unlearned, abstained for some time from divine offices through ignorance or humility. But the Bishop of Tournai already mentioned, formerly abbot of the same church, later came there; having learned the truth, he assured them without hesitation, as a jurist, that your aforesaid sentence, because it had been pronounced by one who was not their judge, possessed no force of validity. The people therefore returned to their own priest. Even if he had knowingly invalidated that priest, so that he might thereby be deprived of the right of his Church, no prejudice could thus be generated against him—just as no prejudice can be generated against a lord by his tenant without the lord’s knowledge or against his will—especially since you were never dispossessed and thus could not seek restoration.

The abbot further declared himself ready immediately and abundantly to prove that the same church possessed the right to institute the canon who ministered spiritual things to the people, that it had both jurisdictions over the people of the borough, and that it had possessed them in the time of your predecessors. He therefore requested that whatever had been attempted in fact by you after the lodging of the appeal be judged void, and that you be restrained from presuming similar acts in future.

[Col. 0089A] Having more fully understood the foregoing and the other arguments through the said hearers—who prudently and faithfully reported to us and to our brethren the petitions and allegations of the parties, reduced to writing—we could not in law adjudge restoration to you. For merely because the people of the said parish, through fear of that sentence, abstained from divine offices for some days, you had acquired no possession among them of parochial jurisdiction; nor was it in any way proved that, when you pronounced the sentence, you possessed parochial jurisdiction over them or had previously possessed it. Nor was it established that you had in any degree been despoiled.

But because full proof could not be given us concerning the other matters advanced on your behalf, we thought fit to commit the cause, under the following form, to our beloved sons the abbots of Vézelay and St. Peter of Auxerre, and the dean of Orléans, etc. At last all the proceedings, authenticated by the seals of the judges, were sent back to us by your beloved son M. N., your procurator, and by the abbot already mentioned, who came before us concerning this matter. We therefore caused those proceedings to be opened in the presence of our brethren, and fully understood their contents, etc.

Since, therefore, your witnesses report that the parishioners of Mont resorted to the tribunal of the Church of Paris, while the witnesses of the other party report that they litigated in the abbot’s court, they do not appear to have spoken contradictory things. The statements of your witnesses may properly be understood of the parishioners of that part of the parish [Col. 0089C] which lies outside the borough and which the said abbot even now acknowledges to be yours; while the statements of the others may be understood of the parishioners of the other part, called the borough, which the said abbot seeks to claim for himself, etc.

Therefore, having carefully heard and more fully understood the depositions, arguments, and other matters advanced on both sides, and since in two articles—namely, institution and removal—it has been lawfully established that the chapel of Mont was in the possession of the abbot, as was also the liberty that the interdict of the Church of Paris should not be observed in the aforesaid parish; and since an apostolic rescript grants to that church that no one except the Roman Pontiff or a legate sent from his side may pronounce a sentence of interdict or excommunication in the borough of Sainte-Geneviève: it appears that you attempted something unlawful and forbidden to you. While the abbot defended possession of his liberty by apostolic authority, no new possession was acquired by you through the sentence which you pronounced, since servitude ought not thus to be created, but rather an existing servitude declared; nor was anything proved in these articles for your side. By the common counsel of our brethren, we therefore adjudge that the abbot himself and his Church are absolved from your jurisdiction and that of the Church of Paris in respect of these matters.

Although, indeed, diverse and varying evidences have been introduced by both parties on the other heads, nevertheless fuller and more explicit proof has been produced for your side. A judge ought to believe what accords with the nature of the affair, so as to confirm the movement of his mind from arguments and testimonies found more suited to the matter and nearer to the truth, and to which the light of truth more readily adheres according to lawful enactments. Since you requested not only that possession, as it were, of parochial jurisdiction be restored to you, but also that the abbot and canons be punished for the aforesaid misconducts by which, as you complained, they inflicted serious injury concerning possession of parochial jurisdiction in the parish of Mont, we, having taken counsel with our brethren, definitively condemn the oft-mentioned abbot and the Church of Sainte-Geneviève, in respect of the aforesaid parish, to you and the Church of Paris in all remaining matters pertaining to possession of episcopal or parochial jurisdiction throughout the whole parish of Mont—except only those matters concerning which a sentence of absolution has been pronounced for the other party.

Nevertheless, from what has prudently been determined in the present possessory proceeding, we do not intend that any prejudice should arise for you or the other party concerning the question of ownership. And lest our sentence, if it lacks effect, seem derisory, etc.

Given at Anagni, 24 December, in the fourth year of our pontificate. [Note: See Letter 100 of Book V, vol. I, col. 1097, and the various documents relating to the same controversy, col. 1185.]

## LI. He grants privileges to the private chapel of William of Montpellier.  
*(1201; Segni.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, VI, documents, 362.]

[Col. 0090C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman WILLIAM, lord of Montpellier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The sincerity of your devotion and your continual solicitude—whereby, as we have learned, you are zealous in works of piety—admonish and move us not to deny you apostolic favour in matters concerning God. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, inclined by your just prayers, we receive under the protection of St. Peter and our own the chapel which, founded in your house by the devotion of your progenitors of illustrious memory, you have enlarged in many respects, together with all the goods which you now reasonably possess; and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. By the authority of these presents we grant that, when a general interdict is laid upon your land, its chaplains—provided that they themselves are neither excommunicated nor interdicted—may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated; and likewise may do so for you, should it happen, God forbid, that you are excommunicated, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

Given at Segni, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

## LV. To all archbishops, bishops, prelates, etc., established throughout France.—For the monastery of Foigny.  
*(1202; Anagni, 17 January.)*

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots, priors, deans, archdeacons, and all prelates of churches to whom these letters shall come, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Not without pain of heart and great disturbance have we learned that in many regions ecclesiastical censure is so relaxed and the severity of canonical sentence so weakened that religious men—and especially those endowed with greater liberty by privileges of the Apostolic See—suffer injuries and robberies everywhere at the hands of wrongdoers, while scarcely anyone is found to assist them with fitting protection and to set himself as a wall of defence in support of the innocence of the poor. In particular, our beloved sons, the … abbot [Col. 0091B] [Note: See the place cited.] and brethren of Foigny, of the Cistercian Order, complaining both of frequent injuries and of the daily failure of justice itself, have asked by apostolic letters that you all be stirred up, so that you may rise with ready magnanimity on their behalf against their wrongdoers in their tribulations, and so that by your protection they may obtain relief from the straits and oppressions which they endure.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and order you all that, after prior warning, if any lay persons have irreverently invaded the possessions, goods, or houses of the aforesaid brethren or of their men, or have unjustly detained what is bequeathed to the aforesaid brethren by the wills of the deceased; or if they have presumed, contrary to the privileges granted by the Apostolic See, to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against the brethren; or to extort tithes on their labour or sustenance in contempt of the privileges of the Apostolic See: you shall publicly strike them with the sentence of excommunication, with lighted candles. But if they are clerics, regular canons, or monks, you shall suspend them from office and benefice, without appeal; and you shall relax neither sentence until they have made full satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren.

Both laymen and secular clerics who have been bound by the chain of anathema for violent laying on of hands shall deserve absolution from that bond when they come to the Apostolic See with letters from their diocesan bishop. In the case of monks and regular canons, the following is to be observed: if brethren of the same cloister lay violent hands upon one another, they shall obtain the benefit of absolution through their own abbot; but if a brother of one cloister presumes to commit such violence upon a brother of another cloister, they shall obtain the benefit of absolution through the abbots of the injured and offending parties. This applies even if some of them, before receiving the religious habit, committed such an act for which they incurred the sentence of excommunication by the act itself, unless their transgression was difficult and heinous—for example, if it extended to mutilation of a limb or shedding of blood, or if violent hands had been laid upon a bishop or abbot—since such and similar offences cannot be passed over without scandal. If, however, they lay hands upon secular clerics, they shall be sent to the Apostolic See for absolution in order to avoid scandal. Moreover, you shall subject to the sentence of interdict those villages in which the goods of the aforesaid brethren or their men are held by violence, for as long as they are so held.

Given at Anagni, 17 January, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

I, the undersigned, delegate of the Lord Keeper of the Seals for the investigation and transcription of the historical monuments of Thiérache and part of the Laonnois, certify that this copy conforms to the original. [Col. 0092B] This 19 April 1788.

Signed: D. R. N. JEANNIN, Religious of St. Michael.

## LVI. To the abbot [Note: See the notes to Letter XXII of this Appendix.] and canons of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris.—By apostolic authority he confirms the settlement entered into between them and the Church of St. Victor concerning the water of the Bièvre.  
*(1202; Lateran, 23 January.)*

[Bréquigny, cited work, p. 1090.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and canons of the Church of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious vows and to grant favourable support to the honourable petitions of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favourable assent to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the settlement made between your Church and that of St. Victor in Paris concerning the water of the Bièvre (*Bevria*), which flows to the mill of Copel, under specified measures: as it was prudently made without wrongdoing, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and observed until now.

Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0092D] Given at Anagni, 23 January, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

Seal.

## LVII. To Walter, Bishop of Luni.—He confirms his agreements and exchanges with the canons of Luni, and all the rights and possessions of the Church of Luni.  
*(1202; Lateran, 7 March.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 850.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WALTER, Bishop of Luni, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Set upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, etc. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Walter, granting with due kindness favourable assent to your just requests, we receive under the protection of St. Peter and our own, after the example of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, the Church of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary at Luni, over which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The parish of St. Stephen of Unsilia, with the chapel of Vallechia and its other chapels; the parish of St. Vitus of the castle of Aginulf; the parish of Massa; the parish of St. Vitalis; the parish of St. Lawrence of Monte Libero; the parish of Carraria; the parish of St. Mary of Sarzana; the parish of St. Andrew of Sarzana; the parish of St. Stephen of Cereto; the parish of Amelia; the parish of Treblano; the parish of Arcola; the parish of St. Venerius; the parish of Ceula; the parish of Rubiano; the parish of Coraja; the parish of Pignone; the parish of St. Andrew of the Castle; the parish of Bolano; the parish of St. Peter of the Castle; the parish of St. Lawrence; the parish of Offlano; the parish of St. Cyprian [Col. 0093C] at the bridgehead; the parish of Viano; the parish of Soleria; the parish of St. Paul; the chapel of St. Mary of Pugnano; the church of St. Margaret of the castle of Verucula; the church of St. Michael of Saxo Albo; the parish of Crispiano; the parish of Venelia; the parish of Bagnone; the parish of Vico; the parish of Turrano; the parish of St. Cassian of Urteola; the parish of St. Alexander at the bridge of Trenusio; the parish of Vignola, with all the chapels which you justly and canonically possess; and the borough of Aventina with its chapels and other appurtenances.

Moreover, the agreements and exchange, entered into between you and our beloved sons, the canons of Luni, both concerning churches and other matters, [lacuna], prudently made without impropriety, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and hitherto peacefully maintained, as contained in an authentic document, we confirm by apostolic authority.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, for the benefit in every respect of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0094A] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. Peter, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. John, bishop of Albano. Gratian, cardinal-deacon of SS. Cosmas and Damian. Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustace. Matthew, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. Jordan, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, title of Pastor. Guy, cardinal-priest of St. Mary in Trastevere, title of St. Callixtus. Hugh, cardinal-priest of St. Martin in Equitius. Cinthius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Prisca. Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Vitalis. [Col. 0094B] Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Susanna.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Blasius, archbishop of Torres, on the Nones of March [7 March], in the sixth indiction, in the year 1202 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

LVIII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0093D] See the note to Epistle XVIII of the Appendix to this collection.] and convent of St. Bertin.—That no one may dare to pronounce against them, their churches, or their chaplains serving in them, a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication without a manifest and reasonable cause. (Year 1202; Lateran, 8 March.)

[From the Archive of St. Bertin, Papal chest, no. 55. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the . . . abbot and convent of St. Bertin, [Col. 0094C] greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant the favour of its goodwill to the honourable prayers of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring favourably with your just petitions, we grant you by the authority of these presents that no one may dare to pronounce against you, your churches, or your chaplains serving in them, a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication without a manifest and reasonable cause. Let no person whatever, therefore, infringe this page of our grant or rashly presume to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, [Col. 0094D] let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of March [8 March], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

LIX. To the abbots of Blangy [Note: [Col. 0093D] He was named Erard, known from documents from 1201 until at least 1208. He is said to have died on 15 September 1211. See the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1591.] and Alciacum [Note: [Col. 0094D]

If the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* are to be trusted, the monastery of Alciacum was then governed either by John I of Béthune or by Simon II; for this is what is read in their work, vol. X, col. 1597:

“X. Simon II, a monk of St. Bertin, governed from the year [Col. 0095D] 1198. Having been chosen abbot of Marchiennes (according to Iperius), he yielded his place to another.

“XI. John I of Béthune, monk of St. Bertin, a man of integrity and holy life, was appointed Simon’s successor. Shortly afterwards—or, according to another reading, after three years (that is, in 1202)—he resigned upon Simon’s restoration to favour.

“XII. Simon, once more appointed to Alciacum, presided for five years and died on the Kalends of May [1 May] 1207.”

Thus far the authors cited above. Yet, in their succession-list of the abbots of Marchiennes (vol. III, col. 397), they do not seem consistent with themselves.]

and to the prior of Hesdin.—That, under threat of ecclesiastical censures, they prohibit the canons of St. Omer from celebrating divine offices in the presence of the excommunicated burgesses of St. Omer, who were excommunicated because of injuries inflicted on the abbot and convent of St. Bertin. (Year 1202; Lateran, 4 April.)

[From the Archive of St. Bertin, Papal chest, no. 57. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1122.]

[Col. 0095A]

We have received the complaint of our beloved sons, the . . . abbot [Note: [Col. 0096D] See the note to Epistle XVIII of the Appendix to this collection.] and convent of St. Bertin, stating that, because of injuries which the burgesses of the town of St. Omer had inflicted upon them, those same burgesses lay under a sentence of excommunication and the town itself under a sentence of interdict by authority of the Apostolic See; nevertheless, the canons of St. Omer in the diocese of Thérouanne rashly presumed to celebrate divine offices in the presence of the excommunicated. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, after prior warning, you compel the said canons, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to make due satisfaction to those brethren concerning this matter and to desist from so rash a presumption. If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, two of you shall nevertheless execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of April [4 April], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

LX. To William, archbishop of Reims and cardinal of St. Sabina [Note: [Col. 0096D] See the note to Epistle XIV of Book III.]; to A., abbot of St. Remigius [Note: [Col. 0096D] Peter of Ribaudimont, of noble birth, abbot of St. Remigius at Reims, is known from documents from 1197 until 1203, when he died on the third day before the Kalends of August [30 July]. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IX, p. 234.]; and to the dean [Note: [Col. 0096D] See the note to Epistle CXLIX of Book V.] of Reims.—That they cause the sentence of excommunication justly pronounced against the burgesses of St. Omer, on account of the seizure of certain marshes belonging to the Bertinians, to be published and observed [Note: [Col. 0096D] See above, at Epistle XLIX of this Appendix.]. (Year 1202; Lateran, 8 April.)

[From the Archive of St. Bertin, Papal chest, no. 58. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0095C]

You should know that it has come to our hearing, as our beloved sons, the . . . abbot and convent of St. Bertin, have reported, that a case concerning certain marshes known to belong to that monastery, and concerning the many damages and injuries which those burgesses inflicted upon the same monastery, had been committed by the Apostolic See to our venerable brother, the . . . bishop [Note: [Col. 0096D] See the note to Epistle XVIII of this Appendix.], and to our beloved son, the . . . archdeacon of Arras. Because of the contumacy of the burgesses, the aforesaid abbot and [Col. 0095D] convent were put into possession of those marshes by delegated judges, with the case reserved to it [Note: [Col. 0096D] “With the case reserved to it”: thus in the copy, erroneously.]. Since the burgesses afterwards presumed to molest them in this respect, they were bound by a sentence [Col. 0096A] of excommunication; and because they persisted in their obstinacy for a year and more, the judges assigned true possession to the aforesaid brethren, renewing the sentence of excommunication against the said wrongdoers.

Wishing, therefore, in our pastoral solicitude to provide for the monastery of St. Bertin, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you cause the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, since it was reasonably pronounced, to be published and inviolably observed; and that, without appeal, on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, you cause the oft-mentioned burgesses to be publicly proclaimed excommunicate throughout the province of Reims until they make suitable satisfaction, and strictly command all persons [Col. 0096B] to avoid them. Carry out the apostolic mandate in such a way that the same abbot and monks obtain their justice through you, and that we may be able to commend your devotion in the Lord. If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, you, brother archbishop, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of April [8 April], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

LXI. To the archbishop of Rouen and his suffragans.—That they defend the abbey of La Lucerne against wrongdoers and assist it in its distress.—“Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the fifth year of the pontificate [1202].”

(*Neustria pia*, p. 797, where only a notice of this bull survives.)

[Col. 0096C]

LXII. To the chapter of Aarhus.—He confirms the establishment of prebends. (Year 1203; Anagni, 3 January.)

[LANGEBECK, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, VI, 388.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Aarhus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

What is prudently ordained for the adornment of the house of the Lord, we desire to be observed all the more firmly insofar as we are the more intent upon the honour and advancement of the churches. Inclining, therefore, to the prayers of you and of our venerable brother, the bishop of Aarhus, we confirm by apostolic authority the establishment [Col. 0096D] of prebends and benefices prudently made by him in your church and confirmed by the late archbishop of Lund, then legate of the Apostolic See, as contained in their authentic [Col. 0097A] letters; and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no person whatever, therefore, infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly presume to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

LXIII. To the prelates of Bremen.—He anathematizes the murderers of C., bishop of Würzburg. (Year 1203; Lateran, 25 January.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburgische Urkunden*, Hamburg, 1842, quarto, p. 295. From the original in the archive at Stade, chest II, no. 14.]

[Col. 0097B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishop of Bremen and his suffragans, and to his beloved sons, the abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established in the province of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The sorrow of holy Church is renewed almost unceasingly, nor is she permitted even a brief respite from continual sighing. For she labours in her lamentation; every night she washes her bed with tears, yet the Lord has not fully heard her supplication. Indeed, she had not yet wiped her cheeks, but her tears were still upon them, and she would not be comforted (Lam. 2), while the blood of A., bishop of Liège, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0097D] Albert, killed in 1192.], still fresh, cried from the earth. And behold, a voice was heard anew in Ramah, much weeping and lamentation (Matt. 2): for, as we have learned, sons of Belial laid sacrilegious hands upon the anointed of the Lord, wickedly murdering C., bishop of Würzburg, of good memory and chancellor of the imperial court.

They had indeed agreed among themselves unjustly to kill a just man and to possess the sanctuary of the Lord as an inheritance. Having conceived pain, they immediately brought forth iniquity. And lest anything necessary to their fraud be lacking—so that, like Judas, they might betray the Son of Man with a kiss—they put aside hostile countenances and concealed beneath the fleece of feigned peace and pretended friendship the malice long conceived in their hearts, which they had been unable to exercise as enemies. [Col. 0097D] Thus, entering as ravening wolves in sheep’s clothing, they immediately rose against the shepherd of the fold and shed the blood for which they had long thirsted.

Nor was this enough for them. But, so that blood might touch blood and deep call unto deep, raging against his now lifeless body, they cut off, as is said, his right hand—the hand by which he had frequently signed the bread and wine to be changed into the Body and Blood of Christ—and, after severing his head, they also cut the crown from the remaining part of his head with drawn swords: the crown which he wore, after the example of the Prince of the Apostles, as a sign of reverence for the Lord. They did not consider that most sacred unction had been poured both upon his head and upon his hands. In another way also, [Col. 0098A] they cut his body into pieces, as though they wished to eat what they had slain, to expose for sale what they had taken in so impious a hunt, or to make his corpse food for the birds of heaven and his flesh for the beasts of the earth.

Consider, therefore, and see whether there is any sorrow like the sorrow of the Church, whose sons—indeed, whose spouses—the wicked slaughter like sheep for the killing, and whose prelates’ blood they pour out seemingly with impunity. If they presume this in the green wood, what will they dare in the dry? If they have committed so wicked a crime against a man distinguished by such nobility, endowed with such dignity, illustrious in such honour, and pre-eminent in such learning and eloquence, what are they believed likely henceforth to commit against lesser prelates of churches and secular [Col. 0098B] princes? What power, justice, or authority will henceforth be safe from such men? For if they have dared such wickedness against the anointed of the Lord, and through him against Christ the Lord, what will they do to lesser men? Will they spare the inferior members, having dared to exercise such cruelty even against the head?

Moreover, what is worse and therefore still more alarming is that, since ministers of the Empire have now twice committed so enormous a crime, this wickedness is being drawn into precedent and the example of such great malignity is being disseminated among others. For Otto of Barchisten first killed the aforesaid bishop of Liège while he was in exile; and now his followers have slaughtered another bishop with such enormity.

Do not, therefore, weep only for those who, as the Apostle testifies of himself, fulfilled in their own bodies what was lacking of Christ’s sufferings; but weep also for yourselves, for henceforth those close to you must be feared as enemies and friends guarded against as enemies, lest the familiar enemy do the greater harm and a man’s enemies be those of his own household (Matt. 10). Flee, therefore, from before the bow, that the elect may be delivered; and, because the beginnings were not resisted, at least resist the intermediate stages, lest the remedy be applied too late if, while you wait for the end, the cause of the disease grows stronger. For we, whoever might hold the monarchy of the Empire, would by no means spare him in so great a crime, but would oppose his undertakings for ecclesiastical liberty, even if for this reason we had to lay down our lives.

Lest the impunity of the crime give anyone boldness to offend, in the name of Almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; and by that power of binding and loosing which the Lord, although we are unworthy, has conferred upon us, we anathematize those who killed the aforesaid bishop, and all those by whose favour, assent, assistance, or command, express or tacit, he was killed; and likewise all who, after the perpetration of the crime, gave or attempted henceforth to give them assistance, counsel, or refuge.

We therefore command your entire body by apostolic letters and, in the power of the Holy Spirit, strictly enjoin under the obligation of obedience [Col. 0099A] by which you are bound to us, that every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, each and every one of you publicly and solemnly proclaim our sentence, publishing both the names of the murderers and those of persons found to have assented by word or deed to the death of the same bishop. Declare the lands of those murderers, and of all who gave, have given, or now give them favour in this matter, subject to sentence of interdict; so that, except for the baptism of infants and penance for the dying, no ecclesiastical sacrament or divine office may be celebrated in them, nor may the bodies of the dead be committed to ecclesiastical burial. From their households, moreover, let nothing be received as offering or alms, and let no sacrament be administered to them except baptism for little children and penance for those suffering at the point of death. Furthermore, wherever they may go, forbid divine offices to be celebrated under the same terms for as long as they remain present.

We have ordered these things to be written with this severity immediately upon receiving the reports; but when we have fully learned the truth, we shall proceed far more severely. Nor shall there be respect of persons with us: rather, we shall expressly proclaim by name, and command others to proclaim, both great and small alike, of whatever dignity or rank, as excommunicated. We further hope and hold almost as certain [Col. 0099C] that He who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished, just as His power has already taken fitting vengeance upon the murderers of the aforesaid bishop of Liège, will likewise take more severe vengeance upon the killers of this bishop and their supporters. Moreover, we will and command under the same severity that, putting aside every favour and fear, you investigate the truth concerning each person with the utmost diligence and do not delay faithfully reporting to us what you discover. But you, brother archbishop, shall faithfully execute our mandate, setting aside every favour and fear; and, by ecclesiastical compulsion and without appeal, shall cause it to be executed by others.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January], in the fifth year of our pontificate.

LXIV. To the abbots of Engelberg and Muri.—That they compel knights who are encroaching upon the property of the Church of Beromünster to make compensation for the damage done. (Year 1203; Lateran, 28 January.)

[NEUGART, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, printed at St. Blasien, 1795, quarto, p. 121; from L. B. de Zurlauben, manuscript *Miscellanies of Swiss History*, vol. III, p. 812.]

[Col. 0100A] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Engelberg [Note: [Col. 0099D] Mount of the Angels, commonly Engelberg, a Benedictine abbey in Switzerland at the foot of Mount Titlis.] and Muri [Note: [Col. 0099D] The Benedictine abbey of Muri flourishes in Aargau.], of the diocese of Constance, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You should know that we have received a report from our beloved sons, the canons of Beromünster [Note: [Col. 0099D] Berona, Beromünster, a collegiate church in the district of Lucerne.], that E. H. of Büttikon [Note: [Col. 0099D] Büttikon, in Lower Aargau, a free estate near Hilfikon, in the parish of Villmergen or Vilmaringen.] and other knights of the diocese of Constance have presumed violently to invade their possessions and build a certain castle upon them. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning, you compel those knights by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to make satisfaction in these matters as justice shall require.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February [28 January], in the fifth year of our pontificate [Note: [Col. 0099D] Innocent III was elected on 8 January 1198 and consecrated on 22 February, from which day the years of his pontificate are to be reckoned.].

LXV. To the abbot of St. Columba, M., archdeacon of Sens, and the master of the schools of Orléans.—Concerning the procurations and visitations of the bishop of Paris. (Year 1203; Lateran, 28 March.)

[*Cartulary of the Church of Paris*, III, 185.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of St. Columba, M., archdeacon of Sens, and the master of the schools of Orléans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to our hearing, as our venerable brother the bishop of Paris has reported, that when he has at times needed to visit the diocese of Paris, [Col. 0100C] as belongs to his office, certain priors and chaplains of the same diocese refuse to provide him the procuration due to him. In defence of their refusal, they allege only that neither they nor their predecessors have paid a procuration of that kind. We, therefore, considering their aforesaid allegation frivolous—since a subject cannot acquire by prescription against his prelate exemption from the procuration due by reason of visitation—command your discretion by apostolic letters that, notwithstanding the aforesaid allegations, if nothing else stands in the way, you cause such procuration to be provided to the same bishop according to the canonical enactments and without appeal, compelling any opponents or rebels, after prior warning, by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal, to desist from their [Col. 0100D] presumption. If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, two of you shall nevertheless execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April [28 March], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

LXVI. To our venerable brother, the bishop of Rodez [Note: [Col. 0100D] The bishop of Rodez, Hugh (of Rodez), is mentioned in documents from at least 1162 until at least 1210. He is said to have lived until 1214, but had previously resigned the bishopric. See the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, col. 208.], and to our beloved sons Hippolytus of Montsalvy and the prior of St. Antonin, in the diocese of Rodez, greeting and apostolic blessing.—That they decide the controversy between the chapters of St. Cecilia and St. Salvi of Albi concerning the church of St. Marciana. (Year 1203; Ferentino, 22 May.)

[We publish this letter from manuscript no. 7392 of the Royal Library, final folio, verso. It is wholly identical with that printed in Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. III, p. 20, col. I, new folio edition. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0101A]

We have received a grave complaint from the chapter of St. Cecilia of Albi, our beloved sons: although they have canonically acquired the church of Blessed Marciana, the canons of Blessed Salvi of Albi, [Col. 0101B] wishing to increase the pension of twenty solidi which they had customarily received from that church as a procuration, presume to harass them unjustly both concerning this and concerning the said church. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning, you compel the said canons by ecclesiastical censure and without appeal to desist from their undue harassment, notwithstanding any letters procured from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice. If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, you, brother bishop, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.

Given at Ferentino, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

LXVII. To the bishop of Rodez, the provost of Montsalvy, and the prior of St. Antonin, in the diocese of Rodez.—Against the canons of Blessed Salvi of Albi. (Year 1203; Ferentino, 22 May.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, folio edition, II, 20.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Rodez, and to his beloved sons, the provost of Montsalvy and the prior of St. Antonin in the diocese of Rodez, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received a grave complaint from our beloved sons, the chapter of the Holy Church [Col. 0101D] of Albi: although they have canonically acquired the church of Blessed Marciana, the canons of Blessed Salvi of Albi, etc., as above.

LXVII bis. Letter of Pelagius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia, to William, bishop of Albi.—On the same subject. (Ibid.)

To his venerable brother in Christ, G., by God’s grace bishop of Albi: P., by the same grace cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

[Col. 0102A] We understand that the canons of the church of Albi acquired the church of Blessed Marciana from certain laymen, who were accustomed to give the canons of Blessed Salvi only twenty solidi for the refection which they owed; and that these canons now demand refection for themselves and all whom they bring with them, by which the Church of Albi is said to be heavily burdened. It therefore seems proper and consonant with reason that you should ensure that they receive twenty solidi from the canons, as they were accustomed to receive from the laymen. We therefore request your affection, in which we place full hope and confidence, that you do not permit the Church of Albi—which we regard as our own, because it was built in honour of Blessed Cecilia—to be burdened, but that you take such steps that the aforesaid canons be content with no more than twenty solidi, [Col. 0102B] so that we may be bound to render you thanks. For we and the chapter of our Church receive them in our prayers and wish, with God and honourably, to assist in every way in their affairs, which we regard as our own.

LXVIII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0101D] See the note to Epistle XLV of Book III.] and convent of St. Denis of Paris.—That they restrain the recklessness of clerics in the town of St. Denis, notwithstanding an appeal lodged by them. (Year 1203; Ferentino, 22 May.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed by us from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of St. Denis of Paris. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.—This bull had long ago been published by DOUBLET in *History of the Church of Saint-Denis*, p. 538. PATRISTIC EDITION.]

[Col. 0102C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the . . . abbot and convent of St. Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You should know that it has come to our hearing that certain clerics living in the town of St. Denis, not fearing to abuse clerical privilege, break down the doors of women by night, burst violently into their houses, and stir up disturbances and quarrels with the burgesses’ sons. The provosts and justiciars of the town are afraid to lay hands upon them for their correction because of the liberty of the clerical order. But if you, son abbot, [Col. 0102D] wish to oppose their recklessness, they immediately resort to appeal, so that under the shelter of our invocation they may both evade canonical punishment and take boldness to offend. Since, therefore, we are bound by the office laid upon us to restrain the recklessness of the perverse, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning and removing the impediment of appeal, you cause those clerics, as pertains to your office, to desist from the aforesaid presumptions and excesses through ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Ferentino, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], in the sixth year of our pontificate.

LXIX. He confirms the foundation of the collegiate church of Mirabel. (Year 1203; Anagni, 5 October.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, Documents, p. 338.]

[Col. 0103A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons and the canons of Blessed Mary of Mirabel, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When a request made to us is just and honourable, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought through the diligence of our office to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favourably concurring with your just prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own your persons and the very church of Blessed Mary of Mirabel, [Col. 0103B] in which you have been canonically established by our venerable brother Maurice, bishop of Poitiers, your diocesan. We receive them with all the church’s appurtenances and other goods, as it now reasonably possesses them or, by God’s favour, may in the future acquire them by just means.

Furthermore, by the gift of the same bishop, we confirm by apostolic authority to you—and through you to that church—the same church, the church of St. Hilary of Mirabel, and the offerings of St. Andrew and of the same castle which that bishop customarily receives on specified feast days, together with the possessions and other revenues that you have acquired both through the generosity of that bishop and through that of the faithful; as well as the liberties and immunities granted by the same bishop to you and to your church, as is more fully contained in his authentic document; and we strengthen by the protection of this present writing both you and all that you justly and peacefully possess. [Col. 0103C] Let no person whatever, therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of October [5 October], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

LXX. To Gerung, provost of the church of All Saints in the Black Forest, of the Premonstratensian Order, in the diocese of Strasbourg, and to his brethren in perpetuity.—He receives them under protection, and their possessions are enumerated [Note: [Col. 0103D] This letter of Innocent should certainly be compared with what the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* report concerning the abbey of All Saints, vol. V, col. 890.]. (Year 1204; Anagni, 5 February.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from the original preserved in the archives of the abbey of All Saints in the diocese of Strasbourg, communicated to us by the late Lord Abbot Grandidier. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0103D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gerung, provost of the church of All Saints in the Black Forest [Note: [Col. 0103D] The monastery of All Saints, of the Premonstratensian Order, still exists today in the Black Forest, [Col. 0104D] and in the diocese of Strasbourg, now Freiburg, in the Duchy of Baden.], and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0104A] Whenever something religious and honourable is requested of us, it befits us to grant it with willing mind and to afford fitting support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid church of All Saints, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order, which is known to have been established in that place according to the Rule of the Lord and of blessed Augustine and the institution of the Premonstratensian Brethren, shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same [Col. 0104B] church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among them, we have thought fit to specify these by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the holding of Rincum; the holding of Haselbach; a wood at Elisweiler, for planting a vineyard, from Henry’s boundary to Erpherad’s boundary; likewise, in the marsh, two rent-free holdings and a fourth part of the fishery at Bustric, granted to your church by pious generosity by the late Duke Welf and Uta, his wife, duchess of Scowenburg [Note: [Col. 0104D] Utha of Schawenburg, wife of Welf, duke of Bavaria.], Duke Hugh of Ulemburch, and [Col. 0104C] the nobleman Duke Berthold of Zähringen [Note: [Col. 0104D] Berthold, duke of Zähringen.], founders of the same place, and afterwards confirmed by Emperor Henry; likewise, acres of land and estates at Appenvilre and Ufholtz, given by Conrad Keseman, Henry Gertine, and Conrad Mesterlin; and the estate at Griseborn, which Conrad, bishop of Strasbourg, of good memory, granted to your church out of piety, with meadows, vineyards, lands, woods, rights of use, and pastures, in woodland and plain, in waters and mills, in roads and paths, and with all its other liberties and immunities. And indeed, concerning your newly cleared lands, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy [Col. 0104D] Roman Church, on the Nones of February [5 February], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1203 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

LXXI. To the provost, dean, and custodian of Minden.—On behalf of the canons of St. Willehad of Bremen. (Year 1204; Rome, at St. Peter’s, 5 February.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburgische Urkunden*, p. 303, from the original in the archive at Stade, chest II, no. II, with the lead seal of Innocent III.]

[Col. 0105A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the provost, dean, and custos of Minden, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The complaint laid before us by our beloved sons Wald[emar] and the other canons of the church of Saint Willehad at Bremen has shown that their provost H., unjustly appropriating to himself for ten years now the revenues of a certain prebend belonging to the aforesaid church, wrongs those same canons concerning their stipends, by conferring, according to his own arbitrary will, the cellarership of that church—which by right belongs to them—upon A., a cleric of Bremen, after an appeal to us had lawfully been lodged. Since, therefore, [Col. 0105B] the foregoing has not been established before us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon the parties, hear the case, and, setting aside the appeal, bring it to a conclusion by means of justice, restoring to its due state whatever shall be found to have been rashly undertaken after the appeal to us was lawfully lodged. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of truth and justice shall stand in the way. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Nones of February, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

LXXII. To the bishop, provost, and dean of Hildesheim.—That they compel the canons of Bremen to produce their privileges. (1204. Lateran, 5 April.)

[Ibid. “Copy-book of the Chapter. Fol. 7b, no. XIII. With this heading: ‘Concerning the stealthy removal and withholding of the privileges of the church of Hamburg by the men of Bremen.’”]

[Col. 0105C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop, and his beloved sons the provost and dean of Hildesheim, greeting and apostolic blessing.

At the complaint of our beloved sons, the canons of Hamburg, it has been reported to us that the canons of Bremen, retaining and suppressing the privileges of the church of Hamburg to their prejudice and detriment, are rashly attempting to break the union between the churches of Bremen and [Col. 0105D] Hamburg, which had been established by our predecessors of happy memory, Benedict and Sergius, and subsequently confirmed by many of their successors. Therefore, desiring to provide for that church, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning, you compel the canons of Bremen by ecclesiastical censure, setting aside any appeal, to produce those privileges; and that, after summoning the parties and hearing the allegations on both sides, you determine what shall be just in these matters, causing what you decree to be firmly observed by the same coercive means. Moreover, if witnesses [Col. 0106A] who have been named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them by like coercion, appeal set aside, to bear testimony to the truth. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of truth and justice shall stand in the way. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, you, brother bishop, together with one of them, shall nevertheless carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

LXXIII. To the bishop of Paderborn.—That he see to the restoration to the archbishop of Bremen of the goods of the Church of Bremen seized by H., Count Palatine of the Rhine. (1204. Lateran, 5 April.)

[Ibid., p. 304. “The original is cited in the Stade Register, box XVII, no. 10.”]

[Col. 0106B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishop and beloved son, the provost of Paderborn, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The lamentable complaint of the venerable archbishop of Bremen has reached us: although with a full heart and unfeigned faith he had devoutly come into allegiance to the king, and it had been prudently ordained by the king himself and confirmed by our venerable brother Ernest, bishop and legate of the Apostolic See, that the ministerials of the Church of Bremen and others who had returned to the king’s allegiance should thereafter peacefully possess what they had quietly possessed up to that time, until it should be decided by [Col. 0106C] judgment whether there was any dispute about these matters between any persons: nevertheless, although that archbishop had committed everything belonging to the Church of Bremen to our and the king’s protection, our beloved son, the nobleman H., Count Palatine of the Rhine, unlawfully seized whatever that archbishop, the canons, priests, and ministerials possessed in the land of Stade and Hadeln [Note: [Col. 0105D] Hadeln.], and, though repeatedly asked by the king himself, by our legate and venerable brother the archbishop of Cologne, and by many others, refused to restore it. Therefore, when the said archbishop achieved nothing with him either by prayers or warnings, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him and an interdict upon the land which he had violently [Col. 0106D] seized. Although our legate had ratified that sentence and ordered it observed, he nevertheless deferred to the count beyond what was due, because the latter promised to restore by a fixed date what he had taken, so that, unless he restored it, he would incur the aforesaid sentence; and he caused that sentence to be relaxed by the same archbishop. And although, for the said count, because he had not performed what he had promised, our legate had once, twice, and three times sought and received postponements for his performance thereafter, he nevertheless refused to restore anything of what he had received. For this reason the archbishop again pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication. And although the legate himself had promised the archbishop by letter that he would henceforth not intervene on the count’s behalf, yet, forgetting his promise and changing his mind, he absolved him in the archbishop’s absence and assigned a fixed day and place at Verden for both parties to examine the case. Furthermore, when the archbishop presented himself before the legate, and perceived that he was opposed to him, inasmuch as he seemed to be inducing and compelling him to enfeoff the count with what he had taken, he appealed to the Apostolic See.

Now, however much we love the aforesaid count in the Lord, since we neither wish nor ought to fail churches and ecclesiastical persons in their rights, attending not to his will but rather to expediency and salvation, [Col. 0107B] we have commanded him by apostolic letters and ordered him, under such coercion as we can impose, to lay aside every excuse, restore in full to that archbishop what he has taken, and henceforth cease molesting him. Nevertheless, if he wishes, he may pursue his legal claim against him by judicial process. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid Count Palatine neglects to fulfill what we have commanded, you restore to its due state whatever you find to have been undertaken after the appeal to us was lawfully lodged; and, setting aside the obstacle of appeal, strike him with a sentence of excommunication, placing under ecclesiastical interdict, by our authority, the land he seized; [Col. 0107C] and solemnly proclaim both sentences on every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, until fitting satisfaction has been made, and order them inviolably observed. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of truth and justice shall stand in the way. If both of you cannot take part in carrying this out, let one of you nevertheless carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

LXXIV. To the prior of La Charité.—He approves the custom of praying for evildoers. (1204. Lateran, 12 April.)

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 795, from the manuscript of La Charité.]

[Col. 0107D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and convent of La Charité, greeting and apostolic blessing.

If the children of men judged justly and diligently considered the grace bestowed upon them by the Redeemer, who gave himself up for us, becoming obedient unto death in order to free us from the jaws of the enemy, they would strive more earnestly to honor the holy Church, his bride, which he consecrated with his own blood, and those who serve therein, and would wholly withdraw their wills from harming them. But, as we relate with sorrow, because sins demand it, men’s wickedness upon earth is now so great, and the audacity of the malicious has grown to such a degree, that they not only stretch greedy hands toward ecclesiastical property and plunder it at the choice of their own will, but even make churches and their possessions a target for the arrow, pursuing religious men with accursed hatred and wickedly disturbing their holy repose. Since such persons, although reckoned Christians by name, are nevertheless alien from Christ’s works, rejoicing when they have done evil and exulting in the worst deeds; and, though often warned, do not wish to desist from their perversity, refusing to understand so as to act rightly, but meditating upon iniquity in their chambers: since, as we have learned from your report, you cannot resist such evildoers yourselves, a custom has taken root in your church that, whenever an evildoer [Col. 0108B] violently occupies property of your monastery or carries it off by robbery, and, having been warned, does not seek to make satisfaction to you, you prostrate yourselves upon the floor of the church during the solemnities of Mass, when the Son is offered to the Father for the sins of the world, and pray for your persecutors, raising your eyes to the Lord and humbly beseeching him to deign to have mercy upon you—he who is near to those who call upon him in truth, fulfills the desires of those who fear him, hears their prayers, and saves them. Therefore, since we are instructed to pray for persecutors not only by the Lord’s command but also by his example, believing the aforesaid custom to be pious, we grant you authority by these presents not to abandon it, [Col. 0108C] but to observe it humbly and devoutly, so that by your prayers the wicked may be recalled from evil and you may enjoy the peace and quiet you desire.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of April, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

LXXV. To Adela, queen of France.—That she may be buried at Pontigny. (1204. Lateran, 24 April.)

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1234.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest daughter in Christ, … the illustrious queen of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious vows and to grant benevolent favor to the honorable petitions of supplicants. Therefore, dearest daughter in Christ, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward the monastery of Pontigny and the brethren who continually serve the Lord there, we mercifully assent to your pious requests and by the authority of these presents forbid anyone, after your death, to presume to bring any impediment upon those brethren, preventing your body from receiving burial in their monastery according to your free disposition. Let absolutely no person, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our prohibition or rashly act contrary to it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0109A] Given at the Lateran, on the eighth Kalends of May, in the seventh year of our pontificate. [Note: [Col. 0109D] What the most pious queen had desired with so devout a heart, she obtained two years later: burial was granted at Pontigny in 1206.]

LXXVI. To the king of England.—He grants permission to ride to preachers crossing the sea with the king. (1204. Lateran, 30 April.)

[Rymer, *Foedera*, etc., I, 91, from the original in the treasury of the Receipt of the Exchequer.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, … the illustrious king of England, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Graciously assenting to your Highness’s requests, we grant the Friars Preachers and Friars Minor, whom you shall take with you overseas, free permission to ride whenever they are requested by you to do so, notwithstanding a contrary statute [Col. 0109B] of their orders.

Given at Lyons. [Note: [Col. 0110D] It should read “at the Lateran,” or the letter should be assigned to Innocent IV.] On the second Kalends of May, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

LXXVII. To Amelinus, bishop of Le Mans, and the abbot of Perseigne, etc.—Concerning the reform of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours. (1204. Lateran, 30 April.)

[*Defence of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours*, 28.]

Amelinus, by God’s grace bishop of Le Mans, and Adam, abbot of Perseigne, to all Christ’s faithful to whom this present document shall come, greeting in the Lord. Know that we have received an apostolic mandate in the following form:

“INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0109C] brother the bishop of Le Mans, and his beloved sons the abbot of Perseigne in the diocese of Le Mans, and Master Guarin, canon of Angers and Le Mans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“From the report of our beloved sons, the subdean and certain canons of Saint Martin of Tours, it has been conveyed to us that, although in former times that church was accounted more distinguished than other Gallican churches by the abundance of its goods and its liberties, it now lies in ashes, desolated by the conflagration caused by the ravages of war. For its own household have despised it: those who hold the greater place in it, both in honors and in the receipt of benefices, such as the priors, chief precentors (capicerii), and provosts, rarely enter the church itself, although by an oath personally taken they are bound to residence and a liege dwelling there. The ordinary canons, moreover, whether because of the deficiency of revenues or because of their greater absence, show themselves negligent concerning the estate of the church and God’s service, taking their example from their superiors, since the same matters are neglected by those who, because of their greater emolument, are bound to provide for them more diligently. Since, therefore, the reform of the condition of this church, which is a special daughter of the Apostolic See, especially devolves upon us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you personally visit that church, investigate matters requiring investigation concerning its condition and the conduct of its persons, and, supported by our authority and notwithstanding any opposition or appeal, correct there what you find needing correction; establish provisions both concerning the residence of its persons and concerning other matters conducive to the benefit of the Church and clerical propriety; and cause what you establish to be firmly observed. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, you, brother bishop, together with one of them, shall nevertheless carry it out.

“Given at the Lateran, on the second Kalends of May, in the seventh year of our pontificate.”

Accordingly, by authority of this mandate, having approached the church, diligently investigated the state of the church and the conduct of its persons, and taken counsel with the church’s priors and other prudent men, strengthened by divine help, we first considered that those matters which we recognized as pertaining to the adornment of the Lord’s house and to reforming the church’s condition for the better should be set forth. Therefore we establish the following concerning the church and its service. If a weekly priest, who is bound to celebrate Mass, is absent through carelessness or negligence, he shall be fined two solidi for every day of the week during which he ought to serve. If a deacon is likewise absent, he shall be fined fourteen denarii; if a subdeacon, twelve; if an acolyte, six. This, however, is said of resident members: visiting priests are fined twelve, a deacon eight, and a subdeacon seven, etc.

LXXVIII. Concerning the bishopric of Carlisle, granted to the archbishop of Ragusa at the request of Pope Innocent III. (1204. Ferentino, 15 May.)

[Rymer, *Foedera*, etc., London, 1816, folio, vol. I, p. 190. Patent Roll, 5 John, no. 11, in the Tower of London.]

[Col. 0110C]

The king, etc., to the venerable father in Christ and dearest brother GEOFFREY, by God’s grace archbishop of York: JOHN, by the same grace king of England, lord of Ireland, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, greeting. We have received the lord pope’s letters in these terms:

“INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, illustrious king of England, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“At the urgent request of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Ragusa, we have thought fit to release him from the care and solicitude by which he was bound to the Church of Ragusa, namely because he could not remain there safely and, if he had access to it, danger of death threatened him.

“Lest that archbishop suffer want in temporal matters, to the discredit of our ministry, we grant, out of the benevolence of the Apostolic See, for the relief of his need, the bishopric of Carlisle and the church of Melbourne, with all their appurtenances, which have been graciously conferred upon him by your munificence and liberality and by the grant of our venerable brother Geoffrey, archbishop of York. We admonish and exhort [Col. 0111A] your royal Serenity that, for the sake of our prayers and in consideration of the pontifical office, you will regard the same archbishop as commended to you, sympathize with his need, aid his poverty, and render the present gifts yet more ample by your illustrious munificence, so that by these acts you may seem to render service to the King of kings, who is a priest forever; for he declares that what is bestowed upon his ministers is bestowed upon himself.

“Given at Ferentino, on the Ides of May, in the sixth year of our pontificate.”

We, therefore, according to the aforesaid request of the lord pope, have granted to the said archbishop of Ragusa the aforesaid bishopric of Carlisle out of royal munificence and liberality, ordering you to obey him in all things as your pastor and bishop. Witness the lord archbishop of Canterbury, at Marlborough, on the tenth day of January.

LXXIX. To the abbot of Foigny and his brethren in perpetuity.—He receives them under protection and confirms their privileges. [Note: [Col. 0111] See the notes to letter XXXIV of this appendix.] (1204. Lateran, 21 May.)

[Bréquigny, ibid., p. 1092.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of Foigny and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of anyone’s rashness either recall them from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall there be inviolably observed for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, [Col. 0111D] or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, acquire by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Sparsey, with its appurtenances; the grange of Gactinise, with its appurtenances; the estate of Landosville, with its appurtenances; the grange of Landosilecourt, with its appurtenances; the grange of Abentonlecourt, with its appurtenances; the meadow of [Col. 0112A] Veagis; the grange called Mare, with its appurtenances; the grange of Villecell, with its appurtenances; the grange of Focutis, with its appurtenances; the cellar at Curpett, with its appurtenances; the grange of Hevercagna, with its appurtenances; whatever you possess in the village of Sainte-Croix; the grange of Hercusot, with its appurtenances; the estate of Marla; the tithes which you possess in the village of Mascotz; the tithes which you possess in the village of Cella; whatever you possess near the city of Laon; and the meadows of Strecs, with lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, rights of common, and pastures, in woodland and plain, in waters and mills, in roads and paths, and with all their other liberties and immunities. Certainly, from the produce of your labors, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense—whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, or in your gardens, shrublands, and fisheries, or from the raising of your animals—let no one presume to demand or exact tithes from you.

It shall also be lawful for you to receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and unencumbered, fleeing from the world, and to retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any one of your brethren, after he has made profession in your monastery, to leave that place without his abbot’s permission; and let no one dare retain one who has departed without letters of release from the community. If anyone should presume to retain him, it shall be lawful for you to pronounce the regular sentence against such monks or conversi. [Col. 0112C] We strictly forbid, moreover, that lands or any benefice granted to your church may be given personally to anyone or alienated in another manner without the consent of the entire chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any grants or alienations are made otherwise than has been said, we decree them void. We further forbid any monk or conversus bound to the possession of your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, to borrow money for any purpose beyond the amount fixed by the prudent judgment of your chapter, unless it be for the manifest benefit of your house. If he should presume to do so, the convent shall not be bound in any way to answer for it. It shall also be lawful for you, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, to use the testimony of your brethren, lest your right be lost in any respect through lack of witnesses.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop or other person to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions; or to presume to come to your houses for the purpose of celebrating ordinations, conducting cases, or calling any public assemblies; or to hinder the regular election of your abbot, or interfere in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, with installing or removing the person who shall then hold that office. If, however, the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when humbly and devoutly requested as is fitting, refuses to bless the abbot who has been appointed and to confer upon you the other things belonging to the episcopal office, it shall be lawful for the said abbot, if he is a priest, to bless his own novices and perform the other acts belonging to his office; and it shall be lawful for you to receive from another bishop everything that has been improperly denied by your own bishop. We add that, in receiving the professions which are made by abbots already blessed or about to be blessed, you are to be content with those forms and expressions instituted from the origin of the Order, without the bishop’s formula and expression [Note: [Col. 0113D] Thus it is read in the copy, incorrectly, it seems.], namely that the abbots themselves ought to profess, without prejudice to their Order, and are not to be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order. For the consecration of altars or churches, for holy oil, or for any ecclesiastical sacrament, no one may dare exact anything from you under pretext of custom or otherwise; rather, the diocesan bishop shall supply all these things free of charge. Otherwise, it shall be lawful for you to approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer who has the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and who, relying upon our authority, shall provide you with what is requested. Should the see of the diocesan bishop happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighboring bishops, provided that no prejudice against your own bishops shall thereby arise in future. Since indeed you sometimes do not have access to your own bishops, if a bishop who is in communion with the Roman See, as stated, and of whom you have full knowledge, should happen to pass through your vicinity, you may by authority of the Apostolic See receive from him blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks. Moreover, if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict against your monasteries or the persons established there, or even against your hired laborers because you do not pay tithes, or for any reason relating to those things granted to you by apostolic [Col. 0113D] favor; or against your benefactors because they have charitably bestowed upon you some benefits or services, or assisted you in labor on days when you work and others rest, we decree that such a sentence, as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See, is to be annulled. Nor shall those letters have force which are shown to have been obtained while concealing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges. Moreover, desiring to provide hereafter with paternal care for your peace and tranquility, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your places or granges [Col. 0114A] to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare to commit violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.
