We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved wholly for the benefit of those uses for whose governance [Col. 0114B] and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, attempts rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend his offense by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge [Col. 0114C] may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Callistus in Santa Maria in Trastevere. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of Saints Martin and [Col. 0114D] Equitius. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Cencius, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis. I, Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0115A] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth Kalends of June, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

I, the undersigned, delegated by Monseigneur the Keeper of the Seals for the research and transcription of the historical monuments of Thiérache and part of the Laonnois, certify that this copy conforms to the original. [Col. 0115B] This 10 April 1788. Signed: D. R. N. JEANNIN, religious of Saint Michael.

LXXX. To the elect [Note: [Col. 0115D] See the note to letter XLV of Book Eight.], dean [Note: [Col. 0115D] This was John III, who is found subscribing documents already from the year 1200. Octavian, legate of the Apostolic See, delegated his authority to him in 1201 to settle the dispute between the churches of Saint-Bertin and Saint-Omer on one side and Guy of Coucy on the other, who claimed for himself the right of advocacy in the village of Caumont. He occurs in a charter of 1209 for the establishment of two chaplaincies of the cathedral church; he was still in office in 1212.], and archdeacon of Arras.—That by ecclesiastical censure they compel the nobleman Philip, count of Namur, and the bailiffs of Baldwin, count of Flanders, in accordance with their promise, to preserve the liberties of the abbot and convent of Saint-Bertin and to render satisfaction for the damage and injuries inflicted upon the said abbot and convent on the occasion of the excommunication of the burgesses of Saint-Omer. (1204. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 23 September.)

From the archive of Saint-Bertin, papal box, no. 59. At the end of the copy D. C. de Witte appended this note: “Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, having departed for the Holy Land in 1202, as has been discussed above in heading and notes 299, Philip, count of Namur and brother of the said count of Flanders, together with several bailiffs of the said count of Flanders, took advantage of this absence to cause damage and make incursions into the lands and garden-plots of the abbey of Saint-Bertin, situated in the diocese of Thérouanne. The abbot and religious of Saint-Bertin therefore submitted their complaints at Rome; consequently, the sovereign pontiff Innocent III issued this present apostolic mandate to the dean and archdeacon of Arras, to oblige the said count of Namur and the bailiffs of the count of Flanders, under penalty of ecclesiastical censure, to indemnify and make satisfaction for all damages and injuries caused by them to the said abbot and religious of Saint-Bertin.” BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1123.]

[Col. 0115C]

The complaint set before us by our beloved sons, … the abbot and convent of Saint-Bertin [Note: [Col. 0116D] See the note to letter XVIII of this appendix.], has shown [Col. 0115D] that, when the burgesses of Saint-Omer in the diocese of Thérouanne had, by our authority, been subjected to excommunication for offenses committed against them, the nobleman … [Note: [Col. 0116D] See above, C. de Witte’s note.] count of Namur, and the bailiffs of the nobleman … [Note: [Col. 0116D] In the same place.] count of Flanders, in the diocese of Thérouanne, violently invading their goods and estates on that occasion, inflicted upon them [Col. 0116A] and their monastery so many and such great losses and burdens that, fearing exile, they were compelled, on the advice of our venerable brother the bishop of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0116D] See the note to letter CLXXXII of Book Nine.], their diocesan, and other prudent men, to accept a day with them. On that occasion the aforesaid bailiffs promised, in order that the sentence of excommunication might be temporarily relaxed, fitting satisfaction for both injuries and damages, and also preservation of their liberties, as the letters of themselves and of those who were present attest; concerning which the complainants assert that they were shamefully defrauded and deceived. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning, you compel the aforesaid count and bailiffs by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, as justice requires, to preserve the liberties of the said monastery in accordance with their promise [Col. 0116B] and render it fitting satisfaction for the damages and injuries. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of truth and justice shall stand in the way. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth Kalends of October, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### LXXXI. To John, [Note: [Col. 0116D] See the note on Letter XVIII of the appendix to this work.] Abbot of Saint-Bertin.—He is granted authority to bless altar cloths and sacerdotal vestments. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 5 October.)

[From the Archive of Saint-Bertin, Papal chest, no. 161. At the end of this copy D. C. de Witte appended the following note: “Since the right of blessing things used at the altar for the holy sacrifice of the Mass belonged to bishops, John, abbot of Saint-Bertin, in order to avoid every difficulty on this matter, entreated the sovereign pontiff—having regard to the great number of altars under his charge—to grant him the faculty of blessing their altar cloths or linens used to cover the altar, as well as sacerdotal garments. Pope Innocent III favorably granted this, by the present bull, to the said John and to all his successors as abbots of Saint-Bertin.” BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0116C]

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and bring to effect the requests which do not depart from the path of reason.

[Col. 0116D] Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, concurring favorably with your just petitions, by apostolic authority we grant to you and your successors the faculty of blessing altar cloths and sacerdotal vestments. Let absolutely no person, therefore, infringe this page of our concession or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third Nones of October [5 October], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### LXXXII. To Peter, prior, and the brethren of Saint Reparata of Lucca.—He confirms their rights and possessions. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 7 October.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 445.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior of Saint Reparata, situated in the city of Lucca, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity, etc.

[Col. 0117B] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Saint Reparata, which serves as the *plebs* church in the city of Lucca and in which you are devoted to divine service, after the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Eugenius, Anastasius, Adrian, and Celestine, Roman pontiffs; and so forth. We have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the hospital of Saint Reparata, situated beside the aforesaid church, with all its rights and appurtenances; the church of Saint Cassian, with all its rights and appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael of Contesora, with all its rights and appurtenances. Likewise, [Col. 0117C] the right which you possess in the church of Saint Justus at the Arch, and in the church of Saint Lawrence of Piciorano. We also confirm to you by authority of the Apostolic See your entire parish and parishioners, and the tithes which you possess.

We decree, moreover, that on those Sundays, and especially on those solemn feasts, upon which the canons of the Major Church customarily come in procession to the said church, should they perhaps, induced by some perversity, refuse to come to that place according to ancient custom, you yourselves shall solemnly celebrate by our authority the principal Mass, Vespers, and the other divine offices which they ought to have celebrated.

Furthermore, you may receive as brethren, without anyone’s objection, educated and respectable clerics from wherever they may come, provided that, if they are unknown, they bring letters of recommendation from their bishops, and provided also that your bishop consents. [Col. 0117D] If the bishop himself maliciously acts contrary to right and refuses to allege a reasonable ground, you shall nevertheless receive those clerics.

We also decree that the burial-place of the house shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving nevertheless the rights of [Col. 0118A] those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We prohibit either the bishop or any other person from introducing new customs into that church against your will, imposing unlawful exactions, or taking your parishioners from you in any manner. We further prohibit anyone from imposing penance upon your parishioners without consulting you, unless they are placed in such an urgent extremity of necessity that they cannot have recourse to you, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 0118B] I, John, bishop of Albano. I, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of October [7 October], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1204 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

### LXXXIII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0117D] See the note on Letter XVIII of the appendix to this work.] and convent of Saint-Bertin.—He confirms certain possessions belonging to them. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 10 October.)

[From the Archive of Saint-Bertin, Papal chest, no. 62. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1125.]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious requests and to bestow benevolent favor upon the honorable prayers of petitioners. [Col. 0118C] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably granting your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen with the protection of this writing:

the land which you lawfully acquired from Nicholas of Clarkes in the vill of Woeserma, together with its comital jurisdiction, which you acquired from Gilbert, castellan of Bergues; likewise, the land in the parish of Longanessa, commonly called Stapleveld, obtained by exchange from (Gerard), provost of Saint-Omer, [Note: [Col. 0117D]

Gerard II, brother of the count of Flanders and provost of Saint-Omer, is known from documents as early as 1180. His successor, Peter of Collemedio, is not mentioned before 1227 by the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 473.

Compare also the letters of Gerard, provost of the church of Saint-Omer, in J. F. Foppens, *Supplement to Miraeus*, vol. VI, p. 216, chap. LII.]

whose fief it was; also the possessions which Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, and William, castellan of Saint-Omer, piously and generously gave you in their fief, as is contained in their authentic instruments; also the lands and revenues in the castellanies of Cassel and Bourbourg, and in all [Note: [Col. 0118D] “And in all”: thus in the copy.] [Col. 0118D] the churches of Saint-Omer and Saint-Folquin which were granted to you and your monastery; furthermore, the churches of Trulleia and Chillam, with chapels and all their appurtenances; likewise the vill of Calmunt, with its estate and comital jurisdiction, as is more fully contained in the authentic writings drawn up concerning it; also the share of possessions which you hold in the same vill through the Church of Saint-Omer, as you justly and peacefully possess them; and likewise the agreements made between you and . . . priest of Stenkerke concerning the tithe of [Col. 0119A] Avencapella, and with the parishioners of Merch concerning the tithes of herring, insofar as they were prudently made without malice, freely accepted by both sides, and hitherto peacefully observed.

Let absolutely no person, therefore, infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixth Ides of October [10 October], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### LXXXIV. To the abbot of Saint Vincent, [Note: [Col. 0119D] Peter I, abbot of Saint Vincent at Senlis, appears in documents from at least 1203 through at least 1212. Concerning him the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1497, write: “With Stephen, archdeacon, and the succentor of the church of Senlis, he was appointed judge in a controversy between the church of Saint-Frambald, etc., in 1207”; this seems indeed to concern this letter of Innocent.] the archdeacon, and the succentor of Senlis.—That they may settle a dispute between the chapter of Saint-Frambald, the count of Dammartin, and others. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 23 October.)

[From the Archive of the church of Saint-Frambald. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1126.]

[Col. 0119B]

From the complaint of our beloved sons, the dean [Note: [Col. 0119D] Hermerus, who had as brothers Hugh, Ralph, and Walter, knights, appears in 1180 as a canon of Blessed Mary, subdeacon, and cantor of Saint-Frambald. In 1185 he is called dean of Saint-Regulus in a certain charter. Soon afterwards Hermerus appears as canon of Blessed Mary, deacon, and dean of Saint-Frambald in 1187; he is still found subscribing under one name in an instrument of 1207. See *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1474.] and chapter of Saint-Frambald at Senlis, it has been reported to our ears that the nobleman [Note: [Col. 0120D] See the note on § LXXXIV of the *Gesta of Innocent*.] . . . count of Dammartin, and his wife [Note: [Col. 0120D] See the note on Letter CLXXXVIII of Book VIII.] . . . , the abbot of Rebais [Note: [Col. 0120D] After Simon, who died in Palestine on 8 July 1204, Stephen assumed the administration of the monastery of the Praise of Blessed Mary—a man, as the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* say (vol. III, col. 304), courageous and vigorous against those who invaded the monastery’s goods. He ruled for four years, and then died on 7 March 1207.] and certain others, monks as well as clerics and laymen, of the dioceses of Senlis, Meaux, and Beauvais, presume to inflict serious injuries upon their movable and immovable property and upon their church.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion [Col. 0119C] to summon those whom you know should be summoned in this matter, to decide the case concerning these things with due finality, without appeal, and to cause what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See that prejudice truth and justice. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, nevertheless two of you shall execute it.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth Kalends of November [23 October], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### LXXXV. To the archbishop of Lund.—He grants permission to absolve a certain reeve. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 13 November.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplom. Suec.* I, 150.]

[Col. 0119D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the archbishop of Lund: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0120A] It has been reported to us on your behalf that a certain priest, while he was accustomed to engage in an abominable act with the wife of one of your reeves, was captured by the reeve. The reeve cut off his nose and wounded his tongue, although he did not lose his speech. Therefore the priest withdrew into the leisure of monks, so that among them he might save his soul.

But because that reeve seeks absolution from us concerning this deed, you have requested permission to absolve him. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if the matter is so, you restore to communion the said reeve, who is avoided as though excommunicated, on condition that he send, in aid of the Holy Land [Col. 0120B] or in aid of the Christians laboring in those regions against the perfidy of the pagans, the expenses which he would have incurred in travelling to the Apostolic See for this matter; and that he furthermore redeem the burden of the journey according to his own means.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of November [13 November], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### LXXXVI. To Stephen, [Note: [Col. 0120D] After Simon, who died in Palestine on 8 July 1204, Stephen assumed the administration of the monastery of the Praise of Blessed Mary—a man, as the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana* say (vol. III, col. 304), courageous and vigorous against those who invaded the monastery’s goods. He ruled for four years, and then died on 7 March 1207.] abbot of the monastery of Los, and his brethren.—They are received under the protection of blessed Peter, and the goods belonging to them are enumerated. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 17 November.)

[We publish this letter, or rather bull, on the authority of a copy carefully transcribed from the Archive of the monastery of the Praise of Blessed Mary (otherwise called Loz), in the diocese of Tournai, and deposited in our chartophylacium by D. Queinfert. It may also be read in Jean François Foppens’s supplement to Miraeus’s diplomatic works (*Aub. Mir., Opera diplomatica*, vol. II, chap. L), though not without some discrepancy, which we have not delayed to note here; notably, the names of the subscribing cardinals are lacking in J. F. Foppens. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1126.]

[Col. 0120C]

It is fitting that apostolic protection be available to those choosing the religious life, lest an attack of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religious observance. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the monastery of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary of Los, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. First, indeed, we decree [Col. 0120D] that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

[Col. 0121A] Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; [Note: [Col. 0121D] Compare the charter of Count Theoderic in Miraeus, vol. I, p. 730, chap. 99.] the abbey grange, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Marcha, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Duremort, [Note: [Col. 0121D] Compare in Miraeus, vol. I, p. 699, the charter by which Theoderic, count of Alsace, and his wife Sibyl make a benefaction to the abbey of Laudes in 1252. There one reads: “For we have consented that the church and abbey of Los, of the Order of Clairvaux, shall possess in perpetuity, at an annual rent of two solidi, the land which Walter of Duremort [Col. 0122D] held from us, and which Stephen of Primeka held from Walter, compelled by the request of Stephen and by concern for our salvation, etc.”] with all its appurtenances; [Note: [Col. 0122D] Miraeus adds: “The grange of Brebant, with all its appurtenances.”] the grange of Esquelio, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Antonio, [Col. 0121B] with all its appurtenances; the grange of Rogirfart, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Templonio, with all its appurtenances.

Certainly, from the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense—whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens, shrublands, and fisheries, or from the raising of your animals—let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved from worldly obligations and flee from the world, and retain them without any objection.

We further prohibit any one of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without the permission of his abbot. Let no one dare retain one who departs without letters of release from your community. If anyone should presume to retain him, you may pronounce the regular sentence against such monks or converts. We strictly prohibit anyone from personally receiving, or otherwise alienating, lands or any benefice granted to your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part; and if any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we judge them void.

We also prohibit any monk or convert bound by profession to your house, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, from standing surety for anyone [Col. 0121D] or receiving a loan from anyone beyond the amount established by the prudent determination of your chapter, except for manifest benefit to your house. If he should presume to do so, the convent shall in no way be bound to answer for it.

Furthermore, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brethren, so that [Col. 0122A] your right may not suffer loss in any respect through lack of witnesses.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit any bishop or any other person from compelling you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit your own property or possessions to secular judgment; from presuming to come to your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, hear cases, or summon public assemblies; or from hindering the regular election of your abbot, or interfering in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, in appointing or removing the person who is abbot for the time being.

But if the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when humbly and devoutly requested as is fitting, refuses [Col. 0122B] to bless the abbot who has been appointed or to grant you the other things belonging to the episcopal office, that abbot—provided that he is a priest—may bless his own novices and perform the other acts pertaining to his office; and you may receive from another bishop everything unlawfully denied by your own bishop. We add that, when receiving professions offered by abbots already blessed or about to be blessed, bishops shall be content with the form and expression established from the beginning of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must make profession while preserving their Order, and shall not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order.

For consecrations of altars or churches, [Col. 0122C] for chrism, or for any other ecclesiastical sacrament, let no one dare extort anything from you under color of custom or in any other way; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things to you without charge. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer who enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and he, relying upon our authority, shall provide what is requested. If the see of the diocesan bishop happens to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without objection receive all the sacraments of the Church from neighboring bishops, provided that no prejudice thereby arises in future against your own bishops.

And because you do not always have a bishop of your own at hand, if a bishop who, as we have said, is in communion with the Roman See and is fully known to you happens to pass through your area, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks.

Moreover, if bishops or other rulers of churches [Col. 0123A] pronounce a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict against your monasteries or persons dwelling therein, or even against your hired laborers because you do not pay tithes, or on any pretext relating to the things granted you by apostolic favor; or if they seek the same sentence against your benefactors because they have charitably rendered you benefits or services, or have assisted in labor on those days on which you work while others rest—we decree that such a sentence is void, as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall those letters have force which are shown to have been obtained while concealing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges.

[Col. 0123B] Wishing also to provide henceforth with paternal care for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosure of your places or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to use violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the privilege of this writing, all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, Roman pontiffs, as well as liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree [Col. 0123C] that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away or retain its possessions once taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] These words are absent in Miraeus.] Therefore, if in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence through fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy [Col. 0123D] body and blood of God and the Lord, our Redeemer [Col. 0124A] Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Octavian, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter X of Book III.] bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter LXIX of Book V.] bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter CXVII of Book VI.] bishop of Albano. I, Peter, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter XXXII of Book V, and the note on Letter I of this appendix.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. [Col. 0124B] I, Jordan, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter LXXIV of Book V.] cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Guy, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter XXVIII of Book III.] cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Callixtus. I, Hugh, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter XLI of Book III and the note on Letter VII of this appendix.] cardinal priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, John, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter XV of Book III.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Cencius, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter XVII of this appendix.] cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter LX of Book V.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis. I, Benedict, [Note: [Col. 0123D] See the note on Letter LIV of Book III.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. [Col. 0124C] I, Gratian, [Note: [Col. 0124D] See the note on Letter VII of this appendix. It should be noted, however, that Oldoinus says that the time of death of Gratian, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, is unknown. Yet it should be investigated whether it can be established from the letter of this appendix to be presented immediately below, in which John, cardinal deacon of the same title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, is found subscribing.] cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0124D] See the note on Letter LX of Book VII.] cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, [Note: [Col. 0124D] See the note on Letter LXX of Book V.] cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace. I, Matthew, [Note: [Col. 0124D] See the note on Letter LIV of Book III.] cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, John, [Note: [Col. 0124D] See the note on Letter XXVII of Book VII.] cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, [Note: [Col. 0124D] See the note on Letter CLXXXIV of Book VII.] subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth Kalends of December [17 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1204 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of [Col. 0124D] Lord Pope Innocent III.

### LXXXVII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0125D] The authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 447, state that Robert, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, of whom we have already spoken in the note on Letter III of this appendix, lived at least until 1204, and mention Robert’s successor John from documents only in 1207. This hitherto unpublished letter of Innocent abundantly proves that, if Robert lived into 1204, he died before the Kalends of December, and that John was appointed in his place in that same year, 1204.] of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.—By apostolic authority he confirms the judgment in which Pope Celestine III had declared void a grant of certain churches, not vacant, to particular clerics. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 1 December.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0125A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son . . . . . . . abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we are bound to give special attention to the advancement and increase of your monastery because it is immediately subject to us, nevertheless, because of the devotion and purity of faith which you and your predecessors have hitherto taken care to show to the Roman Church, we are more effectively moved to hear your petitions and those of your monastery.

[Col. 0125B] Now, as became known to us from the tenor of the rescript of C., our predecessor of happy memory, when R., your predecessor, had brought before him that both he and his predecessors, at the solicitation of certain nobles and contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, had granted certain churches that were not vacant to certain clerics, and that, because of the pensions which the church of Saint-Germain was bound to pay yearly to those clerics, it suffered no small loss and burden, our said predecessor, observing that this was contrary to the sacred canons, annulled the aforesaid grants and released your church from payment of such pensions.

[Col. 0125C] Therefore, favorably granting your just petitions, we ratify what was decreed concerning this by that predecessor of ours and command that it be inviolably observed. Let absolutely no person, therefore, infringe this page of our concession or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of December [1 December], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

### LXXXVIII. To Odo, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint John in Venere.—He confirms their privileges. (1204; Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 2 December.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 715.]

[Col. 0125D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ODO, abbot of the monastery of Saint John in Venere, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0126A] “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God,” teaches us to enter upon the path of uprightness, since the strength of the Lord is straight in a simple way. Therefore a hearing must not be denied to petitioners, because it is our duty to provide for the tranquillity of God’s servants, so that, free from secular disturbances, they may be strong in walking with simple hearts in the way of the Lord.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery, known to have been founded in honor of the Mother of God and Virgin Mary and Saint John the Baptist, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Leo, Victor, Nicholas, Urban, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs; [Col. 0126B] and we strengthen it by the privilege of this document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic Order known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through the grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the said monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; all possessions [Col. 0126C] and other goods which you hold in the counties of Chieti, Penne, Abruzzo, Fermo, and Termoli.

In the county of Chieti: the following cells, namely Saint John in Maltraverso; Saint Zechariah; Saint Benedict; Saint Romanus; Saint Severinus; Saint Mary at the chapel near Ortona; Saints Paul and Peter, with the borough beside it; the churches of Saint George; Saint Philip of the Palace; Saint Angel, with a third part of the port of Ortona; Saint Mary beside the stream called Grivus; in the court of Antean, the church of the holy martyrs Leguntianus and Domitianus, with a thousand *modii* of land adjoining it; in the court of Agrame, Saint Calixtus; the holy martyrs Aurea and Petronilla; Saint Ambrose; Saint Martin; Saint Stephen on the hill; at Gitti; Holy Cross, with twelve *marnatae* [Col. 0126D] of persons; Saint Angel near the town of Septem.

In the court of Saint Nicholas: the cells of Saint John at Rocca with its town; Saint Thomas with its town; Saint Farmanus; Saint Eusanus with its castle; Saint Apollinaris with its castle; Saint Nicholas with its castle; Saint Vitus; Saint Mary in Caldaria with its castle; Saint Mary in Gripta Feninea; Saint Mary of Trodio with its cells; Saint Angel in Pesulo; Saint Angel in Ochreca with its town; Saint Mark; Saint Quiricus; Saint Lucy in Argelli; [Col. 0127A] Saint Pantaleon; Holy Cross in Alveto, in the town of Mucela; Saint Ansuinus; Saint John in Ragio; Saint Paul in Piscaria with the town of Saint Lawrence in Piscaria, together with a fourth part of the crossing of the same river and a fourth part of the port of the same; Saint Nicholas with the town of Sagro; Saint Cansione with the castle of Pallito; Saint Martin of the sons of Theobald; Saint Peter in Banniario with its *fara* and cells, namely Saint Bartholomew of Varanna, Saint Blaise of Monte Nigro, and Saint Nicholas of Plazzano; the churches of Saint Agatha, Saint Pancras, Saint Justin of Casulo, Saint Peter in Lauro, Saint Delinara with its castle, Saint Peter with the castle of Resse, Saint Peter in Parlari, Saint Mary in Valle, Saint Mary in Heremo, Saint Paul, Saint Mary of Rota, Saint Quiricus of Rivo Plano, Saint Mary in Basilica, and Saint Vitus in Fortulae.

[Col. 0127B] The towns, however, are these: Fossa Caeca, the walled castle, Rocca de Sclavis, Giruli, Laternum, Lentiscum, Monte Octaviani, Guastum Meruli, Porcile, Milianica, Castellum Vetus, Ballenianum, the *fara* of Benedict son of Ubertus, the *fara* of the sons of Boderocchus, Monte Saint Silvester, Perranum, Senella, Castellione, Guastum Aymonis, Turricella, half of Collis Martini, Ilex, Divus Justus, Mucella Scorciosa, the estate of Saint Benedict, Morum, Rivus Petri, Pesclorum.

In the county of Penne: the cells of St Mary at Rosano, with the castle of Casa Vetere; of St Michael at Boccaccetto, with its *fara* and cells; and the *fara* of St Michael of Saratico; at Fine, with the *fara* and height of St Peter at Campo Rotondo; St Mary at Lochiano, with its height; St John at [Col. 0127C] Rivosonuli; St John at Aquaviva, with its hamlet; St Pelinus; St John at Ponticlum; St Antinus; St Mary at Rivulo; St Saviour at Casa Nigra; St Margaret at Legoniano; St John at Carpeneto; St Angel at Rivo Turbido; St Mary in the Valley; St Nicholas at Plomba; St Lawrence near Gomanum; St John at the Burnt House; the castle at Mare Speltore; Turrica; Cosenza; Monte Silvano; the town of St Angel; Ilice of the Holy Cross; Casa Laute; Ilice Titilianum; Tezzanum; Scuranum; Monte Gualtieri; Motula; Spatula; Rupta; Arseta; Biferrum; Avianum; Ranchi Silvo; Mitilianum; Casole; Murum Altum; Castle Vedum; Monte Petritum and the church of St John at Gomanum with its castle; Carrum; Bifulcum; the church of St [Col. 0127D] Caesarius; St Donatus at Salinello with the castle of Palme; and St Stephen at Mura; the church of St Angel; Monte Pagani; and the hamlet of St Martin at Gomanum; Gassianum; Ripa of the sons of Azzo; Poggio of Felix Morellus; the entire estate of Padoniano; the entire estate of Bucelliano; one third of the estate of Semproniano.

In the county of Fermo: the cell of St Peter with its ancestral castle; Monterone; half the estate of Supportica; the whole estate of Aquaviva; Monte Bovario; the castle of Rodectarisci; Caprilla; Colmari; the church of St Pastor.

In the county of Ascoli: the entire estate of Salviano.

In the county of Camerino: lands with their cultivators.

On the estate of Cesapalumbo: half the estate of Castelliano; one quarter of the estate of Jano.

In the county of Termoli: the cells of St [Col. 0128A] Martin and St Mary at Coronule, with the castle of Olivastro; the churches of St Januarius, St Victorinus, and St Lawrence; one sixth part of the revenues of the church of St Saviour; at Lesina, the cell of St Archangel; in the suburb of Ferrara, the cell of St Nicholas.

In the city of Ravenna: the church of St Mary at the vineyard of Talliotta.

In the principality of Benevento: the churches of St Mary and St John.

At Mursia: the cell of St Anastasius.

In the city of Ernia: the entire inheritance of Leo Prinninus.

In Dalmatia, near Belgrade: likewise the cell of St Thomas; Talleoneum, market dues and bridge tolls; and tithes and offerings for the dead from all sources, to be held by you without any opposition.

But you are to receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks [Col. 0128B] and other clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you choose. Within the boundaries of the entire abbey, no bishop, unless invited by you, may dare to hold a synod or compel clerics, so that you may understand that this care belongs especially to your solicitude, having been granted to you by the Apostolic See.

When you, now abbot of this place, or any one of your successors, dies, no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of usurpation or force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge, according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, should be elected. The elected person, moreover, shall come to the Roman pontiff to be blessed.

But you, sons, must preserve in every respect the grace conferred upon you, and answer the great benefits of the Apostolic See with worthy deeds, lest you misuse this liberty as an opportunity for the flesh and as a cloak for malice. Rather, the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more earnestly you must strive, with all the strength of mind and soul, to please God.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved untouched and entire, for the complete benefit of the uses for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or [Col. 0128D] secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0129A] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Jordan, cardinal priest of the title of St Pudentiana, [also] called St Pastor. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St Martin in Equitius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca. I, Cencius, of the title of St John and St Paul, Pammachius. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of St Vitalis. I, Benedict, cardinal priest of the Church of St Susanna. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St Eustachius. [Col. 0129B] I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

LXXXIX. He rejects the election of Ecbert as bishop of Bamberg and consecrates him by his own authority. (1204; Anagni, 22 December.)

[USSERMANN, *Episcopatus Bambergensis*, San Blasien Press, 1802, quarto, p. 139, from a copy.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Bamberg, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

When our beloved sons Gundelous, dean; Syboto, archdeacon; Gotfridus and Hertnidus, canons; together with Otto, Marcuald, and Chunrad, ministerials of the church of Bamberg, came into our presence concerning the election which you had made of our venerable Eckenbert, bishop, then your provost, they took care humbly to explain before us and our brethren that, when that church, as it pleased the Lord, had been deprived of its pastor, you considered not only the malice of the times but also the man’s nobility and prudence. Considering that through his skill and power the Church itself might be raised up and receive growth both in spiritual and [Col. 0129D] temporal matters—since its goods had already been given over to plunder and prey through the evil deeds of many who, at the Devil’s instigation, do not cease to rage against ecclesiastical property—you elected him unanimously as pastor in zeal for God, and most humbly petitioned us to deign to confirm his election by apostolic authority.

We caused the manner of the election and the person elected to be diligently examined by our brethren, as is customary. Learning that he had not yet reached thirty years of age, and relying upon the enactment of the Lateran Council, which expressly provides that no one shall be elected bishop unless he has completed his thirtieth year, and that clerics who elect anyone contrary to that rule shall then be deprived of the power of election and suspended from ecclesiastical benefices for three years, we declared his election void and invalid by authority of this decree. We decreed null and without force whatever had followed from or because of it, and likewise pronounced the electors, by authority of the same decree, suspended from ecclesiastical benefices for three years and deprived during that time of the power of election, since in the strictness of justice we could proceed no otherwise.

But because the church of Bamberg is our special daughter, and its needs especially rest upon our care to be provided for with due watchfulness, at the urgent and repeated petition of the aforesaid persons—who, because of the feared condition of that church amid the dangers of the present time, did not cease continually to assail our ears with entreaty—we looked upon it with an eye of mercy. Having taken counsel with our brethren, and dispensing with the defect of age because of urgent necessity and manifest advantage, we granted him to you as pastor by our authority. We first received from him, and also from the aforesaid dean and archdeacon and your other fellow-canons, their corporal oath that, when the bishop of Constance ordained him deacon, they neither knew nor believed that the latter was bound by the bond of excommunication. Then we caused him to be ordained priest by our venerable brother, the bishop of Porto; and we ourselves, laying hands upon him, saw fit to confer the gift [Col. 0130C] of consecration. We also caused the pallium—namely, the fullness of the pontifical office—to be assigned to him, that he might use it on specified days, as is more fully contained in our privilege granted to him. Moreover, in order to show mercy not only to him but also to you, we have seen fit, in the kindness of the Apostolic See, to remit the sentence of suspension which, as stated above, you incurred.

Therefore, sending your bishop back to you with the fullness of our favour, we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters to take care devoutly and humbly to obey him as the spiritual father and shepherd of your souls, faithfully and manfully assisting him in the needs of the church of Bamberg, so that, aided by your devotion and fidelity, he may more effectively pursue the advancement of yourselves and of the Church itself.

Given at Anagni, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth [seventh] year of our pontificate.

LXXXIX bis. To Ecbert, bishop of Bamberg.—He grants him the pallium. (1204; Anagni, 24 December.)

[Same work, p. 140.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ECBERT, bishop of Bamberg, [Col. 0131A] and to his successors canonically promoted in perpetuity.

The words of the Lord’s address, by which it is said to the same keeper of the keys of heaven, “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21), and elsewhere, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22), declare that the governance of all ecclesiastical discipline was specially entrusted to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. For this reason the most holy Roman Church, which by heavenly privilege holds primacy above all others and judges not only earthly but heavenly matters also, customarily both adorns her sons, whom with motherly affection she feeds with the nourishment of the divine law, with various prerogatives, and in her accustomed mercy bestows the honour due upon her [Col. 0131B] members.

For this reason, venerable brother Bishop Ecbert, whom, with the Lord’s cooperation, we ourselves consecrated as bishop, as it were with the hands of Blessed Peter, we grant your person the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office and a sign of humility and justice, for celebrating the sacred solemnities of Mass. You may use it only within the church on the days specified in this present document: namely, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ; the feast of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; the solemnities of the holy martyrs Dionysius and George; the Epiphany and Ascension of the Lord; the Purification of Blessed Mary, ever Virgin; the feast of St Michael the Archangel; the feasts also of Blessed King Henry and Queen Cunegund, whose bodies rest in the same church; the anniversary day of your consecration; the dedications of churches; and solemn ordinations of clerics.

We desire you in every respect to vindicate the character of this pallium, and, God being favourable, to show yourself in all things such a person that the good may find you a gentle corrector and the wicked a merciful one. In that correction, you should know that this order must be observed: love persons and persecute vices. Otherwise, should you choose to act differently, correction may become cruelty, and you may lose those whom you desire to amend. You must cut away a wound in such a way that what is healthy cannot become ulcerated; for if you press the blade in more deeply than the matter requires, you harm the one whom you hasten to benefit. Let gentleness in you also be cautious, not lax; let correction be diligent, not harsh. Let each thus be tempered by the other, so that the good, through love, have what they should fear, and the depraved, through fear, what they should love. Therefore, dearest brother, if you diligently preserve this dignity of the pallium received, you will possess inwardly what you are known to have received outwardly. May divine grace guard your fraternity and always protect it from every adversity.

Because the goods of the church of Bamberg lie in various dioceses or parishes, and certain bishops, as we have learned, are negligent in restraining wrongdoers or disturbers of those possessions, we decree that if such wrongdoers, after canonical warning, refuse to restore what they have taken and cease from their presumption, and the bishops in whose parishes they reside are likewise negligent in correcting them, you may pronounce canonical sentence against them.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority to the same Church, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander and Celestine: the abbey called Münster, with the church of St Sixtus situated in the same town; the church of St Leonard at Gamenare; likewise those of St Peter, St James, and St Martin of Villach; those situated in Canali; and generally all the churches and tithes which the church of Bamberg has hitherto held canonically in other parishes or shall hereafter justly hold. As a further token of greater familiarity and favour, we grant that a cross may be carried before you within the boundaries of the church of Bamberg, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the metropolitan see of Mainz. And as a token, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1203 [1204], in the sixth [seventh] year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

XC. To the abbot of Marseilles.—He grants the use of the mitre. (1204; Rome, at St Peter’s, 25 December.)

[*Antiquité de l’Eglise de Marseille*, III, 27.]

[Col. 0132C]

INNOCENT, bishop, etc., to his beloved son, the abbot of Marseilles, etc.

Considering the devotion and purity of faith which the monastery of Marseilles, over which you are known to preside, has hitherto shown towards the Roman Church, we have judged that your person should be honoured in those matters in which, with God’s help, we are able to do so. Therefore, that you may be more devoutly and diligently intent upon the divine offices, we have seen fit personally to grant you the use of the mitre, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

XCI. Letter of P., legate of the Apostolic See, to the canons of Langres.—Concerning the relics of St Mammas the martyr. (About 1204.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 798, from the autograph.]

[Col. 0132D]

To the venerable father in Christ and dearest friend …, by God’s grace bishop, and to his beloved brethren in Christ, the chapter of Langres: P., by divine permission cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus and legate of the Apostolic See, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

We love your Church with such zeal and charitable affection that we desire and seek to do those things which may contribute to the increase of its honour and exaltation, to the praise of God, and to the glory of the saints. Let your fraternity therefore know from these presents that, among other relics of saints which were surrendered by pilgrims into the hands of the bishop of Troyes of good memory during the capture of Constantinople, the head of the glorious martyr Mammas came into the said bishop of Troyes’s possession. When Gualo of Dampierre, a beloved son in Christ, a devout son and useful member of your Church, a man of honourable life and good repute in the army of the Latins, learned this from that bishop’s account, after the bishop’s death he sought from us, with great insistence and supplication of prayers, the aforementioned relics to be conveyed to your church, which was built in honour of the aforesaid martyr. He had frequently laboured and diligently requested this before.

But, that we might be fully assured concerning the relics, we went to the bishop’s house, where the relics were kept. In the presence of ourselves and many others, we caused a certain monk of our household, skilled in Greek letters, carefully to read a title inscribed in Greek letters on a band of silver wound around the head. Having thereby ascertained in truth that they were the relics of the martyr, we willingly granted and gave them to the aforesaid priest Gualo for your church, since we desire to be found more ready to promote the increase of its honour.

Furthermore, wishing to make both himself and us still more certain concerning the matter, the same Gualo brought into our presence a priest named N., a man of good repute. He asserted before us upon his word of truth that, when a certain Greek abbot and monks, who were in a monastery built under the patronage of that martyr, saw the head of St Mammas, they fell weeping before the relics with great reverence. They begged the priest G. that they might deserve to possess them in their church, promising much money for them.

For further investigation of this matter, we arranged to send a cleric of our household with G. himself and the priest mentioned above to the same monastery. In a truthful report he told us that the abbot and brothers of the aforesaid monastery said to him that the relics which the priest G. had in his possession were those of the blessed martyr Mammas. They had been brought to Constantinople, together with the relics of four saints, by a certain *calogerus*—that is, “a good old man,” namely a monk—from the land in which the martyr himself had suffered. While this *calogerus* was considering where he might honourably place the relics, the monks declared that he was given an answer in a dream: he should bring them to the church of Blessed Mammas, which was then being newly built at the expense of Isaac, emperor of Constantinople, and should not trouble himself to build another church.

The same monks also earnestly begged G., before our aforesaid cleric, to carry the relics to their new church. They said they were prepared to offer him a great exchange for them, promising money or some other more valuable thing, and even to hold G. himself as their perpetual lord if he gave them the relics.

Since, therefore, the oft-mentioned G. was always diligent and attentive both in investigating and obtaining the aforesaid relics and in advancing and honouring your Church, and since, after acquiring them, he left behind whatever honour and advantage he had at Constantinople—indeed, he held the custody of the *cantoria* in the church of the Forty Martyrs, one of the thirty greater provostships, and the custody of another provostship, one among the thirty which he held in that city—and, setting aside many other honours in order to render so great a service to your Church, he strove, abandoning everything else, joyfully to return to you carrying these splendid relics of your great patron, we have judged it appropriate warmly to commend to your fraternity this devout son and useful member of your Church, in consideration of his devotion and worth.

Love him henceforth more affectionately for so beneficial and memorable a service rendered to your Church through him, and take care so to reward his labour and diligence that, from devout, he may become still more devout, and that others, encouraged by his example, may more vigorously gird themselves to bear the burdens of service to your Church. For our part, bearing witness to the truth according to what we have seen and heard, we ask in the Lord that, receiving the aforesaid relics with reverence of honour and every devotion, you may wish to hold them especially dear among the other precious things esteemed by you; that you may render service pleasing to God and acceptable to the martyr himself; that you may also grant us, who have always been solicitous and intend to labour for the exaltation of your Church, a share in your prayers; and that you may inscribe our name in your calendar for remembrance.

XCII. To the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Locus Dei.—He confirms their privileges. (1205; Rome, at St Peter’s, 21 January.)

[LANGEBECK, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, VIII, 182.]

[Col. 0134D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of Locus Dei and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, etc.

Those who choose the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—may it never be—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Locus Dei, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, obtain by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have judged the following should be set down expressly by name:

The site itself on which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances. The church of Logum with all its appurtenances, which the same monastery possessed before it adopted the institutions of the Cistercian brethren. Donations made to you by Radulph, bishop of Ribe, founder of that place, and by his successors Stephen and Omer: namely, all that belonged to the bishopric of Ribe in possessions within the parishes of Loegum and Seem. Also the possessions which Omer, bishop of Ribe, granted to your monastery at Ginnegardth, with lands, woods, meadows, waters, mills, pastures, and their other liberties and immunities. Tithes from Logumherret. The grant made to you by the bishop of Ribe of whatever belonged to him in tithes within Gramherret and Ravenstorpherret; likewise the tithes of Buldorp assigned to you by Walpemar, bishop of Schleswig. [Col. 0135C] And three holdings of land at Harghby.

No one may presume to demand or extort from you tithes of the produce which you cultivate by your own hands and at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens, shrublands, fisheries, or the rearing of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the world, and retain them without any opposition.

Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving that place without permission of his abbot. No one may dare retain one who has departed without the safeguard of your community’s letters. If anyone should presume to retain him, you may pronounce regular sentence against such monks or lay brothers.

We strictly prohibit lands or any benefice granted to your church from being personally granted to anyone or otherwise alienated without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If donations or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we judge them invalid.

Furthermore, we prohibit any monk or lay brother bound by the profession of your house from standing surety for anyone or borrowing money from anyone, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, beyond the sum established by your chapter’s prudent decision, unless it is for the manifest benefit of your house. If anyone should presume to do so, the convent shall in no way be bound to answer for it.

Moreover, in your own cases, whether they contain a civil or criminal issue, you may use the testimony of your brethren, lest your right suffer loss in any matter through lack of witnesses. We further forbid by apostolic authority any bishop or any other person to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit your own property or possessions to secular judgment. Nor may anyone presume to enter your houses to confer orders, hear cases, or summon public assemblies, or impede the regular election of your abbot, or interfere in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, with instituting or removing the person who at the time holds office.

If the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when humbly and devoutly requested as is fitting, refuses to bless the abbot appointed in succession or to confer upon you the other things belonging to the episcopal office, that abbot, if he is a priest, may bless his own novices and exercise the other functions belonging to his office; and you may receive from another bishop all that your own bishop has wrongfully denied you.

We add that, when receiving professions made by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops must be content with the form and wording established from the origin of the Order: namely, that the abbots must profess subject to the preservation of their Order and may not be compelled to make any profession contrary to its statutes.

For consecrations of altars or churches, holy oil, or any ecclesiastical sacrament, no one may dare, under colour of custom or in any other way, to extort anything from you; rather, the diocesan bishop shall confer all these things upon you freely. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer, being in communion with and enjoying the favour of the Apostolic See, who, relying on our authority, shall grant you what is requested.

If the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighbouring [Col. 0136D] bishops, provided that no prejudice is thereby created in the future against your own bishops. And because you do not always have access to your own bishops, if any bishop in communion with the Roman See, as we have said, and fully known to you happens to pass through your district, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks.

Further, if bishops or other rectors of churches pronounce against your monastery, persons dwelling there, or even your hired labourers, a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict because you do not pay tithes; or on any ground arising from the things granted you by apostolic kindness; or pronounce the same sentence against your benefactors because they have, out of charity, rendered you benefits or services, or have helped you in labour on days when you work and others rest, we judge that sentence invalid as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall letters obtained while suppressing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges have force.

Moreover, when the land is under a general interdict, you may nevertheless celebrate divine offices in your monastery, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons. Desiring also to provide by paternal care for your future peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your sites or granges, to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare to commit violence.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority and fortify by the privilege of this present document all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact, wholly beneficial to the uses for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop in the aforesaid Church.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But may all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1205, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

[Col. 0138A] Subscribed by the pope with his bishops and cardinals.

XCIII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0137] See the note to Letter LXXXIV of this Appendix.] of St Vincent at Senlis and his brethren.—He confirms to them possession of the church of Alvers. (1205; Rome, at St Peter’s, 23 January.)

[From the archive of the monastery of St Vincent at Senlis, without number. BRÉQUIGNY, same place, p. 1129.]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant benevolent favour to the honourable prayers of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously concurring with your just requests, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the church of Alvers, with its appurtenances, liberties, [Col. 0138B] and immunities, as you justly and peaceably possess it, and fortify it with the protection of this present document. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

XCIV. To the archbishops, bishops, etc., to whom these letters shall come.—That they are to protect and defend the abbots and brethren of the Premonstratensian Order against wrongdoers and molesters. (1205; Rome, at St Peter’s, 24 January.)

[We publish this letter, or rather bull, from a copy, carefully transcribed from the archives of the Abbey of La Chapelle-aux-Planches and deposited in our Chartophylacium by Dom Brincourt. At the end of the copy he added this note: “The said bull, on parchment and in rather poor condition, is eight inches high and nine inches four lines wide, folded at the bottom by ten lines to receive a cord of red and yellow silk, after which is attached a lead seal fifteen lines in every direction, representing on one side the apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and bearing on the other the inscription: INNOCENTIUS PP. III.” — “I, the undersigned religious, Benedictine, archivist of the Abbey of Montier-Ramey, deputed to search for charters and monuments concerning public law and the history of the French monarchy, certify that the present copy, taken from the charter-chest of the Abbey of La Chapelle-aux-Planches and collated by me, conforms to its original. At the said chapel, 7 February 1789. Signed: Dom Brincourt.” We judged it proper to reproduce here this testimony of a most learned man, especially because this bull may perhaps seem not to follow the style of the other privileges of this kind granted by Innocent. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1130.]

[Col. 0138C] [Col. 0139A]

We have learned, not without grief of heart and great disturbance, that in many regions ecclesiastical censure has become so relaxed and the severity of canonical sentence so weakened that religious men—and especially those endowed with greater liberty through privileges of the Apostolic See—suffer injuries and robberies everywhere at the hands of wrongdoers, while scarcely anyone is found to come to their aid with suitable protection and to set himself up as a wall of defense for the fostering of the innocence of the poor.

In particular, beloved sons, the abbots and brethren of the Premonstratensian Order, complaining both of frequent injuries and of the daily failure of justice itself, have asked by apostolic letters that all of you be stirred up, so that you ought to rise for them in their tribulations against their wrongdoers with such prompt magnanimity that, through our protection, they may obtain relief from the straits and oppressions which they endure.

Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command and enjoin upon all of you that, after prior warning, those who have irreverently seized the possessions, goods, or houses of the aforesaid brethren or of their men, or who unjustly retain things left to the said brethren by the wills of the deceased; or who have presumed, contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See, to pronounce against the brethren themselves a sentence of excommunication or interdict; or to extort the tithes of their labor or sustenance despite the privileges of the Apostolic See—if they are laymen—be publicly subjected to a sentence of excommunication, with lighted candles. If, however, they are clerics, regular canons, or monks, suspend them, without appeal, from office and benefices. You are not to relax either sentence until they have made full satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren.

Both laymen and secular clerics who have been bound by the bond of anathema for the violent laying on of hands, when they come to the Apostolic See with letters from their diocesan bishop, shall deserve to be absolved from that bond by the same See. With regard to monks and regular canons, however, the following is to be observed: if brethren of the same cloister have laid violent hands upon one another, they shall obtain the benefit of absolution through their own abbot; but if a brother of one cloister has presumed to commit such violence against a brother of another cloister, they shall obtain the benefit of absolution through the abbots of the injured party and the aggressor.

This shall also apply if any of them committed, before receiving the religious habit, something for which they would by the act itself have incurred a sentence of excommunication, unless their offense was grave and enormous—for example, if it proceeded to mutilation of a limb or shedding of blood, or if violent hands were laid upon a bishop or abbot—since offenses such as these and similar ones cannot be passed over without scandal. But if they have laid hands upon secular clerics, let them be sent to the Apostolic See to be absolved, in order to avoid scandal.

Moreover, subject to a sentence of interdict the towns in which the goods of the aforesaid brethren or of their men are being violently detained, so long as they are detained there.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February [24 January], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

XCV. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0139D]

This was Hugh, who presided over the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon from 1174 until 1205, when he died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August]. See *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 580.

We judged it worthwhile to append here the French place-names listed in this bull, as they were attached by the learned Dom Grenier at the end of the copy which he deposited in our Chartophylacium; we have added some further identifications from the *Gallia Christiana Nova*.]

, and convent of Saint Vincent of Laon.—Confirmation of their possessions. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 26 January.)

[From the archives of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon, bundle “Bulls and Privileges,” 20, charter 8. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1131.]

[Col. 0140C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Laon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant the favor of its benevolence to the honorable requests of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with your just petitions in gracious assent, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the altar of Bavi [Note: [Col. 0139D] Bavi, a village on the Guise side, now unknown.], with its appurtenances; the altar and half of the estate of Marli [Note: [Col. 0139D]

Marli, a village on the same side, on the left bank of the Oise, in Thiérache.

Baldwin (of Retest or Retel), described in the records as “of pious memory,” obtained in 1146 from the bishop of Laon, Bartholomew, the altar of Marla together with the tithes of Montaigu, Loisy, and Berny. *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 578.]

, with its appurtenances; the church of Lescheriis [Note: [Col. 0140D]

Lescheriis (Leguielles), a village to the left of the road from Guise to Cateau-Cambrésis.

In 1132 Burchard of Guise, with his wife Adelaide, daughter of Baldwin of Suppeio, lord of the castle of Lescheriis, changed the collegiate church of that place into a cell dependent upon Saint Vincent. *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 578.]

; the village called Tile [Note: [Col. 0140D] Tiles, a village on the same side, now unknown.]; the ovens, half the mills, and the annual fair [Note: [Col. 0140D] In 1171 Walter, thirteenth abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon, established an eight-day fair at Lescheriis on the feast of Saint John the Baptist and made James of Guise, advocate of the place, a participant in its proceeds. *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol.
