IX, col. 579.] of Lescheriis; the altar and one measure (*modius*) of grain from the tithe of Yrun [Note: [Col. 0140D] Yrun (Yron), another village on a small stream crossing the road from Guise to Landrecies.]; the altar of Dulcelon [Note: [Col. 0141C] Dulcelon, unknown.]; the altar of Saint Germanus [Note: [Col. 0141C] Saint Germanus (Saint-Germain), a village above Guise, between the road to Bohain and the river Oise.], and one measure from the tithe, together with those parishioners who owe *tallia* and *furca* [a levy and labor-service] in the meadows to the lord of Lescheriis; at Fasti [Note: [Col. 0141C] Fasti (Fati), another village east of Guise, on the left bank of the Oise.], an annual rent of seventy solidi of good money; at Vileires [Note: [Col. 0141C] Vileires (Villiers-lès-Guise), another village on the right of the road to Landrecies.], the revenues of the village and, in the land-rent, five measures, and in the tithe two; the church of Saint John of Vendolium [Note: [Col. 0141C]

Vendolium (Vendeuil), a borough mentioned elsewhere.

In 1088 Ratbod, bishop of Noyon, granted the altar of Saint John the Baptist, situated before the castle of Vendeuil on the river Oise, so that brethren living for God under the rule of Saint Benedict might be established there. [Col. 0141D] *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 576.]

, and the entire tithe of that village, together with the parish church of Linifons [Note: [Col. 0141D] Linifons (Liffontaine).] and the Chapel of the Lepers; the tithe of Saint Nicholas of the Wood, subject to an established rent of three solidi [Note: [Col. 0141D] In 1163 Walter, thirteenth abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon, granted the mill of Montaigu in fief and acquired from the church of Saint Nicholas in the Wood the tithe of Vendeuil, subject to a certain rent. Ibid., col. 579 C.]; the chapel of Saint Peter; ten solidi of good money from the mills of Vendeuil; the cultivated and uncultivated land of Buschoitt; daily one pack-load of dead wood, with one servant, from the woods of the lord of Vendeuil; free right of cartage (*Wionagium*) throughout all his land; at Mayoc [Note: [Col. 0141D] Mayoc, another village between the river Oise and the road from La Fère to Ribemont.], two measures of grain from the tithe; the tithe of your cultivated fields and lands of Lambesch [Note: [Col. 0141D] Lambesch (Lambais), a farm to the left of the road from La Fère to Saint-Quentin.] and Cirisi [Note: [Col. 0141D] Cirisi (Cerisy), ibid., above Liffontaine.]; the village of Dormicurt [Note: [Col. 0141D]

Dormicurt (Dormicourt), a farm near Marle.

In 1147 Baldwin of Retest or Retel, eleventh abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon, obtained from a certain knight Bartholomew the freehold of the manor, subject to a land-rent of the ninth sheaf. *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 578.]

, with all its appurtenances; in that same village, the tithe which you hold from the church of Saint Peter under a rent of sixteen denarii; the estate of Orgival with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Julian of Nova Villa [Note: [Col. 0141D] Nova Villa, Neuville, near Chamouille.], two measures in the tithe of the estate of that same village, a mill, an old fishpond, a meadow situated beneath that fishpond, and a plantation above that same fishpond, together with the tithe of certain lands and vineyards; the tithe of certain cultivated lands of Simon at Camolia [Note: [Col. 0142C]

Camolia (Chamouille), a village of the Laon region mentioned in other notices.

In 1140 Count Walter gave a holding in the village of Camolia; and Walbert of Asci granted the vicariate, or viscounty, of the same place. *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 570.]

and at Vileirs [Note: [Col. 0142C] Vileirs (Villers), unknown.], before the Castle Tower, together with a share in the tithe of that village; half the capons which the same Simon received as rent at Ploiart and Arenci [Note: [Col. 0142C] Ployart and Arency, two villages not far from Chamouille.]; at Nova Villa, one field [Col. 0142A] which the same Simon gave as the endowment of the altar of that village; land which the same Simon bought at Cerni [Note: [Col. 0142C] Cerni (Cerny-en-Laonnois), in the same area.] from the heirs of Odo of Laon; daily one pack-load from the Wood of Bruni for the use-right (*usuagium*) of the monks of Nova Villa [Note: [Col. 0142C] We read that the cell of Nova Villa, toward the Aisne, was founded by Helluin of Tyre in the time of William I, twelfth abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon, who died on the day before the Kalends of October [30 September] 1156. (ibid., B.)]; all the land which Clarembald of Oilli possessed at Dormicurt, granted to you in perpetuity subject to a land-rent of the tenth sheaf; the churches of Firmitas with their appurtenances; one thirteenth of all the goods of that castle; six measures of grain from the mills of that castle; one measure of grain, two measures of *vinaticum* [wine-rent], and ten capons from the revenues of Gobert the younger of Firmitas [Note: [Col. 0142D] Firmitas (La Ferté-sur-Péron), a village on the left bank of the Péron.], from the parishioners of the estate of Ferrières, together with the small tithe and the share of the greater tithe which falls to you; at Moncels [Note: [Col. 0142D] Moncels (Monceaux-le-Neuf), near the source of this river.], three [Col. 0142B] measures of grain for the mills, rent, land-rent, and wood which you and the lord of the village hold in common in that village; a rent of five solidi at Montiniacum [Note: [Col. 0142D] At Montiniacum (Montigny-sur-Crécy), mentioned elsewhere.]; seven measures of grain for your land, which the heir of the late knight Arnulf holds at Chevesne; one measure of grain at Moncels on the Serre [Note: [Col. 0142D] Moncels on the Serre (Monceaux-les-Loups), on this side of the river Serre, toward La Fère.]; the freehold of Saint Quentin [Note: [Col. 0142D] The freehold of Saint Quentin (Anguillecourt-Saint-Quentin), a village to the right of the road from La Fère to Ribemont.], subject to a rent of thirty solidi; at Meschuman [Note: [Col. 0142D] Mechumam (Méchame), a farm above Anguillecourt.], the land of John Picta, which you hold from the monastery of Humolarium under a rent of four solidi, and the land called the Valley of Saint Mary, which you hold at the sixth sheaf; in the court of Mechuma, the viscounty with all its appurtenances; the mayoralty of Acheri [Note: [Col. 0142D] Achery, a village on the river Oise between La Fère and Vendeuil.]; one measure [Col. 0142C] of grain in the same village; at Tumbella [Note: [Col. 0142D] At Tumbella (La Tombelle), a hamlet on this side of Marle.], one measure of grain and one of oats; at Hortincort [Note: [Col. 0142D] Hortincort, unknown; but the place must lie above Marle.], a sluice, to be maintained at your discretion, as it extends in a straight line from your mill to the mill; the mayoralty of Villaris Siccus [Note: [Col. 0143B]

Villaris Siccus (Villers-le-Sec), unknown.

Compare above the note to letter 2 of this appendix [Col. 0143C]. Add, if you wish, what is read in the authors of the *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 576: “At about the same time (about 1097), Anselm of Ribemont, setting out on the holy expedition, came to the monastery of Saint Vincent, repenting of the wrongs he had done to the monks, and in chapter, with his shoulders bare, caused himself to be scourged as a penance. The knight Nethelin joined himself to Anselm, and granted the estate of Simon of Villers-le-Sec, not far from Ribemont, while Helinand, bishop of Langres, near death, confirmed it.”]

, with two measures of grain, half a stone house, half the smoke-right, and its other appurtenances; the mayoralty of Hatencort [Note: [Col. 0143C] Hatencort (Attencourt), a farm between Pierrepont and Marle.]; the mayoralty of Curbis [Note: [Col. 0143C] Curbis (Courbes), a village on the right bank of the Oise, toward La Fère.], with all its appurtenances; the church of Altimons [Note: [Col. 0143C]

Altimons, an unknown village.

In 1095 Rainald, archbishop of Reims, granted the church of Saint Gobert at Altimons in the district of Riche, after expelling, with the consent of Count Hugh I, the clerics who had neglected the care of the place. [Col. 0143D] This gift was later confirmed by Manasses, archbishop of Reims, and by the counts of Riche: Hugh III in 1200, John in 1249, and Galcher in 1262.]

, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Thomas [Note: [Col. 0143D]

Saint Thomas (Saint-Thomas), another village between Corbény and Laon.

In 1081 Adalbero, eighth abbot of Saint Vincent, received from Helinand, bishop of Laon, the place called Saint Thomas, below old Laon, to convert it into a cell. *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. IX, col. 576.]

, with its appurtenances; the vineyard of Colomam; the freehold of Buci [Note: [Col. 0143D] The freehold of Bucy (Bucy-lès-Pierrepont), a village beyond this borough.] and of Riu [Note: [Col. 0143D] Riu, near Bucy, a place unknown on the new map of France.], called the holding of Guy the castellan; eighteen measures of grain by the measure of Marle, which the church of Thenolium [Note: [Col. 0143D]

In 1164 and subsequent years Walter, thirteenth abbot of Saint Vincent of Laon, granted certain properties under rent to the canons of Thenolium. Ibid., col. 579 C.

[Col. 0144B] In 1174 Hugh, fourteenth abbot, showed sincere affection for the canons of Thenolium, more than once granting estates to their monastery under an annual rent. [Col. 0144C]]

owes you annually; the altar of Chivi [Note: [Col. 0144C] Chivi, a village beyond Cerny-en-Laonnois.], with its appurtenances; the altars of Morenis [Note: [Col. 0144C] Morenis (Mauregus), a village between Corbény and Laon.], Cortesis [Note: [Col. 0144C] Cortesis (Courtisis), another near Mauregus.], Fussenis [Note: [Col. 0144C] Fussenis (Fussigny), on the same side.] and Cocci [Note: [Col. 0144C] Cocci (Coussy-les-Aippes), above.], with their appurtenances; the oven of Camolia; two parts of the greater and lesser tithe of Cuverni [Note: [Col. 0144C] Cuverni, an unknown village.]; a third part of both the greater and lesser tithe of Bievre [Note: [Col. 0144C] Bievre, a village above Bruyères.]; the altar of Besni [Note: [Col. 0144C] Besni, an unknown village.], with its appurtenances; and twelve denarii which the canons of Laon owe you annually in recognition of an ancient custom and as compensation for the cemetery.

As you justly and peacefully possess all these things, we confirm them to you and, through you, to your monastery by apostolic authority, and strengthen them by the protection of this present writing. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February [26 January], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

XCVI. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0144C] See the note to letter LXXXIV of this appendix.] and convent of Saint Vincent of Senlis.—By apostolic authority he confirms the agreement made between them and the chapters of Saint Rieul and Saint Frambourg concerning certain revenues, by Peter, former bishop of Arras, and his fellow judges. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 1 February.)

[From the archives of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Senlis, without number. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1134.]

[Col. 0144B]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant the favor of its benevolence to the honorable requests of petitioners. From your account, indeed, we have learned that, whereas the beloved sons, the canons of Blessed Mary of Senlis, in whose church you have from ancient times a specified prebend and receive the annual proceeds of vacant prebends [Note: [Col. 0144C] The church of Saint Vincent of Senlis possesses four prebends, confirmed to it in 1119 by Pope Callixtus II: namely, in the churches of Blessed Mary of Senlis, Saint Rieul, Saint Frambourg, and Saint Evremond of Creil. Clarembald, bishop of Senlis, granted them also the anniversaries, or annual proceeds, of prebends in the churches of Blessed Mary and Saint Rieul [Col. 0144D], as did the canons of Saint Frambourg in their own church. Although these arrangements were confirmed by Louis VI in 1129, they have long since disappeared. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1494; and among the instruments, cols. 210 and 428, charters XIV and LXIII.], were improperly troubling you concerning certain proceeds of your prebend and annual revenues; and whereas the beloved sons William, formerly cantor of Saint Mary and treasurer of Saint Frambourg [Note: [Col. 0144D] William I of Chartres, who in 1197 and 1202 was cantor of Blessed Mary and at the same time treasurer of Saint Frambourg, was in that latter year, 1202, together with Fulk, dean of Orléans, deputed by Philip Augustus to Pope Innocent III concerning Philip’s marriage to Ingeborg. The authors of the *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. X, col. 1479, report this, and immediately add: “William, having become bishop of Noyon, is commemorated in the necrology of Saint Frambourg on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March [19 February].” Yet these most learned authors are inconsistent with themselves, for in their list of bishops of Noyon, ibid., vol. IX, cols. 1005 ff., they assign no place whatever to this William.], and Ivo, dean of Saint Rieul [Note: [Col. 0145D]

“VII. Ivo I, dean, formerly precentor of Saint Rieul, in 1195 and 1197. The necrology of Saint Frambourg makes pious mention of Ivo the first or second: On the Ides of March [15 March], Queen Elizabeth died, who gave us a very honorable chest, one pallium, and renewed for this church the praiseworthy custom of rendering pallia at each birth of queens; for this benefit there are customarily distributed solidi . . . . . . . which Ivo, dean of Saint Rieul, gave.

“VIII. Stephen II is found as dean in 1201, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August [23 July]; perhaps the obituary of Saint Frambourg refers to him as follows: On the sixth day before the Kalends of September [27 August], Stephen, dean of Blessed Rieul and our canon, died.

“IX. Ivo II. Upon his death, in May 1219, Bishop Garin conferred upon William, nephew of Lord Bartholomew of Roga, half the prebend which Ivo had held in the church of Blessed Mary.” [Col. 0146D]

Thus far the authors of the *Gallia Christiana Nova*, ibid., col. 1466. Whether this letter of Innocent concerns Ivo I or Ivo II is difficult to determine.]

, were improperly troubling you concerning the annual proceeds of the prebends belonging to the cantorship of Blessed Mary, the treasurership of Saint Frambourg, and the deanery of Saint Rieul: at length our venerable brother, the bishop of Senlis [Note: [Col. 0146D] See the note to letter CXLV of Book V.], and the beloved sons Hermerus [Note: [Col. 0146D] See above, the note to letter LXXXIV of this appendix.], dean of Saint Frambourg; John Poeta and Reiner, formerly subcantor of Saint Mary; Bartholomew, cantor of Saint Frambourg; and William Rot., arbitrators; and Peter of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0146D] See the note to letter XXV of Book III.], bishop of Arras, together with his fellow judges delegated by the Apostolic See, settled the aforesaid controversies by amicable agreement, as is contained in the authentic documents of the judges and adversaries.

We therefore, yielding to your petitions, confirm by apostolic authority that agreement, as it was prudently made without impropriety, freely accepted by both sides, and hitherto peacefully observed, and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of February [1 February], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

XCVII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0146D] See the note to letter LXXXIV of this appendix.], prior, and cantor of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris.—That they may restrain those molesting the monastery of Saint-Denis. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 10 February.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Denis and communicated to us by Dom Poirier. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0145C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot, prior, and cantor of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Beloved sons, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0146D] See the note to letter XXV of Book III.] and convent of Blessed Denis have shown us by their complaint that P. of Pauceio and W. Cordelin, knights, Morant of Carlou, and certain others of the dioceses of Paris, Chartres, and Orléans do not cease to inflict serious injuries upon them concerning tithes, men, and other property.

Wherefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, after summoning the parties and hearing the allegations on both sides, you shall decide, without appeal, what is canonical; and shall cause what you decide to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. If witnesses who are named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them by like censure, without appeal, to bear testimony to the truth, waiting for no letters from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and justice. And if all of you cannot be present for carrying this out, let two of you nevertheless carry it out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of February [10 February], in the seventh year of our pontificate.

XCVIII. Papal commission against Conrad IV, bishop of Regensburg, concerning the harassment of a feudal house. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 March.)

[RIED, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisponensis*, p. 286, from the original.]

[Col. 0146B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Emmeram, the dean, and the scholasticus of the old chapel of Regensburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As the beloved son W., archdeacon of the church of Regensburg, has shown us by his representation, the beloved son … bishop-elect of Regensburg unjustly burdens and harasses him in many ways concerning a certain house which he is said to hold from the church of Regensburg as a benefice. Wherefore, by apostolic writings we command your discretion that, after prior warning, you compel the said bishop-elect by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to desist from this improper oppression of him. And if all of you cannot be present for carrying this out, let two of you nevertheless carry it out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Nones of March [3 March], in the eighth year of our pontificate.

Lead seal: INNOCENT PP. III.

XCIX. To William, archbishop of Reims.—A privilege granted to the monastery of Saint-Remi for revoking alienations. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 21 March.)

[VARIN, *Archives administratives de Reims*, Paris, 1839, quarto, vol. II, p. 457.—Cartulary of Saint-Remi, fol. 5, no. XXII.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, archbishop of Reims, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is incumbent upon a pastor’s care to provide for his right in such a way that it is not unjustly withheld from him by others, lest he be negligent where he ought to be diligent, since diligence brings increase and negligence brings loss. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, by the authority of this present document we grant that you may canonically restore to your authority and possession—despite any contradiction or appeal whatsoever—the altars, tithes, revenues, jurisdictions, and other things which your predecessor N. of good memory withdrew from your lordship and power by unlawfully granting them in perpetuity to churches and monasteries and to certain persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our grant or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March], in the eighth year of our pontificate.

C. To the prior of Grandmont.—That he may absolve brethren who incurred a sentence of excommunication before assuming the religious habit. [Note: [Col. 0147D] Concerning this letter, hitherto unpublished, see below what Dom Arbellot, canon of Limoges, who most kindly communicated both letters to us, noted on letter 170 addressed to the prior of Grandmont on 1 May 1212. EDITORS OF THE FATHERS.] (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 26 March.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the prior of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant the favor of its benevolence to the honorable requests of petitioners. Your behalf has humbly requested of us that we should deem fit to grant you authority to absolve your brethren who confess that, before assuming the habit of religion in your house, they committed something for which they incurred a sentence of excommunication by the act itself; and likewise those who may hereafter happen to assume the religious habit in that house under a similar circumstance, lest, if they were perhaps sent to the Apostolic See to obtain the benefit of absolution, an occasion for wandering abroad should be afforded to them.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, granting gracious assent to your just petitions, we permit you by the authority of this present document to absolve those of your brethren who are shown to have been bound in this manner by the bonds of excommunication for the violent laying on of hands, unless their offense is grave and enormous—for example, if it proceeded to mutilation of a limb or shedding of blood, or if violent hands were laid upon a bishop or abbot—since offenses of this sort and similar offenses cannot be passed over without scandal.

Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our grant or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April [26 March], in the eighth year of our pontificate.

CI. To the procurators and brethren of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre.—Concerning canons who withhold obedience. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 16 June.)

[Eugène de ROZIÈRE, *Cartulaire de l’église du Saint-Sépulcre de Jérusalem*, published from Vatican manuscripts. Paris, Imprimerie nationale, 1849, quarto, p. 272.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all procurators of the houses and priories of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and their brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Beloved sons, the prior and chapter of the Lord’s Sepulchre have shown us by their complaint that, denying them the due obedience and reverence, you show yourselves rebellious toward them and their messengers in many respects. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command and strictly enjoin upon all of you that henceforth you render due obedience and reverence to the said prior and chapter. Otherwise, we shall hold valid any sentence which they may reasonably judge should be pronounced against you on this account, and, with God as author, we shall cause it to be inviolably observed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June], in the eighth year of our pontificate.

CII. To the clergy of Saint Mary of Marseille.—He safeguards a certain chapel for them. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 11 July.)

[*Antiquity of the Church of Marseille*, Marseille, 1747, quarto, II, 29.]

[Col. 0148C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clerics of the chapel of Saint Mary of Marseille: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant our consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effective completion the wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with your petitions in gracious assent, by the authority of this present document we strictly prohibit anyone from rashly presuming to sell or alienate any of the property of your chapel, which the beloved son Hugh Ferus, citizen of Marseille, is said to have built at his own expense [Col. 0148D] and endowed with extensive property.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our prohibition or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of July [11 July], in the eighth year of our pontificate.

CIII. To Henry, bishop-elect of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0149D] See the note to letter VIII of Book VIII.].—He confirms for him the right of patronage in the cell of Vilmari. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 8 October.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from another copy inserted in an ancient cartulary of the greater chapter of Strasbourg, and communicated to us by the late Dom Abbot Grandidier. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0149A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, bishop-elect of Strasbourg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant the favor of its benevolence to the honorable requests of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, concurring with your just petitions in gracious assent, we confirm to you and, through you, to the church of Strasbourg, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the right of patronage [Col. 0149B] in the cell of Vilmari [Note: [Col. 0149D] See letter L of this appendix.], with its appurtenances, granted to the church of Strasbourg by Count Bertold [Note: [Col. 0150D] This grant was made in 1200 by Henry, count of Neuburg.] and his son, as that church justly and peacefully possesses it. Let no person whatsoever, etc., etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October], in the eighth year of our pontificate.

CIV. To the brethren of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem.—He confirms their possessions in Bohemia and Moravia. (1205. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 5 November.)

[BOCZEK, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, Olomouc, 1836, quarto, vol. II, p. 35, from the original in the archives of the Hospitallers at Prague.]

[Col. 0149C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, . . . prior and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem established in Bohemia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When that which is just and honorable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the diligence of our office, to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclined by your just prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the safeguard of this present writing, your persons and the possessions which have been bestowed upon you in Bohemia and Moravia by pious liberality, or which, God favoring, you may hereafter be able to acquire by lawful means. [Col. 0149D] Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our protection or rashly contravene it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Nones of November, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

CV. To Bonaccursius, provost, and the brethren of St. Genesius in the diocese of Lucca.—He confirms their privileges. (A.D. 1205, Rome, at St. Peter’s, December 5.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, ed. MANSI, III, 426.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0150A] sons BONACCURSIUS, provost of St. Genesius, and his brethren, both present and future, to be canonically appointed, forever.

A petition arising from pious desire ought to be fulfilled with effective support, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may assuredly gain strength. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, since, inspired by divine grace, you have resolved to conform your manner of life and to serve almighty God under the discipline of canonical life and collectively according to the institution of the holy Fathers, we rejoice over your vows with paternal affection. Accordingly, following the enactments of our predecessors of happy memory, Alexander II, Paschal, Eugenius, Anastasius, Alexander, Lucius, Clement, and Celestine, Roman [Col. 0150B] pontiffs, we establish by the authority of this privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed, and receive your church under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves; decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may, with the Lord’s aid, acquire hereafter through grants of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which that *plebs* [parish community] is situated, with all its appurtenances; a fourth part [Col. 0150C] of the tithes of your entire *plebs*; and everything which John, bishop and canon of blessed memory, granted to your church; the house and the lepers’ establishment, with the church of St. Lazarus near the same *plebs*, with its appurtenances; likewise all that has been lawfully given to you by the Lombards of St. Miniato and confirmed by charters; and one third of the alms offered for the dead buried anywhere within the bounds of the *plebs*, as was granted to you and confirmed in writing by our predecessor Paschal of good memory. Also, in the borough, the church of St. Giles with its appurtenances; the churches of St. Christopher, St. Justus, and St. Angel above the borough, with all their appurtenances. In the same borough, moreover, the church of St. Peter; and, in the castle of San Miniato, the church of St. Mary with its appurtenances, [Col. 0150D] in which two churches the divine offices are always to be celebrated by those appointed there through our provision; and whatever right you possess in that same church of St. Mary through the church of St. Christina; likewise the church of St. Bartholomew with its appurtenances, the church of St. Blaise, the church of St. Stephen, the church of St. Lawrence of Nocida, the church of St. Peter above the Fountain, the church of St. Andrew near Castel Ciculo, the church of St. Michael within the walls, the churches of St. James and St. Lucy, the church of St. Donatus of Faugnagna, the church of St. Martin of Castilione, the church of St. Hippolytus of Marzana, the church of St. Mary of Calenzano, the church of St. Quintin, the church [Col. 0151A] of Colle, the church of Capriano, the church of Canneto, the church of St. Mary of Montarso, the church of Monterotondo, the church of Planatole, the church of Brusciano, the church of St. Stephen of Turre, the church of St. Peter of Marcignana, the church of St. Donatus of Insula, the church of St. Angel of Rophia, the church of St. Philip of Pinu, and the church of St. Prosper of Montalprandi, with all their appurtenances; and [the right concerning] anyone who may hereafter happen to build within the territory of a single *plebs*. Also whatever right you possess in the court of San Miniato, of Empoli, of Monterappoli, and in the court of Marrignana.

Furthermore, following the example of Pope Celestine, our predecessor, we add and decree that no one whatsoever may withdraw the aforesaid churches from their customary obedience [Col. 0151B] and due subjection to your church. Nor may anyone ever, by any rashness, build anew a church, oratory, or hospice in your parish without the permission and consent of the bishop of Lucca, and of you and your successors; nor subject one already built to anyone’s authority without the consent of that bishop and of yourselves, without prejudice to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs.

We direct that chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of clerics to be advanced to sacred orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments be supplied to you by the diocesan bishop without an exaction of an oath or any improper practice. Moreover, we grant that the burial place of that establishment shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken nevertheless being preserved. We also decree that, if any of your parishioners chooses and receives burial at another church, the canonical portion due to mother churches from a testament shall be reserved to you. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. By apostolic authority we also decree that no pastor may presume to appoint anyone in your churches without your knowledge and consent; rather, their appointment, according to [Col. 0151D] canonical decrees, as it has hitherto been known to remain, shall always remain in your power. Moreover, we grant to you and your successors, son provost, free authority to correct your subjects, as your predecessors have been accustomed to possess. We likewise confirm to you the rights and ancient reasonable customs of your church hitherto observed, as you now possess them justly and canonically.

Furthermore, we prohibit your bishop from presuming to pronounce a sentence of interdict against you or your churches without just and manifest cause. We confirm by apostolic authority the agreement which Lanfranc, bishop of Fiesole of good memory, is known to have made concerning the church of St. Christopher, by command of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, between B., your predecessor, and Master Guido appointed by the abbot of St. Peter in Ciel d’Oro; it was reasonably made, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and is contained in an authentic document. [Col. 0152A] We further prohibit any layman from daring to assign any church of your *plebatus* [parochial district] to any priest, or even to install him in office; nor may any priest receive or in any manner retain a church from a lay hand. We confirm by apostolic authority the judgment of settlement which Pope Paschal of blessed memory issued concerning the dispute between Anselm, abbot of Ficeclo of good memory, and Guido, your predecessor, son provost, over the church of Grimagneto and certain other [Col. 0152B] churches, as it has hitherto been observed and is contained in an authentic document.

On the death of you, provost of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any craft of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the larger part of the sounder counsel, in the fear of God, shall judge ought to be elected. The person elected shall be presented to the bishop of Lucca and shall promise him obedience, as his predecessors have been accustomed to do; the patrons of the place retaining only the patronage of lawful defense.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0152C] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall hereafter knowingly presume rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his authority and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of the Lord and God, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0152D] Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, on the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1205 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CV bis. To the abbot of Monte Cassino.—He grants that the abbot may, without the obstacle of an appeal, revoke alienations made by his predecessor. (A.D. 1205, Rome, at St. Peter’s, December 9.)

[D. TOSTI, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, vol. II, p. 284. Original, diplomatic chest 5, no. 78.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0153A] son R., cardinal priest of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more directly and without any intermediary the monastery of Monte Cassino belongs to the Roman Church, the more diligently do we wish to safeguard it against injuries. Since, therefore, certain of your predecessors are said wrongly to have alienated certain possessions and other goods of the monastery of Monte Cassino and disposed of them to the grave prejudice of that monastery, by the authority of these presents we grant you that you may lawfully revoke, notwithstanding any appeal, those alienations which you know to have been undertaken to the loss of your monastery. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly contravene it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

CVI. To the bishop of Olomouc.—He confirms letters in which Přemysl, king of the Bohemians, enlarged the liberties and immunities of the church of Olomouc and assigned revenues to its provostship. (A.D. 1206, Rome, at St. Peter’s, January 8.)

[BOCZEK, *Diplomatic and Epistolary Codex of Moravia*, Olomouc, 1836, quarto, vol. II, p. 41; from a mutilated original in the archive of the chapter of Olomouc; copy in paper codex I, fol. 154.]

[Col. 0153C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother . . . bishop, and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Olomouc, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily give consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effectual fulfillment the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ and beloved sons in the Lord, granting favorable consent to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the safeguard of this present writing, to you and through you to your church, the liberties and immunities granted by our dearest son in Christ, P., illustrious king of the Bohemians, to your church and its people; and also the royal chancery and other revenues assigned by him to the provostship of the Church of Olomouc, as you possess them justly and peaceably and as they are more fully contained in the privilege of the same king. For greater clarity, moreover, we have thought fit to insert that privilege itself word for word into this page of ours.

“C. + In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Přemysl, by the grace of God third king of the Bohemians, [address this] to the venerable Robert, bishop of Olomouc, and his successors, and to the Church of Olomouc forever.

“Since it redounds to the glory of royal dignity whenever it honors and exalts holy Church, it has pleased our serenity to provide for its need, so that it may experience the benefits of our kindness and that the rewards of divine favor [Col. 0154A] may thereby come to us. Let both the present age and future posterity know, therefore, that, renewing the ancient privileges of the Church of Olomouc, we decree that all its possessions, whether already held or to be held, whether in Bohemia or Moravia, shall be free from every kind of tribute, toll, levy, and every other exaction. We add that no one may dare to molest the people of the bishopric and church for the building or rebuilding of castles, or for any expedition that may arise, as is contained in the ancient privileges. The right paid for a head or for a thief, or to the prince for *Swod*, or to his beneficed men, we have granted to our venerable father Bishop Robert and his successors and church, to be held in perpetuity. [Col. 0154B] We decree this concerning a thief: if he is caught in wrongdoing while residing on the church’s estates, whether he is seized and convicted before a court, his goods shall remain as a thief’s goods (thus in the text), while he himself shall be punished as the prince sees fit. But if men of the bishopric and church are found guilty of anything before a court, no profit from this shall accrue to us, our judges, courtiers, or beneficed men; rather, satisfaction for the offense shall remain with the bishop and his successors, except insofar as the offender is bound to make satisfaction to his adversary. To state all else briefly: we remit to them every right that pertains to the uses of princes, so that they may enjoy full and perfect liberty, and no one may dare to impose new conditions upon them or alter their rights.

“We release from every claim of ourselves and our successors the village of Kroměříž, with its market and all its rights. Because the envy of preceding princes acknowledged it as, as it were, pledged to the bishop of Olomouc, John, bishop of happy memory, bought it for three hundred marks from our reverend father Robert, who is now the tenth [bishop] from Otto the Black, prince of Moravia. We decree that the bishop of Olomouc and his successors shall have full power to dispose of it as they will, every impediment being removed. Since a custom wholly contrary to divine right had taken root, whereby, upon a bishop’s death, his goods were claimed for the uses of princes, it seemed good to our piety to abolish this abuse, [Col. 0154D] decreeing that the final fate of a deceased bishop must not result in loss to the church, since its patrons, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and the blessed martyr Wenceslas, live eternally with God. Therefore, upon a bishop’s death, all goods of the bishopric and church shall be reserved intact for his successor under the hand of the dean and provost of that church; and no one may dare to occupy, diminish, or claim them for the uses of princes.

“It also happened that from ancient times that church lacked a provost; therefore our father Robert considered it good to appoint in it a provost who would duly provide for the brethren of that church and meet their needs. But since it is fitting that the royal hand rain benefits everywhere, we have bestowed upon that provostship our chancery, together with the village called Vherchi, to which belongs [Col. 0155A] the tenth penny along with the tithe from our ploughlands and from all things pertaining to our benefit, forbidding anyone to dare to alter these things. We also freely and absolutely grant to the canons of that church, according to canonical law, liberty in the election of bishops—a liberty which certain princes were accustomed to hinder—and forbid its impairment hereafter.

“To ensure that all these things remain ratified and unshaken, we have caused this charter of our serenity to be strengthened by our seal and publicly excommunicated by our venerable father Robert on Easter Day. But if anyone acts against this our constitution, let him be heavily punished by the loss of his goods and, at the final judgment, find God with His saints opposed to him. [Col. 0155B] Witnesses of this matter are: Walter, dean of Olomouc and archdeacon of Znojmo; Radoslav, archdeacon of Olomouc; Bosko, archdeacon of Přerov; Esau, archdeacon of Břeclav; Hermann, abbot of Hradisko; Arnust, chamberlain; Willalmus Ussich; Zlauko; Boguslav Odoleni; Boguta and his brother Henry, judge of Olomouc; Medlo, castellan of Olomouc; Sudomirus; Petrus Ross; Predbor Hebky; Sdisslaus Grutowich; Sadiwoy; Donatus; Salizlaus with his son Slawata; John with his brother Preren; Odolen; Rohhche; Radoslaus; Hibirlaw; Swarovich with his brother Sdizlaus; Semizlaus with his sons; Kohhonus; Budisslaus; Pomnen Jarognewich; Bludo; [Col. 0155C] Doben with his brother Nedamirus; Jacob; Lutek; Zbrazlaw; Weliz; Velen; Buz; Bicen; Rathmir; Predbor; Cenakowich; Voysslaw; Sezenca; Luder; Neplah; Skyrben; Sudek; Sobehyrd of Clobuch; Voyteh with his brother Doncamirus; Smil with his brother Andrew; Gron; Ondreick; Boruth son of Wok; Rebor son of Bun; Stanimir son of Wlassin; canons of Olomouc: Wratek, Vlessin, Shignew, Andrew, Chuzeray, Boguslaus, Peter, James Ziffridus, Stephen.

“These things were enacted at Olomouc, in the year 1207 from the Incarnation of the Lord; given through the hand of Rappoto, notary.”

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly contravene it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, [Col. 0155D] let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

CVII. To the brethren of St. John of Jerusalem.—He confirms the immunities granted them by Wladislaus, margrave in Moravia, together with possessions at Kaunice and a chapel at Hrusowan. (A.D. 1206, Rome, at St. Peter’s, April 24.)

[BOCZEK, *Diplomatic Codex of Moravia*, Olomouc, 1836, quarto, vol. II, p. 36; from a bundle of copies of charters in the archive of the Hospitallers at Prague.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0156A] sons, the brethren of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily give consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effectual fulfillment the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favorable consent to your just and devout petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the safeguard of this present writing, the liberties and immunities granted in his land by our dearest son in Christ, Wladislaus, illustrious margrave of Moravia, to your hospital and its people, as they are more fully contained in the privilege of the same margrave; and also your new possessions bestowed upon you by Count Adalbert at Kaunice, together with the chapel at Hrusowan. [Col. 0156B]

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly contravene it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

CVIII. To Hermann, abbot, and the brethren of the church of Blessed Mary at Sayn, of the Premonstratensian order.—He confirms their privileges. (A.D. 1206, Lateran, May 4.)

[HONTHEIM, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, I, 644.]

[Col. 0156C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HERMANN, abbot, and the brethren of the church of Blessed Mary at Sayn, both present and future.

Those who have professed the regular life and chosen the religious life ought fittingly to receive apostolic protection, lest the attack of any rashness either draw them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religious observance.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of St. Mary at Sayn, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree [Col. 0156D] that the canonical order known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may, with the Lord’s aid, acquire hereafter through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the chapel in the castle [Col. 0157A] of Sayn, with certain vineyards in the valley, and tithes at Mettrich and Mensfelden, with all their other appurtenances; and the tithes of newly cleared land at Grisnake and Strumberg, which Henry and Everhard, counts of Sayn of good memory, with the consent of the diocesan bishop, bestowed upon your church out of pious regard; the wood called Burgholtz and the allod at Witersberg; the allod at Engershe; the allod at Heimbach; the allod in the parish of Vallendar; the allod at Thuere; the allod at Ormuntke; and the allod at Hemmingishoven.

Certainly, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics and laypersons, free and released from secular life, and retain them without any contradiction. [Col. 0157B] Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your church, from leaving that place without his abbot’s leave; and no one may dare to retain a person who leaves without the security of your joint letters. If anyone should nevertheless presume to retain him, you may pronounce the regular sentence against those brethren or converts. We strictly forbid anyone personally to give away or otherwise alienate lands or any benefice bestowed on your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or its greater or sounder part. If any gifts [Col. 0157C] or alienations are made otherwise than stated, we decree them void.

We further prohibit any bishop or other person from being permitted to demand or receive from you more for your tithes than their predecessors had required up to this time. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the most holy Roman See, and is willing to provide these things to you without any improper practice. Otherwise, you may apply to whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, who enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and who, relying on our authority, may furnish you with what is requested. If the diocesan see should happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without opposition receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighboring bishops; provided, however, that no prejudice shall thereby be created in the future against your own bishops. We also prohibit anyone within the bounds of your parish from daring to build a chapel or oratory anew without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, without prejudice to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We wholly forbid new and undue exactions to be made by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or any [Col. 0158A] other ecclesiastical or secular persons.

We decree likewise that the burial place of that establishment shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken nevertheless being preserved. Moreover, by our authority you have free power to redeem tithes and possessions belonging by right to your churches that are held by laymen, to lawfully free them from their hands, and restore them to the churches to which they belong. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall [Col. 0158B] commit the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any craft of fraud or force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the larger or sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, judge ought to be elected. Seeking by paternal concern to provide hereafter for your peace and tranquility, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your establishments or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, rashly seizing or killing a person, shedding blood, or exercising violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, all liberties and immunities granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, and other faithful persons. [Col. 0158C]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, to benefit in every way those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0158D] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall hereafter knowingly presume rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his authority and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0159A] I, Cuith., cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Goffred., cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedes. I, Cericius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Benedict, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Leo, cardinal priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Roger, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Rufina. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Sabina. [Col. 0159B] I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum. I, Guido, bishop of Palestrina. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Guala, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Pelagius, cardinal deacon of St. Lucy at the Septa Solis.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary [Col. 0159C] in Cosmedin, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1206 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CIX. To the archbishop and chapter of Narbonne. On the consecration of Fulk, bishop of Toulouse. (A.D. 1206, Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 11.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, ed. LUCA, III, 21.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop and his beloved sons the chapter of Narbonne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it is established that the Church of Toulouse belongs by metropolitan right to the jurisdiction [Col. 0159D] of the Church of Narbonne, although our beloved sons the abbot of Cîteaux, Master Peter of Castelnau, and Brother Ralph, legates of the Apostolic See, admitted the canonically made election of the bishop of Toulouse and had him consecrated by our venerable brother the archbishop of Arles, we nevertheless do not at all wish this to create in the future prejudice to the Church of Narbonne. The Church of Toulouse must render to the Church of Narbonne, as to its metropolitan, the honor due and its customary reverence. Therefore, desiring in this matter to safeguard hereafter the rights of your church, [Col. 0160A] we have thought fit to grant you these present letters as an aid for your protection.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

CX. He confirms the liberties and immunities of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, and grants the right of electing its abbot solely to the brethren of that monastery, or at least to their sounder part. (A.D. 1206, May 27.)

[GUÉRARD, *Cartulary of the Abbey of Saint-Pierre of Chartres*, Paris, 1840, quarto, vol. II, p. 672.]

CXI. He grants the abbot and monks of St. Peter at Chartres permission to recall into their right whatever is found to have been unlawfully alienated from their lordship. (A.D. 1206, May 27.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0160B]

CXII. To the archpriest and Guido of Bagnolo, canon of Bologna.—He entrusts to them the examination of the petition of the abbot of Nonantola that the pope send a foundation stone for the construction of an oratory. (A.D. 1206, Ferentino, July 16.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of Nonantola*, II, 339. Autograph in the archive of Nonantola.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the archpriest and GUIDO OF BAGNOLO, [Note: [Col. 0159D] It is not improbable that this canon Guido of Bagnolo was from Reggio and one of the ancestors of that Guido of Bagnolo, Petrarch’s friend, who is discussed in *Italian Literature* (vol. V, p. 214).] canon of Bologna, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved son, the abbot of Nonantola, humbly [Col. 0160C] petitioned us that, in a certain place known to belong in full right to his monastery, we might deem it worthy to send him a foundation stone for constructing an oratory. But because it is not fully established to us that this can be done without prejudice to another’s right, we direct your discretion by apostolic letters that, having more carefully investigated the truth of the matter, if that place is found to be exempt, you shall, relying on our authority and notwithstanding any appeal, grant him a foundation stone for constructing the oratory.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

CXIII. To the bishop [Note: [Col. 0160D] See the note to Letter XLV of Book VIII.] and archdeacon of Arras.—That they are to investigate injuries inflicted by the lord of Ardes upon the abbot and convent of St. Bertin. (A.D. 1207, Rome, at St. Peter’s, January 23.)

[From the archive of the monastery of St. Bertin, bundle “Papal [letters],” marked Innocent III, no. 26. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1135.]

[Col. 0160D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother . . . bishop, and to his beloved son . . . archdeacon of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been brought to our ears, through the complaint of our beloved sons the abbot [Note: [Col. 0160D] See the note to Letter XVIII of this Appendix.] and convent of Saint-Bertin, [Col. 0161A] that a nobleman, . . . count of Boulogne [Note: [Col. 0161D] See *The Deeds of Innocent*, § LXXXIV, note.], of the diocese of Thérouanne, holds occupied, to the prejudice and injury of that monastery, a certain tract of land which the nobleman . . . lord of Ardes, of the same diocese, held by feudal tenure for the church of Saint-Bertin, on account of the war which he is waging against that lord. For this reason, the same lord of Ardes, in seeking to recover the land from the monastery, has repeatedly acted injuriously and vexatiously toward them.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, after summoning the parties and hearing the allegations on both sides, you shall determine, without regard to appeal, what is just, causing what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. Moreover, if witnesses who have been named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, [Col. 0161B] you shall, by the same coercive authority and with appeal set aside, compel them to bear testimony to the truth, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See which prejudice truth and justice.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

CXIV. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0161D] See the note to Letter CXC of Book VII.] and convent of Compiègne.—He confirms the settlement concerning the parish of Saint-Germain of Compiègne and other matters, made between them and the bishop and chapter of Soissons by the authority of the bishop of Paris. [Note: [Col. 0161D] For the subject of this letter, compare Letter LIII of Book I, TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS, that he may dedicate a chapel granted to him by the provost of Compiègne, and concerning the division of one parish into [Col. 0162D] three. Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of April. See also there Letter LIV, TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS, concerning the same matter. Given as above.] (A.D. 1207; Rome, Saint Peter’s, 26 January.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Saint-Corneille of Compiègne, chest: Spiritual Jurisdiction, fascicle VI, no. 3. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0161C]

Since the Apostolic See received from the Author himself of peace and unity the prerogative of primacy, we, though unworthy, preside over it and are bound by the office of service entrusted to us to uphold in their strength those matters settled by agreement, lest they be drawn back into the uncertainty of renewed litigation. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably granting your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the settlement concerning the division of the parish of Saint-Germain of Compiègne and certain articles established in relation to that settlement, concluded reasonably between you on the one side and our venerable brother N., bishop [Note: [Col. 0162D] See the note to Letter XI of Book III.], and our beloved sons, the chapter of Soissons, on the other, under the authority of our venerable brother O., [Note: [Col. 0162D] See the note to Letter XI of Book III.] [Col. 0161D] bishop of Paris, and our beloved son H., abbot of Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 0162D] See the note to Letter CCVIII of Book VIII.], judges delegated by us; as it was prudently made without impropriety, accepted by both parties, and hitherto observed.

Let no person therefore at all presume to violate this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed [Col. 0162A] Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

CXV. To the chapter of Roskilde.—Confirmation of ten prebends, a third part of the tithes of Giaf, and rights in spiritual and other matters. (A.D. 1207; Lateran, 24 March.)

[LANGEBECK, *Writers of Danish Affairs*, VI, 388.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Roskilde, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and, by the ensuing effect, fulfill requests which do not depart from the path of reason. [Col. 0162B] Accordingly, since Peter, your bishop of good memory, established in your church—which had been, as it were, neglected by his predecessors—ten prebends from his patrimonial goods; and since your beloved son S., your bishop-elect and his successor, granted to your church all the estates within the bounds of the city of Roskilde for your common use, and, from the holdings of Thorp, Waslof, Ostorp, Cattorp and Fiarstorp, Thorstentorp and Ech, one third of the tithes for the augmentation of certain of the aforesaid prebends; and since he also granted you Giaf and every right of exaction, both in spiritual matters and in others, over all your bailiffs and tenants, for yourselves and through you for your church: we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, all these things, as you possess them justly and peacefully.

Let no person therefore at all presume to violate this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

CXVI. To the dean and chief archdeacon of Paris, and to O., scholasticus.—Grant of the altars of Driencourt, Villiers-in-the-Wood, and Lupivivia. (A.D. 1207; Lateran, 26 March.)

[VARIN, *Archives of Reims*, II, 461; Cartulary of Saint-Remi, C, fol. 4 verso, no. XX.]

[Col. 0162D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to . . . the dean and chief archdeacon of Paris, and to O., scholasticus of the cathedral church of Cologne, residing at Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our beloved sons D., canon of Reims, and N., procurator of the monastery of Saint-Remi, appeared in our presence, we appointed our beloved son J., cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, as their auditor. [Col. 0163A] Before him the aforesaid canon alleged that G., archbishop of Reims of good memory, at the petition of the dean and chapter of the church of Reims, acting under an indulgence granted him by the Apostolic See—namely, that he might canonically restore to his own hand and authority altars, tithes, revenues, and other things which W., his predecessor of good memory, had improperly granted to monasteries and certain persons—recalled, on the advice of prudent men, the altars of Lovois, Driencourt, and Villiers-in-the-Wood. These belonged by right to the church of Reims, but W., the aforesaid predecessor, had granted them at his pleasure to the church of Saint-Remi without the consent of the canons of Reims. When Archbishop G. subsequently granted them to the said [Col. 0163B] canon, after taking account of that canon’s fidelity and devotion, the monks of the aforesaid monastery appealed to our tribunal and unjustly occupied the revenues belonging to the aforesaid altars. The above-mentioned canon therefore requested that the gift of those altars made to him be confirmed by apostolic authority and that the revenues received from them in the meantime be restored to him.

The procurator of the monastery, on the other hand, replied that W., formerly archbishop of Reims, had canonically granted the aforesaid altars to that monastery; that this grant was afterwards confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See; and that the monastery had possessed the same altars, almost down to the present time, without any contradiction by anyone. [Col. 0163C] Accordingly, the procurator earnestly requested that we deign to absolve the monastery from the claim of the aforesaid canon.

We have therefore thought fit to commit [this case?] to your examination, commanding by apostolic letters that you shall investigate the truth more fully, both concerning the aforesaid altars and concerning the other altars and other matters regarding which litigation is known to be pending between D. and the monastery; and that, with apostolic appeal set aside, you shall determine what is canonical. Cause what you decree to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure. Moreover, if witnesses who have been named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them by the same coercive authority, with appeal set aside, to bear testimony to the truth, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See without the consent of the parties. [Col. 0163D] If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, nevertheless let two of you carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

CXVII. To Louis, [Note: [Col. 0163D] Louis I, brother of Albert of Hirgis, bishop of Verdun, a man endowed with favor and good character, succeeded Stephen in 1197. He found the monastery so burdened with debt that the greater part of its revenues went to paying interest. Having assumed its care while still young, he endured poverty himself and, avoiding superfluous expenditures, restored it to a sound condition with God’s helping aid. Worn out by old age, he resigned administration on 8 March 1237, and died in the following year, on 16 Kalends of July. *New Gallican Christianity*, vol. XIII, [Col. 0164D] col. 1298.] abbot of the monastery of Saint-Vanne of Verdun, and his brethren.—He receives them under the protection of Saint Peter, and their possessions are enumerated. (A.D. 1207; Viterbo, 22 June.)

[We publish this bull on the authority of a copy faithfully transcribed from the original preserved in the archive of the monastery of Saint-Vanne of Verdun, and deposited in our charter archive by Dom Michael Colloz, subprior of the abbey of Saint-Airy of Verdun. At the end of the copy Dom Colloz appended this note: “The original is written on a parchment one foot eight inches wide and one foot ten and a half inches high. The seal is lost: only threads of silk, half red and half yellow, from which it hung, remain.” But the chronological notes contain a difficulty, which we shall explain. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1136.]

[Col. 0164A]

[Col. 0164B] The authority of the Apostolic See, over which we preside, although unworthy, admonishes us to labor for the condition of churches, and that they may not be disturbed by anyone’s malice, they ought to be strengthened by apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in your monastery according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. [Col. 0164C] Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting it, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; whatever rights you have at Neuville, Mancières, Mucerioles, and the village where salt is made; the chapel at that same Neuville, with its appurtenances, given by Wilric and Theoderic; the allod of Igneis; [Col. 0164D] whatever rights you have at Gaudini Villa; the churches of Walemeis and Mainis, with their appurtenances; the church of Bailvet, the church of Bulleinvilla, and the church of Mont-Saint-Martin, with their appurtenances; the tithe of Moinaville, in the full integrity in which Arnulf, bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0164D] Arnulf (of Chiny), son of Count Albert and Agnes, sister of Count Reynald of Bar, was proclaimed bishop in 1172 from being treasurer of the church of Verdun, with the unanimous consent of the clergy and the acclamation of the people. He was exceptionally experienced in conducting affairs and richly endowed with every kind of learning and with eloquence; he was also distinguished for the finest morals, prudence, and intellect. He died on 14 August 1181, still unconsecrated. Ibid., col. 1206.], [Col. 0165A] is known reasonably to have granted it to us; the allod before the village of Saint-Amand, situated within your ban, given by Gobert, Rainer of Aspermont, Walter, Warner, and their heirs; a cartload of hay in Rambald’s meadow, given by the same men Walter and Warner; the cell of Mont-Saint-Martin, with all its appurtenances, and the allod of Braz, given by Lambert of Sipiencourt.

Likewise, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your monastery the monastery of Luxembourg, as you reasonably possess it by the grant of Arnold, archbishop of Trier, of good memory [Note: [Col. 0165C] This concerns Arnold I, elected archbishop of Trier in 1169. He died on 25 May 1183, highly praised for his love toward the Church and his benevolence toward his subjects. *New Gallican Christianity*, vol. XIII, col. 432.], and as is contained in that archbishop’s authenticated charter. [Note: [Col. 0165C]

Arnold’s diploma concerning the union of the abbey of Saint Mary [Col. 0165D] of Luxembourg, otherwise Blessed Mary of Münster near Luxembourg, is found in Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. II, Documents, p. 378, where it is said to have been given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1178, indiction 11, concurrent 6, no epact, while the lord Alexander, supreme pontiff and universal pope, governed and directed the holy Roman Church, in the fourteenth year of his papacy (rather, the nineteenth), and while the most serene lord Emperor Frederick reigned, and in the eighth year of our own pontificate (that is, Arnold’s), happily.

Bertholet considered this document spurious (*History of Luxembourg*, vol. IV, p. 206).

Hontheim, however, endeavors to defend its authenticity (*Diplomatic History of Trier*, vol. I, p. 606), in the notes: “Bertholet indeed maintains that this charter is spurious, but on grounds which prove nothing other than that this union, so formulated and already decreed, did not take effect, because there is thereafter a continuous and certain succession of abbots of Luxembourg distinct from the abbots of Saint-Vanne of Verdun.” [Col. 0166C]

It does not belong to us to settle this dispute, nor is this the place to submit the authenticity of that diploma to examination. Yet from the following notes the learned reader will understand why we could not pass these matters over in silence.]

Indeed, no one shall presume to demand or exact tithes from you from newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, [Col. 0165B] or from the nourishment of your own animals. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, in a subdued voice and without ringing bells. You may also receive into conversion, and retain without any contradiction, clerics or laypersons fleeing the world who are free and absolved.

On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, provide to be elected. [Col. 0165C] We also decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; while the rights of those churches from which bodies of the dead are taken remain intact.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb [Col. 0166A] the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes fitting satisfaction for the offense, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer [Col. 0166B] Jesus, and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, John, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter CXVII of Book VI.] bishop of Albano. I, John, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter XV of Book III.] bishop of Sabina. I, Nicholas, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter LIV of Book IX.] bishop of Tusculum. I, Guy, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter XXVIII of Book III.] bishop of Palestrina. I, John, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter LXXXIII of Book V.] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill.
