I, Cencius, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter XXXI of Book III.] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. [Col. 0166C] I, Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter IX of Book V.] cardinal-priest of Saint Vitalis, of the title of Vestina. I, Roger, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter XXXI of Book VIII.] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0166D] See the note to Letter LX of Book VII.] cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guy, [Note: [Col. 0166D] Guy, or Wido, a Roman of the Perleone family—not Regulus of Orvieto, from the noble family of Besançon—was first created cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison by Pope Innocent III (in the year of salvation 1205, the seventh of his pontificate, in March according to Panvinio, or in December according to Ciaconius, at Rome in the fourth creation), and was afterwards appointed bishop of Palestrina by Pope Honorius III. He died under Gregory IX, in 1227 according to Aubery, but according to Ughelli on 25 April 1228. Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 13.] cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 0167A] I, John, [Note: [Col. 0167B] See the note to Letter CLXXXIV of Book VII.] cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Guala [Note: [Col. 0167B]

Dom James Guala of Bicheriis, or Becaria, called Qualo by others, a native of Vercelli, regular canon of the monastery of Saint Peter in Ciel d’Oro at Pavia, doctor of both laws, and bishop of Vercelli, governed that church after Albert Cribello had been transferred to Milan, from 1173 until 1185. Pope Innocent III first made him cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico (in the year of salvation 1205, the seventh of his pontificate, in March according to Panvinio, or in December according to Ciaconius, [Col. 0167C] at Rome in the fourth creation), and then cardinal-priest of Saints Sylvester and Martin, of the title of Equitius (in 1211, the fourteenth year of the pontificate, at the seventh creation). As the Albigensian heresy increased daily in Aquitaine, after Peter of Castelnau had been killed, the pope sent this Guala, a man renowned for prudence, learning, and integrity of life, a distinguished jurist and a most zealous defender of the faith, as legate to France. During the last years of Pope Innocent III he was legate in England and remained there for a long time, also under Pope Honorius III. He died as archpriest of the Holy Roman Church under Gregory IX. Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 25.

We thought it all the more worthwhile to report these matters here because we had mistakenly believed that the statements in Letter XXIX of Book VIII concerning G., cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico, were to be referred to Gregory Galganus, who had been invested with the same title by Pope Clement III in 1488 and [Col. 0167D] lived into the time of Pope Innocent III. Compare what we noted there. For from those matters, as well as from what we reported from Oldoini in the notes to Letter XXXI of the same Book VIII concerning Roger, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, a great difficulty arises, which we shall by no means attempt to resolve here.]

cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, [Note: [Col. 0167D] John, formerly a priest of the papal chapel, was made cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian by Pope Innocent III (in the year of restored salvation 1205, the eighth—rather, ninth—year of his pontificate, in December, at Rome, in the fifth creation). He died under Pope Honorius III. Oldoini, ibid., col. 27.] cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Viterbo [Note: [Col. 0167D]

Various discrepancies occur in these chronological notes, from which very serious difficulties arise.

1. The eighth indiction is combined with the twenty-second day of June in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206. But at that time the ninth indiction was certainly in force.

[Col. 0168B] 2. The same twenty-second day of June in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206 is combined with the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate. Yet the tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate, in June, coincided with the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207.

3. The tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate, and the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207, can in June be combined only with the tenth indiction.

Thus there is an error both in the indiction, in the year of the Incarnation, and in the year of Innocent’s pontificate.

[Col. 0168C] The topographical note, “Given at Viterbo,” prevents the letter from being referred back to the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate, A.D. 1206, indiction 9. For in that year, 1206, the ninth of the pontificate, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, Innocent was at Ferentino, not Viterbo. See the letter in Book IX to the Abbess of the Monastery of Saints Innocent and Anastasia of Gandersheim and her sisters, etc., concerning confirmation of privileges, given at Ferentino through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, but in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III.

Indeed, in the tenth year of his pontificate, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, Innocent was at Viterbo, as appears from various letters of Book X. But then it ought to read “in the tenth indiction,” not “in the eighth indiction,” and “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207,” not “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206.”

[Col. 0168D] Now, if anyone considers: first, that this bull of Innocent makes special mention of the diploma issued by Arnold, archbishop of Trier, for the union of the monastery of Saint Mary of Luxembourg with the monastery of Saint-Vanne of Verdun; secondly, that Bertholet regarded this diploma as highly suspect; and thirdly, that various and very serious errors are clearly found in the chronological notes of the bull—he will perhaps admit that some suspicion may arise concerning the authenticity of the bull itself. Add that, in the very words *nihilominus etiam* (“likewise also”), by which the union is confirmed, although this is a very well-known and customary formula elsewhere, there nevertheless seems to be something which does not wholly savor of Innocent’s style. But perhaps we too shall discuss these matters more carefully elsewhere.]

through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1206, but in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CXVIII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0168D] See the note to Letter XVIII of this Appendix.] and convent of Saint-Bertin.—He congratulates them for generously receiving the prior and monks of the church of Canterbury, whom cruel persecution had compelled to live in exile from their own houses. [Note: [Col. 0168D] Compare the various letters of Books VIII and IX.] (A.D. 1207; Viterbo, 25 September.)

[From the ancient cartulary of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, vol. XIX, fol. 64 verso. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1139.]

[Col. 0167B]

We hold it grateful and welcome, and pursue your devotion [Col. 0168A] with due thanksgiving in the Lord, because, as we have learned, you received with pious affection our beloved sons the prior and monks of the church of Canterbury, whom cruel persecution compelled to live in exile from their own houses, and aided them in their necessities as willingly as generously. By this you show more plainly that you both sympathize with their sufferings and share their griefs. Therefore, since you show yourselves true imitators of the Apostles by bearing others’ burdens upon the shoulders of charity, we earnestly admonish and exhort all of you, commanding by apostolic letters that you endeavor to bring more laudably to completion what you have laudably begun concerning the aforesaid prior and monks, so that, besides the reward of eternal recompense, you may obtain [Col. 0168B] an increase of our favor.

Given at Viterbo, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

CXIX. To John, [Note: [Col. 0169D] See above, the note to Letter LXXVII.] abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and his brethren, in perpetuity.—He receives them under apostolic protection, and their possessions are enumerated. (A.D. 1207; Corneto, 8 November.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed by Dom Poirier from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and communicated to us. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1097.]

[Col. 0169A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which we preside, though unworthy, admonishes us that we ought to exercise general care for the condition of all churches and to be especially vigilant for the protection of those which belong particularly to blessed Peter’s jurisdiction and are subject, without any intermediary, to our jurisdiction and guardianship. [Col. 0169B] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your monastery, which is known especially to adhere to the Roman Church, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, the Lord granting it, through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 0169C] In the diocese of Sens: the churches of Emant; Mont-Macheu; Matricoles; Saint-Germain near Musteriolum; Laval; Saint Peter of Old Matrioles; and Balneoles. In the diocese of Paris: the church of Saint-Germain-le-Vieux within the city; the church of Villeneuve; Crona; Valenton; [Col. 0169D] Thodasio; Perodio; Antony; Verrières; Aureinvilla; and Suresnes. In the diocese of Chartres: the churches of Saint-Martin of Drocis; Saint Mary Magdalene of Mont-Calvu; Dom Martin; Laoniarum; Neelfleta; and Septulia. In the diocese of Rouen: the churches of Leodegarii; Vilers; and Longuersa. In the diocese of Soissons: the church of Novigento. In the diocese of Meaux: the churches of Colli; Blessed Mary of Romainvillare; Monteri; and Abeli. In the diocese of Autun: [Col. 0170A] the churches of Gillis; Vilerbichet; and Marri. In the diocese of Bourges: the churches of Britimaco; Neuville; and Lemauso. In the diocese of Poitiers: the churches of Naintriaco and Saint John of the Market of Château-Érard.

We confirm by apostolic authority to you and your monastery the aforesaid churches with all their appurtenances, as you canonically possess them. By the page of this present writing we decree that in them you shall have, without any contradiction, the presentation of priests, as your predecessors and you yourselves are known from ancient times to have had it. If priests instituted in your churches upon your presentation refuse to render account to you concerning temporal matters, [Col. 0170B] you shall have free authority by apostolic authority to withdraw from them the temporalities which they hold from you.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved unimpaired and whole, for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes fitting satisfaction for the offense, [Col. 0170C] let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Sabina. I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 0170D] I, Guy, bishop of Palestrina. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Guala, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Pelagius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy at the Septa Solis. [Col. 0171A] I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Roger, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.

Given at Corneto, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the eleventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0171D] “In the eleventh indiction.” So it is expressly read in the copy, but undoubtedly erroneously. It would seem that “in the tenth indiction” should be read, since it is certain that the tenth indiction coincides with the tenth year of Pope Innocent III’s pontificate. But because it is plainly gathered from the Register of that same tenth year of the pontificate, as may be seen in vol. II of the *Register*, that such an error had become widespread among apostolic scribes—that throughout the entire tenth year of Innocent’s pontificate, when the ninth indiction was connected with the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207—we believe that in this letter too it was written “in the ninth indiction.”], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1207, but in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

CXX. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0172D] See the note to Letter XVIII of this Appendix.] and convent of Saint-Bertin.—He confirms the divisions of the cantorships and personates of Calais and of their other parishes, made by judges delegated from the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1207; Rome, Saint Peter’s, 20 November.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, Papal chest, no. 64. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1140.]

[Col. 0171B]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant benevolent favor to the honorable requests of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just prayers, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the divisions of the cantorships and personates of Calais and of your other parishes, made by judges delegated from the Apostolic See, as they were reasonably and prudently made. Let no person therefore at all presume to violate this page of our confirmation [Col. 0171C] or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

CXXI–CXXII. A privilege providing that the procuration due to prelates shall not exceed the value of four marks. (1208. Lateran, 29 February.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, II, 466. Cartulary of Saint-Remi, A, 45.]

INNOCENT, bishop . . . for perpetual remembrance and observance.

[Col. 0171D] Against the burdens which prelates imposed upon their subjects in procurations owed on account of visitation, canonical enactments had beneficially provided by prescribing that due moderation be observed concerning the number of mounts and persons, the excess of banquets, and other superfluities, so that prelates should not exceed proper limits by demanding too much, nor subjects be burdened by providing excessively [Col. 0172A]; and so that visitation might be for salvation and joy of soul, rather than for the affliction and weariness of those subject to them. But since complaints are still heard concerning such procurations, we, desiring to provide with pastoral concern in this matter so that every occasion of burdening may be removed and all cause for complaint entirely cease, establish by apostolic authority that, when archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, and other prelates visit in person, the churches and places visited shall furnish procurations in foodstuffs and other necessities in moderation, so that, according to the common valuation of goods in the individual places, or according to the expenses incurred for these purposes, they shall in no procuration [Col. 0172B] exceed a total or value of four silver marks. Provided, nevertheless, that the expenses of such procurations shall be made up to that total or below it according to the greater or lesser number of mounts and persons, in proportion to the greater or lesser rank of prelates as fixed at the Lateran Council. Yet in places where there is greater fertility or abundance of goods, and where revenues or ecclesiastical resources are smaller, less shall be spent on those procurations, in proportion to the greater abundance of necessities and the smallness of revenues. If more is spent on such procurations, the prelates receiving them shall be compelled to restore it for the benefit of the churches from which they received them; and those who furnished them shall be compelled to distribute from their own property to the poor double the amount that was thus spent in excess [Col. 0172C], without prejudice to the imposition of another penalty if that should seem expedient. All other provisions known to have been generally established concerning such visitations and procurations shall nevertheless always remain in force.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution and confirmation, or rashly to act against it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CXXIII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0172D] The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1576, identify the abbot of Saint-Evroult as Vulgrin, from documents dating from October 1200 through 1225.] of Saint-Evroult, the dean of Saint-Avitus, and the archdeacon of Orléans.—That they compel the bishop of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 0172D] See letter LIII of Book V, note.] to preserve the instruments of the peace concluded between the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis and the viscount of Châteaudun. (1208. Lateran, 1 April.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed and communicated to us by M. Poirier from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Denis in France.]

[Col. 0173A] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Saint-Evroult, the dean of Saint-Avitus, and . . . . . the archdeacon of Orléans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You should know that the beloved sons, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0173D] See Letter XLV of Book III, note.] and convent of Saint-Denis, have represented to us that it has come to our hearing that our venerable brother, the . . . bishop of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 0174D] See Letter LIII of Book V, note.], refuses to preserve the instruments of the peace solemnly concluded between them and the viscount of Châteaudun concerning the church of Cergy, as his predecessors are said to have preserved them. We therefore commanded him to take care to preserve those instruments with diligent care, as his predecessors are known to have done. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, if the said bishop neglects to fulfil what we have commanded, you shall, after prior warning, compel him by appropriate coercion, without appeal, to do that to which he is bound. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, nevertheless two of you shall carry it out.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CXXIV. To the abbot and brothers of Velehrad.—He confirms the foundation of the monastery of Velehrad and establishes the rights and rules of its brothers. (1208. Lateran, 31 April.)

[BOCZEK, *Codex Diplomaticus Moraviae*, II, 45. From a manuscript paper codex of Velehrad, early fifteenth century, folio, f. 94.]

[Col. 0173C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . the abbot of Velehrad and his brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection present, lest perhaps an assault of anyone’s rashness either turn them back from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Velicard, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. [Col. 0173D] First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is recognized to have been instituted in that place according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brothers, shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 0174A] The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; its granges with their appurtenances; with meadows, vineyards, lands, woods, rights of use, and pastures, on the plain and upland, in waters and mills, roads and paths, and all its other liberties and immunities. Let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of your labor which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens and shrub-grounds, your fisheries, or the increase of your animals. You may also receive into your conversion clerics or laymen, free and released from the world, who flee from it, and retain them without any objection.

Furthermore, we forbid any of your brothers, [Col. 0174B] after making profession in your monastery, to leave that place without his abbot’s permission; and no one may dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from your community. Should anyone presume to retain him, it shall be lawful for you to pronounce the regular sentence against such monks or lay brothers. We strictly forbid anyone to give personally, or otherwise alienate, lands or any benefice bestowed upon your church without the consent of the entire chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. Should any gifts or alienations be made otherwise than as stated, we decree them void.

We further forbid any monk or lay brother bound by profession to your house [Col. 0174C] to stand surety for anyone, or to borrow money from anyone without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter beyond the sum fixed by the prudent decision of your chapter, unless this be for a manifest benefit of your house. If he presumes to do so, the convent shall in no way be bound to answer for it. Further, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of your brothers, lest your right suffer loss in any respect through lack of witnesses.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop or any other person to compel you to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to submit to secular judgment concerning your own goods or possessions [Col. 0174D]; nor may anyone presume to come to your houses to ordain, to hear cases, or to convene public assemblies, or hinder the regular election of your abbot, or in any way interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order, with appointing or removing the person who is abbot at the time. If the bishop in whose diocese your house is founded, when humbly and devoutly requested as is proper, refuses to bless a substitute abbot and confer upon you the other matters belonging to the episcopal office, it shall be lawful for that abbot, provided he is a priest, to bless his own novices and exercise the other functions [Col. 0175A] belonging to his office; and you may receive from another bishop all that has been improperly denied you by your own bishop.

We add that, in receiving professions tendered by abbots already blessed or about to be blessed, bishops shall be content with the form and wording established from the origin of the Order: namely, that the abbots themselves must profess obedience to the bishop, while preserving their Order, and shall not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of their Order. For the consecration of altars or churches, or for obtaining customary dues, or in any other way, he may not dare extort anything; but you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer [Note: [Col. 0175D] Something is missing.], one who possesses the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, who, relying on our authority, may grant you what you request. If [Col. 0175B] the see of the diocesan bishop should happen to be vacant, you may meanwhile freely and without objection receive all ecclesiastical sacraments from neighboring bishops, provided that no prejudice to your own bishops shall thereby arise in the future. Since you sometimes lack ready access to your own bishops, if a bishop in communion with the Roman See, as stated, and known to you beyond doubt should happen to pass through your district, you may receive from him, by authority of the Apostolic See, blessings of vessels and vestments, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of monks.

Furthermore, if bishops or other rulers of churches pronounce against your monastery or persons established there a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict, [Col. 0175C] or pronounce the same sentence against your hired laborers because you do not pay tithes, or because of any of the things granted you by apostolic favor; or against your benefactors because they have charitably bestowed upon you any benefits or services, or have come to work on the days on which you work while others observe a holiday, we declare such a sentence void as pronounced against the grants of the Apostolic See. Nor shall any letters have force which have been obtained while concealing the name of the Cistercian Order and contrary to the tenor of apostolic privileges. Moreover, when a general interdict of the land is in force, you may nevertheless celebrate divine offices in your monastery, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons [Col. 0175D].

Further desiring to provide with paternal solicitude for your future peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your places or granges, to commit robbery or theft, set fire, shed blood, rashly seize or kill a person, or dare to exercise violence. We also confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the privilege of this document, all liberties and immunities granted to your Order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as exemptions from secular exactions reasonably granted to you by kings, princes, or other faithful persons [Col. 0176A].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 0176B] body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But let all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

CXXV. To Peter [Note: [Col. 0176D] See Letter VIII of Book VIII, note.], abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Neuburg [or, Neufbourg], and his brothers.—He receives them under protection and enumerates the property belonging to them. (1208. Lateran, 5 May.)

[From a copy, carefully transcribed from the original preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint Mary of Neuburg and communicated to us by the late Abbot Grandidier. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid.]

[Col. 0176C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Neuburg, and his brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection present, lest perhaps an assault of anyone’s rashness [Col. 0176D] either turn them back from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Saint Mary of Neuburg, in which you are devoted to divine service; and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order recognized to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brothers shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 0177A] The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the grange of Tochendorf, the grange of Hitendorf, the grange of Lobach, the grange of Harthusen, the grange of Dunnenheim, the grange of Dalheim, the grange of Bathenheim, the grange of Wilre, the grange of Erengersvilre, the grange of Selboven, the grange of Sconenvelt, the grange of Mulenbach, [Col. 0177B] the grange of Bretenbach, the grange of Paphenburnen, the grange of Lachen, the grange of Vilenbach, the grange of Honocheit together with Vinchinhoven, the grange of Suvelnheim, and the grange of Heckenheim, with all their appurtenances: namely, fields, meadows, waters, cultivated and uncultivated woods, etc., etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, on the third day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

CXXVI. To the abbot and convent of Westminster.—He grants one year and forty days’ indulgence to all who annually visit the church of Saint Edward at Westminster. (1208. Assisi, 31 May.)

[RYMER, *Foedera, Letters*, etc., I, 101, from the original in the Tower of London.]

[Col. 0177C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Westminster, London, of the Order of Saint Augustine, greeting and apostolic blessing.

At the feasts of the saints, which Christ’s faithful celebrate with votive solemnity, the Almighty is glorified with worthy praises, due honor is rendered to the saints themselves, and spiritual progress is promoted by fitting devotion.

Therefore, we, who bear general care [Col. 0177D] for the faithful themselves, since above all the matters entrusted to our solicitude we are bound to direct our attention to their salvation, earnestly desire that they reverently commemorate those whom the heavenly King, now stripped of their bodies, has clothed in the robe of glory; that they celebrate their feasts with solemn observance and follow them with annual solemnity; and that they prepare themselves more carefully for their veneration in proportion as they perceive it to benefit their souls more. Since we sometimes endeavor, by apostolic generosity, to distinguish those who devoutly observe them with certain spiritual marks—namely, indulgences and remissions.

Accordingly, since your church is said to have been built in honor of blessed Edward, and since we desire that he be revered [Col. 0178A] with due honor, relying on the mercy of almighty God and the authority of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we mercifully remit one year and forty days of the penance enjoined upon all truly penitent and confessed persons who, each year, visit that church on his feast with a pure intention.

Given at Assisi, on the second day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CXXVII. To the burgesses of Saint-Remi of Reims.—A privilege concerning the *assisia*. (1208. Anagni, 2 June.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, II, 472, from the cartulary of Saint-Remi.]

[Col. 0178B] INNOCENT . . . . to his beloved sons, the citizens of the borough of Saint-Remi of Reims.

. . . . We regard as pleasing and acceptable, and greatly commend in the Lord, your devotion in making, as has been reported to us, a certain arrangement which you commonly call an *assisia*, by prudent piety: namely, that you shall annually contribute a fixed amount from your goods to the monastery of Saint Remigius. Therefore, we, who are bound by the office of apostolate laid upon us to foster works of piety, approve this arrangement, as prudently made, and exhort your entire community . . . . to observe it universally. . . . We have commanded the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and the dean and archdeacon of Paris [Col. 0178C] that, if anyone maliciously presumes to hinder this, they shall restrain such presumption through ecclesiastical censure, justice being observed and the obstacle of appeal removed.

Given at Anagni, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CXXVIII. To the abbot of Gerstyn, Henry of Witin, and Tuton of Heiburch, parish priests of the diocese of Passau.—He orders a new inquiry into a certain case of the monastery of Medlice, in which the bishop of Olomouc was said to have issued an unjust judgment. (1208. Viterbo, 21 August.)

[BOCZEK, *Codex Diplomaticus Moraviae*, II, 48.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of Gerstyn, Master HENRY [Col. 0178D] of Witin, and TUTON of Heiburch, parish priests of the diocese of Passau, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Appearing before us, the beloved son, the abbot of Medlice, showed us in a grave complaint that our venerable brother the bishop of Olomouc and our beloved sons, the abbot of Holy Cross and the dean of Saint Agatha, of the diocese of Passau, his co-judges delegated by us, had rendered an unjust judgment against him, although, as is said, no case which appeared to concern him had been committed to them; and by this judgment the aforesaid monastery is known to have suffered considerable loss. Since no one ought to be unjustly burdened, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having summoned those whom you consider should be summoned in this matter, and having made a careful inquiry [Col. 0179A] and learned the truth, you shall determine what is just, setting appeal aside, and ensure that what you decree is firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of truth and justice shall stand in the way. If all of you cannot take part in carrying this out, nevertheless two of you shall carry it out.

Given at Viterbo, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

CXXIX. To Bartholomew, bishop of Chieti.—He confirms all privileges granted to the Church of Chieti by Roman emperors and supreme pontiffs . . . (1208. 19 October.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, VI, 715.]

[Col. 0179B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Chieti, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Placed by the Lord’s disposition on the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are bound, by the office of apostolate entrusted to us by God, to love our brother bishops with sincere charity, preserve for the churches committed to them their rightful claims, labor also for their welfare, and, with the Lord’s help, make beneficial provision for their peace. Therefore, venerable brother bishop in Christ, we graciously grant your just petitions and, following the example [Col. 0179C] of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Nicholas, Paschal, Eugenius, Alexander, and Clement, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Saint Thomas of Chieti, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. We establish that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The parish territory of the Church of Chieti, bounded by ancient and [Col. 0179D] rightful boundaries: namely, from Staffilo between the Mountains and Mount Ursa itself; thence as it goes to Cola and fixes the boundary in the water beneath the ground as far as the Sonuta water; thence as it goes to the Mount of the Head and follows the ridge of the mountain; thence as it proceeds to Mount Sclavi; and thence as it goes into the river called the Trigno as far as the shores of the sea, and along the shore of the sea to Pescara, returning to the former boundary, namely the aforesaid Staffilo.

Furthermore: the city of Chieti itself; the castle of Trivigliano; Villamagna; Montefilardi; the castle of Orni; the castle of Mucela; the castle of Saint Paul; the castle called Furca; the castle of Genesteale; and the castle of Saint Cesidio, with their appurtenances. Beyond Pescara: [Col. 0180A] the castle of Montesilvano; the church of Saint Mary at Rigoli; the castle of Sculcula; the castle of Lastinia; the church of Saint Mary of the Palace; and the church of Saint Justa, with their appurtenances. At Aterno: the parish church of Saints Leontius and Domitian; the church of Saint Thomas; Saint Saviour’s; the church of Saint Jerusalem; and the church of Saint Nicholas, with all their appurtenances; and the tithe of the Bridge and the Port of Nicini.

In Bucelania: the churches of Saint Saviour and Saint Angel, with the count’s tithes; the parish church of Saint Silvester; the count’s tithes in the castle of Saint Angel, in the castle of Three Fronts, and the tithes of the castles which were in the diocese of Chieti under the lordship of Count Robert of Rotello; and what the Church of Chieti holds in the castle of Septi: the church of Saint Mary in Bari; the church of Saint Blaise at Lanciano; the monastery [Col. 0180B] of Saint Martin of Palectu; the church of Saint Leciri at Atissa with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint John at Arclano; the monastery of Saint Angel at Cornacula, with all its appurtenances.

On Mount Oderisius: the church of Saint Nicholas and half the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Saviour and the church of Saint Peter, with their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Maurus with its benefice; the monastery of Saint Salvi; the church of Saint Nicholas of Eremitorio at Ortona; the church of Saint Mary and Saint George, with their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary in the basilica in the city of Luparelli; the parish church of Saint Peter with its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mando in the Palace; the church of Saint James of Turcella with its appurtenances; the monastery [Col. 0180C] of Saint Pancras; the monastery of Saint Mary of Lecto with its hamlet and other appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Martin in the Valley; the monastery of Saint Justus in Cosule.

In the castle of Gessi: the parish church of Saint Mary with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin of the sons of Tresidius; the church of Saint Mary of Casa Candidella; the church of Saint Peter in the castle of Lori; the church of Lori; the church of Saint Mary at Biario; the church of Saint Blaise; the monastery of Saint Peter in Campo; the church of Saint Nicholas of Summo Viculo; the church of Saint Mary of Lacento at Abbatejo; the parish church of Saint Martin with its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Plebe; the parish church of Juliano; the parish church of Saint Cecofidus; the parish church of Pizzo Corbario; the church of Saint Lucy of Argelli; the church of Saint Linus; the parish church of Orcula; [Col. 0180D] the parish church of Saint Mary in the Valley; the parish church of Saint Mary of Caramanico; the parish church of Saint John of Abbatejo; the church of Saint Cesidio; the church of Saint Pontius of Saint Valentine in the castle of Tocco; the church of Saint Mando in Pescle; the church of Saint Eustace; the church of Saint Martin of Fara between the Mountains; the church of Saint John of Pedara; the church of Saint Nicholas of Cantalupo; the church of Saint Saviour of Linari; the church of Saint Mary of Sparpalia; the church of Saint Mary of Ilice; the church of Saint Saviour of Valle Surda; the church of Saint Mary of Valle Corunelli; the church of the Holy Trinity of Fragne; the church of Saint John of Vicaldo with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Troia; and the church of Saint Mary of Tasso.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 0181A] the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, without prejudice to blessed Peter’s right of ownership and to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our grant, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus [Col. 0181B] Christ, our Redeemer, etc., etc. Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

(The subscriptions of eleven cardinals follow.)

Given by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1208 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope.

CXXX. To the abbot and [Note: [Col. 0181D] See the note to Letter CXV of Book IX.] convent of Saint-Vaast of Arras.—He forbids anyone to lend money to any monk without the attestation of their letters. (1208. Lateran, 16 December.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Saint-Vaast of Arras, in the Chapel of Saint Bon. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1140.]

[Col. 0181C]

The concern of our office requires, and piety exhorts, that we take care to provide for the security of churches in such a way that they no longer suffer harm in a matter in which they are known often to have incurred serious loss. Since, as has been reported to us, certain monks of your monastery, without bridle or restraint, abandoning the cloister and roaming through the open field of license, sometimes borrow money in your name and cause you to be compelled to repay it to creditors, sometimes through the king or by other means, we, wishing with paternal concern to safeguard the security of the said monastery, strictly forbid by this document anyone to lend money to any monk without the attestation of your letters [Col. 0181D]. If anyone should hereafter attempt to do so contrary to our prohibition, we decree that the monastery itself shall not be bound to repay that money. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our prohibition, or rashly to act against it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

CXXXI. To Odo [Note: [Col. 0181D] See the note to Letter CXV of Book IX.], abbot of Saint-Vaast, and his brothers.—On confirmation of privileges [Note: [Col. 0182D] Compare the same letter.]. (1208. Lateran, 20 December.)

[From the cartulary of the monastery of Saint-Vaast of Arras. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1141.]

[Col. 0182A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ODO, abbot of Saint-Vaast, and his brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever we are asked for something recognized as suitable to religion and propriety, it is fitting that we readily grant it and offer fitting support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, which is recognized as belonging especially [Col. 0182B] to our jurisdiction, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is recognized to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

[Col. 0182C] Moreover, of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, whether from the sustenance of your animals or from what is contained within the demesne land of your villages—namely, Myolens, Evnanmaynil, and Tanscamp—let no one presume to demand tithes from you. We therefore forbid anyone to presume, without your permission or consent, to bestow upon other churches or monasteries, whether in life or at death, lands or possessions which he holds from your monastery, or to alienate them from it. Furthermore, in the churches which you hold, in accordance with the decree of our predecessor Pope Urban II of blessed memory, you shall choose priests and present them to the bishops in whose parishes your churches are situated; and, if they cannot canonically be rejected by those bishops, they shall receive from them the care of souls and be answerable to them for the care of the people, while rendering to you due subjection in temporal matters.

Moreover, since we ought to adorn with a singular prerogative of honor and dignity, and to strengthen with the privilege of our favor, those persons and their places whom we know to be devoted to Blessed Peter and to ourselves, and whom it is certain belong, without any intermediary, to the jurisdiction of the most holy Roman Church: diligently considering the fervor of most sincere devotion and faith which you and your monastery constantly and commendably show toward that same most holy Roman Church, and especially toward our person; and considering also how the same monastery belongs principally and directly, without any intermediary, to the right and disposition of the Apostolic See—we grant to you, son Abbot, and through you to your successors, out of the customary clemency and kindness of that Apostolic See, the use of the tunic and dalmatic during the solemnities of Mass on the principal feasts, so that, the more you are adorned by the bounty of our gift and favor, the readier you may be found in rendering honor and service to the aforesaid most holy Roman Church. Furthermore, we apostolically confirm to you the altar of Streis, which you reasonably possess by concession of the bishop of Thérouanne.

> [Note: [Col. 0183C] It would be difficult to determine with certainty who the bishop of Thérouanne mentioned here was. The pope seems to speak of him as living; for, when deceased persons are mentioned, the term *quondam* (“formerly”) is almost invariably added. Yet the altar of Streis had already belonged to the monastery of Saint-Vaast before the year 1206, as is shown by Letter CXXI of Book IX, where it is listed among the possessions of that monastery. Lambert, bishop of Thérouanne, who held the see in 1206 and from whom, on the basis of Innocent’s words, this altar might be thought to have been granted to the monastery of Saint-Vaast, had already departed this life in the present year, 1208; nor does the passage appear capable of referring to his successor. For John II, after the church of Thérouanne had been deprived of the support of a bishop on 21 May 1207, was elected bishop and confirmed by the metropolitan, but was not consecrated until 1209. This is inferred from the letter to the abbot of Saint-Geneviève, the archdeacon, and Master P. Peverel, canon of Paris, “On the election of the bishop of Thérouanne,” dated at the Lateran, 29 January, in the eleventh year of the pontificate—that is, 1209.]

[Col. 0183B] We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and intact, to be of every advantage for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall not amend his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But let all who preserve the rights of that place enjoy the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter LXIX of Book V.]

I, John, bishop of Albano.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter CXVII of Book VI.]

I, John, bishop of Sabina.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter XV of Book III.]

I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter LIV of Book IX.]

I, Guido, bishop of Palestrina.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter XXVIII of Book III.]

I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia and Velletri.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter XXIX of Book V.]

I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter XXXI of Book III.]

I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil [Col. 0184B].

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] See the note to Letter LX of Book VII.]

I, Cencius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius.

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] See the note to Letter XVII of the Appendix.]

I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] See the note to Letter XXXII of Book V.]

I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] See the note to Letter CXVII of this Appendix.]

I, Leo, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] See the note to Letter V of Book V.]

I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] See the note to Letter CLXXXIV of Book VII.]

I, Roger, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] See the note to Letter XXXI of Book VIII.]

I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus [Col. 0184C].

> [Note: [Col. 0184C] Octavian, of the counts of Segni, a native of Anagni and of the Hernici, cousin of Pope Innocent III, was appointed chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church and cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, having previously been a priest of the papal chapel and a canon of Saint Peter’s, in the year of restored salvation 1206, in the eighth year of Innocent’s pontificate, in December, at Rome, in the fifth creation. Under Gregory IX he lost the light of life. Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 26.]

I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

> [Note: [Col. 0184D] See the note to Letter CXVII of this Appendix.]

I, . . . cardinal deacon of Saint . . . at . . . of the Sun.

> [Note: [Col. 0184D] Thus in the copy which D. Queinsert caused to be placed in our archive. Undoubtedly one should read: Pelagius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy at the Septa Solis.
>
> For Pelagius Calvani, a Spaniard by nation and a monk by profession, formerly a canon of Saint Peter’s, was first appointed by Pope Innocent III, in the year of restored salvation 1206, the eighth—rather, ninth—year of his pontificate, in December, at Rome, in the fifth creation, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Lucy at the Septa Solis; later, in the year of our salvation 1211, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate, in the seventh creation, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia; and finally was appointed bishop of Albano by the same pope about the year 1212. Honorius made him legate of the Apostolic See for that famous expedition in which Damietta [Col. 0185D] was captured. After undertaking distinguished labors for the Church, he died at Monte Cassino under Gregory IX, on 11 May 1240. Oldoini, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 27.]

.

[Col. 0185A] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 20 December, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

> [Note: [Col. 0186D] “Eleventh”: thus in the copy. But ought not “twelfth” to be read? For in December of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, the eleventh year of Innocent’s pontificate, the twelfth indiction was already running. But on this elsewhere.]

### CXXXII. To the archbishops and bishops established throughout Sardinia.—For the monastery of Monte Cassino.  
*(Year 1208? At San Germano, 6 July.)*

[D. Tosti, *Storia della badia Casin.*, II, 284.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops established throughout Sardinia, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0185B] It is fitting that we show a more extensive concern for the defense of the property of the monastery of Monte Cassino, inasmuch as that place, with all that belongs to it, is known to belong in a special manner to the right of Blessed Peter. Yet what we cannot bring to effect by our own presence, we must take care to accomplish through our brethren the archbishops and bishops. For this reason we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters: take care, for reverence toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, to cherish and uphold the churches and other goods which Saint Benedict possesses in your dioceses; defend them against the molestations of wicked men; and neither inflict, nor permit others to inflict, any injury or diminution upon them. [Col. 0185C] If anyone presumes to assail them, administer full justice against such persons. Moreover, if any of the faithful should wish to confer any of his possessions upon those venerable places, do not presume in any way to forbid or oppose it.

Given at San Germano, 6 July.

### CXXXIII. He confirms the privileges of the abbey of Monte Cassino.  
*(Year 1208?)*

[D. Tosti, *Storia della badia Casin.*, II, 287, from the original. Diplomatic archive, 1, no. 9.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord, the abbot of the venerable monastery of Blessed Benedict of Monte Cassino [Col. 0185D], and to his successors regularly to be appointed in perpetuity.

Since the office of the Apostolic See committed to us makes us debtors to all churches throughout the world, your monastery of Monte Cassino lays us under the greatest obligation, both because of the bodily presence of our most blessed father Benedict, giver of the monastic law, and because among you, by God’s grace, the untiring observance of his commandments has endured down to our own times. Hence our most holy fathers, the Roman pontiffs who preceded us in the Apostolic See, not undeservedly established it as the head of all monasteries [Col. 0186A]; for from it, as from a fountain, flowed the rule of monastic religion. To this is added that this venerable place remains the Roman Church’s sole consolation among her children in adversity and her tireless rest in prosperity. Following, therefore, in the footsteps of our holy fathers Zacharias, Benedict, Leo, Stephen, Alexander, Urban, Paschal, and Callixtus, we decree that the monastery itself and all belonging to it shall always remain at peace and free from the yoke of all mortals, and shall remain under the right and perpetual protection of the Holy Roman Church alone. Among these possessions we have thought fit to specify the following:

First, the monastery of the Lord Savior situated at the foot of Mount Cassino; the monastery of Saint Mary, Virgin Mother of God [Col. 0186B], called Plumbarola [lacuna]. Likewise, the city called San Germano, situated at the foot of Mount Cassino; the castle of Saint Peter, which was called of old the Castle of Cassino [lacuna]. Furthermore, following in the footsteps of our fathers, we declare that the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino is to be preferred to the other monasteries throughout the world; and we ordain that you and your successors shall sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops or princes, and that in judicial proceedings you shall pronounce judgment before the other men of your order. We also grant to you and to your successors the use of sandals, gloves, dalmatic, and mitre on the principal feasts of the year and on Sundays at Mass or in the sitting of a council.

Moreover, both in that venerable monastery itself and in its dependent houses, we forbid any bishop or priest of whatever church, except the Roman pontiff, to presume to exercise any jurisdiction, to excommunicate, to impose an interdict, or to summon to a synod; so that, unless invited by the abbot or prior, he may not even dare to celebrate Mass there [Col. 0186C] [lacuna]. You may receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. Baptism and visits to the sick you shall perform through your own clerics in your towns and villages [lacuna]. Further, by reason of the more abundant goodwill which we bear toward your monastery, beyond the affection of our predecessors [Col. 0186D], we grant permission to you and to your lawful successors that, if anyone violently takes away possessions or goods of your monastery or its dependent houses, and their bishops, after having been thrice summoned by you, entirely refuse to administer justice against them, you may pronounce against those robbers, after a second or third warning, a canonical sentence of excommunication [lacuna].

If, therefore, on any future day an ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power or honor; let that person know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 0187A]. But let all who observe these just provisions have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

### CXXXIV. To Jordan, bishop of Lisieux, and the abbots of Perseigne and Savigny.—That they notify the abbots and monks of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea of the apostolic command concerning the reform of their monastery.  
*[About the year 1208.]*

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 807, from a manuscript of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea.]

[Col. 0187B]

J., by God’s grace bishop of Lisieux, and the abbot of Perseigne, in the diocese of Le Mans, to the venerable and most dear in Christ abbot and convent of Mont-Saint-Michel in Peril of the Sea, greeting in the Lord. We have received the command of the lord pope in these words:

> “INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Lisieux, and to his beloved sons, the abbots of Savigny and Perseigne, of the dioceses of Le Mans and Avranches, greetings and the apostolic [Col. 0187C] blessing.
>
> “Our venerable brother, the bishop of Avranches, has represented to our apostolic office that, although the monastery of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea, situated in his diocese, formerly flourished in spiritual and temporal matters, it has now grievously declined in both through the negligence of its abbot and certain of his supporters. Therefore, unwilling to pass over these matters, if true, by dissimulation, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you personally visit that monastery and diligently investigate the truth concerning these matters and any others which you see should be investigated; and, setting aside appeal, correct whatever you find requiring correction both in head and members, and establish there what is regular [Col. 0187D] and honorable, restraining by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, any opponents or rebels, should there be any. And if not all of you, etc.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, 5 May, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.”

By authority of this command, therefore, we command you that on the morrow of the approaching feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist you appear before us in your chapter-house, so that we may correct such matters, spiritual and temporal, as require correction, and, faithfully carrying out the apostolic command, may establish, with due observance of legal procedure, what must be established concerning the aforesaid matters. Farewell.

The following charges appear below, in which the abbot was undoubtedly found blameworthy, or at least accused:

Concerning his unwillingness to do anything with their counsel. Concerning the fact that the abbey could be adequately maintained from half its revenues. Concerning the consumption and destruction of [lacuna] the church treasury. Concerning the sale and destruction of woods. Concerning revenues taken from the prior, cantor, sacristan, infirmarer, and cellarer. Concerning the devastation and dilapidation of manors. Concerning the tallages of the land of Saint Michael, from which no [Col. 0188B] benefit came. Concerning demesne lands improperly granted away. Concerning the manumission of serfs. Concerning the abolition of hospitality for arrivals. Concerning bread taken from the brothers of our congregation. Concerning his failure to attend either the order or the service of God. Concerning his failure to correct immoral persons and those who managed manors badly. Concerning his insufficient support of religious persons, whom he was accustomed to keep with him. Concerning his swearing many solemn oaths and keeping none of them.

### CXXXV. To John, king of the English.—Concerning the affair of the archbishop of Canterbury.  
*(Year 1208.)*

> [Note: [Col. 0187D] See Letters 90 and 91 of Book XI.]

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 810, from a manuscript of Saint Julian of Tours.]

[Col. 0188C]

Innocent III to John, king of the English.

We have been touched inwardly by grief of heart and disturbed by vehement sorrow, because, although the Apostolic See loved you above other princes with that special prerogative of affection, so that you might in return repay it with reverence and honor, you render hatred for its affection and, as though you had conspired against yourself, spare not your own honor in order that you may detract from ours. Indeed, heedless of your reputation and salvation, to the prejudice of both, you rashly rise up against the disposition of ourselves and [Col. 0188D] the Church—indeed, of God—without considering that you strive in vain to nullify it, since no one can turn aside the outstretched hand of the Most High, and no one can change whatever He has decreed.

Truly, how much and in what manner we have yielded to your royal highness in the affair of the Church of Canterbury, although perhaps in your ingratitude you do not remember it, cannot easily be erased from the memory of the universal Church, which, seeing goodness not overcome by wickedness, marvels at our patience toward you. Alas! What hardness, dearest son, has stopped your ears, so that you have not received the salutary warnings so often impressed upon you by us? What hardness has swallowed up your understanding, so that you have not kept the prudent counsels repeatedly suggested to you by us? You now appear so hardened that you do not feel the growing wound of your injury. You seem so bewitched that you admit neither the help of medicine nor the work of the physician; so that we may almost complain of you with the prophet: “To whom shall we speak, and whom shall we further adjure? His ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear.” You are displeased by the word suggested to you for your salvation. You are weary of the good urged upon you for your honor, since you neither pity the loss of your soul nor are ashamed of that worldly reputation which we would not even call disgrace. Therefore we pity you all the more for such hardness, because, having made yourself cruel toward yourself, you have hitherto most wretchedly refused to pity yourself.

Although the paternal affection from which [Col. 0189B] we say these things to you may perhaps be hateful to you, yet we act toward you in the role of a prudent and loving physician, who beneficially cuts and burns a sick man, even when he is unwilling, unprepared, and resisting. Therefore, God forbid, if we find your disease hardened, you will compel us to employ a more forceful remedy, according as necessary treatment demands. Though perhaps you now shrink from its severity, when health has been restored you will nevertheless praise its effect and bless the skilled physician also.

But that we may still apply the ointment of speech, lest perhaps, once it has been applied, you await harsher measures, we earnestly ask the royal serenity and admonish you through Him who is to come to judge the living and the dead, beseeching you to use sounder counsel and be recalled from so great an error—at least by proceeding in this affair according to the contents of the letters which the son abbot of Beaulieu formerly obtained from us in your name. For beyond doubt, in addition to your earlier fault, this may be imputed to you as a second fault if you appear to withdraw from it: namely, that it was sought with such urgency under the express testimony of your own letters, in which you humbly petitioned us to give firm credence to whatever that abbot should tell us in your name concerning the affair. For this reason you ought, without any difficulty, to fulfill what had been obtained through his diligence—especially since you were finally seen to accept it, when, after what had first been heard from you concerning it, carefully considered and prudently examined, you later caused our delegates to come into your presence as if for the completion of the affair [Col. 0189D].

Therefore, dearest son, do not be obstinate and introduce no difficulty into this affair, lest, God forbid, you bring yourself into a difficulty from which you cannot easily be freed. Otherwise, however sincerely we love your person in the Lord, and although you may perhaps receive canonical discipline indignantly, nevertheless, since when one who is loved is chastised, mercy is then exercised toward him—for love has its wounds, which are sweeter the more bitterly they are inflicted—unless within three months after the receipt, or refusal, of this letter you fulfill what we have set forth, from that time, on the part of Almighty God the Father, Son, and [Col. 0190A] Holy Spirit, and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, whose authority, though unworthy, we possess, we decree you anathematized and cut off from the communion of the faithful. We strictly command our venerable brethren not to delay, appeal being set aside, in publishing that sentence, and to cause it to be solemnly renewed every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lighted, until fitting satisfaction has been made. By the Lord’s authority, we ourselves shall also publish it publicly with our own lips, so that the penalty of one whose fault is known to have offended the universal Church may thus be more certainly and forcefully made known throughout the whole Church.

Moreover, with God’s help we shall proceed against you in many ways if even then you do not hasten to correct your error. [Col. 0190B] Behold, the bow is drawn; flee, dearest son, from the arrow, which does not customarily turn backward, lest, wounded by it, you become gravely sick, so that you may not only be unable to advance to better things, but may scarcely be able to return even to your former condition; for its wound cannot be healed without an ugly scar.

In another hand: Done in the year of grace 1209, when the faithful people undertook the expedition against the Albigensian heretics, Philip reigning in France, and Master Stephen Langton having been appointed archbishop of Canterbury by the lord pope against the will of John, king of England, on account of which his land was placed under interdict.

### CXXXVI. Form of the interdict imposed upon England by Innocent III.

[Marten, ibid., from a manuscript of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea.]

[Col. 0190C]

This is the form of the general interdict established throughout England by Innocent III because of the contumacy of King John.

Clerics, whenever they wish, shall say all the Hours in churches and read the Gospel without any solemnity and without chant, but with the doors closed, so that no layperson may enter, whether for prayer or for any other reason, unless he is some powerful person not excommunicated, who devoutly asks admission and whose refusal might gravely injure the church. Such a person shall then enter alone, but hear nothing from the priest [Col. 0190D] except the word of preaching, that he may obey God more than man, and other such matters.

Likewise, chaplains shall assemble their parishioners every Sunday and on the principal feasts at some cross in the town or in the cemetery, and shall preach to them with all diligence concerning patience and obedience, because Christ became obedient to the Father, etc. And they shall teach that God must be obeyed more than man: “Do not fear those who have power to kill the body,” etc. When the preaching has been completed, the priests shall say prayers most devoutly for the peace of the Church and for the lord king, that the Lord Jesus Christ may direct his feet into the way of salvation and give him a spirit of counsel, so that he may see what must be done according to God and gain strength to carry out what he has seen. They shall also say prayers for the living and the dead, as they were accustomed to do, all kneeling; and they shall most diligently admonish the people to persevere day and night in such prayers, that they may supply the lack of Masses by vigils and prayers. For all who obey the Church of God and enter upon the way of salvation; but those who prove rebellious may fear the vengeance of the Lord, for cursed is the child who resists with his fist a mother striking him.

Chaplains shall also announce feast days, but shall make neither blessed bread nor holy water. Likewise, infants shall be baptized in houses with chrism and anointing and with every due solemnity. All archdeacons and deans shall assemble on Maundy Thursday as they were accustomed, and there they shall be told what they ought to do; but the old chrism shall be kept everywhere [Col. 0191B]. Parishioners shall have a common vessel for baptizing infants, which may be carried through the houses; the baptismal water shall be decently stored, and the vessel carefully guarded.

Whoever requests confession shall have it whenever he wishes, and shall make lawful testimony, with all solemnity, but without the Eucharist and without extreme unction. The bodies of the dead, clerics as well as laypersons, shall be placed wherever their friends wish outside the cemetery, especially where passers-by may be moved by the sight, so that no priest shall be present at the burial of laypersons. But while the body lies in the house, the priest may privately make the commendation of the soul, without cross or holy water. Deceased clerics [Col. 0191C] may properly be placed in marked chests or leaden vessels upon the trees of the cemetery or upon a wall; and the bodies of religious persons shall be placed within their own enclosure, without opening the cemetery earth.

Likewise, the altars in churches shall be stripped. Women shall not be admitted for purification. Betrothals and marriages shall not be contracted. Wherever you see or hear that violence has been done to ecclesiastical property, immediately have the damage assessed and committed to writing; put in writing the names of the offenders; and publicly declare them excommunicated. If they repent, let them be sent to the bishop. Schoolmasters, if laypeople permit them, shall be honorably received and shall read and teach.

Those who were able to receive the Body of the Lord, to whom it was announced [Col. 0191D] that they ought to receive it, and who have treated this with contempt, may not eat meat on Easter Day, nor afterward, without the counsel of a bishop or some authoritative person. Announce this publicly to them, however, without compulsion. Chapters shall be held by deans, and crimes of clerics and laypeople alike shall be rooted out insofar as possible; they may be punished by excommunication. But chapters shall be held in cemeteries or priests’ houses, not in the church itself.

All the bishops of England shall solemnly excommunicate, excepting the persons of the lord king, queen, and the king’s justiciar, whoever lays violent hands upon churches, upon clerical possessions, or upon their chattels; and whoever, against the will of the clerics, purchases anything of their goods from robbers, or receives, removes, carries away, or accepts for safekeeping anything from the house of offenders, unless this is done with the consent of the clerics or for their use [Col. 0192A]. Chaplains shall publicly announce this whenever they preach.

Wherever the Body of the Lord remains, let it be decently reserved in the church until it is stated what ought to be done with it, so that no one, priest or other person, may receive it. Clerics shall place their belongings in churches and cemeteries, where, God willing, they will enjoy peace. If the feast days of the Hospitallers occur, priests shall diligently admonish the people to gather outside the church for their preaching and to observe that confraternity most devoutly. Yet the church doors shall not be opened to them, nor shall they be permitted to bury anyone in the cemetery; but in whatever other ways it may be done, clerics shall assist them and priests shall show them that this is the interdict of the lord pope, which no one can resist. It is so general and so severe that no privilege, no permission for Masses or other liberties, can be observed.

Nevertheless, parishioners shall be bound to pay alms and promised offerings, lest God be more severely angered by their hardness; and when God grants peace to the Church, all things shall be restored both to the living and the dead. All fugitives who seek refuge in the peace of the Church shall be received with all diligence into the Church’s protection. Blessings at meals and thanksgivings may be made in the customary manner [Col. 0192C]. Farewell.

### CXXXVII. To Arnold, prior, and the brethren of Zábrdovice.—He confirms their possessions and privileges.  
*(Year 1209. At the Lateran, 3 April.)*

[Boczek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, II, 52, from the original of the same monastery in the register of the Royal and Imperial Government.]
