INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Arnold, prior, and the brethren of Zaberduwiz, of the Premonstratensian Order, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

When a just and honorable request is made to us, both the rigor of equity and the order of reason require that, through the care of our office, it be brought to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclining to [Col. 0192D] your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves your church, in which you are devoted to divine service, with all the goods which you reasonably possess at present or may hereafter acquire by just means, the Lord granting it. In particular, we apostolically confirm to you and strengthen by the protection of this document the villages of Zyrelitz, Zancowiz, Otradiz, and Borkowaz, and the other villages which you hold justly and peacefully. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation and protection or rashly to act against it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0193A] Given at the Lateran, 3 April, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

### CXXXVIII. Papal commission against the count of Plain and others who obstructed an agreement concerning a sum of money to be paid to the bishop of Regensburg.  
*(Year 1209. At the Lateran, 13 April.)*

[Ried, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisponensis*, p. 296, from the original.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost-major, dean, and scholastic of Eichstätt, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother, the bishop of Regensburg, showed us in his complaint that the nobleman, the count of Plain, the ministerials of the church of Salzburg, F. of Pettau, and certain others of the diocese of Salzburg, whose names are to be expressly stated, are violating and breaking an agreement lawfully entered into between them concerning a certain sum of money which our venerable brother the archbishop of Salzburg is bound to pay him, to the detriment of their salvation. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after prior warning and without appeal, you compel the said count and the others by ecclesiastical censure to observe, as they are bound to do, the agreement which was prudently made without wrongdoing and voluntarily accepted by both parties. And if witnesses who have been named withdraw themselves through favor, hatred, or fear, compel them by the same censure, without appeal, to bear testimony to the truth [Col. 0193C]. If not all of you can be present to carry this out, nevertheless let two of you execute it.

Given at the Lateran, 13 April, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

Lead seal: INNOCENT III, POPE.

### CXXXIX. To the bishop of Regensburg.—Confirmation of a privilege granted by Pope Celestine III in 1192.  
*(Year 1209. At the Lateran, 17 April.)*

[Ried, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisponensis*, p. 297, from the original.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Regensburg, greetings and [Col. 0193D] the apostolic blessing.

In the letters of our predecessor Pope Celestine of blessed memory we have seen the following contained:

> “CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Regensburg, greetings and the apostolic blessing.
>
> “The more duties are incumbent upon the episcopal office,” etc.

See these letters in *Patrologia*, vol. CCVI, col. 965.

Accordingly, inclining to your prayers, we grant you by the authority of these presents the power freely to enjoy the aforesaid indulgence.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of May, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

Lead seal: INNOCENT III, POPE.

CXL. To the abbot and the brethren of the convent of Saints Cosmas and Damian of Monte.—Confirmation of privileges. (1209; Viterbo, 18 June.)

[Farlati, *Illyricum Sacrum*, IV, 8.]

[Col. 0194A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and brethren of the convent of Saints Cosmas and Damian of Monte, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church is accustomed, by the office of its wonted piety, to cherish more earnestly its devoted and humble sons, and, lest they be harassed by the troubles inflicted by wicked men, to foster them like a loving mother with the protection of her defence. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons together with all the goods which you now rightfully possess or may, by just means and with God’s aid, acquire in the future. In particular, we apostolically confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, the churches subject to your monastery, as you justly and peaceably possess them; likewise the gift of the churches of St Peter of Bubniani and St Demetrius of Jadra, with all their appurtenances, granted to you by prudent liberality of those to whom such a gift belonged; and we fortify these things by the safeguard of this present writing.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation and protection, or with rash boldness to oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Viterbo, 14 Kalends of July, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

CXLI. To the archdeacon of Fécamp.—He confirms the immunities of the abbey of Fécamp. (1209; Perugia, 9 August.)

[*Neustria pia*, 245, from the archive of the abbey of Fécamp.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the archdeacon of Fécamp in the diocese of Rouen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Graciously assenting to the prayers of our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Fécamp, of the Order of St Benedict, directly subject to the Roman Church, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, without any difficulty, you shall relax any sentences of suspension, excommunication, or interdict which our venerable brother the archbishop of Rouen, or any other person, may have pronounced against the abbot, monks, or any others subject to them by authority of letters which we have sent concerning the observance of apostolic statutes; and, by our authority, you shall dispense those who have thereby incurred any irregularity.

Given at Perugia, 5 Ides of August, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLII. To the abbot and convent of St Remigius of Reims.—A privilege by which the monastery of St Remigius is exempted from debts unless they are shown to have been applied to the benefit of that monastery. (1209; Anagni, 25 August.)

[Varin, *Archives administratives de Reims*, II, 475, from the cartulary of St Remigius.]

[Col. 0195A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of the monastery of St Remigius of Reims, of the Order of St Benedict, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your indemnity and that of your monastery, by the authority of these presents we grant that you and the priors of your priories shall not be bound to pay any debt contracted or to be contracted, unless the creditors lawfully prove that it was applied to the benefit of the monastery and priories themselves; notwithstanding any letters, renunciations, obligations, acknowledgements, oaths, instruments, and penalties appended or yet to be appended at the time of the contract. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or with rash boldness to oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, 8 Kalends of September, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

CXLIII. To the bishop of Meissen.—On behalf of the abbess of Quedlinburg. (1210; Lateran, 24 January.)

[Leuckfeld, *Antiquitates Quedlinburgenses*. Leipzig, 1713, quarto, p. 227, from the Halberstadt archive.]

[Col. 0195C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Meissen, and to his beloved sons the abbots of Porta and Cella, of the dioceses of Naumburg and Meissen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved daughter in Christ, the abbess of Quedlinburg, showed us in a complaint sent to us that, although the monastery of Quedlinburg, together with all the churches adjacent to it, belongs directly to the Roman Church—as is clearly apparent from the privileges of the Roman pontiffs and of our venerable brothers, the bishops of Halberstadt—the bishop, coming there on Palm Sunday to celebrate more solemnly the offices of divine praise, had repeatedly been provided with a not duly rendered hospitality.

> [Note: Col. 0195D. The passage is corrupt, as are many others below.]

The same bishop, turning this gratuitous reception into an obligation of right and abusing in this matter the favour granted him, came there with such a multitude of persons that, although fish had been purchased to the amount of twenty-five marks of silver, apart from other costly provisions, it was insufficient for those at table. Moreover, on the feast of blessed Stephen the Protomartyr, out of reverence for him, a gold *fertum* was customarily offered, and at the Purification of the Blessed Virgin certain candles were customarily offered freely to the Church of Halberstadt by the abbesses of the aforesaid monastery.

But when the same abbess, having received the grace of blessing through the office of the Apostolic See, perceived that these aforesaid practices caused no small prejudice to herself and her monastery, she caused them to be denied to the people of Halberstadt—especially because the monastery is known, by privileges of the Roman pontiffs, to be free of every burden, while the said people of Halberstadt were demanding as a matter of right what preceding abbesses had shown them out of familiarity and favour.

Now, because both on account of these matters and of other vexations inflicted on that church against the privileges of the Apostolic See, we had, upon the complaint of that abbess, instructed by our letters our venerable brother the bishop of Brandenburg and our beloved sons the abbot of Merseburg and the provost of St Peter of Monte Screno to compel the said bishop—after prior admonition—by such coercion as was appropriate, to desist from the aforesaid burdens and to make satisfaction, as he was bound to do, for the losses and injuries inflicted upon her: meanwhile, after the warning had been given, the chapter of Halberstadt obtained certain letters addressed to our venerable brother the bishop of Halberstadt and his fellow judges, without making any mention of the earlier letters, concerning the hospitality on Palm Sunday, the gold *fertum*, certain candles, and also the obedience which, as they asserted, certain prelates ought to render them. By the tenor of the privileges of the Apostolic See, those prelates are bound to be subject to the aforesaid monastery and, by our special command—as is clearly apparent in the apostolic letters—to render to that monastery and its abbess the reverence and obedience both due and devout. The chapter obtained these letters by suppressing the truth.

When those judges had peremptorily cited the said abbess to appear before them at the city of Hildesheim on the first appointed day, as the letters read in our presence contained, it was alleged before them on behalf of the abbess, before joinder of issue, that the letters obtained wholly lacked binding force, particularly since they made no mention of the earlier letters, and that the determination of such an article ought at least to be settled jointly by arbitrators. But since none of these points could in any way prevail with them, both for that reason and because the place was suspect and remote, and also because she retained the right of appeal, since the abbot of Corvey could not delegate his office to another without the remedy of appeal, and because of certain other burdens, she appealed to our hearing in order to pursue the abandoned appeal, sending to the Apostolic See our beloved son Master Nicholas, our subdeacon and a canon of Meissen.

While he was present in this matter, those judges, taking cognizance of the appeal lodged and declaring it frivolous, presumed to summon the said abbess anew to appear before them. And because they admitted to proceed to her prejudice the bishop-elect and canons of Halberstadt, whom delegated judges, acting by apostolic authority, had prohibited from obstructing the liberty of that church in the aforesaid matters or in others, she again appealed to the Apostolic See, placing herself, the convent, the churches, clergy, ministeriales, and all that belonged to the aforesaid monastery under the protection of the Apostolic See.

But they, despising her appeals, repeatedly renewed, condemned her to pay the expenses of the people of Halberstadt, and decreed that they should be put in possession of all the things they demanded, to the prejudice of the abbess. Although the said abbess had, because of so great a burden, appealed against the said judges to the Apostolic See, fixing for them the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin most recently past as the term, nevertheless, adding oppressions to injury and even disregarding the appeals, they bound her with the chain of excommunication. They caused her publicly to be proclaimed excommunicate to her subjects, commanding the Church of Quedlinburg by their letters to avoid her strictly as excommunicate. But before those letters had been received, they fled to the refuge of appeal.

For this reason, through the same procurator, she humbly petitioned us to deign to direct our letters of command to the aforesaid bishop and chapter of Halberstadt, that henceforth they should not presume, contrary to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, to harass either the monastery itself or its members concerning their goods or the property of clerics and laymen belonging to the said monastery.

On the other hand, our beloved son Master Alexander, procurator of the aforementioned bishop, proposed before us that, since the aforesaid judges had cited the said abbess in the case raised between her on one side and the bishop and chapter on the other, and she was finally found contumacious after having been awaited a second and third time, the judges had for her contumacy pronounced against her, by our authority, a sentence of excommunication. He urgently requested us to command by our letters that the same sentence, having been reasonably pronounced, be observed until suitable satisfaction had been made.

But because the foregoing facts were not established before us, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands as the abbess’s procurator related, you shall decree that the sentence pronounced against her is wholly null, restoring her to her former condition if anything has been attempted against her. Otherwise, after the same sentence has been relaxed in accordance with the form of the Church, summon the parties and hear the case; and, if the parties’ will shall have preceded, bring it to a canonical conclusion with the obstacle of appeal removed, or remit it, sufficiently instructed, to our examination, fixing a suitable term for the parties to appear before us and receive judgment, God willing.

[Col. 0198A] If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, you, brother bishop, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of the others.

Given at the Lateran, 9 Kalends of February, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLIV. To the bishops of France.—On avoiding simony in the reception of monks or nuns. (1210; Lateran, 17 April.)

[Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, I, 817, from the manuscript of St Michael in Peril of the Sea.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of France, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0198B] We have often heard, and from many persons, that in certain monasteries of monks, nuns, and other religious situated throughout your dioceses, a damnable custom—indeed, an abuse condemned and to be condemned—has taken such deep root that scarcely any person at all is received into them without the stain of simoniacal depravity. Therefore, lest we should seem, God forbid, to foster by dissimulation a cry so often repeated, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that each of you, visiting such monasteries in your dioceses once yearly, shall forbid, under threat of anathema, that any person henceforth be received in them through such depravity. You shall always announce this same prohibition in your synods; and concerning those whom you find to have been thus received, you shall, by apostolic authority and with appeal set aside, establish whatever you consider expedient for salvation and uprightness.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of May, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLV. To the abbot and convent of the monastery of Laude.—He confirms for them the annual income of eight measures of grain which Count Baldwin had granted to the church of Laude, upon the lands and meadows of Haia and Skelmis. (1210; Lateran, 29 April.)

> [Note: Col. 0197D. After Stephen—of whom we speak in Letter LXXXVI of the Appendix to this work—who died on 7 March 1207, John II of Warnesson, called “the Lamb” on account of his integrity of life and gentleness of spirit, was chosen abbot of the monastery of Laude. He died on 25 November 1123. *Nova Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 304.]

[From the archive of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Laude. Bréquigny, ibid.]

When what is just and honourable is sought from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the diligence of our office, to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we apostolically confirm to you, and through you to your church, the annual income of eight measures of grain which Baldwin, count of Flanders of illustrious memory, granted in provident piety to your monastery from his lands and meadows of Haia and Skelmis, as you justly and peaceably possess it and as is contained in his authenticated charter; and we fortify it by the safeguard of this present writing. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or with rash boldness to oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of May, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLVI. To Bernard, abbot, and the monks of St Gregory, in the diocese of Basel.—That they are not to confer prebends in their church upon secular persons. (1210; Lateran, 5 May.)

> [Note: Col. 0199D. The abbey of Munster, in the valley of St Gregory, of the Order of St Benedict, still exists today in Upper Alsace and in the diocese of Basel.]

[From a copy carefully transcribed, and communicated to us by the late Abbot Grandidier, from the autograph preserved in the archives of the abbey of St Gregory in the diocese of Basel. Bréquigny, ibid.]

[Col. 0199B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERNARD, abbot, and to the monks of St Gregory in the diocese of Basel, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the duty of our office, we are bound to plant what is useful and graft what is fruitful in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, so also we ought to cut away with the pruning-hook of discretion and authority whatever superfluous things we find. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, guarding against a burden upon your church, we forbid you by apostolic authority to confer a prebend in your monastery upon any secular person unless he has assumed the habit of the monastic religious life. And because we will that this be inviolably observed both by you and by your successors, we fortify it by the safeguard of this present writing. Let no one therefore, etc., etc.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of May, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLVII. To the abbot and convent of St Martin of Glandières.—Confirmation of possessions. (1210; Lateran, 25 May.)

> [Note: Col. 0199D. His name was Walter; his name occurs in documents from the year 1210 through the year 1242.]

[From the archive of the monastery of Longavilla, otherwise Glandières. Bréquigny, ibid., p. 1144.]

When what is just and honourable is sought from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought through the diligence of our office to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting favourably to your just petitions, we receive your monastery, together with all the goods which it now rightfully possesses or may, with the Lord’s help, acquire in the future by just means, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves.

In particular, we apostolically confirm to you: the site of your monastery, with your chapel situated beside that monastery and the liberty of that chapel; churches, villages, holdings, leases, tithes, offerings, annual rents, rent-paying persons, fisheries, freeholds, shares in freeholds, revenues, and all arrangements usefully made between you and your advocates, between you and your households, or between you and your men, together with everything known to be set down by name in the authenticated charter made on these matters by our venerable brother, the bishop of Metz, as you justly and peaceably possess those things and maintain the said arrangements as written above. We fortify them by the safeguard of this present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this our protection and confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

> [Note: Col. 0199D. Bertrand, concerning whom see the note to Letter XXXIV of Book III.]

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of June, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLVIII. To the prior and convent of Novy.—Confirmation of the peace concluded between the count of Rethel and his wife, and the prior and convent of Novy. (1210; Lateran, 3 September.)

> [Note: Col. 0199D. For the subject of this letter, compare what is read in the work entitled *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, new edition, vol. III, p. 632.
>
> “Manasses III, count of Rethel, in 1198 restored to the priory of Novy the communal ovens and a small wood which he had seized, expressing deep regret for this usurpation. After his death, which occurred in 1200, Hugh II, his eldest son, succeeded him in the county of Rethel, together with his wife Félicité of Troyes. Despite the restitution he had made to the priory of Novy, Manasses had still reserved for himself several onerous rights over that house, liable to great abuses: rights of hospitality, lodging, procuration, etc. … Count Hugh reached an agreement with the religious concerning all these matters. … The act is dated September 1205 and signed by the count and his eldest son.”]

[From the cartulary of Novy. Bréquigny, ibid.]

[Col. 0200C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and convent of Novy, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious desires and to grant benevolent favour to the honourable petitions of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favourably assenting to your just requests, we apostolically confirm, and fortify by the safeguard of this present writing, the agreement amicably entered into between you on the one hand and our beloved son the nobleman, the count of Rethel, and his wife on the other, concerning certain procurations remitted to the monastery and other matters, as it was piously and prudently made and voluntarily accepted by both sides, and as is more fully contained in the authenticated instrument drawn up concerning it. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of September, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CXLIX. To Conrad, bishop-elect of Minden.—Concerning the election of Gerard, bishop of Osnabrück, as archbishop of Bremen. (1210; Lateran, 30 October.)

[Lappenberg, *Hamburgische Urkunden*, p. 333, from the original at Stade, chest II, no. 12, to which the lead seal of Pope Innocent III is attached.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the bishop-elect of Minden, the abbot of Lesbern in the diocese of Münster, and the custos of Münster, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brothers the bishops of Lübeck and Livonia, and our beloved son the dean major, together with the other canons of the church of Bremen, informed us by their letters that, whereas they had formerly petitioned us to appoint Waldemar, formerly bishop of Schleswig, archbishop, and this could not be brought to effect, some among them directed the votes of their election toward our beloved son B., major provost of that church. But because his election was not confirmed, they took steps, so far as lay in their power, to provide for their church by considering another person. On this account they have already suffered, and still suffer, grave persecutions and impediments, not only in their goods but also in their persons, at the hands of laymen who for various reasons still adhere to the aforesaid Waldemar.

Since the delay of time past has until now been exceedingly harmful to the church left widowed and almost reduced to nothing, and further delay could be still more destructive, they judged it necessary to persist resolutely in the undertaking they had begun, choosing rather to fall into the hands of men than not to set themselves and their possessions as a wall before the house of God. Accordingly, both they and the said provost humbly requested us in their special letters to deign to grant them as archbishop our venerable brother, the bishop of Osnabrück, their neighbour and a man known to them in every respect. Since he is a man endowed with character and learning, distinguished by nobility of birth, and has hitherto defended manfully the church entrusted to him, the aforesaid church may be restored to its former condition and the insolence of laymen restrained.

Therefore, wishing to provide for the church so long desolate, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after you have investigated and learned the truth concerning these matters, if the case stands thus, you shall enjoin the said bishop by our authority to go to the aforesaid church of Bremen, there to receive its governance in the name of the Lord. Because of the necessity of the time, we have thought fit to grant him this favour: until he receives the pallium, he may retain and govern the church of Osnabrück as its own pastor. We further enjoin the clergy, ministeriales, and people of the said church that, until he receives the pallium, they shall attend upon him as their own pastor as hitherto, and render him the obedience and honour due; restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside.

For we direct our letters to our venerable brothers the suffragans and beloved sons, the chapter and ministeriales of the church of Bremen, commanding that, after he has gone, pursuant to our command conveyed to him through you, to govern the aforesaid church, they shall show him the obedience and reverence due as their pastor and attend upon him humbly and devotedly. Moreover, we will and command that you restrain any opponents or rebels by like censure, with appeal set aside. If not all of you can take part in carrying this out, you, son bishop-elect, shall nevertheless carry it out with one of them, even if you have already been consecrated bishop.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of November, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CL. To the bishops of Lübeck and Livonia.—On the same matter. (1210; Lateran, 30 October.)

[Ibid., p. 334, from the original.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the dean and chapter, and to his venerable brothers the suffragans, and likewise to the noblemen, ministeriales of the church of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From your letters, brothers bishops of Lübeck and Livonia, and sons dean and chapter, it has been disclosed to our apostolic office that, whereas you had formerly petitioned us to appoint Waldemar, formerly bishop of Schleswig, archbishop, some of you directed the votes of your election toward our beloved son B., major provost of your church. But because his election was not confirmed, you took steps, so far as lay in your power, to provide for the same church by considering another person; on this account, etc., as in the preceding letter, as far as the words “so long desolate.” We have directed letters to our beloved sons the bishop-elect of Minden, the abbot of Lesbern in the diocese of Münster, and … the custos of Münster, commanding them that, after they have investigated and learned the truth concerning these matters, if they find the case to be so, they shall enjoin the said bishop by our authority to go to the aforesaid church of Bremen and receive its governance in the name of the Lord, etc., as above, “govern.” We further enjoin the clergy, ministeriales, and people of the church of Osnabrück that, until he receives the pallium, they shall attend upon that bishop as their own pastor, as hitherto, and render him the obedience and honour due, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside.

Therefore we command your whole body by apostolic letters that, after he has gone, upon our command conveyed to him by the same executors, to govern the aforesaid church of Bremen, etc. … you shall attend upon him humbly and devotedly. Otherwise, we direct our letters to the said executors, commanding that they restrain any opponents or rebels by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed.

Given as above.

CLI. To Gerard, bishop of Osnabrück, concerning his election as archbishop of Bremen. (1210; Lateran, 30 October.)

[Ibid., from the original at Stade, chest VII, no. 20, to which the lead seal of the pope is attached.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Osnabrück, greeting and apostolic blessing. The following is the same as in the first letter up to “receive [its governance].” Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when this has been enjoined upon you by the aforesaid executors, you shall go to the said church and receive and faithfully discharge its governance in Christ’s name. Because of the necessity of the time, we have granted you the special favour, etc., as above, through “govern”; directing the aforesaid executors to enjoin the clergy, etc., through “restraining [opponents].” Furthermore, we have thought fit to direct letters to the chapter of Bremen, our venerable brothers the suffragans of the church of Bremen, and its ministeriales, commanding that, etc., as above.

Given as above.

CLII. To the archbishop, dean, and chapter of Bourges.—On the canonization of St William, archbishop of Bourges. (1210; Lateran, 28 December.)

[Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, II, 390, from the cartulary of Bourges.]

[Col. 0203C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges and his beloved sons the dean and chapter, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of your letters we have learned that the mercy of the Redeemer, which glorifies His servants in the kingdom through the eternal reward of faithfulness and sometimes glorifies them in the present life as well, is in these days—when iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold—working frequent miracles in your region through William, of holy memory, your predecessor, brother archbishop, in order to awaken the devotion of the Christian people and increase the faith. At his tomb, by the inspiration of Him who enlightens and inflames the hearts of the faithful, a very great multitude gathers from different parts of the kingdom of the Franks, without anyone prompting or preaching; there many sick persons are restored to their former health.

Accordingly, since so great a lamp, which while it enjoyed the light of this present life shone before all people through the merit of its life and the fragrance of its reputation, ought not to be placed beneath a bushel but rather set upon a lampstand, you sent to the Apostolic See your beloved son Master P. …, chancellor of your church, humbly petitioning us through him that we should have him enrolled among the saints to be venerated.

We, therefore, giving from this praise and glory to the Creator—who, wondrous in His majesty, performing great signs and wonders upon earth through His servants, never ceases wondrously to act, so that they may be imitated as an example of devout conduct, and through their glory may afford us the saving help of everlasting aid—have not at present thought fit to proceed in this matter, since this judgment is divine rather than human. We judge it more prudent to wait until God more and more glorifies him whom He has already begun to glorify, so that at an appropriate time, God granting it, we may proceed more securely to execute so weighty a judgment.

> [Note: Col. 0203D. See Letter 173 below.]

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of January, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CLIII. Bull for the nuns of Parc-aux-Dames. (1210; Lateran.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., X, *Instrumenta*, 227.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess of St Mary of Parc and her sisters, present and future, professing the religious life, in perpetuity.

The Apostolic See ought to extend its protection to those who, under the religious habit, with lamps kindled by works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Parc, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods your monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and those who succeed you. Among these goods we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances and with those things known to belong to the altar of that monastery; the tithes of … and of …; the tithe of five measures at Antilly; the tithe of twelve measures at Raray, and at Neuville and Huelem; the tithe of … belonging to Philip of Nantolio; Einselva; whatever you also possess at Magnevol—lordship, land—and whatever has been granted to the same monastery by the chapters of St Regulus and St Frambald; two measures of grain at Vilers … etc.

Indeed, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of your labours which you cultivate at your own hands or expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands, gardens and shrublands, your fisheries, or the increase of your animals. Moreover, you may receive into conversion in your monastery free and unencumbered women fleeing the world, and retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any of your sisters, after making profession in your monastery, to leave that place without the permission of her abbess; and no one may dare retain a departing sister [Col. 0205B] without the common assurance of your letters. We more strictly prohibit anyone from personally granting lands or any benefice conferred upon your church, or otherwise disposing of them, without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we decree them void. For the consecration of altars or churches, or for holy oil or any other ecclesiastical sacrament, no one may dare extort anything from you under pretext of custom or in any other way; rather, the diocesan bishop shall provide all these things to you without charge. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, being in communion with the Apostolic See [Col. 0205C], who, relying on our authority, shall provide what is requested. Moreover, when a general interdict lies upon the land, you may nevertheless celebrate the divine offices in your monastery, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict. Also, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your sites or granges, from committing destruction or theft, setting fire, shedding blood, rashly seizing or killing a person, or daring to exercise violence. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority all liberties and immunities granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions reasonably bestowed upon you by kings, princes, or other faithful of Christ [Col. 0205D], etc.

We therefore decree . . . I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, bishop of the Church of Porto. I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum. I, Guy, bishop of Palestrina. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Ciricius, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. [Col. 0206A] I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Benedict, cardinal-priest of Saint Susanna. I, Leo, cardinal-priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Pelagius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy at the Septa Solis.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1210, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III. Sealed with a bull.

CLIV. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0205D] See above, note to letter 145.] and convent of Los, otherwise Laude.—On the same subject as in letter 145 above. (1211; Lateran, 21 January.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Laude of Blessed Mary. BRÉQ., ibid.]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant benevolent favour to the honourable prayers of petitioners. [Col. 0206C] As was set before us on your behalf, B., count of Flanders of illustrious memory, for the remedy of his sins, piously and generously remitted to you and to the same monastery eight muids of grain in annual rent, which he had and was accustomed to receive from lands and meadows in the territory of Haia and Skelmis, with the consent of his wife of blessed memory, . . . , as is more fully contained in that count’s charter. Therefore, holding valid what was piously and prudently done by the same count, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 0206D] the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of February [21 January], in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CLV. To the bishop of Maurienne and the prior of Aiguebelle in the diocese of Maurienne.—For the monastery of Savigliano. (1211; Lateran, 26 February.)

[Monuments of National History, Turin, 1836, I, 1175; from an old thirteenth-century copy, Archive of Turin, catalogue 51, bundle 1, no. 6.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 0207A] to his venerable brother, the bishop of Maurienne, and his beloved son, the prior of Aiguebelle in the diocese of Maurienne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received a grave complaint from our beloved sons, the brothers of the monastery of Savigliano: although a dispute had long ago arisen between them and the monastery of Chiusa concerning the subjection of the monastery of Savigliano and other matters, it was settled by apostolic authority through a definitive judgment. Our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory afterwards confirmed that judgment, imposing silence upon the monks of Chiusa concerning the matter. Nevertheless, after troubling the monastery of Savigliano further through many letters, they eventually obtained our letters concerning the same matter addressed to our venerable brother the bishop of Vercelli and our beloved son H. Tortus, canon of Pavia, [Col. 0207B] and secured a contrary judgment. Moreover, having obtained our letters concerning the hearing of the same case, without any mention being made of the aforesaid judgment which our said predecessor is known to have confirmed—the text is defective. [Note: [Col. 0207D] Something appears to be missing.] Since you are four days’ journey from the said monastery of Savigliano, those brothers cannot come before you without grave loss to persons and property. Therefore, unwilling that this litigation should be rendered endless through anyone’s malice, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you are in no way to proceed in this matter.

[Col. 0207C] Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of March [25 February], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

I, William, notary, saw and read the authentic exemplars of these documents. From those exemplars I wrote this present copy, adding or subtracting nothing, except perhaps a letter, syllable, or point; nor did I add, subtract, or alter anything that might increase, diminish, or change the tenor of the earlier documents. Rather, just as the authenticated sealed exemplars contained it, so it is contained in these present documents.

CLVI. To the provost and brothers of the Church of Seclin.—Concerning certain revenues of the chapter of Seclin to be distributed only to those brothers of that chapter who take care to attend all offices and the celebration of masses. (1211; Lateran, 28 March.)

[From the cartulary of the collegiate church of Seclin, which appears to have been written in the thirteenth century. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1146.]

[Col. 0207D]

It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that your predecessor, provost of good memory, son provost, prudently considering how ecclesiastical men might be more strongly encouraged to divine service when prompted thereto by the ecclesiastical benefices they received, wisely ordained with the common consent of the brothers [Col. 0208A] that the altar of Gondelcourt [Note: [Col. 0207D] The altar of Gondecourt is listed among the possessions which Pope Clement III confirmed in 1187 to the collegiate church of Saint Piat, martyr, at Seclin. See J.-F. Foppens, *Supplement to Miraeus*, vol. III, p. 355: “The altar of Gondecourt, with all the revenues which you have there, and arable land.”], the money of Guinelval, and the grain, both wheat and oats, known to arise from the places of Mielentois and Caremban, should be assigned to the use of those brothers who diligently and devoutly attend matins and vespers, the celebration of masses, and every canonical hour; so that they may receive four denarii each day from the said revenues as their daily stipend, and that nothing from them should be provided to others except to those performing the aforesaid offices. Since those things which ecclesiastical prelates are known to have prudently established for the devotion and observance of divine worship ought to be strengthened in perpetuity by the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, [Col. 0208B] we decree valid the aforesaid ordinance, prudently made with the common consent of the brothers concerning the revenues already mentioned, and, confirming it by apostolic authority, ordain that it be observed forever in your church, always saving in all things the command of the Apostolic See. Let no person therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Kalends of April [28 March], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLVII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0208D] Was it still Gerbod, of whom see the note to letter XVII above? Certainly the name of his successor, Thomas I, is not found in the documents before 1214. See *Nova Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1596.] and brothers of Saint Wulmar.—He confirms their possession of certain goods. (1211; Lateran, 17 April.)

[From the Cartulary of the monastery of Saint Wulmar, no. 12. Bréq., ibid., p. 1147.]

[Col. 0208C]

In matters justly requested of us by sons of the Church, we ought to prove accommodating and kind, lest we appear harsh or difficult in matters which, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us, we are bound to perform. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly acceding to your just requests, we confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the wood of Holy Cross, together with its wardenship, situated in the allod of Saint Wulmar, and another wood of the same allod beside the wood called Wrmesberk, as well as every right which your men of Hesdin [Col. 0208D] are known by custom to possess in the wood of that town, in both dead and living timber. You are known to hold all these things both by renunciation and by the gift of Eustace, late count of Boulogne, of good memory, and you possess them justly and peacefully. We have also thought fit to establish by this present writing that, from goods sold by any person in the market of Saint Wulmar, the *venda* shall be paid to you and to the same monastery, as has hitherto been customary, unless the seller is a cleric or knight, who must be altogether free and exempt from such *vendae*. Let no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of May [17 April].

CLVIII. To the provost and brothers of the Church of Marbach [Note: [Col. 0209D] The monastery of Marbach, of the Order of Saint Augustine, still exists today in Upper Alsace and in the diocese of Basel.].—He receives them under protection, and enumerates the goods belonging to them. (1211; Lateran, 4 July.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from the autograph preserved in the archives of the bishopric of Strasbourg, and communicated to us by the late Abbot Grandidier. BRÉQ., ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0209B] sons, the provost and brothers of the Church of Marbach: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church, in fulfillment of its customary duty of piety, is accustomed to love its devoted and humble sons more earnestly and, lest they be harassed by the molestations of wicked men, to shelter them, like a loving mother, under the safeguard of its protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and all the goods which you now rightfully possess or may hereafter acquire by just means, God granting. In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to your church, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing: the eighth part of the tithes, together with the right of patronage of the church at Gerlisheim; estates at Weggelheim, [Col. 0209C] Rimbach, Hundolsheim, Wurtmulein, Phaffinheim, Gebelesvilre, Hadistat, Wochelmisheim, Mobsvilre, Reitholce, Egensheim, Wetelsheim, Sulzbach, Brumatin, Colmere, Kancendale, Ongisheim, Kestenholz, Upper and Lower Crehisheim, Bischovisheim, Tubikein, Kuminigheim, Huseg, Gruzenheim, Elsesheim, and Agintina, with all their appurtenances; and your other goods, just as you possess them rightfully and peacefully. We forbid any cleric or lay brother of your monastery rashly to presume to alienate its possessions by his own authority. Let no person [Col. 0209D] therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Nones of July [4 July], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLIX. To the archpriest and chapter of Pisa.—That they restore ecclesiastical revenues taken from Marsuccus de Caietanis, the pope’s chaplain. (1211; Lateran, 30 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 714.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the archpriest and chapter of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0210A] A complaint submitted to us by our beloved son Marzuccus, your canon, stated that, while he was residing in the service of the Apostolic See by our command, you withdrew his ecclesiastical revenues at your own discretion. Since, therefore, by serving the Apostolic See, he is known also to have rendered actual service to your church, it is fitting that you show yourselves fellow-workers of that See . . . Accordingly, by apostolic writing we command and enjoin your discretion to see that you restore to him without any diminution whatever you withdrew from him on this account. Otherwise, we direct by our letters our venerable brother, your archbishop, after prior warning, to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, to do so.

[Col. 0210B] Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of August [30 July], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLX. Gerard, bishop-elect of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See, to the provost and canons of Piacenza.—He prescribes communal living for them. (1211; 6 October.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 709.]

GERARD, by divine permission bishop-elect of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons, the provost and canons of Piacenza: eternal greeting in the Lord.

By the office of legation entrusted to us, we are obliged to preserve, guard, and renew the commendable and honourable customs [Col. 0210C] of churches, and to destroy and uproot those which conflict with canonical discipline. Therefore, by the authority we exercise, we renew, and in renewing ordain, establish, and confirm, that in accordance with the apostolic commands of Adrian, Lucius, and other Roman pontiffs, and with your praiseworthy ancient custom, you shall eat together in one refectory, hearing divine reading in silence; sleep in a common dormitory, not separately in chambers, except because of illness or in order to devote yourselves to scholarly disciplines; assemble daily in chapter, so that you may deliberate together upon the spiritual and temporal affairs of the Church entrusted to you; and wear round garments, being present in church at the appointed hours before the Lord [Col. 0210D] according to the custom of canons. We also confirm for you the ancient customs which you have in the appointments of wardens, etc. Written.

I, Guala Muricula, notary of the Sacred Palace, wrote this confirmation and, by command of the aforesaid lord legate, authenticated it in the upper chamber of the painted palace, in the diocese of Novara, in 1211, indiction XIV, on 6 October.

CLXI. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0210D] See the note to letter CXLV above.] and convent of Los, otherwise Laude.—He confirms an agreement made between the monasteries of Laude and Saint Salvio of Valenciennes concerning possessions of the monastery of Laude at Frangeres. (1211; Lateran, 29 October.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Laude of Blessed Mary. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0211A] Matters settled by judgment or agreement ought to be strengthened by apostolic protection, lest they fall into the difficulty of renewed litigation. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, acceding to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this present writing the agreement amicably entered into between you on the one part and . . . . . the prior [Note: [Col. 0211D] Guichard, prior of Saint Salvio, is mentioned in 1200. Through Hugh, abbot of Cluny, he brought his monks to a better state of life. He is said to have died in 1220, but perhaps earlier; or he had resigned before his death. *Nova Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, [Col. 0212D] col. 133.] and monks of Saint Salvio of Valenciennes on the other, concerning certain possessions of the grange of Frangeres, insofar as it was prudently made without wrongdoing and freely accepted by both parties, and as is more fully [Col. 0211B] contained in the documents drawn up concerning it. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Kalends of November [29 October], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXII. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0212D] See above, the note to letter CXLV.] and convent of Los, otherwise Laude.—He confirms for them an annual revenue of eight muids of grain, given to them in alms by Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut. [Note: [Col. 0212D] On the subject of this letter, compare letters CXLV and CLIV of this appendix.] (1211; Lateran, 17 November.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Laude of Blessed Mary. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1148.]

[Col. 0211C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Laude, of the Cistercian Order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and grant benevolent favour to the honourable prayers of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly acceding to your just requests, we confirm to you, and through you to the monastery itself, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the annual eight muids of grain which Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, of good memory, granted to your monastery in pious generosity, as you possess them justly and peacefully and as is more fully contained in the charter of that count. [Col. 0211D] Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of December [17 November], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXIII. To the provost and brothers of Saint Evasio of Casale.—Confirmation of privileges. (1211; Lateran, 30 December.)

[DE CONTI, *Historical Notices of the City of Casale*, Casale, 1838, octavo, vol. I, p. 356, from an authenticated transcript preserved in the Archive of Saint Evasio.]

[Col. 0212A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost of the Church of Saint Evasio of Casale and its brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting your petitions [Col. 0212B] a favourable assent with due kindness, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, and, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory—Calixtus, Paschal, Innocent, Lucius, and Urban, Roman pontiffs—we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now rightfully and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings [Col. 0212C] of the faithful, or other just means, the Lord granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

All churches situated in the district of Casale, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Hilary and the house of ecclesiastical labour. At Paciliano, the church of Saint German, etc.; the holding of Radulf Quecca, together with first fruits and a third part of the tithes of the whole place of Casale, and the whole tithe of the lands of the household of Saint Evasio, and the whole tithe of the bishop’s Braidæ; whatever the church at Paciliano is accustomed to provide to your church by right or long custom; the village of Luvintini with its tithes and all its appurtenances. At Saint George, fourteen holdings; one sixteenth part [Col. 0212D] of Torcello; and the tenement formerly held by Peter Crassus, with all its appurtenances. At Montedo, three holdings; at Fraxineto, one and a half holdings. Indeed, let no one presume to take tithes from you of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or of the increase of your animals. You may also receive into your conversion city clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them in your church without any opposition. Furthermore, we forbid [Col. 0213A] any of your brothers, after making profession in your place, to leave the cloister without the permission of his provost; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without the common assurance of letters. As for chrism, etc. Upon your death also, etc. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the use and entire benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If therefore anyone, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0213B] I, John, bishop of Sabina. I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum. I, Guy, bishop of Palestrina. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Conaus, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Benedict, cardinal-priest of Saint Susanna. I, Leo, cardinal-priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Roger, cardinal-priest of Saint Anastasia. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Guala, cardinal-priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, Pelagius, cardinal-priest of Saint Cecilia. [Col. 0213C] I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Kalends of January [30 December], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1211, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent.

CLXIV. To the king of England.—Concerning applying himself to the assistance of the Holy Land. (1211.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 104, from the original.]

[Col. 0213D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, JOHN, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received graciously the letter which your royal highness sent us, and have carefully noted what you signified in it concerning the truce concluded with our dearest son in Christ, Philip, illustrious king of the French.

Since you assert that you concluded this truce in order that you might more readily assist the Holy Land, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord to devote yourself diligently and powerfully to the assistance of that land.

CLXV. Privilege for the nunnery of Saint Peter at Dichkirchen. (1211; Lateran, 26 August.)

[GUNTHER, *Rhenish-Moselle Diplomatic Codex*, II, 107.]

[Col. 0214A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and nuns of Saint Peter at Dichkirchen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to grant benevolent favour to the honourable prayers of petitioners. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, gladly acceding to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this present writing the estate of the village of Bevera which H., former emperor, granted to your monastery in pious devotion, as you possess it justly and peacefully and as is more fully contained in his instrument. [Col. 0214B] Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 6 Kalends of September [27 August], in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXVI. To the bishop and custodian of Strasbourg.—That they proceed cautiously concerning Reimbold’s purification. (1212; Lateran, 9 January.)

[From a copy carefully transcribed from another copy inserted in the old cartulary of the archives of the greater chapter of Strasbourg, and communicated to us by the late Abbot Grandidier. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0214C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop, and his beloved son, the custodian, of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0213] In 1211 Henry was bishop of Strasbourg, and Berenger was *custos* of the cathedral.]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although popular ordeals are conducted before secular judges—such as those of cold water, red-hot iron, or judicial combat—the Church has not accepted judgments of this kind, since it is written in the divine law: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.” Observing this, proceed in such a way concerning the purification of Reimbold, bearer of this letter, who is alleged to be accused of heretical depravity, [Col. 0214D] that this disease, which spreads like a cancer, may be completely cured through your prudent care, so that neither an unjust judgment may burden him nor lax mercy ruin him.

Given at the Lateran, 5 Ides of January [9 January], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXVII. To G., priest.—He confirms a grant of revenues to the altar of Saints Peter and Paul in the Church of Senlis. (1212; Lateran, 11 January.)

[From the Archive of the Church of Senlis. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1149.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0215A] son G., priest: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily assent to the just prayers of petitioners and bring to effectual fulfillment wishes that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, gladly acceding to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, a certain grant of revenues made piously and prudently to the altar of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in the Church of Senlis, for the maintenance of one priest . . . . . depravity. [Note: [Col. 0215D] “. . . . . depravity”; thus in the copy.] Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, [Col. 0215B] let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Ides of January [11 January], in the fourteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXVIII. To the archbishop and chapter of Tyre.—For the chapter of Genoa. (1212; Lateran, 23 January.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 882.]

INNOCENT, etc., to the venerable brother . . . . archbishop, and beloved sons, the chapter of Tyre: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved sons, the canons of Genoa, stated in a petition sent to us that you unjustly forbid the parishioners of the church of Blessed [Col. 0215C] Lawrence, which they are known to possess at Tyre, to be freely buried there and to receive there the ecclesiastical sacraments, to their and their parishioners’ considerable prejudice and grievance. Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your discretion to permit the said church, without molestation, to have free burial for its parishioners and the other ecclesiastical sacraments which are known to belong to it by parochial right. And you, brother archbishop, must take care to watch over yourself and the flock committed to you in such a manner—uprooting vices and planting virtues—that on the last day of strict judgment, before the dreadful Judge who will render to each according to his works, you may be able to give a worthy account.

[Col. 0216A] Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of February [23 January], in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXIX. To the rector and brothers of the Hospital of the House of God at Pinchon.—He receives them under the protection of Blessed Peter and confirms their possessions. (1212; Lateran, 5 April.)

[From the parchment cartulary of the barony of Pinchon (Pecquigny, a borough in the diocese of Amiens, on the left bank of the Somme below the city of Amiens). BRÉQ., ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the rector and brothers of the Hospital of the House of God at Pinchon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its proper effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly acceding to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your house and persons, with everything you now rightfully possess or may hereafter acquire by just means, God granting. In particular, we confirm to you and, through you, to the same house by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the place itself upon which your house is founded and all your possessions and other goods, as you possess them rightfully and peacefully. Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our protection and confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone [Col. 0216C] presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April [5 April], in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXX. To the prior of Grandmont. [Note: [Col. 0215D]

“M. de Burdin, archivist of the department of Haute-Vienne, while examining the papers of the prefecture two years ago, discovered among the bundles of the former republican administration the original copy of a letter of Pope Innocent III, dated in the fifteenth year of his pontificate, on the day of the Kalends of May [1 May 1212], and addressed to the prior of the abbey of Grandmont. It is a letter of recommendation on behalf of Aimeric, a monk of Grandmont, who had left the cloister from levity of mind and who later, moved by repentance, asked to return to the convent in which he had made his vows. When he was refused admission, he went to Rome to cast himself at the pope’s feet, expressed his regrets and his ardent desire to be received again into the cloister. Moved by his tears, Innocent entrusted him with a letter ordering the prior of Grandmont [Col. 0216D] to receive the repentant brother into his house.

“This brief is written on a small piece of parchment to which the pope’s lead seal is attached by a hemp cord. On one side it bears the legend `INNOCENTIVS PP. III`—‘Innocent, Pope III’—and on the other the figures of Saint Peter and Saint Paul: `S. PE.---S. PA.` The handwriting is a very fine diplomatic Gothic minuscule, of great clarity and highly legible despite the abbreviations customary at that period.”

“This brief is not without interest for history, and especially for the history of Limousin. The smallest facts become interesting when great men are involved in them. One likes to see this illustrious pope, who occupies so high a place in history, who gave Europe an impulse against which it could not defend itself, who made kings and the emperor tremble, who compelled Philip Augustus to take back his lawful wife, the unfortunate [Col. 0217D] Ingeborg of Denmark—one likes to see this great pope take an interest in the condition and repentance of a poor monk. This letter recalls the moving Epistle that St Paul wrote to his friend Philemon, urging him kindly to receive his slave Onesimus, who had fled far from his master and who, during that absence, had become a Christian. This brief has never been published; we were able to ascertain this by consulting the collection of Innocent III’s letters edited in two folio volumes by the learned Baluze. Moreover, possession of the original instrument is a treasure for our archives. Everything deriving from this pope, one of the greatest figures of the Middle Ages, possesses historical interest [Col. 0218D]; and a fact, however small, merely because it is connected with a great man, puts on immortality.—M. de Burdin has kindly communicated to us the original copy of another unpublished letter of Innocent III, likewise found in the prefectural archives (see above, under the year 1205, col. 147). This letter is addressed to the prior of Grandmont and is dated the seventh day before the Calends of April, in the eighth year of Innocent’s pontificate.” D. ARBELLOT, canon of Limoges.]

. (Year 1212. Lateran, 1 May.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the prior of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

For our beloved son Aimeric, bearer of the present letter and your fellow brother, who left your cloister through frivolity of mind, we earnestly request and admonish your devotion, commanding you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0217A] that, for reverence for blessed Peter and for ourselves, you receive him as he humbly returns to you, without prejudice to the discipline of the order.

Given at the Lateran, on the Calends of May, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXI. To the canons of Marbach [Note: [Col. 0218D] See below, note on epistle CLVIII.].—He confirms to them possession of certain goods. Year 1212. Lateran, 21 May.

[From a copy diligently transcribed and communicated to us by the late Lord Abbot Grandidier from the original preserved in the archives of the illustrious family of Rapolfstein (in French, Ribeaupierre), at the town of Rapolweiler (in French, Ribeauvillé). BRÉQ., ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0217B] sons, the canons of Marbach: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to bestow the favour of its benevolence upon the honourable petitions of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your church, Weckeltheim and the nine estates, with their appurtenances, just as you possess them rightly and peacefully; and we strengthen this grant by the protection of the present writing. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Calends of June, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXII. To the canons of Pisa.—That, when fifteen days have elapsed, they restore Marzucco, their cleric, whom they had struck from the roll of canons, to his former rank. (Year 1212. Lateran, 22 May.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 714.]

[Col. 0217C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Even if we had asked something great of you [Note: [Col. 0218D] See epistle CLIX.], we did not believe that we should meet with any refusal, especially since we wished to obtain from you by our prayers that to which, if you had any bowels of charity, your own generosity and brotherly compassion ought to have led you. For when we commanded you that you should regard as ratified what had been done concerning provision for our beloved son [Col. 0217D] Marzucco, a cleric—to whom, by special favour, we had granted that he might retain the benefice of your church together with its place until the bishopric of Massa should happen to be restored to a better condition [Col. 0218A]—and that you should not prevent him from freely possessing that benefice according to our concession, nor permit him, so far as lay in your power, to be hindered by others: you, turning deaf ears alike to our prayers and command, after our first letters had been sent to you, removed his bed from the dormitory; after the second, one of you occupied the place where he had lain; after the third, you alleged that you would not answer on this matter unless you had consulted the other canons of Tuscany, and that the Church of Massa, peace having been received, had been restored to a better state.

But because we are unwilling, and ought not, to allow our command, so often repeated, to be evaded, we command you by these apostolic letters [Col. 0218B] and strictly order you in virtue of obedience that you in no way delay to restore to him, within fifteen days, everything received from his benefice after you received our first letters; and that henceforth you do not trouble him concerning that place and benefice, but allow him to possess it peacefully. Otherwise, any opponents shall be suspended from office and benefice, and, in order to make satisfaction to us for their contempt, shall present themselves before us within a month.

Given at the Lateran, the eleventh day before the Calends of June, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXIII. To the dean and chapter of Bourges.—Concerning the canonization of St William, Archbishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0218D] See epistle CLII above.]. (Year 1212. Lateran, 27 May.)

[LABBE, *Bibliothèque des manuscrits*, II, 391, from the archive of the chapter of Bourges.]

[Col. 0218C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Bourges: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with paternal kindness the letters which you sent to our apostolic office concerning the enrolment in the catalogue of saints of William, your late archbishop of pious memory; and we commend your devotion in the Lord, because you aspire with such desire to advance this undertaking. But since the most holy Roman Church is accustomed to proceed in this matter, as one very arduous and belonging rather to divine than human judgment, with much deliberation [Col. 0218D], we have not thought fit to proceed in it at present. Rather, we have decreed that we must still wait, so that He who, as is believed, glorified him in heaven [Col. 0219A] may glorify him further upon earth, to the glory and honour of His name, in such a manner that we may proceed more securely to carry out the aforesaid undertaking.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Calends of June, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXIV. To the dean and chapter of St Theobald of Metz.—Under threat of anathema, he prohibits any cleric of the greater church from presuming to hold a prebend in their church. (Year 1212. Lateran, 27 November.)

[*History of Metz*, III, 171, from the archives of the collegiate church of St Theobald.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and entire chapter of St Theobald of Metz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0219B] When something just and honourable is sought from us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought, through the care of our office, to its due effect—especially where what has been newly planted by the pious generosity of the faithful for service to God ought to be more abundantly filled with the dew of our protection and assistance. Therefore, beloved sons, favourably assenting to your just petition, indulgently regarding your new foundation, and providing for your future tranquillity and peace, we decree by command and prohibit under threat of anathema that no cleric who has obtained a canonical prebend in the greater church shall seek a prebend in your church or presume to hold one; for he would seem to be drawn rather [Col. 0219C] by love of receiving revenues than by a favourable devotion to serve God or a poor church. Moreover, if any ecclesiastical person, knowing this enactment of ours, should rashly attempt to act against it and presume to trouble you, then, if after a second or third warning he does not comply and make fitting satisfaction for the disturbance inflicted, let him know that he is bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Calends of December, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXV. To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, legate of the Apostolic See.—On behalf of the chapter of Genoa. (Year 1213. Lateran, 11 January.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 882.]

[Col. 0219D]

INNOCENT, etc., to the venerable brother . . . . . Patriarch [Col. 0220A] of Jerusalem, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.
