Since the Council of Carthage prohibits any bishop from presuming to accept anything for the small quantity of balsam, blessed for the sacrament of baptism, which is given to churches, we are astonished that, as has come to the hearing of our apostolic office, our venerable brother . . . . the bishop, and our beloved sons the chapter of the Church of St Lawrence at Acre, deny the supply of chrism without payment to the church which our beloved sons the chapter of Genoa declare that they possess at Acre. Since the religion of ecclesiastical propriety abhors such trafficking, as contrary to sacred enactments, we have commanded the said bishop and chapter to desist from so shameful and forbidden a commerce and henceforth [Col. 0220B] to grant chrism freely to the said church. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters effectively to admonish and induce them to do this. And you, brother Patriarch, take care to watch in such a way over yourself and the flock entrusted to you, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of January, in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXVI. To the bishop and chapter of Acre.—Of the same subject as the preceding letter. (Year 1213. Lateran, 11 January.)

[Ibid.]

INNOCENT, etc., to the venerable brother . . . bishop, and beloved sons the chapter of Acre: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0220C] Since the Council of Carthage prohibits, etc., as above.

CLXXVII. To the abbots of St Faron [Note: [Col. 0219D] The monastery of St Faron was then governed by Reginald I; his name appears in very many records from 1214 through 1234. He is said to have died on the thirteenth day before the Calends of June, according to the Necrology. *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1693.] and of Cavea [Note: [Col. 0219D] Herbert, abbot of St Mary at Cavea, also Chagia or Cagia, appears in instruments from 1200 through 1219. Ibid., col. 1717.] and the dean [Note: [Col. 0219D] Ralph, dean of Meaux, is found as early as 1202 and 1203. In 1207, appointed judge by the supreme pontiff together with Geoffrey, bishop of Senlis, and Adam, abbot of Carolus-locus, he settled in September the dispute which had arisen between Odo, bishop of Paris, and the monks [Col. 0220D] of St Denis concerning Argenteuil. He is also mentioned in 1213 and 1214. He is commemorated in the Necrology on 24 July. Ibid., col. 1665.] of Meaux.—He grants them authority to inquire whether the abbot of Cluny was in fact compelled by violence to confer the priory of Benhard upon the son of the bailiff of the Count of Nevers. (Year 1213. Lateran, 23 January.)

[From the archives of the monastery of Cluny. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1150.]

The beloved son, the abbot of Cluny [Note: [Col. 0220D] This was William II, formerly prior of Cluny and of St Martin of the Fields, who was made abbot of Cluny in 1207. In 1214 or 1215, according to modern reckoning, after governing for seven years and the same number of months, he resigned on the Wednesday before Easter. He died in 1222, on the eleventh day before the Calends of October (according to the Sammarthani), or on the third day before the Calends of October (according to the Necrology of the New Monastery of Poitiers). *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1145.], stated in his complaint to us that, when formerly he had gone to the house of Charity and was kept shut up in the town of that place in such a way that access or return [Col. 0220D] of his monks and messengers to him could not be had except through Letheric, bailiff of the noble Count of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0220D] Compare Letters CXLIV and CXCIII of Book Fifteen.], in order to obtain this through the same bailiff, being pressed by necessity, the abbot, contrary to a constitution of the general chapter of Cluny established by apostolic authority, with the consent of the convent of Cluny, conferred the priory of Benhard, belonging to himself, upon Peter, a cleric and son of the said bailiff, to the grave injury of his monastery. He therefore humbly begged us to cause the aforesaid priory, after the truth of the fact had been established, to be restored to the ownership and right of the monastery through discreet men.

But since the foregoing has not been established to our satisfaction, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon those whom you know should be summoned for this purpose, hear the allegations on both sides, and, setting appeal aside, decide what is just; and, imposing canonical punishment upon the abbot himself as he deserves, cause what you decree to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure. If all of you cannot be present for carrying out these matters, nevertheless let two of you carry them out. And you, sons who are abbots, take care to watch in such a manner over yourselves [Col. 0221B] and over the flock entrusted to you, uprooting vices and planting virtues, that on the last day of strict judgment, before the dread Judge who will render to every person according to his deeds, you may be able to give a worthy account.

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Calends of February, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXVIII. To the prior and convent of the monastery of Noyon.—They are received under apostolic protection, and their possessions are confirmed [Note: [Col. 0221D] Compare Letter CXLVIII above.]. (Year 1213. Lateran, 29 March.)

[From the cartulary of Noyon. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1151.]

[Col. 0221C]

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious wishes and to bestow the favour of its benevolence upon the honourable petitions of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favourably assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all goods which you presently possess reasonably or may hereafter, by lawful means and with the Lord’s help, acquire. In particular, we confirm to you and, through you, to your aforesaid monastery, the granges of Barbi and Corni, and everything which you possess in Villeneuve, [Col. 0221D] just as you possess them rightly and peacefully; and we strengthen this grant by the protection of the present writing. Let absolutely no person, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our protection and confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty [Col. 0222A] God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Calends of April, in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXIX. To the dean [Note: [Col. 0221D] See the note to Letter CLXXXVIII of Book Eight.], J., archdeacon of Noyon, and the cantor of Noyon.—He grants them authority to examine the case between W. of Avesnes, on one side, and the Church of Liessies, on the other, concerning certain possessions. (Year 1213. Lateran, 24 May.)

[From the cartulary of the monastery of Liessies, written in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, fol. 68 ff. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0222B] When the procurators of our beloved sons the abbot and convent of Liessies [Note: [Col. 0221D]

Concerning the abbots of the monastery of Liessies in the period with which we are now concerned, the authors of the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 123, give these few particulars:

“VII. Simon, formerly provost of Lagny; deposed in 1194.

VIII. Hugh I, formerly a monk of St Vaast; he governed for three months.

[Col. 0222D] IX. Hugh II of Hestru, died 3 August 1213.”]

, on the one side, and of the nobleman W. of Avesnes on the other, were present before us, we granted as auditor our beloved son B., cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil [Note: [Col. 0222D] Bertrand, also Bertram, cardinal deacon of the title of St George in Velabro, also “at the Golden Veil,” was appointed by Pope Innocent III in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1212, at Rome, in the eighth creation. By command of Pope Honorius III he acted as legate in Gaul for three years against the Albigensians. He then returned to Italy and died under Pope Honorius III. Oldoinus, on Ciaconius, vol. II, col. 36.], before whom the procurator of the said abbot and convent alleged that, after the aforesaid W. had taken the cross intending to depart for the aid of the Holy Land, he had unjustly despoiled the said abbot and convent of Fania, Haia, Lescheres, and four other woods of Villers. The venerable brother, the bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0222D] See note to Letter XIX of Book Five.], diocesan of the place, since he had already learned through witnesses received on the matter by his official that they had been despoiled, [Col. 0222C] pronounced sentences of excommunication upon the nobleman himself, as his contumacy required, and of interdict upon his land.

The said W., however, obtained our letters against the same abbot and convent from the dean of St John at Bourg-Laon and his fellow judges, concerning certain woods of the place whose names were not stated, suppressing the truth. Two of those judges, by apostolic authority, ordered the dean of Avesnes to declare wholly invalid any sentence pronounced against W. or his land by authority of the aforesaid bishop or his official on the occasion of the said dispute; and nevertheless to cite the aforesaid abbot and convent to answer W. on a fixed day and at a fixed place before the same judges. From this manifest [Col. 0222D] grievance, since they sought to revoke the same sentences without prior warning or inquiry into the case, the often-mentioned abbot and convent appealed to our hearing.

Their procurator therefore requested that, after whatever had been attempted by those judges had been revoked as void, we should cause the aforesaid sentences [Col. 0223A] of excommunication and interdict, since they had been pronounced reasonably, to be firmly observed until fitting satisfaction had been made, all obstacle of appeal being removed; and that, through ecclesiastical censure, we should restrain the said W. from wrongs against the aforesaid abbot and convent, both concerning the woods themselves and concerning possessions and other things in which he repeatedly harassed them, and from vexations by his men, whom he oppressed with forced services and other unlawful exactions.

The answer on the other side was that, when the said W. had previously been sued by the named abbot and convent before the official of Cambrai, not by our delegation, concerning the spoliation of certain woods and other things, W.’s procurator, believing that he was being unjustly burdened by the official, lodged an appeal to us. Yet the official, disregarding even a lawful appeal, after letters from us had also been obtained by W. concerning his appeal, caused him to be declared excommunicated and placed his land under interdict. The dean of St John at Bourg and his fellow judges, to whom the nobleman had brought our letters concerning the same matter, decreeing those sentences wholly null, declared that the aforesaid nobleman and his land were not bound by the said sentences; and, wishing to inquire into the principal case, cited the same abbot and convent to appear before them. But they appealed to our hearing without reasonable cause [Col. 0223C].

When the said abbot and convent, cited a second time by the aforesaid judges, presented themselves before them, although the same judges offered to provide them with full justice in these matters, they nevertheless contumaciously withdrew from their presence. The nobleman’s procurator therefore requested that we remit the case for examination by the same judges. But because you could not be fully satisfied concerning these matters and the other things alleged before the aforesaid cardinal, we command you by apostolic letters, with the assent of the procurators of the parties, to summon the parties, hear the allegations on both sides, and, setting appeal aside, decide what is canonical; causing what you decide to be firmly observed through ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0223D]. If witnesses who have been named withdraw through favour, hatred, or fear, compel them by the same censure, all appeal being removed, to give testimony to the truth. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See shall stand in the way, except those obtained with the assent of the parties. If not all of you can be present for carrying out these matters, nevertheless let two of you carry them out.

Given at the Lateran, the ninth day before the Calends of June, in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXX. He receives the monastery of St Peter of Chartres under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Year 1213. Segni, 9 July.)

[GUÉRARD, *Cartulary of Saint-Père of Chartres*, II, 677.]

[Col. 0224A]

INNOCENT, bishop, etc.

We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and monastery . . . together with all that it presently possesses reasonably . . .; and, in particular, we confirm . . . Gisez, Trahone, Braioto, Châteaudun, Bosvilla, and the other priories with their appurtenances. . . .

Given at Segni, the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXI. To the prelates, nobles, and people of Ireland.—That they may persevere in fidelity to the King of England and his heirs. (Year 1213. Lateran, 28 October.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 116, from the original in the treasury of the Receipt of the Exchequer.]

[Col. 0224B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers archbishops and bishops, and beloved sons the abbots and other prelates of churches, and the noblemen, princes, counts, barons, and all knights and peoples established throughout Ireland: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, through the grace of Him who joined together in Himself, as the cornerstone, walls formerly at variance, true peace and complete [Col. 0224C] concord have been restored between kingdom and priesthood in England, we—who are bound to exercise special care and concern for our dearest son in Christ John, illustrious King of the English, and for his kingdom, which by his own grant is known to belong by special right to the Roman Church—wishing to provide for him and his heirs, command and order you by apostolic letters that you take care to persevere with ready mind and sincere heart in fidelity to the king himself and to his heirs, showing yourselves in every way so disposed toward his service that you may deservedly be commended both by us and by him, knowing for certain that we earnestly seek his advantage and honour.

[Col. 0224D] Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Calends of November, in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXII. To the abbot of St Michael of the Castle of the Britons. (Year 1213. Lateran, 22 November.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of the Abbey of Nonantola*, II, 351, from the autograph.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of St Michael of the Castle of the Britons, in the diocese of Bologna [Note: [Col. 0223D] The monastery of St Michael of Castel de’ Britti, in the diocese of Bologna, once belonged to the Camaldolese Order; then, in 1262, it was given to the Frati Godenti. See *Annali Camaldolesi*, vol. V, p. 61, etc.; Melloni, *Acts concerning the Saints of Bologna*, vol. II, p. 62, etc.] and Master T. [Note: [Col. 0223D] This is the celebrated canonist Tancred, who later became a canon and archdeacon of Bologna. The learned Father Abbot Sarti did not begin to find references to him before the year 1214 (*On the Learned Men of the University of Bologna*, vol. I, part II, p. 29). This charter therefore brings the evidence forward by one year and at the same time informs us that, before obtaining his canonry at Bologna, he had a canonry in the church of St Lawrence on the Hill.] [Col. 0225A], doctor of decretals, canon of St Lawrence on the Hill, resident at Bologna: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved sons the abbot and convent of Nonantola stated in a petition sent to us that, when one of their monks was celebrating funeral rites for a deceased person who had chosen burial in the church of St Bartholomew at Spilamberto, which belongs to them by right, the archpriest of the church of St Martin and his accomplices, of the diocese of Modena, laid violent hands upon the monk, not permitting him to celebrate the office for the deceased. When they hoped that this grievance would be relieved through our venerable brother, the bishop of Modena, he added further wrongs to the former ones [Col. 0225B], pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against the vassals of the monastery of Nonantola and all persons who should thereafter choose burial in the aforesaid church.

Therefore, unwilling that the rights of the same monastery should perish, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you publicly declare the said perpetrators of violence excommunicated, all appeal being set aside, and cause them to be avoided by all until they have made fitting satisfaction to the injured party and have come to the Apostolic See to be absolved, bearing testimony from your letters. Moreover, restrain the aforesaid bishop and archpriest from undue harassment of the monastery, lawfully revoking the aforesaid sentence of excommunication [Col. 0225C], with the obstacle of appeal removed. And you, son abbot, take care to watch in such a manner over yourself and the flock entrusted to you, uprooting vices and planting virtues, that on the last day of strict judgment before the dread Judge, who will render to every person according to his deeds, you may be able to give a worthy account.

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Calends of December, in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXIII. To the Bishop of Pistoia and the Abbot of the Holy Trinity of Florence.—In the case between Soffredo, Bishop of Pistoia, and the commune of Pistoia concerning jurisdiction over certain castles. (Year 1214. Lateran, 13 February.)

[ZACHARIA, *Anecdota of the Middle Ages*, Turin, 1755, folio, p. 350.]

[Col. 0225D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother the bishop and beloved son the abbot of the Holy Trinity of Florence: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The case known to be in litigation between the consuls, councillors, and commune of Pistoia on the one hand, and our venerable brother . . . the bishop on the other, concerning jurisdiction over certain castles and men and other things, was obtained by the said bishop to be delegated by us to you, brother bishop. But, in order that judgment may proceed without suspicion, we associate you, son abbot, with the hearing of the case at the request of the other party, and command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 0226A] that in this business you proceed according to the tenor of the earlier letters, with appeal set aside and after due inquiry. And you, brother bishop and son abbot, take care to watch in such a manner over yourselves and the flock entrusted to you, uprooting vices and planting virtues, that on the last day of strict judgment before the dread Judge, who will render to every person according to his deeds, you may be able to give a worthy account.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of February, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXIV. To the abbot and brethren of St Denis.—He receives them under protection and confirms their possessions. (Year 1214. Lateran, 29 March.)

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 543.]

[Col. 0226B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of St Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing, etc.

We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons and the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all goods which you presently possess reasonably or may hereafter, by lawful means and with the Lord’s help, acquire. In particular, we confirm to you and, through you, to your aforesaid monastery, the grange of Chaneueriis and the tithes of Longolio, just as you possess them rightly and peacefully; and we strengthen this grant by the protection of the present writing.

[Col. 0226C] Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Calends of April, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXV. To John, King of the English.—He declares that neither the king nor his chapel may be placed under interdict or excommunicated without a special mandate of the Apostolic See. (Year 1214. Rome, at St Peter’s, 15 April.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 119, from the original in the treasury of the Receipt of the Exchequer.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ JOHN, illustrious King of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The abundant kindness of the Apostolic See is accustomed to pursue with benevolent favour the wishes of faithful persons who render sincere obedience, and more fittingly to adorn with certain honours the persons of illustrious men whom it finds ready and fervent [Col. 0226D] in their devotion. Therefore, in order that, from the special devotion which you are known to have toward the Roman Church and our person, you may perceive that apostolic favour has increased toward you, we decree that your person cannot be excommunicated by anyone, nor your chapel placed under interdict, without a special mandate of the Apostolic See.

You therefore must endeavour so to conduct yourself in these matters that injuries may not arise from the place whence rights arise, and that through abuse—God forbid—you may not be deprived of such a benefit. [The intervening text is materially fragmentary: “me . . . pria . . . juxta . . . cea . . . sanctiones privilegium . . . re . . . tur amittere”; the surviving sense is: “... according to ... enactments, [he] ... deserves to lose the privilege, who abuses the power permitted to him.”]

Let absolutely no person, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page [Col. 0227A] of our enactment or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, the seventeenth day before the Calends of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXVI. To John, King of England.—Concerning a truce to be made between the Kings of England and France. (Year 1214. Rome, at St Peter’s, 22 April.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 120. Patent Roll, 16 John, membrane 17d, in the Tower of London.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ JOHN, illustrious King of the English [Col. 0227B]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the aid of the Holy Land, for which we most ardently strive for the salvation of the Christian people, is impeded by the war being waged between you and our dearest son in Christ Philip, illustrious King of the French, and since innumerable other dangers are feared as likely to arise from it, we, moved by the duty of service of the Apostolic See, intend to intervene for the restoration of peace. We firmly enjoin upon you and upon the aforesaid King of the French—compelling you through ecclesiastical censure, if necessary—that, in order to avoid such great and numerous dangers, you enter into and observe a truce with one another at least until after the general council is held, matters remaining in the condition [Col. 0227C] in which they shall be when the truce itself is confirmed by the parties.

And let two mediators of peace, without malice, be chosen, who shall faithfully negotiate in the meantime for the restoration of concord. If they cannot perhaps bring this about, then submit yourselves to our arbitration, after giving assurances in this regard, so that we ourselves may personally undertake the quelling of the discord.

Therefore we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Royal Serenity in the Lord that, after prudent deliberation on these matters, you do not delay to reply to us through a suitable messenger.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, the tenth day before the Calends of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXVII. To all the clergy of the province of Bremen.—That they publicly declare Waldemar excommunicated. (Year 1214. Rome, at St Peter’s, 30 April.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, p. 344, from the original with the attached lead seal of Pope Innocent III, in box II, no. 10.]

[Col. 0227D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbots, priors, provosts, deans, archdeacons, and other prelates of churches established throughout the province of Bremen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since Waldemar, son of perdition, like a heretic and schismatic, despises canonical censure and regards the keys of the Church as nothing, and, though excommunicated and deposed, presumes to exercise episcopal [Col. 0228A] functions, we strictly command your discretion by apostolic letters that you publicly announce in your churches that the aforesaid Waldemar has been degraded, and that both he and his supporters are excommunicated. And you, sons who are abbots, take care to watch in such a manner over yourselves and the flock entrusted to you, uprooting vices and planting virtues, that on the last day of strict judgment before the dread Judge, who will render to every person according to his deeds, you may be able to give a worthy account.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, the third day before the Calends of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CLXXXVIII. To the peoples of the duchy of Spoleto.—That they should furnish aid and support to Aldrovandino, Marquis of Este and Ancona. (A.D. 1214. Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 5.)

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, I, 327.]

[Col. 0228B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all our faithful established throughout the duchy of Spoleto, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since our beloved son, the nobleman A. [Aldrovandino], Marquis of Este, has, by our counsel and command, entered the March of Ancona in order to restore it to the dominion of the Roman Church and hold it for that Church, we ask, require, and admonish your whole community, commanding you by these apostolic letters, that, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for ourselves, [Col. 0228C] you render him such counsel and assistance in this matter that you may bind him the more firmly to your service, and that we may deservedly commend your devotion for the service rendered us in his person.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

I, Daniel, notary of Rovigo, copied and wrote these letters of the pope at the command of Lord Andrea of Macerata, viscount of Rovigo, for Lord Obizzo, Marquis of Este, adding or subtracting nothing that might alter their sense or meaning, except perhaps a letter or a point in the joining of syllables; in the year of the Lord 1292, indiction V, on the fourteenth day of April.

CLXXXIX. To the podestà and people of the March of Ancona.—That they should obey Aldrovandino, Marquis of Este and Ancona. (A.D. 1214. Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 5.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0228D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the podestà and people of Ancona, the spirit of sounder counsel.

Since our beloved son, the nobleman A., Marquis of Este, has, by our counsel and command, entered the March of Ancona in order to restore it to the dominion of the Roman Church and hold it for that Church, we command you by the authority of these present letters that, wholly withdrawing from the following of the reprobate, accursed, and excommunicated Otto [Col. 0229A] and his supporters, and returning to the Roman Church, your mother, you shall faithfully adhere to that marquis out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for ourselves. You shall humbly comply with him in matters known to belong to the marquis’s right, fully answering to him; and you shall furnish him counsel and assistance so vigorously that it may redound to his and our glory and honour. Since we have firm confidence that, out of reverence for us, he will treat you humanely and kindly, we may deservedly commend your devotion and fidelity. Otherwise, by our letters we give command and instruction to our beloved son R., subdeacon and chaplain, rector of Massa and legate of the Apostolic See, that, setting aside appeal, [Col. 0229B] he compel you to do this as he sees expedient.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXC. To Philip, King of the Franks.—That the king shall no longer tolerate usury in his realm. (A.D. 1214. Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 14.)

[D. d’ACHERY, *Spicileg.*, III, 577.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our dearest son in Christ, PHILIP, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As the soul is better than the body, so spiritual things must be preferred to temporal things. Therefore temporal advantage is not to be sought with spiritual harm, lest spiritual danger arise from the very place from which temporal gain is sought, as Truth testifies when it says: “What profit is it to a man if he gain the whole world, but suffer loss to his soul?” (Matt. 16).

Accordingly, having heard the letters which you and certain of your barons sent against our beloved son R., priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill and legate of the Apostolic See, containing various complaints concerning several matters, we immediately caused both the complaints lodged against that legate and his replies to be set out. We send these enclosed in the present letters, [Col. 0229D] as reasonably moderated, with this brief answer to Your Serenity: although that legate did not receive from us a special mandate concerning usurers, nevertheless the plague of usury has increased in your realm beyond the usual measure, so devouring and consuming the resources of churches, knights, and many others that, unless an effective remedy were applied to so great a malady, they would not be able to contribute to the aid of the Holy Land. For this reason we judged that he should be specially sent. Accordingly, as a spiritual physician, [Col. 0230A] he has, by the counsel of prudent men in various councils, found a salutary remedy for souls against this deadly plague.

Therefore it does not befit your royal prudence—which among the other secular princes is distinguished by the title of Christianity—to obstruct spiritual progress for any temporal advantage, as we regret that you have done by certain letters sent to various communes. We have caused those letters to be enclosed with this page, so that you may retract them upon more prudent counsel. We exhort Your Royal Serenity neither to hinder nor permit hindrance to the exercise of ecclesiastical jurisdiction in your realm. For we command the aforesaid legate that in these matters he shall still employ, so far as he can with God, the necessary moderation, lest in anything [Col. 0230B] he exceed the proper measure; he is not to alter honourable customs and reasonable usages, while reserving the final adjustment of all matters for a general council. We therefore will and command that meanwhile this business proceed modestly on both sides, because then, with the approval of the sacred council, we shall determine concerning these matters and others what we see to be expedient spiritually and temporally.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the second day before the Ides of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCI. To the Master and Brothers of the Order of the Temple.—He absolves them from the claim of the abbot and monastery of Cluny concerning a contract of sale by which the priory of La Charité was said to have been seriously injured.  
[Note: [Col. 0229D] On the subject of this letter, Letters CXCIV and CXLII of Book XV must certainly be consulted.]  
(A.D. 1214. Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 15.)

[From the archive of the Abbey of Cluny. BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1153.]

[Col. 0230C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the master and brothers of the Order of the Temple, greeting and apostolic blessing.

J., syndic, and certain monks of Cluny, appearing before us, alleged that the priory of La Charité, which belongs directly to the Church of Cluny without intermediary, had been enormously injured by the alienation of certain possessions, revenues, and other property which you had bought from it. They requested that we should deign either to revoke such a contract or to restore the monastery itself to its former condition on account of minority. [Col. 0230D] You, on the other hand, requested that the same contract, as lawfully and solemnly concluded, be confirmed by apostolic authority, both at the request of the abbot  
[Note: [Col. 0229D] See the note on Letter CLXVII above.]  
and convent of Cluny, whose authority and consent had intervened in the matter, and of the prior  
[Note: [Col. 0229D] This was William III, who, according to some, was substituted for Geoffrey as prior of Cluny in 1212. See the Letters of Book XV cited above.]  
and convent of La Charité, who asked the same through their letters.

Because the merits and circumstances of the contract were not fully clear to us, we committed the matter for investigation to our venerable brother . . . , bishop of Paris,  
[Note: [Col. 0230D] Peter II of Nemours, called the Chamberlain, son of Walter I, lord of La Chapelle-en-Brie, Villebéon, and Tournanfuye, Chamberlain of France, and Aveline of Nemours. From the treasurership of Tours he was called to the see of Paris in 1208. He died at Damietta in 1218. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 87.]  
and his fellow judges, making mention in the letters of inquiry of letters previously sent concerning the decline of that priory to our venerable brother . . . , Archbishop of Sens, [Col. 0231A]  
[Note: [Col. 0231D] See the note on Letter XLV of Book III.]  
and his fellow judges. Both sets of judges proceeded in execution of the apostolic mandate.

Later, when the parties appeared before us, you earnestly requested confirmation of the contract, while the other party made manifold efforts to challenge it. Because we could not be fully convinced by the matters which the parties sought to advance in support of their respective claims, we instructed our beloved sons . . . , abbot of Sainte-Geneviève of Paris,  
[Note: [Col. 0231D] See the note on Letter XLV of Book III.]  
and . . . , abbot of Bon-Repos,  
[Note: [Col. 0231D] “X. William II, abbot of Bon-Repos, in the years [Col. 0232D] 1205 and 1215, from the charter collection of Calais. He is perhaps the W. recorded there as abbot of Bon-Repos in 1227.” *Nova Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, col. 457.]  
together with . . . , dean of Orléans,  
[Note: [Col. 0232D] Fulk II, dean of Orléans, from 1205 to 1216. Ibid., vol. VIII, col. 1505.]  
that, having carefully heard whatever the parties should present before them within four months from the term set by the prior of La Charité, [Col. 0231B] if it were shown that the priory of La Charité had suffered enormous injury from the sale itself, they should restore it on account of minority and lawfully rescind the oft-mentioned contract; otherwise, they should cause it to be held valid and firm, restraining opponents through ecclesiastical censure.

When the monks’ party failed to prove what it had advanced within the stated term, the judges confirmed the contract by apostolic authority. Finally, our beloved sons Christian, your cleric, and Elias, the procurators of the respective parties, again appeared before us on this account. Your procurator urgently requested that the contract [Col. 0231C] be strengthened by apostolic protection. The opposing party alleged that the abbot of Cluny had been prevented, by the rebellion of the monks of La Charité—who violently expelled him from the monastery before the summons could reach him—from proving his case before the aforesaid judges. For he was unable to produce as witnesses monks and inhabitants of that place who knew the quantity and value of the possessions sold, since they had become rebels. It requested that the proceedings of the aforesaid judges be annulled, as unlawfully undertaken after an appeal to us had been lawfully lodged.

We therefore instructed our beloved sons . . . , abbot of Charlieu,  
[Note: [Col. 0232D] Adam, abbot of Charlieu, is known from documents from 1207 through 1217. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1510.]  
. . . , cantor of Meaux, and Master P. Peverelli, canon of Paris, [Col. 0231D] to proceed in the matter in question notwithstanding the aforesaid proceedings, in accordance with the tenor of the earlier letters.

Before them, your side requested that the other party specify the amount and particulars of the said injury. When its procurator refused to do so, and the judges had ruled [Col. 0232A] that such specification must be made, the said procurator appealed to the Apostolic See. Later, the abbot and convent of Cluny renounced that appeal and requested that their proofs be received. Your party, among other urgent requests, asked that the consent of the prior and monks of La Charité be sought, lest the judgment be illusory. The abbot and convent endeavoured to show that this ought by no means to be done, and again appealed to the Apostolic See. The period of time contained in our letters expired, they having proved nothing on the principal issue. You repeatedly and urgently requested the judges to confirm the contract of the aforesaid sale in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic rescript.

[Col. 0232B] Since they did not undertake to do this, you sent our beloved son Brother Umbert and the same procurator to the Apostolic See on this account. When they and our beloved son the abbot of Cluny appeared before us, we, having more fully understood these and the other matters which they advanced, by counsel of our brethren pronounced you absolved from the claim of the said abbot and monastery of Cluny, imposing perpetual silence on this matter. We do not, however, wish prejudice to arise from this against the monks of La Charité, whose consent was not sought at your party’s request; for, according to lawful enactments, a matter done between some persons ought not prejudice others.

Therefore let no person at all infringe this page of our decision [Col. 0232C] or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Ides of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCII. To the bishops and prelates of the March of Ancona.—That they should provide counsel and assistance to Aldrovandino, Marquis of Este and Ancona, for the recovery of the same March. (A.D. 1214. Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 23.)

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, I, 328.]

[Col. 0232D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops and his beloved sons the abbots and other prelates of churches established throughout the March of Ancona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since our beloved son, the nobleman Al., Marquis of Este, has, by our counsel and command, entered [Col. 0233A] the March of Ancona in order to restore it to the dominion of the Roman Church and hold it for that Church, we command your whole body by the authority of these present letters that, standing manfully by him and faithfully complying with him as with a marquis, you render him counsel and aid so effectively that it may deservedly be pleasing to us and to him and that your fidelity and prudence may thereby be commended.

Finally, brothers bishops and sons abbots, take care to watch over yourselves and the flocks entrusted to you, uprooting vices and planting virtues, so that on the last day of strict judgment, before the dreadful Judge who will render to each according to his works, you may be able to give a worthy account.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0233B] of June, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCIII. To the peoples of the March of Ancona.—That they should be compliant and obedient to Aldrovandino, Marquis of Este and Ancona. (A.D. 1214. Rome, at St. Peter’s, May 23.)

[Ibid., 329.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all persons established throughout the March of Ancona, the spirit of sounder counsel.

Since the reprobate Otto and his chief supporters, especially those who oppose us concerning the patrimony of the Church, [Col. 0233C] are bound by the chain of excommunication; since all have been released from the allegiance which they had rendered to Otto; and since divine judgment has already been made manifest against Otto and his accomplices, we wonder that certain among you are so heedless of the future that they do not fear even now to adhere to Otto and his supporters, blinded as they are and acting against the keys of the Church.

Therefore, since our beloved son, the nobleman Al., Marquis of Este, has, by our counsel and command, entered the March of Ancona in order to restore it to the dominion of the Roman Church and hold it for that Church, we command your whole body by the authority of these present letters that, wholly withdrawing from the following of the said Otto and his supporters and returning to the Roman [Col. 0233D] Church, your mother, you shall faithfully adhere to that marquis out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for ourselves. You shall humbly comply with him in matters known to belong to the marquis’s right, fully answering to him, and you shall furnish him counsel and assistance so vigorously that it may redound to his and our glory and honour. Since we have firm confidence that the same marquis, out of reverence for us, will treat you humanely and kindly, we may deservedly commend your devotion and fidelity.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCIV. To the prior and monks of St. Mary of the Fields of Corbeil.—He confirms their possessions and privileges. (A.D. 1214. Lateran, May 29.)

[DOUBLET, *Hist. de Saint-Denys en France*, p. 543.]

[Col. 0234A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and monks of St. Mary of the Fields of Corbeil, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the persons and monastery of St. Mary of the Fields of Corbeil, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all the ecclesiastical and temporal goods which you now lawfully possess or may hereafter, God granting, acquire by just means. [Col. 0234B] In particular, we confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery by apostolic authority the tithe of the place called Desplanis, lands, vineyards, woods, and your other goods, as you justly and peacefully possess them all.

Therefore let no person at all infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, or rashly oppose it; but if anyone presume to attempt this, [Col. 0234C] etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCV. To the abbot of Cluny.  
[Note: [Col. 0233D] See above the note on Letter CLXVII.]  
—That, notwithstanding appeals unlawfully lodged by his monks, he may punish their offences. (A.D. 1214. Viterbo, June 23.)

[We publish this bull on the authority of a copy which Lord Lambert de Barive caused to be faithfully transcribed from the archive of the monastery of Cluny and deposited in our document repository. He appended to the end of the copy this note: “We have seen, under the seals of the Judge of the Court of Cluny and of that of the Archdeacon of the same place, issued and signed by J. Bochi and de la Pelote, sworn notaries of the said courts, on 19 October 1428, a Bull of Innocent III, issued at Viterbo on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventeenth year of his pontificate—that is, in 1214—providing that the Abbot of Cluny shall have the right of correction over religious persons notwithstanding their appeal to the Holy See, both concerning the faults and scandals which they might commit and concerning the power to punish them by deprivation of their priories, etc.; parchment, sealed with two seals.

“We, the Judge of the Court of Cluny, and we, the Archdeacon of the same place, make known to all who inspect these present letters that we have seen and read, and have caused to be read and collated word for word by our sworn notaries named below, certain apostolic letters of the lord Pope Innocent III of happy memory, sealed with threads of yellow and red silk in the manner of the Roman Church; sound and entire, neither spoiled, cancelled, erased, nor obliterated, nor suspect in any part, but wholly free from every defect and suspicion, containing the form which follows. In testimony of this inspection, since the foregoing is known to us through the faithful report of the sworn notaries of our courts named below, whom we trust and to whose report we give full credit, after they had diligently collated the present transcript or copy with the original letters transcribed above, we have ordered our seals to be affixed to these present letters. Given also for such inspection on the nineteenth day of October in the year of the Lord 1428. The collation was made by us, the notaries named below, of the said original letters with the present transcript or *vidimus*, with our following manual signs as witnesses, in the year and on the day stated above. Signed: Jean Bochi and J. de la Pelote, with flourish.” BRÉQUIGNY, ibid., p. 1155.]

[Col. 0234D]

[Col. 0235B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your devotion has humbly petitioned us that, since grave dissensions and scandals and very many disorders often arise from appeals by monks of your order, because some make appeals merely to frustrate the removal of priories which they waste or the punishment of their offences, we should mercifully grant that no monk of your order may be able to appeal from you in such a fashion. Since the remedy of appeal was devised not as an evasion for the malicious but as a safeguard for the innocent, we grant your devotion by the authority of these present letters [Col. 0235C] that, notwithstanding such appeals, you shall exercise the office of correction over delinquent monks.

Therefore let no person at all infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Viterbo, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCVI. To the people of the city of Ascoli.—That they should no longer refuse to render obedience to Aldrovandino, Marquis of Este and Ancona. (A.D. 1214. Viterbo, September 11.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0235D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the podestà and people of Ascoli, the spirit of sounder counsel.

Since He who resists the proud and breaks the horns of sinners, setting bounds to the sea which its waves may not pass, but against which, beaten back, they overflow into trampling and mire, has abhorred the ingratitude and detested the pride of the reprobate Otto and, by His power, overthrown him—Otto who strove to turn you away from the fidelity and devotion due to the most holy Roman Church, your mother, repaying us in these and other ways hatred for love, offence for favour, and injury for honour—and since we, having released you from the oath which you are said to have sworn to him as unlawful, [Col. 0236A] have solemnly invested our beloved son, the nobleman Al., Marquis of Ancona and Este, with that March by the banner: we wonder, and cannot sufficiently wonder, that you, led by we know not what prudence or relying upon what strength, still lean upon a broken staff and delay returning to the lordship of that Church, your mother; and that you refuse to render the aforesaid marquis oaths of fidelity. By this difficulty in returning you now deserve more blame than you deserved even by departing, since the latter seems to have been done under compulsion, whereas the former is plainly voluntary.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and exhort your whole community, firmly commanding you by these apostolic letters that, without hesitation, you return from the pathless way to the way and turn [Col. 0236B] from the left to the right. Render oaths of fidelity to the said marquis—who will treat you mercifully and kindly—with such cheerfulness and willingness that he may deservedly be moved to love you, and we may be prompted not only to forget the preceding offence but also to show favour and grace.

Given at Viterbo, on the third day before the Ides of September, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCVII. To Eustace de Vesci.—He commands that the King of England suffer no injury because of the discord now at last settled between him and the barons. (A.D. 1214. Lateran, November 5.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 126, from the original in the Tower of London.]

[Col. 0236C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman Eustace DE VESCI, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the grace of Him who made both one, joining the discordant walls together in Himself as the one cornerstone, the discord which formerly prevailed in England between kingdom and priesthood has been entirely settled—the occasion of which is said to have produced confederacies and conspiracies—and since, peace having been restored and concord re-established, the effect ought to cease with its cause, we remember having instructed the earls, barons, and other nobles established throughout England to persevere with sincere heart and pure mind in loyalty to our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious King of the English, and his heirs, conducting themselves in every respect [Col. 0236D] toward his service in such a way as to deserve commendation from both us and him.

Therefore, that this mandate may attain a more effective force, we command your nobility by apostolic letters that, under pretext of those confederacies and conspiracies, you place no obstacle of difficulty in the king’s affairs; neither yourself hindering, nor, so far as lies in your power, permitting others to hinder, the justiciars and other officials of the same king from effectively carrying out the offices entrusted to them.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of November, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

CXCVIII. To Nicholas, Bishop of Tusculum.—Concerning the relaxation of the interdict. (A.D. 1214. Lateran.)

[*Recueil des historiens de France*, vol. XVII, p. 713.]

[Col. 0237A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

Our venerable brother John, bishop of Norwich, and our beloved son Robert Richard de Marisco, archdeacon of Northumbria, together with the noblemen Thomas of Huntingdon and Adam, envoys of our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious King of the English, on the one side; and Master Stephen [corrected to Simon], A. and G., clerical envoys of our venerable brother Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the other side, appearing before us, [Col. 0237B] jointly and firmly asserted that, in order to avoid great loss of property and grave peril to souls, it was exceedingly expedient for both kingdom and priesthood that the sentence of interdict be relaxed without delay.

Therefore we, solicitous in paternal affection, diligently negotiated with them, for the salvation and benefit of all, concerning the things belonging to peace; and at last, with their acquiescence, found and established the form set forth below. The aforesaid king shall cause such a sum of money to be assigned to the Archbishop of Canterbury and the bishops of London and Ely, or to others whom they may wish to appoint for this purpose, counting the payments which the same king is known to have made, that the total may amount to forty thousand marks. [Col. 0237C] Once these have been paid and the security noted below has been furnished, you shall immediately relax the sentence of interdict, every obstacle of appeal and condition—or perhaps, “contradiction”—being removed. Thereafter the king shall cause twelve thousand marks to be delivered to the same persons every year in two instalments: namely, six thousand marks at the commemoration of All Saints, and an equal sum on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, at the church of St. Paul in London, until the entire sum has been paid.

For the faithful performance of this he shall bind himself by his own oath and by letters patent fortified with his seal, and also by the suretyship of the bishops of Winchester and Norwich, the earls of Chester and Winchester, and William Marshal; so that both the heirs [Col. 0237D] of the king and their successors shall be bound. Wherefore we command you by apostolic letters that you do not postpone proceeding in accordance with the form set out above, unless the parties, of their own pure and free will, decide to settle otherwise.

Given at the Lateran . . . .  
[Note: [Col. 0237D] These letters do not exist in Innocent’s Register, nor among the acts of T. Rymer.]

CXCIX. Letter of O., scholastic of Cologne and legate of the Apostolic See, to the illustrious Count of Namur.—Concerning various appearances of crosses while he was preaching the cross, and the multitude of those who took the cross in the province of Cologne. (A.D. 1214.)

[MARTÈNE, *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 1115, from a manuscript of St. Lawrence of Liège.]

[Col. 0238A]

To the illustrious Count of Namur and his noble wife, O., scholastic of Cologne,  
[Note: [Col. 0237D] Oliver, scholastic of Cologne, a very pious and eloquent man, who by authority of the supreme pontiff preached the cross in Frisia, Brabant, Flanders, and neighbouring provinces with great success, together with his disciple Arnold. His letter to Engelbert, Archbishop of Cologne, concerning the capture of Damietta, is found in Bongars. Caesarius of Heisterbach and Albert of Stade write of him.]  
legate of the Apostolic See, present and future salvation.

When I was near the ocean at the edge of the province of Cologne, in the diocese of Münster, on the Friday before Pentecost in the year of grace 1214,  
[Note: [Col. 0238D] Odoricus Raynaldus, from Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, chapter sixty of his history, assigns to this year the following event: while the abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian Order, was zealously exhorting people in the diocese of Rodez, outside the doors of a church—because the narrowness of the place could not contain the multitude—to enroll their names for the army of those who had taken the cross, a cross suddenly appeared in the air before all present, seeming to extend toward the region of Toulouse.]  
and the abbots of the Cistercian, [Col. 0238B] Premonstratensian, and Cluniac orders, together with many other religious, were with me out of reverence for the lord pope, I caused a solemn Mass of the Holy Cross to be sung. The opening of my sermon was: “Far be it from me to glory,” etc. (Gal. 6).

While many thousands of men and women who had come to the sermon sat in a meadow outside the village in Frisia called Bethdum, and the sky was quite clear, a white cloud appeared. In it was a white cross without a human figure, toward the north; then another cross to the south, of the same colour and shape; and thirdly, between and above them, a great light of intermediate colour, having, as it seemed, the form of a human body, of a man’s size. Its outline was naked; its head was upward and its feet downward; [Col. 0238C] its head inclined toward its shoulder, and its arms were not stretched straight out, but raised upward. Nails were visibly apparent through its hands and feet in the same form in which they appear in a representation made by an artisan in a church.

When many ran forward to take the cross, a certain knight who had previously refused to receive it, as soon as he saw the cross, immediately took the cross. One of the inhabitants of the land, seeing this, ran swiftly to me and said, “Now the Holy Land has been recovered,” using the past for the future with almost prophetic certainty. A wealthy girl of eleven years rose to worship; but, compelled by the crowd to sit down, she pointed it out to her mother, grandmother, and many seated round about, who looked upward with great reverence and worshipped [Col. 0238D] for as long as the sign appeared.

This vision lasted for the duration of an appropriate Mass, about the third hour. More than one hundred persons saw this miracle. Later, at another station in the same region, a cross appeared without a human figure, having the colour of a rainbow not set against the sun. The abbot of the Valley [Note: [Col. 0239D] The Valley of St. Peter is a notable monastery of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Cologne, about [Col. 0240D] two hours distant from the city of Bonn, commonly called Heisterbach.]  
of St. Peter, one of his monks, and many of the people of Bethdum saw it.

Then, at another station on the feast day of St. Boniface, near the Frisian harbour called Dokkum, where blessed Boniface received the crown of martyrdom, a great cross appeared. We who were at the station [Col. 0239A] numbered, it is believed, more than ten thousand. The cross was white, and moved gradually in the air as though drawn by a cord, as if showing the route to pilgrims about to sail to the land of promise, between Europe and Africa.

Among the people in whom these events occurred, fifty thousand persons who had taken the cross are counted: eight thousand shield-bearers and one thousand men in mail. Know also that so many ships are being prepared for the expedition of Jesus Christ that we believe more than three hundred cargo ships from the province of Cologne alone [Col. 0239B] will set out, to be filled with fighting men, arms, provisions, and military equipment. We have written this to you because you have beneficially taken the cross for the service of Jesus Christ and, we hope, profitably for the Holy Land; earnestly asking you to show favour to those who have taken the cross and to the judges whom we have appointed at Namur. Farewell.

CC. Ordinance of Philip II concerning those who have taken the cross. (A.D. 1214.)

[D. d’ACHERY, *Spicileg.*, folio ed., III, 577.]

Know that through our beloved and faithful Peter, bishop of Paris, and Guarin, bishop of Senlis, with the assent of the lord legate, we have caused diligent inquiry to be made [Col. 0239C] into the manner in which Holy Church has customarily protected those who have taken the cross and their liberties. Having made this inquiry, they wish the following provisions to be observed, for the good of peace between kingdom and priesthood, until the impending Roman council.

No crusader who is a burgess or peasant, whether a merchant or not, shall be assessed a tallage in the first year in which he has taken the cross, unless the tallage was imposed before he took the cross; and if it was imposed in the first year, he shall be exempt in the second year, unless something is levied for the army. We understand a tallage to have been imposed when it has been announced to someone, or to his household, how much he must pay or contribute in tallage. Since it is established by the custom hitherto prevailing in the kingdom of France [Col. 0239D] that crusaders owe military service, unless they have been exempted by a special privilege of the lord king, we declare that every crusader among those mentioned above is bound to go on campaign, whether he took the cross before or after the summons, provided that he owes military service. If the king judges it expedient that a town send men on campaign, servants rather than those who are of the town shall go. The king may appropriately take from crusaders a payment for the army; but henceforth crusaders shall have the choice of going on campaign if they wish, or of putting their share into the *prisia* [assessment] made for redeeming military service. If they are burdened by the *prisia*, they shall have recourse to the diocesan bishop or his official.

But if a crusader has possessions liable to tallage, he shall pay the tallage as though he were not a crusader; and if he denies that the possessions owe tallage, the matter shall be proved before the diocesan bishop or his official. Concerning crusaders living in communes, we declare that, if the commune takes anything from them for the king’s army, for enclosing the town, for defending a town besieged by enemies, or for a debt of the commune incurred and sworn to be paid before they took the cross, they shall put in their share of the *prisia* just as non-crusaders do. But for a debt contracted by the commune after the assumption of the cross, he shall be exempt while on pilgrimage.

If the bailiffs of the lord king catch a crusader [Col. 0240B] in a flagrant offence for which, according to the custom of the secular court, he ought to be mutilated or lose his life, the Church shall not protect him or his property. But in other, lighter and lesser offences, for which he ought not to be mutilated or lose his life, the bailiff must not seize the crusader’s person or goods, or keep him once seized, without unconditionally restoring him and his goods to the Church when it demands them for the administration of justice. If, however, he is convicted in the Church’s court of an offence for which, according to the custom of secular judges, he ought to be mutilated or lose his life, the Church shall no longer protect either him or his goods. If convicted in the Church’s court of other offences, he shall make amends to the injured party according to the custom of the town [Col. 0240C].

[Col. 0240A] If the lord king grants exemption from military service to any borough, city, or castle, and asks anything of its inhabitants for the army, crusaders shall contribute nothing in the first year.

As to fiefs and holdings subject to rent (*censivae*), a crusader shall answer before the lord of the fief or rent-holding; and if they are aggrieved, they shall have recourse to the bishop or his official. If a crusader sues any Christian concerning a debt, movable property, or bodily injury inflicted upon him, or is sued by Christians concerning the matters aforesaid, he has the choice of suing under whichever judge he prefers, secular or ecclesiastical. No crusader is bound to answer in a secular court, but in an ecclesiastical court, except in matters of fiefs and rent-holdings, concerning which they shall litigate before the lords [Col. 0240D] of the fiefs and rent-holdings. With respect to possession which they have peacefully held for a day and a year, the aforesaid provisions shall be observed until they have completed their pilgrimage. If any new doubts arise concerning the affairs of crusaders, recourse shall be had to the two aforesaid bishops.

For the sake of peace, we will that these provisions concerning crusaders for the land of Jerusalem be observed throughout the entire dominion of the lord king until the council, without prejudice to the rights and customs of Holy Church, and likewise without prejudice to the rights and customs of the kingdom of France, and with the authority of the Holy Roman Church in every respect preserved.

[Col. 0241A] Done at Paris, in the year of the Lord 1214, in the month of March.

CCI. To the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis. — He remits forty days of the penances imposed upon all who devoutly assemble to venerate the relics of Blessed Dionysius. (Year 1215; Lateran, 4 January.)

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 544.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis at Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whether the glorious martyr and bishop Dionysius, whose venerable body rests in your church, [Col. 0241B] is to be regarded as the one called the Areopagite, converted by the apostle Paul, is a matter on which different persons hold different opinions. For some acknowledge that Dionysius the Areopagite died and was buried in Greece, and that another Dionysius preached the faith of Christ to the peoples of the Franks. Others assert that he came to Rome after the death of blessed Paul and was sent into Gaul by Pope Saint Clement; and that another was the one who died and was buried in Greece—both, nevertheless, eminent in deed and illustrious in speech.

But, wishing to prejudge neither opinion, while desiring to honour your monastery—which belongs immediately to the Roman Church—we devoutly send you, through our beloved sons Haimeric the prior and certain other envoys of your monastery sent to the general council, the sacred relic of blessed Dionysius which P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, [Col. 0241C] of happy memory, then legate of the Apostolic See, brought from Greece to the City [Rome]. Thus, when you possess both sets of relics, no doubt shall henceforth remain that the holy relics of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite are held at your monastery.

Receive them, therefore, reverently, rendering us this return: that in your prayers special commemoration of us before God may always be made, and that, according to the offering of those same envoys of yours, the anniversary commemoration of our death may be solemnly celebrated in that monastery. To all who devoutly assemble to venerate these holy relics, we remit by apostolic authority forty [Col. 0241D] days of the penances imposed upon them. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our grant and remission, or rashly to act contrary to it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of January [4 January], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCII. To Abbot Giroldus [Note: [Col. 0241D] Geroldus, or Geraudus, after William II—of whom we have spoken in the note to Letter CLXXVII above—was chosen, with the unanimous voice of all, from abbot of Molesme to abbot of Cluny in 1215, after Easter, or, as the Sammarthani say, on the very day on which William [Col. 0242D] resigned the administration. In 1220 he became bishop of Valence, and later patriarch of Jerusalem. *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1145.] and the convent of Cluny. — He grants the right to elect and install the prior in the monastery of La Charité [Note: [Col. 0242D] Compare the note to Letter CLXXVII above.]. (Year 1215; Lateran, 3 February.)

[From the archive of the monastery of Cluny. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0242A]

Having heard and understood what was laid before us by you, beloved son abbot, on the one hand on behalf of your monastery, and by the monks of La Charité on the other, concerning the election and installation of the prior, we, with the counsel of our brethren, adjudge the right of electing and installing the prior in the monastery of La Charité to you and your successors. On this matter we judge that perpetual silence must be imposed upon the other party. We command that the abbot of Cluny, concerning the installation of the prior, [Col. 0242B] deliberate prudently with the monks of both monasteries who are of maturer age and sounder counsel, and, with their counsel, install the man whom they judge, according to the ordinances of the Rule, ought to be preferred. Yet no necessity shall thereby be imposed on the abbot of Cluny preventing him from following the sounder counsel.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our decision or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of February [3 February], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCIII. To Magnardinus, bishop of Imola. — He confirms the privileges of the Church of Imola. (Year 1215; Lateran, 5 February.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, II, 633, from the autograph.]

[Col. 0242C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MAGNARDINUS, bishop of Imola, and to his successors canonically appointed, etc.

Although unworthy, we have been placed, by the Lord’s disposition, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See. We ought to love our brother bishops, both those near at hand and those far away, with fraternal charity, and to provide with pastoral solicitude for the churches entrusted to them by God. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ Magnardinus, [Col. 0242D] we graciously grant your just requests; and, following the example of Eugenius and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of blessed memory, our predecessors, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Imola, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside. We fortify it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of [Col. 0243A] kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

The abbeys of Saint Mary in Regula, Saint Donatus, Saint Mary in Diaconia, Saint Apostle in the castle of Imola, Saint Peter in Cala, and Saint John in Senno; the hospice of Saint Vitalis; in the city itself, the parish church of Saint Lawrence, and in it for you and your canons one half of all benefices arising from its entire parish in tithes, first-fruits, offerings, and wills. In the castles of Imola: the parish church of Saint Mary with the chapel of Saint Theodore and the other chapels belonging to it; the parish church of Saint Geminianus with its chapels; [Col. 0243B] the parish church of Saint Andrew and the chapel of Saint Paul in the castle of Albori; the hospital of Saint James at Sillero; the parish church of Saint Mary in Guipso, with its rural chapels and its other chapels; the chapel of Saxilion; the tithe of newly cultivated lands in the wood of Pacto within the bounds of your diocese; the parish churches of Saint Mary at Tausiniano, Saint Mary at Timberiaco, Saint Martin at Colina, and Saint Angel at Campiano, with the chapels belonging to them; the parish church of Saint Stephen at Barbiano, with the chapel in the castle of Cunii and its other chapels; the parish churches of Blessed Mary at Centum Licinia, Saint Patrick, and Saint Apollinaris, with the chapels belonging to them; the church of Saint Anastasius at Morediano; the parish churches of Saint Prosper and Saint Mary at Solustra, with their chapels; the whole [Col. 0243C] territory and court of Saint Cassian; the castle and court of Taularia; the castle and court of Aquaviva; and the *massa* of Boloniano, the *massa* Prata, the *massa* Campum; the castle and court called Caput Silicum, and its port with its marshes, watercourses, and fisheries; the port of Petredulo; Rachareta of Runci; the iron-working estate of Liba; the village of Zucharini; the new castle of Fabriaci, with sixteen manses; the castle of Ragnaria, with the entire court and all appurtenances; the *massa* of Adello, Sogorana, Medaxana, and Aureta; the estate of Peculini; the castle of Imola; the *massa* of Plasignani, Valeria, and Cornazani; the castle of Galisterne; the castle of Tonarelli; the court of Saint Martin in Saxo; the estate of Sastilium; the estate of Nunculium, called [Col. 0243D] Casula; the court of the valley of Salve; the castle and court of Monte Alto; the *massa* of Saint Ambrose; the castle of Gauderoncho, with the court of Runci and Rocca; the court of Macerata; the village of Sorbedulum; the castle and court of Petrella; Mount Saint Mary at Guipso with its appurtenances; the castle and court of Corbaria; the castle and court of Fonte Ulicis; the castle and court of Tausinano; the castle called Casale; the public court; the castle and court of Linari; the castle and court of Podioli; Mount Saint Andrew with its appurtenances; the court of Dutia with its appurtenances; the castle and court of Lavatoria; the *massa* of Lilani, Arsizii, and Galisani; in the court of Vitriano, the estate called [Col. 0244A] Capraria and four other estates; and, in the city itself, the toll and public dues.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact, to benefit in every way the uses of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, with the authority of the Apostolic See preserved. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to contravene it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend the wrong by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated [Col. 0244B]; let him be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the Last Judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the severe Judge, may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, etc. I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum. I, Guido, bishop of Palestrina. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Benedict, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 0244C] I, Pelagius, bishop of Albano. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Centius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul and of Saint Pancras. I, Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Gualla, cardinal-priest of Saint Martin, of the title of Equitius. I, Stephen, cardinal-priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

[Col. 0244D] Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Thomas, deacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, bishop-elect of Naples, on the Nones of February [5 February], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1215 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

I, Andrew, who heard the foregoing, have subscribed, etc.

CCIV. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0243D] See the note to Letter XVIII above.] and convent of Saint-Bertin. — He confirms certain possessions to them. (Year 1215; Lateran, 10 February.)

[From the archive of the Monastery of Saint-Bertin, papal chest no. 70. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1157.]

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners [Col. 0245A] and, as the result follows, fulfil requests that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring gladly in your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your monastery, and protect by the patronage of this present writing: the custody of two mills on the river Agniona; a certain holding situated near your court at Wesema, from Hugh of Arras and his sister Mabilia, with the consent of their heirs; the office of notary of Poperinge, from the son and grandson of Lambert; moreover the advocacy of Calmont, from Guido, formerly castellan of Cociaco; likewise the holdings in the borough of Saint-Omer, donated by Giso of Clusa and acquired by you for your monastery; also two sheaves of tithe from Baswrenstem, together with the altar of Poperinge and [Col. 0245B] your other goods. Since you hold all these things justly and peacefully, we confirm them to you.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act contrary to it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of February [10 February], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCV–CCVI. To the magnates of England. — On restoring peace between the king and the barons of England. (Year 1215; Lateran, 19 March.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 125. Patent Roll, 16 John, membrane 1d, in the Tower of London.]

[Col. 0245C]

INNOCENT, etc., to his beloved sons, the magnates and barons of England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We regard it as grievous and distressing that, as we have learned, dissension has arisen between our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, and some of you because of newly raised disputes, a dissension likely to produce grave harm unless it is quickly allayed by prudent counsel and diligent effort.

[Col. 0245D] We wholly condemn this, if, as many assert, you have rashly entered into conspiracies or confederacies against him, and have presumed irreverently to demand from him with arms what, if need be, you ought to have sought from him humbly and devoutly.

Lest, therefore, you should wish to hinder his good purpose by such occasions, we declare by apostolic authority null and void all conspiracies and confederacies undertaken since the dissension arose between kingdom and priesthood. By sentence of excommunication we forbid such things henceforth to be undertaken, prudently admonishing and effectively urging you to take care to appease and reconcile that king by clear tokens of devotion and humility, rendering him the customary services [Col. 0246A] which you and your predecessors have rendered to him and his predecessors. Then, if you think that anything should be requested of him, seek it not insolently but reverently, preserving his royal honour, so that you may more easily obtain what you intend.

We ask and beseech the same king in the Lord, enjoining this upon him for the remission of his sins, that he treat you kindly and graciously receive your just petitions; so that you yourselves, rejoicing with him, may recognize, by the help of divine grace, that he has been changed to a better condition, and that thereby you and your heirs ought to serve him and his successors more readily and devotedly.
