Accordingly, we have thought it proper to entreat and admonish your nobility, commanding you by these apostolic letters to ensure that you conduct yourselves in this matter in such a way that the kingdom of England may rejoice in the peace it desires, and that we may be bound, when necessary, to render you the aid and favour needed in your necessities.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April [19 March], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCVII. To all prelates of churches established throughout England. — He confirms the charter of the king of England granting free election to every church. (Year 1215; Lateran, 30 March.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 127, from the original in the treasury of the Receipt of the Exchequer.]

[Col. 0246C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and beloved sons, all prelates of churches established throughout England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We extol with due praises the magnificence of the Creator, because, after He who is wonderful and terrible in His counsels over the children of men had for some time allowed the spirit of tempest to range, as though in play, by blowing through the flower-bed of His garden, so as thereby to show our weakness and insufficiency, He at once, when He willed, said to the north wind, “Give,” and to the south wind, “Do not withhold”; and, commanding the winds and sea, He made the storm a breeze, so that sailors might find their greatly desired harbour of rest.

For, while a grave controversy concerning the election of prelates had long been carried on between the kingdom and priesthood of England, not without great danger and harm, He for whom nothing is impossible and who blows where He wills at last worked wondrously. Our dearest son in Christ, J[ohn], illustrious king of the English, freely, of his own pure and spontaneous will, with the common assent of his barons, for the salvation of his own soul and of his predecessors and successors, granted and confirmed by his letters that henceforth in every individual church and monastery, cathedral and conventual, throughout the whole kingdom of England, elections of every kind of prelate, greater and lesser, should be free in perpetuity.

We therefore, considering this acceptable and ratified, confirm this grant [Col. 0247A] by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your churches and successors, as we have seen it contained in the letters of the same king, and fortify it with the protection of this present writing.

For the greater and perpetual remembrance of this matter, we have caused the aforesaid royal letters made on this subject to be inserted in the present document. Their tenor is as follows:

> “John, by the grace of God king of England, lord of Ireland, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, earls, barons, and knights, bailiffs, and all who shall see these letters: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Because between us and our venerable fathers, Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all [Col. 0247B] England and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; William, bishop of London; Eustace, bishop of Ely; Giles, bishop of Hereford; Jocelin, bishop of Bath and Glastonbury; and Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, concerning their damages and property taken from them in the time of the interdict, agreement has been fully reached, by God’s grace, through the pure and free will of both parties, we desire not only to make satisfaction to them, so far as we are able according to God, but also to provide wholesomely and beneficially in perpetuity for the entire English Church.
>
> “Therefore, whatever custom has hitherto been observed in the English Church in our own times and those of our predecessors, and whatever right we have hitherto possessed in the elections of any prelates, we, at their request, for the salvation of our soul and of our predecessors and successors, kings of England, freely and by spontaneous will, with the common assent of our barons, have granted and ordained, and by this our present charter confirmed, that henceforth throughout every individual church and monastery, cathedral and conventual, in the whole kingdom of England, elections of all prelates, greater and lesser, shall be free in perpetuity, saving to us and our heirs the custody of vacant churches and monasteries which belongs to us.
>
> “We further promise that we shall neither impede nor permit our agents to impede, nor procure that anyone impede, the free appointment by electors of a pastor over themselves in each and every church and monastery mentioned, whenever they wish after the prelacy has become vacant. Yet they must first seek from us and our heirs permission to elect, which we shall neither deny nor defer.
>
> “And if, perchance—which God forbid—we should deny or defer it, the electors shall nevertheless proceed to make a canonical election; and likewise, after the election has been celebrated, our assent shall be sought, which we shall not deny unless we advance and lawfully prove some reasonable ground why we ought not to consent.
>
> [Col. 0248A] “Wherefore we will and firmly command that no one, when churches or monasteries are vacant, shall in any respect act, or presume to act, contrary to this our grant and ordinance. But if anyone at any time acts contrary to this, let him incur the curse of almighty God and ours.”

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act contrary to it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April [30 March], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCVIII. To all the magnates of England. — That they should pay the scutage customarily owed from ancient times to the king of England. (Year 1215; Lateran, 1 April.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 128, from the original in the treasury of the Receipt of the Exchequer.]

[Col. 0248B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the noblemen, magnates, barons, and knights established throughout England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of the English, has informed us that, whereas your predecessors customarily paid the kings of England from ancient times scutage from the baronies which you hold from him, and you yourselves are known to have paid it to him until recent times, you now refuse, at your own discretion, to pay him the scutage due for the army which he led into Poitou in the preceding year.

Lest, therefore, the pious purpose of the king himself be delayed by such an occasion, we have thought it proper earnestly to admonish and exhort your devotion, commanding you by these apostolic letters to pay him the said scutage, as you are bound to do, without difficulty. This is especially so because he ought not to be deprived without judicial process of possession of the oft-mentioned scutage, which his predecessors and he himself are said to have possessed hitherto, since, while remaining in possession of it, he is prepared to render justice to those who seek it.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April [1 April], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCIX. He grants the county of Melgueil as a fief to the bishop of Maguelone. (Year 1215; Lateran, 14 April.)

[*New Gallia Christiana*, VI, Documents, 367.]

[Col. 0248D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Maguelone: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering the devotion which we know that you and the Church of Maguelone have had toward the Apostolic See, and which we hope you will have in the future, we grant to you and your successors as a fief the county of Melgueil, or Montferrand, which is known to belong to the right or property of the Roman Church, with all its appurtenances. You shall hold it under an annual rent of twenty [Col. 0249A] marks of silver, payable to us and our successors on the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, without prejudice to the other rent which you owe the Roman Church for another cause.

You and your successors shall, on this account, render special fealty to us and our successors; shall acknowledge and hold the county through the Roman Church; and shall henceforth make war and peace concerning it at the command of that Church. You shall in no way presume, without a special licence of the Apostolic See, to grant as a fief or otherwise alienate the castle of Melgueil or the castle of Montferrand, since they are the head of that county. Nor shall you grant any fiefs belonging to that county to anyone living outside the diocese of Maguelone. Let no one, therefore, etc.

[Col. 0249B] Given at the Lateran, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCX. To the abbot and brethren of the monastery at Prüfening, in the diocese of Regensburg. — He confirms to them the churches at Weihenloh and Talmassing. (Year 1215; Lateran, 28 April.)

[RIED, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisbonensis*, p. 309, from the Regensburg cartulary.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery at Prüfening in the diocese of Regensburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See is accustomed to assent to pious desires and to bestow benevolent favour upon the honourable requests [Col. 0249C] of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gladly concurring in your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to the same monastery, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the churches at Weihenloh and Talmassing with their appurtenances, which our venerable brother, the bishop of Regensburg, with the consent of his chapter, has bestowed upon your monastery with pious generosity, just as you possess them lawfully and peacefully.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act contrary to it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0249D] Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April], in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXI. To the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Monte Cassino. — He proposes various measures for their reform. (Year 1215; Anagni, 20 September.)

[D. TOSTI, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, II, 289, from the original, chest 6, no. 8.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Monte Cassino: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Applying due care and concern to the reform of your monastery, we establish the chapters set down below, by whose faithful observance the monastery itself may, by God’s authority, [Col. 0250A] advance both in temporal advantage and in spiritual growth.

First, so that the members may more readily recover when the head is sound, and subjects be formed after the example of their prelate, we have thought fit to decree that the abbot of Monte Cassino shall use footwear and garments according to the Rule of Saint Benedict—namely, cloths such as Raynald and Peter of the Island, abbots of that place of good memory, and other religious abbots there, are known to have used. He shall wholly abstain from meat, unless he is weakened, under medical treatment, sick, or very feeble. When he remains at the upper monastery, he shall attend chapter every day unless an evident cause prevents him. He shall always eat with those guests whom it is necessary and fitting to honour by his presence; [Col. 0250B] and even then neither he nor the monks eating with him shall eat meat.

No entertainers shall under any circumstances be admitted there, or in other places where the abbot takes his meals. Should they perhaps intrude importunately, food shall be given them away from the abbot’s table solely for God’s sake, so that, being content with this, they may be compelled entirely to refrain from foolish antics or words. Neither abbot nor monk shall keep birds or hunting dogs, nor shall they presume to have enamel or gold on saddles, or use gilded bridles in any way. No monastery official (*obedientialis*) shall exceed the number of two mounts and the same number of attendants.

Moreover, when the abbot rides out on urgent business, he shall take a moderate and respectable household. [Col. 0250C] Both at San Germano and at the other castles of the monastery where he happens to stay, three or two of the senior monks—men of proven religious life and reputation—shall always sleep in one chamber with him; while the other monks who are with him eat and sleep in one place, so that no one has a private chamber. Thus Satan’s wiles may better be opposed and the mouths of those speaking iniquity more easily stopped.

The monks residing in the monastery, both officials and others, shall sleep in the common dormitory and eat in the common refectory. No official, or other person serving in the upper [Col. 0250D] monastery, shall keep personal servants or have special dishes prepared for himself; rather, all shall use the common fare, except only the sick. They too shall all eat together in the infirmary, except perhaps those suffering such weakness that they cannot leave their beds without difficulty.

A monk of good conduct, or a layman, shall be appointed under the infirmarian; he shall reside continually in the infirmary and take care, day and night, of each and every sick person. The hospital likewise, after all things taken from it have been restored to it, shall be so reformed that sick and poor persons fleeing to it may receive there the customary relief. Another monk or religious layman shall nevertheless be appointed as hospitaller; remaining in the hospital by day, he shall faithfully minister to the poor by night. [Col. 0251A] Monks of other monasteries, when they come to that monastery, shall be generously provided for just as are the brethren of the place itself.

In the upper sacristy, moreover, there shall be appointed a prudent and upright monk, who shall carefully guard the sacred objects and shall not be removed from that office so long as he serves well and praiseworthily. Priests shall be appointed from among the senior monks fit to carry out this office, so that there may be no scarcity but an abundance of priests in the monastery. Simon of Colle Alto, John of Colimento, John of Campania, and also the monks who presumed, together with Adinulf, former abbot, to conspire or rebel against the Roman Church or the monastery of Monte Cassino, shall always remain in the convent, so that no obedience or office may be entrusted [Col. 0251B] to them until they amend their lives for the better.

Because some of you, to the destruction of your souls, do not fear to possess private property, we decree that they shall be compelled, under oath if necessary, to surrender it for conversion to the uses of the monastery. If henceforth any monk of that place is found to possess private property, he shall be expelled from the monastery without hope of restoration, since we have decreed that all such proprietors are subject to a sentence of excommunication. If private property is found in anyone’s possession at death, he shall be deprived of ecclesiastical burial. But if anything is given specially to any monk by anyone whatsoever [Col. 0251C], he shall surrender it to the abbot or dean; and the abbot or dean shall provide from it for his needs as he judges expedient. Nor shall things assigned for meals, clothing, or other necessities of the monks henceforth be divided among them; rather, they shall be kept by those to whom this responsibility has been entrusted and usefully expended for the monks’ needs. Nor shall any cloistered monk have prebends or revenues outside the cloister; and these shall be entirely taken away from those known to possess them. The dean, moreover, shall not presume to have double garments and special foods; and whenever a monk receives new clothing, he shall return the old.

And since it is now said to prevail among you almost as a custom that, when some quarrelsome or talkative, disobedient monk is found in your community [Col. 0251D], the abbot, avoiding his disturbances, gives him obediences, churches, and other goods of the monastery—whence evil men, as it were deriving profit from their own wickedness, often lapse into worse things, and others also are incited to dissensions and scandals—we will and command that the abbot strive to treat upright, obedient, religious, and serious men with sincere charity; but that he punish dishonourable and disobedient, undisciplined and frivolous men, with the counsel of the dean and elders, according to monastic rules, so that the good may be spurred by good to better things, and the wicked recalled from their wickedness. [The source then has an apparently corrupt repetition: “But let cloistered monks be recalled without malice.”]

Cloistered monks, moreover, shall by no means be granted leave to leave the cloister without a manifest and necessary reason, since it is dangerous [Col. 0252A] for such persons to mingle with gatherings of secular people. Nor, under the pretext of kinship, shall younger monks be allowed to converse with women within the precincts of the monastery unless at least two elderly and reputable monks are present.

In imitation also of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, we decree that the abbot may not alienate or enfeoff the possessions or demesne lands of the monastery; adding that he shall diligently endeavour lawfully to recover for the use of the same monastery both the mills which Abbot Roffredus, of good memory, alienated to the grave injury of the monastery and other things unlawfully alienated, disposed of, or improperly granted from that monastery’s demesne. Let him confer the provostships of its churches upon prudent [Col. 0252B] and honourable monks, whom he shall cause to bind themselves by oath not to alienate their possessions and rights. If they should presume to do so, we decree that they shall be removed permanently from the monastery without hope of restoration, and otherwise severely punished.

Each of the said provosts shall render to the monastery annually fixed, moderate, and customary revenues according to the resources of the churches over which he presides. And so that, as evil men receive punishment for wickedness, good men may receive reward for goodness, the abbot shall not remove from their provostships those provosts whom he has found to have administered well, unless there is a manifest necessity or advantage for the monastery. We command, however, that monks be recalled from castles and villages to the cloister, unless perhaps some are necessary for guarding those fortifications [Col. 0252C] which lie within the boundaries of the abbey; these we permit to remain there temporarily. The abbot shall enjoin upon them, by virtue of obedience, that, living as religiously as they can, they shall show no favour to persons in judgment, but shall administer justice equally to poor and rich, weak and powerful. Those who turn aside to the right or left he himself shall punish with due severity; and if he is negligent or lax in punishing them, he shall experience in his own person the sentence of apostolic correction.

Both the monks entrusted with castles and those entrusted with churches shall personally come to the cloister annually on the feast of the dedication of the monastery, to render an account of their stewardship before the abbot, dean, and others. [Col. 0252D] We decree that this shall also be observed with respect to the monastery’s treasurer, cellarer, infirmarian, hospitaler, and sacristan: those who have acted commendably shall rejoice in the due commendation of the brethren, while those who have acted badly shall be covered with shame and disgrace. Furthermore, the treasurer, cellarer, and infirmarian shall come to the monastery every Saturday, according to the ancient and approved custom, and remain in the cloister with the brethren until Monday; and the abbot also shall endeavour to do this whenever he can suitably do so.

Therefore, we command that the aforesaid chapters be observed inviolably; and, lest anyone be able to excuse himself through ignorance, we will and command that they be read every month in the presence of the abbot and brethren. [Col. 0253A] Let absolutely no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this charter of our constitution or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXII. To the consuls of Modena.—On behalf of the Nonantulans.  
*(1215; Lateran, 23 October.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of the Abbey of Nonantola*, II, 354, from the autograph.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the consuls of Modena, greeting and apostolic [Col. 0253B] blessing.

Since jurisdiction over tithes belongs to the ecclesiastical court, we are compelled to wonder and to be troubled that, as the beloved sons the archpriest and canons of the church of Nonantola have grievously complained to us, you have pronounced definitive judgments against the tenants of certain of their properties, who had been brought before you by our venerable brother the bishop of Modena in a case concerning tithes. Although the beloved sons, the abbot of Santa Maria in Regola at Imola and his fellow judges, by our authority declared those judgments void as having been rendered by judges lacking jurisdiction, you nevertheless strive to put them into execution. Therefore, lest you seem to wish to extend your jurisdiction to the injury of the law, [Col. 0253C] we command your devotion by these apostolic letters that you shall by no means henceforth harass the aforesaid tenants concerning these matters, since we could not endure this with equanimity.

Given at the Lateran, the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXIII. To the bishop of Modena.—On behalf of the Nonantulans.  
*(1215; Lateran, 25 October.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of the Abbey of Nonantola*, II, 353, from the autograph.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Modena, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved sons, the archpriest and canons of the church of Nonantola, [Col. 0253D] have shown us in their complaint that, although you had formerly brought before secular judges the tenants of your properties at Senaida in a suit concerning tithes belonging to the same church, we subsequently caused you, through our delegates—the beloved sons the abbot of Saint Stephen at Bologna and his colleague—to be forbidden to harass the aforesaid tenants concerning these matters [lacuna]. Nevertheless, you caused proceedings to continue in the case and obtained definitive judgments against them. Although the abbot of Santa Maria in Regola at Imola and his fellow judges, [Col. 0254A] by our authority, judged those judgments void and without effect, and firmly prohibited both you and your clergy, under penalty of excommunication, from presuming at any time to use the said judgments, you nevertheless—at which we marvel—are using the aforesaid judgments, having through your syndic brought the said tenants before secular judges concerning the same tithes.

Therefore, that you may not only take thought for your conscience in this matter but also avoid the penalty established by the laws, we command your fraternity by these apostolic letters henceforth to cease from harassing the aforesaid tenants concerning these matters and not to use the aforesaid judgments, lest we be compelled to proceed otherwise against you.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighteenth year [Col. 0254B] of our pontificate.

## CCXIV. To the abbot and brethren of Saint-Denis.—That they may receive tithes and fiefs from the hands of those holding them.  
*(1215; Lateran, 30 October.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 544.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis in the diocese of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your petition presented to us stated that you requested authorization by apostolic authority to receive, as a pledge and to possess freely, the possessions, tithes, and fiefs belonging to your monastery from the hands of those holding them, lest through their fault they [Col. 0254C] be lost to you. Therefore, granting your prayers, we graciously concede what you request, provided that in the meantime you receive no service, on account of those goods, from persons who were previously bound to you in any respect concerning those same things.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Kalends of November, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXV. To the abbot, prior, and provost of Saint Eligius at Noyon.—Confirms a settlement between the prior and convent of Nouvion and the count of Regiteste.  
*(1215; Lateran, 2 November.)*

[Note: [Col. 0253D] The monastery of Saint Eligius at Noyon was then governed by Radulfus II or I, known in documents from 1199 through 1229. Nothing concerning him is recorded in the registers later than 1230. [Col. 0254D] His death is entered in the necrology on the third day before the Kalends of February. *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IX, col. 1068.]

[Note: [Col. 0254D] Compare Letter CXLVIII of the appendix to this collection.]

[From the cartulary of Noyon. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1156.]

There was made known to us by [lacuna] the prior and convent of Nouvion [Col. 0254D] that, whereas formerly a dispute had arisen between them on the one hand and the nobleman [lacuna], count of Regiteste, on the other, concerning certain procurations and other matters which he exacted from them contrary to justice, at length an amicable settlement was reached between them, which they requested should be strengthened by apostolic protection. Therefore, we command your discretion by these apostolic letters to cause that settlement, insofar as it was prudently made without wrongdoing and freely accepted by both parties, to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside. [Col. 0255A] If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, nevertheless let two of you execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Nones of November, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXVI. To the bishop of Auxerre.—On exercising jurisdiction over the abbey of Saint Germanus.  
*(1216; Lateran, 5 January.)*

[LE BEUF, *History of Auxerre*, II, proofs, 45.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

At the request of the former beloved son Master H., your procurator, that the abbot and convent of Saint Germanus [Col. 0255B] at Auxerre be restrained by authority of the Apostolic See from the obstruction which they were causing you in the office of visitation and correction, the procurator of the opposing party answered that the monastery was subject to Cluny; in support of this, its abbot, your beloved son, produced an advocate even in our presence. On these matters we thought fit to commit the case, in a specified form, to our venerable brother the bishop of Troyes and his fellow judges.

At length, when our nephew and beloved son, the abbot of Cluny, was present at the Apostolic See, a certain document of Pope Eugenius of blessed memory was produced before us. It stated, among other things, that canonical reception and correction in the aforesaid monastery at Auxerre belonged to the abbot of Cluny [lacuna]. [Col. 0255C] But because, owing to the parties’ differing and opposing interpretations, it was regarded as doubtful what pertained to correction of the order and what to canonical correction, we declared the aforesaid words as follows: interruption of silence, retention of private property, contempt of obedience in [lacuna], matters which concern the order [uncertain lacuna], negligence in divine service, and other things considered in relation to observance of the monastic rule are said to belong to correction of the order. Criminal accusation, civil suit, and other matters of ordinary jurisdiction, however, are said to pertain to canonical correction. Each, moreover, shall visit and correct, in accordance with the aforesaid declaration, those matters which required correction in the monastery mentioned.

[Col. 0255D] Let absolutely no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this charter of our declaration or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of January, in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXVII. To all those signed with the cross in the province of Bremen.  
*(1216; Lateran, 8 January.)*

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, p. 346, from the original at Stade, bearing the appended lead seal of Innocent III, caps. II, no. 47.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 0256A] to all those signed with the cross in the province of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You who have chosen the Lord—indeed, who have been chosen by Him, the Father of lights, from whom comes every good and perfect gift—that you may be a people especially His own and the sheep of His pasture, serving Him shoulder to shoulder, with one desire and a united will, and beginning under Christ the Prince to wage the Lord’s battles: rejoice and be glad, for now draws near the desired and longed-for day, the time in which it has pleased God to dwell in you; the time, indeed, for executing vengeance upon the nations and rebukes upon the peoples who possess and defile the Holy Land. Like senseless children, they mock and reproach the true Elisha, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” [Col. 0256B] (2 Kings 2); and may you become gracious and a defender to your Christians.

For this reason you have resolved, in accordance with the Apostle’s exhortation, to go outside the camp of your own dwelling, bearing His reproach (Hebrews 13), until the Lord crushes His enemies under your feet, giving them everlasting disgrace and you glorious victory. You must therefore carefully consider that, by living blamelessly, peaceably, and commendably, you render acceptable service to so great a Lord, who has written upon His robe and upon His thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19); who is also the Lord of hosts and King of everlasting glory; who does not accept compelled service but voluntary service, not sorrowful but joyful service; who rejects discordant servants, the proud and harsh also, and embraces the peaceable, humble, and kind.

[Col. 0256C] You should also consider, and must consider, that whereas other valiant warriors fight unto death for a corruptible crown and temporal glory, or to acquire some transitory kingdom, you strive to expose yourselves not for such things but for an incorruptible crown, everlasting glory, and a heavenly kingdom enduring forever. Therefore now, with every joy and exultation, with every desire and affection, you ought eagerly to hasten to obtain the prize of such great blessedness. The right hand of the Saviour displays and unfolds this to you through the banner of His cross, promising not only the aid of His protection but victory and glory.

[Col. 0256D] Therefore we, who desire to be fellow-workers for your crown, so that you may run more freely to obtain the desired palm of this triumph, have decreed, among other measures prudently arranged in the general council for aid to the Holy Land, that for at least four years a general peace shall be observed throughout the whole Christian world. Those at variance shall be brought by the prelates of the churches to a full peace or a firm truce, to be inviolably observed; and those who perhaps disdain to comply shall be most strictly compelled by excommunication in their persons and interdict upon their lands.

Further, lest your holy purpose and aid to the Holy Land be delayed beyond what is due, but may beneficially begin at the fitting time with hastened steps, [Col. 0257A] by the counsel of prudent men fully acquainted with the circumstances of times and places, and with the approval of the aforesaid council, we have determined and by the authority of these presents command that the cross-bearers prepare themselves so that, on the Kalends of June following the next, all who have resolved to cross the sea shall endeavour to assemble in the Kingdom of Sicily: some, as shall be fitting and proper, at Brindisi, and others at Messina and the neighbouring regions on either side. There, with the Lord’s assent, we also intend personally to be present, so that by our counsel and aid the Christian army may be healthfully ordered and depart with divine and apostolic blessing. Those who have proposed to travel by land shall likewise prepare themselves for the same date, meanwhile informing [Col. 0257B] us of this, so that we may grant them a suitable legate from our side for counsel and assistance.

Moreover, that you may bear Christ’s sweet yoke and light burden more willingly and freely, we have decreed in the aforesaid council, for relief of your burdens, that you and the other cross-bearers shall henceforth be exempt from collections, tallages, and other burdens. We receive your persons and goods, after you have taken the cross, and those of the others, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves; and we further decree that you shall stand under the defence of archbishops, bishops, and all prelates of the Church, so that, until the death or return of cross-bearers is known with certainty, their property shall remain whole and undisturbed. If anyone should presume to act against this, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical censure.

[Col. 0257C] We have further appointed as your special protectors, and for others to be signed with the cross in your province, our venerable brother C., formerly bishop of Halberstadt, and our beloved sons Master Conrad [Note: [Col. 0257] Conrad resigned the episcopal dignity in 1208. See the *Chronicle of Halberstadt*.] of Marburg and J., scholasticus (schoolmaster) of Xanten. By these present letters we grant them, for your defence, the authority described above; and we command them zealously to set before Christ’s faithful in your province the word of the cross, and by the aforesaid censure to compel restitution from those who have presumed to retain money promised for aid to the Holy Land, or collected, or to be collected, in chests. We will and command that this money be expended by them, at the proper time, beneficially and prudently through valiant and prudent cross-bearers from the people among whom the aforesaid money has been collected, for persons whose own resources do not suffice to fulfil their vow, as prudent deliberation shall deem expedient. [Col. 0257D] Meanwhile, however, we will that the said preachers, together with suitable and discreet men from the places where the collection is made, shall faithfully preserve the aforesaid alms until the time of distribution.

We further command the same preachers diligently to admonish and induce—beseeching them by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one only true eternal God—kings, dukes [Col. 0258A] and princes, margraves, counts and barons, and other magnates, as well as the communes of cities, villages, and towns, that those who do not personally take part in aid to the Holy Land shall contribute, according to their means, a suitable number of warriors with expenses necessary for three years, for the remission of their sins, as is set out in the general letters.

If any should refuse, being so ungrateful to the Lord our God, let them firmly declare on behalf of the Apostolic See that such persons should know that on this account they will answer to us on the last day of strict judgment before the dreadful Judge. Yet they should first consider with what conscience or security they can appear before Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to whom the Father has given all things [Col. 0258B] into His hands, if they refuse to serve Him, crucified for sinners, in this undertaking as though it were His own and especially personal cause—He by whose gift they live, by whose benefit they are sustained, and indeed by whose blood they have been redeemed.

Now, so that, when all things have been properly arranged and, following Gideon’s example, the useless left at home, we may send those useful and necessary against the Midianites: because by God’s grace the multitude of cross-bearers is numerous—clerics and laypersons, men and women, old and young, weak and strong alike—we wish, by prudent and discerning dispensation, that the vows of certain less useful persons be commuted, redeemed, or deferred. Yet these persons shall nevertheless [Col. 0258C] for a time enjoy the indulgence and be protected by the privilege granted to those departing in aid of the Holy Land. We have thought fit to entrust this responsibility in each diocese to prudent and discerning men whom we consider fit and faithful for the purpose. By other letters we command them, having God before their eyes and carefully investigating the circumstances affecting this undertaking, to carry it out prudently and wisely under public testimony and that of reputable men, carefully providing lest, because of an excess of cross-bearing clerics, the Christian army be burdened and the Church deprived of its due services.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the eighteenth year [Col. 0258D] of our pontificate.

## CCXVIII. Receives the convent of Osterholt under protection and confirms its goods and privileges.  
*(1216; Lateran, 8 February.)*

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, p. 349, from the archives of Osterholt.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the prioress and nuns of the monastery of Osterholt, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When that which is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require [Col. 0259A] that it be brought, through the diligence of our office, to its due effect. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves your persons and the place in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all goods which you now rightfully possess or may hereafter, by just means and by the Lord’s favour, acquire.

In particular, we confirm to you, and through you to the same monastery, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this writing, the estate at Scherembecke, the house at Bremen, and the holdings which you possess near Hiddingwerde, Sutherbroke, Pennyngkbutle, and Duringge, together with their appurtenances, as well as the other goods of the same monastery, insofar as you possess them justly and peaceably. [Col. 0259B] Let absolutely no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this charter of our protection and confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXIX. Forbids that G., a cleric of the diocese of Bremen formerly deposed by Archbishop Hartwig II, be admitted to the chapter.  
*(1216; Lateran, 13 February.)*

[Note: [Col. 0259] Gotschalk, apparently then scholasticus of Bremen.]

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, p. 349, from the original at Stade, chapter II, note 3.]

[Col. 0259C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Paul, the provost of Hilgenrothe in the diocese of Bremen, and the cellarer of Saint Willehad at Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our beloved sons B., provost, and the canons of Bremen, stating that G., a cleric of the diocese of Bremen, was stripped of all ecclesiastical benefices by H., archbishop of Bremen of good memory, because of his offences. When the same cleric complained before us concerning those benefices, we considered it proper to impose perpetual silence upon him. Nevertheless, on the occasion of certain [Col. 0259D] letters of ours obtained in common form concerning certain injuries, he seeks to have a stall in the choir and a place in the chapter restored to him. The said canons have humbly petitioned that provision be made for their church in this matter.

Accordingly, we command your discretion by these apostolic letters that, if the truth supports the foregoing, you shall absolve the said church from such a claim, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside. If all of you cannot be present to carry this out, nevertheless let two of you execute it.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of February, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXX. To Stephen, abbot, and the convent of Monte Cassino.—That no alienations made without the knowledge of the sounder part of the convent are valid.  
*(1216; Lateran, 29 February.)*

[D. TOSTI, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, II, 288, from the original. Diplomatic portfolio 3, no. 34.]

[Col. 0260A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons STEPHEN, abbot, and the convent of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The duty of our office requires that, since we are bound to bear the care and concern of all churches, those things which are wrongly attempted to their prejudice through the insolence of administrators be opposed with provident diligence, and that relief be afforded to their integrity through the benefit of equity. Therefore, since concerning [Col. 0260B] things unlawfully alienated or disposed of to the prejudice of your monastery, the instruments of the alienating abbots appear to be marked by the subscriptions of two, three, or a few monks, and ordinary judges are unwilling in any way to oppose them, we, desiring with paternal solicitude to safeguard the integrity of the same monastery, declare by these presents that instruments made concerning such alienations which lack the subscription of the greater and sounder part of the convent shall have no force to the monastery’s prejudice. [Col. 0260C] Let absolutely no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this charter of our declaration or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of March, in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXI. To the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis.—On redeeming tithes from laymen.  
*(1216; Lateran, 29 February.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 545.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis at Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your devotion petitioned us to grant you leave to redeem tithes from laymen and to possess them peaceably when redeemed. Since laymen have no special right in tithes, [Col. 0260D] we graciously grant your request, but only concerning those tithes held in this way by laymen within your parishes.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of March, in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXII. To the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis.—Grants that they are not bound to furnish procurations to bishops or other prelates.  
*(1216; Lateran, 1 March.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 546.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis at Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your representation informed us that certain [Col. 0261A] bishops and other prelates of churches demand undue procurations from the estates of your monastery situated in the dioceses of those bishops. They say this is owed to them because in those dioceses you receive certain tithes and, from the offerings of parish churches in which you are known to have the right of presentation, receive a fixed portion on many feast-days. But since procurations are owed by reason of visitation, and private oratories have been built on the aforesaid estates which do not pertain to the visitation of the said prelates, you humbly petitioned us mercifully to provide for your protection in this matter. Therefore, acceding to your prayers, by the authority of these presents we grant that you shall not be bound to pay such procurations [Col. 0261B] to the aforesaid prelates unless, in due manner and for the fitting purpose of visitation, they visit those estates which are established to belong by law to their jurisdiction.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of March, in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXIII. To the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis.—Confirms gifts made to them.  
*(1216; Lateran, 7 March.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 546.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis at Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0261C] It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, since the late knight Renaldus of Pomponia, by pious generosity, remitted to the same monastery the obligation to provide ten knights on the feast of Saint Dionysius and five modii of grain from a certain tithe which he received annually from your monastery; and since the late Ferricus gave up to the aforesaid monastery, under divine inspiration, two-thirds of the wine-tithe of Argenteuil, the *minagium*—namely, three mines per modius—ten sextaries of grain, and two-thirds of the tithes and offerings of one of your parishes, all of which he had long unjustly held together with his wife and children: we, [Col. 0261D] assenting to your prayers and approving the aforesaid remission and surrender as piously and prudently made, confirm them by apostolic authority and strengthen them with the protection of this writing.

Let absolutely no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this charter of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of March, in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXIV. Commands the Frisians dwelling in the province of Bremen to expel the excommunicated Waldemar from their territories.  
*(1216; Lateran, 14 March.)*

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, p. 350, from the original at Stade.]

[Col. 0262A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the Frisians not signed with the cross dwelling in the province of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Zeal for justice and the order of brotherly charity require that Christ’s faithful, mutually bearing one another’s burdens and more fully fulfilling Christ’s law, furnish one another with mutual aid at an appropriate time: shaking the yoke of servitude from the necks of the innocent, resisting those who do injury, and more zealously freeing the oppressed [Col. 0262B] from the hands of the wicked, lest, if they are unwilling to disturb the perverse when able to do so, they seem to foster them in the faithlessness of their wickedness.

Since, therefore, the church of Bremen, long held and in some measure enslaved under the yoke of most exacting servitude by the son of perdition, the schismatic Waldemar—excommunicated, deposed, degraded, and condemned by us in a general council—has long pressed us with cries for its liberation and has not yet been able to recover from its distress, although we have expended much care and labour, we earnestly ask and admonish your whole community, commanding you by these apostolic letters and enjoining this upon you for the remission of sins: proceed bravely and powerfully to break [Col. 0262C] the yoke of captivity of the aforesaid church, to cast the aforesaid schismatic out of your territories, and to restrain his supporters, so that you may receive reward from God and fuller praise and favour from us and others.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of March, in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

## CCXXV. To the dean of Saint Frambald and the cantors of Saint Frambald and Saint Regulus, at Senlis.—That they cause a judgment rendered by the bishop of Senlis in favour of the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis in a certain case to be observed.  
*(1216; Viterbo, 18 April.)*

[From a copy carefully transcribed and shared with us by D. Poirier from the autograph preserved in the archives of the monastery of Saint-Denis. BRÉQ., ibid.]

[Col. 0262D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [lacuna], dean of Saint Frambald, and the cantors of Saint Frambald and Saint Regulus at Senlis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Beloved sons, the abbot [Note: [Col. 0261D] See Letter XLV of Book III, note] and convent of Saint-Denis have humbly petitioned us to deign to strengthen by apostolic protection the definitive sentence which, in their favour, our venerable brother …, bishop of Senlis [Note: [Col. 0262D] See Letter CXLV of Book V, note], and his fellow judges, delegated by us, pronounced, as justice required, against N., knight of Flamengeria in the diocese of Laon, concerning certain rents [Col. 0263A] and other matters. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion to cause that sentence, since it is just, to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside. And if not all of you can be present to carry this out, nevertheless let two of you execute it.

Given at Viterbo, 14 Kalends of May [18 April], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXVI. To the Abbess of Saint Mary of Acuis at Marseille.—He takes her under protection and confirms her possessions. (1216; Todi, 29 April.)

*Antiquities of the Church of Marseille*, II, 62, from the archive of the abbey of Saint-Sauveur of Marseille.]

[Col. 0263B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and nuns of Saint Mary of Acuis, etc.

… We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and in particular the church of Saint Mary of Acuis with its appurtenances; likewise the rights which you possess in the fortified places of Alauch and Rocovaira, etc.; Motta beside the river Velna, and in the hospital of the Holy Spirit at Marseille, etc.

Given at Todi, on the third day before the Kalends of May [29 April], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXVII. To the abbess and sisters of Rysebiarg.—He confirms their possessions and privileges. (1216; near Orvieto, 7 May.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplom. Suecan.*, I, 183.]

[Col. 0263C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, … the abbess and nuns of Riesbyarg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, gladly assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own your persons and the monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all the goods which it now rightfully possesses or may hereafter, by just means and through the Lord’s favour, acquire. In particular, we apostolically confirm to you, and through you to that monastery, and fortify by the protection of this writing, Fruoswi, Hindawret, Scotist, Borshogen, Akerbui, Chellestat, Sebui, and the other possessions bestowed upon you by the pious devotion of the faithful, as you hold them justly and peaceably. Let no one therefore presume to violate this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0264A] Given near Orvieto, on the Nones of May [7 May], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXVIII. To the archbishop …—He revokes a sentence of excommunication obtained against the bishop … by A., provost of Saint Willehad, and T. de Walle, canon of Bremen; and confirms the penalty pronounced against the said provost. (1216; Lateran, 9 May.)

[LAPPEMBERG, *Hamb. Urkund.*, p. 350, from the cartulary of the royal archive of Hanover. The beginning is missing.]

… the provost of Willehad and T. de Walle, canon of Bremen, again procured apostolic letters concerning the same affair by a false suggestion. These two—namely, the provost of Saint Willehad and the aforesaid canon T.—were bound by the bond of excommunication because they stubbornly favoured and communicated with the faithless Waldemar, despite the opposition of the provost of the major church and their fellow judge. Although, by authority of our letters, their jurisdiction had been revoked, yet, out of favour for the aforesaid Uldemar (who hated the bishop because he had faithfully carried out the apostolic mandate against him), they pronounced, purely as a matter of fact, a sentence of excommunication against that bishop.

Regarding a certain proceeding and the intrusion of his supporters, the said A., in order to add affliction to the afflicted, procured letters from us addressed to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Magdeburg, outside the province. He concealed both that the aforesaid judges had been entangled in the bond of excommunication because of their communion with the aforesaid Uldemar, and that their jurisdiction had been revoked by the abbot of Lübeck and his fellow judges. He also suppressed the fact that, besides the sentences of excommunication justly pronounced against that same A., which were confirmed by apostolic authority through the abbot of Doberan and his fellow judges, sentences of deposition and excommunication had been pronounced against him and his supporters by the abbot of Rastede and his fellow judges, delegated by us. The aforesaid bishop therefore petitioned us that, since A. and his accomplices, despising the said sentences of deposition and excommunication, presume to celebrate the divine offices, we should lay our hands upon them so heavily [Col. 0264D] that others might learn from their example to abstain from similar conduct.

Therefore, unwilling to leave the rebellion and contumacy of the aforesaid persons unpunished, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if this is so, having declared void whatever you find to have been attempted to the prejudice of the named bishop through authority of letters procured by the aforesaid A., who was bound by excommunication, you shall cause the aforesaid sentences pronounced against that same A. and his accomplices—namely, the sentence of deposition, since it is just, and that of excommunication, since it was reasonably pronounced—to be firmly observed by our authority until fitting satisfaction has been made, all impediment of appeal removed. But if not all of you can be present to carry this out, you, brother archbishop, together with one of them, shall nevertheless execute it.

[Col. 0265A] Given at the Lateran, 7 Ides of May [9 May], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXIX. To the abbot and brothers of Saint Thomas of Paraclete; he confirms their privileges. (1216; Perugia, 30 May.)

[LANGEBECK, *Script. rer. Danic.*, VI, 148.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Saint Thomas of Paraclete, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church, by the duty of its customary piety, is accustomed to love its devout and humble sons more earnestly, and, lest they be harassed by the vexations of wicked men, to cherish them like a loving mother under the protection of her defence. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to your just prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own your persons and the monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, with all the goods which it now rightfully possesses or may hereafter, by just means and through the Lord’s favour, acquire. In particular, we apostolically confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, and fortify by the protection of this writing, the liberties and immunities, tithes, possessions, and other goods granted to that monastery by kings, bishops, or other faithful of Christ through pious and prudent generosity, as you hold them all justly and peaceably. Let no one whatsoever therefore presume to violate this page of our protection and confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0265C] Given at Perugia, on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXX. To the nobles of Uppsala.—He gives thanks for the tribute liberally and devoutly paid. (1216; Perugia, 31 May.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplom. Suecan.*, I, 158.]

[Col. 0265D] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the noble men, barons, knights, and others established throughout the diocese of Uppsala, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because you have liberally and devoutly paid the tribute owed to us—as we have learned from the report of our venerable brother your archbishop, and as the very result plainly demonstrates—we commend your devotion in the Lord and offer you due thanks. We earnestly ask and by these apostolic letters command you to take care to show yourselves so ready and willing to pay that tribute at the proper times that the Apostolic See, and we who, though unworthy, preside over it, may be bound to embrace you more closely with the arms of charity as special sons, and may deserve to obtain from God a fitting reward.

[Col. 0266A] Given at Perugia, on the second day before the Kalends of June [31 May], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXXI. To the abbot [Note: [Col. 0265D] See note to Letter CXV of Book IX] and convent of the monastery of Saint Vaast of Arras.—He confirms the liberty granted them by Louis, eldest son of the king of the French, whereby the free men of their monastery are to be judged by the abbot’s free men. (1216; 1 July.)

[From the Archive of the Monastery of Saint Vaast of Arras. BRÉQ., ibid., p. 1158.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0266B] sons, the abbot and convent of Saint Vaast of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When what is just and honourable is requested of us, both the force of equity and the order of reason require that it be brought to its due effect through the diligence of our office. You have informed us that certain bishops, counts, barons, and other clerics and laymen seek unjustly to subject to themselves your monastery—which belongs to the Roman Church without any intermediary—and also to take away its people and rights. The nobleman L., firstborn son of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the French, to whose lordship and jurisdiction the land of that monastery is said to belong through a royal grant, granted you this liberty: that the free men of the … monastery shall be judged by the free men of the abbot, and the peasants by the aldermen; judgment in all other matters remaining with the free abbot. He also granted to your monastery … which he received from the land, as is said to be more fully contained in the letters of that same L. We therefore, yielding to your prayers, apostolically confirm to you, and through you to your monastery, and fortify by the protection of this writing, the aforesaid liberty and grant, as you hold them justly and peaceably. Let no one whatsoever therefore presume to violate this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0266D] Given … [lacuna] … before the Kalends of July [1 July], in the nineteenth year of our pontificate.

CCXXXII. To the abbot and brothers of Saint-Thibéry (diocese of Agde).—He confirms their possessions and privileges. (1216; near Orvieto.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., VI, Documents, 332, from the archive of Saint-Thibéry.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Thibéry and its brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Though by the office entrusted to us we are debtors to all churches, it is especially fitting that we provide more earnestly for those which belong to blessed Peter and are known to pertain especially to the defence of the Holy Roman Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Sergius, Paschal, Calixtus, Eugenius, and Alexander, receive the aforesaid monastery of Saint Thibéry under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and fortify it by the privilege of this writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods it now rightfully and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means and through the Lord’s favour, acquire, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

[Col. 0267B] Namely, the church of Saint Mary of Gradu in the territory of Agde, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Sulpicius; and the church of Saint John of Castronovo; the church of Saint Martin of Granoleries; the church of Saint Andrew of Roviniac; the churches of Saint John and Saint Susanna of Florentiac; the church of Saint Martin of Fenolet, with their appurtenances; also the church of Saint Peter of Becian, which you obtained, with its tithes and other appurtenances, through the settlement made between you and the abbot and monks of Casa-Dei by Guy of good memory, formerly chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and then legate of the Apostolic See; the church of Saint Mary of Affrian, with its appurtenances. In the bishopric of Béziers, the church of Saint Mary of Sérignan, with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Toulouse, the church of Saint Peter and of the Holy Maidens, with its appurtenances; also the church of Saint Mary of Ciderium, the church of Saint Peter of Campania, and the church of Saint Saturninus of Alamans, with their appurtenances. In Gascony, in the bishopric of Auch, the church of Saint Julian of Galan, with the churches, villages, and all else belonging to it. In the district of Comminges, the church of Saint Mary of Quiriliac and the church of Saint Peter [Col. 0267D] of Puy.

Moreover, we forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person ever to dare, within the aforesaid village in which that monastery is situated and its boundaries, to construct any castle or fortification; or to extort anything by exaction from the people of that village, except for the abbot and his officials; or to exercise the office of vicarius; or, on account of that vicariate, without the permission of the abbot or any person, to claim the field which lies beyond the river Tonge below Severiac. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, let no one be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, the blessing of the abbot, and the ordinations of monks or clerics from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, may grant what you request. No bishop, however, may lawfully demand obedience from you, nor may you presume in any way to render it to anyone except the Roman Church. We further add that no one other than the Roman pontiff and a legate of the Apostolic See may bind the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 0268B] its presiding abbot, or the household which lives from its cellarer’s provision, by a sentence of interdict; but that place, as established by our predecessors, shall always remain under the right and authority of the Apostolic See. As a token of this liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay each year one gold coin to us and our successors.

We decree, therefore, that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all these things shall be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the aforesaid churches, the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If anyone in future knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 0268D] Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum.  
I, Pelagius, bishop of Albano.  
I, Gincio, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, Cencio, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius.  
I, Leo, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Robert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Stephen, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
[Col. 0269A] I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso.  
I, Othonianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.  
I, Gregory, cardinal priest of Saint Theodore.  
I, Reynerius, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
[Col. 0270A] I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo.  
I, Stephen, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.

Given near Orvieto, through the hand of Thomas, cardinal priest of Saint Sabina, in the nineteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

[Col. 0269] YEAR 1198–1216.

CCXXXIII. Ordinance of Lord Innocent concerning the expedition for the recovery of the Holy Land.

(DUCHESNE, *Rer. Franc. Script.*, V, 749.)

[Col. 0269B]

Earnestly desiring to free the Holy Land from the hands of the ungodly, and acting upon the counsel of prudent men who fully knew the circumstances of times and places, with the approval of the holy council we decree that crusaders shall prepare themselves in such a way that, on the Kalends of June next after the coming one [1 June 1217], all who have resolved to cross by sea shall assemble in the kingdom of Sicily: some, as shall be fitting and appropriate, at Brindisi, others at Messina and the neighbouring regions of each. We ourselves, with the Lord’s approval, intend then to be personally present there, so that the Christian army may be beneficially organized by our counsel and aid, to set forth with the divine and apostolic blessing. Those who have proposed to travel by land shall likewise make ready for the same date, informing us meanwhile, so that we may grant them a suitable legate from our side for counsel and assistance.

Priests and other clerics who are in the Christian army, whether subjects or prelates, shall diligently devote themselves to prayer and exhortation, teaching by word and example alike that they must always keep divine fear and love before their eyes, lest they say or do anything that offends the divine majesty. If at any time they fall into sin, let them immediately rise again through true repentance, displaying humility of heart and body, maintaining moderation both in food and clothing, wholly avoiding disputes and rivalries, and utterly putting away rancour and envy, so that, armed with spiritual as well as material weapons, they may fight more securely against the enemies of the faith, placing confidence not in their own strength but in divine power. We grant to these clerics that for three years they may receive their benefices in full as though they were resident in their churches, and, if necessary, may pledge those benefices as security for that same period.

Therefore, lest this holy undertaking be impeded or delayed, we strictly command all prelates of churches that each, in his own place, diligently exhort and induce those who have resolved to take up the sign of the cross, as well as both them and other crusaders, and those who may yet take the cross, to fulfil their vows to the Lord; and, if necessary, without any evasion, compel them by sentences of excommunication against their persons and interdict against their lands. Excepted only are those whom such an impediment befalls that, under the provision of the Apostolic See, their vow ought rightly to be commuted or deferred.

Furthermore, lest anything that may arise be omitted in the cause of Jesus Christ, we will and command that patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and others who have the care of souls shall zealously set before those entrusted to them the word of the cross, beseeching, through the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the one only true eternal God—kings, dukes, princes, marquesses, counts, barons, and other magnates, as well as the communes of cities, villages, and towns, that those who do not personally come to the aid of the Holy Land shall provide, according to their own means, a suitable number of fighting men with expenses necessary for three years, for the remission of their sins, as is set forth in the general letters and as we shall further specify below for greater certainty.

We will that participants in this remission include not only those who furnish ships of their own, but also those who take care to build ships for this work. Should any refuse—if any are so ungrateful to the Lord our God—we firmly declare on behalf of the Apostolic See that they should know that on the last day of strict judgment they will answer us for this before the awe-inspiring tribunal; first considering with what conscience or security they will be able to make confession before Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to whom the Father gave all things into His hands, if they refuse, in this enterprise that is as much His own as their own, to serve Him who was crucified for sinners, by whose gift they live, by whose favour they are sustained, and indeed by whose blood they have been redeemed.

But lest we appear to lay heavy and unbearable burdens upon the shoulders of men which we ourselves are unwilling to move with a finger, resembling those who speak indeed but do not act, behold: from the sums which we have been able to reserve beyond necessary and moderate expenses, we grant and donate thirty thousand pounds to this work, besides the shipping which we provide to crusaders from the City and neighbouring regions. We shall nevertheless assign to this same purpose three thousand marks of silver which remain with us from alms given by certain faithful persons, after other sums had been faithfully distributed for the needs and benefits of the aforesaid land through the hands of the patriarch of Jerusalem, the abbot of blessed memory, and the masters of the Temple and Hospital.

Desiring, moreover, that other prelates of churches and all clerics should share and participate both in the merit and in the reward, we establish with the common approval of the council that all clerics whatsoever, subjects as well as prelates, shall contribute for up to three years a twentieth part of their ecclesiastical revenues to aid the Holy Land, through the hands of those appointed for this purpose by apostolic provision. Certain religious persons, who ought rightly to be exempted from this assessment, are excepted, as likewise are those who, having taken or being about to take the sign of the cross, are personally to depart.

We and our brothers, the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, shall pay the full tenth; and let all know that they are bound, under sentence of excommunication, faithfully to observe this, so that those who knowingly commit fraud in this matter shall incur the sentence of excommunication.

Since, by the just judgment of the heavenly Emperor, those who adhere to His service deserve to enjoy a special prerogative, crusaders, because the time of departure is less than a year away, shall be exempt from levies, tallages, and other burdens. After they have taken the cross, we receive their persons and goods under the protection of blessed Peter and our own; they shall stand under the defence of archbishops, bishops, and all prelates of the Church, with their own protectors specially appointed for this purpose. Their persons and goods shall remain whole and undisturbed until certain knowledge is obtained of their death or return; and anyone who presumes to act otherwise shall be restrained by ecclesiastical censure.

If any persons departing there are bound by oath to pay interest, we command that their creditors be compelled with the same strictness to release them from the oath given and to desist from exacting interest. If any creditor compels them to pay interest, we command that he be compelled by a like penalty to restore it.

[Col. 0271D] We command that Jews be compelled by the secular power to remit interest; and, until they remit it, all communion with them shall be wholly denied by all faithful of Christ under sentence of excommunication. For those unable at present to pay their debts to Jews, secular princes shall provide a useful postponement such that, after their journey has begun, they shall incur no burden of interest until certain knowledge is obtained of their death or return. Jews shall be compelled to credit against the principal, after deducting necessary expenses, the income from pledged goods which they receive meanwhile. For such a benefit appears to entail no great loss, since it postpones payment without extinguishing the debt. [Col. 0272A] Church prelates who prove negligent in administering justice to crusaders and their households should know that they will be severely punished.

Moreover, because corsairs and pirates greatly hinder aid to the Holy Land by seizing and despoiling those travelling to it and returning from it, we bind their special helpers and supporters by the bond of excommunication. Under threat of anathema, we forbid anyone knowingly to have dealings with them by any contract of sale or purchase; and we charge the rulers of their cities and places to call them back and restrain them from this wickedness. Otherwise, since unwillingness to disturb the wicked is nothing other than to encourage them, and one who ceases to oppose a manifest crime is not free from the stain of secret partnership, we will and command that the prelates of churches exercise ecclesiastical severity against their persons and lands.

Furthermore, we excommunicate and anathematize those false and impious Christians who convey arms, iron, and fittings for galleys to the Saracens against Christ Himself and the Christian people; likewise those who sell them galleys or ships; those who perform the office of pilot on Saracen pirate ships; and those who give them advice or aid in engines of war or any other thing to the detriment of the Holy Land. We decree that they be punished by forfeiture of their goods and become slaves of those who capture them. We command that throughout all maritime cities this sentence be renewed on Sundays and feast days, and that such persons shall not be admitted to the bosom [Col. 0272C] of the Church unless they have sent in aid of the aforesaid land all that they received from this condemned gain, together with an equal amount from their own goods, so that by an equitable judgment they may be punished in the matter in which they sinned. If they are unable to pay, their guilt shall otherwise be punished in such a manner that others are deterred by their penalty from presuming to do the like.

Moreover, we forbid all Christians, and under anathema prohibit them, for four years to send or take their ships into the lands of the Saracens who inhabit the eastern regions, so that through this a greater supply of shipping may be prepared for those wishing to cross the sea in aid of the Holy Land, and assistance, which those Saracens have been accustomed to derive from this in no small measure, may be withdrawn from them.

Although tournaments have generally been forbidden under a specified penalty in various councils, nevertheless, because at this time the business of the cross is greatly hindered by them, we firmly forbid their being held for three years under penalty of excommunication.

Since, moreover, it is especially necessary for carrying out this undertaking that Christian princes and peoples keep peace with one another, at the urging of the holy universal synod we establish that a general peace shall be kept throughout the Christian world for at least four years. Through the prelates of churches, those in conflict shall be brought back to a full peace or to a firm truce to be inviolably observed; those who perhaps despise compliance shall be compelled with the greatest strictness by excommunication against their persons and interdict against their lands, unless the malice of their injuries is so great that they ought not to enjoy such peace. If they despise ecclesiastical censure, they may justly fear that secular power will be brought against them by the authority of the Church as disturbers of the cause of the Crucified.
