Therefore, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by that power of binding and loosing which God has granted to us, though unworthy, we grant full pardon of those sins of which they have freely repented in heart and confessed to all who personally undertake this labour at their own expense; and among the recompense of the just we promise them an increase of eternal salvation. To those who do not go there in person but send suitable men at their own expense according to their means and station, and likewise to those who go in person although at another’s expense, we grant full pardon of their sins. We also will and grant that all who suitably provide from their goods for the assistance of that land, or render fitting help and counsel, shall share in this remission according to the quality of their aid and the devotion of their intention. The common universal synod likewise imparts to all who piously undertake this work the suffrage of all its benefits, that it may profit them worthily unto salvation. Amen.

CCXXXIV. To all archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches.—Against forgers and malicious critics.

(MABILLON, *De re diplomatica*, Venetian edition, p. 653, from MS 128 of the Colbert Library.)

[Col. 0273C]

To all archbishops, bishops, and other prelates and clerics of churches, and to all faithful of Christ who shall inspect these present letters.

Formerly, when the die of our bull, by which the heads of the apostles Peter and Paul were stamped, had been broken, we immediately caused another, somewhat similar, to be substituted, lest through the lack of a bull persons and business should suffer loss during the vacancy. But because this substitute [Col. 0273D] represented the images of the same heads larger than usual, and thereby differed noticeably from the former, we afterwards caused another to be made, more suitable for the permanent work of sealing with a bull; by its impression these present letters are authenticated. The other, having been set aside, was to be made by the services of another craftsman and not changed until it should fail through corruption or age. Yet because the pernicious ingenuity of forgers, unless cautious prudence keeps watch against it, might perhaps take occasion from the aforesaid change for malicious action and devise new instruments of wickedness for itself, it must be provided with a more discerning eye, so that, should that hand deadly to itself and to its whole body attempt, within the pestilential workshops of its own hiding-place, [Col. 0274A] to fashion by false dies anything similar—that is, through an appearance copied from genuine exemplars—it may neither deceive the eyes of the discerning examiner nor escape, to the harm of the common good, the punishment of a stern judge.

Therefore we command that, extending the hand of diligent investigation against forgers of our letters, you strive to discover their iniquities so as to bring them into complete hatred; so that this root, which has sprouted through the encouragement of an evil age, may be cut down by the sharp edge of the disciplinary sickle. Whenever apostolic letters are presented to any of you, let careful consideration be given to the person presenting them—especially if he produces a privilege or letters concerning grants or indulgences, which are granted or entrusted by us only from certain knowledge—whether, from [Col. 0274B] his reputation or merits, any scruple of unfavorable suspicion arises concerning his actions.

Then let whoever receives letters of this kind examine them carefully in respect of the bull, thread, parchment, style of composition, handwriting, form, and all other matters in which forgery can be noticed or detected. If a clear indication of forgery appears in them, let them immediately be rejected as false; and let the prelates proceed, with exact diligence and according to the rigor of the canons, against those who procured them or knowingly use them, even to imprisonment and other penalties—against opponents also, etc., if they too refuse to avoid canonical discipline. Provided, however, that no derogation whatever be made from letters sealed with the bull which we have substituted for the broken former one.

Nevertheless, if concerning any such letters [Col. 0274C] reasonable doubt should arise about the genuineness of the bull, let such hesitation be resolved without any difficulty by a careful comparison with other similar bulls concerning which no doubt exists. And so that no frivolous cloak of defense or excuse based on the procurer’s fault or negligence may remain to anyone in this matter, we will and strictly command that each of the prelates, by issuing a public edict of warning, forewarn and instruct his subjects [his subjects], that they carefully examine, with the advice of experts if necessary, the apostolic letters which they intend to use and which they have received into their own hands from hands other than yours [ours] or those of persons known to be appointed to that office; and that they produce them [Col. 0274D] publicly only after they have been approved by strict judgment. But if they find them disapproved, let them immediately destroy or surrender them. And if, after they have begun to use them publicly, those letters should be accused of forgery, let them know that a belated ignorance, if they then plead it, will by no means profit them so as to prevent their being subject to canonical punishment.

Let every one beware, moreover, lest what we have devised in this matter as a remedy turn through abuse into harm. For if, while we are opposing the crime of forgery, some take from this an occasion to act maliciously against persons or affairs, the severity of apostolic discipline will not leave unpunished this grave offense of malice, which can readily be detected.

### CCXXXV. To the abbot of Bec.—That the diocesan of the place may not investigate persons of the monastery.

[MARTEN., *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 819, from the manuscript of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris.]

[Col. 0275A]

You lately petitioned us, as earnestly as humbly, that, since through idle investigations churches often come to ruin both spiritually and temporally, we should, in paternal concern for the protection of your monastery, provide that the diocesan of the place should not proceed to an inquiry against persons of the aforesaid monastery where no cause requires it. But lest, by a slight expedient, one arrive at grave loss—for the door of malicious accusation must be wholly shut, lest anyone be unjustly accused—[Col. 0275B] we, inclined by your just petitions, by the authority of these present letters forbid the diocesan of that place to proceed on his own authority to an inquiry against persons of that monastery, unless someone has been seriously defamed regarding his offenses, not by ill-wishers but by prudent and honorable persons.

### CCXXXVI. To the same.—He grants authority to make one community out of several cells.

(Ibid.)

INNOCENT III, etc.

On your behalf humble supplication has been made to us that, since you have certain small cells in which two or three monks dwell and do not altogether live [Col. 0275C] as befits the honor of the order, we should deem it fitting to grant you permission either to recall those monks, together with the possessions which they hold, to the convent, or newly to establish from them one or more communities. Since therefore it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity, we grant you free authority, without prejudice to another, to do whichever of the aforesaid alternatives you judge more expedient. And you, son abbot, take care to watch over yourself and the flock entrusted to you in such a manner, etc.

Given, etc.

### CCXXXVII. To the same.—He grants authority to absolve certain monks from irregularity.

(Ibid., col. 820.)

[Col. 0275D] From your report we have learned that certain monks of your monastery—some of whom, by violent laying on of hands, incurred the canon of a promulgated sentence; while others entered there simoniacally—without having obtained the benefit of absolution or the favor of a dispensation, received sacred orders and thereafter did not fear to minister in them. Concerned for their salvation, you requested that, since they would have to come to the Apostolic See, and you assert that there is reason to fear that, in coming into our presence, they might wander about and suffer loss of the salvation for whose sake they had come, we should act mercifully in this matter.

But we, having full confidence in your discretion, and also considering that, in favor of religion, we tolerate many things in religious persons [Col. 0276A] which we would not tolerate in others, command by apostolic letters that, after persons who have committed such violence have been absolved according to the customary form of the Church in such cases—unless their offense is difficult or enormous, so that they ought properly to be sent to the Apostolic See—you shall, while observing the general constitution of the council concerning those known to have made a simoniacal entry, act by our authority with respect to the fact that they thus received orders and thereafter ministered in them, as you judge expedient for the salvation of their souls.

### CCXXXVIII. To the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Locus Dei.

[LANGEBECK, *Script. rer. Danic.*, VIII, 189.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0276B] sons, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Locus Dei, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Ribe: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Inclined by the supplication of your devotion, by the authority of these present letters we grant you that you may freely claim, receive, and retain possessions and other movable or immovable goods, except fiefs, which would have fallen, by right of succession or by any other just title, to the free persons of brethren who flee from the world to your monastery and make profession there, if they had remained in the world. Therefore let no one at all presume to infringe this page of our grant, etc. As above.

### CCXXXIX. To the archbishop of Rouen.—He rebukes him for having understood too narrowly a pontifical mandate concerning the conferring of a benefice upon a certain cleric.

[MARTEN., *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 796, from the manuscript of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris.]

[Col. 0276C]

Although we could deservedly rebuke you sharply because you informed us by your letters that many jurists were greatly astonished at the contents of letters which we sent, at the request of R. de Berlaico, elected to the church of Maleville, to our beloved sons the archdeacon, the cantor, and Master A. de Beaford, canon of Évreux; namely, that they contained a mandate contrary to the common law and to the custom of the whole province—this is wholly remote from the truth.

For, setting forth the cause of their astonishment, you asked how [Col. 0276D] that priest could object to another cleric that he possessed several benefices, when he himself possessed several benefices; and how he ought to have been ordained within a year, since he was a scholar and there was great hope concerning him that he ought to attain greater advancement, and he held no other ecclesiastical benefices from which he could be supported.

Certainly, if you had attended more carefully to the tenor of those letters and faithfully explained it to jurists skilled in law, you would have perceived clearly that nothing is expressed in them from which we ought to have understood that the priest held another church, nor that the other cleric was a scholar of whom there was hope that he should attain greater advancement. Even if both had been expressed, neither of them [Col. 0277A] could by law or custom have impeded the form of that mandate: since one who has one church may canonically be appointed to another, provided that he relinquishes the former; and a scholar of whom good hope is entertained ought not to be appointed to a parish church if perhaps he is unwilling or unable to be ordained within a year.

Therefore, wishing that henceforth your brotherhood should be more circumspect concerning the understanding of our letters, we command by apostolic writings that you do not impede them from proceeding in the aforesaid matter according to the form of those letters, especially since in them we took the most diligent care to show deference to you not only in law but also in honor.

### CCXL. To the abbot and convent of Saint Michael of Terrascha.—That the benefice promised to the cleric R. be conferred.

[MARTEN., *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 797, from the manuscript of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris.]

[Col. 0277B]

INNOCENT III, pope, to the abbot and convent of Saint Michael of Terrascha.

Our beloved son R., a cleric, appearing before the Apostolic See, showed us by his statement that, although you had promised that you would provide for him by conferring an ecclesiastical benefice when able to do so—as was clearly demonstrated by letters of the dean of Soissons and his fellow judges, delegated in this matter by the Apostolic See, in which the tenor of your letter of promise was inserted—you have hitherto neglected to do this. Before the aforesaid judges you alleged [Col. 0277C] that such a promise did not bind you in any way, since it appeared to have been made contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, which forbids the promise of a benefice not vacant.

But we, considering that it is one thing for a prelate to promise the conferral of a benefice when he is able, [Col. 0278A] and another thing to promise it when it becomes vacant—since in many cases the opportunity may arise in which the conferral need not be deferred in expectation of a benefice becoming vacant—command by our apostolic writings that you assign a suitable ecclesiastical benefice to the said R. Otherwise, by our letters we have commanded the abbot of Saint John and the dean of Soissons to compel you to this by ecclesiastical censure, without appeal.

### CCXLI. To the archbishop of Torres.—That he procure the restoration of certain churches to the monastery of Monte Cassino. (Lateran, 13 November.)

[D. TOSTI, *Storia della badia Casin.*, II, 285.]

[Col. 0278B] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother A., archbishop of Torres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A report has reached our ears that our brother P., bishop of Ampurias, unjustly holds the churches of Saint Peter of Nugulbi and Saint Elias of Sitim, which had been violently occupied by his predecessor. Since those churches belong by right to Blessed Peter and were granted under an annual rent to the monastery of Monte Cassino by our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Calixtus, and confirmed by his privilege, we command and enjoin you by these present letters to cause the same churches, with all their appurtenances, to be restored to that monastery and [Col. 0278C] left in peace. Thereafter, if the aforesaid bishop considers himself to have any right in them, he may pursue it before us at a suitable place and time.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

[Col. 0277] The three letters which follow had fallen out of their proper place.

### CCXLII. To William, abbot of the monastery of Glanfeuil.—He confirms the monastery’s possessions and privileges, saving the due obedience owed to the abbots of Monte Cassino. (A.D. 1203. Lateran, 23 March.)

[D. TOSTI, *Storia della badia Casin.*, Naples, 1842, quarto, vol. II, 281, from the original, charter chest 2, no. 12.]

[Col. 0277D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Glanfeuil, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Whenever that is requested of us which is recognized to accord with reason and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Popes Urban and Anastasius, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, over which by God’s favor you are known to preside, [Col. 0278C] and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, God favoring it, acquire by concession of pontiffs, grant of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the church of Saint Martin of Saint-Maur; the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius at Bâtheac, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Molo, with its appurtenances; the island of Saint Maur, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary at Dane; the church of Saint Simplicius on the Loire; the churches of Saint Peter at Vodda, of Saint Peter with the village of Fabren, of Saint Lambert of Curallo, of Saint Hilary of Coneorzo with their appurtenances, and of Saint Martin of Sorech; the land of Americ of Averoim; the churches of Saint Just of Vere with their appurtenances [Col. 0279A] and of Saint Mary of Doado; the village of Solonge with its appurtenances; the village called Cru with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Veterinus of Gena, with the mill and its other appurtenances; the church of Saint Cyriacus at Salmosa with its tithes; the church of Saint Maur at Lauduna and the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Vareno; the village of Syndremont with its appurtenances and the village of Lambri with its appurtenances; the island of Blason; in Normandy, the church of Saint Mary of Cingal, the church of Saint Maur situated in the castle of Laudun, the church of Saint Anian, the village of Sindremont, and the church of Saint Peter in the fields.

We also decree that burial in the same place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, saving nevertheless the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, let no one be set over it by any cunning of surreption or by violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the greater part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall be presented to the abbot of Monte Cassino for confirmation and shall receive the gift of blessing from a Catholic bishop whom he shall request by his letters. He and his successors shall promise obedience to the abbot of Monte Cassino and, every five years, shall visit the monastery of Monte Cassino as their head [Col. 0279C] with due humility.

Therefore we decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment [Col. 0279D] of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, subscribe. I, Peter, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, John, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. [Col. 0280A] I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, subscribe. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, shepherd, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Callixtus at Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Martin in Equitius, have subscribed. I, Cencius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Prisca, have subscribed. I, Cencius, cardinal-priest of Saints John and [Col. 0280B] Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, have subscribed. I, Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace, have subscribed. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. [Col. 0280C] I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1202 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

### CCXLIII. To the whole clergy of the province of Bremen.—That they publicly denounce Waldemar as excommunicated. (A.D. 1214. Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 27 April.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg. Urkund.*, p. 344, from the original, with Innocent III’s pendant lead seal, chest II, no. 10.]

[Col. 0280D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbots, priors, provosts, deans, archdeacons, and other prelates of churches established throughout the province of Bremen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since Waldemar, son of perdition, as a heretic and schismatic despises canonical censure and, regarding the keys of the Church as nothing, though excommunicated and deposed, presumes to exercise episcopal offices, we strictly command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic writings publicly to announce in your churches the aforesaid degraded Waldemar and both him and his supporters as excommunicated. [Col. 0281A] And you, sons abbots, take care to watch over yourselves and the flock entrusted to you in such a manner, uprooting vices and planting virtues, that on the last day of strict judgment, before the dreadful Judge who will render to each according to his works, you may be able to give a worthy account.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

### CCXLIV. Bull for Garin, abbot of Saint John in the Valley (diocese of Chartres). (A.D. 1215. Lateran, 18 February.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VIII, instrument 332, from the private archive of M. de Gagneres, in the Royal Library.]

[Col. 0281B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GARIN, abbot of the church of Blessed John of the Valley, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life in perpetuity.

Whenever this, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., we receive the aforesaid church under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing; decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods, etc., shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors; among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

In the church of Blessed Mary of Chartres, the whole revenues [Col. 0281C] for a complete year of the prebend of each brother from the congregation of canons of that church, whenever he leaves it for any reason, so that, however the person may change, the prebendal benefice in its entirety may pass to the uses of your church. The entire prebend which your church holds in perpetuity in the church of Blessed Mary, and which Abbot Albert of blessed memory held when he received the canonical rule; the church of Saint Stephen with its appurtenances, namely the altar of Morenciac with the share of the synod belonging to the altar; the church of Mondonisville with its appurtenances, free from every exaction, synod, and *circada*; the church of Saint Faith with parochial right in the new borough called Castelleth; [Col. 0281D] the church of Luciac; and the portion of a field from that land which Ivo, bishop of Chartres of blessed memory, had previously held; the land of Osanivilla, both episcopal and canonical, with its offerings; the land of Ancherisvilla, in the village of Pontegodani; the priory of the church of that village with all episcopal houses; the entire oat-farrago (mixed fodder crop) and all the bishop’s land which [Col. 0282A] you possess beyond the river Audura; the street which our venerable brother Goslenus, bishop of Chartres, gave you; the gift to your church of the altar of the church of Serneio, made by Goslenus, canon and provost of the church of Saint Mary; the gift to you, made by Hugh, viscount of Chartres, of the vicariate of the Valley and of all the land of Moncellis with all its customary dues; all the land of Eddevilla with its customary dues and fiefs; the church of Ardelecht with all its tenants and land for two ploughs; the church of Saint Nicholas of Curvavilla together with the church of Saint Peter of the same village; the church of Saint Denis of Puteis; Saint Mary of Gohosvilla with its appurtenances; the church of Trembleio with its tithes; the church of Blessed Mary of Teliu with its tithes; [Col. 0282B] the church of Braioso with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saturninus of Camburciac with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Loiniac, with pannage for your pigs; the village of Armentarvilla with the tithe, which you received on lease from the church of Saint Benedict for three measures of wheat and four of oats, payable each year; the village of Albereth and the village of Nerlu; the land of Curvaulmo; and all the other lands which you hold at Chartres; the church of Garneio with land for one plough, which Nivardus of Nonancurte granted to your church for the redemption of his soul; the church of Orrevilla with the tithe which Hugh, son of Guinemar, gave you through the hand of the aforesaid Ivo, bishop of Chartres, in the place called Guoriart; one-half [Col. 0282C] with meadows beside the river Audura, at Saint Priscus’s mill; the meadows which you hold at Ataias from the benefice of Blessed Mary; the land which you hold by right of ownership at the village of Soors. Moreover, the rents of houses, lands, and vineyards, and the tithes of crops and vineyards, which belong to you by right both in the city of Chartres and in its suburb.

Upon the death of you, beloved son Garin, abbot, let no one be set over it by any surreption, cunning, or violence, except one whom the brethren shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine. The person elected shall be presented to the common chapter of Blessed Mary and shall receive the abbacy and the grace of blessing from the bishop of Chartres; and he shall perform his week in the church of Blessed Mary just as the other canons do. [Col. 0282D]

Therefore we decree, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Thomas, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, bishop-elect of Naples, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1215 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III.

[Col. 0283]

## VARIOUS DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE LETTERS OF INNOCENT III

### I. G., bishop of Langres; R., bishop of Chalon; G. of Cîteaux, N. of La Ferté, G. of Pontigny, and O. of Clairvaux, abbots.—Concerning the knights of Calatrava. (A.D. 1198.)

[HENRIQUEZ, *Menologium Cisterciense*, II, 484.]

[Col. 0283A]

To the most reverend lord and Father INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: G., by the same grace bishop of Langres; R., by the same grace bishop of Chalon; G. of Cîteaux, N. of La Ferté, G. of Pontigny, and G. of Clairvaux, the aforesaid abbots: greeting and service of submission and reverence, as devoted as it is due.

We set forth for Your Holiness the course of events [Col. 0283B] concerning the brethren of the military order of Calatrava, now called those of Salvatierra, after the castle of Calatrava itself was occupied by pagans: in what manner they became sons of the house of Morimond, and under what obligation and relationship of filiation a daughter-house is subject to, looks to, and is bound to its mother-house. Thus, if anyone strives to devise anything against this, then, upon seeing our testimony, his entire undertaking may be destroyed by the judgment of apostolic authority.

Since the brethren of Calatrava have professed the Cistercian Order from their very beginning, rejoicing to be designated by this name under which, in nearly every part of Christendom, the name of God is blessed and praised by the faithful, it pleased the master and brethren of Calatrava that in the year of the Lord 1187 the same master should present himself before the chapter of Cîteaux, [Col. 0283C] and there, with letters from the king of Castile and the petitions of the magnates of Spain, should make his and his brethren’s request: that they be incorporated into and more closely united with the same Order of Cîteaux.

Their petition seemed good in the eyes of all; and because it flowed from religious devotion, it was accepted. By common assent and deliberation of the chapter it was prescribed that they should be sons of Morimond, and that the abbot and the same house should possess over them that right of filiation which Cîteaux is known to possess over Morimond: namely, authority to make an annual visitation, to appoint or remove the master who stands in the abbot’s place, to correct faults which occur, exact punishment for offenses, and the like. An institute was delivered to them, and a rule of life prescribed, and regulations concerning food and clothing to be observed by them henceforth, together with the other spiritual observances maintained in the Order. These they accepted with grateful wish and heart, as may be seen in the written copy of the charter made between them and the monks of Morimond, which for this reason [Col. 0284A] we have put together and written here so that the matter may be manifest to you, etc.

### Constitutions of the knights of Calatrava proposed to Innocent III for confirmation

> “Brother Guy, humble minister of Cîteaux, together with the bishops and abbots of the whole chapter, to the venerable brother Nuno, master, and to the whole body of brethren of Calatrava: greeting and the affection of brotherly charity.
>
> “We heartily approve your praiseworthy purpose, by which, converted from the warfare of the world to the warfare of Christ, you have resolved to fight against the enemies of the faith. Giving thanks to almighty God, who draws to himself whom he wills and as he wills, and converts one person in this way and another in that to his service, we humbly pray to him for your progress [Col. 0284B] and increase, in merit and number. As to your request—that you be received into the communion of the benefits of our Order, not as associates but as true brethren—we gladly assent.
>
> “Since you further request that a rule of life be prescribed to you by our authority, we, after taking counsel, have considered that we should not neglect to set out for you a few articles concerning your food and clothing. You may therefore use linen only for undergarments. Have garments moderate, respectable, and suitable, according to the counsel of the lord of Morimond and your master, and a scapular as the habit of religion. You shall sleep clothed and girded, and shall keep continual silence in the oratory, refectory, dormitory, and [Col. 0284C] kitchen. Take the greatest care that, in no garment whatsoever, you may be accused of excess or noted for affected display.
>
> “On three days of the week, namely Tuesday, Thursday, and Sunday, as well as on the principal feast days, you may eat meat. Yet, so far as meat is concerned, you shall be content with one dish and one kind, and shall keep silence at table everywhere. Moreover, we grant your request that no member of our Order may receive any of your brethren without your consent; and you shall be bound by the same rule toward ours.
>
> “When you come to any abbey of our Order, because you know our customs less well, you shall be received not in the convent, [Col. 0284D] but in the guest quarters, honorably and charitably, and as familiarly as possible. We receive as members in the good of the Order the chaplains professed in your house, just as you are.
>
> “Whoever strikes his brother shall not approach arms or horse for six months and shall eat on the ground for three days. Whoever is disobedient to his master shall suffer the same. Whoever is placed in any other obedience shall not gainsay it. Whoever is publicly caught in fornication shall eat on the ground for one year, on bread and water three days in each week; on Friday he shall receive discipline. From the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Easter, all who are at home shall fast three days in every week; but those among the Saracens shall do as the master directs and as is customary. In all these matters we command you to obey your master and make profession to him as to an abbot. Whoever seeks more or less than what is contained here shall be expelled from the house. But we make you free from every exaction of abbots.
>
> “The chaplains who sing Masses for you shall hear your confessions, and you yourselves shall choose them. The master also shall hold chapter for you daily, and you shall observe two Lents. If you are able to build abbeys, the lord of Morimond shall regulate them. The same abbot of Morimond shall provide how they are to be visited once each year, whether by himself or another. Once one has been built, two monks of that same monastery shall live with those brethren as often as necessary.
>
> “Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198.”

Therefore, most holy Father, these things having thus been done and such concessions having been obtained in this manner from the chapter, the same master approached the holy Apostolic See with a certain monk, envoy of the lord of Morimond, and obtained that these things be confirmed for him by an apostolic privilege. The same master [Col. 0285C], and the envoy of Morimond, in procuring the renewal of his privilege from your predecessor of pious memory, Pope Gregory VIII, concerning the abbeys, granges, possessions, and appurtenances which that house possessed, brought back, among the other privileges granted to his house, the house, order, and brethren of Calatrava, with all that belonged to them, by the assistance of the aforesaid privilege. Afterwards, as successive supreme pontiffs succeeded him, and the men of Morimond sought new privileges from new apostolic pontiffs, it came about that the men of Morimond have, in the privileges of four popes—Gregory, Clement, Celestine, and Innocent—the same house, that is, Calatrava, entered in the enumeration of those belonging to them. Therefore we beseech your piety, with all the urgency of prayer that we can, [Col. 0285D] that you confirm by apostolic writings this right of filial relationship over them, which was granted to the house of Morimond with such great deliberation and discernment, lest it suffer mutilation of such a member through the machinations of any malicious persons. Perhaps there will be some among them who come to you seeking, by false representations, letters of emancipation and severance from the order, or of transfer to another house—men who aspire to high things and disdain to be subject to the order, forgetting how great was the humility of their forebears. Those forebears, glorying neither in lineage, nor in riches, nor in arms, nor in frequent victories over the pagans, nor in the rich spoils often carried off, voluntarily subjected themselves, specially and faithfully, to the order of Morimond. Their rash attempt, therefore, must be opposed by apostolic authority [Col. 0286A], lest the aforesaid house be dismembered so ruinously and grievously.

## II. Oath of Fidelity Made by John of Ceccano to the Roman Church for the Protection and Preservation of the Regalia of Saint Peter. (1201.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 621.]

In the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III, the nobleman John of Ceccano swore fidelity to that same Lord Pope Innocent, concerning Ceccano and the whole territory which he holds, in the palace at Anagni before bishops, priests, deacons, and cardinals, with many clerics and noblemen of Anagni present, as well as outsiders and the knights of John of Ceccano himself. [Col. 0286B] And he acknowledged that he held Ceccano and all his other land from the Roman Church. The form of fidelity was as follows:

“I, John of Ceccano, from this hour henceforth, shall be faithful to blessed Peter, to the Roman Church, to my lord Pope Innocent, and to his canonically installed successors. I shall not, by deed, word, counsel, or consent, act so that they lose life or limb, or are seized by an evil seizure. Counsel which they shall entrust to me, whether in person, through an envoy, or by letters, I shall knowingly disclose to no one to their harm. If I learn of certain harm to them, I shall, if able, prevent it; if I am unable, I shall inform them through myself, my letters, or an envoy, or shall tell such a person as I trust will certainly report it to them. I shall help them defend Ceccano and all my other land which I possess, and the other regalia of blessed Peter which he possesses; what he does not possess, I shall help recover; and, once recovered, I shall help retain and defend against all persons. All these things I shall observe in good faith, without fraud or evil contrivance. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.”

After this, placing his hands between the hands of the lord pope himself, he performed liege homage to him. The lord pope then invested him, as a favor, with a gilded silver cup. Later in that same year, the same lord pope, considering the fidelity and service of John of Ceccano and his forebears, assigned to him Sitense Castle as a fief.

## II bis. Concerning Fidelity and Homage Rendered to the Roman Church by Andrew of Calvignano, and the Entrusting to Him of the Custody of the Borough of Dole. (1202.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 623.]

[Col. 0286D]

In the fifth year of Lord Pope Innocent III, the nobleman Andrew of Calvignano rendered fidelity to Lord Pope Innocent concerning the custody of the borough of Dole, in the following manner: in the Lateran palace, before bishops, cardinal-priests, and cardinal-deacons, with the knights and clerics of the said nobleman present, the abbot of Dole and two of his monks, and many others, clerics as well as laymen:

In the name of the Lord. Amen. I, Andrew of Calvignano, lord of the castle of Ralph, from this hour [Col. 0287A] henceforth shall be faithful to blessed Peter, to the Roman Church, to my lord Pope Innocent, and to his successors, etc. (as above). I shall help them defend the borough of Dole, the custody of which I hold from the Roman Church, and the other regalia of blessed Peter which he possesses; what he does not possess, I shall help recover; and, once recovered, I shall help retain and defend against all persons. I shall honorably receive the legates and envoys of the Roman Church and treat them kindly; and throughout all my territory I shall, to the extent of my ability, provide them safe conduct. I shall observe all these things in good faith, without fraud and evil contrivance. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

After this, placing his hands between the hands of the lord pope, he performed liege homage to him. The lord pope then invested him, as a favor, with the custody of the borough of Dole.

## III. Agreement of Emperor Otto with Adolf, Archbishop of Cologne. (September 1202.)

[Published here for the first time from a manuscript in the library formerly of St. Paul’s at Münster and now in the Royal Library at Berlin, containing letters of Innocent III concerning the church of Cologne. We owe fuller information about it to the distinguished Roestell, a diligent supporter of our work, who, at our request, sent us a transcription of both Cologne agreements from it. I have attempted to supply the words printed in italics where they are erased in the manuscript. The cause of this agreement is learned from Godfrey’s annals under the year 1202. PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Leges*, II, 206.] How Adolf swore a second time to King Otto and concerning their settlement.

[Col. 0287B]

[Col. 0287C] The priors, provosts, abbots, deans, and scholastics of Cologne shall swear that in good faith they will induce the Archbishop of Cologne to render steadfast and faithful service to King Otto, and that during the life of King Otto he shall adhere to no other king. If he does not observe this, they shall withdraw the obedience which they owe him and reserve it for the lord pope; but they shall render to King Otto the service owed by them to the archbishop, until the archbishop returns to the service owed by him to King Otto according to the form of his oath.

The nobles of the land who are bound to the Archbishop of Cologne by oaths, those now present and others whenever they can be assembled, shall swear before the king and archbishop that they will induce the Archbishop of Cologne [Col. 0287D] to render steadfast and faithful service to King Otto and that he shall adhere to no other king. If he does not do so, they shall serve King Otto, and not the archbishop, with their castles, lands, and men, until the archbishop comes to his senses and returns to King Otto in the aforesaid manner.

Twenty ministeriales of Saint Peter shall swear for themselves and for the other ministeriales that in good faith they will induce the others to observe the same: that they will induce the archbishop, and the rest as above. If he does not do so, they themselves shall withdraw the service owed to the archbishop and render it to King Otto, until the rest is fulfilled as above.

Twenty-four burghers shall swear for themselves and for the other burghers according to the form [Col. 0288A] of the oath of the ministeriales.

If, however, disagreement should arise between king and archbishop—so that the king says, “The archbishop does not adhere to me in the due and faithful manner,” while the archbishop asserts the contrary—three priors, three nobles, three ministeriales, and three burghers, chosen from among those sworn, shall come together; their statements shall be accepted, whether for the king or for the archbishop. In accordance with the statements of these twelve, all who have sworn shall adhere either to the archbishop or to the king, according to the prescribed form.

Before all else the king shall give his pledge into the hand of the lord legate [Note: [Col. 0287D] Guy, bishop of Palestrina.] that he will ratify the provisions set down above; and likewise shall the archbishop.

King Otto shall free the Aachen mint from Lord Walram [Note: [Col. 0287D] Of Limburg.], and both the king and Walram shall renounce that mint forever. The lord legate, under anathema, shall forbid minting at Aachen—whether there or elsewhere outside the city of Cologne—any coinage in the Cologne standard [Col. 0288B], and shall write to the Roman pontiff asking him to confirm his sentence.

The king shall relinquish the toll at Duisburg and shall never resume it; and the lord legate shall issue a similar sentence, with confirmation from the Roman pontiff.

The king and archbishop, with their household officers, shall treat effectively concerning the destruction of the royal tower [Note: [Col. 0288D] A doubtful word in the manuscript. ROESTELL.] at Werth, together with its toll.

The privilege agreed upon between king and archbishop shall be read publicly, and the king shall publicly declare that he has sworn diligently to observe what is written in the privileges and never to violate it.

The archbishop shall grant the king a truce until the feast of Saint John the Baptist concerning the . . . marks for which he had pledged the estate of Sinzeche to the Duke [Col. 0288C] of Brabant. It shall be at the king’s option either to provide suitable sureties at present or, if the king does not pay the money, that on the feast of Saint John the city of Dortmund shall be the archbishop’s pledge until the aforesaid money is paid to him.

The successors and heirs of deceased priors, nobles, and ministeriales shall render the oaths. If the king wrongfully treats the Archbishop of Cologne or the church of Cologne, the aforesaid four orders shall withdraw their service from the king until he makes satisfaction; and they shall swear this.

The burghers of the city of Cologne shall swear fidelity to King Otto in this form: that from this day forward they shall preserve fidelity to him and guard for him the city of Cologne against every person, [Col. 0288D] so long as he preserves in its right the church of Saint Peter, the Archbishop of Cologne, the priors, nobles, vassals, and ministeriales of Saint Peter, and the city of Cologne.

## IV. Of the King of England.—He Requests That Geoffrey Fitz Peter Not Undertake Pilgrimage before Five Years Have Elapsed. (1204.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 91. *Close Rolls*, 6 John, membrane 6, in the Tower of London.]

To the most reverend Father in Christ, etc., INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, etc., JOHN, by God’s grace [Col. 0289A] king of England, etc., due and devout reverence in all things.

Since we are in such a situation that it would be burdensome for us [to lose] those faithful men of ours who adhere to us most closely, whose fidelity we do not doubt, and by whose counsel our land must be governed and defended by sea; since the days are evil, and day by day our men seem fraudulently and deceitfully to withdraw from our fidelity and service and to rise against us, whereby the condition of our realm, as Your Holiness knows, is disturbed: we supplicate Your Excellency with all the devotion we can, that, having regard for our position, you may be pleased to defer for four or five years the pilgrimage of our beloved and faithful Geoffrey Fitz Peter, [Col. 0289B] our justiciar, who has taken the cross; for his presence is so necessary to us and to our realm that we can by no means do without him.

And we, God willing, shall send both him and the other crusaders to the land of Jerusalem as soon as they have returned to the land [reading uncertain].

May the condition of our estate, therefore, move and induce your fatherhood to this, so that we may deservedly be obliged to give you thanks for it.

Witnessed by myself, at Winchester, the twenty-fourth day of November.

## V. Of Henry, King of Hungary.—Against Certain Persons Who Had Not Accepted the Constitutions Promulgated by the Legate of the Apostolic See. (1204.)

[FARLATUS, *Illyricum Sacrum*, V, 46.]

[Col. 0289C]

To the venerable Father in Christ, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman Church: HENRY, by the same grace king of Hungary, Dalmatia, Bosnia, and Serbia, greeting and faithful reverence in all things.

When John, the humble and faithful chaplain of Your Holiness, came into our presence, bringing with him two of the principal men among those who, as was reported, fostered the condemned sect of heretics in the land of Ban Kulin, we examined the articles of orthodox faith. At John’s exhortation, these articles had not been accepted by those to whom he had been sent. We gave the same articles, contained under our seal, to the son of the lord of that land—namely, the son of the said Kulin, who was then with us—[Col. 0289D] strictly ordering him to cause them, and any other matters which the Roman See should hereafter decree to send them according to God, to be inviolably observed by all in his land.

When he had likewise accepted this according to our will, he subsequently bound himself, by our hand and that of J., Archbishop of Kalocsa, that, should he thereafter knowingly presume to maintain or defend the aforesaid persons, or any other persons, in heresy in his land, he would pay one thousand marks of silver; one half of these would accrue to you, and the other half to our treasury.

Moreover, the aforesaid two principal men who had come with your chaplain John swore in our presence, both for themselves and for their brethren by whom they had been sent, that they would firmly observe forever the constitutions already promulgated and delivered to them by your said faithful legate, etc.

## VI. Instrument Concerning the Castle of Nymphae Delivered to Lord Pope Innocent III. (1204.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 677.]

In the name of the Lord. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204, the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent III, the seventh indiction, on the twentieth day of April: we, Philip and Bartholomew, brothers, sons of the late Lombard, with our sister Lady Aldruda present and consenting to this—she being the widow of our kinsman Scotto—and with her renouncing, conceding, and donating every right, action, or exception which in any manner she appears to possess in all the matters written below, whether by reason of the usufruct of the said property which was left to her by John Paparone, son of her late [husband], or otherwise on account of any matter or cause; before Lord John, Obicio, and Henry, appointed judges beyond the Tiber, Nicholas Tulli, advocate, and the witnesses subscribed below, especially summoned for this purpose: of our own will we renounce and wholly and generally relinquish in every respect, and we confirm in every manner the possession which the lord pope, or another on his behalf, has of the property written below. We do this to you, Lord Octavian, by God’s grace cousin [Col. 0290C] and chamberlain of Lord Pope Innocent III, likewise constituted by his command and as his procurator especially for this purpose, for his use and benefit, and for those of his successors and the whole Roman Church in perpetuity.

That is: the same entire undivided third part—or more, if anything further belongs to us in any way—namely, of the whole castle of Nymphae, with its tenements and appurtenances, within and without. The lord Oddo, son of the late Lord Peter Frangipani, sold, granted in payment, and delivered it to the aforesaid Scotto Paparone, our kinsman, for five hundred and thirty pounds of Parvian denari, as appears from the instrument drawn up in the hand of John Bonus, scrivener; we give this instrument to you for greater security. That third [Col. 0290D] part of the said castle, with every right which the said late Scotto had in it, within and without, belongs to us under the will of John Paparone, our nephew and son of the said late Scotto, as likewise appears from an instrument drawn up in the hand of the said John Bonus, scrivener; we also give that instrument to you for greater precaution.

Whatever right, and whatever personal action, real action, or hypothecary right—whether for bringing an action or raising an exception—we have, or in any manner might have, in the whole said castle with its tenements and appurtenances within and without, and especially in the said third part of that castle which, as stated, belongs to us; namely, whether by right or on account [Col. 0291A] of the aforesaid grant, sale, and transfer in payment made by the aforesaid Lord Oddo to the late Scotto, or also by reason of, or under the right of, the legacy given to us by our aforesaid late nephew in his will: we relinquish, cede, and assign to you, as stated, in a procuratorial capacity for the said lord pope and his successors. Thus whatever we could hitherto bring, plead by exception, or exercise in the said castle or concerning it against any person, in our own right and name, that same lord pope and his successors may exercise, bring, and plead in their own right and name. We constitute him as lord and procurator in his own matter, so that in all things they may succeed to our place, right, and privilege.

[Col. 0291B] We make this relinquishment, grant, and assignment to you, as stated, for five hundred and thirty pounds of good Parvian denari, which, by command of the said lord pope, and on his behalf and out of his money, you pay and discharge to us, as stated, in a procuratorial capacity, for all our right that belongs, or can in any manner belong, to us in the said castle and its appurtenances within and without. Concerning all these things and all our right, we declare ourselves fully discharged and satisfied; and we altogether renounce the exception of unpaid money.

Of these sums, five hundred less eight pounds are from the five hundred pounds of lesser senatorial denari which Bobo Bonfilius held in deposit for the recovery of the aforesaid castle. [Col. 0291C] Therefore henceforth the said lord pope, or another on his behalf, shall have authority and license always to possess our said share of the specified castle with its tenements and appurtenances within and without, and to do with it whatever he wishes.

Moreover, under penalty of double the said sum of money, we promise you, on behalf of the said lord pope, lawful and valid surety that we have not pledged, granted, or otherwise alienated this right of ours and the aforesaid portion belonging to us to any other person.

Furthermore, to you on behalf of the said lord pope and his successors, acting in a procuratorial capacity as stated, we pledge and bind—and, for ourselves, our heirs, and successors, so far as the damage set forth below may arise, shall henceforth possess at sufferance and in his name—all our movable, immovable, and self-moving property and possessions which we have or shall have within the city and beyond it. Nevertheless, if by any pledge, grant, or alienation in any manner made either by us, by our late kinsman Scotto, by John his son and our nephew, or by our sister Lady Aldruda insofar as the usufruct is concerned, the said lord pope or his successors should at any time—God forbid—suffer any loss by law from this cause, whether as expenses or otherwise, then, to the amount of the loss, they may by their own authority and by our mandate, which we hereby give them, [Col. 0292A] recover from such of our property and possessions as they please, by right of pledge and surety, taking and alienating them and thereby satisfying themselves fully.

If we attempt to object, we shall wholly forfeit the right which we have in the same property; and we promise to pay and give double that loss, as the penalty of valid and lawful surety, to the lord pope or his successors through you acting in a procuratorial capacity. In all these matters we renounce every assistance of law, legislation, or good custom established for us in this case, so that we may be able to oppose no right, action, or exception against the said lord pope and his successors for the purpose of invalidating what has been said.

Finally, for ourselves, our heirs, and successors, we promise you, on behalf of the said lord pope and his successors, acting in a procuratorial capacity as stated, to observe and perform everything said above and in no manner to contravene it, under the designation of suretyship and principal obligation, subject to the lawful stipulated penalty of double the entire sum written above. Even if the penalty is paid, this charter shall remain valid.

We requested John, son of Leo, scrivener, to write this in the month and seventh indiction written above. Witnesses: Gerard Scrofani; John, son of Oddo, Roman; Rainerius, son of John Paul; John, son of Bobo Bonfilius; Siginulf of Burrella; Adinulf, son of Oddo.

I, John, son of Leo, scrivener of the Holy Roman Church, having authority to appoint a tutor and curator, to emancipate, to interpose a decree, and [Col. 0292C] to award maintenance, completed and executed this document.

## VII. Of Henry, Brother of the Emperor of Constantinople.—How Emperor Baldwin Was Defeated and Captured. (1205.)

[DUCHESNE, *Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, V, 806.]

To the most holy Father and lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: H., brother of the emperor of Constantinople and governor of the empire, with due humble and devout reverence, kisses of the feet.

Since my brother and lord the emperor has, through several letters and envoys, quite clearly made known to Your Fatherhood the whole progress of the Christian army and the course of our pilgrimage’s hardships, up to this past March [Col. 0292D], I have considered it fitting to disclose to you, as Father and lord, our subsequent events, very unlike the former and indeed, through the demands of our sins, exceedingly miserable.

It happened that the Greeks, who through their habitual great malice and treachery, after every kind of assurance and guarantee, always display betrayal toward us, immediately after the departure of the envoys last sent to you openly revealed the treason which they had long conceived, having rebelled against us. When this became known, my brother and lord the emperor, appropriately attended by only a few—for we were for the most part dispersed among fortifications and frontier districts—left the imperial city, intending to punish the head of the rebellion, namely Adrianople, a most strongly fortified city of Greece, separated only by mountains [Col. 0293A] from the neighbouring peoples of the Vlachs.

For at that time we were divided as follows: the Marquis of Montferrat was beyond Thessalonica with many men; I was on the other side of the arm of Saint George, at Andrometikon, with no few men; Pagan of Aurelia and P. of Bracel were toward Nicaea on the same side; E. of Tric was at Philippopolis with many men; and others were dispersed elsewhere among locations and fortresses.

Now Jannicius, lord of the Vlachs, heard that the Latins had besieged the said city with so small a number of men. The Greeks had secretly summoned him to their aid, in order to inflict greater harm. That Vlach, Jannicius, suddenly rushed upon our men with a multitude of barbarians—Vlachs, Cumans, [Col. 0293B] and others. Our men, most unexpectedly encountering them, pressed forward farther than they ought; at last, hemmed in on every side by the enemy’s ambushes, alas, the lord emperor, Count Louis, Stephen of Perche, and certain other barons and knights were intercepted by the enemy, overwhelmed by so great a multitude, though not without losses to them. I can relate this only with an outpouring of bloody tears.

We truly do not know who was captured and who slain. Yet we have received from our most trustworthy scouts and from reliable report that my lord the emperor is held alive and well, and is, as is said, being treated honorably for the time by that same Jannicius, together with certain others whom, however, we do not yet know specifically.

Know, moreover, that from the day on which we entered Greek territory until the day of that unhappy engagement, whatever multitude met us and our men, though we were very few, we nevertheless always withdrew victorious and in triumph. We believe that the inestimable loss which we then mourn and lament befell us through the ill-considered boldness of our men and the deserts of our sins.

Those who escaped from the battle and evaded the hands of the enemy, after brief deliberation, withdrew from the siege without further loss, together with those who had remained to guard the baggage. As they withdrew to the imperial city, unexpectedly desolate, the Lord suddenly gave such consolation [Col. 0293D] that, as if in a moment, all who had been scattered assembled, as though summoned by God, at a city called Rodosto. The marquis, however, remained faithfully and victoriously in his own regions, while E. of Tric remained unharmed and uninjured by God’s grace in his own district.

Having there reviewed our forces, we began from that point to fortify the cities and castles which seemed capable of being held against the Greek rebellion, and meanwhile advanced as far as Constantinople. Although the loss of persons has brought us mournful misfortune, we nevertheless hope in the Lord and confidently trust that we shall be able for a longer time, in the Lord, to endure whatever plots and assaults our enemies may make, and also to expect aid and assistance from afar.

Yet what we feared has happened; and what public report had declared, we learned also from letters, intercepted by us together with his envoys, containing the alliance of the Vlach with the Turks and the other enemies of Christ’s cross. We sent these letters to your Apostolic See in both languages. [Col. 0294A] Although the wound and ruin inflicted are more grievous than anticipated, no one doubts that it is incumbent upon you to undertake its remedy as Father of all, our patron, and lord. For we labor solely to restore the unity of the Church and to assist the Holy Land; on the fulfillment of these aims depends its exaltation, as the common testimony of all Christians dwelling in the East—and especially of the venerable brethren of the Templars and Hospitallers, both of whom are with us—declares. This restoration seems evidently intended not merely to bring about its liberation, but also to procure the complete overthrow of all pagans and enemies of Christ’s cross. Conversely, its disruption—may the Lord avert it—would not merely remove the hope of recovering the lost part of the Holy Land, but would beyond doubt cut off the hope of retaining even that part which is now devoted to Christian worship.

Recognizing, therefore, that from the beginning our insufficiency is unequal to the height of so arduous an undertaking, we flee to you as the highest, chief—indeed the sole—refuge and foundation of our hope. [Col. 0294C] You alone, above the sons of men, princes, and kings established in however great power, can assist us. With supplicating and devout purpose and mind, prostrate in humble submission at the feet of Your Fatherhood, we implore with tears and all the urgency of prayer we can command that you not delay to extend your customary affection of mercy to your sons, set in such peril and in need, beyond all living persons, of your counsel and aid. We ask this again with greater confidence from the sweetness of Your Fatherhood because, beyond the solemn vow of our pilgrimage, we expend our bodies and lives for the Roman Church; in which matter, besides the common concern of all Christians [lacuna], we know that both we are strictly bound to Your Fatherhood and [Col. 0294D] you to us, as your soldiers and stipendiaries of the Roman Church.

## VIII. Of the Same.—Of Similar Subject Matter.

[DUCHESNE, ibid., p. 807.]

We consider it fitting to reveal to Your Holiness our condition and whatever reports circumstances permit us to communicate through envoys. We believe that it has become sufficiently known to you how, through the demands of our sins, our lord the emperor, after a great part of his men had been killed and captured, was himself captured by the Cumans in the battle of Adrianople—something I cannot say without bitterness of heart and deepest grief.

Afterward, when the princes, barons, and knights of the army chose me as bailli of the empire, I departed from the imperial city with the Christian army. We subdued very many cities and castles that had rebelled against us, fortified our frontier districts, and returned to Constantinople around the feast of Saint Remigius. In the fortification of a certain city called Rossa, we left H. of Teneramunda, a man indeed valiant and prudent, with many knights and sergeants. While they were staying there, around the Purification of the Blessed Mary, word was brought them that the Vlachs had occupied a certain castle near Rossa. Those at Rossa went out armed at night, killed the Vlachs whom they found there, demolished the castle, and returned toward their city with Vlach plunder and their mounts. As they returned, a multitude of [Col. 0295B] Vlachs and Cumans encountered them in ambush near Rossa. Battle being joined on both sides, alas, by divine vengeance nearly all our men were killed or captured. Those who had been assigned to guard the city, about forty knights, withdrew by night with the sergeants and returned safely to us. Thus the Lord, adding scourge to scourge because our perverse deserts required it, showed us the countenance of his indignation.

Nevertheless, because the outcome of wars has always been, is, and will be uncertain, and because it cannot happen that events always go well for combatants, while sad things are often mingled with happy ones, valiant men must not despair. Fortune changes in a short time; the Lord will look upon his own and will soon restore longed-for joys to the desolate. Virtue is proved in difficult circumstances, and dangers themselves make strong men more cautious. For adversity opposed to good purposes is not a judgment of rejection but a test of virtue.

Thus, placed in these straits, we have recourse to you, the father of all—or rather, to speak more truly, our own father in this troubled affair—imploring your aid and counsel, that you may mercifully bring to completion the work mercifully begun through us, necessarily assisting the progress of our undertaking by whatever good means is available. [Note: [Col. 0295] Sympathizing with their misfortunes, the lord pope sent a special envoy to the aforesaid Jannicius for the emperor’s release.]

## IX. Promises of Philip, King of the Romans, to the Pope. (About 1205.)

[Published by Harzheim in *Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 467, from a manuscript of the Ottobonian Library transcribed by Schannat. They seem to be assignable to the year 1205, in which Diethelm, bishop of Constance, is said to have died on 12 April. Certainly they preceded Philip’s letters and embassy that follow below, since these were carried to Rome by Otto of Salem, those immediately following by Martin, prior of Camaldoli, and the third letters finally by Henry of Smalekke. PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Leges*, vol. II, p. 208.]

[Col. 0295D]

I, PHILIP, King of the Romans, ever Augustus, etc. Before Martin, prior of Camaldoli, and Brother Otto, monk of Salem, came to me to negotiate:

1. Concerning peace between Church and empire, I had vowed to God and [Col. 0296A] his saints that I would go overseas to free the Land of Promise from the violence of the nations. Again, after their arrival, having heard their proposal concerning the peace negotiations and the concession of the lord apostolic, I vowed and promised to God and his saints, and to the said prior in the place of the lord apostolic, that at a suitable time, in good faith and without all fraud, I would go there for the Church, the empire, and the liberation of the said land, and, with God’s help, would free that land to the extent of my ability.

Witnesses of this vow are: Diethelm, bishop of Constance; Eberhard, abbot of Salem; Peter, abbot of the borough of the Holy Sepulchre; Brother Otto of Salem; Henry, seneschal of Wittingen; Henry of Smalekke; Henry, marshal of Papenheim; [Col. 0296B] Henry, notary.

Moreover, I promised that I would do all the things written below:

2. All property, both of the Roman Church and of other churches, which our predecessors, kings or emperors, unjustly took or detained, or which I took or unjustly retain, I shall restore and shall permit to be possessed by them quietly and peacefully.

3. I shall forever renounce all abuses which my predecessors exercised in churches—for example, their taking the goods of prelates or of their churches when the prelates died.

4. We shall permit canonical elections of bishops and other prelates, leaving all spiritual matters to the pontiff.

5. Monasteries found to be irregular, insofar as befits imperial majesty, we shall, with the assistance of the lord apostolic, subject to regular communities, namely the Cistercian, Camaldolese, and Premonstratensian orders; and I shall take care that both monastic and clerical orders live in the religious observance and uprightness proper to them.

6. To the extent of my ability, I shall compel the advocates or patrons of churches to cease their exactions, compulsory services, and extraordinary compulsory services.

7. If Almighty God subjects the kingdom of the Greeks to me or to one of my free men, I shall cause the church of Constantinople to be subject to the Roman Church, in good faith and without [Col. 0296D] fraud.

8. I shall always be faithful and devoted to the Roman Church in all things and through all things, and shall be its son and defender.

9. I shall establish a general law and cause it always and everywhere to be observed throughout the whole empire: whoever has been excommunicated by the lord pope shall immediately fall under the imperial ban.

10. Moreover, in order that peace and friendship between myself and the lord pope may always be maintained, and every suspicion entirely removed—so that he may always be to me a most kindly father, and I to him a most faithful and excellent son—I shall give my daughter in marriage to his nephew, [Col. 0297A] and shall cause other male or female members of my kindred, according to his will, to be joined in marriage to his son-in-law.

11. For all my transgressions, at the command and will of the lord pope, I shall make full satisfaction to God and to the Church.

I have sworn that I shall do and observe these things and all the foregoing, in good faith and without any fraud whatsoever, in the presence of the lord bishop of Constance; lord Martin, prior of Camaldoli; lord Eberhard, abbot of Salem; lord Abbot Peter of the borough of the Holy Sepulchre; Brother Odo of Salem, bearer of the present document; Henry, dapifer of Walpur; Henry, marshal of Bappenheim; and Helferic, notary.

## X. Philip’s agreement with the people of Cologne. (1206.)

[From the same parchment codex of the thirteenth century mentioned above. What is printed in slanted type could not be read in the codex and has been supplied by us conjecturally. PERTZ, ibid.]

This is the form of the agreement between King Philip and the citizens of Cologne.

[Col. 0297B]

This is the form of the agreement established between King Philip and the citizens of Cologne. The whole body of Cologne’s citizens shall, in good faith, work through letters and envoys with the lord pope on behalf of Lord Adolf, so that he may obtain the see of Cologne. If this can in any way be obtained from the lord pope, whether by favor or by justice, the city of Cologne shall hold him in esteem and shall serve him, as is due, [Col. 0297C] as its lord.

But if this cannot in any way be obtained from the lord pope, the citizens shall henceforth in no way be troubled by their friends and kinsmen who took part in this agreement, namely: the duke of Lorraine, the count of Guelders, the count of Jülich, the count of the Mount, the count of Hostaden, the count of Kuke, and Hermann the advocate. And whomever the lord king principally, together with the duke of Lorraine and the aforesaid magnates of the land, shall wish to have as bishop, the city shall have him as bishop, except Lord Adolf.

Likewise, the lord king shall confirm by the authentic instrument of his own privilege, and shall inviolably observe, all rights and customs granted to them by privileges from his father or brother, the august emperors, or either of them. Likewise, whatever injury the citizens of Cologne may have inflicted upon anyone, whether in salt, wine, or any other matter, through unlawful exaction, they shall henceforth remain free and absolved in respect of it, without any legal penalty whatever. And whatever injury has been inflicted upon those citizens on account of the war shall remain unavenged and without any complaint.

Likewise, whatever fortifications they may construct from their own resources and with their own walls shall be subject to the will and grace of the lord king. Likewise, any clerics or laymen who wish to remain within this form of agreement shall be safe in both property and person. But those who refuse it shall be regarded as enemies of the empire; no dwelling in the city shall be granted them, nor ought they to enjoy any peace, whether in property or person.

Likewise, all those possessing [Col. 0298A] holdings within the city walls who, during the war, withdrew themselves from the defense of the city shall pay one mark in coin for each mark of income. Likewise, whoever among the citizens has had revenues from the mint or tolls pledged to him by the late Archbishop Adolf or Archbishop Bruno shall receive his debt, and nothing beyond the principal; excepting the fiefs and the toll of Erempozzen, whose holder shall retain the pledges and benefices in the mint according to the privilege granted him by Archbishop Adolf. The aforesaid creditors shall render a definite account of their debt before those whom the magnates of the land shall appoint for this purpose; once the debts have been paid, whatever remains shall be disposed of at the counsel of the king and the aforesaid magnates.

Likewise, the citizens of Cologne have a truce regarding the rendering of fealty to the lord king until Invocavit Sunday; and immediately upon the expiry of that term they shall render him fealty as their lord and king. That this should then be done has been sworn at Cologne by more than two thousand men; and, lest this agreement be violated, the duke of Lorraine and the aforesaid counts have promised on their faith. Likewise, if anyone should presume to burden the citizens of Cologne on account of this agreement, the lord king shall principally support them, and the magnates of the land shall likewise aid them in every way. The burghers also shall stand by the magnates of the land in observing these provisions.

Likewise, they shall henceforth receive none of the unlawful exactions which they were accustomed to impose during the war; and by this form of agreement [Col. 0298C] they shall immediately be restored to the favor of the lord king, and, safe in property and person, shall go throughout the whole empire wherever they wish.

## XI. Philip’s writing and embassy to the pope. (1206.)

[See the *Regesta* of Innocent III, vol. III of this edition, col. 1132.]

## XII. Instrument concerning homage rendered by Count Ildebrandino to Pope Innocent III. (1207.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 613.]

In the name of the Lord, in the year of His Incarnation 1207; in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III, pope; in the tenth indiction; on the last day of July.

If public acts are committed to the memory of letters, the cloud of forgetfulness being removed, they will shine forth under favorable inspection. Therefore I, John of Saint-Laurent, scriniary of the Holy Roman Church, by the command and order of Lord Pope Innocent III, have caused to be written in public letters the liege homage now rendered to the same lord pope in the palace of Montefiascone by Count Ildebrandino—as I saw, heard, and was present—and the fealty formerly rendered to the same lord pope by the aforesaid count, as is set forth below.

Count Ildebrandino confessed in the palace of Montefiascone, before the aforesaid lord pope, in the presence of bishops, cardinals, the prefect of the City, and many clerics and laymen, that he had sworn fealty to the same lord pope, to his successors, and to the Roman Church [Col. 0299A] before the said prefect Peter Saracenus, seneschal of the said lord pope, and Donnico, subdeacon of the same lord, then castellan of Montefiascone.

On the aforesaid month and day, the count rendered liege homage to the said Lord Pope Innocent, before bishops, cardinals, the prefect of the City, and many other clerics and laymen in the same palace, for the castle of Montalto, the county of Roselle, and the other lands which he holds from him, as appears from the privileges of the Roman Church. Before them all, the same lord pope invested the said count with the said castles, county, and lands by means of a silver cup.

Among those present were Lord Theobald de Praefecto; Lord Peter de Colonna; Lord Stephen of Romano Carzoli; Lord Oddo Infans de Colonna; Lord Thomas de Supino; Lord Guido de Colle de Mendi; Transmundus Rubeus, usher of the lord pope; Borgognonus of Viterbo; Capitione, son of John de Tineos; Oddo de Graeco of Orvieto; Guido de Prudezo; Berard de Walmarzo; Bulgarellus de Conversano; John de Conversano; Peter de Olivero; Winezellus of Montefiascone; Bonaccursus; Bonafidanza; and Bartholomew de Donadeis.

I, John of Saint-Laurent, scriniary of the Holy Roman Church, wrote, completed, and authenticated this, as I saw, heard, and was present.

## XIII. Philip Augustus, king of the French, to Pope Innocent III.—He declares that he has inflicted no injury upon the bishop of Cambrai, and does not adhere to Emperor Philip against the Apostolic See, but may form an alliance with Otto’s adversaries. (1208.)

[D. MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 1079, from a Colbert manuscript.]

To the reverend father in Christ and lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme and universal pontiff, PHILIP, by the same grace king of the French, greetings and reverence both due and devoted.

Concerning your command to us regarding the bishop of Cambrai—that we should restore what had been taken from him and cause amends to be made for the injuries which our people inflicted upon that same bishop of Cambrai—let your fatherhood know for certain that neither we nor our people have had or have anything belonging to that bishop; nor is the city of Cambrai part of the kingdom, but of the empire. Nor ought we to make amends for the deeds of those who belong to the empire, just as we would not wish them to make amends for deeds done in our kingdom.

As for your statement that we have abandoned your friendship and adhered to Philip, king of Germany, know without doubt that we do not adhere to the affection of that Philip against you, although we have often been asked to do so; nor do we yet have it in mind. May the Lord place it in your heart and mind not to induce us to adhere to anyone against you.

Furthermore, know that we can lawfully enter into alliance with all those who trouble and oppose King Otto. For while this Otto was count of Poitou, he burned and plundered our land and the churches of our land; nor has he subsequently made satisfaction to us for this. Nor have we had a truce or peace since those evil deeds; and when we made peace with John, king of England, we excluded him from that peace. You should therefore not wonder if we have hated him.
