God alone can inspire us to love those who do evil to us.

As for your command that we hate the bishop of Cambrai, we answer you that we hate no priest and would do evil to no priest—especially to one who is both bishop and priest.

## XIV. Of Philip, king of the French.—For the church of Bourges. (1210.)

[*Patriarchium Bituricense*, in LABBE, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, II, 59.]

To the most holy father in Christ and lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, PHILIP, by the same grace king of the French, greetings and due reverence in Christ.

Although the church of Bourges is slender in resources, it is nevertheless more noble than the other churches of our realm, since, as your fatherhood knows more fully, it possesses the dignity of a primacy. We regard its honor as our own and as belonging to the realm. Therefore, since the archbishop of Bordeaux, not following in the footsteps of his predecessors, is unwilling to show himself so obedient and devoted to the church of Bourges as his predecessors are known to have done, we beg your fatherhood with all the devotion we can that, for God’s sake and at our prayers, you may be pleased to preserve the right of the church of Bourges. Do not permit so great an honor of our realm to be diminished in any respect in this matter, since the church of Bourges alone in the whole realm possesses the dignity of a patriarchate. In its diminution—may God avert it!—we should consider that no slight injury had been done to us and to our realm.

Done at Paris, in the year of the Lord 1210, in May.

## XV. P., count of Auxerre, to Pope Innocent III.—He declares that he holds Malliaci and Vitriacum from the countess of Champagne. (1210.)

[D. MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 820, from the charter archive of Champagne.]

To the most holy father and lord INNOCENT, by God’s providence supreme pontiff, P., count of Auxerre and Tonnerre, kisses of feet both due and devoted.

I make known to your holiness that I hold, and acknowledge that I hold, from my most dear lady Blanche, illustrious countess of Champagne—and held from her predecessors, the lords of Champagne—the castle of Malliaci and Vitriacum, which belongs to the castellany of Malliaci. [Col. 0301A] Although the bishop of Auxerre produces certain letters stating that I hold the aforesaid castle of Malliaci from him, I say and plainly acknowledge that those letters are not genuine and are not sealed with my seal. But I confess that the letters which my aforesaid lady possesses on this matter, stating that I hold the castle of Malliaci and all the fiefs belonging to the castellany of Malliaci from the countess herself, are genuine and sealed with my seal, as the present letters testify, confirmed by the protection of my seal.

Done in the year of grace 1210, in July.

## XVI. Cession by Emperor Frederick II of the county of Fondi to Innocent III. (April 1212.)

[From Cencius’s book of censuses, codex of Saint Angelo, fol. 173, we print the confirmation of the county of Fondi to the Roman Church, published by Raynaldus under 1212, p. 205. PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Leges*, II, 223.]

To the most holy father and lord INNOCENT, supreme pontiff, FREDERICK, by the grace of God and of himself king of Sicily, duke of Apulia and prince of Capua, elected emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus.

Having the most undoubted confidence born of the favor which we have very often experienced from you, by this present document we have thought fit to grant that, when it shall happen that our beloved faithful Richard, count of Fondi, yields to fate, you may freely dispose both of the county of Fondi and of all the land situated on this side of the Garigliano [Col. 0301C]: giving it away or pledging it, retaining or granting it, or entrusting it to whatever person pleases your will. For the record of this our concession, we have ordered this present privilege to be written by the hand of Peter, our notary and faithful man, and have commanded that it be confirmed by our seal, in the year, month, and indiction written below.

Given at Rome, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1212, in April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## XVII. Promise of Emperor Frederick II to Pope Innocent III. (12 July 1213.)

[Previously published by Raynaldus, Goldast, and others. While resident at Rome, I copied it from the original in the Vatican archive; its golden seal is lacking, with a red silk thread remaining; the parchment is corroded in several places by the injury of time. PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Leges*, II, 224.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Frederick II, by divine favor king of the Romans, ever Augustus, and king of Sicily.

We believe and trust that our kingdom is then established when we honor the Most High, from whose hand we have received the goods which we possess. For the more we experience that Lord, who bestows good things upon us, as merciful and wondrous in us, the more we are bound to offer Him sacrifices of deed and devotion. Therefore, recognizing the grace given us by Him, and also keeping before our eyes your immense and countless benefits, dearest lord and most reverend [Note: [Col. 0301D] The authentic text has “most reverend.”] father, protector and benefactor, Lord Innocent, venerable supreme pontiff by God’s grace—through whose benefaction, assistance, and protection we have alike been nourished, protected, and advanced—after our mother, Constance the empress of blessed memory, cast us, as it were from her womb, into your care: to you, most blessed father, and to all your Catholic successors, and to the Holy Roman Church, our special mother, we shall always render, with humble heart and devoted spirit, all obedience, honor, and reverence which our predecessors, the Catholic kings and emperors, are known to have rendered to your predecessors. We wish none of these things to be diminished, but rather increased, so that our devotion may shine more brightly.

Wishing, therefore, to abolish the abuse which certain of our predecessors are known and said sometimes to have practiced in elections of prelates, we grant and enact that elections of prelates shall take place freely and canonically, so that he may be set over the vacant church whom the whole chapter, or its greater and sounder part, considers ought to be elected, provided that no canonical ordinance stands in his way. Appeals in ecclesiastical matters and causes shall also be made freely to the Apostolic See, and no one shall presume to impede their pursuit or procedure.

We also abandon and renounce the abuse which our predecessors were accustomed, by the motion of their own will, to commit in seizing the goods of deceased prelates or of vacant churches. We leave all spiritual matters to you and to the other prelates of churches, to be freely disposed of, so that what belongs to Caesar may be rendered to Caesar and what belongs to God to God, by right apportionment. Concerning the rooting out of the error of heretical depravity, we shall give aid and effective assistance.

We leave to the Roman Church, free and undisturbed, the possessions which it has recovered and which had previously been held by our predecessors or by any others; and we promise in good faith to help it obtain them. As for those which it has not yet recovered, we shall be helpers to the best of our strength in recovering them. Whatever shall come into our hands, [Col. 0302D] we shall endeavor to restore to it without difficulty. These include all the land from Radicofani to Ceprano, the March of Ancona, the duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, the county of Bertinoro, the exarchate of Ravenna, and the Pentapolis, together with the other adjacent lands specified in many privileges of emperors and kings from the time of Louis onward, so that the Roman Church may possess them forever with all its jurisdiction, district, and honor.

Nevertheless, when we come at the summons of the Apostolic See to receive the imperial crown, or for the needs of the Church, we shall receive, by command of the supreme pontiff, provisions or the *fodrum* levy from them. We shall also be helpers in retaining and defending [Col. 0303A] the kingdom of Sicily for the Roman Church and its other rights which are known to belong to it, as a devoted son and Catholic prince.

And so that all these things may be observed by us and our successors, the kings and emperors of the Romans, for you, our aforesaid most holy father Lord Innocent, supreme pontiff of the most sacred Roman Church, and for your successors, and may remain firm and unshaken forever, we have commanded this present written privilege to be secured with the golden seal of our majesty.

The witnesses are these: Siegfried, archbishop of the see of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See; Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg; Berard, archbishop of Bari; Conrad, bishop of Regensburg; Otto, bishop of Würzburg; Manegold, bishop of Passau; Engelhard, bishop of Zeitz; Ottokar, king of Bohemia; Louis, duke of Bavaria; Leopold, duke of Austria and Styria; Hermann, landgrave of Thuringia; Count Albert of Eberstein; Count Adolf of Sowenburc [Note: [Col. 0303D] So the charter; read *Scowenburc*.]; Count Burchard of Mannesfeld; Count Gerard of Diez; Count Louis of Württemberg; Gebehard, burgrave of Magdeburg; Henry of Stahhelburch; Walter of Langenberch; Henry of Chalandrino, marshal of the empire; Walter of Sypf, cupbearer of the empire; Gwalther Gentilis, constable of the kingdom of Sicily; and very many others.

The sign of Lord Frederick II, most invincible king of the Romans (L. M.) and king of Sicily.

[Col. 0303C] I, Conrad, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See bishop of Metz, acting in place of Lord Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, legate of the Apostolic See, and archchancellor of all Germany, have verified this.

These things were enacted in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1213, in the first indiction, in the reign of the glorious Lord Frederick II, king of the Romans and king of Sicily: the first year of his Roman reign and the sixteenth of his Sicilian reign.

Given at Eger, by the hand of Berthold of Niffen, prothonotary of the royal court, on the fourth day before the Ides of July.

## XVIII. Of John, king of the English.—Concerning the agreement between the king himself and Queen Berengaria, former wife of King Richard. (1215.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 137.]

To his reverend lord and father in Christ, the most holy INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, JOHN, by the same grace king of England, etc., greetings and reverence, due to so great a lord and father, with devotion.

We send you, most holy Father, a word-for-word copy of the agreement made between us and Queen Berengaria, whose tenor is as follows:

> “John, by God’s grace king of the English, etc., to all whom this present writing shall reach, greetings.
>
> “Know that we have thus agreed with Lady Queen Berengaria, former wife of Lord King Richard, our brother, concerning her dower which she claimed, and concerning a certain settlement formerly made between us and her over that dower: namely, that whereas she ought to receive from us one thousand marks annually, we now presently give her two thousand marks for all arrears and in payment for the present year; and henceforth we shall give her annually one thousand pounds of good and lawful sterling, namely five hundred pounds at the feast of All Saints and five hundred pounds at the feast of the Ascension. We shall pay this money to her [Col. 0304B] at the house of the New Temple near London.
>
> “The lady queen may also claim her dower from every holder outside the kingdom of England, except ourselves and our successors; and we shall not oppose her in this, unless we are legally bound to warrant it to her. Neither we nor our successors may take into our hand those properties concerning which she has brought their holders to suit. The queen herself may make a settlement at her will with those holders, saving to us and our heirs, after her death, our right.
>
> “We also grant that the queen herself and the members of her household may at all times have free entrance into our land and departure from it; that they may remain there as long as they wish; and that we shall receive both them and all their goods into our safe-conduct and faithful protection, while coming, returning, and remaining, once they have sworn that no harm shall come to us or to the realm through them.
>
> “We also grant that they shall have free passage through all seaports whenever they wish, forbidding any of our bailiffs or men to impede them or to take customary dues from them.
>
> “We make this settlement both for ourselves and for our heirs, decreeing that if—may it not happen!—we or any of our successors should break this agreement, which we cannot do without breach of faith, and, after we or our justiciar, if we are outside the kingdom, have been warned, we do not remedy it within sixty days, we shall be bound to restore her dower to her in full, with every delay and pretext removed.
>
> “Moreover, we have caused our knight Geoffrey Luttrell to swear upon our soul that we shall observe inviolate all that is contained in this charter; and, for greater security, that we shall obtain confirmation of all these things from the lord pope.
>
> “We also ask and humbly petition the lord pope to add to the present settlement whatever safeguards he judges expedient; and we shall hold valid whatever he shall decree concerning it. For we wish all things to be faithfully observed and do not wish the aforesaid queen ever hereafter to be troubled by anyone on this account.
>
> “And it should be known that, at this coming feast of All Saints in the seventeenth year of our reign, we shall pay the said queen the first five hundred pounds of the aforesaid thousand pounds to be paid her annually.
>
> “Witnesses: Lords P., bishop of Winchester; S., bishop of Exeter; Master Pandulf, bishop-elect of Norwich; H., abbot of Beaulieu; Brother Alan Martell; Master P., archdeacon of Salisbury.
>
> “Given by the hand of Master Richard de Marisco, our chancellor, at Dover, on the second day of September, in the seventeenth year [Col. 0305B] of our reign.”

Therefore, reverend Father, since we desire this agreement to obtain the protection of the Apostolic See, we have resolved to pour out our prayers to your holiness, beseeching you, for the greater security of this agreement, to order that such safeguards as you judge expedient be appended to it, and, if it please you, to cause it to enjoy perpetually the protection of the Apostolic See.

At Dover, on the fourth day of September, in the seventeenth year of our reign.

## XIX. Frederick II’s promise to separate the crown of Sicily from the empire. (1 July 1216.)

[After the editions of Raynaldus under 1215 and *Origines Guelficae*, III, p. 830, we have established ours from the *Regesta* of Honorius III in the Vatican archive, vol. I, fol. 35, epistle 146 of the first year. PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Leges*, II, 228.]

To the most holy father in Christ and his lord INNOCENT, supreme pontiff of the most sacred Roman Church, FREDERICK, by the grace of God and of himself king of the Romans and ever Augustus, and king of Sicily, with filial submission, offering in all things the obedience and reverence due to the Apostolic See.

Desiring to provide both for the Roman Church and for the kingdom of Sicily, we promise and grant, decreeing that, after we have received the imperial crown, we shall immediately emancipate from paternal authority our son Henry, whom at your command [Col. 0305D] we caused to be crowned king, and shall entirely relinquish the kingdom of Sicily, both beyond and on this side of the Faro, to be held from the Roman Church, just as we ourselves hold it from that Church alone. Thus from that time we shall neither have nor call ourselves king of Sicily; rather, according to your good pleasure, we shall arrange for it to be governed in the name of our said son, the king, until his lawful age by a suitable person, who shall answer for every right and service to the Roman Church, to which alone the lordship of that kingdom is known to belong. This is so that, because by divine favor we are called to the eminence of the empire, no union of kingdom and empire may at any time be thought to exist if we were to hold both empire and kingdom together, whereby some detriment might arise both to the Apostolic See and to our heirs.

And so that this our promise, grant, and decree may take due effect, we have caused this present document to be secured with our golden seal.

Given at Strasbourg, in the year of the Lord 1216 [Note: [Col. 0305] This should be corrected thus: 1215 in the *Regesta* of Honorius; but 1216 is found in the transcript of Innocent IV, and accords with the fourth indiction.], on the Kalends of July, fourth indiction.

## XX. Of John, king of the English.—He relates the contumacy of the barons and also why, for that reason, he cannot undertake the journey to the Holy Land.

(RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 129.)

To the lord pope, greetings and reverence, due to so great a father and lord, with devotion.

We render manifold thanks to your holiness for your letters addressed on our behalf by your fatherhood to the lord archbishop of Canterbury and his suffragans, as also to the magnates and barons of our land. Know for certain that our barons have in no respect heeded your letters; while the lord archbishop of Canterbury and his suffragans have refrained from carrying your command into effect.

For our part, attending to the foregoing, we declared to our people that our land was the patrimony of Blessed Peter, and that we held it from Blessed Peter, the Roman Church, and [Col. 0306C] from you.

We also added that we were signed with the cross and requested the benefit of the privilege of crusaders, so that our land might not be disturbed and what we proposed to expend in aid of the Holy Land might not be consumed in evil uses. Through W., marshal and earl of Pembroke, and W., earl Warenne, we appealed against those who disturbed the peace of our land.

But because we were crusaders and wished to proceed in all things with humility and gentleness, while preserving our appeal, we offered those barons that we would entirely abolish all evil customs revived and introduced by anyone in our time, and also root out the evil customs that had arisen in the time of King Richard, our brother. With regard to customs introduced in the time of our father, if any existed which burdened them, we would address them by the counsel of our faithful men. But content with neither these nor the other things stated above, they rejected all of them.

Seeing, therefore, that they were plainly striving to disturb our realm, we asked the lord archbishop of Canterbury and his suffragans to execute your command: namely, according to the tenor of your letters, to render us the customary services, and afterward, if they wished to ask anything of us, to ask it humbly and without arms. We asked them to denounce as excommunicated [Col. 0307A] those who, after these offers made to them, disturbed the peace of our realm. And it seemed to the bishop of Exeter and Master Pandulf, who were present, that by law they ought to restrain them by a sentence of excommunication.

But the archbishop replied that he would by no means pronounce sentence of excommunication against them, because he knew well your mind. We likewise thought that he ought to do so, since we had summoned an abundant force from foreign lands to aid our land. He promised us that, if we wished to recall them, he would not only pronounce sentence of excommunication against them, but would also resist them as far as he could. We therefore recalled our force.

Afterward, through our open letters conveyed to them by the lord archbishop of Canterbury and two or three of his suffragans, we offered that we would choose four on our side and they four on theirs, with you appointed as supreme judge concerning all complaints about liberties which they might put forward. We would answer their claims, and whatever you, together with those eight, should decide concerning all that they sought from us, we would accept and uphold.

Although they were unwilling to humble themselves toward us as they should have done, nevertheless, for the service of God and the aid of the Holy Land, we humbled ourselves so far as to make them these aforesaid offers. Furthermore, [Col. 0307C] we offered that, concerning all their petitions, we would grant them the full measure of justice according to the judgment of their peers. They refused this.

Furthermore, lord, on the Friday after the Ascension, Brother William of your household, your familiar, came to us bringing your letters, which stated that, setting aside our journey of pilgrimage, we should have someone of ours represent us before the feet of your holiness at the council, informing your fatherhood of our course and of the progress of our journey.

To this we answer your fatherhood as follows: since, as the foregoing has made known to you, we are oppressed by the perverse disturbances of the aforesaid barons and cannot find in them the good of peace, by which at least we might be brought into harmony and thus pursue our purpose more readily, we cannot inform you with certainty about our journey. One thing we know for certain: many great and noble men, crusaders from distant regions, who have girded themselves to aid the Holy Land, have graciously requested by their letters and envoys that we receive them into our company; because of the aforesaid difficulties, we have not yet been able to give them a definite answer to their requests.

Moreover, reverend Father, in the presence of the aforesaid Brother William, your familiar, and of our venerable brothers the bishops of Worcester and Coventry, [Col. 0308B] we offered the aforesaid barons that, concerning all their demands which they exact from us, we would most willingly submit the matter to you, so that you, who enjoy plenitude of power, might determine what was just. Yet they refuse to make all these arrangements.

Therefore, merciful Father, we have thought fit to set forth these present matters to your lordship, so that, in accordance with your accustomed kindness, you may determine what seems expedient for us.

Witness myself, at Odiham, on 29 May.

## XXI. Of G., prior of Camaldoli.—His monastery having been reduced to ashes, he asks the pontiff for letters of recommendation to obtain assistance from the faithful.

(MARTENE, *Anecdota*, I, 737, from a manuscript of Saint-Alyre at Clermont.)

G., prior of Camaldoli, and all the brothers with him, inform your holiness that, on the day before the Kalends of June, about the middle of the night, an unexpected fire consumed their buildings so suddenly that on the following day they could not make a meal from anything that remained. Thus more than three hundred, monks and lay brothers together, are compelled to beg. They therefore ask your clemency to grant them letters throughout all Italy promising remission of sins, enjoining Christ’s faithful to furnish them charitable assistance.

# PART TWO OF THE WORKS OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF: SERMONS AND SHORTER WORKS

## I. SERMONS
(From the first Cologne edition of 1575. Our recension is supplemented by another twelve sermons of the Pontiff, published from Vatican codices by the late Cardinal Angelo Mai in *Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VI, p. 475, Rome, 1842, 8vo. Here are the words of that most learned man, with which he prefaced his edition: Vatican Codex 700, on parchment, in a small but handsome hand, written shortly after Innocent’s death, contains seventy-nine of his sermons besides the prologue. Only sixty-eight of these and part of another appear in the editions both of Cologne, 1575, and Venice, 1578; the rest had until then remained unpublished. Nor are these written separately or appended at the end, lest anyone perhaps suppose them foreign to the collection; rather, they are intermingled with the published sermons. The unpublished sermons in the order of the codex are IV, V, VII, XXVIII, XXXVI (partly XLIV), XLVII, LIV, LX, LXIV, and LXVII. Of these, Mansi says in the additions to Fabricius’s *Latin Library* that he had also seen two in a double Luccan codex. It is therefore clear that the Cologne editor possessed only an incomplete collection of Innocent’s sermons, while the Venetian borrowed them from the Cologne edition. Thus the number of Innocent’s letters in printed books likewise gradually grew from Sirlet’s edition onward to that of the two editors Bréquigny and Dutheil. Since matters stood thus, I was unwilling wholly to omit a discovery already made, both for Innocent’s own sake and because these sermons suited this volume, which abounds in pontifical records. Yet I shall not commend them in my own words, for the writings of so great a man need no praise; I shall merely note that they were written after his accession to the pontificate, as is expressly stated in the prologue and in chapter 2 of the *Deeds of Innocent*. Finally, in Vatican Ottobonian Codex 132, likewise of the thirteenth century, I read thirty-one sermons of the same Innocent, of which only the last (which is our Sermon XIII), delivered to religious enclosed in cloisters, still awaited publication.

[Note: [Col. 0309] Dom Luigi Tosti published two sermons of Innocent III as unpublished in his *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino* (Naples, 1842), vol. II, p. 293. They are identical with Sermons V and VII below, which we have from Cardinal Mai’s edition. PATROLOGICAL EDITORS.]

[Col. 0309]

## PROLOGUE

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARNULPH, abbot of the Cistercian order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Prophetic authority teaches that blessed are those who sow beside all waters (Isa. 32). “For the seed is the word of God” (Luke 8), and “many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 19). Conversely, “Cursed is he who withholds grain from the people and buries his talent in the earth” (Prov. 11); for the innkeeper who received two denarii from the Samaritan ought to add something besides (Luke 10), and the servant to whom his master entrusted two talents ought to gain something additional (Matt. 15). Golden bells hung from the hyacinth-blue tunic, lest the priest, entering the sanctuary without their sound, should die (Exod. 28).

Among the other matters belonging to the pastoral office, the power of holy preaching is preeminent, as the outstanding preacher teaches: “The Lord did not send me,” he says, “to baptize, but to preach” (1 Cor. 1), according to the saying: “Preach the word; press it in season and out of season; do the work of an evangelist” (2 Tim. 4). Likewise: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10). “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” [Col. 0311] (Isa. 58). For this office the Lord chiefly enjoined upon the apostles, saying: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. 10). “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16).

Preaching is of such power that it calls the soul back from error to truth and from vices to virtues; it changes crooked things into straight, rough places into plains; it instructs faith, raises hope, and strengthens charity; it uproots what is harmful, plants what is useful, and fosters what is honourable. It is the way of life, the ladder of salvation, and the gate of paradise.

A preacher, therefore, ought to possess gold, silver, and balsam—that is, wisdom, eloquence, and integrity—so that he may understand what he says and do what he has said and understood. For “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Otherwise it will be said to him, “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4): he will be like the fig tree that produces leaves without fruit. “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13): either because he adduces testimonies from both the New and the Old Testament; or because he draws discourse alike from the newness of grace and the oldness of sin; or because he treats both rewards and punishments, which are due to those renewed in good or grown old in evil.

On these matters, however, he ought to speak differently according to the diversity of persons and subjects. Hence it is said to the bride in the Song of Songs: “We shall make for you golden ornaments, patterned with silver” (Song 1). By gold wisdom is signified, as Solomon also testifies when he says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21). By silver, however, eloquence is understood, as the Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 118). Thus the flowers of wisdom are fittingly signified by golden ornaments, with which the neck and breast of the Church—that is, its preachers and teachers—are adorned; and they are patterned, that is, distinguished and varied, with silver, namely eloquence, so that the style of discourse may itself vary according to the variety of subject or audience.

For the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect; but among you I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2). And again: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people; as infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). To the wise and perfect, uncreated Truth likewise says: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God” (Luke 8). Conversely, to the unlearned and weak he says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). Therefore he wisely enjoins: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). But be like clean animals, which both chew the cud and divide the hoof (Deut. 14).

A preacher ought to have wine and oil, a rod and manna, fire and water, each to be brought forth appropriately in its place. Above all, he should direct his attention to the instruction of faith and the formation of life, as to foundation and building, confirming what he says by authorities, arguments, and examples, so that “a threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccles. 4). But since the dust of vain glory often clings to the feet of preachers, the preacher must surely shake the dust from his feet (Matt. 10) and wash them with the water of compunction, so that he may be wholly clean, lest, after preaching to others, he himself be rejected (1 Cor. 2).

Would that I myself had done in the office of preaching what I say. But I am beset by so many demands, entangled in so many ties of business, that, divided among individual matters, I must necessarily be found inadequate in each. I am not allowed to contemplate, nor even permitted to breathe; I am so given over to others that I seem almost wholly taken away from myself. Yet, lest through the care of temporal matters—which, owing to the present evil times, weigh heavily upon me—I should altogether neglect spiritual concerns, which press more urgently upon me because of the office of apostolic service, I have delivered and dictated certain sermons to clergy and people, now in Latin and now in the vernacular. At your insistent request, made to me through our common son, Brother Nicholas, my chaplain and your monk, I have endeavoured to send them to your devotion, asking and beseeching you in Christ Jesus that in your prayers you would commend me spiritually to the most just Judge and most merciful Father.

[Col. 0313]

# SERMONS OF POPE INNOCENT III OF THAT NAME, ON THE SEASONS

## SERMON I. FIRST SUNDAY OF THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

Why Christ’s coming was delayed so long; the threefold silence; why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, came; why he assumed a human body only from a woman; why he chose to endure so many insults and sufferings; and the fourfold law.

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313A] “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4).

In the Apostle’s proposed words we must chiefly consider four things: the time and person of the one coming, the manner, and the cause. Concerning the time it is first said: “When the fullness of time had come”; concerning the person it follows: “God sent his Son”; concerning the manner it is added: “Born of a woman, made under the law”; concerning the cause it is supplied: “So that he might redeem those who were under the law.”

The time of fullness is understood as the time of grace, which began with the coming of the Saviour: the time for showing mercy and the year of favour. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (1 John 1). Grace means [Col. 0313B] forgiveness of sins; truth, the fulfilment of promises. Through Christ sins were blotted out, and through him promises were fulfilled.

But why did the physician delay so long before coming to heal the sick person? Why did not one man die earlier for the people, lest the whole nation perish? (John 11). “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

Yet the height of the heavenly counsel ordained that the physician should delay his coming to heal the sick person, lest, if he came too quickly, the sick person should think himself healed not by the physician’s power but by nature’s strength and the mildness of the illness, and thus despise the physician and make light of the disease. For the sinner presumed upon his own strength, saying, “There is no lack of one to act; there is only a lack of one to command.” And again: “Whatever the Lord says to us, we shall do and obey” (Exod. 24). Therefore, so that he might distrust his own power, recognize the greatness of his weakness, and seek the physician’s grace, the Saviour delayed his approach until the sinner should repeatedly cry out: “Come, Lord, and do not delay; release the sins of your people Israel” (Hab. 2).

[Col. 0314A] Yet a more subtle and secret reason for this delay is suggested to us by the Wise Man: “While all things held the middle of silence, and the night in its course had completed half its journey, your almighty Word, Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). Although different people explain this in different ways, it may fittingly be understood that the first silence was under the law of nature, the second under the law of Scripture, and the third under the law of grace.

For God the Creator implanted the natural law in human minds from the very beginning of the world’s creation, containing a twofold command. One was affirmative, teaching the rendering of benefits, as the Gospel says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7). The other was negative, teaching the avoidance of injuries, as is read in Tobit: “Do not do to another what you hate to have done to yourself” (Tob. 4).

But this law was silent from the beginning when Cain killed his brother Abel (Gen. 4), doing to another what he would not have wished done to himself. Thus came the first silence, lasting until Moses, through whom God raised up testimony in Jacob and established a commandment in Israel, giving through him the Decalogue of the law written on two tablets (Exod. 20), one containing love of God and the other love of neighbour. “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22).

But this law was silent from the beginning when the people worshipped the molten calf against the first commandment of the law, worshipping foreign gods (Exod. 32). Thus came the second silence [Col. 0314C] of the law, lasting until Christ, who came in mercy and bestowed the law of grace, writing it in human hearts with the finger of God.

But this law will be silent at the end, when “the son of iniquity is revealed, who exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshipped as God” (2 Thess. 2). And perhaps it is silent already, “because iniquity has abounded and the charity of many has grown cold” (Matt. 24). There is scarcely anyone who does good; scarcely one, even to a single person.

In the first law God gave humanity ability; in the second, knowledge; in the third, will. In the first he gave power through nature; in the second, knowledge through Scripture; in the third, will through grace. God therefore first gave the natural law, by which he might convict the transgressor, lest he perhaps offer the excuse, saying, “I fell because I could not stand” (Ps. 23). But the excuse is removed: through the good of nature he could stand firm in good, but would not. He also first gave the written law, by which he might convict the presumptuous person, lest he perhaps offer the excuse, saying, “I fell because I did not know how to stand.” But the excuse is removed through the teaching of Scripture: he knew how to turn aside from evil, but would not.

Therefore, after both laws, namely at the fitting time, “when the night of sin had taken or completed the middle of its course, your almighty Word came” [Col. 0315B] (Wis. 18), that is, “the Word became flesh” (John 1), and bestowed the law of grace, so that what humanity could do through nature and knew through Scripture, it might fulfil through grace. This is not because some had not possessed grace earlier, but because they were few: more served from fear than from love, more as slaves than as free people. Therefore, when the angel descended, the water was stirred, but only one was healed (John 3). But the true Samaritan, approaching the wounded man, bound up his wounds by pouring in wine and oil—him whom the priest and Levite, though they saw him, had passed by without mercy (Luke 19). Elisha also sent his staff ahead to raise the Shunammite’s son; when the boy did not rise through it, Elisha himself came, fitted himself to the child, and thus the dead boy rose again [Col. 0315C] (4 Kings 4).

Therefore, when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son. He sent him to where he already was, yet sent him according to his humanity to where he was according to his divinity. For “he was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1).

But since “there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5), why did the Father himself not come, or why did he not send the Holy Spirit? Why did he send the Son instead? “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible [Col. 0315D] are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

Yet the height of heavenly counsel ordained that God, who had created the world in his wisdom—according to the saying, “God made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103)—should himself recreate the world in that same wisdom. This is the woman of the Gospel (Luke 13) who lights a lamp in order first to find the tenth drachma that had been lost, while reserving for himself the proper name of sonship, so that he who in divinity was the Son of God might in humanity become the son of man.

Yet a more subtle, though secret, reason for this mission is suggested by the prophet: “If the storm has arisen because of me, cast me into the sea” (Jonah 1). Although this too is explained in different ways by different people, it may fittingly be understood thus. The first storm arose in the empyrean heaven, the second in paradise: the first among angels, the second among human beings. The first storm was the swelling of pride, through which Lucifer wished to ascend to equality with God, as he says: “I shall ascend into heaven; I shall place my throne to the north; and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). But in wishing to ascend, he fell, according to the saying: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who arose in the morning!” (ibid.).

The second storm was the heat of covetousness, through which humanity desired the knowledge of God, as the serpent had promised them: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). But by desiring what was another’s, humanity lost what was its own, according to the saying: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers,” and so forth (Luke 10). These two vices are the root and origin of all evils, of all vices. For of pride it is written: “The beginning of sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10). Of covetousness the Apostle says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6).

But in the holy and undivided Trinity, unity is attributed to the Father, because of origin; equality to the Son, because of the middle; and connection to the Holy Spirit, because of fellowship. The first storm, therefore, which arose among angels on account of equality with God, arose on account of the Son, who according to the Apostle “did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2). But in the Trinity power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, [Col. 0316C] and love to the Holy Spirit. The second storm, which arose among human beings on account of God’s knowledge, likewise arose on account of the Son, who according to the Apostle “is the power and wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1).

Now one who gives occasion for loss is considered also to have caused the loss. Thus the true Jonah—that is, Christ—was spiritually sent into this great and spacious sea, that is, the world, in which he was swallowed by the whale, that is, buried in the tomb. As he says: “As Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly, so shall the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12). Elsewhere he says: “I came into the depths of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68), [Col. 0316D] so that he might restore the things in heaven and on earth—that is, the angelic ruin and the human fall.

God therefore sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law. He was born of a woman, that is, of a virgin: she is called woman in respect of sex, virgin in respect of integrity. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord shall create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the womb of her body” (Jer. 31); and another says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7).

But why did he assume a body from a woman in the likeness of sinful flesh, rather than form a new body for himself from another material, so that, as the first Adam was made by God, the second might likewise be made? “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible [Col. 0317A] are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

For the height of heavenly counsel ordained that, just as death had entered the world through a woman, so life should return to the world through a woman; that from where death arose, life might arise again.

Yet a more subtle and secret reason for this assumption is suggested by the Apostle when he says: “He nowhere took hold of angels, but took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2). Different reasons are assigned by different people for why the Lord assumed not angelic but human nature: whether because the angel fell by himself, having sinned without temptation, while humanity sinned through another, through the devil’s persuasion; or because human nature fell wholly, having sinned in its root, while angelic nature did not wholly sin, since one part remained in its blessedness.

Yet the subtle investigator may fittingly understand also that Adam sinned against the Father, Eve sinned against the Son, and Lucifer sinned against the Holy Spirit. But whoever sins against the Father shall be forgiven; whoever sins against the Son shall be forgiven; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12; Mark 3; Luke 12). Therefore God assumed not angelic but human nature.

What was not assumable remained incurable. For it was healed from the place from which it was assumed; and therefore he assumed body and soul together, so that he might heal [Col. 0317C] soul and body together. It was necessary, then, that he assume flesh from that race which he wished to heal through assumed flesh; and likewise from the seed to which the promise had been made: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22, 26).

He assumed this flesh from a virgin so that he might not contract sin through the desire of the flesh, which he had to remove through purity of flesh. Hence, “When Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1). Other women, indeed, conceive not while betrothed but after marriage; not in the modesty of virginity but in the heat of desire; not unto grace but unto guilt. But she conceived not after marriage, but while betrothed. Hence: “When Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph”; not in the heat of desire, but in the modesty of virginity. Hence: “Before they came together, she was found to be with child”; not unto guilt, but unto grace, because she conceived “by the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Augustine.] The Lord also wished in his conception to fulfil every mode of the human condition. For the first mode of human condition was that a human being should be made neither from male nor female, as Adam was. The second was that a human being should be made not from female but from male, as Eve was. The third was that a human being should be made from male, as Christ was; for it was fitting that, according to his humanity, he should be born from a mother without a mother [Col. 0318A].

God therefore sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law: not simply made, but made under the law—that is, subject to the law. He who established the law subjected himself to it, not from obligation, but solely of free good pleasure. For according to the law he was circumcised on the eighth day and redeemed in the Temple on the fortieth (Luke 2), in order to redeem those who were under the law.

To demonstrate this, there is a law of nature and a law of Scripture; a law of grace and a law of guilt. The Apostle teaches us these in temporal order. The first: “When Gentiles naturally do the things of the law, they are a law to themselves” (Rom. 2). The second: “The law entered in so that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5). The third: “Your boasting has been excluded” (Rom. 3). Through what law? The law of works? No, but through the law of faith. The fourth: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin” (Rom. 7).

Christ was therefore made under the law of sin in order to redeem those under the law of guilt, restoring those who were under the law of Scripture through the law of grace.

But why did God not merely speak and remake us, “as he commanded and they were created” (Ps. 32)? Why did he deign to endure so many sufferings and insults for our redemption? “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! Who has known the mind [Col. 0318C] of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

Yet the height of heavenly counsel ordained that he should redeem the human race by his death, in order that he might kindle his enemies to charity and bring the proud back to humility. For what could kindle us more to charity than that “God did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all”? (Rom. 8). “For no one has greater charity than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 13). What more invites us to humility than that he who “was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death—indeed, death on a cross”? (Phil. 2).

Yet a more subtle and secret reason for this redemption is suggested by the Psalmist: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced” (Ps. 84). Although this is explained differently by different people, it may fittingly be understood that a difficult dispute once raged between mercy and truth. Truth called justice to its aid and counsel; mercy summoned peace as her counsellor and helper. Both jointly chose the judgment of divine wisdom, by whose mediation the dispute might be calmed.

When the parties had therefore been assembled in its presence, mercy, instructed by peace’s counsel, pleaded as follows: Since God, by the decision of his supreme goodness, made humanity in his image and likeness (Gen. 1), it would be unworthy that so worthy a creature should wholly perish, lest God be deprived of his purpose. For he made humanity so that it might know him, love him when known, and possess him when loved, and so become blessed in an inestimable happiness. Why, indeed, should he make a human being whom he wholly knew would perish? There is no utility at all in this; indeed, it would be cruel impiety. Therefore let God not forget to show mercy, nor restrain his mercies in his wrath; rather, let it still please him to show mercy, since, according to the testimony of the Scriptures, he hates none of the things he has made and wishes no one to perish.

Truth, relying on justice’s counsel, replied thus: Since God, by the blameless judgment of equity, shut the gate of paradise because of human sin, placing before the paradise of delight a cherub and a flaming, turning sword (Gen. 3), so that the angel might exclude the devil and the fire humankind, it would be unworthy to reopen it to the unworthy, to give what is holy to dogs, and to cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7). Therefore let him render recompense to the proud (Ps. 93), to each according to his merits. For, according to Scripture’s testimony, “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 52). All are unclean, conceived from unclean seed, and they have continued to sin against him.

To this mercy wisely added in pleading: Although humanity sinned greatly, it afterwards repented perfectly; and therefore what it lost through guilt it ought to recover through repentance. As the Lord himself promised: “At whatever hour the sinner turns,” and so forth, “I shall remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 17).

Truth replied in these words: Although repentance has removed guilt, it has not restored perfect innocence, because there remains the tinder of sin, the weakness of nature, the tyranny of the flesh. Therefore, although sin can remove punishment, it cannot restore glory. “For all have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. 3), lest any unclean person be presented before the divine presence.

While they thus met one another in opposing claims, divine wisdom thoughtfully devised counsels of peace. It saw that justice would be injured unless a sufficient penalty were paid for all, but mercy would perish if each individual were punished with a sufficient penalty. Since God is just and merciful—indeed, since he is mercy and justice—and could act neither against mercy nor against justice, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24), whence the prophet says: “I shall sing to you, Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100), he found a means by which he might satisfy both mercy and justice. He judged, therefore, that he would assume in himself the penalty for all and grant through himself glory to all. Thus “justice and peace have embraced” (Ps. 84).

For no one else was found worthy to open the gate of paradise except the lion of the tribe of Judah, “who shuts and no one opens; opens and no one shuts” (Rev. 3). For scarcely was anyone else’s own justice sufficient even for himself, much less for all; since no one is without sin except God alone, as the prophet says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 144). Therefore God himself became human, so that he might lawfully mediate between God and humanity, since he would be suspect to neither side, bearing the nature of both in one person.

It was therefore necessary that God should redeem the human race by his death, so that, as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many might be made righteous (Rom. 3).

This is the bronze serpent raised up in the wilderness, through which those struck by serpents were healed (Num. [Col. 0320C] 21; John 3).

This is the high priest at whose death those who had fled to the cities of refuge returned to their own homes (Num. 35).

This is he of whom blessed Job says: “He shall catch Behemoth in his eyes as with a hook” (Job 40). In a hook the barb lies hidden beneath the bait; and in Christ divinity lay hidden beneath humanity. Thus Christ caught Behemoth—that is, the devil—as with a hook: when he seized the bait of humanity, he was caught by the barb of divinity. Because he laid hands on one over whom he had no right, he justly lost those over whom he seemed to have some right. Thus, because the devil deceived humanity by a tree, humanity deceived the devil by a tree; and because death entered paradise and expelled its inhabitants, life entered hell and brought out the captives. He therefore took death from our mortality and restored life to us from his own life.

Let praise, honour, and glory therefore be to Christ, who is God blessed above all for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

On the manifold sleep from which we must arise.

[Col. 0319]

[Col. 0319D] “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For our salvation is nearer now than when we believed” (Rom. 13).

[Col. 0320D] The meaning of sleep is variously spread through the Scriptures. We read of the sleep of life and the sleep of death. Now, as life is threefold—bodily, spiritual, and eternal—so the sleep of life is threefold. The first arises from nature; the second from grace; the third springs from glory. Of the first the Lord said in the Gospel: “Sleep now, and rest” (Matt. 27); of the second the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song 5); of the third the Prophet says in the psalm: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same” (Ps. 4).

Likewise the sleep of death is threefold, because death is threefold: bodily, spiritual, and eternal. Of the sleep of bodily death the Lord says: “Lazarus our friend sleeps” (John 11). Of the sleep of spiritual death the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” [Col. 0321B] (Eph. 5). Of the sleep of eternal death the Psalmist says: “He who sleeps shall not add to rise again” (Ps. 40). “For Judas went away and hanged himself with a noose” (Matt. 29).

All rise from the sleep of bodily death; some rise from the sleep of spiritual death; none rise from the sleep of eternal death. For “we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15). Blessed are those who have a share in the first resurrection (Rev. 20), because in hell there is no redemption; and by no means “the wicked shall rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Ps. 1).

Now the sleep of spiritual death occurs in three ways: through negligence, ignorance, and concupiscence. Of the sleep of negligence Solomon says: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise?” (Prov. 6). Of the sleep of ignorance David says: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12). Of the sleep of concupiscence the Psalmist testifies: “They slept their sleep, and all men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 73).

Of this threefold sleep the Apostle says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.” It is as though he said: We must rise from the sleep of negligence. Therefore he adds: “Because our salvation is nearer than when we believed.” We must rise from the sleep of ignorance. Therefore he continues: “For the night has passed, but the day has drawn near.” [Col. 0321D] We must rise from the sleep of concupiscence. Therefore he says: “Not in feasting and drunkenness,” and so forth. And so he concludes—and applies to all these matters—“Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light,” and so forth.

“It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.” But you may say: Since it is always the time to rise from the sleep of sin, according to the prophet’s saying, “At whatever hour the sinner turns,” and the rest, “I shall remember none of his iniquities, says the Lord” (Ezek. 18), what does the Apostle mean when he says, “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep,” as though it were not always the time? Let us therefore hold to what Truth says: “Watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour” [Col. 0322A] (Matt. 25). Accordingly the Prophet exhorts: “Seek the Lord while he may be found,” and so forth (Isa. 53). Let the sinner, then, not flatter himself vainly and say: “I can safely sin for a time, because at whatever hour I turn, the Lord will remember none of my iniquities.” For I do not know the day or the hour. By God’s just judgment it happens that, because a person can turn when he does not wish to, when perhaps he wishes to turn he cannot. For it is then safe for a person to repent when he is still able to sin.

Now therefore—that is, in the present life, or rather in the favorable time—we must rise from the sleep of guilt, because “if he comes in the first watch, or if in the second, or if he comes in the third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants” (Luke XIII).

Therefore let us rise, brothers and children, while we have a favorable time and a fitting hour, from that threefold sleep; for each kind is deadly. Certainly nothing is more friendly to wickedness than negligence. Hence Scripture says: “Cursed is the man who performs the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII). For where Solomon says, “Hand in hand shall not be innocent” (Prov. XI), the contrary counsel is given: Always do some work, so that the devil may find you occupied. [Note: [Col. 0321D] Jerome.] For when David had rested from battles, “and was walking upon the roof after midday, he saw Bathsheba bathing opposite him; he took her and slept with her” (II Kings II). On her account he committed both murder and adultery; and he who conquered in war was at last conquered in peace. Therefore, while you have time, work good toward all (Gal. VI). For a time will come when you will be able to do nothing (John VI). As Truth says: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII).

Rise also, brothers, from the sleep of ignorance, for it too is deadly. Hence Scripture says: “He would not understand, so as to do good; he meditated iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. XXV). And this: “But they did not know my ways, so that I swore in my wrath,” etc. (Ps. XCIV).—“Therefore my people,” says the prophet, “has been led captive, because it had no knowledge” (Isa. V). And: “Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). From this come error, heresy, unbelief, and excuse-making in sins. But the ignorant person shall be ignored, and the negligent person neglected.

We must likewise rise from the sleep of concupiscence, lest perhaps we fall asleep amid the pleasures of the flesh and the enticements of the world; for “he who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. CXX). Carnal life, or worldly conduct, is a kind of sleep. For just as one who dreams that he possesses many riches is sad when he wakes because he finds that he possesses nothing, so one who is rich in this world, when he has passed out of it, will grieve because he will carry nothing away from it with him. “For naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job I).—“For we brought nothing into this world; without doubt, neither can we carry anything away” (I Tim. VI). For we shall carry away from this world nothing with us except our works, as it is written: “Their works follow them” (Apoc. XIV). If these have been good, angels lead them to glory; if evil, they drag them down to Gehenna. Alas, how many and how great are the things mortals ponder concerning the bitterness [variant: uncertainty] of worldly life; yet at the point of death all that they had pondered suddenly vanishes. Hence the Psalmist says: “His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth,” etc. (Ps. CXLV). For the person who remains in sin is like a beast that rots in dung; and one who returns to sin is like a dog returning to its vomit (II Pet. II).

For what do we wretches think about, plan, or do all day long? We weave spiders’ webs. For we wear ourselves out, consume our days, and waste our time in vain pursuits, wicked deeds, pleasures of the flesh, and enticements of the world. Indeed, the Apostle condemns in this passage the concupiscence of both flesh and world, when he forbids revelry and impurity—things in which carnal people, that is, gluttons and the lustful, take greater delight. Again, he says, “contention and envy,” in which worldly people engage, contending with one another over possessions or honors and envying one another on their account.

Therefore it is now time for us to rise from sleep, because our salvation is nearer than when we believed. It is as though he said: We cannot excuse our negligence by saying that what we await is delayed too long, because our salvation is nearer than when we believed. For at the beginning of faith we were cleansed from guilt through baptism; now, through merit, we are worthy of the crown, and therefore we have drawn nearer to salvation. Or salvation is nearer because death is nearer. For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV).

Again, it is now time for us to rise from sleep, because the night has passed and the day has drawn near. It is as though he said: Before Christ’s coming there was a night of the error of unbelief and ignorance; but now, after Christ’s coming, the day of faith, truth, and grace has shone brightly. Thus we can no longer excuse ourselves as though we did not know the hidden truth. For “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I). For the people of the Gentiles, who walked in darkness, saw a great light (Isa. IX). And certainly it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back (II Pet. II); for the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke XII).

Likewise, it is now time for us to rise from sleep, namely because “the world passes away, and its concupiscence” (I John II). Therefore we ought not to walk in revelry and drunkenness, with respect to gluttony; in beds and impurities, with respect to lust; in contention and envy, [Col. 0324B] with respect to anger and jealousy. But let us put on the Lord Jesus Christ, according to the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that we may walk in newness of spirit.

Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness—that is, sins which are committed in darkness, for “he who does evil hates the light” (John III); or those which come from the prince of darkness, that is, the devil; or those which send persons into outer darkness. And let us put on the armor of light, that is, good works, which come from the author of light. For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” Or, they are works which ought to shine “before men, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify our Father who is in heaven” (Matt. III). Or they are works which then pass into the light, through which “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII): namely, so that we may walk honorably, not in the darkness of vices, error, unbelief, and ignorance, but in the day of virtues, faith, virtue, and grace, and may please both God and human beings. Therefore, brothers and children, since we await as near our salvation—that is, the birth of our Savior, who was born for this purpose, “that he might save his people from their sins” (Matt. I)—let us rise from the sleep of sin and cast off the works of darkness, so that we may worthily celebrate his most holy Nativity, through him who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. [Col. 0324D] Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

[Note: [Col. 0323D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[Col. 0323]

[Col. 0323D] “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven” (Dan. VII).

Daniel the prophet, most beloved brothers, whose name is interpreted “man of desire” or “desired man,” while he was held captive in Babylon, revealed these and other things concerning Christ’s incarnation through the Holy Spirit. He explained the king’s dreams and recalled to his memory what he had consigned to oblivion. In these dreams he saw and recognized a small stone cut from a mountain without hands, which grew so greatly that it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Dan. II). This stone signified our Lord Jesus [Col. 0325A] Christ, who today is announced by the prophet Isaiah as a little child, as it is written: “For a little child is born to us” (Isa. IX). He was made little through incarnation, birth, death, and passion; he appeared great and almighty through the glory of resurrection and ascension. Through the truth of miracles he appeared as a great mountain among human beings, and ascended to equality with the Father in order to have a dwelling-place. Concerning his birth, Daniel the prophet foresaw this in his prophecy, saying: “I was watching in a vision of the night,” etc.

All the prophets, most beloved, as though placed in ecstasy, looked ahead to the incarnation of the Son of God; and because Christ’s incarnation was to come after many years, the prophets, beholding it, saw it not openly but as though hidden away. Mother Church considered this in her longing for the Son of God when, looking from afar, she said: “And behold, I see the power of God and a cloud covering the whole earth.” By the power of God coming, we understand the Son of God coming in the flesh; by the cloud, we signify the grace of the Holy Spirit covering the whole earth. Hence it is also added: “Go out to meet him, and say to him: Tell us whether you yourself are the one who is to come among the people of Israel.” And in accordance with this meaning Daniel the prophet says: “I was watching in a vision of the night,” etc. But what is seen in a vision of the night is not known as openly as it is in the brightness of day.

But we ought to know that in divine Scripture “night” is understood in seven ways. First, night is a time opposed to day; for every time established and ordered by God is either day or night. The dialecticians call these two contraries and immediates, because the assertion of one entails the removal of the other. Day was given us for labor, but night for rest. Thus it is written in Genesis: “Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day shall not cease” (Gen. VIII), because they serve humankind. Isaiah uses the word in this same sense, where it is written: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? And the watchman said: Morning comes, and also night. If you seek me, seek; turn back and come” (Isa. XXI). This is to be understood thus: O God, who are the watchman, who willed to be born in the flesh by night, and again permitted yourself to be led to the Passion by night. And the watchman said: Morning comes—morning for my faithful ones, but night for unbelievers. If you seek me, seek with faith and works; turn to me and come.

Second, night is taken for sin, as in the Song of Songs: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” (Cant. III), because while a person is in sins, he cannot prevail in finding God. Third, night is taken for Judas and for the wretched people of the Jews. Hence the Psalmist says: “Night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII). This is to be understood thus: night declares knowledge to night; that is, Judas, who was night, dark and shadowy, delivered knowledge of God—that is, the Son of God—to the night of the Jews. Fourth, [Col. 0326A] night is taken for the time which was under the law, in which the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ was veiled and hidden. Of this night Paul says: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near; let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII). The night has passed—that is, the time which was under the law, which was as it were night, has gone away; but the day has drawn near—that is, the brightness of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ has come.

Fifth, night is taken for the devil, as it is written: “While all things held deep silence, and night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your almighty Word, O Lord, coming from royal thrones, became for us a helper in tribulations” (Wis. XVIII). There were three silences, and likewise there were three courses of the night. For nothing can be called a middle which does not have two adjoining parts; and in this way there are reasonably proved to have been three silences. The first silence extended from the casting of the first parent out of paradise until that time when God gave the law to Moses. Then the first silence was broken after human nature received the divine law. But because it did not long strive to observe it, having abandoned the Creator’s command, as the Psalmist says: “They have all turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none that does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII), the middle silence ensued, in which [Col. 0326C] night—that is, the devil—began his journey; and thus in the second silence it reached its middle course. This silence lasted until angels descended from heaven and announced to the shepherds that God had been born. Then the middle silence was broken when the angelic choir sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II). The third silence was when Christ’s flesh lay in the tomb for three days; but it did not last long, because after the resurrection the congregation of the faithful sang a new song with the Psalmist (Ps. XXXII).

Sixth, night is taken for the life of the present time, because in comparison with eternal life, the life of this age is reckoned night and darkness. Hence in the Psalm: “In the morning I shall stand before you and behold” (Ps. V). [Col. 0326D] And in the Song of Songs: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe deer, feeding among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Cant. II). Seventh, night is taken for the hidden revelation of the prophets, as in the Psalm: “And he made darkness his hiding-place; his tent was around him” (Ps. XVII). By the hiding-place of the Son of God we understand his incarnation, which he placed in darkness—that is, as something holy and hidden—because it was not known to any of the demons that, for you, O Christ, Mary’s womb had been a bridal chamber. “For had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). And according to this meaning Daniel the prophet says: “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven.”

[Col. 0327A] “Cloud” has various meanings in divine Scripture. First, a cloud stands for the Virgin Mary, as it is written: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be shaken” (Isa. XIX). Second, a cloud stands for the infusion of divine grace, as the Psalmist says: “At the brightness before him clouds passed, hail and coals of fire” (Ps. XVII). Third, a cloud stands for divine manifestation: “Behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them” (Matt. XVII). And immediately it is said from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid.). Fourth, a cloud is taken for the blessing of the highest Father, as in the text: “And a cloud received him from their eyes” (ibid.). Fifth, [Col. 0327B] a cloud is spoken of as the prophets; hence: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One, and let the earth bring forth the Savior” (Isa. XLV). And the Psalmist says: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII), that is, obscure knowledge in the prophets. In accordance with this Daniel says prophetically: “And behold, one like a Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven.” “Son of Man” means son of the Virgin Mary, of whom it is said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who ascended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John III). He who is Son of Man in heaven is the same one also called Son of God according to the divine nature, by which he is equal to the Father; and Son of Man according to the human nature, by which he is not equal to him.

[Col. 0328A] His human birth was foretold long beforehand, as in the book of Genesis: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech” (Gen. IV). This is Cain who killed his brother Abel, the impious fratricide who deserved the anathema of eternal curse. Cain is interpreted “possessor,” and signifies Adam, our first parent, who, cast out from God’s possession, needed the mercy of his Creator. But sevenfold vengeance is promised for him, because for his restoration the Son of God willed to be incarnate through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. But for Lamech, seventy-sevenfold vengeance is declared. This is Lamech, who killed Cain and crushed his own child with his hands, as he himself says: “I killed a man for my wound and a young man for my bruise” (Gen. IV). Lamech is interpreted “help,” and signifies Adam, our first parent, because, deprived of God’s help, he longed for the aid of his Creator. But in order that the sin of Lamech—that is, the sin of our first parent—might be cleansed, seventy-sevenfold vengeance is plainly described, because from Adam to Christ there are found seventy-seven generations. From these generations the Son of God, descending according to human nature, on this day by his birth wiped away the sin of Lamech—that is, of the whole world—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

Why Christ is called the great prophet; the fourfold coming of Christ; the fourfold sense of Jerusalem; the fourfold peace; finally, the fourfold renewal of the Church.

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327C] “Behold, a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem.”

The great prophet is understood to be Christ, of whom it is read in Deuteronomy (ch. XVIII): “The Lord shall raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; him you shall hear as you hear me.” And of him it is said in the Gospel: “A great prophet has arisen among us,” and, “Because God has visited his people” (ibid.). Christ is called a prophet both because of his understanding of hidden things and because of his knowledge of things to come: the God of knowledge, the hidden Lord, the investigator of all hidden things, who searches the reins and hearts (Ps. VII), before whose eyes all things are naked and open. “For the word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of spirit and soul, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and there is no creature invisible in his sight” (Col. II). “In him are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Heb. IV). Therefore he is called a prophet because he revealed hidden things, as he says: “All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV); and because he foretold future things, as he says: “I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe” (John XIII).

Therefore he is reckoned a great prophet, not only because he is Lord of the prophets, but because he received the Spirit wholly and always possessed it. For to Christ alone was the Spirit given without measure (John III), “in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II); but the rest receive from his fullness (John I), because “the ointment descends from his head to the beard, and from the beard flows down to the hem of the garment” (Ps. CXXXII). For Christ alone always possessed the abiding Spirit. “Upon whom,” he says, “you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes,” etc. (John I).—“For upon him rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isa. II), and what follows. But the others did not have the Spirit always, but only for a time, according as Elisha said to Gehazi: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden this from me and has not made it known to me” (IV Kings IV).—“For the Spirit breathes where he wills, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

Therefore a great prophet shall come. Sacred Scripture distinguishes four comings of the Redeemer: the first in a cloud, the second in dew, the third in a whirlwind, the fourth in fire. In the cloud of flesh, in the dew of grace, in the whirlwind of death, in the fire of judgment. In the cloud of flesh, that he might redeem the world; in the dew of grace, that he might enlighten the spirit; in the whirlwind of death, that he might reduce the body to ashes; in the fire of judgment, that he might judge the age.

Of the first: “I went out from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XII). He shall come in the cloud of flesh. Hence the prophet: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. LIX), that is, he shall assume flesh free from sins, and he shall enter Egypt, that is, descend into the world. For this is that angel who, according to the Apocalypse of John (ch. X), “came down from heaven clothed with a cloud,” because he came to us with divinity shod, that is, covered with the cloud of flesh.

Of the second: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,” etc. (John XIV). He comes in the dew of grace; hence the Psalmist: “Like the dew of Hermon which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. CXXXII). Hermon is interpreted “exalted light.” For he is Christ, “the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I), first exalted upon the cross and then exalted in heaven. As he himself says in the Gospel: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII). From him the dew of grace descends upon Mount Zion, that is, upon a soul raised aloft by heavenly contemplation. Of this coming it is said through the prophet: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” (Isa. XLV). And again: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece,” etc. (Ps. LXXI).
