Of the third: “When he comes and knocks, let them open to him immediately” (Luke XII). For he shall come in the whirlwind of death. A whirlwind is so called from disturbance. But what disturbs more than death? Hence Scripture says: “O death, how bitter is your remembrance” (Ecclus. XLI). Therefore the Lord says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). And again: “My soul is troubled” (Ps. VI). And what shall I say? “Father, save me from this hour” (John XII).

Of the fourth: “You shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Luke XXI). He shall come in the fire of judgment; hence the Psalm: “Fire shall go before him, and shall burn his enemies round about” (Ps. XCVI); and again: “A fire shall burn in his sight,” etc. (Ps. XLIX). The Church represents these four comings of the Redeemer in the four Sundays of the Lord’s Advent, not only by the number of days but also by the rationale of the offices.

This is also signified through the four verses of the first Advent responsory, namely: “All you earthborn,” [Col. 0330A] etc.; “You who sit upon the cherubim,” etc.; “Lift up the gates,” etc.; “Glory to the Father,” etc.; as the discerning investigator understands, who knows how to suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone (Deut. XXXII).

Therefore a great prophet shall come, etc. You know, most dear ones, that Jerusalem is understood in four ways, according to the four theological senses: historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. For there is a Jerusalem above and below, inward and outward: namely heavenly and earthly, spiritual and bodily. The higher is in the homeland; the lower is on the way. The inward is in the soul; the outward is in Syria. The higher is the triumphant Church, of which the Apostle says: “That Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. IV). [Col. 0330B] The lower is the Church of those who are fighting, of which the prophet says: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem,” etc. (Isa. LX). The inward is the faithful soul, of which it is said: “I shall give salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. XLVI). The outward is wretched Jerusalem, of which it is said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to you” (Matt. XXIII). Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.”

Now there is the peace of sinners, the peace of converts, the peace of the righteous, and the peace of the blessed. The peace of sinners is in vices; the peace of converts in morals; the peace of the righteous in grace; the peace of the blessed in glory. Of the peace of sinners in vices, the Psalmist says: “I was envious of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. XXVII). This peace is seen by the outward Jerusalem—that is, wretched Jerusalem—which sinners now possess, who in vanity come together into one. Of the peace of converts in morals, the Apostle says: “Christ is our peace, who made both one, so that he might create the two walls in himself into one new man, making peace” (Eph. II). This peace is seen by the lower Jerusalem, that is, the Church of those who are fighting, who walk in the house of the Lord in agreement (Ps. LIV). Of the peace of the righteous in grace, the Lord says: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you; not as the world gives do I give to you” (John XIV). This peace is seen by the inward Jerusalem, that is, the faithful soul, because “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience” (Gal. V). [Col. 0330D] Of the peace of the blessed in glory, the Prophet says: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV). This peace is seen by the higher Jerusalem, that is, the Church of those who triumph, because among the elect there is peace upon peace.

Moreover, we earnestly pray for temporal peace, saying: “Give peace, O Lord, in our days”; but because our sins demand it, we almost nowhere possess it, for “we awaited peace and it did not come; we sought good things and behold, disturbance” (Jer. VIII). Jerusalem—that is, the Church—is renewed in four ways: by sacraments, morals, miracles, and commandments.

Of the renewal of sacraments, Moses says in the law: “You shall eat the oldest of old things, and when new things come you shall throw out the old” (Lev. XXVI). The oldest things are moral precepts, the old things legal precepts, and the new things evangelical. Therefore we eat the oldest of old things—that is, we receive moral precepts to be observed for the nourishment of spiritual life—but when the new things come, that is, evangelical sacraments, we throw out the old things, that is, the legal observances: the paschal lamb when Christ’s body comes, and circumcision when baptism comes. For when truth came, the figure ceased, and the shadow vanished when the light shone forth. Hence the Apostle says: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V). O how beneficial is the renewal that changed legal things into evangelical things! For legal things signified but did not justify. Hence the Apostle says: “Abraham received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV). But evangelical things signified and justified. Hence the Apostle says of baptism: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Col. II). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark X). The former showed the disease but did not confer healing. Hence the prophet says: “I gave them precepts that were not good and ordinances in which they would not live” (Ezek. XX). The Apostle agrees with this, saying: “The law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. VII). Indeed, “light entered in so that transgression might abound” (Rom. V.20). But these show infirmity and confer health. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI). This is the Samaritan who, approaching the wounded man, pours wine and oil over him, whereas the priest and Levite had first seen him and left him uncured (Luke XIV).

Therefore a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem. Of the renewal of morals the Apostle says: “Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV). The oldness of the human being means guilt; the newness of the human being means grace. The former is contracted originally from Adam; the latter is freely conferred through Jesus. By the former the mind is deformed; by the latter it is reformed. Therefore let us put off the old man with his deeds—that is, let us lay aside the oldness of guilt which we contracted from Adam, with its deeds, that is, with vices and sins—and put on the new man who has been created according to God: that is, let us assume the newness of grace conferred through Christ, and walk in newness of spirit (Rom. VI), according to the Apostle’s preceding statement: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. IV). Hence elsewhere he says: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V). How beneficial is the renewal that makes vicious persons [Col. 0332A] virtuous!

For human beings had grown so old through sin that they even changed “the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and serpents” (Rom. I). But when Christ came, he destroyed idolatry, according to that prophetic saying: “The Lord alone shall be exalted on that day, and idols shall be utterly broken. On that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his images of gold, which he had made for himself in order to worship moles and bats” (Isa. II). And when he came, “our peace, who made both one and dissolved the middle wall of hostility,” he took away ceremonial observance from the Jews and idolatry from the Gentiles, “so that he might create the two walls in himself, in the cornerstone, into one new man, making [Col. 0332B] peace” (Eph. II) between them and God.

Therefore a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem. Of the renewal of miracles Scripture says: “Renew signs and change wonders” (Ecclus. XXXVI). Signs are sacraments; wonders are prodigies. Therefore the Lord renewed signs—that is, sacraments—and changed wonders—that is, prodigies. For the first Adam was made from virgin earth; the second Adam was made from a virgin woman. The first Adam was male in his very creation; the second Adam was male in his very conception, as the prophet foretold: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the enclosure of her womb” (Jer. XXXI). Eve was formed from the side of the first Adam while he slept. The Church was formed from the side of the second Adam while he died. The first-created man and Eve were two in one flesh (Gen. II); Christ and the Church are two in one body. Those two were one in nature; these two are one in person. O how beneficial is the renewal through which “the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the Gospel!” (Luke VII).

Therefore a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem. Of the renewal of commandments the prophet says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of [Col. 0332D] the land of Egypt; but I shall give my laws into their minds and write them upon their hearts” (Jer. XXXI). The old law was written upon tablets of stone, but the new law upon tablets of the heart. The former was given to the hard-hearted, the latter to the devout; the former to unbelievers, the latter to the faithful. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII). You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. III). O how beneficial is the renewal through which injury is changed into favor! For the old law rendered “eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand [Col. 0333A] for hand” (Lev. XXIV). The new law commands: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also; if he takes away your tunic, give him your cloak as well; if he compels you for a thousand paces, go with him another two” (Matt. V). “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I).

Therefore a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew Jerusalem. [Col. 0334A] “But when the Son of Man comes in the seat of his majesty” (Matt. XIX), then he shall renew Jerusalem—that is, the Church—most perfectly. As John testifies in the Apocalypse (ch. XXI): “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God and surrounded with a robe, like a bride adorned for her husband. And he who sat upon the throne said: Behold, I make all things new.”

## SERMON V. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

[Note: [Col. 0333D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[Col. 0333]

[Col. 0333B] “When John had heard in prison of Christ’s works, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: Are you the one who is to come, or are we to await another?” (Luke VII.)

Perhaps it seems surprising that John the Baptist, who foretold Christ’s coming and pointed him out as present—“Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1); “this is he of whom I told you: One stronger than I will come after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie” (Mark 1)—should now, as though doubting, inquire through his disciples: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” Because of this doubt some have erred, saying that John was damned because, having first believed, he afterwards doubted. But since Christ himself condemned this error, saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? [Col. 0333C] A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet; among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11), we must ask how this passage ought to be understood.

Certainly, the holy Fathers have found this passage expounded in two ways: namely, concerning the coming into the world, which had then already taken place, and concerning the coming to hell, which was then still future. According to the first exposition, John did not doubt, but the disciples doubted. Thus the disciples questioned not on John’s behalf, but on their own, saying: “Are *we* to await another?” They did not say, “Does John await another?” but, “Are we to await another?” For John does not doubt, but we doubt. Yet another evangelist testifies that, when men came to him saying, [Col. 0333D] “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?’” he might answer more fully the question that came from the master’s side.

The sense, then, is this: when John, placed in prison, had heard from his disciples reporting the works—that is, the miracles—of Christ, while they still doubted, John sent them to Christ so that they might ask and hear from him himself. According to the exposition just given, however, not only the disciples doubted, but John too doubted whether Christ would descend to hell in person or through another. Therefore, sending two of [Col. 0334B] his disciples, he said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” As though he were saying: “Just as, by preceding you in birth, I announced you while living to the world, shall I likewise, by preceding you in death, announce you when dead to the dead in hell?”

But against the first exposition there seems to stand what is said here: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” It is not said: “Are you he who *was* to come?” For neither John nor his disciples doubted that Jesus had come into the world, since they saw and heard him performing so many miracles. They therefore knew that he had already come; how, then, could they doubt whether he was to come? Against the second exposition, however, there seems to stand the fact that Christ here mentions only the signs of his first coming, saying: “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed,” [Col. 0334C] and so forth.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we may understand this passage differently, in a new but sound manner, so that the words may agree and the mysteries correspond, so that there may be a base beneath the column and a wheel may be contained within a wheel. Let us say, then, that this passage concerns the coming for judgment. Whether John himself doubted, or, what is safer to suppose, the disciples doubted, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” As though saying: “Tell us whether, just as you came in person into the world for redemption, so you yourself are to come for judgment and recompense; or are we rather to await another who will come?”

Jesus answered and said to them: “Go [Col. 0334D] and report to John what you have heard and seen.” As though he said: “What you heard foretold in the Law, behold, you have seen fulfilled in the Gospel.” For in the Law you heard the prophet proclaim: “Behold, our God will bring the vengeance of recompense. God himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed. Then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened” (Isa. 35). This very thing you see fulfilled through me in the Gospel: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, and the mute speak. Therefore I, who came into the world as Savior, shall come for judgment as recompensing judge, concerning whom [Col. 0335A] the prophet foretold: “Behold, our God will bring the vengeance of recompense; God himself will come and save us” (Isa. 35).

And indeed you ought to believe this, because the signs you heard foretold by the prophet—behold, you have seen them fulfilled through me. Yet more things are done here than were said there, since lepers too were cleansed and the dead raised. Another evangelist likewise testifies: “In that hour he cured many of diseases, wounds, and evil spirits”; and the coming of Christ could never have been prophesied more expressly.

Let the Jew, then, who falsely says that the Messiah has not yet come into the world and is not God, be ashamed. For here it is explicitly said: “God himself will come and save us”; and it is certain that he has come, whose signs of coming are now seen fulfilled. For the blind see, [Col. 0335B] the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor receive the Gospel, and blessed is he who has not been scandalized by me.

Every day Christ works spiritually these miracles which he then worked bodily. For he enlightens the blind when he teaches the true faith to the ignorant; he raises the lame when he trains the negligent for good works; he cleanses lepers when he converts those who err to sound doctrine; he restores the mute when he leads the silent to divine praise; he proclaims the Gospel to the poor when he reveals evangelical truth to the humble; and he raises the dead when he brings sinners to fruitful repentance.

The blind are those who lack the light of truth, of whom it is written: “Leave them alone; they are blind and leaders of the blind. If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” [Col. 0335C] (Matt. 15). The deaf are those who despise obeying the Lord’s commands, of whom it is said: “Like the deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of the enchanter who is charmed by the wise man” (Ps. 67). [Note: [Col. 0335D] Thus the manuscript.] The mute are those who remain silent instead of divine praise, as it is written: “I became mute and was humbled; I kept silence even from good things, and my sorrow was renewed” (Ps. 38). The lame are those who do not walk in the paths of the commandments, as it is written: “How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him” (3 Kings 18).

Lepers are those who corrupt sacred Scripture by heretical perversity. For the flesh of a leper is in some places smooth and in others swollen, in some places reddish, in others [Col. 0335D] black, and in others ulcerated. So too the teaching of heretics is in some places true, in others false; in some places sound, in others perverse; in some places plain, in others obscure. For unless they mixed true things with false, unless they covered the wolf with a lamb, unless Satan’s angel transformed himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11), they would undoubtedly not deceive innocent souls; for, once detected and recognized, they would be avoided. They therefore come in sheep’s clothing, though they are ravenous wolves (Matt. 7); and in a golden cup, under the appearance of nectar, they offer deadly poison.

The dead, moreover, are those who lie in mortal sins, deprived of spiritual life: either like the girl who lay dead [Col. 0336A] in the house (Matt. 9), when the sin of thought still lies hidden in the heart; or like the youth carried out dead beyond the gate, when the sin of speech has already proceeded from the mouth; or like Lazarus, stinking after four days in the tomb (John 11), when the sin of action is repeatedly practiced as a habit. Yet he heals and cures all these maladies, of whom the evangelist testifies: “All who had sick persons afflicted with various diseases brought them to Jesus, and all were healed” (Luke 4).

These miracles now performed spiritually are greater than those then performed bodily. For it is greater for a soul to be healed than for a body, since the soul cannot be healed unless the body consents, whereas the body can be healed without the soul’s consent. The Pharisees too seem to have recognized this: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?”—as though he not only heals bodies but souls as well.

Nor should we pass over in like manner the statement that the poor receive the Gospel, so that he may be shown to have come who said of himself through the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he sent me to proclaim the Gospel to the poor” (ibid.). In this not only is the teacher’s kindness commended, because he did not despise the needy and rejected; the nobility of the disciples is also marked, because they were such—that is, humble in heart—that they deserved to receive saving teaching. As Truth says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them [Col. 0336C] to little ones” (Luke 10).

Thus it is not merely by circumstance but by disposition that the poor receive the Gospel in Christ, so that he may make them evangelists: not those powerful and wise in the world, but the humble and lowly, because God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, lest people perhaps believe that evangelical teaching had been discovered by the wisdom of this world or propagated by the power of this age. “And blessed,” he says, “is he who has not been scandalized by me.”

The Apostle says: “We preach Jesus Christ, and him crucified: a scandal indeed to Jews, but foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1). For Gentile philosophers judged it foolish that one and the same person was believed to be God and man, mortal and immortal, simple and composite, eternal and temporal. [Col. 0336D] But God made foolish the wisdom of the wise and rejected the prudence of the prudent (ibid.), because the argument from contraries shows that the divine mystery prevails. Therefore that proposition seems truer, once it is maintained that a negative does not follow from an affirmative.

The Jews, however, even today are scandalized when they hear that God was scourged, crucified, and died. They disdain to hear that God suffered unworthy things, though for that very reason he ought to be honored by us more worthily: because he deigned to endure things more unworthy for us. This, then, is the stone of offense and rock of scandal (1 Pet. 2), set for the fall and resurrection of many, upon [Col. 0337A] whom every building constructed grows into a holy temple in the Lord. But whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; and upon whomever [Col. 0338A] this stone falls, it will crush him: Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all, God blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. THIRD SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

On the four natural affections of the mind; on the joy of good and evil persons, of heart and flesh; and on what ought to be done in prosperity and adversity.

[Col. 0337]

[Col. 0337B] “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all people; for the Lord is near” (Phil. 4).

We ought to celebrate with great joy the most holy coming of our Redeemer, which the faithful of old awaited with intense longing; for him whom they awaited as promised, we celebrate as presented. For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1).

The joy of the heart we ought to express both by word and deed, but moderately. Therefore the Apostle says: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all people; for the Lord is near.” He teaches, therefore, in what we ought to rejoice when he says, “In the Lord”; for how long, when he says, “Always”; and how, when he says, “Let your moderation be known to all people.” As though he said: moderately. Why? Because the Lord is near. Consider each point carefully, for there is nothing in them that does not breathe a delightful meaning.

Therefore, rejoice in the Lord always. You know, we believe, because you have often seen, that the Roman pontiff uses no embroidered mitre either in Lent or in Advent, except only on that middle Sunday of Lent when at the introit is sung, “Rejoice, Jerusalem,” and likewise on the middle Sunday of Advent when at the introit is sung, “Rejoice in the Lord always.” Each office recalls joy and exultation, and brings gladness and delight. For the present we omit to give you the reason and mystical significance of this practice, because we remember having given it in earlier sermons. “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.”

There are four natural affections of the mind: sorrow, joy, fear, and hope. Sorrow and joy concern the present; fear and hope the future. Sorrow and fear concern evil, while joy and hope concern good. Observe how these four are connected with one another. The first two concern the present; the last two, the future. The first and third concern evil; the second and fourth, good.

Hence people fear, desire, rejoice, and grieve. These are the two millstones, upper and lower, between which the Christian soul must be ground. Concerning them the Law commands: “You shall not take the upper and lower millstone as a pledge” (Deut. 24). Between joy and sorrow, indeed, as between two millstones, we must move through this mortal life, so that sorrow may moderate joy, lest we become dissipated; and joy may moderate sorrow, lest we become crushed in spirit. For excessive sorrow—that is, immoderate and continual sorrow—overwhelms the mind; and excessive joy, likewise immoderate and continual, dissolves the mind. Therefore it is said:

> Introduce joys from time to time amid your cares.

What lacks alternating rest is not lasting. Hear of excessive joy that dissipates: “Lyre and harp and tambourine and wine are at your feasts” (Isa. 5). “Behold joy and gladness: killing calves [Col. 0338C] and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine. ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die’” (Isa. 22). Hear of excessive sorrow that overwhelms: “All hands shall be weakened, and every human heart shall melt; pangs and pains shall seize them; they shall suffer as a woman in labor” (Ezek. 7). The Apostle teaches us to move between these millstones: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12). And another says again: “In the day of good things do not forget evil things” (Ecclus. 11).

When, therefore, some prosperity comes to us, we must take care not to rejoice with excessive dissipation, always mindful of what is written: “Laughter is mingled with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). He knew this who said: [Col. 0338D] “My harp has been turned to mourning, and my organ to the voice of those who weep” (Job 30). Therefore, after the Apostle had said, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” he added, “Let your moderation be known to all people.” As though he said: “Exult with moderation, be glad with measure, and let this itself be known to all, so that your light may shine before people, that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5); so that curtain may draw curtain, and “let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22).

Likewise, when adversity befalls us, we must take care not to grieve with excessive despondency, always mindful of what is said: “Weeping will remain at evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 29); for after the storm he makes calm [Col. 0339A] (Tob. 3). He knew this who said: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have cut away my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with grief” (Ps. 29). For:

> Welcome will come the hour which is not hoped for.

Likewise, between hope and fear, as between two millstones, we ought to move, so that fear may moderate hope, lest we presume, and hope may moderate fear, lest we despair.

> Fly between the two; in the middle you will go most safely.

Through excessive fear the man despaired who said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4). Through excessive hope, on the other hand, the man presumed who “said in his heart, ‘God will not require it’” (Ps. 10). Therefore rejoice in the Lord always—that is, whatever good you do, do with cheerfulness of heart, together with bodily gladness, [Col. 0339B] not from sadness or compulsion. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9),

> and above all friendly faces joined them.

For the Psalmist also says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 36).

But since sorrow and joy are opposites, and one must always rejoice, as the Apostle urges when he says, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” then one must never grieve, since opposites cannot exist together. What then is meant by the Psalmist’s words, “I am poor and sorrowful, and your salvation, O God, has upheld me” (Ps. 68), and the Lord’s saying, “Blessed are you who weep, because you shall laugh” (Luke 6)? Yet rejoicing over one thing and grieving over another are not opposites. Therefore we can at once rejoice in good and grieve over evil.

Although the saying, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” refers not to a continual act but to a continual disposition. Indeed, just as weeping often proceeds from great joy, so joy is often born from great weeping. When the soul is pierced with contrition and crushed over its sins, it sighs and weeps; then, at once receiving hope of pardon, it is healed and enlightened, enlarged and gladdened, so that it can say with the Prophet: [Col. 0339C] “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93). For just as “there is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Ps. 37), since the fire of reason is never extinguished, “so all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44), because “this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

Let us therefore rejoice, not in this world but in the Lord. In another place the Apostle says: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10). The Psalmist likewise exhorts: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright” (Ps. 23). And elsewhere: “The righteous man shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him,” and so forth (Ps. 3). Evil people rejoice in the world; blessed people rejoice in God. The latter rejoice in spiritual and eternal things; the former in carnal and worldly things. The latter rejoice in virtues; the former in vices. Of the former kind it is written: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places. The exultations of God are in their throats, and double-edged swords in their hands” [Col. 0340A] (Ps. 149). Of the latter it is said: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2), and “he glories in malice who is mighty in iniquity” (Ps. 81).

But the joy of the former is everlasting, as it is written: “Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16). The joy of the latter, however, is momentary, as it is written: “They hold tambourine and harp and rejoice at the sound of the organ; they spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend to hell” (Job 21). Oh, how many such people there are in the world today, whom no joy in spiritual and eternal things touches, but only joy in carnal and worldly things. Such was the man who said to his soul in the Gospel: “Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.” But consider what the Lord said to him: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?” [Col. 0340B] (Luke 12). For that rich man who feasted splendidly every day “was buried in hell” (Luke 16).

Therefore, brothers and children, let us rejoice not in this world but in the Lord—that is, in things pertaining to merit and reward, grace or glory, virtue or salvation. The apostles rejoiced in things pertaining to merit; of them it is written that “the apostles went away from the presence of the council rejoicing because they had been considered worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). Hence James exhorts, saying: [Col. 0340C] “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (Jas. 1). But in things pertaining to reward rejoiced those to whom Christ said: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5); whence the prophet said: “But I shall glory in the Lord; I shall rejoice in the Lord my Jesus” (Hab. 3).

Because of these two joys—one possessed from merits, the other from rewards—the Apostle repeats himself, saying:

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice”; or because of the twofold joy of heart and flesh. Of this the Psalmist says: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). The heart exults when it is purified from unlawful desires; [Col. 0340D] the flesh exults when it is cleansed of unlawful deeds. For the Lord says that the ungodly have no joy (Isa. 57), and “there is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Ps. 37).

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, in the Lord, because the Lord is near. He is near in respect of his coming in the flesh, as it is written: “The time for him to come is near, and his day will not be delayed” (Isa. 14). He is near in respect of his coming into the mind, as it is written: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him” (Ps. 144). He is near in respect of his coming in death, because “the days of man are short; the number of his months is with you. A man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state” (Job 14). For “my life, cut off as by a weaver, while I was still beginning, he cut me down” [Col. 0341A] (Isa. 38). He is near in respect of his coming for judgment, because “it is the last hour” (1 John 2), and we are those “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10). “Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25). “For as lightning comes out of the east and appears as far as the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be” (Matt. 24). For “at an hour when you do not expect, the Son of Man will come” (Luke 12).

But since we ought to rejoice because the Lord is near to us in death or judgment, should we not rather fear than rejoice on either account? We should fear indeed, but this is for those who do not love his coming; those who love his coming ought to rejoice. Hence the Apostle said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). And again: “We await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness so that it is conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). May he deign to grant this to us and to you, he who is God above all, blessed for ages.

## SERMON VII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

[Note: [Col. 0341D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[Col. 0341]

[Col. 0341B] “I baptize you with water, but one stands in your midst whom you do not know; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. This is he who is to come after me and has been made before me, because he was prior to me; I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal” (Luke 3).

The Apostolic See, which, by the Lord’s ordering, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful, customarily displays on this middle Sunday of Advent—as also on the middle Sunday of Lent—certain new tokens of a new joy, not only in the office but also in its adornment. There it sings at the introit: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her”; here it sings at the introit: “Rejoice in God always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4). Then the Roman pontiff wears a golden [Col. 0341C] flower resembling a rose; now he wears a mitre and chasuble adorned with gold and gems. We have often set forth the reason for the former practice; now we shall state the intention of the latter.

Certainly, as you will remember if you recall well, we have told you that there are four comings of the Redeemer, which the Church celebrates on the four Sundays of Advent. Two greatly terrify, and two greatly soothe. The coming for judgment and the coming in death terrify; the coming in the flesh and the coming into the mind soothe. For first comes disturbance and afterwards consolation, as the Psalmist says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93). Therefore [Col. 0341D] the Church first celebrates the two comings that terrify, so that she may transfer us from sadness to joy and from fear to love.

Thus, on the first Sunday the last coming is celebrated, and on the last Sunday the first; the second on the third, and the third on the second. This is clearly gathered from the Gospels read in the Masses. For on the first Sunday that Gospel is read in which it is said: “There shall be signs in the sun and moon and stars,” and so forth (Luke 21), by which the coming for judgment is declared. On the second [Col. 0342B] Sunday that Gospel is read in which it is said: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” (Luke 7), by which the coming in death is signified. On the third Sunday the Gospel is read in which it is said: “He who is to come after me has been made before me,” by which the coming in the flesh is expressed. On the fourth Sunday the Gospel is read in which it is said: “The word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness,” by which the coming into the mind is indicated.

On this middle Sunday, therefore, the coming in the flesh is celebrated, concerning which we ought especially to rejoice because of the reconciliation of the human race. To this pertains what John the Baptist first says: “I baptize you with water, but one stands in your midst whom you do not know; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit [Col. 0342C] and fire.” To the exaltation of human nature pertains what John the Baptist adds: “This is he who is to come after me and has been made before me; I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.” Therefore the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always,” because of the reconciliation of the human race; “again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4), because of the sublimity of human nature.

John therefore says: “I baptize you with water, but one stands in your midst whom you do not know; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.” There is, then, a twofold baptism: in water and in fire, but in material water and spiritual fire. The body is cleansed by water and fire; each baptism is sanctified in the spirit. Of the former the Lord says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Of the latter John the Baptist testifies: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

For just as a human being is born according to nature from a woman, but by a man, because the man makes the woman fruitful so that she may conceive, so according to grace a human being is born from water, but by the Spirit, because the Spirit sanctifies the water so that it may purify. For “what is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” [Col. 0343A] (John 3). This fire is charity, concerning which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12). By this fire sins are purged, as the Lord says: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7). For charity covers a multitude of sins.

John therefore baptized in material water, because he cleansed the flesh outwardly; Christ baptized in spiritual fire, because he purified the mind inwardly. The former baptized outwardly as a human being; the latter baptized inwardly as God.

There is, moreover, a threefold baptism: in water, blood, and tears—water for regeneration, tears for contrition, and blood for passion. Of the first the Lord says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Of the second the Psalmist says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. 6). Of the third John testifies: “These are those who came out of tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” [Col. 0343B] (Rev. 7). Yet none of these cleanses unless it has been warmed by the Holy Spirit with the fire of charity. For without charity baptism in water must be regarded as a fiction, baptism in tears as lamentation, and baptism in blood as torment.

Why did John baptize if he did not baptize in the Spirit but in water? For two reasons. First, that he might fulfill the role of the forerunner: for just as he preceded Christ in birth and death, so he might precede him in baptizing and preaching. Second, that by his baptism he might accustom people to receive baptism, because one passes easily from like to like. It is the nature of fire to warm not only things capable of sensation but also insensible things. For this reason John compares Christ’s baptism to fire: because Christ’s baptism not only purifies those already believing but cleanses even those not yet believing.

By this the error of those who say that baptism does not benefit little children is confuted. Wishing to prove this by the authority of the Gospel, they say that Christ said to the apostles: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. [Col. 0343D] He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). A baptized infant who does not believe, they say, is condemned. Further, since sin cannot be forgiven except through charity, an infant who does not love cannot be cleansed from sin through baptism.

But such people are “blind leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15), since they do not observe that original sin, which is always contracted without consent, is one thing, and actual sin, which is never committed without consent, another. What is contracted without consent is therefore remitted without consent. But what cannot be contracted without consent cannot be remitted without consent. Since infants are bound only by original sin, they can, without any consent, be cleansed from that sin [Col. 0344A] by the power of baptism. Far be it that baptism should today be less efficacious than circumcision was of old. For as the divine Law formerly proclaimed concerning circumcision: “The soul whose foreskin’s flesh has not been circumcised shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17), so now the Gospel thunders concerning this sacrament: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3). Therefore, just as by the mystery of circumcision both children and adults formerly escaped the danger of damnation, so now by the sacrament of baptism both children and adults attain entry into the kingdom of heaven. The authorities quoted above, then, which heretics misuse, do not speak of little children, but only of adults. This is evident because little children [Col. 0344B] do not have a multitude of sins, nor is the Gospel preached to little children.

Thus far you have heard what pertains to the salvation of the human race; now hear what pertains to the exaltation of human nature: “He who is to come after me has been made before me.” As though he said: “He who succeeds me in time precedes me in dignity, because he who comes from heaven is above all.” From this passage some have taken occasion for error, saying falsely that Christ is an incarnate angel—namely, one of the great seraphim—who suffered on earth for human beings according to his human nature and suffered in the air for angels according to his angelic nature, so that, according to the Apostle, he might restore the things in heaven and those on earth: that is, the angelic fall and the human fall.

For they say that there are only three rational natures: divine, angelic, and human. If Christ was not made before John according to the divine nature, nor according to the human nature, it follows that Christ was made before John according to the angelic nature, since he was created with the world at the beginning of time. For these three are coeval: angel, world, and time. They are wholly in error, not understanding Scripture or the power of God. Since an angel is not immeasurable, he plainly does not exist everywhere, and therefore is not simultaneously in heaven and on earth. Hence he of whom the narrative speaks said: “No one has ascended into [Col. 0344D] heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). He is not an angel but God, who says of himself: “I fill heaven and earth” (Isa. 23); and who says to the Father of himself: “Glorify me, Father, in your presence with the glory which I had before the world was made” (John 17). For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

Therefore, just as the Word was made flesh, yet was not simply made, so Christ was made before John, yet was not simply made: he was set above John. For this adverb “before” does not signify priority in time but preeminence in dignity, as John himself explains: “He has been made before me,” he says, “because he was prior to me.” For one explanation is the explanation of the other, [Col. 0345A] as he shows more plainly when he adds: “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.”

The humility of the Forerunner and the sublimity of the Redeemer are plainly weighed from this passage. For although John was considered so great that many thought him to be the Christ, he nevertheless regarded himself as so small that he judged himself unworthy even to loosen the strap of His sandals. Yet certainly, “he who humbles himself shall be exalted, and he who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 18);—“for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4). For every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low. “The Lord is exalted and looks upon the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137 [138]).

Indeed, just as there are three persons in one substance—namely, Father, Word, and Holy Spirit—so there are three substances in one person—namely, divinity, body, and soul—mystically signified by the foot, the shoe, and the boot. For just as the shoe covers the foot and the boot, so the flesh covers divinity and soul. And just as the foot is joined to the shoe through the boot, so divinity is joined to flesh through the soul. The soul mediates between divinity and flesh not only by union but also by nature. For divinity is altogether simple, since it lacks both composition of parts and the aggregation of properties. The body, however, is wholly composite, since it has composition of parts and aggregation of properties; while the soul is partly simple, because, like divinity, it lacks composition of parts, and partly composite, because, like the body, it has an aggregation of properties. Concerning this shoe the Lord says through the Psalmist: “Over Idumea I shall stretch out my shoe” (Ps. 59 [60]), that is, “I shall reveal my incarnation to the Gentiles.”

But since this shoe has different straps, because in Christ there are different unions—namely, the union of Divinity with the soul, the union of Divinity with the flesh, and the union of flesh with the soul—why does John mention only one strap and not several? Without prejudice to the majesty of faith, it may plausibly be answered thus: since this shoe is the assumed body, and there are two unions of the body—one by which the body is joined to the soul, the other by which the body is joined to Divinity—only that union which joins the body to Divinity in unity of person is inscrutable. Therefore John declares himself unworthy to loosen only one strap of the shoe.

But let us cease to search out that inquiry in which many have failed; for “man approaches a lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63 [64]); and the investigator of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. Let us humbly beseech the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, that through the merit of faith He may transfer us to the reward of hope—He who with the Father, etc.

## SERMON VIII. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

[Col. 0345]

[Col. 0345C] “On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus too and His disciples were invited to the wedding” (John 2).

“Because it is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6), let us pass over the carnal wedding and discourse upon the spiritual one, so that through things done carnally we may show what ought to be done spiritually. These weddings, then, are celebrated between the human spirit and the grace of the Creator, whenever divine grace is joined to the rational spirit. And lest they be cursed by God as barren, they beget sons and daughters from themselves—that is, affections and actions, or holy desires and righteous works. Concerning wife and offspring together the Psalmist says to the husband and father: “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house. Your children like young olive plants around your table” (Ps. 127 [128]).

He had experienced these weddings who said: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace in me was not empty, but the grace of God always remains in me” (1 Cor. 15). Thus three goods of marriage are found between spirit and grace: faith, offspring, and sacrament. When you hear, “By the grace of God I am what I am,” understand faith, which pertains to uprightness. When you hear, “His grace in me was not empty,” understand offspring, which pertains to fruitfulness. “His grace remains in me”: understand sacrament, which pertains to permanence.

Among sons and daughters, as among brothers and sisters, that wedding-feast is celebrated which blessed Job was accustomed, in a moral sense, to celebrate individually among brothers and daughters (Job 1). Hence these weddings are said to have taken place in Cana of Galilee, because there, through zeal of charity and love of salvation, a person is converted and passes from error to charity and from vices to virtues. For *Cana* means “zeal,” and *Galilee* “passing over” or “migration,” translated from Hebrew into Latin. These weddings are fittingly said to have occurred on the third day, because the first day was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third after the Law. The first was knowledge of virtue under the law of nature; the second, under the law of Scripture; the third, under the law of grace. “For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

Therefore, on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. And the mother of Jesus was there. He Himself and His disciples were invited to the wedding. In this passage Jesus is morally understood as the divine Word, because “He was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). His disciples signify upright manners, because the divine Word instructs and forms them as a teacher. The mother of Jesus signifies the Catholic faith, from which the divine Word is born and proceeds. These are the persons said to have attended this wedding: the divine Word as teacher; upright manners as disciples; and Catholic faith as mother. The bride, for her part, invites to the wedding the graced virtues; the bridegroom, the natural affections.

Not only these persons, however, but also the steward of the feast is said to have been present. In this marriage there is a dining-hall—that is, three tables: the rational power of the natural soul, the irascible power, and the concupiscible power. [Col. 0347B] The first distinguishes good; the second rejects evil; the third desires good. These are the three gifts which natural philosophers morally offered to Christ (Matt. 2): gold, which because of its brightness signifies rationality; incense, which because of its honor signifies the concupiscible faculty; and myrrh, which because of its bitterness represents the irascible faculty. In this dining-hall the higher part of reason, properly called *synderesis*, presides as steward.

When the wine failed at this feast, the mother of Jesus said to Him: “They have no wine.” And He answered: “What is there between you and Me, woman? My hour has not yet come.” Wine in this place, because of its warmth, signifies charity; concerning it the bride says in the Song of Songs: “He brought me into the wine-cellar and ordered charity within me” (Song 2). Wine abounds at the beginning of the wedding, because charity burns fervently at the beginning of conversion. But this wine sometimes fails, because charity sometimes grows cold. This occasionally happens by divine dispensation, so that the alternation of the coming and departing Spirit may be shown—the Spirit who “blows where He wills, and you hear His voice, but you do not know where He comes from or where He goes” (John 3). Or it happens because “the righteous man falls seven times a day and rises stronger” (Prov. 24). Hence the Lord permitted Peter to fall, in order that he might rise stronger and cleanse his threefold denial by confession (Matt. 26).

When the wine fails, the mother of Jesus says to Him: “They have no wine,” because when charity grows cold, faith suggests and urges that the divine Word, by instruction and exhortation, should kindle charity.

And Jesus says to her: “What is there between you and Me, woman? My hour has not yet come.” This word does not proceed from indignation but from discernment. It is as though He said more plainly: Charity, having relaxed, ought for a time to grow lukewarm for the aforesaid reasons, so that when the appropriate time comes it may return more strongly. For a word spoken at its proper time is like apples of gold on beds of silver.

Then the mother of Jesus said to the servants: “Whatever He tells you, do.” For faith commands that whatever the divine Word commands should be done.

Now there stood there six stone water-jars, according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. [Col. 0348A] The six water-jars are the six works which the Lord will commend at the judgment: “I was hungry and you gave Me food; I was thirsty and you gave Me drink; I was a stranger and you took Me in; I was naked and you clothed Me; I was sick and you visited Me; I was in prison and you came to Me” (Matt. 25). They are called stone jars not because of hardness, since works of mercy are not hard, but because of firmness, since mercy is by its origin an unassailable sacrament [the text reads *periculum*]. Scripture says that it “will fight over the shield of the mighty and the spear against Nineveh” (Ecclus. 29). It belongs to those stones of which the Apostle says: “Another builds upon it silver, gold, and precious stones” (1 Cor. 3).

Hence the six jars are fittingly said to have been placed there for the purification of the Jews, because purification signifies the satisfaction of those who trust. For “Jews” is interpreted as “those who trust,” and those who trust must make satisfaction for sins through the six works of mercy. Each of these six jars holds two or three measures, because the six works of mercy admit some of two and some of three distinctions.

For food or drink is threefold: material, sacramental, and doctrinal. Of material food the Apostle says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; and if he thirsts, give him drink” (Prov. 25; Rom. 12). Of sacramental food Truth says: “My flesh is truly food, and My blood is truly drink” (John 6). Of doctrinal food Wisdom declares: “He fed him with the bread of life and understanding, and gave him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15). Therefore we ought to feed the hungry in three ways, and in the same three ways give drink to the thirsty: with nourishment for nature, the sacrament of the Eucharist, and the teaching of Scripture.

Sickness is twofold, namely of heart and body: the one is punishment, the other fault. Of the first the Lord says: “This sickness is not unto death” (John 11); of the second the Apostle says: “Therefore many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11). We visit one sick in body when we correct him in a spirit of gentleness. Likewise, we must visit the imprisoned in two ways, because prison is twofold: one of the body, the other of the heart. Of bodily prison the Evangelist testifies that Herod bound John and put him in prison (Mark 6). Of the prison of the heart the Psalmist says: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141 [142]). You may find similar distinctions in the Scriptures concerning hospitality and nakedness.

The jars hold two or three measures; but the jar is filled with water when mercy is brought to completion: when food is given to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, or clothing to the naked. Concerning this water, according to its effect, Scripture says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Ecclus. 3). Hence the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). But the jar is filled to the brim when a work of mercy is brought to perfection.

Certainly, when mercy is bestowed without charity, it refreshes the recipient but does not benefit [variant: “satisfy”] the giver. Thus it is only water and not wine; for, as the Apostle says, “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). But when mercy is shown out of charity, water becomes wine, because the performance of mercy becomes the working of charity. What was formerly rigid becomes warm; what was formerly lukewarm becomes flavorful; what was formerly pale becomes bright. Thus, morally, water becomes wine. A body naturally disposed to piety becomes meritorious through charity—not so much of eternal wages as of eternal recompense.

The servants, then, who fill the jars with water are liberality and cheerfulness, which administer works of mercy. Of them the Apostle says: “Each one as he has purposed in his heart, not from sadness or necessity. God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). And again: “He who presides, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (Rom. 12). Another says: “Do not delay to do good, because hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13). And again: “Do not afflict the heart of the poor, and do not delay a gift to one in distress” (Ecclus. 4). Therefore Jesus says to them: “Fill the jars with water.”

And when they had filled them, He added: “Draw out now, and carry it to the steward.” When the steward tasted the water made wine, he did not know where it came from; but the servants knew, [Col. 0349C] who had drawn the water. The steward calls the bridegroom and says to him: “Every man sets out the good wine first,” etc.

Then what has been said takes place. The servants are commanded to draw and carry it to the steward, so that he may reasonably approve and commend the fervor of charity. For rational charity does not itself comprehend the source of the charity which God alone works in a human being. Charity does not arise from free choice, as the natural philosopher says, but from God alone, as the faithful Catholic professes. Therefore the steward, as one less understanding the sacrament of grace, says to the bridegroom: “Every man sets out the good wine first. He ought to set out better wine at the end” [the text reads *in principio*, “at the beginning”]; for “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). Yet this may be specially applied to heretics and hypocrites, who display sound doctrine and good works at the beginning; and when people have become drunk—that is, enticed by them—they then put forward what is worse: the poison of error and the leaven of malice.

Let the merely natural person do this. But you, who are spiritual, have kept the good wine until now—that is, you have preserved the fervor of charity; for the more the debt of charity is discharged, the more it is owed. This, then, is the beginning of the signs which Jesus performed in Cana of Galilee, because among works of grace the conversion of the sinner holds first place. Then water becomes wine, because the sinner becomes righteous: as one cold becomes warm, one tasteless wise, one pale ruddy.

It should be known that in these weddings the bridegroom is the Holy Spirit, the bride grace. Jesus is the divine Word, and His disciples are upright manners; the mother of Jesus is Catholic faith; the steward who presides in the dining-hall is the rational faculty, which pre-eminent among the natural powers of the soul. Cana of Galilee is the conversion of the sinner; the third day, the time of grace; water, mercy; wine, charity. Wine fails when charity grows cold (Matt. 24). The six jars are the six works Christ will commend at judgment. They are called stone not because of inflexible hardness, but because of invincible firmness. Each jar holds two or three measures, because each work admits two or three distinctions. The servants are liberality and cheerfulness, which administer works of mercy. Water becomes wine when the effect of mercy is formed by the affection of charity. The steward approves the wine when reason commends charity; nevertheless, he does not know its source, because reason by itself does not know the originating cause of true charity as fully as the servants who draw it, because through their drawing of grace they understand the truth.

But the merely natural person—that is, the heretic or hypocrite—first brings good wine, that is, displays sound doctrine or an upright life, so that once people, enticed by him, have become drunk, he may then add what is worse: the poison of error or the leaven of malice. This, therefore, is the beginning of the signs which Jesus performs in Cana of Galilee, when He justifies the ungodly, converts the unrighteous, and calls back the sinner. And therefore His disciples believe in Him.

For celebrating these weddings, we have beneficially established today’s station at Holy Spirit, in which, as in Cana of Galilee—that is, in the place where there is zeal to pass from vices to virtues—six jars have been placed: namely, the six works of mercy have been established. They are: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, receiving the stranger, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and going to the imprisoned. The mother of Jesus is there, because there the memory of Christ’s most glorious mother is commemorated, in whose honor that church itself is dedicated. Her Son Jesus too, with His disciples, is invited to these saving weddings, because today an image of Jesus Christ is reverently carried by the ministers of the Church to this place, so that His glory may be admired with longing by the faithful people who assemble to celebrate these weddings of piety and mercy.

Therefore, lest anyone return hungry from these weddings, for all who gather in this temptation and henceforth show themselves more generously and cheerfully in celebrating them, one year shall be remitted from the imposed penances, for the fuller obtaining of pardon for sins, so that Christ the bridegroom may thus turn water into wine—He who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. SEPTUAGESIMA SUNDAY  
### On the Heavy Yoke upon the Children of Adam, in Entrance, Progress, and Departure; and on Honorable and Useful Occupation

[Col. 0351]

[Col. 0351A] “Great occupation has been created for all human beings, and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40).

The mother of all human beings is the earth, and that same earth is the burial-place of all human beings. For this reason Job said: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, naked I shall return there” (Job 1). In the words set before us, concerning the state of the human condition, we must chiefly consider three things: entrance, progress, and departure. Concerning progress it is first said: “Great occupation has been created for all human beings”; concerning entrance it is added: “From the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb”; concerning departure it is concluded: “Until the day of burial in the mother of all.” In each state we must consider what is inserted: “And a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam.” It is heavy indeed at entrance, heavier in progress, heaviest at departure.

Thus the prophet rightly wept and said: “Why did I come forth from my mother’s womb, to see labor and sorrow, and for my days to be consumed in shame?” (Jer. 20). For man is formed from earth, conceived in fault, and born for punishment. He does wicked things that are not permitted; shameful things that are not fitting; vain things that are not expedient. He will become food for fire, nourishment for the worm, a mass of rottenness. Behold how heavy a yoke has been created for the children of Adam, from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all.

I shall explain it more plainly and set it forth more fully, showing what man is made from, what man does, and what man will become. Man is formed from dust, mud, and ashes; and, what is more lowly, conceived from most foul seed, in the itching of flesh, the heat of lust, and the stench of wantonness; and, what is worse, in the stain of sin. He is born to labor, fear, and pain; and, what is more miserable, to death. He does wicked things by which he offends God, offends his neighbor, and offends himself. He does shameful things by which he defiles his reputation, his person, and his conscience. He does vain things by which he neglects serious, useful, and necessary things. He will become food for fire, ever burning and unquenchable; nourishment for the worm, ever gnawing and consuming, yet immortal; a mass of rottenness, ever horribly stinking and foul.

If you do not believe me, believe Scripture. “The Lord God,” it says, “formed man from the mud of the earth” (Gen. 3). Hence he says to God: “Remember, I pray, that You made me like clay, and that You will reduce me to dust.” [Col. 0352A] And God says to him: “You are ashes, and to ashes you shall return.”—“I have been compared,” he says, “to mud, and made like ashes and cinders” (Job 30). You have heard what man was formed from; now hear from what he was conceived. “Who,” it says, “can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50 [51]). No one is clean from the filth of sin, not even an infant of one day born upon earth. Hear, then, for what man was born: “The bird is born to flight, and man is born to labor” (Job 5).

“All his days are full of labor and miseries; nor does his mind rest by night. A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14). Such, therefore, man has been made.

But hear what man does: “They glory when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things” (Prov. 2). Therefore God delivered them “to a reprobate mind, to do things unfitting,” things that are not expedient, “filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness, and the other vices and sins” (Rom. 1; the text cites Rom. 2), which Paul enumerates to the Romans. “And when God saw that human wickedness was great upon the earth, and that every thought of the heart was bent upon evil at all times, He repented that He had made man on earth and was touched inwardly with sorrow of heart. ‘I shall destroy,’ He said, ‘the man whom I created’” (Gen. 6). Behold what man has done.

But hear what will happen to him: “His spirit will go forth,” it says, “and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145 [146]).—“You will take away their spirit and they shall fail, and they shall return to their dust” (Ps. 103 [104]).—“He is to be consumed like rottenness, and like a garment eaten by moths” (Job 13).—“Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job 25): the punishment of the wicked person’s flesh is worm and fire. “Their worm,” it says, “shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66). And “the Lord God will give fire and worms into their flesh, that they may burn and feel pain forever” (Judith 16). Truly, therefore, great occupation has been created for all human beings, and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam.

Yet blessed are those occupied with good things, because from good things they shall pass to the best. Miserable are those occupied with evil things, because [Col. 0353A] from evil things they shall pass to the worst. Blessed also are those who bear Christ’s yoke, which is heavy at the beginning but always sweet at the end. Miserable, however, are those who bear the devil’s yoke, which is sweet at the beginning but always heavy at the end.

The Church considers and laments this misery of the human condition. At the Introit she groans and weeps with the prophet, mourning and recalling the human fall: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell encompassed me” (Ps. 114 [116]). Yet lest she despair through excessive sorrow, she immediately recalls the Creator’s mercy in the Gradual: “A helper in due times, in tribulation: let those who know Your name hope in You, because You have not abandoned those who seek You, O Lord” (Ps. 9).

[Col. 0353B] The Lord indicates honorable and useful occupation in the Gospel, by hiring laborers for the vineyard in order to pay them wages (Matt. 20); [Col. 0354A] and the Apostle teaches us in the Epistle to avoid dishonorable and useless occupation: “Do you not know,” he says, “that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. But I run thus, not as toward an uncertainty; I fight thus, not as beating the air,” etc. (1 Cor. 9).

The Prophet distinguishes between yoke and yoke in the Tract: “Out of the depths I have cried to You, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice. If You should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129 [130]). Behold the heavy yoke of the devil, of which it is said through the prophet: “The yoke rotted away because of the oil.” He immediately adds: “Because with You there is propitiation, and because of Your law I have endured You, O Lord” (Isa. 10). Behold Christ’s sweet yoke, of which Truth says: “My yoke is sweet, and My burden light” (Matt. 11).

## SERMON X. ON THE SAME SUNDAY

[Col. 0353]

[Col. 0353B] “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20).

This parable, dearest brothers, is full not of terror but of mercy; not of despair but of confidence; not of bitterness but of sweetness; not of wrath but of grace; not of hatred but of love. For although many are called but few chosen, nevertheless the last were first. Let no one, then, despair because he has sinned long and greatly. Merciful God, because He wills no one of any age to perish, leads some to His worship by calling them to the vineyard: some in childhood, some in adolescence, some in youth, some in old age, and some in extreme old age. To these He will render, in common, an everlasting reward in return for temporal merit.

To recall sinners from vices to virtues more effectively, He often rewards equally those who come later, so that those converted in old age or extreme old age are called to glory earlier than those converted in childhood. Since they love equally, they deserve equally, even though they labor less; for the power of meriting lies not in labor but in charity.

The householder in this passage signifies God the Father; the vineyard, the Church; the laborers, the righteous. The agreement with the laborers concerning a daily denarius signifies the promise made to the righteous of everlasting reward. The five hours signify the five ages: morning, childhood; the third hour, adolescence; the sixth, youth; the ninth, old age; the eleventh, extreme old age; and evening is the end of life. The marketplace is the world; the idle are the negligent; the burden and heat are labor and care; the steward of the vineyard is the man Christ Jesus.

These human ages are fittingly distinguished by these hours of the day. The sun is warm from early morning until the third hour; hot from the third until the sixth; burning from the sixth until the ninth; from then its heat diminishes from the ninth until the eleventh, and from the eleventh until evening, when the sun sets. So natural heat is warm in childhood, hot in adolescence, burning in youth, and thereafter diminishes into old age and extreme old age, until a person inclines toward death.

The householder, then, is God the Father, Creator of every creature, who orders and governs His creatures in His house. He went out early in the morning to hire laborers for His vineyard when, in the first age, He pours the dew of His grace into a child and he works faithfully in His Church. For the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel; in this vineyard Christ is the vine and believers are the branches. “Just as a branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can believers unless they remain in Christ. But he who remains in Him bears much fruit, because without Him he can do nothing. If anyone does not remain in Him, he shall be cast out like a branch and wither; and they shall gather him, cast him into the fire, and he burns” (John 15).

But going out about the third hour, He saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: “Go also into My vineyard, and I shall give you whatever is just.” For God will give His faithful not only what is just, but bestows even more than what is just; because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). He always rewards beyond merit and punishes less than merits deserve.

Of the first, however, it is not said that they were idle, because before childhood there is no time for merit; hence nothing is imputed to an infant for merit. But of the others it is said that they stood idle, because in the other ages negligence is imputed as fault. Idleness is an enemy of virtues and a friend of vices. Thus David, who was always victorious in war, was eventually defeated in idleness, committing both adultery and murder. Because idleness is more condemnable in one worn out by age than in others, since he is closer to death, it is accordingly added with a certain emphasis at the eleventh hour: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” “Because no one has hired us.”

Certainly, no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him, because it is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Yet such persons are not to be despaired of, because He says to them: “Go also into My vineyard.” For “at whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, I shall remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18). And elsewhere He says: “Whether he comes in the first, second, or third watch and finds them thus, blessed are those servants” (Luke 12).

When evening had come, the Lord of the vineyard said to His steward. Evening is the end of life; the steward of the vineyard is the man Christ Jesus, to whom God the Father entrusted the Church for governance. Therefore the Lord says to Him: “Call the laborers and give them their wages,” because the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5), who after death will render to each according to his works, beginning with the last and proceeding to the first. To call laborers to their wages is to receive the righteous into rest.

The thief hanging on the cross came late and labored little, but quickly received much. When he said, “Remember me, Lord, when You come into Your kingdom,” he immediately heard: “Today you shall be with Me in paradise” (Luke 23). Because analogies are adapted to what happens more frequently, it is said that He begins with the last and proceeds to the first. For when adolescents and elders, or young persons and those extremely old, turn to the Lord, the elderly are admitted to the reward before either the extremely old or the young, because according to the course of nature these die sooner than those.

When those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, they received a denarius each. The denarius, which is worth ten ordinary coins, signifies here the everlasting reward rendered for temporal observance of the Decalogue of the Law. Or because the denarius bears the image of the king, everlasting glory is compared to a denarius, in which they shall see their King no longer through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face as He is (1 Cor. 13). We shall be like Him, transformed into the likeness of His image (1 John 3), because “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). Accordingly the Apostle says: “We await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humility, made conformable to the body of His charity” (Phil. 3).

But when the first came, they supposed that they would receive more. Yet they too received a denarius each. And, receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: “These last have worked one hour, and You have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day.” The burden of labor and heat of the flesh are borne especially and principally by adolescents and young people. They bear the burden and heat of the day who are weighed down and burned in this life for God, as the Apostle said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11; the text cites 2 Cor. 2).

But one who does not labor in the Church according to the divine will, and instead wanders about in the world according to the desire of the flesh, is not a laborer in the vineyard but idle in the marketplace. Many questions are customarily raised at this point. How can it be true that those receiving the denarius murmured against the householder, when those receiving the denarius signify the blessed, who receive rest in return for labor, from whom every murmuring has been banished—especially murmuring against God, in whose praises they unceasingly persist? As it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in Your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise You” (Ps. 83 [84]). Nor are such people moved by envy toward their neighbors.

And how did they suppose that they would receive more, when no one is deceived in the first [perhaps *patria*, “the heavenly homeland”], since blessed is he to whom all desired things succeed? Further, how can any blessed person’s eye be evil, when in the heavenly homeland there is no crookedness but most perfect rectitude? And the Apostle says: “Each shall receive wages according to his labor” (Rom. 2). How will he not receive more who labors more? For it is written: “God will render a reward for the labors of His saints.”

One who knows how to distinguish the diverse modes of speaking in Scripture is easily freed from these difficulties of questions.
