This passage is understood hypothetically, as though it said more plainly: Suppose that those receiving the denarius wished to murmur against the householder, saying, “These last have worked one hour, and You have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day.” Certainly the householder could justly repress their murmuring thus: “Friend, I do you no wrong. Did I not agree with you for a denarius? Take what is yours and go.” As though he said: Receive your reward and ascend to heaven as one rewarded, because you will have no just ground for murmuring against Me, since I pay you the wage due to you.

“I wish to give to this last man as I give to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” As though he said: “Am I not permitted, out of goodness, to supply to this man what is less due to him from his labor?” For in granting an equal reward to two who have labored unequally but loved equally, the effect of holiness rather than of equity is more clearly displayed toward the one. But from the fact that many murmured, he gives the moral instruction that, when a multitude sins, correction ought not to be begun with all at once, but separately with one; although it is impossible that one receiving the denarius of eternal reward [Col. 0357A] should murmur against the Lord, or that his eye should be evil. Yet just as, in a lawful power, an impossibility is set aside for the sake of making an arrangement, so here an impossibility is posited for a similar reason, in order to show what a just answer might be.

It is therefore clear that thus the last shall be first and the first last, so that no one at all may despair either because of the length of time of sin, as though habit could not be changed; for God calls to repentance, conversion, and amendment not only children, adolescents, and young men, but also old and decrepit persons; or because of the greatness of sins, as though the ungodly person could not make worthy satisfaction for sins, since God richly rewards even those who labor little. Nor should this [Col. 0357B] excessively discourage anyone: “Many are called, but few chosen,” because within this small number there is a great multitude; for as many human beings are to be saved as there were angels. As it is written: “You have established the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.” Yet they are called few in comparison with the wicked, because “the number of fools is infinite” [Col. 0358A] (Eccles. 1), “and the perverse are difficult to correct.”

Although, from the preceding statement that the first shall thus be last and the last first, it seems immediately to follow that many are called—those of whom it is said, “Call the laborers and pay them their wages”—and then the elect are meant, of whom it is added that, receiving the denarius of heavenly blessedness, they can be understood only as the blessed, who are universally elect. To that complete proposition this conclusion must be added: that the sound of evangelical preaching “has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18), but not all believe Christ’s Gospel. But one who does not believe is already judged. Therefore, since unbelievers are more numerous than believers, without doubt many are called and few chosen—especially since many even among the faithful are damned, [Col. 0358B] namely those who deny the faith by their works; because “it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2).

May Jesus Christ, the steward of the vineyard, exclude us from their number—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON ASH DAY, OR THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

On the dignity and usefulness of fasting; the three solemn fasts, namely those of the Ember Days, Lent, and vigils; and the manner of fasting, the ointment of prayer, and the bestowal of alms.

[Col. 0357]

[Col. 0357C] “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. 6).

The dignity of fasting is commended in many ways: by place, time, and author. For fasting was commanded by God, commanded to Adam, commanded at the beginning, commanded in Paradise: “From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Therefore the first command which God gave to man concerned abstinence from foods. So long as man kept it, he remained steadfast in faithfulness; but when he transgressed it, he fell mortally. From its opposite, therefore, one may understand how good fasting is. “Every soul which does not humble itself on the day of fasting shall be cut off from its people” (Lev. 22).

[Col. 0357D] Thus the usefulness of fasting is assigned in many ways. For fasting is read to have availed for appeasing God’s wrath and obtaining pardon; for avoiding punishment and uprooting wickedness; for preserving purity and repelling ignorance; for attaining victory and obtaining grace.

Fasting avails, then, to appease wrath, as Daniel prayed to the Lord in fasts, eating no desirable bread and tasting neither flesh nor wine: “Turn away, I beseech you,” he says, “your wrath from your city [Col. 0358C] Jerusalem and from your holy mountain. Be appeased, O Lord; attend and act; do not delay.” While he was still speaking, behold, the man Gabriel touched him at the hour of the evening sacrifice and announced that his prayers had been heard by the Lord (Dan. 9).

It also avails for obtaining pardon, as, at the preaching of the prophet, the men of Nineveh proclaimed a fast: “Men and beasts, oxen and sheep, and cattle tasted nothing or drank. And God saw their works, that they had quickly turned from their evil way, and he had mercy concerning the evil which he had said that he would do to them” (Jon. 3).

It avails for avoiding punishment, as Esther (ch. 4), at Mordecai’s counsel, fasted for three days and three nights; and thereafter, entering before the [Col. 0358D] king, obtained the revocation of the sentence which Haman had pronounced against the Jews, that they should all perish.

It avails for uprooting wickedness, as Truth says in the Gospel: “This kind of demons is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17). For that lunatic man ground his teeth, foamed, and wasted away: he ground his teeth through anger, foamed through lust, and wasted away through sloth. Why? The spirit of anger, the spirit of lust, [Col. 0359A] and the spirit of sloth are driven out by prayer and fasting.

It avails for preserving purity, as Daniel and the three boys resolved not to be defiled by the king’s table or by the wine of his drinking, and asked the chief of the eunuchs that they might not be defiled. They ate vegetables and drank water, and their faces appeared more handsome (Dan. 1).

It avails for expelling ignorance, as Paul, at his conversion, for three days and three nights neither saw nor ate nor drank. During those three days he is believed to have learned the Gospel from the Holy Spirit (Acts 9). Hence he boasts that he was taught by God, *theodidactus*, saying: “I neither received it from a man nor through a man, nor did I learn it, [Col. 0359B] but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1).

It avails for attaining victory, as the other tribes, fighting against Benjamin because of the Levite’s wife, were defeated in battle a second time; until, after they had completed a fast, they prevailed and almost utterly destroyed that tribe (Judg. 20).

It avails for obtaining grace, as the Holy Spirit descended upon the fasting apostles on the day of Pentecost, Peter testifying: “These men are not drunk, since it is the third hour of the day” (Acts 2).

But because it would be lengthy to enumerate from the sacred Scriptures each virtue of fasting, let us especially consider this: by temporal fasting we merit the eternal banquet. Accordingly Truth says: “Blessed are you who hunger now, because you shall be filled” [Col. 0359C] (Acts 2). For we shall eat and drink at his table in his kingdom, if we fast from food in the body in such a way that we also fast from vices in the mind. Otherwise fasting has little value, as the Lord, reproaching the Jews, says: “When you fasted for seventy years, did you fast for me?” (Zech. 7). And elsewhere: “My soul has hated your new moons and your fast” (Luke 6). And again: “Behold, you fast for disputes and contentions, and strike wickedly with the fist, and exact payment from all your debtors,” etc. (Isa. 1).

Great and salutary fasting, therefore, is to turn aside from vices. Of this the Lord says through the prophet: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel 1); and elsewhere: “This is the fast which I have chosen: loose the bonds of wickedness, [Col. 0359D] untie the oppressive bundles,” etc. (Isa. 58). Thus the apostles fasted. Of them the Lord says: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them. But days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. 9).

There are three solemn fasts which the Church generally enjoins. The first is the observance of the Ember Days; the second, Lenten abstinence; the third, the vigil of feasts. Each was instituted at fixed times and on fixed days, for definite reasons and causes.

We ought carefully to investigate each of these, so that we may know in due order not only what is done, but how it is done and why [Col. 0360A] it is done. The first fast is that observed in the Ember Days. It takes place four times a year, in groups of three days, for three causes: to carry out a command, to erase sin, and to express a mystery.

This fast is observed to carry out a command, because the law commands—and this is read to have been observed before the law (Exod. 22)—that firstfruits from everything be paid to God. This command is extended also to time: just as there are four seasons of the year and three months in each season, so we fast four times in the year as firstfruits, and on each occasion for three days, to the glory of the Trinity. This fourfold fast had its beginning in the Old Testament, as is read [Col. 0360B] in the prophet: “The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become feast days for the house of Israel” (Zech. 8). But now fasting is more fittingly observed in March, June, September, and December. For in March the world was created and redeemed: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). In June the law was established, the sanctuary instituted, and the Savior’s forerunner born. In September expiation was made, propitiation obtained, and the Redeemer’s mother born. In December the temple was cleansed and dedicated, and the Creator’s only-begotten Son was born.

This fast is observed to erase sin, so that [Col. 0360C] as we sin in four ways under a threefold division, so we may fast four times under a threefold division.

In the first way, we sin against the Father, against the Son, and against the Holy Spirit. We sin against the Father through weakness and frailty; against the Son through ignorance and simplicity; against the Holy Spirit through hardness and malice. For power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and kindness to the Holy Spirit; and their opposites are weakness, ignorance, and malice. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever sins against the Father shall be forgiven; whoever sins against the Son shall be forgiven; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 22).

[Col. 0360D] In the second way, we sin by transgressing the law of nature, the law of Scripture, and the law of grace. This is the threefold silence of which we read: “While all things held deep silence, and night in its course was passing through the middle of its way, your almighty word, O Lord, came from heaven, from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). The first silence began when Cain killed Abel (Gen. 4); the second began when the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play (Exod. 33); the third will be, or perhaps already is, because iniquity has abounded and the charity of many has grown cold (Matt. 24).

In the third way, we sin in heart, in mouth, and in deed. These are the three dead persons whom [Col. 0361A] the Lord raised: in the house, at the gate, and in the tomb. Death in the house is sin in thought; death at the gate is sin in speech; death in the tomb is sin in action.

In the fourth way, sin is distinguished into original sin, venial sin, and mortal sin. These are the serpent, the woman, and the man. The serpent—that is, concupiscence—suggests originally; the woman—that is, sensuality—eats venially; the man—that is, reason—consents mortally. These are the four farthings, concerning the last of which the Lord says: “He shall not go out from here until he pays the last farthing” (Matt. 5), that is, until he pays in punishment what he committed in guilt.

This fast is observed to express a mystery, because, just as a number rises [Col. 0361B] from unity to unity if multiplication by three is performed four times, so the soul ascends from virtue to virtue if it performs a three-day fast four times. Let the first multiplication, then, be three times one: three. Let the second be three times three: nine. Let the third multiplication be three times nine: twenty-seven. Let the fourth be three times twenty-seven: eighty-one. Behold: through such multiplication, number rises from unity to unity, signifying that through such fasting the soul ascends “from virtue to virtue, until it sees the God of gods in Zion” (Ps. 38).

This multiplication is well suited to the soul because of its four states, to which these four multiplications correspond. The first is the state of creation; the second, the state of nourishment; the third, the state [Col. 0361C] of action; the fourth, the state of dissolution. The first multiplication, which flows from one into three, corresponds to the first state; for in the state of creation the soul receives both unity of essence and a threefold set of powers: the irascible power, the concupiscible power, and the rational power. The second multiplication, which rises from three to nine, corresponds to the second state; for in the state of nourishment the soul undertakes the office of governing the human body, which, according to its natural constitution, flows in and out through nine openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, one mouth, and two lower passages. The third multiplication, which rises from nine to twenty-seven, corresponds to the third state; [Col. 0361D] for in the state of action the soul performs visible and bodily actions, which are fittingly represented by twenty-seven, a solid number. It has three dimensions, after the likeness of a human being: length, breadth, and thickness. The fourth multiplication, which after eighty returns to unity, corresponds to the fourth state; for in the state of dissolution the soul, after the variety of this present life, returns to the purity of nature. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 6). By eighty, indeed, the limit of the present life is understood, as the Prophet says: “If in the strong, eighty years; and what is beyond them is labor and sorrow” (Ps. 89). Behold the reasons why we fast at the Ember Days.

[Col. 0362A] The second fast, which is observed in Lenten abstinence, is celebrated once a year, under the number forty, for three reasons: because of a threefold example, because of a divine command, and because of the mystery of the number.

We fast for forty days because Christ, Moses, and Elijah fasted for the same number: before the law, under the law, and after the law—that is, at the beginning of the law, in its middle, and at its end. Before the law, Moses fasted: about to receive the law, he went up the mountain and was there with the Lord forty days, neither eating bread nor drinking water (Exod. 36). Under the law, Elijah fasted: in the strength of the food of one loaf, he walked through the wilderness for forty days, as far as Mount Horeb, the mountain [Col. 0362B] of God (3 Kings 19). After the law, Christ fasted: immediately after baptism he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, and there he fasted forty days and forty nights; afterward he was hungry (Matt. 4). Perhaps for this reason Moses and Elijah appeared to the disciples in the Transfiguration, speaking with Christ (Matt. 17).

For the number forty is holy in the Scriptures (Gen. 7). In the flood, God poured out the waters of the abyss for forty days and forty nights (Num. 13). Moses’ messengers explored the land promised to Israel for forty days (Exod. 16). Israel was fed in the wilderness for forty years by the bread of angels. Jonah prophesied Nineveh’s overthrow within a period of forty days (Jon. 3). Christ too remained on earth for forty [Col. 0362C] days after the resurrection (Acts 1).

We fast at this time rather than another, so that just as an exemplar imitates its model, so the fasting of Christians may follow Christ’s fasting. And as at this time the limbs are loosened toward evil by an abundance of humors, so by abstinence from food may the limbs be restrained for good. And as at this time Adam descended into death through eating forbidden food, so may the Christian ascend to life through abstaining from lawful food, that we may suffer with the suffering Christ (2 Tim. 1). For if we wish to reign with him, we must also suffer with him. Although “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8), yet, purified through abstinence, [Col. 0362D] may we approach the Eucharist more purely; for “whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

We fast for forty days because of the command, since God commanded in the law that tithes be paid from all things, and this command is extended even to time. For the solar year has three hundred sixty-five days and a quarter; a tenth of these is thirty-six and a half days and a tenth part of a quarter. But so that the number of forty days may be completed, a tithe of the tithe is added, which the lesser Levites, by the command of the law, paid to the high priest (Exod. 22). The Church likewise, tithing the tithe of time to Christ—who is the high priest of future good things, a priest forever [Col. 0363A] according to the order of Melchizedek (Heb. 5; Ps. 109)—has taken from thirty-five days three days and a half as the tithe of the tithe, to complete the forty-day number. And because there remained to be tithed only one day and a quarter and the tenth part of a quarter, she therefore deferred the fast with Mass until the night of the holy Paschal Saturday, as is said in the Collect: “O God, who this most sacred night,” etc.

We also fast forty days because of the mystery. The number forty is abundant, and, when its proper divisors are added together, it rises to fifty. Its summed divisors are seven: twenty, ten, eight, five, four, two, and one, which added together make fifty. But fifty signifies rest and remission, because of the fiftieth Jubilee, in which debts were remitted and all things rested (Lev. 25). Therefore we fast for forty days, signifying by this that, just as the number forty reaches fifty by the sum of its parts, so the Lenten fast, with its parts gathered together, leads to eternal rest and remission.

[Col. 0363B] For there are seven parts of spiritual fasting: namely, to abstain from the seven capital vices, from which, as from seven springs, the other vices arise. When these have been dried up by fasting, the remaining streams of vices are dried up. Behold the reasons why we fast in Lent.

The third fast, observed on the vigils of feasts, is enjoined for three reasons. But, to pass over them briefly, it is enough for the present to note this: God commanded in the law (Deut. 16) that at the chief solemnities all should go up to Jerusalem to pray, and should not appear empty before the Lord’s presence, but should offer. Therefore, when we go up at the chief solemnities to Jerusalem—that is, to the Church—to pray, we offer, lest we appear empty before the Lord’s presence; and besides other offerings, we also offer a fast of days.

[Col. 0363C] Thus the first fast is the fast of firstfruits; the second is the fast of tithes; the third is the fast of offerings. In the first fast we render to God the firstfruits of the months; in the second, we pay the tithe of the year; in the third, we give God the offerings of days. [Col. 0363D] Behold at what times, on what days, for what reasons, and for what causes we ought to fast.

But because God pays more attention to the manner in which a thing is done than to the thing done in whatever manner, and considers more how something is done than that it is done somehow, he himself teaches us how we ought to fast: “When you fast,” he says, “anoint your head and wash your face.” Anoint your head: that is, gladden your mind with the ointment of prayer. Wash your face: that is, cleanse your conscience with the water of compassion. Therefore, when you fast, pray and give alms at the same time.

There are especially three vices—vainglory, gluttony, and avarice—by which the first Adam was tempted and defeated; by these same vices the second Adam [Col. 0364A] was tempted and conquered. Opposed to them are the three principal virtues: prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. These are fittingly joined together, because fasting flies to God by these two virtues as by two wings. Hence, after Truth had first spoken in the Gospel of prayer and almsgiving, he immediately added teaching concerning fasting.

But we must take great care lest, perhaps, while we fast, we commit the three aforesaid vices under the pretext of fasting. Some fast from vainglory, some from gluttony (*gastrimargia*), some from avarice. The first are hypocrites, false while fasting; the second are gluttons, ravenous while fasting; the third are greedy, miserly while fasting. The first fast so that what they contain within may be concealed outwardly: outwardly they feign holiness, but inwardly preserve iniquity; unwilling to appear what they are, but wishing to appear what they are not. For they disfigure their faces so as to appear to men to be fasting. But amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.

[Col. 0364B] The second are gluttons, who fast in order to eat more: they eat less often in order to eat more greedily; not for need, but for excess; not to sustain nature, but to stir up appetite. “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them.” The third fast in order to place into avarice what they withdraw from pleasure: they empty the stomach in order to fill the purse; but they store up treasure and do not know for whom they gather it (Ps. 38). Of those who fast in this way it is written: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found,” etc. (Isa. 58).

But when you fast, anoint your head with the ointment [Col. 0364C] of prayer. For prayer is signified by ointment, according to this saying:

> Let not dying flies destroy for you the *figmata* [an uncertain reading, perhaps “fragrant ointments”].  
> Let the pot of your breast continually boil.

“Dying flies destroy the sweetness of ointment” (Eccles. 10): that is, intrusive thoughts take away the devotion of prayer.

This ointment is prepared from various spices: some pertaining to the substance of the things prayed for, others to the manner of those who pray. Seven spices pertain to the substance of the things prayed for. These are the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer, through which two chief things are sought: the attainment of goods and the removal of evils.

[Col. 0364D] Of goods, some are eternal and some temporal. Eternal goods are sought as reward; spiritual goods are sought for merit; temporal goods are sought for support. Of eternal goods it is said: “Let your kingdom come.” Of spiritual goods it is said: “Let your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” Of temporal goods it follows: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Of evils, some are past, some present, and some future. Past evils are to be grieved over; present ones are to be overcome; future ones are to be guarded against. Of past evils it is said: “Forgive us our debts.” Of future evils it is added: “Lead us not into temptation.” Of present evils it follows: “But deliver us from evil.” These are the things for which we ought to pray, but all for the sake of blessedness, as the Lord says: “Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full” [Col. 0365A] (John 16).

Therefore, seven other spices must be mixed with these seven: the seven beatitudes which Christ himself enumerates in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). These spices are crushed by the pestle of discernment in the mortar of memory, lest the ointment be made hard—that is, lest prayer become sin. For there are some who pray for something other than what they ought, and some who pray otherwise than they ought.

The mother of the sons of Zebedee prayed for something other than what she ought. At her sons’ prompting she came to Jesus, prayed, and asked: “Lord, say that these my two sons may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left in your kingdom.” Therefore the Lord answered them: “You do not know what you are asking” (Matt. 20).

The Pharisee prayed otherwise than he ought. Going up to the temple to pray, he prayed this within himself: “Lord, I thank you that I am not like other men: robbers, unjust persons, adulterers, or even like this publican. I fast twice on the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.” For this reason the Lord particularly declared: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Col. 0365B] (Luke 18).

Seven spices pertain to the manner of those who pray. These are the seven virtues: faith, hope, charity, justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Seven other spices must likewise be mixed with these. They are the seven gifts of sevenfold grace, which Isaiah enumerates, saying: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him; the Spirit of counsel and fortitude; the Spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 2).

[Col. 0365C] All these spices are seasoned with the balsam of devotion in the little vessel of wisdom, which is a most sweet fragrance to the Lord, through which worthy incense is offered as an odor of sweetness.

For there are many who pray much, but negligently and without devotion; and the Lord forbids this: “When you pray,” he says, “do not speak much, as the Gentiles do. For they think that they will be heard by their many words.” When such people pray, they speak one thing with their mouth and meditate on another in their heart. Of them the Lord fittingly says: “This people honors me with their lips, [Col. 0365D] but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). Of such persons it is said: “With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed.” They bless with their mouth because they speak the utterances of truth; but in their heart they curse because “they meditate vain things of vanity” (Ps. 61).

Moses and Susanna prayed otherwise: when they were troubled, they cried to the Lord, and he delivered them from their necessities. For they cried out not so much through the earnestness of their voice as through devotion of heart, as the Prophet says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 36). Yet it is fitting that utterance of the mouth accompany devotion of the heart. For what breath does to a coal, utterance does to devotion. Hear through the Prophet: “With my mouth I cried to him, and I exulted beneath my tongue” [Col. 0366A] (Ps. 95).

This ointment must be prepared in a certain secret chamber: that is, in the inner room of conscience. Accordingly the Lord says: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and when you have shut the door, pray to your Father.” The door must be shut lest dying flies enter and destroy the sweetness of the ointment (Eccles. 10). For “death enters through our windows” (Jer. 9). If we pray in this manner, we shall then obtain what the Lord says: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive” (Mark 11). And again: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name shall be done for you” (John 14).

Therefore, when you fast, anoint your head with the ointment of prayer. But also wash your face: wash it with the water of compassion. For almsgiving is signified by water, according to the saying: “As water [Col. 0366B] extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Eccles. 3). Hence *eleemosyna* [almsgiving] is said to derive not only from *elimino*, but from *heli*, meaning “God,” and *moys*, meaning “water.” Thus *eleemosyna*, as though *eleemosyna*, means “God’s water,” because through almsgiving the stains of sins are washed away by God.

This water is divided into three springs. The first flows from the heart, the second from the mouth, and the third from deed. For almsgiving is bestowed in three ways: from the heart through compassion; from the mouth through correction; from deed through generosity. Of compassion of heart the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 2). The sins of neighbors are frying-pans for the righteous. Of correction by the mouth the Lord says: [Col. 0366C] “If your brother sins against you, correct him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother” (Matt. 18). Of generosity in deed the prophet says: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring needy wanderers into your house” (Isa. 58).

Each spring is divided into two streams. The first runs toward ourselves, the second toward our neighbors. Almsgiving must be given in order: first to ourselves, then to our neighbors. For he is cruel and foolish who has compassion on another and does not pity himself; who corrects another and does not amend himself; who assists another and deceives himself. Conversely, Scripture teaches: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30)—“First cast the beam from your own eye, and then you shall take the mote from [Col. 0366D] your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7)—“When you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58).

If we give alms in this way, then indeed we shall merit what the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). Almsgiving indeed provides the greatest confidence before the Most High.

Therefore, beloved, when we fast, let us anoint our heads with the oil of devout prayer and wash our faces with the water of pious compassion, he mercifully granting it whose words are fragrant with the finest ointments, who is the fountain of life, of living water springing up into eternal life (John 4): the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE SAME ASH DAY

On the three bonds of wickedness—namely, those of heretics, sinners, and the damned; on the three cords of sinners by which clerics are for the most part held bound; and on the loosening of those who are bound.

[Col. 0367]

[Col. 0367A] “This is the greater fast which I have chosen: loose the bonds of wickedness; untie the oppressive bundles” (Isa. 58).

If we wish worthily to observe the observance of fasts, let us keep before all others this fast of which the Lord speaks through the prophet: “This is the greater fast which I have chosen: loose the bonds of wickedness,” etc.

We read in the Scriptures of three bonds of wickedness: those of heretics, sinners, and the damned. The bonds of heretics are false doctrines. The bonds of sinners are wicked deeds. The bonds of the damned are eternal punishments.

Of the bonds of heretics the harlot says in Proverbs: “I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread it with embroidered coverings from Egypt” [Col. 0367B] (Prov. 7). For the harlot—that is, heretical perversity—has woven her bed, that is, constructed her teaching, with cords: namely, subtle but twisted deceptions. Thus her correction is like a threefold cord, difficult to break, woven from theological authorities, rhetorical flowers, and dialectical arguments. She perverts sacred authorities, introduces sophistical arguments, and adorns rhetorical speeches. She deceives the simple, so as to entice the wavering and seduce the unsuspecting.

For of such people the Prophet says in the psalm: “For they have destroyed what you have made” (Ps. 10). Heretics destroy the testimonies of sacred Scripture which the Holy Spirit has made, when [Col. 0367C] they pervert them. Moreover, Scripture teaches us that one who speaks sophistically is hateful: “Grace has not been given to him by the Lord, but he has been deprived of all wisdom” (Ecclus. 37). For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1), especially that of those who hold the truth of God in falsehood. Their preaching is not in the manifestation of Spirit and power, but in persuasive words of human wisdom.

These are the tavern-keepers who, according to the prophet, mix water with wine; who serve dragon’s gall (Deut. 32) in Babylon’s golden cup; who travel over sea and land to make one proselyte (Matt. 22). These are the little foxes of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” [Col. 0367D] (Song 2). Samson tied their tails together, setting fire to them in order to burn the crops of the Philistines (Judg. 15). But behold, they now teach openly and preach freely, so that unless their bonds are quickly [Col. 0368A] dissolved, we must fear that not only the weak but even a sound part may be drawn away. Let us therefore loose the bonds of wickedness, because this is the greater fast which the Lord has chosen.

Of the bonds of sinners the prophet says: “Woe to those who draw sins as with a long rope!” (Isa. 5). This rope likewise is joined from three cords. Of these the apostle John says: “Whatever is in the world is either the concupiscence of the flesh, or the concupiscence of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John 2).

Desire of the flesh pertains to pleasures; desire of the eyes, to riches; pride of life, to honours. Pleasures make a man luxurious, riches avaricious, honours proud. By these three cords we clergy are especially bound. For the cord of lust, when sins demand it, holds us so fast bound that we are not ashamed publicly to keep little women in our houses—some of whom were recently shamefully seized and violently dragged away, severely whipped—to the great disgrace of the clergy and grave reproach of priests. Yet the prophet says to us: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). Indeed, in the old priesthood, after his hands and feet had been washed, the priest put on all the breeches (Exod. 19). Certainly, when David was fleeing Saul’s persecution, he came with his men to Nob, to Abimelech the priest, asking that five loaves be given him to drive away hunger. The priest answered him: “I have no common bread at hand, but only holy bread; let the young men eat it, provided that they are clean, especially from women” (1 Sam. 21). For none can worthily eat the holy bread unless they are clean from intercourse with women. Shameful to say, but most shameful to do: let it be said, that it may not be pleasing to do it. Some at night practise the son of Venus in their bedchamber; in the morning they offer the Son of the Virgin at the altar. At night they embrace Venus; in the morning they venerate the Virgin. But if it is true—indeed, because it is true—what the Apostle says: “Fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

Likewise, the cord of avarice, when sins demand it, holds us so bound that many of us are not ashamed to trade or afraid to practise usury. “From prophet even to priest, all pursue avarice; and from the greatest even to the least, all practise deceit” (Jer. 6). But the Lord, having made a whip, drove sellers and buyers from the Temple, poured out the coin of the merchants, and overturned the tables of the money-changers (John 2). For the avaricious priest serves not God but an idol. As the Apostle says: “Avarice is the service of idols” (Eph. 5). For it is written: “Nothing is more wicked than the avaricious man, and nothing more unjust than to love money” (Ecclus. 10), because “covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). From this root comes our indulgence of the sins of those subject to us, like “dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 50), lest they perhaps withdraw from us their offerings, tithes, and firstfruits. From this root comes our seduction of others’ parishioners and invasion of others’ parishes, putting the sickle into another’s harvest and passing beyond the boundaries established by our fathers, so that gain may increase for us from alms.

Likewise, the cord of pride, when sins demand it, holds us so bound that now we prefer to appear proud rather than humble: walking with neck outstretched, eyes raised, head held high; magnifying our fringes, broadening our phylacteries; seeking the first places at feasts, the chief seats in synagogues, and to be called rabbi by men (Matt. 23). Thus we now go forth so adorned that we seem more like bridegrooms than clerics. “Those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 2). But the righteous man chose to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83). The Apostle says, “Not in costly apparel” (1 Tim. 2). For “that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen was buried in hell” (Luke 16). So great is the pride of clerics that they can never humble themselves before their superiors in order to make satisfaction, not imitating him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11)—who “came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20)—but rather him who set his throne in the north in order to be like the Most High (Isa. 14), “who is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41).

These are the oppressive bundles of which, after the prophet had said, “Undo the bindings of impiety,” he immediately added: “Release the oppressive bundles.” For impiety is described as sitting upon a talent of lead. Therefore elsewhere it is read: “My iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37). For “when the wicked man has come into the depths of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18). Let us therefore undo the bindings of impiety, because this is the greater fast chosen by the Most High.

Concerning the bindings of the condemned, the Lord says in the Gospel: “First gather the tares, and bind them into bundles to be burned” (Matt. 13).

And this cord too is made up of three cords: the obscurity of darkness, the bitterness of punishments, and the duration of miseries.

For the fire of Gehenna will always burn and never give light; it will always scorch and never consume; it will always afflict and never cease. “Bind his hands and feet,” he says, “and cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22). “There will be the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched” (Isa. 66). “Let me go,” says Job, “that I may weep a little for my sorrow before I go to a dark land covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10). For the reprobate will endure such distress in their punishments that they will be able to think of nothing except punishments; rather, they will direct the force of their thought where they feel the power of pain. As Solomon says: “There is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in hell, whither you are hastening” (Eccles. 9). “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” Hear John saying in the Apocalypse: “In those days men will seek death and will not find it. They will desire to die, and death will flee from them” (Apoc. 9). “That day: a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and sounding” (Zeph. 1). Let us therefore undo the bindings of impiety, because this is the greater fast chosen by the Most High.

But since it does not suffice for physicians to recognize the cause of sickness unless they endeavour to bring the medicine of health, after showing the kinds of bindings, let us also state the ways of unbinding them. Let us undo the bindings of heretics by faithful teaching; the bindings of sinners by humble repentance;

[Col. 0370C] the bindings of the condemned by final perseverance. For the Apostle says to Timothy: “Give heed to yourself and to doctrine; persist in it. For in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you. For the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods which God created” (1 Tim. 4). The Apostle immediately teaches how this binding is to be undone, saying: “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected” (ibid.). For “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). Let us therefore undo the bindings of heretics through faithful teaching, because this is the greater fast chosen by the Lord.

Moreover, “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and not die, says the Lord. I do not will the death of the sinner, he says, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18). But a sin not undone through repentance immediately draws another after it by its own weight. Thus that cord is made, of which the prophet says: “Woe to those who draw sin as with a long rope!” (Isa. 5). Therefore the Apostle Peter says: “Repent therefore and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3). Let us then undo the bindings of sinners through humble repentance, because this is the greater fast chosen by the Most High. But since a dog returning to its vomit (2 Pet. 2) is a man returning to sin, if, according to the saying of Truth, “Your sins are forgiven you; go, and sin no more” (John 8), because “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). Hence Joseph is described as having had an ankle-length robe among his brothers (Gen. 37), and the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered upon the altar. Let us then undo the bindings of the condemned by final perseverance, through him who is God blessed above all for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. FIRST SUNDAY IN LENT

On the three who tempt—namely God, the devil, and man—and on the matters in which the devil tempted Christ; concerning which, however, he teaches that seven things must be observed; likewise, on the grounds for establishing the devil’s cunning, and on the causes of temptations.

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371B] Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit, that he might be tempted by the devil; and when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry (Matt. 4).

There are three who tempt: God, the devil, and man. But God always tempts toward good; the devil always tempts toward evil (Luke 4); man sometimes tempts toward good and sometimes toward evil. God always tempts toward good because he is always good. The devil always tempts toward evil because he is always evil. But man sometimes tempts toward good and sometimes toward evil, and so forth, because one man is good and another evil. “For God is not a tempter of evils. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. 1).

These three persons are immediately indicated at the beginning: [Col. 0371C] Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit, that he might be tempted by the devil. Jesus was led: behold the man. By the Spirit: behold God. That he might be tempted by the devil: behold the devil. For the divine Spirit led him there where the evil spirit was to tempt him. The divine Spirit led him to fast, but the evil spirit undertook to tempt him. God tempts in order to prove; the devil tempts in order to deceive; man tempts in order to investigate. Of the first it is said: “Prove me, O Lord, and test me” (Ps. 25); of the second we read: “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” (Acts 6); of the third it is written: “Test us, we pray, for ten days” (Dan. 1).

But the devil principally tempts through pleasures, [Col. 0371D] riches, and honours. “For whatever is in the world is either desire of the flesh, desire of the eyes, or pride of life” (1 John 2). Desire of the flesh pertains to pleasures; desire of the eyes, to riches; pride of life, to honours. In pleasures he tempts through gluttony and lust; in riches, through covetousness and avarice; in honours, through pride and boasting. In these three matters the devil tempted Jesus: namely in gluttony, avarice, and boasting. He tempted him in gluttony when he said, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves”; in boasting, when he said, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down”; [Col. 0372B] and in avarice, when he said, “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.”

Observe carefully the cunning of the tempter. For he tempts from different causes, in different places, and by different methods: in gluttony, boasting, and avarice; in the desert, the Temple, and the mountain; by suggestion, argument, and promise. By suggestion when he says: “Command these stones to become loaves”; by argument when he adds: “For it is written: He commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone” (Ps. 90); by promise when he says: “All these things I will give you”—so that the one whom he could not seduce by one cause he might seduce by another; the one whom he had not assailed in one place he might deceive in another; and the one whom he could not deceive by one method he might deceive by another. But he succeeded in no way, because Christ always repelled the tempter and utterly overcame him—not by the sublimity of his power, but by the authority of Scripture. In this he teaches and instructs us that whenever grave temptations arise against us, we should resort to the testimonies of Scripture, in which we find both a mirror at which to marvel and an example to imitate.

Moreover, concerning his temptation we should especially consider seven things, which the Evangelist teaches us to observe: the person, place, time, cause, manner, order, and, after all these, the end. The person who is tempted: Jesus was led by the Spirit that he might be tempted by the devil; [Col. 0372D] the place where he is tempted, because he was led into the desert; the time when he is tempted, because he had fasted forty days and forty nights; the cause for which he is tempted, because afterwards he was hungry; the manner in which he is tempted, because the tempter came and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves”; the order according to which he is tempted, because the devil took him into the holy city, setting him upon the pinnacle of the Temple, and again took him to a very high mountain, showing him all the kingdoms of the world; and the end for which he is tempted, because the devil left him and angels came to him and ministered to him.

[Col. 0373A] With regard to each of these, we must distinguish two things. With regard to the first, we must consider the person of the tempter and the person tempted, because Jesus was led by the Spirit that he might be tempted by the devil. Therefore Jesus is tempted, and the devil tempts. With regard to the second, we must note the solitary place and the frequented place, because in the desert he took him up onto a high mountain, and in the city he set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple. With regard to the third, we must consider the time after baptism and likewise the time after fasting. For after he had been baptized, then, as the Evangelist says, Jesus was led into the desert to be tempted, and he fasted forty days and forty nights. With regard to the fourth, we must note the cause of power, from which he fasted, and the cause [Col. 0373B] of weakness, from which he was hungry. With regard to the fifth, we must consider the method of temptation according to the condition of nature. For when Jesus was hungry, the devil suggested to him: “Command,” he said, “these stones to become loaves.” And according to the authority of Scripture, because when he suggested that he throw himself down, he added: “For it is written: He commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.” With regard to the sixth, we must note the order: after gluttony he tempted him in boasting, and after boasting he tempted him in avarice. For after he had taken him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down,” he again took [Col. 0373C] him to a very high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” With regard to the seventh, we must consider the departure of the evil spirit. For then the devil left him, and kindly spirits came, because angels came and ministered to him. Behold: although the text of the Gospel reading appears simple on the surface, beneath the wax lies honeycomb, beneath the bark the kernel, beneath the ear the wheat.

Let us therefore dig out the well, because it is deep (John 5), and draw water with joy from the fountains of the Saviour (Isa. 12). It was not just any tempter who tempted him, but the devil himself, who is shown to be cunning above all evil tempters by subtlety of nature, antiquity of time, and continual practice of deceiving. By subtlety of nature, as it is said to him: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). By antiquity of time, because he is the first creature—not because he preceded all things, but because none preceded him—as it is said: “How you have fallen, O Lucifer, who arose in the morning!” (Isa. 14). By continual practice of deceiving, because “your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about always seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). This tempter, therefore, so subtle, shrewd, and ancient, tempted not just any man, but Jesus himself, led by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil: not a sinner, but the Saviour, “who did no sin, [Col. 0374A] nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53; 1 Pet. 2). Let the sinner therefore beware, because the Saviour himself was tempted; nor should the righteous be altogether secure, because God himself was tempted. Yet no one should despair when he is tempted, because the Saviour himself was tempted for us, that by his temptation he might conquer ours—he who by his death destroyed ours.

He tempted him not in the marketplace but in the desert; not at the crossroads but in the Temple; not in a low valley but on a lofty mountain. The same one who tempted in paradise tempted in the wilderness. But in paradise he tempted the first Adam and overcame him (Gen. 3); in the wilderness he tempted the second Adam and was overcome. For “there is no power, no wisdom, no counsel against God” (Prov. 21). Therefore let not the monk be secure in the cloister, nor the hermit secure in solitude, because Adam was tempted in paradise and Jesus was tempted in the desert.

He tempted him also not after a feast but after a fast; not after sin but after baptism. For he presses, strives, and labours all the more to seduce great and small alike, righteous and ungodly alike, wise and foolish alike—so that in the seduction of the great the small too may be seduced; in the seduction of the righteous, the ungodly too; and in the seduction of the wise, the foolish too. For it is written: “He sleeps under shade and among reeds in damp places; he drinks up a river and is not amazed; for he is confident that the Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job 40). For when someone is converted from error to truth, [Col. 0374C] from vices to virtues, and from the devil to Christ, then he endures greater temptations against himself and graver persecutions within himself. Thus the Amalekites are read to have severely attacked the children of Israel in the wilderness after their departure from Egypt (Exod. 14). Therefore the Wise Man admonishes and exhorts: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your heart for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). Behold, it is doubtful whether anyone who has had no temptation here will be saved in the future—who knows? Thus from this evil temptation, or rather from the evil one of this temptation, no person is exempted, no place excluded, no time distinguished: everywhere deceit and snare, everywhere pitfall and trap.

[Col. 0374D] Truly, the life of man upon earth is temptation (Job 7). Is it not truly temptation, when manifold enemies everywhere continually lie in wait to seize, pursue to kill: devil and man, world and flesh—the devil with vices, man with beasts, the world with elements, the flesh with senses? Therefore the Apostle weeps and cries: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). And the Psalmist said: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name, O Lord” (Ps. 141). For the devil both takes up causes already found that are suitable for tempting and finds causes to be taken up. To tempt in gluttony, he took up a fitting cause already found: because after Jesus had fasted forty days and forty nights [Col. 0375A] and was afterwards hungry, the tempter approached him and said: “Command these stones to become loaves,” intending, if he could, to draw him into sin by an excessive eagerness for eating, as once Esau, unable to bear hunger, sold his birthright for a dish of lentils (Gen. 30).

Therefore, brothers and children, let us beware of the cunning of temptation, lest perhaps, when we fast, we be drawn into fault by excessive eagerness for eating. For sin is committed not only in various dishes and sumptuous foods, but also by anticipating the proper hour and by immoderate appetite. Thus he did not say, “Command these stones to become meat or fish,” lest perhaps the cunning of the tempter be more easily detected in luxurious and varied foods; but he said, “Command these stones to become loaves,” so that, if impatient of hunger, he changed stones [Col. 0375B] into loaves, an excessive eagerness for eating might be detected. Let those attend to this who, seeking varied flavours, transform substance into accident and nature into art, in order to arouse and revive appetite.

But to tempt in avarice, he found a fitting cause to take up: because the devil led him to a lofty mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” Observe carefully the snares of the enemy. In order to draw him to a fall, he took him up upon a lofty mountain, because the greater the eminence, the graver the ruin. And to arouse and invite desire of the eyes, he showed and promised all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. But after he had first tempted him and had not seduced him through a bodily vice—that is, gluttony—he again tempted him through a spiritual vice, that is, avarice. But the Lord set against the weakness of the flesh the strength of the mind, answering on the authority of Scripture that man does not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. And against covetousness and avarice, which according to the Apostle “is the service of idols” (Eph. 5), he set divine service, [Col. 0376A] answering on the authority of Scripture: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 7), that is, you shall render the service of worship to God alone.

To tempt him also in boasting, he took up a fitting cause and found a suitable place. For he took him into the holy city and set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple, saying: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” There are two things in which men are most accustomed to boast: rank and knowledge—teachers in knowledge, priests in rank. Therefore, intending to tempt him in boasting, he set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple, a place proper to teachers and priests. And because those who boast desire human praise and seek human favour, intending to tempt him in boasting, he took him not to a desert place but to the holy city, so that he might be praised by men with an applause of favour. In order to persuade more readily what he said, he produced prophetic testimony, but twisted it to a foreign meaning, so that the spirit of error might instruct heretical perversity.

Moreover, when he had tempted him from different causes, in different places, and by different methods, and had not succeeded, he departed in confusion. For the devil left him, and angels came and ministered to him. But what did the angels minister—food to one who was hungry? Yet whatever the angels ministered to him, we are morally instructed that, if we take care cautiously to repel the devil’s temptations, [Col. 0376C] angels will assuredly minister to us.

Let us therefore pray, brothers and children, to our Lord Jesus Christ that he who overcame the tempter’s wiles may himself deliver us from the tempter’s snares, and may not permit us to be led into temptation; but if at any time a human temptation should overtake us, may he not allow us to be tempted as far as consent (1 Cor. 10): he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE EMBER DAYS

The Transfiguration of Christ; what the three disciples signify; Christ’s garments; the manifold confirmation of the Transfiguration; and the differing fall of the good and the evil.

[Col. 0375]

[Col. 0375D] Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them apart up a high mountain; and he was transfigured before them (Matt. 17).

Because the Lord is faithful in his promise, he fulfilled what he promised. For he had promised the apostles, saying: “There are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matt. 26), that is, in that glory in which, when the judgment has been completed, he will appear in [Col. 0376D] the kingdom. And behold, he fulfilled the promise: after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, led them apart up a high mountain, and was transfigured before them. For there are six days in which a man must work; but on the seventh day God rested from all the work that he had accomplished (Gen. 2). This Transfiguration is therefore rightly related to have occurred after six days, because future glorification is promised in rest after labour, [Col. 0377A] as it were in the seventh after the sixth (Luke 13). For the same reason Luke appropriately says, “After eight days” (Luke 9), because this Transfiguration is promised for the future in the eighth age of resurrection. Yet even according to the letter there is no disagreement between Matthew and Mark, who teach that such a Transfiguration occurred after six days, and Luke, who says after eight: for the former mention only the intervening days, while the latter included both the first day before them and the final day completing the number.

In the Transfiguration, however, Jesus did not lose the substance of the flesh he had assumed, but displayed the glory of the future resurrection. But before all else one may ask what kind of vision it was: spiritual, or rather bodily. It seems in some respect to have been spiritual, because [Col. 0377B] the disciples were weighed down by sleep. But in sleep a true vision does not appear, only an imaginary one; and therefore that vision seems not bodily but spiritual. Furthermore, since Moses was truly dead (Num. 27; Deut. 32, 34), if he then appeared bodily, it seems that he either rose with a true body or died again; and thus he was punished contrary to justice, without fault—for every death is a punishment—or remained alive forever. In that case Christ, contrary to the word of the Apostle (1 Cor. 15; Col. 10), was not the firstfruits of those who sleep, because he did not rise first, immortal and impassible.

On the other hand, the vision seems to have been bodily, because Holy Scripture clearly distinguishes [Col. 0377C] spiritual vision from bodily vision. When the Gospel records a spiritual vision, it states that it took place in sleep or in ecstasy, as when the angel appeared to Joseph, saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matt. 1). It is expressly said that he appeared in a dream. When Peter saw heaven opened and a certain vessel, like a great sheet, descending from heaven to earth by its four corners, it is expressly said that “an ecstasy of mind fell upon him” (Acts 10). But when it records a bodily vision, it narrates an event, as when it says that an angel of the Lord stood beside the shepherds, the glory of God shone around them, and [Col. 0377D] they were greatly afraid (Luke 2); and where it says that the Magi, seeing the star in the East, came to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. 2). Moreover, unless this vision were true, it would without doubt not have been a true sign of future glorification, because truth is not rightly signified by falsehood. What then shall we say? Certainly that this vision was bodily: for just as he took bodily disciples and led them bodily to the mountain, so he was transfigured before them; and truly his face shone like the sun and his garments became white as snow. Although Peter and those with him were weighed down by sleep, they did not see this vision in sleep, because, as the same Evangelist testifies, when they awoke they saw [Col. 0378A] his majesty and the two men standing with him. Whether Moses assumed an aerial body, as angels do when they appear to men, or truly rose again, he undoubtedly returned whence he had come. And if it is said that he died, that death was not a punishment because he felt no pain from it. Just as after the resurrection, to instruct faith, he displayed signs of mortality even in an immortal body when he showed the opening of his side and the place of the nails, so, to establish faith before the resurrection, he showed signs of immortality in a mortal body: his face shone like the sun and his garments became white as snow.

But because what he showed was wondrous and astonishing, in order that it might be believed more firmly, he wished to establish it by manifold testimony: from heaven and earth, paradise and hell; from God and man; from the living and the dead; through those of former times and those present; through the Law and the Prophets. For Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him. And behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” The voice from the cloud bore testimony to the truth from heaven. The disciples upon the mountain were witnesses to the truth on earth. Moses came from hell, because Christ had not yet led his captives out of the pit in which there was no water (Zech. 9). Elijah came from paradise, where he is believed to remain with Enoch until the final tribulation to come through Antichrist.

[Col. 0378C] That voice proceeded from God the Father: “This is my beloved Son.” That word came forth from the man Peter: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” Elijah was living; Moses dead. The former was living but will die; the latter was dead but will live. Yet both were present: the one as lawgiver, the other as prophet, to bear wondrous testimony to a wondrous thing. Through them, as persons of former times, and through the apostles, as persons present, testimony is borne to the truth. For both those going before and those following cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21). Three apostles and two prophets were brought forward because, according to the divine Law, “every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 17).

[Col. 0378D] Delighted by the glory of the vision—or rather, by the vision of glory—Peter said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” But Peter, seeing glorified humanity, is filled with such joy that he never wishes to be separated from its sight. What then should be thought of those who behold the divinity that glorifies, and with what joy they always desire to cling to it? “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 63). But when he added, “If you wish, let us make here three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah,” he did not know, as another Evangelist says (Luke 9), what he was saying. For a tabernacle is not necessary where, according to the Apocalypse of John, “God Almighty is the Temple, and the Lamb” (Apoc. 21). And [Col. 0379A] he thought that the glory promised after the resurrection in heaven had been restored before the resurrection on earth; but terrified and astonished—or rather placed in ecstasy and carried away in transport—he did not know how to think of future things, because present things delighted him. Therefore he did not deserve to be reproved or even rebuked. But while he was still speaking, behold a bright cloud—not a dark one; for there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial (2 Cor. 6)—overshadowed them, to show that such a vision was not the reality of future glorification but its shadow, so that through the shadow one might come to the reality, as through an image to the thing itself, and through faith to the vision.

Moreover, why this miracle occurred and why this marvel was shown is revealed when it follows: [Col. 0379B] “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” As if he said more plainly: I, who had said, “I repent that I made man” (Gen. 6), now say: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Therefore this is the Son, not another; my Son, not my servant, not one belonging to another; beloved, not cursed; the one in whom I am well pleased, not displeased. Therefore listen to him; do not contradict him.

And hearing this, the disciples fell upon their faces and were very afraid. For the good fall upon their faces, but the evil backward. Of the good who fall it is said: “They fell upon their faces and worshipped the Lord” (Apoc. 4). But of the evil who fall we read: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18). These fall upon their faces through humility; those fall backward through turning away. These understand where they fall; those do not know where they fall. “Blessed, however, is he who is always fearful” (Prov. 28), because “the fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclus. 1). Hence the prophet says to the Lord: “Through fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26).

Therefore, hearing the testimony of the divinity and beholding the glory of majesty, the disciples fell and were afraid, because “man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63), and the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25). Hence the prophet says: “O Lord, I heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. 3); I considered your works and [Col. 0379D] was terrified. But they chiefly feared because Peter had, as it were, compared Jesus with Moses and Elijah by saying, “If you wish, let us make here three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah”; and then they heard the voice from the cloud saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” and understood that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was God. As though they had erred, they fell terrified with fear. But lest they despair from the greatness of their fear, Jesus came to them, touched them, and said: “Rise, and do not be afraid.” He came and touched them because they could not rise by themselves. “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15).

Lifting up their eyes, however, they saw no one except Jesus alone. For if Moses and Elijah had remained with him, [Col. 0380A] the Father’s voice might have seemed uncertain as to whom it had chiefly borne witness. I know, brothers and children, that the literal exposition delights you; but I think that the spiritual exposition will delight you more. Therefore, if you have listened carefully to the letter, listen still more carefully to the spirit. Jesus therefore took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain, etc.

These three disciples signify the three orders of believers in the Church: prelates, the continent, and married persons. They are Noah, Daniel, and Job, whom Ezekiel saw in a vision as being saved (Ezek. 14). But according to the truth of the Gospel, “two are in the field, two in bed, and two at the mill; one of them will be taken and the other left” (Matt. 24). For [Col. 0380B] from every order some are taken to glory and others left for punishment. A place does not make a human being holy; rather, a human being makes a place holy. Jesus therefore took the three disciples and led them up a high mountain, because the Lord received the three orders of believers and led them into heaven—but not all from every order, because he leads them apart, that is, separately, “as a shepherd separates sheep or lambs from goats” (Matt. 25), so that the wicked may be removed lest they see the glory of God, which is promised and given in heaven (Isa. 26); for “the Lord’s throne is in heaven” (Ps. 10), he who says: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may be my minister” (John 17).

That he was transfigured before them signifies that what we now see through a mirror in an enigma, [Col. 0380C] we shall then see face to face, as he is (1 Cor. 13), when we are transferred from figure to truth and led from faith to sight.

“And his face shone like the sun, but his garments became white as snow.” Christ’s garments are all the faithful, concerning whom it is said to him through the prophet: “You shall clothe yourself with all these as with a garment” (Isa. 46). And the Apostle says to them: “As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Rom. 6). Therefore not only did Christ’s face shine like the sun, but his garments also became white as snow. As the Apostle says, “We await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of [Col. 0380D] our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3).

Now, as great as the difference between the brightness of the sun and the whiteness of snow, so great is the difference between the glory of the head and the glorification of the members. There are two forms of glorification: one of the spirit and the other of the body; one by which the body is glorified and another by which the spirit is glorified. For, according to the prophet (Isa. 40), we shall receive double things from the hand of the Lord. The whole person, therefore, will obtain glory in the robe of the mind and the robe of the flesh.

Since the body consists of four elements—earth, water, fire, and air—four properties are said to belong to the robe of the body: brightness, subtlety, agility, and impassibility. And since the spirit has three natural powers—the rational power, the irascible power, [Col. 0381A] and the concupiscible power—three properties are held to belong to the robe of the spirit: knowledge, love, and delight. That wise man recalls and commends both sets when he says: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds; and their Lord shall reign for ever” (Wis. 3). By these words he indicates the properties of the glorified body, as though he said: They shall shine brightly; and, subtle like sparks, they shall run through the reeds with agility; and their Lord shall reign for ever, and they themselves shall be impassible with the Lord.

Next he assigns the properties of the glorified spirit: “Those who trust in him shall understand truth, and the faithful shall rest in love in him, because grace and peace are for God’s elect.” “They shall understand truth”: behold, knowledge. “The faithful [shall rest] in love”: behold, love. “Peace is for the elect”: behold, delight. In order that the Lord might raise hope, establish faith, and kindle love in the apostles concerning the reward of eternal glorification, he displayed in himself both robes and the properties of each. For “his face shone like the sun”: behold, the robe of the body. He did not simply say, “It shone,” but added, “like the sun.” For those four properties are found in the sun: brightness in its substance, because it is fiery and luminous; impassibility in its nature, because it endures perpetually and incorruptibly; subtlety in its ray, because it penetrates glass without obstacle; agility in its motion, [Col. 0382A] because in one day it runs from East to West.

Christ also displayed these properties in his mortal body: subtlety, when he was born of the Virgin (Luke 2); agility, when he walked upon the waters (John 6); brightness, when he was transfigured on the mountain (Matt. 9); impassibility, when he was eaten at the supper (John 19). But the properties of the glorified spirit are commended when it is said: “This is my beloved Son”: behold, love. “In whom I am well pleased”: behold, delight. “Hear him”: behold, knowledge. For he himself also said: “Whatever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). For the more God is known, the more he is loved; and the more he is loved, the more he delights.

[Col. 0382B] Therefore, brothers and children, if we desire to be clothed with the robe of glorification, let us ascend from the valley to the mountain, so that our citizenship may be in heaven (Phil. 3), according to the Apostle’s exhortation: “Seek the things above, not those upon the earth” (Col. 3); not longing for earthly things, but cleaving to heavenly ones. Thus may we ascend “from strength to strength, until we see the God of gods in Zion” (Ps. 83), through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV. THE THIRD SUNDAY IN LENT

Concerning watery places in which the unclean spirit rests; concerning the three brooms by which the house of conscience is cleansed, and the three adornments by which it is adorned; and concerning the seven capital vices.

[Col. 0381]

[Col. 0381C] “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it walks through waterless places, seeking rest and finding none. Then it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came out.’ And when it comes, it finds it swept clean with brooms and adorned. Then it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, having entered, they dwell there. And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Luke 11).

Necessity often prevents what usefulness requires—a circumstance which I am now compelled to experience myself. Usefulness demands that on these holy days I should admonish the people by exhortatory sermons more frequently than usual; but necessity prevents this, because, beyond the ordinary measure—indeed, more than usual—I am occupied with many great concerns, so that I have no leisure free from occupation. What then? Should I decline to do what I can because I cannot do what I would wish to do? Far be it! It is something to advance as far as one can, if one is not permitted to go farther. For the Apostle also says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). I shall therefore say: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it walks through waterless places.”

With regard to the unclean spirit, we must note three things, [Col. 0382C] which Truth itself teaches us to note: its departure, progress, and return—its departure from the person, its progress through places, and its return to the house. Of the first it is said: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person”; of the second it continues: “It walks through waterless places”; and of the third it adds: “I will return,” it says, “to my house from which I came out.” Its departure is always good for a person; its return is always bad. But its progress is sometimes good for a person and sometimes bad: good when temptation is not accepted, bad when it is consented to. Let us therefore see what results from its departure, what occurs in its progress, and what comes from its return.

“When,” it says, “the unclean spirit has gone out of a person,” then the house is swept clean with brooms and adorned. Behold what results [Col. 0382D] from the departure. “It walks through waterless places, seeking rest, but does not find it.” Behold what occurs in the progress. “Then it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, having entered, they dwell there.” Behold what comes from the return. Let us therefore carefully procure its departure, so that our house may be swept clean with brooms and adorned. Let us prudently guard against its progress, so that the unclean spirit seeking rest may not find it. Let us greatly fear its return, lest our last state be worse than our first.

The unclean spirit enters through sin, but goes out through repentance; it enters through vice, but goes out through virtue. For the departure of vice brings about the entrance of virtue—or rather, the entrance of virtue brings about the departure of vice. For “there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial” (2 Cor. 6). “Her many sins,” he says, “are forgiven, because she loved greatly” (Luke 7).

But when the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it then walks through waterless places, while seeking rest in them and not finding it. Watery places are lustful hearts, in which the excess of concupiscence overflows. [Col. 0383B] For of this water the patriarch Jacob is recorded as saying to Reuben: “You have poured forth like water; do not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed” (Gen. 49). For stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant (Prov. 9). In these watery places the unclean spirit rests, as it is written: “It sleeps under the shadow, in the hiding-place of the reed, in moist places” (Job 40).

Waterless places, however, are chaste hearts, aflame with the fire of love; in them not the malicious but the gracious Spirit rests, as it is written: “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my word?” (Isa. 5). The unclean spirit therefore walks [Col. 0383C] through waterless places, confident that the Jordan may flow into its mouth (Job 40). “For it goes about seeking whom it may devour” (1 Pet. 5). But while seeking rest in them and not finding it, it says: “I will return to my house from which I came out.” It is no wonder if the spirit of falsehood lies, or if the spirit of presumption presumes.
