For it still calls its house the one from which it went out, although the house from which the unclean spirit was cast out is no longer the unclean spirit’s. This house is the conscience. Of it the Psalmist says: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100).

When it comes into this house from which it went out through repentance, it finds it swept clean with brooms and adorned: cleansed by the expulsion of vices and adorned by the introduction of [Col. 0383D] virtues. This house is cleansed by three brooms: the broom of compunction in the heart, the broom of confession in the mouth, and the broom of satisfaction in action. By the broom of compunction the heart is cleansed of the stain of sinful contagion; by the broom of confession the heart is cleansed of the filth of perverse speech; by the broom of satisfaction the deed is cleansed of the foulness of evil habit.

It is likewise adorned by three ornaments: gifts, virtues, and works. Concerning them the Prophet says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, clothed round with variety” (Ps. 44). It is adorned with the variety of gifts: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 2). It is adorned also with the variety of virtues: faith, hope, and love; [Col. 0384A] justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. It is further adorned with the variety of works: prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and especially those works of mercy which the Lord will commend at judgment: “I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink,” etc. (Matt. 25).

Then the unclean spirit, as though unable to break into this house alone, goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself. The cunning of the unclean spirit is described to us so that we may take care to employ vigilance. Certainly, when it cannot deceive one way, it attempts to deceive another. For when the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it walks through waterless places. When it cannot deceive by one method, it tries to deceive by another; for, seeking rest and finding none, it says: [Col. 0384B] “I will return to my house from which I came out.” When it cannot deceive alone, it tries to deceive with others; for it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, having entered, they dwell there.

For example, let the following case be supposed. When the spirit of lust, cast out from a person, sees that person furnished with continence and distinguished by honour, so that it is difficult to deceive him through the frailty of the flesh, it resorts to other arts and devises other deceits. First, taking the spirit of pretence, it tries to deceive by hypocrisy; second, taking the spirit of favour-seeking, it tries to deceive by vainglory; third, taking the spirit of ambition, it tries to deceive by covetousness; fourth, taking the spirit of self-exaltation, it tries to deceive by pride; [Col. 0384C] fifth, taking the spirit of presumption, it tries to deceive by arrogance; sixth, taking the spirit of display, it tries to deceive by boastfulness; seventh, taking the spirit of laxity, it tries to deceive by excess. And at last the spirit of lust returns and secretly re-enters. “And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first”: not only because sins that had been forgiven are imputed, but because sins newly committed are added over them.

Yet not even thus should one despair, because Jesus is recorded to have cast seven demons out of Mary (Mark 10): that is, either the seven principal vices, signified by the seven nations cast out of the land of promise, to which are opposed seven petitions, seven virtues, and seven gifts; or rather, spiritual and bodily vices together, which are signified by the number seven because it is composed of three and four. For three refers to the spirit, which has three natural powers: the rational power, by which it discerns good from evil; the irascible power, by which it flees evil; and the concupiscible power, by which it seeks good. Four refers to the body, which consists of four elements—earth, water, fire, and air. Thus the seven demons are understood to have been cast out when bodily and spiritual vices are forgiven: bodily vices, such as gluttony and lust; spiritual vices, such as anger, envy, and so forth.

Let us therefore strive, brothers and children, not to return like dogs to vomit (Prov. 28). For “no one [Col. 0385A] who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). Lot’s wife also, because she looked back, is recorded to have been turned into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19). But because we have failed through our frailty, let us implore the merits of the blessed martyrs Stephen and Lawrence, that they may intercede for us with the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. THURSDAY AFTER THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

Concerning Christ’s justice, power, mercy, prudence, watchfulness, and teaching; concerning the fevers of the Synagogue by which it is held, and simple, double, continuous, and intermittent fever; finally, concerning varieties of illness.

[Col. 0385]

[Col. 0385B] “Jesus, rising from the synagogue, entered Simon’s house. But Simon’s mother-in-law was held by severe fevers” (Luke 4).

Many great things concerning our Redeemer are commended to us in the course of this Gospel reading: justice, power, mercy, prudence, watchfulness, and teaching. Justice, because, rising from the synagogue, he entered Simon’s house; power, because, standing over her, he rebuked the fever and it left her; mercy, because, laying his hands on each one, he healed them; prudence, because, rebuking the demons that cried out and said, “You are the Son of the living God,” he did not allow them to speak; watchfulness, because, “I must,” he says, “evangelize the kingdom of God in other cities also”; teaching, because he was preaching in the synagogues of Galilee.

[Col. 0385C] Rising from the synagogue, therefore, he entered Simon’s house, because he left the unbelieving and came to the faithful. He rejected the synagogue because of unbelief and chose the Church beforehand because of obedience. Simon, moreover, is interpreted “obedient”; his house is the universal Church, entrusted by the Lord to his governance. “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). The Lord commends and recalls its obedience through the prophet: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17). Nothing is more just than that the Lord should reject the unbelieving and disobedient, but receive the faithful and obedient. “For he regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” [Col. 0385D] (Ps. 137). “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4; 1 Pet. 5).

For this reason the apostles are elsewhere recorded as saying to the Jews: “Because you rejected the word of God and made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Therefore, if we do not wish to be rejected but received, let us strive to cast off unbelief and disobedience, and let us strive to take up faith and obedience. For “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 5), and works without faith do not live.

“But Simon’s mother-in-law was held by severe fevers.” The one whom he had previously called the Synagogue he now calls Simon’s mother-in-law. For a mother-in-law is the mother of the wife. The Synagogue is understood as the mother of the Church, which is Simon’s wife, sacramentally joined to him in marriage, [Col. 0386B] as she herself says in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1). For the first believers—[variant: the earliest believers]—were born from the Synagogue, and from it Christ himself also drew his origin according to the flesh. Therefore he himself said: “Salvation is from the Jews” (John 4).

After Christ rose from the Synagogue, leaving it because of unbelief, then Simon’s mother-in-law herself began to be held by severe fevers. He did not say “fever,” but “fevers,” so that it might be understood that she suffered not from one fever only, but from many. The Synagogue, indeed, is chiefly held by two fevers: error and envy. Of the first the Psalm says: “They went astray from the womb; they spoke false things” (Ps. 37). Of the second the Evangelist says (Matt. 27) that they delivered him up through envy.

The fever of error proceeds from cold humour, as it is written: “The Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter” (John 10): a winter of error, unbelief, and ignorance. Hence, when Peter denied him (John 18), he warmed himself at a fire, because it was cold. But the fever of envy proceeds from hot humour, as it is written: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57): the fire of envy, indignation, and hatred. “For fire blazed in their synagogue, and flame consumed sinners” (Ps. 105). Oh, how grievously the Synagogue is tormented by envy when it sees the Church possess kingdom and priesthood, temple and altar, law and prophecy! For the kingdom [Col. 0386D] of God has been taken from it and given to a nation producing its fruits (Matt. 21). Yet it is held in such great error that it does not even then understand the truth. “The ox knew its owner and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel did not know me, and the foolish people did not understand” (Isa. 1).

Thus Simon’s mother-in-law—that is, the Synagogue—is held by these fevers; but the faithful who are in the house pray for her, asking that God may remove the veil from her heart so that she may acknowledge Jesus Christ, who is truth. He, inclined by the prayers of the faithful, stands over her, that is, exalted at the Father’s right hand; for “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, [Col. 0387A] and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

“He rebuked the fever, and it left her.” Not because the fever, as a sensible or rational thing, understood, but because he fulfilled his good pleasure concerning it. “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148). For “the Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. 134). Nothing is more powerful than that even insensible things perceive and obey his command.

Therefore she immediately rose and ministered to them. Although it is natural for those suffering fever, as health begins, to be weak and to feel the discomfort of illness, the miracle overcame nature. For health given by God’s command returns whole and complete all at once. Therefore she immediately rose and ministered to them, so that the miracle may allude to the mystery: for the soul’s health is restored whole and complete all at once. For it is written that he “made the whole person well on the Sabbath” (John 7). This will be fulfilled [Col. 0387B] “when the fullness of the Gentiles enters into faith, and then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 9). For “in those days Judah shall be saved” (Jer. 33), “and the remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 9).

It should be known, moreover, that one fever is simple, another double, another continuous, and another intermittent. A person suffers from a simple fever when troubled by one vice only. Thus there are many who abstain from the others but are defiled by lust. For what the apostle James says, “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2), must certainly be understood in this sense: whoever offends in one point, transgressing one of the divine commandments, has become guilty of all—that is, loses love, without which the rest are not fulfilled. For “the end of the commandment is love” (1 Tim. 1), and love is the perfection of the law (Rom. 13).

But a person suffers from a double fever when entangled in many vices, like that sinful woman from whom the Lord is recorded to have cast seven demons (Mark 16). This does not mean that one who has one vice has all of them, as one who has one virtue has all virtues. For it is otherwise off the road than on the road. All virtues indeed assist one another; but certain vices oppose one another, such as prodigality and avarice, despair and presumption. [Col. 0387D] A person suffers from continuous fever when he perseveres in vice. Such a fever is, as it were, acute and fatal. Of it the Lord says: “You shall die in your sins” (John 8). And perhaps concerning this John the apostle says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (John 5).

But a person suffers from intermittent fever when he sometimes repents of sin but returns to it like a dog to vomit (Prov. 26). Such a person at times suffers from daily, at times tertian, and at times quartan fever, according as the penitent relapses into sin easily, more easily, or most easily. Yet no one should despair, because “they asked him for her, and he rebuked the fever, and it left her.” Certainly, she who could not be healed by her own merits was healed by the prayers of others. Therefore when someone suffers from some grave sin, let him have recourse to the Church, that it may pray for him. For it is written: “When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: Your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 2).

“When the sun had set, all who had persons sick with various infirmities brought them to him, and all were healed.” Christ is the sun of justice, who “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Of him the Prophet says: “The sun knew its setting” (Ps. 103). This sun set when Christ, bowing his head, gave up the spirit (Matt. 27). But before the sun had set, [Col. 0388B] few were healed, because few were converted to faith before Christ’s death. Therefore he himself said: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140). “But when I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself,” because “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12). Therefore, when the sun had set, all who had persons sick with various infirmities brought them to Jesus, and all were healed.

The infirmities of the mind are vices. Hence there are as many varieties of infirmity as there are kinds of vice. Let us enumerate a few among many for the edification of many. Some suffer pains; some swellings; [Col. 0388C] some heat; and some frenzies. Likewise, some are blind, some deaf, some mute, and some lame. Again, some are leprous, some dropsical, some paralytic, and some lethargic. These illnesses are grave, but all are curable through God’s grace.

Pain of heart is hatred, of which it is written: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. 7). This infirmity is grave, because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). Swelling of the mind is pride. Of it it is written: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8); that is, knowledge without love makes a person proud. This infirmity too is grave, because “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). Heat of spirit is lust. Of it the prophet says: “All adulterers are like an oven heated by the baker” (Hos. 7). This infirmity too is grave, because fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God (Heb. 13). Frenzy of heart is anger, of which it is written: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable fury of asps” (Deut. 31). This infirmity too is grave, [Col. 0388D] “because the anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1).

Moreover, let all who have sick persons bring them to Jesus, that they may be healed by the Saviour; for there is no other name given under heaven in which human beings must be saved (Acts 4). Let those struck by fiery serpents look upon the bronze serpent hanging on the wood, that they may be healed (Num. 21). The blind [Col. 0389A] are those lacking the light of truth, concerning whom it is written: “Let them alone; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15). “If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into a pit” (Luke 6). The deaf are those who scorn to obey the Lord’s commandments, of whom it is said: “Like the deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers or spells charmed by the wise man” (Ps. 53). The mute are those who are silent in the praise of God, as it is written: “I was dumb and humbled, and kept silence even from good things” (Ps. 38). The lame are those who do not walk in the path of the commandments, as it is written: “How long do you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him” (2 Kgs. 18).

But let all who have sick persons bring them to [Col. 0389B] Jesus, that they may be healed by the Saviour, for he despises no one and rejects no one. “I am,” he says, “the salvation of my people.” “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I shall refresh you, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). “For everyone who comes to me I shall not cast out” (John 6).

Heretics are lepers: in one part they are sound and in another corrupt, because beneath the appearance of truth they pour in the poison of falsehood. The covetous are dropsical: the more they drink, the more they thirst, like a furnace which, the more wood it receives, the more it consumes. The paralytic are lax in their actions. The lethargic are ungrateful for benefits. [Col. 0389C] But neither should these despair: let them come confidently to Jesus to be healed, because “truly he bore our infirmities and carried our pains; he was wounded for our iniquities and bruised for our crimes. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his wound we are healed” (Isa. 53).

“Demons went out from many, crying out and saying: ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak.” But since the [Col. 0390A] Apostle says, “Whether Christ is preached by anyone, I rejoice, and shall indeed rejoice” (Phil. 1), why did he forbid the demons to speak the truth? Is not a testimony delivered by an adversary stronger? There are three reasons. First, to teach us to flee vainglory, lest we delight in the applause of human favour. Second, to teach us to avoid heretical perversity, so that, by this example, we may forbid heretics to preach even the truth, because they offer the gall of dragons in Babylon’s golden cup (Deut. 32). Third, lest demons, who are spirits of falsehood, be believed when they speak truth. In this we are morally instructed not to desire praise from deceivers and liars, whose praise tends more to insult than to honour.

But the subsequent phrase, “because they knew him to be Christ,” must be rightly understood, lest it seem contrary to the Apostle’s statement that “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2), which some expound as referring to demons. If they had known Christ to be the Lord of glory, they would never have caused him to be crucified through malicious suggestion. For this is the mystery hidden from the ages, but revealed through the Church to principalities and powers (Col. 1). Let the times, therefore, be distinguished, and Scripture agrees with itself. For demons sometimes believed and sometimes doubted. When they saw him undergo human weaknesses, they doubted concerning him, as we read: when [Col. 0390C] he had fasted forty days and forty nights and afterwards was hungry, the tempter came to him and said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matt. 4). But when they saw him work miracles, they believed him to be the Son of God, as elsewhere they are recorded as saying: “Jesus of Nazareth, why have you come before the time to torment us? We know that you are the Holy One of God” (Matt. 8).

## SERMON XVII. THE FOURTH SUNDAY IN LENT

Concerning Christ’s power, wisdom, and kindness; concerning the two miracles and their exposition; concerning the contemplative and active life; finally, concerning the two Testaments and peoples.

[Col. 0389]

[Col. 0389D] “There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?” (John 6).

Three things above all are commended to us concerning our Redeemer in the course of this Gospel reading: power, wisdom, and kindness. Power in the miracle; wisdom in the mystery; and kindness in the service. For what is more powerful than to increase very small things without addition or nourishment? What is wiser than to signify profound causes without speech or writing? What is kinder than to satisfy hungry crowds without request or payment? Certainly, he who had spiritually fed them with the food of teaching also feeds them bodily with the nourishment of nature, so that he who refreshed the spirit may also nourish the body.

This miracle of the multiplication of loaves and fish, by which the Lord satisfied a multitude of people, is recorded as having been performed twice. Yet between the first and second miracle there is much and great difference: various indeed, but not contrary; distinct, but not opposed. In the first miracle he satisfied five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fish, and the disciples filled twelve baskets with the fragments left over. [Col. 0391A] In the second miracle, however, he refreshed four thousand men with seven loaves and a few fish, and the apostles filled seven baskets with the fragments (Mark 8). In the first miracle the kind of loaves and the number of fish are specified; in the second neither is expressed. In the first miracle one boy had five barley loaves and two fish; in the second the disciples had seven loaves and a few fish. In the first miracle five thousand people reclined upon grass; in the second four thousand people reclined upon the ground.

All things are full of divine mysteries and overflowing with heavenly sweetness, if only they have a diligent observer who knows how to suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone (Deut. 32). Let us therefore dig out the well, because it is deep, and draw water with joy from the fountains of the Saviour (Isa. 12).

Indeed, there are two lives, two peoples, and two Testaments: the contemplative and the active life, the Jewish and Gentile peoples, the New and Old Testaments. The five senses serve the active life. The Jewish people has twelve prophets, twelve tribes, and twelve patriarchs. The Old Testament is contained in five books and two tablets. The contemplative life, moreover, is served by seven gifts. The Gentile people has seven Churches, seven angels, and seven deacons. The New Testament consists in the four Gospels.

Thus the first miracle, by which [Col. 0391C] five thousand people were satisfied from five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets were filled with the remaining fragments, pertains to the Old Testament, with its five Mosaic books and two tablets of the law; likewise, to the active life with its five senses, and to the Jewish people with its twelve prophets, twelve tribes, and twelve patriarchs.

At the second miracle, however—by which four thousand people were refreshed from seven loaves and a few fish, and seven baskets were filled with the fragments left over—belong the contemplative life, with its seven gifts and certain virtues; the Gentile people, with its seven Churches, seven deacons, and seven angels; and the New Testament [Col. 0391D], with its four Gospels. Behold, we have briefly begun the web of our discourse—if only we may be able to weave it adequately. Let us therefore ask wisdom of the Lord, who “gives generously to all and does not reproach” (James 1), in case the key of David may deign to open—the key which shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts (Rev. 5).

The five barley loaves are the five books of the Old Testament. The two fishes are the two tablets of the divine Law, taking the container for the thing contained by metonymy. The one boy who had the five loaves and the two fishes is Moses, who presented the five books and the two tablets: pure indeed in himself, but instructing a childish people. The marrow of barley “is covered beneath a hard husk, and the spirit of the Law is concealed beneath the hard letter [Col. 0392A]. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (1 Cor. 3). Let us see why those loaves are described as having been barley loaves. Such loaves are broken when they are expounded. Then they are truly multiplied, so that they can satisfy the multitude of the hungry people. They are expounded in two ways: literally, according to history, and spiritually, according to allegory. For the book shown to Ezekiel was written within and without (Ezek. 3). Thus the Lord broke the two fishes and the five loaves when he opened the disciples’ minds so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). He gave thanks when he said to the Father: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). He blessed when [Col. 0392B] he approved the Mosaic Law: “If you believed Moses,” he says, “you would also believe me, for he wrote of me” (John 5). He ordered them to be set before the people when he taught that the ancient Law should be venerated, declaring that he had come not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5).

Yet five thousand people are satisfied from the five barley loaves and two fishes, because from the five books of the Old Testament and the two tablets of the divine Law, through the literal exposition of history, are nourished animal-minded persons leading the active life. The five senses serve that life: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Such are the carnal Jews, who desire only sensible things and take delight solely in bodily senses. Hence, since “the natural person does not receive the things that are of God [Col. 0392C], but the spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2), twelve baskets are heaped with the fragments that remain. For spiritual men are filled from the subtler mysteries of the Law, which animal-minded persons do not perceive, receiving the meaning of the twelve prophets, who spoke not carnally but spiritually.

You have heard the exposition of the first miracle; hear also the exposition of the second, lest you be able to say, “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4)—although it is not I who break it, but he whom the disciples recognized in the breaking of bread (Luke 24). The seven loaves are the seven chief gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, which Isaiah enumerates, saying (ch. 11): “Upon him shall rest the spirit [Col. 0392D] of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” The few small fishes are other, lesser virtues, nevertheless necessary for the feast of contemplation. The disciples possessed these loaves and fishes. Of them it is written: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power from the Spirit on high” (Acts 2). These loaves are believed to have been not barley but wheat loaves, because “he gave them bread from heaven; he sent them grain in abundance” (Ps. 77). Therefore, the loaves made of wheat are the gifts in which contemplative men delight.

Contemplative men break these seven loaves spiritually when they are compelled to interrupt the leisure of contemplation—which is served by the gifts of the sevenfold Holy Spirit [Col. 0393A]—for the duty of preaching, in order to serve their neighbours’ benefit; and when what they learn in the leisure of contemplation by reading and meditating, they expound in the labour of preaching, admonishing and exhorting. The four thousand persons who are satisfied from the seven loaves and the few fishes are spiritual people who keep Christ’s teaching, contained in the four Gospels; through the preaching of teachers they are nourished by spiritual grace. For “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God that proceeds from his mouth” (Matt. 4). The fragments that remain are the secret mysteries of contemplation, which the simple do not attain (Deut. 8). Seven baskets are filled from them: that is, the seven trumpet-sounding angels [Col. 0393B], namely the prelates of the seven Churches which the Apostle John describes in the Apocalypse (chs. 9, 12). Such were the apostles, to whom Truth itself said: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries [Col. 0394A] of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables” (Luke 8). The seven deacons also belong to these, chosen by the apostles, men full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to distribute provisions at the tables (Acts 6).

Observe, then: in the first miracle people reclined upon grass, and in the second miracle people reclined upon the ground. For animal-minded people who lead the active life lie upon the softness of the flesh. For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40). But spiritual men, who pursue the contemplative life, stand upon the firmness of the mind, withdrawn from earthly things and intent upon heavenly ones, according to the Apostle’s exhortation: “Seek the things that are above, not those upon earth. Set your minds on things above [Col. 0394B], where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3). He who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. LAETARE SUNDAY, OR ON THE ROSE

Why the Roman pontiff presents a golden flower to the faithful people on Laetare Sunday, why it is displayed in the basilica of the Holy Cross, and what the fourfold Jerusalem is.

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393C] “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her; rejoice with joy, you who were in sorrow, that you may exult and be satisfied from the breasts of your consolation” (Isa. 66).

Today’s solemnity, brothers and children, is celebrated according to an ancient custom of the Apostolic See, for which, if you remember well, we set forth a twofold explanation last year. But because some among us wish to grasp with their understanding what they perceive by sight, we wish to repeat certain things, so that we may take care to add others.

There is, indeed, a twofold reason why on this day the Roman pontiff presents a golden flower to the faithful people in this place: one according to the letter, the other according to the spirit. In it we must chiefly consider six things: the person and the cause, the matter and [Col. 0393D] the form, the time and the place.

You know, dearest friends, that the corruptible body cannot endure amid continual anxieties unless from time to time a remedy of refreshment intervenes. Hence it is said:

> Introduce joys among your cares from time to time.  
> What lacks alternating rest is not lasting.

Therefore Truth says in the Gospel: “I have compassion on the crowd, because behold, they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat; and if I dismiss them fasting, they will fail on the way” (Mark 8). Therefore, lest the faithful people fail under unceasing labour because of the severity of Lenten abstinence, on this middle Sunday some solace of refreshment is introduced, so that the anxiety, being moderated, may be borne more lightly. [Col. 0394C] For today’s office is wholly full of rejoicing, wholly filled with exultation, wholly heaped with joy: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her; rejoice with joy, you who were in sorrow, that you may exult and be satisfied from the breasts of your consolation.” At the close of every phrase delight overflows, joy resounds, gladness is impressed: “Rejoice, Jerusalem”; “rejoice with joy”; “that you may exult and be satisfied.”

For this day presents love after hatred, joy after sorrow, and satisfaction after hunger: love after hatred, whence, “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her”; joy after sorrow, whence, “Rejoice with joy, you who were in sorrow”; satisfaction after hunger, whence, “that you may be satisfied from the breasts [Col. 0394D] of your consolation.” These three things are jointly signified in the three properties of this flower which we visibly present to you: love in its colour, delight in its fragrance, satisfaction in its taste. For the rose, beyond other flowers, delights by its colour, refreshes by its fragrance, and strengthens by its taste: it delights the sight, refreshes the smell, and strengthens the taste.

But since “the spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 3), let us pass from carnal things to spiritual. This flower signifies that Flower who says of himself in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 1); and of whom the prophet says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 2). Truly the Flower of flowers, because the Holy of holies, who beyond all other flowers—that is, [Col. 0395A] beyond all other saints—delights by his colour in the sight, because he is “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44), into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1). He refreshes by fragrance in the smell, because “your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments”; the young women loved him because “they run after the fragrance of his ointments” (Song 1). He strengthens by taste in the palate, because the bread he himself gives is his flesh for the life of the world (John 6), possessing every delight and every sweetness of taste (Wis. 16). For he is the one who, as you heard in the Gospel, satisfied five thousand people from five loaves and two fishes (John 6).

There is a threefold material in this flower: gold, musk, and balsam. Yet through the balsam [Col. 0395B], musk is joined to gold. So there is a threefold substance in Christ: divinity, body, and soul. Yet through the soul the body is joined to divinity, because the divine nature is of such subtlety that it would not be fitting for it to be united to a body formed from the mud of earth unless a rational spirit intervened. The bearer of this flower is the Saviour’s vicar, namely the Roman pontiff, Peter’s successor and the vicar of Jesus Christ. For Jesus says to Peter: “You, follow me” (John 12). This should be understood not only of the manner of martyrdom, but also of the order of teaching. “You shall be called Cephas,” he says (John 1), which is interpreted “head.” Thus, head from head, as Peter from rock. And “the head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, the head of Christ [Col. 0395C] is God” (Eph. 5). For just as the fullness of the senses abounds in the head, while in the other members there is some portion of that fullness, so the others are called to a share in solicitude, but Peter alone was taken into the fullness of power, so that he may be shown to be the vicar of him who says of himself in the Gospel: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). Hence Jesus says spiritually to Peter: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

Thus the Roman pontiff presents this flower not at every time, but only on this Sunday, which is the seventh from the Sunday called Septuagesima. For Christ is seen not at every hour, but only in the seventh [Col. 0395D] age by those who are comforted in blessed rest. In the sixth, indeed, Christ is seen through faith; but in the seventh Christ is seen by sight. “No human being shall see me and live,” he says (Exod. 33). Since no one has ever seen God (1 John 4), this must be understood as referring to this mortal life. For in the blessed life he is seen no longer in a mirror, in an enigma, but face to face, as he is (1 Cor. 13). Therefore he says to the apostles: “I will manifest myself to them” (John 14).

There are six days in which a human being may work. But on the seventh day God rested from all the work that he had done (Gen. 2). Thus the number seven signifies rest. Hence the seventh day, seventh week, seventh month, and seventh year are holidays in the Law; above all, the Jubilee which follows the sevenfold cycle. Rightly, therefore, this flower is displayed to the faithful people only on the seventh Sunday, because Christ is seen by holy souls only in the seventh age. Therefore this flower is not displayed for viewing in just any place, but fittingly in this basilica, called that of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, which bears the type and presents the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says in the Epistle you heard: “That Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4). [Col. 0396A] There holy angels and blessed souls contemplate Christ. To her it is rightly said: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her.”

Jerusalem is understood in four ways, according to the four theological [Col. 0396B] senses: historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. Jerusalem is higher and lower, inward and outward. The higher is in the homeland; the lower is on the way; the inward is in the soul; the outward is in Palestine. Of the higher it is written: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose sharing is into one and the same” (Ps. 121). To the lower it is said: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 6). Of the inward it is written: “I will give salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. 46). To the outward it is said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (Matt. 23). To which Jerusalem, then, does the prophetic utterance rightly apply: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her”? Not to the outward Jerusalem, held captive because of its sins; to it rather belongs what is related in Lamentations (ch. 1): “The ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the solemnity. Her enemies have become the head.” [Col. 0396C] But it applies chiefly to the higher Jerusalem, of which it is rightly said: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places” (Ps. 149). To these it is said: “Rejoice with joy, you who were in sorrow.” “For God shall wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall no longer be mourning, or crying, or any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 7, 21).

For when the prophet had said, “Rejoice, Jerusalem,” he immediately showed who ought to rejoice when he said, “Assemble, all you who love her”; how they ought to rejoice when he added, “Rejoice with joy, you who were in sorrow”; and why they ought to rejoice when he added, “That you may exult and be satisfied from the breasts of your consolation.”

Therefore all who love her ought to assemble for rejoicing: that is, not heretics but Catholics; not dogs but sheep. For love is a fountain proper to itself, in which the stranger has no share. The person who truly wishes to rejoice in this assembly has love in his heart, mindful of what is written: “When the king entered the wedding feast to see those reclining, and saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment, he ordered him to be cast out and thrust into the outer darkness [Col. 0397A]” (Matt. 20). Therefore the prophet says: “Assemble, you who love her.”

Moreover, many rejoice in body while grieving in heart, displaying outward joy but carrying inward mourning. For “the wicked have no joy, says the Lord” (Isa. 48), and “there is no peace in the bones because of sins” (Ps. 37). Therefore, after the prophet had said, “Rejoice, Jerusalem,” he immediately added: “Rejoice with joy, you who were in sorrow.” It is as though he said: Let inward gladness accompany outward joy, so that our heart and flesh may exult in the living God (Ps. 83). For “this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). “That you may exult and be satisfied from the breasts of your consolation.” “I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when your [Col. 0397B] glory appears” (Ps. 16).

It is clear, therefore, that the two breasts of consolation are the two kinds of glorification: namely, the robe of the mind and the robe of the flesh. Of them the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower; from the time when I became before you as one finding peace” (Song 8). By the breast of glorification in the mind, holy souls are satisfied in the seventh age of those at rest; by the breast of glorification in the flesh, incorruptible bodies shall be satisfied in the eighth age of those rising again. Therefore it is said: “Give portions to seven, and indeed also to eight” (Eccl. 11). To the number seven are to be given portions of glorification in the heart; to the number eight, portions of glorification in the body.

The portions of glorification in the heart are three: knowledge, love, and delight. Concerning these the Wise Man declares: [Col. 0398A] “Those who trust in him shall understand truth, and the faithful shall rest in love with him, because gift and peace are for God’s chosen ones” (Wis. 3). The portions of glorification in the body are four: brightness, subtlety, agility, and impassibility. Concerning these the same Wise Man declares: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds; they shall judge nations,” and so forth (ibid.). It would be good if we could remain here, so that we might be permitted to meditate upon and contemplate these kinds of glory and glorification. But behold, a great and burdensome occupation holds us back and calls us away—varied indeed, and, would that it were not also vain; for “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1)!

Let us therefore ask, brothers and children; let us ask in believing prayer, “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith [Col. 0398B]” (1 Tim. 1), lifting pure hands without deceit to God, that the Lord may lead us from the sacrament of the thing that we celebrate to the reality of the sacrament that we await. There is life without death, day without night, certainty without contingency. There will be security without fear, delight without pain, tranquillity without labour; beauty without deformity, strength without weakness, uprightness without perversity; love without malice, truth without falsehood, happiness without misery; joy which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 63). May the Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us—he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

On the threefold washing and the six kinds of cleansing.

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0397C] “One who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13).

There is a threefold washing: in water, in tears, and in blood. Each of these is twofold. For there is one washing of material water and another washing of spiritual water. The washing of material water is baptism, concerning which the Lord says: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3); and, “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). The washing of spiritual water is almsgiving. Of it Scripture says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 29); and, “Give alms,” he says, “and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

[Col. 0397D] Likewise, there is one washing of tears that proceed from the eyes, and another washing of tears that proceed from trees. From the eyes they flow for lamentation. Of these the Prophet says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears [Col. 0398C] I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6). From trees they proceed for sacramental use, as we read that the Samaritan, approaching the wounded man, poured wine and oil over him (Luke 10).

Likewise, there is one washing of blood in suffering, and another washing of blood in mystery. The blood of suffering was poured out once on the cross, as it is written: “Jesus entered once into the Holy Place, not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9). But the blood of mystery is drunk often from the cup, as Truth says: “Drink from this, all of you. For this is the cup of the New Testament in my blood. As often as you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me” (Matt. 26). Thus he washed us from our sins [Col. 0398D] in his blood.

There are, therefore, six kinds of cleansing, which the Church represents today (Rev. 1): the cleansing of material water in the washing of feet, for the example of humility; and the cleansing of spiritual water in the feeding [Col. 0399A] of the poor, for the duty of compassion—as you heard when the Gospel was read: Jesus rose from supper, laid aside his garments, girded himself with a linen cloth, poured water into a basin, washed the disciples’ feet, and said: “I have given you an example, that you too may do likewise.” Likewise, the cleansing of tears that flow from the eyes in lamentation is represented in the reconciliation of penitents, celebrated today; and the cleansing of tears proceeding from trees for sacramental use, in the making of chrism, which is consecrated from oil and balsam. Again, it represents the cleansing of blood which, although poured out only once on the cross, is nevertheless drunk often from the cup. Of these two, the Roman pontiff represents one when, today, after the table of the Lateran altar has been removed, he consecrates the Eucharist within the altar itself, thereby recalling that [Col. 0400A] under the Law the high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood once each year.

Behold, we have briefly indicated the mysteries of today’s solemnity, which we cannot pursue because of both the crowd’s tumult and the length of the office. But “one who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.” Many have been washed from evil deeds who nevertheless have not been washed from wicked thoughts. Thus many wash their hands, yet do not wash their feet. Accordingly, one whose hands are washed from the effect of sin should wash his feet from the inclination to sin; and thus let him be wholly clean. For this cleanness the washings mentioned above were instituted. May he make us worthy to celebrate them worthily, who graciously instituted them: Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XX. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399B] “After his passion Christ presented himself alive to the apostles by many proofs; for forty days he appeared to them and spoke of the kingdom of God” (Acts 1).

Wishing, dearest brothers, I wish—if I can—to distinguish the proofs by which the Lord demonstrated the truth of his resurrection by irrefutable reasoning: namely, by the frequency of his appearances and the testimony of angels; by the showing of his wounds and the eating of food; by the exposition of the Scriptures; and by the working of miracles. Christ showed the truth of his resurrection by the frequency of his appearances, since in the Gospel he is described as having appeared ten times after the resurrection: first to Mary Magdalene, when he said to her, “Do not touch me,” and so forth (John [Col. 0399C] 20); second, to her and the other women, when they approached, held his feet, and worshipped him (Matt. 28); third, to Simon Peter (Luke 24); fourth, to the two disciples going to Emmaus (ibid.); fifth, to the other disciples, when after eight days he came where they were assembled, and Thomas was with them (John 20); sixth, to seven disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, when Jesus stood on the shore while they were fishing (John 21); seventh, to the eleven disciples, when they went into Galilee to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them (Matt. 28); eighth, in the upper room, where the eleven disciples were reclining, and so forth (Luke 22); ninth, when he led the eleven disciples out toward Bethany on the Mount of Olives [Col. 0399D] and, while they watched, ascended into heaven. On account of these appearances the Apostle says: “He was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once” (1 Cor. 15). “Then he was seen by James. Last of all, as by one born untimely, he was seen by Paul himself.”

[Col. 0400B] Why, however, did Christ show himself after the resurrection first to women rather than to men, and among women first to Mary Magdalene and then to the other women, while among men first to Peter and then to the other disciples? Let this be the reason, if a better one cannot be given: because woman sinned before man, and the other women sinned in Eve, while the other men sinned in Adam. Therefore Christ appeared first to women and afterwards to men in the prescribed order, so that as death proceeded through fault, life might likewise proceed through grace.

It should certainly be understood that Christ is said to have appeared to his disciples for forty days after his resurrection not because he appeared to them on each of the forty days, but because he appeared frequently during the forty days. Thus John the Evangelist testifies of the third day of appearances—not the third appearance itself, but the third day on which appearances occurred—when he says: “This was now the third time that Jesus manifested himself to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. He manifested himself in this way: Simon Peter and the others were together,” and so forth (John 21). [Col. 0400C] Therefore, there can be no doubt whatever concerning God’s truth when it has been presented to the eyes of many; and he also often made it manifest, for the greater strengthening of faith, through angelic testimony. First, when the angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached, rolled away the stone, sat upon it, and said to the women: “He has risen; he is not here” (Mark 16). Second, when “Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw two angels sitting in white, one at the head and one at the feet, where Jesus’ body had been laid” (John 20); and, “behold, two men stood beside them in shining garments and said to them: Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen” (Luke 24). Third, when, while they watched, he was lifted up [Col. 0400D] and a cloud received him from their eyes. [Col. 0401A] “And behold, two men stood beside them in white garments and said: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up to heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, shall so come as you saw him going into heaven.” Since “every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three” (Matt. 18; 2 Cor. 13), it is plain that in this matter the testimony of angels ought to be believed.

But lest anyone should be able to doubt in any way on this matter, he preserved the marks of the wounds in his body when he said to the disciples: “See my hands,” and so forth (Luke 24). Because of the nature of his glorified body, the Lord preserved the scars of wounds in his body not only so that the faith of the apostles might be more firmly established by them, but also that he might present them, in interceding for us, to God the Father, showing what manner of death he suffered for us, and so intercede more effectively for us.

Further, lest his resurrection might be regarded as phantasmal, as though performed by magical art rather than divine power, he also willed, because of the nature of his incorruptible body, to eat with the apostles after his resurrection. First, when he said: “Have you anything here to eat?” And they offered him a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb (ibid.); second, when the seven disciples had come down from the boat and saw coals, with fish laid on them, and bread, and so forth; third, when, while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, and so forth.

It should be known that the foods the Lord ate before death he digested, but those he received after the resurrection he consumed. Just as thirsty earth absorbs water in one way and fire in another: the former drinks it in, the latter consumes it. For the body which, by reason of its subtlety—one of the four properties of the glorified body—entered through closed doors, and which, by reason of the nature of flesh, did not vanish but blossomed anew in rising, showed itself tangible. If there is a miracle in either case, the one suffices to prove the other. What then is written? “And because in the breaking of bread he suddenly withdrew himself from the eyes of the two disciples; and after eight days Jesus came, the doors being closed, and said: Peace to you” (Luke 24); [Col. 0401D] third, when he said to the disciples: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat,” and so forth (John 21); fourth, when, as the apostles watched, he was lifted up, a cloud received him, and he was borne into heaven (Luke 24), where he sits at the right hand of God.

The miracles fittingly correspond to the truth. For it was fitting that an earthquake should take place in his resurrection, since an earthquake is recorded at his death; that, rising, he should enter to the disciples through the closed womb of a virgin [something is missing]; that those who miraculously caught fish should more miraculously become fishers of human beings; and that he should ascend wondrously into heaven, as he would descend still more wondrously. These are the proofs of the Lord’s resurrection, concerning which Luke the Evangelist testifies in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “After his passion, he presented himself alive by many proofs,” and so forth.

And just as there were forty [Col. 0402A] days after he rose from the dead until he ascended into heaven, so there were forty hours from the time he died on the cross until he was raised from the tomb. For on Friday at the ninth hour, bowing his head, he yielded up his spirit; and on the first day of the week, at the first hour, he rose from the dead and came to life. Four hours thus remained on Friday—the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth—while the day of the Sabbath and two nights, one preceding and the other following, had thirty-six hours; thus all the hours together amounted to forty. It is clear, therefore, from the foregoing that Christ lay in the tomb for three days and nights, though not for three whole days: on Friday at least for one hour, on Saturday for ten, and on Sunday for part of one. Hence [Col. 0402B] Truth wisely and carefully says in the Gospel: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so also shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12). He does not say “for three days and for three nights,” but “on three days and three nights.” For it is one thing to be on a day and another to be throughout a day. Something is on a day when it exists during some part of that day; but it is throughout a day when it exists through its various parts.

But how is it true that he lay in the tomb for three days and three nights, when only two nights intervened? It should therefore be known that, just as day is called the brightness of the air when the sun shines over the earth, so night may be called the darkness of the air when the sun does not shine upon the earth. Yet from the sixth hour, at which the Lord was crucified, until the ninth hour, at which he gave up his spirit, “darkness came over the whole earth, and the sun was darkened” (Luke 23). It is therefore clear that at the ninth hour, because of the darkening of the sun, the air was darkened. Accordingly, the ninth hour, at which Christ died, is understood to have been night; so that, just as Christ’s death took only one hour from the last day, so it took only one hour from the first night.

But since a night of this sort—that is, the darkness of the air—preceded the burial, which, as we read, was performed when it was already late on the Preparation, before the Sabbath, according to this interpretation one must understand by the heart of the earth what Truth says: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so also the Son of Man [will be] in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12).

Moreover, according to this interpretation, by the heart of the earth one should understand not so much the chamber of the rocky tomb as the centre of this inhabited zone. “For here ‘heart’ means ‘middle,’” as is said in the Psalm: “But our God, our king before the ages, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 37 [read: Ps. 73/74]); because in that place the Lord was crucified, died, was buried, and rose again.

For until Christ’s resurrection, day preceded night, as is read: “Evening came, and morning: one day” (Gen. 1); and this suits the mystery well, because in humankind the day of virtues preceded the night of vices. But at Christ’s resurrection night began to precede day, because light followed the night of guilt, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). Therefore the night that lay between Saturday and Sunday is counted twice: once on account of the natural order, in which day preceded night; again on account of the spiritual order, in which night preceded day. Thus, although there were two nights, if one is counted twice, they are understood to have been three for the reason stated.

Besides, whatever the wording may be, the sense is, according to a certain manner of speaking, “for three days and three nights,” that is, for three intervals of days and nights, because he was in the heart of the earth for two whole nights and one whole day. Although he is believed to have risen at some hour of the Lord’s Day: “Rising early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons” (John 20). The Psalmist agrees: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn” (Ps. 56 [Vulgate numbering 57]). For both the Gospel and the Creed state that he rose on the third day. It follows that he did not rise in the night, but in the day.

Yet Matthew the Evangelist both differs and agrees when he says: “At the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came to see the tomb, etc.” (Matt. 28). Certainly *vespere* (“evening”) means the end of the day, that is, twilight; and the end of the night, that is, dawn. But so that the Evangelist might determine of which *vespere* he spoke, he immediately adds: “which dawns toward the first day of the week,” as though he had said: at the dawn that was between the night of Saturday and Sunday.

The practice of the Church also agrees with this opinion: in commemorating the Sunday resurrection, it sings the morning praises. Therefore the Lord rose at dawn, that is, when the sky was growing bright from the eastern regions. By this the apparent discrepancy among the Evangelists concerning the women’s arrival at the tomb is resolved. Matthew says that they came at the evening of the Sabbath, which was dawning toward the first day of the week; Luke says, at very early dawn; John, in the morning while it was still dark; and, conversely, Matthew says, when the sun had already risen. Here “the sun having already risen” is understood as the whole dawn, as Matthew himself explains when he says: “And very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, the sun having already risen.” It is clear, therefore, that they came both when the sun had already risen and yet before full light, while it was still dark: that is, at dawn, when, from the sun’s rising, the sky becomes white in the eastern regions, while darkness still remains in the western regions. For at that hour, if one looks eastward, one perceives the rising sun; but if one looks westward, one cannot distinguish the light because of the darkness.

But if it is asked whether Christ appeared after his resurrection naked or clothed, the answer must be that he appeared clothed. For the angel who came to announce his resurrection also appeared clothed in a white robe, because his garment was like snow.

So that we may state this in the words of one of the three Evangelists: not only new but also ancient paintings of churches testify to this very thing, asserting that the practice began with the primitive Church itself.

But if someone asks in what garments he appeared, it is certain that they were not those which he wore while he was still passible and mortal, and for which they cast lots at the cross, as the Lord had foretold: “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (Ps. 21 [Vulgate numbering 22]). Hence, if it is asked where Christ received that garment, I too ask where the angel received his white robe. But the Psalmist gives a fitting determination, saying: “The Lord has done whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. 134 [Vulgate numbering 135]). And such as he sits in heaven, such will he appear in judgment, when they shall see him whom they pierced (John 19).

Perhaps human thought still presses upon the mind, asking where the Lord was for the forty days after his resurrection when he was not staying with the disciples. It may plausibly be answered that he was in the earthly paradise, where Enoch and Elijah are, since that place is worthier and more delightful, together with the souls of the saints whom he brought forth from hell, until, ascending into heaven, “he led captivity captive” (Eph. 11 [read: Eph. 4]), as he is read to have said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

But from this statement another question arises: whether, on the very day of his death, Christ’s soul immediately descended into hell, so that it at once despoiled it by bringing the souls of the saints out of hell into paradise. Yet, although it cannot properly be said in this way, that body ascended from the tomb and soul from hell at the same time, according to that saying of the Psalmist, “You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15 [Vulgate numbering 16]), I think that Christ’s soul, as soon as it left the body, became impassible, since it was immediately free from every cause of suffering. For then it could suffer neither through association with another, nor because of sin, nor from its own nature—unless perhaps this seems to stand in the way: that just as Christ’s body and soul began together to be subject to suffering, because that body was at once ensouled in being formed and formed in being ensouled, so Christ’s body and soul also received impassibility together, so that, when the soul was restored to the body, it was glorified together with it.

But hear the counsel of the Wise Man: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not search into things stronger than yourself” (Ecclus. 3); for those who search by searching fail. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be wise beyond measure,” etc. (Rom. 12).

Therefore Christ presented himself by many proofs for forty days, appearing to them and speaking of the kingdom of God. I should still like to distinguish what those things were which Christ spoke to the apostles concerning the kingdom after his passion. But first it must be distinguished that in Scripture “the kingdom of God” is called the universal Church, the heavenly homeland, right faith, and sacred Scripture: the first on earth, the second in heaven, the third in the heart, the fourth in the book.

Concerning the kingdom it is written: “The angels shall go forth and gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13). Of the kingdom of the homeland it is found: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (ibid.). Scripture says of the kingdom of faith: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). Of the kingdom of Scripture one reads: “The kingdom shall be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruit” (Matt. 21). But Christ himself may also be understood as the kingdom of God, according to this: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matt. 12). And immediately after his resurrection the kingdom of God may be understood, according to what he says: “I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26).

Although the kingdom of God is thus distinguished in many ways, Christ nevertheless spoke to his apostles after his resurrection of the kingdom of God in four ways according to this distinction. Hear of the first, namely the kingdom of the universal Church: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). He entrusted this kingdom to Peter when he said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” And when Peter answered him for the third time, “Lord, you know that I love you,” he commanded him again, saying: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

Hear of the second, that is, the kingdom of the heavenly homeland: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” etc. (John 20). And again: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28).

Hear of the third, that is, the kingdom of faith: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). And again: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

Hear of the fourth, that is, the kingdom of Scripture: “Beginning with Moses and the prophets, he interpreted to them the things concerning himself”; and therefore again: “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled. Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scripture” (Luke 24).

Behold, we have briefly set forth those matters concerning Christ’s resurrection which pertain, according to faith, to the instruction of knowledge. Greater, however, are those which pertain according to morals to the instruction of life; these are taught elsewhere by the very agent himself, who teaches all knowledge, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER.

On the goodness of Christ the shepherd; the threefold meaning of “soul” in Scripture; the threefold nourishment with which Christ feeds us; and the hireling, the wolf, and the sheep.

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405C] “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his soul for his sheep” (John 10).

The proposed model of the parabolic comparison concerning the hireling and the shepherd, wolves and sheep, greatly terrifies me, brothers and children; for woe is me if perhaps I am a shepherd in name and a hireling in deed; if merit differs from office, if life disagrees with speech. For he is the good shepherd because he gives his soul for his sheep. And who he is, the Lord shows when he says: “I am the good shepherd.” For who is good as he is? Good in nature, good in effect, good in office.

For to be good is nothing other than to be, since his goodness is his essence. Therefore he himself is good by nature; a human being is good by grace. He himself is good essentially; a human being is good accidentally. For this reason he said: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10). He is good in effect because “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1), who is the fountain and source of good things. For this reason he said: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11). For “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 2 [read: Gen. 1]). He is good in office because the good shepherd gives his soul for his sheep.

And he indeed gave his soul not only for the righteous, but also for the unrighteous: “For Christ died for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Pet. 3). Not only for friends, but also for enemies: because “when we were enemies, we were reconciled in his blood” (Rom. 5). “For he washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). O what great grace, what a gift: that the righteous should give his soul for the unrighteous, the friend for enemies—indeed, the Lord for servants, God for human beings, the Creator for creatures.

Let us therefore take heed lest we be ungrateful for so great a grace, and prove unworthy of so great a gift. For “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). Therefore he is the good shepherd in nature, in effect, and in office.

But the good shepherd gives his soul for his sheep. The term “soul” is taken in three ways in Scripture. “Soul” means spirit, according to: “I have power to lay down my soul, and to take it again.” It means life, according to: “He who loves his soul shall lose it” (John 12). It means blood, according to: “The soul of the flesh is in the blood” (Lev. 17). In each of these senses Christ gave his soul for his sheep. For he gave his soul—that is, his spirit—on the instrument of the cross. He gave his soul—that is, his life—at the point of death. He gives his soul—that is, his blood—in the cup of the chalice.

For he who gave himself for us as the price to redeem us from death gives himself to us as food, to nourish us unto life. Therefore he is the good shepherd who gave his soul for his sheep. A shepherd is so called from feeding. And he feeds us in three ways: with the nourishment of nature, the food of doctrine, and the pasture of the Eucharist.

He feeds us with the nourishment of nature, he who “gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater” (2 Cor. 9); who “gives food to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. 146 [Vulgate numbering 147]); who says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, What shall we eat, or what shall we drink? Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 6). Therefore he is the good shepherd.

He feeds us with the food of doctrine, who feeds us with the bread of life and understanding, and “gives us to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15). For “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8). For this reason he speaks in parables: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9). Therefore he is the good shepherd.

He feeds us with the pasture of the Eucharist, who says in the Gospel: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. For the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6). May he feed us in the future with the banquets of glory, of which the Psalmist said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16 [Vulgate numbering 17]). For “in the voice of exultation and confession is the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41 [Vulgate numbering 42]). “You shall eat,” he says, “and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22). And: “To the victor I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2). Therefore he is the good shepherd because he gives his soul for his sheep.

But the hireling, who is not a shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The hireling is one who holds the place of a shepherd but does not perform a shepherd’s work; who feeds the sheep for a wage not spiritual but temporal, not true but false, not eternal but passing: namely, for earthly profit, worldly glory, and human favour. But “Amen, I say to you, he has received his reward” (Matt. 6).

Whether someone is a shepherd, and whether the sheep are truly his own, may be tested by this proof: “If anyone has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need and closes his bowels against him” (1 John 3), he certainly is not a shepherd but a hireling. For if he does not give his sheep earthly substance, how would he give his soul for them? “Skin for skin,” it says, “and all that a man has he will give for his soul” (Job 2).

Such a person sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf is the devil; the wolf is the heretic; the wolf is the tyrant. Of the first it is said: “The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.” Of the second one reads: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7). Of the third it is written: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (Luke 10). The heretic snatches; the tyrant scatters; but the devil both scatters and snatches. He scatters through violence and snatches through fraud, because he is violent as a lion and deceitful as a dragon.

The hireling sees any one of these wolves coming, leaves the sheep, and flees—not always by changing location, but often by withholding protection. For he hides, is silent, and endures when he sees injustice, violence, and faithlessness inflicted upon the powerless, orphans, and needy, as a mute dog unable to bark (Isa. 46 [read: Isa. 56]). Alas, how many such hirelings we have and lament [variant reading: “see”] in the Church today! Because, while they have the name and office of shepherd but not the merit, heretics gain strength, tyrants rage, and the faithless persecute. For scarcely anyone is found who places himself as a wall for the house of Israel or stands in opposition on the day of the Lord (Ezek. 13). “For the harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” (Luke 10). Although we see many in name, we nevertheless see few in deed. Therefore the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep, since “our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5).

But the hireling flees because he is a hireling, and the sheep are no concern of his. “But I,” says the Lord, “am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and mine know me.” I know mine by approval, love, and governance; mine know me by devotion, obedience, and imitation. “For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2). Conversely, he says to the reprobate: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” But his sheep follow him and know his voice. They do not follow a stranger, but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.

“As the Father knows me and I know the Father.” The Son knows the Father through himself, but we know through him, as he says elsewhere: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11). Likewise John says: “No one has ever seen God except the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 4 [read: John 1]).

This text can be understood in two ways, because it may be construed in two ways. First, it may be said as one sentence: “I know mine, and mine know me, as the Father knows me and I know the Father.” Thus a likeness of knowledge between shepherd and sheep is indicated, corresponding to that between Father and Son. But this knowledge is love, as John the Evangelist testifies, saying: “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2). Therefore Truth says: “He who loves me will keep my word” (John 14). Thus the sense is: as the Father loves me and I love the Father, so I love my sheep and they love me. The evident proof of this love is that “I lay down my soul for my sheep.” For “no one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his soul for his friends” (John 15).

Likewise: “My sheep hear my voice,” because “a people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obey me” (Ps. 17 [Vulgate numbering 18]).

Or it may be understood by dividing it under another clause. For he had said before: “I know mine, and mine know me”; now he shows by whose agency and for what end he knows them. By whose agency: because “as the Father knows me and I know the Father.” For what end: because “I lay down my soul for my sheep.” As though he had said more plainly: What the Father wills, I also will. Therefore, in accordance with the Father’s good pleasure, I lay down my soul for my sheep.

It has been shown what a shepherd ought to be; it must therefore be shown what sheep ought to be. Three things are especially commended in a sheep: gentleness, innocence, and usefulness. For it is written: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before one who shears it, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). Everything that comes from a sheep is useful: milk and wool, hide and flesh, offspring and dung, which enriches the soil.

Such should the faithful be: gentle, so that they may not return evil for evil, nor curse for curse, following his example (1 Pet. 3): “When he was cursed, he did not curse; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2). They should be innocent, so that they offend no one, harm no one, injure no one; but rather love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, and pray for those who persecute and slander them, following the example of him who makes his sun rise upon good and evil and sends rain upon righteous and unrighteous alike (Matt. 5). They should be useful, so that they render to their shepherds milk and wool, or dung and offspring—that is, first-fruits, tithes, and offerings. “For the labourer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. 5). For this reason the Apostle said: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9).

It follows: “And I have other sheep that are not from this fold; them also I must bring, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.” The Lord therefore had sheep both justified by grace and predestined to life. Of the justified he had said before: “I know mine, and mine know me.” Of the predestined he adds: “I have other sheep that are not from this fold.” The first had already been gathered from the Jewish people; the second were still to be gathered from the Gentile people. Yet both were to be assembled, so that there might be one fold and one shepherd: that is, one Church and one Lord. “For he is our peace, who made both one, so that two walls coming from opposite directions might meet in one cornerstone” (Eph. 2).

Any sheep found outside this fold is exposed to the bites of wolves, since all who were not in the ark perished in the flood (Gen. 4 [read: Gen. 7]). Moreover, some sheep are sluggish, some diseased, and some wandering. The good shepherd, therefore, must prick the sluggish, support the diseased, and gather the wandering. These three functions are well signified by the shepherd’s staff, which is sharp at the end, straight in the middle, and hooked at the top: sharp, that it may prick sluggish and fat sheep; straight, that it may support diseased and weak sheep; hooked, that it may gather back sheep that wander and go astray.

The Lord entrusted his sheep to Peter to be fed (John 21), repeating the command three times; he appointed Peter as his shepherd in his place.
