For this reason today’s station is celebrated in his basilica, to the praise and glory of Jesus Christ, the supreme shepherd of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE SOLEMNITY OF THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.

On the three solemnities—Passover, the Feast of Tabernacles, and Pentecost—and how we ought to celebrate them; finally, on the three classes of those who celebrate them.

[Col. 0409]

[Col. 0409D] “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. 4).

Formerly three solemnities were celebrated in the Law—not the only ones, but the principal ones—namely Passover, Pentecost, and Scenopegia: that is, the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of tabernacles. We too celebrate them in the Gospel, not according to the letter but in the spirit: Passover in the resurrection; Scenopegia in the ascension; Pentecost in the sending of the Paraclete.

For Christ led captivity captive when, rising again, he brought his bound ones out of the pit in which there was no water (Zech. 9). He ascended on high (Ps. 67 [Vulgate numbering 68]) when he was exalted above the heaven of heavens toward the east. He gave gifts to human beings when he poured out the Holy Spirit upon all flesh. Therefore Christ, ascending on high, gave gifts to human beings, because “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

Passover is indeed called a passing-over, because the angel passed through Egypt, destroying Egypt’s firstborn from human being to beast; but he passed over the houses of the Hebrews, harming none of them, because they had been marked with the blood of the lamb (Exod. 12). Then the people of Israel set out on their journey to pass from Egypt into the wilderness. But “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). Our houses are touched with his blood when our hearts are marked by faith in the Passion—a faith which the devil alone cannot destroy in the person who lives inwardly by faith.

John the Evangelist defines this passing-over, saying: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come that he should pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own, loved them to the end” (John 13). Therefore, rising again, he passed from death to life, from labour to rest, from the world to the Father. For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6).

Scenopegia means the pitching of tents, because Israel dwelt in tents in the wilderness for forty years (Deut. 16). In remembrance of this the Jews still celebrate Scenopegia, dwelling in tents. But the tent is Christ’s assumed body, in which divinity lies hidden beneath humanity; of it the Psalmist says: “He has set his tent in the sun” (Ps. 18 [Vulgate numbering 19]). Christ did not pitch this tent while in mortal flesh, because “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (ibid.), passing from place to place in order to fulfil the ministry he had undertaken. But he then pitched his tent when, “taken up into heaven, he sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16), resting in the Father’s patrimonial goods, “until he makes his enemies the footstool of his feet” (Ps. 109 [Vulgate numbering 110]).

*Pentēkonta* (πεντήκοντα) in Greek, *asiarco* [Hebrew as printed], means “fifty” in Latin; hence that solemnity is called Pentecost, which is observed in remembrance of the Law given on the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt (Exod. 20). But we celebrate Pentecost in honour of the Spirit, the Paraclete, who was given to the apostles on the fiftieth day after Christ rose from the dead (Acts 2). He is indeed the saving light, written by the finger of God not on tablets of stone but in human hearts (2 Cor. 3), of whom John says: “The anointing will teach you about all things” (1 John 2). And Christ says in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 15 [read: John 16]).

We celebrate the solemnity of this day with honour, recalling that, when the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, “there suddenly came from heaven a sound of the Holy Spirit coming with might” (Acts 2). But in order that every act of Christ may be a lesson for the Christian, let us seek not only allegory, which instructs the soul in knowledge, but especially tropology, which instructs the mind in salvation.

For Christ rose that we might rise; he ascended that we might ascend; he gave the Paraclete that we might be consoled. For *Paraclete* means “advocate” or “consoler.” But he rose from the dead after three days; then, after forty days, he ascended into heaven; from that point, after ten days, he gave the Paraclete. All things are full of divine mysteries, and each overflows with heavenly sweetness—if only they have a diligent observer who knows how to draw “honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone” (Deut. 31 [read: Deut. 32]).

Let us therefore rise, brothers and children; let us rise from the dead after three days. The first resurrection is the remission of sins, of which John says: “Blessed are those who have a part in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20). We arrive at this by the path of three days, by which the children of Israel went out of Egypt in order to sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness. “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50 [Vulgate numbering 51]).

Therefore the path of the first day, by which we advance toward the resurrection of the soul, is the examination of sins: when the sinner inquires into and investigates the manner, number, and other circumstances of sins, according to: “I will think upon my sin” (Ps. 3 [read: Ps. 37/38]). This is the first day, this the first illumination of the mind. The second follows it: namely, the recollection of offences, when the sinner sets before himself the manner, number, and other circumstances of offences, according to: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. 5 [read: Ps. 50/51]). This is the second day, this the second illumination of the mind.

The third in turn follows: namely, contrition for vices, when the penitent sinner crushes all vices through sorrow, as he says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93 [Vulgate numbering 94]). Immediately, therefore, the girl is raised in the house (Matt. 9), the young man at the gate (Luke 7), Lazarus in the tomb (John 11). For at whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, “I will remember none of all his iniquities: he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33), says the almighty Lord.

This, therefore, is Passover, or the solemnity in which we celebrate the saving passage from death to life, from evil to good, from darkness to light, from vices to virtues. Then the soul passes from the darkness of Egypt to the pillar of cloud that overshadows by day and the pillar of fire that shines by night (Exod. 14), when through repentance the sinner lays aside the inner darkness of which the Apostle says: “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1), and takes on the light of truth, which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1), which cools through the cloud and illumines through the fire.

But forty days after the resurrection we ought to ascend, so that, establishing “ascents in [our] heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83 [Vulgate numbering 84]), we may ascend from strength to strength until we see the God of gods in Zion. Therefore let us produce worthy fruits of repentance (Matt. 3), especially prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, so that, just as through sin we offend three—God, ourselves, and our neighbour—so through satisfaction we may please three: prayer being directed to God, fasting borne upon ourselves, and almsgiving distributed to our neighbour.

You know, dearly beloved, that forty is the special and proper number of satisfaction; therefore we include under this number the observance of Christian warfare, through which, in order to make satisfaction to the Lord for what we have committed, we pay the tenth part of the whole year. For, to pass over this number’s other significations, which are manifold in the Scriptures, Jonah granted the Ninevites this span [Col. 0413B] of time, that they might turn to the Lord and make satisfaction for what they had committed: “Yet forty days,” he says, “and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jon. 1). For it is an abundant number, rising by the aggregation of its parts to fifty, which, by the rationale of the jubilee, signifies full remission; because, if we thus ascend, after ten days we shall receive the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. For the ten days are the observance of the Decalogue, which is wholly fulfilled in love of God and neighbour; for “charity is the fullness of the law” (Tim. 2), and “the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 2).

For its commandments too are written on two tablets: three on one, which indicate the love of God. Of these the first concerns the Father: [Col. 0413C] “You shall have no strange god”; the second, the Son: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”; the third, the Holy Spirit: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day, which is the sanctification of true rest” (Exod. 20). Therefore, not inappropriately, on the fiftieth day, which is the first after the seventh week, he was sent into the apostles, to establish them in that rest of peace. Of this Truth says in the Gospel: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14). Therefore, after these ten days—that is, after the tenfold observance of God’s commandments—we receive the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete: not because we had not received the Paraclete Spirit before, since “the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts through [Col. 0413D] the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 15), but because we receive him more abundantly and for another purpose. Thus the apostles received the Holy Spirit on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, when the Lord said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20); and yet they received the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day. For “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2).

The purpose for which they received the Holy Spirit on that day was shown through visible figures; for “there appeared to them divided tongues as [Col. 0414A] of fire, and one sat upon each of them” (ibid.). Fire expressed steadfastness, and the tongue knowledge; for fire consolidates and strengthens a soft and fragile vessel, while the tongue expresses and expounds the affection of the mind. The Holy Spirit was given to the apostles for steadfastness, so that, clothed with the power of the Spirit from on high, they might be witnesses in Jerusalem and Samaria and to the uttermost part of the earth (Luke 24; Acts 1). He was given for knowledge, so that the apostles might speak in diverse tongues the mighty works of God, in order that their sound might go forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Rom. 10). Hence elsewhere it is read: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. 1).

Thus we, brethren and children, if we keep the commandments of the Decalogue, assuredly receive the Holy Spirit [Col. 0414B] in fiery tongues, so that there may be blazing fire in the heart and a sounding tongue in the mouth. Of this fire the Lord says: “From on high he sent fire into my bones” (Lam. 1); likewise: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). And elsewhere: “Fire shall always burn upon my altar” (Lev. 6). Solomon expounded this fire when he said: “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8). Therefore let the fire burn in the heart, so that the tongue may fittingly sound in the mouth. For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous acts, and take my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49). Certainly, when a man’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is held in contempt, and it is said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4); “Hypocrite, first cast out [Col. 0414C] the beam from your eye, and then you will cast out the mote from your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7). “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2.)

Three orders of the faithful in the Church celebrate these three solemnities: beginners, who rise through humble penitence; those making progress, who ascend through abundant righteousness; and the perfected, who are consoled through final perseverance. These three ranks of the faithful are signified by the three fifties of psalms. The first ends in penitence, which that fiftieth psalm teaches: “Have mercy on me, O God.” The second ends in righteousness, which that hundredth psalm expresses: “Mercy and judgment I will sing to you, [Col. 0414D] O Lord.” The third ends in perseverance of praise, which the final psalm expounds: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” These three states are the three chambers of Noah’s ark (Gen. 9). These are the three days of which the Lord says: “Today I cast out demons, tomorrow I perform cures, and on the third day I am consummated” (Luke 13).

Therefore, dearly beloved, let us celebrate these solemnities not so much with the body as with the heart, because the remnants of thoughts shall keep a festival day for the Lord (Ps. 75), through the inspiration of the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father and the Son (John 16). With whom he is the living and true God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE SOLEMNITY OF HOLY PENTECOST

On the twofold melting and the difference between things melted; on the wisdom and charity of the apostles; and on the fact that these two should be joined in the office of preaching, so that the preacher may teach by word and example.

[Col. 0415]

[Col. 0415A] “The earth was melted, and all who dwell in it; I established its pillars” (Ps. 74).

There is a twofold melting: one of the good, of which the Bride says in the Song: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5); the other of the wicked, of which the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Like melted wax they shall be removed” (Ps. 57). Moreover, some things melt only through moisture, while others melt through heat and moisture. Through heat, as wax; through moisture, as salt; through heat and moisture alike, as snow. Again, some things, when they melt, remain; others, when they melt, perish. Wax and tallow melt and remain; snow and ice melt and perish.

Thus certain wicked persons melt only through heat: namely, those dissolved by spiritual desires, which proceed from the heat of the heart, as by anger or envy. Of them it is read that “they burned in their desires” (Dan. 13), inflamed by Gehenna. Others melt only through moisture: namely, those dissolved by bodily desires, which proceed from the moisture of the flesh, as by gluttony or lust. Of them it is read that Behemoth sleeps in moist places, trusting that Jordan will flow into his mouth (Job 40). Others melt through heat and moisture alike: namely, those dissolved both by spiritual desires and bodily lusts. Of these, that the punishment may resemble the fault, Scripture says that “from snowy waters they shall pass to excessive heat [Col. 0415C]” (Job 24). David says of them: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57). Jacob says of these: “You have been poured out like water; do not increase, because you ascended your father’s bed” (Gen. 48).

Some of them melt and remain, like those who sin and repent, because through penitence they are restored. For “in whatever hour the sinner, having turned, groans, he shall live and shall not die, says the Lord” (Ezek. 18). Others melt and perish, like those who sin and never repent, because they are condemned for their impenitence. For “when an impious man has died, there shall be no hope concerning him” (Prov. 11). O how dangerous is this manner of melting: that one should die [Col. 0415D] in sin! Behold, the world is almost wholly melted by vices; it is almost wholly melted in sins. For “iniquity has abounded, and the charity of many has grown cold” (Matt. 24).—“For people glory when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2). Because “when the impious man comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). And indeed, the longer God sustains them in the present through patience, the more grievously he will punish them in the future through justice; for, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, “God gave them time to repent, and they abused it” (Job 24).

Wax at fire first softens, secondly melts, thirdly vanishes. Thus also the devil, who is the instigator of evils, first kindles the fire of temptation, through which the soul, more melted, softens like wax when it begins to take delight. Secondly, he kindles the fire of temptation more strongly, through which the soul, more melted, melts like wax when it begins to consent. Thirdly, he kindles the fire of temptation more and more strongly, through which the soul, more and more heated, utterly vanishes like wax [Col. 0416B] when it begins to commit the deed. For “sin, when it has been consummated, brings forth death” (Jas. 1), on account of which it is written: “As wax before the face of fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67).

Therefore, brethren and children, let us seek the Lord while he may be found; let us call upon him while he is near (Isa. 55), lest perhaps we be among those of whom the Prophet declares beforehand: “The earth was melted, and all who dwell in it.” But that we may be among those of whom the Lord says: “I established its pillars.” By the name *earth* human flesh may be understood, which was formed from the clay of the earth. To it the Lord says: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3). Those dwelling in it may be understood as those living in the flesh, of whom Scripture says: “They dwell in houses of clay and have an earthly [Col. 0416C] foundation” (Job 4). Such men Christ found when he came, and left behind when he ascended. For “all have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 13). But lest the whole earth, having melted, should perish, God established its pillars when, on the fiftieth day after his resurrection, he clothed the apostles with the power of the Holy Spirit from on high (Acts 1 and 2). They are denoted by the name of pillars, because through them the Church is upheld, as the Apostle Paul also says, since Peter, James, and John seemed to be pillars (Gal. 2). “For unless the Lord had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom” (Isa. 1).

“The earth was melted, and all who dwell in it. But the Lord established its [Col. 0416D] pillars.” For this strengthening the pillars themselves pray, saying: “Establish, O God, what you have wrought in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem” (Ps. 67). For “when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting, etc. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2).

Before the apostles received the Holy Spirit, as though melted by fear, they fled after abandoning Christ (Matt. 26). But when they received the Paraclete Spirit, as though strengthened by the power of the Spirit from on high, “they went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). Hence Peter, who had first denied him at a maidservant’s voice (Matt. 26), afterwards bore Christ’s name before kings and rulers, steadfastly affirming that one must obey God rather than men (Acts 5).

The wicked melt through vices and sins; but the good [Col. 0417B] are strengthened through virtues and gifts. The former melt through the heat of desire and the moisture of concupiscence; the latter are strengthened through the heat of charity and the moisture of wisdom. For “there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire” (Acts 2). He mentions two things—fire and tongue—representing invisible realities through visible forms. Fire lives in what is dry; the tongue remains in moisture. Fire signifies charity, but the tongue expresses wisdom. Of the heat of charity Solomon says in the Song: “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8). Of the moisture of wisdom he says in Proverbs: “Deep water is speech from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing torrent is the fountain of wisdom” (Prov. 17). Among virtues charity is chief; among gifts wisdom is first. Of the former the Apostle says: “The greater of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13). Of the latter the prophet says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, etc., shall rest upon him” (Isa. 2).

Therefore Christ on this day poured these two—the first and the chief—into the apostles through the Holy Spirit, under the figure of fire and tongue; he was about to send them into the world to preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16). Charity forms one’s life, and wisdom forms doctrine. These two must be joined in preaching, so that a man may teach not only by word but also by example. For “when a man’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is held in contempt”; and it is said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4); “Hypocrite, first cast out [Col. 0417D] the beam from your own eye, and then you will cast out the mote from your brother’s eye” (Luke 6); “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2). “Jesus therefore began to do and to teach” (Acts 1), “leaving us an example, that we should follow his steps; he committed no sin,” so that integrity might be in our life; “neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2; Isa. 53), so that truth might be in doctrine. For “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Hence pomegranates with golden bells hung from the high priest’s garment (Exod. 18).

Let the fire of love therefore first burn in the heart, that thereafter the tongue of preaching may sound in the mouth (Matt. 12). For “when there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, then they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2). Behold, they now see fulfilled what they had formerly heard promised: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (John 14).

In this passage fire and tongue are joined, since “there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire” (Acts 2). In the Gospel which you heard, love and speech are joined, because “he who loves me [Col. 0418B] will keep my word” (John 14). In the Psalm spirit and doctrine are likewise joined: “Strengthen me with a willing spirit. I will teach transgressors your ways” (Ps. 50). From this threefold testimony it may be known that, just as tongue, speech, and doctrine are one, so fire, love, and spirit are one. For “our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4); “God is charity” (1 John 4); and “charity is poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). He is the love of the Father and the Son, the affection and bond of both, to whom this day’s solemnity is especially dedicated.

Because the earth and all its inhabitants were melted, God established its pillars. But again, because God established its pillars, the earth and all its inhabitants were melted. For after the apostles had received the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and addressed the people, expounding to them the prophecy of Joel and other prophetic testimonies. Hearing these things, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brethren?” But Peter said to them: “Do penance, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.” Thus [Col. 0418C] there were baptized and added on that day about three thousand souls (Acts 2). Behold, these men were melted through both heat and moisture: through the heat of penitence and the moisture of baptism. Of the heat of penitence the Psalmist says: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze forth” (Ps. 38). Of the moisture of baptism the Lord says: “Unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3).

Therefore, brethren and children, we who have already been melted through the water of baptism, let us yet be melted through the heat of penitence, that our sins may be blotted out, by the gift of the Paraclete Spirit, who is the true remission of sins, and who with the Father and the Son lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

On the twofold baptism commended to us in the Gospel; how the apostles were baptized in the Holy Spirit; and when we are baptized in the Spirit.

[Col. 0419]

[Col. 0419A] “John indeed baptized with water; but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1).

For a twofold baptism is commended to us in the Gospel: namely, in water and in fire; but in material water and spiritual fire, lest either the water extinguish the fire or the fire consume the water. John the Baptist spoke of both baptisms: “I baptize you in water; but one stands in your midst, who baptizes you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3; Luke 3). Yet each baptism is sanctified in the Word, and each is sanctified in the Spirit. For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). Every firmness and every power is bestowed by God the Father, through the Word, in the Holy Spirit. For “there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. And these three are one” (1 John 5).

John indeed baptized with water only. Since he was merely a man, he could consecrate water neither through the Word nor through the Spirit. But Jesus baptizes in the Spirit, because, being God from God, through the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father (John 15), he himself sanctifies and purifies the soul into which he pours the Holy Spirit. Observe carefully how baptismal water is sanctified in the Word. “Baptize,” he says, “all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). For the name—that is, the invocation of the Trinity—[Col. 0419C] sanctifies the water, so that, washing the body, it may purify the heart. Thus he said: “Cleansing her,” that is, the Church, “by the washing of water in the word of life” (Eph. 5). For the word comes to the element, and a sacrament comes into being.

Observe also carefully how baptismal water is sanctified in the Spirit, as Truth testifies when he says: “Unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3). For just as a human being is born by nature from a woman, but from a man, because the man makes the woman fruitful so that she may conceive, so by grace one is born again from water, but from the Spirit. For the Spirit sanctifies the water so that it may purify. For that which is naturally from flesh is flesh; but that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

[Col. 0419D] But baptism of fire likewise is sanctified both in the Word and in the Spirit, as the epistle reading which you heard shows: “When,” it says, “the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, [Col. 0420A] and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2). When you hear that divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, observe baptism in fire. When you hear that they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, observe sanctification in the Spirit. When you hear that they began to speak in various tongues, observe sanctification in the Word.

For today was fulfilled what the prophet had foretold in the person of the Church: “From on high he sent fire into my bones” (Lam. 1). From on high—that is, from heaven—he sent fire, that is, the Holy Spirit, in fiery tongues. “Into my bones,” that is, into the apostles, through whom the entire body of the Church is upheld; and at that time he made them bones—that is, strong, steadfast, and mighty—as he had promised them: “You shall receive,” he said, “the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judaea and Samaria and even to the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 2).

This fire is the Holy Spirit, of whom Scripture says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4): love, charity, and affection. Of this fire the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). Fire illuminates by its brightness and purifies by its heat. The Holy Spirit illuminates the mind through wisdom and purifies it through charity; by these the soul is baptized—that is, purified—in the Spirit: through wisdom from the darkness of ignorance, and through charity from the stains of guilt. Therefore we are baptized in the Spirit when the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5). Of this baptism the Lord foretold through the prophet: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2). The apostles therefore rightly received this baptism, in accordance with the Lord’s promise to them: “John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence.”

On the fiftieth day after the immolation of the paschal lamb, when the Passover had been celebrated, the children of Israel departed from Egypt through the Red Sea, the Egyptians having been drowned and the Hebrews delivered; and when Moses had gone up Mount Sinai to stand before the Lord while the people waited at the foot of the mountain, on that very fiftieth day they began to hear thunder and see lightning flash. The whole people saw also the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain; and then the Lord [Col. 0421A] gave the law to the children of Israel, written on stone tablets by the finger of God (Exod. 19).

These things are full of divine mysteries and resound with heavenly sacraments. For today the shadow brought forth light and the figure truth. After the immolation of Christ, who is the true paschal Lamb, of whom the Apostle says, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5), and after that *pascha*—that is, passage—had been celebrated, of which John says, “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13), the children of Israel—that is, Christian peoples, seeing God through faith—depart from Egypt, that is, from the darkness of vices, through the Red Sea, that is, through the sacrament of baptism reddened by Christ’s blood. In it, the Egyptians having been drowned—that is, sins having been blotted out—the Hebrews are delivered—that is, the faithful are justified.

This is fulfilled when, after the day of the Lord’s Passion, baptism, initiated by the paschal mysteries, is consecrated, in which catechumens are born again. And when the true Moses—that is, Christ—had ascended the mountain, that is, heaven, to sit at the right hand of God the Father (Mark 16), on the fiftieth day after Passover, which is called Pentecost, thunder began to be heard and lightning to flash. For “suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house [Col. 0422A] where they were sitting; and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one sat upon each of them” (Acts 2).

You may now recognize how the shadow brought forth light and the figure truth. When you hear that a sound suddenly came from heaven, understand that thunder was heard. But when you understand that divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, recognize flashing lightning. And when you hear that God gave the law to the waiting children of Israel, understand that he gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles, as he had commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem but to await the promise of the Father, “which,” he said, “you have heard through my mouth: for John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence.”

This is the law of grace, [Col. 0422B] written on the tablets of the heart and by the finger of God, as the Lord himself had promised: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you” (John 13). This is the anointing which, according to John (1 John 1), teaches us concerning all things. May the Lord Jesus Christ anoint us through the Holy Spirit with this anointing, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths (Isa. 2), until, ascending from strength to strength, we see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83).

## SERMON XXV. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

[Col. 0421]

[Col. 0421C] “From on high he sent fire into my bones” (Lam. 1).

These are the inward words of the Church speaking through the prophet Jeremiah. The One on high is the Father; the sender is the Son; the fire is the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Father, who is most high because he is the principle without principle, who is from none and from whom are all things, the Psalmist says: “The Lord is high, and he regards the lowly; and he knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137). Concerning the Son, who is sent because he is sent by the Father and sends the Holy Spirit, Truth himself says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, he will bear testimony concerning me” (John 11). Concerning the fire, which is the Holy Spirit, the love of the Father and the Son, the pledge and bond of both, Scripture says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. [Col. 0421D] 4).

From on high, therefore—that is, from the Father—the Son sent fire, that is, the Holy Spirit, into the mouths of his ministers. Thus the Church speaks, namely in the apostles, through whom the body of the Church is upheld; at that time he made them, who had been carnal, as it were bones. That is, he made the fearful strong when he clothed them with the power of the Spirit from on high, so that they might all be witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judaea and Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth (Acts 1). Of this fire the Lord says: “I came [Col. 0422C] to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12).

It should be noted that the Spirit was sent in threefold manner. First, in a dove; secondly, in a breath; thirdly, in fire. Of the first it is written that, when Jesus had been baptized in the Jordan, heaven was opened, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son,” etc. (Matt. 3). Of the second it is written that “when Jesus said to the apostles, ‘Peace be with you,’ he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,’” etc. (John 20). Of the third it is written: “There suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. [Col. 0422D] And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one sat upon each of them” (Acts 2).

The first sending took place at baptism, the second at the resurrection, the third at Pentecost. In the first sending the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” In the second sending the Son’s word was heard: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.” In the third sending the Spirit’s sound was heard, [Col. 0423A] because there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind. All these things are full of divine mysteries and pregnant with heavenly sacraments. But since the well is deep, from where shall I draw water? I shall therefore say, through the inspiration of him “who breathes where he wills, and no one knows whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3).

I say, then, that he was sent in the dove upon Christ for judgment and manifestation; in breath he was sent into the apostles for judgment and discernment; in fire he was sent into the disciples for strength and confirmation. The dove lacks the bitterness of gall and abounds in fruitfulness of offspring. Thus this shows that Christ lacks every bitterness of vices and abounds in every fruitfulness of virtues. The Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove, because he is the one “who committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2); “in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2); and “from whose fullness we have received” (John 1), because he baptizes in the Holy Spirit, removing sins and vices and conferring graces and virtues. As [Col. 0423B] John the Baptist bore witness, saying: “I saw the Spirit descending and remaining upon him; this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit; and I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (ibid.).

The Father’s voice was therefore heard at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3), because through baptism from water and the Holy Spirit we are born again as children of God, vices being laid aside and virtues assumed, receiving the spirit of adoption in which we cry: “Abba, Father” (Mark 14). For “unless a man is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3), so that he may be the child of him from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.

Moreover, just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (John 15), so breath proceeds from the lungs and heart. When breath is emitted, if the mouth is closed, it cools the air; if the mouth is opened, it warms the air. Thus, when a spiritual authority pronounces judgment, if the mouth is closed—as when, according to what is written, a sinner is bound by excommunication or interdict—he is undoubtedly cooled, because he is frozen in evil. For it is just that “he who is filthy, let him be filthy still” (Rev. 22). But if the mouth is opened, so that a sinner is absolved from excommunication, the penitent is undoubtedly warmed, because he is kindled toward good. For it is fitting that “he who is righteous, let him be justified still” (ibid.). In this judgment discernment of spirits is most necessary, lest they should, contrary to the apostolic rule, call good evil or the reverse, making darkness light and light darkness (Isa. 5), killing souls that do not die or giving life to souls that do not live.

The Son’s word was therefore heard at the resurrection, when he said to the apostles: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” [Col. 0424A] (John 20), because through forgiveness of sin the soul rises from the death of guilt, of which the Apocalypse says: “He who has a part in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20). For the Father gave all judgment to the Son, who says of himself: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11).

Fire principally does two things: it warms and it shines. Because it warms, it signifies charity; because it shines, it signifies wisdom. Of the warmth of charity Solomon says: “Love is strong as death, and jealousy is hard as hell. Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8). Of the brightness of wisdom he likewise says: “Wisdom is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of divine majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. 7). The Holy Spirit was therefore sent to the apostles in fire so that they might shine through wisdom and be warm through charity. For charity forms life, and wisdom forms doctrine; these two must be joined in preaching, so that one may teach by word and by example. For “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

These two were necessary for the apostles, who were about to go forth into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature. Therefore, when divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, then “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2). The Spirit’s sound was heard at Pentecost in order to show that, just as on the fiftieth day after the typical Passover the law of the letter was given to the children of Israel from Mount [Col. 0424C] Sinai with lightning and thunder (Exod. 20), so on the fiftieth day after the true Passover the law of grace was given to the apostles from on high, indeed in fire and sound. “For the Spirit breathes where he wills, and no one hears him, nor knows whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3).

To show how great the difference is between servants and the Lord, the Holy Spirit was sent upon Christ in a living thing, in a dove; upon the apostles, in an inanimate thing, in the breath of wind and fire. For, as a living thing is preferred to inanimate things, so Christ surpasses the apostles in this respect—indeed, by far more. For “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who shall be like the Most High among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88). Therefore, in this threefold vision were heard the voice of the Father, the word of the Son, and the sound of the Spirit, so that it might thereby be shown that this Paraclete was sent in time not only by the Father and the Son, but also by himself; for the works of the Trinity are undivided.

Yet there is this difference between eternal procession and temporal mission: eternally he proceeds by receiving nature; temporally he is sent by giving grace. Therefore, because he received his nature not from himself but from the Father together with the Son, he is sent eternally by the Father; he proceeds not from himself, but from the Father and the Son. But because he gives grace together with the Father and the Son, he is sent temporally not only by the Father and the Son, but also by himself. Eternally the Holy Spirit proceeds from another, but not into another; temporally, however, he is sent by another and into another.

[Col. 0425A] For the Greek errs in saying that he is called the Spirit of the Son because he eternally proceeds into the Son; rather, as the Latin believes, he is called the Spirit of the Son because he eternally proceeds from the Son—because it is only the Son who has him from the Father from eternity. Indeed, the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father into the Son because he eternally effects nothing in him; for, according to his eternal nature, the Son is neither illuminated nor sanctified by him. But he is called the Spirit of the Son because he proceeds from the Son, just as he is called the Spirit of the Father because he proceeds from the Father; not because he eternally proceeds into the Son, just as neither does he proceed into the Father.

Holy Scripture testifies to both. For Christ says in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). And the Apostle says: “The Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you” (Rom. 8). The same Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4); and again: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8 [the printed text reads Rom. III]).

Who, what, and how great this Spirit is is demonstrated by sacred testimonies. For it is written that he is “the intelligent Spirit, artificer of all things: holy, one, manifold, subtle, mobile, undefiled, pure, gracious, loving the good, keen, unhindered, beneficent, humane, kindly, steadfast, secure, intelligible, pure. … For the Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts without understanding, and will be reproved by iniquity coming upon it. [Col. 0425C] For the spirit of wisdom is kindly and will not acquit a blasphemer of the words of his lips; for God is witness of his inmost parts, the true searcher of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue” (Wis. 1, 7).

Elsewhere it is written of this Spirit: “Renew a right spirit within my inward parts”; and, “Strengthen me with a sovereign spirit” (Ps. 50); “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right land” (Ps. 142), and so forth.

Hear what Truth says to the apostles concerning the Spirit: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and will remind you of everything that I have said to you” (John 14).

“If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth; for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16), and so forth.

*Paraclete* means “advocate” or “comforter,” as the Apostle says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8), because he makes us intercede. To this the Prophet says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93).

[Col. 0426A] Hear another discourse upon this Spirit: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be accursed’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit. Now there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for benefit. To one is given through the Holy Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

The same Apostle says elsewhere: “The love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. [Col. 0426B] 5). “The Lord is Spirit. But where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3): for “those who are led by the Spirit of God are not under the law. For the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, gentleness, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no law” (Gal. 5).

This is the Spirit of whom it is written at the beginning of Genesis (ch. 1): “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” And of whom Gabriel says to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). This Spirit is love, concerning whom John the Apostle says: “God is love; and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). For “whoever is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6), since this Spirit is an anointing.

[Col. 0426C] Of him the same John says: “His anointing will teach you concerning all things” (1 John 2). And Peter the Apostle says of it: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom he anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 4). As he himself testifies through the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Isa. 61).

This Spirit is the finger of God, of whom Truth says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 11). Of him Pharaoh’s magicians said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8).

This Spirit is the divine gift, of whom the Lord says: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me to drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him to give you the water of life” (John 4). Indeed, this Spirit is unquestionably consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son, as John the Evangelist testifies: “There are three,” he says, “who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5).

[Col. 0426D] They are one in nature, one in name, one in power. “Baptize,” he says, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). He does not say, “in the names,” but “in the name,” because the three have one name, one nature, one power. Without doubt he is God: he fills all things, contains all things, can do all things, and knows all things. It is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world; and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. 1), possessing all power and beholding all things. For “by the Word of God the heavens were established” (Ps. 32), and so forth.

[Col. 0427A] “Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103). Oh, how sweet this Spirit is, how delightful, how pleasant! He knows who has tasted. “Taste,” he says, “and see how sweet the Lord is!” (Ps. 33).

Therefore let us ask him, brothers and children, with heart and unfeigned faith alike (1 Tim. 1), that through his mercy he may pour himself into us and, by dwelling within us, make us into a temple of glory. He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Son unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

On the severity and kindness of God; on the rich man and the steward; on God’s call and its effect; on debt and debtors; on what wheat and oil signify; on the children of this age and of light; and on the mammon of iniquity.

[Col. 0427]

[Col. 0427B] “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, who was accused before him as though he had squandered his goods” (Luke 16).

You have often heard how this parable may be understood in summary. But I do not think that you have yet heard how it ought to be understood in detail. Let us therefore set aside what others have expounded and pursue what is to be expounded by us.

God, then, because he is just and merciful (Ps. 114), displays in this parable both severity and kindness: severity, because he removed the wasteful steward from his stewardship; kindness, because, though offended by the steward, he commended his prudence. The rich man is Christ, who is rich in all things and above all (Rom. 10): his is “the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23).

A steward is so called as the guardian of an estate. He is the ruler of the Church, who ought to guard the estate—that is, the Church. Christ has many stewards, because he has appointed many rulers in the Church. Among them one is good and is commended when it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25). Another is evil and is condemned when it is said: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you begged me. Ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?” And he handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt (Matt. 18).

[Col. 0427D] Such was this steward, who was accused before his lord as though he had squandered his goods. He appeared blameworthy in two respects and on account of two things: because he had corrupted his reputation and because he had squandered his master’s property. Alas, how many such prelates are in the Church today! When they should be “an aroma of life unto life,” they have become “an aroma of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2); and when they should be stewards, they themselves have become squanderers.

A prelate of the Church ought to have a good name not only from those within, but also from those without (1 Tim. 5): that is, not only from members of the household but also from strangers; not only from believers but also from unbelievers. Thus he may have a garment woven of twisted fine linen (Exod. [Col. 0428B] 28). For “a good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22).

How gravely, therefore, he sins if he stains his reputation, and how greatly he deserves punishment if, through the demands of his own faults, he is bespattered by an evil report, is plainly inferred from this passage. For that steward who was accused before his lord as though he had squandered his goods heard from his lord: “Give an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to be steward.”

It is not said that he had squandered his master’s goods, but that he had done so *as though* he had squandered them. Yet after rendering his account, he is said to be removed from the stewardship: like one who, having been accused of dilapidation, is suspended from the office of administration even after presenting his accounts, so that the bad reputation may cease, lest it be a scandal among the people of God to have such a prelate over them.

But you will say: if the master certainly knew that the steward was a culpable squanderer, why did he command him to render an account when he knew he could not render one worthily? But if he could render his account worthily, why did he impose upon him, as one guilty, the punishment that he could no longer be steward? Perhaps from this passage certain religious men have drawn a certain rule of their order: that after a prelate among them has been accused, they remove him from the office of prelacy without any investigation, although an accounting ought often to be required of one plainly judged guilty, so that by it it may be known in what respects he has sinned and may appear what remains and what has been dispersed.

[Col. 0428D] Therefore the master summoned the steward, saying to him: “What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship; for you will no longer be able to be steward.” Almost the same was said to Hezekiah: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (Isa. 38).

This summons is inspiration, according to what is said elsewhere: “You will call me, and I shall answer you” (Job 13). For then Christ calls the guilty prelate, saying to him, “What is this that I hear about you? Your reputation is evil, and it has come to me,” when he inspires his mind to reflect upon his fault and repent, so that by making worthy satisfaction in the present he may be able to render a worthy account in the future. Therefore he says: “Give an account of [Col. 0429A] your stewardship”; that is, show yourself worthy, so that you may be able to render a worthy account of your stewardship. “You will no longer be able to be steward,” because I will withdraw you from this life, after which there will be no time for stewarding but a time for receiving.

See how merciful and kind the Lord is. Truly, he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live (Ezek. 18). For he rebukes in order to correct, and makes known in order to pardon.

What is the effect of this calling is shown next, where it says: Therefore the steward said within himself, as though pierced by divine inspiration: “What shall I do? Where shall I turn, a sinner? Because my master is taking the stewardship from me”—that is, withdrawing me from the present life, after which I shall not be able to steward or accomplish anything.

By his speaking within himself it is shown that the master also called him inwardly. But the master called through the stirring of inspiration; the steward responds through the effect of compunction. Yet he does not dare direct his answer to him before whom he greatly blushes for his fault. Instead, he turns the answer toward himself, in order to punish in himself what he sinned against him.

“What, therefore, shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship from me? I am not able to dig; I am ashamed to beg.” For after this life there is no place for doing work, but for receiving according to one’s work; nor is it a time for begging merit, but for receiving according to merit. For then each will receive according to what he has done in the body (2 Cor. 6 [probably 2 Cor. 5:10]). “Bind his hands and feet,” he says, “and cast him into the outer darkness” [Col. 0429C] (Matt. 22). With hands and feet bound, they cannot work.

That gluttonous rich man, buried in hell, begged in vain for a drop of water from the finger of the poor Lazarus (Luke 16). And the foolish virgins wished in vain to beg oil from the prudent ones (Matt. 25). Alas, what shame before all the elect and the reprobate, before God and his angels, to appear naked in judgment without the garments of good works! What disgrace, what confusion, what embarrassment! Truly, “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31), because “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4).

Although our first parents were alone in paradise, when they knew themselves to be naked they sewed fig leaves and made themselves coverings, and hid themselves in the midst of paradise (Gen. 3). But no reprobate person at judgment will be able either to beg clothing for himself or to dig himself a hiding place. For then the books will be opened and the hidden things of darkness made manifest. And perhaps therefore he says: “I am not able to dig; I am ashamed to beg.” But “the Lord is near to all who call upon him” (Ps. 144). Therefore, what the anxious steward should do, the Lord himself mercifully inspired.

“I know,” he says, “what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses”—not material houses on earth, of course, but spiritual houses in heaven. Of these Truth says: “In my Father’s house are many dwellings” (John 14): namely, that those among whom I may merit a place may receive me there.

[Col. 0430A] Therefore, having summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” He said: “A hundred measures of oil.” That debt is the punishment owed for sin, as is read elsewhere: “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty” (Luke 7). And for this reason we ask in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6).

By the steward’s asking the debtor how much he owed his master, it is mystically shown that a priest ought to inquire of the penitent into the quantity and quality of the sin, lest shame cause him to conceal it; for confession is more easily drawn out through questioning. Yet he must beware not to question in such a way as to instruct the penitent concerning unknown and monstrous modes of sinning, because:

> We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> —Ovid, *Amores*, book III, elegy 4, line 17.

But because the Lord commended this steward for prudence, let us see how prudent he was in deed and speech. He recognized himself as a sinner and turned himself to repentance, so that he might make satisfaction for his sin in order to obtain forgiveness. Therefore he forgave his debtors so that God might forgive him, his debtor. Accordingly, he summoned his master’s debtors as though they were his own debtors, because he too, as a prelate of the Church, was his vicar. He forgave one half the debt and another one fifth.

For one owed a hundred measures of oil, and another a hundred *cors* of wheat. But to the debtor of a hundred measures of oil he forgave fifty; and to the debtor of a hundred cors of wheat he forgave twenty, so that the former remained indebted for fifty measures and the latter for eighty cors.

[Col. 0430C] Oil in this passage signifies a shining reputation, as is read elsewhere: “Your name is oil poured forth” (Song 1). Wheat signifies earthly property, as is said elsewhere: “That he may give them in due season their measure of wheat” (Luke 12). Therefore, whoever stains a shining reputation spoils the oil, and consequently owes a hundred measures of oil: that is, a great punishment for a corrupted reputation. But whoever squanders earthly property scatters the wheat, and consequently owes a hundred cors of wheat: that is, a great punishment for squandered property. For the greatness of the number expresses the greatness of the debt.

Yet it is far more dangerous to squander inward than outward property, as is read of the prodigal son: he went into a far country and there squandered his property with harlots (Luke 15).

Therefore he said to him who owed a hundred measures of oil: “Take your note of indebtedness”—that is, employ the necessary caution, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Your sins are forgiven you; go, and sin no more” (John 8)—lest you return like a dog to its vomit. Therefore, “sit down quickly”: that is, immediately, from this moment, cease from sinning. And “write fifty”: that is, know that half of the debt will be forgiven you by me through that power of the keys which the Lord granted me: “Whose sins,” he says, “you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20).

[Col. 0431A] “Write,” he says—that is, retain it firmly in your heart as though written down, lest you be ungrateful for so great a grace. Likewise he said to him who owed a hundred cors of wheat: “Take your letters”—that is, write this upon the tablets of your heart, so that it can no longer be erased.

Now, when the one who corrupted a shining reputation owed as much as the one who squandered earthly property—for the former owed a hundred measures of oil and the latter a hundred cors of wheat—why did he forgive the former more and the latter less? For he forgave the former half and the latter one fifth. But it must be known that a cor is a larger measure than a *cadus*; therefore he forgave more to the one who owed more by measure, and less by number to the one who owed less. For a greater sin must be punished more, and a lesser sin less. Squandering is a greater sin than defamation; for squandering is both the fault of the one squandering and the punishment of the one despoiled, whereas defamation is more a fault than a punishment.

This may also be understood differently: oil may signify mercy and wheat fortitude, according to the saying: “That he may make the face glad with oil, and that bread may strengthen the heart of man” (Ps. 108 [the printed text]; bread is made from wheat). Therefore, whoever does not have compassion on the wretched spoils the oil because he denies mercy, and consequently owes a hundred measures of oil: that is, a full and perfect measure of punishment for mercy denied. Likewise, whoever yields to adversities scatters the wheat and loses fortitude, and consequently owes a hundred cors of wheat: that is, a full and perfect measure of punishment for lost fortitude.

[Col. 0431C] But the debt of him who denied mercy, when it is forgiven, is reduced to fifty, which is the number for mercy to be shown, on account of the fiftieth Jubilee. The debt of him who lost fortitude, however, when it is forgiven, is reduced to eighty, which is the number up to which strength was accustomed to endure. As it is written: “But if in powers, eighty years; and the greater part of them is labor and sorrow” (Ps. 130 [the printed text]).

Observe the prudence of the one forgiving, not only in this but also in forgiving those who owed in the same manner as he did. For he himself was indebted both because he had been accused before his master and because he had squandered his goods. Thus he forgave persons who had both corrupted their reputation and squandered property.

Therefore the master praised the steward of iniquity—not because he was then wicked, but because he had been wicked, just as Simon was called “the leper” (Mark 14), not because he then was such, but because he had been such. He praised him, I say, not because he had been wicked, but because he had acted prudently: “for the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.”

The children of this age are those who serve this age. But the children of light here are called hypocrites, who, though they are angels of Satan, transform themselves into angels of light (2 Cor. 11) and “do their righteous acts in order to be seen by men” (Matt. 6). Thus elsewhere they are called stars falling from heaven.

[Col. 0432A] Yet the children of this age—that is, lovers of the world, who sin through love of the age—are more prudent in their generation, that is, in their condition, than the children of light, that is, hypocrites. For although the former are more intent upon unlawful things and the latter abstain more from lawful things, the former nevertheless sometimes recognize that they are evil and turn from evil; while the latter, because they always wish to appear good, rarely turn toward good.

“And I say to you: make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” This is the fruit, the reward, the prize of the foregoing parable: that everlasting glory may be acquired through temporal almsgiving.

In the Syrian language, *mammon* means riches. Therefore the Lord commanded us to make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity: that is, to distribute unjust riches to the poor, so that through their distribution iniquity may be wiped away, in accordance with Daniel’s counsel: “Redeem your sins by alms” (Dan. 4); for “as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving resists sin” (Ecclus. 3). “Give alms,” says the Lord, “and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

[Col. 0432B] Now since God does not accept unjust gifts—as it is written, “God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (Gen. 4); for “he who offers sacrifice from the goods of the poor is as one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father” (Ecclus. 34)—and since the Law commands, “You shall not offer in the house of the Lord your God the price of a dog or the wages of a prostitute” (Deut. 23), why does the Lord command in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” as though he accepted alms distributed from unjust deeds?

But riches are here called the mammon of iniquity, not because they are unjust, but because they are customarily acquired by injustice. They take their name from what occurs more frequently. Or riches are called the mammon of iniquity because the wicked Mammon presides over them: that demon who tempts a person by riches, as that evil one tempted Christ by riches—though without success—when “he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said: ‘All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me’” (Matt. 4).

Or rather, one must distinguish between one kind of iniquity and another. There is a kind of iniquity from which riches may lawfully be distributed to the poor, as from military service or performing entertainment, because they pass into the ownership of the possessor. And there is a kind of iniquity from which riches acquired may not lawfully be distributed to others, as from theft or usury; in these cases ownership is not transferred, and therefore they must be restored as another’s goods, because sin is not forgiven unless what has been taken is first restored.

[Col. 0432D] Zacchaeus distinguished this well when he said: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). Therefore he says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail”—that is, depart from this life, or when your own merits fail—“they may receive you,” that is, you may be received through their merits, “into eternal dwellings,” that is, perpetual homes, of which it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; unto age upon age they shall praise you!” (Ps. 82).

[Col. 0433A] From this it is clearly inferred that, just as one person can merit grace for another—as is read of Jesus, that “when he saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Your sins are forgiven you’” (Mark 2)—so one can merit glory for another, as is maintained here: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

But whether, when someone gives alms to an unjust person whom he nevertheless considers just, that person may merit glory or grace for him—so that the giver of alms is not unjustly deprived of his merit—or whether, because that person displeases God, he cannot move God to grant grace or glory; or, if he can, whether one and the same work ought to be judged meritorious for another; or whether by it there may be for one a merit of death and for another a merit of life, just as good and evil proceed from God and the devil—these matters can be asked and doubted. But the solution of these questions must be postponed, because it is not our present purpose to resolve questions of this sort.

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE FEAST OF THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

On the different kinds of God’s house and dwelling places; and on what, where, how, and why one ought to worship.

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433B] “I will enter, O Lord, into your house; I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear” (Ps. 5).

The Lord and Creator of all, whose majesty is immeasurable, sublimity uncircumscribed, and power uncreated, has many and various houses, and very many diverse dwelling places in those houses: universal and particular, special and singular, higher and lower, inner and outer.

The universal house of God is the whole fabric of the world, of which Solomon says: “We know, Lord, that you have built for yourself an everlasting house: heaven and earth together with the sea” (2 Chron. 6). The particular house of God is holy mother Church, of which it is written: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days” (Ps. 92). The special house of God is the glorious Virgin Mary, of whom the prophet says: “I saw, and behold, the glory of the Lord filled the house of God” (Ezek. 43).

[Col. 0433C] The singular house of God is the assumed humanity of the Savior, of which it is written: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. 9). The higher house of God is heavenly blessedness, of which it is written: “I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Isa. 56). The lower house of God is the basilica of prayer, of which the Lord says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Luke 19). The inner house of God is a pure conscience, of which the Psalmist says: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100). The outer house is that which is inhabited and its household, or Holy Scripture, of which it is written: “We walked in the house of the Lord with one accord” (Ps. 54).

Since, then, from among so many and various houses, the faithful man enters the house of God in order to worship at the holy temple, we must consider what, where, how, and why one ought to worship.

Certainly the Father is to be worshipped, the Son is to be worshipped, and the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are to be worshipped, because all together and each severally are the one and only God: Spirit uncreated, immeasurable, unchangeable, supremely powerful, supremely wise, supremely good.

[Col. 0434B] He is Spirit because he does not consist of parts; uncreated because he did not begin in time; immeasurable because he is not circumscribed by place; unchangeable because he is not altered in disposition; supremely powerful because nothing is impossible to him; supremely wise because nothing is unknown to him; supremely good because there is no envy in him.

From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things: all things are created by power, formed by wisdom, and preserved by care; by power, the Father, the efficient cause; by wisdom, the Son, the efficient cause; by care, the Holy Spirit, the completing cause. For “there are three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5), although each is personally distinguished by his own property: the Father by generation, the Word by sonship, the Holy Spirit by procession. The three are one in their principle; all are wholly what each is in nature, power, will, and in every respect that is predicated according to substance.

[Col. 0434C] For although the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, yet the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; their glory equal and their majesty coeternal. Therefore the worship of the whole undivided Trinity is one and equal.

This may rightly be understood in the Lord’s saying: “True worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4). For whoever worships God truly worships the Father in spirit, but also in truth—that is, in the Son, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). “I,” he says, “am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10). Therefore the Father is to be worshipped in the Son, the Son is to be worshipped in the Father, and the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped in both.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be worshipped [Col. 0435A] in the lower house, the inner house, and the outer house: that is, in the sacred basilica, in a pure conscience, and in Holy Scripture; so that at last they may be worshipped in the higher house, that is, in the heavenly homeland, of which it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; unto age upon age they shall praise you!” (Ps. 83).

But since God is everywhere, not only by power but also by essence, why is God to be worshipped more in a temple than in another place? For his dominions are in every place, as the prophet says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). And the Psalmist says of him: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138). Likewise, when the Samaritan woman asked Christ for the resolution of the question that was very often debated concerning the place of worship: [Col. 0435B] “Our fathers,” she said, “worshipped on this mountain; and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.” Jesus answered her: “Woman, believe me: the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem; but true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4). As though he said: I do not prefer one place to another; let God be worshipped everywhere, provided it is in spirit and truth—that is, for spiritual and true things, namely eternal things.

Yet although God is to be worshipped everywhere, he is especially to be worshipped in the temple, according to the words: “Worship the Lord in his holy court” (Ps. 28). He is also especially to be worshipped toward the east, [Col. 0435C] as is read in the Book of Wisdom: “One ought to worship at the rising of the light” (Wis. 16), so that, as we worship God, there may rise for us “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), Christ our God, the Sun of righteousness (Mal. 4). For it would have been pointless for a temple to be made for the Lord with such zeal and labor, unless the Lord received worship there more graciously. For we read that, after the temple had been built and dedicated, Solomon worshipped the Lord (3 Kings 8), asking that whatever Jew or Gentile should enter the temple, praying for sins or crying out to the Lord in any tribulation, might be heard by the Lord in those things which he justly requested. The Church still preserves this form of prayer, praying thus at the dedication of a temple: [Col. 0435D] “that whoever enters this temple to seek benefits may rejoice that he has obtained all things.”

For the angels of God stand by faithful worshippers in holy temples, that they may offer their devout prayers to the Lord, according to the words: “In the sight of angels I will sing psalms to you, and I will worship toward your holy temple, and I will give thanks to your name, O Lord” (Ps. 137). Hence the angel said to Tobias: “I offered your prayer to the Lord” (Tob. 12). The relics of the saints also rest in holy temples; through their prayers they obtain for us what we cannot attain through our own merits. Therefore, brothers, carefully consider how attentive and devoutly you ought to worship the Lord in the temple before the relics of the saints and in the presence of God’s angels. Hence it is necessary that we worship the Lord not only [Col. 0436A] in the sacred basilica, but also in a pure conscience.

God is to be worshipped from a pure heart, not as some worship him, who glorify God in prosperity but blaspheme him in adversity. Of them the Prophet says: “They will give thanks to you when you do good to them” (Ps. 48).—“But if they are not satisfied, they will murmur” (Ps. 58).

God is to be worshipped from a good conscience, not as some worship him, who sin most grievously against God and nevertheless offer sacrifice to him. Of them it is written: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49). That covenant, indeed, of which Truth says: “This is my blood of the new covenant” [Col. 0436B] (Mark 14).

God is to be worshipped with unfeigned faith, not as some worship him, who speak rightly but live wickedly, to whom the Lord reproaches, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29; Matt. 15; Mark 7). For they speak, and do not act.

Therefore God is to be worshipped with heart, mouth, and deed (Rom. 10): with the heart through devotion, loving him above all; with the mouth through confession, praising him above all; with deed, serving him above all. But since some have zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, lest through simple ignorance we be held in grave error, let us worship according to the judgment and authority [Col. 0436C] of sacred Scripture.

For sacred Scripture distinguishes two kinds of worship: *latria* and *dulia*. We ought to render *latria* to the Creator; but we may render *dulia* to certain creatures. By *latria* we ought to revere the Creator alone above all things; by *dulia* we may venerate certain creatures among all things. Temples, altars, priesthoods, sacrifices, feasts, and ceremonies belong to *latria*; as the eminent doctor Augustine says, these are to be offered to God the Creator alone. Of this worship it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6; Matt. 4), that is, you shall render the service of worship to God alone. Those who act otherwise do not offer the worship of *Theosebia* [godly devotion], but incur the crime of idolatry, serving the creature [Col. 0436D] as though it were the Creator and changing the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man (Rom. 1).
