For we read (Acts 14) that, when Paul and Barnabas had healed a certain lame man, “the crowds raised their voices, saying: ‘Gods made like men have come down to us.’” Wishing to sacrifice to them, they brought bulls for a victim. But when Paul and Barnabas heard that divine honors were to be paid to them, they tore their garments, saying that they were mortal human beings, who had rather come to call them back from idolatry. Likewise, when John wished in a vision to worship an angel, the angel forbade him, saying: “Worship God. For I am your brother and fellow-servant of your brothers” (Rev. 19).

[Col. 0437A] Since, therefore, holy people and angels do not wish to be worshipped in any way, what is it that some, under a pretext of piety and a show of religion—to say nothing of other things—worship various images, as though it were permissible to worship something made by hands? For “the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 134).—“Let all who worship carved images be confounded, and those who glory in their idols” (Ps. 96). How severely the perversity of this crime is condemned is most clearly declared in the books of the prophets, and especially in the Book of Wisdom. For brevity’s sake I pass over their testimonies here, recalling only what Moses said to the people of Israel: “Lest perhaps, deceived by error, you worship [Col. 0437B] those things which the Lord your God created” (Deut. 4).

Hence it was that King Hezekiah, devout and prudent, broke in pieces the bronze serpent which Moses had raised in the wilderness, so that those bitten by serpents might be healed by looking upon it (Num. 21). Although it had previously stood as a figure of human redemption, yet after much time had passed the people, contrary to the commandment of the law, were burning incense to it; and he scattered its dust in the torrent Cedron (4 Kings 18).

Moreover, brothers, there is one image of God the Father, which we ought to venerate with the same worship as the Father: namely, the only-begotten Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who is “the brightness of his glory and the express image of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1). We ought to worship not only his divinity but also his humanity, [Col. 0437C] according to the words: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98). But other images we may venerate not with *latria* but with *dulia*: not on account of the image, which can do nothing of itself, but on account of that which is imaged, who can do all things of himself; not so that we, who have been made in the image and likeness of God, may remember ourselves as being like images which we ourselves made in our own image and likeness; but so that for God’s sake we may bow before sacred images—he who for our sake “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2).—“For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18).

For when we see images, we bow, not in order to place our hope of salvation in them, [Col. 0437D] but so that, stirred to remembrance, we may show in deed the devotion which we bear in our heart toward God himself. For, as was said, we may render *dulia* to creatures, holy and sacred things: namely, angels, human beings, and sacraments. Concerning the worship of angels, we read that Abraham, lifting up his eyes in the valley of Mamre, saw three and worshipped one of the angels (Gen. 18). Likewise Lot, meeting two angels [Col. 0438A] entering the city, worshipped them, asking them to turn aside as guests into his house (Gen. 19).

Why then was John forbidden to worship an angel? Because Christ, as man, had now been exalted above angels. Concerning the worship of people, we read that Jacob, seeing Esau coming, went before both companies and bowed himself to the ground seven times (Gen. 33). Jacob’s sons also worshipped Joseph in Egypt (Gen. 43). Why then did Mordecai refuse to worship Haman? Because Haman wished divine worship to be rendered to himself (Esther 3). Concerning the worship of sacraments, the Church says: “We worship your cross, O Lord.” Hence elsewhere it is read: “Christians devoutly venerate and worship sacred images.” Yet more truly we worship God before an image [Col. 0438B] than the image before God; hence it is commanded: “You shall not worship before the altar” (Isa. 36). It does not say “the altar,” but “before the altar.”

And the Prophet says: “I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear.” Not in human fear, of which the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10). Nor in servile fear, of which John the apostle says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4). But in initial fear, of which the Wise Man says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). And in filial fear, of which David the prophet says: “The holy fear of God endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 18).

[Col. 0438C] Why God is to be worshipped, the same prophet has taught us, saying: “Come, let us worship and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us, because he himself is the Lord our God” (Ps. 94). Because he himself is God, that is, Creator; because he himself is Lord, that is, Redeemer; because he himself is ours, that is, Savior. Then indeed he will be most truly our Savior, when he shall be all in all (Col. 3), that is, the sufficiency of each individual. Therefore he is God, who created us from nothing. He is Lord, who redeemed us with his own blood. He is ours, who saved us by his own gift. In creating, he gave us nature; in redeeming, he bestowed grace; in saving, he will bring glory.

Therefore we have what is to be worshipped: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Where it is to be worshipped: [Col. 0438D] in the sacred basilica, in a pure conscience, and in divine Scripture. How it is to be worshipped: from the heart, with the mouth, and by deed. Why it is to be worshipped: because of creation, redemption, and salvation. May the Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. AT THE CONSECRATION OF THE ALTAR.

On the dedication of the temple of our body and the consecration of the altar of our heart; and on what the things done at the consecration of an altar signify.

[Col. 0439]

[Col. 0439A] “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 6).

If you desire to become participants in this solemnity, to which you have gathered with desire, you ought to strive that whatever is done materially in the consecration of a temple may all be fulfilled spiritually in us. For “the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3),—“built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom all the building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Eph. 2). Yet for the present we shall give you milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor. 3), because solid food belongs to the perfect (Heb. 5), and we speak wisdom among the perfect (1 Cor. 2). But among you [Col. 0439B] we judge ourselves to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (ibid.). For “like newborn infants, desire milk, that you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2). Let us therefore take a few things out of many, whose meaning we may briefly expound to you for edification.

The temple that has been dedicated is understood as the body; the altar that has been consecrated is understood as the heart. The Apostle says of the temple of the body: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” The Lord spoke in the same sense when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; but he said this concerning the temple of his body (John 2). Concerning the altar of the heart the Lord commands: “The fire on [Col. 0439C] my altar shall always burn” (Lev. 6). For the fire that continually burns on the altar is charity, which continuously burns fervently in the heart. For “many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 7). Therefore, according to the Prophet, keep a solemn day in crowded assemblies, even to the horn of the altar (Ps. 117), because “the remnant of thought shall keep a feast-day for the Lord” (Ps. 75).

Therefore let the temple of our body be dedicated by abstinence, and cleansed from the defilements of gluttony; let it be dedicated by continence, that it may be purified from the pollutions of lust. For every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but one who commits fornication sins against his own body. Consider, brothers and children, how grave a sin it is to violate the temple of the Holy Spirit by adultery, to take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute. Hence it is read that adultery holds the first place among punishments. Therefore crucify your flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), lest sin reign in your mortal body (Rom. 6), following the example of the Apostle, who says of himself: [Col. 0440A] “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become a reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

Let the altar of the heart be consecrated through the conception of fear; let it be consecrated through the affection of love; let it be consecrated, that it may be completed for the better. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). Of this another prophet says: “From your fear, O Lord, we have conceived and borne the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 25).—“But the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1).—“For charity is the fulfillment of the law” (Rom. 13). Let the altar of the heart be consecrated in you, that you may conceive holy desires. Let the temple of the body also be dedicated, that you may bring forth righteous works, so that with a pure heart and chaste body you may sacrifice to [Col. 0440B] God “not in the leaven of old malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

The altar is consecrated in this order: a slab is laid upon it, the table is anointed, incense is burned, the altar is clothed; and finally the sacrifice is celebrated. Relics are deposited: these are examples left to us for imitation. We deposit them in a casket when we retain them in memory for imitation, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4).—“For Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

But what does it mean that the relics of the saints are placed in the casket with three [Col. 0440C] grains of incense, except that we ought to retain the examples of the saints in memory in the faith of the Trinity? For “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11).—“For the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. 10). The slab placed above signifies charity, of which the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). Of its breadth the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118). For the commandment of charity is broad, extending even to enemies, according to the Lord’s command: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5). Love with the heart, do good by deed, [Col. 0440D] so that there may be in you “a threefold cord,” which “is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4). Therefore the slab is placed upon the relics, because charity, which covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4), is kindled by the examples of the saints.

The table is anointed, so that charity may show mercy. For anointing signifies mercy, according to [Col. 0441A] the words: “Anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. 5). Hence the Samaritan, approaching the wounded man, poured wine and oil over him (Luke 10). But what does it mean that the table is anointed in six places—namely, in the middle, at the four corners, and in front—except that we ought to exercise charity through the six works of mercy recounted in the Gospel: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. 25)?

After the anointing incense is burned, so that the fame of a good work may spread to neighbors. Of this the Apostle says: “We are the sweet savor of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2), so that curtain may draw curtain (Exod. 36), and “let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). But what does it mean that incense is burned in five places, namely at the four corners [Col. 0442A] and in the middle, except that we ought so to exercise the five bodily senses that our light may shine before people, so that, seeing our works, they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 6)?

Now the altar is clothed when the pure heart of a person is adorned with good works. Of these Solomon says: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccl. 9), that is, let your works be clean. Upon an altar consecrated in this order, a sacrifice acceptable to the Most High is offered: namely, that of which the prophet says in the Psalm: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50). Or also that of which he says elsewhere: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49).

## SERMON XXIX. EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL READING ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY.

On the Redeemer’s two goings forth, and on his voluntary assumption of our mutability; on two kinds of sinners; on four obstacles to salvation and four aids to salvation; finally, on what must be done in order that Jesus may be seen, and on the giving of alms, the virtues of Zacchaeus, and the threefold house.

[Col. 0441]

[Col. 0441B] “Jesus, having gone out, was passing through Jericho. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus; he was chief of the tax collectors, and he was rich. And he sought to see Jesus, who he was, but could not because of the crowd, because he was small in stature” (Luke 19).

There are two goings forth of the Redeemer: one eternal and the other temporal; one hidden and the other manifest; one according as he was born of the Father, and the other according as he was born of his mother; one in the form of God and the other in the form of a servant. The prophet recalls and commends both when he says: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you shall go forth one who shall rule my people Israel; and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5).

Jesus, therefore, having gone out, was passing through Jericho, because he went forth from the Father and came into the world (John 18). Yet he went forth not by abandoning the divine nature in which he remains hidden with the Father, but by assuming human nature, in which he appeared manifestly from his mother. Jericho, according to its interpretation, means “moon”; and because of its revolutions and mutability it signifies the world, which is always turning and changing. “For I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit; and I saw that nothing remains under the sun” (Eccl. 1). One is born and another dies; one is raised up and another cast down; one increases and another diminishes; one rejoices and another is sorrowful; one becomes poor and another rich; one becomes lord, [Col. 0441D] and another becomes servant. “A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries. Like a flower he comes forth and is crushed; he flees like a shadow, [Col. 0442B] and never remains in the same state” (Job 14).

Jesus, therefore, having gone out, was passing through Jericho. For he who first went forth from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the mother, from heaven to earth, was always and is the same, as he himself says of himself through the prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3). The same one, after going forth from the Father and coming into the world, voluntarily assumed our mutability and freely subjected himself to our changeability; for he hungered, thirsted, was afraid, suffered pain, and finally underwent the cross and death. “For when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. 4). When he said on the cross, “I thirst,” they gave him gall for food and gave him vinegar to drink in his thirst (John [Col. 0442C] 19). He himself likewise testifies of himself through the prophet: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1).—For Jesus “began to fear and to be weary” (Mark 14),—“began to be sorrowful and sad” (Matt. 26),—and became “obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).

Therefore Jesus, to whom according to the divine nature nothing is added and from whom nothing is taken away, because he has nothing in himself except himself, nor is what possesses other than what is possessed, nor what is possessed other than what possesses—except that, “made in the likeness of human beings, he was found in appearance as a man” (ibid.)—he assumed our changeabilities and took upon himself our defects for us.

[Col. 0442D] And therefore, having gone out, he was passing through Jericho. “And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus; he was chief of the tax collectors, and he was rich. And he sought to see Jesus, [Col. 0443A] who he was, but could not because of the crowd, because he was small in stature.”

There are two kinds of sinners. Some despair of God’s mercy, saying wretchedly with Cain: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 4). Since their sickness is hopeless, their healing too is despaired of; for “when the wicked has come into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18). But others hope in divine mercy, saying mercifully with David: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50); and because they seek salvation, they obtain healing.

For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost. Such was this Zacchaeus, who, although he was chief of the tax collectors and was rich, nevertheless sought [Col. 0443B] to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, because he was small in stature. Four obstacles seemed to stand in his way, preventing him from seeing Jesus: first, he was chief of the tax collectors; second, he was rich; third, he could not because of the crowd; fourth, he was small in stature.

Those were called tax collectors who exacted public taxes, and their business can scarcely, or never, be carried on without sin. Thus the chief of the tax collectors was an exacter of the treasury. Therefore, just as the chief of robbers shares in robbery, so he was a participant in the tax collectors’ public business, from which he acquired riches for himself by right and wrong alike. For it is not the possession of riches that is blameworthy, but their misuse; hence the Prophet says: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61). For Abraham was rich (Gen. 13), David wealthy (2 Kings 12), and Job prosperous (Job 1), and they were found righteous and pleasing to God. Yet it is difficult to possess riches and not love them, just as it is difficult to be in fire and not burn. Therefore Truth says: “It is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 9); but what is believed impossible among people is considered possible with God (Matt. 19), who does not despise the rich, since he too is rich.

Thus Zacchaeus sought to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, because he was small in stature. So long as the crowd presses in, Jesus cannot be seen, especially as to who he is—except perhaps by faith, but not by sight. Therefore he said: “I will manifest myself to them” (John 14). For “this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17).—“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

Morally, one is small in stature who can persist only a little—that is, who easily falls, either weak through the frailty of the flesh or bound by the fetter of habit. We know and lament that there are many such people: evil deeds which they commit displease them, but drawn or overcome by frailty or habit, they do what they detest, because “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit desires against the flesh” (Gal. 5). [Col. 0444A] Yet they sin more under the Lord than against the Lord, always thinking of repentance and trusting in mercy. Such was Zacchaeus, who desired to see Jesus, as one meditating upon pardon, yet could not because of the crowd—as one held back by guilt, resisting by reason but yielding to sensuality.

To this belongs what the Psalmist says: “My soul has desired to desire your justifications” (Ps. 118). One desires to desire God’s justifications who does not yet desire perfectly, but desires in order to desire perfectly. So some grieve because they cannot grieve, but grieve in order that they may grieve—that is, so that ineffective grief may bring about effective grief. For in sinners there first occurs something by which, though they are not yet justified, they are nevertheless found worthy—that is, capable—of justifications [Col. 0444B].

Zacchaeus therefore sought to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, because “dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. 10). For the crowd caused disturbance, whether it consisted of evil people, malicious thoughts, or malignant demons, who always entice, suggest, and drag people into sin. Hence we read that when the blind man cried, “Have mercy on me, Son of David,” those going before rebuked him to be silent; but he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Luke 18). For the more strongly the disturbance of demons, thoughts, or people rises up against us, the more insistently we ought to persist in repelling temptations of this sort, lest through ignorance or negligence we fall asleep unto death; rather, through attentiveness [Col. 0444C] and watchfulness, we should rise again to life.

This is shown by the example of Zacchaeus, who ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree in order to see Jesus, because he was to pass that way. Therefore let no one, because he has been overtaken by some sin, despair through negligence or be negligent through despair; but, running ahead, let him climb the sycamore tree. Behold Zacchaeus, solicitous for his salvation, found four aids against four obstacles, by four remedies. Because he was rich, he gave half his goods to the poor; because he was chief of the tax collectors, if he had defrauded anyone, he restored fourfold; again, because he was small in stature, he climbed a sycamore tree; and because he could not see because of the crowd, [Col. 0444D] he ran ahead, and thus left the crowd behind him.

So also, brothers, whenever in the way of God we are hindered by adversaries, let us cleverly and diligently resort to fitting aids, and let us not fail on the way; rather, being unencumbered, let us advance to our homeland. Zacchaeus, therefore, ran ahead and left the crowd behind him, because a sinner wishing to hasten toward pardon ought to leave behind evil people, malicious thoughts, and maligning demons, all of which we said were signified by the crowd. He must neither cling to these, yield to these, nor assent to those; but the more they attack, the more he must resist, so that he may instead overcome those attacking him, following the example of him whom the crowds going before rebuked all the more to be silent, but who cried out all the more: “Son of David, have mercy [Col. 0445A] on me.”

Therefore let the cry of devout petition overcome the nature of impious suggestion, so that the spirit may prevail against the flesh; and when one has been separated from the wicked, divided from the faithless, and distinguished from the perverse, let him climb the sycamore tree, so that he may see Jesus passing by from it.

The sycamore is a tall tree and, as some say, a “foolish fig” (*ficus fatua*; printed *facua*). It is indeed the cross of Christ, which is considered foolishness by unbelievers: “We preach,” says the Apostle, “Jesus Christ, and him crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). Another Scripture also sets before us the ascent of this tree: “I will climb the palm tree,” it says, “and take hold of its fruits” (Song 7). The palm, which is a sign of victory, signifies faith in the cross, [Col. 0445B] of which John says: “This is the victory which conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5). It comprehends “with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. 3). The fruit of this tree is purple and has a blood-like juice, because the fruit of life which hung upon the cross poured out its blood for us.

Therefore whoever wishes to see Jesus passing by, let him climb the sycamore tree. For Jesus—that is, Savior—cannot be seen except from the place of salvation, that is, from the cross, through which “God, our King before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73), in the place of Calvary. Hence, when Moses saw the Lord’s back parts, we read that he stood in the cleft of the rock (Exod. 33). Since the rock signifies Christ, according to the words, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), the clefts of the rock rightly signify the wounds of Christ. Therefore elsewhere it is read: “In the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall, show me your face” (Song 2), because whoever wishes to see Christ’s face must stand in the clefts of the rock, that is, in Christ’s wounds, through faith in the passion and cross.

Zacchaeus, therefore, climbed the sycamore tree in order to see Jesus, because he was to pass that way. “Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid. Therefore, because of the Jews’ Preparation, since the tomb was near, they laid Jesus there” (John 19). Hence he passed [Col. 0445D] from death to life, from the world to the Father, as John says: “Jesus knew that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father; having loved his own, he loved them to the end” (John 13).

“And when Jesus came to that place, looking up, he saw him.” From eternity he saw him with the gaze of predestination, in the manner in which he said to Nathanael: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1). But when in the fullness of time he came to the place of Calvary, where he willed to be crucified for the salvation of sinners, looking up he saw Zacchaeus and other sinners with a gaze of compassion, in order graciously to redeem and save them by looking upon them.

And behold, when Zacchaeus had climbed the sycamore tree [Col. 0446A] in order to see Jesus, we read that Jesus, looking up, saw him, because unless he had first been seen, how could he see Truth? Just as unless the light of a lamp or of the sun first strikes a person’s eyes, however much the person opens his eyes, he cannot see the lamp or the sun. But Christ is Truth; Christ is the sun; Christ is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Hence we read: “The Lord looked upon Peter, and immediately he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22).

And the Lord said to Zacchaeus: “Zacchaeus, come down quickly, because today I must remain in your house.” His ascent is commended, because he ran ahead and climbed up. His descent too is commended, because he came down quickly. He climbed through faith, to see Jesus; [Col. 0446B] he descended through humility, to receive him. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). For “he who descended is the same as he who ascended” (Eph. 7). And Jacob saw a ladder whose summit touched the heavens, and angels ascending and descending by it (Gen. 28).

Therefore, come down quickly, because today I must remain in your house. As though he said: You are now enlightened by faith; therefore see by faith. Once the darkness of error has been driven away, it is fitting not for me but for you—for I do not need your goods, but without me you can do nothing—that I make my dwelling in your house, not as a guest for a day, [Col. 0446C] but as a permanent inhabitant; for “whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). In a house, indeed, not so much material, built of stones, as spiritual, fashioned from virtues.

He obtained more than he hoped for. For he was content, having climbed the tree, to see Jesus; but Jesus not only showed himself to Zacchaeus to be seen, but also deigned to lodge in his house. From this it is plainly inferred and concluded that he both forgives what the conscience fears and adds what prayer does not dare presume. Moreover, because “not hearers of the law but doers are righteous before God” (Rom. 2), Zacchaeus was not a slow and forgetful hearer, but a zealous and diligent doer: he came down quickly and received him joyfully.

By this the Christian is morally instructed not to carry out the divine command with delay or slowness, weariness or idleness, according to what the Apostle says: obedience without delay. Nor should he perform divine service with sadness or pain, murmuring or complaint, because, according to the same Apostle: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9).

Accordingly, he hurried down and received him joyfully. And when they all saw it, they murmured that he had turned aside to a sinful man. Some murmured out of envy, others out of ignorance; but both kinds of murmuring were unjust, as though anyone should complain because a physician turned aside to a sick person. So likewise the Savior deigned to turn aside to a sinner. [Col. 0447A] Hence, when the Pharisees said to the apostles, “Why does your master eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus, hearing them, said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9). And Peter, astonished by the novelty of the miracle, said to the Lord: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5), when he ought rather to have said: “Enter unto me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,” since unless light approaches, darkness does not depart. But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” How much the Savior’s presence had accomplished is shown by the effect of salvation. [Col. 0447B] For he who had been unjust through fraud became righteous through faith; and he who had been chief of the tax collectors and was himself rich became the father of the needy and himself poor. Hence not without reason is his name called Zacchaeus, which is interpreted “justified.” “Behold,” he says, “Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” Since, indeed, “if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4, LXX), Zacchaeus, as provident and discerning, both offered rightly and divided rightly: for he gave half his goods to the poor, and if he had defrauded anyone of anything, he restored it fourfold. He gave what was his own and restored what belonged to another; for sin is not forgiven unless what has been taken away is restored. And: “He who gives alms from the robbery of a poor man is as one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Ecclus. 34). God does not accept unjust gifts, especially those derived from sacrilege or theft, robbery or usury; in these cases ownership is not transferred, and wrath rather than mercy is provoked. Some, though they have much, give little; though they have what is dear, give what is worthless; though they have their own property, give another’s; though they ought to give to the needy, give to actors. But Zacchaeus both offered rightly and divided rightly: giving not little but much, for he gave half; not what was worthless but what was dear, for he gave half his goods; not another’s but his own, for he gave half his own goods; not to actors but to the needy, for he gave half his goods to the poor.

[Col. 0447D] At every time we ought to aid the needy, but especially at this time, in which God has brought barrenness and famine, displaying mercy and making justice manifest in one and the same matter: so that, while he scourges us through the privation of famine because of our sins, he may show the rigor of his justice; and while he presents an opportunity to assist the poor, he may furnish a ground for mercy. Thus, when we have borne God’s scourge patiently and assisted the needy generously, we shall certainly be delivered through justice and crowned through mercy. But whoever, at such a crisis of necessity, is not content even to retain only what is superfluous, should know that he deserves as many deaths as there are poor persons dying through his avarice; [Col. 0448A] or at least that he should be punished by as many penalties as the supplicants are afflicted by sufferings. For “if anyone has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes his compassion against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3). Nor should anyone excuse himself, since it suffices that each person give according to his own means. If he has much, let him bestow abundantly; if little, let him gladly endeavor to share even from the little (Tob. 4): so that he deprives necessity of something and takes everything away from superfluity, restoring another’s property in full—not always merely singly, but sometimes fourfold.

For another’s property is sometimes stolen knowingly through deliberate contrivance, sometimes unknowingly through negligence. When another’s property [Col. 0448B] was knowingly stolen, if the thing still existed, it was restored double according to the justice of the law; if it no longer existed, it was restored fourfold, as is commanded in Exodus (ch. 22). But if another’s property was stolen through ignorance, the principal was repaid, with a fifth part added. The same was done concerning stolen property when the theft remained concealed and the thief voluntarily confessed and made restitution, as is found in the book of Numbers.

Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.” A son, indeed, not by flesh but by faith; not by succession but by imitation, according to what Truth says: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John 8).—“Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15; Rom. 4; Gal. 3). Zacchaeus, however, obeyed [Col. 0448C] Jesus, and it became salvation for him. Abraham received the angels of the Lord in hospitality (Gen. 18); Zacchaeus, however, received the Lord of angels. Abraham rejoiced that he might see his day; he saw it and was glad (John 8). Zacchaeus, however, climbed a sycamore tree in order to see him passing by, and coming down received him joyfully. Rightly, then, has salvation come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and save that which was lost.

In this man, then, who was justified, the fullness of the virtues is variously displayed: faith, hope, charity, justice, fortitude, prudence, temperance, obedience with humility, hospitality with cheerfulness, mercy with generosity. Faith, because he ran ahead [Col. 0448D] and climbed the sycamore tree; hope, because he sought to see who Jesus was; charity, because he received him joyfully; justice, because he restored fourfold; fortitude, because he stood and spoke to the Lord; prudence, because he not only gave to the poor but restored to those he had defrauded; temperance, because he did not distribute everything but gave half; obedience with humility, because he hurried down; hospitality with cheerfulness, because he received him joyfully; mercy with generosity, because he gave half his goods to the poor and made restoration to those he had defrauded.

For through faith he ran ahead and climbed the sycamore tree: he climbs the sycamore tree who exalts faith in the cross. Through hope he sought to see who Jesus was; he saw and rejoiced. For this reason the Lord says: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11). Through charity he received him joyfully; for charity rejoiced because it received truth. Through justice he restored fourfold, because no one is justified from guilt unless he restores what belongs to another. Through fortitude he stood: he did not lie prostrate as one weak, but stood as one strong. For Jesus too, in order to strengthen Stephen, did not appear to him sitting, but standing: “Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). Through prudence he gave to the poor and restored to those he had defrauded: he gave what was his own and restored what was another’s. Therefore those sin gravely who do not pay tithes and firstfruits to priests, but distribute them to the needy according to their own will. Through temperance [Col. 0449B] he gave not everything but half; he gave what was superfluous and retained what was necessary, as the prophet says: “When you see one naked, cover him; and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58). Through obedience he acted quickly, for it is written: “Obedience without delay.” Through humility he came down, since “whoever humbles himself shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 18). Through hospitality with cheerfulness he received him joyfully, because “God loves a cheerful giver.” Through mercy with generosity he gave half his goods to the poor, and therefore “his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111). For it is written: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11 [the printed citation reads 2]); [Col. 0449C] because “as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3).

Which of us, beloved, I do not say strives to distribute half, but even a fourth, a sixth, or a twelfth to the poor? When does he, according to the counsel of Jesus Christ, sell all that he has and give it to the poor (Matt. 19), when he does not even pay the tithe which he is bound to pay as a debt? (Matt. 18). Certainly iniquity has abounded and the charity of many has grown cold (Matt. 24). But Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor, and if he had defrauded anyone of anything, restored it fourfold.

From these virtues that house is constructed in which Jesus deigns to dwell. “Hurry,” he says, “come down; for today I must stay in your house.” [Col. 0449D] There is the house of the Godhead, the house of man, and the house of the devil: the house of God by grace; the house of man by nature; the house of the devil by guilt. Of the first it is written: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, unto length of days” (Ps. 92); of the second it is said: “Those who dwell in houses of clay and have an earthly foundation” (Job 4); of the third it is written: “I will return to my house from which I came out” (Matt. 12).

The roof of vices is pride, which is the beginning [Col. 0450A] of sin (Ecclus. 10); the door is concupiscence, which wages war against the soul; the floor is avarice, which is the service of idols (Gal. 5); the four side-walls are the four kinds of sinners, namely: the sin of frailty through incapacity; the sin of simplicity through ignorance; the sin of security through negligence; and the sin of malice through envy. In the house of nature, reason is the foundation, memory the roof, understanding the door, will the floor, and the four side-walls the four natural affections: fear and hope, sorrow and joy.

Hence men desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve. In the house of grace, faith is the foundation. Of it the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” [Col. 0450B] (Heb. 11). Charity is the roof, of which James says: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (James 5). Obedience is the door, of which the Lord says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19). Humility is the floor, of which the Psalmist says: “My soul clung to the pavement” (Ps. 118). The four side-walls are the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. These are the four equal sides of the city in the Apocalypse (ch. 20). The windows are hospitality with cheerfulness and mercy with generosity. This is the house of which the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Col. 0450C] (John 14).

But this sacred basilica too is a house of the Godhead and a temple of God, of which the Lord says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Isa. 56; Matt. 21). Into this house Jesus comes today through the grace of dedication and the efficacy of consecration. For it is read that, when Solomon’s temple had been dedicated and the priests were saying, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever” (1 Chron. 16), a cloud filled the house of the Lord and overshadowed the faces of the priests, so that they could not see one another. And Solomon said: “The Lord said that he would dwell in a cloud” (1 Kings 8). He said it—that is, he showed it by deed—because on Mount Sinai he appeared in a cloud (Exod. 19), and he went before Israel in a cloud [Col. 0450D] (Exod. 14), and he passed before Moses, placed in the cleft of the rock, in a cloud (Exod. 33). The mystery is clearly expressed, but is to be expounded elsewhere.

For the rest, brothers, because “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15), let us imitate Zacchaeus, so that Jesus may deign to dwell in our house—he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0451]

**SERMONS OF POPE INNOCENT III, OF THAT NAME, ON THE SAINTS.**

**SERMON I. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD. On the manifold meaning of “word,” the fourfold sense of “flesh,” and why the Word became flesh.**

[Col. 0451A] “The Word became flesh and dwelt in us” (John 1).

According to the ordinary understanding of speech, “word” is taken in many ways. There is a word conceived in the heart, a word uttered by the mouth, and a word written with a pen. An understanding is conceived in the heart, a sound uttered by the mouth, and a sign written with a pen. Understanding is in the mind, sound in the air, and a sign in an image. But since “the spirit is that which gives life,” let us pass from carnal things to spiritual things; “for the flesh profits nothing” (John 6).

There is a human word and a divine Word. A human word, once uttered, passes away; the divine Word, once begotten, remains. Of the former the poet says:

> Once sent forth, a word flies irrevocable.  
> [Col. 0451B] (Horace, *Epistles* I.18.71.)

Of the latter the Prophet says: “The word of the Lord remains for ever; the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation” (Ps. 32). The Word of God the Father is the Son of God, through whom “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (ibid.). For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 33). For as understanding is expressed through a word, so the Father is made known through the Son, according to what he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I have glorified you upon the earth; I have made your name known to the people whom you gave me from the world” (John 17). Therefore the Son himself is called the Father’s discourse. For it is written: “Your almighty discourse, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18); and elsewhere: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar” (Isa. 31).

This Word is conceived, uttered, and written: conceived according to the divine birth; uttered according to the human birth; written according to the gracious birth. According to the divine birth, conceived from the Father; according to the human birth, born from the mother; according to the gracious birth, written in the mind. He is born from the Father eternally, from the mother temporally, and in the mind spiritually. Eternally he is conceived from the mystery of divinity; temporally he is uttered from the mother’s womb; spiritually he is written by the finger of God. Of the Word conceived according to divine birth from the Father, John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Of the Word uttered according to human birth from the mother, Isaiah speaks (ch. 9): “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel.” Of the Word written according to gracious birth in the mind, Luke testifies (ch. 3): “The word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zachariah, in the wilderness.”

There is a heavenly Word, an inward word, and an outward word. The heavenly Word is God [Col. 0452B] and flesh; the inward word is spirit and life; the outward word is seed and sword. The Word is God according to eternity, because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The Word is flesh according to humanity, because the Word became flesh and dwelt in us. The Word is spirit for those who understand, life for those who believe; hence: “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6). The Word is seed in the propagation of virtues; hence: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8). The Word is a sword in cutting away vices; hence: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

Indeed, the Word becomes flesh, bread becomes flesh, and man becomes flesh. The Word becomes flesh through union, bread becomes flesh through conversion, and man becomes flesh through commingling: through personal union, sacramental conversion, and carnal commingling. Of the first it is said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; of the second it is read: “The bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6); of the third it is written: “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh.

By the term “flesh” there is sometimes designated [Col. 0453A] nature, sometimes person, sometimes frailty, and sometimes carnality. Nature, when it is said: “One kind of flesh is that of fishes, another of birds, another of beasts” (1 Cor. 15); person, when it is said: “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Luke 3); frailty, where it is said: “My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6); carnality, where it is said: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore, when it is said, “The Word became flesh,” by “flesh” is understood either outward condition or humanity. For the Word became flesh—that is, God was incarnate—because “he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1).

And thereby the following question is resolved: since a human being sufficiently consists of soul and body, why is the Word said to have become flesh on account of one part, but not said to have become soul on account of the other, especially since there is a greater likeness between Word and soul than between Word and flesh? Because “incarnate” signifies condition, that is, clothed in flesh, which befits the Word; whereas “ensouled” signifies life, that is, made alive by a soul, which does not befit the Word. For the Word is not made alive by the soul, but rather gives life to the soul. Or, by synecdoche, the Word is said to have become flesh—that is, God became man. For “a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86), according to what is elsewhere said: “I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2).

Before the Word became flesh, he dwelt far [Col. 0453C] from us; but once the Word became flesh, he dwelt within us—not only by grace, but also by nature. For this is “our God,” who, according to the Prophet, “was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch 3), bone from our bones and flesh from our flesh. But he dwells in those whom the Holy Spirit has made a temple, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). Therefore the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14); and again: “I shall be with you,” he says, “until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

[Col. 0453D] The Word became flesh for four reasons: to humble the proud, to reconcile enemies, to redeem servants, and to nourish friends. “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in outward condition as a man” (Phil. 2). What the Apostle calls “emptied,” the Prophet calls “shortened.”—“The Lord,” he says, “will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Ps. 10). The vice of pride had to be expiated by the virtue of humility, since contraries are cured by contraries: the greatness of the virtue of humility had to correspond to the greatness of the vice of pride. Now the vice of pride was so great that man wished to be like God, as the serpent had promised him: [Col. 0454A] “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). Therefore the virtue of humility had to be so great that God became like man, as the Apostle says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of man, and found in outward condition as a man.”

Therefore the Word became flesh in order to give us an example of humility, so that we who departed in pride might return in humility. “For pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). By it the angel sinned in heaven, saying: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). By it man sinned in paradise, to whom it was said: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” [Col. 0454B] This vice is first in the sinner and last in the penitent: when it approaches, sin is committed; when it departs, sin is forgiven. For as soon as we despise the divine command, so soon do we become proud against the Lord; and as soon as we are pierced with compunction for sin, so soon are we humbled before God. Therefore the Word became flesh so that, as God humbled himself for man, the Lord for the servant, the Creator for the creature, so man might humble himself for God, the servant for the Lord, the creature for the Creator; for “whoever humbles himself shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14).—“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4).

There was a grave discord of enmity between God and man, because man by sinning withdrew and took from God the servant whom he had delivered and subjected to the devil. Therefore peace could not reasonably be made between them unless man restored the loss he had inflicted. But man had nothing with which he could worthily compensate God for the loss; for whatever a rational creature might render to God in return for rational substance taken away would be less. Yet man could not restore man worthily, because he had taken away one who was just and innocent, and found no one except a sinner. Seeing, therefore, that man could not escape the yoke of condemnation by his own power, God first came before him by mercy alone, so that afterward he might also deliver him through justice. Therefore, in order that God might be appeased by man, God freely gave man what man would render to God as a debt. [Col. 0454D] He gave man a man, whom man might restore for man; and, in order that the recompense might be worthy, this man was not merely equal to the former but greater.

Therefore the Word became flesh so that God-man might be given to men, as Isaiah foretold: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9), so that he might lawfully mediate between God and man. For if he belonged to only one nature, he would not be common to both, and consequently would not be fit to restore the covenant of peace between them. “For a mediator is not of one,” as the Apostle says (Gal. 3). For this reason, at Christ’s birth, the multitude of the heavenly host sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2).—“For he is our peace, who made both one” [Col. 0455A] (Eph. 2), the cornerstone who joined two walls from opposite directions in one new man (ibid.).

God could have delivered man by power through a word alone, but he preferred to redeem him by a price through justice, so that he might invite him not to power but to justice. And it was just that man should be redeemed from the debt of guilt by the price of punishment, appeasing through punishment him whom he had offended through guilt. No one’s punishment could suffice as the price of human redemption for all, especially since everyone was a debtor to punishment, not only because of committed iniquity, but also because of contracted stain. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, [Col. 0455B] and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13).

Therefore the Word became flesh so that, in the most pure flesh, wholly free from guilt, by bearing a punishment not owed, he might pay God the price of human redemption, “becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).—“For we were redeemed not with corruptible gold or silver, but with a great price, the blood of an immaculate lamb” (1 Pet. 1). This is the high priest at whose death those guilty persons who had fled to a city of refuge returned safely to their own possessions (Num. 45 [as printed]). Therefore he took upon himself the punishment for all, so that through himself he might give glory to all, as Isaiah bears witness, saying: “He was wounded [Col. 0455C] for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed. Truly he bore [Col. 0456A] our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53).

Moreover, he gave the flesh he assumed not only as a price for us, to redeem us from death, but also gave it to us as food, to nourish us unto life. As he himself promises: “The bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6), so that, just as death had entered the world through food, life might return to the world through food. For just as bodily life cannot subsist without bodily food, so spiritual life cannot be nourished without spiritual food: “Unless you eat,” he says, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid.).

Therefore the Word became flesh so that what was food of angels according to divinity might become food of men according to humanity; so that man might eat the bread of angels (Ps. 77), “having in itself every delight and every sweetness of flavor” (Wis. 10).—“But let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of this bread and drink from the cup. For he who eats this bread unworthily eats judgment unto himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11). [Col. 0456B] For just as the good man acquires life by enduring death, so the evil man incurs death by receiving life. Therefore, brothers, let us not be ungrateful for so great a grace; rather, let us render most worthy thanks to our Redeemer for so great a grace, humbly beseeching that he who became a participant in our nature (1 Cor. 9 [as printed]) may make us participants in his glory: Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed above all things for ages of ages. Amen.

**SERMON II. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY. How “new” is understood in many ways in Scripture; concerning the threefold newness accomplished in Christ’s birth, and his three names.**

[Col. 0455]

[Col. 0455D] “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the enclosure of her womb” (Jer. 31).

In Sacred Scripture “new” is understood in many ways. For “new” is said of that which renews, and “new” is said of that which has been renewed; “new” is said of what is recent, and “new” is said of what is unfamiliar; “new” is said of what is last, and “new” is said of what is miraculous. “New” means renewing, according to: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13). “New” means renewed, according to: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21).—“And he who sat upon the throne said: Behold, I make all things new” (ibid.). “New” means recent, according to: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Mark 2). “New” means unfamiliar, according to: “They shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents” (Mark 16). “New” means last, according to: “Then you will begin with shame to occupy the lowest place” [Col. 0456D] (Luke 14). “New” means miraculous, according to: “Renew signs and change wonders” (Ecclus. 36).

Therefore the Lord will make a new thing upon the earth. For “this has been done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. 117). In all these ways the Lord made a new thing upon earth, because a woman encompassed a man in the enclosure of her womb. “For then a great prophet came, and he himself renewed Jerusalem” (Jer. 38). Then the Lord consummated the new covenant over Jerusalem, the house of Israel, and the house of Judah, not according to the covenant he gave their fathers when they came out from the land of Egypt. Then this was fulfilled: “You shall eat the very old things of old, and, when new things come, you shall cast away the old” (Lev. 26).

For then the Lord made a new thing in person, a new thing in nature, and a new thing in grace. In person, because he made a new thing in the mother and in the offspring; in nature, because he made a new thing in the sign and in the manner; in grace, because he made a new thing in the covenant and in the gift. He made a new thing in the mother, because a virgin bore a man, a star brought forth the sun, a daughter conceived her father, a creature gave birth to the Creator: at once mother and daughter, bearer and handmaid; she who gave birth with her integrity intact and conceived in virginity. These things had been prefigured by fire in the bush, fruit on the rod, and dew on the fleece. “For he came down like rain upon the fleece, and like drops distilling upon the earth” (Ps. 71). This is the closed gate in the house of the Lord, and no man entered through it (Ezek. 44). This is she who first and alone escaped the curse of the law expressed in the words, “Cursed is the barren woman in Israel” (Exod. 23), and fulfilled the purpose of virginity; for “before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0457B] (Matt. 1).

He made a new thing in the offspring, because the Lord became a servant; the eternal one became a child; the exalted one became a little one; the immeasurable one became localized; the simple became composite; the immortal became mortal; the Father of his mother and the son of his daughter. He descended into his mother but remained with his Father. He assumed humanity but retained divinity. For “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,” etc. (Phil. 2). “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Strong, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). To his mother Zion it is said: “A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” [Col. 0457C] (Ps. 86).

Behold that miraculous and unfamiliar new thing which the Lord made upon earth, when a woman encompassed a man in the enclosure of her womb. Therefore “sing to the Lord a new song, because the Lord has done marvelous things” (Ps. 97). He made a new thing in the sign; for when Christ was born, a star appeared more brightly, according to Balaam’s prophecy: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24). Octavian Augustus is said to have seen in heaven a virgin carrying a son at the Sibyl’s manifestation, and thereafter he forbade anyone to call him lord, because “the King of kings and Lord of lords” had been born (Rev. 17). Hence the poet:

> Behold, a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* IV.7.)

[Col. 0457D] A fountain of oil flowed most abundantly for a whole day from the tavern of the veterans, signifying that he would be born on earth who was anointed with oil above his companions (Ps. 44). The Temple of Peace utterly collapsed. For the Romans, because of the perfect peace that was to prevail over the whole world under Augustus, had built a marvelous Temple of Peace. When they asked how long it should endure, the answer was given: “Until a virgin bears a child.” They replied joyfully: “Then it will be everlasting, because a virgin will never give birth.” But God destroyed the wisdom of the wise and rejected the prudence of the prudent (1 Cor. 1), for at the hour of the Lord’s birth it utterly collapsed.

For when full and perfect peace universally abounded throughout the whole world—a thing which had never happened before and did not happen again for long afterward—there was born God, Strong One, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. Hence the Prophet says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away” (Ps. 71). And another prophet likewise: “There shall be peace in our land when he comes” (Mic. 5).—“For he is the peace of God which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4).—“He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2); at whose birth the multitude of the heavenly host sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2).

He did something new in manner, because in his birth he fulfilled the mode of the human condition. For the first mode was that a human being should be made neither from male nor from female, as Adam; the second, that a human being should be made from male, not from female, as Eve; the third, that a human being should be made from male and female, as Abel; the fourth, that a human being should be made from female, not from male, as Christ, as the Virgin wondered when she said to the angel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1). And just as there are three persons in unity of substance, so he brought it about that there should be three substances in unity of person: so that, as the Trinity of persons does not divide the substance, so the Trinity of substances does not divide the person. For as a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ. Behold that new, recent, and final thing which the Lord did upon the earth: a woman encompassed a man in the bosom of her womb. Therefore, “Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done wonderful things” (Ps. 97). [Col. 0458B–C]

He did something new in the covenant, because in a virginal womb God joined human nature to himself in marriage. In one person he represented bridegroom and bride, as the prophet says: “As a bridegroom he placed a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with a crown” (Isa. 61). “For he has placed his tent in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18). Hence that nuptial song resounds: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; and: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” (Song 1).

The mystery of this marriage is signified by the name foretold by the prophet: “His name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7). For he is called Jesus, he is called Christ, he is called Emmanuel. Jesus according to the divine nature; Christ according to the human nature; Emmanuel according to both. For Jesus is interpreted “Saviour,” and he, insofar as he is God, saved his people from their sins (Matt. 1). Hence in the song of Habakkuk (ch. 3): “But I will rejoice in the Lord; I will glory in God, my Jesus.” Christ is interpreted “anointed,” and he, insofar as he is human, “was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.” Hence in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1). Christ is so called from *chrism*; and chrism is principally made from oil; hence his name is called oil. And because all the faithful are called Christians from Christ, his name is therefore “oil poured out.” [Col. 0458D–0459A]

Emmanuel is interpreted “God with us” (Matt. 1), namely, God-man or man-God. For in order to mediate lawfully between God and humanity, as one who would be suspect to neither party, he was made God-man, bearing in one person the nature of both. “For a mediator is not of one; but God is one” (Gal. 3): at once rich and poor, priest and victim, judge and advocate. “For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who intercedes for us; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2), who in all things is heard because of his reverence (Heb. 5). He asks himself, and he himself hears himself. He, the servant, asks himself, the Lord; he, God, hears himself, the human being.

He did something new in his gift, because God became human so that humanity might become God. God descended from heaven to earth so that humanity might ascend from earth to heaven. God became a servant so that humanity might become free. God became mortal so that humanity might become immortal. God became poor so that humanity might become rich. “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” (John 3). For “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). “Hardly does anyone die for a righteous person; though perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. But God commends his love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us; and when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through his death” (Rom. 5). [Col. 0459B–0460A]

Behold that renewed and renewing novelty which the Lord did upon earth, when a woman encompassed a man in the bosom of her womb—enclosing in the womb him by whom she was encompassed in the world. A virgin woman, an undefiled woman, encompassed the true God, the perfect man, who “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8); who says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). And to whom the prophet says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138). Above all things, not elevated; beneath all things, not cast down; among all things, not enclosed; outside all things, not excluded.

Other women conceive infants; but this woman encompassed a man in the bosom of her womb. Then time brought forth eternity; place conceived immensity; number comprehended infinity. Therefore, “Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done wonderful things.” But that you may worthily sing a new song to the new King, “put off the old human being with his deeds, and put on the new, who is created according to God” (Col. 3). “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough. Not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5): through the granting of him who is God, blessed above all things for ever.

## SERMON III. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

On the three births of Christ, which the Church represents in the three Masses on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity; and on the six names of Christ, and why they are neither more nor fewer.

[Col. 0459]

> [Col. 0459C] “A child is born to us and a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9).

Just as the Catholic faith confesses three substances in Christ—divinity, flesh, and spirit—so Sacred Scripture attests three births in him: divine birth from the Father, carnal birth from the mother, and spiritual birth in the mind. From the Father, God is born; from the mother, flesh was born; in the mind, spirit is born. From the Father, the way; from the mother, the truth; in the mind, the life. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). From the Father he is born always; from the mother he was born once; in the mind he is born often. O wondrous novelty and new miracle: that the selfsame one should be born always, once, and often.

He is born of the Father always, because that generation is eternal. Of it the Father says to the Son: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109). For Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1), first-born before every creature, who says of herself through Solomon: “Before the abysses were made, I was already conceived; before the hills, I was brought forth” (Prov. 8). [Col. 0459D–0460C] For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

He was born of the mother once, because that generation is human, concerning which the prophet says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7); and elsewhere: “The Lord shall make something new upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the bosom of her womb” (Jer. 31). For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

In the mind he is born often, because that generation is gratuitous, concerning which Scripture says: “For those who fear God the sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. 4). “I stand,” he says, “at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I shall enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3).

According to the eternal birth, Christ has a Father without a mother; according to his humanity, Christ has a mother without a father; according to the gratuitous birth, Christ has both father and mother, as he himself attests when he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12). [Col. 0460D]

The Church today represents these three births of Christ in three Masses: the first in the Mass sung at night; the second in the Mass sung at dawn; the third in the Mass sung by day. For the eternal birth is wholly hidden, so that the prophet says of it: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). To signify this, the first Mass is sung at night.

Because the carnal birth is partly hidden and partly manifest—hidden with respect to its manner, manifest with respect to its fact—the wondering Virgin said to the angel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” And the angel answered her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High,” etc. (Luke 1). To signify this, the second Mass is sung at dawn.

But the spiritual birth is more clearly manifest, as Christ declares when he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14). For Christ is conceived through affection, born through effect, and nourished through progress. To signify this, the third Mass is celebrated by day. [Col. 0461A–B]

Therefore a child is born to us. Yet from the Father he is born to us for creation, in the mind for justification, from the mother for salvation: for creation, that he might give nature; for justification, that he might give grace; for salvation, that he might give glory. Thus he was born to us from the Father for creation, according to what is read: “God said: Let there be light” (Gen. 1)—that is, he uttered the Word, namely, he begot the Son, through whom he made light. For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

For justification he is born to us in the mind, according to what is read: “For those who fear God the sun of righteousness shall arise,” that is, the light that justifies, namely, that light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (ibid.). For salvation he was born to us from the mother, according to what is read: “You shall indeed bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1). “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). [Col. 0461C]

“And a son is given to us.” He was given to us by God in order that he might be returned by us to God as a debt. For between God and humanity there was a grave discord of enmity, because humanity, by sinning, withdrew and took away from the Lord the servant whom it had handed over and subjected to the devil. Therefore peace could not reasonably be made between them unless humanity restored the damage it had inflicted.

Yet humanity had nothing with which it could worthily compensate God for the damage; for if it gave back something from rational creation in exchange for the rational substance taken away, it would be less. But it could not worthily restore a human being, because it had taken away one who was righteous and innocent, and it found no one except a sinner. Therefore, seeing that humanity could not by its own power escape the yoke of condemnation, God first came to meet it by mercy alone, so that he might afterward also liberate it through justice. Thus, in order that God might be appeased by humanity, God freely gave to humanity what humanity was bound to give back to God. [Col. 0461D]

He therefore gave a human being to humanity, whom humanity [or: God] might restore for humanity; and, in order that the recompense might be worthy, he should be not only equal to the first, but greater. For this reason “the Word was made flesh,” so that God-man might be given to human beings, as Isaiah foretold: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us.” A Son spiritually, as the Apostle says: “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8); and again: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4). Thus God, who had created the world in his wisdom, according to the saying, “You have made all things in wisdom, O Lord” (Ps. 103), might himself recreate the world in that same wisdom.

This is the evangelical woman (Luke 15) who lights a lamp in order to find the tenth drachma which had been lost. He reserved for himself the proper name of sonship, so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might become the Son of man in humanity. Therefore a child is born to us, that we may be reborn; and a son is given to us, that we may be redeemed: that we may be reborn into grace and redeemed into glory; reborn from water and redeemed in blood. For “unless one is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, one shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3); and: “We were redeemed not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb” (1 Pet. 1). [Col. 0462A–B]

“And his name shall be called Wonderful.” Six names of this child are counted, neither fewer nor more. For you know, brothers and children, that according to the arithmetical rules of numbers, one number is deficient, another perfect, another superabundant. A deficient number is one whose parts, added together, make up a smaller sum—for example, eight. Its parts are four, which is its half; two, its quarter; and one, its eighth: added together, these make seven.

A perfect number is one whose parts, added together, make up the same sum—for example, six. Its parts added together are three, its half; two, its third; and one, its sixth: together these make the same sum, namely six. A superabundant number is one whose parts, added together, make up a greater sum—for example, twelve. Its parts added together are six, its half; four, its third; three, its quarter; two, its sixth; and one, its twelfth: together these make a greater sum, namely sixteen. [Col. 0462C–D]

Therefore, because this child is God, to whom these names belong, and in God nothing is deficient, as though weak, nor anything superabundant, as though superfluous, but all is entirely perfect, as eternal: these names which belong to him according to the divine nature are accordingly designated under the perfect number. For nothing is added to God, so that anything should be superabundant in him; nor does anything depart from him, so that anything should be diminished from him. Rather, he always remains the selfsame, having in himself nothing diverse, just as he has nothing opposed; he has nothing variable, just as he has nothing contrary. He has in himself nothing but himself; nor is the possessor different from what is possessed, nor is what is possessed different from the possessor—although the possessor himself possesses no habit, nor is he possessed as a habit by anything, except that “being made in the likeness of human beings, he was found in outward appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2). Therefore he himself testifies of himself through the prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3). [Col. 0463A]

Moreover, since there are three perfect numbers—the first below the first limit, namely below ten, that is, six; the second below the second limit, namely below a hundred, that is, twenty-eight; and the third below the third limit, namely below a thousand, that is, four hundred and ninety-six—why are the names designated under this perfect number alone, namely six? Is it because “God is spirit” (John 4), and therefore supremely simple? Thus, lest this multiplicity of names indicate anything composite in him, they are comprehended under the number which alone is perfect among monads, that is, among simple numbers: six. Hence on the sixth day God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment (Gen. 2); and when the sixth age had come in the fullness of time, on the sixth day at the sixth hour he redeemed the human race.

Therefore his name shall be called Wonderful. Truly he is glorious, God in his saints, wonderful in majesty, performing wonders; and it is said of him according to his humanity in the Gospel that “all marvelled at his teaching and answers, and at the glorious things done by him” (Luke 13). To him it is spiritually said: “Renew signs and change wonders” (Ecclus. 36). [Col. 0463B–C]

“And his name shall be called Counsellor,” because he devised the counsel of peace, as he himself testifies: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” (Jer. 29). Of him the prophet says: “The counsel of the Lord remains for ever, the thought of his heart from age to age” (Ps. 32). “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

“And his name shall be called God.” Therefore this child is called God, Mighty. The name of divinity is understood in Scripture in many ways: substantively, according to nature; adoptively, according to grace; by office, according to function; usurpatively, according to vice. According to nature: “Hear, Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. 6). According to grace: “I said: You are gods, and all of you children of the Most High” (Ps. 81). According to office: “You shall not speak ill of gods, nor curse the ruler of your people” (Exod. 22). According to vice: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95).

But this child is called God substantively, according to nature.
