So that the heretic may be confounded and the Jew ashamed, let testimonies be brought forward from both the Old and the New Testament, so that a wheel may be contained within a wheel and a base may stand on a pillar. Since “every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19), let John say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Let Thomas say: “My Lord and my God” (John 20). Let Paul say: “Being in the form of God, he did not think equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2). Let David say: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Let Jeremiah say: “This is our God, and none other shall be esteemed beside him. After this he was seen on earth and conversed with human beings” (Bar. 3). And let Habakkuk say: “I will glory in the Lord and rejoice in God, my Jesus” (Hab. 3). [Col. 0463C–0464A]

For because humanity wished to be like God, as that serpent promised: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3), it was necessary that God should become human. As the Apostle says, he “was made in the likeness of human beings and found in outward appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2), so that the greatness of the vice of pride might be matched by the greatness of the virtue of humility. [Col. 0464B]

“And his name shall be called Mighty.” “Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle” (Ps. 23). For he is wisdom that conquers malice. “He reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8). Wisdom is Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). He reaches mightily from end to end—that is, from the empyrean heaven to hell—casting proud angels down from the empyrean and leading righteous souls out of hell. And he orders sweetly all things, that is, the intermediate things lying between the empyrean and hell, by redeeming the wretched and justifying sinners.

He is the true David, mighty of hand, who conquered the bear, overcame the lion, and struck down the Philistine (1 Sam. 17). He is the true Samson, who killed a lion’s cub, slew a thousand men with an ass’s jawbone, and carried away the gates of Gaza with their posts (Judg. 14, 16); he is the stronger one who came upon and overcame the armed strong man (Luke 11). [Col. 0464C]

“And his name shall be called Father of the age to come.” He is Father and giver, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “Your heavenly Father will give a good spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11). For he came to give the faithful not present things but future things; not earthly but heavenly things; not passing but eternal things; not the ground, but the pole; not the world, but heaven—so that, as Father of the age to come, he might bestow the paternal inheritance upon his children. Therefore he taught us to pray: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6). “My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world” (John 18).

In that kingdom there is life without death, day without night, certainty without “perhaps”; there will be security without fear, joy without pain, tranquillity without labour; beauty without deformity, strength without weakness, rectitude without perversity; love without malice, truth without deception, happiness without misery; joy which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of a human being” (1 Cor. 2). [Col. 0464D]

“And his name shall be called Prince of Peace.” “For he is the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4); “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2), making peace in one new human being, peace for those near and peace for those far off. At his birth the multitude of the heavenly host sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 1). Concerning his passion he said to the apostles: “I leave peace to you; I give you my peace—not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14). After the resurrection he said to the same disciples: “Peace be to you,” and again said to them: “Peace be to you” (John 20), for the peace of time and the peace of eternity. May he himself lead us to that peace, he who is God above all things, blessed for ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0465A–0466A]

## SERMON IV. ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0465]

> [Col. 0465B] “After eight days had been completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus—the name called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2).

Since you have heard the circumcised word concerning the circumcised Word, let us also say some circumcised word concerning this circumcised Word. For this is the shortened word which the Lord made upon the earth (Rom. 9), the word which he sent into Jacob and which fell upon Israel (Isa. 9): would that it may prove fruitful in our heart and not depart empty from our mouth.

Therefore Christ was circumcised so that the Christian might be circumcised in spirit. For, as he himself says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). Therefore the prophet says: “Circumcise your hearts and not your bodies” (Joel 2). And, as the Apostle says: “Circumcision of the heart is in the spirit, not in the letter; its praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2).

The mystery of circumcision ought to have been observed until the sacrament of baptism was substituted for it. For he who now cries in the Gospel, “Unless one is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, one shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3), formerly cried in the Law: “The male whose foreskin has not been cut away shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17). Therefore, since Christ was to come “unto his own,” and “his own did not receive him” (John 1), he had to be circumcised, lest the Jews use circumcision against him “to excuse excuses in sins” (Ps. 140), and say: “You are uncircumcised; you must perish from your people. You are a transgressor of the Law; we will not hear you against the Law.” [Col. 0465C–D]

Therefore he himself said: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5). Christ, then, was circumcised only in body, because he had nothing in his heart to be circumcised; just as he was baptized only in flesh, because he had nothing in his mind to be baptized. “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Nor did he contract sin, because “the Lord ascended upon a light cloud” (Isa. 19), that is, he assumed flesh exempt from sins. In accordance with this, the angel said to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore also the holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

> [Col. 0466B] “After eight days had been completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus—the name called by the angel before he was conceived.”

This name Jesus was not only announced beforehand by an angel but was also foretold by a prophet: “I,” he says, “will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult in God, my Jesus” (Hab. 3). Therefore the name Jesus belongs to the divine person according to the human nature; from which it follows that, if he is Jesus, he is God; and if he is Jesus, he is human; and therefore, if he is Jesus, he is God-man or man-God.

Indeed, this name *Jesus* has two syllables and five letters, three vowels and two consonants. It also has three inflections, through which it is declined: *Jesus, Jesu, Jesum*; from these is composed the word *sum* (“I am”). Two end in consonants, and each is singular: one belongs only to the nominative case, the other to the accusative; the third inflection ends in a vowel and is common to four cases: genitive, dative, vocative, and ablative. A great mystery and a difficult sacrament: let us therefore dig out the well, because it is deep, and draw water from the fountain of the Saviour (Isa. 12). [Col. 0466B–C]

Therefore this name *Jesus* has two syllables because Jesus has two natures, namely divine and human: divine from the Father, from whom he was born without a mother; human from the mother, from whom he was born without a father. Hear the divine nature: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Hear the human nature: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). Hear again the divine nature: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Hear the human nature: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). Of both natures the prophet says: “A human being was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86). Likewise another prophet: “Bethlehem, from you shall come forth a ruler who shall govern my people Israel; and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 10). Behold, there are two syllables in this one name because there are two natures in this one person. [Col. 0466C–D]

It should be noted that a vowel is that which gives voice by itself; a consonant is that which produces sound from another. Therefore by the three vowels is signified divinity, which, though one in itself, sounds forth in three persons. For “there are three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5). By the two consonants is signified humanity, which, although it has two syllables—namely flesh and soul—does not sound by itself but rather with another, to which it is joined in the power of personhood. For as a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and humanity are one Christ.

And indeed he is God and human; but he sounds forth by himself insofar as he is God. He does not sound forth by himself insofar as he is human, because the divinity, in assuming, retained the right of personhood; but the humanity, in being assumed, did not receive the right of personhood. For neither person assumed person, nor nature nature, but person assumed nature. [Col. 0467A]

This name *Jesus* has the same vowels as that name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, which was written on the gold plate hanging upon the front of the high priest’s mitre: namely *I, E, V*, or *Ioth, Eth, Vau*. They call it the ineffable name of God, and therefore do not dare pronounce it, but write and pronounce in its place the name *Adonai*. That name consists of four letters, *I, E, V, E*; or rather of three, because one is repeated.

Truly that name is ineffable, not with respect to sound but with respect to understanding, because the mystery of Trinity and Unity designates three persons in one substance. Thus Abraham is described as having seen three and is read to have worshipped one. The two seraphim cry one to another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts” (Rev. 4). John therefore says: “There are three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). [Col. 0467B–C]

This name has such power, as the most learned Hebrews assert, that if it is divided into three words, each of them signifies what the whole signifies: if one says *Ie, Eu, Ue*, each is a name of God, as is likewise the whole, *I, E, Ue*. For it is wonderful: each of the three persons, just as the nature itself, is one God.

But the middle letter alone is doubled in this name, because only the middle person has a twofold relation in the Godhead. For the Father is neither made nor begotten by anyone, yet another is from him. But the Son alone both is from another and has another from him. The Holy Spirit is from another, and no one is from him; but the Son alone is both from him and has another from him. [Materially uncertain: the relations in this sentence are transmitted inconsistently.]

It is fitting, therefore, in these distinctions, that the second is taken only from the first, and the third is taken from the first together with the second. For since the first ends in *E*, namely *Ie*, the second begins with *E*, namely *Eu*; and since the second ends in *U*, *Eu*, the third begins with *V*, namely *Ve*. It itself ends in *E*, from which the second begins and in which the first ends, because in the Godhead the Son is from the Father alone, but the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from both. [Col. 0467D]

Although Christ is α and ω, first and last, beginning and end, these vowels α and ω alone are not found in the name *Jesus*. But why? Because the same thing which is signified by the two syllables of this name is elsewhere designated by these two vowels: namely, the divine nature, according to which he is beginning, and the human nature, according to which Christ is end. For he who made humanity insofar as “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” Christ according to the Apostle is “the end for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10), and he says of himself: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

Yet in this name *Jesus* there is something worthy not only of consideration but also of veneration: although it has two syllables, its first alone is the name of him whose name it is, namely *Ie*, which, as stated above, is a name of God. For although Jesus has two natures, one of them nevertheless is himself, namely the divine nature. This is aptly designated in the personal name *Jesus* by the same vowels of which that essential name called the Tetragrammaton consists, because the very nature which exists essentially in the three persons is present, wholly and fully together, in this one. [Col. 0468A–B]

But perhaps you wonder why this name is declined through three inflections. Observe that Christ bent—or, so to speak, declined—himself in three ways: through passibility, patience, and passion; through passibility, which he graciously assumed; through patience, which he openly displayed; and through passion, which he willingly accepted. “For he was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53).

Do you wish to hear how Jesus bent and declined himself? If you do not believe me, believe the Apostle: for, he says, “although he was in the form of God, he did not think equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself”—that is, humbled, bent, and declined himself—“taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in outward appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2). He bent and declined himself even further: he wrote with his finger upon the earth, and his mother laid him down in a manger.

But because he so greatly bent and declined himself, “God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those under the earth” (ibid.). Render each thing to its corresponding thing: because he declined himself, “therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name”; and because he bent himself, therefore “every knee of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those under the earth bends to him.” [Col. 0468B–D]

Thus, from the three final letters of those three inflections is composed the word *sum* (“I am”), which truly and properly belongs to him according to the most excellent glory, as will here be shown: he is the one who says of himself in the Old Law, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). Understand Jesus as though saying: “I, Jesus, am; I am God,” for Jesus is the name of God; as if he said: “Manifestly I am God, and I do not change.” He himself expressed this in the Gospel when he said: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8); and again: “It is I; do not be afraid” (Luke 24). [Col. 0469A]

Of these three inflections, two end in consonants: the nominative in S and the accusative in M; the third in a vowel, namely U, which is common to four cases: genitive, dative, vocative, and ablative. By the two consonants, as was said above, Christ’s human nature is signified, which consists of two substances, namely soul and flesh; and Christ, according to his human nature, is found, so to speak, to have been nominative and accusative. He was nominative with respect to the office of preaching which he carried out; accusative with respect to the penalty of the Passion which he endured. For the office of preaching is indicated by his saying: “Father, I have made known your name to the people whom you gave me from the world” (John 17). But the penalty of the Passion was involved in this: [Col. 0469B] he is recorded as having been accused of many things before Pilate.

But Christ, who is signified by a vowel according to his divine nature, exists according to that same nature, as it were, as genitive, dative, vocative, and ablative. As genitive he creates nature; as dative he bestows glory; as vocative he calls out grace; as ablative he removes unto punishment. Of these, he accomplishes the first two in the present and the latter two in the future.

For he shows himself to be genitive when he says: “Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” (Isa. 66); for “my Father is working even now, and I am working” (John 5). He proves himself to be dative when he says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14). He shows himself to be vocative when he says: “Come, [Col. 0469C] blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). He shows himself to be ablative when he adds: “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.). For then he removes the wicked from the midst of the righteous, so that the ungodly may be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.

But because among consonants semivowels are more worthy than mutes, these two consonants, S and M, by which the human nature in Christ—that is, soul and flesh—is signified, are not mutes but semivowels. For among all creatures human nature is more noble in Christ, as the Psalmist says: “You have crowned him with glory and honour, and have set him over the works of your hands; you have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. 8). For although he is made lower than the angels by so much as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs (Heb. 1), nevertheless, insofar as he assumed passible flesh, he was made a little lower than the angels, since angelic nature is impassible.

Appropriately, the second of those semivowels is a liquid, namely M, in the accusative case: because Christ, as it were, himself endured the Passion of death [reading uncertain; the Latin is defective]. [Col. 0470B] Therefore the Apostle, expounding that prophetic saying, “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, O Lord” (ibid.), declares that he was made a little lower than the angels: “We see Jesus, because of the Passion of death, crowned with glory and honour, so that by the grace of God he might taste death.”

And note that, just as among the Hebrews that ineffable name is written one way and pronounced another—for it is written with these four letters, I, E, V, E, and pronounced *Adonai*—so among the Latins that most excellent name is written one way and pronounced another. It is pronounced *Jesus* and written IHS with a title placed above it. The mystery is expressed, but is to be expounded elsewhere: many will pass through it, and its meaning will be manifold. This, then, is the holy and glorious name [Col. 0470C] invoked over us: “Nor is there any other name under heaven in which we must be saved” (Acts 4): a sweet name, a delightful name, a lovable name, indeed a saving name, through which may the Lord himself save us, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0469D] From the edition of Angelo Mai.]

[Col. 0469]

[Col. 0469D] “This is the day which the Lord has made: let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117).

Although the Lord makes all days, what day is so celebrated and solemn that it is said especially of it, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” and so forth? This is the day of the Lord’s resurrection, on which Christ, rising from the dead, granted us hope of security and certainty, and the glory of resurrection unto immortality: so that where the exaltation of the head has gone before, there the body of humility may follow. For although many rose before Christ, he nevertheless rose first, immortal and impassible. Hence he is called “the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. 15), and “the firstborn of the dead” (Rev. 1). For “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer [Col. 0470D] have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

Therefore this is a day without night, life without death, on which Christ rose from the dead and, descending into hell, swallowed up death and bit hell, as is read in the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13).

Now “day” is called the bright sun over the earth, that is, the brightness of the air resulting from the sun’s shining upon the earth. This sun is Christ, of whom it is written: “For those who fear God the sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. 4), that is, the sun which makes righteous—the “light,” namely, “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). He says of himself in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world; whoever walks in the day does not stumble” (John 11). This sun set upon the altar of the cross when Jesus, “bowing his head, [Col. 0471A] gave up the spirit” (John 19). Of this setting the Psalmist says: “The sun knew its setting” (Ps. 103); and the material sun also recognized it and submerged its own brightness. For “from the sixth hour,” when the Lord was crucified, “until the ninth hour,” when he gave up the spirit, “darkness came over the whole earth” (Matt. 27), “and the sun was darkened” (Luke 23). But when he rose on the third day, a new day shone upon the world, because “God, the Lord, has shone upon us” (Ps. 117).

There are twelve hours of the day; and this day, that is, the brightness of the Lord’s resurrection, has twelve hours: namely, twelve appearances of the risen Lord himself, by which his resurrection is most clearly proved.

The first hour was when he appeared to Mary Magdalene, who thought him to be the gardener, and said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20). The second hour was when he appeared to the women and said to them: “Greetings!” But they came near, held his feet, and worshipped him (Matt. 28). The third hour was when he appeared to Peter. The fourth hour was when he appeared, in the form of a traveller, to two disciples going to Emmaus, and they recognized him in the breaking of bread. The fifth hour was when he appeared to the eleven disciples, Thomas being absent, standing in their midst, and said: “Peace to you; do not be afraid” (John 20). The sixth was when he appeared again to his disciples, Thomas being with them, and showed them his hands and [Col. 0471C] side. The seventh was when he revealed himself to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, standing on the shore, and said to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find” (John 20). The eighth was when he appeared to the eleven disciples in Galilee, on the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, and said to them: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28). The ninth was when Jesus appeared to the eleven disciples as they reclined at table and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead. The tenth hour was when he led them out toward Bethany, to the Mount of Olives, and “while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1).

There were also two further hours in which he appeared, so that the twelvefold number of hours might be completed. [Col. 0471D] Of these the Apostle says: “He was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once, then by James” (1 Cor. 15). But these two hours are not read in the Gospel, except that it is read in the Gospel called *According to the Hebrews* that, after the Lord had given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, he came to James and appeared to him. For James had sworn that he would not eat bread from the hour when he had drunk the Lord’s cup until he saw the Lord risen from those who sleep. Last of all he was seen by Paul also, as by one untimely born; but this appearance occurred after he had ascended into heaven, and therefore it does not belong to the hours of the day.

Yet it is likely that he appeared before all others to his most glorious mother, although this is not read in the Gospel: so that she whom the death of her son had grieved more than all others might be gladdened by his resurrection before all others. Perhaps today’s station is celebrated in this basilica of hers to signify this. [Col. 0472A]

The hours may also be designated differently, according to the distinction of the five hours which the Lord assigned in the Gospel (Matt. 9), when he sent labourers into his vineyard: namely, early morning, the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. Under these are included the other seven hours, so that there are eleven hours of the day.

The first hour, therefore, was the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection made by the testimony of angels; and it includes two hours. One was when “the angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled back the stone and sat upon it” [Col. 0472B] (Matt. 28)—and “the angel answered the women: Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here” (Mark 21 [OCR error for 16]). The other was when Mary Magdalene “bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid” (John 20)—and “behold, two men stood beside them in shining clothing and said to them: Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen” (Luke 14 [OCR error for 24]). Therefore, since every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Deut. 19; Matt. 18), it is evident that this testimony of angels should be believed.

[Col. 0472C] The third hour was the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection made by the eating of food; for otherwise it might have been thought phantasmal, as though produced by magical art rather than divine power. For a body raised phantasmatically cannot eat food; consequently, the eating of food is a most certain argument of a wholly true resurrection. To signify this, John the Evangelist records that at the supper made with Jesus in Bethany, six days before Passover, where Lazarus had been dead, Lazarus—who had been dead—was one of those reclining at table (John 12). And when the Lord had raised the girl, he ordered that she be given something to eat (Mark 5).

But this manifestation includes three hours. One was when he said to the apostles: “Have you anything to eat?” [Col. 0472D] And they brought him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. “When he had eaten before them, he took what remained and gave it to them” (Luke 24). Another was when the seven disciples came down from the boat onto land and saw coals laid out, fish placed upon them, and bread; and he said to them: “Come, dine.” And none of those reclining dared ask him, “Who are you?” knowing that he was the Lord (John 21). The third was when Jesus appeared to the eleven as they reclined and, “eating with them, commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father” (Acts 1).

The sixth hour was the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection made by the showing of miracles. This likewise includes three hours. First, that at his resurrection “many bodies of the saints who had slept rose, and came into the holy city and appeared to many” [Col. 0473A] (Matt. 27). Second, that “there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled back the stone and sat upon it; and the guards, terrified by fear of him, became as dead men” (Matt. 28). Another was when, at the Lord’s word, the disciples cast their net on the right side of the boat. When he entered among the disciples though the doors were shut, and when he truly went up into heaven borne by clouds, this entrance and ascent seem not so much miraculous as natural to a glorified body, because of the subtlety and agility which a glorified body naturally possesses.

The ninth hour was the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0473B] made by the showing of the wounds, which Christ retained in his impassible body and showed to the disciples so that they might believe that he whom they knew to have been wounded on the cross was the very same one raised from death. This itself includes two hours. One was when he said to the apostles: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands, side, and feet (Luke 24). The other was when he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful” (John 20).

The eleventh hour of this day was the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0473C] made by the exposition of the Scriptures. [Col. 0474A] This likewise includes two hours. One was when he said to the disciples on the way: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he expounded to them the Scriptures concerning himself (Luke 24). The other was when he said to the apostles: “These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: all things written concerning me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets must be fulfilled.” Then he opened their understanding to comprehend the Scriptures, and said to them: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day” (ibid.).

Behold, we have expounded in two ways the twelve hours of this votive and festal day, so that from these hours there may arise a natural day of twenty-four hours, which the Lord has made for us to rejoice and be glad in it. [Col. 0474B] Let us rejoice in heart and be glad in body, as it is written: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83). The heart rejoices when it knows itself freed from evil thoughts; the body is glad when it feels itself cleansed from unclean deeds. For “it is not for the wicked to rejoice,” says the Lord (Isa. 48), and “there is no peace in the bones because of sins” (Ps. 37). Therefore, if we desire worthily to celebrate the day of the Lord’s resurrection, let us cleanse our hearts and bodies, that we may beneficially rejoice and be glad in it; through him who, with the Father, etc.

## SERMON VI FOR SUNDAY

[Note: [Col. 0473D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[Col. 0473]

[Col. 0473C] “Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18).

Although the Pharisee went up to the temple to pray, he commended himself and accused his neighbour. He commended himself in three respects: for singular righteousness, saying, “I am not like other people”; for bodily abstinence, saying, “I fast twice in the Sabbath”; and for legal observance, saying, “I give tithes of all that I possess.” But he accused his neighbour in three respects: of adultery, injustice, and robbery. Thus, after saying in his own commendation, “I am not like other people: robbers, adulterers, and unjust,” he immediately added, in accusation of his neighbour, “or even like this tax collector: a robber, adulterer, and unjust man.”

But, in the manner of the proud, wishing [Col. 0473D] to set himself arrogantly and uniquely above all others, he began: “I am not like other people”—as though saying: “I alone am righteous; all the rest are unrighteous.” The Pharisee is not reproved for giving thanks [Col. 0474C] to the Lord that he was not a robber, adulterer, and unjust man, or because he fasted twice in the Sabbath and gave tithes from everything he possessed; but because he proudly boasted that he was not like other people, as though he alone were righteous. For by “Sabbath” is meant a week, according to Hebrew usage, because they name the other days from the Sabbath, as “the first of the Sabbath,” and so the rest; so that “twice in the Sabbath” means twice in the week.

The Apostle did not think in this way. He said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4). The Psalmist likewise testifies: “Who understands transgressions?” (Ps. 18). Therefore he prays: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults” [Col. 0474D] (ibid.). Solomon also says: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean, and I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. 20). For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1), since “we all stumble in many things” (James 3).

Listen, arrogant Pharisee, who rashly boast of your righteousness, to blessed Job humbly speaking of himself: “Even if I were innocent,” he says (Job 9). You affirm this very thing in your boasting, that you are not like other people—a robber, adulterer, and unjust man. You would have acted more wisely had you humbly accused yourself, in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18). For the one who accuses himself, God will excuse; and the one who excuses himself, God will accuse. In human judgment, indeed, the person who confesses his sin—

[Note: [Col. 0475D] Something is missing.]

—as in the saying, “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Job 40). Hence in the Psalm: “I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness [Col. 0475B] of my sin” (Ps. 31).

Certainly, in this parable a dispute between accuser and defendant is argued before a judge. The Pharisee is the accuser; the tax collector is the humble and devout defendant; the judge is righteous and truthful. The former, as proud and arrogant, says: “I am not like other people: robbers and unjust men.” He added, “or even like this tax collector.” The latter, humble and devout, stood at a distance and would not lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” But the judge, as righteous and truthful, having heard the confessions of the parties, pronounced judgment in the case: “Amen, I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.” He gave the reason for the sentence: [Col. 0475C] “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.” This man confesses himself a sinner, and God forgives his sin; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4).

This tax collector is especially commended in three respects: because he stood at a distance, because he would not raise his eyes, and because he beat his breast. By these are denoted the three things necessary to a penitent: shame, fear, and sorrow. Out of shame he stood at a distance; out of fear he did not raise his eyes; out of sorrow he beat his breast. Thus he blushes, is afraid, and groans because of the foulness, multitude, and greatness of his sins. Therefore, distrusting his own righteousness and trusting in divine mercy, he prays briefly: “God,” he says, “be merciful to me, a sinner.” [Col. 0475D] But a short prayer wins a long forgiveness, for “this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.”

In striking the breast there are three things to be noted: the blow, the sound, and the touch. Through these are signified the three things necessary to true penitence: contrition of heart, signified by the blow; confession of the mouth, signified by the sound; and satisfaction by works, signified by the touch. Therefore penitents customarily do and ought to strike their breasts.

You therefore, whoever you are, Christian, learn, when you go up into the temple, not to boast of yourself in a vainglorious and proud manner or accuse your neighbour, but to praise devoutly and humbly to beseech God, accusing your own wickedness with shame, [Col. 0476A] fear, and sorrow alike, because of the multitude and greatness of your sins. Thus you too may obtain from God true forgiveness through humble penitence, after the example of this man who went down to his house justified rather than the other—not because this man was justified by the other, but rather accused by him, but because in comparison with the other he appeared righteous, or less unrighteous.

[Note: [Col. 0475] Correct; for it is a Hebraism, as is known to beginners in the sacred language.]

Thus it is said to Jerusalem through the prophet: “Bear your shame, because you have surpassed your sisters in your sins, acting more wickedly than they; for they have been justified by you” (Ezek. 14). Or, while that man remained on the height of pride, this one departed and went down to his house, in order to dwell within the abode of humility, justified by God.

[Col. 0476B] But carefully beware lest, when you hear that the Pharisee was condemned by the Lord, you suppose that he sinned because he gave tithes of everything he possessed or because he fasted twice in the Sabbath. There is certainly no sin in these things: it is good to give tithes of everything, just as it is good to fast twice in the Sabbath, that is, in the week. Rather, he sinned especially because he proudly boasted that he was not like other people: a robber, adulterer, and unjust man. This clearly proves that arrogance or pride is a greater sin than adultery or robbery.

Tithes must therefore be given from all that is possessed, that is, received—not only from greater things but also from lesser—according to what Truth says elsewhere: [Col. 0476C] “Woe to you, Pharisees, who tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect judgment and the love of God! These things you ought to have done, without omitting the others” (Luke 11).

Observe also carefully that, although the Pharisee was arrogant and proud, he had not yet broken out into such audacity or pride as to confess that his good qualities existed from himself, as those are recorded to have said: “Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” (Ps. 11). Rather, he acknowledged them to come from him from whom “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). Thus he gave thanks to him for his good things. Therefore the madness of those who presume to assert that human beings are made by God, [Col. 0476D] but good by themselves—attributing nature to God and ascribing virtue to themselves—must be wholly rejected.

The tax collector stood at a distance and did not dare lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Since most of you must follow the example of the humble tax collector, let us be instructed why this tax collector stood at a distance and did not dare look toward heaven. I think that, if he had been questioned, he would immediately have answered: “I stand at a distance because I am ashamed and blush; I fear to look toward heaven and am afraid to approach the altar, especially for four reasons, which I shall explain in order.

“The first reason [Col. 0477A] is that I am foul and fetid with criminal and unspeakable stains of sin, so that my soul is more abominable and unclean than leprous flesh. For I am a tomb whitewashed outside, but within full of every impurity and of dead men’s bones” (Matt. 23). “I am a four-days-dead corpse, stinking in the tomb” (John 11)—indeed, to speak in this way, a corpse dead for four ages, because through four stages of life, from infancy to old age, I have emitted in the tomb of evil habit the most foul stench of my conduct, like “a beast rotting in dung” (Joel 1). I am truly dead, because I am wholly separated from true life, that is, from God. Therefore I stand at a distance because I am ashamed and afraid to approach, lest by the stench of my foulness I offend the divine majesty all the more. Therefore, “all [Col. 0477B] day long my shame is against me, and confusion of face has covered me” (Ps. 43).

“The second reason is that I am ungrateful and undevoted toward God for absolutely all the goods and gifts granted and bestowed upon me by him. For all gifts—whether bodily, spiritual, or natural—are gratuitous. What I am, that I live, that I move: I have received all this from him, from whom ‘every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.’ Yet I have always repaid him with offences for grace, evil deeds for benefits, injury for honour: a human being to God, a servant to his lord, a creature to its Creator; forgetful and ungrateful for that inestimable grace, that God himself was made a servant for me, the Creator was made a creature for me, and Life himself endured death for me, in order to redeem me from death unto life. For ‘though he was in the form of God, he did not think equality with God robbery. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being made in the likeness of a human being; and, found in appearance as a human being, he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross’ [Col. 0477C] (Phil. 2). Therefore I stand at a distance because I am ashamed and afraid to approach, lest by my lack of devotion and ingratitude I offend the divine majesty all the more. Hence, ‘All day long my shame is against me, and confusion of face has covered me.’

“The third reason is that I have always abused God’s patience, despising the riches of his goodness and long-suffering. For God’s kindness led me to repentance; but I, according to the hardness of my heart and my impenitent heart, have stored up wrath for myself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2). “He has hitherto invited and waited for me to look back and return to him; yet I have always estranged and removed myself from him, going” (Ps. 44) after the vanities and desires of my heart, going into a far country, where by living luxuriously I squandered my substance (Luke 15), despised his commandments, and turned aside from his counsels. I did not consider that, if he wished, he could destroy me by a word alone or cast me down by a mere nod.

“Certainly, since no creature could bear so many and such great injuries and offences so long with equanimity without taking vengeance upon them, if it had the power and opportunity to avenge itself, surely the Creator alone is known to be so patient; and from this he is proved omnipotent. [Col. 0478A] He gave me time to repent, but I abused it. Therefore I stand at a distance because I am ashamed and afraid to appear, lest by my great abuse and great contempt I offend the divine majesty all the more. Thus, ‘My shame is against me, and confusion of face has covered me.’

“The fourth and final reason is that I have been unfaithful, false, treacherous, and perjured toward God himself, my God: I have kept neither resolution, promise, vow, nor even oath, but have always returned ‘like a dog to its vomit’ (Prov. 26). At baptism I renounced the devil and all his pomps, but after baptism I turned back to the pomps of the devil. In penitence I repeatedly promised that I would not again commit deeds to be wept over; but after penitence I again committed without number deeds to be wept over. I did not cease to sin, and I took no care to make satisfaction.

“Certainly, to recover bodily health I have often endured strict and burdensome diets, always taken the harshest and most grievous draughts, and even suffered iron and fire; yet for recovery of the soul’s health I have scarcely been willing to undergo anything difficult. Why is this, except that I hoped less faithfully for the salvation of my soul? Is it not evidence of unbelief that, to obtain a temporal advantage, I have endured many and [Col. 0478C] great labours, but to gain an eternal reward have scarcely been willing to undertake even a light labour? Therefore I stand at a distance, because I blush and am afraid within myself, lest I offend the divine majesty. Hence, ‘All day long my shame is against me, and confusion of face has covered me.’

“What, then, shall I do? I cannot flee; I am afraid to approach. But let necessity overcome shame, and boldness conquer fear. Therefore ‘I shall arise,’ and now at last ‘I shall go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ Nor am I worthy to behold the height of heaven because of the multitude and foulness of my iniquities. ‘Make me,’ at least, ‘as one of your hired servants’ (Luke 15), [Col. 0478D] and do not allow me to die in my sins—you who died for the sins of all.

“O Lord our God, I flee to you; I cry to you, fountain of mercy and harbour of salvation. My soul is like earth without water before you (Ps. 142), dry and parched. But ‘as the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God’ (Ps. 41). Therefore I beat my breast; and in that very striking I carefully attend to three things: the blow, the sound, and the touch. By these I understand spiritually the three things necessary for true penitence: contrition of heart, signified by the blow; confession of the mouth, signified by the sound; and satisfaction in deed, signified by the touch. For as I have sinned in three ways—in heart, word, and deed—so I ought to repent in three ways: by compunction of heart, in which is sorrow; by confession of the mouth, in which is shame; and by satisfaction in deed, in which is labour.

[Col. 0479A] “Therefore let the penitent beware lest he repent deceitfully while thinking that he repents truly. For since to repent is to undergo punishment, surely the person who does not undergo punishment does not repent. Therefore the Psalmist said: ‘I have laboured in my groaning,’ and so forth (Ps. 6). He would not have said, ‘I have laboured in my groaning,’ of rare and slight groaning, but of groaning prolonged and continual; for one does not labour in groaning if he laughs as soon as he groans. Surely he is not penitent who does not undergo punishment but instead makes light of it, passing from groaning to laughter. But the one who said, ‘All day I went about grieving; I roared from the groaning [Col. 0479B] of my heart, and my pain is always before me’ (Ps. 37), laboured in groaning.

“Nor must one weep only once, but often. Therefore he says: ‘Every night I shall wash my bed’ (Ps. 6). Nor only a little, but much. Therefore he adds: ‘With my tears I shall drench my couch’ (ibid.). Where there is drenching, there is an abundance of moisture. Therefore he does not say ‘on nights,’ but ‘through the nights’; he does not say ‘through some,’ but ‘through every one,’ in order to show that he has a prolonged and continual weeping, reproving the hardness of those who can scarcely and rarely be softened to tears. For that person has a stony breast, a heart of stone, and iron within, who produces no groans, emits no sighs, and sheds no tears for himself—not so much for his body, which will die, as perhaps for his heart, which is already dead. Let him therefore know himself to be culpably hard and harshly blameworthy who mourns the bodily death of his friend but does not weep for the spiritual death of his own soul.

“Consider rather the tears of that sinful woman who, ‘standing behind at the Lord’s feet, watered his feet with tears and wiped them with the hair of her head’; and do likewise if you wish to hear with her: ‘Your sins are forgiven you’ (Luke 7).

“Or by ‘night’ is understood sin, which darkens the mind and obscures it with the gloom of sins; and by ‘bed’ is understood the conscience, in which the spirit sleeps when it rests from the disturbance of vices. Thus he says: ‘I shall wash my bed,’ that is, I shall cleanse my conscience, ‘through every night,’ that is, through every sin, [Col. 0479D] namely, from all sins. For each individual sin the penitent ought to offer an individual sacrifice, in order to offer, according to the divine Law, a fitting sacrifice for sin (Lev. 5)—that, indeed, of which it is elsewhere written: ‘A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God’ (Ps. 50), in which every impure thing is washed away today.

“Therefore let the penitent beware lest, if in confession he produces a sound, a hiss comes forth instead. For the person who reveals some sins and conceals others, or confesses one part to one person and another part to another, or states the deed but suppresses its manner, or minimizes and excuses the crime—that person certainly does not produce a sound but emits a hiss. But one who confesses truthfully ought to confess every circumstance of sin: the degree to which he sinned, the place, time, number, person, age, knowledge, rank, order; whether easily, frequently, openly, or persistently.

[Col. 0480A] “Just as pus gathered beneath the skin increases swelling and pain until, when drawn out through an opening, the swelling and pain are relieved, so the rot of sin, heaped up in the hidden place of the heart, inflates and disturbs the soul until, cast out through confession, the distress of inflation and disturbance is immediately eased. From this not only is the spirit certainly made cheerful, but the body too rejoices, as it feels itself now relieved of the great weakness by which it was previously burdened.”

Moreover, a penitent is not accustomed to strike his breast with only one finger or two [Col. 0480B], but with all of them together; for just as the hand has five fingers, so satisfaction has five parts: the power of prayer, abstinence from food, generosity in almsgiving, labour in work, and the roughness of clothing. Of these the Psalmist says: “I clothed myself in sackcloth; I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV);—“I have been exercised, and my spirit failed for a little while” (Ps. LXXVI);—“My eyes have failed” (Ps. LXVIII);—“I was troubled and did not speak” (Ps. LXXVI). Would that, in striking my breast, I had done what I said, so that I might safely say: God, be merciful to me, a sinner; “Lord, have mercy” (Ps. XL). I confess and acknowledge [Col. 0480C] that my crimes are so many and so great that, if you wished to deal with me according to what my deserts require, you could most justly both put me to shame in the present and condemn me for ever. But you, God, be merciful to me, a sinner; Lord, have mercy. Certainly no punishment would be sufficient, nor any vengeance proportionate, if fire descended from heaven and consumed me wholly, or if the earth opened its mouth and swallowed me alive. But you, God, be merciful to me, a sinner; Lord, have mercy. Therefore, “do not enter into judgement with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII). For “if you mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. CXXIX). But you, God, be merciful to me, a sinner; Lord, have mercy. [Col. 0480D] Unless I knew you to be most merciful and most devoutly compassionate, most clement and most gracious, most patient and most gentle, I should indeed utterly lose confidence and wholly despair. But you, Lord, be merciful to me. Although I wholly distrust and despair of my own merits and powers, yet in your loving-kindness and mercy, O God, I place the fullest hope and confidence. Therefore let your loving-kindness overcome my ungodliness, and let your mercy conquer my misery. For “against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L), O Jesus Christ, Saviour of the world, who are blessed above all for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE FEAST OF ST SYLVESTER, SUPREME PONTIFF

On the dignity, holiness, and usefulness of St Sylvester; on the kingdom and priesthood of the Roman pontiff; on the priority of priesthood over kingship; and, finally, on the necessity for a priest of the splendour alike of knowledge and of life.

[Col. 0481]

[Col. 0481A] “Behold a great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous; and in the time of wrath he became reconciliation.” (Office of the Church, from Ecclesiasticus CXLIV.)

In the words set before us, three things concerning blessed Sylvester are especially commended to us: dignity, holiness, and usefulness. His dignity is stated first: “Behold a great priest”; his holiness follows: “Who in his days pleased God and was found righteous”; his usefulness concludes: “And in the time of wrath he became reconciliation.” Thus holiness follows dignity, and usefulness follows holiness, because one who holds the place of dignity ought to possess the merit of holiness; and one who possesses the merit of holiness ought to perform the work of usefulness—lest one who is highest in rank be lowest in merit, and one innocent in heart be useless [Col. 0481B] in deed. Alas, how many such people there are in the Church today: exalted in rank, but base in merit, and useless to others. Would that I too were not one of them, “appointed for the fall” rather than “for the rising again of many” (Luke II). May the Lord avert this, he “who is able to raise up children to Abraham from stones” (Matt. III).

Blessed Sylvester, therefore, was a priest not merely great but greatest, exalted by pontifical and royal power. He was the vicar of him who is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Apoc. XIX), “a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX), so that the words of the blessed Apostle Peter [Col. 0481C]—their first and chief predecessor—may be understood spiritually as spoken to him and his successors: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II). For the Lord chose these men to be priests and kings. For the distinguished Emperor Constantine, by divine revelation through blessed Sylvester, was cleansed of leprosy in baptism; and he handed over and relinquished to him the City and the Senate, with their persons and dignities, and the whole kingdom of the West, himself withdrawing to Byzantium and retaining for himself the empire of the East. He wished also to confer upon him the crown from his own head; but Sylvester, out of reverence for the clerical crown—or rather from humility—refused to wear it. Nevertheless, in place of a royal diadem, he uses a circular gold-fringed headpiece. By pontifical authority he appoints patriarchs, primates, metropolitans, and bishops; [Col. 0481D] by royal power he establishes senators, prefects, judges, and notaries. Thus the Roman pontiff uses a crown as a sign of empire and a mitre as a sign of pontificate; but he uses the mitre always and everywhere, whereas he uses the crown neither everywhere nor always, because pontifical [Col. 0482A] authority is earlier, worthier, and more extensive than imperial authority.

For priesthood preceded kingship among the people of God, since Aaron, the first high priest, preceded Saul, the first king [variant: “consecrated him”]; Noah likewise preceded Nimrod, since Scripture says of Nimrod that Babylon was the beginning of Nimrod’s dominion (Gen. X). But Noah built an altar to the Lord and offered burnt offerings upon it (Gen. VIII). Speaking of priests and kings, moreover, Scripture calls priests gods and kings princes: “You shall not speak ill of the gods,” it says, “and you shall not curse the ruler of your people” (Exod. XXII). And although the Apostle says concerning the king, “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake: whether to the king as pre-eminent, or to governors as sent by him” (I Pet. III), the Lord himself says to Jeremiah [Col. 0482B] the priest, one of the priests of Anathoth: “I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and destroy, and to build and plant” (Jer. I). But to Peter—and in Peter to Peter’s successors—the Lord said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI). He who said “whatever” excepted nothing. For this reason elsewhere he said: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI), making no distinction between these sheep and those, in order to show that one who refuses to have Peter as shepherd has no claim at all upon his sheep. To him alone he also said: “You shall be called Cephas” (John I), which is interpreted “head,” wherein the fullness of the senses resides; for, while the others [Col. 0482C] were called to share in the burden of care, Peter alone was taken into the fullness of power.

Blessed Sylvester, then, was Peter’s successor and Jesus Christ’s vicar. Therefore he truly was a great priest, who in his days pleased God. Not so much in the days of time as in the days of virtues: the former pass away in their changing course, while the latter endure in stability. For the individual virtues are individual days that illumine the mind; of these it is read mystically that Job’s sons held feasts on each of the days (Job I). Yet two things are especially necessary for a priest: the splendour of life and the splendour of knowledge, so that he may shine alike by example and by teaching. For “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I), [Col. 0482D] leaving priests an example that they should follow his footsteps: “who committed no sin,” so that there may be uprightness in life, “nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II), so that there may be truth in doctrine; for “whoever does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0483A] (Matt. V). Hence pomegranates hung from the pontifical garment together with golden bells (Exod. XXVIII). A priest must shine in good works for the sake of example. Therefore it is said elsewhere: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V); and again: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII). He must also excel in knowledge for the sake of instruction. Thus it is said: “You are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world. No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matt. V); for “day pours forth speech to day, and night makes knowledge known to night” (Ps. XVIII).

[Col. 0483B] Perhaps these are the two days concerning which the Evangelist testifies that Jesus remained with the Samaritans for two days (John IV): namely, because the Samaritans remained enlightened by Christ both through the example of his life and through the word of his teaching. Neither of the two should suffice a priest without the other. For if a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is held in contempt, and it is said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV);—“Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast out the speck from your brother’s eye” (Luke VI);—“You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. II). Certainly, “if the priest who has been anointed sins, he causes the people to offend” (Lev. IV); and “if an enchanter is bitten by a serpent, [Col. 0483C] who will heal him?” (Ecclus. XII). “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments, and a harsh judgement shall be made upon those who rule” (Wis. VI).

These are the two days, namely life and knowledge, in which blessed Sylvester pleased God and was found righteous, as history plainly attests. For he endured much to acquire the merit of life, and established much for the instruction of knowledge. He also became reconciliation in a time of wrath, reconciling sinners to pardon and those at discord to peace. For until his time the wrath of pagans against Christians blazed so fiercely that Christians were slaughtered everywhere like sheep for the slaughter: “They were stoned, they were cut asunder, they died by the slaughter of the sword; they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted—men of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. XI). But through blessed Sylvester Christians were reconciled to pagans, [Col. 0484B] because, once the most devout Emperor Constantine had been baptized, peace and liberty were given to the Church of God. From that time the Church began to spread, and Isaiah’s prophecy to her began to be fulfilled: “Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together and come to you. Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise at your side” (Isa. LX). He was truly the vicar of him of whom the Apostle says: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. We entreat you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. V). For priests are mediators between God and man, and therefore they ought to be such as are pleasing to God and acceptable to men. May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed above all for ages of ages, make us such through the merits and prayers of blessed Sylvester. [Col. 0484C] Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE SOLEMNITY OF THE MANIFESTATION OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

On the most holy marriage between Christ and the Church—promised, sworn, fulfilled, consummated, confirmed, and declared; on the three manifestations; on the coming and gifts of the Magi and their meaning; and, finally, on the allegorical exposition of the Gospel and the houses in which Christ is found.

[Col. 0483]

[Col. 0483D] “When the Magi saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshipped him; and, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matt. II).

The most holy marriage between Christ and the Church, promised to the patriarch Abraham, then sworn to King David, then fulfilled to Mary the mother, is today consummated, confirmed, and declared. It was consummated in the Magi’s adoration, confirmed in the baptism in the Jordan, and declared in the miracle of the wine. Long ago God promised the patriarch Abraham that all nations would be blessed in his seed (Gen. XVI), and swore to King David that he would set one of the fruit of his womb upon his throne (Ps. [Col. 0484D] CXXXIII). But what he had promised and sworn he fulfilled to Mary the mother, since “he set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII);—for “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). That marriage is read as consummated today when the Gentiles joined themselves to Christ through faith in the adoration of the Magi. For behold, Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” It is read as confirmed today because the Father’s voice was heard over Christ at his baptism in the Jordan: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). It is read as declared today when Christ turned water into wine at a wedding, because “Jesus did this as the beginning of signs in [Col. 0485A] Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory; and his disciples believed in him” (John II).

The Church commemorates and venerates all three together today. For on the thirteenth day after his birth Jesus was worshipped by the Magi; on the same day, in his thirtieth year, he was baptized by John in the Jordan; and then, once a year had elapsed, on the same day he changed water into wine. Therefore, brothers and children, let us rejoice and exult—not in this world, but in the Lord—as it is said: “Let him who glories glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I). And as we sang in jubilation: “Today the Church is united to her heavenly Bridegroom; today Christ washed her sins in the Jordan; the Magi hasten with gifts to the royal wedding; and the wedding-guests rejoice as water is made wine.” Therefore this day, as is found in the more ancient codices, is called *Epiphaniarum*, “of manifestations,” in the plural, [Col. 0485B] because Christ was manifested today through the sign of the star, through the Father’s word, and through the miracle of the wine. Hence some distinguish these three manifestations by particular [variant: “spiritual”] names, calling *Epiphany* the manifestation made from above through the star, from ἐπί (*epi*), “above”; *Theophany*, the manifestation made by God at baptism, from θεός (*theos*), “God”; and *Bethphany*, that made within a house at the wedding, from *beth*, “house,” and *phane*, “illumination.”

Let us rejoice, then, brothers and children; let us rejoice in the Lord. For the Magi too “rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” Because they saw the star, they rejoiced; but because the star which they had seen in the east went before them, [Col. 0485C] they rejoiced with great joy; and because they found the child with Mary his mother, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. According to the historical account, these three Magi were three kings, not diviners but philosophers, so called from the greatness of their knowledge; for those whom the Greeks call philosophers, the Persians call Magi. They were successors in the teaching of Balaam, who had learned of the star by his prophecy, when long ago he proclaimed in the Spirit: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. XXIV). They came from the regions of Persia and Chaldaea, where the river Saba is found, from which the Sabæan region also takes its name. As David had foretold: “The kings of Arabia and Saba shall bring gifts” (Ps. LXXI). It is believed that they hastened from lands so remote in so short a time upon dromedaries—animals of extraordinary swiftness—according to the prophet’s words: “A flood of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah” (Isa. LX).

Accordingly, these three kings assembled by agreement, as was their custom when investigating their doctrines, and saw a certain wondrous star above the land of Judaea, remarkable and distinct in many respects. The sun’s light did not overshadow it; it was not in the firmament among the stars, nor in the ether among the planets; rather, it remained motionless in the upper air, near the earth. Warned by this sign, they believed that in Jerusalem had been born the king of whom Balaam foretold: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise from Israel, and from Jacob shall come one who shall rule” (Num. XXIV). [Col. 0486A] Therefore the Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, thinking to find the newborn king in the royal city. But those who had been assured of the time by the sign of the star deserved to be assured of the place by the oracle of prophecy. For thus it had been written by the prophet Micah: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall go forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from days everlasting” (Mic. V).

And behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them. They supposed that the star which they had seen in the east was over Judaea; and it, which had first stood motionless until they came to Jerusalem, began to move and went before them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was. And entering the house—that is, the lodging of which the Evangelist says, “because there was no room for them in the lodging” (Luke II)—[Col. 0486B] they found the child with Mary his mother. This is the cornerstone, to whom two walls came together: one from the Jews, namely the shepherds, at the angel’s word; the other from the Gentiles, namely the Magi, at the star’s sign: “that there may be one fold and one shepherd” (John X). Both indeed were on earth, but were instructed from heaven, because the King of heaven had been born on earth. The star ran to the star, because the star descended into the star. “I am,” he says, “the bright and morning star” (Apoc. XXII). And falling down—the lesser kings before the King, the Magi before the Teacher—they worshipped: servants, the Lord; human beings, God; the great, a little child, or rather, more truly, the little, the great. For this child was he of whom Isaiah foretold: [Col. 0486C] “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and dominion has been placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX). And because they believed this child, whom the star served, to be God, they fell down and worshipped him.

And, opening their treasures, the Magi offered the Lord gold, frankincense, and myrrh, in accordance with Sabæan custom; yet they signified by the gold that he was King, by the frankincense that he was God, and by the myrrh that he was mortal. For gold is paid to a king as tribute; frankincense is offered to God in sacrifice; while myrrh is used for the burial of a dead person, because it keeps worms away from dead bodies. Hence Joseph brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes in order to anoint Jesus’ body (John XIX). [Col. 0486D] Not one gift from each, but all gifts from all: for each offered gold, believing him to be King and Lord of lords; each offered frankincense, believing him to be God of gods and Creator of creatures; and each offered myrrh, believing him to be mortal for the dead and destined to die for mortals. Or rather, in the three gifts they designated three substances in Christ: deity, flesh, and soul.

Pharaoh’s Magi performed the first and second signs among the plagues of Egypt, but failed at the third, saying to Pharaoh: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII). That is, natural philosophers, guided by reason, attained knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom they called *Togatum* and *Noima*; [Col. 0487A] but without the teaching of faith they did not at all attain knowledge of the third person, namely the Holy Spirit. He is called the finger of God, in accordance with the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke II). Hence another Evangelist says, in place of “finger,” “by the Spirit” (Matt. XII). Therefore they named God’s finger, whom they did not know; and thus they could not perform the third sign. But these men, enlightened by faith, believed that “there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one” (I John V). Therefore these same three kings, in faith in the Trinity, offered three gifts. Whoever comes to knowledge of the indivisible Trinity without preaching or reading has had it revealed not by human reason but by divine inspiration—as did the man reported to have said: “The first Monad generated the second Monad; the first and second reflect their own ardour into themselves.”

Moreover, according to allegory, the three Magi signify the three orders of the faithful in the Church: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, prelates, the continent, and the married—who possess faith in the Trinity and whom Ezekiel saw in a vision as being saved (Ezek. XIV). And according to the Gospel parable, two are in the field, two in the bed, and two at the mill; one of each is taken and the other left (Matt. XVIII). These, seeing the star—that is, understanding Gospel preaching, which shines in the night of the world against the darkness of error and ignorance, as the Psalmist says, “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” [Col. 0487C] (Ps. CXVIII)—rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. As the prophetic saying has it: “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance for ever, because they are the exultation of my heart” (ibid.). For this is the treasure hidden in the field, “which, when a man finds it, he hides; and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matt. XIII). For one who understands and loves, the teaching of Gospel preaching indeed contains much exultation and sweetness: it refreshes and delights, cheers and nourishes the mind. Hence the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

“And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.” Whoever wishes to find Jesus should enter [Col. 0487D] the holy Church, a pure conscience, and Holy Scripture. For Jesus is found in these houses; among the many, these are especially houses of God. Of the first it is written: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days” (Ps. XCII); of the second it is said: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” (Ps. C); of the third it is written: “We walked with one accord in the house of the Lord” (Ps. LIV). The heretic therefore seeks in vain, since Christ is by no means found outside the house of the Church. For this reason he himself said to the Jews: “You shall seek me and shall not find me” (John VII). Jesus’ parents sought him, “and found him in the temple, in the midst of the teachers, asking” and answering. To those who sought him he said: “Did you not know [Col. 0488A] that I must be in the things of my Father?” (Luke II). Therefore, entering this house, the faithful found the child Jesus with Mary his mother, believing that he who created the star according to divine power was born of the Virgin according to assumed human nature.

“And falling down, they worshipped him.” The good fall upon their faces, but the evil fall backwards. For of the good who fall it is written: “They fell before the throne upon their faces and worshipped God” (Apoc. V). But of the evil who fall it is written: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John XVIII). Those who fall upon their faces fall under Christ and before Christ as subjects and devotees; hence: “The peoples shall fall beneath you” [Col. 0488B] (Ps. XLIV), and: “Let us fall down before God” (Ps. XCIV). Thus, falling down in submission and devotion, they worshipped him—him, namely, of whom Scripture says: “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Luke IV). Indeed, it shows where he is to be worshipped when it says, “And entering the house”; and it shows how he is to be worshipped when it adds, “They offered him gifts, gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

Now, since God alone is to be worshipped with that worship which is called or termed in Greek *latria*—a worship to which altars, temples, and sacrifices belong, things to be dedicated, consecrated, and offered to God alone, certainly not to angels, apostles, or martyrs, but to God alone in their honour, because this service is owed not to the creature but to the Creator—[Col. 0488C] (thus, in the Apocalypse, the angel forbade John to worship him, saying: “Worship God, for I am your brother and fellow-servant of your brethren” [Apoc. XIX]; and when Paul and Barnabas had healed a lame man at Lystra in Lycaonia, and the crowds wished to sacrifice victims to them, they tore their garments and went out into the crowds, forbidding them to worship them [Acts XIV]; and Mordecai testifies that he feared to worship the exceedingly proud Haman, lest he transfer the honour of his God to a human being and worship anyone except his God [Esth. XIII])—what does it mean that the Magi are said to have worshipped not God but a child? Although he is truly God, he is nevertheless a child not according to his divine nature, but according to assumed flesh; according to this he is also not maker but made, as Paul testifies: “Who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I), and as the Psalmist declares, “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). [Col. 0488D] Moreover, Moses commands in the Law that no one, deceived by error, should worship those things that the Lord his God made (Deut. IV). Yet if God alone is to be worshipped, and this child is God, as the prophet Isaiah testifies—“A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty”—then this child who was born to us is to be worshipped as God. He is worshipped in one and the same worship with the Father who begot him and the Spirit who proceeds, as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” [Col. 0489A] (John IV). For such is the personal union between the divine and human natures that, in the hypostasis of the Word, because of the divinity that assumes it, the assumed humanity also is worshipped, according to the prophetic saying: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. XCVIII). Other sacred or holy things, however, are not to be worshipped with *latria*, but venerated with *dulia*, lest perhaps, under the appearance of piety, θεοσέβεια (*theosebeia*, “reverence for God”) be turned into idolatry, and vice thus enter in the place of virtue.

Therefore, having opened their treasures—not, of course, treasures of money, from which are produced those gifts “that blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words [Col. 0490A] of the righteous” (Deut. XVI), but treasures of wisdom, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel that “every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. XIII), and Solomon says, “In the treasures of wisdom is the signification of discipline” (Ecclus. I)—the faithful offer him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Gold of contemplation in faith; frankincense of prayer in hope; myrrh of compassion in charity. This is a fitting order and an ordered fitness: first the soul contemplates through faith; then it prays in hope; finally it has compassion in charity.

## SERMON IX. ON THE FEAST OF THE CONVERSION OF ST PAUL THE APOSTLE

On Paul’s drawing, on God’s great mercy and patience toward sinners, and on why no one should despair.

[Col. 0489]

[Col. 0489B] “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI).

I have often spoken to you by divisions and distinctions for the instruction of knowledge; but now I have spoken to you by warnings and exhortations for the formation of the life that is in Christ Jesus. For “knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (I Cor. VIII). “No one,” says the Son, “comes to me unless my Father draws him.” This saying is truly true, because it is the word of the Word of truth, of the Word who was in the beginning with God: “For it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. IX). “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing, because without me nothing was made; for a branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine” (John XV). [Col. 0489C] And “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. I).

A human being can indeed sin by himself, but cannot rise again by himself. Before he sins, he is whole, and therefore can cast himself down; but after he has fallen, he is broken, and therefore cannot rise by himself. For when “a man goes down from Jerusalem to Jericho, he falls among robbers, who strip him and, after inflicting wounds, depart leaving him half-dead” (Luke X). No one, therefore, comes to the Son unless the Father draws him. We find a clear example of this saying in the conversion of St Paul, who was drawn so that he might draw in Christ and draw to Christ. But from where, how, and to where was he drawn?
