Hear briefly whence he was drawn: “Saul,” it says, “still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, approached the chief priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that, if he found any men or women of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts IX). [Col. 0489D] Hear how he was drawn: “And as he journeyed, suddenly a light from heaven shone around him; and falling to the ground, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad. And trembling and astounded, he said to Jesus: Lord, what do you want me to do?” (ibid.). [Col. 0490B] Hear to where he was drawn: “He was baptized,” it says, “and immediately, entering the synagogues, he preached Jesus, that he is the Son of God. And he grew stronger and stronger, confounding the Jews and proving that he is the Son of God” (ibid.).

Thus he was drawn from the depth of shame that lay hidden in his heart, for “Saul was breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.” He was drawn from the depth of shame that was evident in deed, when [Col. 0490C] “he went to the chief priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that, if he found any,” and so forth. You see, then, that he was drawn from the depth of perversity which he endured and from the depth of perversity which he inflicted. He was drawn by the spirit of fear and through the radiance of heavenly illumination, because “suddenly a light from heaven shone around him”; and through the trembling of inward inspiration, because, trembling and astounded, he said: “Lord, what do you command me to do?” The light that came upon him blinded him in body so that the light entering him might illuminate him in mind; light brought blindness, and blindness brought light.

He was drawn also to the sacrament of faith, because he was baptized and remained with the disciples for several days; and to the office of preaching, [Col. 0490D] when, entering “the synagogues, he preached Jesus, that he is Christ.” From Saul he became Paul; from persecutor, preacher; from wolf, lamb. And the light shone around him in such a way that it illuminated his mind. This is the man of whom it is said in the blessing of the patriarch Jacob: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, [Col. 0491A] and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX). You have, then, whence Saul was drawn: from the shame of heart and deed; how he was drawn: through heavenly illumination and inward inspiration; and to where he was drawn: to the sacrament of faith and the office of preaching.

Therefore let no one despair because of the multitude or magnitude of sins; for God not only receives penitents, but even draws sinners. For “from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI). Let no one at all despair, because God “is patient and merciful, and ready to relent concerning evil” (Joel II); gentle and mild, and abundant in mercy toward all who call upon him; for “he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XVIII). For [Col. 0491B] “there is greater joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke XV); because “he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners”; because “those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. IX).—“For he came to seek and save that which was lost” (Luke XIX). At whatever hour the sinner shall be converted and shall groan, “I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII): at whatever hour—whether in childhood, youth, or old age—that is, always, while he lives. Likewise, at whatever hour he shall be converted—that is, as often as he repents—in accordance with what Truth says to Peter, when he asks how often a brother who sins is to be forgiven: “I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” [Col. 0491C] (Matt. XVIII). Nor does he say, “He shall be converted and make satisfaction”; but he says, “He shall be converted and groan,” because sin is forgiven in contrition, according to that prophetic saying: “I said, I will confess my injustice to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Ps. XXXI).

Cain sinned greatly when he killed Abel, but he sinned more grievously when he said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. IV). For far be it that human iniquity should be greater than God’s mercy, since a falling away from the good, which is iniquity, cannot be compared with the supreme good, which is God’s mercy. Therefore let no one despair of divine mercy, since “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).—“For he saved us, not by works of righteousness which we had done, [Col. 0491D] but according to his mercy” (Tit. III).—“First,” says the Apostle, “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man; but I obtained mercy, so that Christ Jesus might display in me all long-suffering, for the instruction of those who are to believe” (I Tim. I).

For this reason the epistles of Paul and the psalms of David are used in the Church more frequently than the other Scriptures: so that, when sinners hear that Paul, a blasphemer and persecutor, was made an apostle, and David, an adulterer and murderer, was made a prophet, they may trust that through God’s mercy they will merit not only forgiveness but also attain glory. For who can doubt that God wishes to have mercy on one whom [Col. 0492A] he made so great and excellent in creating, and whom he made so great and excellent also in redeeming? Great is what he created, but greater is what he redeemed. In creating, man was made in the image and likeness of God; in redeeming, God was made in the image and likeness of man. Of the former it is said: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. I); of the latter it is said: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II).

Indeed, to possess God’s likeness is greater than to possess man’s likeness; yet it is greater that God was made in the image and likeness of man than that man [Col. 0492B] was made in the image and likeness of God: greater in respect of condescension, and greater also in respect of usefulness. Who, then, can distrust that God will have mercy on one whom he made in his own image and likeness, whom he set over the birds of heaven, the beasts of earth, and the fish of the sea? (Gen. I.) For “he placed all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field; the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. VIII). Who can doubt that God will have mercy on one for whom “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man; becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross?” (Phil. II.) For “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” [Col. 0492C] (Rom. VIII); he who so “loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” (John III).

Otherwise Christ was born and suffered in vain, rose from the dead in vain, and ascended into heaven in vain. Far be it! This is the Catholic faith; for his blood always cries to the Father on our behalf, and he is heard in all things because of his reverence. “For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (I John II), who always intercedes for us, displaying the marks of his passion. And he himself is truly the propitiation for our sins. “For we have been redeemed, not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb” (I Pet. I).

Who, hearing such benefits of the Redeemer, would not [Col. 0492D] be drawn to him? If a stone heard, it too would surely be drawn; indeed, from stones God raises up children to Abraham (Matt. III). “For he sends forth his crystal like fragments of bread” (Ps. CXLVII); and he converts from Bashan (Ps. LXVI). Set before your eyes the woman who was a sinner in the city, from whom he cast out seven demons (Luke VIII). Set before your eyes the thief who, because of murder and sedition, had been sent to prison—indeed, who was suspended on a cross (Luke XXIII); and you will certainly see that one must never despair of God’s mercy.

Although “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV), nevertheless, that we may know that “mercy exalts itself above judgment” (Jas. II), as oil floats above wine, let us compare [Col. 0493A] mercy and justice with one another, and we shall see clearly that it is just for God to spare, but not merciful for God to punish. It is indeed just that he should spare, because God cannot fail to be merciful; indeed, divinity itself is mercy. Yet God likewise cannot fail to be just, since deity itself is justice. Therefore the nature of deity requires that he both spare through mercy and punish through justice. But nothing is just except what reason requires; therefore it is just that he should spare and punish. Who, then, would despair of mercy, when justice itself supports hope? Divine justice, nevertheless, and not human justice. For “establishing their own justice, they are not subject to the justice of God” (Rom. X).

Therefore no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him. Although the works of the Trinity are undivided, what is common to the three is nevertheless attributed to the Father [Col. 0493B] because of his principal authority; or rather, because, since in the Trinity power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit, whatever pertains to power is rightly appropriated to the Father. And certainly nothing manifests divine power more clearly than to justify the ungodly—that is, to draw the sinner—according to what is read: God most especially displays his omnipotence by sparing and having mercy. For to justify is greater than to create: in creation nature is given, but in justification guilt is removed and grace bestowed.

Behold, brothers and children, a mirror has been set before us for admiration; an example has been set before us for imitation, that we may turn to the Lord, so that he may turn [Col. 0494A] to us and we may turn to him. May he draw us from the depth of confusion, which lies hidden in the heart through perverse thought, is made apparent in the mouth through wicked speech, and prevails in action through evil habit. That is, may he raise the girl in the house, the young man outside the gate, and the man four days dead in the tomb, through the spirit of fear; for “the fear of the Lord expels sin” (Ecclus. I), as the prophet says: “Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI).

For when the sinner begins to consider within himself the greatness, multitude, and foulness of his sins, and reflects upon the judge’s power, from which he cannot escape; wisdom, from which he cannot hide; and justice, which he cannot corrupt—when he sees what punishment, how great a punishment, and what manner of punishment awaits sinners in Gehenna—he immediately [Col. 0494B] stands aghast and fears, conceiving compunction in his heart, giving birth to confession in his mouth, and nourishing satisfaction in his deeds, so that he may now say: “Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation.”

And thus he is drawn to the path of truth through avoidance of prohibited things, performance of commandments, and supererogation in counsels: so that on the first step he may be drawn from evil to good; on the second, from good to better; on the third, from better to best. May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages, grant this to you and us through the prayers and merits of most blessed Paul. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE SAME FEAST

### On the threefold death; the threefold resurrection; the threefold life; and the will of God.

[Col. 0493]

[Col. 0493C] “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XXX).

In the conversion of St. Paul, the Lord showed us a manifest example of this saying. He not only received him as he came, but drew him back as he fled. Let us therefore consider in him, brothers, the death which the Lord did not will, the conversion which he effected, and the life which he bestowed: death of guilt, conversion of repentance, life of grace. “Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the chief priests and asked them for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any men or women of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts IX). Behold the death of guilt, which the Lord did not will.

“And as he was journeying, suddenly [Col. 0493D] a light from heaven shone around him; and, falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ And he said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you persecute. [Col. 0494C] It is hard for you to kick against the goad.’ And trembling and astonished he said, ‘Lord, what do you want me to do?’” (ibid.). Behold the conversion of repentance, which the Lord effected. “And when he had been baptized, entering the synagogues he preached Jesus, that he is the Son of God, declaring that he is the Christ” (ibid.). Behold the life of grace, which the Lord bestowed.

True, then, is what Truth says: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.” Therefore God does not will the death of the sinner, because God did not make death; and he did not make death because “what was made in him was life”; because he himself is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). God also does not will the death of the sinner because the death of sinners is most evil; and it is most evil because “when an ungodly man dies, [Col. 0494D] there shall be no hope for him” (Prov. II). And there is no hope because in hell there shall be no redemption.

Therefore we sinners give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, because you do not will the death of sinners, but that [Col. 0495A] they be converted and live. I shall tell you what that death of the sinner is which you, Life, do not will. Do you not put to death and make alive? Are not death and life in your hand? What then? Do you will those whom you do not will to be sinners to die? Yet you do not will those whom you will to die to be sinners; because you hate guilt, but inflict punishment. Or must a distinction be drawn between death and death? Certainly a distinction must be drawn.

For death is bodily, spiritual, and Gehenna’s death. Bodily death extinguishes nature; spiritual death takes away grace; Gehenna’s death prevents glory. Therefore the first death is evil, the second worse, and the third most evil. The first death is evil because of punishment, the second worse because of guilt, and the third most evil because of both punishment and guilt. Of the first it is written: “Who is he that lives and shall not see death?” [Col. 0495B] (Ps. LXXXVIII), as though to say: There is absolutely no one who does not incur death of the body. Of the second it is written: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (I John III), as though to say: There is a certain mortal sin for which one must not pray, because it “is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII). Of the third death it is written: “Like sheep they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII); as though to say: just as a sheep does not pluck up grass, but grazes, so that the grass may always grow again for pasture, so hell does not consume man but afflicts him, so that man may always live unto death.

All rise from bodily death; some rise from spiritual death; none rise from Gehenna’s death. “For we shall all rise, but we shall not [Col. 0495C] all be changed” (I Cor. XV).—“Blessed are those who have a part in the first resurrection” (Apoc. XX), because “the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Ps. I). Now I understand more fully, Lord Jesus Christ, that you do not will the death of guilt; for you said: “O death, I shall be your death; O hell, I shall be your bite” (Hos. III).

This death occurs in the following order. First a person is disordered, then becomes sick, then dies; after this he is carried out, and finally buried. He is disordered in thought, becomes sick in delight, dies in consent, is carried out in deed, and buried in habit, in which he decays and stinks. The spirit therefore dies in consent, and then the dead girl lies [Col. 0495D] in the house (Matt. IX). He is carried out in deed, and then the dead young man is brought out beyond the gate (Luke VII); he is buried in habit, and then the man four days dead stinks in the tomb (John IX), because then the soul, like a beast of burden, rots away in dung (Joel II).

Oh, if the soul dead in sins could be seen—by what stench it is defiled, with what filth it reeks, how detestable and abominable it would appear! Yet even so one must not despair, because you, Lord, raised these three dead persons: the girl in the house, the young man outside the gate, and Lazarus in the sepulchre. There is only one kind of this death from which no one rises, namely final impenitence; concerning which perhaps you said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII). But to the rest the Apostle cries: “Awake, you who sleep, [Col. 0496A] and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V).

The death of Gehenna follows the death of guilt: an immortal death, a living death, in which those who were dead to their own life will live unto death; those who had life and lost it will seek it and not find it. Hear John speaking in the Apocalypse: “In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them” (Apoc. IX). O death, how sweet you would be to those for whom you were so bitter! Those who vehemently hated you alone will desire and long for you alone.

Therefore we sinners give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, because you do not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. “At whatever hour the sinner is converted, he shall live life and shall not die,” says the Lord (Ezek. XVIII). At [Col. 0496B] Jonah’s preaching the men of Nineveh proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, “and God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way, and he relented concerning the evil which he had said that he would do to them” (Jonah III).—“For he is patient and merciful, and ready to relent concerning evil” (Joel II). Therefore let us sinners turn to the Lord, because the Lord will immediately turn to us. “For he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX), because “he came to seek and save that which was lost” (Luke XIX). However great our misery may be, his mercy is greater. Far be it that we should despair with Cain, saying: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. IV). On account of this he went away as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth.

[Col. 0496C] Now there is a threefold life, just as there is a threefold death: the life of nature, the life of grace, and the life of glory. Of the life of nature blessed Job says: “Remember me, O God, because my life is wind” (Job VII); of the life of grace the prophet says: “The righteous lives by faith” (Hab. II); of the life of glory the Wise Man declares: “The righteous shall live for ever, and their reward is with the Lord” (Wis. III). The first is good, the second better, and the third best. Therefore let the sinner turn from the death of guilt to the life of grace, and escape from the death of Gehenna to the life of glory. For God always holds out his hands to receive sinners, because he does not will the death of the sinner but that he be converted and live.

But since nothing resists the divine will—for [Col. 0496D] “whatever he wills, he has done in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. CXXXIV)—if God does not will the death of the sinner but that he be converted and live, how is it that very many sinners not only are not converted so as to live, but are even perverted so as to perish? For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). Perhaps, then, those whom he does not will to die are converted and live, whereas those whom he wills to die are perverted and perish? For, as the Apostle says, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. IX). He himself also testifies through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I).

What, then, does the Apostle mean when elsewhere he says: “God wills all men to be saved” (I Tim. II)? And the prophet says to him: “You hate none of the things [Col. 0497A] which you have made, O Lord” (Wis. XI).—“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI.)

Yet the will of God is understood in several ways: namely, as good pleasure and as sign. His good pleasure is one, but the signs are diverse. Hence it is said: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX). Among these are counsel and commandment. Thus God wills—that is, counsels—that all people be saved; and he wills—that is, commands—that the sinner be converted and live. But his counsel and commandment are not always fulfilled. Yet whoever is converted according to his counsel and commandment shall live; but whoever is not converted shall die.

Furthermore, since a sinner cannot be converted without God’s operative grace—for, as the Apostle says, “It is not of one who wills or runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. IX)—and [Col. 0498A] since no one can merit operative grace, because, as the same Apostle says, if it is from merits, it is no longer from grace, it seems that a person should not be blamed if he is not converted, since God does not bestow grace. But it is one thing to merit and another to demerit. No one can merit grace, but anyone can demerit grace; and therefore a person is not altogether blameworthy if he does not at present merit grace, but he is certainly blameworthy if he demerits grace.

Therefore, brothers, if any one of you is overtaken in some fault, let him by no means despair. Meanwhile let him do whatever good he can, so that God may enlighten his heart unto repentance; open his eyes so that he may behold the light of the sun; soften the wax so that it may receive the impression of the seal. Let him make himself receptive, so that God may stamp upon him the form of his likeness [Col. 0498B] and impart the power of his grace. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT MARY

[Note: [Col. 0497D] From the edition of Angelo Mai.]

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497C] “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI).

In the words set before us we must chiefly consider three things: the root, the rod, and the flower. The root is David; the rod, the Virgin; and the flower is Christ. David, however, is called the root of Jesse not as one from whom Jesse proceeded, but as one who proceeded from him—just as Christ himself is called the root of Jesse: “There shall be,” he says, “a root of Jesse, who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Rom. XV). For in different respects the Father is called the root of the Son, and the Son is called the root of the Father. Thus Christ too is called the seed of Abraham: “In your seed,” he says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

But you will say: since the promise concerning Christ’s incarnation was made earlier to Abraham than [Col. 0497D] to David, why is Christ said to be born rather from the root of Jesse than from the root of Abraham? Let this threefold reason be given, unless a better can be given. The saying is to be explained on account of excellence of dignity, the more pointed expression of likeness, and the firmness of the promise.

For although Abraham possessed dignity as the chief patriarch, David possessed greater dignity as the most excellent of kings and an outstanding prophet. He was indeed the first king chosen and confirmed by God; for Saul had not been chosen but forced upon the people, and did not merit confirmation, but rather rejection. Hence, although fourteen kings occurred in the succession of generations from David to the Babylonian captivity, Matthew nevertheless calls David alone “king,” by antonomasia. And although Deborah the prophetess and Samuel the prophet preceded him, and many other prophets followed him, David nevertheless is called “prophet,” by antonomasia, just as Paul is called “apostle”; for the others prophesied, as it were, through figures and visions, through dreams in an enigma, whereas to David the spirit of prophecy was revealed openly. Hence he said: “I have understood beyond the elders” (Ps. CXVIII); and: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Moreover, a more express likeness is found between David and Christ than between Christ and Abraham. Hence Christ is very frequently understood through David in the Scriptures. For of David it is written: “I found David my servant; I anointed him with the oil of my salvation” (Ps. LXXXVIII). And it is also said: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of salvation above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). Thus this one came forth from that one: prophet from prophet, king from king, anointed one [Col. 0498D] from anointed one—Jesus the Nazarene, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit (Acts X); who says of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to bring good news to the poor” (Luke IV); who has written upon his garment and his thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Apoc. XVII); of whom it is elsewhere said: “I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a king shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth” (Jer. XXIII).

He is the great prophet of whom Moses spoke: “God shall raise up a prophet from among your brothers; hear him as you hear me” (Deut. XVIII); and another says: “Behold, a great prophet shall come, and he himself shall renew the kingdom” (Ecclus. XLVI). Truly great, because he is the Lord of prophets, of whom the Gospel says: “A great prophet has risen among us” (Luke VII).

Although it was promised to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), on account of which the Apostle says [Col. 0499A] that “God assumed not angels, not archangels, but the seed of Abraham” (Heb. II), this was nevertheless promised more clearly, more certainly, and more expressly to David—not by a simple word, but with an oath interposed: “The Lord,” he says, “swore truth to David, and he shall not fail in it: of the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI). For many swear, but not truth; and many swear truth, but do not keep it. Yet God both swore to David, swore truth, and kept that truth; for, he says, he shall not fail in it: “Of the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne”—not yours, I say, but mine. Therefore, since heaven is my throne, I shall establish him not so much upon your earthly throne as upon my heavenly throne, [Col. 0499B] so that this man may sit at my right hand.

And for that reason David is mentioned and placed before Abraham in Christ’s genealogy. “The book,” he says, “of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. I). These are the two pillars which the true Peaceful One placed in the vestibule of the temple before the entrance. A cord of twelve cubits encircles them, and Christ, the door, opens from their midst; he says of himself: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved; he shall enter and go out and find pasture” (John X).

One pillar—that is, David—is encircled by a cord of twelve cubits, that is, by the company of the twelve patriarchs. For just as the twelve patriarchs, his grandsons, descended carnally from Abraham, so twelve prophets, his imitators, proceeded spiritually from David. David, therefore, is the root of which the evangelical prophet foretold: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.” This is the “little rod of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense” (Song III), the rod which blossomed and bore fruit, because the Virgin believed, conceived, and bore Christ.

Concerning this rod Balaam prophesied, saying: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel, and from Jacob shall come one who shall rule” (Num. XXIV). The star—that is, Mary, whose name is interpreted “star of the sea”—is also the rod which bore this flower; and he himself is the one “who shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXI). For “the Lord is his name” (Ps. LXVII): a rod of humility, a rod of virginity, and a rod of fruitfulness. These three are fittingly signified in the words set before us. For when you hear “root,” understand humility; when you hear “rod,” recognize virginity; when you hear “flower,” attend to fruitfulness. In these three respects this rod is especially commended.

Thus, when the angel foretold her fruitfulness—“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII)—and she responded to him concerning virginity, “How shall this happen, since I know not a man?” (Luke I), at last understanding that neither virginity hindered fruitfulness nor fruitfulness took away virginity, as the angel declared: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you,” she immediately concluded from humility: [Col. 0500A] “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word. He has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” (ibid.).

Nor is it the rod of indignation and vengeance, of which it is written: “Assyria is the rod of my fury, correction, and destruction” (Isa. X).—“And I shall visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. LXXXVIII). It is not the rod of correction and destruction, of which it is written: “Shall I come to you with a rod?” (I Cor. IV).—“He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. XIII). Rather, it is the rod of support and consolation, of which this may be understood: “Your rod and your staff have comforted me” (Ps. XXII).

From this rod came forth the rod of truth and power, of which it is written: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength from Zion” (Ps. CIX).—“And you shall rule them with a rod of iron” (Ps. II). It is the rod through which the true Moses performed wonders in Egypt and in the wilderness: surely a rod from the root of Jesse.

David, therefore, is the root of Christ. For, as the Apostle says, “He was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I). But Christ is the root of the Church, of whom it is written: “He rose like a shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground” (Isa. LIII). The Church, in turn, is the root of the saints, of which it is said: “If the root is holy, so also are the branches” (Rom. XI), that is, the ministers.

Furthermore, perseverance is the root of good persons, of which it is written: “These have no roots, because they believe for a time, and in time of temptation fall away” (Luke [Col. 0500C] VIII). The root is the faith of preachers, of which it is said: “Though its root be sown in the earth, at the scent of water it shall bud” (Job XIX). Faith is the root of virtues, as the Apostle says: “Rooted and founded in faith” (Eph. III). Or it is humility, of which it is said: “The righteous man sends down his root” (Isa. XXXVII). But the root of wisdom, the word of God, is not in high places.

Therefore the devil is the root of the wicked, of whom it is said: “From the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk” (Isa. XIV); and elsewhere: “The roots of junipers shall be their food, and its roots shall be thickened upon heaps of rocks” (Job XXX). Against this it is said: “The axe is laid to the root” (Matt. III). Furthermore, evil obstinacy in sins, or love of earthly things, is a root of evil, concerning which it is said: “I saw the fool firmly rooted, and immediately cursed [Col. 0500D] his beauty” (Job V). But “every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. XV). Conversely, of wisdom it is written: “Send down roots among my chosen ones, and I took root among an honored people” (Ecclus. XXIV).

It follows: “And a flower shall rise from his root.” Why is it that the flower is not said to have risen from the rod, but rather from the root, from which the Virgin too proceeded? Certainly the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, preferred to say that the flower rose from his root rather than from the rod, in order to distinguish the stages of ascent, to indicate the summit of exaltation, and to destroy the poison of error.

For in Christ’s genealogy there are twenty-eight stages of ascent from the root [Col. 0501A] to the rod—that is, from David to the Virgin Mary, from whom Christ, who is called Jesus, was born (Matt. I). Through these stages of ascent the flower rises from the root to the rod, in which the ascent ends. And although, according to the nature of the flesh, Christ descended from David, yet incorporeally he rose above him according to the excellence of dignity. Therefore the prophet himself significantly foretold that the flower would rise from his root, so that his throne might be understood to be far more exalted than David’s throne, as much more excellent as he inherited a name more different from David’s. Hence it is fittingly said through the prophet: “Upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom” (Isa. IX). He does not say *on the throne*, but *upon the throne*; nor *in the kingdom*, but *upon the kingdom*: so that it may be shown that David’s was earthly and temporal, whereas Christ’s is eternal and heavenly.

This is the meaning to which the angel’s words to the Virgin are to be referred: “The Lord will give him the seat of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever” (Luke I), so that the sign is used for the thing signified.

Moreover, by the statement that the flower rose from the root, the error of the impious Manichaean is destroyed. He presumed to assert that Christ did not possess natural and true flesh, but shadowy and phantom flesh; and he falsely inferred this because Christ is said to have been conceived not from flesh or blood, but from the Holy Spirit. “That which is born of flesh is flesh, and that which is born of spirit is spirit” (John [Col. 0501C] III). Against this, the prophet, speaking expressly, foretold: “A flower shall rise from his root,” in order to show that his root and flower are of the same nature, and thus that Christ is a true man, just as David was a true man.

Furthermore, lest it should be thought that Mary had been transferred by adoption from one family to another, just as a rod is sometimes transferred by grafting from one root to another, the prophet, in order to indicate the truth more surely and expressly, says that the flower shall rise from his root. For just as David reigned after many persecutions, so Christ, after his passion, entered into the glory of the Father.

Through the genealogies which Matthew and Luke set forth, it does not seem to be proved that Mary was of the stock of David, nor even of the tribe of Judah—granting also as certain that, according to the law, persons of different tribes might be joined to one another in marriage, while inheritances and portions might not be joined. For the two tribes, priestly and royal, could lawfully be united to each other by a marital bond; hence Mary is read to have been a kinswoman of Elizabeth, who was of the daughters of Aaron. Thus Joseph, who was of the royal stock, namely of the house and family of King David, could lawfully be united to her. But even if it be granted that Joseph and Mary were of the same tribe, namely Judah, it is nevertheless not proved that they were of the same family; for, just as Joseph descended from David’s stock, so Mary might have descended from the offspring of his loins, or even from other families of the same tribe. Therefore the prophets, filled with the Holy Spirit, wished openly to proclaim that Christ would be born from David’s stock and royal seed. Thus Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” that is, from King David, who indeed was Jesse’s son and of the royal line; “and in Christ a flower shall rise from his root.” And elsewhere: “I shall raise up for David a righteous shoot, and a king shall reign; he shall be wise and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. And this is the name by which they shall call him: the Lord our righteous one” (Jer. 23). Where the Latin has *Dominus* (“Lord”), the Hebrew has *Adonai*, which is a name of God and in Hebrew is used only of God. Hence it is proved that this shoot of David, namely Christ, is God. Likewise in the Apocalypse one of the elders said to John: “Do not weep; behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered,” etc. (Rev. 5). Paul also writes to Timothy: “Remember that the Lord Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (2 Tim. 2).

Yet from what is read at the end of Numbers concerning the sons of Machir and the daughters of Zelophehad, it can sufficiently be shown that women possessing a share of an inheritance had to marry men not only of their own tribe but also of the same family. Hence it is written there: “Let all men take wives from their own tribe and kinship, and let all women take husbands from the same tribe, so that the inheritance may remain in the families” (Num. 36). Joachim and Anna had no male heir; rather, their firstborn was the Virgin Mary. Therefore the principal share of the inheritance unquestionably belonged to her. Since the holy woman married a righteous man, she surely married, according to the law, a man of the same tribe; and the Virgin Mary was of the same tribe and family.

But how do they say that this flower rose, rather than descended, since Christ, insofar as he is incarnate, descended rather than rose? For he is the living bread who came down from heaven (John 6). He also says of himself: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5). And through the prophet it is said to him: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 54 [probably 64]). This is said in order to preserve the propriety of expression: because in the propagation of a race an ascent takes place, and therefore, when he spoke of a shoot, he wished and ought to use the word “ascent.” For there was to be a progress from the lower to the higher, and therefore it had to be called an ascent. Nevertheless, he who descended is the same as he who ascended, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). For “his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its highest point; and there is none who can hide himself from his heat.” Hear of his descent: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped; he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). But hear how greatly he ascended: “Therefore,” he says, “God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

Nor should you wonder if this flower rose by descending, because, being true God and man, he himself rose as man into God. Of this ascent the prophet says: “God shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isa. 14 [probably 19]). Therefore he rose from his root. In the Song of Songs he says of himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2). There are indeed flowers of truth and grace, and flowers of vanity and guilt. Of the former it is written: “Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come. Sustain me with apples; strengthen me with flowers, for I languish with love” (ibid.). Flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her. Of the latter it is said: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. 40). “A human being, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; like a flower he comes forth and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14). “In the morning may he flower and pass away; in the evening may he fall, grow hard, and wither” (Ps. 89). Of these it is written: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither, and let no flower of time pass us by” (Wis. 2). Of the former it is said: “They shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 19 [probably 91/92]).

[Col. 0503C] But this flower of glory, this flower of flowers, came to plant the former and uproot the latter: to plant virtues and eradicate vices. Oh, if we could worthily praise this flower—and if not worthily, at least not unworthily! Surely this flower has a most beautiful colour, a most fragrant scent, and a most delightful taste. Therefore, dearest brothers, although not as much as we wish, yet as much as we are able, let us behold this flower’s pleasant and beautiful colour; let us take in this flower’s refreshing and delightful fragrance; let us taste this flower’s pleasing and pure flavour. Of the colour of this flower the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5): white in his conception, ruddy in his Passion. Since he is “the brightness of eternal light,” “the spotless mirror of God’s majesty,” and “the image of his goodness,” God’s majesty and the image of his goodness could certainly not be darkened by the stain of any sin. Therefore “he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

Nor did he contract sin, because he paid what he had not taken. For his mother Mary was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit, as the angel had foretold her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”; therefore that which shall arise from you, wholly clean and wholly white, “shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). For the Lord has clothed himself with splendour. To him the Prophet says: “You are beautiful in form beyond the children of men; grace is poured out upon your lips. In your comeliness and beauty, attend, prosper, proceed, and reign” (Ps. 44). For you are the sun of righteousness (Mal. 4), you are “the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), whose beauty sun and moon marvel at, “into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1), and in wonder say: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? Why is your clothing red, like that of one treading in a winepress?” (Isa. 53 [probably 63]). For, as is written elsewhere, “his garment was sprinkled with blood” (Rev. 19), not blood that defiles but that cleanses, according to the text: “They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 22). Although through the disgrace of his contemptible Passion he appeared without beauty or glory—hence the prophet says of him, “We saw him, having neither form nor beauty”—his beauty and comeliness nevertheless remained even when they did not appear.

Thus this flower neither lost its bloom nor merely came into bloom, but flowered and flowered again: it flowered in conception, free from fault, as he himself testifies through the Psalmist: “My flesh flowered again, and of my own will I shall confess him” (Ps. 27). Of this flower’s fragrance the Bride likewise says in the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine, like the finest ointment. In the fragrance of your ointments we run” (Song 1). Hence the wisdom of God says of itself: “Like cinnamon and fragrant balsam I gave forth an odour; like choice myrrh I gave the sweetness of fragrance” (Ecclus. 24). Isaac, perceiving this flower’s fragrance in the Holy Spirit, said: “Behold, the odour of my son is like the odour of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27). By its fragrance the dead rise, the sick are healed, and the weak are strengthened.

Moreover, this flower is without doubt the living bread that descended from heaven, containing within itself every delight and the sweetness of every flavour (Wis. 16), sweeter to the soul that loves it than honey and the honeycomb (Ecclus. 24). Of it the psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33); and the apostle Peter says: “If indeed you have tasted how sweet the Lord is” (1 Pet. 2). This same flower is called the wisdom of God: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24). For such is the sweetness of this flower that satiety provokes hunger and intoxication brings on thirst. Blessed are the eyes which now behold this flower through faith and shall at last contemplate it by sight: seeing him not in a mirror, in an enigma, but face to face (1 Cor. 13)—with the eyes of the body, man; with the eyes of the heart, God. May he mercifully bring us to that everlasting vision, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## SERMON XII. ON THE FEAST OF THE PURIFICATION OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EVER-VIRGIN MARY

On the letters, signs, and messengers sent beforehand before Christ’s coming; on the three paths of the three messengers and the threefold peace; why we carry lighted candles at the Purification; likewise, on the Lord’s threefold coming and the threefold temple to which he comes, and on the building of the temple.

[Col. 0505]

[Col. 0505A] “Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before your face; and immediately the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the Covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3).

The King of kings and Lord of lords was about to come into his own for the salvation of his people, yet his own were not going to receive him (John 1). Therefore, lest they should plead ignorance of his coming as an excuse for their sins, he sent beforehand the signs of his coming, addressed letters to them, and sent messengers before his face. By these three things—letters, signs, and messengers—he clearly declared his coming. For he who, when he had come, is read to have sent them out two by two before his face, ought not to have come alone or suddenly. He therefore sent beforehand signs, that is, mysteries of figures; he directed letters, that is, testimonies of the Scriptures; he sent messengers, namely the persons of the prophets.

For he was prefigured in types: Isaac, born of a barren woman (Gen. 21), prefigured Christ to be born from a Virgin. The rod put forth leaves (Num. 17) and bore fruit, because the Virgin conceived and bore Christ. The fire in the bush (Exod. 3), the manna in the wilderness (Exod. 10), and the rain on the fleece (Judg. 6) likewise prefigured this. He was foretold in the Scriptures, as in Genesis: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49). And elsewhere: “The Lord shall come like an oak, who is in Shiloh, when it has been divided from itself into twelve parts” (Amos 2). And in the secret writings of Jeremiah: “After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Baruch 3). He was announced through the prophets, as by Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7); by Habakkuk: “If he delays, wait for him; for he who is coming shall come and shall not delay” (Hab. 2); and by Daniel: “Seventy weeks are shortened, that transgression may be brought to an end, everlasting justice be brought in, and the Holy of Holies be anointed” (Dan. 9).

Yet wretched Synagogue did not observe such manifest signs; blind Judaea did not understand such open letters; unbelieving people did not receive such truthful messengers. Therefore, when “he came into his own, his own did not receive him” (John 1). Through the prophet he complains of them, saying: “The ox knew its owner and the ass its master’s manger, but Israel did not know me” (Isa. 1). Hence he says to them in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me” (John 5). “For he wrote of me: God shall raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers,” etc. (Deut. 18). Again: “You shall see your life hanging before your eyes, and shall not believe in your life” (Deut. 28).

He sent these messengers a long time beforehand. But at the last, when he was now about to come, he sent three eminent and illustrious messengers close at hand. The first prepared the way of the Incarnation; the second, the way of the Nativity; the third, the way of preaching. By the first way he came to the saving temple; by the second he came to the material temple; by the third he came to the spiritual temple.

Of the first messenger it is written in the Gospel: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And, coming to the virgin, he gently greeted her: ‘Hail,’ he said, ‘full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women’” (Luke 1). Hail, because through you the name of Eve shall be changed. She was full of sin, but you are full of grace. She withdrew from God, but the Lord is with you. She was cursed among women, but you are blessed among women. The fruit of her womb was the accursed Cain, but the fruit of your womb shall be the blessed Jesus. Through her death entered the world, but through you life returned to the world; for you shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Jesus (ibid.). “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1).

Having given the greeting, he immediately foretold the coming of his Lord: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). When these things had thus been accomplished, the Holy Spirit immediately came and prepared a threefold way before the Lord’s face. The first was the virgin’s consent; the second was cleansing of the flesh; the third was formation of the body. The first was the consent of the virgin’s mind; the second was cleansing of the flesh from the tinder of sin; the third was the formation of the body from the most pure blood. For when the angel had told the wondering Virgin the manner and order of conception, she immediately, burning with the highest ardour of desire, consented; and at the prompting of the Holy Spirit she answered: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). Blessed is she who believed, because all things were fulfilled in her. For the author of faith could not be conceived from an unbelieving woman; and therefore the first way, namely the Virgin’s consent, had to be prepared.

Immediately the Holy Spirit came upon her. He had indeed come to her before, when in her mother’s womb he cleansed her soul from original sin; but now he also came upon her in order to cleanse her flesh from the tinder of sin, so that she might be wholly without wrinkle and stain. Thus he wholly extinguished in her, as I think, the tyrant of the flesh, the weakness of nature, the tinder of sin, so that thereafter there could arise in her members no motion from the law of sin against the law of righteousness; nor could the flesh desire against the spirit, in her in whom “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4), was to dwell bodily. Therefore the second way, namely the cleansing of the flesh, had to be prepared.

Then from the most pure blood of the most glorious Virgin, by a certain spiritual operation, he formed the Redeemer’s body; without any interval of time he created a new soul by infusing it, and the Word assumed it together with the body. Thus he became man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh. Therefore, when this threefold way had been prepared for the Lord, the power of the Most High immediately descended into her and united itself to the body through the mediation of the soul. The soul mediates not only by union but also by nature. Divinity is altogether simple: it lacks multiplicity of parts and possesses a concrete unity of properties. The body, however, is wholly composite: it has multiplicity of parts and a concrete unity of properties. The soul is partly simple, because, like divinity, it lacks multiplicity of parts; and partly composite, because, like the body, it possesses a concrete unity of properties. Hence the divine nature is read to be of such subtlety that it was not fitting for it to be united to a body formed from the clay of the earth except through the mediation of a rational essence.

Thus he immediately came to his holy temple, namely the saving temple. Of it he says in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” But he said this of the temple of his body (John 2). This temple is holy—that is, sanctifying—not sanctified, that is, cleansed from sin, because “he committed no iniquity, nor was guile found in his mouth” (Isa. 53). Nor did he contract sin, because “what he did not take away, he paid” (Ps. 68). “God ascended upon a light cloud,” that is, assumed flesh free from sin, “and entered Egypt” (Isa. 19), that is, he came into the world. He came by the Incarnation, because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). “For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2).

Moreover, just as he did not come suddenly, so he did not come alone. With him came the spirit of power and the spirit of charity. By power he was able to be incarnate; by charity he willed to be incarnate. Of power it is written: “Your all-powerful word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18), bearing the stern command. And what power is greater than this: that the eternal made himself temporal, the simple composite, and the immortal mortal? Certainly no word is impossible with God. Since it was greater for God to become human and be conceived of a virgin than, God having become human, to be born of a virgin, why then is Christ’s Nativity celebrated with greater solemnity than his conception? Is it because the conception was hidden but the birth was manifest? Or rather because of the reason of the mystery: that the Virgin’s conceiving Christ bodily in her womb signifies that the faithful soul ought to conceive Christ by faith in the mind; while the Virgin’s bearing Christ into the world signifies that the faithful soul ought to bear Christ in action. “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 3 [probably 2]). But faith lives when it works through love. Therefore birth is considered more solemn than conception.

Of charity it is written: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” (John 3). He gave a Son, not a servant; he gave his only-begotten and best Son; he did not give him back, because “not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3). Yet he did not merely give but handed him over, because “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). “No one has greater love than that a person should lay down his life for his friends” (John 14 [probably 15]). O immeasurable charity of God: he who made man without man became man for man. Hence Christ is also said to have been born of the Holy Spirit, not because the Spirit generated him paternally, but because Christ was born of the Virgin through the Spirit’s spiritual operation. Although the works of the Trinity are undivided, the work of love is specially attributed to the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son, the affection and bond of both. But in the Incarnation charity clearly shines forth: not only because God, in ineffable charity, made his only-begotten Son incarnate, but also because the Virgin, out of an excessive ardour of charity, conceived the Word of God when she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). You have, therefore, the first messenger, the first way, the first coming, and the first temple.

But after the first messenger came the second, who appeared to the shepherds and said: “I announce to you great joy, because Christ the Lord is born in the city of David” (Luke 2). He too prepared a threefold way before the Lord’s face: first, by preparing a servant for attendance; second, by preparing a place in the lodging; third, by preparing a cradle in the manger. For the angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1). The lofty counsel of heaven wisely arranged that the Virgin should have a bridegroom, not only to remove the reproach of fornication, not only to deceive the deceitful devil, but also that he might be a comfort to the Virgin and render service to her in childbirth.

Later, amid the crowd of people who had gathered to register, he prepared an exceedingly cramped place for the Virgin about to give birth. Of this the evangelist says: “Because there was no place for him”—that is, no other place—“in the lodging.” Finally he prepared for him a cradle in the manger, in which the Virgin laid the child (Luke 2). Of this the prophet says: “You shall be made known in the midst of two animals” (Hab. 3). For it is not incredible that he prepared this, he “who makes his angels spirits and his ministers burning fire” (Ps. 103).

But why is it that, while the angel rejoices with the shepherds, God is born as man in the manger of an ox and an ass? What is this, I say, except that he indicates to us a threefold peace? You know, dearly beloved, that before the Redeemer’s coming there were three walls of hostility. The first was between God and man, the second between angel and man, and the third between man and man. By disobedience, man had offended his Creator; through his fall he had impeded the restoration of the angel; through diverse rites he had separated himself from his fellow human being. For the Jew cultivated ceremonies, while the Gentile practised idolatry; and each disliked the other’s rite. But when “our peace came, he made both one,” destroyed the walls of hostility (Eph. 2), and joined the converging walls in himself, the cornerstone, so that henceforth there might be “one fold and one shepherd” (John 10). He therefore took away sin and reconciled man to God; repaired the fall and reconciled man to angel; destroyed the rites and reconciled man to man.

Thus, according to the Apostle, he restored those who are in heaven and those who are on earth; and for this reason that multitude of the heavenly host sang: “Glory to God in the highest,” that is, glory from the angels to God, “and on earth peace to human beings,” Jews and Gentiles, “of good will” (Luke 3 [probably 2]). Hence also the angel speaks and rejoices with the shepherds: because peace between angels and human beings has been restored. God is born as man because peace between God and human beings has been restored. He is born in the manger of an ox and an ass because peace between human beings has been repaired. For the ox prefigures the Jewish people, and the ass the Gentile people, according to: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass” (Deut. 22), that is, with Jew and Gentile.

When these things had taken place, “the Lord, the Ruler, came to his holy temple” (Mal. 3): to the material temple, of which the Gospel says, “This temple was forty-six years in building” (John 2); and the Psalm says, “We have received your mercy in the midst of your temple” (Ps. 47). He came by offering, as the Gospel reading appointed for this day declared, because “when the days of Mary’s purification were fulfilled, they took Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord” (Luke 2), etc. He was offered because he himself willed it; but he was offered by his mother in the temple, he who offered himself to the Father on the cross. He was redeemed in the temple, he who redeemed on the cross. But he gave himself as a ransom for the world, whereas the world gave a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons as ransom for him.

He is read to have been redeemed twice: once from the priests, with a dove or turtledove; likewise from the ministers, with a drachma or a stater (Matt. 17). Yet he was not redeemed as a matter of obligation, but only by free good pleasure. For under the law no one was bound to be redeemed except a firstborn opening the womb (Lev. 12), whereas he did not open the Virgin’s womb. For this “is the closed gate” (Ezek. 44), and no man passed through it.

Why, then, do we carry lighted candles at this feast? This may be inferred from the Book of Wisdom, where idolaters are read to perform dark sacrifices. The Gentiles dedicated the month of February to the infernal gods because, as they thought—though they erred—Proserpina had been carried off by Pluto at the beginning of that month. Since they believed that her mother Ceres had searched for her throughout Sicily, around Etna, through the entire night with lighted torches, they too, in remembrance of her, went about the city at night with lighted torches at the beginning of the month. Hence that festival was called *Amburbale*, the city-circling rite. Since the holy Fathers could not completely eradicate this custom, they ordained that lighted candles should be carried in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Thus what was formerly done in honour of Ceres is now done in honour of the Virgin, and what was formerly done in honour of Proserpina is now done in praise of Mary.

For this reason also, at the Purification of the Virgin we carry lighted candles, so that, purified by grace, we may deserve to enter the wedding feast with lighted lamps, like the prudent virgins (Matt. 25). Furthermore, just as he did not come suddenly, so neither did he come alone. With him came the spirit of humility and the spirit of poverty. Humility offered him; humility laid him in the manger; poverty wrapped him in poor cloths; poverty redeemed him for a paltry price. O wondrous mercy and wondrous condescension of the Lord! He became poor, he whose are “the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23). He who was exalted was humbled, because “the Lord is great, and great is his power; and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146). You have, therefore, the second angel, the second way, the second coming, and the second temple.

But after the second messenger came the third, of whom the angel Gabriel said: “He shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to prepare a perfect people for the Lord” (Luke 1). John is called an angel, not by the property of his nature but by the character of his office. In the same way Christ himself is subsequently called an angel, according to: “And immediately the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the Covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3). Truly he is great: herald of the Judge, voice of the Word, friend of the bridegroom, lamp of the sun; and because of his dignity he deserved to be called not merely a prophet, but more than a prophet (Matt. 2 [probably 11]).

For he was the boundary of what preceded and what followed: “the law and the prophets [were] until John” (Luke 16), while the Gospel and the apostles begin from John. Together with those who preceded him, he foretold Christ as future: “He who shall come after me has been made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie” (John 1). Together with those present, he showed him as present: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid.).

He prepared the way before the Lord’s face—a threefold way, I say, for baptism is read to be threefold: of washing, of compunction, and of Passion; of washing in water, of compunction in tears, and of Passion in blood. He prepared the first way by baptizing, the second by preaching, the third by dying. He baptized the body outwardly but not the mind inwardly; hence: “I baptize in water, but one stands in your midst who baptizes you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3). He preached repentance but did not bestow forgiveness. Hence: “Do repentance, for the kingdom of heaven shall draw near” (Luke 3). He died for righteousness, but did not himself justify, because Herod caused John’s head to be cut off in prison (Mark 6).

The Lord therefore immediately came to his holy temple, to the spiritual temple, of which the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3). After baptism and fasting he gathered those whom he chose from the world, whom he made the temple of the Holy Spirit, “a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). But then, just as he did not come suddenly, so he did not come alone. With him came the spirit of integrity and the spirit of truth: he displayed integrity in deeds and truth in words. For “he committed no sin”—behold the spirit of integrity—“nor was guile found in his mouth” (Isa. 53)—behold the spirit of truth. He performed singular works, as he himself testifies: “If I had not done the works which no other has done,” etc. (John 15). He uttered saving words, as Peter testifies when he says: “Lord, you have the words of eternal life,” etc. (John 6).

“The Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the Covenant whom you desire, therefore came to his holy temple” (Mal. 3). This is a metaplasm, a change of grammatical form: earlier the Father spoke to the Son, “Behold, I send my angel,” etc.; now he turns his address to those who desired the Son’s coming, saying: “Come, Lord, and do not delay; forgive the crimes of your people Israel.” And elsewhere: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth,” etc. (Isa. 16). Of these the Lord says to the apostles: “Many kings and prophets wished to see the things that you see, and did not see them,” etc. (Luke 10). The Church represents their desire in those antiphons, “O Emmanuel,” etc., “O root of Jesse.”

[Col. 0511D] But because it is the spirit that gives life, let us set forth something spiritually concerning Christ’s spiritual coming. For we read in the Scriptures of three comings of Christ: present, past, and future; the present in holiness, the past in humility, the future in majesty. First he came into the world for redemption; secondly he comes into the soul for sanctification; thirdly he shall come in judgment for recompense. Of the first he says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16); of the second he said: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14); of the third he says: “You shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power,” etc. (Luke 21). The first has been spoken of; the second must be spoken of. But in this coming an angel is sent before Christ’s face to prepare the way for him.

This is that familiar and spiritual messenger of whom the prophet says: “From your fear, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26). This fear prepares the journey of three days by which the children of Israel departed from Egypt (Exod. 14); that is, by which penitents depart from the darkness of sins. The journey of the first day is the examination of vices; the journey of the second day is remembrance of sins; the journey of the third day is contrition for transgressions. For in the penitent there first comes a subtle examination, which diligently considers and investigates the number and kinds of vices, as the penitent himself says: “I shall declare my iniquity, and I shall be anxious concerning my sin” (Ps. 37). After this follows mournful remembrance, which recalls and attends to the shamefulness and circumstances of transgressions, according to: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50). Weighty contrition follows, which wipes away and cleanses the stains of sins, as he says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93).

When this threefold way has been prepared for the Lord through fear, he immediately comes through grace to his holy temple, that is, into the soul of the penitent, in order to sanctify it. He does not come alone, but the Father and the Holy Spirit come with him, as he himself testifies: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

[Col. 0512C] They make this dwelling in the following order. They lay the foundation, arrange the bases, raise the columns, set the architraves upon them, place the capitals above, build up the walls, arrange the windows, put on the roof, insert the door, lay the pavement, and divide the temple into two chambers. All these things, brethren, are full of spiritual mysteries.

For the foundation is faith in Christ. Founded upon it, the faithful soul stands firm in stable solidity against the spirits of storm and whirlwind. Of this the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI).—“For whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV).—“But the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. II; Rom. I; [Col. 0512D] Heb. X). Hence in Genesis: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV).

Upon this foundation seven bases are arranged in order: that is, the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer—three pertaining to the present life, three to the future life, and the middle one pertaining to both. “Let thy kingdom come,” he says, “thy will be done,” etc. (Matt. VI). Upon these bases seven columns are firmly raised: that is, the seven gifts of sevenfold grace, which Isaiah, enumerating them upon Christ, says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI). Concerning these Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house; [Col. 0513A] she has hewn out seven columns” (Prov. IX). Hence also the seven eyes in one stone, and the seven golden lamps in the lampstand, according to the prophecy of Zechariah (Zech. III).

Upon these seven columns are placed architraves, and upon the architraves capitals: that is, seven virtues and seven beatitudes, which Christ himself enumerates, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek,” etc. (Matt. V). For the eighth beatitude returns to the beginning. Four walls are built up for this structure: that is, the four cardinal virtues—justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. The side of justice faces east, through which Christ, the sun of justice, rises upon those who fear God. The side of fortitude faces north, through which we resist adversities, which [Col. 0513B] according to the prophet are opened from the north (Jer. I). The side of temperance faces south, through which we restrain the enticements by which desires blaze up. The side of prudence faces west, through which we turn away from things tending toward decline and avoid the snares of those who set. These four sides are equal, so that the building may be square.

In these walls five windows are arranged: that is, the five senses understood spiritually—sight, understanding; hearing, obedience; smell, discernment; taste, delight; and touch, action. Through these spiritual senses [Col. 0514A] life enters in, just as, conversely, death enters through the bodily senses, as the prophet says: “Death entered through the windows” (Jer. IX). The roof placed above is “charity,” surpassing the other virtues, “which covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV).

The door set into the eastern side is hope, through which we enter to perform righteousness. Its two gates are abstinence and continence. The gate of abstinence must be closed, lest perhaps Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks, enter and overthrow the whole of Jerusalem. The gate of continence must be closed, lest foreign women enter and overturn Solomon’s mind (3 Kings XII). Within, moreover, the pavement is laid: that is, humility, concerning which we read: “My soul clung to the pavement” (Ps. CXVIII).

This temple [Col. 0514B] is divided into two chambers. The inner one is wisdom, by which the soul clings to the contemplation of heavenly things. The outer one is knowledge, which attends to the ordering of earthly things. The inner is contemplative; the outer, active. In the inner chamber Mary sat at the Lord’s feet, hearing his words; in the outer, “Martha was busy about much service” (Luke X). Let us therefore also strive to bring forth worthy fruits of repentance (Matt. III), so that the Angel of the Covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, may make us such a temple for himself—he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. FOR THE FEAST OF ST GREGORY, POPE, THE FIRST OF THAT NAME

What is required for a testament, and concerning Christ’s testament; concerning the four kinds of Scripture, signified by the four rivers flowing from Paradise; concerning the twofold priesthood; and concerning the pontifical vestments with which the pontiff of the Old Testament was clothed.

[Col. 0513]

[Col. 0513C] “The Lord established for him an everlasting covenant, gave him a great priesthood, and made him blessed in glory” (Ecclus. XLV).

[The foregoing words commend to us three things concerning our blessed pontiff and outstanding teacher: the knowledge of charity, the excellence of dignity, and the glory of holiness. Regarding the first it is said beforehand: “The Lord established for him an everlasting sacrament.” Regarding the second it is added: “He gave him a great priesthood.” Regarding the third it is further stated: “He made him blessed in glory.” [Note: [Col. 0513] Mai prints the material enclosed in brackets from a Vatican manuscript.]]

A testament is the just determination of one’s own will concerning what a person wishes to be done with his possessions after death. A testament requires suitable witnesses, before whom the testator may appoint heirs and dispose of his property. It also requires a notary to write out the testament, so that only then, after the testator’s death, the testament may be irrevocable.

All these things, brethren, we can find in Christ’s testament. Because he was more perfect, and therefore wished to make a more perfect testament, when he was soon to die he employed not merely [Col. 0514C] seven witnesses but all the apostles as his witnesses. To them he also said: “You shall be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the end of the earth” (Luke XXIV). Before them he appointed not only one heir but all the elect as his heirs. According to the Apostle, they are heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ (Rom. VIII); concerning them he had said through the Prophet: “I have made a covenant with my chosen ones” (Ps. LXXXIII). Thus he disposed the kingdom of heaven to them by testament, as he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Hence he said to the apostles: “I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII).

[Col. 0514D] Finally, setting forth the substance of the testament, “he took bread, blessed it and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat: this is my body. Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be poured out for [Col. 0515A] many for the remission of sins” (Luke XXII). A notary was also present—not only one, but Matthew and John—who wrote that testament, that is, the Gospel, as one of them says in his subscription: “This is the disciple who wrote these things” (John XXI).

This testament, therefore, is everlasting, because it was confirmed by the death of the testator. Therefore the Old Testament was bound in law to cease, according to what is written: “When new things come, you shall cast away the old” (Heb. IX). And again: “Behold, I make all things new” (Apoc. II). Hence the prophet says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant which I gave to their fathers when I led them out of [Col. 0515B] the land of Egypt; but I shall give my laws into their minds,” etc. (Jer. XXXI).

Although he disposed this testament to all the elect, he did so especially to the apostles and their vicars, to whom he entrusted the primacy of the kingdom. The Psalmist says: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV);—“who order his covenant over sacrifices” (Ps. XLIX). Blessed Gregory truly ordered his covenant over sacrifices. As the universal Church maintains, he wisely established the norm and rule of the offices, both concerning the sacrifice and concerning the other mysteries. He expounded the New and Old Testament more profitably [Col. 0515C] and understood them more subtly, so that the words which the Bride says in the Song of Songs fittingly apply to him: “All fruits, new and old, I have kept for you, my beloved” (Song VIII). For indeed the New and Old Testament had in some measure flowered through other interpreters, but through him it bore fruit fully. For he is the learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, who brought forth new things and old from his treasury (Matt. XIII). He is the innkeeper who brought out two denarii, received from the Samaritan, for the healing of the wounded man (Luke X).

From the spring of Scripture he brought forth four streams of exposition. Of these it is read mystically: “A river went forth from the place of delight to water Paradise. It is divided into four heads: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates” (Gen. II). The place of delight is fittingly understood as [Col. 0515D] the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son, the affection and bond of both.

Concerning him it is written: “You shall make them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV). The river proceeding from it is sacred Scripture, which was issued and expounded through the Holy Spirit. For as that river was divided into four heads—Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates—so sacred Scripture is divided into four kinds: history, allegory, anagogy, and tropology.

Gihon is interpreted “gaping of the earth,” signifying history, because the ancients gaped after earthly things, since earthly things were promised according to history; for example: “I shall give you a land [Col. 0516A] flowing with milk and honey, grain and wine and oil” (Exod. XIII), and similar things.
