Pishon is interpreted “change of speech,” signifying allegory, according to which the letter is changed into spirit: one thing sounds in the letter and another is contained in the spirit. Tigris is interpreted “swift,” signifying anagogy, for the understanding of which the mind is made swift and comprehension easy, because it treats especially of things above and heavenly: that is, the Trinity of persons and the orders of angels. Euphrates is interpreted “fruitful,” signifying tropology, through which the soul is planted in morals, sprouts in virtues, and bears fruit in works.

By these rivers blessed Gregory watered Paradise—that is, he made the Church fruitful: “He stretched out his bow and made it ready; and in it [Col. 0516B] he prepared instruments of death; he made his arrows for those that burn” (Ps. VII). In a bow there are two things, wood and string, joined one to another. But hard wood is bent by a soft string. The hard wood is the Mosaic law, concerning which the apostle Peter says: “Why do you test us by putting upon us a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts XV). The soft string is the Gospel law, concerning which the Lord says: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. II). The hard yoke is bent by the soft string, because the Mosaic law is tempered by the Gospel law. That law rendered eye for eye, hand for hand, tooth for tooth (Lev. XXIV). This law commands: “If anyone strikes you [Col. 0516C] on one cheek, offer him the other also. If anyone takes your tunic from you, give him your cloak as well. If anyone compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him two more” (Matt. V).

Furthermore, the Bride says in the Song: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the choicest ointments” (Song I). And the Bridegroom says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. II). Wood and string are joined together because the New and Old Testaments agree. For “wheel is contained in the midst of wheel” (Ezek. I), and the two cherubim look toward each other, their faces turned toward the propitiatory seat (Exod. XV).

In this bow blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0515D] *Book of Morals*.] prepared instruments of death against opposing heretics, in order to catch the little foxes [Col. 0516D] that destroy the vineyards (Song II), having indeed different mouths but tails tied together (Judg. XV), because they agree together in vanity. He made his arrows for those who burn—that is, for sinful Catholics—so as to lead wandering sheep back to the folds and pasture them in pleasant thickets. The *Book of Morals* stands like a quiver full of these instruments and arrows.

“The Lord therefore established for him an everlasting covenant, and gave him a great priesthood” (Ecclus. XLV). Priesthood is twofold. One is visibly given outwardly in ordination; the other is visibly given inwardly in justification. One is of [Col. 0517A] dignity; the other is of holiness. Concerning the first the Lord says to Moses: “Bring near to yourself your brother Aaron and his sons, that they may minister to me in the priesthood” (Exod. XXVIII). Of the second Peter says: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II).

The Lord bestowed both upon blessed Gregory—not only a great priesthood but the greatest. He adorned him with the vestments of virtues and raised him to the summit of the apostolic see. Although all the apostles commonly received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and thereby all bishops received them, so that whatever they bind on earth through use of the keys should be bound in heaven, and whatever they loose on earth should be loosed in heaven (Matt. XVI), nevertheless blessed Peter principally received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and therefore [Col. 0517B] his successor, so that he may bind the others but cannot be bound by the others. For to him alone it was said: “You shall be called Cephas” (John I), that is, “head.” For just as in the human body the head alone has the fullness of the senses, while the other members receive a share of that fullness, so in the ecclesiastical body the other bishops are called to a share of the solicitude, but the supreme pontiff is assumed into the fullness of power.

Moreover, blessed Gregory preferred to be of benefit rather than to preside, so that power was more a burden than an honor to him. He was one of those concerning whom it is written: “The rams are clothed with sheep, and the valleys shall abound with grain” (Ps. LXIV). He was clothed with the ornaments of virtues signified by the pontifical vestments, so that he might be one of those of whom it is said: “May your priests be clothed with righteousness, and may your saints rejoice” (Ps. CXXXI).

There were in the Law (Exod. XXXVIII, XXXIX) eight—or, more correctly, seven—pontifical vestments, signifying in this very way the grace of the Holy Spirit: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. XI). The pontiff was clothed in them in the following order.

After first washing his hands and feet, he put on *monachasim*, that is, the drawers, signifying that the priest, with his works and affections cleansed by the tears of repentance, must take up continence in order to offer a sacrifice without blemish, holy and pleasing to God (Rom. XII). Our [Col. 0517D] pontiff, however, because he ought to possess unceasing continence, does not put on drawers during the sacrifice, but sandals. It is as though it were said: “He who has washed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John XIII). By hands works are signified, according to the words: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. CXLIII). By feet affections are signified, according to the words: “Shake the dust from your feet” (Matt. X).

Second, he put on the *cathemone*, that is, the linen garment, signifying that the priest must put on innocence, so that he may not do to another what he does not wish done to himself (Matt. VII). For linen signifies innocence because of its whiteness, according to the words: “At all times let your garments be [Col. 0518A] white” (Ecclus. IX).

Third, he girded himself with a belt, signifying chastity, by which he must be girded around the loins in order to restrain desire. Hence Truth says: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII).

Fourth, he put on the *poderim*, that is, the ankle-length garment, signifying that the pontiff must put on perseverance, because “he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X). For perseverance is signified by the ankle because of its extremity, according to the words: “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III). Pomegranates with golden bells hung as fringes (Exod. XXVIII). By the pomegranate is understood action; by the golden bell, preaching. These two [Col. 0518B] must be united in the priest, lest he enter the sanctuary without them and die. “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts I), leaving priests an example that they should follow his footsteps (1 Pet. II). He committed no sin, so that there might be uprightness in conduct; nor was deceit found in his mouth (ibid.), so that there might be truth in preaching.

Fifth, he put on the *ephod*, that is, the shoulder-garment, signifying that the pontiff must put on patience, so that in patience he may possess his soul (Luke XXI). For by the shoulders we carry burdens, according to the words: “He bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant under tribute” (Gen. XLIX). It had two edges joined together on each side at the upper ends, signifying that the pontiff [Col. 0518C] must possess the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor. VI), so that he is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity.

It also had two onyx stones set in the shoulders, upon which were engraved the twelve names of the sons of Israel—six on one and six on the other (Exod. XXVIII). By the two onyx stones are signified truth and sincerity: truth by their brightness, sincerity by their solidity. By the sons of Israel are signified holy desires and righteous works, according to the words: “Cursed is the man who has not left seed in Israel.” By the number six perfection is signified, because on the sixth day God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment. Therefore, the six names of the sons of Israel engraved on one stone and six upon the other signified that the priest’s desires [Col. 0518D] and works must be made perfect, not “in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. V), so that sincerity may shape the intention and truth the end.

It also had two chains of the purest gold joined to one another, which were put onto two hooks (Exod. XXVIII), signifying that the pontiff must have two affections of charity, toward God and toward neighbor. Of these it is commanded: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI; Luke X). For as gold surpasses all metals, so charity surpasses all virtues. The Apostle says of it: “The greater of these is charity” (1 Cor. XIII). The two hooks are intention and end, upon which the chains are placed, so that he may love both God and [Col. 0519A] neighbor “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. I); and may love both God and neighbor for the sake of blessedness—God for his own sake, and neighbor for God’s sake.

Sixth, he put on the *logion* (Exod. XXVIII), that is, the rational garment or breastpiece, signifying that the pontiff must put on discernment, through which he distinguishes light from darkness and right from left, because “there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial” (2 Cor. VI). The breastpiece was square, signifying that he must distinguish between four things: between true and false, lest he go astray in belief; and between good and evil, lest he go astray in action. It was also double, because he must discern for two—namely, for himself and for the people—lest, if [Col. 0519B] the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit (Luke VI).

It also had four rows of stones (Exod. XXVIII), signifying that the pontiff must possess the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. In each row, however, it had three stones, signifying that in the first he must have faith, hope, and charity; in the second, modesty, gentleness, and kindness; in the third, peace, mercy, and generosity; in the fourth, watchfulness, diligence, and long-suffering. Stones also signify virtues, according to the words: “Another builds with gold and silver and precious stones” (2 Cor. III).

The highest ornament of the head was the *cydaris* or tiara, which the pontiff put on last, signifying humility. Of it the Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV, XVIII). He wore it on his head, signifying that the pontiff must bear humility in his mind, after the example of our head, who says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). For the head signifies the mind, according to the words: “Anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. VI).

From the *cydaris* a golden plate hung down upon the forehead, signifying wisdom. Upon it was written the tetragrammaton, that is, the name of four letters: *Joth, He, Vau, Heth*—that is, “the beginning of life, of the Passion, this one” [reading uncertain]. As though speaking more plainly: he whose person this [Col. 0519D] pontiff bears, namely Christ, is the beginning—that is, the author—of life, of the passion—that is, of life restored through the Passion; because “by dying he destroyed our death, and by rising he restored life” (Preface of the Church). It is a lovable, delightful, and saving name: a name which heals, refreshes, and enlightens, of which it is written: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore young maidens loved you” (Song I). There is no true wisdom in which the name of so great a mystery is not engraved.

For the most part, the vestments were woven in *polymitus* work, that is, variegated work, because of the variety of virtues. Of this it is written: “The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, clothed round about with variety” (Ps. XLIV). They were woven from four precious colors: purple, scarlet, fine linen, [Col. 0520A] and hyacinth-blue. By purple is signified the pontifical authority of royal dignity, which must walk on the royal road, lest it turn aside to the right or stray to the left—lest it bind the worthy or loose the unworthy. By scarlet, a fiery color, is signified pontifical teaching, which like fire ought both to shine and to burn; for this reason it is said to be twice dyed. It must shine by promise: “Everyone who leaves father or mother,” etc., “shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX). It must burn by threat: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. VII).

By fine linen of outstanding whiteness is signified the brightness of reputation, which ought to be twisted or spun, so that the pontiff may have good testimony, according to the Apostle, “both from those who are within [Col. 0520B] and from those who are without” (1 Tim. III). By hyacinth-blue, the color of the air, is signified serenity of conscience, which the pontiff should possess within himself, as the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. I).

Blessed Gregory was clothed with all these things, so that he might be a great priest who in his days pleased God and “was found righteous, and in the time of wrath became reconciliation” (Ecclus. XIV). Therefore the Lord made him blessed in glory. He has already made him blessed in soul, and he has also made him blessed in body. For the saints shall have a twofold robe of glorification: one of the spirit and the other of the flesh.

[Col. 0520C] The robe of the spirit consists in three things: knowledge, love, and delight. Concerning knowledge, Truth says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). For in it the saints know even as they are known, seeing “not through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face” (1 Cor. XIII); understanding as it is the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity. From this comprehensive knowledge is born the highest love, by which the saints love God “with their whole heart, with their whole mind, with their whole soul” (Matt. XXII; Luke IX). And with the heart—that is, with the understanding—they love the Son wholly, that is, without error; with the mind—that is, with the memory—they love the Father wholly, that is, without forgetfulness; with the soul—that is, with the will—[Col. 0520D] they love the Holy Spirit wholly, that is, without opposition.

From this highest love is born the highest delight, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II). Yet concerning it we read: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places” (Ps. CXLIX).

The robe of the flesh consists in four things: brightness, subtlety, agility, and impassibility. Of these the Lord says: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke VI); and elsewhere: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run about like sparks among reeds, and their Lord shall reign for ever” (Wis. III). They shall shine, being bright; and like sparks, being subtle; they shall run among reeds, being agile; and their Lord [Col. 0521A] shall reign for ever: they shall be impassible. “For God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more; neither mourning nor crying nor any pain, because the former things [Col. 0522A] have passed away” (Isa. XXV; Apoc. VII).

May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages, bring us to this grace through the merits and prayers of blessed Gregory. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. FOR THE SOLEMNITY OF THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EVER-VIRGIN MARY

Concerning the various senses of “heaven”; concerning the stages of Christ’s descent and ascent; and how we ought to descend.

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521B] “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

When I carefully consider who I am that speaks, or of whom I speak, I judge it better to be silent than to speak. For I, a mute man, speak of the Word; earth speaks of heaven; a sinner, of the Savior. Yet, although God says of the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my Covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. LIX), still, because the creature ought not to fall silent in the praises of the Creator, permit me, brethren, to put something from the foregoing words into the treasury for the praise of the Redeemer.

These words should be weighed with so much the subtler consideration as they are fruitful in a more profound understanding. For upon the surface of the letter it seems [Col. 0521C] that Christ alone ascended into heaven, just as he alone descended from heaven, although many have ascended into heaven with him or after him. Many, therefore, are to ascend, so that where the exaltation of the head has gone before, there the humility of the body may follow, as he himself says: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may be my minister” (John XII).—“Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Eph. IV): namely, the saints, because, held suspended by the divine vision, they were detained in the darkness of hell. Of them it is written: “He brought out his bound ones from the pit in which there was no water” (Zech. IX).

But if we wish carefully to attend to the bark of the letter, beneath it we shall find the kernel of subtle understanding.

[Col. 0521D] For “heaven” is understood in sacred Scripture in various ways. At times it signifies the height of divinity, as when Lucifer says: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will set my seat toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Since Lucifer was established in the empyrean, there was no higher heaven into which he could ascend. But he understood heaven as the height of divinity, into which he desired to ascend so as to be like the Most High.

Thus heaven can fittingly be understood here also, so that the meaning is this: no one—that is, no human being ever, however holy, even though sanctified from the womb—has ascended into heaven, that is, into the sublimity of divinity, so as to be God, except him who descended from heaven, that is, from the height of divinity, so as to be [Col. 0522B] man: namely, the Son of Man, who remains in heaven as God. For he did not so descend from heaven as not to remain in heaven, because he was not so made man as to cease to be God. Rather, he is at once rich and poor, God and man: God, begotten of God before the ages; man, born of man within time.

Likewise, in the Psalm it is read: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its highest point” (Ps. XVIII). This, brethren, was fulfilled today, when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).—“Today the Lord made a new thing upon the earth: a woman encompassed a man” (Jer. XXXI) in the womb of a virgin. A woman, yet untouched; a mother, yet a virgin. In her womb she encompassed a child, yet a man; an infant, yet God. O truly new thing which the Lord has made upon the earth today: a star conceived the sun, a creature the Creator, a daughter the Father. Today he made the eternal temporal, the simple composite, and the immortal mortal. Today he renewed the mystery of the Trinity, so that there are three substances in unity of person, just as there are three persons in unity of substance; so that he who was born of the Father without a mother might be born from a mother without a father. Today he descended and ascended simultaneously; but God descended into man, and man ascended in God.

God therefore descended; man ascended. But because Christ is God and man, he simultaneously descended and ascended. Christ’s descent, however, was the assumption of [Col. 0522D] the form of a servant, of which the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II). In this descent, as upon a ladder, many steps are set. Let us therefore distinguish his steps, so that they may be recounted to another generation. The first step is the capacity for suffering which he assumed; the last is the Passion which he endured. Between the first and last are different gradations of steps.

To the first belong the deficiencies of humanity which he took upon himself: fear and pain, hunger and thirst, poverty and labor. To the last belong the punishments inflicted by men which he endured. For he was seized and bound, struck and scourged, mocked and reproached, cursed and condemned, crucified and pierced with a lance. Behold, the alabaster vessel was broken and the house filled with the fragrance of ointment (Matt. XXVI). But in order that the fragrance of the ointment may breathe forth more sweetly, the stages of these deficiencies must be set out, since the stages of the punishments are apparent.

Thus he confesses in the Psalm that he descended to the stage of fear: “The dread of death fell upon me; fear and trembling came upon me” (Ps. LIV). Concerning this same thing the Gospel says: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark XIV). O wondrous condescension of Christ! For us he feared whom angels fear, whom archangels tremble before, before whom every knee bends—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings (Phil. II).

He also testifies through the prophet that he descended to the stage of pain: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I). Hence the Gospel says: “My soul [Col. 0523B] is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). O wondrous mercy of the Lord! He suffered grief for sinners and wept for the wretched—he whose joy is always full, whose gladness never fails, through whom the Father and he himself played before the Father upon the circle of the earth (Prov. VIII).

He descended to the stage of hunger and thirst, as he himself testifies: “They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). The Gospel says of the same: “When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. IV). O ineffable dispensation of the Redeemer! The fountain of life thirsts; the food of angels hungers; the bread of life, who descended from heaven, of whom, if anyone tastes, he shall live for eternity (John VI).

[Col. 0523C] He confesses that he descended to the stage of poverty: “I am poor,” he says, “and sorrowful” (Ps. LXVIII). The Gospel says of the same: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII). O great example of humility! He was made poor, whose are the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it (Ps. XXXII).

He descended to the stage of labor, saying himself: “I labored in crying out,” etc. (Ps. VIII). And in the Gospel he is said to have grown weary on the journey (John IV). But who is so hard, whose breast is so iron, whose body so stony, that he can keep in his sighs and restrain his groaning when he hears that his Creator, his Redeemer, [Col. 0523D] descended humbly through these stages—he who “became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II)? Let him know himself culpably hard who laments the insults and sufferings of a friend, yet when he hears of so many punishments of Christ, so many insults and reproaches, is not moved to groaning and sheds no tears. For he did not descend for himself but for us, and gave his life as a redemption for the world.

But he who descended is the same who ascended. Of this ascent the prophet says: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root” (Isa. XI). Then, as if defining the stages of his ascent, he adds: “And the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit [Col. 0524A] of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (ibid.).

Elsewhere, too, describing the steps in this ascent, the same prophet says: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX). This is he who ascended to the rank of supreme authority, as he himself testifies: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). For “whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea, and in all the abysses” (Ps. CXIII). He had, indeed, steps of ascent not only through the gifts which he received at his conception, but also through the miracles which he performed by his own power. Therefore, he ascended through the miracles [Col. 0524B] which he performed in heaven, through those which he performed on earth, and through those which he performed in water. And in these three realms he performed miracles in being born, preaching, and dying. When he himself was born, a new star appeared in the east, because the Sun of righteousness arose (Mal. II), whom the Magi, led by the star, came with gifts to adore (Matt. II). At Rome, moreover, the Temple of Peace marvellously collapsed, because he was born who came not to bring peace but a sword (Matt. X). For when complete peace had been restored to the whole world under Augustus Caesar, the Romans built the Temple of Peace. When they asked how long it would endure, the reply was: “Until a virgin gives birth.” Rejoicing, they concluded: “Therefore it will endure for ever, since a virgin will never [Col. 0524C] give birth.” But immediately, at the hour of the Lord’s birth, it fell utterly to the ground. Then, too, the river Tiber received into itself a stream of oil flowing from an oil-shop, because the river of delight was born, of whom it is written: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song I).

He likewise ascended these steps by preaching. For at the Transfiguration the voice of the Father was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear him” (Matt. III). He also, to pass over his other miracles, raised Lazarus, four days dead, from the earth (John XII). He walked upon the waters with dry feet (Mark VI). When he died upon the gibbet of the cross, the sun was darkened, the earth trembled, and water flowed from his side [Col. 0524D] (Luke XXIII).

These are deeds which no one else ever performed or could perform; and therefore no one ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.

But we also, brethren, if we wish to reign with him, must suffer with him; and if we wish to ascend, we must descend (II Tim. II), because “he who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV). But the devil, because he wished to ascend through pride, not only descended but fell, as it is written: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning” (Isa. XIV). And of the same one: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke I). Let us therefore descend through [Col. 0525A] humility, and in that descent arrange our steps according to the example of the Lord. First, indeed, we ought to descend through subjection; secondly, through compassion; thirdly, through self-abasement. Subjection contains three steps: the first is to subject oneself to a superior; the second, to subject oneself to an equal; the third, to subject oneself to an inferior. We descend to the first through due necessity; to the second through mutual charity; to the third through overflowing humility. Christ descended to this step when he washed the disciples’ feet (John XIII), and when he placed his head—dreaded by the angels—under the hands of the Baptist, saying: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. III), that is, overflowing humility. He taught the apostles, and us in them, to descend to this same step, [Col. 0525B] saying: “He who is greatest among you shall be the servant of all,” setting himself before them as an example, “because the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. XX). Hence the one highest in the Church calls himself the servant of the servants of God.

Compassion, however, is divided into two steps. The first is compassion for oneself; the second, compassion for one’s neighbour. Of the first it is said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX). The Apostle descended to the second step when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. II). Let us also descend, weeping over the misery of this life, sighing for future glory, groaning for our own sins, and weeping [Col. 0525C] for those of others.

Self-abasement likewise contains two steps. The first is rejection of the world; the second, rejection of oneself. John exhorts us to the first, saying: “Little children, do not love the world, nor those things which are in [Col. 0526A] the world. For whatever is in the world is the lust of the flesh” (I John II)—with regard to gluttony and lust—“and the lust of the eyes,” with regard to riches and possessions. But it is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIX). And there is “the pride of life,” with regard to honours and dignities. Yet we are lifted on high so that we may fall more grievously. To the second step the Lord invites us, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX).

And in all these matters we must descend in heart, speech, and deed: so that we exclude pride from the heart, boasting from the mouth, and vain glory from our actions. If we descend in this way, we shall ascend more worthily from evil to good, [Col. 0526B] from good to better, and from better to best. The first ascent belongs to beginners, the second to those making progress, the third to those who have attained their goal. The first ascent is to justification, the second to perfection, and the third to glorification.

The first ascent has three steps: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. We ascend to the first through sorrow, to the second through shame, and to the third through labour. The second ascent likewise has three steps. The first is avoidance of what is forbidden; the second, fulfilment of the commandments; the third, supererogation beyond the counsels. The third ascent is distinguished by a double step. First comes ascent to the glorification of the soul; secondly, to the glorification of the body. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant us [Col. 0526C] to ascend to these, he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PREPARATION

Why Christ is bound with the ungodly; and why Christ, not Barabbas, must be chosen. That is, Christ rather than sin; that all sinners prefer Barabbas to Christ; and that they can abstain from sin if they do not love sin more than Christ.

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525D] “Whom do you wish me to release to you—Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” (Matt. XXVII).

These words, beloved, which you have often heard and often read, plainly raise the question: by whom was it asked? Pilate asked it of the Jews. But why did he ask it? He was a judge, and by virtue of his judicial authority had several prisoners bound in his prison. Yet he had this custom: on the day of Passover, partly in honour of that solemnity and partly to preserve the friendship of the Jews, he permitted one of those whom he held bound to depart freely each year, on the aforesaid day, at their request. Accordingly, among the other prisoners was one named Barabbas. But we know very well why Barabbas was bound: he was a robber and had committed murder in a sedition [Col. 0526D]. But what had Jesus deserved? Why was he judged among criminals? Was he not the very one who, by an ineffable will, granted pardon to criminals, and who by his bodily presence raised the dead? O wickedness! “What fellowship has light with darkness?” (II Cor. VI). But Christ is bound again with the ungodly in order that what had been said of him might be fulfilled: “And he was reckoned with the ungodly” (Isa. LIII). Mercy is counted among the ungodly, yet mercy is not changed into ungodliness; rather, ungodliness itself is afterwards transformed into piety.

Pilate therefore says to the Jews: Which of the two do you wish released to you? Behold, Jews, the choice between Christ and the robber is placed in your judgment. Choose whom you wish; reject whom you wish. Christ “committed no sin, nor was deceit found [Col. 0527A] in his mouth” (I Pet. II). But Barabbas was notorious for the crime of robbery and stained with the blood of murder. Behold: you celebrate the Passover with unleavened bread, and reject leaven. Choose, therefore, innocent and pure Christ; reject the robber, leavened with many iniquities. Reject the man who kills, and receive the man who saves. Reject, I say, him who killed the living; receive him who gives life to the dead.

Yet let us see whom you chose; let us hear what you said: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John XVIII). A choice which love did not make: I think you did not even love the one whom you chose. Nor did you wish Barabbas to be released for any other reason than that Christ might be crucified. “Not this man, but Barabbas.” Not this man—alas for the pain! The robber’s name is spoken; Christ is not deemed worthy even of being named. Yet he was burdensome for them to name because he was burdensome for them to behold.

But, dearly beloved, why do we declare these things? Why do we examine so carefully both Pilate’s question and the Jews’ answer? Certainly because, after the likeness of this question, we wish to pose another question. That question was put to the Jewish people so that ours might be put to the Christian people. But because there are good and bad among the Christian people, in this present sermon we do not pose it to the good—rather, to those who are bad and are called sons of men. Let us therefore set two things before them: sin and Christ. Say, then, sons of men: Which of the two do you wish released—sin or Christ? Good or evil? Truth or vanity? Iniquity or justice? [Col. 0527C] Or, to state more expressly what we mean: which of the two do you wish released—a prostitute or Christ? The flesh of a harlot, or the flesh of the Son of Man? Flesh which grants eternal life, or flesh which brings everlasting death? Which do you prefer: by eating Christ’s body, to abide in him; or, by cleaving to a harlot, to make your body and hers one? For Christ speaks thus of his own body: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him,” etc. (John VI). But the Apostle says this concerning the body of a harlot: “He who cleaves to a harlot becomes one body” (I Cor. VI). Say, sons of men, [Col. 0527D] what do you love? Answer what you have chosen of the two. Apply discernment, if you can, make your choice, and then give your answer. I make the question plain to you; it requires neither necessary nor profound discrimination. We set before you good and evil, a prostitute and Christ, and ask which of the two you choose above all.

O sons of men, why do you hesitate? Why do you not answer promptly? Why, except because you are sons of men? And what are sons of men except sons of carnal people—those who love carnal things and have a carnal understanding? Are you not those of whom it is written: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV). Certainly this is why you do not choose the good: you are heavy of heart and [Col. 0528A] love vanity. “How good is God to Israel!” (Ps. LXXII). But to whom? Not to those crooked in heart. O heavy-hearted sons of men, what is it that rises above your head? Whence comes such heaviness in your heart? This is indeed that of which it is written: “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead” (Zech. V). The man in the Psalm laboured beneath this burden of iniquity when he said: “For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Ps. XXXVII). They also were pressed by this weight, of whom it is said: “They sank like lead in mighty waters” (Exod. XV). This iniquity, therefore, O heavy-hearted sons of men, not only weighs down your hearts but has stopped your mouths so that you do not answer us. And would that at least [Col. 0528B] you kept silent and answered nothing, and, although you despised Christ, did not choose the prostitute!

But if you ask how or when you despise Christ, how or when you choose the prostitute, call to mind the time of your confession; remember what you say at the time of communion. Let us suppose someone comes to a priest, confesses his sins, and says: “I confess, Lord, that I have sinned: I have offended my father and mother; I have lied, sworn falsely, and seized what belongs to others by theft and violence.” The priest says to him: “Do you repent of having done these things, and do you wish henceforth to abandon them?” And he replies: “I repent of them from my heart, and gladly abandon them.” The priest says: “See,” he says, “whether you have done more. Tell me whether you have ever touched a woman.” [Col. 0528C] And he replies: “Who is there, lord, who does not do this? Who is there who abstains from this sin?” The priest says: “Do not speak so, friend, do not speak so. Unless you confess this sin as you have the others, and unless you promise amendment in this as in the others, know for certain that you will neither receive Christ’s communion worthily nor attain eternal life after this temporal life. Therefore confess this sin also, promise amendment, and then receive communion.” And he replies: “O lord, I am very weak; I cannot abstain from a woman, and therefore I do not dare promise what I know I cannot keep.” “Vow,” he says, “and render to the Lord your God” (Ps. LVII); “and it is better not to vow than to vow and not render” (Eccles. IV).

The priest replies: [Col. 0528D] “I do not demand that you make a vow which you have not made, but that you render what you promised. Did you not renounce the devil and his works in baptism? Is not fornication a work of the devil? Thus, if according to our counsel you promise not to fornicate, you do what you ought to do; if you do not promise it, nevertheless you always ought to do it. Finally, rendering a vow while not owing it is properly called a free gift, not a vow; for that person makes a vow who freely promises that he will do what he does not owe. But one who promises not to fornicate does not make a vow—that is, he does not promise what he does not owe—but resolves to render what he owes. Therefore, when I urge you to abstain from fornication and preserve chastity, I do not demand a vow, but require a debt. As for what you say, ‘I am weak; I cannot abstain [Col. 0529A] from a woman’: examine what you say and see whether you certainly can. For I believe you could if you wished; you could if you loved God as much as you love your eye.

“Behold, I put a question to you; give a true answer. If temptation now came upon you and incited you to lust; if the devil urged you on; if the flesh tickled you; if even a woman thrust herself upon you shamelessly and irreverently, exposing her whole self for sin—then, in the very heat of temptation, if you knew for certain that you would lose an eye if you sinned with her, tell me, before God, what would you do? Would not a certain horror immediately spread through your body, and would not that heat of lust which had occupied your whole being be extinguished? Would you not recoil from that woman? Would you not even strike her with your fist? [Col. 0529B] Now consider what you are accustomed to say: ‘I would abstain if I could.’ Behold, you can, because you fear to lose an eye. What you can do for the sake of an eye, you cannot do for God—unless it is because you love your eye more than God? Is an eye worth more than God? Therefore do not say what you are accustomed to say: ‘I would abstain if I could.’ Instead say: ‘I could if I wished.’ Correct your will, love chastity, and you will receive the power to be continent. But if you profess yourself weak, why do you not run to the physician? If you suffer sickness, why do you not embrace health? If you see yourself powerless, why do you not receive the Almighty? O unhappy one, look upon yourself and despise yourself; look up and receive him. He will be your all if he comes to you; he himself will treat you, he himself will heal you, [Col. 0529C] and he himself will grant strength. For he is physician, salvation, strength, and health. Consent to our counsel, abandon fornication, make a promise of chastity, and then you will receive communion. [Col. 0530A] If you choose one, you cannot have the other; choose, therefore, what you wish.”

O sons of men, attend to what this companion of yours answers; see what he chooses. “If,” he says, “I cannot otherwise receive communion unless I promise chastity, I prefer to defer communion rather than make a promise beyond my capacity.” O foolish answer! O Jewish choice! What did the Jews answer Pilate? “Not this man, but Barabbas.” What does the son of man answer the priest? If we examine the meaning of his words, what else does he answer but: “Not Christ, but the prostitute”? For what else does he say when he says: “I prefer to defer communion rather than promise chastity”? O how dangerous it is to defer! O unhappy is this delay, when can you know what you can endure? Would it not be better for you to suffer temptation than to defer communion? Endurance of temptation would make you blessed; but this postponement of communion does not absolve guilt—it increases it. “Blessed is he who endures temptation” (Jas. I); but woe to one who postpones communion out of love for sinning.

Renounce, sons of men, Jewish impiety; follow Christian piety; love justice; cleanse your conscience. If you wish to escape eternal damnation, flee fornication. But you wretches not only fail to repel it when it is present and pressing; what is worse, you seek it when absent and hold it when it flees. But what is it to flee fornication except to avoid occasions for fornication? Flee these, therefore; choose Christ, so that in this present life [Col. 0530C] you may worthily receive his communion, and in the life to come may attain his possession—he who lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE SOLEMNITY OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST

How John the Baptist was great in many ways.

[Col. 0529]

[Col. 0529D] “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. XI).

He who praises and glorifies God is himself praised and glorified by God, as he himself testifies: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Luke XII). For Peter said to Christ: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI), and Christ says to him: “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (ibid.). Thus John said of Christ: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I), and Christ says of him: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen.” They confessed the truth concerning Christ; Christ declared their dignity, [Col. 0530D] because the confession of truth merits a declaration of dignity.

How great John was is attested by both the prophetic and the Gospel reading. He was great in predestination, great in annunciation, great in conception, great in nature, great in person, great in grace, great in office, great in merit, great in mystery, great in dignity, great in power, great in brilliance, great in reputation, great in preaching, and great in passion.

He was therefore great in predestination, according to what the Lord says to him through the prophet: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. I). “For the Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II), that is, he predestined his own. By contrast, he says to the reprobate: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII). In the same sense the Lord says to Nathanael: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I knew you” (John I). But since God knows all things before they happen, why does he say particularly of John: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you?” (Jer. I). When what belongs commonly to many is attributed particularly to one person, it must be understood antonomastically—that is, as a pre-eminent designation. God knew John more fully, because he predestined for him greater grace in the present and fuller glory in the future.

He was great in annunciation, because “an angel appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense: ‘Do not fear,’ he said, ‘Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. And behold, Elizabeth your wife shall bear you [Col. 0531B] a son, and you shall call his name John; and you shall have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth’” (Luke I). The same angel—namely Gabriel—announced John’s birth to his father and Jesus’ birth to his mother, announcing in each case a great miracle: the birth of a virgin and that of a barren woman. Concerning John he speaks not of conception but of birth; concerning Jesus he foretells both birth and conception. To Zechariah the father it is not foretold: “Your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John” (ibid.); but to Mary the mother it is foretold: “Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (ibid.). For John was conceived in sin; but Christ alone was conceived without sin. Yet both were born in grace, and therefore the Nativity of each is observed; but the conception of Christ alone is celebrated.

He was great in conception because he was conceived not at nature’s demand but through the working of grace, since Zechariah was old, “and Elizabeth was barren, and both had advanced in their days” (ibid.). Behold another Isaac: born of an old man, conceived of a barren woman, foretold by an angel, named beforehand by that angel himself; father of Jacob, who begot the twelve patriarchs (Gen. XVII, XXVIII). The one was of Abraham, the other of Zechariah; the one of Sarah, the other of Elizabeth; each of an old man, each of a barren woman; each announced and named beforehand by an angel—the one Isaac, the other John. At Isaac’s birth Sarah said: “The Lord has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me” (ibid.); [Col. 0531D] at John’s birth, when neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had shown, or magnified, his mercy toward Elizabeth, they rejoiced with her, as the angel had foretold Zechariah: “You shall have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke I). But Zechariah became mute because he did not believe the angel; Abraham, however, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as faith unto righteousness” (Gen. XV). Isaac, as a carnal father, carnally begot Jacob; John, as a spiritual father, spiritually begot Christ. The former begot twelve patriarchs, the latter twelve apostles; the former was great, but the latter greater: for among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen.

He was great in nature because he was born of a priestly [Col. 0532A] family. “There was,” it says, “in the days of Herod king of Judaea, a priest named Zechariah, of the course of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth” (Luke I). Noble from noble parents, and righteous from righteous parents, because “both were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (ibid.).

He was great in person because “he went before God in the spirit and truth of Elijah, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (ibid.). For this reason the Lord also said of him: “He is Elijah who is to come” (Matt. XI). John announced the first coming; Elijah will announce the second. John suffered persecution from Herod on account of Herodias, Herod’s wife; Elijah suffered persecution from Ahab on account of Jezebel, his wife.

Great in grace: hence he was called John, a name interpreted “the grace of God,” because he was filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb (Luke I), the Lord saying to him through the prophet: “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. I). He was reborn before he was born, regenerated before he was begotten; thus, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb (Luke I).

He was great in office. In accordance with the prophetic word, he answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God’” (John I). He “turned the hearts of fathers to their children and the unbelieving to the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke [Col. 0532C] I). He is the voice of the Word, the herald of the Judge, the bridegroom’s friend, the lamp of the Sun, the end of the Law, and the beginning of the Gospel.

He was great in merit because “he drank neither wine nor strong drink” (ibid.), and “he had a garment of camel hair and a leather girdle about his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey. Moderate in abstinence, because he drank neither wine nor strong drink, and his food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. III). Chaste in continence, because “he had a garment of camel hair and a leather girdle about his loins” (ibid.), so that “his loins might be girded and lamps burning in his hands” (Luke XII).

He was great in mystery: for “the Law and the prophets were until John, and from him the kingdom of heaven has been preached” (Luke XVI). But from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men seize it. He himself testifies to the meaning of the mystery concerning himself: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices with joy because of his voice” (John III). For which reason he also says elsewhere: “He who comes after me has been made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John I).

He was great in dignity, as the Father says of him to the Son: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you” (Mal. III). John was called an angel not by a property of nature but by the dignity of his office. Truth itself extolled his excellence, saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” For John, together with the prophets, spoke of the future: “Behold, one mightier than I shall come” (Mark I); and, more than a prophet, he showed him present: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

He was great in power, as the Lord says of him in the person of the prophet: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, that you may pluck up and destroy, ruin and scatter, build and plant” (Jer. I); for the hand of the Lord was with him. He was great in brilliance, because “he was a burning and shining lamp” (John I), concerning whom the Father says through the prophet: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. CXXXI). “For there was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came to bear witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him” (John I).

He was great in reputation: for when the people were supposing and all were considering in their hearts concerning John [Col. 0533B] whether perhaps he himself was the Christ, John answered them all, saying: “I baptize you in water; but one mightier than I is coming after me, who will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke III). The people considered him exalted, but he answered that he was humble, saying: “I must decrease, but he must increase” (John III); for “he who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV).

He was great in preaching because “John came into all the region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. ‘Bring forth,’ he said, ‘fruits worthy of repentance’” (Luke III); and: “Repent,” he said, “for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III). An outstanding preacher, for he preached especially those things through which true remission of sins is granted: baptism and repentance (Matt. III).

He was great in passion because he suffered imprisonment for truth and was at last beheaded: baptized in blood, he who baptized in water (John I).

There is, moreover, a threefold baptism: in water, in tears, and in blood—water for regeneration, tears for compunction, blood for passion. John prepared each of these before the Lord’s face, by baptizing, preaching, and dying. Therefore, among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen. [Col. 0533D] What then? Is not Christ, who was born of a woman, greater? As he himself says to his mother: “Woman, behold your son” (John X). But Christ was born of a woman according to sex, not according to sexual embrace; born of a woman according to outward form, not according to sensual softness. Or “prophet” is to be understood when it is said, “None greater than John the Baptist has arisen,” namely, no greater prophet. As the Lord himself had said before: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matt. XXI). For although Christ is somewhere called a prophet, as: “Behold, a great prophet will come”; and again: “A great prophet has arisen among us” (Luke VII), he should nevertheless be called not so much a prophet as the Lord of the prophets.

But what does the following mean: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John the Baptist”? To omit uncertain and obscure explanations, let us state plainly and fully at once: in the kingdom of heaven, [Col. 0534B] that is, in the heavenly homeland, only angels were present when Christ said these things, because he had not yet ascended on high and led his captivity captive (Ps. LXVII). The prophet, speaking of Christ, testifies that angels are greater than men: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII). For they are immortal, while these are mortal; they are incapable of suffering, while these are capable of suffering; they are blessed, while these are wretched; they triumph, while these are soldiers. Therefore, he who was then least in the kingdom of heaven was greater than John the Baptist.

We therefore, brethren and children, who have assembled to celebrate his nativity, if we take care to celebrate it worthily, should certainly hope that, the greater he is with God, the more he will intercede for us [Col. 0534C] with him. But we must take the greatest care that, as we rejoice outwardly at his nativity, we may rejoice inwardly at his nativity; for “the remnant of thoughts shall keep festival to the Lord” (Ps. LXXV). “But the ungodly are not to rejoice” (Isa. XLVIII), says the Lord, as the Psalmist testifies: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins; my conscience reproaching me” (Ps. XXXVII). Therefore let us cleanse the soul of the stains of sins, so that we may worthily celebrate the joy of so great a solemnity. For one who shines outwardly and is foul inwardly is like, as the Lord says, a sepulchre whitened on the outside but within full of every uncleanness (Matt. XXIII). Let us pray, therefore, brethren and children; let us all pray, each individually, that through the intercession of blessed [Col. 0534D] John the Baptist Jesus Christ our Lord may grant us the joy of the eternal solemnity—he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE SAME FEAST

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533D] “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men seize it” (Matt. XI).

Perhaps it seems strange to some that the kingdom [Col. 0534D] of heaven is seized by violence. But it cannot seem strange to those who, for the kingdom of heaven, crucify their members with their vices and desires [Col. 0535A] (Gal. V); who, for the sake of divine words, keep to hard paths; who deny themselves in order to follow Christ and walk by the narrow way that leads to life. O what force such a person applies to himself! What violence he inflicts! What a struggle he undertakes, when, though rich in worldly goods, he makes himself poor for God and chooses to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than dwell among sinners! (Ps. LXXXIII). For flesh contends, nature resists, and habit opposes; yet grace conquers, spirit prevails, and reason rules, when it carefully considers what Christ truly promises: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

A happy conflict, a blessed struggle, a glorious battle, when the spirit fights against the flesh in order to obtain [Col. 0535B] the kingdom of heaven. Thus it fights against nature in order to conquer, prevail, and triumph. This war cannot be waged without great strength, grave difficulty, and much violence. A person reared in riches shrinks from poverty and embraces wealth, because poverty is hard and riches pleasant. But conversely, one who has already learned to bear Christ’s yoke loves want and despises riches, knowing that riches prick the soul and enervate the body. He has learned from him who calls riches thorns (Luke VIII), because they prick, tear, and afflict: they are not acquired without labour, possessed without fear, or lost without pain. Therefore, “Blessed are the poor [Col. 0535C] in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

Such was John the Baptist, who left the world with its riches and sought the wilderness with its poverty, because he was in the wilderness until the day of his manifestation to Israel. He was unwilling to exercise the priesthood in his father’s place, in order to receive priestly and legal revenues, tithes, and firstfruits; for he abandoned everything from which he might have received anything. Therefore it is rightly said that from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and violent men seize it, since John showed in himself, by the Spirit, an example of how this might be done.

When someone suffers injury without cause, receives an insult, or sustains loss, and for the sake of the kingdom of heaven does not rise in anger, is not carried away [Col. 0535D] into rage, and does not turn to revenge, he surely does great violence to himself, imposes much force upon himself, and inflicts a great and severe restraint upon himself. So strong is this virtue, so virtuous this strength, that a man conquers his own conqueror when he overcomes himself; for, in Solomon’s saying: “The patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who takes cities” (Prov. XVI). In this contest, indeed, he is defeated who commits an injury against his neighbour; and he conquers who endures an injury for God’s sake, as Truth says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI). Such was John the Baptist, who endured imprisonment for righteousness and at last was beheaded for righteousness. He endured it without murmuring or resistance, although he was [Col. 0536A] so great a man, and of such character, that Herod feared him, as the Gospel reading attests. Therefore it is rightly said that from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. John displayed in himself a clear example.

There is another kind of struggle, in which one must resist more cautiously: namely, when the breeze of favour caresses with praise, applause resounds, and the flatterer’s tongue speaks smooth words—lest it snatch a person upward, lift him to the highest place, and raise him on high. Rather, let him reckon himself lower, present himself as humbler, and show himself smaller. For who is there whom praise does not delight and exalt, and reproaches do not cast down and sadden? To prevent this, modesty is necessary: it restrains the violent impulse of self-exaltation and prudently moderates [Col. 0536B] the excess of arrogance, so that inwardly the oil of the heart may not make the head fat (Ps. CXL). Such was John the Baptist. Although everyone thought him to be Christ, he refused, against conscience, to yield to public report and so vainly exceed himself; rather, against public report, he chose to yield to conscience, that he might truly remain below himself. Yet when people proclaimed him exalted, believing him to be Christ, he answered that he was humble: “I am not he,” he said, “but after me is coming one who was made before me, whose sandal I am not worthy to untie” (Matt. III). It is rightly said that from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it; for John displayed a clear example in himself so that this might happen.

[Col. 0536C] What shall I say about gluttony? What shall I recount about lust? How difficult it is for the gluttonous person to be restrained by the bridle of abstinence; how burdensome for the lustful person to be constrained by the girdle of abstinence, since without much exertion he cannot alter carnal habit. This enemy is familiar; and therefore one more easily avoids an enemy of this kind—not far away but near; not outside but within. For “his strength is in his loins” (Job XL); and strength against this enemy requires a new combat, because when it is fled from, then it is put to flight. Whoever, therefore, for the kingdom of heaven embraces sobriety and pursues chastity, abstaining from feasts and restraining himself from enticements, certainly does great violence to himself [Col. 0536D] and undertakes a severe struggle, since “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). Where the struggle is greater, there the crown is more precious; and where the conflict is more grievous, there the triumph is more glorious.

Such was John, who despised delights, rejected feasts, and avoided enticements—chaste, sober, and restrained. For it is written of him that “he had clothing of camel’s hair and a leather girdle round his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. III). Thus he plainly deserved the testimony of Truth: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, more than a prophet; [Col. 0537A] for among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist.” Therefore it is rightly said that from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it, because John the Baptist displayed a clear example in himself so that this might happen.

Oh, how difficult it is to change an ingrained habit, especially to pass from sweet things to bitter, from pleasant things to troubles, from prosperity to adversity! How much violence a man surely does to himself when he passes from feasts to fasting, from sleep to vigils, from leisure to hardship, from delights to miseries, from rest to labour, from joy to lamentation, from freedom to servitude—believe one who has learned it by experience.

There is yet another domestic struggle: the more familiar it is, [Col. 0537B] the more grievous. Nor does it seem a small one, because it is waged against little ones, that they may be seized and dashed against the rock. For who could avoid awareness of evil thoughts, whom importunate thoughts do not trouble? “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Ecclus. X); they are the birds swooping down which Abraham drove away from the sacrifice (Gen. XV). It is not in a person’s power that they should not arise; but it is within a person’s strength that they should not grow. Little ones grievously afflict; grown ones violently destroy. We cannot avoid feeling the first stirrings, although we can avoid consenting to them. Often obscene thoughts creep in against a person’s will, so that he cannot think without shame—to say nothing of those that are vain and profane—and they cannot be driven out [Col. 0537C] without great effort, especially through the power of holy prayer.

He does great violence to himself in doing what is necessary for the kingdom of heaven. For concerning the former it is commanded: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V). Concerning the latter it is commanded: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). The struggle is severe, but the victory is great, when carnal and spiritual affection contend with one another. If, in this struggle, spiritual affection conquers carnal affection, then indeed the wild cows which had left their calves at home, drawing the new cart upon which they bore the ark of the Lord [Col. 0537D] placed upon them, go straight along the road leading to Beth-shemesh; and they proceed by one route, going and lowing, so that they turn neither to the right nor to the left (1 Sam. VI). Thus the kingdom of heaven suffers violence from such persons, and violent persons of this kind seize it; because through the violence they inflict upon themselves, in passing from vices to virtues, they deserve to obtain the kingdom of heaven.

But although it is said that from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence not only for the reason explained above, but also because “the Law and the Prophets were until John, and from him the kingdom of heaven has been proclaimed” (Luke XVI): the Mosaic Law permitted temporal riches, whence Truth says: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Lev. XX)—grain, wine, oil, [Col. 0538A] dew, and rain. But the Gospel Law enjoins temporal poverty: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX); because “unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). The Mosaic Law returned evil for evil, retaliation for retaliation; but the Gospel Law returned good for evil, blessing for cursing. “If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other; if he takes your tunic, give him your cloak” (Matt. V), and so forth. The Mosaic Law enjoined marital union: “Cursed,” it says, “is the man who leaves no seed in Israel; and cursed is the barren woman who does not bear children.” But the Gospel urges virginal chastity: “There are eunuchs,” it says, “who have made themselves eunuchs [Col. 0538B] for the kingdom of heaven. Let him who can receive this receive it” (Matt. XIX).

These things are indeed severe, but to those who love they are counted light, because love overcomes all things. “Come to me,” he says, “you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light.” For “the Law was given through Moses; therefore grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I). Thus from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent persons seize it. They plainly seize it and acquire it by force.

The Lord willingly permits this violence to be done to him: he is moved to grant benefits not only by devout prayers but even by importunate cries, as he himself teaches in the Gospel. For if the friend [Col. 0538C] who asked to be lent three loaves persists in knocking, “I say to you, even if he does not rise and give to him because he is his friend, nevertheless because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs” (Luke II [probably XI]). Therefore he wishes to be entreated with importunate prayers, so that what seems to have been obtained through much insistence may be held dearer. Likewise, it is remarkable that the angel who wrestled with Jacob was compelled to bless him; as that same angel says: “Let me go, for dawn has come.” He answered him and said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” But he said: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; for if you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?” And [Col. 0538D] he blessed him in the same place (Gen. XXXII).

But if the fathers of the Old Testament were such men, why is it said that from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffered violence, when before John the Baptist’s time the kingdom of heaven also suffered such violence from those who despised riches, avoided enticements, and scorned delights?

Yet it is said for this reason also: what was then done rarely by a few is now done frequently by many, who strive in companies and press forward emulously in great numbers to pass into the kingdom of heaven. This may plainly be seen in those who, having scattered all their possessions for the Lord’s sake, deny themselves, take up the cross, and follow Christ. Therefore let us strive, dearest brethren, to inflict violence upon ourselves for the kingdom of [Col. 0539A] heaven, “that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, righteously, and godly in this age, awaiting the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Tit. II). May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us through the prayers and merits of blessed John the Baptist—he who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

[Note: [Col. 0539D] From Angelo Mai’s edition.]

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0539B] “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent persons seize it” (Matt. XI).

The kingdom of heaven, or kingdom of God, dearest brethren, is understood in many ways. One kind is lower and another higher; one is inward and another outward. The lower is on the way; the higher is in the homeland. The inward is in the heart; the outward is in the book. The lower is the army at war; the higher is the choir of those who triumph. The inward is right faith; the outward is Holy Scripture. So that the foundation may stand beneath the column, let us set examples beneath each of these. Of the lower kingdom it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls” (Matt. XIII). Of the higher it is said: “They shall come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII). Of the inward [Col. 0539C] kingdom it is written: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII). Of the outward it is said: “The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits . . .” (Matt. XXI).

The lower kingdom suffers violence in order to seize the higher kingdom, because through the battle waged on the way one reaches the crown bestowed in the homeland; as the Apostle says: “He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. II). Likewise, the inward kingdom suffers violence in order to seize the higher kingdom, because through faith of the soul one comes to the understanding of Scripture; as the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” Certainly, unless our soul believed that three persons are one God, would it understand what Scripture says: [Col. 0539D] “Two seraphim cried one to another: Holy, holy, holy, the God of hosts” (Isa. VI)? Nor would it understand that Abraham is described as having seen three, and is read to have worshipped one (Gen. XVIII).

Likewise, unless the soul believed that God the Father eternally begot God the Son, would it understand what Scripture testifies: “With you is sovereignty on the day of your power, amid the splendours of the saints; from the womb before Lucifer I begot you” (Ps. CIX)? Nor would it understand that Wisdom speaks of herself in Proverbs: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning; the abysses did not yet exist, and I was being brought forth; and I was with him arranging all things” (Prov. VIII).

Again, unless the soul believed that God became man, it would never understand [Col. 0540B] what Scripture says: “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). Nor would it understand what is written: “From you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, shall come forth a leader who will be ruler in Israel; and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. V). Therefore, unless the soul believed that Mary bore Christ Jesus, it would never understand what is elsewhere written: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI). There are many such things, but let these few among many suffice, so that we may pass to others.

This soul suffers great violence in believing, because what it believes is almost unbelievable, so that faith may have merit where human reason offers no proof. Hear the prophet marvel at such matters: [Col. 0540C] “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her labour came, she bore a male child” (Isa. LXVI). Who, I ask, has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? Therefore elsewhere he says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII). Such violent persons, then, who through faith inflict violence upon nature, seize the kingdom of heaven—that is, they understand the mysteries of the Scriptures.

This violence begins from the days of John the Baptist, because the Law and the Prophets were until John, and from him the kingdom of heaven has been proclaimed. Until John the Baptist the literal sense prevailed in the Scriptures, but from the days of John the Baptist spiritual understanding shone forth in the Scriptures. Thus John the Baptist himself, when asked who he was, disclosed one of [Col. 0540D] Scripture’s mysteries and answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight the ways of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet says” (John I). Therefore, the one who wishes to understand the mysteries of Scripture must inflict great violence upon himself, because they cannot be understood without much study and watchfulness, much sweat and labour, much meditation and reading. Therefore the Lord says: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III), because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV). Therefore from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent persons seize it.

Perhaps it seems strange to some that the kingdom of heaven is seized by violence, etc., as above.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE SAME FEAST

On John’s threefold birth—carnal, sacramental, and spiritual—in which many rejoice.

[Col. 0541]

[Col. 0541A] “Elizabeth your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John; and you shall have joy and gladness, and many shall rejoice at his birth” (Luke I).

What we read and understand to have been foretold by Gabriel, behold, we see fulfilled in John and rejoice in it: for many rejoice at his birth. The angelic word, however, yields a threefold meaning, according to John’s threefold birth: carnal, sacramental, and spiritual. Carnal according to history; sacramental according to allegory; spiritual according to tropology. Or: carnal according to nature, sacramental according to figure, and spiritual according to grace. To the carnal birth according to nature belongs what you heard in the Gospel: “Elizabeth’s time to give birth was fulfilled, [Col. 0541B] and she bore a son.” To the sacramental birth according to figure pertains what is said through the prophet: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. I). To the spiritual birth according to grace pertains what the angel says: “He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.”

According to history, many rejoice at John’s birth: not only Christians but also Agarenians [Muslims], who, believing that he was a prophet, celebrate his birth and exult. Heretics and Jews alone are excluded from this joy because they lack this faith. In some regions, girls today represent that joy by singing psalms with cymbals and wearing little crowns. [Col. 0541C] In other regions, boys collect bones, burn them, and play by the fire. Although the custom is vain, its intention is sound.

According to allegory, moreover, Isaac’s birth prefigured John’s birth. For each was born of an old man, each of a barren woman, and each was both announced and named beforehand by an angel: Isaac in the one case, John in the other. At Isaac’s birth Sarah said: “God has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me” (Gen. XXI). At John’s birth, the neighbours and relatives, hearing that God had magnified his mercy with Elizabeth, rejoiced with her. But Zechariah, because he did not believe the angel, was made mute; Abraham, because he believed God, had it reckoned to him as righteousness. Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, [Col. 0541D] and Jacob begot the twelve patriarchs (Gen. XVII); likewise Zechariah begot John, John begot Christ, and Christ begot the twelve apostles. But between Christ and John the order of generation was altered: Zechariah begot John according to the flesh, whereas John begot Christ from water according to the Spirit.

[Col. 0542A] Hear the mystery and understand the sacrament: “The Law and the Prophets were until John, and from him the kingdom of heaven has been proclaimed” (Luke XVI). Until John, human beings were born according to nature from flesh; but from John onward human beings are reborn from water through the Spirit, because unless one is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. “What is born from flesh is flesh; and what is born from Spirit is spirit” (John III). For the moment, it is enough to have tasted a little of so great a mystery, because not everything ought to be explained to everyone. As Truth says: “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Matt. XIII; Luke VIII).

Many also rejoice at John’s birth according to tropology: namely, all who receive and preserve with cheerfulness of mind the grace of God being born within them. Of this the Psalmist spoke and prayed: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a ruling spirit” (Ps. L). For John is interpreted “the grace of God,” which is conceived through affection, born through effect, and nourished through progress. For concerning John himself his mother said: “As soon as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the child leaped for joy in my womb, because he was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb” (Luke I).

The same angel—Gabriel—who announced John’s birth to his father announced Jesus’ birth to his mother, announcing in both cases a miracle, the birth of a virgin and of a barren woman. But he foretold not John’s [Col. 0542C] conception, but his birth; whereas of Jesus he foretold his birth and, together with it, his conception.
