For to Zechariah the father it is foretold: “Elizabeth your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John” (ibid.); but to Mary the mother it is foretold: “You shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (ibid.). Why is this, except because John was conceived in sin, while Christ alone was conceived without sin? Yet both were born in grace; therefore both their births are observed, but Christ’s conception alone is celebrated.

But let us not seek examples far away, since morally we can find Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth in each of us. She bears him a son, and his name ought to be called John: “And he shall have [Col. 0542D] joy and gladness, and many shall rejoice at his birth” (ibid.). Elizabeth, Zechariah’s wife, may be understood as the flesh joined to the spirit. For as a husband corrects and governs his wife, so the spirit ought to correct and govern the flesh, lest it grow wanton and incur the guilt of fornication. She shall bear him a son [Col. 0543A] when the spirit performs a good work through the service of the flesh: if, for example, it gives alms, clothes the naked, feeds the hungry, visits the sick, or buries the dead. Then his wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of his house; his children, like young olive shoots around his table (Ps. XII). His name ought to be called John, that is, God’s grace, because no one ought to ascribe a good work to himself, but to the grace of our God. As the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty, but his grace always remains in me” (1 Cor. XV). And he shall have joy and gladness, because he shall rejoice and exult in the good work that gladdens and brightens the mind. For “a woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow; but when she has borne a male child, she no longer remembers [Col. 0543B] the anguish because of joy, because a human being has been born into the world” (John XVI).

And many rejoice at his birth: namely, all good people, who will rejoice with their neighbour in his good. Therefore Truth says: “Let your light shine before men, so that, seeing your [Col. 0544A] good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Therefore it must be most carefully provided that we who rejoice outwardly, dancing in body, may rejoice inwardly, exulting in mind; for “the remnant of thought shall keep a feast to the Lord” (Ps. LXXV).—“But the wicked shall not rejoice, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII).—“Nor is there peace in my bones because of sins” (Ps. LXXV). Therefore let us cleanse our souls from the stains of sins and vices, so that we may worthily celebrate the joy of so great a solemnity; lest perhaps we be among those “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II), “who hold the tambourine and harp and rejoice at the sound of the instrument, but in a moment descend to hell” (Job [Col. 0544B] XXI). Rather, let us be among those who enter “into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. XL). Through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED PETER

[Note: [Col. 0543D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[Col. 0543]

[Col. 0543C] Jesus said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He says to him: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI).

Although all the apostles deserved to be greatly honoured by God, because it is said of all the apostles, “Your friends have been exceedingly honoured, O God; their authority has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII), blessed Peter the apostle especially deserved honour because faith and charity shone pre-eminently in him. For the merit of his most steadfast faith won for him the keys from the Lord; and the merit of his most fervent charity won for him the Lord’s sheep in trust. Before granting the keys, the Lord questioned him about faith: “Who do you say that I am? Simon Peter answered and said: ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God.’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,’” and so forth: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI). Before entrusting the sheep, he questioned him about charity: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He says to him: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you,” and so forth, up to: “Feed my sheep.” He inquired especially concerning these virtues because among the virtues faith is first and charity is chief: faith is the foundation and charity the roof; faith begins, and charity brings to completion. Therefore it is written: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI). Of charity it is written: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV). Of faith it is written: [Col. 0544C] “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI). Of charity it is said: “If I distribute all my substance as food for the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII). Faith is great, but charity is greater, because, according to the Apostle, “Now remain faith, hope, charity—these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (ibid.).

In granting the keys he questioned him about faith, because the keys are entrusted only to believers. Those who think wrongly concerning them in the present will assuredly suffer evil in the future, because “he who does not believe is already judged” (John III). In entrusting the sheep he questioned him about charity, because he is a hireling and not a shepherd who feeds the sheep from desire of gain rather than [Col. 0544D] love of God. But in questioning about faith, he questioned once, because there is one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. IV). In questioning about charity, he questioned three times, because out of charity a person ought to love three things: God, himself, and his neighbour. “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God” (Matt. XXII): this is the first; “as yourself” (ibid.): this is the second; “you shall love your neighbour” (ibid.): this is the third.

But perhaps you will say: although Peter is questioned three times about charity, he is questioned not about his charity toward himself or his neighbour, but only toward Christ. Let us inquire, then, more closely why the Lord asked Peter three times: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” When he answered the third time, “Lord, you know that I love you,” the Lord for the third time commanded [Col. 0545A] him: “Feed my sheep.” Why, too, did he say only the first time, “Do you love me more than these?” And why was Peter grieved only at the third question? Why, moreover, did he say twice, “Feed my lambs”?

Since Peter had denied the Lord three times out of fear, it was fitting that he should likewise confess the Lord three times out of love, so that a threefold confession might answer for the threefold denial, lest his tongue serve love less than it had served fear; and so feeding the Lord’s flock might become an office of love, as denying the Lord of the flock had been a sign of fear. By saying, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?”, however, the Lord seems to have asked two things at once: whether Peter loved him and whether he loved him more than the others. Peter, remembering the common proverb, “Whom a snake has bitten often fears a lizard,” because he had once, without measuring his own strength, answered too boldly and presumptuously: “Even if all are scandalized, I will not be scandalized” (Mark XIV); “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI)—and afterwards, being scandalized, had denied him at the voice of a single maidservant—now answers prudently and cautiously, leaving aside what is doubtful and holding to what is certain. Therefore he does not answer the doubtful question, namely whether he loved him more than the others, but the certain one, namely that he loved him, saying: “Lord, you know that I love you.” Since in the first instance Peter answered this prudently and cautiously, the Lord did not question him further on that point.

He asks three times whether Peter loves him, and commands him three times to feed, because of the three reasons for loving and the three modes [Col. 0545C] of feeding. For it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your soul” (Deut. VI): God, namely the Creator, who by creating gave nature; Lord, namely the Redeemer, who by redeeming bestowed grace; Lord, namely the Saviour, who by saving confers glory. Then he shall be most truly yours, when he is all in all (1 Cor. XV), the fruit, reward, and prize of each person.

Thus he says: “Simon, son of John, do you love me as Creator, Redeemer, and Saviour?” And Peter says: “I love you with all my heart and with all my soul” (Deut. VI). With the heart, that is, the understanding; wholly, that is, without error. With the mind, that is, the memory; wholly, that is, without impiety. For whoever confesses the divine nature and denies the human, like Manichaeus; or confesses the human but denies the divine, like Arius, certainly does not love him with his whole heart as Peter loves him, who confesses both divine and human natures, as is said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). Christ means “anointed” according to his humanity. Hence the Psalm: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). He is the Son of God, anointed according to his divinity; hence: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II).

But those who glorify God in prosperity and blaspheme in adversity certainly do not love him with all their mind, because they are readily forgetful and ungrateful for his benefits; like those of whom it is written: [Col. 0546A] “They will praise you when you do them good; but if they are not filled,” and so forth (Ps. LVIII). Those, however, who wish “to serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI) certainly do not love God with all their soul, because there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor agreement of Christ with Belial (2 Cor. VI).

Or because the Lord said of himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), he asks Peter for the third time: “Simon, do you love me more than these?”—as though he said: “Do you love me as the way, the truth, and the life? For I am the way, as an example to those who act rightly; I am truth, as instruction to those who preach soundly; and I am life, as the sacrament of divine communion to those who receive worthily. If you love me as truth, feed them by the grace and example of right action; for this is what Wisdom said: [Col. 0546B] ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me’” (John IV). “Feed them by the teaching of holy preaching, for this is the food of which I said: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God’” (Matt. IV). “Feed them by the sacrament of divine communion, for this is the food of which I said: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’” (John VI). Feed my sheep, therefore, so that love of God may be proved through love of one’s neighbour. “For he who does not love the neighbour whom he sees—how can he love God, whom he does not see?” (1 John IV).

There are three orders of sheep whom you must feed from charity: virgins, continent persons, and [Col. 0546C] married persons. Therefore he commands: “Feed my lambs”—as though to say, feed virgins and continent persons, who are signified by lambs. By sheep, however, which bear offspring, are signified those who serve carnal generation. Such is one order of believers in the Church, namely married persons. Therefore he commands once, “Feed my sheep”—as though to say, feed married persons, who are signified by sheep. Peter was grieved, then, because for the third time he said to him, “Do you love me?”, as though he doubted this; and therefore Peter answers him: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you”—as though to say: You cannot doubt, since you know all things.

But because in Christ’s sacrament remembrance of his death is made, as the Apostle says: “Whenever [Col. 0546D] you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. XI); and death brings sadness, as the Lord says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Phil. II), therefore Peter is said to have been grieved on the third occasion, when the sacrament of that death is commemorated which became a cause of life for believers. For married persons are signified on the third occasion by the sheep, and their sorrow is no small matter because of the tribulation of the flesh which, according to the Apostle, they suffer (1 Cor. VI). Thus Job, who signifies married persons, is appropriately interpreted as “sorrowing.”

If you love me, then do not feed yourself: feed my sheep, not yours, so that you seek my glory in them, not your own; my gains, not yours. Therefore, in order to carry out the office of shepherd beneficially, be Simon, son of John [Col. 0547A]: ascribe the virtue of obedience not to your own merits but solely to divine grace. For Simon is interpreted “obedient,” and John is explained as “God’s grace.” Feed them, moreover, not idly, not perfunctorily, not carelessly, because they are mine—that is, purchased at the price of my blood. For “the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X). Therefore they were bought at a great price, not with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb. And therefore you must feed them attentively and diligently.

Consider carefully what is said through the prophet concerning wicked shepherds: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel,” he says, “who fed themselves and did not feed my flock; they ate the milk, but did not feed my flock. What was weak you did not strengthen; what was sick you did not heal; what was broken you did not bind up; what was cast away you did not bring back; what was lost you did not seek. Therefore my sheep were scattered and became food for every beast: ‘but I will require their blood from your hand’” (Ezek. XXXIV).

When you feed by example, take prudent care not to perform your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them; “otherwise you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VI). Rather, let “your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V), so that curtain may draw curtain, and “let him who hears say, ‘Come.’” Surely, pastors deserve as many deaths as the examples of perdition which they pass on to the sheep. For when a subject sees his prelate sin, he is easily corrupted by the example and puts it forward as an excuse for his own fault: it is enough for the disciple to be like his master; for the son cannot do anything except what he has seen his father doing. Thus, by one and the same sin the prelate both condemns himself and destroys the people. For if the anointed priest sins, he causes the people to sin (Lev. IV).

When you feed by instruction, prudently beware of heretical perversity, lest perhaps you mix water with wine, lest you offer the dragon’s gall in Babylon’s golden cup. “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search out things stronger than yourself” (Ecclus. III), because “those searching by scrutiny have failed” (Ps. LXIII). And the investigator of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. Beware also lest you give what is holy to dogs, or cast pearls before swine (Matt. VII). Yet neither should you give solid food to little ones, following the example of him who says: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons; as little children in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). “For we speak wisdom among the perfect”; but “among you I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

But when you feed with the sacrament of the Eucharist, admonish the people, saying: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (I Cor. XI). For just as one who endures death well acquires life, so one who receives life badly incurs death. Remember him who entered the wedding feast without a wedding garment: by the Lord’s command, with hands and feet bound, he was cast into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched (Matt. XXII).

Such ought you to be, brothers, who are pastors. But you also, children, strive diligently to be truly gentle and innocent sheep, so that you do not return evil for good, nor curse for curse [Col. 0548C] (I Pet. III), after the example of him “who, when he was cursed, did not curse; when he suffered, did not threaten” (I Pet. II). Be useful and fruitful, rendering milk and wool to your pastors—that is, firstfruits and offerings—which, behold—*Dominus nobis* [thus the codex; uncertain]—you cannot retain without danger to yourselves. “For the laborer is worthy of his wages” (I Tim. V). Therefore the Apostle said: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX). Therefore, while you have time, sow in blessings, that you may reap eternal life. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

It teaches that one’s own reputation ought not to be neglected, and discusses at length Peter’s blessedness, dignity, and power.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547D] Jesus was questioning his disciples, saying: “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” etc. (Matt. XVI).

Because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X), the Lord questioned his disciples—not because he who knows all things was ignorant of anything, but so that from their very answer he might take occasion both to confirm faith and to reward confession. Thus, when Peter said, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God,” the Lord at once confirmed his faith, replying: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Then, rewarding his confession, he added: “And I say to you”—whose saying is doing—“that you are Peter, and upon this rock [Col. 0549A] I will build my Church; and to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

Yet he first asked about the opinion of others so that he might reject their error. For “there is no fellowship of light with darkness” (II Cor. VI), and truth cannot be planted unless falsehood is uprooted. He therefore says: “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” He has given us a clear example that we should not be content with conscience alone, but should also be concerned for reputation: that we may strive to possess and preserve a clear conscience toward God and an unclouded reputation toward our neighbor. For “a good name is better than great riches” (Prov. XXII).

To him who asked about the opinion of others, they replied: “Some say John the Baptist; others Elijah; others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” Because Christ was baptizing [Col. 0549B], people thought—but were mistaken—that John the Baptist had been raised. Or they thought him one of the two prophets who, in crossing the Jordan, prefigured baptism: Elijah (III Kings XVII) or Elisha (IV Kings II). They thought him Jeremiah (ch. I), because he is read to have been sanctified in the womb. And they could similarly be mistaken about the others, just as Herod had been mistaken about John: “This,” he said, “is John the Baptist; he himself has risen from the dead, and therefore powers work in him” (Matt. XIV).

“But you, who do you say that I am?” As if he said: You, who are not carnal but spiritual, and who therefore ought deservedly to be called not men but rather gods, as it is written in the Psalm: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” [Col. 0549C] (Ps. LXXI). “Who do you say that I am?” He asks prudently and distinctly. As though saying more plainly: Men think this of the Son of Man; but what do you think of me? Yet what could men made gods think of God made man, except what Peter, first and chief among all, answered for all, saying: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.”

As if to say: You are not John the Baptist, beheaded in prison; you are Christ. You are not Elijah, taken up into paradise (IV Kings II); you are the Son of God. You are not Jeremiah, though sanctified from the womb; you are the Son of the living God. You are not one of the prophets, buried in a cemetery. Jesus replied to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Bar-Jonah is a Hebrew name, composed of the complete word *Bar*, meaning “son,” and the corrupted form *Joanna*, meaning “son of John.”

Indeed, the Gospel reading commends to us, in blessed Peter, with a certain singular prerogative, three things: blessedness, dignity, and power. Of blessedness it says: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Of dignity it adds: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” Of power it continues: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

You are blessed, therefore: now by merit, at last by reward; now in hope, at last in possession; now with the blessedness [Col. 0550A] of the journey, at last with the blessedness of the homeland; now with the blessedness of faith [variant: hope], at last with the blessedness of hope [variant: rest]. For flesh and blood—that is, any carnal person, puffed up by the wisdom of the flesh—has not revealed this to you; “but my Father who is in heaven,” who inhabits heavenly minds and illuminates them with the light of truth. For “he has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI), such as Peter was: not proud but humble. Hence Simon is blessed; it means “obedient”; Bar-Jonah means “son of John,” and John means “God’s grace,” because the virtue of obedience proceeds from divine grace.

This blessedness consists especially in knowledge and love, that is, in faith and charity. Of these, one is first among the virtues and the other chief. For the Apostle says of faith: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI). Behold, faith is first. But of charity the same Apostle says: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII). Behold, charity is chief.

Of faith it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God, because the just person lives by faith” (Heb. XI; Hab. II). Of charity it is said: “If I distribute all my possessions as food to the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” [Col. 0550B] (I Cor. XIII). Behold, both are necessary. For the Lord says of faith: “Your faith has made you whole; go, and sin no more” (Matt. IX). He says likewise of charity: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII).

The Lord required both from Peter: faith, when he granted him the keys; charity, when he entrusted the sheep to him (John XXI). In granting the keys, he asked concerning faith: “But you, who do you say that I am?” Peter replied: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” In entrusting the sheep, he asked concerning charity: “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” And he answered: “Lord, you know that I love you” (ibid.).

But he required faith by asking only once, because “there is one God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV). In requiring charity, however, he asked three times at once, because in charity we ought to love three: God, ourselves, and our neighbor. “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord [Col. 0550D] your God”—behold the first—“and as yourself”—behold the second—“you shall love your neighbor” (Deut. XI; Matt. XXII)—behold the third. Therefore, when the Lord had asked Peter for the third time, “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” and he had answered for the third time, “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI), he also for the third time commanded him to feed the sheep. As though saying: Feed them by word, feed them by example, feed them by protection. Feed them by the word of preaching, by the example of conduct, and by the protection of defense.

O good shepherd, holy shepherd, outstanding shepherd: because you laid down your life for your sheep, as the Lord himself foretold, “When you were younger, you girded yourself and went where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish. This he said, signifying [Col. 0551A] by what death he would glorify God” (ibid.). Hence elsewhere he said to him: “Follow me” (Matt. IX). As if saying: Follow me in the manner of death, namely, on the gibbet of the cross.

In granting the keys he asked concerning faith, because keys are granted only to the faithful. Of such persons it is said: “Those who think [variant: serve] wickedly in the present will surely think wickedly in the future; for whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III). But in entrusting the sheep he asked concerning charity, because he is not a shepherd but a hireling who feeds the sheep from greed for gain rather than from love of God (John X).

What Peter’s faith was, and how great it was, is surely shown by his own answer: “You are,” he said, “Christ [Col. 0551B], the Son of the living God.” For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). He confesses in Christ two natures and one person. He confesses the human nature when he says, “You are Christ,” which means “anointed,” according to his humanity, as the Prophet says to him: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). He confesses the divine nature when he says, “the Son of the living God.” For no one can naturally be someone’s son without possessing that person’s nature: just as one cannot be the Son of Man unless one is human, so one cannot be the Son of the living God unless one is God. Hence the Father says to the Son: “You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Ps. II). Speaking of his unity with the Father according to his divine nature, he said: “I and the Father [Col. 0551C] are one” (John XVIII).

But just as between Father and Son there is diversity of persons but unity of nature, so between divinity and humanity there is diversity of nature but unity of person. For as rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ. Therefore Peter answered: “You are Christ,” not “Christs”; “you are the Son,” not “sons.” For he who in divinity was the Son of God is the same one who in humanity became the Son of Man. For “nature” is the name of a kind, while “person” is the name of a legal status.

“You,” therefore, in distinction from another; because “many false prophets will come in your name, saying, ‘I am Christ’” (Mark XIII). But you alone are so, not merely supposedly but substantially. John too was regarded as Christ, which he himself denied: “I am not Christ,” he said; “but he who comes from above is above all” (John I). You are Christ—that is, the Anointed One—not by a human anointing, according to which there are many christs, as it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Ps. LXXXVIII), but by a divine anointing, according to which there is only one Christ. For “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” [Col. 0551D] (Ps. LXIV). Therefore he himself said through the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Isa. LXI).

You are the Son, not adopted but true, because he said to you: “You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Ps. II). Hence you are not only the Son of Man but also the Son [Col. 0552A] of God—not of a dead god, like the gods of the Gentiles, who “have mouths and do not speak; eyes and do not see; ears and do not hear; hands and do not touch; feet and do not walk” (Ps. CXIII). Rather, you are Christ, Son of the living God, who, living in himself, gives life to all things: “in him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII).

The Lord did not permit this great faith to fail under any temptation. Thus, when at the time of his passion he said to blessed Peter, “Simon, behold, Satan has asked for them, that he might sift them like wheat,” he immediately added: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have at some time turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII). For although he once doubted, and therefore the Lord rebuked him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” [Col. 0552B] (Matt. XIV), yet, because his faith grew strong in its firmness, the Lord immediately delivered him from the danger of the sea.

This true and holy faith did not proceed from a human invention but from divine revelation. Therefore Christ added: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Upon this faith the Church is founded on the rock; therefore the Lord added: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

This dignity is seen in two respects: blessed Peter is both foundation and head of the Church. Although Christ is the first and chief foundation, as the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid, besides which no other can be laid, and that is Christ” [Col. 0552C] (I Cor. III), nevertheless there are secondary and subordinate foundations, namely the apostles and prophets, as the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II), of whom it is elsewhere said through the Prophet: “Its foundation is in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). Among them blessed Peter is first and chief; and to him alone the Lord says: “You shall be called Cephas” (John I). For *Cephas*, though in one language it means “Peter,” in another is said to mean “head.” For just as the fullness of the senses resides in the head, while in the other members there is some part of that fullness, so the others were called to share in the burden of care, but Peter alone was taken into the fullness of power.

Thus, when the Lord spoke simultaneously to all the apostles, he said universally: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John XX). But when he spoke to Peter alone, he said particularly: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven,” because Peter can bind the others, but cannot be bound by the others, being the first and highest teacher and prince of the Church. Even if this is read as having been said to all the apostles together, it is nevertheless not read as said to the others without him, but as said to him without the others, so that he, unlike the others without him, is understood to be able to do this by the fullness of power.

This is also why, when it was said generally to the others, “Cast out the nets for a catch,” it was said particularly to Peter, “Put out into the deep” [Col. 0553A] (Luke IV). And when after the resurrection the others came to the Lord by boat, Peter alone girded himself with his tunic and cast himself into the sea (John XXI). From this new bestowal of a name the Church has derived the practice that, when Peter’s successor is elected, a new name is given to him.

But it is commonly asked when this name was bestowed on him: whether when, according to John, Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon, son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which means Peter; or when, according to Matthew, Jesus said to him, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Yet there he seems more to have foretold it, while here more to have confirmed it. For there it says, “You shall be called”; but here, “You are.” Still, it must be maintained without doubt that the name Peter was bestowed on him at the choosing of the Twelve. Mark testifies accordingly (ch. III): “And he gave Simon the name Peter, and gave John and James the names Boanerges.”

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it”: that is, the vices and sins which lead into hell. For neither perversity nor adversity can in any way overthrow the Church. As Truth says: “The winds blew, the floods came, and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon a rock” [Col. 0553B] (Matt. VII). Therefore the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0553C] Power is especially displayed in two things: the absolution of sinners and the working of miracles. Although Peter received, together with the others, the common power to forgive sins, nevertheless not without rational cause is he alone read to have asked Jesus: “If my brother sins against me, shall I forgive him up to seven times?” (Matt. XVIII). And to him alone Jesus is read to have replied: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (ibid.). For the number seven signifies universality, since all time is comprehended in the seven-day number. What, then, does this number seven multiplied by itself signify here, if not every sin of all persons? Thus Peter alone is commanded that, if his brother sins against him, he should forgive him not merely seven times but up to seventy times seven, because Peter alone can forgive on earth every sin of all persons. Indeed, there are certain sins whose absolution is reserved to Peter alone.

This is he who possessed such power for working miracles (Acts III, IV) that it is written of him: “The multitude of men and women believing in Christ increased, so that they brought the sick into the streets and laid them on beds and pallets, that, as Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some one of them and they might be delivered from their infirmities. A multitude also came together from the towns near Jerusalem, bringing sick persons and those troubled by unclean spirits; and all were healed” [Col. 0553D] (Acts V). In him was truly fulfilled what Truth says: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV).

There is indeed one key of David, “which shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts” [Col. 0554A] (Apoc. III), which entrusted two keys to Peter alone because of that most excellent faith which truly recognized two natures in the one Christ. Therefore, through the keys he received, Peter both shuts and opens: he shuts when he binds; he opens when he absolves. “And whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

“A key discerns and judges; it shuts and opens for those entering and leaving. The first key is understood as the knowledge of discerning and judging; the second key is understood as the power of binding and absolving. The key of knowledge is necessary for discerning between [Col. 0554B] leprosy and leprosy, good and evil, light and darkness, holy and profane” (Deut. XVII). For “woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. V), “making alive souls that do not live and putting to death souls that do not die.”

Yet knowledge of discernment is not always a key. For although some know how to discern, they nevertheless cannot exercise discernment, because they do not possess the key of power; without it, knowledge is not a key. Let the shepherd of the Church therefore see to it that he does not receive the key of power without the key of knowledge, because it is written in the Prophet: “You have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, that you may not exercise priesthood for me” [Col. 0554C] (Hos. IV). For “the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. II). He who refused to understand so as to act rightly “devised iniquity on his bed” (Ps. XXXV). Against such persons the Lord says: “They have not known my ways; therefore I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter into my rest’” (Ps. XCIV).

Thus the key of knowledge was necessary to Peter along with the key of power, so that whatever you bind on earth may be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth may be loosed in heaven. What then? Does not a priest sometimes, through a just error, bind someone on earth who, because innocent, is not bound by God in heaven? Certainly, even if the key of knowledge is brought to bear in such a bond, it is not knowledge [Col. 0554D] unmixed [variant: mixed] with falsehood, but a certain opinion which, though just, is nevertheless false. Yet when a sentence of binding is passed justly in intention and in due order, the person thus bound on earth is nonetheless bound also in heaven, because the heavenly court approves and confirms that binding. Such a person is therefore both loosed and bound in heaven, just as he is both bound and loosed on earth: bound by the sentence, loosed from fault.

There is therefore a twofold binding: binding of fault and binding of sentence. Hence it often happens that these acts of loosing do not always accompany one another equally. The Lord himself symbolically indicated this in the loosing of Lazarus: he first raised the dead man, and then commanded the apostles to loose the man whom he had raised. The priest looses not merely by declaring one loosed, and binds not merely by declaring one bound; rather, he binds and looses by withdrawing or restoring the Church’s suffrages and the divine sacraments.

Perhaps now, as he promised, he entrusted the keys of the Church to Peter alone, in a special and principal sense; but after the resurrection he entrusted them generally and commonly with the others, when he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” [Col. 0555A] (John XX).

Let him therefore who receives the keys have faith; let him who receives the sheep have charity. The sheep must indeed be fed in three ways, because he is commanded a third time to feed them. For there are three orders of the faithful in the Church: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, prelates, the continent, and married persons [Col. 0555B]—whom Ezekiel saw saved in a vision. The prelate must feed them by word, example, and sacrament: by the word of doctrine, the example of life, and the sacrament of the Eucharist.

Thus blessed Peter fed the sheep entrusted to him, [Col. 0556A] whom the world rejoices to have as its father in general, but whom the city glories to have as its patron in particular. Through him it became the teacher of truth, though it had been the head of error; and it is now far more eminent in apostolic teaching than it formerly was in imperial rulership. Even the Roman ruler himself is known to be subject to its teaching. In it heavenly authority now flourishes, where earthly power once flourished; it has advanced to that height of dignity that its judgment pronounced on earth is observed also in heaven. It likewise possesses judicial power over souls, so as to be able both to loose and to bind them.

Let us therefore, brothers and children, pray to him as our Father and patron, that, through his merits, he may loose us from the bonds of sins and bring us into the heavenly kingdoms: through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE SAME FEAST

How the sea should be understood as the world, the ship as the Church, the deep of the sea as Rome, and the net as preaching.

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555C] When Jesus had entered one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and, sitting in the boat, taught the crowds, when he ceased speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and cast out the nets for a catch.” Simon replied: “Master, though we have labored all night, we have caught nothing; yet at your word I will cast the net.” When they had done this, they enclosed an abundant multitude of fish (Luke V).

If many waters are many peoples (Apoc. XIX), then the great sea is certainly the whole world. Of it we read: “This sea, great and broad in expanse: there are creeping things without number, little living things with the great; there ships pass through” (Ps. CIII). For just as the sea is always turbulent and bitter, so the world abides always in bitterness and disturbance. Nowhere are there peace and security; nowhere rest and tranquility; everywhere are fear and trembling, everywhere labor and sorrow. “For the world lies in evil” (I John V). “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” [Col. 0555D] (Prov. XIV). Deservedly, then, the Apostle cried: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). And the Psalmist said: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. CXLI). “For the bird is born to flight, and man is born to labor” (Job V). “All his days are full of labors and miseries; even by night his mind does not rest” (Eccles. II). “Great travail has been created for all human beings, and a heavy yoke upon all children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. XL).

In this sea the greater fish devour the smaller; and in the world the greater people oppress the lesser. “Those who devour my people like food for bread have not called upon God; there they trembled with fear,” etc. “The wild ass is the lion’s prey in the wilderness; so the poor are the pasture of the rich” [Col. 0556C] (Ecclus. XIII).

> Whatever mad kings do, the Achaeans suffer the penalty.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14)

The depth of this sea, of which Christ says to Peter, “Put out into the deep,” is Rome, which held and holds primacy and dominion over the whole world. Divine condescension chose to exalt it so greatly that, just as in the time of paganism it alone held lordship over all Gentiles, so in the time of Christianity it alone might hold teaching authority over all the faithful. Therefore God wisely provided what was fitting and worthy—indeed, fittingly provided what was worthy—that he who was prince of the Church should establish his see in the city which held the world’s sovereignty. Therefore the Lord says to Peter: “Put out into the deep.” As though saying: Go to Rome; transfer yourself and yours to that city, and there cast out the nets for a catch.

Behold clearly how greatly God loved this city: it should be both priestly and royal, imperial and apostolic, possessing and exercising not only dominion [Col. 0557A] over bodies but also teaching authority over souls. It is now far greater and worthier by divine authority than it formerly was by earthly power: through the former it holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven; through the latter it governed the reins of the world. And lest the honor of so great a dignity—or rather, the dignity of so great an honor—should for any reason pass to another city, but should remain in this city under an everlasting law according to the divine disposition: when Peter, fleeing the persecution of unbelievers, had left the city, the Lord appeared to him near the city. Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” He replied, “I am going to Rome to be crucified again.” Peter understood this as said of himself—that the head might be crucified in the member—and returned to the city, which at last he consecrated with his blood on the gibbet of the cross.

He had as companion the most blessed Paul. Thus, although it is said to Peter alone, “Put out into the deep,” it is added in the plural, “Cast out the nets for a catch,” because Peter alone, as universal prince of the Church, ascended to the height of supreme prelacy, but he, together with Paul, cast out in the city the nets of preaching to catch human beings. It is also believed not to have been without divine providence that where two brothers according to the flesh, Remus and Romulus, who bodily founded this city, lie buried in honored tombs, there two brothers according to faith, Peter and Paul, who spiritually founded this city, rest buried in glorious basilicas: Peter on the side where Romulus is buried, and Paul on that where Remus is buried, so that, stationed at either end, they may protect this city by their patronage [Col. 0557C]. Therefore one went out into the deep, but both cast out the nets for a catch.

Moreover, as the ship is the Church, the sea the world, and the deep Rome, so the net signifies preaching. A net is joined together from varied threads and cords, and preaching is confirmed by varied authorities and arguments. The prudent preacher should shape his discourse according to the diversity of matters and persons: now speaking of virtues, now of vices; sometimes of rewards, sometimes of punishments; at times of mercy, at times of justice; sometimes simply, sometimes subtly; according to history and according to allegory; according to anagogy and according to tropology; through authorities and arguments; through comparisons and examples, so that:

> Let every particular thing fittingly occupy the place allotted to it.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry* 92)

These are the threads, these the cords from which the net is joined together—that is, by which preaching is confirmed. The outstanding preacher teaches this when he says of himself: “We speak wisdom among the perfect; but among you I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II). And again: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons; as little children in Christ [Col. 0558B] I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III).

Fish, birds, and beasts are caught in nets. Fish are caught in water, birds in air, and beasts on land. Fish signify the lustful, birds the proud, beasts the violent. Therefore, when a preacher forms a discourse against lust, pride, and violence, introducing authorities, arguments, comparisons, and examples in order to recall the lustful to continence, the proud to humility, and the violent to gentleness, then he casts out the nets of preaching to catch fish in the water, birds in the air, and beasts on land. Those caught he does not kill but gives life to; he does not slay but feeds; he does not abandon but guards.

These nets the most blessed Peter and Paul cast out together for a catch. Through their preaching Rome was converted from error to truth, from vices to virtues. Rome, therefore, ought to venerate all the blessed apostles together, but should honor these two especially and chiefly as its first and principal ones, as its own fathers and patrons, so that, helped by their merits and prayers, it may now be preserved safely on earth and at last happily crowned in heaven [Col. 0558C]. Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE MOST BLESSED MARY MAGDALENE

How human mortality committed offense in seven ways, how the devil afflicts a human being in three ways; likewise, how Mary Magdalene was beset by seven demons, and concerning her sin, penitence, and satisfaction.

[Col. 0557]

[Col. 0557D] “Where offense abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V).

The apostolic saying proposed to you is certainly fulfilled in Mary Magdalene, in whom offense abounded and grace abounded still more.

Human mortality committed offense in seven ways: in three kinds and four forms—in the heart [Col. 0558D], in speech, and in deed; through ignorance and inability, through negligence and envy. Perhaps these are the seven demons which, according to Gospel testimony, Christ cast out from Mary Magdalene: namely, the sin of thought in the heart; the sin of utterance in speech; the sin of execution in deed; the offense of simplicity through ignorance; the offense of frailty through inability; the offense of complacency through negligence; and the offense of malice through envy. For one must not believe that she was afflicted bodily by seven demons, but spiritually by seven vices.

The devil harasses a human being in three ways. First, through guilt, by taking away gratuitous gifts; second, through punishment, by injuring natural endowments; third, through loss, by bringing dangers upon him. Of the first it is written: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, who stripped him and, after inflicting many wounds, went away, leaving him half dead” (Luke 10). Of the second it is written: “Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute” (Luke 11)—that is, judging from its effect, because it had made the man mute. Of the third it is written [Col. 0559B] that Satan struck Job (ch. 1), from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, with a grievous sore, after first taking everything away; so that, sitting on a dung-heap, he scraped away the discharge with a potsherd.

Thus the seven demons harassed Mary Magdalene through guilt, because they had led her astray in seven ways, not merely into wrongdoing but also into sin. A distinction is made between wrongdoing (*delictum*) and sin (*peccatum*): wrongdoing consists in omission, sin in commission. Wrongdoing is not doing what ought to be done; sin is doing what ought not to be done. Hence in Leviticus (chs. 1, 10) the Lord strictly commanded sacrifices to be offered both for sin and for wrongdoing.

Therefore she committed wrongdoing and sin in heart; wrongdoing and sin in speech; wrongdoing and sin in deed. She committed wrongdoing in [Col. 0559C] heart when she rejected the good thoughts descending upon her; she sinned in heart when she received evil thoughts rising within her. For good thoughts descend from God, as the apostle James says: “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1). Evil thoughts rise from the human being, as the Lord says to the apostles: “Why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” (Luke 24 [printed: 26]).

She committed wrongdoing in speech when she kept silent about the truth; she sinned in speech when she uttered falsehood. Of the first the prophet says: “Woe is me, because I kept silent!” (Isaiah 6). Of the second the Psalm says: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 7). She committed wrongdoing in deed when she omitted the good; she sinned in [Col. 0559D] deed when she committed evil. Conversely it is commanded: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalms 33, 36).

Her sin, moreover, was great, abundant, and notorious. It was great because Christ cast seven demons out of her. It was abundant because “many sins were forgiven her” (Luke 7). It was notorious because “the woman in the city was a sinner” (ibid.). Everyone had access to her, nor did anyone suffer rejection by her. But where wrongdoing abounded, grace abounded beyond measure. For because her sin was great, she made satisfaction with great sorrow; because it was abundant, she made satisfaction with much labor; because it was notorious, she made satisfaction with remarkable shame. These are the three things that accomplish worthy satisfaction: sorrow in the heart, shame in speech, and labor in deed. Thus, according to Solomon’s Wisdom [Col. 0560A], “By the things through which a person sinned, by those things let him be tormented” (Wisdom 2).

Coming therefore, as a sinner, to the fountain of mercy to be absolved [variant: “washed”], deeply troubled with sorrow, she watered his feet with tears. Confounded by conspicuous shame, “she stood behind, beside his feet, and kissed them” (Luke 7). Ashamed to appear before the Lord’s face, yet silent with her mouth, she cried with her heart: “Lord, you know my folly; my crimes and my wrongdoings are not hidden from you” (Psalm 68). See: she who is not ashamed before the dinner-guests is ashamed before the Lord, because they look outwardly, but the Lord looks inwardly. And indeed she was much more disgraceful within, in conscience, than outwardly, in reputation. With much devout labor, “she brought an alabaster vessel of ointment and anointed his feet” (Luke 8). [Col. 0560B]

Nor did she do this only once, but more often. First, when she anointed the Lord’s feet in the house of Simon the Pharisee (John 12); second, when she poured ointment over his head in the house of Simon the leper (Matthew 26); third, when she bought spices, so that she might come and anoint Jesus’ head (Mark 16). There is a profound mystery in these things, but it must be explained elsewhere. Thus she cleansed the wrongdoing of her heart with tears, the wrongdoing of her mouth with kisses, and the wrongdoing of her deeds with ointments. “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76). For just as she had presented her members to serve impurity unto iniquity, so, according to the Apostle’s exhortation (Romans 6), she presented them to serve righteousness unto sanctification.

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, [Col. 0560C] taste, smell, and touch. In these five senses wrongdoing abounded in Magdalene; in these five senses grace abounded beyond measure. She did wrong with her eyes, because the fornication of “a woman lies in the lifting up of her eyes” (Ecclesiasticus 26). But she made satisfaction with her eyes, according to what is written: “Mary stood weeping at the tomb” (John 20). While she therefore wept, she bent down and looked into the tomb.

She did wrong with her ears because she turned her hearing toward tales of vanity. But she also made satisfaction with her ears, as it is written: “Mary sat beside the Lord’s feet and heard his words” (Luke 10). She did wrong with her nostrils: “A gold ring in her nostrils: a beautiful and foolish woman” (Proverbs 11 [printed: 2]). But she also made satisfaction with her nostrils, as it is written: “Mary took a pound of precious pure nard ointment, [Col. 0560D] and anointed Jesus’ feet, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12).

She did wrong with her lips, because “the lips of a prostitute drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil” (Proverbs 5). But she also made satisfaction with her lips, as it is written: “Mary, standing behind beside the Lord’s feet, kissed them” (Luke 7). She did wrong with her hands, because “a foolish woman destroys with her hands the house that has been built” (Proverbs 14). But she also made satisfaction with her hands, as it is written: “Mary washed Jesus’ feet and wiped them with the hair of her head” (Luke 7).

But in these matters she did wrong and sinned through ignorance and frailty; she did wrong and sinned through negligence and malice. Yet where wrongdoing abounded, grace abounded beyond measure. For against the wrongdoing of ignorance [Col. 0561A] she received knowledge in the contemplation of God; and against the sin of frailty she acquired steadfastness in Christ’s Passion. Again, against the wrongdoing of negligence she exercised the devout service of action; and against the sin of malice she rendered the kindly office of love.

She is commended by the Lord for her knowledge of contemplation: “Mary,” he says, “has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10). For she sat beside the Lord’s feet and listened to his word. She is commended for firmness of mind by the fact that, when the disciples had fled after abandoning Christ, Mary followed Christ as far as the cross: “For there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene” (John 19).

She is commended [Col. 0561B] for the service of action by the Lord: “Why,” he says, “do you trouble this woman? She has done a good work for me. For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial” (Matthew 26). She is commended for the office of love by the fact that “many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7). “For charity covers a multitude of sins” (Proverbs 10). Mary loved the Lord because the Lord loved Mary, as Scripture says: “Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus” (John 11). Mary wept for the Lord because the Lord wept for Mary, as Scripture says: “When Jesus saw Mary weeping, he troubled himself and wept” (John 11 [printed: 20]). But she wept, [Col. 0561C] seeking the living among the dead; he wept, calling the dead man back to the living, as is written [Col. 0562A]: “Jesus therefore, again groaning within himself, cried with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lazarus, come forth.’ And immediately he who had been dead came out” (John 11).

Wrongdoing therefore abounded in Magdalene because she had been entangled in many vices. Grace also abounded beyond measure because she was adorned with every virtue. For certain vices oppose one another, so that some cannot coexist with others; but all virtues support one another, so that some cannot be possessed without the others.

Henceforth, brethren, because “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Romans 15), let us, following the example of blessed Mary Magdalene, turn to the Lord; for he is gracious and greatly merciful, and ready to relent from evil (Joel 2). “For he [Col. 0562B] does not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezekiel 18). Therefore, following her example, let there be in us sorrow of contrition in the heart, shame of confession in speech, and labor of satisfaction in deed: so that through the sorrow of contrition the sin of thought may be erased, and the girl be raised in the house (Matthew 9); through the shame of confession the crime of speech may be washed away, and the young man be raised at the gate (Luke 7); through the labor of satisfaction the offense of action may be cleansed, and Lazarus be raised from the tomb (John 11). May he mercifully grant this: he who first mercifully disclosed to his blessed Mary Magdalene the joy of his resurrection (John 20), our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. [Col. 0562C] Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE FEAST OF ST PETER IN CHAINS

An allegorical exposition of this day’s Epistle.

[Col. 0561]

[Col. 0561C] “King Herod laid hands upon certain persons of the Church, in order to afflict them. He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. And seeing that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also.”

[Col. 0561D] Since we plainly see the history, let us thoroughly investigate the allegory: seeking the spirit beneath the letter as the kernel beneath the bark, because “it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). For as in an image we attend not so much to the panel as to the painting, so in exposition we ought to attend not so much to the history as to the figure. For the history, like a panel, does not always correspond equally to the painting; the thing signified in allegory is sometimes evil and the signification good, and conversely.

Therefore King Herod laid hands upon certain persons of the Church in order to afflict them. Herod is the devil; the Jews are demons. The former is king of the Jews; the latter, king of demons, for “he is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41). Thus King Herod laid hands in order to afflict certain persons of the Church [Col. 0562C], because the devil exercises power in order to scourge some members of the congregation of the faithful.

He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword when he seduces a righteous person: the brother of John, as it were the kinsman [Col. 0562D] of grace, because no one is righteous except through grace. He kills him with the sword when he separates him from Christ the head, because “the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11).

“And seeing that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also.” “Demons rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2). Therefore, seeing that the killing of James pleased the Jews—that is, the devil perceiving that the seduction of a righteous person pleased the demons—he proceeded to seize Peter also: not any righteous person, not any sort of believer, but Peter himself, the prelate of the Church. “He swallows up a river and is not amazed, and he is confident that the Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job 40). For choice food is his nourishment; indeed, “if the priest who is anointed sins, he causes the people to offend” [Col. 0563A] (Leviticus 4).

Now it was the days of Unleavened Bread. As the eminence of a person aggravates sin, so the solemnity of a time increases wrongdoing; and therefore Herod did not proceed to seize Peter at just any time, but in the days of Unleavened Bread, when, because of the greater solemnity, a fault is a greater sin if it is committed. Did not Herod seize Peter when Peter, contrary to his promise, denied Christ three times? He did indeed seize him, but did not kill him, because “the Lord looked upon Peter” (Luke 22).

Therefore, brethren, let us consider both the manner of capture and the order of deliverance, so that we may take care not to be caught; and, if perhaps we have been caught, may provide for our own liberation. For when Herod had seized [Col. 0563B] Peter also, he put him in prison. Thus, when the devil seduces a prelate, he leads him into habitual practice, so that he stinks like one four days in the tomb. For evil habit is a grave prison, from which no one is easily brought out unless freed by God’s grace, because “when the wicked man comes into the depth of vices, he despises” (Proverbs 18).

He handed him over to be guarded by four squads of soldiers—that is, he entrusted him to be held by four chief demons. For just as there are four principal virtues, namely justice, courage, prudence, and temperance, so there are four principal ways of sinning, through which demons cause human beings to sin and seduce them: through frailty and simplicity; through malice and heedlessness; or through incapacity and ignorance; through craftiness and negligence. Through incapacity or frailty, against courage; through ignorance or simplicity, against prudence; through craftiness and malice, against justice; through negligence or heedlessness, [Col. 0563C] against temperance. There is no sin that is not committed in one of these ways.

These are the four farthings, of the last of which Truth said in the Gospel: “He shall not come out from there until he has paid the last farthing” (Matthew 5), that is, until he pays in punishment whatever he committed in guilt. He therefore handed him over to four squads of soldiers to be guarded, intending after Passover to bring him forth to the people. During the feast he did not wish to bring him [Col. 0563D] forth to the people—that is, to hand him over to demons for punishment, so that, because “sin when completed brings forth death” (James 1), they might thrust him into hell.

And Peter was indeed kept in prison. This happens mystically when a prelate is cherished in evil habit. But prayer was made to God without ceasing by the Church for him. From this it is evident how powerful “the prayer of a righteous person is, provided it is persistent” (James 5 [printed: 3]); for behold, through prayers a sinner is freed from evil habit. From this too it follows that the universal Church ought to pray without ceasing for the supreme pontiff.

Now when Herod was about to bring him forth, Peter in that very night was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. He who lies in guilt sleeps in night. [Col. 0564A] For “he who does evil hates the light” (John 3), and therefore Peter was sleeping in that very night between two soldiers, bound with two chains. The two chains are cupidity and concupiscence, one of the mind and the other of the flesh; the two soldiers are two demons who tempt through the desire for possessions and the desire for women. Thus Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and guards before the door were keeping the prison.

The door through which one enters the prison is the act through which one enters habit; therefore the prison door is guarded when habitual sin is frequently practiced. Those who guard the prison before the door are freedom to sin and pleasure in sin. For nothing nourishes evil habit more than the delight of guilt and [Col. 0564B] the impunity of punishment.

“And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by, and a light shone in the dwelling.” Thus far you have heard the manner of capture; henceforth hear the order of deliverance. Herod seized Peter and put him in prison. But the angel of the Lord—not an instigator or enemy, but a visitor and guardian—stood by to protect and liberate him. Therefore the light of grace shone in the dwelling, which had been darkened by the shadows of sins. And, striking Peter’s side with the lance of charity, of which the Bride says in the Song of Songs (ch. 2), “I am wounded by love,” he roused him from the sleep of sin, saying, “Rise quickly,” as the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Ephesians 5).

“And the chains fell [Col. 0564C] from his hands.” Then chains fall from our hands when cupidity and concupiscence fall away from our acts, so that neither cupidity may still desire nor concupiscence still lust. And the angel said to him: “Gird yourself and put on your sandals.” It is not enough for us to abandon evil unless we also do good; hence it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33). Therefore, after the chains have fallen from his hands, he is told: “Gird yourself and put on your sandals,” as if it were said: Bind yourself with the girdle of continence against concupiscence, and take up examples of justice against cupidity.

As the Lord commands: “Let your loins be girded and lamps [Col. 0564D] burning in your hands” (Luke 12). For feet are acts and sandals are examples, concerning which the Lord surely says: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5). From this, morally, it may be understood that religious men, when necessity demands, can sometimes mitigate the strictness of their rule, because Peter loosened his belt in prison.

And he said to him: “Put your cloak around yourself and follow me.” Garments are works, concerning which it is elsewhere said: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Ecclesiastes 9), that is, let your works be pure. He, therefore, puts his garment around himself and follows the angel who adorns himself with good works and follows Christ. “And going out, he followed [Col. 0565A] him, and did not know that what was done through the angel was real, but thought that he saw a vision.” Whatever is done in time is vanity, not reality, in comparison with eternity: not a waking state, but a sleep. Solomon testifies: “I saw vanity in all things, and that nothing remains under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 2). The Psalmist too says: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Psalm 75).

But when a person awakens in the future life, then he will return to himself, because he will return from what is alien to what is his own. When the soul is distracted by human and worldly occupations and stretched thin by secular cares, then it is alienated from itself, as though going into a far country, when it is not brought back to think [Col. 0565B] of God and to meditate upon itself—what will happen freely after this life—because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9). Then it truly returns to itself and will be able to say: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod,” and so forth.

Having passed the first and second guard, they came to the iron gate leading to the city, which opened to them of its own accord. The angel is said to pass with Peter because [Col. 0566A] he made him pass the first and second guard—that is, pass beyond the will to sin and the freedom to sin, by which the sinner is held in evil habit. The iron gate is harsh persecution, concerning which the Prophet says: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Psalm 16). This leads to the city because “narrow is the way which leads to life” (Matthew 7). “Which opened to them of its own accord,” because “God is faithful, who does not allow his faithful ones to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation provides the means of escape” (1 Corinthians 10 [printed: 1]).

“And, going out, they proceeded one street.” They went out, namely, from this world, “in which, as long as we are here, we wander from the Lord as in a street” (2 Corinthians 5). And immediately the angel departed from him, because after this life, [Col. 0566B] when one arrives there, no visitor or guardian is necessary, because “God is all in all” (Colossians 3 [printed; cf. 1 Corinthians 15]).

Therefore, brethren and children, let us pray without ceasing to the Lord that he may send his angel to rescue us from the hand of Herod and from every expectation of the Jewish people: Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. ON THE FEAST OF ST LAWRENCE THE MARTYR

On the works, miracles, and torments of blessed Lawrence; on the manifold kinds of fire; on God’s visitation; on how blessed Lawrence was free from avarice, pride, and ambition, yet patient and courageous; and finally, a comparison between Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and blessed Lawrence, archdeacon of Christ’s Church.

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565C] “You have tested my heart, O Lord, and visited me in the night; you have examined me by fire, and iniquity has not been found in me” (Psalm 16).

There are three things that gloriously commend blessed Lawrence: works, miracles, and torments—righteous works, radiant miracles, cruel torments. Because of these three he cried to the Lord in prophetic words: “You have tested my heart” by righteous works; “you visited me in the night” by radiant miracles; “you examined me by fire” through cruel torments. You tested my heart by righteous works, because I have already spent your treasures which you entrusted to me: “He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for age upon age” (Psalm 111 [printed: 3]).

You visited me in the night by radiant miracles, because my night contains no darkness, but all things shine in light. For Lawrence did a good work when, by the sign of the cross, he gave light to the blind. You examined me by fire, through cruel torments, because on the gridiron I did not deny you as God, but, placed upon the fire, I confessed you, O Christ. For as his bodily limbs were stretched on the gridiron and the attendants placed coals beneath it, Christ’s Levite taunted them.

“You have tested my heart” by righteous works, because a tree is known by its fruit: “A bad tree cannot bear good fruits” (Matthew 7). “You visited me in the night” by radiant miracles [Col. 0566C], because God is wonderful in his saints; he himself gives strength and power to his people (Psalm 67). “You examined me by fire” through cruel torments. For “blessed is the man who endures temptation; because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James 1). Therefore, “You have tested my heart,” and so forth.

There are three kinds of fire: spiritual, artificial, and natural. Yet among these there is a manifold diversity of nature. For some fire does not burn but gives light; some does not give light but burns; and some both gives light and burns. The empyrean fire does not burn and gives light; the fire of hell does not give light but burns; the fire of a furnace both gives light and burns.

Again, some fire always lives and never dies; some sometimes lives and sometimes dies; some dies as soon as it lives. The fire of a star always lives and never dies; the fire of a forge sometimes lives and sometimes dies; [Col. 0566D] the fire of lightning dies as soon as it lives. Likewise, one fire feeds and consumes; another consumes and is not fed; another feeds and does not consume. Ordinary fire feeds and consumes; solar fire consumes and is not fed; Gehenna’s fire feeds and does not consume. For it is written: “Like sheep they are set in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Psalm 48); but “people will desire to die, and death will flee from them” (Revelation 9).

But because investigating the natures of things is more philosophical than theological, we, who ought to be spiritual, should proceed with spiritual matters. There is a fire of guilt: the rancor of envy, or the burning of concupiscence, concerning which it is written: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Psalm 57). And elsewhere: “Fire rose up and burned the beautiful things of the desert” (Joel 1).

The fire [Col. 0567A] of punishment is the pain of compunction or the sorrow of compassion. Of it it is said: “By doing this, you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (Romans 12); and elsewhere: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze” (Psalm 38). The fire of grace is the fervor of charity or the brightness of truth, concerning which it is written: “I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12). And elsewhere: “From on high he sent fire into my bones” (Lamentations 1).

Likewise, there is diabolical, angelic, and divine fire. Of the first it is said: “Fire fell from heaven” (Job 1), according to the saying: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Of the second it is written: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103). Of the third it is written: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4).

Again, there is the fire of persecution, the fire of rebuke, and the fire of purification. Of the first it is written: “You tested us, O God; you examined us by fire as silver is examined” (Psalm 65). Of the second [Col. 0567C] it is said: “If anyone kindles a fire and the fire destroys crops, the one who kindled the fire is liable” (Exodus 22). Of the third it is written: “Fire will test what sort each person’s work is” (1 Corinthians 3).

Further, there is the fire of sacred teaching, the fire of a cauterized conscience, and the fire of eternal vengeance. Of the first it is written: “The Lord came from Mount Paran, and in his hand was a fiery law” (Deuteronomy 33). Of the second it is written: “I will bring forth fire from your midst, and it will devour you” (Ezekiel 28). Of the third it is said: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire,” and so forth (Matthew 25).

Moreover, there is the fire of mystical sacrifice, concerning which it is written: “Fire shall always burn on my altar” [Col. 0567D] (Leviticus 6); the fire of heavenly protection, concerning which it is said: “He spread a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night” (Psalm 104); and also the fire of divine judgment, concerning which it is written: “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Psalm 49).

Because “the judgments of God are a great deep” (Psalm 35), the fire of divine judgment is sent for many causes: for vengeance, as in “The Lord rained sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19); for signification, as in “Fire passed by, but the Lord was not in the fire” (3 Kings 19); and for testing, as in: “Lord God of our fathers, hear me today, so that this people may learn that you are the Lord my God. And fire descended [Col. 0568A] from on high and consumed the burnt offering and the wood” (3 Kings 18).

There is a good fire, of which John says: “I baptize you in water; but one stands in your midst who baptizes you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3). There is also an evil fire, of which the prophet says: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isaiah 66 [printed: 61]). Since sacred Scripture distinguishes so many kinds of fire, by what fire does the glorious martyr and Levite Lawrence testify in prophetic words that he was examined? “You have tested my heart,” he says, “and visited me in the night; you examined me by fire, and iniquity was not found in me.”

He was indeed examined by the fire of persecution and the fire of love: by the fire of persecution in his body, by the fire of love in his heart; by the fire [Col. 0568B] of persecution amid adversity, by the fire of love amid prosperity. For God tested him and visited him: he tested him in the day and visited him in the night; he tested him in prosperity and visited him in adversity. In prosperity he was humble and merciful; in adversity he was courageous and patient. In neither did he fail; in both he advanced. “For all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Romans 8).

God, moreover, visits in two ways: by granting grace and by inflicting vengeance. Of the first it is written: “Through the tender mercies of our God, in which the Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). Of the second it is written: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges” (Psalm [Col. 0568C] 88).

But among all forms of prosperity, two things especially tend to corrupt the human heart: wealth and dignities. Wealth makes one greedy; dignities make one proud. Moreover, sacred Scripture teaches us that “the root of all evils is cupidity” (1 Timothy 6), and “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10). “For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare” (1 Timothy 6). “A person who, when in honor, did not understand is compared with senseless beasts and made like them” (Psalm 48).

For cupidity has seduced and condemned many. Achan perished by stoning because he took gold and silver from the accursed spoil of Jericho (Joshua 7). [The printed text has “Achior.”] Gehazi was struck with leprosy because he asked for and received gold, silver, and garments in Elisha’s name (4 Kings 5). Judas hanged himself with a noose because he sold the blood of the righteous one (Matthew 27). “For he was a thief and, having the money-box, carried what was put into it” (John 12).

Not so, not so blessed Lawrence. Though he had the Church’s treasures laid up—neither few nor small, but so many and so great that even the Roman emperor would intensely have desired them—he did not keep them for himself or hand them over to relatives, but “scattered and gave to the poor”; and therefore “his righteousness remains for age upon age” (Psalm 111). Let those consider this who luxuriously consume the resources of the Church, the patrimony of the Crucified One, upon their own pleasures, or distribute it without restraint to enrich their relatives, while neglecting the poor and despising the needy. [Col. 0569A] For “whoever has this world’s goods and sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him—how does the charity of God remain in him?” (1 John 3).
