God made the rich not so much for the poor as the poor for the rich, because the rich profit more by what they distribute than the poor by what they receive. “Make friends for yourselves,” he says, “from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). In the same way, he does not so much make use of good people for bad people as of bad people for good people, because grain was not made for the flail, but the flail for the grain.

Pride also has lifted up and cast down many. Nebuchadnezzar, because he arrogantly boasted of his power, lost his kingdom and, among the beasts, ate hay like an ox (Daniel 4). Sennacherib, because he set his mouth against heaven and spoke proudly against God, was killed by his sons in the temple of Nisroch (4 Kings 19; Isaiah 37). Haman, because he wished divine honor to be bestowed upon himself, was hanged on the gallows (Esther 7).

Not so, not so blessed Lawrence. Although he was archdeacon of the apostolic see, highest after the first—or rather, first after the highest—he sought out holy poor people through districts and lanes, through houses and crypts, washed their feet, and cherished them with kisses, following the example of his Master, who, after washing the disciples’ feet, added: “I have given you an example, that you also should do likewise” (John 13).

[Col. 0569C] Among adversities too, two things especially tend to overthrow the human heart: losses of possessions and dangers to persons—the former through worldly fear, the latter through human fear. Herod, fearing that he would lose his kingdom, killed innocent children (Matthew 2). Likewise the Jews, fearing that the Romans would come and take away their place and nation, took counsel to seize and kill Jesus (John 12). Peter, who had said, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew 26), denied him at a servant-girl’s voice, out of fear of death. Marcellinus also, who for a long time had been a confessor, offered incense to idols through fear of suffering.

Of such persons it is written: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back [Col. 0569D] on the day of battle” (Psalm 77). For many who put their hand to the plow (Luke 9), and looked back with Lot’s wife, were turned into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19).

Not so, not so blessed Lawrence. When he saw Bishop Sixtus and his deacons being led to the torments of martyrdom, strong and undaunted he cried: “Where are you going without your son, Father? Where, holy priest, are you hastening without your deacon? Do not leave me behind, holy Father, for I have now spent your treasures which you entrusted to me.” He was not ambitious for honor or greedy for rank, as though he desired his superior’s death in order that he himself might ascend to leadership after him. For he did not wish to succeed his superior, since he wished to die with his superior; but he desired “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Col. 0570A] (Philippians 1), not fearing those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, but fearing him who can send body and soul into Gehenna (Matthew 10).

For, clothed with the power of the Spirit from on high, he proved so strong and endured so patiently that, amid torments so dreadful and severe that it is horrible not only to recount them but even to hear them, he said to the tyrant: “Learn, wretch, that your coals afford me not burning but refreshment. See, wretch: you have roasted one side; turn over the other and eat.” Thus he confessed Christ without fear and followed him with love, so that in dying he might triumph over death and in living might reign with life (Luke 24). God tested him like gold in a furnace (Wisdom 3), “so that the testing of faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by [Col. 0570B] fire, might be found unto praise and glory and honor” (1 Peter 1), because iniquity was not found in him.

For since opposites placed beside one another shine forth more clearly, let us set before us Pharaoh, who failed alike in prosperity and adversity, so that by comparing the two we may exalt his vice and this man’s virtue. Pharaoh was king in the land of Egypt; this man was an archdeacon in the Church of Christ. He was a tyrant of bodies; this man a physician of souls. He was ruler of temporal things; this man minister of spiritual things. He utterly forgot Joseph’s benefits; this man continually remembered God’s gifts. He held God’s people in slavery; this man had the Church’s treasure under his authority. He afflicted the people with harsh forced labours; this man distributed the Church’s treasure [Col. 0570C] in generous gifts. Moses and Aaron came to him to free God’s people; Decius and Valerian rose up against this man to plunder the Church’s treasures. Ministers of God against the servant of the devil; ministers of the devil against the servant of God. Decius and Valerian thundered with threats; Moses and Aaron flashed with miracles (Exod. IV). The former imposed cruel commands; the latter gave counsel. Yet Pharaoh would not yield to sound counsel, nor would Lawrence obey cruel commands. He proudly scorned God’s name; this man humbly proclaimed it. He afflicted the people ever more severely; this man distributed the treasure ever more liberally. At last Moses and Aaron wonderfully struck Pharaoh with ten plagues; Decius and Valerian [Col. 0570D] tortured Lawrence with ten torments.

For blessed Lawrence was first shut up in prison; second, beaten with scorpions; third, bound with chains; fourth, scourged with clubs; fifth, burned with heated plates; sixth, mangled with leaded scourges; seventh, laid out and stretched upon the rack; eighth, battered with stones; ninth, compressed by forks; tenth, roasted in flames. But Pharaoh could not be brought back by plagues; Lawrence could not be bent by torments. The former was hardened more and more in evil; the latter was strengthened more and more in good. Moreover, since they were opposites in life, they were also opposites in death. For Pharaoh, upon his chariot, was submerged by waters (Exod. XIV); Lawrence, upon a gridiron, was burned by fire. The former passed from snowy waters to burning (Job XXIV); the latter passed from fire [Col. 0571A] to refreshment. The former descended into the company of demons; the latter ascended into the company of angels.

Furthermore, brethren, because “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV), let us take the example of blessed Lawrence: mercy and humility in prosperity; courage and patience in adversity. Let us be merciful in heart, merciful in speech, merciful in deed: in heart through compassion, in speech through correction, in deed through assistance. Let us be humble toward superiors, equals, and inferiors: toward inferiors through due necessity, toward equals through mutual charity, toward superiors [Col. 0572A] through abundant humility. Let us be strong in heart, strong in speech, strong in deed: in heart against fear, in speech against shame, in deed against toil. Let us be patient amid losses, reproaches, and scourges, lest we conceive grief, give birth to fury, or nourish resentment; but, in accordance with the Lord’s command, let us love our enemies, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute and slander us (Matt. V). Through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. ON THE SAME FEAST

On the threefold gridiron; likewise on the gridiron of penitents, the perfect, and martyrs; on the twofold confession and the manifold altar.

[Col. 0571]

[Col. 0571B] “You shall make a bronze gridiron in the form of a net; at its four corners there shall be four rings, which you shall place upon the ledge of the altar” (Exod. XXVII).

We read of three gridirons in Scripture: one upon which the flesh of sacrifices was roasted; another upon which unleavened loaves were baked; and another upon which condemned persons were burned. Of the first we find in Exodus: “You shall make a bronze gridiron in the form of a net, and you shall place it upon the ledge of the altar.” Of the second it is read in Leviticus: “If the sacrifice is from the gridiron, fine flour shall be mixed with oil” (Lev. III). Of the third the historian says: “They stretched the limbs of the body upon the gridiron.” Upon this gridiron the glorious martyr and Levite Lawrence was burned by cruel fire—or rather by fiery cruelty. Yet within him [Col. 0571C] burned the fire of love, which cooled without the fire of heat: the inward fire tempered the outward; but the outward fire kindled the inward. “For love is strong as death, and jealousy hard as hell. Waters cannot quench charity” (Cant. VIII). Therefore blessed Lawrence cried out to the Lord in a pure voice: “Upon the gridiron I did not deny you as God; applied to the fire, I confessed you, Christ: ‘You have proved my heart and visited it by night; you have examined me by fire, and iniquity has not been found in me’” (Ps. XVI).

Let the first gridiron, then, be that of penitents; the second, that of the perfect; the third, that of martyrs. To the gridiron [Col. 0571D] of martyrs belongs the first passage which you heard in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). The grain of wheat is the Word of God, on which human beings and holy angels feed. This grain fell into the earth when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). For “the Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell [Col. 0572B] into Israel” (Isa. IX). Therefore it fell when Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II). But it died when Christ “became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (ibid.). It bore much fruit because “therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings—and every tongue confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid.).

Before this grain of wheat had died, it bore little fruit, as he himself says in the Psalm: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. CXL). But after it died, it bore much fruit [Col. 0572C], as he himself said in the Gospel: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII). Thus it is read of the children of Israel in Exodus that “the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and increased” (Exod. I). There is also a Word of God which is God: “The Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). And there is a Word of God which is not God, of which Scripture says: “Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII; Matt. IV). The Word of God which is God, unless it had fallen into the earth and died, would assuredly have borne no fruit (John XII), because birth would have profited nothing unless redemption had profited. But the Word of God which is not God, if it falls into the earth [Col. 0572D] and dies, bears no fruit whatever. Hence we read that the seed which “fell by the wayside did not grow, because the birds of heaven ate it” (Luke VIII).

To the gridiron of penitents belongs the second passage which you heard in the Gospel: “Whoever loves his life shall lose it; but whoever hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life” (John XII). Now, if, according to prophetic testimony, “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X), and, according to the Lord’s saying, “he who hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life” (John XII), then it seems to follow that whoever loves iniquity keeps his soul for eternal life. Far be it. For just as there is good love and bad love, so also there is good hatred. Good love is that of which the Lord says: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI). Bad love is that of which the Apostle says: “In those days people will be lovers of themselves” (II Tim. III). Good hatred is that of which the Psalmist says: “I have hated the wicked, and I have loved your law” (Ps. CXVIII); and again: “I hated them with perfect hatred, and they became enemies [Col. 0573B] to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Bad hatred is that of which John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III); and elsewhere: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. LXXIII). Therefore, whoever loves badly loses; and whoever hates well keeps. For whoever hates well keeps here; and whoever loves badly hates here. It is not said simply, “Whoever hates his life keeps it,” but with the addition: “Whoever hates his life in this world”—that is, in the pleasures, lusts, and seductions of this world—so as to hold them hateful, crucifying his flesh with its vices and lusts: he “assuredly keeps it for eternal life” (John XII). Conversely, “whoever loves his life” [Col. 0573C], with “in this world” understood—that is, loves it for this world’s pleasures, lusts, and seductions, so as to delight in them, following after lusts—he indeed “shall lose it” (ibid.) in the hell of eternal fire.

To the gridiron of the perfect belongs the third passage which you heard in the Gospel: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall my servant also be” (John XII). Elsewhere the Lord is recorded as answering: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX; Mark X; Luke XVIII). Therefore perfection consists in following Christ: the naked following the naked, the poor the poor. Although he is Lord of all, having written on his garment [Col. 0573D] and upon his thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. XIX), he nevertheless became so poor that he says of himself in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX). Hence, “when he was born, there was no room for him in the inn” (Luke II). He therefore first states the merit when he says, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me”; and immediately promises the reward when he adds, “Where I am, there shall my servant also be” (John XII). At once he remained on earth according to his humanity and reigned in heaven according to his divinity; hence he himself said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). And [Col. 0574A] therefore he promised not an earthly kingdom but a heavenly one, saying: “Where I am, there shall my servant also be” (John XII). “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). What indeed is more honourable, glorious, and blessed than that a human being should be with God, a servant with his lord, a creature with the Creator? “Today,” he says, “you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII)—as though he had said more plainly: Today you shall be with me, which is to be in paradise.

“You shall therefore make a bronze gridiron in the form of a net; at its four corners there shall be four rings, which you shall place upon the ledge of the altar.” Thus the gridiron [Col. 0574B] had four lateral corners and four corner-rings; it also had ribs arranged in a net, so that through the openings of the gridiron the kindled fire might rise and burn the sacrifice placed upon it. Let us therefore shake out the chaff and gather the wheat; break the shell to draw out the kernel; press the honeycomb to taste the honey. The kindled fire is the pain of compunction; the gridiron laid over it is the labour of satisfaction. Of this fire the Psalmist says: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire shall blaze” (Ps. XXXVIII). When the sinner reflects on the future judgment, the fire of grief is kindled in his heart, fearing to fall into the hands of the living God, who exacts the debt down to the last farthing (Matt. V). For he renders to each according to his merits (Rev. XX). He therefore runs and hastens to the priest, that he may impose the gridiron of satisfaction, upon which the sinner may burn his carnality with the fire [Col. 0574C] of contrition, so that he may say with the Prophet: “My bones were crushed as in a frying-pan, because I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. C).

By the four corners of this gridiron understand the four parts of satisfaction: prayers, almsgiving, fasting, and vigils. For we sin in four ways: through ignorance and frailty, through negligence and malice. Perhaps these are the farthings of which Truth says in the Gospel: “He shall not come out from there until he has paid the last farthing” (Matt. V): that is, until he has paid in punishment whatever he committed in fault.

Conversely, we must make satisfaction in four ways. [Col. 0574D] Against frailty, by fasting (Matt. IV); against ignorance, by prayer; against malice, by giving; against negligence, by keeping watch. These are the worthy fruits of repentance which the Lord mentions and commends in the Gospel: “This kind of demon,” he says, “is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII; Mark IX). “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI). “Keep watch, for you do not know at what hour the thief will come” (Matt. XXV; Mark XIII; Luke XII).

Into these four corners four rings must be set: namely, the four chief virtues—justice, courage, prudence, and temperance. In prayer, prudence, lest “prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII). In fasting, courage, that one may reach Mount Horeb of God [Col. 0575A] (III Kings XIX). In almsgiving, justice, that one may find a just person to whom to give. In vigils, temperance, lest one fail in temptation.

The ribs of the gridiron are works of mercy, which the Lord will commend at the judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; thirsty, and you gave me to drink; naked, and you clothed me; a stranger, and you received me; in prison, and you visited me” (Matt. XXV). Penitents ought to apply themselves to these works and abound in these fruits.

But the perfect person also [Col. 0575B] kindles a fire for himself and places a gridiron over it. The fire is the ardour of love; the gridiron, the pain of compunction. Of this fire Truth says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke XII). Of this gridiron it is read: “The sins of neighbours are the frying-pan of the just.” For he is perfect who loves his neighbour as himself and has compassion upon his neighbour as upon himself. He has compassion upon himself because of his sojourn in the present life and the delay of the life to come, as the Psalmist says: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt among the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. CXIX). This is the upper and lower spring which Caleb gave his daughter Achsah as a dowry (Josh. XIII). But he has compassion upon his neighbour in adversities and perversities, as the Apostle testifies: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. XI). These are the four corners into which four rings must also be set. In the sojourn of the present life: contempt for the world, according to John’s saying: “Do not love [Col. 0575C] the world, nor the things which are in the world” (I John II). In the delay of the future life: desire for heaven, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). In perversity: correction, as Truth commands: “If your brother sins against you, correct him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. XVIII). In adversity: assistance, as the prophet urges: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house” (Isa. XXXVIII).

“You shall therefore make a bronze gridiron in the form of a net.” Bronze, since it is a resonant metal, signifies confession. Now confession is twofold [Col. 0576A]: confession of praises and confession of sins. Of the first it is said: “Confess to the Lord with the harp; sing to him upon the ten-stringed psaltery” (Ps. XXXII). Of the second we read: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. V). Therefore each gridiron ought to be bronze: the former on account of the confession of sin performed by the penitent; the latter on account of the confession of praise performed by the perfect person.

“You shall therefore make a gridiron, and place it upon the ledge of the altar.” Scripture speaks of manifold altars: upper and lower, inner and outer. Each kind is twofold. For the upper altar is the Trinity of God, concerning which it is read: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (Exod. XX). There is also the upper altar, the triumphant Church, of which it is said: “Then they shall place calves upon your altar” (Ps. L). The [Col. 0576B] lower altar is the Church militant, concerning which we read: “If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones” (Exod. XX). There is also the lower altar, the table of the Temple, of which it is said: “Keep the solemn day amid dense branches, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII). The inner altar is a pure heart, concerning which it is commanded: “The fire upon my altar shall always burn” (Lev. VI). There is also the inner altar, faith in the Incarnation, concerning which it is commanded: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. XX). The outer altar is the altar of the cross, that is, the altar of burnt offering, upon which the evening sacrifice shall be burned. There is also the outer altar, the Church’s sacraments, of which it is written: “Your altars, O Lord of hosts” (Ps. LXXXIII), and so forth.

Since there are so many altars, upon the ledge of which altar [Col. 0576C] is the gridiron commanded to be placed? Surely the gridiron upon the ledge of the altar is repentance upon purity of heart, because “a troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. L). Let us therefore make for ourselves, dearest brethren, the gridiron of repentance, upon which we may offer sacrifice for sin, burning our carnality with the fire of compunction, so that afterwards we may sacrifice a sacrifice of praise—not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (I Cor. V)—through the merciful grant of him who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE SOLEMNITY OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EVER-VIRGIN MARY

How blessed Mary is a castle, what sort of castle she is, and how Christ entered it; and on the two sisters, the active and contemplative life.

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575D] “Jesus entered a certain castle, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary, who, sitting beside the Lord’s feet, heard his word” (Luke X).

The castle which Jesus entered is the Virgin Mary [Col. 0576D], when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I), as the angel promised her: “The Holy Spirit,” he said, “shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore the holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

[Col. 0577A] Now since Christ is true God and true man—God begotten of God before the ages, and man born of man in time—whatever is truly attributed to him applies either according to his divine nature, according to his human nature, or according to both. According to the divine nature he is called Jesus, which means “Saviour.” According to the human nature he is called Christ, which means “anointed.” According to both he is called Emmanuel, which means “God with us” (Matt. I).

Since entering is to approach from outside to within, one may ask—and even doubt—according to which nature he entered this castle, that is, the virginal womb. Not according to his divine nature, since he himself moves all things without moving and is always wholly everywhere, as he says of himself through the prophet [Col. 0577B]: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). Likewise: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. III). But neither according to his human nature, since his mother Mary received nothing externally into her womb, but conceived solely inwardly in the womb, as Isaiah plainly testifies: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII; Matt. I). For she is, according to Ezekiel (ch. XLIV), “the closed gate in the house of the Lord, and no man has entered through it.” But Christ was a man from his very conception, as the prophet Jeremiah testifies: “The Lord,” he says, “will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the enclosure of her womb” (Jer. [Col. 0577C] XXXI). What, then, shall we say? How, then, did he enter that castle? The Apostle gave sound counsel when he said: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think unto sobriety” (Rom. XII). And another says: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search into things greater than yourself” (Ecclus. III). “For the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. XXV). For “let a person approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII).

Yet, without prejudice to the majesty of faith, we may answer that, since philosophers call the beginning of being an entrance into substance, every thing which has a beginning likewise has an entrance. Hence, since the Word of God, according to the humanity he assumed, began to be in the virginal womb, assuredly according to that same humanity he entered it—not coming from outside, but assuming within. In this manner of speaking Truth itself testifies: “I went out from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI), not because he came from outside the world, but because he proceeded within the world. Jesus therefore entered a certain castle [Col. 0577D]. For the fortification of a castle two things are necessary: a wall and a tower—the wall outside and the tower within. For the castle’s guarding two things are likewise fitting: a watchman and a defender—the watchman to contemplate and the defender to act.

Let us therefore ask whether this castle was such. Certainly, in this spiritual castle, which is Mary the Virgin, Mother of God, the outer wall is bodily virginity; the inner tower is humility of heart. For “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be [Col. 0578A] exalted” (Luke XIV). Accordingly the Virgin herself testifies: “He has cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke I). Of the wall of virginity she says to the angel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (ibid.). For “before they came together, she was found with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I). Likewise, of the tower of humility, she says to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word; for he has regarded the humility of his handmaid. For behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke I). O happy virginity, adorned by humility! O happy humility, honoured by virginity! Humility adorns virginity, lest it be proud; virginity honours humility, lest it be despised. Virginity is humble, lest it be exalted [Col. 0578B]; humility is virginal, lest it be despised. For we read of both wise virgins and foolish virgins (Matt. XXV). The wise are humble; the foolish are proud. Thus this castle has the wall of virginity against the assault of lust; it has the tower of humility against the attack of pride. These are the enemies which frequently and violently assail wretched humanity: outwardly, lust of the flesh; inwardly, pride of mind. Of these the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not merely against flesh and blood”—behold lust—“but against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI)—behold pride. From the latter proceed shameful things which are unfitting; from the former proceed shameful things which are unlawful; from both proceed vain things which are unprofitable.

Whenever lust of the flesh attacks you [Col. 0578C], go to this castle; cling to the wall of virginity; entreat Mary. Who has ever invoked her and not been heard by her? Whenever pride of mind assails you, come to this castle; climb the tower of humility; entreat Mary. Who has ever invoked her and not been heard by her? She is “the mother of fair love and holy hope” (Ecclus. XXIV), who prays for the wretched, pleads for the afflicted, and intercedes for sinners.

In this castle dwell two sisters, who guard the castle: Martha and Mary. Martha labours and works; Mary rests and contemplates. The former [Col. 0578D] labours and works lest the castle be taken through negligence; the latter rests and contemplates lest the castle be seized through ignorance. Ignorance gives birth to error of heart; negligence brings forth torpor in action. Through error of heart we sin in matters of belief; through torpor in action we sin in matters of practice. Now, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI); and “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II). Let the contemplative life, then, keep watch, that it may destroy ignorance, since “the ignorant person shall be ignored” (I Cor. XIV). Let the active life labour, that it may put negligence to death, since “cursed is he who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII). Hear the Virgin labouring: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I were seeking you in sorrow” (Luke II). Hear the Virgin contemplating: “Mary kept [Col. 0579A] all these words, pondering them in her heart” (ibid.). Whenever negligence makes you sluggish, invoke Martha; act with Leah. Whenever ignorance makes you obscure, call upon Mary; keep watch with Rachel (Gen. XXVIII).

Jesus therefore entered a certain castle, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house, because Jesus came not to rest but to labour; not to joy but to sorrow; not to peace but to struggle; finally, he came to death. Hear of his labour: “I laboured crying out; my throat became hoarse” (Ps. LXVIII). “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe me” (Isa. LXV); therefore he is also said to have been “wearied from the journey” (John IV). Hear of his sorrow [Col. 0579B]: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I). “My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). “For he began to be afraid and troubled” (Mark XIV). Hear of his struggle: “Being in agony,” he says, “he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke XXI). Hear also of his death: “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). “For he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

Hear how Jesus himself busied himself with frequent ministry and was troubled about many things: “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of him who sent me” (John IV). “I have a baptism with which to be baptized [Col. 0579C], and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke XII). Martha therefore truly received him into her house. Hence, according to the flesh, he was born not of Rachel but of Leah. But Mary sat beside the Lord’s feet and heard his word. The Lord’s two feet are the two affections of the mind: fear and love—holy fear and chaste love. Holy fear provides the beginning, for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX). Chaste love prepares the end, for “the end of the commandment is charity” (I Tim. I). Mary therefore chose the better part, which shall not be taken from her, because “charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII), and “the holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” (Ps. XVIII).

Martha stood and busied herself in order to feed the Lord; Mary listened in order to be fed [Col. 0579D] by the Lord. The former did so in order to feed the Lord with bodily food; the latter in order to be fed by the Lord with spiritual food, because “human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from God’s mouth” (Matt. IV). Indeed, as much better as the soul is than the body, so much more sweetly does spiritual food taste in the mind than bodily food in the belly. “How sweet are your words, O Lord,” he says, “to my throat, more than honey and honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). Martha said to the Lord: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.” For her sake the Lord replied: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, [Col. 0580A] which shall not be taken from her.” Martha said this not as though she envied Mary because she laboured while Mary rested, but because the active life, when it is insufficient to itself because of the difficulties of affairs or the ambiguities of cases, seeks the contemplative life’s assistance: that what it cannot accomplish by labouring or acting, the contemplative life may obtain by praying and supplicating. For when Moses prayed on the mountain, Joshua conquered in the valley (Exod. XVII). Nor did the Lord answer her as though he were reproving Martha by commending Mary; rather, he preferred the best to good things, one thing to many, and what is everlasting to what is passing.

“Martha,” he says, “you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her.” Works of mercy [Col. 0580B] belong to the active life, which the Lord will commend at judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. XXV). He also commended Mary for the duty of burial: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has done a good work for me. For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it to bury me” (Matt. XXVI). These things are good, and one must not cease from them so long as they are necessary. But when the lack arising from misery has ceased, the effect of mercy will likewise cease, because mercy is shown to the miserable. And when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial shall be done away (I Cor. XIII). That is best which shall remain eternally. Mary therefore chose the better part, which shall not [Col. 0580C] be taken from her, because “this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). This certainly now begins in contemplation through faith and will at last be perfected in glorification through sight. “For now we know in part and prophesy in part; but then we shall know as we also are known, seeing not through a mirror in an enigma, but beholding face to face” (I Cor. XIII).

Hear how the Apostle Paul, as one active, was anxious and troubled about many things: “Who,” he says, “is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? My daily pressing concern is care for all the churches” (II Cor. XI). But hear how the same man, as contemplative, [Col. 0580D] “was caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (ibid.). As to the one thing, he aspired when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. II). But he endured the other as necessary when he added: “To remain in the flesh is necessary because of you” (ibid.). Therefore those things about which Martha busies herself are necessary, and that which Mary chose is necessary. But the former are necessary in the sense of useful; the latter is necessary in the sense of indispensable. Thus logic teaches that one thing is contingent truth and another necessary truth. A contingent truth is true in such a way that it can fail to be true; a necessary truth is true in such a way that it cannot fail to be true.

When the Virgin [Col. 0581A] said to her Son, “Son, why have you done this to us?” Behold, your father and I were seeking you in sorrow” (Luke II), did she not seem, as it were, to say with Martha: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me”? And when he answered: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things which are my Father’s?” (ibid.), did not the Lord seem, as it were, to answer Martha: “Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; yet one [Col. 0582A] thing is necessary. Mary therefore has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her.” The Prophet desired and sought this one thing when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI). One is preferred to many, because as all things proceed from one, so all things ought to proceed toward one: namely, toward him who is α and ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

On the characteristics or qualities of dawn, moon, and sun, and how they apply to Mary.

[Col. 0581]

[Col. 0581B] “Who is she who comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?” (Cant. VI.)

Since dawn is the end of night and the beginning of day, the Virgin Mary is fittingly signified by dawn: she was the end of condemnation and the beginning of salvation; the end of vices and the beginning of virtues. For just as death entered the world through a woman, so life had to return to the world through a woman. And therefore what Eve condemned, Mary saved, so that from the source whence death arose, life might rise again. Eve consented to the devil and ate the forbidden fruit, according to the words: “She took of the fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband” (Gen. III); Mary believed the angel and conceived the promised Son, according to the words: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke I). [Col. 0581C] Eve ate the fruit unto death, as had been foretold to her: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II); Mary conceived a Son unto salvation, as had been announced to her: “You shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I). Eve gave birth in sorrow, according to the words: “I will multiply your sufferings and your conceptions, and in sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. III); Mary brought forth in joy, according to the words: “I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all people; for today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke II). Eve was produced from man alone, since the Lord God fashioned into a woman the rib which he had taken from Adam, [Col. 0581D] “but he made man and woman” (Gen. II); Mary, however, was produced from man and woman, but brought forth a man alone: “For the Lord has made a new thing upon the earth: a woman has encompassed a man in the womb of her womb” (Jer. XXXI). Eve was produced without fault, but brought forth into fault; Mary, however, was produced in fault [Note: [Col. 0581D] Pope Innocent III could hold this view concerning a matter not yet defined by the Church, which is now [Col. 0582D] an article of faith, namely: Mary was conceived without stain. PATROLOGICAL EDITION.], but brought forth without fault. Eve was called *Eva*; to Mary it was said, *Ave* (“Hail”), because through her the name of Eve was changed. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace, the Lord is with you” [Col. 0582B] (Luke I). As though he said: Eve was full of sin, but you are “full of grace.” Eve was cursed among women, but “blessed are you among women” (ibid.). The fruit of Eve’s womb was the cursed Cain, but the fruit of your womb will be the blessed Jesus. Cain enviously killed his brother Abel (Gen. IV); but Jesus was enviously killed by his brothers.

Dawn, after driving away darkness, displays light to the world; but you, having destroyed vices, brought forth the Savior to the age. For through you “the people” of the Gentiles, “who walked in darkness, saw a great light; upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. IX)—that light, namely, “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). You therefore are the rising dawn: that is, the end of night and [Col. 0582C] the beginning of day; the end of condemnation and the beginning of salvation.

Beautiful as the moon. As those who discourse upon the natures of things reasonably maintain, the moon is cold and moist. Because it is cold, it signifies virginity; because it is moist, it signifies humility. Fire, from which dryness comes, being as it were light, naturally seeks heights. Water, however, from which moisture proceeds, being as it were heavy, naturally seeks low places. Thus the coldness and moisture of the moon are Mary’s virginity and humility: for she was cold against the heat of lust, and moist against the arrogance of pride. The moon is fully beautiful when it is round; and Mary was fully beautiful when she was fruitful in offspring. Happy the virginity which humility adorned; happy [Col. 0582D] the humility which virginity honored. But far happier than either is the fruitfulness which virginity and humility together adorned and honored. Therefore, lest virginity should incur that curse of which it is said, “Cursed is the barren woman who does not bear” (Exod. XXIII; Deut. VII), fruitfulness accompanies it; and lest fruitfulness should contract that uncleanness of which we read, “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” (Job XIV), virginity accompanies it. [Col. 0583A] And lest either virginity or fruitfulness should receive that sentence of which we read, “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XIV, XVIII), humility accompanies them both. The Evangelist commends and recounts these three together in Mary: “When Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I). Great humility: for the mother of Jesus was betrothed to Joseph. Holy fruitfulness: for she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. Pure virginity: because, before they came together, she was found to be with child—not that they ever afterward came together in carnal intercourse, for she was a virgin before giving birth, a virgin in giving birth, and a virgin after giving birth. “For this is the gate [Col. 0583B] in the house of the Lord, shut, and no man has entered through it” (Ezek. XLIV). This is “the enclosed garden and sealed fountain” (Song IV). This is the burning bush, yet not consumed (Exod. III). Concerning fruitfulness, the angel Gabriel foretold to her: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke I). But concerning virginity she replied: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (ibid.). When she heard that neither virginity hindered fruitfulness nor fruitfulness took away virginity—“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”—she immediately added from humility: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). Thus Mary was beautiful as the moon: a virgin, humble [Col. 0583C] and fruitful.

Chosen as the sun. Two things are especially commended in the sun: brightness and heat. Because it shines, it signifies wisdom; because it is warm, it signifies charity. For of wisdom we read that it “is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. VIII). Of charity we read that “there is a fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI)—and, “Many waters cannot extinguish charity” (Song VIII). Mary was therefore chosen in order that she might shine and be warm as the sun: shine through wisdom and be warm through charity; for the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke I). The Holy Spirit is charity, of whom it is said: “God is charity” [Col. 0583D] (I John II). And the power of the Most High is wisdom, of which we read: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (Acts VIII). Hear Mary questioning from wisdom: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke I). Hear her answering from charity: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). Hear wisdom in Mary: “Mary,” it says, “kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (ibid.). Hear charity in her: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (ibid.). Therefore the Holy Spirit came upon her, in order to give her in conceiving bodily the affection of charity. Hence we read that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. And the power [Col. 0584A] of the Most High overshadowed her, in order to give her understanding of wisdom for conceiving in her heart. Hence we read: “Blessed are you who believed, because all things have been fulfilled for you by the Lord” (ibid.). In her body she conceived “the Word, which was made flesh and dwelt in” (John I) her. In her heart she conceived “the Word” which “was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God” (ibid.). She was therefore chosen as the sun, inasmuch as “he set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom, proceeds from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII).

Terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps. For it is written that “wisdom conquers malice” (Wis. VIII), and between them a great and severe conflict is waged in this mortal life. For on wisdom’s behalf the choir of virtues fights [Col. 0584B] and conquers; but on malice’s behalf the army of vices fights and resists, because “there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial” (II Cor. VI). The camp of vices follows pride as its leader, of which Scripture says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X). But the camp of virtues follows humility as its leader, of which Mary says: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke I). Therefore the battle-line of camps—that is, the fullness of virtues—was so ordered in the Virgin that she could truly say of herself: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar, and ordered charity within me” (Song II), so that, after the fullness of divinity [Col. 0584C] of wine-ness dwelt bodily in her (Col. II), she wholly conquered malice. For, as I strongly suppose, from that time the tinder of sin, the infirmity of nature, and the sting of the flesh in her were not merely lulled but entirely extinguished, so that thereafter the flesh did not desire against the spirit; rather, being full of grace, she appeared terrible to vices and demons.

She therefore is the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps. The moon shines at night, dawn at daybreak, and the sun by day; but night is sin, daybreak repentance, and day grace. Therefore, whoever lies in the night of sin should look upon the moon and entreat Mary, that she may, through her Son, illuminate that person’s heart unto compunction. For who has invoked her in the night and was not heard by her? She [Col. 0584D] is “the mother of fair love and holy hope” (Ecclus. XXIV). Whoever rises to the daybreak of repentance should look upon the dawn and entreat Mary, that she may, through her Son, enlighten that person’s heart unto satisfaction. For who has devoutly invoked her and was not heard by her? She is “the mother of fair love and holy hope” (Ecclus. XXIV). Since “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job VII)—for the world is placed in evil (I John V), the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. VI), the eye despoils the soul (Lam. III), and death enters through the windows (Jer. IX)—our wrestling is not only against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against the rulers of this darkness (Eph. VI). For our adversary, [Col. 0585A] the devil, “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V). Whoever feels assault from enemies—whether from the world, the flesh, or the devil—should look upon the ordered battle-line of camps [Col. 0586A] and entreat Mary, that she may, through her Son, “send help from the sanctuary and defend him from Zion” (Ps. XIX). May he grant this, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE FEAST OF THE NATIVITY OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EVER-VIRGIN MARY

On the fisherman’s implements—namely, rod, line, hook, and bait—what we ought to understand by them, and why the devil is called by the names of various animals.

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585B] “He shall take Behemoth in his eyes, as with a hook” (Job XL).

The words which I have spoken, dearest brethren, are the Lord’s words to Job: few, yet many; small, yet great; brief, yet extensive. Few in letters, but many in meanings; small in syllables, but great in figures; brief in expression, but extensive in significance. For all are full of their mysteries and overflowing with heavenly sweetness—provided, however, that they have a diligent examiner who knows how to draw “honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone” (Deut. XXXI). “But I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (I Cor. III), because “as newborn infants you desire milk, that you may grow unto salvation” (I Pet. II).

In a fisherman’s implement we must note four things: rod, line, hook, and bait. The prophet defines what [Col. 0585C] this rod is, saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI). This is the little rod of smoke, of the spices of myrrh and incense (Song III). “The rod blossomed and brought forth fruit” (Isa. VII), because the Virgin conceived and bore Christ; therefore I would call this rod Mary. A rod has pliancy, straightness, and length: pliancy, so that it may not be hard; straightness, so that it may not be crooked; length, so that it may not be short. Mary, however, has virginity, humility, and charity: virginity without concupiscence, humility without pride, charity without malice. Of virginity the prophet says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII; Matt. XIII). For the angel Gabriel was sent [Col. 0585D] by God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, “to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke I). Of humility blessed Mary herself says: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” (ibid.). “Upon whom,” God says, “shall my spirit rest, except upon one who is humble, quiet, and trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). Of charity she says in the Song: “Support me with apples, adorn me with flowers, for I languish with love. For the king brought me into the wine-cellar and ordered charity within me” (Song II).

To this rod is joined the line, which Matthew the Evangelist describes: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0586B] son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. I). I would therefore call this line the genealogy. For just as a fisherman’s line is joined together from diverse threads, so the Redeemer’s genealogy is woven from diverse persons: men and women, Jews and Gentiles, righteous and sinners; for “all have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. III). Moreover, he says in the Gospel: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. II). Therefore they cried out, saying: “Come, Lord, and do not delay; forgive the crimes of your people Israel. Send forth the Lamb, Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. XVI).

To this line the hook is attached, as the Evangelist specifies in saying: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” [Col. 0586C] (Matt. I). I would therefore call this hook Christ: iron through power, sharp through wisdom, curved through diligence. For through power he subdues and overcomes; through wisdom he penetrates and investigates; through diligence he holds fast and preserves. Of the first the Psalmist says: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and break them like a potter’s vessel” (Ps. II); of the second the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV); of the third the Lord says: “This is the will of my Father: that I lose none of all that he has given me” (John V). Bait was placed around this hook when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). For the hook concealed in bait is God veiled in flesh. [Col. 0586D] I would therefore call this bait flesh, in accordance with which Christ compares himself to a worm: “I am,” he says, “a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. XLI). He is called a worm because of the lowliness of his abasement and because of the particular nature of his conception. “We,” says the prophet, “considered him as though a leper, struck by God and humbled; but who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. LI). For just as a worm is born without seed, so Christ was born of a virgin. The fisherman cast this hook into the sea to catch a fish when God sent Christ into the world to catch Behemoth, that is, the devil; for when the devil took the bait of humanity, he was caught [Col. 0587A] by the hook of divinity. Hence the prophet says: “On that day the Lord visited with his hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan the bar-serpent, and Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he shall kill the sea-monster which is in the sea” (Isa. XXVII). Therefore he says in the Psalm: “I came into the depths of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me” (Ps. LXVIII). When, therefore, the devil suggested that Christ be killed, he then deserved to be made captive by Christ, according to that prophetic saying: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. XII). For the devil entered Paradise and cast out its inhabitants; Christ descended into hell and brought out its captives. Since the devil laid his hand upon him in whom he had no right at all, he justly lost those over whom he seemed to have some right. But lest the devil should appear [Col. 0587B] to have been deceived by fraud when he is said to have been caught with a hook, the text first says: “He shall take Behemoth in his eyes, as with a hook.” For deceit is not imposed on one who knows and wills. For the devil, by knowing Christ, feared him; and by fearing, knew him. “What,” he says, “have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come before the time to destroy us? I know that you are the Holy One of God” (Luke VIII). And again: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me” (Matt. V). Yet his habitual greed drew him, and recklessness impelled him, to thirst for Christ’s blood and desire his flesh.

The interpretation of the name *Behemoth* signifies a beast. Because of his different properties, the devil is called by the names of different animals. He is called by the names of beasts because of violence and [Col. 0587C] oppression; by the names of creeping things because of cunning and deception; by the names of fishes because of luxury and excess. For by these four modes he especially tempts and overcomes. He is called a bird, as in: “Will you play with him as with a bird?” And by a specific name he is called a partridge, as in: “The partridge cried out and gathered what it did not bear” (Jer. VII). Thus demons are called birds, as in the Gospel: “The birds of heaven ate it” (Luke VIII). He is called [Col. 0588A] Behemoth, that is, a beast, as in: “Behold Behemoth, which I made with you.” And by a specific name he is called a lion, as Peter says: “Your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V). He is called a wolf, as in: “The wolf comes, and the hireling flees” (John X). Thus demons are called beasts, as in the Psalm: “Do not deliver to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. VI). He is called a serpent, as in: “On that day the Lord shall visit Leviathan the bar-serpent” (Isa. XXVII). For *Leviathan* means “their addition,” because he promised to add glory to the first parents: “You shall be,” he says, “like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). And by a specific name he is called a snake, as it is said: “By his laboring hand the twisting snake was brought forth” (Job XXVI). He is called a dragon, as in: “This dragon which you formed to play with it” (Ps. CIII). Thus demons, because they deceive in different ways, are called by different names of creeping things, as in: “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk,” etc. (Ps. XC). Again: “He shall suck the head of asps, and the tongue of the viper shall kill him” (Job XX).

He is called a fish, under whose figure a huge fish came forth to devour Tobias (Job V). And by a specific name he is called a sea-monster, as in: “The Lord shall kill the sea-monster which is in the sea” (Isa. XXVII). In all these instances he is called Satan, that is, “adversary,” as in: “Satan stood at his right hand, to oppose him” (Zech. V). He is called Belial, that is, apostate, transgressor, and without a yoke, as it is said: “What fellowship [Col. 0588C] has Christ with Belial?” (II Cor. VI). He is called devil, that is, accuser, or “flowing downward,” as in the Psalm: “Let the devil stand at his right hand, and let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII).

The devil, therefore, is strong and cunning; but one stronger and more cunning came upon him, plundered his goods, and brought forth captives (Luke XI): the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages.

## SERMON XXX. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

What we ought to understand by the two seraphim; concerning the three armies that cry out; and concerning the five places in which human spirits dwell.

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587D] “Two seraphim cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; all the earth is full of glory” (Isa. VI).

The two seraphim, one of which cried to the other, are the two Testaments, one of which corresponds to the other. For “a wheel is contained in the midst of a wheel” (Ezek. I), and the two cherubim look upon one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat (Exod. XXV). Hence the one Testament begins in this way: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I); [Col. 0588D] the other: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (I John V). What is written less openly in the former is related more openly in the latter. In the former it is written: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts”; in the latter it is related: “There are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.” Apart from the mystery of unity and trinity, which these words evidently and excellently commend, they also suit today’s solemnity fully [Col. 0589A] and plainly. For God, three and one, has three armies in three places: one triumphing in heaven; another fighting in the world; a third lying in purgatory. Of these three armies the Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). These three armies distinctly cry with the seraphim: Holy Father, holy Son, holy Spirit. To the Father is attributed power, which belongs to the army fighting on the way; to the Son, wisdom, which belongs to the army triumphing in the homeland; to the Holy Spirit, mercy, which befits the army lying in punishment. The first army is in praise, the second in struggle, and the third in fire. Of the first we read: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII). Of the second it is said: “The life of man upon earth is warfare, and his days are like the days of a hired laborer” (Job VII). Of the third the Apostle says: “Fire shall test what sort each person’s work is” (I Cor. III).

Certainly there are five places in which human spirits dwell: the highest, which is of the supremely good; the lowest, which is of the supremely wicked; the middle, which is of the good and the wicked; and between the highest and the middle, one which is of those moderately good; and between the middle and the lowest, another which is of those moderately wicked. The highest, which is of the supremely good, is heaven, where the blessed are. The lowest, which is of the supremely wicked, is hell, where the damned are. The middle, [Col. 0589C] which is of good and wicked alike, is the world, where the righteous and sinners are. Between the highest and the middle is that of the moderately good, Paradise, where Enoch and Elijah are—living indeed, but still [Col. 0590A] destined to die. Between the middle and the lowest is that of the moderately wicked, where those are punished who did not repent on the way, or who bore some venial stain at death. They are called wicked for this reason: partly because of the evil of punishment, partly because of the evil of fault. Yet although there are five places, the armies of the Lord dwell in only three. For those who are in hell do not belong to God’s army, but to the army of Zabulus, to whom it shall finally be said: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). Those who are in Paradise, although they belong to God’s army, do not by themselves make up an army, since they are two. But the middle army today offers praises for the army triumphing in heaven, and tomorrow pours forth prayers for the army lying in purgatory: for the former it offers praises, because it reigns in glory; for the latter it pours forth prayers, that it may escape punishment. [Col. 0590B] O how reasonable and salutary is the institution of this observance! Who would not gladly offer praises to the indivisible Trinity for the saints, by whose prayers and merits we believe that we are helped, so that where they are, we too may be? Who would not gladly pour forth prayers to the indivisible Trinity for the dead, since he too is destined to die, in order to do for others in this life what he wishes to be done for himself after this life? Therefore all the earth is full of his glory, because the sound of this solemnity, through which God is glorified in the saints, has gone out into all the earth (Ps. XVIII), which under the one solemnity of All Saints venerates the merits of all the saints [Col. 0590C] to the praise and glory of the indivisible Trinity, who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. DELIVERED ON THE SAME FEAST IN THE MONASTERY OF SUBIACO

Who are pure in heart, and how they are blessed; the twofold character of blessedness; the threefold vision of God; and finally, how the heart is to be cleansed.

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589D] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

The words uttered by the Word are plain yet full, eloquent and fruitful alike—provided, however, that they have a diligent examiner who knows how to thresh grain from chaff and draw honey from the honeycomb. The foregoing words stir the mind with certain questions, so that it may conceive a fuller understanding. For Solomon testifies: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean, and I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. XX). For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I), since “we all offend in many things” (Jas. III). How, then, are the pure in heart blessed, if no one can say that he has a clean heart and is free from sin? But it is one thing to have and another to say, or one thing to say and another to have. Indeed, holy men and righteous people have a clean heart when they have been cleansed from mortal sins and purified from grave vices—such as those of whom Truth himself said: “He who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean. And you are clean, but not all” (John XIII). Otherwise, the Psalmist would have prayed in vain when he said: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Wash me more abundantly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. L). Although frail man cannot be entirely without venial sins, since even the moon is not wholly without a spot and “the righteous man falls seven times a day” (Prov. XXIV), yet rises stronger, nevertheless through the grace of God, which works principally, [Col. 0591A] and free will, which soundly cooperates with it, he can refrain from grave offenses. A person is called clean here not because he is altogether clean, but because he must be cleansed more and more; for no one is so clean in this life that he cannot be cleaner in it. “Every branch,” he says, “that bears fruit, he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” (John XV). Yet no one should say, as though boasting, that he has a clean heart; rather, “let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X), because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job VII), and therefore before the end of the battle one must not boast of victorious success. “For our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V); and daily the demon, the world, and the flesh fight against wretched man: the demon with vices, the world with the elements, the flesh with the senses [or: desires]. “Blessed therefore is he who is always fearful” (Prov. XXVIII), because “the fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclus. II). Therefore one ought rather to fear and beware than to boast or presume. But “let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (I Cor. II), not in exaltation but in humility, as the Apostle boasted, saying: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (II Cor. XII). Nor is this contrary to what he says elsewhere: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). For that glory was not his from himself but from God—that is, the testimony of a free conscience—lest he should vainly boast [Col. 0591C] in God if he presumed to boast contrary to the testimony of a right conscience; as hypocrites vainly boast, being like whitewashed tombs outwardly but within full of every filthiness and the bones of the dead (Matt. XXIII). For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful” (Wis. I). Or, “Who can say, ‘I have a clean heart and am pure from sin’?” (Prov. XX), as though to say, “Such a person is rare.” For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). The good, indeed, are few in comparison with the wicked, because “the number of fools is infinite, and the perverse are corrected with difficulty” (Eccles. I). “But who understands transgressions?” (Ps. XVIII). Hence, after the Apostle said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” he immediately added: “Yet I am not thereby justified” [Col. 0591D] (I Cor. IV). Therefore the Psalmist said: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. XVIII). For elsewhere it is also read: “No one knows whether he is worthy of hatred or love” (Eccles. IX). This should rather be understood concerning predestination or reprobation, as the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I), because God predestined Jacob and rejected Esau. Therefore, blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. But how are those blessed who are still in battle and misery? Who was purer than Paul, who nevertheless said: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). The Psalmist agrees with him, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison, that it may confess your name, [Col. 0592A] O Lord” (Ps. CXLI). If he was wretched, how then was he blessed? For there is nothing under the sun except vanity and affliction of spirit (Eccles. I). Indeed, we are more able to experience our misery than to express it. But blessedness is twofold: one of the way, the other of the homeland. The blessedness of the way consists in hope; the blessedness of the homeland consists in reality [variant: merit]. The former consists in faith, the latter in sight; the former consists in merit, the latter in reward; the former consists in grace, the latter in glory. Of this blessedness it is written: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII). Of that blessedness it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for age upon age they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII). These walk, but those dwell; these labor, [Col. 0592B] but those rest; these exercise themselves in the law, but those delight in praise. Therefore the pure in heart are blessed: now through hope, at last through reality; now through faith, at last through sight; now through merit, at last through reward; now through grace, at last through glory—for they shall see God.

Contrary to this, John seems to have said in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1). And God says in the Law: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Yet Isaiah seems to contradict these words when he says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6); and Jacob: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my life was preserved” (Gen. 32).

Perhaps someone might reply and say that God cannot be seen [Col. 0592C] according to the divine nature, but was seen according to the human nature, as Jeremiah indicates: “This is our God,” he says, “and none other shall be accounted equal to him” (Baruch 3). “Afterward he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings.” It is therefore true that “no one has ever seen God” (John 1) according to the purity and simplicity of the divine nature, because God is an invisible spirit. Yet it is also true that God was seen according to the image and likeness of human nature, because he became a visible human being.

But this distinction of vision does not bear upon the meaning of the present statement, since many have seen, and will see, in God the human nature, though they neither were nor will be blessed—such as Herod, Pilate, Judas, and Caiaphas. So too those of whom it is said: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19). They will see him not for salvation but for condemnation, because the wicked person will be taken away lest he see the glory of God. “Blessed, therefore, are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20).

The distinction should rather be made as follows: one kind of vision is bodily, another enigmatic, and another comprehensive. Bodily vision resides in sense; enigmatic vision in an image; comprehensive vision in intellect. Of the first it is said: “My eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 1); of the second: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13); and of the third it is added: “But then we shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 15).

By bodily vision no one has ever been able, or will be able, [Col. 0593A] to see the Godhead, because God is not a body but spirit. By enigmatic vision, however, God is in some measure seen in the present life—not by direct sight but by faith, and not fully but imperfectly. By comprehensive vision he is seen purely by the holy angels and blessed souls, who know even as they are known.

It is therefore true that “no one has ever seen God” (John 1), but this must be understood of bodily vision. It is likewise true that he says: “No human being shall indeed see me and live” (Exod. 33), but this must be understood of this mortal life. This was fittingly signified in Moses, who, standing in the cleft of the rock, saw the Lord’s back parts but did not behold his face. For just as, when a human being is viewed from behind, one knows indeed that it is a human being but not which human being; so we now know that God exists, but do not know what [Col. 0593B] he himself is. We certainly know that he is God, but we do not know what he is.

The ancient fathers therefore saw the Lord enigmatically, through a certain likeness of a human vision, appearing rather to sense or imagination. But blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. He does not say, in the present tense, “They see,” but, in the future, “They shall see,” because he is seen more fully and perfectly in the future. Yet he is also seen in the present through the effect of inspiration, contemplation, prayer, meditation, reading, and preaching, by which the soul is raised up to behold God.

The heart, however, must be cleansed both of deadly sins and of worldly cares, [Note: [Col. 0593] Alternatively: “so that it may be able freely to behold God; for one entangled in deadly sins is blind, and one caught in worldly cares is one-eyed,” etc.] lest God be seen by bleary eyes. For “if your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, [Col. 0593C] your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6). Thus one beholds the eternal light less, another not at all. For “the one who does evil hates the light and walks in darkness” (John 3).—“But the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it at all” (John 1).—“Their foolish heart was darkened,” says the Apostle (Rom. 1); and the more a person sins, the more he is darkened, until from inward darkness he is cast into outer darkness, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, where the worm shall not die and the fire shall not be quenched” (Matt. 22).

Let him therefore depart from Egypt who wishes to sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness; let him be cleansed from the darkness of vices, because God [Col. 0593D] “is light, and there is no darkness at all in him” (1 John 1). Alas, if anyone saw the sinful soul—how foul, how stinking, how murky, how dark it is—surely it would appear more abominable and detestable than leprous flesh.

Likewise, whoever wishes freely to contemplate God must cleanse the heart of worldly cares. For as long as it is divided by worldly actions and distracted by earthly occupations, as though cast down upon the ground, it cannot look up to heaven. This is aptly signified in Zacchaeus, who, being chief of the tax collectors and himself rich, wanted to see who Jesus was; but because of the crowd he could not, since he was small in stature (Luke 19). He was chief [Col. 0594A] of the tax collectors and therefore occupied with revenue business. He was small in stature because, intent upon earthly things, he was cast down to the ground and not raised toward heaven. Therefore, owing to the crowd—that is, the entanglement of worldly anxieties—he could not see who Jesus was, until, passing beyond the crowd, that is, abandoning worldly occupations, he climbed the sycamore tree, that is, approached faith in the life-giving cross. Concerning this, with all the saints, he grasped what is its length and breadth, what its height and depth are (Eph. 3).

Let the dead flies which spoil the sweetness of ointment be driven away (Eccl. 10); that is, let importunate thoughts, which take away the sweetness of contemplation, be excluded. And let the little ones be dashed against the rock (Ps. 136): that is, let the first impulses be checked against Christ, so that the soul, ascending from strength to strength, may see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83).

Let the mind therefore place beneath itself all earthly things, in which there are vanity and affliction, and rise beyond them to investigate heavenly things, in which are true happiness and perfect blessedness: considering and admiring, in that heavenly court, the orders of angels, the assemblies of patriarchs, the choirs of prophets, the crowns of apostles, the palms of martyrs, the companies of confessors, and the fruit of virgins—resting in peace, rejoicing in praise, shining in light, secure without fear, at rest without labor, joyful without pain. Let it consider how great are their knowledge, delight, and love; how great their beauty, rectitude, and strength; how great their impassibility, incorruptibility, and [Col. 0594C] immortality; and that God himself “is all in all” (1 Cor. 15), the reward and prize of each one.

And if, in investigating these things, the mind is carried away with some taste of sweetness, then indeed it contemplates. How sweet it is to contemplate in this manner, he who has tasted knows more fully.

Yet there is a still sweeter taste of contemplation: namely, to investigate the union of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is the love and delight of both, proceeding from both; yet neither later than nor less than either, as consubstantial with and coeternal with each. For just as in Christ there are three substances in one person, so in God there are three persons in one substance. In the three substances there is “another thing,” but not “another person.” But in the three [Col. 0594D] persons there is “another person,” but not “another thing”; for the three are one, which is eternal and simple. For it has neither beginning nor end, but is beginning without beginning and end without end—as though the beginning were directed toward the end and the end toward the beginning.

Nor does it have a multitude of parts or a composite aggregation of properties, because it has nothing in itself except itself; nor is the possessor one thing and the thing possessed another, nor is the thing possessed one thing and the possessor another—although no possession of the possessor himself is greater or lesser. Although in the one who is one substantially there is another and another, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But in the one who is one personally, because there is both “another thing” and “another person,” there are earlier and later, greater and lesser, [Col. 0595A] namely the eternal, the new, and the old: the Godhead eternal, the soul new, the flesh old.

Among these matters it is exceedingly sweet and delightful, in this supreme and true good, to investigate the power that created all things; the wisdom that ordered all things (Wis. 8); and the goodness that governs all things. From it, through it, and in it all things subsist—great, beautiful, and useful. Thus by greatness you may investigate the powerful One; by beauty, the wise One; by usefulness, the good One. Yet the one and same One created, ordered, and governs. In him power is not one thing, wisdom or goodness another; so that, just as there is unity in nature, there is also distinction in persons. But let us cease to pursue the inquiry; for “a human being approaches the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63), and “the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25).

Blessed, therefore, are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Comprehensive vision is indeed the perfect blessedness of the soul, because “this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). For that person is perfectly blessed to whom all desired things come to pass. Certainly, whoever sees God possesses whatever he desires.

Do you delight in wisdom? If you see God, [Col. 0595C] you have what you desire, because God is most perfect wisdom, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8).—“In him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2). Do you delight in beauty? If you see God, you have what you desire, because God is most perfect beauty, “upon whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1). The sun and moon marvel at his beauty.
