Do you delight in peace? If you see God, you have what you desire, because he himself is most perfect peace, who made both one, whose peace surpasses all [Col. 0596A] understanding. Do you delight in light? If you see God, you have what you desire, because God is the most perfect “light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1), and “he himself dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6). Do you delight in strength? If you see God, you have what you desire, because God is most perfect strength. Nothing is impossible to him, nothing resists his will; he is strong and mighty above all gods.

If perhaps you delight in sweetness, he is supreme sweetness, of whom Scripture says: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30). “Taste,” Scripture says, “and see that the Lord is sweet, gentle and upright, kind and merciful” (Ps. 33). But why linger over individual things? Whatever good you desire, [Col. 0596B] if you see God, you possess it in him. Since he is the supreme good, in him is the fullness of every good; if you see him, you comprehend him; if you comprehend him, you possess him.

To attain and obtain this supreme good, you have left the world and chosen the wilderness—not just any wilderness, but the one chosen by our blessed father and patron Benedict, in which he established the monastic life and ordered the monastery. You are bound to observe its ordinances [alternatively, its Rule] not only because of your vow but also because of the place.

Therefore, brothers, cleanse your hearts, that you may be able to see God. The heart must be cleansed with those brooms by which that house was cleansed from which the unclean spirit went out, and which he afterwards found swept clean and decorated. [Col. 0596C] Repentance is a good broom; almsgiving is a good broom; fasting is a good broom; prayer is a good broom; vigils are good brooms. With these brooms cleanse the houses of your hearts, that you may be able to see God. May he grant this, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0595]

## Sermons of Pope Innocent III

For the birthdays and feast days of the holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, which they call the Commons.

### First Sermon: On the Apostles

On the singular prerogative, honor, and veneration of the apostles, and especially on the three things that commend their honorable primacy.

[Col. 0595D] “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. 138).

In what could anyone be more honored than in being truthfully called a friend of the true God? For if it is regarded as honorable even to be enrolled among the friends of an earthly king, how much more honorable should it be considered [Col. 0596D] to be the friend of the heavenly King? Among intimate friends there ought to be a sharing of fortunes, a communication of secrets, and a communion of wills; by these a faithful friendship is proved. For this is characteristic of friends: that nothing is private between them.

Christ bound the apostles to himself by so indissoluble a love that he regarded their fortunes as his own, as he said to them: “Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever receives you receives me” (Luke 19). Thus he said to Saul: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9). To Peter also, when he asked, “Lord, where are you going?” he replied: “I am going to Rome to be crucified again.”

Though he himself reigned impassibly in heaven, he nevertheless called himself passible [Col. 0597B] on earth, because he regards what is his as belonging to his own, and what belongs to his own as his. For there is no dissimilar fortune for those whose effect is alike; nor is the lot different for those who have one soul. Hence he said: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my minister may be. Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they too may be with me: that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them, that they may be one as we are one” (John 17).

He also joined his apostles to himself by such sincere friendship that he made them privy to his secrets. “I shall no longer call you servants,” he said, “but friends, because a servant does not know what his master does. But I have called you friends, because everything whatsoever that I heard from my Father [Col. 0597C] I have made known to you” (John 15). And again: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8). Therefore he himself said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 2).

But how can it be true that he made known to the apostles everything whatsoever that he heard from the Father, when elsewhere he says: “I have many things to say to you which you cannot bear now” (John 16)? We must consider who said this: assuredly he who spoke and things came to be; who knows all things before they happen; to whom future things are past—or rather, to whom all things are present, both past and future—because “he who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18).

Christ therefore made certain things known to the apostles insofar as concerned himself, which were to be made known to them insofar as concerned them. “When he comes,” he said, “the Spirit of truth, he will teach you all truth” (John 16), because “he will teach you concerning all things, and you shall all be taught by God” (John 6). Christ, therefore, as a true friend revealed hidden things to his apostles; and they, as true friends of their Lord, fulfilled his good pleasure, as he said to them: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15). For if “anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14); and “whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 22). Therefore, stretching out his hands toward his disciples, he said: “This is [Col. 0598A] my mother, and these are my brothers” (Luke 18).

Indeed, he laid down his life for them, and they laid down their lives for him. “Skin for skin, and all that a man has, he will give for his life” (Job 2).—“But no one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). The apostles surely sat at the table of their rich friend (Prov. 23), and therefore prepared for him such things as they had received from him. For he had drunk for them, and therefore they drank for him the cup of suffering, according to the Psalm’s saying: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me? I shall take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

“The apostles therefore went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). For his disciples remembered what they had heard from their master saying: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too shall confess him before my Father” (Luke 12); for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10); and “whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his own majesty and that of the Father and the holy angels” (Luke 9). Therefore the Apostle said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world!” (Gal. 6).

Although, then, all saints are honorable before God and venerable in the Church, [Col. 0598C] the apostles are nevertheless to be honored and venerated principally and especially, because they deserved familiarly to see and hear God’s salvation, as the Lord himself declares: “Blessed are those who see what you see and hear what you hear. Amen, I say to you: many kings and prophets wished to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke 10).

By the singular grace of this intimate prerogative, the Lord calls them both brothers and friends (John 15): brothers, as co-heirs of good things; friends, as sharers in secrets. “I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I shall praise you” (Ps. 21). Likewise: “I say to you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill [Col. 0598D] the soul” (Luke 12).

Foreseeing their primacy, the Prophet declared in the Psalm: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened.” There are indeed many things that commend the honorable primacy of the good apostles; but among all these, three are chief: dignity, authority, and power.

Concerning dignity, Truth says to the apostles: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials; and I appoint for you a kingdom, as my Father appointed one for me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22). O how great is the Lord’s condescension, how great the servant’s dignity: namely, that the servant cleaving to the Lord should be established in the kingdom, eat the bread of life which descended from heaven, [Col. 0599A] and drink the wine which flowed from Christ’s side upon the altar-table in the kingdom of the Church Militant (John 16).

Of these, too, it is said to the bride through the Psalmist: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth” (Ps. 64). For the twelve apostles were born to the Church in place of the twelve patriarchs and likewise in place of the prophets; and she appointed them rulers over all the earth. For they are “the princes of the peoples who were gathered with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 16).

Moreover, this primacy does not confer domination but grants ministry; for domination is forbidden and service commanded. As the Lord says to the apostles: “The rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. But not so among you; rather, the greater among you shall be as the younger, and the leader as the servant” (Luke 22). Therefore the Prince of the Apostles said: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5), because “whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14, 18). “For the Lord on high looks upon lowly things, and knows lofty things from afar” (Ps. 112). Therefore it is said: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3).—“Have they made you a ruler? Do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32). For the humbler the eminence, the more exalted the humility; and therefore let those who wish to be exalted be humble.

The Lord recalls and commends authority to the apostles, saying: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). They were made not so much princes of bodies as judges of souls. For at the regeneration, “when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).—“For the Lord comes to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3).—“Her husband is noble in the gates when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 1).

The number twelve is sacred: in the twelve apostles, twelve prophets, twelve patriarchs; in twelve scouts, [Col. 0599D] twelve princes, twelve tribes; in twelve springs, twelve stones, twelve thrones; in twelve hours, twelve months, twelve years; in twelve signs, twelve stars, twelve gems; in twelve gates, twelve corners, and twelve foundations; in twelve rods, twelve cubits, and twelve baskets; in twelve bowls, twelve dishes, and twelve mortars; in twelve oxen, twelve heifers, and twelve rams.

It is an abundant number, consisting of two sixes, signifying the perfection of thought and work, or of mind and body; of three multiplied by four, and four by three, signifying faith in the undivided Trinity and the teaching of the four Gospels; or three Catholic theological virtues and four civic virtues [Note: [Col. 0599D] Something appears to be missing here.]; from the five senses, which concern the body, and the sevenfold gifts, which concern the spirit.

Thus Christ first, with five barley loaves (John 6), on account of the active life served by the bodily senses, and afterward with seven wheaten loaves, on account of the contemplative life served by the gifts of the spirit, satisfied the multitude of the people through the hands of the apostles (Matt. 15). This number, when its parts are added together, increases into sixteen, which consists of ten and six, signifying the fulfillment of the commandments. For there are ten [Col. 0600B] commandments of the Law, which we fulfill in six days, increasing into the perfection of love, which according to the Apostle is known to have sixteen properties. “For love,” he says, “is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own things; is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices with truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails” (1 Cor. 13).

Power is commended and recalled when it is said: “Jesus, having summoned his twelve apostles, gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to cure every disease and [Col. 0600C] every infirmity” (Matt. 10). Hence he said to them: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to the mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matt. 17). For “whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14), because “all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9).

Therefore the disciples returned with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10). For the saints conquered kingdoms through faith (Heb. 11), because “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5). These are they at whose trumpet-blast the walls of Jericho fell (Josh. 6), who in their preaching converted the world from error to truth and from vices to virtues, going into all the world [Col. 0600D] and preaching the Gospel to every creature, teaching all nations to keep whatever God commanded them. Hence they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed (Mark 16). For “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18).—“They proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds” (Ps. 63).

These are the watchmen of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me; when I had passed them by a little, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song 3). Of them the Lord also says through the prophet: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set guards; all day and all night they shall not cease praising the name of the Lord” (Isa. 62).

These are the witnesses, of whom it is written that the apostles gave testimony to Jesus Christ with great power (Acts 4), as he had promised them: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).—“And you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1). Thus, when the apostles had been forbidden to preach in the name of Jesus, they answered: “One must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5). For “there is no other name under heaven in which human beings must be saved” (Acts 4).

These are the heavens of which the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32). For “the Spirit of the Lord adorned the heavens” (Job 26), and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them; and “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues, [Col. 0602A] as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2).

Certainly, although Christ is the first and chief foundation of the Church, of whom the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid, apart from which no other can be laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3), the apostles are nevertheless second and subordinate foundations, of whom the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. 86). Hence the Apostle says: “You are now no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household; built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2).

But since we are unable adequately to set forth the praises of the apostles in worthy proclamations, [Col. 0602B] let us turn to prayers, humbly imploring that those who received from the Lord such dignity, authority, and power, and who merit to obtain whatever they ask in the Savior’s name, may themselves intercede for us by their merits and prayers with him who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages.

### Second Sermon: For the Common of Apostles

On the different cities of God: namely, the heavenly, earthly, spiritual, and bodily.

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601C] “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. 126).

The King of kings, dearest brethren, has different cities in different regions: namely, a heavenly and an earthly city, a spiritual and a bodily one. The heavenly city is the Church of the triumphant; the earthly, the Church of those who fight; the spiritual, the faithful soul; the bodily, wretched Jerusalem. Of the first it is written: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose sharing is in unity itself” (Ps. 121); of the second: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. 47); of the third: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45); of the fourth: “Jesus, seeing the city, wept over it” (Luke 19).

But now I would rather weep over it than say anything. For whose breast is so iron, whose heart so stony, that he does not utter groans and pour out tears when he carefully considers its calamity, so as to be able to say with the prophet: “The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn feast; and her enemies have become head” (Lam. 1). O unhappy outcome—or rather, calamity come to pass. “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a keeper’s hut in an orchard” (Ps. 78). They have poured out the blood of your servants around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them (Jer. 14). “You have made us a reproach to our neighbours, a derision and scorn to those around us” (Ps. 43). Our enemies taunt us, saying: “You trusted in the wood, but behold, he could not save himself” (Matt. 27). Where now is your glorying? Your hope has utterly perished. “Fools, return to your heart, and at last become wise” (Ps. 113).

But you, Lord, answer for us; indeed, answer for yourself, lest our adversaries agree together and say: “Our hand, and not God, has done all these things” (Deut. 32). For unless you guard the city, those who guard it watch in vain. “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15).

The heavenly city, however, is not fortified by guards, because it is not attacked by enemies. In it are security without fear, joy without pain, day without night, life without death. O “how great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30), such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). Blessed is the soul to which it is granted not only to inhabit this city through glory, but also to approach it through grace; not only to behold it through sight, but to conceive it through faith.

Now a city built upon a mountain has a foundation and walls, towers and gates, guards and enemies (Isa. 34). The mountain upon which this city stands is Christ, who grew from a small stone into a great mountain—the mountain upon the summit of the mountains—to whom all nations flow, and of whom he himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). He is the first and chief foundation, as it were the foundation of foundations, of whom the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid, other than which no one can lay another, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3). Upon this foundation the apostles and prophets arise as secondary foundations, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 68).

The walls of the city are all the faithful, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, concerning whom the prophet says: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed guards” (Isa. 62). Yet Christ too is the wall of walls, of whom it is written: “Zion, the city of our strength: the Saviour shall be set in it as a wall” (Isa. 26). Among these walls the perfect rise like towers, pre-eminent in the excellence of their merits, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Let peace be in your strength and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121). Yet Christ too is the tower of towers, of whom it is written: “He has become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” (Ps. 60).

The gates of the city are the teachers of the Church, who bring the nations into the faith, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. 86). Yet Christ too is the door of doors, who says of himself: “I am the door” (John 10), and so forth. The guards of the city are the rulers of the Church, the holy apostles and apostolic men, concerning whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me” (Song 3). Yet Christ too is the guardian of guardians, of whom it is written: “The king of Seir cries to me: ‘Watchman, what of the night?’” (Isa. 21).

In this way, most beloved brethren, the spiritual city has a foundation and walls, towers and gates, guards and enemies. The foundation of the soul is faith, of which the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11). For it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not remain” (Isa. 7).

The soul’s four walls are the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. The wall of justice faces east, through which for those who fear God “the Sun of righteousness rises” (Mal. 4), who “enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1). The wall of fortitude faces north, through which we flee the things of the west, which, according to the prophet, are opened from the north (Jer. 1). The wall of temperance faces south, through which we restrain the allurements by which the heat of desire burns. The wall of prudence faces west, through which we flee the things that lead to setting, lest we perish unhappily with them.

The towers of the soul are the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, which Isaiah enumerates, saying: “Upon him shall rest the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). But, to pass briefly over the matter: charity is the soul’s gate, hope its doorway, and the remaining virtues its bulwarks. The soul’s guards are angels, of whom Truth says: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18).

Each city has many enemies: higher and lower, inner and outer. The higher are malicious demons; the lower are hostile people; the inner are fleshly desires; the outer are worldly allurements. Of the higher the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6); of the lower the Psalmist says: “Sinners have built upon my back; they have prolonged their iniquity” (Ps. 128); of the inner Paul says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5); of the outer John says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for whatever is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John 2).

Unhappy is the person surrounded by so many enemies and attacked by so many foes. Therefore the Apostle cried: “Unhappy man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Certainly, unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain; for “it is not of one who runs or one who wills, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

Against these four enemies the rulers of the Church must carefully keep the four watches of the night; for “shepherds were keeping the watches of the night over their flock” (Luke 2): namely, the first silence of night, cockcrow, the midnight watch, and the pre-dawn watch, during which the guards of a besieged city keep watch in turns. The first watch of the night, then, must be kept against the higher enemies—that is, against the deceits of demons; the second against the lower enemies—that is, against the cunning of people; the third against the inner enemies—that is, against fleshly desires; the fourth against the outer enemies—that is, against worldly allurements.

For the first enemy, like a crafty serpent, deceived Eve; the second, like a deceitful fox, devours the vineyards; the third, like flattering Delilah, ensnares Samson; the fourth, like an enchanting Siren, draws sailors in. Hence perhaps the night office was divided into four parts: three nocturns and morning praises. As tradition relates, divided according to the four watches of the night, the Church of old sang it against the persecutions of the four enemies. The first enemy persecutes through diabolical suggestions; the second through heretical corruptions; the third through empty pleasures; the fourth through worldly ambitions.

But, to leave aside the others, the Church has among human beings themselves various enemies: the impious and schismatics, unbelievers and heretics. Those who strive to divide the head from the members, the father from his sons, and the shepherd from his sheep have not yet entirely abandoned schism; but unless they cease, they shall receive a portion with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive (Num. 16). Nor have heretics yet disappeared, “whose speech spreads like a cancer” (2 Tim. 2), because they offer the venom of asps and the gall of dragons in Babylon’s golden cup (Jer. 51). Mixing falsehood with truth, under the pretext of religion they pour the poison of wickedness into the simple. “They come in sheep’s clothing, though they are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7).

Let us therefore persist diligently and keep watch attentively, so that “we may catch the little foxes that destroy the vineyards: having indeed different mouths, but tails bound together with one another” (Song 2); because “they agree together in vanity” (Ps. 61). If we guard temporal riches carefully, how much more carefully ought we to guard spiritual riches. Whoever steals faith steals life, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1). Whoever takes away charity takes away God, because God is charity. May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed above all for ages of ages, guard his city from these enemies through the merits and prayers of blessed N., the apostle. Amen.

## SERMON III. FOR THE COMMON OF EVANGELISTS

Concerning the fourfold sense of paradise, according to which the words of the theme are expounded in four ways: historically, allegorically, morally, and anagogically.

[Col. 0605B]

“A river went out from the place of delight to water paradise; it is divided into four heads: Pishon and Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates” (Gen. 2).

A fourfold paradise is found in Holy Scripture: higher and lower, inner and outer. The higher is heavenly; the lower is earthly; the inner, spiritual; the outer, bodily. The heavenly is in the homeland; the earthly, on the way; the spiritual, in the mind; the bodily, in the east. Of the higher paradise it is said to Lucifer: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). Of the lower it is said to the angel of Ephesus: “To the conqueror I shall give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2). Of the spiritual it is written in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). Of the bodily it is written in Genesis: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.”

According to this fourfold understanding of the name “paradise,” the proposed words can be expounded in four ways: historically, allegorically, morally, and anagogically. Historically, a certain spring bursts forth from the midst of paradise to water the grasses and trees of paradise. Proceeding from paradise, it is carried into four heads, which are the four rivers of paradise.

Allegorically, the river which goes out from the place of delight is evangelical preaching, which proceeds from the Lord Jesus Christ. He is the fountain of life, in whose light we shall see light, from whom every true delight generally flows. “Come to me,” he says, “all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and you shall find rest for your souls, for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. 33).

This preaching is rightly compared to a river, not only because it refreshes, washes, and makes fruitful, but because a river is called flowing water. As Solomon says: “Deep water is the words from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing torrent is the fountain of wisdom” (Prov. 18). It has flowed so far and wide that it has filled the whole world, according to what the Lord himself commanded the apostles, saying: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). Therefore, “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18).

It waters paradise—that is, it makes the Church fruitful—according to the Apostle’s words: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase” (1 Cor. 3). For this is the fountain of gardens, the well of living waters flowing mightily from Lebanon (Song 4). This river is divided into four heads because the preaching of Jesus Christ is distributed into the four Gospels. Although many wrote Gospels—for, as Luke testifies, “many have undertaken to arrange a narrative of those things which have been fulfilled among us” (Luke 1)—only four were received by the Church: those of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

This occurred for several reasons. First, to show the harmony of the two Testaments. For just as in the Old Testament there was one lawgiver, namely Moses; four major prophets, namely Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel; twelve minor prophets; and many other wise men, such as Job, David, Solomon, and Jesus [Sirach], so in the New Testament there was one lawgiver, namely Christ; four Evangelists, namely Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; twelve apostles; and many other teachers, such as Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and Gregory. Thus it may be shown that “wheel is contained within wheel” (Ezek. 1), and that the two seraphim look toward one another with their faces turned toward the propitiatory [mercy-seat] (Exod. 25).

Second, because of the mystery of Aminadab’s chariot, of which the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My soul was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6). Aminadab means “spontaneous of God.” This is Christ, “who became obedient unto death” (Phil. 2), and “was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53). His chariot is evangelical teaching, by which Christ’s fame is borne throughout the whole world. Its four wheels are the four Evangelists. Because of this chariot the bride—that is, the Church—is troubled with saving grief unto repentance.

Third, it signifies the liberation of the human race from fourfold death—that is, from fourfold transgression. The first transgression was that of the commandment in paradise; the second, transgression of natural law; the third, transgression of written law; the fourth, transgression of the Gospel. Or rather: the sin of frailty through incapacity; the sin of simplicity through ignorance; the sin of security through negligence; and the sin of malice through envy. For in these four ways of sin the soul dies—that is, it is separated from God—perhaps by reason of the mystery of the square. For as the square is more solid and stable than other shapes, so among all teachings the Gospel endures more solidly and stably. For the square stands firm on every side, and the Gospel, because of its stability, is called eternal; by its grace a person is made square in morals—that is, strengthened in virtues.

The Gospels of these men rather than of others were received, both because they described evangelical history more carefully and clearly, and because, although they wrote things at times varied, they never wrote things contrary; although at times different, never opposed. Since these four were prefigured by the figures of the four living creatures in the vision of John (Rev. 4) and Ezekiel, Matthew is represented by the human being, because his purpose is especially concerned with writing Christ’s humanity. Thus his book begins with Christ’s human birth: “The book,” he says, “of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1).

Mark is represented by the lion, because his purpose is especially concerned with describing Christ’s resurrection. Hence his Gospel is read pre-eminently on the day of the Resurrection. For it is said that a lion, with a great roar, rouses its cubs on the third day. Thus God the Father, by immeasurable power, raised his Son on the third day. “Therefore Mark also begins with a cry, saying: ‘The voice of one crying,’ and so forth” (Mark 1). This is “the strongest lion among beasts, which fears no encounter” (Prov. 30); how great his holiness was is clearly shown by his tunic, preserved in this very church of his.

Luke is represented by the calf, because his purpose is especially concerned with writing Christ’s Passion, in which Christ offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father: himself both priest and sacrifice. For a calf was the priest’s sacrifice. Thus he begins with the priesthood, saying: “In the days of Herod, king of Judaea, there was a certain priest,” and so forth (Luke 1).

John is represented by the eagle, because while the others walked with the Lord upon earth, he flew into heaven to describe Christ’s divinity and said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). These four principal purposes are signified by the figures of those four living creatures. Each of them, according to Ezekiel’s vision (ch. 1), has four faces, because all treat of each subject, although some treat more principally of particular subjects—especially since all treat of Christ, to whom those four figures belong. For he was a human being in being born, a calf in dying, a lion in rising again, and an eagle in ascending.

These are Pishon and Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates. Pishon means “change of mouth,” and signifies John, who changes his mouth when he descends from divinity to humanity or ascends from humanity to divinity. Thus, after saying of divinity, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” he next descends to humanity, saying: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

Gihon means “gaping of the earth,” and signifies Matthew, who describes Christ’s human generation, of which the Prophet says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked forth from heaven” (Ps. 84)—that is, Christ was born from Mary. Tigris means “swift,” signifying Mark, who more swiftly—that is, more briefly—describes evangelical history than the others. The figure of the lion is suitably applied to him, for it is a most swift animal. Euphrates means “fruit-bearing,” signifying Luke, to whom, according to the prophetic vision, the figure of the calf is applied, for it serves in cultivating crops; and he himself describes the blessed fruit of the womb.

These four are also signified by the four rings of the ark, which were round and golden (Exod. 25). In gold brightness is signified; in roundness eternity, because the round has neither beginning nor end. They are aptly signified by golden rings, since they describe Christ’s eternal brightness and bright eternity. By the two rings on the left are signified the two Evangelists who did not receive the teaching of the Gospel from Christ: one from Peter, namely Mark; the other from Paul, namely Luke. By the two on the right are signified those two whom Christ himself taught: Matthew and John.

Some, however, understand Matthew and John by the two rings on the left, since they adhered to the Lord while he was still capable of suffering and mortal; and Mark and Luke by the two on the right, since after the Ascension they adhered to Christ, now made immortal and incapable of suffering. For the left signifies mortality and the right immortality, according to the words: “His left hand is under my head and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). For this reason, in paintings in churches Paul is placed at the right and Peter at the left of the Saviour.

Morally, the river which goes out from the place of delight is the infusion of grace, proceeding from the Holy Spirit, who is the delight of the Father and the Son, their love and bond. Of him the Psalmist says: “You shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35). It waters paradise—that is, it makes the mind drunk—according to what is said earlier in the Psalm: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house” (ibid.).

[Col. 0609A]

It is divided into four heads—that is, into the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Morally, these are the four rivers of paradise, concerning which Truth says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). But he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive.

Anagogically, the river which goes out from the place of delight is the abundance of blessedness that proceeds from the enjoyment of God. It waters paradise—that is, it gladdens the homeland—according to the saying: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45). It is divided into four kinds: two belonging to the robe of the body, and as many belonging to the robe of the soul. To the former belong brightness and impassibility; to the latter, knowledge and delight.

Of the brightness of the body it is written: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). Of the impassibility of the flesh it is written: “God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; and there shall no longer be either mourning or crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21). Of the mind’s knowledge Truth says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). There we shall know as we also are known, seeing not through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face (1 Cor. 13). Of the delight of the heart the Psalmist says: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. 149).

There our joy shall be fulfilled, surpassing every sense. May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed above all for ages of ages, grant us to attain it through his ineffable mercy, by the merits and prayers of the most blessed N., the evangelist. Amen.

## SERMON IV. FOR THE COMMON OF ONE MARTYR

Concerning self-denial and its five degrees; and concerning the mystery and sacrament of the holy cross.

[Col. 0609C]

“Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9).

To those wishing to go after Christ, two things are chiefly said: namely, to deny themselves and to take up the cross after Christ. This is “to turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36), so that where the loftiness of the head has gone before, the humility of the body may follow. This denial has five degrees, because a Christian ought to deny not only what belongs to others, but what is his own; not only his own things, but himself; not only himself, but his own self; not only his own self, but his very self.

He denies what belongs to others who neither keeps what is offered to him nor desires to take it away; hence Zacchaeus says: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). He denies his own things who neither clings to what he has acquired nor longs to acquire more; hence Peter says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19). He denies himself who chastises the desires of the flesh; hence Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery” (1 Cor. 9). He denies his own self who empties the desires of the mind; hence David says: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. 130). He denies his very self who renounces his own will; hence Jesus says: “Not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14).

Therefore, when the glutton becomes sober, the lustful chaste, the greedy generous, the proud humble, the angry gentle, and, to speak generally, when the criminal becomes virtuous, then he denies his very self, so that he can say with the Apostle: “I now live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). But when an impious person turns from impiety, he can indeed say: “I am not what I was,” because he is no longer such in guilt, although he is the same in nature, according to that prophetic saying: “Turn the impious, and they shall not be” (Prov. 12).

Whoever, therefore, wishes to go after Christ, let him deny his very self. But if, according to Truth’s testimony, it depends upon the human will that, by denying his very self, a person may go after Christ, why does the Apostle say: “It is not of one who wills, nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9)? This is said because a good work belongs more principally to God’s mercy than to a human will. For divine mercy not only precedes and prepares, but also follows and accompanies the human will. It precedes by inspiring and follows by helping; it prepares so that the will may begin and accompanies it so that it may finish.

Of mercy that precedes, the Prophet says in the Psalm: “His mercy shall precede me” (Ps. 58). Of mercy that follows, he says elsewhere: “Your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22). For grace works principally, and free choice cooperates secondarily, as the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me has not been empty” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore Truth says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny his very self, take up his cross, and follow me.”

He says “his own,” that is, voluntary rather than forced; willing rather than unwilling; through the virtue of patience rather than through the servitude of compulsory labour. For forced service does not please him who requires the heart rather than the hand, the will rather than the act. Jesus willingly bore the cross, of whom it is written: “Bearing his cross for himself, he went out to the place called Calvary” (John 19). Simon of Cyrene bore the cross unwillingly, of whom it is written that “they compelled him to carry Jesus’ cross” (Matt. 27).

O how profound is the mystery of the cross; how lofty its sacrament! It is written that Moses, at the Lord’s command, raised up a bronze serpent as a sign; those bitten by serpents were healed when they looked at it (Num. 21). Christ himself explains this in the Gospel, saying: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish” (John 3).

It is also written that when Joseph brought Manasseh and Ephraim to Jacob, placing the elder at his right and the younger at his left so that he might bless them in due order, Jacob changed his hands—that is, crossing them in the form of a cross—and placed his right hand upon the head of the younger Ephraim and his left upon the head of the elder Manasseh, and said: “The angel who rescued me from all evils, bless these boys” (Gen. 48), and so forth.

Ezekiel heard the Lord saying to the man clothed in linen, having a writer’s inkhorn at his loins: “Pass through the midst of the city, and mark a *tau* on the foreheads of the men who mourn and groan” (Ezek. 9). After this he said to seven men: “Pass through the midst of the city and strike everyone upon whom you do not find the *tau*” (ibid.). “Let not your eye spare anyone.” John likewise saw “an angel coming up from the rising of the sun, holding the seal of the living God; and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: ‘Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have marked the servants of our God upon their foreheads’” (Rev. 7).

Hence, when the Lord struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, he passed over the houses of the Hebrews unharmed because he saw blood upon the lintel and upon both doorposts (Exod. 12). While Moses held his hands stretched out, Israel, fighting, overcame Amalek (Exod. 17).

The wood cast into the waters at Marah sweetened the bitter waters (Exod. 15). And when wood was cast into the Jordan, the iron that had fallen off floated up (4 Kings 6). This is the tree of life in the midst of paradise (Gen. 2), concerning which the Wise Man declares: “Blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes to pass—salvation” (Wis. 14). For God reigned from the wood; indeed, “he set right the world, which shall not be moved” (Ps. 95). Those who said, “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2), did not know the sacraments of God, nor did they comprehend “what is the length and breadth, height and depth” (Eph. 3).

Therefore the cross restores health, bestows blessing, distinguishes from unbelievers, delivers from dangers, drives out enemies, and makes victors. The cross is the mystery of faith, the support of hope, the key of knowledge, the form of justice, the magnificence of kings, the glory of priests, the support of the needy, the consolation of the poor, the guide of the blind, the staff of the lame, the hope of the despairing, the resurrection of the dead.

The cross is taken up both spiritually and materially. Spiritually it is taken up in two ways: through the compassion of the mind and through affliction of the flesh. Therefore the Apostle says: “They have crucified their members with their vices and desires” (Gal. 5); and again: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). Whenever a person is tortured in heart by compassion for a neighbour, he certainly takes up the cross with the Apostle, who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). But whenever he is tortured in body, afflicting his very self, he likewise takes up the cross with the Apostle, who says: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

Materially also the cross is taken up in two ways: as a sign of religion and as the punishment of suffering. As a sign of religion, certain religious persons bear the cross to show that they are spiritually dedicated to the service of the crucified one. As punishment, both some good and some evil persons, who are suspended upon crosses for justice or for an offence, bear it—just as two thieves were crucified beside Jesus’ cross, one at the right and the other at the left (Matt. 27).

There were four pieces of wood in the Lord’s cross: the upright stake, the transverse beam, the support beneath, and the title above. There were also four nails, by which the hands were fastened and the feet fixed; there was also the lance by which the side was opened; and there was a crown of thorns placed around the head.

[Col. 0612C]

All these things, brethren, can also be assigned spiritually in the spiritual cross. For the four timbers of the cross are the four virtues of the mind: faith, hope, perseverance, and patience. Of these the Apostle says: “That you may comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth, height and depth” (Eph. 3). The length of the cross is perseverance, of which the Lord says: “Whoever perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). The breadth of the cross is patience, of which Truth says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21). The depth of the cross is faith, of which the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11). The height of the cross is hope, of which the Psalmist says: “In your word I have hoped beyond hope” (Ps. 118).

Thus Christ’s cross had one upright timber in length and another transverse one in breadth. By these two timbers were mystically signified those which the poor widow of Zarephath gathered (3 Kings 17). And fittingly the upright stake had a support below and a title above, because perseverance proceeds from faith to hope, as an upright stake from the support beneath to the title above. Understanding this, Job says: “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see God. I myself shall see him and not another, and my eyes shall behold him. This hope is laid up in my bosom” (Job 19).

For unless the cross has the foundation of faith and the title of hope, it is certainly only punishment and not merit. That patience pertains to the cross is sufficiently evident in itself, because the patient endure torment amid adverse tribulations; hence the Apostle James says: “Tribulation works patience” (Jas. 1). Concerning perseverance likewise it is written: “Be faithful unto death, and I shall give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2). Moreover, according to the Apostle, “no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). Perseverance, therefore, which crowns, itself has a contest, so that it rightly pertains to the cross.

On these two pieces of wood the Christian must nail his two feet and two hands, with four nails. The four nails are the four principal virtues: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. The feet are the affections of the mind [Col. 0613B], of which the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5). And the Lord says to the Apostles: “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13); and again: “Shake the dust from your feet” (Mark 6). Thus the two feet are the two affections of the mind: fear and desire. For the chief inclination of the mind lies either in fleeing what it fears or in choosing what it desires.

The foot of fear must be nailed with the nail of fortitude, lest the fearful person collapse because of adversities. For when fear in Peter was not fixed with the nail of fortitude, he denied at a servant-girl’s voice (Luke 22); but when it was fixed with the nail of fortitude, he preached the Lord’s name before kings and governors [Col. 0613C]. Yet fear itself is a certain nail, of which the Psalmist says: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118 [119]). But one nail is fixed by another when fear is strengthened by fortitude.

The foot of desire must be nailed with the nail of justice, lest the covetous person stray into unlawful desires. For if desire is not fixed, then the flesh desires against the spirit; if it is fixed, the spirit desires against the flesh. Thus the Christian must fasten his nails to the cross, lest he either collapse through fear or wander through covetousness.

The spear with which the side must be wounded is charity, of which the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by charity.” The side lies next to the heart, by whose power we love; and it must therefore be wounded, so that its effect may go forth [Col. 0613D], not only toward friends but also toward enemies, as the Lord commands: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5).

The crown of thorns is repentance itself, to be placed around the head—that is, the mind—of which the Psalmist says [Col. 0614A]: “I was turned in my misery while the thorn is driven in” (Ps. 31 [32]). This crown consists of three thorns: contrition, confession, and satisfaction. The first pierces the heart because of vain thought; the second pierces the mouth because of vain speech; the third pierces the hand because of wrongful action. The first pierces through grief, the second through shame, the third through labour.

The hands are works, of which the Psalmist says: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle” (Ps. 143 [144]). And Solomon: “She gave him wool and flax, and worked according to the counsel of her hands” (Prov. 31). Thus there are two hands, two kinds of works: namely, the work of will and the work of necessity. For every work is voluntary or necessary [Col. 0614B].

The hand of voluntary work must be nailed with the nail of prudence, lest, being crooked, it perform works of darkness. For when Saul’s hand was not fixed with the nail of prudence, Saul persecuted the Church; but when Paul’s hand was fixed with the nail of prudence, Paul suffered for the Church.

The hand of necessary work must be nailed with the nail of temperance, lest it be stretched too loosely toward excess and superfluity. Necessary works are sleeping, eating, and the like; these we must regulate with moderation, so that we temper sleep with prayers and vigils, and food with almsgiving and fasting. With these, as with mighty weapons, we shall be able to overcome our enemies.

For we read that when Israel fought Amalek in the wilderness, Israel prevailed while Moses prayed; but when he ceased, Israel was defeated (Exod. 17). We also read that when the other tribes fought Benjamin because of the Levite’s wife, they were defeated in battle twice, until, after a fast had been proclaimed and humbly observed, they almost utterly destroyed that tribe (Judg. 20) [Col. 0614C].

Moreover, it is not enough for anyone to deny himself and take up his cross unless he follows Christ. For there have been certain philosophers, and there are certain heretics, who have denied themselves and endured severe sufferings; yet this did not profit them, nor does it profit them unto salvation, because they do not follow him who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), namely Jesus Christ, who suffered for us, leaving an example that we should follow in his footsteps: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2) [Col. 0614D].

Therefore, brothers, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, let us crucify our members with their vices and lusts, so that, by following Christ, we may attain eternal life, through his grant—he who is God blessed above all things for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. FOR THE COMMON OF ONE MARTYR

Concerning the twofold crown of the saints, and their precious stones and flowers.

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613D] “You have placed, O Lord, upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Ps. 20 [21]).

[Col. 0614D] The crown of the saints is twofold: one by which they are crowned on the way, another by which they are crowned in their homeland; [Col. 0615A] one given for merit, the other given as reward; one of virtue and grace, the other of salvation and glory; one belonging to those who fight, the other to those who triumph.

The crown of virtue is silver, illumined by the brightness of grace; the crown of salvation is gold, illumined by the splendour of glory [variant: “irradiated”]. Of the first the Psalmist says: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Ps. 64 [65]), that is, you will multiply virtues in the time of grace; whence he adds: “And your fields shall be filled with abundance” (ibid.). Of the second the Apostle says: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4), that is, the reward which will be rendered for merits; whence he adds: “Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” (ibid.).

Both around the rim and at the summit of the crown are precious stones and very beautiful flowers, together with pearls and gems arranged in marvellous variety [Col. 0615B]. Each adjacent stone has two paired flowers, between which are set smaller gems, surrounded by the finest pearls.

The crown of virtue has around its rim four principal stones, that is, the four civic virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Justice is at the front, prudence at the back, temperance on the right, and fortitude on the left. The positions suit the stones well: what lies in front is certain; what lies behind is doubtful; what lies to the right is prosperous; what lies to the left is adverse. Justice must be exercised in matters certain; prudence must be employed in matters doubtful; temperance is needed in prosperity; fortitude is necessary in adversity.

These are the four fingers concerning which Exodus commands: “You shall make a chased crown four fingers high, and above that crown a little golden crown” (Exod. 25) [Col. 0615C]. Justice has two associated virtues, discernment and rectitude; prudence, watchfulness and caution; temperance, continence and abstinence; fortitude, constancy and magnanimity.

Between these flowers stand four smaller gems: the four natural affections, grief and joy, fear and hope, of which it is written:

> Hence men fear, desire, rejoice, and suffer grief.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.733)

Justice directs hope; prudence moderates [Col. 0615D] grief; temperance shapes joy; fortitude strengthens fear. Around the gems on the rim shine seven pearls, that is, the seven gifts of sevenfold grace, which Isaiah enumerates, saying: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, etc., shall rest upon him” (Isa. 2).

At the summit of the crown are arranged three principal stones, namely the three theological virtues: hope, faith, and charity. Above these is set the fear of the Lord, Scripture saying: “You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward shall not be made void. You who fear God, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened” (Ecclus. 2).

These stones too have adjacent flowers: faith has sincerity and truth; hope, patience and perseverance; charity, kindness and generosity; fear, obedience [Col. 0616A] and reverence. Between these flowers stand three smaller gems: the natural powers of the soul, the rational power, the irascible power, and the concupiscible power. The first distinguishes good from evil; the second rejects evil; the third chooses good. Faith enlightens reason; hope strengthens the irascible faculty; charity forms the concupiscible faculty.

Around these gems likewise shine seven pearls, namely the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer: three pertaining to the present life, three to the life to come, and the middle one pertaining to both.

But the crown of salvation is far more precious and worthy. It has four principal stones around its rim and three chief stones at its summit. The principal stones around the rim are the four properties [Col. 0616B] of the glorified body: brightness, subtlety, agility, and impassibility. Of these Truth says: “They shall give into your bosom good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6). “For the righteous shall shine, and shall run swiftly like sparks among reeds, and their Lord shall reign for ever” (Wis. 3); and they themselves shall be impassible with the Lord. “For God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, etc.” (Rev. 21).

For in the homeland there will be joy without grief, security without fear, rest without labour, life without death, day without night, certainty without perhaps, strength without weakness, rectitude without perversity, beauty without deformity.

Christ showed these properties of the glorified body, as evidence of future glorification, even in mortal flesh [Col. 0616C]. He showed brightness when he was transfigured on the mountain and “his face shone like the sun” (Matt. 17); subtlety when, “with the virginal seal closed,” he came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber (Ps. 18 [19]); agility when he crossed over the water with dry footstep (John 6); impassibility when he gave his body and blood to the disciples at supper (Matt. 26).

The chief stones at the summit are the three properties of the glorified soul: knowledge, love, and delight. After the Wise Man had said, “The righteous shall shine, etc.” (Wis. 3), he immediately added: “Those who trust in him shall understand truth, and the faithful shall rest in love in him; for gift and peace are for God’s elect” (ibid.) [Col. 0616D].

For the saints possess comprehensive knowledge, by which they know even as they are known: seeing not through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face (1 Cor. 13), the Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity; reading in the Word of life, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (John 17). Of this knowledge Truth says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (1 Cor. 13).

From this comprehensive knowledge proceeds the highest love, by which the saints love God “with their whole heart, with their whole mind, and with their whole soul” (Matt. 22). “With the mind,” that is, with memory, they love the Father “wholly,” that is, without forgetfulness; “with the heart,” that is, with the understanding [Col. 0617A], they love the Son “wholly,” that is, without error; “with the soul,” that is, with the will, they love the Holy Spirit “wholly,” that is, without opposition. For through charity they cleave so completely to the divine will that they will nothing at all except what they know God wills.

From this highest love is born ineffable delight, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). Of it the Psalmist says: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places” (Ps. 149) [Col. 0618A]; and again: “I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and praise, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41 [42]).

May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed above all things for ever and ever, bring us to that exultation and those feasts through the merits and prayers of the holy martyr N. Amen.

## SERMON VI. FOR THE COMMON OF SEVERAL MARTYRS

Concerning twofold tribulation, by whom it is inflicted, and the many great tribulations endured by the holy martyrs; finally, concerning the threefold washing of regeneration, the threefold robe, and blood.

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617B] “These are they who came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7).

Most beloved brothers, Scripture speaks of a twofold tribulation: one of faults and vices, the other of punishments and torments; one of adversity, the other of perversity. Of the first it is written: “They were made few, and were afflicted by tribulation of evils and sorrow” (Ps. 106 [107]); of the second: “They cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and he delivered them from their necessities” (ibid.).

Oh, how grievous is the tribulation of sinners, who always bear within themselves “the worm of conscience, which does not die, and the fire of reason, which is never extinguished” (Isa. 66). “There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 57). For “when the wicked man comes into the depth [Col. 0617C] of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18); and “by the things through which a man sins, by those he is also tormented” (Wis. 2).

Pride puffs up; avarice pricks; envy gnaws; anger inflames; gluttony distresses; lust dissolves; lying binds; murder stains—and so do the other monstrosities of vices. Thus the things that are pleasures of sin to a human being become instruments of punishment to God.

Three enemies inflict this tribulation: the world, the flesh, and the devil. The world, sweet like a siren, drowns those who sail; the flesh, flattering like Delilah, ensnares Samson; the devil, raging like a lion, kills travellers. Of the first Truth says: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John 15). Of the second the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5). Of the third [Col. 0617D] it is written: “Your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5).

These are the three deceptive sophists who miserably reason falsely with the unwary. The world supplies the major premise, the flesh adopts the minor premise, and the devil draws the conclusion. The world supplies worldly enticements; the flesh accepts unlawful desires; the devil concludes with everlasting torments. The world provides the wood, the flesh applies the spark, the devil kindles the fire. The first enemy must be despised, the second restrained, the third overcome.

Against the first it is commanded [Col. 0618B]: “Do not love the world, nor the things which are in the world; for whatever is in the world is either the lust of the flesh, or the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John 2). These are the pieces of wood supplied by the world. Against the second it is commanded: “Flee fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2). This is the spark supplied by the flesh. Against the third it is likewise commanded: “Take up the shield of faith, that you may be able to extinguish the fiery darts of the evil one” (Eph. 6). This is the fire kindled by the devil.

The glorious martyrs came forth from this tribulation “by a journey of three days, that they might sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness” (Exod. 3). The way of the first day is the avoidance of prohibitions; the way of the second day is the performance of commandments [Col. 0618C]; the way of the third day is the supererogation of counsels (Job 4). By the first way is fulfilled this commandment: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Matt. 7). By the second way is fulfilled this precept: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (ibid.). By the third way is fulfilled this counsel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19). Of these ways it is written: “I will exercise myself in your commandments and consider your ways” (Ps. 118 [119]).

But in this very life they suffered many and great tribulations. They were afflicted in heart, afflicted in speech, and afflicted in deed. They were afflicted in heart through sorrows and griefs; in speech through insults and terrors; in deed through straits and labours. Through the pains of contrition and the sorrows of compassion; through the terrors of threats and the insults of mockery; through the labours of affliction and the straits of suffering.

Of tribulations of heart the Psalmist says [Col. 0618D]: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50 [51]). And the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). Of tribulations of speech the Lord says through the prophet: “I have endured insults [Col. 0619A] and terrors from them, and the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior” (Jer. 20); and elsewhere: “All who saw me despised me; they spoke with their lips and shook their head” (Ps. 21 [22]). Of tribulations of deed the Psalmist speaks in the person of the martyrs: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been considered like sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43 [44]); and again: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 65 [66]).

For while the saints are pilgrims from the Lord in this valley of tears, they are afflicted in many ways and by various persons, in many places and at diverse times. The Apostle quite expressly indicates the diversity of the ways and places, saying: “The saints endured mockery and scourges, moreover also chains and prisons; they were stoned, sawn apart, tempted, put to death by the sword; they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, on mountains, in caves and caverns of the earth” (Heb. 11) [Col. 0619B].

It is as though he said: They were afflicted by so many, such great, and such diverse means—not only in cities but also in deserts; not only in plains but also on mountains; not only in houses but also in caves; not only in prisons but also in caverns of the earth. They endured the tribulations of this world from beasts, from human beings, and from demons.

They were afflicted by beasts, as the Psalmist says: “They gave the mortal remains of your saints, etc., to the beasts of the earth” (Ps. 78 [79]). They were afflicted by human beings, as it is written: “When people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123 [124]) [Col. 0619C]. They were afflicted by demons, as the Apostle testifies: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6).

They are afflicted not only by strangers but also by parents and relatives; not only by outsiders but also by members of their own household; not only by enemies but also by friends. Truth proves this, saying: “You will be handed over by parents and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death” (Luke 21).

Moreover, they were afflicted before the law, under the law, and after the law: before the law the patriarchs were afflicted; under the law, the prophets; after the law, the apostles [Col. 0619D], and likewise the martyrs. For Truth says: “Behold, I send to you prophets, priests, and scribes; and some of them you will kill, scourge, and crucify, so that upon you may come all righteous blood that has been shed, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 22).

Before the law, Abel; under the law, Zachariah; after the law—that is, in the time of grace—prophets, priests, and scribes. Hence the Church laments, saying: “Often have they attacked me from my youth; yet they could not prevail against me. Sinners built upon my back,” etc. (Ps. 128 [129]).

Let us therefore, brothers, imitate in them the virtues of heart and deed, and detest in ourselves the frailty of mind and flesh. They endured for Christ [variant: “for sin,” Col. 0620A] cold and nakedness; but we dress in double garments and clothe ourselves in costly attire. They endured for Christ hunger and thirst; but we consume diverse dishes and feast on delicacies. They endured for Christ vigils and labours; but we rest for ample hours and sleep in long slumbers. They endured for Christ straits and pains; but we enjoy worldly pleasures and delight in the allurements of the flesh.

Alas for me! What shall I, wretched man, say or do when that most strict Judge comes, who “will render to each according to his works?” (Matt. 16). This is a terrible place; for “if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4). “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them” (Ps. 33 [34]) [Col. 0620B].

These, then, are they who came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. The washing of justification is threefold: in tears of regeneration, in water of redemption, and in blood of suffering. Of the first the Psalmist says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6). Of the second Truth says: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Of the third John testifies: “He washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1).

Likewise there is a threefold robe: the first, of innocence; the second, of grace; and the third, of glory. Of the first the father says to his servants: “Quickly bring forth the first robe and put it on him,” etc. (Luke 15). In saying “first,” he indicated a second; for “first” is said in relation to “second” [Col. 0620C]. Of the third it is written: “The Lord loved him and adorned him; he clothed him with a robe of glory” (Ecclus. 15).

This threefold robe is washed in that threefold washing—or rather, the person clothed with the robes is washed. Yet each robe is washed in the blood of the Lamb. But there is blood of guilt, blood of punishment, and blood of pardon. Of the first blood it is written: “Blood touched blood” (Hos. 4). From this blood the Psalmist asks to be delivered when he says: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50 [51]). Of the second blood it is written: “They poured out the blood of your saints around Jerusalem” (Ps. 78 [79]). For this blood the choir of martyrs asks vengeance, saying [Col. 0620D]: “Avenge our blood which has been shed, O our God” (Rev. 6). Of the third blood it is written: “This is the blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26).

By this blood the human race has been redeemed, because “we were redeemed not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb” (1 Pet. 1). The malignant dragon instils the first blood through wicked suggestion; the impious dog draws the second blood through savage affliction; the most pure Lamb sheds the third blood because of exceeding love. For he so loved us that he shed his blood for us. “No one has greater charity, etc.” (John 15).

“What then shall I render to the Lord for all that [Col. 0621A] he has rendered to me? I shall receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115 [116]). Thus our martyrs rendered to him, who came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb: not the lamb of the flock, not the lamb of the law, nor the lamb of the daily sacrifice, but the Lamb of the King, who takes away the sins of the world. Of him it is said: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16).

Samuel sacrificed the lamb of the flock at Mizpah, asking that lightning, clouds, and thunder be given from heaven; and on that day the Lord delivered Jerusalem from the hand of the Philistines (1 Sam. 7). The children of Israel sacrificed the lamb of the law at the borders of Rameses, smearing the doorposts and lintels with its blood [Col. 0622A]; and on that night the Lord delivered their firstborn from the destroyer (Exod. 12). The lamb of the daily sacrifice was offered by the priests morning and evening, “as a most sweet savour to the Lord” (Num. 28).

These are they who came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Since “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15), let us also, by the example of the holy martyrs, wash our robes—that is, our works—in the blood of the Lamb, that is, in faith in Christ’s Passion; he mercifully granting it, who is God blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON VII. FOR THE COMMON OF SEVERAL MARTYRS

Concerning the various furnaces of the good and the evil, their instruments, and how the holy martyrs were tested in the furnace of patience.

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621B] “The Lord tested the elect as gold in a furnace” (Wis. 3).

Holy Scripture distinguishes for us various furnaces: one of the good, in which the righteous are purified; and another of the evil, in which the reprobate are tormented. Of the first it is written: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter” (Ecclus. 27); of the second: “The smoke of the pit rose like the smoke of a great furnace” (Rev. 9).

But each furnace is twofold: one interior, of the mind; the other exterior, of the flesh. The interior furnace of the blessed is the affliction of repentance, through which penitents are purified from iniquity; their exterior furnace is the tribulation of patience, through which the patient are tested in charity. In the latter gold is tested; in the former silver is purified.

But the interior furnace [Col. 0621C] of the evil is the worm of conscience, through which the impious are spiritually tormented on account of guilt; their exterior furnace is the fire of Gehenna, through which the reprobate are bodily tortured in punishment. In the latter iron is burned; in the former lead is consumed.

Materially, in a material furnace, there are bellows, fire, and coal; tongs and a sprinkler. These may be assigned spiritually in the spiritual furnace. In the furnace of repentance, the breathing bellows are the fear of reflection; the burning fire is the pain of compunction; the glowing coal is the shame of confession; the gripping tongs are the labour of satisfaction; the dripping sprinkler is the love of justification. For the penitent reflects in fear, is pricked in grief, confesses in shame [Col. 0621D], makes satisfaction with labour, and is justified by love.

Yet the order of this justification should be observed. Fear proceeds and introduces love; love follows and brings in grief; grief approaches and produces shame; shame proceeds and brings forth labour. For the sinner fears as he reflects upon judgment, knowing the Judge to be most powerful, most wise, and most just.

He is most powerful indeed, because “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32 [33]) [Col. 0622B]; he calls the stars and they say, “Here we are” (Baruch 3); “he makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103 [104]). Nothing at all resists his will (Rom. 9); no word is impossible for him (Luke 1); winds and sea obey him (Matt. 8); and “every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” bends to him (Phil. 2).

He is most wise because “all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4); he searches hearts and reins (Rev. 2); he “numbers the drops of rain and the sand of the sea” (Ecclus. 1). The God of knowledges, the Lord who foreknows all and knows each individual, knows all things and penetrates all things, the hidden searcher of every hidden thing. “And it shall be,” he says, “on that day that I shall search Jerusalem with lamps” (Zeph. 2).

He is most just, because God is a just, mighty, and long-suffering judge; just and terrible above all gods (Ps. 7), exacting what is his down to the last farthing (Matt. 5). He turns aside from the path of rectitude neither for a price, nor for love, nor for hatred; but always proceeds by the royal road, leaves no evil unpunished, and no good unrewarded. “For he shall judge the world in equity” (Ps. 95 [96]) [Col. 0622C], and “who shall stand to see him?” (Mal. 3).

Blessed are those who will be presented as judges in that judgment, not as persons to be judged. “For it is exceedingly dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10).
