Therefore the prophet David cried: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142 [143]). If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where shall the impious and the sinner appear?

As he considers these things and others like them, how greatly the sinner is troubled by godly fear, how violently shaken by trembling, knowing the Judge to be most powerful, from whom he cannot flee [Col. 0623A], as the prophet says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138 [139]); most wise, from whom he cannot hide, as the Prophet says: “The Ancient of Days sat, and books were opened before him” (Dan. 7); most just, whom he cannot corrupt, as the Prophet says: “He will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61 [62]).

Who, then, would not fear that tribunal, in which the same one will be accuser and witness, advocate and judge? He will say to those who are on his left: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat; I was thirsty, and you did not give me to drink. For when you did not do it to one of my least ones, neither did you do it to me” (Matt. 25).

At these words the bellows of fear breathe, and kindle the fire of grief in the furnace of the penitent, according to that prophetic saying [Col. 0623B]: “From your fear, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26). “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, O Lord, have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 51 [52]).

For the penitent grieves, sighs, and groans, not only because he has committed evil, but also because he has omitted good; not only because he has deserved condemnation, but also because he has forfeited glorification. “For one who offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 1). “For the end of the commandment is charity, from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1). Whoever therefore sins against charity fulfils no commandment.

Let him know himself to be culpably hard and harshly blameworthy who mourns the bodily death of his friend but does not mourn the spiritual death of his own soul, which, once charity is extinguished, immediately overwhelms it [Col. 0623C]. Therefore let him grieve, groan, and weep, because “a troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50 [51]). Let him cry often and say: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity” (ibid.). “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). I have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea; but according to your great mercy remember me, O God: “for I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always before me” (Ps. 27 [38]) [Col. 0623D].

Now the fire of sorrow, blazing in the furnace of the penitent, kindles the coals of confession. The redness of the coal is the shame of confession, concerning which it is written: “Tears wash away the fault which shame prevents one from confessing with the mouth.” With how much shame, do you suppose, a person confesses before another what he cannot even contemplate within himself without great shame? Yet he ought to have been far more ashamed to commit abominable disgraces before God, who sees all things, than to reveal before a man who hears him the disgraces he has committed. But one must fear and take care lest the confusion of shame hinder the purity of confession. For the sinner ought to confess every circumstance whatsoever of the sin: how he sinned more grievously in place, time, number, and person; [Col. 0624A] according to age, knowledge, rank, and order; whether easily, frequently, openly, or persistently. All these aggravate the crime; and therefore he ought to confess each one, lest he either lessen the offence or excuse the sin. For the shame of confession is no small part of satisfaction, which the Prophet, out of charity, wished upon his enemies when he said: “Let all my enemies be ashamed and exceedingly troubled; let them turn back and be very quickly ashamed” (Ps. VI). Let them be ashamed in confession, troubled in contrition, converted in satisfaction.

Thus, when the coals have been kindled in the furnace of repentance, the sprinkler of love lets fall its drops, by which the fire of sorrow is more vehemently kindled, and the silver of the heavenly image, which had been [Col. 0624B] corrupted by sin, is purified through the power of love, according to what Truth says: “Her many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke VII).—“For charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV). Love of the world introduces sin, but love of God dismisses sin. Covetousness kindles one toward guilt, but charity rises toward pardon. The Prophet desired to be sprinkled with this sprinkler when he said: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L).

Finally, the tongs of satisfaction must be applied, to cleanse from the furnace of repentance the dross of sins. Tongs are joined by two arms, and satisfaction consists of two parts: one by which we avoid guilt, and the other [Col. 0624C] by which we complete repentance. Of the first, Truth says: “Go, and sin no more” (John VIII). For he is a mocker and not penitent who still does what he repents of. “The dog returns to its vomit,” and penitents to sin (Prov. XXVI). Of the second John says: “Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III). These are chiefly prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. For sin offends three—God, ourselves, and our neighbour—and by three acts of satisfaction they are appeased: prayer is directed to God, fasting is borne by ourselves, and almsgiving is distributed to our neighbour.

In this first furnace the Lord purified His martyrs as silver, as they themselves cry in the Psalm: “You have tested us, O God; You have examined us by fire as silver is examined” (Ps. LXIII). But [Col. 0624D] in the furnace of patience, the blowing bellows are the terror of threats; the burning fire is the heat of persecution; the glowing coal is the blood of suffering; the constricting tongs are the horror of affliction; the dripping sprinkler is the strength of protection. For cruel tyrants threatened the holy martyrs with every kind of torture unless they forsook Christ and adhered to idols, thinking to terrify them by torments when they could not soften them by flatteries. But they, keeping Christ’s commandments, despised the threats of rulers. Thus it is written of the blessed apostles that, when they preached the word of God boldly, the chief priests threatened them, ordering them not henceforth to speak in this name. But clothed with the power of the Holy Spirit from [Col. 0625A] on high, they answered more boldly: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V); as Truth Himself testifies: “Do not fear,” he says, “those who kill the body,” etc. (Matt. X).

The bellows of threatening therefore blew violently; but, once the threat was despised, they kindled the fire of persecution more fiercely. Of this the martyrs boast: “We passed,” they say, “through fire and water, and You led us into refreshment” (Ps. LXV).—“The saints indeed endured mockeries and scourgings, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, sawn apart, tempted, died by slaughter with the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and [Col. 0625B] hollows of the earth” (Heb. XI).

But because the flame of persecution could not overcome in the martyrs the fire of charity—“for love is strong as death” (Cant. VIII), and “many waters cannot quench charity” (ibid.)—persecution itself, blazing more fiercely, shed the blood of the saints through diverse torments, as it is written: “They poured out the blood of the saints around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them” (Ps. LXXVIII).—“These are they who came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. VII).

Yet, for suffering to become glorious, the constricting tongs were necessary—that is, the horror of affliction—which made martyrdom glorious. For the sense of the flesh does not desire anything except what delights the flesh’s appetite. Hence it happens [Col. 0625C] that they merit through death because dying did not delight the martyrs. “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI). Truth proves this, who, near His passion, said to the apostles: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (ibid.).—“Jesus began to fear and to be distressed; he began to be sorrowful and downcast” (Mark XIV). Hence also, after His passion, He said to the apostle Peter: “When you have grown old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John XXI). But lest the martyrs fail through the horror of suffering, He let fall upon them the sprinkler of divine protection, protecting and strengthening them, according to what is written: “You have protected me, O God, from the assembly of the wicked and from the multitude of those who work [Col. 0625D] iniquity” (Ps. LXIII). Human frailty would indeed succumb unless divine mercy protected it. Hence that voice cried to God: “Keep me, Lord, as the pupil of Your eye; protect me beneath the shadow of Your wings from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me” (Ps. XVI).

In this second furnace the Lord tested His martyrs as gold, so that the testing of faith, much more precious than gold tested by fire, might “be found unto praise and glory and honour” (1 Pet. I).—“O how great is the abundance of sweetness which the Lord has hidden for those who fear Him” (Ps. XXX); “neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II).—“Rejoice,” he says, “and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. V).—For the righteous shall live forever, [Col. 0626A] and their reward is with the Lord, and their care is with the Most High. Therefore “they shall receive a kingdom of splendour and a diadem of beauty from the hand of God” (Wis. V).—“The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). They shall shine and run about like sparks among reeds. They shall judge nations and rule peoples, and their Lord shall reign forever. But the reprobate shall be cast “into a furnace of burning fire” (ibid.), that they may be tormented inwardly in the furnace of conscience and outwardly in the furnace of Gehenna.

In this inner furnace, moreover, each of the furnace’s instruments may be described. The bellows are the agitating memory; the fire is the torturing conscience; the coal is insufficient repentance; the tongs are the tormenting anguish; the sprinkler is the darkening [Col. 0626B] ignorance. For the memory of sins will trouble the reprobate, according to what is written: “They shall come timidly into the thoughts of their sins, and their iniquity shall bring them across against their will” (Wis. IV), so that with the greatest disturbance they may recall what they did with the greatest delight. Conscience of offences will torment the wicked, as it is written: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI), so that the goad of conscience may prick them to punishment, whom the sting of wickedness impelled to guilt. The damned will repent, but uselessly, according to what is written: “They shall say among themselves, repenting: ‘We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us. What did pride profit us, and what did boasting of riches [Col. 0626C] contribute to us? All these things have passed like a shadow, but we have been consumed in our wickedness’” (Wis. V). Thus their own iniquity will displease them so much that no righteousness will please them.

Anguish will torment sinners, as it is written: “Seeing, they shall be troubled with dreadful fear, groaning through anguish of spirit, and saying: ‘We fools considered the life of the saints madness. Behold how they have been numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints’” (ibid.). Ignorance will darken the wretched, according to what is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” For the damned will scarcely, rarely, or never raise their minds to think of God; rather, they will direct the force of their thought where [Col. 0626D] they feel the force of pain. In this furnace lead is burned up: namely, that upon whose talent impiety sits.

But in the punishments of Gehenna three things must especially be foreseen: darkness, bitterness, and duration—darkness of darkness, bitterness of punishments, and duration of miseries. Of these the Lord says in the Gospel: “Bind his hands and feet, cast him into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII);—“where there will be a worm that does not die and a fire that is not extinguished” (Isa. LXVI).—Job says: “Let me go, that I may weep a little for my pain before I go to a dark land, covered with the gloom of death; a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death and [Col. 0627A] no order dwell, but everlasting horror abides” (Job X). “For the fearful,” says the Lord, “and unbelieving, and accursed, and murderers, and fornicators, and sorcerers, idolaters, and liars, their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur” (Rev. XXI). In it they shall be tormented day and night for ages of ages. “For when an ungodly man dies, there shall be no hope concerning him” (Prov. XI). Then they shall live for death, because they are dead [Col. 0628A] to life: “they shall seek death and shall not find it” (Rev. IX), because they had life and despised it.

May the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages, deliver us from these punishments of the wicked and bring us to those joys of the saints through the merits and prayers of the blessed martyrs. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE FEAST OF MANY MARTYRS

[Note: [Col. 0627D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[Col. 0627]

[Col. 0627B] “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

The vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles rebukes and reproves in this passage those who believe in Christ delicately: they wish indeed to have glory with Christ in heaven, but do not wish to endure sufferings for Christ on earth. Not so, not so. If we wish to reign with Him, we must also suffer with Him. For if we are companions in sufferings, we shall also be companions in the resurrection (2 Cor. I), because “no one shall be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. II). And where the struggle is greater, there the crown is greater. “For narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII); hence the Psalmist said: “For the words of Your lips, I have endured hard ways” [Col. 0627C] (Ps. XI). For if neither a vinedresser can receive the fruit of the vineyard nor a farmer the fruit of the field without diligence and labour, how much less can anyone receive the kingdom of God without labour and diligence? It is granted not to the idle but to the diligent, as Truth testifies when He says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI).

But lest anyone say that he does not wish to endure the sufferings of this present time because they are grievous, prolonged, and of little use, the Apostle meets the objection by saying that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us. As though he said more plainly: They are not prolonged, because they are sufferings of time—that is, temporal sufferings—which cannot remain long. For everything temporal is enclosed within a short span of time, as [Col. 0627D] Solomon testifies when he says that nothing remains beneath the sun (Eccl. II). Hence the Psalmist: “A thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday, which has passed” (Ps. LXXXIX); and the apostle Peter: “Before God, a thousand years are as one day” (2 Pet. III). So too a centenarian, when he dies, however long he may have lived, scarcely reckons himself to have lived one day. For future things are born, present things die, and whatever is past is wholly dead.

Nor are they grievous, because they are sufferings of this time, in contrast to those which are to come [Col. 0628B] in the time of Antichrist, of whom the Lord says: “Then there shall be great tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be; and unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved, but for the sake of the elect they shall be shortened” (Matt. XXIV). Either sufferings are grievous and quickly end, or they are light and easily borne. Therefore, although absolutely all sufferings, however grave, are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us, the sufferings of this present time are far less so, since in comparison with those which are to come in the time of Antichrist they are light. Nor are they useless because they are not worthy to be compared with future glory, etc.

Certainly, they are not comparable in respect of time, because these sufferings are transitory, whereas that [Col. 0628C] glory is everlasting. Hence the apostle Peter says: “The God of all glory, who called us into His eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will Himself perfect, preserve, and strengthen you” (1 Pet. X). For “the momentary and light affliction works beyond measure an immense weight of glory in the heights.” For as great as the distance between flesh and spirit, between heaven and earth, so great—indeed, far greater—is that between transitory and perpetual, between eternal and temporal.

Nor are they comparable in respect of place, because these sufferings are endured on earth, whereas that glory is bestowed in heaven. After we were expelled from our homeland, “the earth brings forth thorns and thistles for us” (Gen. [Col. 0628D] III), and upon it “we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (2 Cor. V), like exiles in a valley of miseries and tears. “I am a sojourner upon the earth,” he says (Ps. CXVIII), “and a pilgrim like all my fathers.” Hence Jacob says: “The days of my pilgrimage are few and evil; they have not reached the days of my fathers, during which they were pilgrims” (Gen. XLVII). Therefore blessed Peter exhorts us: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. II). Who, however, placed in exile would not gladly return to his homeland? Or who, placed in prison, would not desire liberation? Hear Paul cry with tears: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). And David entreating with tears: “Bring my soul out of prison, [Col. 0629A] Lord, that it may confess Your name” (Ps. CXLI). Therefore we who desire to live in the world and remain in the flesh have undoubtedly, in this respect, lost our senses and abandoned reason—like pilgrims desiring to remain in exile and prisoners wishing to be kept in prison. Not so, not so the Apostle, who said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I), wishing to return from exile to his homeland. Therefore the sufferings endured in this exile of pilgrimage are not worthy to be compared with [Col. 0629B] the future glory that shall be revealed in that kingdom of blessedness.

Nor, again, are these sufferings comparable in respect of price, because God rewards incomparably more than anyone can deserve. For, as Truth Himself says: “Whoever leaves house or field for My name’s sake,” that is, is willing to suffer poverty for Me, “shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX). Therefore do not be wearied or burdened by enduring sufferings for Christ; rather endure them with equanimity and gladness, because the sufferings of this present time are not worthy, etc. Hear also Peter saying: “Rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice at the revelation of His glory” (1 Pet. IV).—“For Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow His footsteps” (1 Pet. II). He said of Himself: “Christ had to suffer” (Luke XXIV), and thus enter into His glory.

Christ’s passion alone was wholly commensurate; the other sufferings are not commensurate, although some are worthy and others altogether unworthy. For Christ’s passion was commensurate with the glory that He merited not only for Himself but for us, because, although Christ is true God and true man, God Himself descended to suffering as far as the man Himself ascended to glorification. For He who descended is the same as He who ascended. Hear the Apostle understanding and affirming this concerning Him: “Although He was in the form,” he says, “of God, He did not judge equality with God a thing to be seized; He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. II). [Col. 0629D] Behold how far He descended: from equality with the Father to death on a cross. “For which reason God also exalted Him and gave Him a name above every name,” etc., “and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid.). Behold how far He ascended: from death on a cross to the glory of God the Father.

The other sufferings are not commensurate, because the least glory possessed in the homeland is greater than any punishment endured on the way. Therefore Truth says: “He who is least in the kingdom [Col. 0630A] of heaven is greater than John the Baptist” (Luke VII), because the least reward of attainment is greater than any merit of one on the journey. Yet some sufferings are worthy, such as those of which Truth says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). And again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been tested he shall receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love Him” (James I). But other sufferings are wholly unworthy for obtaining glory: those, namely, which evildoers endure for their crimes. Of them the apostle Peter says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or accursed person, or coveter of what belongs to others; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, [Col. 0630B] but let him glorify God in this name” (1 Pet. VI). Hence “the apostles went away rejoicing from the council’s presence because they were counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

Therefore do not be sad but rejoice; do not grieve but be glad, if you endure sufferings for the Lord, as the apostle James exhorts, saying: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (James I). This must be understood soundly of outward temptations, which are punishments, not of inward temptations, which are faults. We must therefore endure for Christ suffering of heart, mouth, and deed: pains, insults, and terrors; distresses and labours; hunger and thirst; cold [Col. 0630C] and nakedness; and, if necessary, persecution even to death. Let us then be sad and grieve not only for our own perversity or perversities but also for the adversities of others, following the example of him who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. XI). “My bones were crushed as in a frying-pan.” For just as a fish is fried in a pan, whether it is turned to one side or the other, so the soul ought to be afflicted in conscience whether it thinks upon others’ sins or recalls its own.

But [Col. 0630D] one must utterly avoid, as an immense crime, glorying in evil. For “he who glories in malice is surely mighty in iniquity” (Ps. LI), since it is a greater offence to glory in evil than to do evil. Hence Scripture, heightening the sin, speaks of some people thus: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked words” (Prov. II). And again: “They proclaimed their sins like Sodom” (Isa. III). Therefore, brothers, you ought not rejoice but grieve over evil; not glory but be saddened, because such grief shall be turned into joy, as the Lord promises: “Blessed are you who weep, because you shall laugh” (Luke VI); and again: “Blessed are those who mourn, because they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). Indeed, if we wished to rejoice, we would have no material for joy, because the earth is corrupted and full of iniquity: “Iniquity has abounded, and the charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). “The wickedness of men is great upon the earth, and every thought [Col. 0631A] of the heart is intent upon evil” (Gen. VI). Therefore “the earth and all its inhabitants have melted away” (Ps. LXXIV). On every side are distresses, and everywhere pains.

Therefore endure insults and terrors for Christ, because “blessed shall you be when men hate you, curse you, and speak every evil against you falsely” (Luke VI). For if you are reproached in Christ’s name, you shall be blessed, provided that, when you receive an insult or hear detraction, you do not at once blaze up into reproaches or immediately burst forth into vengeance, because “in your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI). Certainly, you can never confound adversaries better than if, when they strike you on one cheek, you offer the other (Matt. V), following the example of Him [Col. 0631B] “who, when He was reviled, did not revile; when He suffered, did not threaten” (1 Pet. II). If you drink poison in this way, it shall not harm you; for by enduring rather than inflicting injury, you will conquer. So it is written: “I suffered insults and terrors from them, and the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior” (Jer. I). Oh, how greatly that mind rejoices with itself which has been able to endure injury with equanimity; and how greatly that fury is confounded which inflicted injury without producing any disturbance in another! Just as art is foiled by art: the one inflicted the injury not in order that he should not be disturbed by the other, but in order to disturb him greatly; yet the other bore the injury so that he was not disturbed by him at all. Thus the disturber became disturbed.

Do not fear to endure distresses and labours [Col. 0631C] for Christ, for He Himself says to His faithful: “Come to Me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

What, then, brothers—what shall we say of ourselves? When we ought to endure cold and nakedness for Christ, we clothe ourselves in double and costly garments; when we ought to tolerate hunger and thirst for Christ, we eat diverse courses and feast on delicate foods; when we ought to endure vigils and labours for Christ, we rest in ample leisure and sleep long in slumber; when we ought to endure distresses and pains for Christ, we enjoy worldly pleasures and delight in the enticements of the flesh. We must indeed fear lest at last we hear what was once said [Col. 0631D] to that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly each day: “Son, remember that you received good things,” etc., “and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted and you are tormented” (Luke XVI).

Do not, O man, fear cold and nakedness for Christ, because “when this mortal shall put on immortality” (1 Cor. XV), you shall receive a precious robe without price—not indeed one woven of fine linen and purple, hyacinth and scarlet, but one composed of the four properties of the glorified body: subtlety, agility, brightness, and impassibility. Of these it is written: “The righteous shall shine and run about like sparks among reeds, and their Lord shall reign forever” (Wis. III); for “God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there shall be no more mourning, crying, or any pain [Col. 0632A], because the former things have passed away” (Rev. XXI). Nor fear, for Christ’s sake, to endure hunger or thirst, because when He “passes by, He shall minister” (Luke XII), He will offer His faithful inestimable delights. The more these are tasted, the more eagerly they will be desired, because when tasted they do not produce disgust but engender desire. They contain three foods—not bread, wine, or flesh, but knowledge, love, and praise—by which the soul, seeing God, is unspeakably satisfied: “I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when Your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI). Nothing is sweeter than to know God as Three and One; nothing pleasanter than to love the one true God; nothing more delightful than to praise God [Col. 0632B] as Creator and Saviour.

Therefore the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us. In it there shall be life without death, day without night, certainty without contingency; security without fear, delight without pain, tranquility without labour; beauty without deformity, strength without weakness, rectitude without perversity; goodness without malice, happiness without misery; joy which “neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II). Therefore it is said that this glory shall be revealed in us because it is now hidden and concealed, so much so that we are unable even to understand it, much less explain it. “How great,” he says, “is the abundance of Your sweetness, O God, which You have hidden for those who fear [Col. 0632C] You!” (Ps. XXX). “To him who conquers I shall give hidden manna” (Rev. II), far sweeter and more pleasant than that concerning which the Wise Man declares: “You gave them bread from heaven without labour, containing in itself every delight and sweetness of every flavour” (Wis. XVI). For our manna shall surely be our God, “all in all” (Eph. I), who will have, for each person, the flavour that his soul desires. “Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). He will be tasted fully and perfectly when the soul contemplates Him, “no longer through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face as He is” (1 Cor. XIII), because “this is eternal life: that they may know You, the only God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent” (John XVII). Since He is the highest good, in Him is every fullness of the blessed. Therefore whoever has God alone possesses utterly every good.

But some, deceived by error, think that this saying is not true because it is hidden; saying, yet falsely, that the glory of the resurrection will not come. To refute their error, the testimonies of the New and Old Testaments suffice, as do also the arguments and analogies introduced by certain philosophers. But for the present we offer this one point to crush their madness: their belief, if it is true, profits them not at all; if false, it harms them greatly. For belief that human beings will not rise again does no good if they do not rise again, and does much harm if they do rise again. [Col. 0633A] The contrary belief, however, if true, does the greatest good; but if false, does the least harm. For belief that the resurrection will come greatly profits if human beings rise again, and does no harm if they do not rise again. Thus one must by all means maintain the belief which, if true, profits most and, if false, harms least.

Moreover, if anyone, drawn or assisted by another, does good or evil with him and through him, does not each, before the most just judge, deserve reward for good or punishment for evil? Certainly. Since body and soul stand in this relation, God, the just, mighty, and patient Judge, [Col. 0634A] “who will render to each according to his merits” (Rom. II), will reward or punish the soul when, after this life, it is reunited with the body—when there will be a place for receiving, just as in this life there is a place for meriting. This could not happen unless the body rises; and it certainly shall rise. This will occur not in this world, where evils often befall the good and good things the wicked, but in the world to come, where the good shall receive only good things and the wicked only evil things. Body and soul shall receive incomprehensible and ineffable gifts, through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON THE FEAST OF MARTYRS

[Col. 0633]

[Col. 0633B] “My soul is troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Cant. VI).

The prophet Jeremiah’s lament is: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. I). The triple *ah* signifies a triple weakness: deficiency of conscience, eloquence, and wisdom. If Jeremiah laments and fears to preach—he, the most distinguished of prophets, who also bore the most excellent testimony concerning the Son of God made man, saying: “After this He was seen upon earth and conversed among men” (Bar. III)—if the prophet Jonah, sent to preach to the Ninevites, fled to Tarshish (Jonah I), who am I, who am neither prophet nor son of prophet, indeed not even a child, that I should ascend the mountain to announce to the Jews and Jerusalem their crimes; that I should speak the mighty acts of God with uncircumcised [Col. 0633C] lips—unrepentant while speaking of repentance, guilty while speaking of innocence, polluted while speaking of holiness, cold while speaking of charity, when a cold breast cannot set another aflame? Yet, because “little children asked for bread and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. IV), and because water often flows through stony channels to fertile beds, and lye washes even though it is not itself washed, I rise to speak—yet readier to listen.

Therefore, having begged at the very threshold of this sermon your pardon for a threefold—indeed manifold—insufficiency, and having invoked the help of Him who inspired the hearts of prophets, I shall sow for your hearing a brief seed-plot of God’s word, and, would that it may bear abundant fruit.

“My soul is troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab.” [Col. 0633D] These are the words of the Bride in the Song of Love; and she speaks in the person of the whole human race, as though the human race said: My soul—that is, this present life, according to Job’s saying, “In whose hand is every living soul” (Job X); and in the Song of Songs, “Tell me whom my soul loves” (Cant. I). And *anima* (“soul”) is said to derive from ἐν (*en*, “in”) and αἷμα (*haima*, “blood”) [Col. 0634B] [Note: [Col. 0633D] In presenting this etymology, Innocent perhaps has Leviticus XVII.14 in view; although the passage there concerns the soul of beasts. [Col. 0634D] Innocent immediately follows a tropological interpretation.], because it is in blood—that is, in sin. Hence the Psalm says: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. LIV), because this life is almost wholly spent in sin; hence not even an infant of one day is without sin.

It has troubled me with the agitation of busyness and distraction, of which the Gospel says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke X), because of the chariots of Aminadab. *Aminadab* is interpreted “spontaneous one of my people.” He is “Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI), the true Aminadab, who for the salvation of the whole human race “was led as a sheep to slaughter and was offered because He Himself willed it” (Isa. LIII). There are four chariots of this Aminadab by which the human race is borne: elemental, worldly, temporal, and affective. [Col. 0634C] The first consists in the four wheels of the elements; the second in the four quarters of the world—east, west, south, and north; the third in the four times of the world: namely, the time of derivation, from Adam to Moses; of recall, from Moses to Christ; of return, from the Incarnation to the Ascension and lasting until the end of the world; and the fourth in the four affections, which are joy, hope, sorrow, and fear.

Concerning these chariots the prophet Zechariah says: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains; and the mountains were of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, in the second black horses, in the third white horses, and in the fourth dappled horses” (Zech. [col. 0634D] IV). The first chariot, namely the four elements, came forth from between the two bronze mountains, which are matter and form, enduring like bronze. Its horses are red on account of the two principal elements, namely fire, which glows red, and earth, which is naturally red; hence Adam was formed from red earth in the field of Damascus. The horses of the second are black [col. 0635A] on account of earthly habitation, which is black and dark; hence Job says: “In darkness I have spread my bed” (Job XVII); and in the Song of Songs: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song I). The name of Adam prefigured this chariot of the four cardinal points of the world, which the human race was to possess: it is compounded from the four names of the cardinal stars [Note: [col. 0635] The manuscript reads *stolarum* (“of stoles”). But I preferred *stellarum* (“of stars”), that is, of the cardinal points; for “stole” has no relevance here], namely ἀνατολή, “east,” δύσις, “west,” ἄρκτος, “north,” and μεσημβρία, “south”; the name Adam is composed from the initial letters of these names. Likewise the general name *homo*, “man,” is composed from these four names, east, west, south, north: *h* being used in place of *s*, as *septem* for ἑπτά, “seven,” and *sex* for ἕξ, “six.” The horses of the third are white because they draw toward eternity, in which there is ineffable brightness and light, according to the saying: “God inhabits [col. 0635B] inaccessible light” (1 Tim. VI); its horizon and circumference are time, as the Psalmist says. The horses of the fourth are dappled because of the variations of affection. And these four chariots came forth “from between two mountains,” which are beginning and end.

Our bride speaks in her own person, for the Church militant says: “My soul,” etc., that is, my righteous elect. Hence in Genesis: “All the souls of Jacob’s household that entered Egypt were seventy” (Gen. XLVI). This soul is called from ἀνά, meaning “upright,” and *imago*, meaning “likeness.” Hence in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). “It disturbed [col. 0635C] me”: it troubled me with the disturbance of desire, of which the Psalm says: “My soul is greatly troubled” (Ps. VI), “because of the chariots.” There are two chariots by which the Church is conveyed. One is that of commemoration, which recalls the four seasons of the world by varying the Church’s annual offices in fourfold fashion. The season of derivation is in Septuagesima; the season of return from Easter to Pentecost; from then until Advent, the season of pilgrimage; assign the season of return to the period up to the Octaves of Epiphany; from Abraham until Septuagesima, the season of pilgrimage. On account of this chariot it is said in the Psalm: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises” (Ps. XLVI). The other has four wheels, that is, four [col. 0635D] states: clerics, penitents, innocents, and confessors. The Holy Spirit indicates these orders in the Song of Songs, where he says: “Who is this that rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle?” These are the four colors in the covering of the tabernacle: purple, fine linen, scarlet, and hyacinth-blue. Upon these chariots the ark of the covenant is brought back from Gibeah to Jerusalem; and the Queen of the South comes from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. She enters Jerusalem; that is, the Church militant, which advances toward the heavenly Jerusalem to contemplate the supreme Solomon.

[col. 0636A] Again she speaks in the person of every righteous person: “My soul is with you,” namely, my spirit; hence in Ezekiel: “All souls are mine; and the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). This soul is called from *a*, which is alpha and signifies the Father; νοῦς, which is “mind” and signifies the Son; and *amor*, “love,” which signifies the Holy Spirit. For it is named from the three persons, since the trace of the Trinity shines especially in the soul because of its three powers: irascible, rational, and concupiscible. The irascible power expresses spiritedness and power, and thus looks to the Father; the rational power expresses wisdom and thus belongs to the Son; the concupiscible belongs to the will and thus looks to the Holy Spirit, who is the will of both. “It disturbed me,” [col. 0636B] that is, my body, by ruling it, “because of the chariots of Aminadab.” These four chariots are the four cardinal virtues, formed by charity. In this fiery chariot Elijah was taken up into heaven (4 Kings II). Again the bride speaks in the person of the penitent: “My soul,” that is, my sensuality, which [lacuna] is occupied with earthly things. For man is earthly by nature, just as he is heavenly by reason. “It disturbed me” with the disturbance of suffering, of which the Psalm says: “My spirit is distressed within me; my heart is troubled within me” (Ps. CXLII).

“Because of the chariots of Aminadab.” There are two principal chariots. The first and more important turns upon four wheels: remission of sins, [col. 0636C] contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. These four are indicated by four words, namely: “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. L). And in the Song of Songs, it is repeated four times: “Return, return, that we may look upon you.” In it sits the Ethiopian eunuch, to be baptized by Philip, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. VIII). This chariot succeeds Pharaoh’s chariot, and it swallows it up. The latter likewise has four wheels, the four kinds of sin: delight, consent, speech, and deed. It is submerged in the Red Sea, that is, in baptism, or penitence, or the fire of Gehenna. The second chariot consists in fourfold satisfaction: fasting, vigils, prayers, and alms; these too are signified by four words in the Psalm: [col. 0636D] “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXVI). This cart creaks with prayers and carries hay, that is, the withering and drying-up of the human body, according to the prophet Amos (ch. II): “Behold, I press down beneath you, as a cart creaks when loaded with hay.” This chariot is set against the iron cart of Damascus, which likewise has four wheels: sin of speech, thought, deed, and final impenitence. Thus the prophet Amos says, “For three crimes of Damascus”—namely speech, thought, and deed—“and for the fourth”—namely final impenitence—“I will not turn [col. 0637A] it back, because it threshed Gilead with iron carts” (Amos I). In this cart sits every son of perdition, every sinner, and he is carried to Babylon, that is, to eternal damnation.

The Savior himself consecrated this chariot of fourfold satisfaction by his deeds and sayings. He prefigured its first wheel, fasting, when he fasted, through Moses and Elijah. And through the prophet Jonah: “Sanctify a fast; yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III). Therefore this number, forty, is penitential, because it is produced from ten multiplied by four; and everyone who sins mortally transgresses the Decalogue and the four Gospels, for “whoever offends in one point is made guilty of all” [col. 0637B] (Jas. II). He dedicated the second wheel, vigils, when, keeping watch in the garden on the night in which he was betrayed, he said to his disciples: “Watch and pray now, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI). And elsewhere: “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch” (Mark XIII). He dedicated the third, prayer, when in that same garden he prayed, “and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground” (Luke XXII); and when he said: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV), when one should always rest. He consecrated the fourth wheel, almsgiving, when on the cross he bestowed the alms of prayer upon those crucifying him, praying for them; and when he said: “Give alms, [col. 0637C] and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI).

Therefore, if you sit or have sat in Pharaoh’s chariot, that is, in the chariot of sins, come down. Hear the counsel of the prophet Isaiah, who says: “Come down; sit upon the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans; you shall no longer be called tender and delicate. Take millstones, grind flour; uncover your veil, bare your legs, cross the rivers” (Isa. XLVII). As if he said: Transgressing soul, barren in good, descend from the pride of sins by renouncing sins; and after the remission of sins you shall no longer remain in sinful delight. Grind flour: that is, grind, crush, and annihilate the hardness of sin by contrition of heart, scattering the clouds of sin like ashes; because [col. 0637D] “a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L). Uncover your veil; strip off your footwear, that is, your sins, by which, rushing through the fields of license from sin into sin, we were running toward Babylon. Confess, according to the saying: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Job XL). And again: “Reveal your way to God” (Ps. XXXVI). Cross the rivers of carnal pleasures, of which the Psalm says: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. CXXXVI). Cross in the aforesaid chariot of penitence: fasting, keeping vigil, praying, and giving alms. For just as a bodily wound is healed by four remedies—first, cleansing and flesh-drying agents; second, repellents; third, [col. 0638A] strengthening agents; fourth, scar-forming agents—so the wound of sin must first be bound and poulticed with fasts, which dry up and cleanse the moisture of carnal pleasures; second, with vigils, which repel and drive back threatening harms; third, with prayers, which by their power and frequency strengthen the wound; fourth, with alms, which, like oil, float above all good things, because mercy is greater than all burnt offerings, and which level and soothe the place of the scar.

Nor is a fast of the taste from food and drink sufficient. For in this way the miser fasts so as not to spend; the Epicurean, so that he may reserve his luncheon for a splendid dinner; the hypocrite, so that he may appear devout. Rather, one must fast also with the other senses: with sight, from shameless and unlawful spectacles, [col. 0638B] because death enters us through the windows of the eyes. Thus Jeremiah: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. III). And in the Psalm: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. XVIII). Likewise with hearing, from idle tales and buffoonish speech, lest our ears itch. Likewise with touch, from soft and luxurious things, from silken and purple garments; for “those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. XI), not of the highest King. Hence the rich man in the Gospel, “who was clothed in purple and fine linen, was buried in hell” (Luke XVI). Rather, the chief fast is that of the heart from vices; it alone is holy and sanctifies the aforesaid bodily fasts. Thus the prophet Joel: “Sanctify a fast; call an assembly” (Joel I). Likewise bodily [col. 0638C] vigils in nocturnal studies—such as are customary with scholars—are not sufficient; one must also keep watch in churches, in one’s heart, over one’s flock of virtues and thoughts, lest cattle-rustlers carry them off and thieves break through into your house and sheepfold. Thus in the Gospel: “If the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into” (Matt. XXIV).

Likewise vocal prayer is not sufficient: that is, praying or singing psalms in choir while the mind wanders and conducts business in the marketplace. Such prayer is lame, and a lame offering is forbidden to be offered to the Lord. The Lord reproves those who pray in this manner through Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX). Again, giving bodily alms to the poor is not enough [col. 0638D] unless you give from a cheerful heart. For God examines the heart, not the hand; and “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX). It is not enough to free a poor person from temporal need, from bodily death, if you do not free yourself from spiritual death, the death of sin; that is, ordered charity begins with oneself. First have mercy upon your own soul by repenting, confessing, and making satisfaction. Do not delay, because delay draws danger to itself.

> He who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, 94.)

For it is just that “the one who is filthy should become filthier still,” as is read in the Apocalypse (ch. XXII). Do not say: “I am frail; I cannot do it now. Later I shall repent, next year; God is merciful; at the end [col. 0639A] I shall repent, like the thief on the cross, and I shall be saved.” How can anyone be secure about a year—indeed, about a month, indeed about the next day, indeed about the present hour? For even the present hour offers no certain assurance. Nothing is more certain than death; nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. Let that Gospel saying terrify you: “Fool, your soul shall be required of you; and perhaps this is the eleventh hour” (Luke XII).

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. VI); it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. Behold, Christ cries upon the cross: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is a sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I). You cannot reign with him unless you are willing to suffer with him—not for him, dying as a triumphant one, but for yourself, dying and, unless you repent, destined to perish. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Daughters of Jerusalem, [col. 0639B] do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves” (Luke XXIII). Do not fear temporal satisfaction; fear eternal damnation. Again: “He will flee from weapons of iron; he will rush upon a bow of bronze” (Job XX). The iron weapons are penitential works, [col. 0640A] strong against the devil; the bronze bow is the irremediable impenitence of eternal damnation. Fear this bow, the lake from which “blood came out as high as the horses’ bridles,” as is read in the Apocalypse (ch. XIV). Where is death? It is mortal not to have been able to die; where there is nothing but “woe, woe,” the son of Eve knows how to speak. But because these things, though true, are terrible, and ears are dull toward terrors and thunderclaps, as Tully says: “Pity ought to be brief, because nothing dries more quickly than a tear.” Let us come to the end. Let us descend, brothers, from Pharaoh’s chariot; let us cast stones out of the street; let us flee from the land of the north; let us mount the chariot of the Ethiopian eunuch, and also the chariot of fourfold satisfaction, so that at last in Elijah’s fiery chariot we may pass to the heavenly Jerusalem, to songs of joy, [col. 0640B] to joys which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II), through the granting of him to whom belong honor and dominion through endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. FOR THE COMMON OF ONE CONFESSOR

On the sleep of vices and the watchfulness of virtues; on how we ought to keep watch; on the four ways in which the Lord comes; and on why the Lord altered the order of the watches.

[col. 0639]

[col. 0639C] “Watch, because you do not know when the master will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest he come suddenly and find you sleeping” (Mark XIII).

The soul sleeps in vices in two ways and keeps watch in virtue in two ways. It sleeps through error and ignorance; it sleeps through sluggishness and negligence. Against the first manner the Psalmist prays: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. XII); against the second Solomon inveighs: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise? You will sleep a little, you will slumber a little, and want will come upon you like a traveler” (Prov. VI). Both sleeps are damnable and deadly; for “the ignorant person shall be ignored, and the negligent person shall be neglected” (1 Cor. [col. 0639D] XIV). While guilt is unknown, penitence is not done, and therefore forgiveness is not granted. While care is neglected, medicine is not sought, and therefore recovery is despaired of. For it is read in the Book of Kings that the two men, chiefs of the brigands, “Rechab and Baanah came and entered the house of Ish-bosheth, who was sleeping on his bed at noon; and the female gatekeeper of the house, while cleaning wheat, fell asleep. They struck him in the groin, and he died; and, taking away his head, they departed” (2 Kings IV). Certainly, “whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” [col. 0640C] (Rom. XV); for “all these things happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. X). Behold, both Ish-bosheth and the gatekeeper were sleeping (2 Kings IV). The gatekeeper, who cleans wheat from darnel, grain from vice, is the guard of the mind, or vigilance [Note: [col. 0639] Alternatively: “It is reason itself, which discerns good from evil, virtue from vices, which,” etc.], which, should it perhaps fall asleep through ignorance and fail to guard the doors of the house—that is, the bodily senses—the two chiefs of brigands, namely the spirit of avarice and the spirit of pride, which are the two principal vices (for “the root of all evils is avarice” [1 Tim. VI], to which every unlawful desire belongs; and “the beginning of every sin is pride” [Ecclus. X], to which every wicked presumption belongs), enter the house and at once strike Ish-bosheth as he sleeps—that is, the negligent mind—in the groin: they kill it through carnal pleasure; [col. 0640D] for nothing is more friendly to pleasure than idleness. The poet too recognized this when he said:

> The question is why Aegisthus became an adulterer:  
> the cause is ready at hand—he was idle.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, 161)

Ish-bosheth is therefore well interpreted as “man of confusion,” because one who neglects to keep watch deserves confusion. Therefore always do some work, so that the devil may find you occupied. For this reason the Lord commands: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour the thief will come” (Matt. XXIV); and the Apostle says: “Brothers, be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil [col. 0641A] goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. V). Moreover, we ought to keep watch through faith of heart and through diligence in work: through faith of heart against error and ignorance; through diligence in work against sluggishness and negligence. For “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI), and “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II). Therefore, “while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be children of light” (John XII). And while you have time, “work good toward all, especially toward those of the household of faith” (Gal. II). A time will come when you will be able neither to act nor to see. “Bind his hands and feet,” he says, “and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII). Bound hands cannot act; those cast into darkness cannot see. Watch therefore, because you do not know [col. 0641B] when the Lord will come. And although nothing is more certain than death, nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death; and since it is always uncertain to us, let it always be suspect to us, so that we may always be pleased to live as though we must always die. Therefore we do not know when the Lord comes. The Lord comes in four ways. The first and last time he comes once; the second and third, often. First he comes into the world for redemption; last he will come in judgment for recompense. Second, he comes into the mind for sanctification; third, he comes into the flesh for dissolution. Of the first it is said: “I came forth from the Father, and I came into the world” (John XVI); of the last: “You will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power [col. 0641C] and majesty” (Matt. XXIV); of the second: “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV); of the third: “When he comes and knocks, let them open to him at once” (Luke XII). He comes in order to receive the soul that he gave; he knocks in order to announce near death through the distress of the flesh. But you do not know when the Lord will come: in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. By the four hours are understood the four ages—childhood, adolescence, youth, and old age—in which the one who is negligent and ignorant sleeps, while the one who believes and works keeps watch. Furthermore, one who sleeps in one age should at least wake in another; for at whatever hour the sinner is converted, “he shall live and shall not die, says the Lord” (Ezek. XVIII). For if he comes in the first watch, and if he comes in [col. 0641D] the second watch and finds them thus, those servants are blessed. Yet let no one abuse the patience of his long-suffering any longer; for the more he endures in the present, the more severely he will punish in the future. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the goodness [col. 0642A] of God leads you to repentance? By your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God” (Rom. II). Now, since morning seems to signify human childhood, cockcrow adolescence, midnight youth, and evening old age, why does the Lord reverse and alter the order? For he does not say, “In the morning, at cockcrow, at midnight, or in the evening,” but: “In the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning.” The Lord, however, keeps the necessary order according to the degree in which each is more bound to watch: the old man more than the young, the young more than the adolescent, and the adolescent more than the child. Or rather: since, when a man is born to misery, night then begins for him, but when he dies to salvation, day then begins for him, evening, [col. 0642B] which is the beginning of night, rightly signifies childhood; morning, which is the end of night, signifies old age. Therefore the Lord mentions evening before morning, so that we may pass from night to day—that is, from the misery of the present life to the glory of the life to come. Hence the Psalmist testifies: “They have slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV). It must be asked, however, why, since man has six ages—infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and extreme old age—the Lord, omitting the first and last, mentions only the middle ones. Yet, though these are left unspoken, provision has been made for them by a necessary reason. For he had previously given two commands: “Watch,” namely, “and pray; you do not know when the Lord will come.” In the first [col. 0642C] age, although a person does not know when the Lord will come, he has no need to watch, because an infant is not ordinarily accustomed to sin at that age. In the last age, although he needs to watch, a decrepit person nevertheless knows that the Lord comes at that age, because that age ends in death. Though all are commanded to watch, according to the saying, “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch,” this command especially concerns the prelates of the Church, according to the saying: “He commanded the doorkeeper to watch.” For the doorkeeper is he to whom the keys of the Church are entrusted, and who is bound to keep watch both for himself and for the people, lest, if a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit (Luke VI). To him the Lord also says through the prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood from your hand” [col. 0642D] (Ezek. XXXIII).—“For the shepherds were keeping the watches of the night over their flock” (Luke II). Watch, therefore, because “blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke XII).

## SERMON XI. ON THE FEAST OF CONFESSORS

[Note: [col. 0641D] From the edition of Cardinal Mai.]

[col. 0641]

[col. 0641D] “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased my Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII).

[col. 0642D] Since elsewhere divine Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. XXVIII), and “he who is without fear cannot be justified” (Eccles. VIII), perhaps your thought says within you: What does it mean that we are told, “Do not fear, little flock”? I thought that you would say such things in your hearts, since it is also written: “Fear God, all his saints, because those who fear him lack nothing” (Ps. XXXIII).—“Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man” (Eccles. XII). Brothers, different kinds of fear must be distinguished: human, worldly, natural, servile, initial, and final. The first two are vices; the last two are virtues; the two in the middle are neither vices nor virtues. Human fear is that by which someone turns from good to evil in order to avoid temporal danger, like Peter, who denied life lest he incur death, forgetful of what [col. 0643B] he had heard from his Master: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X). Worldly fear is that by which someone turns from good to evil in order to avoid temporal inconvenience, like Herod, who killed the innocent lest he lose his kingdom (Matt. II). “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII). Natural fear is that by which every person naturally dreads suffering, as even Christ himself did, of whom it is written that “Jesus began to be afraid and wearied, to be sorrowful and distressed” (Mark XIV). Servile fear is that by which someone restrains his evil mind from sin, not through love of righteousness but through dread of punishment; and of this fear it is written: “There is no fear in charity, but [col. 0643C] perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John IV). Initial fear is that by which someone turns from evil partly through love of righteousness and partly through dread of punishment; of it it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Eccles. I). Final fear is that by which someone turns from evil solely through love of righteousness; of it it is written: “The fear of the Lord has set itself above all things” (Ecclus. XXV).

Therefore, when you are told, “Do not fear, little flock,” understand this of worldly or human fear: namely, do not turn from virtue to vice on account of bodily danger or temporal inconvenience. Therefore do not fear, little flock, because you are little—because you are few or poor. You may be few in number, but not in merit; poor in possessions, but rich in virtues. Certainly, if you love God, you are not alone, because you have the whole Trinity within you, as the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” [col. 0643D] (John XIV). For “God is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV). If you love God, you are not alone, because you have a multitude of angels with you. Recall, brothers, what Elisha said to his servant: “There are more with us than with them” (4 Kings VI), because an army of angels had descended to protect Elisha. And the angel Raphael said to Tobias: “When you prayed with tears, I offered your prayer to the Lord” (Tob. XII). Hence the Psalmist said: “In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you” [col. 0644A] (Ps. CXXXVII). Therefore, if you love God, you are not alone, because the undivided Trinity is present with you and multitudes of angels are with you. Nor are you poor, since Scripture says: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI). “The rich have lacked and hungered, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. XXXIII). Hence, when the Lord said to the apostles: “When I sent you without purse and bag and sandals, did you lack anything?” they answered, “Nothing” (Luke XXII). Seek, therefore, first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or how shall we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all [col. 0644B] these things” (Matt. VI). Because he is Father, he wills it; because he is heavenly, he can do it. Therefore he knows, can, and wills; consequently, without doubt he will give what is expedient for your salvation. He indeed “gives food to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. CXXXVI); he will give food through his ravens; he will give food to you who remain in the desert—food to white persons through black, to righteous persons through sinners, to cloistered persons through seculars. Moreover, why should you fear fewness, when in leaving the world you have fled the multitude? Why should you fear poverty, when in renouncing yourselves you have despised riches?

Therefore do not fear, little flock—provided, however, that you are a flock not of swine, who hurled themselves into the sea (Luke VIII), but “of shorn sheep that have come up [col. 0644C] from the washing” (Song VII). Swine are those who trample divine sacraments underfoot; of them it is written: “Do not cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII). Swine are those who embrace the uncleannesses of the flesh, because of “the washed sow in the wallow of mire” (2 Pet. II). Swine are those who do not chew the cud—that is, who do not meditate upon the law of the Lord—and such persons, according to the Law, are not fit to be eaten by him who, when he is eaten, eats; for in his heart he prepares for himself food, eating [text uncertain]. Take care, therefore, take care not to be a herd of swine plunging into the sea (Luke VII), lest you again immerse yourselves in this great and wide sea—that is, in the cares and enticements of this age—where there is “the broad and spacious way that leads to death” (Matt. VII). But be a flock of sheep, [col. 0644D] not of any kind, but “shorn sheep that come up from the washing” (Song IV). Sheep are the innocent, of whom it is written: “These who are sheep, what have they done?” (2 Kings XXV). Sheep are the obedient, of whom the Lord says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X). Sheep are the patient and meek, of whom it is said: “Like a sheep led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). And you, brothers, ought to be sheep through innocence, so that you do not render “evil for evil, nor curse for curse” (1 Pet. III). You ought to be sheep through obedience, so that without delay, together and without complaint, you obey not only divine commands but also the ordinances of the Rule. You ought to be sheep through meekness and patience, so that [col. 0645A] in your patience you may possess your souls (Luke XXI), following the example of him who “when he suffered did not threaten; when he was cursed, did not curse” (1 Pet. II), who became obedient to God the Father unto death, even death on the cross (Phil. II), and who was subject even to his mother (Luke II), setting himself before us as an example: “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

Thus you ought not to be a flock of swine but a flock of sheep; nor simply of sheep, but of shorn sheep, their fleece laid aside, lest wool wound you, for it produces worms, or hairs entangle you, for they cling to thorns. Certainly, you were shorn when you left behind for Christ not only your own possessions but also your own will, following the example of him who said: “Behold, [col. 0645B] we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. XIX). Again, you were shorn not only when you left your native soil for Christ, but also when you came into a foreign land, following the example of him to whom it was said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land which I shall show you” (Gen. XII). But take care, beloved, lest wool grow again upon you and you desire to return into Egypt to the pots of meat, or melons and garlic (Exod. XXVI), lest perhaps—God forbid—you die in the graves of craving. Whenever such wool grows again, therefore, let it at once be shorn, so that you may be a flock “of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song IV). You came from the first washing when you were born again of water and the Holy Spirit [col. 0645C] (John III); but you ought often to come from the second washing, that you may wash your bed every night and water your couch with tears (Ps. VI), offering to God the sacrifice of a troubled spirit not only for your own sins but also for those of others. He does not despise those who weep, not only because of their dwelling in this life or on this road, but also because of love for the homeland [col. 0646A] toward which you ought to pant with all your affections; so that you who once had dry land may now have watered land, following the example of Achsah, who received from her father Caleb the upper and lower springs as her dowry (Josh. XV).

For it is certain that, if you are a flock of shorn sheep that come from the washing (Song IV), you need not fear being a little flock, because the Father has been pleased in you. It is read that God the Father is pleased in the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII). The Father is pleased in the elect, whence: “My Father has been pleased in you.” A righteous man is pleasing to God, whence: “He pleased God and was found righteous” (Ecclus. XLIV). God the Father is pleased in the Son, in whom, as the Only-begotten wholly like himself, he delights above all others. God the Father is pleased in the elect, whom he predestined as co-heirs of the Only-begotten to the kingdom (Rom. VIII). The righteous person pleases God when, as obedient and devout, he fulfills his good pleasure. First and greatest is that the Father is pleased in the Son; second and middle, that the Father is pleased in the elect; third and last, that the righteous person pleases God. Strive therefore, brothers, strive to please God by fulfilling his good pleasure with all your strength, so that he may be pleased in you by mercifully granting you his kingdom: a kingdom of peace and tranquillity, a kingdom of delight and joy, a kingdom of light and brightness, a kingdom of eternal blessedness and happiness. In it, with the holy angels [col. 0646C] and blessed souls, may you deserve always to see him, know him, love him, and possess him—three and one, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the eternal, living, and true God, who is blessed above all things for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. FOR THE COMMON OF A VIRGIN

On the fourfold understanding of the kingdom of heaven; the wicked and righteous merchant, the perverse and holy merchant; the manifold distinction of pearls, especially the threefold distinction, each of which is sought well by some and badly by others.

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645D] “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls. And, when he had found one precious pearl, he gave all that he had and bought it” (Matt. XIII).

The kingdom of heaven, whose definition is variously scattered through the Scriptures, is one thing above us, another below us, another within us, and another outside us. That which is above us is understood as the Church of the triumphant; that which is below us, as right faith; that which is within us, as the divine law; that which is outside us, as the Church of those on active service. Of the first it is said: “They shall come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII); of the second: “The angels,” that is, the reapers, “shall go out and gather from his kingdom all [Col. 0646D] stumbling-blocks”; of the third: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII); of the fourth: “The kingdom shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

Therefore, in this passage the kingdom of heaven is understood as the Church of those on active service: namely, of those who can say of themselves, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). This kingdom—that is, the Church—is said to be like a merchant seeking fine pearls. But there is a wicked and perverse merchant, and there is a righteous and holy merchant. Of wicked and perverse commerce the Psalm says: “Because I have not known commercial dealings, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. LXX); but of honorable and [Col. 0647A] holy commerce the Lord says: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke XIX).

Hence too that man who went abroad divided his goods among his servants. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one. He who had received five talents gained another five; and he who had received two gained another two (Matt. XXV). When the master returned, he commended such profit: “Well done,” he said, “good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a few things, I shall set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord” (ibid.). But he who bound up the money entrusted to him in a napkin and hid it was rejected by his lord, who said to him: “Wicked servant, ought you not to have entrusted my money to the bankers at interest?” etc. (ibid.). Interest is made perfect when through merits we attain rewards, when through temporal things we gain eternal things.

Therefore, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls. Scripture contains a manifold distinction or division of pearls, or precious stones. For the prophet says: “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. XXVIII). And he immediately enumerates nine kinds of stones, on account of the nine orders of angels. Moses likewise set twelve kinds of stones in the breastpiece of judgment (Exod. XXVIII), on account of the teaching of the twelve apostles. For Paul says in his Epistle: “One builds with wood, hay, straw; another with gold and silver and precious stones” (I Cor. III). Likewise, in the Apocalypse of John: all the precious stones of its wall, and the towers of Jerusalem, shall be built with gems (Apoc. XXI).

[Col. 0647C] For our edification, however, it is enough to distinguish three kinds of pearls. There is the pearl of knowledge in Scripture, the pearl of grace in the Church, and the pearl of glory in the homeland. The first is bought at the price of meditation and reading; the second, at the price of contrition and confession; the third, at the price of thought and action. The first is bought by him of whom it is said: “His delight was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. I). The second is bought by those to whom it is said: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI). [Note: [Col. 0647D] Something appears to be missing here.]

Yet it seems truer that through grace one comes to pardon than that through pardon [Col. 0647D] one comes to grace, as Truth itself testifies when it says: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII). Moreover, each of these pearls is sought badly by some and well by others. Thus the heretic seeks the pearl of knowledge badly; the Catholic seeks it well. The former seeks it in order to attack the truth; the latter, in order to defend the truth. The former seeks it in order to empty faith of its content; the latter, in order to confirm faith. The former seeks it in order to mix water with wine and offer dragon’s gall in a golden cup; the latter seeks it in order to catch “the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song II): foxes indeed having different faces, but their tails bound together (Judg. XV), because they agree together in vanity.

[Col. 0648A] Yet there are certain Christians, as we ourselves have frequently heard and understood, who invoke the pearl of knowledge not for the defense of truth but for the assertion of falsehood, so that they may receive merchandise [variant: “life”] in exchange for a pearl. Of them the Psalmist says: “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to your law, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII).

The ambitious person also seeks the pearl of grace badly; the devout person seeks it well. The former seeks it through Simonian perversity; the latter through Catholic purity. The former seeks it in order to practice fraud; the latter in order to bring praise to completion. The former hears with Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII); the latter hears from the Lord: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. X). For the Lord drove sellers and buyers out of the Temple, overturned the tables, and poured out the coins of the money-changers [Col. 0648B] (Luke XIX), leaving us an example, that we should expel Gehazi-like persons and Simoniacs from the Church, because they have no share in the kingdom of Christ and God.

The Jew also seeks the pearl of glory badly; the Christian seeks it well. The former seeks it by byways, and therefore never finds it; the latter by the way, and therefore reaches it. The former is like a blind man with veiled face; the latter like one who sees with unveiled face. For there is one and only one way by which one comes to the homeland: namely, that way which says of itself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

There are therefore many pearls, but one is precious. When a man finds it, he sells all that he has and buys it. He gives temporal things in order to acquire eternal things; earthly things in order to acquire heavenly things; he gives everything, [Col. 0648C] not only what is his but himself—not only his own resources but also his own will—according to the saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross” (Luke IX), etc. Hence Peter said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. XIX). Thus everything is sold in order that one thing only may be bought.

“Martha, Martha,” says the Lord, “you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary” (Luke X). The Prophet sought this one pearl when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. XXVI). How precious this pearl is, we cannot conceive, much less explain; for “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what [Col. 0648D] God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II). But lest we remain altogether silent, let us say that this pearl is the one God, who is all in all, the reward of all and the recompense of each individually. This is that denarius paid to all who labor in the vineyard (Matt. XX). And it is rightly called a pearl because of the splendor of knowledge in which eternal life consists: “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

Let no one despair because of poverty when he hears of a precious pearl, for it is bought easily.
