The widow bought it with the two small coins which she put into the treasury (Mark XII); another bought it with a drink of a cup of cold water, which he gave in the name of [Col. 0649A] a prophet (Matt. X); the thief hanging on the cross bought it with a single word, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” For immediately he heard: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke XXIII). Therefore let no one despair, for where means are lacking, the will is sufficient.

Therefore let us give what we can: earthly things for heavenly, transitory things for eternal, that we may buy the precious pearl from the Lord; he granting it, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0649]

# SERMONS OF POPE INNOCENT III OF THAT NAME, ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

## FIRST SERMON AT THE CONSECRATION OF A PONTIFF

On the dignity, danger, and sin of the priest; what is to be understood by the calf and the tabernacle; and on true repentance for all sins, and full confession and satisfaction for them.

[Col. 0649B] “If the priest who is anointed shall sin, causing the people to offend, he shall offer to the Lord for his sin an unblemished calf, and he shall bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord; he shall lay his hand upon its head, and shall sacrifice it to the Lord” (Lev. IV).

The words which I have spoken to you, dearest brethren, are words of the Lord speaking to Moses in Leviticus concerning the expiation of a priest’s crime. There are four kinds of persons: priest, ruler, people, and individual soul. Moreover, just as the sin of the priest is described first, so it is judged greatest: both because of the dignity of his office and because of the perversity of his example. The first is marked when it says, “If the priest who is anointed shall sin”; the second when it adds, “causing the people to offend.” For, in the words of the satirist Juvenal:

> Every vice of the mind bears in itself a crime  
> so much more conspicuous as the sinner is considered greater.

Many things are slight in subjects which are grave in prelates; and many things venial for laypersons are mortal for clerics. For if an enchanter is struck by a serpent, who will heal him? (Ecclus. XII). And if a priest sins, who will pray for him? Indeed, the higher the rank, the graver the fall. For from him to whom more is entrusted, more is required. “A severe judgment shall be made for those who rule” (Wis. VI).

To you, priest, “it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke VIII). But “the servant who knows his master’s [Col. 0649D] will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII). To you, priest, have been given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven (Matt. XVI). But woe to you if you put to death souls that should not die, or give life to souls that should not live (Ezek. XIII).

To you, priest, [Col. 0650B] it has been given to consecrate bread and wine into the body and blood of Jesus Christ. But “if you eat unworthily, you eat judgment to yourself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (I Cor. XI). And what of the fact that by your sin you cause the people to offend? Through you, “the name of God is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. II). “For the son cannot do anything unless he sees his father doing it” (John V). And he pleads in excuse: “It is enough for the disciple to be like his master” (Luke VI). Why, says the layman, should I not commit adultery when the priest fornicates? Why should I not lend at interest when the priest lends at interest? Certainly, the priest deserves as many deaths as the examples of perdition which he passes on to the people.

If the head is sick, the whole body will be weak; for “the whole head is sick and the whole heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I). When heretics see us sinning, they teach that alms ought not to be given to us, citing for this the authority of sacred Scripture, which says: “Let alms sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give.” It does not say, “Until you find an adulterous, drunken, envious, proud, perjured, greedy, usurious priest,” and the like; but it says, “Until you find one to whom you may give.” Offerings too, tithes and first-fruits, are to be given to ministers of God, not servants of the devil; for “he who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John VIII).

When heretics see us sinning, they teach that our preaching ought not to be heard, proving this by the authority [Col. 0650D] of sacred Scripture, which says: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX). When one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things. For when a man’s life is despised, it remains for his preaching to be held in contempt, and for it to be said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” [Col. 0651A] (Luke IV). “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Luke VI).

Likewise, when the Prophet was to be sent to preach, he was first cleansed from iniquity, and his mouth was touched by a live coal taken with tongs from the altar (Isa. VI). When heretics see us sinning, they teach that we cannot perform ecclesiastical sacraments, adducing the authority of Scripture which says: “I shall curse your blessings, and when you multiply prayer I shall not hear you” (Mal. II); “for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I). Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean (Lev. V). Therefore let our light shine before men, that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

[Col. 0651B] “For if the priest who is anointed shall sin, causing the people to offend, he shall offer to the Lord an unblemished calf for his sin.” It is not enough for the priest to offer for his sin a turtledove or pigeon, kid or lamb, goat or sheep; rather, he must offer a calf—not any calf, but an unblemished one; not anywhere, but at the entrance of the tabernacle; not before just anyone, but before the Lord; not in just any manner, but he shall lay his hand upon its head and sacrifice it to the Lord.

The individual soul that sins is commanded to offer a female goat; the ruler who sins is commanded to offer a male goat. But for both the priest’s sin and the sin of the multitude, an unblemished calf is commanded to be offered. Hence it is inferred that the sin of a priest is equated with the sin of the whole multitude, because the priest in his own sin causes the entire multitude to sin. Therefore let the priest offer an unblemished calf for sin, because a great fault must be expiated by a great victim.

Morally, by the unblemished calf we understand a contrite spirit, because “a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. L). This calf, this victim, this sacrifice must be offered to the Lord for sin, so that the calf which by sinning had been untamed through pride may by repenting be tamed through humility, and take upon itself Christ’s yoke, of which he says in the Gospel: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI). Then God will accept the sacrifice of righteousness; “then you shall lay calves upon his altar” [Col. 0651D] (Ps. L).

Therefore let the priest bring the calf to the entrance of the tabernacle by confession with the mouth; let him lay his hand upon its head by satisfaction in deed; and let him sacrifice it to the Lord by contrition of heart: so that the sin of thought may be washed away in the heart, the sin of speech in the mouth, and the sin of action in habitual practice. Thus the girl may be raised in the house (Matt. IX), the young man at the gate (Luke VII), and Lazarus in the tomb (John XI).

Therefore let the priest bring the calf to the entrance of the tabernacle. If by the tabernacle we understand the body, in which, according to the Apostle, “we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V), then by the entrance of the tabernacle we must surely understand the mouth of the body, of which David says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” [Col. 0652A] (Ps. CXL). The calf is brought to this entrance when the secret of the heart proceeds to confession by the mouth. “Speak,” he says, “your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII). “For the righteous man at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” (Prov. XVIII).

He who accuses himself before God, God excuses him. And he who excuses himself before God, God accuses him. Let us return to the Gospel; there we shall find an example: “Two men went up into the Temple to pray” (Luke XVIII), etc. There is a great difference between the confession of a crime made in a human tribunal and that made in the divine one. For the former condemns, while the latter justifies. In that tribunal, when the accused confesses, he is punished; in this one, he is absolved. Therefore the Prophet prays: “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII).

But one must take great care not to bring to the entrance of the tabernacle a fox instead of a calf. For he who reveals some of his sins and conceals others; or confesses one part to one person and another part to another; or states the deed but suppresses his intention in it; or minimizes and excuses the crime—such a person surely brings not a calf, but a fox. For “foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests” (Luke IX). But we, according to the Prophet, should “render the calves of our lips” (Hos. XIV), confessing every circumstance whatsoever of sin: the place, the time, the number, the person; the age, [Col. 0652C] knowledge, rank, and order; whether it was done readily, frequently, openly, or perseveringly, according to the ways in which we sinned more grievously.

For this is commanded: that the calf be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle before the Lord, who searches “the kidneys and hearts” (Apoc. II), before whose eyes all things are naked and open (Heb. IV), from whom no secret is hidden and no concealed thing escapes notice. In a human tribunal, when the accused confesses his sin, the judge is informed; in the divine tribunal, when the accused confesses his sin, the Lord forgets it. For at whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, “I shall not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII), says the Lord.

Therefore let the priest to whom the sinner confesses take care, since the confession is made not to a man but to God, lest perhaps after hearing it he remember the sin. That is, let him not indicate by word or sign that he knows the offense; for it is not said that the calf is to be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle before a man, but before the Lord. For the priest who reveals a sin commits a graver sin than the person who commits it.

It follows: “And he shall lay his hand upon its head.” By the calf’s head is signified the ruling faculty of the mind, that is, reason, according to the saying: “Anoint your head and wash your face.” By the hand is understood action, according to the saying: “My soul is always in my hands” (Matt. VI). We lay our hand upon the calf’s head when we subordinate action to reason, so that, according to the Apostle, “our worship may be rational” and we may “bear fruits worthy [Col. 0653A] of repentance” (Rom. XII).

The hand has five fingers, and satisfaction has five parts: roughness of clothing, abstinence from food, the power of prayer, interruption of sleep, and generosity in almsgiving (Luke II). Of these the Prophet says in the Psalm: “I clothed myself with sackcloth, and humbled my soul in fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV); and: “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Ps. CXVIII). Yet in all these matters one must lay one’s hand upon the calf’s head, so that one’s worship may be rational: lest the beast, if excessively burdened, collapse, or, if insufficiently burdened, become wanton (Rom. XII).

Let the measure of punishment correspond to the measure of fault, with the character of the penance weighed: it should not be so light that one grows presumptuous, nor so heavy that one despairs. “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. As you presented your members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, so present them to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. VI). Woe to those who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel; who bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on men’s shoulders, yet will not move them with one of their own fingers (Matt. XXIII).

Therefore let the priest lay his hand upon the calf’s head and sacrifice it to the Lord. To sacrifice the calf is to crush the heart, so that, according to the Apostle, it may die to sin and live to righteousness (I Pet. II). When it is thus killed, then it is justified [variant: “made alive”]; when it is thus struck, then it is healed. “I,” says the Lord, “shall kill and I shall make alive; I shall strike and I shall heal” (Deut. [Col. 0653C] XXXII). Therefore let our calf be put to death, let it be sacrificed, so that henceforth it may not revive for guilt. For he is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he repents of. “A dog returned to its vomit” (II Pet. II) is a penitent returned to sin.

Moreover, there are some who bring the calf but do not sacrifice it: these are those who repent of one sin but delight in another. Yet a person repents in vain unless he repents of all sins, because God does not halve forgiveness. For he made the whole man sound on the Sabbath (John VII); again, he cast out seven demons at once (Mark XVI), the number seven signifying the totality of forgiven crimes; likewise, from another he drove out a legion of demons (Luke VIII), showing that, whatever sins there are in one person, one must repent of them all. If, according to the Gospel saying, forgiven sins too return because of one sin, how much more are unforgiven sins retained because of one sin? “If therefore the priest who is anointed,” etc.

[Col. 0654B] Therefore, dearest brethren, let us live not only chastely but cautiously. Chastely, lest we defile the anointing of the order which we have received; for this reason it says: “If the priest who is anointed shall sin”—as though saying: Let him not sin, lest he defile the anointing. Or this is added to exclude those who, though of priestly descent, could not be anointed or serve because of bodily blemishes.

Cautiously, lest by our example we corrupt others; for this reason it says, “causing the people to offend”—as though saying: Let him not sin, lest by sinning he corrupt the people. Or, according to the Hebrew truth: “If the priest who is anointed shall sin to the guilt of the people,” that is, so basely as one of the people—which is exceedingly condemnable in a priest. Therefore let us preserve holiness of heart [Col. 0654C] and body, as befits God’s ministers and priests, with the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. AT THE CONSECRATION OF THE SUPREME PONTIFF

On the primacy of the Apostolic See, that it is from God, and on the eminent power of the Roman pontiff: that he is a servant, not a lord; and on the office of the faithful servant who is set over the Lord’s household, and the threefold food which he is bound to give the household.

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653D] “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time?” (Matt. XXIV).

Truth itself plainly shows what kind of person he ought to be who is set over a household, and in what manner he ought to be set over it. He ought indeed to be faithful and prudent, that he may give them food at the proper time: faithful, certainly, in giving food; prudent in giving it at the proper time. It is likewise plainly stated who appoints him, namely the Lord; whom he appoints, namely a servant; what kind he appoints, namely one both faithful and prudent; over what he appoints him, namely over a household; why he appoints him, namely that he may give them food; and when, namely at its proper time.

Let us therefore weigh each word. For since they are the words of the Word, there is nothing in them that does not have weight, [Col. 0654D] but all are weighty with fruitful meaning. The Lord, then, is not just any lord, but he who has written on his garment and thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Apoc. XIX), of whom it is read that “the Lord is his name” (Ps. LXVII). By himself he established the primacy of the Apostolic See, so that no audacity can oppose its establishment.

As he himself testifies: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI). Since he himself is both founder and foundation of the Church, surely the gates of hell cannot prevail against it, because its foundation remains immovable. Of it the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid, other than which no other can be laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Col. 0655A] (I Cor. III).

Therefore, although Peter’s little ship is often tossed by great waves in the midst of the sea, especially when Jesus sleeps in it, nevertheless it is never submerged. For Jesus commands the winds and sea, and there comes a great calm, so that men wonder and say: “What kind of man is this, that winds and sea obey him?” (Matt. VIII). For this is that lofty and stable house of which Truth says: “The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house; and it did not fall, because it was founded upon the rock” (Matt. VII)—namely, upon that rock of which the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

It is therefore clear that the Apostolic See does not fail in tribulation but is enlarged by God’s promise, so that it can say with the Prophet: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV). It prospers, trusting in the promise of him who said to the apostles: “I shall be with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Moreover, “if God is with us, who is against us?” (Rom. VIII). Therefore, since this institution is not from man but from God—or, more truly, since this institution is from the God-man—the heretic or schismatic labors in vain, the faithless wolf labors in vain, to destroy the vineyard, tear the tunic, overturn the lampstand, and extinguish the lamp, according to the word of Gamaliel, the honored teacher of the law, who says: “If this counsel is from men, it will be dissolved; but if it is from God, you cannot dissolve it, lest perhaps you be found to be resisting God” (Acts [Col. 0655C] V). “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me” (Ps. CXVII).

For I am that servant whom God has appointed over his household—but would that I were faithful and prudent, to give it food at the proper time!

Certainly I am a servant, indeed a servant of servants—would that I were not one of those of whom Scripture says: “He who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John VIII), and of whom it says: “Wicked servant, I forgave you every debt” (Matt. XVIII); and again: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII)—but one of those to whom the Lord says: “When you have done all things well, say that we are unprofitable servants” (Luke XVII).

I acknowledge myself to be a servant and not a lord, according to what the Lord says to the apostles: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise power among them are called sorcerers. But you are not so; rather, he who is greatest among you shall be servant of all, and he who is foremost, like a minister” (Luke XXII). Therefore I claim ministry for myself; I do not usurp lordship: following the example of that first and chief predecessor who said, “Not lording it over the clergy, but having become from the heart an example to the flock” (I Pet. V); and also of him who said, “Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one less wise: I more” (II Cor. XI).

It is a great honor that I have been appointed over the household; but it is a heavy burden, because I am the servant of the entire household. “I am a debtor to the wise and the foolish” (Rom. I). Many can scarcely serve one person worthily, still less can one person serve all worthily. “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn? Apart from those things which are outward, [Col. 0656A] there is my daily pressure, the care of all the churches” (II Cor. XI). How many distresses and pains, how many anxieties and labors I endure, I can endure more than I can express. I do not wish to exaggerate what I endure, lest I become less able to endure what I pile up. “Day utters to day how many labors I endure, and night declares anxieties to night” (Ps. XVIII). “My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” (Job XVI).

Yet, although I fail through frailty, “my sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III), “who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach” (Jas. I). Therefore, although “the way of a man is not in himself,” nevertheless I hope that my steps may be directed by him (Jer. X), who raised blessed Peter as he walked upon the waves lest he sink (Matt. XIV), and who “turns crooked things into straight and changes rough things into level ground” (Isa. XL). You have heard the condition; hear the obligation.

Since I am a servant, I ought to be faithful and prudent, that I may give food to the household at the proper time. God chiefly requires three things of me, denoted by these words: faith of heart, prudence in action, and food of the mouth. That is, I must be faithful in heart, prudent in action, and give food by speech. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). For “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV). “Without [Col. 0656C] faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. II), because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV).

For unless I myself were strengthened in faith, how could I establish others in faith? This is known to belong especially to my office, as the Lord declares: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXII). He prayed and obtained, because he was heard in all things on account of his reverence. Therefore the faith of the Apostolic See has never failed in any disturbance, but has always remained whole and undefiled, so that Peter’s privilege might remain unshaken.

Faith is so necessary to me that, although concerning other sins I have God alone as judge, I could be judged by the Church for the sin alone which is committed against faith. For “he who does not believe has already been judged” (John III). I do indeed believe, and most certainly believe, that I believe Catholicly, trusting that my faith ought to save me, according to the promise of him who says: “Your faith has saved you; go, and sin no more” (Luke VIII).

But “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II). That faith lives which works through love, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Heb. X). “For it is not hearers of the law, but doers, who are righteous before God” (Rom. II); “for if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man contemplating the face of his birth in a mirror” (Jas. I).

Therefore neither does faith suffice without prudence, nor [Col. 0657A] prudence without faith. It is necessary, then, that I be faithful and prudent; for it is written: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matt. 10). O how necessary prudence is for me, that my service may be reasonable (Rom. 12), that my left hand may not know what my right hand does (Matt. 6); that I may thus distinguish between leprosy and non-leprosy, between good and evil, between light and darkness, between holy and profane; lest I call evil good, or good evil (Deut. 17); lest I make darkness light, or light darkness (Isa. 5); lest I put to death souls that do not die, or give life to souls that do not live (Ezek. 12). Rightly, therefore, among the pontifical ornaments the *logion* is especially commended, which was square and double; and the discernment of the pontiff—which [Col. 0657B] it prefigured both in place and in name—ought to distinguish between four things: between truth and falsehood, lest he err in matters of belief; between good and evil, lest he err in matters of action. He ought to distinguish on behalf of two, namely himself and the people, lest, if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit (Matt. 13).

“It was square on account of the fourfold sense which the pontiff ought to have in the Scriptures: the historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. It was also double on account of the twofold Testament, which it is not expedient for the pontiff to ignore; because ‘the letter kills, but the spirit gives life’ (2 Cor. 3).” Square, on account of the New Testament, which is contained in the four Gospels; likewise double, on account of the Old, which is inscribed on two tablets. O how great must be that [Col. 0657C] one prudence which is compelled to answer every kind of prudence: to untie the knots of questions, unlock the hidden places of doubts, disclose the merits of cases; observe the proper order of judgments, expound the Scriptures, preach to the peoples, rebuke the restless, strengthen the weak, confound heretics, confirm Catholics. “Who is this man? We shall praise him” (Ecclus. 31). Therefore the Lord significantly says: “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant?” (Matt. 24). Such must be the man who is set over the household.

Indeed, I have been set over the household, so that, as my position is most eminent, so my merit may be most eminent. Yet it adds greatly to the praise of the mighty Lord that through his lowly servant [Col. 0657D] he accomplishes his good pleasure, so that nothing may be ascribed to human strength, but everything attributed to divine power. But who am I, or what is my father’s house, that I should sit above kings and hold the throne of glory? For to me it is said in the Prophet: “I have set you over nations and kingdoms, that you may uproot and destroy and scatter and dissipate, and build and plant” (Jer. 1). To me also it is said in the Apostle: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven,” etc. (Matt. 16). Though he spoke to all the apostles, he said particularly: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained” (John 20). But when he spoke to Peter alone, he said universally: “Whatever you bind [Col. 0658A] on earth shall be bound also in heaven,” etc.; because Peter can bind the others, but cannot be bound by the others. “You,” he says, “shall be called Cephas” (John 1), which is interpreted “head”; because, just as in the head resides the fullness of all the senses, while in the other members there is some share of that fullness, so the others were called to a share in solicitude, but Peter alone was assumed into the fullness of power.

You now see, therefore, who this servant is who is set over the household: surely the vicar of Jesus Christ, successor of Peter, the Lord’s Anointed, god of Pharaoh; set midway between God and man, below God but above man; less than God but greater than man; judging all men and judged by no one; declaring in the Apostle’s voice: “The one who judges me [Col. 0658B] is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4). Yet let the office of servitude humble him whom the height of sublimity exalts, so that his sublimity may be humble and his humility sublime; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4).—“He who humbles himself shall be exalted, and he who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14).—“Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Isa. 40). Sound counsel: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). And: “They have made you a ruler: do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32).—“This is the lamp set upon a lampstand” (Ecclus. 26), so that the sheep that are in the house may see (Matt. 5). But “if this light becomes darkness, how great will that darkness be?” (Matt. [Col. 0658C] 6).—“This is the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savour, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5). It is good for nothing thereafter except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men.

Hence, from him to whom more is entrusted, more is required; for he has more cause for fear than grounds for glorying: being about to render an account to God not only for himself, but for all who have been entrusted to his care. But absolutely all who belong to the Lord’s household are placed under his care. For he does not distinguish between this household and that, nor is it said in the plural, “over households,” as though there were many; but in the singular, “over the household,” as though there were one, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd (John 10).—“One,” he says, “is my dove, [Col. 0658D] my perfect one” (Song 6); likewise there is but “one seamless tunic, which was not divided” (John 19). Only one ark existed, within which all who were there “are recorded as having been saved in the flood under one ruler. But all who were found outside it perished in the flood” (Gen. 6).

Now he is set over the household for this purpose: that he may give it food in due season. The Lord Jesus Christ established Peter’s primacy before the Passion, during the Passion, and after the Passion. Before the Passion, when he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 14). During the Passion, when he said: [Col. 0659A] “Simon, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have once turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22). After the Passion, indeed, when for the third time he commanded: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21).

In the first, the sublimity of power is expressed; in the second, constancy in faith; and in the third, the feeding of the flock—things which are most clearly set forth here with respect to Peter. Constancy in faith, when it says: “He set [him] over the household.” The feeding of the flock, when it says: “That he may give it food.” He is bound to give food: namely, the food of example, of word, and of sacrament. It is as though he said: Feed them by the example of life, by the word of doctrine, by the sacrament of the Eucharist; by the example of conduct, by the word of preaching, by the sacrament of communion.

Concerning the first, Truth says: [Col. 0659B] “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4). Of the second, Scripture says: “He fed him with the bread of life and understanding, and gave him the water of saving wisdom to drink” (Ecclus. 15). Of the third, the Lord says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). I am bound to give the household the food of example, that my light may shine before men, so that, seeing my good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).—“For no one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may shine on all who are in the house” (ibid.). Therefore elsewhere the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 2). Let curtain draw curtain, and let him who hears [Col. 0659C] say: For if the priest who has been anointed sins, he causes the people to transgress. For

> Every vice of the soul bears a crime  
> So much the more conspicuous in itself,  
> The greater the sinner is held to be.  
> —Juvenal

But I am also bound to give the household the food of the word, that by dispensing it I may multiply the talent received, and so accomplish the work of an evangelist. For, according to the Apostle’s word, “God did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel” (1 Cor. 13); that the little dogs may eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table; because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 5). Lest perhaps that saying be uttered because of me—or rather, against me: “The little ones asked [Col. 0659D] for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4).

I am likewise bound to give the household the food of the sacrament, that in it it may receive life and by it escape death, he himself saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever. And the bread which I shall give is my flesh [Col. 0660A] for the life of the world. For unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6). I am indeed bound to give this threefold food, but in due season; because, according to Solomon’s proverb, “All good things [are] in their season” (Ecclus. 3). I am first bound to give the food of example, then the food of the word, so that I may worthily give the food of sacrament. For “Jesus began to do and to teach, leaving us an example that we should follow in his steps” (Acts 1).—“He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). For “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

For this reason pomegranates with golden bells hung from the pontifical garment (Exod. 28). For if I teach [Col. 0660B] and do not act, it will rightly be said to me: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4). And: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7).—“You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2). But God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my just ordinances, and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49). Certainly, if a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too should be held in contempt. “I have become all things to all men,” says the Apostle, “that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9).—“Rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep, so that our service may be reasonable” (Rom. 12).—“We speak wisdom among the perfect. [Col. 0660C] But among you I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2).—“As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For solid food belongs to the perfect” (1 Cor. 3). Let a man therefore prove himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of the cup; for “he who eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

Behold, brothers and sons, I have set before you to eat the food of the word from the table of sacred Scripture, expecting this recompense from you, asking this return from you: that you may lift pure hands to the Lord without disputing, and ask in believing prayer that Jesus Christ our Lord—who is God above all, blessed for ever and ever—may enable me worthily to fulfil this office of apostolic service, which is unbearable for my weak shoulders, to the glory of his name, the salvation of my soul, the advancement of the universal Church, and the benefit of the whole Christian people. Amen.

## SERMON III. AT THE CONSECRATION OF A PONTIFF

On the four kinds of betrothal and the praises of the Roman Church; on the spiritual marriage of a bishop with his Church, and the goods of marriage.

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659D] “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

[Col. 0660D] The groomsman says these things of the bridegroom; the voice speaks of the Word, the lamp of the sun, John of Christ. For Christ is the bridegroom, and the Church is the bride whom he has. Of [Col. 0661A] him David says: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18), etc. Solomon speaks of the bride: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride” (Song 6).

For we remember that we distinguished four kinds of betrothal in the little book which we published on the fourfold kind of marriage: the first, between a man and a lawful woman; the second, between Christ and holy Church; the third, between God and a righteous soul; the fourth, between the Word and human nature. Of the first marriage the first-created man, awakening, prophesied: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother,” etc. (Mark 10). Of the second marriage John speaks in the Apocalypse: “Come, I will show you the bride, the new wife of the Lamb” (Rev. 21). Of the third marriage the Lord says [Col. 0661B] through the prophet: “I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and compassions” (Hos. 2). Of the fourth marriage the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Go forth, daughters of Jerusalem, and see King Solomon in the diadem,” etc. (Song 3).

In this fourfold kind of marriage something is found equally worthy of admiration and veneration. By the first, two become one flesh; by the second, two become one body; by the third, two become one spirit; by the fourth, two become one person. Of the first, authority testifies: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Therefore Truth added: “Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. 19). Of the second the Apostle says: “Although all the members of the body are many, nevertheless they are one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 13). Because of this union he adds elsewhere: “For we have all been baptized into one body” (ibid.). Of the third, Scripture says: “He who clings to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6). Because of this union the apostle John says: “He who remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). Of the fourth, the Catholic faith confesses that, as a rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ. Because of this ineffable union the Evangelist testifies: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

Therefore the first union is rightly called carnal; the second [Col. 0661D] sacramental; the third spiritual; and the fourth personal: carnal, as we have said, between a man and a lawful woman; sacramental, between Christ and holy Church; spiritual, between God and a righteous soul; personal, between the Word and human nature.

Therefore, he who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. I have become the Bridegroom’s friend, to whom the Bridegroom graciously says: “Friend, come up higher” (Luke 24); having become the successor of him who, in a threefold answer, said to the Bridegroom: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21). Would that I loved the Bridegroom as I have been loved by the Bridegroom! For what more could he have done for me, whereby he might love me more? He has heaped upon me the goods of nature, [Col. 0662A] multiplied in me the gifts of grace, bestowed spiritual benefits on me, and added temporal ones; I hope, indeed, that he will grant eternal ones. “If one must glory, it is indeed not expedient” (2 Cor. 12), because “from him to whom more is entrusted, more is required” (Luke 12), according to the rule of truth.

Standing, therefore, I rejoice because of his voice; but because of which voice? Is it because of that which he said to me in Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven?” (Matt. 16). Or because of that which he spoke to me in the prophet: “I have set you over nations, that you may uproot and destroy and build and plant?” (Jer. 1). But this voice ought to make me afraid rather than glad. For I know him who said: “A severe judgment shall be made upon those who rule” (Wis. 6); and Scripture therefore warns and says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3).—“They have made you a ruler; do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32); and the Lord in the Gospel: “He who is greatest among you shall be servant of all; and he who is first, as one who ministers” (Luke 22).

And because of which voice ought I to rejoice? Surely because of that in which the Lord says to the apostles: “I will be with you all days, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28). And especially to Peter: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded that he might sift you like wheat,” etc. (Luke 22). This is the Bridegroom’s voice, for which I rejoice; because, just as he foretells to Simon the battle who promises victory, so he imposes an office who provides help. He foretells the battle when he says: “Satan has demanded that he might sift you like wheat.” He promises victory when he adds: “But I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (ibid.). For “this is the victory which conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5). He imposes an office when he says: “Strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22). He provides help when he says: “I have prayed for you, Peter” (ibid.).—“For he is heard in all things because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).—“The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me” (Ps. 117).

Therefore he who has the bride is the bridegroom. Am I not a bridegroom, and each one of you a friend of the bridegroom? [Col. 0662D] Certainly. A bridegroom, because I have the noble, rich, exalted, beautiful, chaste, gracious, most holy Roman Church, which, by God’s ordering, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful. She is Sarah more mature, Rebekah more prudent, Leah more fruitful, Rachel more pleasing, Hannah more devout, Susanna more chaste, Judith more courageous, and *Edissa* [uncertain name] more beautiful. “Many daughters have gathered riches, but this one alone has surpassed them all” (Prov. 31). With her I have a sacramental marriage; with her, a nuptial union. A marvellous thing: I, who promised celibacy, have contracted a marriage; but this marriage does not impede celibacy, nor does the fruitfulness of this spouse take away the chastity of virginity. John was pleasing in celibacy; Abraham was pleasing in marriage. [Col. 0663A] Would that I might be pleasing in both, that I might bear with exultation the sheaves of each!

Carnal marriage, that which is between a man and a woman, is customarily called initiated, ratified, and consummated: initiated in betrothal, ratified in consent, consummated in union. So too spiritual marriage, which is between a bishop and a Church, is called initiated in election, ratified in confirmation, consummated in consecration. But the marriage which I, the bridegroom, contracted with this bride of mine was simultaneously initiated and ratified; for when the Roman pontiff is elected, he is confirmed, and when he is confirmed, he is elected. Do you not remember what you read concerning him in the canon? That the person elected, as true pope, obtains authority to govern the Roman Church and dispose [Col. 0663B] of all its resources.

Certainly, when I contracted this marriage, the son took the mother as wife; but where I contracted it, the father had the daughter as wife. In carnal marriage, relatives are excluded and outsiders admitted; but in spiritual marriage, at first sight, outsiders are regularly excluded and relatives admitted. Concerning the exclusion of relatives from carnal marriage, you have read the canon’s provision: “We deny that all relatives by affinity may enter into a marital union.” But canonical authority hands down, concerning the exclusion of outsiders from spiritual marriage, that clerics are free to refuse if they see that they are being overburdened, and need not fear to reject those who may happen to be thrust upon them against their will. Therefore the canon provides [Col. 0663C] that no one from among carnal priests or deacons be consecrated to the height of the apostolate.

Today, therefore, you celebrate with me for the first time the anniversary day on which this spiritual marriage was consummated, although I was consecrated in the apostolic see on the very day on which the blessed apostle Peter was placed in the episcopal chair. But as the light of the sun does not allow the light of a star to be seen alongside it, so that solemnity does not permit this one to be celebrated with it. Thus the lesser yields to the greater, because the lesser succeeds the greater. I therefore contracted the marriage and celebrated the nuptials by consecration.

The three principal goods of marriage are faith, offspring, and sacrament. Faith pertains to chastity, offspring to fruitfulness, and sacrament to permanence. [Col. 0663D] For the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church have always kept such faith with one another that the saying of Truth in the Gospel may fittingly be applied to them: “I know my sheep, and mine know me” (John 10); they do not follow but flee a stranger, because they do not know the voice of strangers. The strangers are heretics and schismatics, whom the Roman Church does not follow, but pursues and drives away. But she knows and hears her own: not an apostate but an apostolic man; not a Cathar but a Catholic; receiving and rendering the marital due—receiving from him the due of providential care, and rendering the due of reverence. For “the man does not have power over his own body, but the woman does; likewise the woman does not have power over her own body, but the man does” (1 Cor. [Col. 0664A] 7).

But since the Roman Church renders the due of reverence to absolutely no one except the Roman pontiff, who after God has no other superior, what does this mean: that the Roman pontiff is bound to render the due of providential care not only to the Roman Church, but indeed to every Church whatsoever? “I am debtor to wise and foolish alike,” says the Apostle (Rom. 1); and: “My daily pressure: concern for all the Churches” (2 Cor. 11). What is judged by equal measures, so that, according to what is read in the Old Testament, one man could have several [wives]? Have you not read that Abraham had Sarah as his wife, yet she introduced her maidservant Hagar to him? In doing this she did not commit adultery, but fulfilled a duty (Gen. 16). So too the Roman [Col. 0664B] pontiff has the Roman Church as his bride, yet she introduces to him the Churches subject to her, so that they may receive from him the due of providential care; because the more that is rendered, the more is owed. But what then happened in the flesh now happens in the spirit, because “it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6).

But can not one bishopric have two bishops, and one bishop have two bishoprics? Not to seek examples far away: one and the same man is bishop of Ostia and Velletri [the printed text is defective: “Hostiensis et Vellucensis … episcopus”], so that both Churches were at the same time married to the same man. Again, the Church of Hippo, which was joined to Valerius, was also married to blessed Augustine while Valerius was still alive; Augustine did not so much succeed as [Col. 0664C] join Valerius. But by what reasoning these things can occur while the law of marriage remains intact, you may investigate, you who delight in investigating questions; another concern keeps me occupied.

Against this marriage between bishop and Church, let her bear religious offspring for Christ, so that his wife may be like a fruitful vine at the sides of her house, “her children like shoots of olive trees,” etc. (Ps. 127). For this reason the Apostle says: “My little children, whom I am again in travail with until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4). And Leah, having once given mandrakes, “hired Jacob to go in to her; and she conceived and bore” (Gen. 30). Those whom Christ regenerates he instructs with saving teachings and forms by upright admonitions; “he feeds them with the bread of life and understanding, and gives them the water of saving wisdom [Col. 0664D] to drink” (Ecclus. 15).—“Come,” he says, “and eat my bread, and drink the wine which I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9): the heavenly bread and the cup of salvation, from which whoever tastes shall live for ever, “containing every delight in itself and the sweetness of every flavour” (Wis. 16).

But the sacrament between the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church remains so firm and stable that they can never be separated from one another except by death; because when her husband dies, the woman, according to the Apostle, “is released from the law of her husband” (Rom. 7). But this husband, bound to his wife, seeks no release; he does not yield; he is not deposed. For “before his own master he either stands or falls” (Rom. 14).—“The one who judges is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4). Yet [Col. 0665A] on account of fornication the Roman Church could dismiss the Roman pontiff. I do not mean carnal but spiritual fornication, because the marriage is not carnal but spiritual: that is, on account of an error of unbelief; for “he who does not believe is already judged” (John 3). And it is in this respect that the Gospel passage you have heard is understood: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its savour, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5). Nevertheless, I would not readily believe that God would permit the Roman pontiff to err against the faith, for whom he prayed spiritually in Peter: “I,” he says, “have prayed for you, Peter,” etc. (Luke 22).

Therefore he who has the bride is the bridegroom. This bride did not marry empty-handed, but bestowed upon me a precious dowry without price: namely, the fullness of spiritual things [Col. 0665B] and the breadth of temporal things, the greatness and abundance of both. For the others were called to a share in solicitude, while Peter alone was assumed into the fullness of power. As a sign of spiritual things she bestowed a mitre upon me; as a sign of temporal things she gave me a crown: the mitre for priesthood, the crown for kingship; making me the vicar of him who has written upon his garment and thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19), and who is “a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). She bestowed upon me an ample dowry; but whether I have given her any bridal gift, judge for yourselves. I do not wish presumptuously to assert it. She sought one ignorant [Col. 0665C] and accepted one reluctant—opposing at first, but consenting at last—because consent alone between lawful persons makes marriage.

From this it seems to follow, however marvellous it may appear, that someone can belong to a Church before he is its bridegroom, [Col. 0666A] just as someone can be the bridegroom of a Church before he is its pontiff. For when, by the provision of a superior, a bishop is rightfully given to those who wrongfully withhold [consent], before they consent to him, he is surely their pontiff by the authority of the grant. But perhaps he does not yet seem to be their bridegroom because of the absence of consent, by which she is bound to consent and enter into the marriage covenant with him. But when he is received through election, he surely becomes their bridegroom by the mutual consent of electors and elected, especially once the election is confirmed. Yet before he is consecrated, he shall not claim either the name or the office of pontiff. But whether this is so, let our inquiry determine.

In spiritual matters a distinction can be made between bride and husband, and between bridegroom and wife: that the elected man is called bridegroom before confirmation, namely before he “knows” her—that is, before he administers; but he is called husband after confirmation, and especially after consecration, when he administers fully. Or rather, bridegroom or bride is said with regard to virginity, spouse with regard to fruitfulness. “For,” says the Apostle, “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11).

Therefore, he who has the bride is the bridegroom. But you, brothers and sons, who are friends of the Bridegroom and rejoice with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice, lift pure hands to God without disputing and, “with a pure heart and unfeigned conscience” (1 Tim. 1), pray that I may so render [Col. 0666C] to the Church the marital due that, when the Bridegroom comes, I may deserve, with the wise virgins and with lamps lit, to enter the wedding feast (Matt. 25). May he grant this, who is God above all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. AT THE CONSECRATION OF A PONTIFF

That charity and wisdom are necessary to a teacher, and what salt ought to be in a prelate; on twofold vanity and the diversity of things that lose their savour.

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665D] “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savour, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing thereafter except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men” (Matt. 5).

Truth, which cannot be deceived and does not wish to deceive, advances in the words set forth a certain terrible and irrefutable argument, by proposing, assuming, and concluding. It proposes an office, assumes a defect, and concludes punishment. It proposes the office when it says: “You are the salt of the earth.” It assumes the defect when it adds: “But if the salt loses its savour, with what shall it be salted?” It concludes punishment when it infers: “It is good for nothing thereafter except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men.” Therefore let him who bears the office take care not to incur the defect, because he will not escape punishment. “For the powerful shall powerfully suffer torments, [Col. 0666D] and a severe judgment shall be made upon those who rule” (Wis. 6). Certainly, the greater the eminence, the heavier the fall. For:

> Every vice of the soul bears a crime  
> So much the more conspicuous in itself,  
> The greater the sinner is held to be.  
> —Juvenal

Therefore Christ says: “You are the salt of the earth.” Among virtues and gifts, two are as it were especially and principally necessary to us: charity and wisdom. Charity serves the formation of an upright life; wisdom, the instruction of true doctrine. For “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” “For Jesus began to do and to teach, leaving us an example that we should follow in his steps” (Acts 1). [Col. 0667A] “He committed no sin,” so that uprightness might be in our life, “neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2), so that truth might be in doctrine. Hence “pomegranates with golden bells” hung from the pontifical garment (Exod. 28), lest one entering the sanctuary without them should die.

For there are many—would that I myself not be among their number—who speak but do not act. “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them upon men’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their own finger” (Matt. 23). But to such a man it is said: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4).—“Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7).—“You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. [Col. 0667B] 2).

These two, namely charity and wisdom, are commended in salt, which is made from two things: heat and moisture; for moisture is thickened by heat so as to become salt. By heat charity is signified, of which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12).—“Many waters cannot extinguish charity” (Song 8). By moisture wisdom is understood, of which Solomon says: “The words from a man’s mouth are deep water, and the overflowing torrent is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. 18). Therefore the pontiff ought to be the salt of the earth, so that through charity he may form the people by the example of his life, and through wisdom instruct them by the word of doctrine.

[Col. 0667C] Salt principally does three things: it seasons foods, dries meats, and makes the ground barren. To the first belongs what blessed Job says: “Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without being seasoned with salt?” (Job 6). To the second pertains what is said of the fish in Tobit: “Its flesh was salted” (Tob. 6). To the third refers what the Psalmist says: “He made a fruitful land into a salt-marsh because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it” (Ps. 106). Such ought the salt in a prelate to be: that it may season foods, dry meats, and make the ground barren. It must season the food of doctrine, concerning which Truth says: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season?” (Matt. 24); it must dry the flesh of concupiscence, concerning which [Col. 0667D] the Apostle says: “The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5); and it must make barren the ground of wickedness, concerning which the Lord says to Adam: “Cursed is the ground in thy work; thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for thee” (Gen. 3).

The food of doctrine is unsavoury if it has not been seasoned with the salt of wisdom—namely, that wisdom of which the Apostle says: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). Hence no doctrine has a good savour which does not resound with Christ, who is the savour, sweetness, and delight of the soul. “Let your speech,” says the Apostle, “be seasoned with salt” (Col. 4). For speech is insipid when it is not seasoned with the salt of spiritual wisdom.

Thus, when the sons of the prophets said to Elisha: “Behold, the dwelling-place of this city is excellent, [Col. 0668A] but the waters are very bad, and the land also is barren,” he said to them: “Bring me a new vessel and put salt into it.” And he said: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be in them death or barrenness” (4 Kings 2). Elisha is Christ; the city, the Law; the water, the letter; the salt, wisdom; the vessel, the preacher; the land, the Synagogue. The dwelling-place of this city, therefore, is excellent because, according to the Apostle, “the Law is holy, and the commandment holy” (Rom. 7); but the water is very bad, because “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3); and therefore the land is barren—that is, the Synagogue is unfruitful—because the Law brought no one to perfection.

The new vessel is the preacher of the Gospel, such as the Apostle Paul was, of whom the Lord said: “This man shall be a vessel of election unto me” (Acts 9). He is called a [Col. 0668B] new vessel on account of the new doctrine, concerning which Truth says: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Matt. 9). Into this vessel is put the salt of which the Lord says to the apostles: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9). From this new vessel Elisha pours salt into the spring, that he may heal the waters, so that there may be “in them no more death or barrenness” (4 Kings 2): for through the Gospel Christ sends preachers into the letter that is passing away, because “it is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 2 [as printed]). Thus at the wedding he changes water into wine, and removes the veil from the face of Moses, so that with unveiled face one may behold the glory of the Lord.

For the prelate must not only season foods, but also dry meats: that he may chastise his body and bring it into servitude [Col. 0668C] (1 Cor. 9), lest perhaps, after preaching to others, he himself should become a reprobate. For unless the flow of carnal concupiscence is dried up, the carnal man certainly rots in dung like a beast, and stinks in the tomb like one four days dead. Therefore the Psalmist said: “Pierce my flesh with thy fear, for I have feared thy judgments” (Ps. 118). Fear is the best nail, fastening the flesh to the cross. As it is written: “They crucified their members with vices and concupiscences” (Gal. 5), because “the fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclus. 1); and of it it is again said through the Prophet: “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Ps. 26).

It is also written that victorious [Col. 0668D] kings sowed destroyed cities with salt, so that no further growth might arise in them. The victorious kings are holy preachers, concerning whom the Apostle says: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms” (Heb. 2 [as printed]). The destroyed cities are the nations converted to the faith, from which the kingdom of the devil has been destroyed. Of this destruction the Lord speaks through the prophet: “I have set thee over nations and kingdoms, that thou mayest pluck up and destroy and scatter and overthrow” (Jer. 1). Therefore we must sow these destroyed cities with salt, lest any further growth arise in them, lest henceforth thorns and thistles of vices should spring up. Hence the Lord commands in the Law: “In every sacrifice you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2); that is, in everything that you say or do, employ wisdom, [Col. 0669A] lest you offer the Lord anything insipid or unsavoury.

“But if the salt has lost its savour, with what shall it be salted?” There are two kinds of vanity: one of nature, which is the mutability of our condition; the other of fault, which is vice and sin. Of the first the Apostle says: “The creation was made subject to vanity, not willingly” (Rom. 18 [as printed]); and Ecclesiastes says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (ch. 1). Likewise the Psalmist: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38). Of the second the same Psalmist says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4). And again: “The sons of men are deceitful in balances, that they may themselves deceive together through vanity” (Ps. 71 [as printed]); likewise: “Their days failed away in vanity, and their years in haste” [Col. 0669B] (Ps. 77).

No one escapes the first vanity, as is written concerning blessed Job: “Man, born of woman and living for a short time, is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow” (Job 14). But the Lord’s saying, “If the salt has lost its savour, with what shall it be salted?” concerns the second vanity. It is as though he said: If a prelate has become dissolved into vice, by whom will the people be instructed?

Now some lose their savour in heart, some in speech, some in deed: in heart, those who believe wrongly; in speech, those who teach wrongly; in deed, those who live wrongly. Of the first the Apostle says: “They became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1). Of the second the Psalmist says: “Each one spoke vain things to his neighbour; with deceitful lips, and with a double heart, they spoke evil” [Col. 0669C] (Ps. 2 [as printed]). Of the third Solomon says: “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity, because the perverse are difficult to correct, and the number of fools is infinite.”

But some lose their savour only through moisture; others through heat and moisture together. They lose it through heat who are dissolved by spiritual desires, as by anger or envy; of these it is written: “They burned in their concupiscences, inflamed by Gehenna” (Dan. 13 [as printed]). They lose it through moisture who are dissolved by carnal desires, such as gluttony and lust; of these it is written: “Behemoth sleeps in moist places, [Col. 0669D] confident that Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40). They lose it through heat and moisture together who are at once dissolved by spiritual desires and by carnal concupiscences; of these, so that the punishment may resemble the fault, Scripture says: “From snowy waters they shall pass to excessive heat” (Job 24). Of the former David says: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57). Of the latter Jacob says: “Thou hast been poured out like water; thou shalt not increase, because thou didst go up to thy father’s bed” (Gen. 49).

If salt has thus lost its savour in a prelate, with what shall the people be salted? As if to say: With nothing; because, according to the testimony of the divine Law, if the priest who is anointed sins, he causes the people to offend (Lev. 4). The sin of a prelate, therefore, is harmful to others and dangerous to himself. [Col. 0670A] It is harmful to others because, if the salt has lost its savour, with what shall it be salted? It is dangerous to himself because it is good for nothing further except to be cast out—that is, deposed from office—and trampled by men—that is, despised by the people. Or, “cast out and trampled by men” means excommunicated and avoided. Or again, it is cast out because it sinned against itself, and trampled by men because it sinned against its neighbour.

How this may be understood concerning any other prelate is sufficiently clear; but how it should be understood concerning the Roman pontiff is not so evident. For a servant, according to the Apostle, “stands or falls to his own master” (Rom. 14). Hence the same Apostle says: “Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant?” (ibid.). Therefore, since the Roman pontiff has no master other than God, however much he may lose his savour, who can cast him out or trample him underfoot, when it is said to him: “Gather thy cause into thy bosom”?

Yet he should not flatter himself vainly because of his power, nor rashly glory in his exaltation or honour; for the less he is judged by man, the more he is judged by God. I say, the less, because he can be judged by men—or rather shown to have been judged—if he should lose his savour into heresy; for “he who does not believe is already judged” (John 3). In this case, indeed, the saying concerning him must be understood: if the salt has lost its savour, it is good for nothing further except to be cast out and trampled by men.

What, then, does it mean when it says, “It is good for nothing further”? Does not the Lord say: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and not die” (Ezek. 18)? Did not the shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, come to seek the hundredth that had perished, and, having found it, carry it back upon his shoulders? (Luke 15). Did not the woman light a lamp and overturn the house in order to find the lost drachma? (ibid.). And after each parable the Lord added: “There is greater joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine just persons who need no penance” (ibid.). Did not David lose his savour when he committed adultery and murder? Yet he was not cast out or trampled by men; rather, with his sin forgiven, he remained in the kingdom (2 Kings 2 [as printed]). Did not Peter lose his savour, he who denied Christ three times? [Col. 0670D] Yet not only did he not lose the apostleship, but he also received primacy (Matt. 26).

What, then, does it mean when it says: “If the salt has lost its savour, it is good for nothing further except to be cast out and trampled by men”? But it is one thing to lose savour in one’s actions and another to lose savour in one’s beliefs. He who loses savour in deed, provided that he does not lose it in faith, is always restored to grace if he repents, and is often restored to rank. But he who loses savour in faith so as to become a heretic or apostate can indeed be restored to grace, but is restored to rank only with difficulty, because a scar remains from leprosy of this kind once contracted. For Peter denied not in heart but in speech.

But lest salt should lose its savour in me—a thing exceedingly harmful and dangerous—you, brothers and sons, should implore the most merciful [Col. 0671A] Father with devout prayers, that he who foretold to blessed Peter, “I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith may not fail; and thou, once converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22), may strengthen in me, his unworthy and undeserving successor, that faith [Col. 0672A] which works through love, to the glory of his name, to the salvation of my soul, and to the advancement of the universal Church: Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. TO THOSE IN THE CLOISTER

[Note: [Col. 0671D] From Cardinal Mai’s edition.]

[Col. 0671]

[Col. 0671B] Addressing those in the cloister, Scripture says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell as one!” (Ps. 132). And elsewhere the Psalmist says in the person of those in the cloister: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26). Although among natural philosophers unity is marked by most celebrated mysteries, among theologians it is subject to sacraments no less great. Without spiritual unity, grace is possessed neither in the present nor glory bestowed in the future; without unity, all religion expires; without unity, heavenly love languishes; without unity, faith perishes; without unity, obedience fails. Unity produces harmony in divine things, concord among angels, and obedience in Churches.

[Col. 0671C] Unity is threefold: there is supercelestial unity, celestial unity, and subcelestial unity. Supercelestial unity is in the concord of the Trinity, where there is unity that unites and is united; there is also unity that unites but is not united, and unity that is united but does not unite. Unity that unites and is united is the Holy Spirit, who unites the Father with the Son; hence he is called one with the Father and the Son, and elsewhere is called the kiss and love of the Father and the Son. And he is united because he is united with the Father and the Son through the divine nature. Unity that unites but is not united is the divine nature, because it unites the three persons with one another, but is not itself united to them, because it is not a person. Unity that is united but does not unite is the Father, because he is united with the Son and the Holy Spirit, but neither of them with him. Of the unity that unites and is united it is said: “Now, Holy Spirit, make us one with the Father and the Son.” [Col. 0671D] Of unity not united it is said: “In the Father, unity,” etc.

Celestial unity is in the concord of angels, and it is threefold: unity of nature, unity of grace, and unity of glory. Unity of nature, because all are ministering spirits; unity of grace, because they are confirmed in grace; unity of glory, because all are glorified in eternal blessedness. In this threefold unity there is diversity in the governance of dignities, in the ministries of offices, and in the knowledge of the mysteries of hidden things. There is there harmonious dissonance, consonant discord, diverse unity, united diversity, consenting disagreement, uniting diversity.

But subcelestial unity ought to exist in the Church, and it is threefold: unity of faith, unity of charity, and unity of obedience, so that inferiors obey superiors and superiors, by a measured custom, condescend to those beneath them. To indicate the merit of this unity, one man who went down into the pool was healed (John 5); one son of a widow was raised (Luke 7); the ark is completed in one cubit (Gen. 6). One man is sent to announce victory to David (2 Kings 1). One who announced to Job the death of his children was delivered from danger. Unity embraces all things that pertain to ecclesiastical unity. Singularity gives form to all things. For there is “one God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4), one law, one king, one grace, one glory.

Among those in the cloister there should likewise be a threefold unity: unity of religious observance, unity of possessions, and unity [Col. 0672C] of charity. Unity of religious observance requires that they be uniform in clothing, uniform in food, uniform in fasts, and uniform in vigils. But certain irregular persons exempt themselves from the rule of this unity, desiring to recline upon softer beds, attend fewer vigils, employ little or no silence, and eat more delicate foods.

For some monks embellish a coarse habit in one way or another—whether by shaking off its dust or by a certain elegant arrangement of its parts—because they fit their feet more tightly into their shoes, tighten their sleeves, or turn their hoods back over their ears. They seek, as far as they can, more delicate foods, and as much as possible alter, if not the material, at least the form: for if one wishes beans or other plain foods to be prepared in one fashion, another wishes them in another. Some break silence, if not with words, at least with signs, and so redeem tales made of words by a multitude of signs. Some either omit or interrupt the vigils.

There must also be unity in possessions, so that all things are held in common. For a monk ought to have nothing as his own in possession, because neither ought he to have anything as his own in willing. That he ought to have nothing as his own in property, let him understand from the example of Ananias, who expired at Peter’s feet because he held something back as his own (Acts 5). And for the instruction of those in the cloister the Lord says: “Unless a man renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). Nor is it enough to renounce one’s own things in property unless one also renounces them in will. Hence Peter says of this renunciation of the will: “Behold, we have left [Col. 0673A] all things and followed thee” (Matt. 19).

The cloistered person, therefore, who desires to have something as his own looks back with Lot’s wife (Gen. 19), puts his hand to the plough but draws it back, and, with Dinah the daughter of Jacob, seeks the adornments of foreigners (Gen. 38 [as printed]). Therefore he who excepts something for himself from the common practice of possession purchases the place of Judas, traitor and thief. O cloistered person, who hast left many things in the world, do not return to the world through desire for a single coin. Let not desire for one coin ensnare thee whom a treasury of riches did not deceive. Fear lest the devil’s snare catch thee in the least thing, when it did not deceive thee in the greatest.

Let the monk also cast away his own will, so that, as there is community in religious observance, so there may be community in will; that not only may all things be common to them as regards property, [Col. 0673B] but also as regards disposition; that all may agree in one will and consent in one charity; so that it may truly be said of them: “They had one heart in God and one soul” (Acts 4). The cloistered person is also bound to possess unity of charity, so that he finds his own advancement in his neighbour’s progress and mourns his own loss in his neighbour’s failing. Let the wiser instruct the less learned; let the healthy feel compassion for the sick; let the unharmed rejoice with the healthy. Thus let the cloistered life be an image of the heavenly life: where, just as in eternal life unequal brightness is joined to equal joy, so in the cloistered life unequal [Col. 0674A] gifts are joined by the mutual bond of love.

From this threefold unity the cloistered person is called a monk, as it were a guardian of unity. If he does not preserve the first unity, he becomes irregular; if the second, an apostate; if the third, a schismatic.

Therefore in cloistered communal life let there be unity that unites and is united: that is, a prelate uniting subjects by authority, and a subject united by charity. Let there be unity that is united but does not unite: that is, a subject who, although he does not unite others, nevertheless joins himself to others in charity. Let there be unity that unites but is not united: that is, charity, firmly attaching itself in the present to no one alone. Let there be in them unity of nature, that they may love nature in themselves; unity of grace, that they may share with one another the grace bestowed upon them; unity of glory, that in one hope they may tend toward the glory of eternal life. [Col. 0674B] Let there be unity of faith, lest they be heretics; unity of charity, lest they be schismatics; unity of hope, lest they be obstinate in a particular manner; so that it may be said of them: “Behold, how good”—with respect to human opinion—“and how pleasant”—with respect to the delight of the mind—“for brothers to dwell as one” (Ps. 132): as one in religious observance, as one in possessions, as one in charity. Thus may we be able to attain that unity of which the Psalmist says: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26).

## SERMON VI. DELIVERED AT THE GENERAL LATERAN COUNCIL

[Note: [Col. 0673] From Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. 22, p. 968; as also Sermon VII.]

[Col. 0673]

[Col. 0673C] “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,” that is, before I die (Luke 22).

Because “for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1), I do not refuse—if it has been ordained by God—to drink the cup of suffering, should it be offered to me, whether for the defence of the Catholic faith, the aid of the Holy Land, or the condition of ecclesiastical liberty; although I desire to remain in the flesh until the work begun is completed. Nevertheless, not my will but God’s be done. And therefore I said to you: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.”

Human desires are many and various: who could adequately set them forth? Yet all may be reduced to two kinds, namely spiritual and carnal: the spiritual concerns [Col. 0673D] heavenly and eternal things; the carnal, temporal and earthly things. Of the former the Prophet says in the Psalm: “My soul has desired to long for your ordinances at all times” (Ps. 118). And the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I had desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2). Of the latter the Apostle says: “Flee the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2); [Col. 0674C] and another says: “Keep evil desire far from me” (Ecclus. 23).

But I call upon the testimony of him who is the faithful witness in heaven that it was not with carnal but spiritual desire that I desired to eat this Passover with you: not for earthly advantage or temporal glory, but for the reform of the universal Church, and above all for the liberation of the Holy Land. It was principally and especially for these two purposes that I summoned this sacred council.

But perhaps you will say: What is this Passover which you desire to eat with us? For *pascha* is understood in different ways in the divine Scriptures: for a day, as in, “The day of unleavened bread, which is called Passover, drew near”; for an hour, as in, “On the fourteenth day at evening is the Lord’s Passover” (Lev. 3); for the lamb, as in, “The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover had to be slain”; [Col. 0674D] for unleavened bread, as in, “They did not enter the praetorium, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover” (John 18); for the feast, as in, “Before the feast-day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13); and also for Christ himself, as in, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5).
