Certainly [Col. 0675A], in Hebrew Passover is called *phase*, that is, “passage” or “transition” (Exod. 12); in Greek, *paschein* (πάσχειν), that is, “to suffer”: because through sufferings we must pass to glory, according as Truth himself said: “Christ had to suffer, and so enter into his glory” (Luke 24). For if we wish to reign with him, we must also suffer with him, although “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

This Passover, which is *phase*, that is, transition, I have desired to eat with you. Of it Exodus says: “They shall eat it hastily; for it is the *phase*, that is, the passage of the Lord” (Exod. 12). For it is read in the Book of Kings, and is stated most clearly in Chronicles, that in the eighteenth year of the reign of King Josiah the temple was restored and [Col. 0675B] the *Phase* was celebrated, such as had not occurred in Israel from the days of the judges and kings (4 Kings 24; 2 Chron. 35).

Would that this history might be a parable of the present time: that in this eighteenth year of our pontificate the temple of the Lord, which is the Church, may be restored; and that *Phase*, or Passover—namely, this solemn council—may be celebrated, through which there may be a transition from vices to virtues, such as truly has not occurred in Israel from the days of the judges and kings, that is, from the times of the holy Fathers and Catholic rulers, among the Christian people who see God through faith.

And I confidently hope in him who promises his faithful ones, saying: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18). For he himself is present in our midst to celebrate [Col. 0675C] this Passover: we who have gathered in this basilica of the Saviour in the name of the Saviour, for matters pertaining to salvation.

Now there is a threefold Passover, or *Phase*, which I desire to celebrate with you: bodily, spiritual, and eternal. Bodily, that there may be a passage to a place, for the liberation of pitiable Jerusalem; spiritual, that there may be a passage from one state to another, for the reform of the universal Church; eternal, that there may be a passage from life into life, for the attainment of heavenly glory.

Concerning the bodily passage, pitiable Jerusalem cries to us through Jeremiah in the Lamentations: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1). Therefore, all you who love me, pass over to me, that you may free me [Col. 0675D] from such great misery. For I, who once was mistress of nations, have now been made tributary; I, who once was full of people, now sit as though alone. “The ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the solemn feast” (ibid.); her enemies have become chief; all the holy places have been profaned; and the Lord’s sepulchre is without glory, though it used to be glorious.

Where the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, was worshipped, the son of perdition, Muhammad, is now worshipped. Foreign sons insult me and reproach the wood of the cross, saying: “You trusted in the wood; behold, now let it help you, if it can.” O what shame, what confusion, what reproach: the sons of the slave-woman, the most contemptible Hagarites, hold our mother—the mother of all the faithful—in slavery! [Col. 0676A] It is of her, indeed, that the Psalmist says: “Of Zion it shall be said: Man after man has been born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86); there God our king, before the ages, deigned to work salvation in the midst of the earth.

What then shall we do? Behold, beloved brothers, I entrust myself wholly to you; I place myself wholly before you, prepared, in accordance with your counsel, if you judge it expedient, to undertake personal labour and to go to kings, princes, peoples, and nations; and even beyond this, if by a loud cry I can rouse them to rise up to fight the Lord’s battle and to avenge the injury done to the Crucified One, who for our sins has been driven from the land and from his seat, which he purchased with his blood and in which he accomplished all the mysteries of our redemption.

Whatever [Col. 0676B] others may do, we priests of the Lord should take up this undertaking in a special manner, helping and assisting the needs of the Holy Land in persons and resources. Thus no one at all should remain who is not a participant in so great a work, lest anyone be deprived of so great a reward. For long ago, in a similar case, God brought salvation to Israel through priests, when through the Maccabees—priests, indeed, the sons of Mattathias—he freed Jerusalem and the temple from the hands of the ungodly (1 Macc. 9).

Concerning the spiritual passage, the Lord says to the man clothed in linen, who had a writer’s ink-horn at his loins: “Pass through the midst of the city, and mark *Tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations done in its midst” (Ezek. 9). Then [Col. 0676C] he said to the six men having instruments of destruction in their hands: “Pass through the city after him, and strike down everyone upon whom you do not find *Tau*. Let not your eye spare anyone; and begin at my sanctuary” (ibid.).

The man clothed in linen, having the writer’s ink-horn at his loins, ought to be the one who speaks: a man flourishing in virtues, such as that man of whom Scripture says: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was simple, upright, fearing God, and departing from evil” (Job 1). Clothed in linen—that is, adorned with honourable conduct and good works. Thus elsewhere it is said: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Ecclus. 9), that is, let your works be clean. For linen signifies purity and honour on account of its whiteness, to which it is brought by the mortification and crushing of the flesh; and from it the priestly garment was made under the Law.

The eminent and supreme writer is the Holy Spirit, the finger of God by which the tablets of the Covenant were written. Of him the Psalmist says: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44). The ink-horn of this writer is the gift of knowledge: through the pen of the tongue, the ink of teaching is brought forth and inscribed upon the parchment of the heart. [Col. 0676D] The loins are the seat of desire; concerning them the Lord commands: “You shall gird your loins” (Exod. 2); and the Psalmist prayed to the Lord: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. 25).

Therefore he has the writer’s ink-horn [Col. 0677A] who, through the gift of knowledge given him by the Holy Spirit, restrains and represses the desires of the flesh, so that his life may not disagree with his teaching, lest it be said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4); “You who preach that one ought not steal, do you steal? You who teach that one ought not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2). Therefore Truth says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12).

Hence he is commanded to pass through the midst of the city and mark *Tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve. T is the final letter of the Hebrew alphabet, expressing the shape of the cross as it was before Pilate placed the title over the crucified Lord; it was also wonderfully signified by the blood of the lamb placed upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses. He bears this sign upon his [Col. 0677B] forehead who displays in action the power of the cross: so that, as the Apostle says, he “crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5), and says with the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

Such people certainly grieve and groan over all the abominations committed in the midst of the city, because their neighbours’ sins are frying-pans for the righteous. “Who,” says the Apostle, “is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore the man clothed in linen, having the writer’s ink-horn at his loins, must pass through the midst of the city and mark *Tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the [Col. 0677C] abominations committed in its midst. For the supreme pontiff, established as watchman over the house of Israel, must pass through the entire Church, which is the city of the great King, the city set upon a mountain, examining and investigating the merits of each person: lest they call good evil or evil good; lest they put darkness for light and light for darkness (Isa. 5); lest they kill souls that do not die or make alive souls that do not live (Ezek. 11).

And therefore, in order that he may distinguish and discern between those persons, he must mark *Tau* upon the foreheads of the men who grieve, so that he may show that those who grieve and groan over the abominations perpetrated in the midst of the Church are marked with *Tau* upon their foreheads. Such people certainly grieve over guilt and groan over disgrace because of the abominations committed in the midst of the city; for abomination has now proceeded so far that guilt is disgraceful and disgrace itself is guilt.

Hence, if we diligently dig through the wall, as the prophet is commanded to do (Ezek. 12), we shall see greater abominations, most wicked abominations, which some practise in the temple. [Col. 0677D] The six men, each having instruments of destruction in his hand, ought to be you, men of virtue: six indeed because of the mystery of the number, so that you may be perfect in work and speech. For the number six is perfect because it is made up from the sum of its parts. Hence on the sixth day God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment (Gen. 1). [Col. 0678A] And when, in the fullness of time, the sixth age had come, on the sixth day, at the sixth hour, he redeemed the human race. Therefore he spoke six final words on the cross.

The instrument of destruction which you ought to hold in your hands for destroying the wicked is pontifical authority, which you ought to exercise in deed for the destruction of the unjust, following the example of the Psalmist, who says: “In the morning I slew all the sinners of the earth, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all those who work iniquity” (Ps. 100). Of these instruments it is said elsewhere: “He bent his bow and made it ready; and in it he prepared instruments of death; he made his arrows fiery” (Ps. 7).

You are therefore commanded: “Pass through the midst of the city, following him”—namely the supreme priest—as your leader, prince, and master, [Col. 0678B] so that you may strike by imposing interdicts and suspensions, excommunications and depositions, according as the character of the offence requires, everyone upon whom you do not find *Tau* marked by him who shuts and no one opens, who opens and no one shuts (Rev. 3). For those who are marked must not be harmed, as it is said elsewhere: “Do not harm the earth, the sea, or the trees until we have marked the servants of our God upon their foreheads” (Rev. 17).

But concerning the rest it is said: “Let not your eye spare anyone” (Ezek. 9), so that there may be no respect of persons among you, remembering what Moses is recorded to have said to the Levites: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join me. Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go to and fro from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each one kill [Col. 0678C] his brother, his friend, and his neighbour.” And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses (Exod. 32). You too should act in the same way.

Moreover, strike in such a way that you heal; kill in such a way that you give life, following the example of him who says: “I shall kill and I shall make alive; I shall strike and I shall heal” (Deut. 32). “And begin,” he says, “at my sanctuary” (Ezek. 9). “For it is time,” as the blessed Apostle says, “for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord” (1 Pet. 4).

For every corruption among the people proceeds principally from the clergy, because “if the priest who is anointed sins, he makes the people guilty” (Lev. 4). Indeed, when laypeople see them sinning shamefully and monstrously, they too fall into iniquity and crimes by their example. When anyone rebukes them, they immediately excuse themselves, saying: “The son cannot do anything except what he sees the father doing” (John 5); and, “It is enough for the disciple to be like his master” (Matt. 10). [Col. 0678D] That prophetic saying has been fulfilled: “As is the people, so is the priest” (Hos. 4); indeed, “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23).

From this also evils have arisen among the Christian people. Faith perishes; religion is disfigured; liberty is thrown into confusion; justice is trampled down; heretics spring up; schismatics grow insolent; the faithless rage; the Hagarites prevail.

But concerning the eternal passage the Lord says: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watchful. Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and, passing by, [Col. 0679A] will minister to them” (Luke 12). Of this passage the martyrs rightly boast in the Psalm, saying: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 65).

This Passover above all others I desire to eat with you in the kingdom of God. Now there is bodily eating and spiritual eating. Of the former it is said: “Give them something to eat” (Matt. 14); of the latter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). Again, there is eating of guilt and eating of punishment; of the former it is said: “They ate the sacrifices of the dead” (Ps. 105); of the latter we read: “My sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32).

Again, there is doctrinal eating and penitential eating. Of the former it is said: “I have food to eat which you do not know” [Col. 0680A] (John 4); of the latter we read: “They ate ashes like bread” (Ps. 101). There is, moreover, eucharistic eating and eating of glory. Of the former it is said: “He who eats me shall live because of me” (John 6); of the latter we read: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14).

By this final kind of eating I especially desire to eat this Passover with you, so that we may pass from labour to rest, from sorrow to joy, from unhappiness to glory, from death to life, from corruption to eternity; through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. DELIVERED AT THE GENERAL LATERAN COUNCIL

[Col. 0679]

[Col. 0679B] “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the appearance of gold” (Ps. 67).

Two things are necessary for our merit: namely life and teaching—the one for ourselves, the other for our neighbours. “For Jesus began to teach and to do” (Acts 1), leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps, he “who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found” (1 Pet. 2): “he committed no sin,” so that there may be uprightness in life; “and in whose mouth no deceit was found,” so that there may be truth in teaching. These two are commended to us in the words set before us. Concerning life, it first says, “If you sleep”; teaching follows, “among the midst of the lots.” Hence it is that pomegranates [Col. 0679C] with golden bells hung from the pontifical garment (Exod. 28). By the pomegranate is understood action; by the golden bell, preaching. These two must be joined in a priest, lest he enter the sanctuary without them and die.

But because reward is attained through merit, reward is rightly promised after merit. A twofold reward is promised: one in the present and the other in the future. For godliness has the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come, so that one may receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life: a hundredfold in the present, eternal life in the future. Concerning the present it first says: “The wings of the dove are silvered.” Concerning the future it adds: “And the hinder parts of her back are in the appearance of gold.” “For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace [Col. 0679D] and glory” (Ps. 83). He grants grace in the present for merit; he will grant glory in the future for reward.

Now sleep is twofold: one sleep of death, the other of life; but each is divided. There is a sleep of bodily death, and this is punishment; and there is a spiritual sleep, and this is guilt. Of the first the Lord says to the apostles: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps” (John 2); and the Apostle says: “I do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep,” etc. (1 Thess. 4). [Col. 0680B] Of the second David says: “Will one who sleeps not add that he may rise again?” (Ps. 40); and the Apostle says: “Arise, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ shall illuminate you” (Eph. 5).

This is incurred in three ways: through ignorance, negligence, and desire. Of the sleep of ignorance the Psalmist says: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12). Of the sleep of negligence Solomon says: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you arise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, you will doze a little, you will fold your hands a little in order to sleep; and poverty will come upon you like a traveller, and want like an armed man” (Prov. [Col. 0680C] 6). Of the sleep of desire David says: “They have slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 73).

Moreover, a sleep of life is also read of in Scripture as twofold: one of bodily life proceeding from nature, the other of spiritual life proceeding from grace. Of the first the Lord said to the apostles: “Sleep now and rest” (Matt. 26); of the second, the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song 5). So we too, beloved, should watch and sleep: we should sleep from evils and keep watch in good things.

For the perfection of life consists in two things: avoiding vices and practising virtues, according to the saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” [Col. 0680D] (Ps. 36). By the one we avoid punishment; by the other we acquire reward. These two are appropriately understood through sleep. For sleep, as those who discourse upon the natures of things affirm, is the repose of the animal powers, while the natural powers remain active. But we who are spiritual can find these things spiritually in the spirit.

For there are three natural powers in the soul: the rational power, [Col. 0681A] the concupiscible power, and the irascible power. Rationality is like a digestive power, distinguishing good from evil, light from darkness, and holy from profane. The concupiscible faculty is like an appetitive power: it chooses the good, seeks light, and pursues the holy. The irascible faculty is like an expulsive power: it rejects evil, repels darkness, and refuses the profane.

Conversely, there are three animal defects in the soul: ignorance, negligence, and concupiscence. Ignorance opposes rationality; negligence, the irascible faculty; concupiscence, the concupiscible faculty. It is chiefly from these three vices that we must sleep. For from negligence comes an offence; from concupiscence comes sin; from ignorance arise both offence and sin. There is a difference between an offence and sin: offence consists in omission, sin in commission. An offence is not doing what ought to be done; sin is doing what ought not to be done. [Col. 0681B]

We must sleep from ignorance, especially from ignorance of the commandments in the divine precepts and of the offices in the ecclesiastical sacraments; these two we cannot ignorantly neglect without danger. For it is written: “But they did not know my ways, so I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest. They did not know or understand; they walked in darkness” (Ps. 95). But God says to the prophet: “You have rejected knowledge, and I shall reject you, so that you may not exercise the priesthood for me” (Hos. 4). “And my people have been led captive because they had no knowledge; [Col. 0681C] their nobles have perished from hunger, and their multitude has dried up with thirst” (Isa. 5). “He did not wish to understand so as to do well; he meditated iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. 35). “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

Let us therefore especially beware of ignorance, we to whom it has been given by office to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, while the rest receive them in parables (Matt. 13). For we ought to be oxen ploughing; the rest are asses grazing nearby. As we sing to God, we promise: “I shall meditate upon your ordinances; I shall not forget your words” (Ps. 118). We ought to be the light of the world. But if the light that is in us becomes darkness, how great will the darkness be? We ought to be the salt of the earth. “But if salt loses its savour, with what will it be salted? It is good for nothing further except to be cast out and trampled underfoot by people” (Matt. 5). [Col. 0681D]

Therefore let ignorance be at rest, and let rationality be active, according to the saying: “Let your service be rational” (Rom. 12); and: “Be ready to give an account to everyone who asks you concerning the faith that is in you” (1 Pet. 3). For this is the *logion*, or “rational [breastpiece],” which the high priest wore upon his breast, on which were written *urim* and *tummim*, that is, “manifestation and truth” (Exod. 28). For upon the breast of the priest there ought to be manifest knowledge of truth, according to that prophetic saying: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

Now the breastpiece was four-cornered, because the priest ought to distinguish [Col. 0682A] between four things: truth and falsehood, lest he err in belief; good and evil, lest he err in action. It was also doubled, because he must distinguish for two persons—for himself and for the people—lest, if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit (Matt. 15). Let us therefore sleep from ignorance, because “he who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120). He will not sleep with respect to punishment unless we sleep with respect to guilt.

We must also sleep from negligence, especially in prayer, which concerns the Lord, and correction, which concerns one’s neighbour. These two cannot be neglected without sin. Some pray so negligently and irreverently that with their mouths indeed they speak heavenly things, but in their hearts meditate on earthly ones. To them the Lord reproaches through the prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 26). Of such persons it is written: “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed” (Ps. 61). With their mouths they bless who speak words of truth; but with their hearts they curse who meditate empty vanities.

Others pray so hastily and indiscreetly that, omitting the middle, they utter only the head and tail. But how will God hear someone who does not hear himself? Whoever prays in this way does not incline God to pardon, but provokes him to anger. “But when you pray, enter into your chamber and, with the door shut, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6). Enter the chamber of your heart, shutting the door of the senses, lest dead flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment. [Col. 0682C] Pray to your Father, not with much speaking, as the Gentiles do, who suppose that they are heard because of much speaking, but “with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1).

Thus Moses and Susanna prayed (Dan. 13): they cried to the Lord, and he delivered them from their necessities. They cried not so much through exertion of voice as through devotion of heart, as the Psalmist says: “Delight in the Lord, and he shall give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 56). Hence the Apostle also says: “Singing and making melody in your hearts” (Eph. 3). For God is not so much a hearer of the voice as of the heart; nor must he be reminded by cries, since he searches the reins and hearts (Ps. 7).

This Hannah, bearing the type of the Church, is read to have observed: not through a loud petition but through devout prayer she obtained what she asked. It is read in the Book of Kings that “Hannah spoke in her heart, and only her lips moved, while her voice was not heard at all” (1 Kings 1). Hence the Psalm says: “What you say in your hearts, be contrite upon your beds” (Ps. 4), because “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50). [Col. 0682D]

Nevertheless, it is fitting that verbal utterance should accompany devout affection: for what breath does for coal, utterance does for devotion. Hear the Psalmist: “With my mouth I cried to him, and I exalted him beneath my tongue” (Ps. 65). Therefore, beloved, when you pray, stand before the Lord our God contrite, humble, and devout—[Col. 0683A] without movement, laughter, or loud guffawing. Do not cry out too loudly or hurry too much, but pronounce distinctly so as to be understood, because “cursed is the person who performs the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48).

Therefore, “serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 1), especially in the sacrifice in which the memorial of Christ’s death is celebrated. “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). And the Apostle says: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 2). Negligence is sin in every office, but in the sacrifice it is perilous, because “he who eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid.).

Let us likewise beware of negligence [Col. 0683B] in correcting sinners. For some are “dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56), smoothing over the vices of sinners either from love of gain or fear of frailty: from love of gain, lest perhaps they lose offerings or tithes; from fear of frailty, lest perhaps they incur resentment or hatred. Against such persons it is said through the prophet: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow and make pillows under the head of every age” (Ezek. 12). Again: “They built a wall, but those men coated it again” (ibid.). “Your prophets saw foolish and false things for you; they did not expose your iniquity to provoke you to repentance” (Isa. 56).

On the other hand, it is commanded: “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58). Hence the Apostle said to the Ephesians: “My hands are clean from the blood of all of you, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20). Hear the prophet: “Woe is me, because I have kept silence: for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people with unclean lips” (Isa. 6).

John did not fear Herod so as to refrain from freely rebuking him concerning Herodias, whom he held as wife while her husband Philip was still alive. Therefore let negligence be at rest, and let the irascible faculty be active, according to the saying: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Eph. 4; Ps. 4); that is, be angry with vices, lest you sin. This is that zeal by which Christ, inflamed, [Col. 0683D] cast those selling and buying from the temple (John 2), in accordance with the saying: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68); and by which Phinehas, stirred up, pierced with a spear the Jew coupling with a Midianite woman (Num. 25).

Therefore the discerning priest should exercise severity toward rebels and the obstinate, but show compassion toward the humble and penitent. Do not follow him [referent uncertain], leaving the half-dead man in his wounds—the man whom the Samaritan brought to the inn and poured wine and oil upon (Luke 20). And in the ark of the tabernacle were kept both the rod and manna.

We must also sleep from every concupiscence, especially from desire for things, which proceeds from avarice, and desire for women, which arises from lust. For it is written: “Nothing is more wicked than the miser, and nothing more unjust than to love money” (Eccl. 10). [Col. 0684A] It is the saying of the wise man, confirmed by the Apostle, who says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, the devil’s snare, and many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a human being into ruin and destruction; for covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). And elsewhere: “Avarice is the service of idols” (Eph. 5).

Hear what the prophet says against covetous priests: “Her rulers judged for gifts, her priests taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money” (Mic. 3). “Hell and destruction are never filled; likewise, human eyes are insatiable” (Prov. 27). “The leech has two daughters, saying: Bring, bring” (Prov. 30).

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* 14.139

“But the world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2). “Therefore let us not fear when a man has become rich and the glory of his house has been multiplied; for when he dies, he shall take none of these things, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48). [Col. 0684B] Nor do I say this because it is unlawful to possess riches, but because it is unlawful to cling to riches, according to the saying: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61).

Therefore let none of you entice another’s parishioner or invade another parish. For it is commanded that no one put a sickle to another’s harvest (Deut. 33), [Col. 0684C] nor overstep the boundaries which our fathers established. Nevertheless, let us beware of desire for women; for “wine and women make wise men apostatize” (Ecclus. 19).

And because of a woman’s beauty many have perished. “Her house is the way to hell, penetrating to the innermost regions of death” (Prov. 7). Passion and wantonness always go before her; stench and uncleanness always accompany her; pain and repentance always follow her. “For the lips of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but in the end she is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. 5). The enemy is familiar: he dwells not far away but near, not outside but within; for “his strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40).

[Col. 0684D] He is never driven away except by flight; never slain except by mortification. But we who have been established in sacred orders are now bound by necessity to preserve chastity. For it is written that, when David fled Saul’s persecution, he came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest, asking that five loaves be given him to drive away his hunger; and the priest replied: “I have no common bread at hand, but only holy bread. If the young men are clean, especially from women, let them eat” (1 Sam. 21). He did not say, If they have faith, hope, and charity; if they have justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance; if they have the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

[Col. 0685A] Rather, he said: “If they are clean, especially from women, let them eat,” because none can worthily eat holy bread unless they are clean from intercourse with women. Let concupiscence therefore be at rest, and let the appetitive power be set aflame, according to the saying: “My soul has longed to desire thy justifications at all times” (Ps. 118). Let it be set aflame through the three principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity—so that the rational faculty may be enlightened through faith, the irascible faculty strengthened through hope, and the appetitive faculty formed through charity. Let it be enlightened by the truth of faith, so that the rational faculty may drive out the error of ignorance; strengthened by the steadiness of hope, so that the irascible faculty may exclude the torpor of negligence; formed by the sincerity of charity, so that the appetitive faculty

[Col. 0685B] may extinguish the heat of concupiscence.

Let us therefore sleep “between the middle portions,” that is, in the midst of the *cleroi*, according to Greek idiom. Literally, we exist between the middle portions of the whole world; therefore our works cannot remain hidden, whether they are good or evil. “Let your light therefore shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5), so that curtain may draw curtain, and he who hears may say, “Come.”

Yet we can understand this otherwise. For κλῆρος (*klēros*) in Greek is interpreted as “lot” or “inheritance”; hence clerics are so called because they have obtained a share in the Lord, according to the saying: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15). There is a threefold inheritance: lowest, middle, and highest. The lowest is earthly, concerning which

[Col. 0685C] it is written: “He gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his servant” (Ps. 135). The middle inheritance is sacred Scripture, concerning which it is said: “I have acquired thy testimonies as an inheritance for ever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart” (Ps. 118). The highest is heavenly blessedness, concerning which it is written: “The measuring-lines have fallen to me in splendid places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (Ps. 15). Each of these inheritances has its middle portions. Earthly possession consists of movable and immovable things; sacred Scripture, of spirit and letter; heavenly blessedness, of the robe of the mind and the robe of the flesh.

We must sleep among these middle portions, among these middle inheritances, in different ways. For there is a middle which touches both extremes; there is a middle which touches neither extreme; and there is a middle which touches only one of the extremes.

[Col. 0685D] For example, the middle which touches both extremes is the air, which, being between heaven and earth, touches both; the middle which touches neither extreme is the sun, which, being between heaven and earth, touches neither; and the middle which touches only one extreme is a tree, which, being between heaven and earth, touches only one. In this manner we must sleep among these middle portions, among these middle inheritances.

Let us therefore sleep among the middle portions of earthly possession through the irascible power, so that we may rest in neither of its parts,

[Col. 0686A] according to what is written: “Little children, do not love the world, nor the things which are in the world” (1 John 2). Let us sleep among the middle portions of sacred Scripture through the rational power, so that we may rest in only one of its parts, as it is written: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Let us sleep among the middle portions of heavenly blessedness through the appetitive power, so that we may rest in both parts, according to what is written: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5): rejoice for the robe of the heart, and exult for the robe of the body.

If we sleep thus, then indeed we are the silvered feathers of the dove. As the dove signifies the Church, so the dove’s feathers signify the priests

[Col. 0686B] of the Church, who raise her to heavenly things by word and example. Hence the bridegroom says of the bride in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my perfect one” (Song 6). Describing her feathers perfectly, the prophet says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). Silvered feathers are those instructed by the divine utterances, according to the saying: “The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tested by fire, tried in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11). Hence it is said elsewhere: “Your eyes are like doves washed with milk, sitting beside abundant streams” (Song 5).

There are feathers of virtue, feathers of contemplation, and feathers of teaching. Of the first it is written: “He flew upon the feathers of the winds” (Ps. 17); of the second it is said:

[Col. 0686C] “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54); of the third it is written: “The wings of one were joined to those of another” (Ezek. 1). Moreover, there are true feathers and false ones. True are the feathers of the righteous, signified by the feathers of the heron; false are the feathers of hypocrites, signified by the feathers of the ostrich. For it is written in Job: “The feather of the ostrich is like the feather of the heron and the hawk” (Job 39).

We are feathers when, despising worldly things through the irascible power, we sleep among the middle portions of earthly possession. Let us be feathers of the dove when, desiring heavenly things through the appetitive power, we sleep among the middle portions of everlasting blessedness. Let us be silvered feathers

[Col. 0686D] when, understanding divine things through the rational power, we sleep among the middle portions of sacred Scripture. And let us not merely be, in the present life, silvered feathers of the dove, but let “the hind parts of her back” be in the appearance of gold. As the back signifies the labor of the present life, according to the saying, “Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 128), so the hind parts of the back signify the rest of the life to come, according to the saying: “There shall be no more mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21). Therefore the hind parts of the back—that is, rest after labor—will be in the appearance of gold, that is, in the glory of contemplation, fittingly signified by the brightness of gold; for this reason:

[Col. 0687A] “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Wis. 3). To this glory may the Lord

[Col. 0688A] Jesus Christ bring us, who is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Notice concerning the following sermon

[MAI, *Spicilegium Romanum*, VI, p. 578.]

[Col. 0687]

At the end of the earlier Innocentian codex there appears, among other items, a sermon of Master Romanus, Cardinal, On Penance, or Confession. Romanus was a cardinal-priest under Paschal II, at the beginning of the twelfth century, according to the catalogues cited by Cardella. Another Peter, slightly earlier, was a Roman cardinal-priest under Alexander II, according to Panvinio, after the middle of the eleventh century; nevertheless, the name Peter is prefixed to this one. This Romanus was nevertheless a contemporary of Cardinal Atto. A third Romanus, cardinal-priest, is likewise listed in the catalogues under Celestine III, at the end of the twelfth century. There were also Roman cardinal-deacons; nevertheless, this sermon seems more properly to be attributed to a priest than to a deacon. Indeed, a splendid epitaph of Romanus, apparently cardinal-priest, is recited by Rondinini at the church of Saint Clement, p. 281. All these preceded the pontificate of Innocent III, although one almost reached it. I have therefore not declined to append here this sermon, which presents an image of sacramental penance as it already existed at that time.

## Sermon of Master Romanus, Cardinal, on Penance

[Col. 0687]

[Col. 0687B] “Come from Lebanon, my sister, my bride; come from Lebanon, come: you shall be crowned” (Song 4).

Thus it is read in the Song of Songs; and Christ, the bridegroom and brother of holy Church, speaks to his sister and bride. God, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, seeing that the soul created by him, having fallen, cannot return unless drawn, calls her back, saying: “Come,” etc. He calls her sister because he made her in his image and likeness with respect to reason and understanding; he calls a human being bride with respect to baptism, because in baptism the human being is joined to him as a bride. God infused the soul by creating it, and created it by infusing it. And because it has fallen in three ways—namely, by thinking, speaking, and acting—he recalls it three times, saying, “come, come, come”; and twice he says “from Lebanon,”

[Col. 0687C] that is, from the whitening of body and soul. And “you shall be crowned,” because after the cleansing of body and soul comes the crown.

As light was made on the first day, so divine grace must first be infused after a fall. On the second day the waters above the firmament were divided from those below it; so, after grace has been received, through faith and works as intermediaries, virtues are separated from vices. On the third day, “the earth brings forth green herb and fruit-bearing tree, yielding fruit according to its kind” (Gen. 1). The earth is holy Church, bringing forth green herb—that is, holy preachers—who bear fruit according to their kind by converting sinners through their preaching.

Or Christ loved the faithful soul as a brother loves a sister, or as a son loves father or mother; for “he emptied himself” (Phil. 2) for her, assuming our humanity. He loves us more than a husband loves his bride; for he was willing to be crucified for

[Col. 0688B] our salvation, which a husband would by no means do. And as a husband does not wish anyone to share his wife, so neither does Christ wish anyone to share the faithful soul. Yet if she departs from him by sinning, he calls her back, saying through Ezekiel: “You have committed fornication with your lovers” (ch. 16); nevertheless, return to me at last.

The soul dies in three ways: first, through thought, and it is raised by God’s grace through contrition of heart, as was the girl in the house raised by the Lord. Second, it dies through evil speech and is raised by the Lord through true confession, as the widow’s son was raised at the gate (Luke 7). Third, it dies through evil action, but it is raised by the Lord, like Lazarus (John 11), through satisfaction. These are the three days’ journeys by which we must return to

[Col. 0688C] our Creator, so that we may offer him a sacrifice of praise—as Abraham offered sacrifice on the third day after completing his journey (Gen. 22). These are the three days’ journeys which the Hebrews—that is, the children of Israel—asked of Pharaoh, saying: “We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the Lord” (Exod. 3). Hebrews are those who pass from vices to virtues; Pharaoh, that is, the devil, opposes them. The wilderness is this world, in which are beasts and creeping things without number, that is, diverse kinds of sins. In this wilderness let us sacrifice to the Lord in a safe place, that is, in the cloister of religion. The three journeys are also so called because of Peter’s threefold denial and threefold confession, and because of the three persons of the Trinity.

The first journey is contrition of heart, which is necessary. For as delight attended evil thought, so bitterness ought to follow in satisfaction; for by the art of medicine, contraries are cured by contraries.

[Col. 0689A] The second journey is confession of the mouth, which is necessary in order that sin may be healed by spiritual medicine; for in confession all things are washed away, as the apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another that you may be saved” (Jas. 5).

There are fifteen steps of confession, just as there are fifteen Songs of Ascents, and there were fifteen steps by which one ascended to Solomon’s temple. And so that we may come to the temple of the true Solomon, that is, Christ, let us ascend by these fifteen steps. They are these: confession ought to be voluntary, true, shamefaced, self-accusatory, prompt, frequent, deliberate, personal, naked, whole, undivided, secret, straightforward and ordered, general, special, and individual.

It must be voluntary; hence: “I shall sacrifice to thee willingly and confess thy name, O God” (Ps. 53).

[Col. 0689B] It must not be compelled, as happens at the end, when the sinner is powerless and forgetful of conscience because of the straits of death. Hence Augustine says: “When one confesses because sin is abandoning the person rather than the person sin, I neither praise nor blame it.” And Solomon says: “Confess while you are well, and while living you shall confess” (Ecclus. 17).

It must be true; for one who falsely accuses himself out of humility, though previously righteous, makes himself a sinner. It must be shamefaced; for shame is a great part of penance, yet no one ought through shame to omit confession. It is better to blush before the priest alone, who is Christ’s vicar,

[Col. 0689C] than before all who will be present at judgment; for then the books will be opened—that is, the consciences of each individual will lie open to every individual—except those matters which have been covered through confession. They will be covered from the devil, who writes down our sins—for everyone has a devil lying in wait for him—and from God, who will not remember our iniquities; they will also be hidden even from the priest to whom confession is made. For he does not dare reveal what he has heard; if he did, he ought to be deposed without mercy. The Prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31).

Confession must be self-accusatory; for the righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech, and ought not name another. Confession must be prompt, lest the sinner wish to confess when he cannot do so.

[Col. 0689D] Hence the saying:

> Delay harmed the prepared.

It must be frequent, for the righteous person falls seven times a day. It must be deliberate; for in confessing, the sinner must state all the circumstances of every sin whatsoever. These are:

> Who, what, where, with whose assistance, why, how, when.

[Col. 0690A] It must be personal, for one must confess one’s own sins, not another’s. Confession must be naked, for the sinner must openly and distinctly confess whatever he has done. It must be whole; for a divided confession is no confession. A wound is not healed as long as the iron remains hidden in it, and Christ healed completely those whom he healed. It must be undivided, lest the confessor tell one part to one priest and another part to another; for in so doing he is a hypocrite, since he wishes to appear righteous. It must be secret; for one who makes public his sin before all condemns himself, because:

> The case of a matter confessed need not be defended.

But one who confesses secretly frees himself. It must be straightforward and ordered, so that confession is made in the order in which the sin was committed. It must be general,

[Col. 0690B] so that one says generally: “I have sinned through pride, avarice, lust,” and so on with the rest. Then one descends to particulars, saying: “In this species of lust, whether in fornication, adultery, or incest,” and so on with the rest. Then one descends to individual instances, saying: “In this species of lust I sinned in this manner.”

These matters also must be observed in confession, so that one may thus come to the third journey, namely satisfaction in deed. This must be voluntary, humble, cheerful, secret, and proportionate. Voluntary, because we must willingly offer the sacrifice of penance and praise: of penance, I say, because no evil goes unpunished. Either it is punished in this age, and more lightly, or

[Col. 0690C] in purgatory. If it has been punished insufficiently in this age, there the punishment is greater than the most severe punishment in this age; for there, whatever is to be tortured is cast wholly into the fire. As blessed Gregory says, that fire differs from our material fire in violence and heat as much as material fire differs from painted fire.

We offer the sacrifice of praise to the Lord, for we ought to praise the Lord in all things. Penance must be humble, lest the penitent despise anyone whom he sees to have less grace. It must be cheerful, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). It must be secret, so that the penitent may avoid vain glory. It must be proportionate, so that the measure of penance corresponds to the gravity of the fault. Either a human being punishes in this life, or

[Col. 0690D] God in the future; but “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10). When these three journeys have been accomplished, we shall be able to sacrifice to the Lord and to reach the promised land with the children of Israel, who are called “men seeing good things.” May he deign to grant this to us who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## II. Short Works

[Col. 0691]

## Dialogue between God and the Sinner. Notice

(MAI, *Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VI, p. 562.)

### Notice

I found another work of Innocent in the Vatican Library, inserted in Palatine manuscript 365 and entitled *Dialogue of Innocent III between God and the Sinner*. Whether he wrote this dialogue before or after his pontificate, I do not know; for Innocent does not speak of himself in it, but introduces the person of any sinner speaking with God. Nor should anyone wonder that this dialogue is not listed among the *Gesta*, for many other published and unpublished writings of Innocent were unknown to the author of the *Gesta*. Let the Christian Church therefore receive from us this further work of the great pontiff, which, while demonstrating the profoundly devout mind of its author, likewise stirs the piety of its readers and earnestly urges amendment of life.

## Dialogue between God and the Sinner

[Col. 0691A] Because the pious and merciful Lord, most beloved brethren, permits—indeed, is pleased—to be invoked by miserable mortals, courage rises also in me, though unworthy and a sinner, to cry out to God with a loud voice and invoke his mercy. Therefore do not find it burdensome if, since it may, with the Lord’s help, advance the fruit of repentance, I set before the ears of your charity a kind of dialogue, a conversation between the sinner and God. For the Most High does not disdain such conversations of his servants, as Job says to him: “Speak, and I will answer thee; or certainly I will speak, and do thou answer me” (Job 13).

Therefore, while he looks on from heaven and sits on the height of his glory, as the immutable God with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration,

[Col. 0691B] I, lying prostrate upon the earth and humbly clinging to the pavement, shall assume the person of a sinner in this conversation all the more fittingly because, beyond others, I confess and acknowledge myself to be guilty, blameworthy, unclean, and sinful. Beginning, then, and opening the desire of my mind, I speak to him in these words:

### The Sinner to God

Eternal God, whose nature is goodness and whose work is mercy, who even when angry remembers mercy: by what words can I worthily invoke thee, so that thou mayest deign mercifully to hear one invoking thee? I know that my Redeemer, thy Son, teacher of truth and wisdom, when one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach me to pray,” said: “Say: Our Father who art in heaven” (Luke 11). If therefore, Lord, I invoke thee in prayer thus,

[Col. 0692A] may I receive that the saying proved in me by thy faithful prophet may be fulfilled:—

### God to the Sinner

Certainly thy Son, consubstantial and coeternal with me, taught thee to pray thus. But because thou dost not present thyself to me as a son, thou canst not worthily invoke me in the aforesaid prayer as Father. For the prophet speaks in my person: “If I am a Father, where is my love?” (Mal. 1). If, however, thou, the human being whom I created, didst love me as Father, thou wouldst keep my commandments as a son who loves his father; for the performance of a work is proof of love.

But when I consider the whole human race and the entire condition of those living in the flesh, scarcely anyone is found among prelates and subjects, kings and

[Col. 0692B] ministers, cloistered religious and professed persons, masters and servants, clerics and laypeople, who fulfils my will by carrying out my commandments and shows me filial love as to a father. Every sex and age has corrupted its way, in following its own concupiscences and despising all evangelical tradition and teaching.

### The Sinner to God

Thy knowledge, Lord, has proved wondrous against me, and I shall not be able to attain it. Thou shuttest my mouth and stoppest it with thy arguments, so that I do not dare rush forward to invoke thee with the words of the aforesaid prayer. “Yet I speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). I shall change my words, in case my invocation may be found worthy in thine ears. To invoke thee, I shall take up the prayer of thy faithful prophet David, to whom thou didst bear thy testimony, saying: “I have found a man according to my heart” (Ps. 88).

[Col. 0693A] Thus, Lord, I shall cry to thee in prayer: “Have mercy on me.” And I likewise have said: “Lord, have mercy on me”; and elsewhere: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, and hear my prayer” (Ps. 4).

### God to the Sinner

That prayer does not sound well in thy mouth, because thou dost not have me as Lord, because thou dost not fear me as a servant ought to fear his lord, although thou canst not deny that thou art my servant. I who said through the prophet against disobedient sons, “If I am a Father, where is my love?” (Mal. 1), cried through the same prophet against servants without fear: “If I am a Lord, where is my fear?” (ibid.). That thou dost not fear me, or dost not have me as Lord, I can readily prove to thee.

For if thou wert alone in some secret place with a woman alone, whom thou greatly lovedst, ready and ardently inflamed toward her to fulfil bodily lust, wouldst thou not, if someone whom thou feared burst in, immediately abandon the work begun and flee for fear of him? Or at least, lest thou be seen by him, wouldst thou not, through shame and fear or modesty, if thou couldst, run to some hiding-place? Yet for my sake thou dost not cease to do such things before my eyes, although thou knowest that they displease me and that I forbid thee to do them. For the prophet says of me: “Am I a God nearby?”

[Col. 0693C] (Jer. 23). “Behold, I am a God afar off. If a person hides himself, shall I not see him?” Thus thou art shown to fear that man more than me—indeed, to fear him as lord, although he is a mortal and corruptible man like thyself, while thou art proved to despise me, who am almighty and eternal and, whether thou wilt or no, thy Lord. It is therefore not fitting for thee worthily to invoke me thus, saying: “Lord, have mercy.”

### The Sinner to God

Thou convincest me, O Lord, plainly, and thy argument reaches an irrefutable conclusion. As I speak to my Lord, I—a human being, corruption, and a son of man, a worm—there comes to my mind, Lord, the prayer of the sinner and publican, which thou in mercy didst accept when, praying in the temple and unwilling to lift his eyes to heaven, he struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). Following his example and using like words, I shall cry to thee, in case thou hearest one who invokes thee thus

[Col. 0693D] and showest mercy to my sin, for it is great.

### God to the Sinner

If I am the Lord thy God—who alone certainly am God—thou seemest altogether to cry to me mockingly, using the words of the aforesaid prayer to invoke me, since thou worshippest something besides me as God and chiefly directest thy affection toward it. For that is thy god which is loved by thee more. If thou art avaricious, thou worshippest and lovest money as God, like an idolater. For avarice, as my Apostle testifies, “is the service of idols” (Eph. 5). If thou art a glutton or a belly-slave, thy belly is thy god, because thou carest for those things which chiefly inflame the greed of the belly. The aforesaid Apostle says: “These are they whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3).

[Col. 0694A] Therefore, if thou hast another god besides me—namely, that vice which thou lovest more than me, who am the true God—thou dost not worthily invoke me to show mercy to thee. Rather, it appears that thou wouldst mock me and invoke God as though in irony, if, rendering to another the worship and love due to me, thou shouldst cry to me: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18), when this foolish notion is contrary to Scripture, which says: “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6).

But thou dost as an adulteress does, who, having on one side her lawful husband, receives on the other her lover. For thou, like an immodest harlot, despisest me, who am thy bridegroom, and expellest me from the chamber of thy soul, where I should rest with thee in delightful and holy love, because my delights are to be with the children of men.

[Col. 0694B] Not without injury to me dost thou introduce the devil as an outside lover, to play wantonly with him in thy concupiscences and desires. Of these Scripture truly says: “The bed is narrow, so that one falls off” (Isa. 28). Therefore I leave the bed and have withdrawn from thee, because the soul, shamelessly cleaving to another in her fornications, has abandoned me, the husband of her youth, to whom she ought to have clung inseparably.

Moreover, when dost thou think thou canst invoke me so that I may answer thee, when I am not in thee? Why dost thou pass by with closed eyes and not attend to the force of the prophet’s saying: “Thou shalt call, and the Lord shall hear thee” (Isa. 58)? To invoke (*invocare*) is so called as though to pray within (*intus orare*), that is, to cry aloud to him who is within.

[Col. 0694C] Certainly, if by frequent knocking thou cried at the door of a house in which no one was present, thou couldst cry all day; and because no one was inside to hear thee, no one would answer thee crying out, however loudly and frequently. So it is with me: when I have left the dwelling of thy soul, from which thou hast compelled me to depart because of its uncleanness, I have become far from thee and can no longer hear the cry of thy voice, much less favorably hear thee while thou dost what displeases me.

### The Sinner to God

What then, most merciful Lord, shall I do, so that thou mayest return to me, from whom, alas, thou hast removed thyself because of my iniquities? So that, dwelling within,

[Col. 0694D] thou mayest answer when I invoke thee, and I may be saved—I who had been abandoned by thee—when it is written: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118).

### God to the Sinner

Hear the counsel of holy Scripture; if thou dost it, thou shalt immediately bring me back to the lodging of thy soul, so that I may hear thee when thou callest. Have contrition of heart, and grieve deeply because by thy sins thou hast offended me, according to what the prophet says to thee and thy like: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). Again: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33).

In that contrition also firmly resolve to confess thy sins truthfully to a priest, as the prophet David says: “I said, I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31).

[Col. 0695A] From this thou canst plainly understand how great and incomparable is my mercy, which, in response to such a purpose, remits and forgives all crimes. But when opportunity to confess has been granted thee, as the prophet says and cries: “Do thou declare thy iniquities, that thou mayest be justified” (Isa. 43); likewise the Apostle: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5). And my Son, as the angel of great counsel, came to save his people from their sins. He significantly and figuratively enjoined the confession expressly commanded by his apostle when he said to those healed by him of bodily leprosy: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17). By this he indicated that the penitent who is contrite with the purpose

[Col. 0695B] of confessing has been cleansed from the filth of sins in the soul, as from spiritual leprosy; but, since the penalties of the debt remain, let such persons humbly approach the sacrament of confession, devoutly submit themselves to the judgment of priests, and make satisfaction in deed according to what the priests command.

### The Sinner to God

Great and ineffable, Lord, is the power of contrition, through which thou dost justify the impious and wondrously makest good out of the perverse. But I, a sinner, cannot merit it; nor shall I be able to obtain it in any measure except through the infusion of thy grace. For I do not know what contrition is, but I do know that it is the gift of thy grace alone, from whom, as from the Father of lights, descends every good gift and every perfect gift

[Col. 0695C] (Jas. 1). Why then, Lord, dost thou require me to make myself good through contrition, when I cannot make myself such? Since, as guilty and defiled, I cannot even merit it except through the inestimable grace of thy mercy.

### God to the Sinner

Do not err or deceive thyself. I do not require thee to make thyself good, which I know thou canst not do, since this belongs to me; rather, by applying thy free will to me and meditating upon divine benefits, make thyself capable of receiving me. If thou dost this, since it lies within thee, thou shalt without doubt receive the infusion of my grace, which in my goodness I am always ready to give to anyone who effectively wills to receive it.

[Col. 0695D] Although that capability in the sinner precedes the infusion of my grace not by merit but by fitness. Hence Augustine says: “Something precedes in sinners which, although they are not justified, nevertheless makes them worthy of justification and capable of it.” It is as with one whose eyes are shut: nothing is required of that person for seeing except to do what lies within, namely, open the eyes; for the brightness of the sun is ready outside and will immediately illuminate the opened eyes for sight. By such an example, consider plainly that divine grace stands ready to pour itself into a human being; it requires only the fitting readiness found through the application of free will.

### The Sinner to God

I plainly acknowledge, Lord, that the unsearchable height of thy knowledge wonderfully instructs

[Col. 0696A] and teaches me. Therefore I shall diligently meditate upon thy benefits, most merciful God, by which thou hast bound me to thee in many ways, directing my understanding and applying myself to thee, however feebly I can, like dry land to thee; in case through such thoughts thou, Father of mercies, mayest find me fit to receive the dew of thy grace, which I have not merited, and mayest deign to infuse it. With its help, awakened to good, I may be able sufficiently to be crushed in heart over my committed impieties, with the purpose of humbly confessing them. Although this very meditation on thy benefits cannot arise in my mind from myself without thee, as the Apostle says: “We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3).

[Col. 0696B] Yet what shall I, wretched man, do? For, moved by thy grace, I often resolve to confess; but many things occur which hinder me and call me back from fulfilling my purpose. The first hindrance is the great shame which is against me all day, and the confusion of my face which has covered me. Many times I intend to approach a priest; but because the things I have committed are exceedingly shameful, I turn from this purpose out of embarrassment. Many times I have resolved to go to a priest, and have gone intending devoutly to reveal my iniquity; but when I stood at his feet, my conscience pricking me, sudden confusion fell upon me, and my spirit, disturbed within itself, began to waver and say: “Alas, what shall I do? Shall I recount my crime? Can I recount it?” And so, with my shame prevailing,

[Col. 0696C] I set confession aside, withdrew from the penitential tribunal without the medicine of salvation, and my scars were corrupted and made worse by my foolishness.

### God to the Sinner
You are judged exceedingly foolish and undiscerning when, like the moon, you change, and through shame and embarrassment abandon the confession of your sins. It is praiseworthy if you are ashamed and modesty overtakes you when you recall your crimes, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “I am confounded and blush, because I have borne the reproach of my youth” (Jer. 31). But you must take every care that such shame does not turn you back from confessing sin; for shame of this kind [Col. 0696D] increases guilt rather than lessens it, since it does not allow the penitent to disclose in confession what he has committed. There is shame that brings glory, and shame that brings guilt. It is blameworthy if it excludes confession; it is praiseworthy if it makes one ashamed in such a way as also to accompany confession. For to reveal sin without blushing is a sign of boastfulness rather than devotion. Why, fool, are you ashamed to say once what you were not ashamed to commit many times?

Yet, if you are tempted, speak beforehand and say: “I shall not be ashamed to confess to God in his minister—who is a mortal man like myself—that which cannot be hidden from the eyes of His majesty. I shall not be ashamed to reveal my guilt to a man in this present life, when I know that, if I do not disclose it to him, it will be manifest to all on the day of judgment. But if [Col. 0697A] I reveal it here, God in His immeasurable goodness will cover and conceal it; and He will make me one of the blessed, ‘whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered’ (Ps. 31).”

## THE SINNER TO GOD

You have comforted me, Lord, by your words and strengthened me by holy sayings; and I shall no longer refrain through shame when I approach your minister to disclose my transgressions through confession. But there is another thing, my Lord, which presents a great obstacle to my confessing: namely, fear of punishment. I have sinned, Lord, beyond the number of the sand of the sea, and my sins have multiplied. Therefore I greatly fear approaching confession, because, if the measure of punishment is to be imposed according to the measure of guilt, I may be burdened with so great a load of satisfaction [Col. 0697B] as, in the estimation of my crimes, ought to be laid upon me, that, even if I lived for a very long time, I, most wretched man, could not fulfil it.

## GOD TO THE SINNER

Your folly still does not leave you, and a thought devoid of discernment has risen into your heart. You must never believe that God commands a human being what is impossible, or orders you to bear a punishment that you cannot endure. My vicar, the pope, whom I have appointed in my place on earth as your judge, will mitigate the sorrow of the penitent, taking account of the circumstances of the sins. Since he has received from me the power both to bind and to loose—by ministry indeed, not by authority—[Col. 0697C] he will moderate the punishment according to the judgment of his discretion, and impose such penance that through it, with my cooperation, you may grow in righteousness. He may also find in you such sorrow, bitterness, and forcefulness of contrition that thereafter you may trust in God’s goodness for the remission of the greater part, or perhaps the whole, of the imposed punishment.

But you, whom fear of present punishment draws back from the intention of confessing, why do you not consider and turn over in your mind that, however long the punishment of this life may be, it is brief compared with the eternal; however bitter it may be, it is sweet when compared with the punishment of hell? Therefore it is better for you to repent here than afterward to be tortured intolerably and most bitterly. Let there not happen to you what Job says: “He who fears frost, [Col. 0697D] hail shall fall upon him” (Job 6); and he who fears temporal punishment will assuredly incur eternal punishment. Likewise, “He shall flee iron weapons and fall upon a bronze bow” (Job 20). Present punishment, which soon passes and is consumed, is denoted by iron weapons, which are consumed by rust; but eternal punishment, which cannot end, is denoted by a bronze bow, since bronze is incorruptible.

Penance is most fruitful in this world, but in the future utterly fruitless—indeed, destructive. That saying also of the Apostle ought to give you comfort and strongly encourage you to endure temporal punishment: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). Likewise: “This light and momentary affliction [Col. 0698A] of ours works in eternity a sublime weight [of glory].”

## THE SINNER TO GOD

Your sayings, Lord, are delightful to your servant, sweeter to my mouth than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 118), though I am unworthy to gaze upon their height. Do not disdain, I beg, still to bear with a little of my folly. Behold, Lord, neither shame for guilt nor fear of punishment will now hinder confession in me. But there is another thing that delays me somewhat—or rather, turns my heart back from confession: attachment to, or desire for, temporal things.

I consider within myself and speak to my mind: if I have confessed my offences to a priest, perhaps he will command me to go to Jerusalem, or undertake the toil of some pilgrimage, [Col. 0698B] or at least to visit churches and, remaining there for a longer time, devote myself to frequent prayer. Yet meanwhile I might devote myself to temporal gain and to many acquisitions, increasing the resources of this world both for myself and my household. But if I possess anything, it will be necessary rather to diminish than increase it, until the pilgrimage undertaken can be completed, or for as long as I must be occupied with spiritual exercises. Therefore it is more useful for me to desist from confession than to obstruct the pursuit of worldly acquisition.

## GOD TO THE SINNER

That thought which has seized you is vain—indeed, it is a temptation of Satan. In order to drive that thought far from you, remember what the Gospel Scripture [Col. 0698C] proclaims: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Matt. 24). The pregnant are perverse souls that conceive in their minds, as though from seed of wickedness injected by the devil, through illicit desires for temporal things or consent to some iniquity. Nursing souls are those who do not cease through avarice to heap up earthly delights, or who, taking pleasure in the iniquities they have committed and persisting in them, put off repentance.

Without doubt death will come upon them, and they shall go down alive into hell, because wickedness is in their dwellings and in the midst of their minds. Certainly, if you thought soundly, when these worldly things solicit you toward their desire, you ought to reflect that whatever objects of desire are seen in the world are transitory, whereas those promised by God are [Col. 0698D] eternal: these are earthly, those heavenly; these small, those great; these false, those certain; these lowest, those highest; these least, those greatest. These are acquired with labour, preserved with fear and anxiety, and lost with pain and distress. Although there is labour in acquiring those things, because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11), yet their possessors can in no way be stung by anxiety concerning their preservation, nor tortured with pain at their loss or destruction, because “there rust or moth does not destroy, nor do thieves break in and steal” (Matt. 6).

## THE SINNER TO GOD

Do not be angry, Lord, if even on this occasion I, a most worthless creature, now take upon myself the boldness to speak in the presence of your majesty; [Col. 0699A] and if, as in other matters, I find in the abyss of your wisdom counsel for what I am about to propose, as one set in perplexity. There is still something that greatly shakes me and sets before me a more difficult obstacle to confession than the rest, from which I fall into despair because of the grave difficulty of resisting sin.

Wretched I, I remember that I have fallen many times; and afterward, repenting, I rose with your help. But unable to stand, I relapsed and returned many times to the same thing, returning again and again like a dog to its vomit and a sow to wallowing in mire (2 Pet. 2). Therefore, since I am slippery and unstable, like wax bent toward vice, I despair of my own steadfastness; and for that reason I utterly desist from confession, [Col. 0699B] thinking that it profits nothing if I am raised and rise again only to fall soon, and distrusting that I can stand even for a short interval of time. I think, moreover, that I cannot easily obtain forgiveness, since, though often raised up, I have often relapsed into sin and am found ungrateful and undevout toward Him who raises me.

## GOD TO THE SINNER

In what you now propose, you prove yourself not so much senseless as mad. For you do right if you distrust yourself and, observing your frailty and placing no confidence in your own powers, think that after you have risen you cannot hope to stand by your own strength. But you must hope in me: although you are weak and feeble in yourself, [Col. 0699C] I can nevertheless, if I will through my mercy, establish one who is weak and strengthen one however infirm so that you do not fall.

Why should you despair of me, who do not will the death of the sinner but rather that he be converted and live (Ezek. 18), who am certainly merciful and surpassing in goodness over wickedness? Take heed: if you despair of me, you incur the unforgivable sin, which is sin against the Holy Spirit. No sin is comparable to it, because it alone is believed to be remitted neither in this age nor in the age to come. Take heed: if you despair of me, you offend me all the more grievously insofar as you have attempted more cruelly to extinguish my power and take from me the goodness that I possess not as an accidental gift but by nature, and so to separate my omnipotence [Col. 0699D] from me for the time being.

For I am He of whom it is said: “God, whose characteristic it is always to have mercy and to spare.” I am He to whom the congregation of the faithful cries: “God, who most of all manifests your omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy.” Why, unhappy one, should you despair of me? I count it joy for myself and for my angels over one sinner who repents. Leaving ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, I sent their shepherd to seek the one that was lost and, when found, to carry it upon his shoulders. I gladly received the returning prodigal son; I gave him the finest robe and a ring, prepared a great feast for him, and killed the fatted calf (Luke 15).

I am He who, like a mother, opens the bowels of compassion to children even when they sin; who bears patiently with those who offend me many times, [Col. 0700A] even to the end of life, and, delaying punishment so that they may repent, waits patiently. Concerning me the prophet indeed cries, saying: “Hear, house of Jacob and remnant of Israel: you have been carried from my womb and borne from my belly. I have made, and I will bear; even to grey hairs I will carry” (Isa. 46).

Why should you despair of me, who, after creating man in order to make him a partaker of my glory, sent my only-begotten one into the world out of the exceeding love by which I loved him? He redeemed man, sold under sin, not with corruptible gold and silver but with his precious blood, which he abundantly poured out for him.

Know and see, you who refuse to confess because, by repeating too often the very same things you have often confessed, you have shamefully corrupted your ways: [Col. 0700B] although it is evil and bitter for you to have forsaken the Lord your God, it is shown to be far worse to persevere in evil, to set aside love for Him, and continually to withdraw yourself and turn your face away from Him. Why do you not consider that you fall often and rise often, and that it is less evil to fall and rise alternately than to remain continually in sin? For by God’s goodness, when you rise in this way, death may overtake you in a good present state, so that you may be saved. But if you persist in sin and are found perverse at the end of your life, without doubt you will be carried away to eternal punishments for condemnation; for, as Scripture says, the Lord judges the ends of the earth and final works (Ps. 95).

And if a tree has fallen to the north [Col. 0700C] or to the south, it would, I think, prefer first to be drawn out of the mire and afterward to fall again than to remain continually in it. Likewise, one suffering from some fever—would he not judge it more grievous to suffer it continuously than to be tormented by it intermittently? Thus you too, with two evils set before you—namely, to fall into sin and consequently rise from it, or to persist in evil without turning back and without reverence—ought rather to flee the second than the first.

Therefore do not, as one who distrusts and despairs of God, draw yourself back from confession. Rather, as often as you suffer this misery by committing again what you have confessed, nevertheless confess the same things again. For just as water cleanses a garment, however often it is soiled, whenever it washes it, removing its filth and making it as new, [Col. 0700D] so confession, whenever one has recourse to it, restores to the soul the brightness of purity that it loses through repeated sin.

When you confess your sin and drive the poison of wickedness from your soul by confession’s antidote, I shall immediately return to it as to my home, from which I had formerly gone out. Thereafter, if you call upon me, I shall hear you and, as one dwelling within, answer your cry without delay.

## THE SINNER TO GOD

Lord God of my salvation, the words that you speak are words of eternal life, and the counsels you urge are salutary. Therefore, helped by you, I shall devoutly seek your minister and pour out my heart before him like water; I shall open my lips in his presence, speaking [Col. 0701A] in the bitterness of my soul. Like one putting his finger into his throat, I shall search my conscience by examination and shall not cease until I vomit out that bitter pus of my sins, hidden within me, over wormwood and gall. Thus, when the putrefaction has been vomited out and cast away—the abominable stench of which had [Col. 0702A] caused you to leave the dwelling-place of my mind—may you graciously deign to return and dwell there with the inestimable fragrance of your ointments, according to your holy and ineffable promise; you who are blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0701]

# THREE BOOKS ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD, OR ON THE MISERY OF THE HUMAN CONDITION

(Edition of the Works of Innocent III, Cologne, 1575, folio, p. 421.)

## BOOK ONE

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0701B]

To the lord father most dear, P., by God’s grace bishop of Porto: Lotharius, unworthy deacon, grace in the present and glory in the future.

The little leisure which, amid many troubles, I recently seized on the occasion you know of, did not pass wholly idly for me. To humble pride—which is the head of all vices (Ecclus. 10)—I have written, however inadequately, on the lowliness of the human condition. I have dedicated the title of this present little work to your name, asking and requesting that, if your discernment finds anything worthy in it, you ascribe it wholly to divine grace.
