But if your fatherhood should suggest it, with Christ’s favour I shall describe the dignity of human nature. [Note: [Col. 0701] The Book on the Dignity of Human Nature has not yet been discovered.] Thus, by this work the proud may be humbled, [Col. 0701C] and by that the humble may be exalted [or: may rejoice].

## CHAPTER ONE. On the wretched entry into the human condition

“Why did I come forth from my mother’s womb, to see toil and sorrow, and for my days to be consumed in shame?” (Jer. 20). If he whom the Lord sanctified in the womb (Jer. 1) spoke such words of himself, what words shall I speak of myself, whom my mother bore in sins? “Alas for me,” I shall say, “my mother, why did you bear me, a son of bitterness and sorrow? Why did I not die in my mother’s womb? Why did I not perish at once when I came forth [Col. 0702B] from the womb? Why was I received on knees and nursed at breasts?” (Job 3)—born “for burning [or: shame] and food for fire” (Isa. 9). “Would that I had been slain in the womb, so that my mother might have been my grave and her womb an everlasting conception” (Jer. 20). “For I should have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb” (Job 10). “Who then will give my eyes a fountain of tears?” (Jer. 9), that I may weep for the wretched course of the human condition and the damnable outcome of human dissolution?

Therefore I considered with tears what man is made from, what man does, and what man will become [or: will do]. Certainly, formed from earth, conceived in guilt, born for punishment, he does wicked things that are not lawful, shameful things that are not fitting, and vain things that are not expedient; he will become food for fire, fodder for worms, a mass of putrefaction. I shall explain this more plainly and expound it more fully.

Man is formed from dust, mud, and ashes—and, what is baser, from the foulest semen; conceived in the itching of flesh, the heat of lust, and the stench of lechery—and, what is worse, in the stain of sin; born for toil, pain, and fear—and, what is more wretched, for death. He does wicked things by which he offends God, his neighbour, and himself; shameful things by which he pollutes his reputation, conscience, and person; vain things by which he neglects serious matters, useful matters, and necessary matters. He will become food for fire, which ever burns and burns unquenchably; food for the worm, which ever gnaws and devours immortally; a mass of putrefaction, which ever stinks and is horribly foul.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the baseness of man’s very material

Thus the Lord God formed man from the slime of the earth, which is baser than the other elements, as appears in Genesis 2. He made the planets and stars from fire; he made breaths and winds from air; he made fish and birds from water; he made human beings and beasts from earth. Considering aquatic things, man will find himself base; considering airy things, he will recognize himself as baser; considering fiery things, he will judge himself basest. Nor can he make himself equal to heavenly things, [Col. 0703B] nor dare he prefer himself to earthly things, since he finds himself equal to beasts and recognizes himself as like them.

“For one is the death of human beings and beasts, and the condition of both is equal; man has nothing more than a beast. They arose from earth, and together they return to earth” (Eccl. 3). These are not the words of just any man, but of Solomon, the wisest of men. What, then, is man but mud and ashes? Hence man says to God: “Remember, I pray, that you have made me like mud, and that you will reduce me to dust” (Job 10). Hence God says to man: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3). “I have been compared,” Job says, “to mud, and I have been made like ashes and cinders” (Job 30).

Mud is made from water and dust, both remaining; but ash is made from wood and fire, both perishing. The mystery is expressed, but should better be expressed elsewhere. Why, then, do you who are mud grow proud? Why, you who are dust, exalt yourself? Why, you who are ashes, glory?

## CHAPTER THREE. A distinction concerning conception

Perhaps you will answer that Adam himself was formed from the slime of the earth, but you are begotten from human seed. Yet he was formed from earth, but virgin earth; you, however, are begotten from seed, but unclean seed. “For who can make clean that which is conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14). Who is man, that he should be spotless and appear righteous, born of a woman? “For behold, I was conceived [Col. 0703D] in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50). Not in one iniquity only, not in one offence only, but in many iniquities and many offences: namely, in his own offences and iniquities, and in the offences and iniquities of others.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the conception of an infant

There is a twofold conception: one of seeds and another of natures. The first occurs in acts committed; the second in conditions contracted. For parents commit in the first, while offspring contract in the second. For who does not know that even marital intercourse is never undertaken wholly without the itching of flesh, the heat of lust, and the stench of lechery? Hence the seed conceived is defiled, stained, and corrupted; from it the soul, when at last infused, contracts the stain of sin, the blemish of guilt, and the filth of iniquity. Just as liquid poured into a corrupt vessel is corrupted, and whatever touches something polluted is itself polluted by that very contact.

For the soul has three natural powers, or three natural faculties: the rational, to distinguish good from evil; the irascible, to reject evil; and the concupiscible, to desire good. These three faculties are originally corrupted by three opposite vices. The rational faculty by ignorance, so that it does not distinguish good from evil; the irascible faculty by anger, so that it rejects good; the concupiscible faculty by concupiscence, so that it desires evil. The first begets an offence; the last gives birth to sin; the middle generates both offence and sin. For an offence is failure to do what ought to be done; sin is doing what ought not [Col. 0704B] to be done.

These three vices are contracted from corrupt flesh through three natural enticements. In carnal intercourse, the perception of reason is lulled so that ignorance is sown; the itch of lust is stirred so that anger is propagated; the appetite for pleasure is satisfied so that concupiscence is contracted. This is the tyrant of the flesh, the law of the members, the tinder of sin, the sickness of nature, the nourishment of death, without which no one is born and without which none dies; and although it sometimes passes away in guilt, it always remains in act. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

O grievous necessity and unhappy condition! Before we sin, we are bound by sin; and before we commit an offence, we are held by an offence. “Through one man sin entered [Col. 0704C] into this world, and through sin death passed to all human beings” (Rom. 5). Have not “the fathers eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children been set on edge?” (Jer. 31; Ezek. 18).

## CHAPTER FIVE. By what food the conceived child is nourished in the womb

But consider by what food the conceived child is nourished in the womb: assuredly by menstrual blood, which ceases to flow from the woman after conception so that the conceived child may be nourished from it within her. This is said to be so detestable and unclean that, through contact with it, crops do not germinate, shrubs wither, grasses die, trees lose their fruit; and if dogs eat of it, they become rabid. Conceived fetuses contract the defect of the seed, [Col. 0704D] so that lepers and those suffering from elephantiasis are born from this corruption. Hence, according to Mosaic law, a menstruating woman is reckoned unclean (Lev. 10); and if anyone approaches a menstruating woman, he is commanded to be put to death (Lev. 12). And because of the uncleanness of menstruation, it is commanded that a woman who bears a male abstain from entering the Temple for forty days, but if she bears a female, for eighty days.

## CHAPTER SIX. On an infant’s weakness

“Why, then, is light given to the wretched, and life to those who are bitter of soul?” (Job 3). Happy are those who die before they are born, feeling death before knowing life. Some are born so deformed and monstrous that they seem not human beings but rather abominations. Perhaps it would have been better for them had they never come forth to be seen, since they are displayed as monsters and shown for a spectacle. Very many, moreover, are born with limbs diminished and senses impaired: the grief of friends, the disgrace of parents, the shame of relatives.

Why should I say this particularly of some, when we all are born without knowledge, without speech, without strength—tearful, weak, feeble, scarcely differing from brute beasts, indeed possessing less in many respects? For they walk as soon as they are born; but we not only do not walk erect on our feet, but do not even crawl bent over on our hands.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On the pain of childbirth and the infant’s wailing

[Col. 0705B]

All of us are born wailing, so that we may express our misery. For a newly born male says “A,” but a female “E”:

> Saying E or A, all who are born from Eve.

What then is *Eva* [Eve] but *heu ha*—“alas, ah”? Both are interjections of one in pain, expressing the greatness of sorrow. For before sin she was entitled *virago* [woman, female counterpart of man]; after sin she deserved to be called *Eva*, from the time when she heard it said to her: “In pain you shall give birth” (Gen. 3). For there is no pain like that of a woman in labour. Thus Rachel died from the excessive pain of childbirth and, dying, called her son Benoni, that is, “son of sorrow” (Gen. 31). The wife of Phinehas, when sudden pains came upon her, gave birth and died at the same time; and at the very point of death [Col. 0705C] she called her son Ichabod (1 Sam. 4). “A woman, like a shipwrecked person, when she gives birth has sorrow; but after she has borne a child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16). Thus she conceives with uncleanness and stench, gives birth with grief and pain, nurses with distress and labour, and guards with diligence and fear.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. On human nakedness

Naked he goes out, and naked he returns. Poor he comes, and poor he departs. “Naked,” Job says, “I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job 1). “We brought nothing into this world; without doubt, neither can we carry anything away” (1 Tim. 6). But if anyone enters clothed, let him consider [Col. 0705D] what garment he brings forth. Shameful to say, more shameful to hear, most shameful to see: a foul little skin stained with blood. This is that barrier of which Tamar said in childbirth: “Why has the barrier been broken through because of you?” For this reason she called his name Phares, which is interpreted “division” (Gen. 38).

## CHAPTER NINE. What fruit man produces

O unworthiness of the base human condition; O unworthy baseness of the human condition! Examine herbs and trees. They produce from themselves flowers, foliage, and fruits; but alas, you produce from yourself nits, lice, and worms. They pour out from themselves oil, wine, and balsam; but you produce from yourself spittle, urine, and excrement. They breathe out from themselves sweetness of fragrance; but you emit from yourself the abomination of stench. Such as the tree is, such is the fruit. “For an evil tree cannot bear good fruit” (Matt. 7 and 12).

For what is man according to his bodily form except a kind of inverted tree? His roots are his hair; his trunk, his head with its neck; his stem, his breast with his belly; his branches, his thighs with his shins; his foliage, his fingers with their joints. This is the leaf carried away by the wind and the stubble dried by the sun (Job 13).

## CHAPTER TEN. On the discomforts of old age and the brevity of human life

At the beginning of the human condition, human beings are recorded to have lived nine hundred years and more (Gen. 6). But gradually, as human life declined, the Lord said to Noah: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be one hundred and twenty years” (Gen. 6). This can be understood either as the limit of life or as the period allowed for repentance. From then on, people are very rarely recorded to have lived longer; but as human life was cut shorter and shorter, the Psalmist said: “The days of our years are seventy years; but if in the strong, eighty years, and what is beyond them is labour and sorrow” (Ps. 89).

“Will not the fewness of my days end in a short time?” (Job 10). “Our days pass more swiftly than a web is cut down by the weaver” (Job 7). “Man, born of woman and living for a short time, is filled with many miseries. [Col. 0706C] He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14). For few now reach forty years and very few sixty.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN. On the discomforts of old age

But if anyone reaches old age, his heart is immediately afflicted and his head shakes; his spirit languishes and his breath stinks; his face wrinkles and his stature bends; his eyes grow dim and his joints totter; his nostrils run and his hair falls; his touch trembles and his ability to act fails; his teeth rot and his ears grow deaf. An old man is easily provoked and difficult to calm; quick to believe and slow to disbelieve; tenacious and greedy, sad and querulous; quick to speak and slow to hear, [Col. 0706D] yet not slow to anger. He praises the ancients and despises the moderns; he criticizes the present and commends the past; he sighs and is anxious, grows numb and weak. Hear the poet Horace:

> Many disadvantages beset an old man.  
> —Horace, *On the Art of Poetry*

Moreover, let neither old men glory over the young nor young men behave insolently toward the old, because what we are, this man was; and what he is, we shall someday be.

## CHAPTER TWELVE. On the labour of mortals

“Thus a bird is born to fly, and a human being is born for labour” (Job 5). All his days are filled with labours and miseries, nor does his mind rest even at night. And what is this but vanity? [Col. 0707A] No one is without labour beneath the sun, none without defect beneath the moon, none without vanity in time. Time is the duration of mutable things. “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes (ch. 1), “and all is vanity.”

O how varied are human pursuits, how diverse their occupations! Yet all have one end and the same result: labour and affliction of spirit. “A great occupation has been created for all human beings, and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40).

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On the pursuit of the wise

Let the wise search out and investigate the heights of heaven, the breadths of earth, and the depths of sea; let them dispute concerning each thing and treat all things, always learning or teaching. And what will they find from this occupation except labour, pain, and affliction of spirit? He who said this knew it by experience: “I gave my heart to know prudence and learning, errors and folly; and I learned that this was labour and affliction of spirit, because in much wisdom there is much vexation, and he who adds knowledge adds pain” (Eccl. 1).

Although an investigator must labour through many sleepless vigils and attend diligently to labours and sweats, scarcely anything is so trivial, scarcely anything so easy, that a person understands it completely and grasps it with clarity—unless perhaps this is perfectly known: that nothing is perfectly known, although an insoluble refutation follows from this. Indeed, “the corruptible body [Col. 0707C] weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9).

Hear what Solomon thinks about this: “All things are difficult; man cannot explain them in speech” (Eccl. 1). “There is a man who by day and night takes no sleep in his eyes, and he cannot discover any reason for the works of God. And the more he labours to seek, the less he will find” (Eccl. 8). “Those who search by searching fail, for man shall approach a deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63). “For a searcher into majesty shall be oppressed by glory” (Prov. 25). For the more one understands, the more one doubts; and he seems to himself to be wiser who is more foolish. Therefore part of knowledge [Col. 0707D] is to know that one does not know. “God made man upright, but he has involved himself in endless questions” (Ecclus. 7).

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN. On the various pursuits of human beings

Mortals run and hurry about through hedges and paths; climb mountains, cross hills, fly over rocks, traverse the Alps, pass over pits, enter caverns, search the bowels of the earth, the depths of the sea, the uncertainties of rivers, the shadows of forests, and the trackless places of solitude. They expose themselves to winds and rain, thunder and lightning, waves and storms, collapses and precipices. They forge and smelt metals, carve and polish stones, cut down and plane timber, spin webs and weave garments, cut [Col. 0708A] them and sew them; build houses, plant gardens, cultivate fields, dig vineyards, light ovens, construct mills, fish, hunt, and catch birds.

They meditate and think, deliberate and arrange, complain and litigate, plunder and steal, deceive and trade, contend and fight; and they do innumerable such things in order to heap up riches, multiply gains, pursue profits, acquire honours, elevate dignities, and extend powers. And these things too are labour and affliction of mind. If I am not believed, let Solomon be believed: “I magnified my works: I built houses for myself and planted vineyards for myself; I made gardens and orchards, and planted them with trees of every kind; I built pools of water to irrigate the forest of growing trees; I possessed male and female slaves and had a great household; I also had herds and great flocks of sheep, beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem. I heaped up for myself gold and silver and the wealth of kings and provinces. I acquired male and female singers and the delights of the children of men, cups and little pitchers for service in pouring wine; and I surpassed in riches all who were before me in Jerusalem. When I turned to all that my hands had made and to the labours at which I had sweated in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of mind in all things, and that nothing remains under the sun” (Eccl. 1).

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN. On diverse anxieties

[Col. 0708C]

O how great is the anxiety that torments mortals! Care afflicts them, worry troubles them, fear terrifies them, trembling shakes them, horror overspreads them, pain afflicts them, sadness disturbs them, and disturbance [or: tribulation] makes them sad. Poor and rich, slave and master, married and continent, finally good and bad—all are afflicted by worldly torments and tormented by worldly afflictions. Trust the teacher who speaks from experience: “If,” he says, “I should be wicked, woe is me; and if righteous, I shall not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery” (Job 10).

## CHAPTER SIXTEEN. On the misery of the rich and poor
[Col. 0708D] For the poor are oppressed by want, tortured by hardship, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness; they are demeaned, waste away, are despised, and put to shame. O wretched condition of the beggar! If he asks, he is confounded by shame; if he does not ask, he is consumed by need; yet necessity compels him to beg. He charges God with injustice, because He does not distribute rightly; he accuses his neighbor of malice, because he does not give full assistance. He is indignant, murmurs, and utters curses. Consider on this point the judgment of the Wise Man: “It is better,” he says, “to die than to be in want” (Ecclus. 40).—“Even to his neighbor the poor man will be hateful” (Prov. 14).—“All the days of the poor are evil; the brothers of a poor man hate him; even his friends have withdrawn far from him” (Prov. 19); because

[Col. 0709A]

> While you are fortunate, you will count many friends;  
> If the times become cloudy, you will be alone.  
> (Ovid, *Tristia* I.9.3.)

Shame upon it! A person is judged according to fortune, when fortune ought rather to be assessed according to the person. A man is thought as good as he is rich, and as bad as he is poor, whereas he ought rather to be judged as rich as he is good, and as poor as he is bad. But the rich man is dissolved by excess and made unbridled by boasting; he runs wherever he pleases and falls into what is unlawful. Even the things that had been instruments of sinful pleasure become instruments of punishment. Labor in acquiring, fear in possessing, and grief in losing continually weary, trouble, and afflict his mind. “For where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6). But we shall speak more fully of this below.

## Chapter XVII. On the misery of servants and masters

The servant performs service, is terrified by threats, exhausted by forced labor, afflicted by blows, and stripped of his possessions. If he has nothing, he is compelled to acquire it; and if he has something, he is compelled not to have it. The master’s fault is the servant’s punishment; the servant’s fault is the master’s spoil:

> Whatever madness kings commit, the Achaeans pay the penalty.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14.)

The wild ass in the wilderness is the lion’s prey; so too the poor are the pasture of the rich. O most extreme condition of slavery! Nature bore men free, but fortune made them slaves [Col. 0709C] (Ecclus. 13). A servant is compelled to suffer, and no one is permitted to suffer with him; he is forced to grieve, and no one is allowed to grieve with him. Thus he is so little his own that he is no one to himself. Wretched are those who follow military camps, for it is wretched to live on another’s plunder.

If a master is cruel, he must be feared because of the wickedness of his subjects; if he is gentle, he comes to be despised because of their insolence. Thus fear afflicts the severe master, while contempt makes little of the gentle one. Cruelty produces hatred, and familiarity produces contempt; for the care of those close to him wears him out, and household concern troubles him. He must always be prepared and everywhere defended, so that he may forestall the snares of evildoers, repel the injuries of attackers, crush enemies, and protect citizens. [Col. 0709D] Nor is its own evil sufficient for the day; rather, day pours forth labor to day, and night announces anxiety to night (Ps. 18). Thus days are spent laboriously, and nights pass sleeplessly.

## Chapter XVIII. On the misery of the continent and the married

If fire can fail to burn, flesh can fail to desire; for however much it is punished [variant: “fought against”], that Jebusite can nevertheless never be expelled:

> Drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will always return.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.10.24.)

“For not all,” he says, “receive this saying, but he who can receive it, let him receive it” [Col. 0710A] (Matt. 16). Hence, when God Himself commanded concerning certain priestly garments that Moses and Aaron should clothe his sons, He did not command this solely concerning the breeches; rather, He said that they themselves should use breeches when they entered the tabernacle of testimony (Exod. 18).

The Apostle also says: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same state, lest Satan tempt you through your lack of self-control. For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7). Therefore Satan’s angel fights against continence: he carnally goads and grievously buffets; he kindles the fire of nature by the breath of suggestion, supplies material, grants opportunity, and furnishes occasion.

[Col. 0710B] Appearance too fights against it: what is suddenly seen is readily desired. Thus, when David was walking after midday upon the palace of the royal house, and saw Bathsheba bathing opposite, “he sent and took her, and slept with her; for she was a woman exceedingly beautiful” (2 Kings 12). Moreover, he who has a wife is concerned with the things of the world and is divided. He is drawn apart through many straits and cut up among varied anxieties, so as to seek and provide necessities for children and wife, male and female servants. “Such persons, therefore, have tribulations of the flesh” (1 Cor. 7).

A wife insists on having costly adornment [variant: “attire”] and varied household furnishings, so that her finery is often worth more than her husband’s estate. Otherwise, [Col. 0710C] night and day she weeps and sighs, chatters and murmurs. For there are three things that do not permit a man to remain in his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife. “That woman,” she says, “goes out more splendidly dressed and is honored by everyone; but I, most wretched of women, am alone despised in the gathering of women and scorned by all.” She wants alone to be loved, alone to be praised; she regards another woman’s affection as hatred of herself and suspects another’s praise to be her own disgrace. Everything she loves must be loved; everything she hates [variant: “despises”] must be hated. She wants to prevail but cannot bear to be overcome. [Note: [Col. 0709D] Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*.] She does not endure to serve, but endeavors to rule. She wants everything to be possible and nothing to be impossible.

If she is beautiful, she is readily loved; if ugly, she is not readily desired. But what many love is difficult to guard, and it is burdensome to possess [Col. 0710D] what no one deigns to have. One man solicits her by his beauty, another by intelligence, another by wit, another by generosity; and that which is assailed from every side is captured in some respect [variant: “provoked”]. A horse and an ass, an ox and a dog, a garment and a bed, even a cup and a little pitcher, are tested before they are purchased; but a bride is scarcely shown at last, lest she displease before she is taken. Yet, whatever chance brings her, she must always [variant: “necessarily”] be kept.

Whether ugly, foul-smelling, sick, foolish, proud, angry, or defective in whatever other way, a wife cannot be dismissed by her husband except for fornication alone. Nor may the man who dismisses her take another, nor may the dismissed woman be joined to another. [Col. 0711A] For “whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever takes a dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. 5).—“But if a wife departs from her husband, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and likewise a husband, if he departs from his wife” (1 Cor. 7).

The burden of marriage is exceedingly heavy. For, as Solomon says, “he is foolish and impious who keeps an adulteress” (Prov. 18), and he is a patron of disgrace who conceals his wife’s crime. But if he dismisses an adulteress, he is punished without fault of his own, because while she lives he is compelled to remain continent. On this account Christ’s disciples said: “If this is a man’s case with his wife, it is not expedient to marry” (Matt. 19). Who has ever been able calmly to endure a rival? Suspicion alone grievously afflicts the jealous man. For although it is written, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 3), the husband’s jealousy does not permit two persons in one flesh.

## Chapter XIX. On the misery of the good and the wicked

“The wicked have no joy,” says the Lord, because a person is tormented by the very things through which he sins (Isa. 38, 37). For “the worm” of conscience “does not die,” and “the fire” of reason [variant: “terror”] “is not extinguished” (Isa. 66). For I have seen those “who work iniquity, sow sorrows, and reap them, who perish at God’s breath and are consumed by the spirit of His wrath” (Job 4).

Pride puffs up, envy gnaws, avarice spurs on, anger kindles, gluttony oppresses, lust dissolves, lying binds, [Col. 0711C] murder stains. So too the other monstrosities of vices: the things which are a person’s sinful pleasures are God’s instruments of punishment.

> The envious man wastes away at another’s abundant prosperity; but  
> Sicilian tyrants found no greater torment  
> Than envy.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.57.)

For vice corrupts nature, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “They became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their own bodies; and since they rejected having God in knowledge, [Col. 0711D] God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are unfitting” (Rom. 1). Yet “all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).—“For the saints endured mockings and beatings, moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tested, and died by the sword for the Lord. They wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—persons of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and caverns of the earth” (Heb. 2). “In dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers from false brethren; in labor and hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many distresses, in cold and [Col. 0712A] nakedness” (2 Cor. 11).

For the righteous person “denies himself” (Luke 9), “crucifying his members with their vices and desires” (Gal. 5), so that the world is crucified to him and he to the world. “He does not have here an abiding city, but seeks the one to come” (Heb. 12). He endures the age as an exile, shut up in the body as in a prison. “I am,” he says, “a resident alien upon the earth, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 118).—“Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more” (Ps. 38).—“Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119).—“Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). For [Col. 0712B] the sins of neighbors are frying-pans for the righteous. This is the watered land which Caleb gave to his daughter Achsah as a dowry (Josh. 15).

## Chapter XX. On the enemies of man

“Human life upon earth, therefore, is warfare” (Job 7). Is it not real warfare, when manifold enemies continually lie in wait on every side, to capture and pursue in order to destroy: demon and man, world and flesh? The demon attacks with vices and desires; man with beasts; the world with the elements; flesh with the senses. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). But “our struggle is not against flesh [Col. 0712C] and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against the rulers of this darkness” (Eph. 6).—“For your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). The flaming darts of the wicked one are kindled. “Death enters through the windows” (Jer. 9); the eye plunders the soul (Lam. 3); “the world fights against the senseless” (Wis. 5).—“Nation shall rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom; there shall be great earthquakes in various places, plagues and famines, terrors from heaven, and storms” (Luke 21).

The earth produces thorns and thistles (Gen. 3), water storms and waves, air tempests and thunder, fire flashes and lightning. “Cursed,” He says, “is the earth in your work; it shall produce thorns and thistles for [Col. 0712D] you. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth; for earth you are, and into earth you shall go” (ibid.).—“The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it” (Ps. 79). Wolf and bear, leopard and lion (Jer. 5), tiger and wild ass, crocodile and griffin, serpent and snake, basilisk and asp, horned viper and dragon, scorpions and vipers; likewise nits and lice, ants and fleas, gnats and flies, hornets and wasps, fishes and birds. For we who were created to rule over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing that moves on the earth are now given to them as prey and handed over to them for food (Gen. 1). For it is written: “I will send among them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of creatures that crawl upon the earth and of serpents” (Deut. 3).

## Chapter XXI. On the prison of the soul, which is the body

“Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Certainly he does not wish to be led out of prison who does not wish to leave the body; for the body is the soul’s prison. Of this the Psalmist says: “Lead my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141). Nowhere are rest and tranquillity; nowhere are peace and security. Everywhere are fear and trembling; everywhere labor and pain. So long as flesh lives, it will suffer pain, and the soul will mourn over itself.

## Chapter XXII. On the brief joy of man

[Col. 0713B] Who has ever spent even one whole day pleasantly in his own delight without being troubled in some part of the day by the accusation of conscience, an onset of anger, or a stirring of desire? Whom has the bitterness of envy, the ardor of avarice, or the swelling of pride not tormented? Whom has no loss, offense, or suffering disturbed? Whom, finally, has no sight, sound, or act offended?

> A rare bird on earth, and most like a black swan.

Hear on this point the judgment of the Wise Man: “From morning until evening the time will change” (Ecclus. 18).—“Various thoughts succeed one another, and the mind is carried in different directions” (Job 20).—“They take up tambourine and lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the instrument; they spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to hell” [Col. 0713C] (Job 21).

## Chapter XXIII. On unforeseen grief

For sudden sorrow always follows worldly [variant: “human”] joy. What begins in gladness ends in mourning. Worldly happiness is indeed sprinkled with many bitternesses. He knew this who said: “Laughter will be mingled with grief, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). Job’s children experienced this: while they ate and drank wine in the house of their eldest brother, suddenly a violent wind came from the desert region and shook the four corners of the house; as it collapsed, it crushed them all (Job 1). Rightly, therefore, their father said: “My lyre has been turned to mourning, and my instrument to the voice of those who weep” (Job 30).—“For it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). Consider this wholesome counsel: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evil things” (Eccl. 11).—“Remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Eccl. 7).

## Chapter XXIV. On the nearness of death

The last day is always regarded as the first, and the first day is never regarded as the last. Yet one ought always to live as though one must always die. For it is written: “Remember that death does not delay” (Ecclus. 14). Time passes and death approaches. A thousand years before the eyes of the dying are like [Col. 0714A] yesterday, which has passed. Future things are always being born; present things are always dying; and whatever is past is wholly dead.

For while we live we are always dying, and only then do we cease to die when we cease to live. It is therefore better to die to life than to live to death, because mortal life is nothing but living death. Hence Solomon says: “I praised the dead more than the living, and I judged happier than both the one who has not yet been born” (Eccl. 4). Life flees swiftly and cannot be held; death, however, meets us urgently and cannot be prevented. This is the remarkable thing: the more it grows, the more it decreases, because the farther life advances, the nearer it comes to its end.

## Chapter XXV. On the terror of dreams

[Col. 0714B]

The time granted to rest is not granted to be restful: dreams terrify and visions disturb. Although what dreamers dream is not truly sad, dreadful, or laborious, they are nevertheless truly saddened, terrified, and exhausted, to such an extent that they sometimes weep in sleep and are very often troubled on waking. If they see something pleasant, they are nonetheless saddened on waking, as though they had lost it.

Observe what Eliphaz the Temanite says concerning this: “In the horror of a nocturnal vision, when sleep is accustomed to overtake men, dread and trembling seized me, and all my bones were terrified; and when a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end.” Consider [Col. 0714C] Job saying: “If I say, ‘My bed will console me, and I shall be relieved while speaking with myself on my couch,’ you will terrify me through dreams and shake me with horror through visions” (Job 7).

Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream that terrified him greatly, and the visions of his head disturbed him (Dan. 2). Many concerns are followed by dreams, and where there are many dreams, there are very many vanities. Dreams have caused many to err, and those who hoped in them have fallen. For shameful images often appear in dreams; through nocturnal illusions not only is the flesh defiled, but the soul also is stained. Hence the Lord says in Leviticus: “If there is among you a man defiled in a nocturnal dream, let him go outside the camp and not return [Col. 0714D] until he has washed himself with water before evening; and after sunset let him return to the camp” (Lev. 19).

## Chapter XXVI. On compassion for friends

O how great a grief troubles us, how great a trembling shakes us, when we feel the losses of friends and fear dangers to parents! At times the healthy person is more disturbed by fear than the sick person by illness. The one is more afflicted voluntarily by the feeling of grief than the other unwillingly by the effect of sickness. That poetic saying is true:

> Love is a thing full of anxious fear.  
> (Ovid.)

Whose breast is so iron, whose heart so stony, [Col. 0715A] that he does not utter groans or shed tears when he beholds a neighbor’s or friend’s illness or death [variant: “death”], so as not to suffer with the sufferer and grieve with the grieving? Jesus Himself, when He saw Mary and the Jews who had come with her to the tomb weeping, groaned in spirit, troubled Himself, and wept—perhaps not because the man was dead, but rather because He recalled him from death to the miseries of life. But let him know that he is culpably hard and harshly blameworthy who mourns the bodily death of his friend yet does not weep for the spiritual death of his own soul.

## Chapter XXVII. On sudden misfortunes

[Col. 0715B] Suddenly, when one does not expect it, misfortune occurs, calamity rushes in, illness attacks, death cuts one off—which [variant: “because”] no one escapes. Therefore “do not boast about tomorrow, not knowing what the coming day will bring forth” (Prov. 27).—“Man does not know his end; but as fishes are caught on a hook and birds caught in a snare, so men are caught in an evil time, when it suddenly comes upon them” (Eccl. 9).

## Chapter XXVIII. On the innumerable kinds of illnesses

Not in all the ages since the world began has medical skill been able to discover as many kinds of illnesses and varieties of sufferings as human frailty has been able to endure. Shall I call the intolerability of diseases tolerable, or their tolerability intolerable? Better to join both expressions. For it is intolerable because of the severity of suffering, and tolerable because of the necessity of enduring it. From day to day human nature is corrupted more and more. Thus many remedies that were once healthful experiments are now deadly because of nature’s own decline.

Both worlds have now grown old: the macrocosm and the microcosm, that is, the greater world and the lesser world. And the longer the old age of each is prolonged, the more grievously the nature of each is disturbed.

## Chapter XXIX. On the various kinds of tortures

What shall I say of the wretched, who are punished through innumerable [Col. 0715D] kinds of tortures? They are beaten with clubs and slaughtered with swords; burned in flames and crushed beneath stones; torn with claws and hung on gibbets; tortured with tigers [variant: “claws”] and scourged with scorpions; bound with chains and strangled with nooses; thrust into prisons and worn away by fasts; hurled down and drowned; flayed and pulled apart; cut and undermined. “Those destined for death, to death; those for the sword, to the sword; those for famine, to famine; and those for captivity, to captivity.” A cruel judgment, a monstrous punishment, a sorrowful spectacle: they are given as food to the birds of heaven, the beasts of the earth, and [Col. 0716A] the fishes of the sea. Alas, alas, alas, wretched mothers, who bore such unhappy sons! (Jer. 15).

## Chapter XXX. On a certain horrible deed: namely, a woman who ate her own child

It is fitting, therefore, to recall that horrible deed which Josephus describes concerning the Jewish siege. [Note: [Col. 0715D] Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book VII, chapter 13.] A certain woman, noble in wealth and family, together with the rest of the multitude that had gathered at Jerusalem, endured the common fate of the siege. The tyrants had wholly seized the remainder of her property, which she had brought from her house into the city. If anything remained of her great wealth on which she might sustain a very scant daily subsistence, the raiders’ attendants rushed in at every moment and carried it off. On this account great anguish, arising from a kind of indignation like madness, wore the woman down, so that she sometimes provoked the robbers to kill her by curses and abuse.

But since no one, whether angered or moved to pity, killed her, and since any food perhaps sought by her was sought by others, and there was now nowhere any means of obtaining it, dreadful hunger pressed upon her entrails and marrow. As want drove her onward into the madness of hunger, she adopted the most wicked counsel and armed herself even against the laws of nature. For she had at her breasts a little son; holding him before her eyes, she said: “You are the child of an unhappy mother—O child more unhappy still! For whom shall I preserve you amid war, famine, and the plunder of robbers? Even if life could be hoped for, [Col. 0716C] you will nevertheless be weighed down by the yoke of Roman slavery [variant: “I am weighed down”]. Come now, therefore, my son: be food for your mother, fury for the robbers, and a tale for the ages—the one thing lacking to complete the calamities of the Jews.”

Having said this, she immediately cut her son’s throat; then, placing him on the fire, she roasted him, consumed one half, and kept the other half covered. And behold, at once the robbers rushed in, having caught the smell of the cooked flesh. They threatened her with death unless, without delay, she showed them the food which they perceived had been prepared. Then she said: “I have saved the best portion for you,” and immediately uncovered the child’s remaining limbs. But suddenly great horror seized them; their limbs stiffened, and, as if through hardness of heart, their voice was choked in their throats. She, however, with a savage countenance and more savage than the robbers themselves, [Col. 0716D] said: “The offspring is mine, the son is mine, the deed is mine. Eat: for I ate first, I who bore him. Do not make yourselves either more devout than a mother or softer than a woman. But if piety overcomes you, curse my food; I who have already fed on such things shall feed on them again.” After this, terrified and trembling, they departed, leaving this one food, out of all her possessions, to the wretched mother.

## Chapter XXXI. That the innocent is sometimes punished and the guilty acquitted

Let no one who knows himself free from guilt trust that he is exempt from punishment. “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). For often the innocent is condemned and the guilty acquitted; the devout are punished and the wicked honored; Jesus is crucified and Barabbas set free. Today [Col. 0718A] a just and quiet man is considered useless, a religious man a hypocrite, and a simple man a fool. “For the simplicity of the righteous is mocked” (Job 12): a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich.

# Book II: Treating of the culpable course of human conversion

[Col. 0717]

## Chapter I. What people commonly desire

[Col. 0717B]

People chiefly desire three things: riches, pleasures, and honors. From riches proceed wicked things; from pleasures, shameful things; from honors, vain things. Hence the Apostle John says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). The desire of the flesh pertains to pleasures; the desire of the eyes to riches; the pride of life to honors. Riches generate greed and avarice; pleasures bring forth gluttony and lust; honors nourish pride and boasting.

## Chapter II. On greed

[Col. 0717C]

“Nothing, therefore, is more wicked than the greedy man, and nothing more unjust than to love money” (Ecclus. 10). It is a saying of the Wise Man, confirmed by the Apostle, who says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, into the devil’s snare, and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition. For greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). It commits sacrileges and thefts, practices robbery and plunder, wages wars and murders; buys and sells simoniacally, unjustly asks and receives; trades and lends at interest unjustly; persists in deceit and threatens fraud; breaks an agreement and violates an oath; corrupts testimony and perverts judgment.

## Chapter III. On unjust gifts

[Col. 0717D]

Consult Isaiah, the evangelical prophet: “All,” he says, “love gifts and pursue rewards; they do not judge for the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not come before them” (Isa. 1). They do not precede rewards, because they do not judge from love of justice; rather, rewards precede them, because they judge from love of money. For they always follow a gift, a promise, or an expectation; and therefore they do not judge for the orphan, from whom nothing is given, promised, or hoped for.

O faithless rulers, companions of thieves: all you who love gifts and pursue rewards will never shake a gift from your hand unless you first banish greed from your breast. The prophet says of you: “Her rulers are like wolves seizing [Col. 0718B] prey and greedily pursuing gain” (Ezek. 22).—“Her rulers judged for gifts, her priests taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money” (Mic. 3). Behold, the Lord commanded the opposite through Moses in the Law: “You shall appoint judges and teachers in all your gates, that they may judge the people with righteous judgment and not turn aside to either party. You shall not accept a person or gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just. But you shall pursue what is just, justly, and you shall live” (Deut. 16).

He says two things, “just” and “justly.” Some indeed pursue what is just justly; others pursue what is unjust unjustly. Again, some pursue what is just unjustly; others pursue what is unjust justly.

## Chapter IV. On respect of persons

[Col. 0718C]

“Woe to you” who, corrupted by entreaty or payment, drawn by love or hatred, “call good evil and evil good, putting darkness for light and light for darkness” (Isa. 5), “putting to death souls that should not die and keeping alive souls that should not live” (Ezek. 13). For you do not consider the merits of cases, but the merits of persons; not laws, but gifts; not justice, but money; not what reason dictates, but what will desires; not what the law establishes, but what the mind craves. You do not incline your mind to justice, but incline justice to your mind; not so that what is lawful may please you, but so that what pleases you may be lawful.

Your eye is never so single that your whole [Col. 0718D] body may be full of light (Matt. 6); rather, you always mix in some leaven by which you corrupt the whole lump (1 Cor. 5). You neglect the cause of the poor with delay, but promote the cause of the rich with urgency. With the former you show severity; with the latter you make allowances out of gentleness. You look upon the former with difficulty; you deal with the latter favorably. You hear the former negligently; you listen to the latter attentively. The poor man cries out and no one hears; the rich man speaks and all applaud. “The rich man has spoken and all have been silent, and they carry his word up to the clouds; the poor man has spoken and they say, ‘Who is this?’ And if he stumbles, they will overthrow him” (Ecclus. 13).

The man suffering violence cries out, and no one hears; he raises his voice, and there is no one to judge. Yet if you happen to take up the poor person’s cause, you support him slackly; but when you undertake the rich person’s cause, [Col. 0719A] you help him obstinately. You despise the poor and honor the rich; you rise respectfully for the latter and tread the former contemptuously underfoot. “If a man wearing a gold ring and fine white clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothes also enters, and you attend to the man clothed in splendid apparel and say to him, ‘Sit here in a good place,’ but say to the poor man, ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool,’ do you not judge among yourselves and become judges with wicked thoughts?” (Jas. 2).

For the prophet speaks of you and against you: “They have become great and rich, fat and sleek; they have not pleaded the cause of the orphan and have not judged the case of the poor” (Jer. 5), as the Law commands: “There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as well as the great. You shall accept no person, because judgment belongs to God” (Deut. 1).—“For there is no respect of persons with God” (Acts 10).

## Chapter V. On the sale of justice

But you neither give favor freely nor render justice justly, because unless something comes to you, nothing proceeds from you; nor is it given unless it is sold. You often delay justice so long that you take more than the whole from litigants, because the cost of the expense is greater than the benefit of the judgment. What then will you be able to answer Him in strict judgment, who commands: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10)? Profit is in the chest, loss in [Col. 0719C] the conscience: you pursue money but make the soul captive.

But “what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world yet suffers loss to his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?” (Matt. 16).—“A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem? He will not give God his propitiation or the price of the redemption of his soul; he has labored forever, and shall he yet live to the end?” (Ps. 45). Hear, rich men, what the Apostle James says against you: “Come now, rich men, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have decayed, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days. Behold, the wages of the laborers who harvested your fields, which have been withheld by you, cry out; and their cry has entered the ears of the Lord of hosts” (Jas. 5).

Therefore Truth commands: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy and where thieves break in and steal” [Col. 0719D] (Matt. 6).

## Chapter VI. On the insatiable desire of the greedy

O unquenchable fire! O insatiable greed! What greedy person was ever satisfied with his first desire? When he obtains what he wished for, he desires greater things; he always sets a limit to acquiring and never to what he has acquired. The greedy man’s eye is insatiable and will not be satisfied with any measure of wickedness. “The covetous man will not be filled with money, and he who loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. 5). Hell and destruction are never filled; likewise, the eyes of men are insatiable. “The leech has two daughters, which say, ‘Bring, bring’” (Prov. 30). For

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> (Juvenal, XIV.139.)

## Chapter VII. Why the greedy person cannot be satisfied

Do you wish, greedy man, to know why you are always empty and never filled? Consider this: your measure is not full, since however much it contains, it remains capable of holding more. But the human soul is capable of God, since “he who is joined to God is one spirit with God” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore, however much it contains, [Col. 0720B] it is never full unless it possesses God, of whom it is always capable. If you wish, then, greedy man, to be satisfied, cease to be greedy; for so long as you are greedy, you cannot be satisfied. “For there is no agreement of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial” (2 Cor. 6), because “no one can serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6).

## Chapter VIII. On the false name of riches

O false happiness of riches, which truly makes a rich man an unhappy son. For what is more unhappy [variant: “false”] than worldly resources, which are called riches? To be rich and to be needy are opposites. Yet worldly resources do not take away need but bring it [Col. 0720C] upon one. Solomon says, indeed, that a little is more sufficient for the poor man than very much for the rich, because “where there are many riches, there are many who consume them” (Eccl. 5). I myself frequently find by experience how many and how great magnates are in need. Wealth, therefore, does not make a person rich but needy.

## Chapter IX. Examples against greed
How many has covetous desire deceived! How many more has avarice destroyed! Balaam’s ass rebuked him and crushed the feet of its rider, because, captivated by desire for the promises made to him, he had intended to curse Israel (Num. 22). The people stoned Achan because he took gold and silver from what had been placed under the ban (Josh. 7). Naboth was killed so that Ahab might possess his vineyard (3 Kings [Col. 0720D] 21). Gehazi was struck with leprosy because, in Elisha’s name, he asked for and received gold, silver, and garments (4 Kings 5). Judas hanged himself with a noose because he sold and betrayed Christ (Matt. 27). Sudden death destroyed Ananias and Sapphira because they withheld from the apostles part of the price of their field (Acts 5). “And Tyre built herself a stronghold, heaped up silver like dust and gold like the mud of the streets; but behold, the Lord will take possession of her, strike down her strength into the sea, and she shall be consumed by fire” (Zech. 9).

## Chapter X. On the excessive anxiety of the covetous

Why should anyone strive to gather possessions when the one who gathers cannot remain? For “he comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14). Why should he desire much, when little is enough? “Having food and clothing,” he says, “let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6). Why should he seek necessities with much anxiety, when they offer themselves without great difficulty? Hear what Truth says on this matter: “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? What shall we drink? Or with what shall we be clothed? For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6; Luke 12).—“For I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread” (Ps. 36).

## Chapter XI. On avarice

[Col. 0721B]

Tantalus thirsts amid waters; the miser is needy amid wealth [Note: [Col. 0721D] Horace.]. For he possesses only as much as he does not possess, since he never uses what he has acquired but always gapes after further acquisitions. Solomon says: “One is as though rich while having nothing, and another as though poor while possessing great riches” (Prov. 13).

The miser and hell alike consume and do not digest; they receive and do not give back. The miser neither sympathizes with those who suffer nor assists or pities the wretched; rather, he offends God, himself, and his neighbour. For he withholds from God what is owed, denies his neighbour what is necessary, and deprives himself of what is fitting. He is ungrateful toward God, impious toward his neighbour, and cruel toward himself. “For the greedy and exceedingly grasping man possessions are without reason; and for the envious man, what use is gold? He who is evil to himself—how shall he be good to others? Nor shall he take delight in his own goods” (Ecclus. 14).—“Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, yet shuts his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3.) For he does not love his neighbour as himself when he lets him perish from hunger and be consumed by want; nor does he love God above all things when he prefers gold and sets silver before him.

## Chapter XII. Why avarice is slavery to idols

The Apostle rightly defines it: “Avarice is the service of idols” (Eph. 6). For as the idolater serves an image, so the miser serves a treasure. The former diligently enlarges the worship of idolatry, while the latter gladly increases his heap of money. The former tends an image with every care; the latter guards his treasure with every concern. The former places his hope in idolatry; the latter fixes his hope upon money. The former fears to mutilate an image; the latter fears to diminish his treasure.

## Chapter XIII. On certain characteristics of avarice

The miser is quick to ask, slow to give, and shameless in refusing. If he spends anything, he considers it wholly lost; sorrowful, complaining, and morose, he sighs and frets anxiously. He holds possessions hesitantly and spends unwillingly. He magnifies what has been given, but cheapens what is to be given; he gives in order to gain, but does not gain in order to give; lavish with another’s property, but sparing with his own. He empties his stomach in order to fill his chest; he emaciates his body in order to extend his profit. He keeps his hand clenched for giving but stretched out for receiving; closed for giving but open for receiving.

Moreover, “the possessions of the unjust shall dry up like a river” (Ecclus. 40), because he who gathers wickedly soon scatters. It is a just judgment that what comes from evil should arrive at evil; and that what does not proceed from good should not come to good. Therefore the miser possesses condemnation both in this life and in the life to come.

## Chapter XIV. On the unjust possession of riches

[Col. 0722B]

True, therefore, is what the Wise Man declares: “Gold and silver have destroyed many” (Ecclus. 8).—“He who loves gold shall not be justified” (Ecclus. 31). “Woe to those who pursue it. Behold, sinners who abound in this age have obtained riches” (Ps. 72). Hence Truth itself commanded the apostles: “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts” (Matt. 10); for just as a camel cannot enter through the eye of a needle, so it is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19). “For narrow is the way and constricted the gate that leads to life” (Matt. 7). Therefore the Apostle, following the rule of Truth, said: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3).—“Woe to you who join house to house and couple field to field, even to the boundary of the place” (Isa. 5).—“The earth is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to its treasures” (Isa. 2).—“Because of the iniquity of his avarice, I was angry and struck him” (Isa. 57).

## Chapter XV. On lawful riches

Abraham, however, was rich; Job was wealthy; David was prosperous. Yet Scripture says of Abraham: “He believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15); of Job, “There was none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing [Col. 0722D] God and departing from evil” (Job 1); and of David, “The Lord found a man according to his own heart” (1 Kings 16).

But they were “as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6), in accordance with the Prophet’s saying: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61). We, however, possess everything as though possessing nothing, according to the Psalmist’s words: “The rich have been needy and hungry” (Ps. 33). For it is easier to find one who loves riches and does not have them than one who has them and does not love them. For it is difficult to be in fire and not burn; more difficult still to possess riches and not love them. Hear the prophet Jeremiah: “From the least to the greatest, [Col. 0723A] all pursue avarice; and from prophet to priest all practise deceit” (Jer. 6).

## Chapter XVI. On the uncertainty of riches

Every covetous and avaricious person strives and labours against nature. For nature brings a person poor into the world, and nature leads him poor out of the world. The earth received him naked and will receive him naked again; but the covetous person desires and takes pains to become rich in the world. “I will tear down my barns,” he says, “and build larger ones; and there I shall gather all that has grown for me, and all my goods” (Luke 12). But he was told: “Fool, this night your soul shall be demanded of you; and whose shall be the things you have prepared?” (ibid.).—“You store up treasure and do not know for whom you gather it” (Ps. 38).—“They have slept their sleep, [Col. 0723B] and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75).—“When the rich man sleeps, he carries nothing away; he shall open his eyes and find nothing” (Job 27).—“Therefore do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied, for when he dies he shall take none of these things, nor shall the glory of his house descend with him” (Ps. 48); rather, he will leave his riches to strangers, while their tombs are their houses for ever.

The Wise Man likewise testifies: “He who unjustly heaps up from his heart gathers for others, and another shall luxuriate in his goods” (Ecclus. 14). Alas—the one whom he had as an enemy, he leaves as his heir.

## Chapter XVII. On gluttony

[Col. 0723C]

“The beginning of human life is water and bread, clothing, and a house covering nakedness” (Ecclus. 29). But now, for gluttons, the fruits of trees are insufficient, the kinds of legumes insufficient, the roots of herbs insufficient, the fish of the sea insufficient, the beasts of the earth insufficient, the birds of heaven insufficient. Spices are sought, aromatics are bought [variant: “prepared”], fattened fowls are reared, and creatures are caught for food; they are carefully cooked by the craft of cooks and richly prepared by the service of attendants. One crushes and strains; another mixes and makes ready. Substance is changed into accident, nature into art, so that satiety may become hunger and disgust may recall appetite: to provoke gluttony, not [Col. 0723D] to sustain nature; not to supply necessity, but to satisfy greed.

Yet the pleasure of gluttony is so brief that in extent of place it scarcely occupies four fingers, and in duration scarcely as many moments. Moderation is despised and excess sought, through diversity of flavours and variety of foods. Greed knows no measure, and variety [variant: “voracity”] exceeds bounds; and in these things the mind is weighed down, the stomach disturbed, and the senses oppressed. From them come not health and soundness, but sickness and death. Hear the Wise Man’s judgment on this matter: “Do not be greedy at every banquet, and do not pour yourself out upon every food. For in many foods there will be sickness, and because of gluttony many have perished” (Ecclus. 37).—“Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both this and that” (1 Cor. 6).

## Chapter XVIII. Examples against gluttony

Gluttony exacts a costly tribute but returns the vilest payment; for the more delicate the foods, the fouler the excrement. He acts more shamefully who takes food in shamefully, producing a horrible wind above and below and emitting an abominable sound. Gluttony shut paradise (Gen. 3), sold Esau’s birthright (Gen. 25), hanged the baker (Gen. 41), and beheaded the Baptist (Mark 6). Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks, burned the Temple and overthrew Jerusalem (4 Kings 25). At the banquet Belshazzar saw a hand writing against the wall, “Mene, [Col. 0724B] Tekel, Peres,” and that same night he was killed by the Chaldeans (Dan. 5). “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32); but “their food was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God rose against them” (Ps. 77).—“Those who fed delicately perished in the streets” (Lam. 4). That rich man who feasted splendidly every day was buried in hell (Luke 16).

## Chapter XIX. On drunkenness

What is more shameful than a drunkard? His mouth stinks, his body trembles; he promises much, betrays secrets, loses his mind, and his face is transformed. “For there is no secret where drunkenness rules” (Prov. 31).

Horace (*Epistles* I.5.19):

> What man have fruitful cups not made eloquent?

Wine, moreover, is not enough; nor cider, nor beer. Rather, mead, syrup, and claret are carefully made—with much labour, great concern, and no small expense—but from them arise contentions and brawls, lawsuits and quarrels. “For much wine drunk,” as the Wise Man says, “produces irritation, anger, and much ruin” (Ecclus. 31). From it come acts of fornication. “Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. 4). Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, wherein is dissipation” (Eph. 5). And Solomon says: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness tumultuous” (Prov. 20). The sons of Rechab and the son of Zechariah did not drink wine or strong drink, nor anything that could intoxicate [Col. 0724D] (Jer. 35; Luke 1).

## Chapter XX. Examples against drunkenness

For drunkenness uncovered shameful nakedness (Gen. 9), committed incest (Gen. 19), killed a king’s son (2 Kings 13), and slew a commander of an army (Judg. 13). Therefore Solomon truly says: “Those who give themselves to drink and contribute to drinking parties shall be consumed” (Prov. 23); and Isaiah says: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness, and drink until evening so that they burn with wine. Harp and lyre, tambourine and flute, and wine are at your banquets. Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, men strong at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 51).—“Behold, joy and gladness: killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating [Col. 0725A] flesh and drinking wine. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And the voice of the Lord of hosts was revealed in my ears: This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die” (Isa. 22).—“Woe to the crown of Ephraim’s pride. Priest and prophet have not known: overwhelmed by drunkenness, they have been swallowed up by wine; they did not know the seer and did not understand judgment” (Isa. 28).

Shame indeed! When a certain presbyter was asked for a blessing before the Gospel lesson was to be proclaimed, he was said, belching out the previous day’s debauch and the night’s drunkenness, to have declared in a loud voice: “May the king of angels bless the servants’ drink.”

## Chapter XXI. On lust

[Col. 0725B]

Moreover, a shameful mother gives birth to a still more shameful daughter; for it is just that “he who is filthy should become filthier still” (Rev. 22).—“For all adulterers are like an oven heated by the baker. The princes began to rage from wine” (Hos. 7). A belly richly filled readily embraces Venus. O utter shamefulness of lust! It not only effeminates the mind but also enfeebles the body; it not only stains the soul but disfigures the person. “For every sin whatever a man commits is outside his body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6). Ardour and wantonness always precede it; stench and uncleanness always accompany it; pain and repentance always follow it. “For,” Solomon says, “the lips [Col. 0725C] of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood, and her tongue sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. 5).

## Chapter XXII. On the universality of lust

It is an intimate enemy, dwelling not far away but near; not externally but within. For “his strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). It is never driven out unless fled from; never slain unless mortified. As a cause it demands freedom and abundance; but for its effect it requires [variant: “finds”] opportunity and proximity. It corrupts every age, confounds every sex, dissolves every rank, and perverts every [Col. 0725D] station. It attacks old and young, male and female, prudent and simple, superiors and inferiors—even, in the last generation, priests, who embrace Venus at night but venerate the Virgin in the morning.

Shameful to say, but most shameful in deed: let it be permitted to say what one has no wish to do. At night they pursue the son of Venus in their beds; in the morning they offer the Son of the Virgin at the altar.

## Chapter XXIII. On the various kinds of lust and their punishments

Who can adequately explain its many kinds? It overthrew Pentapolis with its neighbouring region (Gen. 19). It destroyed the Sodomites and Shechem with his people, the ravishers of Dinah (Gen. 34); struck Er and Onan, the sons of Judah (Gen. 16), that is, the unclean; pierced through with a dagger the Jew and the Midianite woman (Num. 25), that is, fornicators; destroyed the tribe of Benjamin for the Levite’s wife (Judg. 19–20), that is, adulterers; and struck down in battle the sons of Eli the priest, that is, violators (1 Kings 2, 4). It killed Amnon at a banquet (2 Kings 13). Finally, it killed Uriah (2 Kings 11), stoned the elders (Dan. 13), cursed Reuben (Gen. 35, 49), seduced Samson (Judg. 19), and perverted Solomon (3 Kings 11).

Therefore it is true what is written: because of a woman’s beauty many have perished. For “wine and women make wise men apostatize and rebuke the sensible” (Ecclus. 19). It has cast down many wounded; and all the strongest have been slain by it. Its house is the way to hell, penetrating into the innermost places of death (Prov. 7). It enervates strength, [Col. 0726B] diminishes the senses, consumes days, and pours out wealth.

## Chapter XXIV. On intercourse contrary to nature

It produces a shameful transformation (*morphosis*), which nevertheless the Apostle does not blush to name. “Therefore,” he says, “God gave them over to shameful passions. For their women exchanged the natural use for that which is contrary to nature. Likewise also the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires toward one another, males committing shameful acts with males” (Rom. 1).

What is more shameful than those who commit this shamefulness? What crime is more criminal than this? For in the Law the intercourse of a male with a male and intercourse [Col. 0726C] of a human being with an animal are joined as though equal. Thus it is read in Leviticus: “You shall not have intercourse with a male as with a woman, because it is an abomination. You shall not have intercourse with any beast, nor defile yourself with it” (Lev. 18). An equal punishment is prescribed for both: “Whoever,” it says, “lies with a male as with a woman, both have committed an abomination; they shall surely die. Kill the beast also” (Lev. 20). Let him who has ears hear—or rather, let him who is foolish come to his senses.

## Chapter XXV. On the punishment of this crime

The punishment teaches what this fault deserved. “For the Lord rained sulphur and fire from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Gen. 19). The Lord did not wish to entrust execution [Col. 0726D] of this punishment to any angel or human being, but reserved to himself vengeance for this crime, according to the words: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32). Therefore the Lord rained from the Lord—that is, from himself—not rain or dew but sulphur and fire: sulphur upon the stench of lust, fire upon the burning of desire, so that the punishment might resemble the fault. Nor is he said to have sent it, but to have rained it, so that by this very word he might indicate the greatness and abundance of the punishment. His eye spared no one, but he destroyed all alike.

He also turned Lot’s wife into a pillar of salt because she looked back; and he transformed not merely the cities but all the surrounding regions into the Dead Sea and a salt valley. “For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10), who, the greater the patience he displays through his forbearance, [Col. 0727A] inflicts the harsher vengeance through his severity.

## Chapter XXVI. On the ambitious man

The covetous person gathers wealth, and the miser preserves it; the glutton tastes pleasures, and the lustful person practises them; the ambitious person desires honours, and the proud person exalts them. The ambitious man, however, is always fearful, always watchful lest he say or do something displeasing in people’s eyes. He pretends humility, feigns integrity, displays affability, shows kindness; he follows and serves, honours everyone, bows to all, frequents courts, visits nobles, rises and embraces, applauds and flatters. He knows well the poetic saying:

[Col. 0727B]

> Though there be no dust, still he shakes it off.  
> —Ovid

He is eager and ardent wherever he thinks he can please; restrained and lukewarm wherever he believes he may displease. He disapproves of evils and detests wrongdoing, yet approves and disapproves different things with different persons, in order that he may be judged suitable, considered acceptable, praised by people, and approved by each individually.

And behold, within himself he endures a grave battle and difficult conflict: iniquity strikes at his mind, while ambition restrains his hand [variant: “evil”]; what the former suggests should be done, the latter does not permit to be done. Yet mother and daughter—iniquity and ambition—conspire with one another. For the mother stands openly, while the daughter does not resist in secret. The one claims the public sphere for herself; the other, the private. Therefore the ambitious man willingly [Col. 0727C] speaks of the office for which he strives, saying: “O when will that man rule who is strict in justice, merciful in compassion, who does not turn aside through love or hatred, who is not corrupted by prayer or payment, who trusts the faithful and gives heed to suppliants, who is humble and kind, generous and gentle, steadfast, wise, patient, and shrewd?”

## Chapter XXVII. On the excessive desire of the ambitious

Perhaps one who makes no progress by this art has recourse to another: he summons Simon and approaches Gehazi; through the latter he strives to buy from the former what he cannot obtain on his own. He begs and promises, offers and gives; shame on it! He strives to obtain favour which he could not obtain freely [variant: “to obtain by fair means or foul”]. Nor does he yet desist, [Col. 0727D] but presses on and violently assaults an honour, shamelessly snatching at dignity, through the votes of friends, the support of relatives, and such a burning passion for condemnation, such a lust for presiding, that he neither recoils from schism nor fears scandal.

But leprosy struck Gehazi (4 Kings 5), and Simon perished through money (Acts 8). Korah with his companions was taken by fire, and the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram alive (Num. 16). “Therefore let no one assume an honour for himself, unless called by God as Aaron was” (Heb. 5).

## Chapter XXVIII. An example of ambition

A clear example of ambition is found in Absalom. When he aspired to the kingdom, “he made for himself [Col. 0728A] chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him. Rising early in the morning, Absalom stood beside the entrance of the gate. Every man who had a case and came for judgment before the king, Absalom called to himself and said: ‘From what city are you?’ When he replied, ‘Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel,’ Absalom answered him: ‘Your words seem to me just and good; but there is no one appointed by the king to hear you.’ Absalom would also say: ‘Who will appoint me judge over the land, so that all who have a case may come to me and I may judge them justly?’ But whenever a man came near him and greeted him, he stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and kissed him. Thus he acted toward all Israel who came for judgment to be heard by the king; and he won over [Col. 0728B] the hearts of the men of Israel. When Absalom had gone to Hebron, he sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying: ‘As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, say: Absalom has become king in Hebron.’ And the conspiracy became strong, and the people gathering together increased with Absalom” (2 Kings 15).

## Chapter XXIX. On the short and miserable life of magnates

But suppose that he is raised on high and advanced to the summit: cares immediately grow, anxieties accumulate, fasts are extended, vigils prolonged; by these nature is corrupted and the spirit weakened. Sleep is impaired, appetite is lost, strength is debilitated, the body grows thin; and thus, failing in himself, he does not merely halve his days but brings a miserable [Col. 0728C] life to a still more miserable end.

True is that poetic saying:

> [Lacuna] great things collapse upon themselves, and it is denied to the highest  
> to stand long [lacuna] they are raised aloft,  
> that they may fall with a heavier fall.

But truer is the prophetic saying: “I saw the wicked highly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon. I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36).—“Before his days are fulfilled he shall perish; his cluster shall be injured like a vine in first bloom, and like an olive casting off its flower” (Job 15). Hear the Wise Man’s judgment on this: “Every dominion is a short life” (Ecclus. 10).

## Chapter XXX. On the various characteristics of the proud

[Col. 0728D]

As soon as the ambitious man is eager for honour, he is lifted up into pride and runs unchecked into boasting. He does not care to be useful, but glories in presiding. He supposes himself better because he has risen to be superior. Yet it is not rank that makes one good, but virtue; not dignity, but honourable conduct. He scorns former friends, ignores yesterday’s acquaintances, despises old companions; he turns away his face, raises his gaze, lifts his neck, displays arrogance, speaks grandly, and meditates lofty things. He does not endure subordination but strives to rule; hostile to superiors, burdensome to subordinates. He does not bear inconveniences, does not defer what he has conceived; he is rash and bold, vainglorious and arrogant, grave and importunate.
