## Chapter XXXI. On pride and Lucifer’s fall

[Col. 0729A]

O pride, unbearable to all and hateful to everyone: among all vices you are always first and always last. For every sin is committed when you arrive and abandoned when you depart. For it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10).—“Death’s firstborn” (Job 18). For amid the very beginnings of things it raised a creature against the Creator, an angel against God; yet it immediately cast him down, because he did not stand in the truth—from innocence into sin, from delights into miseries, from the empyrean heaven into the darkened air.

Hear the prophet: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have fallen to the earth, [Col. 0729B] you who wounded the nations, you who said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven and exalt my throne above the stars of God; I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14).—“You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of God’s paradise. Every precious stone was your garment [variant: “covering”]: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, carbuncle, sapphire, emerald, and gold. The workmanship of your adornment and your settings was prepared on the day you were created. You were a spread-out and protecting cherub, and I placed you on God’s holy mountain. You walked amid fiery stones, perfect [Col. 0729C] in your ways from the day of your creation until iniquity was found in you. You sinned, and I cast you out from the holy mountain of God. Your heart was lifted up in your beauty, and I cast you down to earth” (Ezek. 21).—“The cedars were not taller than he in the paradise of God. The fir trees did not equal his height, and the plane trees were not equal to his branches. No precious tree of paradise was comparable to him and to his beauty, because I made him beautiful in his many thick branches” (Ezek. 31).—“He is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41).

He is “the great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon his heads seven diadems; his tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them down to earth. And that great dragon was cast down—the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceived the whole world—and he was cast down to earth, [Col. 0729D] and his angels were cast down to earth with him” (Rev. 12). Of him Truth also says: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10). For “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14).

## Chapter XXXII. On human arrogance

O proud presumption and presumptuous pride, which sought not only to make angels equal to God but also presumed to deify human beings! Yet those whom it raised, it cast down; and those whom it exalted, it humbled. Thus the Lord says to the prophet: “Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: [Col. 0730A] because your heart has been lifted up as though it were the heart of God, and you have said, ‘I am God,’ though you are a human being and not God, therefore I shall bring against you the strongest of the nations, and they shall kill you, and you shall die in the destruction of the slain” (Ezek. 28).

Nebuchadnezzar, because he proudly boasted of his power, said: “Is this not Babylon, which I have built for myself as a royal house [variant: ‘at last’] by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendour? While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: your kingdom shall pass from you, and I shall drive you out from among human beings; your dwelling shall be with the wild beasts, you shall eat grass like an ox, and seven periods shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of human beings and gives it to whomever he wills.’ That same hour the word was fulfilled concerning Nebuchadnezzar” (Dan. 4).

Therefore true is what is said in the Psalm: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48). Pride overthrew the tower and confused language (Gen. 11), struck down Goliath (1 Kings 17), hanged Haman (Esther 7), killed Nicanor (2 Macc. 15), destroyed Antiochus (1 Macc. 9), drowned Pharaoh (Exod. 14), killed Sennacherib (4 Kings 19), and cut off Holofernes’ head (Judith 13). “God has destroyed the seats of proud rulers and dried up the roots of proud nations” (Ecclus. 19).

## Chapter XXXIII. On the abomination of pride

[Col. 0730C]

How detestable pride is, the Lord himself testifies through the prophet, saying: “I detest the pride of Jacob” (Amos 6).—“And the Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: ‘If I forget all their works unto the end’” (Amos 8). Therefore, among the six things that the Lord hates and the seventh which his soul detests, Solomon puts first “haughty eyes” (Prov. 6), that is, pride. And Isaiah says: “The day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every proud and lofty person, and upon every arrogant person; and the height of men shall be humbled; upon all the tall and erect cedars of Lebanon, upon all the oaks of Bashan, upon all high mountains and all elevated hills, upon every [Col. 0730D] lofty tower and every fortified wall; and the loftiness of human beings shall be bowed down and the height of men humbled” (Isa. 2).—“Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit, and its lofty and glorious ones shall descend into it” (Isa. 5).—“The Lord of hosts has planned this, to bring down the pride of all its glory” (Isa. 23). Job likewise says: “Though his pride ascend to heaven and his head touch the clouds, he shall perish at last like dung” (Job 20).

## Chapter XXXIV. Against the arrogance of the proud

Almost every vicious person loves one like himself; but the proud person hates one who is exalted. Thus Solomon says: “Among the proud there are always quarrels” (Prov. 13), and “where pride is, there also is reproach” (Prov. 5). The proud man longs for novelty and disdains familiar things. He considers it a great thing if he deigns to speak, a greatest thing if he rises and embraces someone. He values the dignity granted by him more than he values the person made dignified; he never wishes to employ paternal affection, but always to employ the authority of dominion. “His pride, his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength.”

The passage from the Gospel comes back to mind: “A dispute arose among the disciples of the Lord Jesus as to which of them appeared to be greater. And Jesus said: ‘The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority among them are called benefactors; but you are not to be so. Rather, the greater among you shall be as the younger, and he who [Col. 0731B] precedes as one who serves’” (Luke 22). And as Peter, chief of the apostles, says: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but being made from the heart an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5).—“The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23). Therefore one is God and one is Lord. All others are not lords but servants: dominion is forbidden them, and service enjoined upon them. Hear the Wise Man on this: “They have made you ruler: do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32).

## Chapter XXXV. An example against the deceit of the ambitious

The sons of Zebedee, who through their mother’s intervention sought honour from Christ—“Say,” she said, “that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom”—deserved to hear: “You do not know what you ask.” For one reaches the kingdom not through honour but through burden. Hence the Lord adds: “It is not mine to give to you”; as though to say: It is indeed mine to give, but not to you—that is, to ambitious persons such as you are (Matt. 20). Although authority is from God, the proud person nevertheless does not reign from God, according to that prophetic saying: “They have reigned, and not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8).

## Chapter XXXVI. On the characteristics of arrogant persons

The proud man “loves the first seats in synagogues, [Col. 0731D] the first places at banquets, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people” (Matt. 23). He wishes to be addressed not by a personal name but by a title of rank; he wishes to be honoured not as a human being but as a lord. He sits high, walks loftily, wants everyone to rise for him and each person to bow.

Now a certain philosopher, wishing to mock the arrogance of a king, saw him sitting high upon his royal throne. He threw himself on the ground and worshipped him as a suppliant; then immediately, without invitation, he went up and sat beside the king. The king was greatly astonished, and, since he knew him to be a philosopher, asked why he had done this. The philosopher replied: [Col. 0732A] “Either you are God or a man: if God, I ought to worship you; if a man, I may properly sit beside you.” But the king turned the reply against the philosopher: “Indeed, if I am a man, you ought not to have worshipped me; if I am God, you ought not to have sat beside me.” The one answered wisely, but the other evaded him shrewdly.

## Chapter XXXVII. On superfluous adornment
God made for our first parents garments of skin [otherwise, loincloths] after their sin (Gen. 3), and Christ says to Christians: “Do not possess two tunics” (Matt. 10). But according to John’s counsel: “Let him who has two tunics give one to him who has none” (Luke 3). Yet the proud man, that he may seem magnificent, is eager [Col. 0732B] to be clothed in double garments, dressed in soft fabrics, and adorned with costly things. But what is a person adorned with precious things except a tomb whitewashed outside but full of filth within? (Matt. 23). Hyacinth and purple, scarlet and fine linen, rot in mud; gold and silver, stones and gems, become foul in mire. Dignity and power lie ill in the dust; honor and glory sit ill in ashes. Why, then, do you proudly broaden your phylacteries and make your fringes splendid? That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen was buried in hell (Luke 16). Dinah, daughter of the patriarch Jacob, before she went out—as Josephus says [Note: [Col. 0731D] Josephus, *Antiquities*, chap. 28.]—to buy the adornment of local women (Gen. 34), remained a virgin. But when she went out, Shechem, son of King Hamor, violated her by force. Holofernes, [Col. 0732C] who sat upon a couch woven of purple, fine linen, gold, emerald, and precious stones, was slain by Judith. She, though she had previously worn sackcloth, then put on pleasing adornment (Judith 13). Hear the Wise Man’s counsel on this matter: “Never glory in your clothing” (Ecclus. 2); and the Apostle: “Not in costly apparel” (1 Tim. 2); “nor let there be inwardly the arranging of hair, or the wearing around of gold, or the adornment of garments” (1 Pet. 3).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Against excessive adornment.

Consider what the Lord threatens through the prophet against excessive adornment: “Because the daughters of Zion have been haughty and have walked with [Col. 0732D] outstretched necks, going with glances of their eyes, the Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion and will lay bare their hair. On that day the Lord will take away the ornament of their footwear, the little moons, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, turbans, hair-bands, anklets, chains, perfume-vessels, earrings, rings, and jewels hanging upon the forehead; changes of garments, little cloaks, linen cloths, pins, mirrors, fine linen garments, headbands, and veils. And instead of a sweet fragrance there shall be stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; instead of a breast-band, sackcloth” (Isa. 3). Behold, a just punishment is rendered for the fault: that they are punished in the very thing in which they sinned.

[Col. 0733A] Hear yet another prophet concerning these matters: “O Tyre, variegated fine linen woven in Egypt was your sail; hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elishah became your clothing [otherwise, covering]. They exchanged ivory and ebony tusks at your price. Because of the multitude of your works, they displayed in your market a gem [the text reads *guttam*, perhaps *gemmam*], purple, embroidered cloths, fine linen, silk, and *chadchod* [Note: [Col. 0733] *Chadchod*, a Hebrew word for a certain precious stone.] . Dedan were your merchants in carpets for sitting; and you were exceedingly filled and glorified. But now you have been broken in the sea, and in the depths of the waters your riches have been reduced to nothing, and you shall be no more forever” (Ezek. 27).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How more deference is shown to clothes than to virtues.

[Col. 0733B] When a certain philosopher came to a prince’s court in contemptible clothing and, after knocking for a long time, was not admitted—indeed, whenever he attempted to enter, he was repelled—he changed his clothing and assumed finery. Then, at his first call, the entrance was opened to him. Going before the prince, he began reverently to kiss the cloak he wore. The prince, astonished, asked why he did this. The philosopher replied: “I honor that which honors me, because what virtue could not accomplish, clothing obtained.” O vanity of vanities: more honor is shown to clothes than to virtues, more to attractiveness than to integrity.

## CHAPTER XL. On the application of colors [otherwise, to the eyes].

An artificial appearance is laid on, and the natural face is covered over, [Col. 0733C] as though human workmanship surpassed the Creator’s art. Not so, not so. “Consider,” says the Lord, “the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor, neither do they spin; yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of them” (Matt. 6). Far be it that artificial color should be comparable with native color. Indeed, when the face is painted with counterfeit color, the mouth is corrupted by an abominable stench. “Every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38). For what is more vain than combing the hair, smoothing the locks, dyeing the cheeks, anointing the face, extending the eyebrows? Since “favor is deceitful and beauty is vain” (Prov. 31). “All flesh is grass, and all [Col. 0733D] its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40), because “it withers quickly like grass” (Ps. 36).

But I pass over personal adornment, lest I see some grow angry more maliciously than truthfully. What is more vain than adorning a table with painted tablecloths, ivory-decorated knives, golden and silver vessels, cups [otherwise, tubs] and napkins [otherwise, cloths], bowls and serving-dishes, little dishes and spoons, forks and salt-cellars, basins and little pitchers, caskets and fans? What benefit is there in painting ceilings, enriching poles, covering a vestibule with hangings, laying carpets beneath the feet, arranging a bed swollen with feathers, covered with silks, draped in curtains, or even with a canopy? For it is written [Col. 0734A]: “When a man dies, he shall not take all these things, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48).

## CHAPTER XLI. On the uncleanness of the heart.

There is no one who can glory in purity of heart, since “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3). “And if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Who can say with the Apostle: “I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4)? Who is this man, that we may praise him? Behold, “among the saints none is unchangeable; the heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job 15), and “in his angels he found perversity” [Col. 0734B] (Job 4). How much more abominable and useless is man, who drinks iniquity like water? (Job 15). “Therefore God repented that he had made man on the earth, because human wickedness was great upon the earth and every thought of the human heart was continually inclined to evil; and, touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, he destroyed the man whom he had created” (Gen. 6). Moreover, “iniquity has abounded, and the charity of many has grown cold” (Matt. 24). “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Pss. 13, 51).

Almost the entire life of mortals is full of sins committed by mortals, so that scarcely can one be found who does not turn aside to the left, who does not return to his vomit, who does not rot in dung. [Col. 0734C] Indeed, rather, “they glory when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2), “filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, avarice, malice; full of envy, murders, contention, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insulting, proud, exalted, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy” (Rom. 1). With such people, and worse, this world is filled: it abounds in heretics and schismatics, faithless persons and tyrants, simoniacs and hypocrites, ambitious persons and the greedy, plunderers and robbers, violent men and extortioners, usurers and counterfeiters, impious persons and sacrilegious men, traitors and liars, flatterers and deceivers, garrulous [Col. 0734D] and crafty men, gluttons and drunkards, adulterers and incestuous persons, effeminate and unclean persons, slothful and negligent men, vain and prodigal people, impetuous and angry men, impatient and inconstant people, poisoners and diviners, perjurers and accursed persons, presumptuous and arrogant people, unbelieving and despairing persons—finally, entangled in every vice. Moreover, “as smoke fails away, so shall they fail; and as wax melts before fire, so sinners shall perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67).

## CHAPTER XLII. On the pains which the wicked suffer in death.

The wicked suffer four pains in death. The first pain is bodily anguish, so [Col. 0735A] great and so severe as neither was nor is found in the present life before that dissolution. This is evident in some, though not all, who tear themselves apart because of excessive pain. For violent is the force—strong and incomparable—when those bonds and vital knots between body and soul are broken. Hence the Prophet laments: “The pains of death surrounded me” (Ps. 114). There is no limb, no joint in the body that is not altogether enveloped by that inexpressible pain.

The second pain is when, the body now almost exhausted and its strength spent, the soul then sees much more freely, in an instant, all the good or evil deeds that it has done; all are brought back before its inward eyes. This pain is so great, [Col. 0735B] and this review [otherwise, recollection] so severe, that the soul, greatly troubled, is compelled almost to hate itself. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Torrents of iniquity troubled me” (Ps. 17). For torrents come with great force and seem to overthrow [otherwise, destroy] everything; so at death the wicked person will suddenly see every good or evil work he has done.

The third pain is when the soul begins to judge itself so justly that, for each of its iniquities, it sees all the punishments due in Gehenna threatening it. Hence the Psalm says: “The pains of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me” (Ps. 17).

[Col. 0735C] The fourth pain is when the soul, still placed in the body, sees evil spirits ready to seize it. There is then such pain and fear that the wretched soul, though about to leave the body, flees back as long as it can, in order to purchase time from its captivity before it leaves the body. For this reason Zephaniah the prophet says (chap. 1): “From the first gate a cry goes forth, and from the second a howling.” The first gate is said to be when an evil soul, as soon as it leaves the body, is as soon seized by evil spirits for eternal punishments. The second gate is said to be when, after the day of judgment, the wicked will be punished in body and soul [Col. 0736A] without end. For in the first separation of body and soul the wicked are punished in the soul alone; after judgment, however, they will be punished in soul and body. Hence it is said: “Break them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Christ’s coming at the day of each person’s death.

Both the good and the wicked, before the soul departs from the body, see Christ set upon the cross. The wicked see him to their confusion, that they may be ashamed that, through their own fault, they were not redeemed by Christ’s blood. Hence it is said of the wicked in the Gospel: “They saw him whom they pierced” (John 19). This is understood both of Christ’s coming at the Judgment and of his coming on the day of each person’s death. [Col. 0736B] The good, however, see him for rejoicing. We have this from the Apostle’s words: “Until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. 6), that is, until the day of death, when [otherwise, because] Christ set upon the cross appears to both good and wicked alike. Christ himself says of John the Evangelist: “Thus I will that he remain until I come” (John 21), namely, until I come at his death.

For four comings of Christ are read of: two visible and two invisible. The first visible coming was in the flesh, when he was born of the Virgin. The other visible coming is at the Judgment, when he will judge good and wicked, when he will place the sheep at the right and the goats at the left. The first invisible coming occurs in the mind [Col. 0736C] of the righteous through grace; hence Christ says of the righteous person: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). Thus the soul of the righteous is God’s seat and dwelling, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is God’s seat,” because God sits in it through grace. The second invisible coming is at the death of each faithful person. Hence John in the Apocalypse, desiring to be freed from the prison of the body and to come to Christ, says: “Come, Lord Jesus” (Rev. 22), namely, at my death; hence it is said that on the day of his death Christ comes to meet him.

# BOOK THREE. On the misery of the human condition.

[Col. 0735]

## CHAPTER I. On the rottenness of corpses.

[Col. 0735D]

“His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145). O how many and how great are mortals’ thoughts amid the uncertainty of worldly provision; yet at the point of sudden death, all that they have thought suddenly vanishes. “They were taken away like a declining shadow, and shaken out like locusts” (Ps. 108). Therefore his spirit shall go forth, not willingly [Col. 0736D] but unwillingly, because with pain he will leave what he possessed with love. Whether he wills it or not, a limit is appointed for him which cannot be passed (Job 14), in which earth will return to earth. For it is written: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). It is natural that what is made of matter should be dissolved into matter. “You shall take away their spirit and they shall fail, and they shall return to their dust” (Ps. 103). “When a man dies, he shall inherit beasts, serpents, and worms” (Ecclus. 19). [Col. 0737A] “For all shall sleep in the dust, and worms shall cover them” (Job 21). “As a garment, the worm shall eat them; and as wool, the moth shall devour them” (Isa. 51). “He shall be consumed as rottenness, and as a garment eaten by the moth” (Job 13). “I said to rottenness,” says Job, “You are my father; and to worms, my mother and my sister” (Job 17). “Man is rottenness, and the son of man” (Job 25). How foul a father, how base a mother, how abominable a sister!

For a human being is conceived from blood decayed through the heat of lust, and funeral-like worms will at last attend the corpse of that same lust. Alive, he generated lice and maggots; dead, he will generate worms and flies. Alive, he produced dung and vomit; dead, he will produce [Col. 0737B] decay and stench. Alive, he fattened one human being; dead, he will fatten many worms. What, then, is more fetid than a human corpse? What more horrible than a dead person? He whose embrace was most delightful in life will be burdensome even to behold in death. What, then, do riches profit? What feasts? What delights? What honors? Riches will not free one from death; feasts will not protect from death, nor pleasures from the worm; honors will not rescue one from stench. He who just now sat glorious upon a throne now lies despised in a tomb; he who just now shone adorned in a hall now lies foul and naked in a grave; he who just now fed on delicacies in a banquet chamber is now consumed by worms in the sepulcher.

## CHAPTER II. On the sorrowful remembrance of the damned.

[Col. 0737C]

“The vengeance of the flesh of the ungodly is worm and fire” (Ecclus. 7). Each is twofold, inward and outward: inward, which gnaws and burns the heart; outward, which gnaws and burns the body. “Their worm,” he says, “shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66). “The Lord will give fire and worms into their flesh, that they may burn and feel them forever” (Judith 16). The worm of conscience will tear them in three ways: memory will afflict them, late repentance will trouble them [otherwise, punishment will embitter them], and anguish will torment them. For they will come, trembling, into remembrance of their sins, and their iniquities will arraign them face to face, saying: “What did pride profit us? And what did the boasting of riches [Col. 0737D] contribute to us? All these things passed away like a shadow, and like a ship that passes over the troubled water, whose track, after it has passed, cannot be found” (Wis. 4). Thus we too, having been born, immediately cease to be; certainly we can show no mark of virtue, but we have been consumed in our wickedness. With great turmoil they will recall what they did with excessive pleasure, so that the goad of memory may sting for punishment those whom the prick of wickedness spurred to guilt.

## CHAPTER III. On the useless repentance of the damned.

Saying within themselves in repentance, they will say: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine for us” (Wis. 5). “Then they will begin to say to the mountains: [Col. 0738A] Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us” (Luke 23). They will repent unto punishment, but will not turn unto pardon. For it is just that those who would not do so when they were able should not be able when they wish to do so. The Lord gave a place for repentance, and they misused it. Therefore the rich man who was tormented in the flame said to Abraham: “I beg you, father, send Lazarus to my father’s house. For I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments.” When Abraham had answered him, “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them,” he added: “No, father Abraham; but if someone from the dead goes to them, they will repent” (Luke 16). He too was repenting in hell; but because he knew that repentance to be useless, he begged that this be announced to [Col. 0738B] his brothers, so that they might practice repentance fruitful in this age. For repentance benefits a person when that person is still able to sin.

## CHAPTER IV. On the diverse punishments of hell.

The punishments of hell are diverse according to diverse sins. The first punishment is fire; the second is cold [otherwise, frost]. Of these the Lord said: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13): weeping because of the smoke of fire, gnashing of teeth because of cold. The third will be stench. Of these three it is said in the Psalm: “Fire, sulphur, and a blast of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10). The fourth is unceasing worms, whence Isaiah: “Their worm shall not die, and [Col. 0738C] their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66). The fifth is striking hammers, whence Solomon says: “Condemnations are prepared for blasphemers [otherwise, mockers], and hammers striking the bodies of fools” (Prov. 10). The sixth is palpable darkness, outward and inward, whence Job: “A land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death, etc.” (Job 10); and elsewhere: “I shall go to a dark land covered by death’s gloom” (ibid.). And in the Psalm: “They shall never see light” (Ps. 48); elsewhere: “The wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2). The seventh is the shame of sinners: “Then, as is read in Daniel, the books shall be opened” (Dan. 7), that is, people’s consciences shall be manifest to all. The eighth is the horrible sight of demons, who will be seen amid [Col. 0738D] the scattering of sparks rising from the fire. The ninth is fiery chains, by which the ungodly will be bound in every limb.

The first punishment belongs to the lustful; the second to the malicious; the third to the luxurious; the fourth to the envious and those who bear hatred; the fifth to those who did not deserve to be chastised by scourges in this age because “they tempted and provoked the Lord” (Ps. 77) by the multitude of their iniquities. Hence it is written: “The sinner provoked the Lord; according to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek him” (Ps. 10). The sixth belongs to those who, walking in darkness, despised to come to the true light, namely Christ; the seventh to those who confess their sins and despise repentance; the eighth to those who in this [Col. 0739A] age gladly see evil and do it; the ninth to those who have poured themselves out through each individual vice, who walk in their desires and follow their lusts.

## CHAPTER V. On the ineffable anguish of the damned.

“They shall be troubled at a horrible fear, groaning because of anguish of spirit, and saying: These are those whom once we held in derision and made a likeness of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. Behold how they have been numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints” (Wis. 5). It will be a punishment of the wicked to behold the glory of the blessed, perhaps indeed after the end of Judgment. The blessed likewise will see the reprobate [Col. 0739B] in torments, according to the words: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the ungodly” (Ps. 57). But the reprobate will not see the blessed in glory, according to the words: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). Such things sinners will say in hell, because “the hope of the ungodly is like down carried away by the wind, like thin foam scattered by a storm, like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the remembrance of a guest of one day” (Wis. 5).

## CHAPTER VI. On the fire of Gehenna.

The fire of Gehenna is fed neither by wood nor kindled by breath, but was created by God inextinguishable from the beginning of the world. For it is written: “A fire that is not kindled shall devour him” (Job 20). It is believed [Col. 0739C] to be beneath the earth, according to Isaiah’s words: “Hell beneath was troubled to meet your coming” (Isa. 14). But every place is punitive for the reprobate: they always bear their torment with them and everywhere encounter punishment against themselves. “I will bring forth,” he says, “fire from your midst, which shall consume you” (Ezek. 28). The fire of Gehenna will always burn and never give light; always scorch and never consume; always afflict and never fail. For among the infernal regions there is the utmost obscurity of darkness, immeasurable bitterness of punishments, and infinite eternity of miseries. “Having bound his feet and hands,” he says, “cast him into the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22).

[Col. 0739D] Individual limbs will undergo their own punishments for their own sins, so that they may be punished in that in which they sinned. For it is written: “By the things through which a person sins, by these he shall also be tormented” (Wis. 11). Thus the one who had sinned with the tongue was tortured in the tongue. Therefore he himself cried: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16). By fingers is understood activity, for we work with our fingers. It is as though he said: If I had the least of Lazarus’s works, I would feel a lesser punishment.

## CHAPTER VII. On the darkness of hell.

The reprobate will be enveloped not only by outward but also by [Col. 0740A] inward darkness, because they will lack both spiritual and bodily light. For it is written: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26), who alone will then be “in everlasting light” (Isa. 60). The reprobate will endure such anguish in their punishments that they will scarcely be able to think of anything besides the punishments; rather, they will direct the force of their thoughts wherever they feel the power of pain.

Indeed, a certain disciple is reported to have appeared after death to his teacher. When the teacher understood that he was damned, he asked him whether any questions were debated in hell. He is said to have replied: “In hell the sole question is what is not punishment.” Solomon also says: “There is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in hell, whither you hasten” [Col. 0740B] (Eccl. 9). For there will be in the reprobate such forgetfulness of mind, such blindness of soul, such confusion of reason, that they will rarely or never be able to rise to think anything about God, much less to aspire to make confession. For “from the dead, as from one who is not, confession has perished” (Ecclus. 7). It is written: “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell” (Ps. 113). “Hell shall not confess you, nor shall death praise you” (Isa. 38).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the disorder of punishments.

“Let me alone, Lord,” says Job, “that I may weep a little for my pain before I go to [Col. 0740C] the dark land covered with death’s gloom: a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10). There will indeed be order in the quantity of punishments, because “with the measure with which they have measured, it shall be measured back to them” (Luke 6), so that those who sinned more grievously may be punished more grievously. “For the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6). But there is no order in the kinds of things, because they will pass from snowy waters to excessive heat [otherwise, fire] (Job 1), so that the sudden change of contraries may bring more severe torment. I have learned by experience that if someone who has been burned immediately applies something cold, he feels a more burning torment.

## CHAPTER IX. On the unfailing nature of torments.

[Col. 0740D]

“Like sheep they are placed in hell, and death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48). This is said by comparison with animals which do not pull up grasses by the roots, but pluck only their tops, so that the grass may grow again for food. Thus the ungodly, as though fed upon by death, will revive for death, in order to die eternally. Ovid:

> Thus the ever-renewing liver of Tityus, though never consumed,  
> does not perish, so that it may often perish.  
> (*Pont.* I.2.41)

Then death will be immortal; then the dead will live, who are dead to life. They will seek death and not find it, because they had life and lost it. Hear John saying in the Apocalypse (chap. 9): “In [Col. 0741A] those days people shall seek death and shall not find it; they shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them.” O death, how sweet you would be to those for whom you were so bitter! Those who most vehemently abhorred you alone will longingly desire you alone.

## CHAPTER X. Why the reprobate will never be freed from punishments.

Therefore let no one flatter himself and say: “God will not be angry to the end, nor will he be indignant forever” (Ps. 102), but “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144), because when he is angry he will not forget to have mercy, nor has God hated anything that he made (Wis. 2)—taking as an argument for error what the Lord says through Isaiah the prophet: “They shall be gathered in the gathering [Col. 0741B] of one bundle into the pit, and shall be shut up in prison, and after many days they shall be visited” (Isa. 24). For a person sinned for a time; therefore God will not punish forever.

O empty hope, O false presumption! Let no one, deceived by vain error, believe that he can be redeemed at any price, since in hell there is no redemption. Sinners, therefore, shall be gathered into the pit and shut up in prison, namely in hell, where they will be tormented without bodies until the day of Judgment; and after many days—namely, after they rise with their bodies on the last day—they shall be visited, not for salvation but for vengeance, because after the day of Judgment they shall be punished more severely. Thus elsewhere it is said: “I will visit [Col. 0741C] their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88).

God is angry with the predestined only temporarily, because “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12); of them the saying is understood: “He will not be angry to the end,” etc. (Ps. 102). But God is angry with the reprobate eternally, because it is just that God should avenge in his eternity what the wicked person transgresses in his own eternity. For although the capacity to sin leaves him, he nevertheless does not abandon the will to sin. For it is written: “The pride of those who hate you rises forever” (Ps. 73). The reprobate, already despairing of pardon, will not be humbled; rather, the malice of hatred will grow so greatly in them that they will wish him altogether not to exist, through whom they know themselves to exist so unhappily. They will curse the Most High and blaspheme the Exalted One, complaining that he is cruel, who creates them for punishment and is never inclined to pardon. Hear John saying in the Apocalypse (chap. 16): “Great hail came down from heaven upon people, and people blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it was made exceedingly great.” Therefore the will of the damned, although it has lost the effect of power, will always retain the disposition of malice; and in hell this will itself will be punishment which in the world had been sin—although perhaps there too it is sin, but not meriting punishment. Therefore, because the ungodly person will always have within himself guilt arising from fault, he will always feel [Col. 0741D] against [otherwise, concerning] himself torment arising from punishment, because what he did not erase by repentance God will not remit by pardon. It belongs, then, to great justice in judging that those who never wished in life to be without sin should never be without punishment in Gehenna. They would indeed have wished, had they been able, to live without end; they so wish who never cease to sin while they live.

## CHAPTER XI. Testimonies concerning eternal punishments.

[Col. 0742A]

“Who,” says Isaiah, “among you can dwell with everlasting burnings?” (Isa. 33). “These shall be smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day and night; it shall not be extinguished, but its smoke rises forever” (Isa. 65). Jeremiah likewise says: “I will give you over to everlasting reproach and eternal disgrace, which shall never be erased by forgetfulness” [Col. 0742B] (Jer. 23). Daniel says: “Those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, others to reproach, that they may see forever” (Dan. 12). Solomon also says: “When an ungodly person dies, there shall be no hope for him” (Prov. 11). His destruction shall come, and he shall suddenly be broken and shall have no further remedy. And John the Apostle says: “If anyone worships the beast and its image, he shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath and shall be tormented with fire and sulphur; and the smoke of their torments shall rise unto ages of ages, and whoever worships the beast and its image shall have no rest by day or night” (Rev. 14). Truth itself confirms these things, when at the Judgment it will judicially reject the damned [Col. 0742C] [otherwise, those to be damned], saying: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). If, according to divine judgment, “every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19), how much more shall the proposed truth be established by the mouth of so many and such great men.

## CHAPTER XII. On the day of Judgment.

“Behold, therefore, the day of the Lord shall come, cruel and full of indignation, wrath, and fury, to make the earth a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of heaven and their splendor shall not spread their light; the sun has been darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not shine in its light. I will visit evils upon the world and their iniquity upon the ungodly. I will bring the pride of unbelievers to rest, and I will humble the arrogance of the mighty. Therefore all hands shall be weakened, and every human heart shall waste away and be crushed. Pangs and pains shall seize them; they shall suffer pain like women in labor; each shall be astonished at his neighbor; their faces shall be burned countenances” (Isa. 13). [Col. 0742D] “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and sounding, because the Lord shall make a swift end of all who inhabit the earth” (Zeph. 1). “And that day shall come suddenly like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole [Col. 0743A] earth” (Luke 21). For “as lightning goes out from the east and appears even to the west, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24). “For the day of the Lord shall come like a thief in the night. And when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, as pain upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the tribulation preceding Judgment.

“But a great tribulation shall precede, such as has never been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24). “For nation shall rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there shall be great earthquakes in places, pestilences, [Col. 0743B] famines, terrors from heaven, and great signs. And there shall be signs in the sun, moon, and stars; and on the earth distress of nations through bewilderment at the roaring of the sea and waves, people withering through fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world” (Luke 21). “For false Christs and false prophets shall arise and perform great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24). “Then the man of sin shall be revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God; whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2).

Moreover [Col. 0743C] “Elijah the prophet shall be sent before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he shall turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the heart of children to their parents” (Mal. 4). Enoch also will come with him, and “they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth. And when they have completed their testimony, the beast that rises from the abyss shall make war against them, conquer them, and kill them; and their bodies shall lie in the streets of the great city which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. And after three and a half days the spirit of life shall enter into them” (Rev. 1).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the signs preceding Judgment.

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days [Col. 0743D] the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken; and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn over themselves” (Matt. 24).—“The kings of the earth and princes, and commanders and rich men, and the mighty, and every slave and free person, will hide themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains; and they will say to the mountains and rocks: Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come. And who shall be able to stand?” (Rev. 6).—“And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds and from the heights of heaven to their ends” (Matt. 24). Then “the Lord himself, at the command and [Col. 0744A] voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven” (1 Thess. 4). And “all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and the good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but the evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5).—“Death and hell will give up their dead who are in them” (Rev. 20).—“Behold, he comes in the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (Rev. 1); “and then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power, great authority, and majesty” (Luke 21).

The Lord will come to judgment not only with angels and apostles, but also with the senators of his people. Thus Solomon says: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. 31). For they too will sit [Col. 0744B] “upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).—“I watched,” Daniel says, “until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down. His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels like burning fire. A swift river of fire went forth from before him. Thousands upon thousands ministered to him, and ten times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7). Hence the Psalmist also says: “Our God will come openly; our God will not be silent. Fire will burn in his presence, and a mighty tempest around him” (Ps. 46 [citation as printed: LXLVI]).—“Cloud and darkness are around him; righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne” (Ps. 49).—“And [Col. 0744C] he summoned heaven above and earth, that he might judge his people” (Ps. 49). For “all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; and he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER XV. On the power, wisdom, and justice of the Judge

O how great then will be the fear and trembling, how great the weeping and groaning! For if “the pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod” (Job 26), and “the angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isa. 33), what will sinners do? “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4). Therefore the Prophet cries: “Do not enter into judgment [Col. 0744D] with your servant, O Lord, because no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142).—“For if you should observe iniquities, O Lord, who could endure?” (Ps. 120).

For who would not fear a Judge most powerful, most wise, and most just? Most powerful, whom no one can escape; most wise, from whom no one can hide; most just, whom no one can corrupt. “If strength is sought, he is most mighty; wise in heart and strong in power. If equity of judgment is sought, no one would dare give testimony for me; if I wished to justify myself, my own mouth would condemn me; if I showed myself innocent, it would prove me perverse, even if I were blameless” (Job 9).—“He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148). He calls the stars, and they say, [Col. 0745A] “Here we are” (Baruch 3).—“He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. 103); whose “will nothing at all resists” (Rom. 9);—for whom “no word is impossible” (Luke 1); before whom “every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bends” (Phil. 2).

Therefore no one can flee him, as the Prophet says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138). He searches the reins and hearts (Jer. 17), before whose “eyes all things are naked and exposed” (Heb. 4), and who “numbers the drops of rain and the sand of the sea” (Ecclus. 1). He is the Lord, the God of knowledge, foreknowing all things and knowing each individual thing, the hidden investigator of every hidden matter. Therefore no one can hide from him, as the Apostle says: [Col. 0745B] “There is no creature invisible in his sight” (Heb. 4). He is the righteous Judge, strong and patient (Ps. 7), who turns aside from the path of uprightness neither through prayer, nor payment, nor love, nor hatred; but, always proceeding on the royal road, passes over no evil unpunished and leaves no good unrewarded. [Note: [Col. 0745C] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book V.] Therefore no one can corrupt him, as the Psalm says: “You will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the divine judgment

Who, then, would not fear that examination in which one and the same person will be accuser, advocate, and judge? He will accuse when he says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me [Col. 0745C] food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink.” He will act as advocate when he adds: “Inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these least ones of mine, you did not do it to me either.” He will judge when he declares: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

Witnesses will not be needed in that judgment, because then “the hidden things of darkness” will be made manifest (1 Cor. 4).—“For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10). Then the books of consciences will be opened (Dan. 7), and the dead will be judged from the things written in the books according to their works: “for their works follow them” (Rev. 14). How great will be the shame of sinners! How great the confusion when their most abominable crimes will be plain and manifest to all! “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Isa. 58 [citation as printed]). From that sentence there can never be an appeal [variant: a revocation or appeal]. For “the Father gave all judgment to his Son” (John 22 [citation as printed]).—“He shuts and no one opens; he opens and no one shuts” (Rev. 3).—“For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 58).

## CHAPTER XVII. That nothing will benefit the condemned

Then wealth will not benefit them, honours will not defend them, and friends will not aid them. For it is written: “Their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath” (Ezek. 7). “All the kings of the earth will weep and mourn when they see [Col. 0746B] the smoke of their burning, because of fear of their torments” (Rev. 18). What, then, will you do on the day of the Lord’s wrath, on the day of visitation and calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee? “Each person will bear his own burden” (Gal. 6).—“The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18).

O how harsh and exacting is that judgment, in which an account must be rendered not only of deeds but also “of every idle word which people have spoken, on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12); in which “the debt, with interest, will be exacted to the last farthing” (Matt. 18).—“Who, then, will be able to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3).—“Then the Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom [Col. 0746C] all scandals and those who commit iniquity, and bind them in bundles to be burned, and cast them into the furnace of burning fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13): groaning and wailing [variant: lamentation], mourning and torment, gnashing and crying, fear and trembling, pain and toil, heat and stench, darkness and anguish, bitterness and harshness, calamity and destitution, distress and sorrow, oblivion and confusion, writhings and stings, bitterness and terrors, hunger and thirst, cold and scorching heat, sulphur and burning fire for ages of ages. May God, who is blessed for ages of ages, deliver us from these. Amen.

[Col. 0745]

# LITTLE TREATISE ON ALMSGIVING OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

(From the edition of the works of Innocent III, Cologne, 1575, folio, p. 198.)

## CHAPTER ONE. “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11)

[Col. 0745D]

No one could commend almsgiving more worthily than Truth itself has commended it, which declares that all things are cleansed through almsgiving. Thus the name fittingly accords with its effect and with the interpretation of truth. For *eleemosyna* (“almsgiving”) is said to derive from *elimino*, “I remove,” or from *eli*, which is [Col. 0747A] “God,” and *moys*, which is “water”; because through almsgiving God removes the stains of sins and washes away the filth of vices. Almsgiving, indeed, is the relieving of one in need with an eye to mercy; and Sacred Scripture shows how great its fruit is. For almsgiving cleanses; almsgiving delivers; almsgiving redeems; almsgiving protects; almsgiving intercedes; almsgiving obtains; almsgiving perfects; almsgiving blesses; almsgiving justifies; almsgiving raises again; almsgiving saves.

Hear examples of each in order, and attend in an orderly manner to each example, so that you may obtain the fruit of almsgiving. “Give alms,” says the Lord, “and behold, all things are clean for you.” Behold how almsgiving cleanses. The angel Raphael said to Tobias: [Col. 0747B] “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good, better than storing up treasures of gold; for almsgiving delivers from death. It is that which purges sins and causes one to find eternal life” (Tob. 12). Behold how almsgiving delivers. Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar: “May my counsel please you, O king: redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercies shown to the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offences” (Dan. 4).

But Tobias, because while travelling “throughout all his kindred he distributed from his possessions to each according to his ability, fed the hungry, gave clothing to the naked, and diligently provided burial for the dead,” when the king ordered him killed, “fled naked and lay concealed, because many loved him” [Col. 0747C] (Tob. 1). Behold how almsgiving protects. “Hide almsgiving,” it says, “in the bosom of the poor man, and it will pray for you” (Ecclus. 29); because “water extinguishes blazing fire, and almsgiving resists sins” (Ecclus. 3). Behold how almsgiving intercedes.

“Cornelius the centurion, a devout man who feared God, gave many alms to the people and prayed to God continually. In a vision he clearly saw an angel of God saying to him: Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God” (Acts 10). Behold how almsgiving obtains. The Lord likewise says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have great treasure in heaven” [Col. 0747D] (Matt. 19). Behold how almsgiving perfects.

“The third year,” says the Lord, “you shall set apart another tenth of all that is produced for you at that time and store it within your gates. And the Levite, who has no other possession with you, and the stranger, orphan, and widow within your gates, will come and eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you do” (Deut. 14). Behold how almsgiving blesses. “He scattered abroad, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever; his horn will be exalted in glory” (Ps. 111). Behold how almsgiving justifies.

When Tabitha, who was full of good works and alms, had died, “all the widows stood around Peter weeping and showing him the tunics [Col. 0748A] and garments that she made for them. He knelt and prayed, and said: Tabitha, arise. But she opened her eyes and, seeing Peter, sat up” (Acts 9). Behold how almsgiving raises again. “Zacchaeus, standing, said to the Lord: Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold. Jesus said to him: Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke 19). Behold how almsgiving saves.

## CHAPTER II. The effects of almsgiving demonstrated in many ways by testimonies from Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0748B]

There are also many other effects of almsgiving, which you may learn from the testimonies set forth below. Why then do you anxiously seek, why do you uneasily investigate, what deed will earn you eternal life? At the judgment the Lord commended works of mercy, for which he himself will grant the merciful an eternal kingdom. “Come,” he says, “blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in; naked and you clothed me; sick and you visited me; in prison and you came to me. Amen, I say to you: inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me” (Matt. 25).—“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5); for “with the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you” [Col. 0748C] (Matt. 7).

That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly each day, because he did not pity the beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate covered with sores, longing to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything, died and was buried in hell. Therefore, when after death he himself begged for mercy—“Father Abraham,” he said, “have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame”—he could not obtain mercy, because before death he had refused to show mercy. Therefore Abraham replied to him: [Col. 0748D] “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, whereas you are tormented. And in all these things a great chasm has been established between us and you” (Luke 16).

That servant who would not have mercy on his fellow servant, as his master had had mercy on him, was handed over to torturers until he should repay the entire debt (Matt. 18). Likewise, to the rich man who planned to enlarge his barns and gather abundant produce there, the Lord says: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” (Luke 12). So it is with one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. Therefore the Lord commanded: “Sell what you possess and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure [Col. 0749A] in heaven” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

He gave the same command in the Law: “If one of your brethren who dwell within the gates of your city, in the land that the Lord your God will give you, falls into poverty, you shall not harden your heart or close your hand, but shall open it to the poor person” (Deut. 15). Likewise: “There will not be lacking poor people in the land where you live. Therefore I command you to open your hand to your needy and poor brother who lives with you in the land” (ibid.). For according to the testimony of the apostle John: “Whoever has the goods of this world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his compassion against him—how [Col. 0749B] does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3).

Mindful and observant of this command was blessed Job, who said: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame, a father to the poor and a comforter of the sorrowful” (Job 29).—“Have I denied the poor what they wanted, or made the eyes of the widow wait? Have I eaten my morsel alone, without the orphan eating from it? For compassion grew up with me from my infancy, and it came with me from my mother’s womb. Have I despised a passerby because he lacked clothing, or a poor person without a covering? Have not his sides blessed me because he was warmed by the fleece of my sheep?” and so forth (Job 31).

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Break [Col. 0749C] your bread for the hungry, and bring needy wanderers into your house. When you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58). You have heard the command concerning merit; hear the promise concerning reward. “Then your light will break forth like morning, and your salvation will rise before you; your righteousness will go before your face, and the glory of the Lord will gather you. Then you will call, and the Lord will hear; you will cry, and he will say: Behold, I am here. Likewise, when you pour out your soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, your light will rise in darkness, and your darkness will be like noon; and the Lord your God will always give you rest,” and so forth (ibid.).

The widow of Zarephath is commended because she fed Elijah. From that day the jar of flour did not fail, and the vessel of oil was not diminished, until [Col. 0749D] the day when the Lord gave rain upon the earth (3 Kings 17). Obadiah is commended, who hid and fed one hundred prophets, fifty by fifty. Therefore, delivered from fire, he deserved to be granted the spirit of prophecy (1 Kings 18 [citation as printed]). Hospitality is commended in Abraham and Lot, who received even angels as guests (Gen. 18). It is commended in Mary and Martha, who made a supper for Jesus six days before Passover (John 12). It is commended in the two disciples going to Emmaus, who recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread (Luke 24). The apostle Paul made collections among the Gentiles in order to send them to the saints at Jerusalem (1 Cor. 16).

Observe that the Lord made the rich not so much for the poor as the poor for the rich, because the poor person benefits the rich more [Col. 0750A] than the rich person benefits the poor. For the rich person gives the poor a temporal alms, but the poor person returns to the rich an eternal reward. Hence Solomon says: “One who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him in return” (Prov. 19). And another wise man likewise says: “A man’s almsgiving is like a purse with him, and it will preserve a person’s favour as the pupil of the eye; afterward it will rise and repay them their recompense, returning it upon each one’s head; it will fight upon the shield of might and upon the spear against your enemy” (Ecclus. 17).

Observe also that, in other matters, what is loved more dearly is kept more carefully; but the one who loves almsgiving more gives it more generously. Such is the debt of love: the more it is paid, [Col. 0750B] the more it is owed. Moreover, when you give alms on earth, you lay them up in heaven; and when you bestow alms upon another, you preserve them for yourself. Thus through almsgiving you give aid to another in such a way that you acquire merit for yourself; you help another in such a way that you advance your own good.

You will carry nothing at all of all temporal possessions with you from this life except almsgiving alone, which you send ahead to heaven through the hands of the poor. For, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 6), “we brought nothing into this world; without doubt, neither can we take anything away.”—“Naked,” says another, “I came forth from my mother’s womb; naked I shall return there” (Job 1). But when you distribute to the poor, you lay up treasure in heaven, as Truth testifies when it says: “Lay up [Col. 0750C] treasures for yourselves in heaven, where thieves neither dig through nor steal, and where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6).

What, then, is more welcome or more precious than almsgiving, which does not abandon its giver when all else abandons the one who keeps it? In the recipient it extinguishes thirst, drives away hunger, and covers nakedness. But in the giver it extinguishes guilt, drives away blame, and covers sin. O how worthy a recompense: that because almsgiving covers another person’s bodily nakedness, it may cover your own mental iniquity. “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31).

## CHAPTER III. Almsgiving performed in sin does not avail for merit or attain its effect, yet is preparatory for obtaining God’s grace

[Col. 0750D]

But if almsgiving is of such power—or rather, if such is the power of almsgiving—let people then do whatever they please, provided only that they persist in almsgiving, secure in the truth which says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 2 [citation as printed]). Are all things, then, clean for people who give alms while drunkards, adulterers, murderers, and persons entangled in every other kind of filthy vice? May they therefore freely practise their vile acts and pursue their pleasures, if almsgiving suffices to redeem sins, if it suffices to cleanse offences? Absolutely not, because Scripture testifies: “Whatever an unclean person touches will be unclean” (Lev. 15).

For when the Wise Man had first said, “Do not despise prayer and almsgiving,” [Col. 0751A] he immediately added: “Do not say, ‘God will look upon the multitude of my gifts, and when I offer to God Most High, he will receive my offerings’” (Ecclus. 7). For givers are not pleasing because of their gifts; rather, gifts are pleasing because of their givers. Hence it is written that “God looked upon Abel and his gifts” (Gen. 4). He first said, “upon Abel,” and afterwards, “upon his gifts,” because God attends more to the manner in the deed than to the deed in the manner—that is, to how something is done rather than to what is in any manner done.

Consider carefully what the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (Rom. 13 [citation as printed]). Therefore true almsgiving proceeds from true love. For this is the command of love: “You shall love [Col. 0751B] your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22). To this belongs the saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7). Therefore, just as we wish others to help us in our necessities, so we ought to help others in theirs, so that we may love our neighbours as ourselves.

Unless the branch of almsgiving springs from the root of love, it has neither richness nor moisture by which to produce sweet and ripe fruit. For true almsgiving is the fruit of love. “But love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 6 [citation as printed]). Truth says of it: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7). Almsgiving which proceeds from love, therefore, cleanses from vices and redeems from sins.

But perhaps you object that Cornelius the centurion did not yet possess faith in the Mediator, without which he could not be righteous, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1); nor could he “have love without faith, since without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 2 [citation as printed])—that is, faith in Jesus Christ, Mediator of God and humankind. For those going before and those following cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 18 [citation as printed]). Yet Cornelius, through almsgiving, deserved to come both to the sacrament of faith and to faith in the sacrament, as the angel told him: “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God” (Acts 10). Therefore he commanded him to summon Simon Peter, [Col. 0751D] who, when he came at the Spirit’s command, instructed and baptized him (ibid.).

Furthermore, since Nebuchadnezzar was wicked, Daniel would have given him counsel in vain to redeem his sins by almsgiving unless he could through almsgiving be delivered from his iniquities (Dan. 4). Likewise, since, according to the testimony of the angel Raphael, almsgiving is of such efficacy (Job 12 [citation as printed]) that it delivers from death and purges sins, this cannot be understood of temporal death, since all of us without exception are bound by the necessity of dying, from the time when the first man incurred the punishment of that threat: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2). For “God did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all” (Rom. 8), undoubtedly to death, because “he became obedient for us unto death, even death [Col. 0752A] on a cross” (Phil. 2).

It remains, therefore, that the angelic saying should be understood of eternal death: either the death of guilt, which comes first as its cause, or the death of Gehenna, which follows as its punishment. Thus almsgiving delivers a person from the death of the soul, provided it is understood in any sound sense whatsoever. But it does not deliver from that death which is not owed to the soul, since that would not be a matter of great power or strong efficacy. It therefore delivers a person from the death owed to the soul. Now death of the soul is owed only to the wicked, who are entangled in mortal sins. Such persons, therefore, are delivered from the death of the soul through almsgiving.

From these perplexing difficulties you may be delivered by the distinction that, just as certain things are preparatory to sin, so certain things are preparatory to [Col. 0752B] grace. For in a righteous person a malignant suggestion comes first, and a wrongful delight follows. Although it is not yet mortal but venial, it nevertheless weakens the mind and prepares it for consent; when consent arrives, it makes the person sin mortally, since consent itself is a mortal sin. In these matters we are daily renewed according to the spirit, matters which once occurred literally in the first human being. The serpent—that is, concupiscence—makes the original suggestion. The woman—that is, delight—eats venially. The man—that is, reason—consents mortally.

Likewise, in an ungodly person certain preparations for grace come first; they soften the mind as fire softens wax (Ps. 67), so that it may receive the image of the seal—that is, the likeness [Col. 0752C] of God—through the impression of grace that comes upon it. Hence it is written: “Meanwhile, do whatever good you can, that God may enlighten your heart unto repentance.” For such servile fear—although it may be said of it that “there is no fear in love, but perfect love casts fear out” (1 John 4)—is nevertheless itself said to expel sin: the fear of the Lord expels sin, and one without fear cannot be justified. Since, therefore, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Ecclus. 1), it is certainly preparatory to grace; and it introduces love beforehand, as a thread leads the yarn [*cetam*, uncertain reading], as is said through the prophet: “From your fear we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26).

Thus almsgiving given apart from love, or rather before love, does indeed profit, [Col. 0752D] although it does not suffice: it is preparatory, though not meritorious, for grace or salvation; nevertheless, through it one comes to grace and salvation. For it renders a person capable, suitable, and fit—like one thirsting, panting, or drawing near to the fountain of saving grace—through which one is delivered from death, cleansed from guilt, and redeemed from sin.

## CHAPTER IV. That almsgiving is better than fasting and prayer, and that no one is excused from it

Fasting is good, but almsgiving is better, because what fasting takes away, almsgiving gives. Otherwise, what fasting removes from pleasure, it restores to greed. But one who gives alms spends entirely on another whatever he takes away from himself. Through fasting [Col. 0753A] one’s own flesh is afflicted; through almsgiving another’s is refreshed. The former supplies hunger; the latter provides satisfaction.

Again, prayer is good, but giving is better, because almsgiving does both: descending to one’s neighbour and ascending to God. Hear on this the saying of the Wise Man: “Shut up almsgiving,” he says, “in the heart of the poor, and it will pray to the Lord for you” (Ecclus. 29). For one does not cease praying who does not cease doing good, since it is better to pray by deed than by speech.

But you will say: “I am poor, needy, and destitute” (Rev. 3); I have no bread, no clothing, no means by which I can give anything away. Yet observe that, before God, good will suffices where fitting means are lacking. He attends not so much to the amount [Col. 0753B] of the gift as to devotion in the deed; he weighs more from how much than how much. For Jesus, looking on, saw rich people casting their gifts into the treasury. But he saw a certain poor widow casting in two small coins, and said: “Amen, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all. For all these gave gifts to God from their abundance; but she, from what she lacked, cast in all the livelihood that she had” (Mark 12).

Elsewhere the Lord says: “Whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, amen, I say to you, shall not lose his reward” (Matt. 10). Thus Tobias says: “According to your means, be merciful. If you have much, give abundantly; if little, strive gladly to share even that little. For you lay up a good reward for yourself in the day of necessity. For almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death, and will not permit the soul to go into darkness. Almsgiving will be a great confidence before God for all who practise it” [Col. 0753C] (Tob. 4). Poverty, therefore, must not excuse itself, because it is enough that the will be rich where resources are poor.

## CHAPTER V. What should be the order, measure, cause, and end of giving alms

It remains now for you to consider diligently four matters concerning almsgiving: namely, its cause and end, its measure and order. Its cause: that it be done from love; its end: that it be done for the sake of blessedness; its measure: that it be done cheerfully; its order: that it be done according to rule.

Almsgiving must indeed be given from love, for love stands to almsgiving as a tree does to its fruit. “For a good tree cannot bear bad fruits, nor can a bad tree bear good fruits” (Matt. 7). Therefore the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore let no one vainly deceive himself into thinking that almsgiving without love can suffice for salvation. Though almsgiving distributed apart from love can avail for three things: for capacity to receive grace, for mitigation of eternal punishment, or for obtaining some [Col. 0754A] temporal good.

When, therefore, anyone gives alms, he ought to give them for eternal blessedness, not for worldly favour or human recompense. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself, as hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, so that they may be honoured by people. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6).

This is not contrary to what the Lord says elsewhere: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5). First, because [Col. 0754B] the intention can remain hidden while the action is open: so that, because of the hidden intention, the left hand does not know what the right hand does; and, because of the open action, those seeing the good works may glorify the Father. Second, because no one ought to do a good work in order that he himself may be glorified by people, but that people may glorify God. Hence the first is forbidden and the second commanded.

Again elsewhere Truth says: “When you give a luncheon or a supper, do not invite your friends, or your brothers, or your relatives, or wealthy neighbors, lest perhaps they in turn invite you back and you receive repayment” (Luke 14). Therefore elsewhere it is said: “Go, eat rich foods and drink sweet wine, and send a portion [Col. 0754C] to those who have prepared nothing for themselves” (2 Esdras 8).—“But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14). This is the end, this the reward, this the prize for which almsgiving must be done.

Moreover, almsgiving should be given not sadly, but cheerfully; not slowly, but promptly. As the Apostle teaches, saying: “Each one should give as he has resolved in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). And again: “He who presides, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (Rom. 12). For above all a good countenance should accompany it. Nor should you think contrary to this what a certain Wise Man says: [Col. 0754D] “Give what pains you.” For by this he meant to commend a magnificent gift, or rather to invite one to give magnificently. Do not lose all merit because of a sorrowful face; rather, by a cheerful expression obtain an acceptable reward. Bestow a blessing of deed when you can; but when you cannot, return a blessing of word. “Do not provoke the poor man, nor disturb him” (Ecclus. 4), mindful of what is written and commanded: “My son, do not add complaint to benefits, nor, in every gift, the sadness of an evil word. Does not dew cool the heat? So also a good word is better than a gift. Behold, is not a good word above a good gift? Yet both are with a justified man. A fool will reproach harshly, and the gift of an undisciplined man makes the eyes waste away” (Ecclus. 18).

Moreover, [Col. 0755A] he gives twice who gives quickly. Therefore do not delay to do good, because “hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13).—“Do not afflict the heart of the needy, and do not delay a gift to one in distress” (Ecclus. 4).—“Before death, do good to your friend; and according to your means stretch out your hand to the poor. Do not deprive yourself of a good day, and let no portion of a good gift pass you by. Remember that death will not delay. Therefore do good without delay while you can, because perhaps, when you wish to do good, you will be unable, and another will luxuriate in your goods” (Ecclus. 14). To this pertains what Jesus said to Judas according to John: “What you are doing, do quickly.” For some thought, because Judas had the purse, that Jesus had told him to give something to the needy (John 13). How indeed could they have thought this unless they had frequently [Col. 0755B] heard Jesus telling Judas to give promptly to the needy?
