Therefore do not defer the good you have conceived, for from morning to evening the weather changes, and the mind is carried off in different directions. Nor leave its execution to your heir, for he will scarcely repay you with praise, much less with reward. Besides, in giving alms observe an ordered rule.

For almsgiving is threefold: that of the heart, the mouth, and the deed. From the heart it is given through compassion; from the mouth through correction; from the deed through generosity. Of the first the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). For we greatly console the afflicted when we suffer with those who suffer and grieve with those who grieve. [Col. 0755C] Of the second Truth says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother” (Luke 17). You have helped one who errs not a little if, after correction, you have called him back to uprightness. Of the third the prophet says: “Break your bread for the hungry, and [bring in] the needy, etc.” (Isa. 58). You bring him into an earthly house, and he will bring you into the heavenly hall.

Yet this threefold almsgiving must be given in order: first to ourselves, then to our neighbors. For he is cruel and foolish who has compassion on another and no mercy upon himself; who chastises another and does not amend himself; who aids another and despises himself. On the contrary, it is commanded: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30).—“First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck from [Col. 0755D] your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7).—“When you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58). Therefore first show almsgiving to yourself by having mercy upon yourself. Correct yourself; aid yourself; for “he who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Ecclus. 14). Know, therefore, that you are culpably hard and harshly blameworthy if you mourn the bodily death of your friend and do not mourn the spiritual death of your own soul.

After yourself, give alms to your neighbors; and among them also keep order, preferring believers, members of your household, and relatives. Thus the Apostle says: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6). For this is required by ordered charity, of which the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar and ordered charity within me” (Cant. 2). [Col. 0756A] But among these the righteous should be preferred, if the remaining circumstances are equal. Perhaps, then, you will object that the Lord says: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6); for He excluded no one when He included all. Accordingly, elsewhere He says: “Love your enemies, do good, etc., and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (ibid.). Love with the heart, pray with the mouth, do good by deed, just as your heavenly Father “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5).

Since every person, good as well as evil, is our neighbor by reason of nature, and since by divine command we are bound to love our neighbors as ourselves, it certainly seems that we are bound, wherever possible, to assist every needy person; especially since [Col. 0756B] doing good to enemies appears to have greater merit than doing good to friends, according to the saying of Truth: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even tax collectors do this?” (ibid.). Likewise Tobit: “Give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person. Thus it will come about that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you” (Tob. 4).

On the other hand, Truth itself testifies: “Whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matt. 10). He does not say indefinitely, “whoever receives a person,” but specifically, “whoever receives a righteous man,” as elsewhere it is read: “Let your alms sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give” (Ecclus. 12). Hence elsewhere [Col. 0756C] Scripture says: “If you do good, know to whom you have done it, and there will be much grace in your good deeds. Do good to the righteous, and you will find great repayment; and if not from him, certainly from the Lord. For it does not go well with one who persists in evils and does not give alms; for the Most High hates sinners and has mercy on the penitent. Give to the merciful, and do not receive the sinner; render vengeance to the impious and sinners. Give to the good, and do not receive sinners. Do good to the humble, and do not give to the impious” (ibid.). Likewise Tobit: “Set your bread and wine upon the burial of a righteous man, and do not eat and drink from them with sinners” (Tob. 4).

Thus almsgiving would very often be delayed if one always had to distinguish between good and evil persons. [Col. 0756D] But why, in giving alms, should you not prefer the righteous person to the wicked, when by his merits and prayers he can obtain more for you from the Lord? Certainly good should be done to good and evil alike, to righteous and impious, to friends and enemies, when necessity requires and means permit; but in such cases the circumstances must be weighed, so that it can be discerned when, how, where, and to whom assistance ought rather to be given. For it may happen that at times a bad person ought to be helped more than a good one, if he is oppressed by greater need, especially when aid cannot be postponed without danger. And although doing good to enemies is of great merit, because then the mind most forcibly constrains itself for God’s sake—hence, “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize [Col. 0757A] it” (Matt. 11)—nevertheless, if parents are in need, I think they should rather be assisted, on account of that special commandment: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20). This is understood to have been promulgated not so much for rendering reverence as for providing support.

Although, therefore, good should generally be done to all neighbors, it should be done more abundantly to the good than to the bad, to the righteous than to the impious, unless some special exception, after weighing the circumstances as I have indicated, qualifies the general rule. But the saying, “Let your alms sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give” (Ecclus. 12), according to the context of the letter refers to paying tithes to a priest. Its sense is: “Until you find a righteous person to whom you may give,” [Col. 0757B] that is, a priest to whom you owe it. For a priest is bound to be righteous, besides being under command to do so, by reason of his office—although some manuscripts read *a righteous person*. The Jews, moreover, divided three tithes, which they also called alms; but this is not the place to discuss them.

What is elsewhere read, “Give to the merciful and do not receive a sinner,” and again, “Do good to the humble and do not give to the impious” (ibid.), must certainly be understood according to the rule: persons must be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved. Thus the sinner is forbidden to be received and the impious person forbidden to receive, namely lest through such reception or gift the impious person be encouraged in sin. Therefore such persons are not to be assisted insofar as their fault is fostered; [Col. 0757C] but they are to be assisted insofar as their nature is sustained.

Moreover, carefully observe that unless you give the alms of the heart, God does not accept the alms of deed, as He himself testifies: “If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your offences. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matt. 6). Thus He taught and commanded prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (ibid.). For this reason, in the same sermon He had commanded: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, when you return, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. 5). You see plainly [Col. 0757D] that God does not approve the gift of deed unless you first offer the gift of the heart.

You wisely bestow the alms of the heart when either you forgive one who has offended you, or make satisfaction to one you have offended, so that neither he retains resentment or hatred in his heart against you, nor you against him. Thus the statement, “because your brother has something against you,” may be understood in either sense: either that he has grounds for resentment or hatred against you because perhaps you have offended him, in which case you must make satisfaction to him, that you may be reconciled with him; or that he has committed an offence against you, because of which you are stirred to resentment or hatred against him, in which case you must forgive him, that you may reconcile him to yourself.

For resentment and hatred of heart you must wholly dismiss on account of the offence, [Col. 0758A] whether he asks forgiveness or not, whether he makes satisfaction or not, because by divine command you are bound to love an enemy. Hence the apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). The best almsgiving, therefore, is to pardon sinners, forgive debtors, and have mercy on the wretched. Of it Truth says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6).—“I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Matt. 9).—“For mercy exalts itself above judgment” (Jas. 2); and: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

It remains to say from what resources alms should be made. Clearly, from those things which you possess justly and have acquired reasonably, according to the saying of the Wise Man: [Col. 0758B] “Do not offer wicked gifts, for God will not receive them” (Ecclus. 35). Likewise: “He who offers a sacrifice from the plunder of the poor is as if he sacrificed a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclus. 34). Again: “You shall not offer in the house of the Lord your God the price of a dog or the wage of a prostitute” (Deut. 23). There are many such passages in Scripture, but these suffice, because “every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 17).

Yet the Lord seems to have taught the contrary in the Gospel: “Make for yourselves friends,” he says, “from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). Ecclesiasticus likewise reads: “Do not be greedy in unjust riches” (Ecclus. 5). But among [Col. 0758C] things acquired unjustly, some are such that ownership passes, and some such that it does not. From things in which ownership passes—for example, trade, military service, and the like—alms may lawfully be given; for, although you offended by acquiring them unlawfully, once they have become yours, you may nevertheless give from them as from your own goods. But from those things in which ownership does not pass, such as theft, robbery, sacrilege, and usury, it is not lawful to give alms; for since they belong to others, not to you, you are bound to restore them to those whose they are, not to dispose of them against their owners’ will.

Thus Zacchaeus properly distinguished: “Behold,” he says, “I give half my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). [Col. 0758D] What is said in the Gospel about the mammon of iniquity (Luke 16), and in Ecclesiasticus about unjust riches (chapter 14), applies to those unjust acquisitions in which ownership passes, from which alms may lawfully be given—although they may also soundly be understood in another way, but that interpretation does not pertain to the present little book. Refer the other authorities to those unjust acquisitions in which ownership does not pass. Although the schoolmen commonly dispute concerning a prostitute’s wage—which, if it is said to pass into the prostitute’s ownership (Deut. 23)—it must certainly be said that, by reason of its mystical significance, like the price of a dog, it is forbidden to be offered in the house of the Lord.

But because “not hearers of the law, but doers, are righteous before God” (Rom. 2), I ask, exhort, [Col. 0759A] entreat, and admonish you, brother—whoever you are, Christian—if you wish to be what you are called, to endeavor to do what you have heard. Hold it certain that almsgiving offered “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith” (1 Tim. 1) gives great confidence before the Most High, and itself is a healing remedy against every danger.

## CHAPTER VI. Perseverance is necessarily required for almsgiving, as for every good work.

Since neither almsgiving, nor fasting, nor prayer can please God or be meritorious for a person unto the blessed life without perseverance, a few words must therefore here be added concerning the virtue of perseverance. First, in the following authorities, everyone is admonished to perseverance. For [Col. 0759B] our Lord Jesus Christ says: “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10); and elsewhere: “If he perseveres in knocking until the end, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, nevertheless, because of his importunity, he will rise and give him as many as he needs” (Luke 11 [printed “II”]). The Apostle says: “All run in the race-course, but one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9); and “he who has contended lawfully shall be crowned” (2 Tim. 2). Elsewhere it is said that the Lord judges the ends of the earth (Ps. 9); and: “Where the tree falls, whether to the south or to the north, there it shall remain” (Eccl. 11). For the end, not the battle, crowns.

From this we must proceed thus: it is not great merely to begin good, [Col. 0759C] but to bring it to perfect completion. Many undertake great things but fail on the way; many leave Sodom but look back (Gen. 19); many depart Babylon but linger on the road and do not arrive at the eternal city of peace. Perseverance does not shrink from undertaking great things, nor does it weary of what it has begun. It steadies the wavering; it crowns the combatant; it leads to the prize and to the harbor; it gives form to the work and rule to the action. It is Joseph’s long robe, reaching to life’s end (Gen. 37); it is the priestly robe, reaching down to the feet (Exod. 28); it is the tail of the victim which we are bound to offer God (Lev. 3); it is the heel of good action which we must guard against the serpent’s bite (Gen. 3). It is the virtue that [Col. 0759D] pleads before God on behalf of prayer, that shapes every good vow; by it martyrs win their laurels, by it virgins receive their crowns. It brings difficult matters to ease and conquers every difficulty; it is the garment without wrinkle, the tunic without stain (Eph. 5); it makes good action of one color and virtue uniform.

It should be noted that there is, so to speak, one perseverance that is temporary and another that is final. Temporary perseverance flourishes for a time and blooms in a time of perversity; it is comparable to grass, which is now green and now thrown into the oven (Luke 12), now blooms, now is crushed, now consequently [Col. 0760A] dies (Jas. 1). “This flower comes forth and is crushed; it flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14). Final perseverance, however, is that which lasts to the end. It is a living fountain, a sealed garden (Cant. 4), in which no stranger shares, which always flows and always springs forth faithful labors, so that those in cloisters may possess it, virgins retain it, widows be shaped by it, and all rest in it.

The devil sometimes incites a person to good in order to draw a worse evil out of the good. Perseverance prevails against this assault of the devil, so that good beginnings may be closed with a good end. For to begin good things and conclude them with an evil end is to fashion monsters. That action is a chimera which has its beginning from reason but its end from sensuality. [Col. 0760B] For when this is done, “a painter paints a horse’s neck onto a human head, and so introduces varied and fruitless feathers.” [Note: [Col. 0759D] HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, verse 1.] Therefore beware, O man, lest your action produce monsters or bring forth portents. For the fruit of a living being is monstrous if its end does not correspond to its head. There are some whose life is a wondrous monster: their good beginning displays, as it were, a human head; then their middle descends into lust and displays a goat’s belly; finally, turning aside into rapacity, it shows a she-wolf’s feet. Ah, man! What does it profit you to begin well and not conclude with a good end? For you not only lose the good of virtue, but also incur loss and deserve punishment. It is better [Col. 0760C] not to know the way of truth than to turn back after knowing it (2 Pet. 2). After such inconstancy you are accused of fickleness, incur apostasy, and set aside steadiness of mind.

O man, through perseverance you redeem the shortness of life and permit no time to pass in vain. It belongs to a composed mind to be able to stand firm in good and remain in good. Nothing is so useful as to conclude a good work with a good end. Perseverance brings tender good to maturity; perseverance carries advanced good on to maturity. Perseverance does not seek a childish spirit but an adult one: it seeks mature character, not tender and unarmed dispositions.

If you wish to attain perseverance, accustom yourself always to good, so that habit, which is a second nature as it were, may produce perseverance in life, and fellowship with good people [Col. 0760D] may bring forth long-suffering. If perseverance does not adorn your whole life, at least let final perseverance close your end. If you have offered the flower of youth to the devil, at least sacrifice the dregs of old age to your God. At evening the day’s serenity is praised; at the end, the condition of a good work. See from how great a good Judas fell, because he did not persevere in good (Matt. 26); see what Solomon lost through inconstancy and instability of mind (3 Kings 11); into how great a calamity Saul fell (1 Kings 13). Against one who proposes good but does not bring it to completion stands that Gospel saying: “Behold, this man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14).

[Col. 0761A] How great the merit of perseverance is may be inferred from the heinousness of the opposite vice. For of impenitence it is said that the punishment of this sin is so great that it cannot submit itself to the humility of seeking forgiveness. This is the sin against the Holy Spirit; this is the sin unto death, of which John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone [Col. 0762A] should pray for it” (1 John 5). But impenitence is born of despair or arises from presumption; and, insofar as it lies in itself, it either detracts from God’s justice or diminishes God’s mercy. Blessed, therefore, is perseverance, which excludes impenitence, drives out obstinacy, eliminates contempt, and overcomes hardness of heart.

[Col. 0761]

## ENCOMIUM OF CHARITY, BY INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

(*Works of Innocent III*, ed. 1575, Cologne, folio.)

Charity makes almsgiving, like every good work and the other works of piety, pleasing to God and fruitful for humanity.

[Col. 0761B] As I am about to append here an encomium of charity at the end, I consider it worthwhile first to establish and commend it from Sacred Scripture. These are the authorities which set forth the form of charity: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole mind, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6; Matt. 22). Likewise John says: “God is charity; whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (John 14). Likewise Peter: “Above all, maintaining continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4). Likewise Paul: “Charity is patient, is kind, does not behave perversely” (1 Cor. 13). Likewise Solomon: “Hatred stirs up quarrels, and charity produces love” (Prov. 10). Likewise Augustine: “Whatever we do without charity profits us nothing; we expend foolish and empty effort if we do not have charity, which is God.” Likewise Gregory: “The more the heart of the sinner is burned by the fire of charity, the more abundantly the rust of sins is consumed.”

From these we must proceed thus: Who, endowed with Ciceronian eloquence, who furnished with every form of wisdom, is sufficient to express the praises of charity and set forth its virtues to the smallest detail? This is charity, which teaches us to flee enticements, trample pleasures, restrain the desires of the flesh, break unlawful desires, despise human things, and finally reject every allurement. Of it the Bridegroom says in the Song of Love: [Col. 0761D] “Set me as a seal upon your heart, for love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Cant. 3). For death extinguishes the living, but hell does not spare even the dead. Love, therefore, is strong as death: for as death destroys bodily sensation, so love punishes the inclination of fleshly desire. Jealousy is hard as hell, because it compels those whom the desire for eternal things draws inwardly [Col. 0762B] not only to reject pleasant things but also to endure adversities, in order to obtain what it loves.

This is the charity that made Abel a martyr and brought Abraham out of his land. This preserved Joseph in Egypt. This is the flame which quenched the flame for the three boys in the furnace (Gen. 4, 13, 41; Dan. 3). This is the greatest of all good things: nothing foreign, harsh, or confused tastes pleasant to it; it strengthens the other virtues by the protection of its perfection. Whoever is grafted into its root neither fails in greenness nor disappears from fruitfulness, because he does not effectively lose the work of fecundity. Of it Isidore says: “No reward is reckoned without the love of charity. Although one believes rightly, yet without charity he cannot attain blessedness, [Col. 0762C] because the power of charity is so great that even prophecy and martyrdom are believed to be nothing without it. Charity holds the primacy among all virtues. Hence it is called by the Apostle the bond of love, because all virtues are bound together by its bond. Love the Lord, therefore, so that you may choose; love better, that you may live healthfully. Love God, that you may choose to be with God; love better, that you may become one with him. Therefore through love love what you love, if you desire to arrive more safely, and hasten that you may lay hold of it. Thus through love you run; through love you lay hold. Again, the more you love, the more fully you embrace. Therefore through love look above to that from which love itself comes to you. [Col. 0762D] Love itself is the course, the arrival, the abiding, the blessedness. Love God, therefore; choose the Lord; run; lay hold; possess; enjoy. This is the most excellent, surpassing way, which straightens crooked paths and shows straight ones.”

This is charity, which prevailed so greatly over God that it brought him from the seat of supreme majesty to the weakness of our humanity; wounded [Col. 0763A] the impassible, bound the unconquerable, drew the immutable, and made the eternal mortal. If charity could do so much in God, how much should a human being be able to do in himself? If God endured so much for humanity, what will a human being refuse to endure for God? Be ashamed, O man, not to submit to charity, which subjected the Creator of the world to itself; do not be ashamed that charity has subjected clay to itself when it subjected even the potter.

It is not jealous; it does not behave perversely (1 Cor. 13). From the one in whom it dwells it uproots the root of vices. Charity is the origin of all virtues; it illuminates the human mind, cleanses the conscience, gladdens the soul, and shows God. The soul in which charity dwells is not puffed up by pride, ravaged by envy, tormented by anger, blinded by avarice, scattered by evil sorrow, [Col. 0763B] inflamed by gluttony, or defiled by lust. It is always clean, always tranquil, always chaste, always joyful, always peaceful, always kind, always modest; secure in adversity and not exalted in prosperity.

This is the spiritual cross which each person is bound to carry, so that by taking up this cross he may follow Christ’s footsteps. Its height is raised toward God; its breadth extends even to an enemy; its length reaches to life’s end; its depth savors the immeasurable divine goodness. This is the charity that is merit to the combatant and reward to the victor, [Col. 0764A] which is thus begun on the way and completed in the homeland. This is “fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). Charity brings forth, as it were, a created Trinity: in this Trinity, love of God is as the Father; from it proceeds the love by which a person loves himself, as offspring from a parent; and from both proceeds love of neighbor, as the Holy Spirit from both. These loves are one in the substance of charity, but distinct in their proper persons.

Beware, therefore, O man, if you wish to pursue love, lest you be deceived by love’s shadow. For there is a love of fortune, which comes with prosperity and departs in adversity. This is how the carnal person loves God: he praises God only when God has done him good. There is a love of nature, by which one sensually loves one’s own nature and God. [Col. 0764B] There is a love of grace, which alone has this: it loves God so that he may be possessed as reward. The first is deficient, the second productive, the third perfecting. The first belongs to charity, the second to sensuality, the third to reason. The first belongs to falsity, the second to the humble sinner, the third to the justified person. O man, consider how sweet is the love of God and how impure the love of this age. Love of God is the mother of all virtues; love of the world is the mother of all vices. In the latter love all things are imperfect; in the former all things are perfect.

[Col. 0763]

## SIX BOOKS OF INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF, ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE EVANGELICAL LAW AND THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST

(*Edition of the Works of Innocent III*, Cologne, 1575, folio.)

## ORDER OF MASS

[Col. 0763C]

**PRIEST.**—In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.—Amen.

I will go in to the altar of God.

**MINISTERS.**—To God, who gives joy to my youth.

**PRIEST.**—Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy people; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man.

[Col. 0764C]

**MINISTERS.**—For you, O God, are my strength. Why have you cast me off, and why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?

**PRIEST.**—Send forth your light and your truth: they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.

**MINISTERS.**—And I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth.

[Col. 0765A]

**PRIEST.**—I will praise you on the harp, O God, my God. Why are you sorrowful, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?

**MINISTERS.**—Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.

**PRIEST.**—Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

**MINISTERS.**—As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, unto ages of ages. Amen.

**PRIEST.**—I will go in to the altar of God.

**MINISTERS.**—To God, who gives joy to my youth.

**PRIEST.**—Our help is in the name of the Lord.

**MINISTERS.**—Who made heaven and earth.

[Col. 0765B]

**PRIEST.**—*(Bowing.)* I confess to almighty God, to blessed Mary ever-virgin, blessed Michael the archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the saints, and to you, brothers, that I have sinned exceedingly in thought, word, and deed *(he strikes his breast three times)*, through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. Therefore I pray blessed Mary ever-virgin, blessed Michael the archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the saints, and you, brothers, to pray for me to the Lord our God.

**MINISTERS.**—May almighty God have mercy upon you, and, having forgiven your sins, bring you to everlasting life.

[Col. 0765C]

**PRIEST.**—Amen. *(Then the ministers repeat the confession.)*

**PRIEST.**—May almighty God have mercy upon you, and, having forgiven your sins, bring you to everlasting life.

**MINISTERS.**—Amen.

**PRIEST.**—*(He signs himself with the sign of the cross.)* May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us pardon, absolution, and remission of our sins.

**MINISTERS.**—Amen.

**PRIEST.**—*(Bowing.)* O God, by turning toward us you will give us life.

**MINISTERS.**—And your people will rejoice in you.

[Col. 0765D]

**PRIEST.**—Show us your mercy, O Lord.

**MINISTERS.**—And grant us your salvation.

**PRIEST.**—O Lord, hear my prayer.

**MINISTERS.**—And let my cry come unto you.

**PRIEST.**—The Lord be with you.

**MINISTERS.**—And with your spirit.

**PRIEST.**—*(Ascending to the altar.)* Let us pray.—Take away from us, we beseech you, O Lord, our iniquities, that with pure minds we may be worthy to enter into the Holy of Holies.—Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

*(He kisses the middle of the altar.)*—We pray you, O Lord, by the merits of your saints, whose relics are here, [Col. 0766A] and of all the saints, that you may deign to forgive all my sins. Amen.

**INTROIT.**—He fed them with the fat of wheat, alleluia; and satisfied them with honey from the rock. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.—Psalm: Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.—Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. *(Alternately with the ministers, he says:)* Lord, have mercy. Lord, have mercy. Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy. Lord, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.

Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will. We praise you; we bless you; we adore you; we glorify you. We give you thanks for your great glory. Lord God, heavenly King, God the almighty Father. Lord, only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ; Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father. You who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. You who take away the sins of the world, receive our supplication. You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us. For you alone are holy; you alone are Lord; you alone are Most High, Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen.

**PRIEST.**—The Lord be with you *(turning toward the people).*

**MINISTERS.**—And with your spirit.

**PRIEST.**—Let us pray.—O God, who under a wondrous sacrament left us a memorial of your Passion, grant, we beseech you, that we may so venerate the sacred mysteries of your Body and Blood as continually to experience within ourselves the fruit of your redemption.—Through [Col. 0766C] Christ, etc.

A reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 11). Brothers, I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and, having given thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat: this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise also the cup, after supper, saying: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.” For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty [Col. 0766D] of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person test himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.

**MINISTERS.**—Thanks be to God.

SACERDOS. — From the rising of the sun even to its setting, great is my name among the nations. — And in every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name, because great is my name among the nations. — Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you.

(Bowed in the middle of the altar.) Cleanse my heart and my lips, almighty God, who cleansed the lips of the prophet Isaiah with a burning coal; so deign, in your [Col. 0767A] gracious mercy, to cleanse me, that I may worthily proclaim your holy Gospel. Through Christ. — The Lord be with you.

MINISTERS. — And with your spirit.

SACERDOS. — The continuation of the holy Gospel according to John. (Chapter VI.)

MINISTERS. — Glory to you, O Lord.

SACERDOS. — At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me shall himself live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven: not as your fathers ate manna and [Col. 0767B] died; he who eats this bread shall live for ever.

MINISTERS. — Praise to you, O Christ.

(The priest kisses the Gospel.) May our offences be blotted out through the words of the Gospel. (Then to the middle of the altar.)

I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made. Who for us human beings and for our salvation [Col. 0767C] came down from heaven. And was incarnate of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary: AND WAS MADE MAN. He was also crucified for us; under Pontius Pilate he suffered and was buried. And on the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures. And he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. And he shall come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom shall have no end. And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son; who together with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified; who spoke through the Prophets. And [I believe] in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church.

I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. And I await the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the age to come. Amen.

[Col. 0767D] The Lord be with you (turned towards the people).

MINISTERS. — And with your spirit.

SACERDOS. — Let us pray. — The priests of the Lord offer incense and bread to God; therefore they shall be holy to their God and shall not profane his name, alleluia.

(Offering the host upon the paten.) Receive, holy Father, almighty everlasting God, this spotless host, which I, your unworthy servant, offer to you, my living and true God, for my countless sins, offences, and negligences; and for all those standing around; and also for all faithful Christians, living and dead: that it may avail for my salvation and theirs unto everlasting life. Amen.

(He blesses the water.) O God, who wonderfully created the dignity of human [Col. 0768A] nature and more wonderfully restored it, grant that through the mystery of this water and wine we may be made sharers in the divinity of him who deigned to become a partaker of our humanity, Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with you, etc.

(Offering the chalice.) We offer you, Lord, the chalice of salvation, imploring your clemency, that in the sight of your divine majesty it may rise, with an odour of sweetness, for our salvation and that of the whole world. Amen.

In a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart may we be received by you, Lord; and so may our sacrifice be made today in your sight, that it may please you, O Lord God. Come, sanctifier, almighty everlasting [Col. 0768B] God, and bless this sacrifice prepared for your holy name.

(The priest washes his hands, saying:) I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will encompass your altar, O Lord,

That I may hear the voice of your praise and recount all your wonders.

O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.

Do not destroy my soul with the wicked, O God, nor my life with men of blood,

In whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is full of gifts.

But I have entered in my innocence: [Col. 0768C] redeem me and have mercy on me.

My foot has stood in the right way; in the assemblies I will bless you, O Lord.

Glory to the Father, etc.

(Bowed in the middle of the altar.) Receive, holy Trinity, this offering which we offer to you in memory of the passion, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ our Lord; and in honour of blessed Mary, ever Virgin; of blessed John the Baptist; of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; and of these saints, and of all your saints: that it may avail to their honour and to our salvation; and may they deign to intercede for us in heaven whose memory we keep on earth. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

[Col. 0768D] (Turned towards the people.) Pray, brethren, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable to God the almighty Father.

For through the mystery of the Word made flesh, a new light of your radiance has shone upon the eyes of our mind: so that, while we know God visibly, through him we may be drawn into love of things invisible. And therefore, with angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, and with all the host of the heavenly army, we sing the hymn of your glory, saying without end:

Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth.

[Col. 0769B] Heaven and earth are full of your glory.

CANON OF THE MASS.

Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly pray and ask you to accept and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices, which above all we offer to you for your holy catholic Church: deign to grant her peace, to guard, unite, and govern her throughout the whole world, together with your servant our Pope N., our bishop [Col. 0769C] N., and all orthodox believers and those who profess the catholic and apostolic faith.

COMMEMORATION FOR THE LIVING. — Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, N. N., and all those standing around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is recognized; for whom we offer to you, or who offer to you, this sacrifice of praise: for themselves and all who belong to them; for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and safety; and they render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.

WITHIN THE ACTION. — In communion with, and venerating the memory above all of, the glorious and ever Virgin Mary, mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs Peter and Paul, Andrew, James, John, [Col. 0769D] Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Thaddaeus, Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian, and all your saints: through whose merits and prayers grant that we may in all things be defended by the help of your protection. — Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen. — Therefore, Lord, we beseech you graciously to accept this offering of our service, and that of your whole household; order our days in your peace; command that we be delivered from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of your elect. — Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

Deign, O God, we beseech you, to make this offering in every respect blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, [Col. 0770A] and acceptable, that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands; and, raising his eyes to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat of this, all of you:

FOR THIS IS MY BODY.

In like manner, after supper, taking this noble chalice also into his holy and venerable hands, again giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink from it, all of you:

[Col. 0770B] FOR THIS IS THE CHALICE OF MY BLOOD, OF THE NEW AND ETERNAL COVENANT: THE MYSTERY OF FAITH: WHICH SHALL BE POURED OUT FOR YOU AND FOR MANY FOR THE REMISSION OF SINS.

As often as you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.

Wherefore, Lord, we your servants, and also your holy people, remembering the same Christ your Son, our Lord, his so blessed passion, and likewise his resurrection from the dead and his glorious ascension into heaven, offer to your supreme Majesty from your own gifts and grants a pure host, a holy host, a spotless host: the holy bread of eternal life and the chalice of everlasting salvation.

Upon which deign to look with a gracious and serene countenance and to accept them, as you deigned to accept [Col. 0770C] the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and the offering made to you by your high priest Melchizedek: a holy sacrifice, a spotless host.

(Profoundly bowed.) — We humbly beseech you, almighty God, command these offerings to be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your altar on high, in the sight of your divine Majesty, that all of us who, by participation at this altar, receive the most sacred body and blood of your Son, may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

COMMEMORATION FOR THE DEAD. — Remember also, Lord, your servants, men and women, N. N., [Col. 0770D] who have gone before us marked with the sign of faith and sleep the sleep of peace. To them, Lord, and to all who rest in Christ, we beseech you to grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

To us also, your sinful servants, who hope in the multitude of your mercies, deign to grant some share and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs: John, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia, and all your saints. Into their company, we beseech you, admit us, not as one weighing merit, but as the bountiful giver of pardon. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

[Col. 0771A] Through whom, Lord, you always create all these good things, sanctify, give life, bless, and grant them to us. Through him, and with him, and in him, is to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all honour and glory.

Through all ages of ages.

The beginning of the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0772D] MINISTERS. — Glory to you, O Lord.

SACERDOS. — In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him; and without him nothing that was made was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings. And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was a man sent from God whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light. The true light was that which enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who [Col. 0773A] received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name: who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God. AND THE WORD [Col. 0774A] WAS MADE FLESH, and dwelt among us. And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

MINISTERS. — Thanks be to God.

ON THE SACRED MYSTERY OF THE ALTAR. SIX BOOKS.

[Col. 0773]

PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0773B] There are three things in which the divine law chiefly consists: commandments, promises, and sacraments. In the commandments is merit; in the promises, reward; in the sacraments, assistance. For by the sacraments we are helped toward both ends: both to carry out the commandment and to obtain the promise. Yet among all sacraments, that is plainly the chief which is most sacredly celebrated in the office of the Mass upon the table of the altar. It represents that banquet of the Church at which the father kills the fatted calf for his returning son (Luke XV), setting forth the bread of life (John VI) and the wine which Wisdom has mixed (Prov. IX).

Christ himself instituted this office when he established a new covenant with his heirs, appointing for them a kingdom as his Father appointed one for him, so that [Col. 0773C] they might eat and drink at his table in his kingdom; and this is what the Church consecrated. For while they were at supper, Jesus took bread, and, giving thanks, blessed and broke it; and he gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me (Luke XXII; Matthew XXVI; Mark XIV).

Thus formed by this institution, the apostles began regularly to celebrate the most sacred mystery, preserving the form which Christ had expressed in words and retaining its material elements in acts, as the Apostle testifies to the Corinthians: “I,” he says, “received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, [Col. 0773D] broke it and said: Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be given for you” (I Cor. II).

Therefore blessed Peter the apostle is said to have been the first to celebrate Mass at Antioch, where only three prayers were said in the earliest beginning of the nascent Church. The other elements, however, are recorded as having been added at different times and by different persons, as, with the worship of the Christian religion increasing, they seemed more fittingly appropriate.

For this office is found to be arranged with such providence that it contains, for the most part, the things done through Christ and in Christ, from Christ’s descent from heaven until his ascension into heaven; and it represents them, both in words and signs, in a certain wondrous manner. The office itself [Col. 0774B] consists of four things: persons, actions, words, and material things. There are three ranks of persons: those celebrating, those ministering, and those standing around. There are three kinds of actions: gestures, acts, and movements. There are three varieties of words: prayers, chants, and readings. There are three classes of material things [variant: *maneries*]: ornaments, instruments, and elements.

All these are full of divine mysteries, and each overflows with heavenly sweetness, provided that they have an attentive observer who knows how to draw honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone (Deut. XXXII). But who knows the order of heaven and will establish its principles upon earth? (Job XXXVIII). The well is deep, and I have nothing with which to draw water (John IV), unless he who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them (James I) stretches forth [Col. 0774C] his hand, so that I may draw the water passing through the midst of the mountains (Ps. CIII) with joy from the fountains of the Saviour (Isa. XII). Knocking, then, I shall knock, if perhaps the key of David may deign to open (Apoc. III), so that the king may bring me into the wine-cellar (Song I), in which he may show me that heavenly pattern which was shown to Moses on the mountain (Exod. XXV), in order that, through his revelation, I may be able to expound the most sacred office of the altar—he who makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom X), whose Spirit blows where it wills, distributing to each as it wills (John III; I Cor. XII)—to the praise and glory of the Trinity, to the advancement and benefit of readers, and to pardon and forgiveness for [Col. 0774D] my sins.

Therefore, if anything worthy is found in this little work, let it be wholly ascribed to divine grace. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James I). If anything unworthy is found, let it be attributed to human insufficiency. For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wisdom IX). I have proposed, however, to follow the custom of the apostolic see—not that which it is read to have had formerly, but that which it is known to have now—which, by the Lord’s ordering, is mother and teacher of the other Churches.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0775]

CHAPTER ONE. On the six orders of clerics.

[Col. 0775A]

When the bishop of the apostolic see solemnly performs the rites of the Mass, he has with him six orders of clerics: bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, and singers, thereby showing through the sacrament of the number itself the perfection of this office. For the number six is perfect, because it is produced by the sum of its parts. Hence on the sixth day God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment (Gen. I); and when, in the fullness of time, the sixth age had come, on the sixth day likewise, at the sixth hour, he redeemed the human race (Gal. IV). We also read of six kinds of ministers in the Old Testament: high priests, priests, Levites, Nethinim, gatekeepers, and psalm-singers. Artaxerxes for the most part distinguished them in the letter which he sent to Ezra the scribe: “We make known,” he says, “concerning all priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, Nethinim, and ministers of the house of God, that no tax, tribute, or provision shall in any way be imposed upon them” (I Ezra VII).

CHAPTER II. On chief cantors and singers.

David, preeminent among the prophets, wishing to enlarge more solemnly the worship of God, established singers to sing before the ark of the covenant of the Lord with musical instruments and modulated voices. Among them the chief were Heman, Asaph, and Hethan. But Heman was first of all, and his role in the Church is now held by the chief cantor, who is set over the singers. Hence it is read in Chronicles: “These are those whom David set over the singers of the house of the Lord, standing in their order for the ministry: of the sons of Kohath, Heman the singer, son of Joel; and at his right Asaph, son of Berechiah; but at the left Ethan, son of Chushi” (I Chron. VI). Singers ought therefore to sing in harmonious voices and sweet melody, so that they may be able to stir the minds of their hearers to devotion to God.

CHAPTER III. On acolytes and what their ministry is.

Acolytes, who in Latin are called candle-bearers (*ceroferarii*), may take an example of their ministry from Aaron and his sons. For it is written in Exodus: “Command the sons of Aaron to offer most pure oil from olive trees, beaten in a mortar, so that a lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of testimony; and Aaron and his sons shall set it in place, so that it may shine before the Lord until morning” (Exod. XXVII). What the priests did then, acolytes now do in the ministry of lamps. Indeed, in the law of Moses we read that many things were added and changed, not only in the New but also in the Old Testament. Hence David is reported to have said in the book of Chronicles: “It shall no longer be the office of the Levites [Col. 0776A] to carry the tabernacle and all its vessels for ministry” (I Chron. XXIII). Acolytes carry lighted candles while the Gospel is read, not in order to illumine the darkness of the air, but to display to their neighbours works of light.

The Lord testifies that he holds this office when he says: “I am the light of the world. He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John VIII).

CHAPTER IV. On subdeacons.

Subdeacons represent in the Church the role of the Nethinim. Concerning them it is read in Ezra (I Ezra VIII) that David gave the Nethinim for the ministries of the Levites. Hence they are called in Greek *hypodiacones* [subdeacons], and from their order came that Nathanael whom the Lord commended in the Gospel: “Behold,” he says, “a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile” (John I). Nethinim means those serving the Lord in humility. Concerning them the fathers rightly decreed that those who handle the sacred mysteries ought to observe the law of continence, as it is written in the Prophet: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII).

The Lord deigned to exercise their office when, after supper with his disciples, he poured water into a basin, washed the disciples’ feet, and dried them with the linen cloth with which he was girded (John XIII).

CHAPTER V. On deacons.

The order of deacons took its beginning from the tribe of Levi. Hence the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Bring near [Col. 0776C] the tribe of Levi, and make them stand before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him and keep watch, and observe everything belonging to the worship of the multitude before the tabernacle of testimony, and guard the vessels of the tabernacle while serving in the ministry” (Num. III). From twenty-five years of age and above, they were commanded to serve in the tabernacle, as being of an age strong enough to bear burdens, so that they could carry the ark of the covenant, the table of the offering, and the vessels of the tabernacle. This is also recalled in the New Testament, when a stole is placed on the deacons’ left shoulder, and on fast-days the chasuble is folded over that same shoulder. For whatever labour we endure in this life, we carry as it were on the left, until we pass from the left [Col. 0776D] to the right, where we may have rest.

For this reason, too, the cardinal deacons carry the table of the Lateran altar upon their shoulders on Maundy Thursday and carry it back on Saturday: as Levites, they always carry the supreme pontiff as the ark of the covenant. In the New Testament, however, the order took its beginning from the apostles, who chose seven men of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit, as deacons, appointing them by the laying on of hands after prayer (Acts [Col. 0777A] VI). These are the seven angels sounding trumpets in the Apocalypse (chapter VIII); these are the seven golden lampstands; these are voices of thunder, who announce peace, preach the Gospel, prepare the table, offer the Eucharist, and so forth. Although these things are humble, they nevertheless belong pre-eminently to their ministry.

Christ exercised this office when, after supper, he distributed the consecrated sacraments with his own hands, and when he awakened the sleeping apostles to pray: “Watch,” he said, “and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII).

CHAPTER VI. On greater and lesser priests.

The institution of the priestly order took its origin from the old law, according to what we read that the Lord commanded Moses: “Bring near to you Aaron your brother with his sons from among the children of Israel, that they may exercise the priesthood for me” (Exod. XXVIII). Nevertheless, priests are read to have existed before the Law. Thus Melchizedek is read to have been priest of God Most High, and Abraham paid him tithes from all the spoils, as to a priest (Gen. XIV; Heb. VII). There were many lesser priests, who were commonly called Nazareans. But there was one high priest, whom they specifically [variant: imperially] called the *Arabarchus*. Moreover, David established twenty-four priests, sixteen from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar (I Chron. XXIV); yet he set one over all of them, whom he appointed chief of the priests. He assigned to each, by lot, the weeks of his respective turn; the eighth of these fell to Abijah, from whose stock Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, descended (Luke I). But in the New Testament Christ himself established greater and lesser priests: namely, the twelve apostles (Matt. X) and the seventy-two disciples, whom he sent two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was to come (Luke X). For just as Moses set high priests over peoples to govern them under the Law, but chose men of the next order and second rank to assist them in their fellowship and work—(for into Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s sons, he poured the abundance of his fatherly fullness, so that the ministry of priests might suffice for saving sacrifices and the sacraments of more frequent service; and in the wilderness he propagated Moses’ spirit among the minds of seventy prudent men, whom Moses employed among the people so that he might easily govern their innumerable multitudes [Num. IX])—so also Christ added disciples to his apostles, through whom they filled the whole world with their preaching. The greater priests, that is, bishops, therefore hold the place of the apostles; the lesser priests, that is, presbyters, hold that of the disciples.

CHAPTER VII. On the meaning of the names bishop and presbyter.

The name bishop conveys more burden than honour. *Episcopus* means “overseer” in Greek; in Latin he performs the office of a watchman, as the Lord says to the prophet: “Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel” (Ezek. III), so that he may not attend carelessly but provide diligently for the people committed to him. For this reason the Apostle says: “He who desires the episcopate desires a good work” (II Tim. III). He does not say “honour,” but “work,” because a bishop is chosen not so much to preside as to be of benefit. A presbyter, however, is named not from age but from prudence. For *presbyter* in Greek means “elder” in Latin. Old age is venerable not because it is long, nor because it is reckoned by the number of years; rather, a person’s understanding is gray hair, and an unstained life is the age of old age (Wisdom IV). For the Lord also says to Moses: “Gather to me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and teachers” (Num. II).

CHAPTER VIII. On the primacy of the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0778B] But Christ set one above all the apostles, namely Peter, to whom he entrusted the primacy of the whole Church before his Passion, at the time of his Passion, and after his Passion. Before the Passion, when he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and to you I shall give the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16). For although he said to all the apostles in common: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20), yet he granted principally to Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16). Peter can bind the others, but cannot be bound by the others. For to them it was said particularly: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them”; but to him it is said universally: “Whatever you bind,” and so forth.

[Col. 0778C] At the time of the Passion, moreover, when he had said concerning them all in the plural, “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat” (Luke 22), he nevertheless added, specifically concerning Peter: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail”; and immediately he added: “And when you have once turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22). It therefore belongs to Peter, as to a master, to strengthen the rest, since his faith failed in no temptation. For the faith of the Apostolic See, founded with stable firmness upon the solid rock, has never been capable of being stained by any filth of errors; but, remaining without

[Col. 0778D] wrinkle or blemish, it has, as times required, cleansed others of the blemishes of error.

After the Passion, when he had asked Peter three times, “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” and he had answered three times, “Lord, you know that I love you,” he commanded him a third time, “Feed my sheep”; and immediately added, “Follow me” (John 21). For Peter followed Christ not only in the manner of his martyrdom, but also in the rank of his teaching office. Christ showed this when he said: “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1). For although *Cephas* is interpreted in one language as “Peter,” in another it is explained as “head.” For as the head possesses the fullness of the senses, while the other members receive a share in that fullness, so the other priests are called to share in solicitude, but

[Col. 0779A] the supreme pontiff is assumed into the fullness of power.

Hence also, not without the sacrament of a great mystery, when Christ had questioned all the apostles, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter alone, as first and foremost, answered for all: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). And when all the apostles together were terrified by fear of danger, Peter alone went down fearlessly to walk upon the waves of the sea to the Lord (Matt. 14). And when many of the disciples had gone back, saying, “This saying is hard,” Jesus said to the twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?” Simon Peter answered him: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (John 6).

[Col. 0779B] And when Jesus had looked upon the disciples, he said to Simon Peter: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone,” and so forth. When Peter said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? As many as seven times?” Jesus replied: “I do not say to you, as many as seven times, but as many as seventy times seven” (Matt. 18). And when all the apostles took flight, Peter alone, drawing his sword, struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear (Luke 22). And after the Resurrection, while the other disciples came by boat to the Lord, Peter girded himself and cast himself into the sea, so that he might come to him through the waves (John 11 [apparently John 21]). Therefore Christ too, when he had risen from the dead, appeared first to Peter before the other apostles, because, according to the Apostle, he “was seen by Cephas, then by the eleven; thereafter he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once” (1 Cor. 15).

## CHAPTER IX. On the agreement and difference of powers between bishops and presbyters

But bishops and presbyters differ in this: it belongs to all priests in common to catechize, baptize, preach, consecrate, loose, and bind. But it pertains especially to pontiffs to ordain clerics, bless virgins, consecrate bishops, impose hands, dedicate basilicas, depose those to be degraded, hold synods, make chrism, and consecrate vestments and vessels.

[Col. 0779D] The hands of presbyters are anointed by the bishop so that they may recognize through this sacrament that they receive, through the Holy Spirit, the grace of consecrating. Hence, when the bishop anoints them, he says: “Deign, O Lord, to consecrate and sanctify these hands through this anointing and our blessing, so that whatever they consecrate may be consecrated, and whatever they bless may be blessed, in the name of the Lord.”

The hands of presbyters are also anointed so that they may exercise works of mercy, according to their ability, toward all. For hands signify works, and oil signifies mercy. Hence the Samaritan, approaching the wounded man, poured wine and oil upon him (Luke 10). Nevertheless, both the greater and the lesser priests jointly fulfill in certain respects the role of the supreme pontiff, that is,

[Col. 0780A] of Christ, while they pray for sins and reconcile sinners through penance. Hence the Apostle said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and he has placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5).

For priests are mediators between God and human beings: they convey God’s commands to the people by preaching, and present the people’s vows to God by supplication. Therefore priests ought to be such that they are pleasing to God and acceptable to human beings. For, as Pope Alexander says: “The worthier Christ’s priests are, the more readily are they heard in the needs of the people for whom they cry out.” And the Apostle says: “A mediator is not of one” (Gal. 3). For one who is not at peace with both parties through the bond of fellowship and friendship cannot reconcile those who are at discord. If someone who is himself unacceptable is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things.

[Col. 0780B] After the invocation of the Holy Spirit, they receive the stole over both shoulders, so that they may understand from this that they are armed with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor. 6), in order that they may be neither broken by adversities nor exalted by prosperities. Hence, when they receive the stole, the bishop says to them: “Receive the yoke of the Lord; for his yoke is sweet and his burden light” (Matt. 11). It is sweet in prosperity and light in adversity.

They likewise receive the chalice and paten from the hand of the pontiff, so that by these instruments

[Col. 0780C] they may recognize that they have received the power to offer propitiatory sacrifices. Hence, when the bishop gives them these things, he says: “Receive the power to offer sacrifice to God and to celebrate Mass, both for the living and for the dead, in the name of the Lord.”

The Lord Jesus Christ exercised the office of priest when, after supper, by divine power he changed bread and wine into his body and blood. “Take,” he said, “and eat: this is my body. Do this in remembrance of me” (Matt. 26). But he exercised this office more excellently when, for the sins of humankind, he offered himself upon the altar of the cross, himself both priest and victim.

## CHAPTER X. On the common and special vestments of pontiffs and priests

[Col. 0780D]

This commonality and special character of the powers of bishops and presbyters is denoted by the very number of the common and special vestments. There are six vestments common to bishops and presbyters: the amice, alb, girdle, stole, maniple, and chasuble. For there are likewise six matters in which the power of bishops and presbyters is shared: catechizing, baptizing, preaching, consecrating, loosing, and binding.

There are nine special ornaments of pontiffs: stockings, sandals, the cincture, tunic, dalmatic, mitre, gloves, ring,

[Col. 0781A] and staff. For there are nine functions in which the special power of bishops consists: ordaining clerics, blessing virgins, consecrating bishops, imposing hands, dedicating basilicas, deposing those to be degraded, holding synods, making chrism, and consecrating vestments and vessels.

The pallium, however, belongs properly to metropolitans, primates, and patriarchs, so that by it they may be distinguished from other bishops and possess a privileged dignity. Thus in both the New and the Old Testament it is established that pontiffs possess special vestments in addition to common ones. But there were four common and four special vestments there; here, however, there are six common and nine special. Mystical reasoning required this. For the former were given to carnal and worldly persons; the latter to spiritual and perfect persons.

[Col. 0781B] The number four is suited to flesh because of the four humors, and to the world because of the four elements. But six is suited to the perfect, because it is a perfect number, being equal to the sum of its parts. Hence on the sixth day God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment (Gen. 1). Nine is suited to spiritual persons because there are nine orders of angels, which, according to the prophet (Ezek. 28), are denoted by nine kinds of stones. Thus there are fifteen ornaments of the pontiff, signifying by their very number the fifteen degrees of virtues, which the Psalmist distinguished through the fifteen Songs of Ascents. For priestly vestments signify the virtues with which priests ought to be adorned, according to that prophetic saying:

[Col. 0781C] “May your priests be clothed with righteousness, and may your saints exult” (Ps. 131).

## CHAPTER XI. On the legal vestments according to the historical sense

There were four legal vestments common both to the lesser priests and to the chief of priests. The first was called *manathasim* in Hebrew, *perizōmata* (περιζώματα) in Greek, and may be called *femoralia*, “breeches,” in Latin; it was woven of twisted fine linen. The second was *cathemone*, which we call a linen garment or under-tunic, but which Moses called *abanec*. The Hebrews, however, after their departure from Babylon, called it *emissan*; it was of fine linen and double.

The third was the belt—that is, a girdle or cincture—about four fingers broad, woven in such a netlike way that it appeared like the skin

[Col. 0781D] of a viper, and made of fine linen, scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-blue. The fourth was the tiara, which the Hebrews call *manephei* and we call an *infula*; it differs greatly from the *cidaris*, that is, the pontifical mitre, and represents, as it were, the form of a rounded helmet (Exod. 28 throughout).

In addition to these, the pontiff used four distinctive vestments. The first was a hyacinth-blue tunic, which he called *nathir* in Hebrew, *podērēs* (ποδήρης) in Greek, and a “garment reaching to the ankles” in Latin. It had pomegranates for fringes, with eighty little golden bells arranged alternately, so that the sound might be heard when the pontiff entered the sanctuary, lest perhaps he die.

The second was the *ephod*, that is, the shoulder-piece, woven from the four aforementioned colors and gold,

[Col. 0782A] sleeveless and shaped like a short tunic, with a square opening on the breast, a palm’s breadth in size, into which was inserted the *logion* (λόγιον), of the same dimensions. In its upper part—that is, upon the shoulders—two onyx stones were fastened with gold; on them were engraved the twelve names of the sons of Israel, six upon one and six upon the other. The ephod with which Samuel and David are said to have been clothed was another, made of linen, and was properly called *ephobar*.

The third was called *heusen* in Hebrew, *logion* (λόγιον) in Greek, and *rationale* in Latin, “breastpiece,” which the pontiff wore on his breast. It was called the breastpiece of judgment because there was a stone in it by whose radiance they knew that God was favorable to them. The breastpiece was square and double, woven from the four aforesaid colors

[Col. 0782B] and gold, and had twelve stones in four rows. In the first were sard, topaz, and emerald; in the second, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; in the third, ligure, agate, and amethyst; in the fourth, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl. On these were written the twelve names of the sons of Israel, one on each stone. These two names were also written upon it: *purim* and *tymim*, that is, “truth” and “teaching.”

The *logion* was attached to the shoulder-piece at the upper part by two rings and two golden chains, inserted into two hooks fixed beneath the two aforementioned onyx stones in the shoulder-piece. At the lower part, however, the ephod was fastened by two golden rings with two joints or hyacinth-blue chains.

The final ornament of the head was the *cidaris*, that is, a mitre rising to a point, with a golden circlet bearing pomegranates and flowers.

[Col. 0782C] From it hung over the forehead a golden plate, called the *petalum*, in the form of a half-moon. On it was engraved: “Aioth [variant: Anoth] Adonai,” that is, “the holy name of the Lord”; the Tetragrammaton, that is, of four letters: Joth, He, Vau, Heth. But lest the plate move when the pontiff moved, it was fastened with a transparent hyacinth-blue ribbon or tie, whose ends hung down behind.

Our pontiff, therefore, has sandals in place of breeches, an alb in place of the linen garment, a girdle in place of the belt, a tunic in place of the ankle-length garment, an amice or stole in place of the ephod, a pallium in place of the *logion*, a mitre in place of the *cidaris*,

[Col. 0782D] and a cross in place of the plate. Some of these differ in form from the former, but are the same in figure.

## CHAPTER XII. On the symbolism of the legal vestments according to allegory

Adorned with these vestments, the pontiff represented the image of the entire world. The linen breeches fittingly represented the earth, because linen comes forth from the earth. The belt, with its bands and little vessels, denoted the encircling course of Ocean. The hyacinth-blue tunic represented the air by its very color. The bells signified the sound of thunder; the pomegranates represented flashes and bolts of lightning.

The four vestments of the lesser priest and the four of the supreme pontiff denoted by their number the four parts of the microcosm and the four parts of the macrocosm—that is, the four humors and the four elements.

[Col. 0783A] The ephod, by its variety, displayed the starry heaven. The gold woven into the colors signified that vital color penetrates all things [perhaps “the vital principle,” for *color*]. The two onyx stones denoted the sun and moon, or the two hemispheres; the twelve gems of the breastpiece represented the twelve signs of the zodiac. The breastpiece was in the middle because all things are full of reason, by which earthly things adhere to heavenly ones. Indeed, the ordering of earthly things, of the seasons, of heat and cold, and the twofold moderation between them, proceeds from the course and reason of heaven. By the rings, chains, and hooks are signified the connections of the elements, humors, and seasons. The *cidaris* signified

[Col. 0783B] the empyrean heaven; the plate placed above it signified God presiding over all things.

The authority of the Book of Wisdom confirms this allegory, saying: “Upon the long robe which he wore was the whole world; and the glorious deeds of the fathers were engraved in four rows of stones; and your majesty was written upon the diadem of his head” (Wis. 18).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the legal vestments according to tropology: on the breeches

The priest put on these legal vestments in this order (Exod. 29). Having first washed his hands and feet, he put on the *manathasim*, that is, the breeches, signifying that the priest, having cleansed his works and affections by the tears of repentance, ought to undertake continence,

[Col. 0783C] so that he may offer “a victim unspotted, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. 12). Our pontiff, however, because he ought to possess continual continence, does not put on breeches at the sacrifice, but sandals; as if it were said: “He who has washed needs only to wash his feet, and is wholly clean” (John 21 [apparently John 13]).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the linen garment

Second, he put on the *cathemone*, that is, the linen garment, signifying that the priest ought to put on innocence, so that he does not do to another what he does not wish done to himself (Matt. 7). For linen, because of its whiteness, signifies innocence, according to the saying: “At all times let your garments be white” (Eccl. 9).

## CHAPTER XV. On the girdle

[Col. 0783D]

Third, he girded himself with the belt, signifying chastity, because he ought to be girded about the loins in order to restrain concupiscence. Hence Truth says: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 11).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the tunic

Fourth, he put on the *tunica poderis*, that is, the ankle-length tunic, signifying that the pontiff ought to put on perseverance; because “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). For the heel, because it is the extremity, signifies perseverance, according to the saying: “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 1).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the pomegranates and golden bells

[Col. 0784A]

Pomegranates and golden bells hung as fringes. By the pomegranate is understood action; by the golden bell, preaching. These two must be joined in a priest, lest he die by entering the sanctuary without them. For Jesus “began to do and to teach” (Acts 1), leaving priests an example that they should follow the footsteps of him who “did no sin,” so that there may be uprightness in conduct; and “no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2), so that there may be truth in preaching.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the shoulder-piece

Fifth, he put on the ephod, that is, the shoulder-piece,

[Col. 0784B] signifying that the pontiff ought to put on patience, so that in patience he may possess his soul (Luke 21). For we bear burdens upon the shoulders, according to the saying: “He bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant under tribute” (Gen. 49).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the two edges

It had two edges joined at either side of the upper ends, signifying that the pontiff ought to possess the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor. 6), so that he may not be raised up by prosperity or cast down by adversity.

## CHAPTER XX. On the two onyx stones

[Col. 0784C] It also had two onyx stones set in the shoulders, on which were engraved the twelve names of the sons of Israel: six on one and six on the other. The two onyx stones signify truth and sincerity: truth by their brightness, sincerity by their solidity. The sons of Israel signify holy desires and just works, according to the saying: “Cursed is the man who does not leave seed in Israel” (Deut. 27). The number six signifies perfection, because God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment on the sixth day (Gen. 2).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the twelve names of the sons of Israel

That six names of the sons of Israel were engraved

[Col. 0784D] on one stone and six on the other signifies that a priest’s desires and works ought to be perfected “not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5), so that sincerity may shape the intention and truth the end.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the two chains

It also had two chains of purest gold, joined to one another, which were inserted into two hooks, signifying that the pontiff ought to possess two affections of charity, namely toward God and toward neighbor. Of these it is commanded: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind; and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6; Matt. 12). For as gold surpasses all metals,

[Col. 0785A] so charity surpasses all virtues. Of it the Apostle says: “The greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the two hooks

The two hooks are intention and end, into which the chains are inserted, so that he may love both God and neighbor: God for his own sake, and neighbor for God’s sake, “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the breastpiece
