Sixth, he put on the *logion* (λόγιον), that is, the breastpiece, signifying that the pontiff ought to put on discernment, by which he may distinguish light from darkness,

[Col. 0785B] the right from the left. For “there is no agreement of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial” (2 Cor. 6).

## CHAPTER XXV. On the squareness and doubleness of the breastpiece

The breastpiece was square, signifying that the pontiff ought to distinguish four things: truth from falsehood, lest he go astray in matters of belief; and good from evil, lest he go astray in matters of action. It was also double, because he ought to discern on behalf of two, namely himself and the people, lest, if a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into the pit (Matt. 15).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the four rows of stones

It also had four rows of stones, signifying that the pontiff ought to possess four principal

[Col. 0785C] virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the twelve stones

In each row it had three stones, signifying that in the first the pontiff ought to possess faith, hope, and charity; in the second, modesty, gentleness, and kindness; in the third, peace, mercy, and generosity; and in the fourth, vigilance, diligence, and long-suffering. For stones signify virtues, according to the saying: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work shall be made manifest” (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the *cidaris*

[Col. 0785D]

The supreme ornament of the head was the *cidaris* or tiara, which the pontiff put on last, signifying humility, concerning which the Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18). He wore it upon his head, signifying that the pontiff ought to bear humility in his mind, following the example of our head, who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). For the head signifies the mind, according to the saying: “Anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. 6).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the golden plate

From the *cidaris* hung over the forehead a golden plate, signifying

[Col. 0786A] wisdom, by which the pontiff ought to excel, according to the saying: “His head is finest gold” (Song 5).

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Tetragrammaton name of the Lord

On this golden plate was written the Tetragrammaton name of the Lord—that is, the name of four letters: Ioth, He, Vau, Heth, meaning “the beginning of the passion of this life.” As if it were said more plainly: He whose person this pontiff bears, namely Christ, is the beginning—that is, the author—of the life of the Passion, that is, of life restored through the Passion; because by dying he destroyed our death and by rising again restored life.

The name of the Lord written upon the golden plate was *Anoth, Adonai*, that is, “the holy

[Col. 0786B] name of the Lord,” the Tetragrammaton, which is called ineffable, not because it cannot be uttered, but because it signifies an ineffable reality.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the variety of workmanship

For the most part these vestments were woven in *opus polymitum*, that is, variegated work, on account of the variety of virtues. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the four colors

The vestments were woven from four precious colors: purple, scarlet, fine linen, and hyacinth-blue.

By purple, the pontifical power is signified as a royal dignity,

[Col. 0786C] which ought to proceed by the royal road, lest it turn aside to the right or stray to the left: lest it bind the worthy or loose the unworthy.

By scarlet, a fiery color said to have been dyed twice, is signified pontifical teaching, which, like fire, ought both to shine and to burn. It ought to shine by promise, as: “Everyone who has left house, or father and mother, and so forth, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 10). It ought to burn by threat, as: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 7).

By fine linen, of surpassing whiteness, is signified the brightness of reputation, which ought to be twisted, so that the pontiff

[Col. 0786D] may have a good testimony, according to the Apostle, both from those within and from those without (1 Tim. 3).

By hyacinth-blue, the color of the air, is signified serenity of conscience, which the pontiff ought to have within himself, according to the Apostle’s saying: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the vestments of the evangelical priest

The vestments of the evangelical priest signify one thing in the head and figure another in the members. For both head and members are designated by the name of priest. To the head the Psalmist says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). But to the members the Apostle says: “You

[Col. 0787A] are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore their mysteries must first be expounded insofar as they pertain to the head, and then insofar as they pertain to the members.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On pontifical vestments insofar as they pertain to Christ

The pontiff, then, in the service of the altar, representing the person of Christ his head, of whom he is a member, while putting sandals on his feet, signifies that footwear of the Lord’s Incarnation of which the Lord says in the Psalm: “Into Idumea I shall extend my sandal” (Ps. 59), that is, among the Gentiles I shall make my Incarnation known. For the Divinity came to us shod, in order that the Son of God might exercise the priesthood for us.

By the straps with which the sandals themselves are fastened to the feet, we understand the same thing that John the Baptist signified by the sandal-strap when he said: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Matt. 3).

[Col. 0787B] Therefore by the sandal-straps we understand the ineffable union and indissoluble bond by which the divinity of the Word joined itself to our flesh. The feet, however, are joined to the sandals by means of the stockings, because the divinity is united to flesh through the mediation of the soul. For as a foot supports the body, so the Divinity governs the world. Hence the Psalmist says: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98).

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the amice, where the reason is given why the same thing in Christ is signified by the footwear of the feet and by the covering of the head

[Col. 0787C]

The amice, with which the priest covers his head, signifies what is described in the Apocalypse: a mighty angel of God descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud (Rev. 10). And in Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a white cloud” (Isa. 19). When the Son of God, the angel of great counsel, came for the salvation of the world, he was clothed with a cloud when he concealed his divinity in flesh. For “the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). The amice of the priest thus signifies this hiding-place of the flesh. It is expressed still more clearly by that linen cloth with which the supreme pontiff covers his head.

And it is fitting that the same thing be signified by the footwear of the feet and by the covering of the head:

[Col. 0787D] because the Divinity lay hidden in flesh and was made known through flesh. For while God was known in Judaea and his name great in Israel, he extended his sandal into Idumea (Ps. 59) and revealed his righteousness before the sight of the Gentiles (Ps. 97).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the alb

The alb, a linen garment far removed from the garments of skin made from dead animals, with which Adam was clothed after sin (Gen. 3), signifies the newness of life which Christ both possessed, taught, and bestowed in baptism. Of this the Apostle says:

[Col. 0788A] “Put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who was created according to God” (Eph. 4). At the Transfiguration his face likewise shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow (Matt. 17). For Christ’s garments were always clean and white, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his tongue” (1 Pet. 2; Isa. 53).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the belt or girdle

The priestly belt signifies what John the Apostle says: “I turned and saw one like a son of man, girded about the breasts with a golden belt” (Rev. 1). By the golden belt is signified Christ’s perfect charity, which the Apostle calls “the charity of Christ surpassing knowledge”

[Col. 0788B] (Eph. 3), burning in the heart and radiating in action.

Its cincture signifies what Isaiah, speaking of Christ, foretold: “Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the cincture of his reins” (Isa. 11 [the text reads II]). For the Lord is just and loves just deeds; his face has beheld equity (Ps. 10). The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works (Ps. 144). Its two ends are the two natural parts of justice, which Christ both did and taught: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4); but “whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7 [the text reads IX]).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the stole

[Col. 0788C] The stole, which rests around the priest’s neck over the amice, signifies the obedience and servitude which the Lord of all underwent for the salvation of his servants. For although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as robbery. Rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2). He neither contracted the cause of mortality by origin nor committed it in action, because he paid what he had not stolen (Ps. 68). For the Father gave him the cup—not as judge, but as Father; from love, not anger; by will, not necessity; through grace, not vengeance.

This is that Jacob who, obeying the command of his father Isaac and the counsel of his mother Rebecca, served Laban so that he might take Rachel and Leah in marriage (Gen. 28 and 29 [the text reads XXXIX]).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the tunic

[Col. 0788D]

The ankle-length tunic, which in the old priesthood was hyacinth-blue, with bells and pomegranates hanging from its lower part so that the pontiff proceeded wholly sounding, signifies Christ’s heavenly teaching. Those people had knowledge of it to whom God said through the prophet: “Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion” (Isa. 40). Yet the chief weaver of this garment of evangelical teaching was the wisdom of God, Jesus Christ; and he gave it to his apostles: “Everything,” he said, “that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

[Col. 0789A] This, therefore, was signified by that tunic of the Lord which the soldiers were unwilling to divide, because it was seamless, woven from above throughout (John 19): judging that it would be a very great loss if anyone should attempt to tear evangelical teaching apart by heresies.

## CHAPTER XL. On the dalmatic

Over this tunic the pontiff puts on the dalmatic, which by its shape signifies Christ’s broad and generous mercy, which he above all both taught and bestowed. “Be merciful,” he says, “as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6). “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). “Judgment without mercy shall be shown to one who does not show mercy, because mercy exalts itself above judgment” (Jas. 2). Therefore, “forgive, and you shall be forgiven”; and thus, he says, you shall pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6).

[Col. 0789B] He is therefore that Samaritan, our neighbor, who showed us mercy, pouring wine and oil upon our wounds (Luke 10). For through the bowels of his mercy, the Dayspring from on high visited us (Luke 1 [the text reads X]). He saved us not from works of righteousness which we did, but according to his mercy (Titus 3). He came for sinners in order to grant pardon for sins. “I desire mercy,” he says, “and not sacrifice” (Matt. 9).

## CHAPTER XLI. On the gloves

The gloves are skins of kids, which Rebecca put around Jacob’s hands, so that the hairy hands might present the likeness of the elder brother (Gen. 27).

[Col. 0789C] The skin of a kid is the likeness of sin, which mother Rebecca—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—placed around the hands of the true Jacob, that is, around Christ’s works, so that Christ might exhibit the likeness of the elder, that is, the first Adam. For Christ assumed the likeness of sin without sin (Rom. 8), so that the mystery of the Incarnation might be hidden from the devil. For in the likeness of sinners he hungered, thirsted, suffered pain and fear, slept, and labored. Hence, after he had fasted forty days and forty nights and afterward hungered, the devil came to him and tempted him in the likeness of the first Adam (Matt. 4). But by the same means through which he had conquered the first, he was conquered by the second.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the chasuble, including discussion of its front and back parts

The chasuble or planet of the great priest is the universal Church, concerning which the Apostle says: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). This is that garment of Aaron, upon whose hem the ointment descends; but it descends from the head to the beard, and from the beard to the hem

[Col. 0789D] (Ps. 132). For not all of us received from the fullness of his Spirit (John 1): first the apostles, afterward the rest. That the chasuble, though single and whole, is in a certain manner divided into front and back portions by the stretching out of the hands signifies both the ancient Church, which preceded Christ’s Passion, and the new Church, which follows his Passion.

[Col. 0790A] For both those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the maniple

That the priest wears the maniple on the left signifies that Christ attained the prize while on the way. For the maniple signifies a reward, as it is written: “They shall come, coming with exultation, bearing their sheaves” (Ps. 125). By the left hand the present life is understood, according to the text: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). Yet Christ simultaneously [Col. 0790B] enjoyed and merited: he enjoyed in the homeland, he merited on the way. For he simultaneously comprehended and ran the course, because he was simultaneously both in the homeland and on the way. “No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the mitre

The pontiff’s mitre signifies that of which the Prophet, speaking of the Son, says to the Father: “You have crowned him with glory and honour, O Lord, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8). This, therefore, is that name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld (Phil. 2). For on the golden [Col. 0790C] plate of the high-priestly tiara was engraved the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, whose mystery we have touched upon above. By the mitre, therefore, we understand that supreme honour bestowed upon Christ’s humanity by reason of his divinity. For the footstool is worshipped because of the foot: “Worship,” he says, “his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98).

## CHAPTER XLV. On the staff

The pontiff’s rod signifies Christ’s power, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The rod of your kingdom is a straight rod; because you loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 44). For this reason [Col. 0790D] he says elsewhere: “You shall rule them with an iron rod” (Ps. 2). The hardness of iron signifies the rigor of equity, because Christ will shatter sinners like a potter’s vessel. Yet Christ’s power is not only a rod but also a staff, because he not only corrects but also sustains. Hence the Psalmist: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22).

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the ring

The ring of the finger signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the articulated and distinct finger suggests the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8); and elsewhere: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 2). The golden and circular ring signifies the perfection of his gifts, [Col. 0791A] which Christ received without measure, since in him “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). For he who comes from heaven is above all; to him God did not give the Spirit by measure (John 3). “He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining,” he says, “is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1). For upon him rests the Spirit of wisdom and understanding (Isa. 2), etc. He himself, however, distributes from his fullness according to differing gifts: to one, according to the Apostle, giving the word of knowledge; to another, gifts of healing; to another, the working of miracles (1 Cor. 12), etc. This the visible pontiff also imitates, appointing some as priests in the Church, others as deacons, others as subdeacons, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the five psalms to be said while the bishop prepares himself

[Col. 0791B]

A bishop about to celebrate the solemnities of Mass first says certain psalms and prayers, in accordance with the Psalmist’s exhortation: “Let us go before his face with confession, and rejoice before him in psalms” (Ps. 94). He says these five psalms: “How lovely” (Ps. 23), “You have blessed” (Ps. 84), “Incline” (Ps. 85), “I believed” (Ps. 115), and “Out of the depths” (Ps. 129), so that he may cleanse by the prayer of five psalms whatever uncleanness he has incurred through transgression of the five senses. For they contain certain things fittingly applicable to those celebrating the mystery of the altar and [Col. 0791C] the sacrament of the Eucharist.

In the first: “My soul has longed for and fainted after the courts of the Lord. Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God. O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob. Look upon us, O God our protector, and look upon the face of your Christ.”

In the second: “Restore us, O God our saviour, and turn your wrath away from us. Will you be angry with us for ever? Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation. Yet his salvation is near those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.”

In the third: “Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication. All nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord. I will confess to you, O Lord my God, with my whole [Col. 0791D] heart, and I will glorify your name for ever.”

In the fourth: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. You have broken my bonds, O Lord; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise and call upon the name of the Lord. I will pay my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, O Jerusalem.”

In the fifth: “Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication. My soul has waited upon his word; my soul has hoped in the Lord. For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.”

The prayers which he adds plainly concern the obtaining of purity and protection for heart and body.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On pontifical vestments as suited to the members: here, on hose and sandals

[Col. 0792A]

Meanwhile, the pontiff’s feet are shod with hose and sandals in preparation for the Gospel of peace, whose beauty the Prophet admired when he said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Ps. 52). The sandals have a complete sole underneath, but above they have perforated leather; for the preacher’s steps ought to be protected below, lest they be defiled by earthly things, according to the saying: “Shake the dust from your feet” (Matt. 10); and open above, so that they may be revealed for the knowledge of heavenly things, according to the prophetic saying: [Col. 0792B] “Unveil my eyes, and I shall behold the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118).

That the sandals are open in some places and closed in others signifies that evangelical preaching ought neither to be revealed to everyone nor concealed from everyone, as it is written: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8). “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). He is first clothed with hose extended up to the knees and fastened there, because the preacher ought to make straight paths with his feet and strengthen weak knees; for “he who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the washing of hands

[Col. 0792C]

Next he washes his hands bodily, so that he may cleanse his actions spiritually, on the authority of the Psalmist, who says: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will compass your altar, O Lord” (Ps. 25). It is not the dirt of the hands that defiles the divine sacraments; rather, if anyone eats and drinks unworthily, he eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 2). For eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person. But those things which proceed from the mouth come forth from the heart, and these defile a person: evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, fornications, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things which defile a person (Matt. 15). Hence one must earnestly strive that not so much the outward [Col. 0792D] defilements of the hands as the inward defilements of minds may be cleansed.

## CHAPTER L. On the amice, including the two ties by which it is fastened before the breast

Having therefore washed his hands, he takes the amice, which is spread all around over the shoulders. By it strength in works is signified. For the shoulders are strong for performing works, according to the saying concerning the patriarch Jacob: “He bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant paying tribute” (Gen. 49). The two little vessels—or ties—by which the amice is fastened before the breast signify intention and end; these must shape the work, lest it be done “in the leaven of malice and wickedness,” but “in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5). For the priest [Col. 0793A] ought not to be idle, but should persevere and toil in good works, as the Apostle says to Timothy: “Labour as a good soldier of Jesus Christ” (2 Tim. 2).

## CHAPTER LI. On the alb

The alb, fittingly adjusted to the limbs of the body, shows that there ought to be nothing superfluous or disordered in the priest’s life. By its bright whiteness it signifies purity, according to the text: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccles. 9). It is made of byssus or linen. Hence it is written: “Byssus is the righteousnesses of the saints.” For just as byssus or linen, worn down by much beating, acquires by art [Col. 0793B] the whiteness which it does not possess by nature, so human flesh, chastened by many mortifications, obtains by grace the purity which it does not possess by nature. Hence the priest, according to the Apostle, chastises his body and brings it into slavery (1 Cor. 9), lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate. This garment is described as having been tight in the old priesthood, because of the spirit of servitude in fear. In the new it is loose, because of the spirit of adoption in freedom (2 Cor. 3). That it has gold embroidery and is adorned with gems in diverse places and with varied workmanship for beauty suggests what the Prophet says in the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. 44).

## CHAPTER LII. On the girdle and cincture

[Col. 0793C]

Therefore the alb ought to be girded around the loins with a belt, so that the priest’s chastity may not be loosened by any goads of incitement. Hence: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). For lust holds sway in the loins. Thus the Lord, speaking of the devil, makes this clear: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). The loins, then, must be girded through continence. They must also be bound tightly through abstinence, since “this kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17). Hence the Apostle also says: “Stand, having girded your loins with truth” (Eph. 6).

## CHAPTER LIII. Why the Roman pontiff puts on the *orale* after the alb, and the cross after the *orale*

[Col. 0793D]

The Roman pontiff, after the alb and girdle, puts on the *orale*, which he wraps around the head and folds back over the shoulders, following the order of the legal high priest. After the close-fitting linen garment and belt, that priest was clothed with the ephod, that is, the shoulder-garment, whose place is now occupied by the amice. And because the sign of the cross succeeded the golden plate, in place of the plate which that pontiff wore on his forehead, this pontiff wears a cross upon his breast. For the mystery contained in the four letters of the golden plate he has unfolded in the four parts of the shape of the cross, as the Apostle says: “That you may comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. 3). Therefore the Roman [Col. 0794A] pontiff sets before his breast a certain cross, suspended from the neck on little chains, so that the sacrament which the former bore on his forehead this one may store up in his breast; for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

## CHAPTER LIV. On the stole

After this the priest places upon his neck the stole, which is otherwise called the *orarium*, to signify that he has taken upon himself the yoke of the Lord. Descending from the neck over the front, it adorns the right and left sides, because through “the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left” (2 Cor. 6)—that is, in prosperity and adversity—the priest ought to be armed. For the stole signifies wisdom or patience, concerning which it is written: [Col. 0794B] “You have need of patience, that you may obtain the promises” (Heb. 10). And again: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21). Hence the stole is bound with the girdle by certain fastenings, because virtues are joined to virtues, lest they be disturbed by any assault of temptation.

Moreover, according to the decree of the Council of Braga, the priest ought, from one and the same *orarium*, to form the sign of the cross upon his breast, pressing at once his neck and both shoulders. Whoever does otherwise shall incur the due penalty of excommunication—unless, perhaps, someone should say that this decree has been abrogated by the contrary custom of the Roman Church.

## CHAPTER LV. On the tunic

[Col. 0794C]

Then the pontiff puts on a *podērēs* tunic, that is, an ankle-length tunic, signifying perseverance. Hence Joseph is described as having had an ankle-length tunic among his brothers (Gen. 37). Although the other virtues run in the race, perseverance receives the prize; for “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). Hence the command: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2). In the old priesthood this garment had pomegranates with golden bells in place of fringes, whose mystery we have explained above.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the dalmatic

Over this tunic the bishop puts on the dalmatic, so called because it was discovered in Dalmatia. Its form signifies generosity, because it has broad and extended sleeves [alternative reading: “generosity has hands extended”]. Hence, according to the Apostle, a bishop must not be greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable (1 Tim. 3). Therefore he should not have a hand extended to give a collection and to receive it, but should do what the Prophet urges: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58). Perhaps for this reason deacons use dalmatics in a special way, because they were principally chosen by the apostles to minister to tables as an office (Acts 6).

The dalmatic ought to have two scarlet stripes, on either side, before and behind, [Col. 0795A] from top to bottom, so that the pontiff may have ardour toward God and neighbour in prosperity and adversity, in accordance with the precept of the Old and New Testaments: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself” (Deut. 6; Matt. 22). Hence John says: “Beloved, I write to you not a new commandment, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning”; and again: “I write to you a new commandment,” etc. (1 John 2). On the left side the dalmatic also customarily has fringes, signifying the cares of the active life which a bishop ought to have for those subject to him, as the Apostle says: “Apart from those things which are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches” (2 Cor. 2).

## CHAPTER LVII. On gloves

[Col. 0795B]

Because many people spoil a good work that they perform through vain applause, the bishop immediately covers his hands with gloves, so that his left hand may not know what his right hand does (Matt. 6). Thus the glove fittingly signifies caution: it performs the work publicly while keeping its intention hidden. For although the Lord said, “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.)—for which reason the glove has a golden circle above it—he nevertheless commanded: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them; otherwise [Col. 0795C] you shall have no reward with your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the chasuble or planet

Finally, over all the vestments he puts on the chasuble or planet, which signifies charity. For “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4), and the Apostle says concerning it: “I show you a still more excellent way: if I speak with the tongues of men and angels but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal” (1 Cor. 13). This is the wedding garment of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22).

That the amice is turned back over the opening of the planet indicates that every [Col. 0795D] good work must be referred to charity. For “the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned” (1 Tim. 1). That it is divided by the extension of the hands into a front and a back signifies the two arms of charity, namely toward God and toward neighbour. “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself” (Deut. 6). “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22). The breadth of the planet signifies the breadth of charity, which extends even to enemies; hence: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118).

## CHAPTER LIX. On the maniple

Moreover, because sloth often creeps into minds well ordered and devoted to divine worship, rendering the soul drowsy through a certain sluggishness—as the Psalmist says: “My soul has slumbered because of weariness” (Ps. 118)—a small cloth is placed on the left hand, called a maniple or *sudarium* (“sweat-cloth”), with which one may wipe away the sweat of the mind and shake off the sleep of the heart, so that, after weariness or sluggishness has been driven away, one may diligently keep watch over good works. Thus the maniple signifies watchfulness, concerning which the Lord says: “Watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 14); hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, and my heart watches” (Song 5).

## CHAPTER LX. On the mitre

The pontiff’s mitre signifies [Col. 0796B] knowledge of both Testaments. Its two horns are the two Testaments; its two fringes are spirit and letter. The golden circle, which embraces the front and rear parts, indicates that every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven brings forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. 13). Therefore the bishop must carefully beware of wishing to be a teacher before he knows how to be a disciple, lest, if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit (Matt. 15). For it is written in the Prophet: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not exercise priesthood for me” (Hos. 4).

## CHAPTER LXI. On the ring

The ring is the sacrament of faith, by which Christ has [Col. 0796C] betrothed his bride, the holy Church, so that she may say of herself: “My Lord, that is, Christ, has betrothed me with his ring.” Bishops and prelates are its guardians and tutors, bearing the ring as a sign in testimony. Of them the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me” (Song 5). The father gave this ring to his returning son, according to the saying: “Put a ring on his hand” (Luke 15).

## CHAPTER LXII. On the staff, and why the supreme pontiff does not use a pastoral staff

The staff signifies pastoral reproof [alternative reading: “correction”]; hence the consecrator says to the consecrated: [Col. 0796D] “Receive the staff of pastoral office.” And the Apostle says of it: “Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4). That it is pointed at the end, straight in the middle, and curved at the top signifies that the pontiff ought by it to prick the slothful, guide the weak, and gather the wandering. A certain versifier expressed this in one verse:

> Gather the wandering, support the sick, spur on the sluggish.

The Roman pontiff, however, does not use a pastoral staff, because the blessed apostle Peter sent his staff to Eucharius, first bishop of Trier, whom he dispatched with Valerius and Maternus to preach the Gospel to the Germanic people. Maternus succeeded him in the episcopate, having been raised from death by the staff of Saint Peter. The Church of Trier preserves that staff [Col. 0797A] to this day with great veneration.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the pallium, in which its material and form are expounded according to their mystery

[Col. 0797A]

The pallium, used by the higher-ranking bishops, signifies the discipline by which archbishops ought to govern themselves and their subjects. By this is gained the golden necklace which those who contend lawfully receive, concerning which Solomon says in Proverbs: “Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother, that grace may be added to your head and a necklace to your neck” (Prov. 1).

[Col. 0797B]

The pallium is woven of white wool; above it has a circle binding the shoulders, and two bands hanging down on either side. It has four purple crosses, before and behind, right and left; but on the left it is double and on the right single. All these things are filled with moral mysteries and pregnant with divine sacraments. For, as Scripture testifies: “In the treasures of wisdom is the signification of discipline” (Ecclus. 1). In wool harshness is noted; in whiteness kindness is signified. For ecclesiastical discipline exercises severity toward the rebellious and obstinate, but displays mercy toward penitents and the humble. Therefore it is made not from the wool of just any animal, but only from that of the sheep, a gentle animal. Hence the Prophet: “He was led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53).

Hence wine and oil are both applied to the wounds of the half-dead man whom the Samaritan brought [Col. 0797C] to the inn: by wine the wounds are bitten, and by oil they are soothed (Luke 10), so that one who is responsible for healing wounds may apply the bite of severity in wine and the gentleness of mercy in oil. This is also signified by the ark of the tabernacle, in which, together with the tablets, a rod and manna are contained (Heb. 9). For in the mind of a ruler, along with knowledge of Scripture, there ought to be a rod of strictness and manna of sweetness, so that severity may not rage immoderately and mercy may not indulge more than is fitting.

The circle of the pallium by which the shoulders are bound is the fear of the Lord, through which works are restrained lest they decline into unlawful acts or relax into superfluities. For discipline restrains the left hand from unlawful things through fear of punishment, while it moderates the right hand from superfluities through love of justice. “Blessed, therefore, is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). For, according to the sentence of the Wise Man, “fear of the Lord repels sin” (Ecclus. 1), while one who is without fear cannot be justified. Hence the pallium is frequently fitted both before the breast and over the shoulders.

The four purple crosses are the four civic virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Unless these are dyed purple by the blood of Christ’s cross, they vainly claim for themselves the name of virtue and do not lead to the true glory of blessedness. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: “Unless your justice abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). This is the king’s purple tunic, dyed [Col. 0798A] [alternative readings: “joined”; “bound”] in the channels, which Solomon mentions in the Song of Songs (ch. 7).

Therefore one adorned with the glory of the pallium, if he wishes to be what he is called, ought to have justice on the front, so as to render to each what is his; prudence on the back, so as to avoid what is harmful to each; fortitude on the left, so that adversities may not cast him down; and temperance on the right, so that prosperity may not exalt him. The two bands, one behind the back and the other extending before the breast, signify the active and contemplative life. The prelate ought to exercise them in such a way that, following Moses’ example, he now ascends the mountain and there philosophizes with the Lord, now descends to the camp and there attends to the needs of the people, taking careful care that, although he has often given himself to others, he sometimes restores himself to himself (Exod. 24, 34). [Col. 0798B] Thus he may both busy himself with Martha in much service and, with Mary, hear the word of the Saviour (Luke 10).

Both, however, weigh downward, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9). Therefore the pallium is double on the left but single on the right. For the present life, understood by the left hand, is subject to many troubles; but the future life, signified by the right, is always gathered into a single rest. Truth itself signified this when he added: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her for ever” (Luke 10).

The pallium [Col. 0798C] is double on the left so that the prelate may be strong in enduring the troubles of the present life; it is single on the right so that, in seeking the rest of the future life, he may sigh with his whole desire, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26).

The three pins fastened to the pallium—before the breast, over the shoulder, and behind the back—signify compassion for neighbour, administration of office, and strictness of judgment. The first pierces the mind through grief, the second through labour, the third through fear. The first pierced the Apostle when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not [Col. 0798D] burn?” (2 Cor. 18). The second is: “Apart from those things which are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches” (1 Pet. 4). The third: “If the righteous man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (2 Cor. 11). No pin is fastened over the right shoulder, because in eternal rest there is no sting of affliction, no spur of piercing. For God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because former things have passed away (Rev. 21).

The pin is golden, sharp below and round above, and contains a precious stone, because the good shepherd is indeed afflicted on earth for the care of the sheep, but will be eternally crowned in heaven, where he will possess that precious pearl [Col. 0799A] of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls; when he found one precious pearl, he went away and sold all that he had and bought it” (Matt. 13).

The pallium is called the fullness of pontifical office because in it and with it the fullness of pontifical office is conferred. For before a metropolitan is adorned with the pallium, he ought neither to ordain clerics, consecrate pontiffs, or dedicate churches, nor to be called archbishop.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the armour of virtues

These are the arms which the pontiff ought to put on when about to fight against spiritual wickedness. For, as the Apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, [Col. 0799B] but mighty through God for the destruction of strongholds” (2 Cor. 10). The same Apostle says of them in another Epistle: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil. Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of justice, and having shod your feet in preparation for the Gospel of peace; in all things taking the shield of faith, by which you may quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

Therefore let the bishop provide carefully and the priest attend diligently that he may not bear a sign without its meaning, or wear a garment without virtue, lest perhaps he be like a tomb whitewashed on the outside but within full of every uncleanness (Matt. 23). Whoever is adorned with [Col. 0799C] sacred vestments but is not clothed with honourable manners, the more venerable he appears to people, the more unworthy he becomes before God. Thus pontifical glory is now commended not by the honour of garments, but by the splendour of souls. For those things which formerly delighted fleshly eyes instead demanded that the things signified within them be understood: so that what those coverings signified in the gleam of gold, the brightness of gems, and the variety of manifold workmanship may now shine forth in conduct and actions. For among the ancients the forms of the signs themselves held reverence, but among us the experiences of realities are surer than the riddles of figures. Then indeed valleys abound in grain when rams are clothed with sheep (Ps. 44).

## CHAPTER LXV. On the four principal colours by which vestments are to be distinguished according to the character of days

[Col. 0799D]

There are four principal colours by which the Roman Church distinguishes sacred vestments according to the character of the days: white, red, black, and green. For four colours are also said to have existed in the legal vestments (Exod. 28): byssus, purple, hyacinth-blue, and scarlet. White vestments are worn on the feasts of confessors and virgins, red on the solemnities of apostles and martyrs. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5): white in confessors and virgins, [Col. 0800A] ruddy in martyrs and apostles. Both these and those are the flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys.

White vestments, therefore, ought to be used on the feasts of confessors and virgins because of integrity and innocence. For his Nazarites have been made white and always walk with him in white. For they are virgins and follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14). For the same reason white is to be used in the following solemnities: namely, on the feasts of angels, of whose brightness the Lord says to Lucifer: “Where were you when the morning stars praised me?” (Job 38); at the Nativity of the Saviour and of the Forerunner, since each was born pure, that is, free from original sin. For the Lord ascended upon a light cloud—that is, he assumed flesh [Col. 0800B] immune from sins—and entered Egypt (Isa. 19), that is, he came into the world, in accordance with the angel’s words to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore the holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

John, although conceived in sin, was nevertheless sanctified in the womb, according to the prophetic saying: “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1). For the angel also says to Zacharias: “He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1). At Epiphany, because of the radiance of the star that brought the Magi, according to the prophetic saying: “Nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the splendour of your rising” (Isa. 60). At Hypapante, because of the purity of Mary, who, according to Simeon’s canticle, offered “a light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of his people Israel” (Luke 2). At the Lord’s Supper, because of the preparation of chrism, which is consecrated for the cleansing of the soul; for the Gospel reading especially commends purity on that solemnity: “He who has washed does not need [Col. 0800C] except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean”; and again: “If I do not wash you, you shall have no part with me” (John 13).

At the Resurrection, because of the angel who witnessed and announced the resurrection, who appeared clothed in a white robe (Mark 16); of whom Matthew says that his appearance was like lightning and his garment like snow (Matt. 28). At the Ascension, because of the white [alternative reading: “bright”] cloud in which Christ ascended. For two men also stood beside them in [Col. 0800D] white garments and said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” etc. (Acts 1).

This also should not be noted idly: although, at the consecration of a pontiff, vestments are to be used by the consecrators and ministers in accordance with the character of the day—for the person being consecrated always uses white—at the dedication of a church white must always be used, whatever day the dedication is celebrated. For at a pontiff’s consecration the Mass of the day is sung, but at the dedication of a basilica the Mass of the dedication is sung. For the Church is also called by a virgin’s name, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). Of her the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come” (Song 4).

[Col. 0801A]

Red vestments, however, ought to be used on the solemnities of apostles and martyrs because of the blood of suffering which they shed for Christ. For they are those who came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 7). On the feast of the Cross, on which Christ shed his blood for us, the Prophet says: “Why is your garment red, like that of those treading in the winepress?” (Isa. 63). Or, on the feast of the Cross, it is better to use white, because it is a feast not of the Passion but of the Finding or the Exaltation.

At Pentecost, red is used because of the ardour of the Holy Spirit, who appeared over the apostles in tongues of fire. For divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, [Col. 0801B] and rested upon each one of them (Acts 2). Hence the prophet: “He sent fire from heaven into my bones” (Lam. 1). Although red ought to be used for the martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul, white is nevertheless to be used for their Conversion and their Chair. Likewise, although white is to be used at the Nativity of Saint John, red is to be used at his Beheading.

When the feast of one who is both martyr and virgin is celebrated, martyrdom takes precedence over virginity, because it is the sign of most perfect charity, as Truth says: “No one has greater charity than that one should lay down his life for his friends” (John 14). Accordingly, at the commemoration of All Saints some use red vestments; others, however, like the Roman curia, use white, since the Church says, not so much within that solemnity as concerning it, that the saints, according to John’s Apocalypse (ch. 7), stood before the Lamb clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands.

[Col. 0802A] Black vestments are to be used on days of affliction and abstinence, for sins and for the dead: namely, from Advent until the vigil of Christmas, and from Septuagesima until the Saturday of Easter. For the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon. Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me” (Song of Songs 1). On the day of the Innocents, however, some maintain that black vestments should be used, while others maintain that red should be used. The former do so on account of sorrow, because “a voice was heard in Ramah, great weeping and lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children and unwilling to be comforted, because they are not” (Jer. 31). For the same reason, songs of joy are omitted, and the mitre is not worn with gold embroidery. The latter do so because of the martyrdom which the Church principally commemorates when it says: [Col. 0802B] “The saints beneath the throne of God cried out: ‘Vindicate our blood which has been shed, O our God’” (Luke 18; Rev. 6). Therefore, on account of the sorrow indicated also by the silence of joyful songs, the mitre worn is not adorned with gold embroidery; but on account of martyrdom red vestments are used. Today we use violet, as on *Laetare Jerusalem*: on account of the joy signified by the golden rose, the Roman Pontiff wears a mitre adorned with gold embroidery; but on account of abstinence he uses black—indeed, violet—vestments.

It remains, therefore, that on ferial and ordinary days green vestments should be used, because green is an intermediate colour between white, black, and red. This colour is expressed where it is said: [Col. 0802C] “Henna (*cyprus*) with nard; nard and saffron” (Song of Songs 4).

The remaining colours are referred to these four. Scarlet belongs to red, violet to black, and saffron-yellow to green. Although some refer roses to martyrs, saffron to confessors, and lilies to virgins.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0801]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the bishop’s approach to the altar

[Col. 0801C]

Adorned with these vestments, the bishop proceeds to the altar, [Col. 0801D] led on either side by two persons—namely, a priest and a levite—with a subdeacon going before, carrying the closed book of the Gospel until the bishop reaches the altar; there he kisses the book when it is opened. All these things are full of divine mysteries. For the bishop represents in himself that high priest of whom the Apostle says: “Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands” (Heb. 9), that is, not of this creation, and so forth.

## CHAPTER II. On the priest and deacon who lead the bishop on either side

The priest and levite signify the Law and prophecy, according to the parable of the wounded man proposed by the Lord himself: “A certain priest went down by the same way and, seeing him, passed by; likewise also a levite” (Luke 10). Moses and Elijah appeared on the mountain with Christ, speaking with him, as figures of the Law and prophecy [Col. 0802C] [Col. 0802D] (Matt. 17). Therefore the priest and levite lead the bishop because the Law and prophecy announced and promised Christ. For Moses says in the Law: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as you hear me” (Deut. 18). And Isaiah: “Behold, the great prophet will come, and he himself will renew Jerusalem” (Isa. 66).

## CHAPTER III. On the subdeacon who goes before carrying the closed book of the Gospel

The subdeacon who goes before signifies John the Baptist, who went before Christ in the spirit and power of Elijah, “to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke 7). He carries before the high priest the book of the Gospel [Col. 0803A] because John began the preaching of the Gospel before Christ: “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 2). That the book is kept closed until the high priest reaches the altar and is then opened signifies what is described in the Apocalypse: that no one was found worthy to open the book written within and without, sealed with seven seals, except “the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David,” who opened the book and loosed its seven seals (Rev. 14). The altar signifies the Church, according to the Lord’s saying in Exodus: “If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones” (Exod. 20). In forbidding the cutting of stones in the altar, he condemns the division of believers, lest the Church be divided by errors and schisms.

## CHAPTER IV. On the high priest who reaches the altar

[Col. 0803B]

The book, then, is opened when the bishop reaches the altar. For where Christ gathered the primitive Church of the apostles, teaching and preaching, he revealed the mysteries of Scripture: “To you,” he says, “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8). Hence after the resurrection he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). The bishop therefore acts more fittingly when he himself opens the book of the Gospel, although Christ also disclosed the mysteries of Scripture through his ministers. That the bishop kisses the book of the Gospel signifies that Christ preached peace in the Gospel. “My peace,” he says, “I give to you; peace I leave to you; not [Col. 0803C] as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14).

## CHAPTER V. On the procession of the Roman Pontiff from the secretarium to the altar

When a stational solemnity is celebrated, the Roman Pontiff proceeds in procession from the secretarium to the altar with the six aforesaid orders, signifying that Christ “went forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). For this order of procession represents the sequence of Christ’s genealogy, which Matthew the Evangelist describes (ch. 1). In it are found six orders of persons from whom Christ drew his origin according to the flesh and came forth into the world: namely patriarchs and prophets, kings [Col. 0803D] and princes, shepherds and leaders. Abraham was a patriarch; David, a prophet; Solomon, a king; Solomon, a prince; Judah, a shepherd; Zerubbabel, a leader.

## CHAPTER VI. On the two deacons who lead the Pontiff

The two deacons who lead the Pontiff signify Abraham and David, to whom the promise of Christ’s incarnation was made. To the former it was promised: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22); to the latter: “Of the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne” (Ps. 131). For this reason the Evangelist expressly places these two first in Christ’s genealogy: “The book,” he says, “of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). These are the two columns which the true peacemaker placed in the vestibule of the temple [Col. 0804A] before the door (2 Chron. 3), which a cord of twelve cubits encircles: that is, whom the faith of the twelve apostles embraces. From between them Christ, the door, is opened to believers (John 10).

## CHAPTER VII. On the cloth carried above the Pontiff, fastened to four staffs

Four ministers carry above the Pontiff a cloth fastened to four staffs; for this reason these ministers are called *mappularii*, “cloth-bearers.” The cloth, figured with diverse images, signifies Holy Scripture, distinguished by many mysteries. It is carried stretched out above the Pontiff upon four staffs because Holy Scripture is expounded concerning Christ in four ways: according to history, [Col. 0804B] allegory, tropology, and anagogy. This is the river of Paradise which goes forth divided into four heads (Gen. 2). This is the table of the offering, which stands raised upon four feet (Exod. 25). It is carried stretched out above the Pontiff to show that he has come of whom the Law and the prophets wrote. For Christ himself, beginning with Moses and the prophets, interpreted in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24). Hence elsewhere he says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote concerning me” (John 5).

## CHAPTER VIII. On candles and incense

Thus two lights are borne before him with incense, because the Law and the prophets, together with the Psalms, foretold [Col. 0804C] Christ’s coming, as Christ himself attests when he says: “All things must be fulfilled which are written concerning me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms” (Luke 24). At greater solemnities, however, seven candlesticks are carried before the Pontiff. This displays what John describes in the Apocalypse: “I turned,” he says, “and saw seven golden candlesticks, and in the midst of the golden candlesticks one like the Son of Man, clothed in a long robe” (Rev. 1), so that by this he may be shown to be the one upon whom the sevenfold Spirit of grace rested, according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit [Col. 0804D] of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

## CHAPTER IX. On the fire which the Pontiff sets to a bundle of tow in the choir

In certain basilicas, near the middle of the choir, a bundle of tow is hung upon a column, to which the Pontiff applies fire so that it is suddenly burned before the people. By this he commemorates the second coming, when Christ will judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. For “fire shall blaze in his presence, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 49). Therefore, lest anyone be wrongly secure: he who in the first coming makes himself gracious will terrify in the second. For he who came in the first to be judged [Col. 0805A] will come in the second to judge. Or rather, since according to the Apostle James our life is “a vapour appearing for a little while” (Jas. 4), the Pontiff applies fire to the tow lest, as he proceeds in glory, he should take delight in temporal glory. For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40; 1 Pet. 1).

## CHAPTER X. On the primicerius, who kisses the Pontiff’s right shoulder

When the Pontiff approaches the altar, the *primicerius* of the school of singers comes forward and kisses his right shoulder before those standing by. For when Christ was born into the world, that angel with whom there came to be a multitude of the heavenly host praising God made his birth known to the shepherds (Luke [Col. 0805B] 2). Of him the prophet says: “A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, and dominion has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9).

## CHAPTER XI. On the three priests who reverently bow before the altar, kissing the Pontiff’s mouth and breast

The three priests who reverently meet the Pontiff as he comes before the altar and, bowing, kiss his mouth and breast signify those three Magi who came to Jerusalem saying: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” And, falling down, they worshipped him when they had found him; and, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. 2). By the double kiss they confess the twofold nature in Christ, namely divine and human: the divine [Col. 0805C] as hidden in the breast, which the Magi also mystically figured through their offered gifts. For a kiss is a sign of reverence, as Esther is read to have kissed the top of the king’s sceptre (Esth. 5).

## CHAPTER XII. On the arrangement of the procession

This procession is arranged “like an army drawn up in order” (Song of Songs 6). For the greater and stronger, like guards of the army, go before and follow behind; the lesser, as weaker, are gathered in the middle. Bishops and priests go before; the Pontiff and deacons follow; subdeacons and acolytes are gathered in the middle. The singers, like trumpeters, go before the army, in order to rouse and summon it to battle against [Col. 0805D] demons. Of this battle the Apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). Hence the Psalmist: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemn feast” (Ps. 80). Therefore the cross, like a royal standard, is sent forward and borne before them, “that those who hate him may flee from his face” (Ps. 67). Far be it from us, therefore, to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to us, and we ought to be crucified to the world! (Gal. 6).

## CHAPTER XIII. On confession and the striking of the breast, in which three things are noted: the blow, the touch, and the sound

[Col. 0806A]

Because “the righteous man is the accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18), when the Pontiff reaches the altar and returns to himself, before beginning the sacred office he confesses his sins with those standing by, first saying that psalm which is manifestly recognized throughout as belonging and fitting to this purpose: “Judge me, O God,” and so forth, in order that, separated from an unholy nation and delivered from the unjust man (Ps. 42), he may enter worthily unto God’s altar. This must be noted concerning this confession: sins are to be confessed not specifically, as some do with insufficient prudence, but generally, because this confession is not secret [Col. 0806B] but public. We strike our breasts when confessing sins, so that, following the example of the tax collector who struck his breast saying, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18), we may go down justified to our house. In the striking are three things: the blow, the sound, and the touch. By these are signified the three things necessary in true repentance: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction by deed. For just as we sin in three ways—by thinking in the heart, speaking with the mouth, and committing deeds—so we must repent in three ways: by sorrow in the heart, shame in the mouth, and labour in deeds.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the incense which the priest presents in a vessel, and the bishop places in the censer

[Col. 0806C] Therefore, when about to approach the altar, the Pontiff puts incense into the censer, thereby signifying what is written: that an angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand, which he filled with fire from the altar; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer it from the prayers of the saints (Rev. 8). The angel is Christ; the golden censer, his immaculate body; the altar, the Church; the fire, charity; the incense, prayer, according to the prophet’s words: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). Thus the angel—that is, Christ—came; he stood before the altar, that is, in the sight of the Church; he held a golden censer, that is, an immaculate body, full of fire, that is, charity; and much incense, that is, prayers, was given to him by the faithful, [Col. 0806D] so that he might offer them—that is, present them to the Father—from the prayers of the saints. It does not say merely “prayers,” because Christ does not heed every prayer, but only from all those that pertain to salvation. Hence, when Paul asked the Lord three times to remove from him the sting of the flesh, the Lord answered: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Cor. 12), for power is made perfect in weakness. Therefore the bishop puts frankincense in the censer because Christ inspires prayer in the soul, so that through him incense worthy to be an odour of sweetness may be offered. He goes before us in the blessing of sweetness, so that our merit may be his gift, because he receives only what he bestows. “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing; for the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine” [Col. 0807A] (John 15). The priest, however, presents incense to the bishop because the Law prepared that precious *thymiama*—incense—which is offered to the Most High as an odour of sweetness. Concerning it the Lord adds in Exodus: “You shall not make such a composition for your own use, because it is holy to the Lord. Any man who makes a similar thing in order to enjoy its fragrance shall perish from among his people” (Exod. 39). There have been those who said that if the censer descends from the altar, other incense should then be placed in it without a blessing and offered to men, as though the former concerned *latria*—worship due to God—and the latter *dulia*—veneration. Yet it is better understood according to the spirit than according to the letter. For “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3).

## CHAPTER XV. On the threefold kiss: of the mouth, the altar, and the breast

[Col. 0807B]

Then, approaching the altar, the bishop kisses the sacred altar, signifying that Christ, when he came, united the holy Church to himself, according to that bridal song: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1). For in a kiss mouth is joined to mouth; and in Christ not only is humanity united to divinity, but the bride also is joined to the bridegroom, according to the prophetic saying: “He adorned me like a bridegroom with a crown, and adorned me like a bride with jewels” (Isa. 61). Hence John: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). For “he placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself goes forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18). Then the bishop turns and kisses the deacons, to show that in Christ’s coming there came [Col. 0807C] the peace which the prophets had promised. Thus David says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away” (Ps. 71). Another prophet likewise says: “There will be peace in our land when he comes” (Jer. 2). And therefore, when Christ was born, the voice of angels rang out: “And on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2). For a kiss sometimes signifies peace, as the Apostle says: “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (Rom. 16). “And may the God of peace be with you all. Amen” (Rom. 15). The deacon then immediately bows and kisses the bishop’s breast, signifying that the prophets foretold the coming peace by divine inspiration. For John too, reclining upon Christ’s breast (John 13), drank the streams of the Gospel [Col. 0807D] from that sacred fountain of the Lord’s breast itself.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the censing by which the Pontiff censes the altar and the priest the bishop

Therefore the bishop, receiving the censer from the deacon, censes the sacred altar because Christ, assuming a body, of the stock of the prophets, made of the seed of David according to the flesh, cherishes the Church with his prayers, as he prays in the Gospel: “Holy Father, I pray for them, and not for them only, but also for those who will believe through their word” (John 17). That the deacon receives the censer in order to cense the bishop morally teaches that, if we wish worthily to offer the incense of prayer, we must hold the censer of the incarnation. For without faith [Col. 0808A] in the mediator human beings cannot please God (Heb. 2), but according to the word of his promise: “Whatever they ask in prayer believing, they shall receive” (Matt. 21). For by the censer is understood the incarnate Word.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the form of the censer, and the twofold reason for censing, spiritual and literal

For just as the upper and lower parts of a censer are joined by three chains, so there are three unions in Christ, by which divinity and humanity are joined: the union of flesh with soul, the union of divinity with flesh, and the union of divinity with soul. Some assign a fourth union: that of the deity with the composite made jointly of soul and flesh; for some censers have four chains. Moses speaks particularly to Aaron concerning this censer: “Take the censer, and having taken fire from the altar, put incense upon it” (Num. 16). Apart from the mystical reason, the altar is also censed so that every malice of the demon may be driven away from it. For the smoke of incense is believed to have power to put demons to flight. Hence, when Tobias asked the angel what remedy was provided by the things he had commanded to be kept from the fish, he answered: “If you place a piece of its heart upon coals, its smoke drives out every kind of demon” (Tob. 6).

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the antiphon said at the introit, why it is repeated with the glory of the Trinity inserted, and who established that it should be sung

[Col. 0808C]

Meanwhile the choir sings the antiphon at the introit, repeating it after the glory of the Trinity has been inserted. Just as the priest’s entrance signifies Christ’s coming, so the antiphon said at the introit signifies the longing for his coming. Concerning this the Lord says to the apostles: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13; Luke 10). The choir enlarges its soul and sings the introit with jubilation, because prophets, patriarchs, kings, priests, and all the faithful awaited Christ’s coming with great longing, crying and entreating: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, [Col. 0808D] from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). “Come, O Lord, and do not delay; forgive the offences of your people Israel.” Thus that righteous and aged Simeon blessed and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2). Therefore the introit is sung in the person of those through whom Christ entered the world, as the Apostle says: “And when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: ‘Let all the angels of God worship him’” (Heb. 1). The repetition of the antiphon signifies the multiplication of the cry. Hence the prophet: “Command, command again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little there” (Isa. 28). “If he delays, wait for him, because he will surely come and will not delay” (Hab. 2). The insertion of the glory signifies [Col. 0809A] an appeal for favour. For in order more readily to obtain what they awaited, they cried out glorifying the whole Trinity: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84). “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” (Ps. 79). At last the Holy Spirit heard their cry, anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions, and sent him to evangelize the poor, as the Son himself testifies through the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me and sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isa. 61; Luke 4). Thus the introit represents this longing of the ancients, not according to the literal sense, but by the jubilation of its melody. Pope Celestine established that all 150 psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, which had not previously been done; only the Epistle and Gospel were read. Thus introits, graduals, offertories, and communions were selected from the psalms and began to be sung with melody at Mass in the Roman Church. *Antiphon*, in Greek, means “a responsive voice,” because two choirs alternate in turn the melodies of their chants.

## CHAPTER XIX. On *Kyrie eleison*, why it is sung nine times, and why *Kyrie eleison* is said six times and *Christe eleison* three times

When, therefore, the time of fullness and mercy has now come, as the Psalmist foretold: [Col. 0809C] “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because the time has come to have mercy upon her” (Ps. 101), the choir fittingly adds in song: *Kyrie eleison*, which means, “Lord, have mercy.” Hence the prophet: “Lord, have mercy on us, for we have waited for you” (Isa. 33). It is said here nine times, against nine kinds of sin. There is original, mortal, and venial sin: that is, serpent, woman, and man. For the serpent—that is, concupiscence—suggests originally; the woman—that is, delight—eats venially; the man—that is, reason—consents mortally. Again, there is the sin of thought, speech, and commission: of thought in the heart, of speech in the mouth, of commission in the deed. This is death in the house, death in the gate, death [Col. 0809D] in the tomb. Again, there is sin of frailty, simplicity, and malice: frailty through incapacity, simplicity through ignorance, malice through envy. This is sin against the Father, sin against the Son, and sin against the Holy Spirit. Therefore the choir says three times to the Father, *Kyrie eleison*; three times to the Son, *Christe eleison*; and three times to the Holy Spirit, *Kyrie eleison*. But the Father and the Holy Spirit are addressed under one and the same title only because the Father and the Holy Spirit are only of the same nature; the Son, however, is addressed under another, because although the Son is of the same nature as they, he is also of another, “a giant of twofold substance.” Or it is said nine times so that the tenth order, [Col. 0810A] restored from human beings, may be joined to the nine orders of angels.

Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0809D] Gregory I.] ordered that *Kyrie eleison* be sung at Mass by the clergy, whereas among the Greeks it was sung by the whole people.

## CHAPTER XX. On *Gloria in excelsis*, the threefold peace, and who established the singing of the angelic hymn at Mass

Immediately follows the angelic hymn, bearing witness to Christ’s temporal birth. It is first intoned by the one who represents the Angel of Great Counsel. The choir continues it in song, because “suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: ‘Glory [Col. 0810B] to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will’” (Luke 2). This hymn belongs not only to angels, but also to human beings rejoicing together because that woman who had lost the tenth drachma had now lit a lamp to find the lost drachma; and because the shepherd, leaving ninety-nine sheep in the desert, had now come to seek the hundredth sheep which he had lost (Luke 13).

Before Christ’s birth there were three walls of enmity: the first between God and humankind, the second between angel and humankind, the third between human being and human being. For by disobedience humankind had offended the Creator; by its fall it had hindered the restoration of the angels; by diverse rites it had separated itself from humankind. The Jew [Col. 0810C] practised ceremonies; the gentile practised idolatry; and each found the other’s rite displeasing. But true peace, coming, made both one; it destroyed the walls of enmity and joined the converging walls in itself as the corner-stone (Eph. 2), so that henceforth there might be one fold and one shepherd (John 10). Thus it took away sin and reconciled humankind to God. It repaired the fall and reconciled humankind with God and angel. It destroyed the rites and reconciled human being to human being. It therefore restored, according to the Apostle, “the things in heaven and the things on earth” (Col. 1). For these reasons the multitude of the heavenly host sang: “Glory to God in the highest”—that is, among the angels—“and on earth peace to Jews and gentiles, people of good will” (Luke 2). [Col. 0810D] Hence too the angel speaks with and rejoices together with the shepherds, because peace between human beings and angels has been restored. God is born as man because peace between God and humankind has been restored. He is born in the manger of ox and ass because peace between human beings has been repaired. For by the ox the Jewish people, and by the ass the gentile people, are figured, according to the words: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1).

Pope Symmachus established that *Gloria in excelsis* should be sung at Mass both on Sunday and on the feasts of martyrs. Telesphorus, the ninth from blessed Peter, had ordered this hymn to be sung at the nocturnal Mass of Christ’s Nativity [Col. 0811A]—which he himself also established—and added to it what follows the angels’ words; although many maintain that Saint Hilary of Poitiers added these words.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the candlesticks and cross placed above the middle of the altar

To signify, therefore, the joy of the two peoples rejoicing at Christ’s birth, two candlesticks are set at the horns of the altar, bearing lighted tapers with the cross placed between them. For the angel says to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people; for a Saviour has been born to you,” and so forth (Luke 2). This is the true Isaac, whose name means “laughter” (Gen. 21). The light of the candlestick, however, is the faith of the people. For the prophet says to the Jewish people: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 60). To the gentile people the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). For at Christ’s birth a new star also appeared, according to Balaam’s prophecy: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24). Between the two candlesticks the cross is placed in the middle of the altar, because Christ is the mediator in the Church between the two peoples, the corner-stone (1 Pet. 2), who “made both one” (Eph. 2): to him came the shepherds from Judaea and the Magi from the East.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the priest’s movement from one side to the other

[Col. 0811C]

The Pontiff, intending to pray, ascends to the seat and, standing, pronounces the collect, which he reads from the open book. For according to the Gospel testimony, Jesus came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; and, according to his custom on the Sabbath day, entered the synagogue and stood up to read. The book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him. Unrolling it, he found the place where it was written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me and sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isa. 61). And when he had folded the book, he gave it back to the minister and sat down. According to the practice of other bishops, moreover, when the bishop prays, he stands at the right side of the altar.
