In this he signifies what had been prophesied: “God shall come from the south” (Hab. 3). And since [Col. 0811D] joyful things are signified by the right, and sorrowful things by the left, the Pontiff first approaches the right side of the altar in order to show the joy of the Lord’s Nativity. Then after the Gospel he turns to the left, in order to signify the sorrow of the Passion. But he returns again to the right, in order to announce the joy of the resurrection. Ezekiel represented this very thing in his description of the four living creatures. “The face of a man,” he says, “and the face of a lion were on the right side of all four” (Ezek. 1). For by the man the Nativity is signified; by the lion, the resurrection; by the ox, sacrifice. Therefore the face of the man and the face of the lion were on the right, while the face of the calf was on the left, because Nativity and resurrection brought joy, but the Passion inspired sorrow. On this account [Col. 0812A] Christ himself said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 20). Therefore the priest ought to pray facing east, because “the Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1; Zech. 4). Of him it is written: “Behold, the man whose name is the East [*Oriens*]” (Jer. 23); and an argument for this is found in the Book of Wisdom: “One ought,” it says, “to worship at the rising of light” (Wis. 16). This is not because the divine majesty is locally situated in the east, though it is essentially everywhere: “I fill heaven and earth,” he says (Isa. 66); but because for those who fear God the sun of righteousness will rise (Mal. 4), which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). For Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6) and Moses’ tabernacle (Exod. 26) are read to have had their entrance on the east. Since under the Old Testament the entrance [Col. 0812B] into the temple was from east to west, this signified that all before Christ’s Passion tended toward the setting—that is, toward hell after death. But now the entrance into the temple is from west to east, signifying our rising and ascent to glory. In those churches whose door is on the west, however, the priest standing before the altar always turns toward the people during the greeting, so that he may worship facing east—except at the preface and the fraction, when, wholly intent upon prayer, he has his heart lifted up to the Lord and performs the sacrament of the Eucharist.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the removal of the Pontiff’s mitre

When about to pray, the bishop removes his mitre because, according to the Apostle [Col. 0812C] (2 Cor. 2), a man ought to pray with uncovered head, so that no veil of malice may stand between him and God, and so that, with unveiled face, he may behold the Lord’s glory.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the greeting of the Pontiff and priest to the people

Therefore the Pontiff begins with the greeting to the people, saying: “Peace be to you,” using the blessing of him whose high-priesthood he exercises. But when an inferior priest greets the people, he says: “The Lord be with you.” This is the phrase which Boaz is read to have said to the reapers (Ruth 2), and Boaz is understood also to have prefigured the Saviour because he took Ruth the Moabite as his wife. The choir answers both: “And with your spirit.” This is taken from Paul’s Epistle to Timothy: [Col. 0812D] “The Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “be with your spirit” (2 Tim. 4). To show that he is Christ’s vicar, the bishop says the first time: “Peace be to you,” because this was Christ’s first utterance to the disciples when he appeared to them after the resurrection. Afterwards, however, following the pattern of the other priests, he says: “The Lord be with you,” in order to show himself one of them. Moreover, the people are greeted seven times in the Mass, so that, after the seven capital vices have been cast out, they may receive sevenfold grace.

## CHAPTER XXV. That a priest ought not to celebrate with fewer than two persons present
It is established in the sacred canons that no presbyter should presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass unless two persons are present and respond to him, so that he himself may be counted as the third. For since he says in the plural, “The Lord be with you,” and in the secret prayers, “Pray for me,” it is plainly fitting that his greeting be answered by more than one person. Yet a case of necessity is one thing, and contempt for religion another. It should also be piously believed—and is confirmed by sacred authorities—that angels of God stand by those who pray, as the prophet says: “In the presence of angels I will sing praises to you” (Ps. 137). And the angel said to Tobias: “When you prayed with tears, I offered your prayer to the Lord” (Job 12). The canon likewise contains: “We humbly beseech you, almighty God, command that these things be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your altar on high,” etc.

Certainly every human being has his own angel for protection. Thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when the maid who ran to the door announced Peter’s arrival, they said: “It is his angel” (Acts 12). And the Lord, speaking in the Gospel of little children, says: “Their angels always behold the face of the Father” (Matt. 18). Therefore we have as companions in reason those whom we shall have as fellows in glorification.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On prayer and its conclusion

After the greeting has been given, by which the hearers are made attentive, he adds the prayers, which are signified in the Apocalypse (ch. 8) by the smoke of incense ascending before the Lord from the hand of the angel. For Christ, true man, destined to suffer for us—whose voice is that: “You did not require burnt offerings and offerings for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39)—always prayed for us through the Word united to himself. According to the Apostle, “in the days of his flesh,” offering “prayers and supplications to God, who was able to save him from death, with a strong cry and tears,” he “was heard in all things because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

The words added at the end of the prayer, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” signify what he himself says in the Gospel: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name shall be done for you” (John 15, 19). For God’s eternal benefits cannot reach us by any other way than through him who is the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2), just as by means of a crystal we direct fire from the distant sun onto food placed beneath it.

This is taken from the Epistle to the Romans: “We glory,” he says, “in God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5). The ensuing words, “who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God,” may be understood simply, but not unwisely: “who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God,” that is, together with the Holy Spirit. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Or: “in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, who is the unity of Father and Son, the love and bond of both.

“Through all ages of ages” may be understood either consecutively or antonomastically: consecutively, as “generations of generations”; [Col. 0814A] antonomastically, as “Song of Songs.” “Amen” expresses the disposition either of one who wishes or of one who affirms. For at the end of the Psalms, where we say, “Let it be, let it be,” the Hebrew says, “Amen, amen.” Christ also often says in the Gospel, “Amen, amen, I say to you”; that is, “Truly, truly, I say to you,” according to what he says elsewhere: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes’” (Matt. 5). Thus it refers either to the form of the prayer, so that what is prayed for may be desired, or to the manner of the conclusion, so that it may be affirmed.

For example, when the priest prays, “Grant us, we beseech you, Lord, health of mind and body,” the people answer with a wish: “Amen,” that is, “Let it be.” Or when the priest concludes, “Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages,” the people answer affirmatively: “Amen,” that is, “It is true.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. Why prayers are called collects, and how many are to be said in Mass

The prayers said near the beginning of Mass are called *collects*, because the priest who serves as an ambassador to God for the people gathers and sums up in them the petitions of all. More properly, however, those prayers are called collects which are made over the gathering of the people while the people assemble in order to proceed from one church to another for the making of a station.

The authors of prayers were many and varied, and their number and diversity grew so greatly that the Eighth African Council, in which blessed Augustine took part, decreed as follows: no petitions, [Col. 0814C] prayers, Masses, prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands are to be said unless they have been approved in council. Pope Gelasius too is said to have arranged prayers composed both by himself and by others. Blessed Gregory, setting aside those that seemed excessive or unsuitable, brought together reasonable ones, adding many fitting and necessary prayers of his own.

Some, however, exceeding measure and order, multiply prayers to such an extent that they produce weariness and disgust in their hearers; whereas, on the contrary, the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you pray, do not use many words, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking” (Matt. 6; Luke 12). Therefore, when the apostles said to him, “Lord, teach [Col. 0814D] us to pray,” he taught them a concise prayer: “Our Father who art in heaven,” etc. (ibid.). Priests, therefore, following the form of this prayer, should not exceed the number seven in Mass. For Christ comprised in seven petitions all necessities of body and soul.

But because

> “God delights in an uneven number,”  
> —Virgil

some carefully observe the practice of saying an odd number of prayers in Mass: one, three, five, or seven. One or three, because of the sacrament of unity or the mystery of the Trinity; five or seven, because of the Lord’s fivefold Passion or the sevenfold Spirit of grace. For God detests division and discord. [Col. 0815A] Hence, although he blessed the works of the other days, he is not read to have blessed the works of the second day, because the number two departs from unity and the other divisible numbers derive their origin from it.

Care must also be taken that, if a collect for the dead is joined to others, it be said not last but next to last, or before the next to last; for the end ought to bend back to its own beginning. In a Mass for the dead, however, a prayer for the living should not be inserted, except that common prayer: “Almighty everlasting God, who [art] of the living,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the extension of the priest’s hands in Mass

Standing to pray, the bishop raises and extends his hands, while ministers stand on either side supporting them, and a priest before him holds the sacramentary. The Law indeed intimates this sacrament. For it is read in Exodus (ch. 17) that, when Israel fought against Amalek in the wilderness, Moses went up to the top of the hill; and whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed. But if he lowered them even a little, Amalek overcame. Aaron and Hur supported his hands on both sides. Thus it came about that his hands did not grow weary until sunset; and Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword.

For this reason the priest extends his hands when he prays in Mass. For Christ too, when he had spread out his hands on the cross, prayed for his persecutors and said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23), [Col. 0815C] teaching morally that Christ is always ready to receive penitents, as he himself promised: “Whoever comes to me, I will not cast out” (John 6).

When the true Moses, that is, Christ, raises his hands—that is, grants help and consolation—Israel, that is, the Church, prevails. “For if God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8). But if he lowers his hands even a little—that is, if, because sins require it, he withdraws help and consolation—Amalek, that is, the devil, prevails. For it depends “not on one who wills or one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

But because Christ promised the Church, “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28), therefore Aaron—that is, “mountain of strength”—and Hur—that is, “fire of charity”—support his hands: so that in strength he may bear help and out of charity consolation, lest his hands grow weary until sunset, that is, until the end of the world. Thus, under Joshua’s leadership—that is, Christ’s leadership—Israel puts Amalek and his people to flight: that is, the Church overcomes the devil and the army of demons by the edge of the sword, that is, by the power of prayer. For “the sword is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

Therefore, whoever wishes by the power of prayer to overcome the devil must raise his hands—that is, raise his actions toward God—so that his conduct may be in heaven (Phil. 3). Hence: “Raise the drooping hands and strengthen the weak knees” (Isa. 35). “The lifting up of hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 40). “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good” (Job 12). But “faith without works [Col. 0816A] is dead” (Jas. 2). Let us therefore raise pure hands without dissension (1 Tim. 2), seeking the things above, not the things on earth, where Christ sits at the right hand of God (Col. 3).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the epistle that precedes the Gospel

The Epistle which precedes the Gospel signifies the office of the forerunner, which John exercised before Christ: he went before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways. As he himself testifies: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. 3). John, therefore, was as it were a subdeacon, that is, an under-minister of him who says of himself: “I came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20).

For the Law, like a pedagogue, received God’s infant people under the care of Moses, teaching them to await the coming of him whom John, by word and finger, showed as present in the flesh to that same people now grown up, so that, led by him, they might follow him into the kingdom. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

The Law preceded the Gospel as shadow precedes light, rod precedes spirit, fear precedes charity, beginning precedes perfection, the command of one ruling precedes the counsel of one loving. “For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (ibid.). The Epistle, moreover, is the voice of the Law, confessing its own imperfection through John’s testimony and sending men on to evangelical perfection: “This is he,” it says, “of whom I told you: He who comes after me has been made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loose. I must decrease, but he must increase. He was not the light, but [came] that he might bear witness to the light. The true light was that which enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid.). For the Law led no one to perfection (Heb. 7).

Therefore one acolyte accompanies the subdeacon reading the Epistle, but both subdeacon and acolyte accompany the deacon reading the Gospel: because few followed John’s preaching, but very many received the preaching of the Gospel. Hence the disciples are read to have said to John: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he baptizes, and all are coming to him” (John 3). Thus, when Jesus knew [Col. 0816D] that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making more disciples than John, he left Judea, etc. (John 4).

Since John was the boundary between what preceded and what followed, standing between apostles and prophets—for “the Law and the prophets were until John,” and from him “the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it” (Matt. 11)—therefore the Epistle is not always read from the prophets nor always from the apostles, but is sometimes taken from the Old Testament and sometimes from the New. For John, whose voice the Epistle represents, foretold Christ’s coming together with the ancients: “He who comes after me has been made before me”; and, together with the moderns, showed Christ present: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.”

The Greek word *epistola* is called in Latin *supermissio* or *superrogatio* (“an addition” or “something added over and above”), a name well suited to apostolic letters, which have been added over and above the Gospel and from which epistles are read more often. For the apostolic order is understood through that innkeeper to whom the Samaritan entrusted the man stripped by robbers, wounded, and left half dead, producing two denarii and saying to him: “Take care of him; and whatever you spend in addition, I will repay you when I return” (Luke 10).

## CHAPTER XXX. On the reverence shown by the subdeacon to the bishop after the Epistle has been read

The fact that the subdeacon approaches the priest with the acolyte after reading the Epistle signifies that John, when he had heard in prison of Christ’s works, sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or do we await another?” (Matt. 11), so that through the miracles they had seen they might know that Christ had now come. Hence Jesus answered them: “Go, report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor receive the Gospel” (ibid.).

And because “the right hand of the Lord has wrought might” (Ps. 127), the subdeacon kisses the priest’s right hand. Because, through the miracles he had seen, he knew this to be the one of whom his master had foretold: “He who comes after me has been made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loose,” he bows at the feet and kisses the sandal of the Roman pontiff. The priest blesses the subdeacon because Christ commended John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. Amen, I say to you, among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 3).

The subdeacon approaches the priest after the end of the reading, but the deacon before its beginning, and shows reverence, because the Law received its end in Christ, but the Gospel took its origin from him. For the Law and the prophets were until John; the Gospel and the apostles are after John.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the gradual

But because John preached repentance—“Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven is at hand”; and again: “Produce fruits worthy [Col. 0817D] of repentance” (Matt. 3)—the gradual rightly follows the Epistle, since it signifies the lament of repentance. For this reason it is removed from the office during the days of Pentecost, because those days signify the future happy state of the Church in God’s kingdom, when Christ’s threshing-floor, cleansed by the winnowing fan in his hand, will have its grain stored in the barn of eternal blessedness.

It is called a *gradual* from the steps of humility, as being appropriate to one who has not yet ascended “from strength to strength,” but is still set in the valley of tears (Ps. 83), though he has already disposed ascents in his heart. Therefore those act more rightly who do not render the gradual with festive or elaborate musical voices, but sing it simply and mournfully, as though it were a grave and harsh chant.

Yet the responsory called the gradual may be referred to the calling of the apostles, when, at Christ’s call, “Come after me,” they answered not merely in word but in deed, because leaving everything they followed him (Matt. 2). Thus the gradual is sung because the apostles walked after the Lord, disciples after their master. The gradual, therefore, is sung after the Epistle because, after John’s preaching, disciples followed Christ.

As John the Evangelist describes it: “John,” he says, “was standing with two of his disciples; and looking at Jesus as he walked, he said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.’ And the two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus. Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who had heard John and followed him.” He sang the gradual when he found his brother Simon and said to him: “We have found the Messiah,” which is interpreted “Christ”; and he brought him to Jesus. Philip likewise sang the gradual when he found Nathanael and said to him: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph of Nazareth, of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets [wrote]: come and see” (John 1).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Alleluia

Consolation follows mourning: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). Therefore Alleluia is sung after the gradual. It signifies the ineffable joy of angels and human beings rejoicing in eternal blessedness, that is, always praising [Col. 0818C] God. For: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). “The sound of feasting is in the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 41).

What *alleluia* means is explained by Psalm 112: when “Alleluia” is prefixed in its title, the psalm at once begins by expounding the title: “Praise the Lord, you servants.” The poverty of the present life can by no means deserve to possess this ineffable joy; but, tasting it beforehand in hope, it thirsts and hungers for what it has tasted, until hope is changed into reality and faith into sight. Therefore this Hebrew name has remained untranslated—that is, it was not translated—so that it might signify rather than express a joy foreign to this life by a word likewise foreign.

Its mystery, like a certain drop of joy from the riches of the heavenly Jerusalem, first flowed down through the Holy Spirit into the minds of the patriarchs and prophets, and afterwards more fully into the mouths of the apostles. Since, then, Alleluia is as it were the proper word of future blessedness, it is rightly used more frequently at the time when Christ, rising again, bestowed upon us hope and the merit [variant: promise] of that same blessedness.

Formerly, however, it was not the custom of the Roman Church to sing it at Mass in other seasons; but this was established—or rather restored—by blessed Gregory. For from the time of Pope Damasus, though it had previously existed, the same custom had lapsed. Finally, when he perceived that some were murmuring about this and certain other matters, as though he were following the custom of the Church of Constantinople, he did not disdain to give his reason: “In none of these matters have we followed another Church. For the practice that Alleluia should not be said here is reported to have been taken from the Church of Jerusalem, according to the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory; and therefore in this matter we have rather cut off the custom which had been handed down here from the Greeks.”

We sing Alleluia, therefore, after the gradual: the song of joy after the mourning of repentance. Striving earnestly to express the greatness of the consolation laid up for those who mourn, we rather jubilate than sing, and we prolong one short syllable of a worthy word into many neumes, so that the mind, astonished by the pleasing sound, may be filled and caught up to that place where there will always be life without death, day without [Col. 0819B] night, certainty without uncertainty, delight without pain, security without fear, peace without toil, strength without weakness, uprightness without perversity, beauty without deformity, truth without deceit, charity without malice, blessedness without misery.

Yet Alleluia may be referred to the exultation of those who rejoiced at Christ’s miracles, praising the Lord and saying: “For we have seen marvelous things today” (Luke 5), and, “The Lord has visited his people” (Luke 7). Then Alleluia was sung in jubilation, when all the people, seeing, gave praise to God, and all the people rejoiced in all the glorious things done by him (Luke 10). The seventy-two also returned with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (ibid.).

Hence Alleluia is not sung from Septuagesima until Easter, because in a time of sadness the song of joy ought not to be sung, according to that prophetic saying: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136). For Septuagesima spiritually represents the time of Babylonian captivity, in which, sitting and weeping beside the rivers of Babylon, they hung their instruments upon the willows (ibid.). The Tract is then sung, which, both by the harshness of its notes and the length of its words, signifies the misery of our present sojourn. Of this the Psalmist says: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What kind the verse ought to be, and how it is inserted

[Col. 0819D]

The fact that, with a verse inserted, Alleluia is sung twice signifies that, after joy has intervened, the saints will receive the twofold robe of glorification: that of mind and flesh, or of heart and body. For with the robe of the mind the saints “shall exult in glory” and “rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. 149); with the robe of the flesh “the righteous shall shine forth, and run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3).

Therefore the verses should sound nothing sinister or sad, but altogether joyful and sweet, such as: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in majesty” (Ps. 92); “The Lord reigns; let the earth exult” (Ps. 96); “Make a joyful noise to God” (Ps. 99); “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91). For God “shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, [Col. 0820A] and there shall no longer be either mourning or crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Apoc. 21). The same thing is signified by the fact that in certain churches the sequence is sung after Alleluia with sweet jubilation and pleasing melody.

It should further be noted that, in the office of Mass, the diversity of three languages comes together, so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2). This is also shown by the title of the cross, which was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the priest’s sitting while the Epistle is read and the gradual sung

[Col. 0820B] Until this point the priest sat silent, signifying that while John preached, Christ in some fashion remained silent, because he did not preach openly. But, as the Evangelist relates: “After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God” (Mark 1).

Or, because sitting belongs to a victor, the priest’s sitting signifies Christ’s victory, who after fasting conquered the devil: for the tempter left him, and angels came and ministered to him (Matt. 4).

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the priest’s movement from one side of the altar to the other when he is to read the Gospel

After these things have been duly prefaced, the priest approaches the left side of the altar and proclaims the Gospel, signifying that Christ came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9). The righteous are signified by the right hand, sinners by the left. Hence at the judgment the Lord will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left (Matt. 25).

Some nevertheless say here that the priest stands on the right at the beginning of Mass, then turns to the left when he proclaims the Gospel, and toward the end returns again to the right, because the worship of faith was first among the Jewish people; then passed to the Gentiles; and toward the end will return again to the Jews through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, who “will turn the hearts of fathers to their children” (Mal. 4), because “in those days Judah shall be saved and the remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 9).

But since the priest who proclaims the Gospel represents the person of Christ himself, and Christ preached not to the Gentiles but to the Jews, as he himself says in the Gospel, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15), let the prudent hearer consider whether that statement is correct.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Why the deacon who is to read the Gospel kisses the bishop’s right hand

Moreover, when a bishop celebrates, everything is performed more solemnly. The deacon, having kissed the bishop’s right hand, receives the book of the Gospel from the altar and asks the bishop for a blessing; once it is given, he proceeds [Col. 0821A] to the lectern, with candle-bearers going before, carrying lighted tapers and a censer with incense.

Now the figure changes: the deacon, who previously represented the prophet, now represents the evangelist. For “the Law and the prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of heaven is preached” (Matt. 2). This is a deep well; but if it is diligently dug out, we shall draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior (Isa. 12).

The deacon therefore kisses the bishop’s right hand because the preacher ought to proclaim the Gospel for eternal glory, of which the bride says in the Song of Songs: “His right hand shall embrace me” (Song 8). For the angel who came to announce the glory of Christ’s resurrection sat at the right, clothed in a white robe (Mark 16). Although, according to the Apostle, those who sow spiritual things may reap material things (1 Cor. 9), preaching must not be sown for material and earthly things, but for spiritual and eternal things; for “he who sows in blessings shall also reap eternal life from blessings” (2 Cor. 9). A hireling is one who, in the office of preaching, seeks not an eternal reward but temporal advantage.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. When the hands and feet of the supreme pontiff should be kissed

Moreover, the subdeacon or deacon kisses not the hands but the feet of the Roman pontiff, in order to show the highest reverence to the supreme pontiff and to indicate that he is the vicar of him whose feet that woman who had been a sinner in the city kissed (Luke 7). For “the footstool of his feet is to be adored, for it is holy” (Ps. 98); women holding his feet worshipped him when he rose from the dead (John 20).

Generally, no one should kiss the hands of the supreme pontiff except when receiving something from his hands or giving something into his hands, so that it may be shown that in both cases we ought to give him thanks. For as he always gives what is his own, so he never receives what belongs to another. He himself touches with his hands no offering other than the offering of bread, except one offered for the dead. He receives this in his hands in order to rebuke the error of those who teach that alms do not avail the dead.

[Col. 0821D] He touches bread because of reverence for the sacrifice which is made from bread, since he is the vicar of him who says of himself: “I am the living bread, who came down from heaven” (John 6). He receives other offerings at his feet because of what is found in the Acts of the Apostles: they brought the prices of the things sold and laid them at the feet of the apostles (Acts 4).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the blessing which the deacon asks for and receives

When the deacon receives the book of the Gospel, he asks a blessing from the bishop because no one should preach unless he is sent, according to the Apostle: “How shall they preach unless they have first been sent?” (Rom. 10). And the Lord says to the apostles: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest that he may send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. 9; Luke 10).

Isaiah also, when he heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send? And who will go from among you?” answered: “Behold, I am here; send me.” And the Lord said: “Go, and say to this people: Hearing, hear,” etc. (Isa. 6).

The bishop visibly blesses the deacon who is to read the Gospel, which he did not do for the subdeacon who was to read the Epistle, because Christ, remaining invisible, invisibly sent and taught the Law and the prophets, which are signified by the Epistle: “Go,” he says, “preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand’” (Matt. 10). But after he was seen on earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3), he visibly sent the apostles and evangelists. “And they went forth and traveled through the villages, preaching the Gospel and healing everywhere” (Luke 9).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On receiving the book of the Gospel from the altar

The text of the Gospel is taken from the altar because “from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2)—not, of course, the Mosaic Law, which once went forth from Mount Sinai, but the evangelical law, of which the prophet says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a new covenant upon the house of Israel and upon the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I gave to their fathers when I led them out of the land of Egypt. But I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them upon their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jer. 31).

For the Mosaic Law was written on tablets of stone, but the evangelical law is written upon tablets of the heart by the finger of God (2 Cor. 3). For the former was given to hard people, who had a heart of stone; but the latter is given to the obedient, as he himself says in the Psalms: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17).

## CHAPTER XL. On those who precede the deacon with candles and incense

The deacon sends ahead candle-bearers with tapers and incense because the preacher ought to give forth from himself the fragrance of a good reputation. According to the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2). For when someone’s life is despised, it remains for his preaching to be held in contempt; and it is said: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4). “First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7).

He must also kindle desire and joy in the hearts of his hearers, so that they may listen willingly and obey gratefully. Who would not desire good news, and who would not rejoice in good news? For the Gospel, by the interpretation of its very name, signifies good news.

Or, through the fact that the bishop sends two acolytes before the deacon who is to read the Gospel, carrying candles and incense, it is indicated that Christ sent two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was to come, bearing before them the brightness of miracles and the fragrance of virtues. Hence, when they returned, they said: “Lord, even demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10). Christ’s “faces” here are suitably understood as the apostles, who showed peoples the form of his teaching. Therefore he said to them: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10).

Or the censer and candlestick precede the Gospel book because power and renown went before Christ’s teaching, as the Evangelist testifies: “Jesus went forth in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report about him went out through the whole region; and he taught in their synagogues” (Luke 4).

## CHAPTER XLI. How the subdeacon follows when going and precedes when returning with the Gospel

The deacon goes before as teacher, while the subdeacon follows as hearer. The former goes before to preach; the latter follows to minister, because “the laborer is worthy of his wage” (Luke 10), according to the Lord’s command in the Law: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. 25).

After the reading, however, the subdeacon, as though sufficiently instructed, goes before carrying back the Gospel, because he receives the reward of the Gospel for his ministry, according to what the Lord himself promised in the Gospel: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. 10). For this reason the deacon sends him ahead to the bishop: to show that he brings back the fruit of preaching, concerning which the Lord commanded: “I have appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John 15).

In some churches, however, the subdeacon precedes the deacon, carrying a cushion to place beneath the book so that it may rest softly. By the cushion placed beneath one who is weary for rest is signified the consolation of life: namely, that hearers should supply necessities to the preacher as a recompense for his labor. For, as the Apostle says: “Those who serve at the altar share with the altar” (1 Cor. 9).

## CHAPTER XLII. Why the deacon ascends the lectern by one side and descends by another

The deacon proceeds in silence, carrying nothing except the book of the Gospel, because of the Lord’s command: “Greet no one, and carry nothing on the way” (Matt. 10). The subdeacon ascends the lectern by one way and the deacon by another, because the former progresses in the increase of knowledge by teaching, the latter by learning; or because the minister progresses in the increase of righteousness by the merit of his work, and the preacher by the merit of his speech, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35).

But they return to the bishop by the same way, because the reward is attained by final perseverance, as the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10, 24). And because preaching does not suffice without works—“Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1)—the preacher returns by the same way through which the minister had approached.

Or the deacon who is to read the Gospel goes forward by one side and comes out by the other because the apostles first preached to the Jews and afterwards to the Gentiles, as they say to the Jews: “Because you have rejected the word of God and made yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

## CHAPTER XLIII. Why the Gospel is read toward the north
The deacon therefore ascends the ambo to proclaim the Gospel, in accordance with that prophetic saying: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength” (Isa. XL). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. X). For the Lord himself also went up the mountain in order to preach the Gospel; and, opening his mouth, he taught his disciples, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. III), and so forth. He turns his face before him [Col. 0824B] toward the north, in order to show that Christ’s preaching is directed especially against him who said: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). For, according to the prophet, every evil will be disclosed from the north upon the inhabitants of the earth (Jer. I). Therefore the Gospel is read toward the north, so that “the north wind may arise and the south wind come” (Song IV): that is, so that the devil may flee and the Holy Spirit may draw near. Hence the deacon fortifies himself with the sign of the cross, lest the devil, who lies in wait for good works, take devotion from his heart or speech from his mouth.

Thus the priest or deacon, when he is about to read the Gospel, ought to sign himself on the forehead, to sign himself on the mouth, and to sign himself on the breast, as though saying: “I am not ashamed of Christ’s cross, but with my heart [Col. 0824C] I believe what I preach with my mouth.” “We preach,” says the Apostle, “Jesus Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (I Cor. I). But we ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom is salvation (Gal. VI), because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his own majesty, and that of the Father, and of the holy angels” (Luke IX). He ought also to sign the book and kiss it; the deacon or presbyter kisses the book after the Gospel has been spoken, and not before, as though saying: “This is the book of the Crucified One, through whom we have received reconciliation.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the mystery of the cross and its manifold effect

O how profound is the mystery of the cross! How lofty is the sacrament! For we read that Moses, at the Lord’s command, raised up a bronze serpent as a sign; those who had been bitten by serpents were healed when they looked upon it (Num. XXI). Christ himself expounded this in the Gospel, saying: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life” (John III).

We also read that, when Joseph brought Manasseh and Ephraim to Jacob, placing the elder at his right and the younger at his left, so that he might bless them in order, Jacob crossed his hands—that is, interlaced them in the form of a cross—placing his right hand upon the head of Ephraim the younger, and his left upon the head of [Col. 0825A] Manasseh the elder, and said: “May the angel who delivered me from all evils bless these boys” (Gen. XLVIII), and so forth.

Ezekiel likewise heard the Lord saying to a man clothed in linen, who had a scribe’s inkhorn at his loins: “Pass through the midst of the city and mark Tau upon the foreheads of the men who grieve and groan” (Ezek. IX). After this he says to seven men: “Pass through the middle of the city, and strike everyone upon whom you do not see Tau. Let not your eye spare anyone” (ibid.). John also saw an angel ascending from the rising of the sun, bearing the seal of the living God; and he cried in a loud voice to the four angels to whom it had been given to harm the earth and sea: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have marked the servants of our God upon their foreheads” (Rev. VII).

Hence also, when [Col. 0825B] the Lord struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, he passed over the houses of the Hebrews without harm because he saw blood upon the lintel and upon each doorpost (Exod. XVIII). While Moses held his hands stretched out, Israel, fighting Amalek, prevailed (Exod. XVII). Wood cast into Marah sweetened its bitter waters (Exod. XV). And, when wood was cast into the Jordan, the iron that had fallen in floated up (IV Kings VI). This is the tree of life in the midst of paradise (Gen. III), concerning which the Wise Man declares: “Blessed is the wood through which righteousness is accomplished, because God has reigned from the wood” (Wis. XIV). For he made firm the circle of the earth, which shall not be moved (Ps. XCII). Those who said, “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. II), did not know the mysteries of God, nor did they comprehend what is [Col. 0825C] the breadth and length, what the height and depth (Eph. III).

Therefore the cross restores health, bestows blessing, distinguishes from the faithless, frees from dangers, drives out enemies, and makes victors. The cross is the mystery of faith, the support of hope, the key of knowledge, the form of righteousness, the magnificence of kings, the glory of priests, the support of the needy, the consolation of the poor, the guide of the blind, the staff of the lame, the hope of the despairing, and the resurrection of the dead.

## CHAPTER XLV. How the sign of the cross is to be made

The sign of the cross is to be made with three fingers, because it is impressed under invocation of the Trinity, of which the prophet says: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” [Col. 0825D] (Isa. XL). It should descend from the upper part to the lower, and pass from the right to the left, because Christ descended from heaven to earth and passed from the Jews to the Gentiles.

Some, however, make the sign of the cross from the left to the right, because we ought to pass from misery to glory, just as Christ passed from death to life and from hell to paradise; especially so that they may mark themselves and others alike, in one and the same manner. Yet it is clear that, when we make the sign of the cross over others, we mark them from their left to their right. But if you attend carefully, even over others we make the sign of the cross from right to left, because we do not mark them as though they had turned their backs, but as though they were presenting their faces.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the greeting prefixed to the Gospel

[Col. 0826A]

The deacon therefore, standing in the ambo, greets the people, saying, “The Lord be with you,” observing what the Lord commanded: “Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace to this house” (Matt. X; Luke X). The people, standing—something they had not done while the epistle was read—answer devoutly and attentively: “And with your spirit.” Then the deacon, in order to render them well-disposed and receptive, immediately adds: “The continuation of the holy Gospel,” and so forth. They too answer with reverence and honor: “Glory to you, O Lord,” glorifying the Lord because he has sent them the word of salvation, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: “And they glorified the Lord, saying: Therefore God has granted repentance unto life even to the Gentiles” (Acts II).

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the preeminence of the Gospel

[Col. 0826B] Indeed, just as the head surpasses the body and the other limbs serve it, so the Gospel excels the whole office, and its other parts accord with it by intelligible reason. It is the Word of the Word, the Speech of the Speech, the Wisdom of Wisdom: the Word of the Word which was in the beginning with God, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John I); the Speech of the Speech who came from the royal seats (Wis. XVIII), bearing a commanding decree, living and efficacious, and more penetrating than every two-edged sword (Heb. IV); the Wisdom of Wisdom which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. VIII).

It is the paradise [Col. 0826C] of delights, the garden of spices, the wine-cellar, the upper chamber of life, the table of offering, the chariot of Amminadab, the tower of David, the treasury of the temple, the householder’s treasure. “This is the fountain of gardens, the well of living waters that flow in a rush from Lebanon” (Song IV). Therefore let the deacon strive to show himself pure in heart, clean in speech, and chaste in deed, so that he may worthily proclaim the most holy Gospel; for the well of living waters—that is, evangelical preaching—does not flow in a rush, that is, freely, except from Lebanon, that is, from a chaste heart and a stainless mouth. “For praise is not fitting in a sinner’s mouth” (Ecclus. XV). But God says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant [Col. 0826D] into your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX).

Here Moses does not speak (Exod. IV), he who from yesterday and the day before was not eloquent, but had become slow and impeded of tongue from the time that he heard the Lord speaking to him. Here Isaiah does not speak, who says of himself: “Woe is me, because I have been silent, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa. VI). Here Jeremiah does not speak, who says: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. I). Rather, here the Father speaks in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages (Heb. I).

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Why, after the Gospel, the book and censer are brought back to the bishop

After the Gospel has been read, the book and censer are brought back to the bishop [Col. 0827A], because all good things ought to be referred back to him from whom all things proceed. Hence many psalms are entitled, “Unto the end, a Psalm of David.” For Christ is the end that brings to completion but does not consume, the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. The bishop therefore smells the incense and kisses the codex, because Christ approves and accepts what he himself has inspired and taught. For God receives nothing except what he accomplishes, nor rewards anything except what he gives. For, as all things he makes are good, so nothing is good except what he makes. Thus “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I).

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Creed sung after the Gospel

[Col. 0827B] Since one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X), the Church, to show that it has received the word of the Gospel in its heart, immediately sings aloud with its mouth the Creed of faith. The bishop nevertheless begins it, to signify that every good proceeds from Christ. For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I). Therefore, lest that heavenly musician say, “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matt. II), the Catholic choir answers the teaching of the Gospel with a harmonious voice and solemn rejoicing professes the Catholic faith.

*Symbolum*, in Greek, means in Latin either “indication” or “contribution”: both because it indicates the full rule and perfect account of faith, and because it gathers together in one the articles of faith. For it is handed down that, after the apostles had received the holy Paraclete and were about to depart to preach the Gospel, they conferred together concerning the articles of faith and resolved that, just as all were in harmony in one faith, so all should preach one faith in harmony. Thus, when they composed the *Symbolum*, each contributed one *bolum*, that is, one portion. Hence, according to the catalogue of the apostles, it is known to contain twelve portions. Therefore the Creed after the Gospel shows faith after preaching. Thus John says: “As he was saying these things, many believed in him” (John VII); for according to the Apostle, “faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. X). Pope Damasus decreed [Col. 0827D] that the Creed should be sung at Mass, by decree of the holy universal synod held at Constantinople.

## CHAPTER L. On the twelve parts of each Creed, both the Apostles’ and the Constantinopolitan

I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.

And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.

Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.

Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.

[Col. 0828A] He descended into the lower regions; on the third day he rose from the dead.

He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.

From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

I believe in the Holy Spirit.

The holy catholic Church, the communion of saints.

The forgiveness of sins.

The resurrection of the flesh.

And life everlasting. Amen.

The Constantinopolitan Creed is likewise known to contain twelve clauses.

I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.

[Col. 0828B] And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made.

Who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, and was made man.

He was also crucified for us under Pontius Pilate; he suffered and was buried.

And he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.

And he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

And he will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

[Col. 0828C] And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son; who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified; who spoke through the prophets.

And in one holy catholic and apostolic Church.

I confess one baptism for the forgiveness of sins.

And I await the resurrection of the dead.

And life in the age to come. Amen.

These are the twelve loaves, fresh and warm, which were set before the Lord upon the table of offering (Lev. XXIV). These are the gifts which the leaders of the tribes offered on twelve days at the consecration of the altar (Num. VII). For the number twelve [Col. 0828D] is consecrated in many ways: in the twelve apostles, twelve prophets, twelve patriarchs, twelve spies, twelve leaders, twelve tribes, twelve springs, twelve stones, twelve seats, twelve hours, twelve months, twelve years, twelve signs, twelve stars, twelve gems, twelve gates, twelve corners, twelve foundations, twelve rods, twelve cubits, twelve baskets, twelve bowls, twelve dishes, twelve mortars, twelve oxen, twelve little lions, and twelve rams.

It is also an abundant number, composed of two [Col. 0829A] sixes, signifying the perfection of thought and work, or of mind and body; and of three multiplied by four and four by three, signifying faith in the indivisible Trinity and the teaching of the four Gospels, or the three theological virtues and the four civic virtues. This number, enlarged by the sum of its own parts, grows into sixteen, which consists of ten and six and signifies the fulfillment of the commandments: for there are ten commandments of the Law, which we fulfill in six days, rising to the perfection of charity, which, according to the Apostle, is known to have sixteen qualities: “Charity,” he says, “is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, [Col. 0829B] does not think evil, does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices together with truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER LI. On the days upon which the Creed is to be said at Mass

The Creed ought to be sung at Mass only on those solemnities of which some mention is made in the Creed: namely, on every Sunday; at the Nativity of the Lord; the Epiphany of the Lord; the Lord’s Supper; Easter; the Ascension; Pentecost; all feasts of blessed Mary; the Holy Cross; angels; apostles; dedications of churches; and the commemoration of All Saints—although that itself is a feast of dedication.

It is sung within the octave of the Nativity of the Lord, [Col. 0829C] except on the day of the Innocents, when songs of gladness are silent: both because “a voice was heard in Ramah, of weeping and great lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children” (Jer. XXXI; Matt. II); because the Innocents descended into hell; and also because they confessed not by speaking but by dying. Yet it is sung on the octave itself because of the glory of the resurrection, which the octave signifies.

It is sung within the octaves of Epiphany, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, the apostles Peter and Paul, and the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. Thus, although the Creed is not sung on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist or on the feast of Saint Lawrence, it is nevertheless sung in their octaves, because they fall within the octaves of the Apostles and of the Assumption. For this reason the preface concerning the apostles is sung in the octave of Saint John, and the preface concerning the Assumption in the octave [Col. 0829D] of Saint Lawrence.

All these are commemorated in the Creed, though some obscurely: the Epiphany, which is the feast of baptism, concerning which the Creed contains, “I confess one baptism”; the Lord’s Supper, which is the solemnity of the Eucharist, to which refers what the Creed contains, “the communion of saints”; and angels, who should be understood by the name “heaven,” when the Creed says, “Creator” or “maker of heaven and earth,” according to the saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I), that is, the angelic and human natures.

Some, however, think that the Creed should not be sung on feasts of angels, because angels have never had faith, but sight: they do not believe, but know. The dedication of churches is indicated by the clause, “the holy catholic Church”; for then the catholic Church is sanctified and, so to speak, made catholic when it is dedicated. The resurrection of the dead, contained in the Creed in the words “I await the resurrection of the dead,” refers to octaves.

Yet on the second feast of Agnes the Creed is not sung, because, although it is celebrated on an octave day, it is not a feast of the octave. Hence it is neither written in the calendar nor announced in church as an octave. Some not unreasonably sing the Creed on each day of Eastertide, as on every Sunday, from the day of the resurrection to the feast of the Ascension. Some also sing the Creed on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, calling her the apostle of the apostles, because she properly, or first, announced to the apostles the joy of the resurrection (John XX). Yet some things are mentioned in the Creed whose commemorations do not include the singing of the Creed, such as the Passion and Burial, because the office of those days does not follow the rule of other offices.

## CHAPTER LII. By whom, and where, the Creed is to be sung

Since Christ did not come to preach to the Gentiles but to the Jews, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Accordingly he commanded the apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X), until after the resurrection [Col. 0830C] he commanded the same men: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI).

Therefore, when the Roman pontiff celebrates solemnly, the Creed of faith is sung not by the singers in the choir but by the subdeacons at the altar; and they respond generally to all the parts, until the pontiff says: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” For until after Christ’s resurrection, only the Church of the Jews—represented by the subdeacons, who stand above at the altar—believed with the heart unto righteousness and confessed with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X). But thereafter the singers in the choir respond and sing everything, because after the resurrection the Church of the Gentiles, represented by the singers who stand below in the choir, received Christ’s faith and offered praises [Col. 0830D] to the Savior.

Between the Gospel and the sacrifice, however, the choir sings the offertory, because between preaching and the Passion the Gentile people sang, offering the vow of faith, when the Canaanite woman came out from the regions of Tyre and Sidon, cried out, and said: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” At last, commending her faith, the Lord said: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you desire” (Matt. XV).

## CHAPTER LIII. On the offertory

When the priest is about to say “Let us pray,” he first says, “The Lord be with you,” because unless the Lord is with us, we cannot pray for our salvation. Then [Col. 0831A] the offertory is sung, taking its name from offering, because while it is sung the priest receives offerings from the people or victims from the ministers. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. I). The order is fitting: after preaching come faith in the heart, praise in the mouth, and fruit in action—faith in the Creed, praise in the offertory, fruit in the sacrifice. Therefore the offering is sung, because a sacrifice of praise is offered. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will go round about and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of joyful proclamation; I will sing and say a psalm to the Lord” (Ps. XXVI). And in Paralipomenon: “When they offered the burnt offerings, they began to sing praises to the Lord and to sound together upon the various instruments which King David had devised” (Par. XXIX).

## CHAPTER LIV. On the silence after the offertory

[Col. 0831B]

After this the priest seeks the solitude of silence, as the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion approaches. This signifies that Jesus was no longer walking openly among the Jews when they were devising to kill him, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples. Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council and said: “What shall we do, because this man performs many signs? If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation.” But one of them, Caiaphas by name, being high priest in that year, said to them: “You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish.” From that day therefore [Col. 0831C] they planned to kill him (John XI). The priest’s silence thus signifies Christ’s hiding-place.

## CHAPTER LV. On the washing of hands before the sacrifice is offered

It should be noted that, after the priest has said, “Let us pray,” he does not immediately add the prayer; rather, before approaching the altar, he washes his hands, so that with washed hands he may receive the offering, offer incense, and pour forth prayer. For it is written in Exodus: “You shall make a bronze basin and place it in the tabernacle of testimony by the altar; and, water having been put into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it when they are about to enter the tabernacle of testimony and when they are about to approach the altar” (Exod. XXX).

Therefore, although the bishop had already washed his hands when he was about to enter the tabernacle, he washes his hands again when he is about to approach the altar, so that, ever more and more cleansed, he may offer a spotless, holy victim pleasing to God [Col. 0831D] (Rom. XII). Hence the Psalmist, though cleansed, asked to be cleansed further: “Wash me more abundantly from my injustice, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. L).

The priest, then, who is about to offer the victim, ought to wash his conscience with tears of repentance, according to the words: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Ps. VI). For Christ too, before offering the true and unique sacrifice upon the altar of the cross, shed compassionate tears at Lazarus’s resurrection, as the Evangelist testifies: “Jesus,” he says, “groaned in spirit, troubled himself, and wept” (John XI).

## CHAPTER LVI. On the corporals, and why one part is spread out and another folded

Meanwhile the deacon arranges upon the altar the corporal cloths, which signify the linen cloths in which Jesus’ body was wrapped. The part folded over the chalice signifies the cloth that had been upon his head, separately wrapped in one place. Concerning these, only the following is found in the canon:

> “With the consent of all we decree that no one dare celebrate the sacrifice of the altar upon a silk cloth or one that has been dyed, but upon pure linen [variant: *linteo*], [Note: [Col. 0831D] *De consecratione*, distinction, canon 1.] produced and woven from earthly flax, consecrated by a bishop, just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud.”

Yet something else may also be signified in them. For the cloth called the corporal is twofold: one cloth, which the deacon spreads completely over the altar; another, which he lays folded over the chalice. The extended part signifies faith; the folded part signifies understanding. For this mystery ought to be believed, but cannot be comprehended, so that faith may have merit where human reason provides no proof. Let us therefore believe with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith (I Tim. I). But let us not presume to investigate, because “those searching with searching have failed” (Ps. LXIII). For it is written [Col. 0832C] that “the searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. XXV). For those who said, “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” went back and no longer walked with Christ (John VI).

## CHAPTER LVII. On the offering and incense; why the priest moves and circles the incense three times; and why the altar is incensed completely on every side

Then the priest rises and approaches the altar to receive the mystical offering from the ministers. This signifies what John the Evangelist recounts: “Jesus, six days before the Passover, came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom Jesus raised. They made him a supper there, and Martha served” [Col. 0832D] (John XII). Once the offering has been received, incense is immediately burned, by which is indicated what the Evangelist at once adds: “Mary therefore took a pound of costly ointment of pure nard and anointed Jesus’ feet; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (ibid.).

That the priest moves the incense over and around three times signifies that Mary displayed and applied ointment three times about Jesus’ body: first, when she anointed his feet in the house of Simon the Pharisee (Luke VII); second, when she poured ointment upon his head in the house of Simon the leper (Matt. XVI); and third, when she bought spices so that she might come and anoint Jesus, now laid in the tomb. For an intention is reckoned as a deed when it did not depend upon the person herself whether she completed what she had begun.

That the whole altar is incensed on every side signifies that this deed spreads through the whole Church in every direction, as the Lord himself testifies: “Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, what she has done shall be spoken of in memory of her” [Col. 0833A] (ibid.). In a moral sense, the incense of devotion must be burned in the censer of the heart by the fire of charity, so that it may emit a sweet fragrance. Scripture says of this: “To exercise the priesthood, and to have praise in his name, and to offer him worthy incense as a sweet fragrance” (Ecclus. XLV). For the priest receives this incense—that is, Christ accepts it—and with it incenses the sacrifice and the altar.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the manner and order of offering the sacrifice, and the mixing of water and wine

But it is pleasing to explain further the mystery of the offering. The subdeacon prepares the chalice, placing bread and wine in it, because indeed the Law—which is fittingly represented here by the subdeacon—foreshadowed the mystery of this offering, teaching that Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine. For he was priest of God Most High (Gen. XIV). Expounding this, the Prophet says to Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

The deacon receives the prepared chalice and sets it upon the altar, because the Gospel, of which the deacon is the figure, commended this rite of sacrifice to the Church, which, as we said above, is represented by the altar [Col. 0833C]. Yet first the deacon hands the paten with the host to the bishop, and the bishop himself places it upon the altar, signifying that Christ himself first instituted this sacrament and handed it over to the Church for celebration, saying: “For this is my body, which shall be given for you; do this in remembrance of me” (I Cor. XI).

The bishop mixes water with wine in the chalice because Christ reconciled the people in his death. For it is written that many waters are many peoples (Rev. XI). But Christ poured out his blood for the people, as he himself testifies: “This is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. XXVI). And blood and water came forth together from Christ’s side, so that neither might Christ be without the people nor the people without Christ. For when water is mixed with wine, Christ and the people are united.

But the Mosaic Law also prefigures this mystery, as the Apostle explains, saying: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). Therefore the subdeacon hands the bishop the cruet containing water, which the bishop pours into the chalice, so that, just as water is not separated from wine, the people may never be separated from Christ. The chalice is placed on the right side of the offering, as though about to receive the blood which is believed—or seen—to have flowed from Christ’s right side. For as bread is transubstantiated into body, so certainly wine is transubstantiated into blood.

Moreover, when the priest takes the paten and cruet, chalice and censer—the paten with the host, the cruet with [Col. 0834A] water, the chalice with wine, and the censer with incense—he makes the sign of the cross over them, so that through the power of the cross every company [variant: “endeavor”] of diabolical malice may flee, lest it prevail in any way against priest or sacrifice. For this reason he also moves and circles the incense and sacrifice at the altar in the form of a cross, so that the malignity of diabolical deceit may be driven away by both the sign of the cross and the incense of the censer, as we have said and shown above that both are effective for this purpose.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the paten upon which the sacrifice of bread is offered

The paten, so called from *patendo* (“being open”), signifies a broad and spacious heart. Upon this paten—that is, upon the breadth of charity—the sacrifice of righteousness ought to be offered, so that the soul’s burnt offering may be rich. The apostles had this breadth of heart when Peter said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” All the disciples likewise said this to Christ. Therefore the Lord added: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI).

But the breadth of heart fled from them and lay hidden when all the disciples, abandoning their master, fled and hid. Therefore, after receiving the offering, the priest conceals the paten beneath the corporal, or the subdeacon, standing back from the altar, holds it wrapped up behind him. By this are signified the disciples’ flight or hiding-place: when the true sacrifice was offered, they fled, leaving Christ, and hid, just as he himself had foretold: “You will all suffer scandal because of me this night. For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” [Col. 0834C] (ibid.).

Therefore, when the priest is about to announce the blessing (*eulogium*) of the Lord’s resurrection, he takes up the paten again, because, when it was evening on that first day of the week and the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst and said to them: “Peace to you” (John XX), gathering back the sheep who had fled in fear.

## CHAPTER LX. On the priest’s bowing

Then the priest, bowing, prays first for himself and then for the people, urging the people to pray for him: “Pray for me, brethren.” For we ought to pray for one another, according to the Apostle, so that we may be saved [Col. 0834D] (James V). For the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Amen I say to you, if two or three agree upon any matter on earth, whatever they ask shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

Christ too prayed first for himself and then for the people, saying: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you. Holy Father, preserve those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are” (John XVII). By bowing, the priest signifies Christ’s humiliation, who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death—indeed, death upon a cross (Phil. II).

At last the priest says the prayer which he had interrupted, because then Christ finally returned to Jerusalem, to the house of prayer which he had left for a time when [Col. 0835A] he withdrew to Ephraim. For the Gospel says: “When Jesus came to Jerusalem, he entered the temple of God and cast out those selling and buying in the temple, saying: My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI).

## CHAPTER LXI. On the preface
For Jesus was now again walking openly; and so, on the next day, when the great crowd that had assembled for the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, they took palm branches and went out to meet him, crying: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (John 12). Therefore the priest raises his hands and voice, saying aloud: “For ever and ever.” The end of the prayer is the beginning of the Preface [Col. 0835B], by which the priest indicates that Christ is the cornerstone (1 Pet. 2), who made both one (Eph. 2), comprising Jews and Gentiles, so that there might be one fold and one shepherd (John 10). Hence, after the praise of the Jews, the Evangelist describes the faith of the Gentiles. “Now there were,” he says, “certain Gentiles among those who had come up to worship on the feast-day. These asked Philip, saying: ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus’” (John 12).

When the priest is about to say the most worthy prayer, he first offers a greeting, wishing that we may be such persons as the Lord may deign to remain with, and may celebrate with us that banquet to which the woman brought an alabaster jar of costly genuine nard ointment and poured it upon the head of the reclining Lord (ibid.). Hence the priest immediately [Col. 0835C] adds: “Lift up your hearts.” And the choir adds: “We have them lifted up to the Lord,” so that the Church, like the woman truly bearing ointment, may lift her heart upward to the very divinity of the Word and, reaching by faith that Head equal to God the Father, anoint it with the ointment of Catholic confession.

The priest continues its praise, saying: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” And the choir responds: “It is fitting and just.” For we ought to render thanks to almighty God through Christ our Lord, believing and confessing that through him angels praise his majesty, dominations adore, and powers tremble. Indeed, to pour out this ointment is to confess this mystery of the Godhead, which John the Evangelist compounded from the marrow of the Gospel-spices [Col. 0835D]: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

The Church fittingly concludes this proclamation of holy confession by singing, together with angels and human beings, this hymn of a devout heart: “Holy, holy, holy.” This prayer, or hymn, contains words spoken partly by angels and partly by human beings. For it is read in Isaiah that the seraphim cried one to another and said: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6). It is likewise read in the Gospel that those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” [Col. 0836A] (Matt. 21). The voice of the angels commends the mystery of Trinity and unity in God; the voice of human beings proclaims the sacrament of divinity and humanity in Christ.

Yet the office of the Preface may be referred to that occasion when Jesus went up into the large furnished upper room. There he spoke much with his disciples and, giving thanks, offered a hymn to God the Father (Luke 22), which John the Evangelist describes until Jesus went out across the brook Cedron; of this Matthew says: “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matt. 26). Pope Gelasius composed tracts and hymns and dictated the Prefaces of the sacraments in cautious and polished language. Sixtus, however, ordained that the hymn “Holy, holy, holy” should be sung.

## CHAPTER LXII. Exposition of the Same Preface

[Col. 0836B]

The priest therefore exhorts us to have our hearts lifted up to the Lord, according to the Apostle’s exhortation: “Seek those things which are above” (Col. 3), and not those which are upon the earth [variant: “set your minds”]. For “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. 6). Many indeed speak of heavenly things with their mouths while meditating upon earthly things in their hearts; the Lord reproaches them through the prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). Thus in every prayer it is sinful—but in this prayer perilous—for the heart to be divided from the mouth, or the mouth from the heart; for one who does not listen to himself is not heard by God either.

The choir, therefore, replying, professes that it has accepted the priest’s admonition when it says: “We have them lifted up to the Lord.” Let it therefore take diligent care not to lie damnably to the Holy Spirit by having its heart cast down toward the world. After making them attentive and devout, the priest exhorts them to give thanks to the Lord our God. For he is God, that is, Creator; he is Lord, that is, Redeemer; and he is our Jesus, that is, Saviour. Then he will be most truly ours, when he will be all in all—that is, the sufficiency of every individual—because he is God, who created us from nothing; he is Lord, who redeemed us by his blood; he is ours, who saved us by his own gift. In creating, he gave us nature; in redeeming, he gave us grace; and in saving, he will bestow glory.

The choir [Col. 0836D], in responding, approves and affirms the priest’s words: “It is fitting and just.” It is fitting with respect to the Lord, because he is the Lord our God; it is just with respect to us, because we are his people and the sheep of his pasture (Ps. 99). “Truly it is fitting and just, equitable and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give thanks to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God,” etc. It is fitting, because you made us by sheer will; just, because you redeemed us through pure mercy; equitable, because you justify us freely; salutary, because you glorify us eternally: that we should give you thanks everywhere, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, always. Hence the Psalmist: “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 102); and again: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33).

“Through Christ our Lord.” For we have with the Father an advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous Lord, who intercedes for us and is himself the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2), who is heard in all things because of his reverence (Heb. 5). Through him, as mediator, we offer praise; through him, as advocate, we render thanks; through him angels praise your majesty, dominations adore, and powers tremble. Through him, then, they praise, adore, and tremble—through whom all things were made, through whom all orders of spirits were created. For God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made (Gen. 1). He spoke by the Word and made by the Word, because “by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32). “And in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.
