All things were made through him [Col. 0837B], and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

They praise: hence the Psalmist, “Praise him, all his angels” (Ps. 148). They adore: hence Ezra, “The host of heaven adores you” (2 Esdr. 9). They tremble: hence Job, “The pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his coming” (Job 20). They are said to tremble not with fearful dread, since they are perfectly blessed, but from the emotion of wonder, or in the service of obedience, since, according to the Apostle, they are all ministering spirits sent forth for service (Heb. 1). The heavens are said to praise God because they furnish material for praise. Hence the Prophet: “Let the heavens of heavens and the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148). Or here by “heavens” he understands thrones, because the Lord says: “Heaven [Col. 0837C] is my seat” (Isa. 66).

*Seraphin* means “burning” or “kindling,” because above the rest they burn and are kindled in charity. This name is found both as neuter and as masculine: it ends in *-n* in the neuter, as in this place, “blessed *Seraphin*”; it ends in *-m* in the masculine, as in the prophet: “The seraphim cried one to another” (Isa. 6). But since there are nine orders of angels, why are only six named in the Preface, with three omitted? Do not the omitted ones, together with the rest, glorify and adore the divine majesty? Far be it! For “the powers of heaven” include them all. Hence the Psalmist: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their host by the spirit of his mouth” (Ps. 32). And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23).

Or perhaps this was provided by a reason that is hidden but certain. Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0837D] Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.] teaches that there are three orders of angels, placing three in each so that the likeness of the Trinity may be shown as impressed upon them. There are three higher, three lower, and three middle orders. The higher are seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; the middle, dominations, principalities, and powers; the lower, virtues, archangels, and angels. Yet from each grouping one order is removed: from the higher, cherubim; from the middle, principalities; and from the lower, archangels. This is because, in comparison with the eternal Trinity—whose majesty is especially commended here—every other trinity is found diminished and imperfect. For “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” [Col. 0838A] (Ps. 88).

For some trace of the uncreated Trinity shines forth in every creature: in angel, in human being, and in the world. Thus the prophet says to the angel: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” (Ezek. 28). Scripture says of the human being: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1). The Apostle says of the world: “The invisible things of God are understood, from the creation of the world, by the things that are made” (Rom. 1). Every trinity, whether spiritual in the angel, corporeal in the world, or spiritual and corporeal in the human being, displays a certain likeness of the divine Trinity; nevertheless, it does not attain the truth of that likeness itself.

For God is uncreated Spirit, immeasurable, unchangeable, supremely powerful, supremely wise, and supremely good: uncreated, because he did not begin in time or from time; immeasurable, because he is not circumscribed by place; unchangeable, because he is not altered in deed [variant: “disposition”]; supremely powerful, because nothing is impossible to him; supremely wise, because nothing is unknown to him; supremely good, because there is no envy in him. “From whom are all things, in whom are all things, through whom are all things” (Rom. 2): from whom all things are created powerfully, through whom all things are formed wisely, and in whom all things are preserved diligently. They are created through power, formed through wisdom, and preserved through care: created through the power of the Father, the efficient cause; formed through the wisdom of the Son, the ordering cause; perfected through the care [Col. 0838C] of the Holy Spirit, the completing cause.

For “there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 3). They are three personally, each distinct by his own relation: the Father by generation, the Word by sonship, and the Holy Spirit by procession. They are one effectively [variant: “essentially”]: all wholly one in nature, power, and will, and in every respect whatever is predicated according to substance. Angels praise, dominations adore, and powers tremble before this eternal and undivided Trinity; with them also are joined our voices. For almighty God created two rational creatures, angelic and human, that they might devote themselves to divine praises and render him thanksgiving; while they celebrate together with equal desire, they are joined like the higher and lower strings of a heavenly lyre. Of this John says: “And I heard the voice of harpists playing on their harps, and they sang as it were a new song” (Rev. 14).

With supplicating confession—without proud presumption, but with humble praise—they say: “Holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth” (Isa. 6). “Holy” is said three times and “God” once, so that the mystery of Trinity and unity may be confirmed. Not only did the seraphim cry this beneath God’s exalted throne, according to the prophet, but also the four living creatures, according to the Apocalypse (ch. 6), around the throne, had no rest day or night, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty.” He is called holy—that is, sanctifying, not sanctified. Hence: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” [Col. 0839A] (Lev. 10 and 20). Holy is the Father, as the Son says: “Father, sanctify in truth those whom you have given me, because you are holy” (John 17). Holy is the Son, as the angel declares: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1; John 20). Holy is the Spirit, as Christ says: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.”

He is called “Lord God Sabaoth,” that is, “Lord of hosts”—namely, of angels and human beings—whose ordered array is terrible as an army in battle formation (Song 11). God has as many hosts on earth as there are orders in the Church; he has as many in heaven as there are orders among the angels. “Heaven and earth are full of your glory” [Col. 0839B]. By the names heaven and earth, angels and human beings are declared full of divine grace; or, literally, heaven and earth are filled with divine glory, because deity [variant: “divinity”] is everywhere. Hence the Prophet: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138). Above all things, yet not raised up; beneath all things, yet not cast down; within all things, yet not enclosed; outside all things, yet not excluded. Thus it is found in Job (ch. 11): “It is higher than heaven—what will you do? Deeper than hell—how will you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea” [Col. 0840A].

But because it is necessary for eternal salvation also to confess the mystery of the Incarnation, there fittingly follows: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” “I,” he says, “have come in the name of my Father” (John 5). The Father’s name is the Son, of whom the prophet says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar” (Isa. 30). “Hosanna in the highest.” *Hosanna* is a Hebrew word meaning “Save, I beseech you,” compounded from *osi*, meaning “save,” and *anna*, an interjection of entreaty; or *osi* and *anna* are two words uttered elliptically. *Hosanna* is said twice because of the two portions of salvation, the robe of the mind and the robe of the flesh, with which the saints are made blessed in glory. This verse of praise is found in Psalm 117. For what the crowds said, “Hosanna,” is what is said there: “O Lord, save me”; and the same words are followed by: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 5).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0839]

## CHAPTER I. On the Silence after the Preface

[Col. 0839B]

After the acclaimed proclamation follows secret [Col. 0839C] silence. For, as John the Evangelist relates, after Jesus had been honourably received by the crowds with psalms and praises, he went away and hid himself from them (John 12). This was not from the fearful terror of one fleeing, but from the office of divine dispensation, because his hour had not yet come. When it did come, he went willingly to the Passion. “Rise,” he said, “let us go; behold, he who will betray me is at hand” (Matt. 20). For “he was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53). Thus, when the cohort and attendants came with lanterns, torches, and weapons to seize him, Jesus, knowing all things that would come upon him, went forward and said to them: “Whom do you seek?” They answered him: “Jesus of Nazareth.” He said to them: “I am he” (John 18).

Therefore, that hiding-place of Christ is represented by this secret [Col. 0839D] silence, in which, when the tumult of words ceases, devotion alone, intent upon God, is directed toward him.

Then the priest ought to enter the chamber of his heart and, having shut the door of the senses, pray to God the Father—not with many words, like the Gentiles, who think that they are heard through much speaking (Matt. 6), but with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith (1 Cor. 1). For God hears not the voice but the heart, nor must he be reminded by cries, because he searches the reins and hearts (Jer. 17). Hannah, prefiguring the Church, is recorded to have observed this: she obtained what she asked, not by clamorous petition, but by silent devotion. For it is written in the Book of Kings that Hannah spoke in her heart, and only her lips moved, [Col. 0840B] while her voice was not heard at all (1 Sam. 1). Likewise in the Psalms: “Speak in your hearts, and be pierced with compunction in your chambers” (Ps. 4). God is Spirit [Col. 0840C], and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4).

Lest dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment (Eccl. 4), let them be driven away by the fan of the Spirit, so that, when the south wind comes, it may blow through the garden and the spices may flow forth (Song 4). That is, lest intrusive thoughts take away the devotion of prayer, let them be repelled by the inspiration of grace, so that the Holy Spirit, coming, may make the mind fruitful and virtues may abound. Moreover, lest the most holy words become cheapened when nearly everyone, knowing them by common use, sang them in streets, lanes, and other unsuitable places, the Church decreed that this supplication, which is judged secret, should be said secretly by the priest. It is therefore reported that, before the custom which later prevailed, when certain shepherds sang it in a field, they were struck by divine judgment.

## CHAPTER II. Those Whose Commemoration Is Observed in the Secret

In the Secret is recalled the memory of the Passion: namely, of those things done during the week before Easter, from the tenth day of the first month, when Jesus came to Jerusalem, to the seventeenth, when he rose from the dead. Therefore, in most sacramentaries, an image of Christ is painted between the Preface and the Canon, so that not only the understanding of the text but also the sight of the picture may inspire remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. And perhaps it was done by divine providence, though not arranged by human design, that the Canon should begin with the letter **T**, which by its shape shows and expresses in figure the sign of the cross. For **T** signifies the mystery of the cross, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Mark *Thau* upon the foreheads of the men who mourn and groan” (Ezek. 9).

## CHAPTER III. The Three Signs Made over the Offering and the Chalice

“You, therefore, most merciful Father.” On the same day when praises were acclaimed to Christ by the crowds—namely, the tenth day of the first month, when, according to the Law, the typical lamb was brought into the houses of the Hebrews (Exod. 12)—the true Lamb entered Jerusalem. Beset by most wicked butchers, he was sought for death by many snares. He was handed over by three: by God, by Judas, and by the Jew. Of the first handing-over the Apostle says: “God did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all” [Col. 0841B] (Rom. 8). Of the second it is written in Matthew (ch. 26): “Judas sought an opportunity to hand him over.” Of the third it is read in John (ch. 28): “Your nation and your chief priests handed you over to me.”

The first was from grace, because “he loved us and gave himself up for us” (Eph. 5). The second was from avarice, because they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver, and from then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over without the crowds (Luke 22). The third was from envy, for Pilate knew that they had handed him over out of envy (Matt. 27). God therefore handed him over as a gift; Judas for a payment; the Jew as an unblemished sacrifice—one which, indeed, the Jews did not offer, but the Gentiles did. For the kingdom was taken away from the Jews and given to the nation producing its fruits (Matt. 21).

To signify this, the priest makes three crosses over the offering and chalice while saying: “These gifts, these presents, these holy unblemished sacrifices.” He commemorates that handing-over which God made as a gift, Judas for a payment, and the Jew as an unblemished sacrifice. Yet each handed him over unto death, even death on the cross (Phil. 2); for although the agents were different, what was effected was one and the same. This threefold handing-over began when the Son, coming to Jerusalem by the decree of God the Father, the counsel of the Holy Spirit, and also his own good pleasure, exposed himself to the Passion. When he came, he there disclosed why he had come: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” [Col. 0841D] (John 12). He said this to signify by what death he would die.

Or rather, because the works of the Trinity are undivided, the whole may be referred to the undivided Trinity, which as a whole handed Christ over to death, so that as a whole it might redeem us from death through Christ. For a *donum* is the gift of the giver, a *munus* the present of the recipient, and a *sacrificium* the sacrifice of the offerer; and the Father gave, the Son offered, and the Holy Spirit received. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ, through the Holy Spirit, offered himself without blemish to God” (Heb. 9). Yet each gave, offered, and received. But by distinction, the Father is said to have given because of authority, the Son to have offered because of humanity, and the Holy Spirit to have received because of loving-kindness.

O generous grace, gracious generosity: what God gave as a gift, he received from us as an offering; for the same things are both sacrifices and gifts. They are gifts bestowed upon us and offerings presented by us; indeed, the same sacrifices are at once gifts and offerings. For what is offered upon sacred altars is called both *munera* and *dona*. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar, go first and be reconciled with your brother” [Col. 0842A] (Matt. 5). And the Apostle says of the high priest that he offers gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb. 5). Daniel too said to Belshazzar: “Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your presents to another” (Dan. 5).

The repeated use of words is an incitement to pious devotion or an ineffable commendation of the sacrament. No single term can be found that can worthily name so great a sacrament, except what is called in Greek *eucharistia*, interpreted as “good grace” or “thanksgiving.” They are called gifts, presents, and sacrifices in the plural because bread and wine, before they are consecrated, are diverse kinds of substances, and the substances of their appearances are diverse. But when heavenly consecration has come, the appearances indeed remain, but the substances are changed; thus the containers are diverse, but what is contained is one. For the same thing is contained under both appearances, although the two substances are not each changed into the same thing, as will be shown more clearly and fully below.

They are also called holy and unblemished, because bread and wine signify the most holy body and immaculate blood of Jesus Christ. They are not called *illibata* (“untouched”) as though they had not yet been tasted; rather, they are called *illibata*, that is, immaculate, which must be offered without stain of heart and body, so that the heart may be cleansed from iniquity and the body from impurity. For, as the Apostle says, “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the chalice of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that chalice. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore many are weak and feeble among you, and many sleep” [Col. 0842C] (1 Cor. 11).

## CHAPTER IV. The Three Sacrifices of the Church

Moreover, there are three sacrifices of the Church, signified in the Old Testament by the mercy-seat, the censer, and the altar: the sacrifice of repentance, the sacrifice of righteousness, and the sacrifice of the Eucharist. Of the first the Psalmist says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50); of the second: “Then you shall accept the sacrifice of righteousness” (ibid.); of the third: “I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115). Flesh is slain upon the altar; incense is burned beneath the censer; blood is brought to the mercy-seat. Flesh is slain in contrition, incense is burned in devotion, and blood is brought for redemption: upon the altar of the body, beneath the censer of the heart, and to the mercy-seat of God the Father.

In those sacrifices bread, wine, and water are offered spiritually. In the sacrifice of repentance there are wine of sorrow and compunction, water of grief and weeping, and bread [Col. 0843A] of labour and affliction: sorrow in the heart, grief in the mouth, labour in deed. In the sacrifice of righteousness there are bread of strength and constancy, wine of uprightness and prudence, and water of gentleness and temperance: strength amid adversities, uprightness amid injustices, gentleness amid reproaches. In the sacrifice of the Eucharist there are bread of unity, wine of charity, and water of faithfulness: bread for the body, wine for the soul, and water for the people, as will be shown more clearly and fully below.

Among these sacrifices, the first leads out, the second leads along, and the third leads in. The first leads beginners, the second those progressing, and the third those perfected: from Egypt, through the wilderness, into the homeland—from the Egypt of confusion, through the wilderness of pilgrimage, into the homeland of glorification. The priest offers these three sacrifices in the Mass: the first in confession, the second in the Preface, and the third in the Canon. For according to the prophet there are also three things that God requires of a human being: “To love mercy, to do judgment, and to walk diligently with God” (Mic. 6). Therefore let one who wishes to offer the sacrifice of repentance love mercy; let one who wishes to offer the sacrifice of righteousness do judgment; and let one who wishes to offer the sacrifice of the Eucharist walk diligently with God.

## CHAPTER V. For Whom the Sacrifice Is to Be Offered

“First of all, therefore . . .” Here one must first inquire to whom and for whom, in what manner and for what reason, we ought to offer the sacrifice of praise. These four points can be clearly discerned from the Canon itself: to whom, namely, to God alone and the undivided Trinity; for whom, for the holy Catholic Church, that is, for all the orthodox; in what manner, in the unity of faith, namely, in the communion of saints; and for what reason, for temporal, spiritual, and eternal benefits, yet all for God’s sake.

The first is noted where it says: “They render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God”; the second: “For your holy Catholic Church”; the third: “Communicating and making commemoration” [variant: “venerating”]; the fourth: “For the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and preservation.” Therefore the sacrifice of praise is offered both generally for all and specially for certain prelates and subjects, where it says: “Together with your servant, our Pope, and all orthodox believers”; for the men and women standing there: “Remember, O Lord, your male and female servants”; for priests and those standing by: “And all those present”; and for those who offer this sacrifice to you: for us and all who are ours, where it says: “For themselves and all who belong to them.”

“First of all,” that is, principally, we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church, that is, the universal Church spread throughout the whole world but united by the sacraments of faith; that you may deign to grant it peace, so that it may have peace from heretics and schismatics; to gather together what is scattered among pagans and unbelievers; to preserve it from vices and demons; and to govern it in prosperity and adversity. Yet “grant peace,” “gather together,” “preserve,” and “govern” seem to mean the same thing. For he grants peace when he unites the minds of the faithful, so that, through charity poured out by the Holy Spirit, the multitude of believers may be of one heart and one soul [Col. 0844A] (Acts 4). He preserves when he governs amid the dangers of the world, so that, sending help from the sanctuary, he may protect it from Zion (Ps. 19).

Although seven Churches are written of in the Apocalypse (Rev. 1), nevertheless in the Song of Songs there is but one dove (Song 6). For Wisdom has built herself a house and cut out seven pillars (Prov. 9). Therefore the Church is one, distributed into seven orders or distinguished by seven gifts of grace, and he grants it peace and gathers it together; he preserves and governs it, who for its governance and protection has set one person over all, so that all may be governed by one, as the body by its head. For him prayer is immediately made: “Together with your servant, our Pope.” Hence it is clear, as Pelagius says, that those are separated from the whole world who, through any disagreement, do not customarily make mention of the Apostolic Pontiff during the sacred mysteries. Those who are not of the Roman diocese are also said to pray for their own pontiff, so that they may preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4).

The Apostle also teaches Timothy that one must pray for the ruler: “I beseech,” he says, “first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are established in high position, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity” [Col. 0844B] (1 Tim. 2). For just as there are two lives, heavenly and earthly—one by which the spirit lives from God, the other by which the flesh lives from the spirit—while each life is nourished in order that it may subsist, the heavenly by spiritual things and the earthly by bodily things, so there are two powers, ecclesiastical and worldly: one governs spiritual matters and the other governs bodily matters. The former acts through clerics, the latter through laypeople, so that the former may be free for heavenly matters with respect to the soul and the latter for earthly matters with respect to the body.

After both powers, prayer must be made for all orthodox believers, who under both powers revere and cultivate the Catholic and apostolic faith. The orthodox are so called as being “rightly glorious,” because they glorify God through the confession of right faith. Although only one person offers the sacrifice, he nevertheless says “we offer” in the plural, because the priest sacrifices not merely in his own person but in that of the whole Church. Therefore, in the sacrament of Christ’s body nothing greater is effected by a good priest and nothing less by a bad one, provided that the priest stands with the others in the ark and observes the form handed down by the dove. For it is accomplished not by the merit of the priest but by the word of the Creator. Thus the priest’s wickedness does not hinder the effect of the sacrament, just as the weakness of a physician does not corrupt the power of medicine.

Although the working work may sometimes be unclean, the worked work is always clean. Yet just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things are unclean to the unclean (Titus 1). Thus an evil person, when he receives life, incurs death; conversely, a good person, when he undergoes death, acquires life. For “he who eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself” [Col. 0844D] (1 Cor. 11).

## CHAPTER VI. At What Place the Names of the Living Ought to Be Recited

[Col. 0845A]

“Memento famulorum famularumque tuarum et omnium circumstantium” — “Remember your servants, both men and women, and all who stand around.” From this joining of words it is plainly inferred that here there is, as it were, a place in which the priest ought specially to name whomever he wishes. Yet he ought here to recite the names of the living, since in what follows there will occur a place where he may make a special commemoration of the dead.

Hence it is clearly apparent how holy and salutary it is to be present at the mysteries of the Mass, since the sacrifice of the Eucharist is offered especially for those standing around. Therefore it is provided in the canons that all the faithful who assemble in church for the sacred solemnities should hear the writings of the Apostles and the Gospel [Col. 0845B; Note: [Col. 0845D] On Consecration, distinction I, chapter “All the Faithful”]. Those, however, who do not remain until the Mass is completed should, as persons stirring up disturbances in the Church, suitably be deprived of communion.

But since the Lord is ignorant of nothing and can forget no one, why do we ask that God remember us? God is said to know those whom he approves: “The Lord knows those who are his”; and he is said not to know those whom he rejects: “I do not know you” (Matt. I). Again, he is said to forget the wicked when a wicked person turns to good: “If the ungodly man does penance, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII). And he is said to forget the good when a good person turns to evil: “If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness, I will not remember any of his righteous deeds” (ibid.).

God therefore sometimes remembers in order to show mercy [Col. 0845C]: “Remember me, O God, because my life is wind” (Job VII). Sometimes he remembers in order to punish: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXXVI). Thus we ask not merely that he remember, but here we ask that he have mercy on us, according to the words: “Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, which are from everlasting” (Ps. XXIV).

“Whose faith is known to you, and whose devotion is acknowledged.” As though it said: You are propitious to the faithful and devout; you alone see into consciences, knowing who believe rightly and love you devoutly, as the searcher of reins and hearts, the God of knowledge, the hidden examiner of all hidden things (Ps. VII). Before whose sight no creature is invisible [Col. 0845D] (Heb. IV).

“For whom we offer, or who offer to you.” That is: Remember, Lord, those for whom we offer, but also the priests who offer. For when a priest offers for the people, he offers no less for himself. Or it says, “for whom we offer, or who offer to you,” because not priests alone offer, but all the faithful as well. For what is performed especially through the ministry of priests is done universally through the desire of the faithful.

It is called a sacrifice of praise, according to the Apostle’s words: “Whatever you do, do all for the praise of God, that God may be praised in you” (Col. III). Or it is called a sacrifice of praise because, when we offer anything to God, we render back to him what is his; we do not give him what is our own [Col. 0846A]. Hence: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine and its fullness. Therefore sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX).

Or rather, it is called a sacrifice of praise because above all we ought to praise God for this: that he not only gave himself for us as a price, but also gave himself to us as food—by the price to redeem us from death, and by the food to nourish us unto life. Hence: “He who eats shall live because of me” (John VI).

“For themselves and for all who are theirs”: namely, for blood-relatives or relatives by marriage, household members, or friends. Although we are bound also to love enemies, according to the saying, “Love your enemies” (Matt. V), we must nevertheless preserve the order of charity, according to: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar and ordered charity within me” [Col. 0846B] (Song II). For the Apostle also says: “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. VI).

## CHAPTER VII. On the three temporal, spiritual, and eternal goods for which the sacrifice of praise is offered

“For the redemption of their souls.” That is: not for temporal gain and earthly desire, but for the hope of salvation and preservation—that is, for salvation or preservation hoped for; for “by hope we were saved”—for health of mind and soundness of body. For each health comes from him who says: “I am the salvation of the people” (Isa. LI).

Yet each form of health arises from the redemption of the soul, that is, the remission of sin [Col. 0846C]; just as, conversely, weakness of both proceeds from the guilt of sin. This accords with the saying of Truth: “Behold,” he says, “you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

There are, moreover, three goods of the human being: bodily, spiritual, and eternal; that is, lowest, middle, and highest goods, for which the priest says that he offers. For bodily goods, that is, preservation; for spiritual goods, that is, redemption; for eternal goods, that is, salvation. The Lord himself teaches us to pray for these three things: for eternal goods: “May your kingdom come”; for spiritual goods: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth”; for bodily goods: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI).

Therefore we offer sacrifice [Col. 0846D] for eternal goods, that they may be given us as reward; for spiritual goods, that they may be given us for merit; for bodily goods, that they may be given us as assistance—so that through these and those we may arrive at those eternal goods.

At times we offer sacrifice to God only for his own sake, because he himself is the Lord our God. Hence the Prophet: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXVII). But since the Apostle says, “Power is made perfect in weakness,” and again, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. XII), why do we offer a sacrifice of praise for bodily health? So that, when health has been preserved for us or restored to us, we may give thanks in the Church.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the sacrifice of the altar is offered equally to the whole Trinity

[Col. 0847A]

“They render to you their vows,” when we give what is ours and render back what is another’s. How do they render vows if the vows are theirs, rather than give them? Or, if they render them, how are they theirs, rather than another’s? Certainly, a good vow belongs both to man and to God: to God because of the agency of grace, to man because of freedom of will. Therefore the Apostle says: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV); and again: “We are God’s fellow-workers” (ibid.).

“To the eternal, living, and true God.” For men, demons, and images are called gods: men by adoption, demons [Col. 0847B] by usurpation, images by designation. By adoption, as in: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXI). By usurpation, as in: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. XCXV [probably XCVI]). By designation, as in: “They called the works of human hands gods” (Wis. XIII).

The first are true and living, but not eternal; the second are living, but neither eternal nor true; the third are neither true, nor eternal, nor living. But he alone is eternal, living, and true—indeed, Truth, Life, and Eternity—who is God by essence, who says of himself: “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isa. XLV).

Although this prayer is directed especially to the Father, because of the authority of the principle. For the Son likewise taught us to pray: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI). [Col. 0847C] Accordingly, at the beginning of the Canon it is said: “Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly ask and beseech you.” Yet the sacrifice of praise is offered equally to the indivisible Trinity: to the Father, to the Son, and to the Spirit of them both. As their majesty is indivisible, so also is their worship indivisible.

This accords with the teaching of Truth: “True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John IV). For whoever strives truly to worship God should worship the Father in the Holy Spirit and in Truth, that is, in the Son; because the Father is essentially in the Son, the Son naturally in the Father, and the Holy Spirit substantially in both, according to: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV and XVII).

[Col. 0847D] Therefore the words “to the eternal, living, and true God” may be distinguished, though not indiscriminately, so that what is common according to essence may be appropriated according to our knowledge. Eternity is appropriated to the Father by reason of his being the principle: the Father is from no one, and all things are from him—the Son by generation, the Holy Spirit by procession, and all other things by creation. Truth is appropriated to the Son, who says of himself: “I am the truth” (John XIV), and of whom the Psalm says: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV). Life is appropriated to the Holy Spirit, as is contained in the Creed: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” The worship of the whole indivisible Trinity, then, is undivided; and it is chiefly offered in the sacrifice.

## CHAPTER IX. On the threefold commemoration of the saints made in the Canon

[Col. 0848A]

“Communicating . . .” The Secret, which according to different usages is also called the Canon and the Action, is seen not to have been composed all at once by one person, but gradually by many; this is also inferred from the fact that commemoration of the saints is repeated three times within it. Yet this too redounds to the praise and glory of the Trinity.

For in the second commemoration those are supplied who among the earliest saints seemed lacking in the first. But in the commemoration made before the consecration of Christ’s body, the intercession of the saints is sought. In that made after the consecration of Christ’s body, fellowship with the saints is implored [Col. 0848B]. For before the body of Christ—which is the universal Church—is consecrated, that is, before the kingdom comes, we need, on our journey, the intercession of the saints, so that by their merits and prayers we may be fortified by the help of divine protection. But when Christ’s body has been consecrated, that is, when the kingdom has come, we shall attain fellowship with the saints in our homeland, so that we may have society and a share with the holy apostles and martyrs.

On the journey, we communicate with the saints through the faith which they had and which we have. We have faith and hope; they have sight and possession. We run the course; they possess the prize. We fight on the journey; they triumph in the homeland. Therefore we communicate with and venerate the memory of the apostles and martyrs, and especially of the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God [Col. 0848C], so that through their intercession we may be brought from faith to sight, come from the course to the prize, and pass from the journey to the homeland.

In this commemoration of the saints, the Church observes what antiquity was accustomed to do: in its prayers it recalls the memory of the fathers, so that, through the assistance of their merits, it may more readily obtain what it asks. Thus Moses, interceding for the sinful people, introduced the memory of the fathers: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants” (Exod. XXXII). Thus Azariah is recorded to have prayed in the furnace: “Do not, we beseech you, take away your mercy from us, O Lord our God, for the sake of Abraham your beloved, Isaac your servant, and Israel your holy one” (Dan. III).

[Col. 0848D] For the merits of fathers greatly assist their children. Hence, when Hezekiah sought divine help, he heard: “I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (4 Kings XIX). And elsewhere: “Behold, I will tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand; nevertheless one tribe shall remain to him for the sake of David my servant, that a lamp may remain for David my servant before me in Jerusalem all days” (3 Kings XI). Hence: “For David your servant’s sake, do not turn away the face of your anointed” (Ps. CXXXI).

And because outside the unity of the Church there is no place for offering the sacrifice of unity, we share in the memorials of the saints in the sacrifice, so that we may offer sacrifice in the communion of saints. For as one bread is made from many grains [Col. 0849A], so one body is made from many members. Thus one Church consists of many faithful persons. For it is written: “No foreigner shall eat of them, because they are holy” (Exod. XXIX). Therefore we admit to eat this Lamb only one joined to our household: namely, every member of the household of faith, from prince to common people, from the populace to the tax collector.

## CHAPTER X. Why no commemoration of confessors is made in the Canon

It should be asked why there is no commemoration of confessors in the Canon, although among the saints the Church venerates their memory magnificently. A probable answer may be given: the Canon was composed before the Church celebrated the memorial of holy confessors [Col. 0849B]. For almost all the saints commemorated in the Canon preceded Sylvester, except John and Paul, Marcellinus and Peter, who followed shortly after him.

The Church, however, began to venerate the memory of holy confessors after the time of blessed Sylvester. Episcopal sees too, which according to the arrangement of blessed Peter the Apostle were in ancient times established in individual cities, were dedicated by ancient devotion not in memory of confessors but in honour of apostles and martyrs, and especially of the Blessed Virgin.

The ecclesiastical histories also record that Saint Boniface, who was fourth after blessed Gregory to hold the bishopric of the city of Rome, obtained by his prayers from the Emperor Phocas the gift to Christ’s Church of the temple in Rome which had formerly been called the Pantheon by the ancients. Having removed all its impurity, he made it a church of the Mother of God and of all Christ’s martyrs.

[Col. 0849C] The Canon is inferred to have preceded this, because the catalogue of apostles is not arranged in it as it is found in more corrected manuscripts. For in earlier editions, as Jerome says, not only was the order of the Evangelists changed, but there was also a confused mixture of words and sentences.

It is handed down that Pope Gelasius, the fifty-first from blessed Peter, who lived one hundred and sixty years after Sylvester, was principally responsible for arranging the Canon. But, as blessed Gregory asserts in the *Register*, Scholasticus composed that prayer which is called over the Eucharist in the Secret [Col. 0849D].

## CHAPTER XI. That sacrifice ought to be offered to God alone; whence the two kinds of service are distinguished

“This offering of our service . . .” There are two kinds of service. One is owed to God the Creator alone and is called *latria*; the other is rendered to creatures and is called *dulia*. The Lord defines both kinds when he says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII).

To *latria* belong temples, altars, priesthoods, sacrifices, and such things, which are to be offered to God alone, who is “glorified in the council of the saints, great and terrible above all who are around him” (Ps. LXXXVIII). For temples are not dedicated to saints in honour of God, but rather to God in honour of saints; altars are consecrated, priesthoods established, and sacrifices offered not to saints but to God, lest, if it be otherwise, not divine worship (*theosebia*) but idolatry be committed [Col. 0850A].

Thus God commanded in the Law: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. VI); and you shall render to God alone the service of worship.

“And dispose our days in your peace.” Blessed Gregory is said to have added these three prayers to the Canon: “Dispose our days in your peace,” through him who for us was delivered into the hands of those who hate peace; “deliver us from eternal damnation,” through him who for us was condemned to temporal death; and “number us among the flock of your elect,” through him who for us was reckoned among the wicked.

[Col. 0850B] There is a peace of sinners and a peace of the righteous; a temporal peace and a peace of eternity. Temporal peace is sometimes granted to good and bad alike. But eternal peace is never given except to the good, because “there is no peace for the ungodly,” says the Lord (Ps. XLVIII). Of the peace of sinners the Psalmist says: “I was envious of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII). Against this peace the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. X).

Of the peace of the righteous the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience” (Gal. V). This peace the Lord left to the apostles, saying: “Peace I leave with you” (John XIV). Of temporal peace the Prophet says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace” (Ps. LXXI). The Church unceasingly asks for this peace: “Give peace in our days, for there is no other who fights for us except you, our God” [Col. 0850C].

Of eternal peace the Lord said to the apostles: “My peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you” (John XIV). This is, according to the Prophet, peace upon peace, of which the Psalmist says: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV).

For this threefold peace we pray three times in the Mass: “Dispose our days in your peace”; “Graciously grant peace in our days”; “Grant us peace”—so that from temporal peace, through peace of heart, we may pass to eternal peace. For this reason too, the priest kisses the altar three times during Mass: at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.

## CHAPTER XII. On the five signs made a second time over the offering and chalice, and on Christ’s sale; on the person of seller, sold, and purchaser

[Col. 0850D]

“This offering . . .” On the fourth day of the week Judas, one of the Twelve, deceived by the devil, committed an enormous sacrilege when he sold the Son of God to the Pharisees for thirty silver shekels, as compensation for the loss he had incurred on account of the pouring-out of ointment: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” But he said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief and, having the money-box, carried what was put into it (John XII).

Each silver piece was worth ten ordinary denarii; and thus Judas compensated with thirty silver pieces for the loss of the ointment, which had been worth three hundred denarii [Col. 0851A]. But if we say that the silver pieces were ordinary denarii, then we say that Judas sold Christ as a cheap slave for thirty denarii, which is one tenth of the three hundred denarii the ointment was worth. Therefore the Lord speaks contemptuously through the prophet: “They weighed out my wages, thirty silver pieces, the price at which I was valued by them” (Zech. II).

Thus, to signify the amount of the price for which Christ was sold, the priest here makes three crosses together over the offering and chalice, when he says: “Blessed, enrolled, ratified.” For both three hundred and thirty are products of multiplication by three. Afterwards, to signify the sale and purchase, he separately makes two crosses: one over the offering and another over the chalice, when he says [Col. 0851B]: “May it become the body and blood.”

As though he said: That sale was cursed, proscribed, void, unjust, and detestable; but may you, O God, deign to make this offering blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable. For Judas “loved cursing, and it came upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.” But may you, O God, deign to make this offering enrolled, through which you may enroll us among the elect. Judas hanged himself with a noose, and another received his episcopate (Acts I). But may you, O God, deign to make this offering reasonable, through which the service of our servitude may become reasonable. Judas rendered evil for good and returned hatred for love. But may you, O God, deign to make this offering acceptable, through which you may make us acceptable to yourself.

Therefore [Col. 0851C] the priest makes three crosses together over the offering and chalice because Christ did three things together concerning the bread and wine: he took, blessed, and gave. Afterwards he makes one cross especially over the offering because Christ said: “Eat; this is my body”; and another especially over the chalice because he said: “Drink; this is my blood.”

In this sense the following words are properly added: “Who, the day before he suffered.” Or rather, because Judas sold Christ to be crucified to the priests, scribes, and Pharisees. Therefore the priest, marking the three purchasers together, makes three crosses together over the offering and chalice when he says, “Blessed, enrolled, and ratified.” But, to signify separately the seller and the one sold, he makes two separate crosses over the offering and the chalice when he says: “That it may become body and blood” [Col. 0852A].

We ask, therefore, that God make this offering blessed, enrolled, and ratified: that he may consecrate, approve, and confirm it into a reasonable victim and an acceptable sacrifice, so that for us—that is, unto our salvation—the bread may become the body and the wine the blood of the most beloved Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Or we pray that God may deign to make this offering *ascripta*, “enrolled”: that is, such that no forgetfulness can erase it from his remembrance; and *rata*, “ratified”: that is, such that no change can overthrow it from his remembrance. We ask that it be made *rationabilis*, “reasonable”: that is, such as accords with divine reason. For there is a difference between *rationabile* and *rationale*: *rationabile* is said of that which proceeds from reason, while *rationale* is said of that which uses reason.

Or: may you, O God, deign in every respect to make this offering blessed—that is, to transform it into that victim which is in every respect blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable. The saving victim is called blessed, that is, free from every cause of curse, whether original or actual, mortal or venial. As Elizabeth says to the Virgin: “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke I).

It is called enrolled [Col. 0852B], that is, signified in ancient figures and writings: both in the paschal lamb (Exod. XII) and in the heavenly manna (Exod. XVI), both in Isaac being offered and in Abel having been offered (Gen. IV). For, as John says, “This is the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. XIII).

It is called ratified, as though not transitory like the old sacrifice which passed away and the new which succeeded it, but enduring forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Gen. XIV; Ps. CIX; Heb. IX). It is called reasonable, as though not animal, as the legal sacrifice was: one which could not cleanse from sin by the blood of bulls and goats, but which cleanses consciences from dead works by its own blood. It is called acceptable, as though not that of which the Prophet says: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering” (Ps. XXXIX), but as the Lord says: “A sacrifice of praise shall honour me” (Ps. XLIX). According to this exposition, the following is rightly added: “That it may become the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0851]

## CHAPTER I. On the sacrament of the Eucharist

[Col. 0851D]

Behold, now that we approach the highest summit of the sacrament and penetrate to the very heart of the divine sacrifice, whatever we strive to express scarcely appears to have any weight: the tongue fails, speech disappears, genius is surpassed, understanding is overwhelmed [Col. 0852D]. “For who knows the order of heaven and establishes its ordinances on earth?” (Job XXXVIII). Yet let us knock at the door, in case the key of David may deign to open it (Rev. III), so that the friend may lend us three loaves, which will be especially necessary for this banquet (Luke XI). For faith asks and receives Life; hope seeks and finds the Way; charity knocks and opens Truth. For he is the Way, the Truth, and the Life (John XIV).

## CHAPTER II. On the different figures of the Eucharist which preceded it in the Old Testament

[Col. 0853A]

“Who, the day before he suffered . . .” On the fifteenth day of the first month, which was then a Friday, the Lord suffered; and on the preceding night, namely at evening on the fourteenth lunar day of the first month, in order to fulfill the figures of the Law, after the typical Passover he instituted the sacrament of his body and blood and handed it over to the Church for frequent celebration.

For thus it had been prefigured in Exodus (ch. XII): “On the tenth day of the first month let each person take a lamb according to his families and households, and keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening. And they shall take of the lamb’s blood [Col. 0853B] and place it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they will eat it; and they shall eat that night flesh roasted by fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” And shortly after: “For it is the *phase*, that is, the passing-over of the Lord” (ibid.).

John the Evangelist defines this passing-over when he says: “Before the feast-day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end; and, when supper had been made, he completed those things which had been prefigured” (John XIII).

Egypt is the world; the destroyer is the devil; the lamb is Christ; the lamb’s blood is Christ’s Passion; the houses are the bodies of souls; the lintel of the house is the heart’s thoughts. We stain the latter with blood through faith in the Passion, and the former with blood through imitation of the Passion [Col. 0853C], setting the sign of the cross within and without against hostile aerial powers. Finally, we eat the flesh of the Lamb when in the sacrament we receive Christ’s true body; and we eat unleavened bread—that is, sincere works—with wild lettuces—that is, the bitterness of penitence.

As manna was given to the Hebrews after their passage through the Red Sea, when the Egyptians had already been drowned (Exod. XVI), so the Eucharist is given to Christians after the washing of baptism, when sins have already been removed: so that through baptism we may be cleansed from evil, and through the Eucharist preserved in good. For as manna led that people through the wasteland of the pathless desert to the land of promise, so the Eucharist leads this people through the pilgrimage of the present life to the homeland of paradise. Hence it is rightly called *viaticum*, “provision for the journey,” because, refreshing people on the way, it leads them to their homeland.

Certainly, what manna prefigured is fulfilled in the Eucharist. For however small or great a portion someone receives, the person receives the whole Eucharist; just as happened with manna, “for he who had gathered more had no surplus, nor did he who had prepared less find less” [Col. 0853D]. Thus that heavenly bread was a figure of it, concerning which the wise man declares: “He provided bread from heaven without labour, containing every delight in itself and the sweetness of every taste” (Wis. XVI).

Christ himself, as it were, explains this of himself: “I am,” he says, “the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever. And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI). Hence the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X).

## CHAPTER III. Why the sacrament of the body and blood was established under the species of bread and wine

“He took bread.” Melchizedek is the first recorded as having celebrated the rite of sacrifice, offering bread and wine; for he was priest of God Most High (Gen. XIV). Hence David says to Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). Thus the evangelical sacrifice preceded the legal one, not only in dignity but also in time, as the Apostle [Col. 0854B] shows more fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews (ch. VII).

Christ instituted bread and wine as the sacrifice of his body and blood because, as bread above other bodily foods and wine above other bodily drinks strengthen and gladden the human heart (Ps. CIII), so Christ’s body and blood above other spiritual foods and drinks refresh and nourish the inner person. Hence: “How excellent is your inebriating cup” (Ps. XXII). In these two consists full and perfect refreshment, as he himself testifies: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John XII).

The bread ought to be made from wheat, and the wine from the vine. For Christ compared himself to wheat when he said: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John XII); and to the vine when he said: “I am the true vine” (John XV). Moreover, neither a cluster of grapes nor a grain of wheat ought to be offered unless the former has been pressed into wine or the latter reduced to bread, because Christ gave himself as bread and compared himself to wheat.

Because Christ took bread and the chalice into his holy and venerable hands, the priest too, following Christ’s example, takes bread and chalice into his hands and blesses each separately with the sign of the cross. Yet when the priest blesses several offerings at once, he takes one into his hands for all. For all the offerings together are changed into one body of Christ.

## CHAPTER IV. On unleavened and leavened bread

[Col. 0854D]

Bread that is not leavened, but unleavened, ought to be offered in sacrifice, both on account of the historical event and on account of its mystery. For thus it is commanded in Exodus: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day, at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread; for seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread, that person shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether strangers or natives of the land. You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread” (Exod. XII). Therefore, since Christ supped with his disciples on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, and ate the paschal lamb—certainly according to the legal rite, with unleavened bread and wild lettuces—it is evident that at that hour leavened bread was not found in the houses of the Hebrews. [Col. 0855A] Thus he undoubtedly consecrated unleavened bread into his body.

For leaven signifies corruption, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V). Therefore, in order that this sacrament may be shown to contain nothing corrupt or corrupting, but to be wholly pure and purifying, we consecrate not leavened but unleavened bread. For, according to the Apostle: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (ibid.).

But the Greeks, obstinate in their error, prepare it from leavened bread, maintaining that on the Preparation Day the moon was in its fourteenth day, on which the true Lamb was sacrificed, so that the figure of the Law might be fulfilled. [Col. 0855B] Therefore, foreknowing that he would suffer on that day, the Lord, on the preceding evening, anticipated the necessary time for eating the Passover, because leavened bread could then be eaten; and they themselves make the Lord’s body from leavened bread. For John the Evangelist also testifies that before the feast day of Passover Jesus supped at night with the apostles; he also says that on the Preparation Day the Jews did not enter the praetorium, lest they be defiled, but might eat the Passover (John XVII, XVIII). He also called the Sabbath after the cross “a great Sabbath day,” which is not usually said unless a feast coincides with the Sabbath. And Luke says that the women prepared ointments on the Preparation Day, which they would not have been allowed to do on a feast day (Luke XXIII). Matthew likewise relates that the chief priests and elders [Col. 0855C] of the people had resolved to kill Christ, but not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.

Yet the things that have been said do not accord with their assertion, if they are properly understood. For “Passover” is said of a day, a feast, a lamb, and an hour. Of a day, as here: “The feast day of unleavened bread, which is called Passover, was approaching” (Luke XXII). Of a feast, as here: “Before the feast day of Passover” (John XIII). Of a lamb, as here: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Matt. XIV). Of an hour, as here: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place” (Matt. XXVI).

The paschal feast day was the fifteenth day of the moon, according to: “On the fifteenth day you shall celebrate a feast to the Most High Lord” (Lev. XXIII). For the fourteenth was not solemn except at evening. Before this feast day the Lord [Col. 0855D] celebrated the Passover with the apostles. For, as Matthew says (ch. XIV), “On the first day of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” And when evening had come, he reclined with the twelve. Mark specifies the first day of unleavened bread, saying: “When they sacrificed the Passover” (Mark IV). And Luke says: “On which it was necessary for the Passover to be slain” (Luke XXII). It is therefore evident that Christ kept the Passover with the apostles on that day on which, by the Law, it necessarily took place: namely, at evening on the fourteenth moon of the first month. Anyone who carefully consults the table of calculation may establish this without doubt.

They called the Sabbath day “great” during the three week-long feasts, whichever of the seven days it fell upon. [Col. 0856A] For all were solemn; and although not as much as the first and the last, nevertheless throughout the seven days they had to remain clean in order to eat unleavened bread. Hence, on any of the seven days they could not enter the praetorium lest they be defiled, but ate the Passover—that is, ate during Passover. Or unleavened bread itself may be denoted by the name “Passover.”

The assertion that the women are said to have prepared ointments on the feast day, the Preparation Day, presents no obstacle, because they were not under the Law but under grace. Yet Luke says that they kept silence on the Sabbath according to the commandment. And it was commanded in the Law that on the first and last days of unleavened bread they should do no work, except what pertained to eating. Besides, no one would then have sold spices, even to persons wishing to buy them [Col. 0856B] so that they might come and anoint Jesus. Therefore, lest any doubt remain, Luke should be reconciled with Mark, so that it may be understood that the women, returning, prepared spices and ointments according to Luke—not then, but, according to Mark, after the Sabbath had passed. What if they had prepared them long before, since they had often heard that the Lord’s coming was near? Does not Mary Magdalene already seem to have prepared them, and by inspiration to have anticipated the mystery of anointing, as Truth testifies when he said: “By pouring this ointment upon my body, she has done it for my burial” (Matt. XXVI)? And again: “Let her keep it for the day of my burial” (John XII). But she completed later the ointment which she had begun earlier.

Moreover, the design of the priests could not prevail against the design of God, who [Col. 0856C] had ordained that the true Lamb should be sacrificed in the paschal days; and just as the typical lamb was eaten by the Jews at night on the fourteenth moon of the first month, so the disciples ate the true Lamb alive at the same hour. Even if what the Greeks contend concerning the moon were true, one must nevertheless believe that the Lord observed the rite of the Law in this matter as in others—he who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. V), “born of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. IV).

But they again object that when truth came, the figure ceased, and the shadow vanished when the light shone forth. Therefore, when our Passover was reached, the things which had preceded in type ceased, according to the saying: “When new things come, [Col. 0856D] you shall cast away the old” (Lev. XXVI). And the Apostle says: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V). Therefore Christ prepared the true Passover without wild lettuces, and likewise without unleavened breads, lest he retain the old rite in the new sacrifice and thereby teach us to Judaize. For both were commanded together in the Law: “They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces” (Exod. XII).

We must therefore know that the Church has not rejected all customs of the ancient Law, but has retained some of them by prudent consideration. Hence the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you” (Cant. VII). For she still observes the full face of the moon, lest Passover be celebrated during its waning. She still prepares [Col. 0857A] the oil of anointing and burns the incense of sweetness; she still pays tithes and firstfruits; she still has a candlestick, lamps, vestments, vessels, high priests, and Levites.

For if unleavened bread must be rejected because the Law permitted it, by the same reasoning leavened bread must be rejected, because the Law decreed in Leviticus (ch. VII): “They shall offer leavened loaves with the sacrifice of thanksgiving which is offered for peace offerings.” Likewise: “At Pentecost you shall offer loaves of firstfruits from two tenths of leavened fine flour” (Lev. XXIII). The Church gladly adopts not only from legal enactments but also from the writings of the gentiles whatever she recognizes as rightly said or done in them; and, as with a captive woman, she cuts off the nails and superfluous hair, so that, cleansed of foreign superfluity, she may be worthy to enter the bridal chamber of truth [Col. 0857B] (Deut. XXI). Legal customs, therefore, have not been wholly abolished, nor destroyed by the arrival of opposites; rather, they have sometimes been changed for the better.

For when God changed circumcision, he did not introduce its opposite, that is, foreskin; rather, he brought forth something better, namely baptism. For, as the Apostle says, “circumcision is nothing, nor does uncircumcision avail anything,” but rather “faith working through love” (Gal. V). But unleavened and leavened bread are wholly opposed, as immediate contraries. It was therefore unfitting that God, as though contrary to himself, should reject unleavened bread and adopt leavened bread, as though preferring what is less good.

Nor should what they say have force: namely, that they offer leavened bread because leavened bread, as they claim, signifies the fervor of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0857C] by whose coming Christ’s body was conceived from the Virgin’s flesh, as the angel foretold: “The Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I). They derive this meaning of leaven from that evangelical parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened” (Matt. XIII). For leaven plainly signifies both the swelling of the virgin’s womb and the bond of union.

Yet it much more devoutly suggests that, according to the Apostle, he took a body without sin from the sinful mass: as though he had taken unleavened bread from leavened bread; and that between Christ and [Col. 0857D] the people, just as between wheat and water in unleavened bread, there is nothing of the old lump or of alien corruption—so that there is nothing between them of malice and wickedness. For by wheat Christ is signified, and by water the people, according to: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John XII); and: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. XXXII). Water without leaven, mixed with wheat, signifies a people without sin joined to Christ. Yet it may also signify this: that as unleavened bread is made from a pure lump without leaven, so Christ’s body was conceived without sin from the undefiled Virgin.

Moreover, this alone would suffice the Latins against the Greeks: the corruption of heresies [Col. 0858A] leavened the Church of Constantinople, so that it produced not only heretics but even heresiarchs. But no storm of heretical perversity has been able to shake the Roman Church, founded with firm stability upon the rock of apostolic faith. Rather, she has always preserved with uncorrupted faith what she received from the apostles themselves, who, being present in person, both instructed her in sacred doctrines and taught her the rule of ecclesiastical observance. From the blessed apostles Peter and Paul themselves—whom she had while living and guards when dead—she received this rite of sacrifice, which she has hitherto maintained in inviolable observance.

But after the Greeks divided the Lord’s seamless tunic, in order to introduce the scandal of perpetual division, they rashly changed the rite of sacrifice. Leo IX refuted them, in various heresies, by a letter addressed to the emperor of Constantinople. [Col. 0858B] Among other things they called the Latins *azymites*, “users of unleavened bread,” though they themselves ought more truly to be called *fermentarii*, “users of leavened bread.”

## CHAPTER V. On the three words that seem to have been added to the form of consecration

“Having lifted up his eyes to heaven.” Three matters are indeed mentioned here in the canon which none of the Evangelists describes: “having lifted up his eyes to heaven,” “of the eternal Testament,” and “the mystery of faith.” Who, then, was of such presumption and audacity as to attempt to insert these from his own heart? Certainly the apostles received this form of words from Christ himself, and the Church received it from the apostles themselves.

For the Evangelists omitted many things, both of the Lord’s words and of his deeds, which the apostles nevertheless supplied. [Col. 0858C] An example is what the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “He was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once; then he was seen also by James; last of all, as by one born untimely, he was seen also by me” (I Cor. XV). For among the Evangelists themselves, some things are omitted by one and supplied by another. Thus, while three Evangelists mention, “This is my body,” Luke alone (ch. XXII) adds, “which shall be delivered for you.” And while Matthew (ch. XXVI) and Mark (ch. XIV) say “for many,” Luke says “for you”; but Matthew adds, “for the remission of sins.”

Nevertheless, the things added in the canon can be confirmed from other places in the Gospel. For John, describing the raising of Lazarus, [Col. 0858D] testifies that Jesus, having lifted his eyes upward, said: “Father, I thank you, because you have heard me” (John XI). Elsewhere the same writer says: “Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, glorify your Son’” (John XVII). If, then, he lifted his eyes to heaven to the Father when he recalled Lazarus’s soul to his body, how much more should it be believed that he lifted his eyes to heaven to the Father when he converted bread and wine into his own body and blood? In both cases, however, he did this for our instruction. Therefore we too should not cast down the eyes of our heart to the earth, but lift them to heaven if we wish to obtain what we pray for.

“Giving thanks.” From this also is gathered why it is called the sacrifice of praise: because Christ established it while giving thanks. [Col. 0859A] Yet he gave thanks not for himself, but for us—that is, for the future restoration of humankind.

## CHAPTER VI. How Christ consecrated, and under what form

“He blessed.” Since at the utterance of these words, “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. XXVI), the priest consecrates, it is judged credible that Christ also consecrated by speaking the same words. Some, however, have said that Christ consecrated when he blessed, construing the sentence in this order: “He took bread, he blessed”—with the words “This is my body” to be understood—and then he broke it and gave it, and said: “Take and eat”; and he repeated, “This is my body.” Thus he first uttered those words in order to confer on them the power of consecration, and then uttered them again in order to teach the apostles the form of consecrating.

Others have said that he both consecrated the sacrament and instituted the form after the blessing, when he said, “This is my body,” understanding that blessing to have been either some sign impressed upon the bread or some word pronounced over the bread. Against them appears to stand the fact that he broke it before saying, “This is my body.” Nor is it credible that he gave it before consecrating it. Certainly, it may be said that Christ consecrated by divine power and afterward expressed the form under which later persons should bless. For he himself blessed by his own power; but we bless by the power which he imparted to the words.

## CHAPTER VII. On the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine

[Col. 0859C]

When the priest pronounces those words of Christ, “This is my body, and this is my blood” (Matt. XXVI), bread and wine are converted into flesh and blood by that power of the Word by which “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I); by which “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created”; by which he changed a woman into a statue (Gen. XIX), and a rod into a serpent (Exod. IV); by which he changed springs into blood and water into wine (John II). For if Elijah’s word could bring down fire from heaven (IV Kings I), could Christ’s word not change bread into flesh? Who would dare [Col. 0859D] think this of him, for whom no word is impossible (Luke I), through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made? (John I).

Certainly, it is greater to create what does not exist than to change what does exist; and far greater to bring forth from nothing what does not exist than to transform into something else what does exist. Will no one doubt the former, and will anyone doubt this? Far be it! Incomparably greater is the fact that God so became man that he did not cease to be God, than that bread so becomes flesh that it ceases to be bread. The former happened once through the Incarnation; the latter happens continually through consecration.

But someone may say: “I am entirely certain that he can do this, but not certain in any way that he wills to do it.” Let such a person observe that, when Christ had taken bread, he blessed it and said: “This is [Col. 0860A] my body.” Truth said this; and therefore what he said is altogether true. Thus what was bread when he took it was his body when he gave it. The bread, then, had been changed into his body, and likewise the wine into his blood.

For the Lord’s saying, “This is my body,” must not be understood in the heretics’ manner—or rather, their senseless manner—as “This signifies my body,” just as the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” that is, “the rock signified Christ” (I Cor. X). This would have been said more suitably of the paschal lamb than of unleavened bread. For the paschal lamb undoubtedly prefigured the Lord’s body, but unleavened bread signified a work of purity. Just as John the Baptist’s saying, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I), so Christ’s saying, “This is [Col. 0860B] my body,” was defined by the addition, “which shall be delivered for you” (Luke XXII). Therefore, as Christ’s body was truly being delivered, so it was truly shown—not in a figure which had already ceased, but in the truth which had now come.

Certainly, when the Jews disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”, Jesus said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John VI). Therefore he says, “Amen, amen,” that is, “in truth,” so that what he said—“Unless you eat the flesh,” and so forth—may be understood not figuratively but truly; and, to express the truth more fully, he adds: [Col. 0860C] “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid.).

But because I desire to have eternal life, I truly eat Christ’s flesh and truly drink his blood: namely, that flesh which he drew from the Virgin, and that blood which he shed on the cross. I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that in this sacrament I eat our Lord Jesus Christ himself, relying on the authority of the saying: “Whoever eats my flesh shall live because of me” (ibid.). For when he is eaten, he is not divided into parts, nor is he torn under the sacrament as flesh sold in a butcher’s market; rather, he is received unharmed and eaten whole. He lives when eaten because he rose when slain; when eaten he does not die, because he rose [Col. 0860D] never to die. For Christ, rising from the dead, dies now no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died once to sin; but in that he lives, he lives to God (Rom. VI).

For as the widow of Zarephath ate daily and the flour from the jar and the oil from the vessel never diminished (III Kings XVII), so the universal Church daily receives and never consumes the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ under the different appearance of the sacrament. Therefore, as Christ’s body is eaten daily and neither fails nor diminishes, so bread daily passes into Christ’s body, but that body itself neither grows nor increases in any respect. For flesh and blood are not materially formed from bread or wine; rather, the matter of bread or wine is changed into the substance [Col. 0861A] of flesh and blood, and nothing is added to the body, but it is transubstantiated into the body.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the whole body exists under the whole appearance

But whether parts pass into parts, the whole into the whole, or the entire into the entire, he who does it knows. I burn in the fire what remains; for we are commanded to believe and forbidden to investigate. Yet if the importunity of the questioner persists, I shall grant, without prejudice to faith, that the entire bread is converted into the entire body, so that no part passes into any part of the body.

But I judge, while preserving the majesty of faith, that where bread has been consecrated, the whole body exists under the whole appearance. For as so great a body is miraculously enclosed beneath so small an appearance, so the whole body is miraculously [Col. 0861B] contained in each part. I infer this from the fact that, into however many parts the appearance is divided, beneath each part Christ is whole: whole in the large, whole in the small, whole in the unbroken, whole in the broken.

I know, nevertheless, that some say that so long as the appearance of bread remains whole, the whole body exists under the entire appearance. But when it is divided, it begins to be whole in each division. Just as, while a mirror is whole, only one image of the person looking into it appears; but when it is broken, as many images appear as there are fractures in it. Yet since God gave those words the power that, at their utterance, the Lord’s body begins to exist under the sacramental appearance, and since those words are not uttered in the breaking, let them attend carefully and answer for themselves how the body [Col. 0861C] of Christ—which before the breaking was not whole in each part, but existed wholly under the entire appearance—after the breaking in some manner withdraws into individual parts and begins to be separately in each part what it was integrally in the whole.

Although the Lord’s body is in a place locally, it is nevertheless asked whether in the sacrament it is locally situated: that is, whether it makes a local distance and has a local position, so that one should say that it lies, sits, or stands. But many other questions can be raised concerning the present matter; it is better to leave them untouched than rashly define them. For “the beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned” (Exod. XIX). In such matters it is safer to stop short of reason than to go beyond reason, lest perhaps—may it not be!—“the bones of the king of Edom be reduced to ashes” (Amos II).

## CHAPTER IX. On the breaking, where it is said why breaking and crushing take place

“He broke.” Many are accustomed to ask, but few to understand, what Christ then broke at the table and what the priest now breaks at the altar. Some have said that, just as after consecration the real accidents of bread remain, so also does the real substance of bread, because just as a subject cannot exist without accidents, so accidents cannot exist without a subject.
