> [Note: [Col. 0861D] This opinion was condemned under this pontiff at the Lateran Council, as is evident from the treatise *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith* [Col. 0862D]. It had also been condemned much earlier by St Ambrose.]

The being of an accident is nothing other than inhering. But, while the substances of bread and wine remain, at [Col. 0862A] the utterance of those words Christ’s body and blood truly begin to exist beneath those appearances, so that beneath the same accidents both bread and flesh, wine and blood, are truly received: one of these is demonstrated by sense, the other believed by faith. These persons say that the substance of bread is broken and crushed, adducing in support the Apostle’s words: “The bread which we break” (I Cor. X); and Luke: “On the first day of the week, when we had assembled to break bread” (Acts XX). They readily solve that question asking what is eaten by a mouse when it gnaws the sacrament: according to them, the substance of bread is eaten, beneath which Christ’s body immediately ceases to be.

But the mode of signifying which the noun “accident” has in natural philosophy corresponds to the mode of existing which an accident, understood in the sense of the noun, has in theological truth. [Col. 0862B] For just as the term *white* signifies an accident in a substance—that is, in adherence—while the term *whiteness* signifies an accident without a subject—that is, in existence—so before consecration an accident is in a subject, because it exists in another. But after consecration an accident is without a subject, because it exists through itself. For the substance passes away, but the accidents remain; and it is not called an accident with the force of a participle, but must be understood with the force of a noun.

For just as the substance of the body is there where the form of the body is not seen, so the form of bread is seen where the substance of bread is not; nor is there any other bread there except Christ’s flesh, which is sometimes designated by the name of bread. Accordingly the Lord says: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI); and [Col. 0862C] the Apostle: “As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup” (I Cor. XI). We must not seek nature in grace, nor customary practice in a miracle.

Not only accidental but even natural properties seem to remain: such as the small quantity which, by satisfying, drives away hunger, and the vinous quality which, by satisfying, extinguishes thirst. Therefore let us say that the appearance of bread is broken and crushed, but Christ is received and eaten—referring what denotes corruption to the appearance of bread, and what denotes reception to Christ’s body.

## CHAPTER X. On Berengar’s confession

For Berengar was suspected of heresy, [Col. 0862D] and, lest a serpent remain in the grass, for fuller expression he confessed before Pope Nicholas and many bishops that the bread and wine placed upon the altar, after consecration, are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of Christ; and that they are sensibly handled and broken not only sacramentally but also in truth by the hands of priests, and crushed by the teeth of the faithful.

Yet Christ’s body is neither divided into parts nor torn by teeth, since it is immortal and impassible. But St Augustine shows in what thing the breaking or crushing takes place, saying: “When Christ is eaten, he refreshes and does not diminish. Nor, when we eat, do we make a part [Col. 0863A] of him; although in the sacrament this is so done. For Christ also rebukes the carnal understanding of the disciples, who thought that his flesh was to be divided into parts and torn by bites, like other flesh. It is called the appearance of bread, not because it is so, but because it was so; just as Simon was called the leper, not because he was such, but because he had been such.”

## CHAPTER XI. What is also eaten by a mouse when it gnaws the sacrament

But if it is asked what is eaten by a mouse when it gnaws the sacrament, or what is burned when the sacrament is cremated, the answer is that, just as the substance of bread is miraculously converted when the Lord’s body begins to exist beneath the sacrament, so in some miraculous manner it returns when his body ceases to be there. This does not mean that the former substance of bread returns, which passed into flesh; rather, in its place something is miraculously created, although the accidents of this [Col. 0863B] can be gnawed without a subject just as they can be eaten.

Here, despite the miracle, an argument is falsely drawn from things conjoined or related, just as elsewhere it is falsely drawn from contraries. For there are here color and taste, quantity and quality, although nothing is colored or flavored, quantified or qualified by the other. A miracle overcomes nature, and a dispensation derogates from law.

Certainly, in God’s nature there is a Trinity of persons: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the hypostasis of the Son there is a trinity of substances: namely, divinity, body, and soul. In the sacrament of the body there is a trinity of species: [Col. 0863C] namely, bread, wine, and water. In God’s nature there is neither accident in substance nor substance in accidents; in the hypostasis of the Son there is accident in substance and substance in accident; in the sacrament of the body accident is not in substance, but substance subsists beneath accident.

## CHAPTER XII. What kind of body Christ gave at the supper

“He gave.” It is customary to ask what kind of body Christ gave at the supper: mortal or immortal, passible or impassible, and the other matters belonging to this question. I profess that divine sacraments are more to be revered than investigated, judging the simplicity of faith sufficient. One may say that he gave such as he willed, and again [Col. 0863D] that he alone knows what kind he gave.

Yet some have said that, just as he who gave was truly the same person as he who was given, so in that which was given he was immortal and impassible, just as he visibly bore and invisibly was borne— invisibly with respect to the form of the body, not with respect to the species of the sacrament. For in that which he bore, what he was appeared; but in that in which he was borne, he himself, as he was, was not seen, because the appearance of bread and wine veiled the form of flesh and blood. This is that true David who was borne in his own hands before Achish, king of Gath (I Kings XXI). Because one who was immortal was given, one who was incorruptible was eaten.

These persons accordingly grant, as a consequence, that if some portion of the sacrament had been reserved during the three days of Christ’s death, the same body [Col. 0864A] would both lie dead in the tomb and remain alive beneath the sacrament. It suffered upon the altar of the cross, yet was not injured beneath the appearance of bread.

But since it is judged incredible that according to the same nature he was at once mortal and immortal—though this was fitting according to the same person—others have said that Christ certainly was mortal, but by will and not by necessity. For inasmuch as he was free from every fault, he was free from every penalty; since he had no sin, he owed nothing to death. Yet he voluntarily endured mortality because he willed to endure death. For if he had not assumed mortality, he could not have died at all. Therefore, to show that he was mortal not by necessity but by will, when he wished [Col. 0864B] he laid aside mortality and received immortality.

For it is read in the Gospel that, when the Jews had led Jesus to the brow of the hill in order to throw him down, he passed through their midst and went away (Luke IV). While he was being led away, he endured being held as passible; but when he was about to be thrown down, he passed through their midst as impassible. For there are four proper qualities of the glorified body: brightness, subtlety, agility, and impassibility. Of these it is written: “The righteous shall shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wisdom III); and: “God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall be no more mourning or crying” (Apoc. XXI). Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, [Col. 0864C] and running over” (Luke VI).

Christ individually received each of these before, in rising from the dead, he assumed the nature of the glorified body. He received subtlety when he was born from the Virgin; brightness when he was transfigured on the mountain; agility when he walked upon the sea; impassibility when he was eaten at the supper. For just as he showed a sign of passibility in an immortal body when, after the resurrection, he showed his hands and side, so in a mortal body he showed a sign of impassibility when, before the Passion, he offered flesh and blood. Yet it may be granted without prejudice to faith that he gave such a body as he then had: namely, mortal and passible—not that he could suffer in the sacrament, but that he could suffer while under the sacrament.

But now he is received by us as immortal and impassible. Yet he does not now have greater efficacy, just as he does not have greater power. Therefore, that he was eaten while passible and yet was not injured was not a matter of human nature but of the divine power by which he was able to do whatever he willed.

## CHAPTER XIII. Whether Judas received the Eucharist
He gave [it] to his disciples. It is commonly disputed whether Judas received the Eucharist with the others. For Luke shows Judas to have been present with the others, mentioning the betrayer immediately after the cup, saying: “This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood, which shall be poured out for you. Yet behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke 22). But all who were present received the Eucharist, as Mark testifies when he says: “And they all drank from it” (Mark 14), in accordance with Christ’s own command, as Matthew testifies: “Drink from this, all of you” (Matt. 26). On the other hand, it is argued that Judas was not present. For according to Matthew, Jesus said immediately to those drinking the cup: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (ibid.). Therefore Judas was not there, since he would not drink with him in the kingdom.

Moreover, when speaking of those drinking, he excluded no one when he said, “which shall be poured out for you”; but he excluded many others when he said, “which shall be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” Hence, when according to John Christ had said to the apostles, “You will be blessed if you do these things,” he immediately made an exception: “I do not speak of all of you; I know whom I have chosen” (ibid.). And again: “You are clean, but not all” (John 13).

What, then, are we to maintain in this case? Perhaps, without prejudice to other views, what John suggests: that when Judas had received the morsel of bread, he went out immediately—for it was night (ibid.). Christ, however, gave the Eucharist after the other foods. Luke’s mention of the betrayer after the cup can be understood as a recapitulation. For sacred Scripture often narrates later what had happened earlier. Thus Matthew mentions, two days before Passover, the alabaster vessel of ointment which, according to John, a woman poured out in the house of Simon the leper six days before Passover.

[Col. 0865C] But if it is granted that Judas received the Eucharist—as most interpreters grant—it must be asked for what reason the saving physician gave to a sick man a medicine which he knew would be deadly to him. For he knew that “whoever eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself.” Was it in order to teach by his own example that a priest ought not deny communion to one whose crime, though known to him, is not nevertheless manifest to the Church, lest he prove not a corrector but a betrayer? Hence it is found prescribed in the canon: “Let the steward of the Lord not forbid the rich of the earth to eat at the Lord’s table; but let him warn them to fear the exacting Judge.”

Let this stand, if no better answer can be given. Yet since it is a lesser evil to become suspected of a crime than to commit a crime, and since, of two evils, if one must be faced, the lesser is to be chosen, why should a discerning priest not deny the Eucharist to a guilty person, so as to incur the lesser evil in order to avoid the greater—that is, so that he may become suspected, lest the other eat unworthily? Certainly, since no one ought to commit a mortal sin in order that his neighbor may not commit another mortal sin, it is preferable for the priest not to betray the sinner than for the latter not to sin. Rather, the latter ought to choose, by abstaining, to become suspected than, by communicating, to eat unworthily.

But if it is asked whether Christ gave the Eucharist to Judas for good or for evil: indeed, he does not seem to have given it for good, lest his intention have been frustrated—for, as the prophet testifies, he “did all that he willed” (Ps. 113). [Col. 0866A] Judas received it not for good but for evil; yet Christ does not seem to have given it for evil either, since Christ is not the author of evils, but their avenger. The truest answer is that, if the proposition denotes intention or disposition, the statement “he gave it for evil” is false; but if it indicates consequence or effect, it is true.

But Christ handed Judas a dipped morsel. Hence the Church has ordained that the Eucharist not be given dipped. This was likewise ordained for the extirpation of the heresy which taught that Christ exists whole under neither species, but whole only under both together. Nor should it be understood that Christ gave the Eucharist to the betrayer under the form of a dipped morsel of bread; rather, by the dipped and offered morsel [Col. 0866B] he identified his own betrayer, perhaps signifying his deceit by the dipping of the bread.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the two ways of eating the Eucharist

“Take and eat.” It should not be understood that the disciples served themselves the body they received from the Lord’s hand; rather, he who consecrated also ministered it, as though he said, “Eat, and eat again,” thereby indicating the twofold eating of this sacrament. For Christ’s body is eaten in two ways, because it is understood in two ways: the true body which he drew from the Virgin and which hung upon the cross, and the mystical body, which is the Church of Christ, enlivened by the Spirit.

Of the true body the Lord says: “This is my body, which shall be given for you” (Luke 22). Of the mystical body the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one bread and one body” (1 Cor. 10). Christ’s true body is eaten sacramentally—that is, under the species. The mystical body is eaten spiritually—that is, in faith under the species of bread, in the faith of the heart. Of sacramental eating the Lord says: “Take and eat: this is my body which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11). In this manner both good and evil persons eat Christ’s body. But only the good eat it unto salvation; the evil eat it unto judgment. For if evil persons did not eat Christ’s body, the Apostle would not have said: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body” (ibid.). Judas too is reported to have received the Eucharist with the others.

[Col. 0866D] Of spiritual eating the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). In this manner only the good eat Christ’s body. Hence: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6). For whoever abides in charity abides in God, and God in him (1 John 4). Hence: “Why do you prepare tooth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten.” Whoever believes in God eats him; whoever is incorporated into Christ through faith—that is, made his member, or more firmly established in the unity of his body—eats him. Elsewhere, what is eaten is incorporated, and the eater incorporates it. But here, what is eaten incorporates, and the eater is incorporated. Christ indicates both modes of eating where he says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). For unless Christ’s flesh is eaten spiritually, it is eaten not unto salvation but unto judgment.

## CHAPTER XV. What becomes of Christ’s body after it has been received and eaten

Perhaps the mind is still troubled by the question: what becomes of Christ’s body after it has been received and eaten? Such are the thoughts of mortals that they scarcely wish to rest, especially concerning matters which ought not to be investigated. Hear the counsel of the Wise Man: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search out things stronger than yourself; but always consider what God has commanded you, and do not be curious about his many works” (Ecclus. 3).

[Col. 0867B] If bodily presence is sought, let it be sought in heaven, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. Yet for a time he displayed bodily presence in order to invite us to spiritual presence. While the sacrament is held, eaten, and tasted, Christ is bodily present to sight, touch, and taste. So long as bodily sense is affected, bodily presence is not removed; once bodily sense fails in receiving it, bodily presence is no longer to be sought, but spiritual presence must be retained. Once the administration has been completed, Christ passes from the mouth to the heart. For it is better that he proceed into the mind than descend into the stomach. He is food not of the flesh but of the soul. He comes to be eaten, not consumed; tasted, not incorporated. He is eaten by the mouth, but [Col. 0867C] not digested by the stomach. He refreshes the mind, but does not pass out into excrement.

Therefore the Lord’s saying, “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is discharged into the privy” (Matt. 15), must plainly be understood as spoken not of spiritual food but of bodily food.

## CHAPTER XVI. If evacuation or vomiting occurs after receiving the Eucharist alone

But if, perhaps, evacuation, flux, or vomiting should occur after the reception of the Eucharist alone, it is produced by bodily accidents and humors, since among the humors, without the matter of any food whatever, they may either flow out as excrement or be expelled in vomiting. Therefore, when after the office of administration something is perceived again—

> [Note: [Col. 0867] Here some passage seems to be lacking, perhaps to be supplied thus: “It is not referred to the reality of the body or blood, but to the corruptibility of the species.”]

[Col. 0867D] Thus the species serves its proper function, so that the truth of the likeness may everywhere be preserved. For where the likeness failed, there would be no sacrament; rather, it would reveal itself there and remove the place of faith, and it would no longer be believed that it ought not happen in this way. Accordingly, in relation to us it preserves in every respect the likeness of corruptible food; but in relation to itself it does not lose the reality of an inviolable body. The species is sometimes gnawed away or stained, but the reality is never corrupted or defiled. Whenever you see such a thing, do not fear for it; but be concerned for yourself, lest you be harmed if you believe wrongly.

But if it is asked [Col. 0868A] whether Christ locally descends from heaven or ascends into heaven when he displays or withdraws bodily presence, or whether in some other way he begins or ceases to be under the sacramental species, I answer that we ought not be curious in such matters, lest we presume beyond our capacity and fail to comprehend. The Apostle gave wholesome counsel: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. 12). I do not know how Christ approaches, and I do not know how he departs; he knows who knows nothing imperfectly.

## CHAPTER XVII. When transubstantiation occurs

“For this is my body.” If, upon the utterance of these words, “This is my body,” bread is changed [Col. 0868B] into body, and upon the utterance of those words, “This is my blood,” wine is changed into blood, then, since the former words are uttered before the latter, bread is changed into body before wine is changed into blood. But is body without blood, or blood without body? Therefore some say that, when the whole has been said, the whole has been accomplished, being unwilling or unable to determine the precise instant of the conversion itself.

Others say, and well, that although at the utterance of the preceding words bread is changed by nature into body, and at the utterance of the following words wine is further changed into blood, nevertheless body is never without blood nor blood without body, just as neither is without soul. [Col. 0868C] Rather, under the form of bread blood exists in the body through the change of bread into body, and conversely. This is not because bread is changed into blood or wine into body, but because neither can exist without the other. Therefore blood is under the species of bread, not by the power of the sacrament but by natural concomitance, according to Brother Giles.

But it is asked: what did Christ point to when he said, “This is my body”? Not bread, for it was not true of bread that it was his body; nor body, for he had not yet uttered the words upon whose utterance he changed bread into body. What then? Logicians raise a similar objection when it is said, “This wine is dead,” on the supposition that at the utterance of the subject it is wine and at the utterance of the predicate it is dead. But as far as east is from west, so great is the difference between miracle and nature. Therefore he easily frees himself from the snare of this question who says that Christ consecrated when he blessed. If an objection is raised concerning the priest, who consecrates when he pronounces those words, the answer is that the priest points to nothing, because he uses those words not declaratively but recitatively. In the same way Christ says: “I am the true vine” (John 15); “I am the light of the world” (John 8); and innumerable similar things.

But again it is asked what he pointed to when he said, “Eat of this, all of you.” Although in none of the four Evangelists is this read concerning the body, but [Col. 0869A] only concerning the blood: “Drink of this, all of you.” For once he had broken the bread, if he pointed to some of the fragments, they ought not all to eat that fragment, since he distributed individual portions to each. If he pointed to the body, they could not eat it “of this,” but that body, since Christ’s body is not eaten in parts but wholly. Rather, according to Tyconius’s rule, it must be understood that Scripture frequently appears to speak of one thing but speaks of different things, as in: “He blessed, broke, and gave”: he blessed the bread, broke the form, and gave the body.

> [Note: [Col. 0869] On Tyconius’s seven rules, see St Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book III, near the end.]

In the same way, when he said, “Eat of this, all of you,” the pronoun indicates the whole body and the preposition indicates the divided form, so that the sense is: “Eat this whole body under a divided form.” For the form alone is divided into parts, while the whole body is eaten whole. Similarly, what follows may be understood: “This is my body,” that is, that which I offer under this form.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the form of the words

It is further asked whether addition, omission, transposition, or alteration, if it should occur in that form of words which Christ expressed, impedes the effect of consecration or not. For example, by adding: “This is my body, which I took from the Virgin”; by omitting: “This is body”; by transposing: “My body this is”; by inserting: “This indeed is my body”; or by altering: “This is the body of Jesus.”

Certainly God made man upright, but he has entangled himself in countless questions. Therefore, setting aside these matters, which sometimes overturn the mind rather than build it up, let this be known for certain: one who attempts any of these things in any fashion sins gravely, especially if he intends to alter the form or introduce heresy. For the form of words expressed by Christ must be preserved wholly unaltered, although, according to the philosopher, transposed nouns and words signify the same thing. Let not what is useful be spoiled by what is useless.

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether bread is transubstantiated into Christ

Now since bread is transubstantiated into a rational, animate body, it seems that bread is transubstantiated into a human being, and by the same reasoning [Col. 0869D] is transubstantiated into Christ, and thus into the Creator. Thus a creature daily becomes the Creator.

Some wished to maintain that bread is transubstantiated into Christ, yet not into the Creator, because Christ is spoken of according to his human nature, according to which bread is transubstantiated into him. For just as Christ is said to be eaten because his body is eaten, so bread ought to be believed changed into him because it is converted into his body. “I am,” he says, “the living bread which came down from heaven; and the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6). Therefore Christ calls both himself and his flesh by the name of bread, in order to show thereby that [Col. 0870A] just as bread is truly changed into his flesh, so it is truly changed into him.

Yet, as in other matters, so also here I profess that the divine sacraments are to be venerated rather than investigated. For it is written: “Do not eat of it anything raw, nor boiled in water, but roasted with fire” (Exod. 12). And, according to the force of the inference, this does not follow: “If bread is transubstantiated into a human body, therefore bread is transubstantiated into a human being,” because the body is not a human being but a part of a human being.

## CHAPTER XX. On the manner of transubstantiation

It is asked whether, before consecration, one should grant “the bread will be Christ’s body,” or, after consecration, “that which was bread is Christ’s body.” [Col. 0870B] This seems to follow from the fact that one who becomes a priest will be a priest, and one who has become a priest is a priest. Likewise, what becomes a body will be a body, and what has become a body is a body. For who would say that this is that, if this will never become that?

Augustine also teaches that before consecration there are bread and wine, formed by nature; but after consecration there are flesh and blood, consecrated by blessing. And Ambrose says on these words: “What was bread before consecration is now Christ’s body after consecration.” For if bread neither will become Christ’s body nor something else, bread will be nothing there; and thus bread is annihilated, and therefore becomes neither Christ’s body nor something else.

But if it is said that bread will be Christ’s body, it immediately follows that there will be another [Col. 0870C] Christ’s body which was neither born, nor suffered, nor died, nor was buried. Moreover, when different loaves are pointed out, it will have to be granted that this too will be that same thing and will not be the same thing; therefore this will become that—yet again, this will be bread and will not be Jesus’ body, which is wholly impossible. Furthermore, if that which was bread is Christ’s body, then surely Christ’s body is that which was bread; therefore Christ’s body either was bread or is bread. Diverse and innumerable such conclusions could be drawn, wholly at variance with truth.

For these and other questions, which can be raised concerning the present point more subtly than usefully, there are those who say that bread is called changed, converted, transubstantiated, or passed into Christ’s body for the reason that Christ’s body begins to be under the same accidents in place of bread. Grammarians similarly say that *a* is changed into *e* when a past tense is formed from a present—*ago, egi*—because in place of the letter *a*, the letter *e* is put.

Others have expressly said that the very essence of bread is truly changed into the substance of Christ’s body, and bread is not reduced to nothing, because it ceases to be what it was but is changed into something else, since it begins to be what it was not. This conversion occurs not by union but by transition, because one essence does not join another as an increase, so that through what is added that to which it is added becomes something greater; rather, what is added becomes one with that to which it is added. [Col. 0871A] Nor does the body receive the being of bread; bread receives the being of body, because bread passes into body, not body into bread.

Therefore, when it is concluded that there will be another Christ’s body which was neither born nor suffered, if the relation is made to the predicate, the statement is false; if to the subject, it is true, but the conclusion does not follow from it. Thus it does not follow: “Christ’s body was neither born nor suffered,” just as it does not follow: “Something is the Father which neither begot nor breathed forth; therefore the Father neither begot nor breathed forth.” Nor does this follow: “This and that will be the same, and they are not the same; therefore this will become that.” Rather it would more correctly be inferred: “Therefore this will become something which that will be.”

Thus the Father and Son are the same, yet the Father is not the Son, but is that which the Son is. Although this will be that, it will never be true that this is that, because this ceases to be this and begins to be that—just as what is healthy will be sick, because what is healthy ceases to be healthy and begins to be sick. Although that which was bread is Christ’s body, Christ’s body is not something which was bread, because that which was bread is wholly other than it was; but Christ’s body is wholly the same as it was. Thus the unrighteous one who was Saul is Paul, yet Paul is not the unrighteous one who was Saul.

What occurs naturally in accidents occurs miraculously in natures. There is a twofold conversion: substantial and formal. For as form is sometimes converted without substance, so substance is sometimes converted without form, and sometimes each together with the other. [Col. 0871C] Substance is sometimes converted into that which comes to be and was not, as a rod into a serpent (Exod. 7), and then form is converted along with substance. Sometimes it is converted into that which already was and does not come to be, as bread into the Eucharist, and then substance is converted without form.

But let us cease to search out the searchings (Ps. 63), for “the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25). For man approaches the deep heart, and God shall be exalted (Ps. 63). Just as ineffable is that union by which God became man, so ineffable is that conversion by which bread becomes flesh. Yet bread should not be said to be incarnated because bread becomes flesh. For the Word, remaining what it was, became flesh by assuming flesh; it did not pass into flesh. But bread, ceasing to be what it was, becomes flesh by passing into flesh, not by assuming flesh.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why the Eucharist is consecrated under a double species

Likewise, although both—that is, body and blood—are received under either species, nevertheless both species are consecrated, and neither is superfluous, in order to show that Christ assumed the whole of human nature in order to redeem it wholly. Bread refers to flesh, and wine to soul, because wine produces blood, [Col. 0872A] in which is the seat of the soul. Moses indeed testifies that flesh is offered for the body, but blood for the soul. Hence it is read in Leviticus, chapter 17: “The soul of the flesh is in the blood.”

Therefore bread and wine are offered in the sacrifice, which avails for the safeguarding of flesh and soul, lest, if only one species were received, salvation be thought to pertain only to one of them. And although blood is received with the body under the species of bread, and the body with the blood under the species of wine, nevertheless blood is not drunk under the species of bread, nor is body eaten under the species of wine. For just as blood is not eaten and body is not drunk, so neither is drunk under the species of bread or eaten under the species of wine. And even if it seems admissible that body is received by drinking or [Col. 0872B] blood by eating, there is a mode of receiving flesh and blood in which neither is both eaten and drunk.

## CHAPTER XXII. Whether bread without wine, or wine without bread, can be consecrated

But it is asked whether bread without wine, or wine without bread, may be consecrated—not whether it ought to be, but whether it can be. Since at the utterance of these words, “This is my body,” bread is changed into flesh, and at the utterance of those words, “This is my blood,” wine is changed into blood, if, after the utterance of the former and before the utterance of the latter, an impediment happens to the priest so that he cannot proceed, then bread seems to have been changed into flesh while the wine has not been changed into blood.

[Col. 0872C] What, then, should be judged to be done in this case? Should another priest repeat the whole from the beginning, so that consecration is repeated over the bread? Or should he begin only from the point where that priest left off, and thus divide the mystery of unity? Concerning this, the Council of Toledo is read to have decreed as follows: “We have judged it fitting that, when the mysteries are consecrated by priests at the time of Masses, if an event of some illness occurs by which the priest cannot complete the mystery of consecration that he has begun, it shall be lawful for another bishop or presbyter to carry out the consecration of the office begun, so that another may willingly succeed after the preceding priest to complete it” (Cant. VII).

Now, since there is disagreement among theologians regarding the time of consecration—some saying that when the whole has been said, the whole has been done; others saying that bread is changed into body first and wine into blood afterwards—most, proceeding more safely, affirm that another priest ought to repeat and complete the consecration. For, as authority teaches:

> [Note: [Col. 0871D] *On Consecration*, distinction IV, chapter “Cum itaque.”]

what is not known to have been done before is not called repeated. But lest that repetition or division of the sacrament occur, and lest any scruple of error or doubt remain, it is judged more advisable and safer that such an offering be most carefully reserved, and that the whole office be celebrated over another offering.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Whether, under compulsion of necessity or upon an intervening contingency, the matter of bread alone can be consecrated into the Eucharist

[Col. 0873A]

And if wine cannot be found, or is lacking through some contingency, it is asked whether, under compulsion of necessity or upon an intervening contingency, the matter of bread alone can be consecrated into the Eucharist, just as the Eucharist ought to be reserved under the species of bread alone. There are indeed some who say that, since word and element make the sacrament, neither the form of the words nor the matter of the things expressed by Christ can be changed or divided. For just as wine without bread, so bread without wine is in no way consecrated, since each belongs to the substance of the sacrament. Hence, whether water is put into the chalice in place of wine [Col. 0873B] or barley is made into bread in place of wheat, just as neither by itself, so neither together with the other, is transubstantiated into flesh or changed into blood.

For if bread without wine or wine without bread could be changed into flesh or blood, then in regions where one or the other cannot be found, one could lawfully be consecrated without the other. For ignorance excuses less than necessity, and negligence less than difficulty. Others, however, say that since Christ first converted bread into flesh and afterwards changed wine into blood, as the text of the Gospel reading shows, both bread without wine and wine without bread can be consecrated. Yet one who through negligence or ignorance omits either species commits a grave offense; more grave still is the offense of one who does so knowingly or voluntarily, especially if he intends to alter the form or introduce heresy.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Precaution when a priest discovers after consecration that wine was omitted

What then should a priest do who discovers after consecration that the wine has been omitted? Some say that he ought to add wine and repeat the consecration over that alone. Others say that, once wine has been added, he ought to put in the consecrated bread, as on Good Friday, and thus receive the sacrifice. But I always judge that in doubtful matters what is safer ought to be preferred.

## CHAPTER XXV. On different priests celebrating over the same host

[Col. 0873D]

When several priests sometimes concelebrate, if perhaps they do not all pronounce the consecratory words at the same time, it is asked whether the one alone who pronounces them first consecrates. What then do the others do? Do they repeat the sacrament? It could therefore happen that the one principally celebrating does not consecrate, while one who celebrates secondarily does consecrate; and thus the pious intention of the celebrant would be frustrated.

Certainly it may be said, and plausibly answered, that whether the priests utter the words earlier or later, their intention must be referred to the instant of the bishop’s utterance, with whom [Col. 0874A] they concelebrate while he celebrates principally; and then they all consecrate and accomplish it together. Although some agree that the one who pronounces first is the consecrator, the intention of the others is not frustrated, because what they intended has been done.

The cardinal presbyters customarily stand around the Roman pontiff and celebrate together with him. When the sacrifice has been completed, they receive communion from his hand, signifying the apostles, who reclined with the Lord and received the sacred Eucharist from his hand. In their concelebration they show that the apostles then learned from the Lord the rite of this sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the hour of institution

[Col. 0874B] “After supper.” On the fourteenth moon of the first month, at evening (Exod. 12), Christ celebrated the Passover with the apostles according to the type of the Law. Having said of it: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 12), he immediately showed why he said this: namely, in order, by ending the old Passover, to substitute the sacrament of the new Passover.

For, taking bread, he blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat, for this is my body which shall be given for you.” Likewise the cup, after he had supped, saying: “Drink from this, all of you: this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Do this in remembrance of me” [Col. 0874C] (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 21).

Thus formed by this institution, we continually celebrate in mystery that which was once offered as the price. For when the reality came, the figure ceased, and the sign was removed from the midst, since there was no longer something to be signified as future, but something present to be received. Yet the figure remained until what had previously been set forth in likeness was fulfilled in reality.

For this reason also Christ gave his body and blood to the apostles after supper: that they might commend this sacrament more firmly to memory as the final command of a testator. Hence, making a last testament for his heirs: “You,” he says, “are those who have remained with me in my trials; and I appoint for you a kingdom, as my Father appointed one for me, [Col. 0874D] that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

It is clear, therefore, that when the apostles first received the Eucharist, they did not receive it fasting. Yet the Church is not therefore to be reproached because it is always received by those fasting. For it pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should first enter the Christian’s mouth, as this custom is observed everywhere.

> [Note: [Col. 0873D] See St Augustine, *Letter to Januarius*.]

For it does not follow, because the Lord gave it after food, that those who have breakfasted or supped should receive it, as did those whom the Apostle rebukes, saying: “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper; for each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat, [Col. 0875A] and one is hungry while another is drunk” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore the Savior handed on the Eucharist after supper for the reasons stated; but he left it to the apostles to determine the subsequent order in which it was to be received.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Christ’s body is wholly in many places at once

“Taking also this excellent cup.” The container is put metonymically for its contents. For one and the same [sacrifice] is offered by all, then and now, here and elsewhere: wholly in heaven and wholly on the altar; at once seated at the right hand of the Father and remaining under the sacramental species. You marvel that, according to the power of the sacrament, the Word of God exists wholly and simultaneously in different places. Yet you do not marvel that, according to the nature of a voice, a human word is wholly and simultaneously in the ears of different persons.

[Col. 0875B] Why do you seek nature in Christ’s body, when he himself was born of a Virgin beyond nature? Therefore Christ is one in different places just as he is whole in different parts. That he consecrated wine in the cup is clear from what he himself added: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine” (Luke 22).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Why Christ’s blood is called the new covenant

“This is the blood of the new and eternal covenant.” The Old Covenant, dedicated with the blood of goats and calves, promised temporal things to humankind; but the New Covenant, consecrated by Christ’s blood, promises eternal things. Therefore that covenant was old and transitory, while this one is new and [Col. 0875C] eternal. Or it is proved eternal—that is, perpetual—by the very fact that it is called new, that is, final. For a person’s final testament remains unalterable, because it is ratified by the death of the testator, as the Apostle teaches: “A testament,” he says, “is confirmed in the case of the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the testator lives” (Heb. 9).

Moreover, “covenant” means not only Scripture but also promise, as the Apostle says: “Therefore he is mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promise of an eternal inheritance” (ibid.). In this sense it is said: “This is my blood of the new and eternal covenant” (Matt. 26), that is, the confirmer of the new and eternal promise. As the Lord himself promises: [Col. 0875D] “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6).

Hence not even the first covenant, as the Apostle says, was dedicated without blood. For after the entire commandment of the Law had been read, Moses took the blood of goats and calves and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: “This is the blood of the new covenant, which God has commanded to you” (Heb. 9; Exod. 24). See how fittingly Moses spoke beforehand the words which Christ used at supper.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whether water mixed with wine is changed into blood
But it is asked whether the water mixed with the wine is converted into blood. If it is converted, then the sacrament is blood—indeed, the blood of the people, for “many waters are many peoples” [Col. 0876A] (Rev. XIX); and for this reason water is mixed with wine, that the people may be united to Christ. For blood and water came forth from Christ’s side (John XIX). If it is not converted, where does it remain after the consecration? And how is it separated from the wine with which it had been mixed into one? Moreover, the priest does not offer blood alone in this sacrament if, after consecration, pure water remains; therefore, after one reception he ought not to communicate again on the same day, as though he had first drunk water. For this reason, after the priest has vomited, he does not sacrifice again on the same day, because he receives pure wine. Or perhaps, just as wine is changed into the sacrament of redemption, so water passes into the sacrament of washing, since both flowed forth together from Christ’s side. Who would dare to define this? [Col. 0876B] But it is utterly impious to suppose what some have presumed to say: namely, that the water is converted into phlegm. For they falsely maintain that not water but a watery fluid—that is, phlegm—came from Christ’s side, failing to observe that from Christ’s side flowed the Church’s two chief sacraments: the sacrament of redemption in blood and the sacrament of regeneration in water. For we are not baptized in phlegm but in water, according to the Gospel’s declaration: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John III).

To some, however, it does not seem absurd that the water together with the wine passes into blood, on the ground that water, through admixture, passes into wine, and wine, through consecration, passes into blood. For who [Col. 0876C] doubts that water passes into wine when a small amount of water is poured into much wine? Otherwise, the entire substance of the wine would be changed because of a drop of water, so that a certain mixture would result that was neither water nor wine. By the same reasoning, all the water of a spring or river would be changed into the appearance of confession because of a small drop of wine; nor could that bread be consecrated into the Eucharist which had been made from wheat to which perhaps one grain of barley or oats had been mixed.

But what if more water than wine is added: will the sacrament be invalid? Certainly, so much wine ought to be placed there that the water, once mixed, retains the flavor of wine. Although the best wine ought to be sought with diligent care for offering the sacrifice, a defect in the wine [Col. 0876D] does not stain the purity of the sacrament. Therefore, whether new wine, called must, or sour wine, called vinegar, is offered in the sacrifice, the sacrament is effected and consecrated by divine power.

## CHAPTER XXX. Whether Christ, rising again, resumed the blood which he shed on the cross

Let this also be examined: whether Christ, when he rose from the dead, resumed that blood which he shed on the cross. For if not a hair of your head perishes, how much more did that blood not perish which belonged to the reality of his nature. What, then, shall be said of the circumcised foreskin or of the severing of the navel? Did it likewise return, in Christ’s resurrection, to the integrity of human [Col. 0877A] substance? It is believed to be preserved in the Lateran Basilica, namely in the Holy of Holies. Although some say that Christ’s foreskin was brought from Jerusalem by an angel to Charlemagne, who took it and placed it at Aachen. But afterwards Charles the Bald placed it in the church of the Savior at Carosium. Yet it is better to entrust the whole matter to God than rashly to define anything further.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On wine added after consecration

But if other wine is poured into the chalice after its consecration, it indeed does not pass into blood, nor is it mixed with the blood; rather, mixed with the accidents of the earlier wine, it is poured all around the body which lies hidden under them, without moistening what surrounds it. [Col. 0877B] Yet those accidents seem to affect the one thing added, as is inferred from this: if pure water is added, it takes on the taste of wine. It happens that accidents change their subject, just as the subject happens to change accidents. For nature yields to miracle, and power works above customary order. Some, however, wished to maintain that, just as pure water becomes blessed by contact with holy water, so wine becomes consecrated and passes into blood by contact with the sacrament. Reason offers no support whatever to their assertion.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Whether wine without water is consecrated into blood

It is asked whether what is done is invalid if [Col. 0877C] water is perhaps omitted. For it is laid down in the Canon that the Lord’s chalice cannot consist of water alone, nor of wine alone, unless both are mixed. [Note: [Col. 0877D] On Consecration, distinction 2, chapters 1–3.] And Cyprian says: “The Lord’s chalice is not water alone nor wine alone, just as the Lord’s body cannot be flour alone, unless both have been united and consolidated into the structure of one bread.”

Some affirm this firmly, saying that, just as water cannot be consecrated without wine, so wine cannot be transubstantiated without water, since both flowed together from Christ’s side (John XIX). Others, however, grant that if someone, without intending to introduce heresy, has omitted the water through forgetfulness or ignorance, he should indeed be rebuked severely and gravely; nevertheless, the sacrament is not invalidated. [Col. 0877D] Therefore the preceding assertion—that wine alone cannot be offered—must be qualified, because it admits an exception in this way: it cannot be offered unless this happens simply or through ignorance; or “cannot” means “ought not,” since that which is not done lawfully is not said to be possible. For the Greek Church too is said not to add water to the sacrament.

Cyprian says [Note: [Col. 0878D] In *Letters*, book II, letter 3]: “If any of our predecessors, through ignorance or simplicity, failed to observe what the Lord taught us to do by example or instruction, the Lord’s pardon may be granted in indulgence of his simplicity. But we cannot be forgiven, now that we have been instructed by the Lord to offer the Lord’s chalice mixed [Col. 0878A] with wine, according to what the Lord offered.” From this, therefore, it is inferred that Christ handed to his disciples at supper wine mixed with water.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Whether leavened bread is transubstantiated

It is asked whether one who sacrifices with leavened bread effects the sacrifice, especially if he does this negligently or ignorantly. For it has been sufficiently shown above that Christ consecrated unleavened bread when he instituted the sacrament. Yet many still sacrifice with leavened bread, and the Roman Church communicates with them as truly Catholic. But the resolution of this question is deferred, so that it may be treated more suitably elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Why the Eucharist is received under another appearance

[Col. 0878B]

Christ instituted that the sacrament of his body and blood should be received under another appearance for three reasons: to increase merit, to sustain the senses, and to avoid ridicule. To increase merit, because one thing is seen there and another is believed to be present, so that faith may have merit where human reason provides no direct experience. To sustain the senses, lest the mind recoil from what the eye saw, since we are not accustomed to eat raw flesh or drink human blood. To avoid ridicule, lest the pagan mock when the Christian does this, so that truth may thus be present and ridicule absent.

Therefore Christ proposed that the Eucharist be received under the appearance of the principal food [Col. 0878C], so that the senses might be sustained by one thing and faith built up by another. The senses are sustained by one thing when they perceive what is customary; faith is built up by another when, in what it sees, it recognizes the nature of that which it does not see. The appearance of bread and wine is offered so that, in receiving Christ’s body and blood, we may be taught that there is perfect refreshment; for complete refreshment consists of food and drink. And bread and wine are principally the substance of food and drink.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That the sacrament of the altar is at once reality and figure

*Mystery of faith.* From these and other words of Scripture, some have thought to derive a support for error, saying [Col. 0878D] that in the sacrament of the altar there is no reality of Christ’s body and blood, but only an image, appearance, and figure, because Scripture sometimes calls what is received at the altar a sacrament, mystery, and example. Such people certainly fall into the snare of error, because they neither receive God’s sacraments reverently nor understand the authorities of Scripture properly, “knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. XXII).

For is the sacrament of the altar not reality because it is a figure? Then neither is Christ’s death reality because it is a figure; nor is Christ’s resurrection reality because it is a figure. For the Apostle plainly declares that both the death and resurrection [Col. 0879A] of Christ are figure, image, and likeness, saying: “Christ died for our offenses and rose for our justification” (Rom. IV). And the Apostle Peter: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. II). Therefore Christ’s death was an example that we might die to sin, and his resurrection an example that we might live to righteousness. Does it follow that it was not reality? Then Christ did not truly die and did not truly rise; but far be it that his death or resurrection was not real. For the prophet foretold concerning him: “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our pains” (Isa. LIII). Therefore the sacrament of the altar is both reality and figure.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament

[Col. 0879B]

There are, indeed, three distinct things in this sacrament: visible form, the reality of the body, and spiritual power. The form is that of bread and wine; the reality, flesh and blood; the power, unity and charity. The first is seen by the eye, the second believed by the mind, the third perceived by the heart. The first is sacrament and not reality; the second is sacrament and reality; the third is reality and not sacrament. But the first is the sacrament of a twofold reality; the third is the reality of a twofold sacrament; while the second is the sacrament of one thing and the reality of another.

For the form of bread signifies both kinds of Christ’s flesh: that is, the true and the mystical. It both contains and signifies the true flesh; it signifies the mystical flesh, [Col. 0879C] but does not contain it. Just as one bread is made from many grains and one wine flows together from diverse grapes, so Christ’s body is composed of many members, and ecclesiastical unity consists of diverse persons: the predestined, called, justified, and glorified. For “those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified” (Rom. VIII). Therefore the Apostle says: “We, being many, are one bread and one body” (1 Cor. X). As a type of this, the ark of the Lord was made of *setim* wood, which is incorruptible and very like the white thorn (Exod. XXV).

Wine, insofar as it is liquid and red, signifies the likeness of blood. Insofar as it is warm and fragrant, it signifies and displays the property of charity. For wine produces blood and stirs up charity, because it gladdens and expands the heart of the drinker. It is therefore clear that the substance of Christ’s body and blood is both sacrament and reality: the reality of one sacrament and the sacrament of another reality. It is the reality of the first, because it is signified and contained by the first—namely, the visible form; and it is the sacrament of the third, because it signifies and effects the third—namely, ecclesiastical unity.

The Lord’s saying, “You always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me” (Matt. XXVI), must therefore be rightly understood, lest it seem contrary to what he says elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). We have Christ with us under the appearance of the divine sacrament; but we do not always [Col. 0880A] have him with us in the proper form of his person. It is therefore called the mystery of faith because one thing is seen there and another believed. The appearance of bread and wine is seen; the reality of the Lord’s flesh and blood is believed.

What is here called “mystery of faith” is elsewhere called “spirit and life.” For spirit is mystery, according to: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. III). Faith is life, according to: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. I). Hence the Lord says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That the appearance of bread and wine is understood as sacrament for two reasons

But since consecration effects the sacrament, [Col. 0880B] and after consecration there is no bread or wine on the altar, what bread is the sacrament of the body, or what wine the sacrament of the blood? If it is said that the bread which was there, or the wine which existed, is the sacrament, certainly neither is the sacrament of the body or blood, because bread has passed into body and wine into blood. But if it is said that the remaining appearance is the sacrament, it neither consists of grains nor flows together from grapes, since an accident does not proceed from these, but substance does. What likeness, then, shall we assign between the sacrament of a reality and the reality of a sacrament? For if sacraments did not have a likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not properly be called sacraments. Thus the sacrament of baptism, which is the outward washing of the flesh, has a likeness to what it signifies, the inward washing [Col. 0880C] of the mind.

Certainly, this sacrament bears a likeness to the body insofar as the bread represents a likeness. Therefore the appearance of bread is the sacrament of the body, not only by reason of the thing signified but also by reason of the thing contained.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Whether the form of bread and wine, or the appearance of the accidents and the reality of the body, are distinct sacraments

But it is asked whether the appearance of bread and the reality of the body are one sacrament or different sacraments. For it is written: “May your sacraments, we pray, accomplish in us what they contain”; and elsewhere: “Grant that this sacrament of your body and blood [Col. 0880D] may not be guilt unto punishment for us.” Moreover, since they signify the same holy thing, they seem to be the same sacrament. But since they are different signs, they seem to be different sacraments.

There are, certainly, some who say that the form of bread and wine is one sacrament, not because of one thing signified but because of one thing contained. The appearance of bread and the reality of the body, however, are one sacrament, not because of one thing contained but because of one thing signified. They must grant that, just as different things are the same sacrament because of the same thing signified, so the same thing is different sacraments because of different things signified.

Against them it is objected that, if the appearance of bread and the reality of the body are the same sacrament, and if the appearance of bread is the sacrament [Col. 0881A] of the body, then the reality of the body is the same sacrament, and thus a sacrament is its own sacrament. This does not follow, because the appearance of bread is one sacrament whose reality is the body, and another sacrament whose reality is not the body, since there are two different things signified.

Others say that, whether the things signified are different or the things signifying are different, the sacraments are always different. They must grant that on the altar there are at least four sacraments: the appearance of bread, the appearance of wine, the reality of flesh, and the reality of blood. Further, since the accidents of bread and wine are different—taste, smell, weight, color, quantity, and shape—it seems that each separately is a different sacrament. For by what reasoning is one rather than another to be called a sacrament? But of what is smell or taste the sacrament? It may suitably be answered that all taken together are one sacrament of the Eucharist, because no individual accident signifies the whole by itself; rather, all together represent the appearance of bread, which contains and signifies Christ’s body.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the distinction of signs, showing that “sacrament” is said actively and passively

Signs are of two kinds: natural and conventional. Natural signs signify according to nature. Some signify what follows through what precedes, as clear weather in the morning is signified by evening redness. Others signify what precedes through what follows, as fire is signified by smoke or ashes [Col. 0881C]. Conventional signs signify by imposition. Some are signs of a sacred thing, such as the bronze serpent raised in the wilderness (Num. XXI); others are signs of a non-sacred thing, such as a triumphal arch erected at a crossroads.

Among signs of a sacred thing, some are sacred, such as baptism; others are not sacred, such as the Paschal lamb. The sacred ones are signs of the New Testament; the non-sacred ones, of the Old. Although both are signs of a sacred thing—that is, they signify a sacred reality—both are not sacred signs, that is, signs that justify; although some have said that the legal rites justified. For this is the difference between legal and evangelical sacraments: the former signified only and did not justify, while the latter signify and justify.

But “sacrament” is sometimes taken broadly and sometimes strictly. Broadly, every sign of a sacred thing, whether sacred or not, is called a sacrament; hence legal signs are called sacraments. Strictly, only a sacred sign is called a sacrament. “Sacrament” is also said both actively and passively: as signifying the sacred, or as the sacred thing signified. For by the name “sacrament” the sign of a thing is sometimes called, and the reality signified is sometimes called, in different ways. Insofar as sacrament is understood as the reality signified, it is called sacrament from *sacred* and *secret*: as it were, a sacred secret.

Therefore the appearance of bread is called sacrament actively—that is, as signifying the sacred; but the unity of the Church is called sacrament passively—that is, as the sacred thing signified. The Lord’s body is called sacrament in both ways [Col. 0882A]: as the sacred thing signifying and as the sacred thing signified.

## CHAPTER XL. That a sacrament consists of three things: things, actions, and words

A sacrament consists of three things: things, actions, and words, according to property, likeness, and interpretation. A lion, by its property, signifies the devil; hence: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. V). Sowing, by likeness, signifies preaching; hence: “The sower went out to sow his seed, and some fell on good ground, some upon rock, and some among thorns” (Luke VIII). Emmanuel, by interpretation, [Col. 0882B] signifies Christ; hence: “His name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted “God with us” (Matt. I). A thing may be baptismal water, or water; an action, the sign of the cross; a word, the invocation of the Trinity. Each is found in this most excellent sacrament: the thing, namely body and blood; the action, namely eating and drinking; the word, “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. XXVI).

## CHAPTER XLI. That Christ’s blood shed for the remission of sins is understood in two ways

“Which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins.” It was shed for the predestined alone with regard to efficacy, but it was shed for all human beings with regard to sufficiency. For the shedding of the blood [Col. 0882C] of the just one for the unjust was so abundant in value that, if the whole human race believed in redemption, the bonds of the devil would hold no one at all.

Sin is remitted in two ways: with respect to the guilt incurred by fault, and with respect to the debt of punishment. The guilt incurred by fault is remitted through faith in the blood, because we are justified from guilt; the debt of punishment is remitted through the price of the blood, by which we have been redeemed from punishment. “All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way. And the Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all. He was wounded for our iniquities, crushed for our crimes; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. Truly he bore our infirmities” (Isa. LIII). Therefore, because the just one was punished unjustly, the unjust are justly set free. For he took punishment upon himself for all, in order to give grace through himself to all.

## CHAPTER XLII. That reception of the Eucharist should not be deferred too long

“Whenever you do these things.” In receiving Christ’s body and blood, great discernment must be exercised. We must beware lest, if it is deferred too long, we incur danger of death, as the Lord declares: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI). But if anyone receives unworthily, he incurs the judgment of condemnation, as the Apostle testifies: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and [Col. 0883A] drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. XI). Therefore, according to the voice of the same Apostle, “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (ibid.).

Thus a great necessity of living well seems to us, or is imposed upon us, lest by receiving the Lord’s body unworthily we receive judgment, or by refraining from receiving it we nevertheless incur danger. For the Lamb must necessarily be received so that we may be protected from the destroying angel; nor can we depart from Egypt unless, in celebrating the Passover, we eat the Paschal lamb (Exod. XII).

Let one person say that communion ought to be received daily; let another say that it ought not be received daily. Let each do what he devoutly believes ought to be done. For Zacchaeus (Luke XIX) and that centurion did not quarrel with one another or set himself above the other: one of them joyfully received Christ in [Col. 0883B] his house, while the other said, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII).

Hear what Augustine thinks on this matter: “To receive the Eucharist daily,” he says, “I neither praise nor blame; yet I exhort people to receive on every Lord’s day. If, however, the mind has an inclination toward sinning, I say that it is made more burdened by receiving the Eucharist than purified. And although a person may be stung by sin, if he has no will to sin further and makes satisfaction by tears and prayers, let him approach securely. But I speak this of one who is not burdened by mortal sins. For it is prescribed in the canon that all who do not wish to be deprived of the Church’s lights should communicate at least three times a year: at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas.”

## CHAPTER XLIII. That the sacrament of the altar is a commemoration of Christ’s death

[Col. 0883C]

“Do this in remembrance of me.” In this sacrament the remembrance of Christ’s death is renewed for us daily, as the Apostle explains, saying: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. XI). Therefore he himself said to the apostles: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII).

The Lord left us this final remembrance of himself, as though someone setting out on a journey were to leave some pledge with one whom he loves, so that whenever that person looked upon it, he ought to remember the traveler’s friendship. For if he loves perfectly, he cannot look upon it without great tears [Col. 0883D] or longing. Therefore the Savior instituted this sacrament because the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father, and because what he said to the apostles was true: “Where I go, you cannot come” (John XIII). For when Peter said, “Lord, where are you going?” he answered, “Where I go, you cannot follow me” (ibid.). Bequeathing to them a fitting inheritance, he entrusted to them a visible remembrance of himself: “Do this,” he said, “in remembrance of me.”

For he did not judge the remembrance afforded by Scripture alone sufficient for healing the lethargic sick person whom he had come to cure. For how great a part of us can grasp that remedy, fragrant with the finest ointments, in the Gospel—the Word which was in [Col. 0884A] the beginning with God, through whom all things were made, and which became flesh and dwelt among us (John I)? To chew over that Word is indeed a health-giving remedy, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. XVIII), sweet to the palate of a loving soul. But so great a food belongs to very few, and is nourishment for the mind alone; by it the soul will then be most fully satisfied when it tastes the Word itself in eternal blessedness.

But he who assumed body and soul in order to heal both soul and body, by the provident art of charity compounded his spices, with which he might stir the lethargic mind of the sick through a daily renewed remembrance of its salvation; and might accustom the toothless—that is, the people without teeth, who could not chew the ancient Word and eternal Beginning as solid food—to sip this most sweet prepared liquid in the sacrament of bread and wine [Col. 0884B].

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the different reasons for the institution

The Wisdom of God, which makes itself known through visible things, wished clearly to show that it is the food of souls; therefore it offered the assumed flesh as food, so that through the food of humanity it might invite us to taste divinity, of which the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). Christ therefore gives his whole self to us as food: as he refreshes us with his divinity, which we spiritually taste with the heart, so he refreshes us with his humanity, which we bodily eat with the mouth. Thus he transfers us from visible to invisible things, from temporal to eternal, from earthly to heavenly, from human to divine.

“I am,” he says, “the living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI): behold, the food of divinity. “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh”: behold, the food of humanity. Therefore the bread of angels became the food of human beings (Wis. XVI), according to that prophetic saying: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII). Thus we who receive the food of divinity according to the soul may also receive the food of humanity according to the flesh; for, just as rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ.

And because the human being incurred death through tasting, he likewise acquires life through tasting, so that life might rise from that very source from which death arose. For it was said concerning the former: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II). But concerning the latter it is said: “If anyone [Col. 0884D] eats of this bread, he shall live forever” (John VI). That mortal food hung upon the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; this life-giving food hung upon the tree of life, which is in the midst of Paradise. That was the tree of disobedience, toward which the human being stretched out his hand in order to become like God, as the serpent promised him: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). But this is the tree of obedience, upon which God stretched out his hands and became human, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

Therefore, in order to show his charity toward us [Col. 0885A] and kindle our charity toward him, he who gave himself as a price for us also gave himself to us as food. Through the price he gave himself for us unto death; through food he gives himself to us unto life, in order to destroy our death by his death and nourish our life by his life. This bread, if worthily eaten, enriches; this cup, if worthily drunk, intoxicates—not the body but the heart, not the belly but the mind. Hence: “How glorious is your intoxicating cup” (Ps. XXII).

Through the power of this sacrament all virtues increase, and the fruits of every grace abound. For he who is the fountain and origin of all virtue and grace is received in this sacrament whole and entire. Through the mystery of the cross he rescued us from the power of sin; through the sacrament of the Eucharist he frees us from the will to sin. For if the Eucharist is received worthily, it frees from evil and strengthens in good; it removes venial sins and guards against mortal sins. Therefore, when in the Lord’s Prayer we first say, “Give us this day our *epiousion*, that is, supersubstantial, bread,” we immediately add, “And forgive us our debts, and lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen” (Matt. VI). For through this heavenly bread we are freed from evils past, present, and future.

He therefore gave us this sacrament of salvation so that, because we sin daily and he can now die no more, we may daily obtain remission of sins through this sacrament, which we receive in memory of his death. For he not only washed us from [Col. 0885C] our sins in his blood when he shed his blood for us on the scaffold of the cross; he also washes us daily from our sins in his blood when we receive his blood in the cup of the chalice.

Therefore, when Christ was about to ascend to the Father, because he had promised the apostles and their followers, “I will be with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII), he wished to remain with them not only through indwelling grace, nor merely through his divine essence, but also through bodily presence. And so he instituted this sacrament, in which he is present with us under another form indeed, but truly in his proper substance.

For it was fitting that God should more expressly mark the human being whom [Col. 0885D] he formed and made in his image and likeness. Therefore the heavenly height of counsel ordained that, just as there are three persons in unity of substance—Father, Word, and Spirit—so there should be three substances in unity of person: divinity, [Col. 0886A] body, and soul. Therefore, since Christ according to his divine nature exists in things in three ways—locally in heaven, personally in the Word, sacramentally on the altar—so, just as according to divinity he is wholly and essentially in all things, according to humanity he is wholly sacramentally in many places.

By the power of this sacrament it becomes possible for those who are of earth to ascend into heaven. For the Savior himself says: “No one ascends into heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven, who is in heaven” (John III). One and the same is the Son of God who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who ascends into heaven: Christ Jesus. To him, as to their head, are joined all the members of the body: all who through faith in this sacrament preserve [Col. 0886B] the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. IV).

And as one body, one person, one Christ with his members ascends into heaven, he speaks joyfully, representing the glorious Church to God: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II), showing that she has come together with him into one person. “The two,” he says, “shall be one flesh” (ibid.). But this, as the Apostle says, is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church (Eph. V), which the Eucharist both effects and signifies, according to the Lord’s saying: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI).

Through what he receives from us, we receive from him what is his; we are joined by so indissoluble a bond that he who is one with the Father through ineffable unity becomes one with us through wondrous union, and through this, with him as our common mediator, we are made one with the Father. “Holy Father,” he says, “keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are. But I pray not for them only, but also for those who shall believe in me through their word, that they too may be one in us, and that the world may believe that you sent me” (John XVII).

Unity prays for union: the Word is one with the Father in nature; the human being is one with the Word in person; the members are one with the head. The first is in righteousness, and afterwards in glory, because “he who is joined to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. VI). Therefore, that they may be one in righteousness, “let the world know that you sent me” [Col. 0886D]; and that they may also be one in glory, “I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see the glory which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John XVII).

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0885]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the signs made third over the offering and the chalice

[Col. 0885D]

Hence also, “being mindful.” For the Lord himself had commanded that we should do this in remembrance of him. Therefore the Church has set forth three things to be commemorated there: namely, his blessed Passion, likewise his resurrection from the dead, and also his glorious ascension into heaven. [Col. 0886D–0887A] The first of these, that is, the Passion, kindles charity; the second, the resurrection, strengthens faith; the third, the ascension, gladdens hope. For what more greatly inflames charity in us than that God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all? (Rom. VIII.) And Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II). What more firmly confirms faith in us than that Christ rose from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep? For since death came through a human being, resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being. As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ (I Cor. XV). What more enlarges hope in us than that Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings (Eph. IV), so that where he is, there also may be his servant? [Col. 0887B]

Because the Church says that she is mindful of the Lord’s Passion, she immediately recalls a more bitter representation of that Passion, recollecting in five crosses the five wounds. Then she proceeds through the parts of the Lord’s Passion, as the following exposition will make clear. From this point, therefore, until the corporal is removed from over the chalice, the Passion of the Lord is commemorated.
