For when the priest says, “A pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” he makes the fivefold sign of the cross over the offering and chalice, signifying those openings of the living rock in which the immaculate dove fruitfully makes her nest. While, amid the aforesaid five signs of the cross, faithful memory holds and contemplates the five wounds of her Beloved—namely, two of the hands, as many of the feet, and one of the side. [Col. 0887C]

The priest makes three of these jointly over the offering and the chalice, because in three phrases both are understood together. For in making the sign of the cross, the bread is never separated from the chalice, unless it is separately named in the Canon. Yet the upright portion of the cross should be made over the bread alone, while its transverse portion ought to extend as far as the chalice, because the upright part of the cross supported Christ’s body, and the transverse arms were stretched out.

## CHAPTER II. Why signs are made over the Eucharist after consecration

[Col. 0887D]

Here arises a question which ought not to be passed over in silence. Since consecration has been fully and perfectly performed—for the material of bread and wine has already passed into the substance of flesh and blood—why is the sign of blessing still made over the blessed and most fully consecrated Eucharist, or another word of consecration uttered? Indeed, certain things are subsequently added in the Canon which seem to suggest that transubstantiation has not yet been completed.

On this question I should prefer to be taught rather than to teach, and to report an opinion rather than put one forward. Yet because I have been unable to find anything said by the elders on this matter, I shall state what I think, faith being preserved and without prejudice to a better opinion. For in the Canon the words signify one thing and the signs indicate another. The words principally concern the consecration of the Eucharist; the signs principally concern recollection of the history. We use words to consecrate bread and wine into the body and blood of Jesus Christ; we use signs to recall what was done concerning Christ during the week before Easter.

Thus, as regards the order of consecrating the Eucharist, it is plain that this section, “Who, on the day before he suffered,” ought to have been placed at the end of the Canon, because consecration is completed in it. But because this would have hindered the order of the history being recalled—since what happened in the middle would have been placed at the end—the prudent arranger of the Canon, in order to preserve the historical order, compelled as it were by a certain necessity, placed this section, “Who, on the day before he suffered,” in the middle, like the heart of the Canon, so that what follows may be understood to precede, according to that figure by which what follows in narration often precedes in sense. Or rather, so that both the wording and the history might preserve their proper order. [Col. 0888A–B]

Let it therefore be said that the signs concern the recollection of the history. But the words do not concern the consecration of the Eucharist; rather, they concern the Eucharist already consecrated, in this manner: “We, thy servants”—that is, the priests—“and thy holy people”—that is, the Christian people; for what the people do by desire, the priests perform sacramentally—“offer unto thy excellent majesty,” that is, majesty more splendid than all others. For if the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII), how much more splendidly does the divine majesty shine forth.

“Of thy gifts,” that is, of the fruits of the fields, with respect to the bread consecrated into flesh; “and of thy bounties,” that is, of the fruits of trees, with respect to the wine consecrated into blood. Of these and of those, I say, we offer a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim: that is, the Eucharist, free from every fault or sin—original, venial, and mortal; or pure in thought, holy in speech, immaculate in deed—because “he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII). [Col. 0888C–D]

That is, “the holy bread”: that is, sanctifying bread; the giver of eternal life with respect to the robe of the body; and “the chalice of perpetual salvation,” with respect to the robe of the soul. According to the saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (John VI).

“Upon which do thou vouchsafe to look with a propitious and serene countenance, O Lord”: that is, with a gracious regard. Not that his countenance is ever changed; rather, God illuminates and makes serene his countenance over us when he displays and declares his mercy toward us. According to the Psalmist: “May he make his countenance shine upon us and have mercy on us” (Ps. LXVI).

## CHAPTER III. Concerning New-Testament figures which preceded in the Old Testament

[Col. 0889A]

“As thou didst deign to accept the gifts of Abel . . .” This adverb “as” indicates likeness, not equality of degree. For this sacrifice is far more acceptable than that which Abel offered, that which Abraham offered, or that which Melchizedek offered. For the reality seems greater than the shadow, truth than the figure. We must therefore attend to the likeness itself rather than to the degree.

We are like Abel in offering, if, while offering rightly, we also divide rightly; because Cain did not do this, he sinned (Gen. IV). He rightly offered to God what was his and what he owed him, but he kept himself for himself; withdrawing his heart from God, he divided wrongly. But righteous Abel offered to God an acceptable whole burnt-offering in his heart, because he did not keep himself for himself, but wholly subjected and devoted himself to God. Therefore God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts; but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look (ibid.). He first looked upon Abel and afterwards upon his gifts, because the offerer did not please him on account of the gifts, but the gifts pleased him on account of the offerer. [Col. 0889B]

Likewise Abraham, in outstanding faith, first offered his whole self to the Most High; and therefore, when he brought what was to be offered, he offered pleasing victims. In order that we might knowingly imitate this, God required from him his paternal affections. “Take,” he says, “your only-begotten son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him as a whole burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you” (Gen. XXII). And immediately he found him ready and obedient—or rather, he showed him to us.

Likewise Melchizedek, unless he had first offered himself as a sacrifice acceptable to God, could not have foreseen the causes of things to come, in contemplation of which he first offered the mystical sacrifice of bread and wine. For he was priest of God Most High (Gen. XIV). Therefore, as we stand ready to offer, if we first divide rightly, let us offer ourselves in sacrifice: slaughtering ram-like fierceness for the sake of the way, bull-like savagery, and goat-like lust. As we sang in the Psalm: “I will offer thee fat whole burnt-offerings with the incense of rams; I will offer thee bulls with goats” (Ps. LXV). Then, like Abel’s gift, Abraham’s sacrifice, and Melchizedek’s victim, the Lord will accept our vows. [Col. 0889C–D]

But we ought to behold likeness not only in the offerers, but also in the offerings themselves. For those ancient sacrifices prefigured this new sacrifice. What is expressed by Abel’s gift, offered from the firstborn of the flock, if not Christ, “the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom. VIII)? For as Abel was slain enviously by his brother, so Christ was maliciously killed by the Jewish people. For according to the Apocalypse of John, “he is the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (Apoc. XIII).

What is signified by Abraham’s offering of his beloved and only son, if not the Passion of the Lord? Of him the Apostle says: “God did not spare his beloved Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, XVII). Melchizedek’s offering, however, so exactly foreshadowed the new sacrifice that it was foretold of Christ: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). Being in every respect, according to the Apostle, made like unto the Son of God, “he remains a priest for ever” (Heb. VII). [Col. 0890A]

Abel is called a boy, not so much from youth as from purity, according to the saying: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen; I have put my Spirit upon him” (Isa. XLII). Abraham is called patriarch, not so much of the Israelite people as of the Christian people: of the former by flesh, of the latter by faith, according to the saying: “Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but you shall be called Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations” (Gen. XVII). Melchizedek is interpreted “king of righteousness,” then “king of Salem,” that is, of peace, because of what is written: “In his days righteousness shall arise and abundance of peace, until the moon be taken away” (Ps. LXXI). “A holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim”: Pope Leo added this to the Canon. [Col. 0890B]

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the signs made fourth over the offering and chalice

“Most humbly we beseech thee . . .”

After the hymn had been said, Jesus went out after supper to the Mount of Olives, across the torrent Cedron; and going a little farther, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.” Then a second and a third time he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground. Then he came to his disciples and said: “Rise, let us go; behold, he who will betray me draws near.” But the betrayer gave them a sign, saying: “Whomsoever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him.” And immediately, coming up, he kissed him (Luke XXII; John XVIII). [Col. 0890B–C]

Therefore, because Jesus fell down praying and saying, “Father, if it be possible,” the priest bows and prays, saying, “Most humbly we beseech thee . . .,” representing by the kiss of the altar the kiss of the betrayer. And because, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, saying the same words three times, the priest makes three crosses: the first and second distinctly over the offering and chalice, saying, “the most holy body and blood of thy Son”; the third by signing himself on the face, when he says, “may we be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.” [Col. 0890C–D]

Perhaps he makes the cross over the body on account of the sweat of the body, and over the blood on account of the drops of blood; and because he fell on his face in prayer, he makes the cross upon his own face. Or rather, by the two crosses which the priest makes over the body and blood are signified the bonds and the scourges: the bonds by which the body was bound, and the scourges by which his blood was beaten. For concerning the bonds it is written: “The servants of the Jews seized Jesus, bound him, led him away bound, and delivered him to Pilate” (Mark XV). Concerning the scourges it is written: “Pilate took Jesus and scourged him” (John XIX), “by whose bruise we are healed.”

By the third cross, which the priest makes upon his own face, is recalled the passage concerning those who spat in his face, struck his face with their palms, and, covering his face, said: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is he that struck thee?” (Luke XXII). [Col. 0891A]

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the ministry of angels, who are always present at the sacrifice

“Command these to be borne by the hands . . .”

These words are of such depth that human understanding can scarcely penetrate them. For blessed Gregory also, a worthy interpreter of so great a sacrament, speaks in one place about them, as about something ineffable, almost ineffably: “Who among the faithful,” he says, “can doubt that, at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened, the choirs of angels are present in the mystery of Jesus Christ, things lowest are joined to things highest—that is, earthly things are joined to heavenly—and one thing is made from things invisible and visible?” [Note: [Col. 0891D] Pope Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 58.]

Elsewhere he says: “At one and the same time and instant, it is borne up to heaven by the ministry of angels to be joined to Christ’s body, and yet is seen before the priest’s eyes upon the altar.”

Nevertheless, preserving the hidden sacrament of the heavenly oracle, these words may be understood, though more simply, yet more safely, as follows: “Command these”—namely, the vows and prayers of the faithful—“to be borne by the hands of thy holy angel,” that is, through the ministry of angels, according to what the angel said to Tobias: “When you prayed with tears, I offered your prayer to the Lord” (Tob. XII); “to thy high altar,” that is, into the sight of thy divine majesty. [Col. 0891B–C]

Moreover, as blessed Augustine explains, the angel is not said to offer our prayers to God as though God then first learns what we desire, since God knows all things before they happen; but because a rational creature needs to refer temporal causes to eternity, either by asking what is to be done concerning itself, or by consulting what it ought to do, so that what it has learned must be performed at God’s command, it may report to us either openly or secretly. From this it is also plainly apparent that angels are always present at, or attend, the sacrifice.

Many kinds of altar are found in Scripture: higher and lower, inward and outward. Each kind is twofold. The higher altar is the Trinity of God, concerning which it is written: “Thou shalt not go up by steps unto my altar” (Exod. XX). There is also the higher altar, the triumphant Church, of which it is said: “Then they shall lay calves upon thy altar” (Ps. L). The lower altar is the Church militant, concerning which it is said: “If thou make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stones” (Exod. XX). There is also the lower altar, the table of the Temple, concerning which it is said: “Keep the solemn day in thick crowds, even unto the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII). [Col. 0891D]

The inward altar is a clean heart, concerning which it is commanded: “Fire shall always burn upon my altar” (Lev. VI). There is also the inward altar, faith in the Incarnation, concerning which it is commanded: “Ye shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. XX). The outward altar is the altar of the cross, that is, the altar of whole burnt-offering, upon which the evening sacrifice was burned. There is also the outward altar, the ecclesiastical sacraments, concerning which it is written: “Thine altars, O Lord of hosts” (Ps. LXXXIII). What things he asks to be borne to the high altar he specifies by adding: “That as many as . . .” [Col. 0892A]

“Remember, O Lord.” Our devout mother the Church prays not only for the living but also for the dead, and commends them through the intercession of the sacred offering, most certainly believing that that precious blood, which was shed for many for the remission of sins, avails not only for the salvation of the living but also for the absolution of the dead who depart to the Lord with the sign of faith. Not that faith or hope exists where there is both appearance and reality. For faith is done away with, but charity never fails (I Cor. XIII). Rather, “the sign of faith” is understood as the mark of Christianity, by which believers are distinguished from unbelievers, according to the saying: “I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel” (Apoc. VII). [Col. 0892A–B]

“And sleep in the sleep of peace,” according to the saying: “In peace, in the selfsame, I will sleep and rest” (Ps. IV). Sacred Scripture frequently calls the dead sleepers, because as sleepers awaken, so the dead shall rise. Therefore the Apostle says: “I would not have you ignorant concerning those who sleep, that you may not grieve as others who have no hope” (I Thess. IV). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Lazarus our friend sleeps” (John XI).

“To them, O Lord, and to all who rest in Christ.” At this point the priest ought to make special commemoration of whichever dead persons he chooses. “A place of refreshment,” where there is no heat of punishments; “of light,” where there is no darkness of shadows; “and of peace,” where there is no conflict of punishments. For God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints (Apoc. XXI). “But they shall delight in the abundance of peace; they shall be pleasing before the Lord in the light of the living” (Ps. LV). [Col. 0892B–C]

“To us also, sinners.” For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I). Although at all times we ought sincerely to acknowledge ourselves as sinners, we ought especially to do so when the most holy mystery is celebrated for the remission of sins.

“To those hoping in the multitude of thy mercies,” according to the Psalmist: “According to the multitude of thy mercies, O Lord, blot out my iniquity” (Ps. L). God’s mercy is only one thing—indeed, none other than God himself, who is merciful—but his dispositions are many, and these are called mercies. Hence: “Remember thy mercies, O Lord, and thy compassions which are from eternity” (Ps. XXIV).

Moreover, since God himself is all in all (I Cor. XV), he is the salvation, reward, and glory of each person. “I am the salvation of the people,” he says (Ps. XXXIV). What then is meant by the phrase, “vouchsafe to grant some share and fellowship,” as though not all were to receive the same denarius? Certainly, although the reward of each is one and the same—namely, God himself, in whose knowledge eternal salvation consists, according to what he says in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they may know thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John XVII)—nevertheless, according to the difference of merits, some enjoy the divine vision more and others less. For “star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV); and therefore the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV). It is as with one sun, whose light all share, some more and some less, according to the difference among those who behold it. [Col. 0892D–0893A]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the second commemoration of the saints

“With John, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas . . .”

In this second commemoration of the saints, those who seemed to be lacking from among the earliest saints in the first are, for the most part, supplied. But how is John repeated, and why is Stephen, associated with John, placed before Matthias and Barnabas?

Certainly, John is included in the first commemoration and numbered with the others because of the dignity of his apostleship. In this commemoration, however, he is repeated and associated with Stephen because of the privilege of celibacy. For they are virgins and follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Apoc. XIV), and for that reason are placed before the others. John’s virginity is especially commended because Christ on the cross entrusted his mother, a Virgin, to the disciple, a virgin. “From that hour the disciple took her into his own home” (John XIX). [Col. 0893B]

Stephen’s virginity is especially commended because he was appointed by the apostles to the ministry of widows, and by being set over women deserved testimony to the most untainted chastity (Acts VI). John, however, might be understood not as the Evangelist but as the Baptist, were it not for the preceding words, “with thy holy apostles and martyrs.” From this one infers that only apostles and martyrs are indicated, although John the Baptist may deservedly be counted among the martyrs.

“Not an evaluator of merit”: because thou dost not repay according to the strict demands of merits, but either by punishing less or rewarding more than each person has deserved. Hence: “Do not deal with us according to our sins” (Ps. CII); and elsewhere: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke VI). [Col. 0893B–C]

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the signs made fifth over the body and blood, and at the side of the chalice

[Col. 0893D]

“Through whom, O Lord, thou dost ever create all these good things.” For through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made (John I). “And God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I). Therefore thou createst by establishing nature; thou sanctifiest by consecrating matter; thou quickenest by transubstantiating the creature; and thou blessest by increasing grace.

But the reference of the pronoun is broad, as is the tense of the verb. For the present tense, used broadly, does not retain its ordinary present use. “All these things,” then—that is, bread, wine, and water—thou dost ever create good according to their primordial causes; thou sanctifiest them according to their sacramental causes; thou quickenest them, so that they pass into flesh and blood; and thou blessest them, so that they confer charity and unity. [Col. 0894A]

“Through him,” as through a mediator; “with him,” as with an equal; “in him,” as in one consubstantial. For in the Father authority is indicated; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, communion. Authority is in the Father because of the principle; equality in the Son because of the middle; communion in the Holy Spirit because of fellowship.

The Lord was crucified at the third and sixth hours: at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, as Mark recounts (chapter XV); at the sixth hour by the hands of the Gentiles, as John recounts (chapter XIX). And about the ninth hour, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit (John XIX).

To recall the crucifixion which took place at the third hour through the tongues of the Jews, crying three times, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke XXIII), and again, “Away, away, crucify him” (John XIX), the priest makes three crosses over the offering and chalice when he says, “Thou sanctifiest, quickenest, and blessest.” [Col. 0894A–B]

To recall the crucifixion which, after an interval of three hours, took place through the hands of the Gentiles—for the soldiers crucified Jesus—the priest again makes three crosses with the host over the chalice, saying, “Through him, and with him, and in him.” Afterwards, to signify the separation of flesh and soul when the Lord died, he makes two crosses at the mouth of the chalice, saying, “To thee, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.” For although in Christ there are three united substances—namely, divinity, body, and soul—only two, body and soul, were separated in death. The divinity was neither divided nor separated from either; therefore the Lord’s death is signified not by three crosses but by two. [Col. 0894B–C]

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the extension of the Savior’s hands upon the cross

Therefore the priest extends his hands over the altar-table because Christ stretched out his hands upon the altar of the cross, according to the prophetic saying: “I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe me” (Isa. LXV). Yet this can be figured more subtly and profoundly.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the three sufferings which Christ endured

For the three crosses signify the three sufferings which Christ endured on the cross: passion, fore-suffering (*propassio*), and compassion. Passion in the body, fore-suffering in the mind, compassion in the heart.

Concerning the suffering of the body, the Lord says through the prophet: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I). “They pierced my hands and my feet, and numbered all my bones” (Ps. XXI). Concerning the fore-suffering of the mind, the Lord says to the apostles: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Jesus “began to be afraid and to be distressed; he began to be sorrowful and sad” (Matt. XVI; Mark XIV). From compassion of heart he prayed to the Father for his crucifiers: “Father,” he said, “forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII). For “had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). [Col. 0894D–0895A]

The priest therefore makes these three crosses with the host over the chalice because Christ endured such sufferings in his body upon the instrument of execution; for the chalice signifies the Passion, according to what the Lord himself says: “Lord Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI).

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the water and blood which flowed from Christ’s side

The two crosses which the priest makes at the side of the chalice signify the two sacraments which flowed from the Lord’s side: namely, the water of regeneration and the blood of redemption, according to John’s testimony: “One of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came forth” (John XIX). [Col. 0895A–B]

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the rending of the veil

The corporal is removed from over the chalice because “the veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom” (Matt. XXVI). Indeed, what had been written concerning him was until then closed, as is said of certain persons: “And that saying was hidden from them”; when it was fulfilled, it was also revealed. For the wood cast into Marah sweetened the bitter waters (Exod. XV).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Christ’s burial and the elevation of the sacrifice

Then the deacon approaches and raises the sacrifice a little from the altar, which both he and the priest set down. For Joseph of Arimathea came, and Nicodemus also came; having obtained Jesus’ body from Pilate, they took it down and buried it. And because he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb (Matt. XXVI), the deacon replaces the corporal over the mouth of the chalice. [Col. 0895C]

## CHAPTER XIII. It is shown why the deacon kisses the altar-table and the bishop’s shoulder

Because “his place was made in peace” (Ps. LXXV), the deacon kisses the altar-table. And because “government was made upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX), the deacon kisses the bishop’s shoulder, so that in each action he may signify Christ: both that he rested after death and that he conquered after death, according to what he himself foretold in the Psalm: “In peace, in the selfsame, I will sleep and rest” (Ps. IV); and elsewhere: “O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite!” (Hos. XIII).

For Christ triumphed over death through death. Since he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross, therefore God exalted him (Phil. II). This was also figured in Christ’s carrying the cross upon his shoulder. [Col. 0895C–D]

## CHAPTER XIV. Epilogue concerning the number and rationale of the signs made over the offering and chalice

The sacrifice, therefore, is signed seven times in the Canon. The first time, three times, where it says: “These gifts, these offerings, these holy unblemished sacrifices,” because of Christ’s threefold handing-over: by God, by Judas, and by the Jew.

The second time, five times, where it is said: “Do thou, O God, vouchsafe in all respects to make this offering blessed, enrolled, ratified, that it may become body and blood,” because of the five persons: the seller, the one sold, and the purchasers—namely, the priests, scribes, and Pharisees.

The third time, twice, where it says: “Jesus, taking bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to the disciples” (Matt. XXVI); likewise, “this excellent chalice”; again, “giving thee thanks, he blessed it”: because of the blessing of bread transubstantiated into flesh and of wine transubstantiated into blood. [Col. 0896A]

The fourth time, five times, where it says: “A pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation”: because of the five distinct wounds, two of the hands, as many of the feet, and one of the side.

The fifth time, twice, where it says: “The most holy body and blood of thy Son”: because of the bonds by which the body was bound and the scourges by which the blood was beaten.

The sixth time, three times, where it says: “Thou sanctifiest, quickenest, and blessest”: because of the crucifixion performed at the third hour through the tongues of the Jews, crying three times, “Crucify him” (Mark XV).

The seventh time, five times, where it says: “Through him, and with him, and in him, is to thee, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.” Three times over the chalice, because of the three sufferings which Christ endured—passion, fore-suffering, and compassion—and twice at the side of the chalice, because of the water and blood which flowed from Christ’s side. [Col. 0896B–C]

Among these seven occasions, the sacrifice is signed twice on two occasions, three times on two occasions, five times on two occasions, and on the seventh occasion twice and three times: altogether five times five, that is, twenty-five. This number, multiplied by itself, always returns into itself if multiplication is continued indefinitely. However greatly the sacrament of the Eucharist is multiplied, it is always the same sacrifice.

In this sacrament also the five bodily senses are exercised: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, concerning colour, flavour, odour, breaking, and receiving. Yet the flesh must pass into spirit, because “it is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John VI). Hence the five spiritual senses of the soul should abound: the sight of understanding, the hearing of obedience, the smell of discernment, the taste of delight, and the touch of action. Of these it is found in the Gospel: “Lord, thou deliveredst to me five talents; behold, I have gained another five” (Matt. XXV). [Col. 0896C–D]

The number two and the number three also fittingly correspond to the sacrament. Two, because of flesh and blood; three, because of bread, wine, and water. Two, because of the double manner of eating: sacramentally under the appearance of bread, and spiritually in faith of heart; three, because of the three distinct things in this sacrament: visible form, reality of body, and spiritual power. The form is that of bread and wine; the reality, that of flesh and blood; the power, that of unity and charity—so that the number three through the number two, that is, faith in the Trinity through love of God and neighbour, may work. [Note: [Col. 0897] See P. Lebrun, *Literal Explanation of the Ceremonies of the Mass*, preface, p. XII, octavo.]

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the utterance of the voice and the striking of the breast

Moreover, not only the making of the cross, but also the utterance of the voice, indicates the events that occurred beside the cross. For when the point is reached, “To us also, thy sinful servants,” the priest, slightly raising his voice and striking his breast, breaks the silence, representing the contrition and confession of the thief at that moment of the Lord’s Passion, when he rebuked the other and said: “We receive the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing evil.” And he said to Jesus: “Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom.” Therefore Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to thee: today thou shalt be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). [Col. 0897A]

Or, by raising the voice and striking the breast, is expressed what the centurion and those with him did: seeing what took place, “they feared exceedingly, saying: Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII). “And all the crowd who had come together for this spectacle returned, striking their breasts” (Luke XXIII).

Because Jesus, crying with a loud voice, gave up the spirit, the priest raises his voice in saying: “For ever and ever.” And because the women lamented, weeping for the Lord, the choir responds, as if lamenting, “Amen,” representing the faithful who mourned and bewailed the Lord with contrite heart; or, formerly, Abel’s parents, who mourned him slain by the wrath of his envious brother (Gen. IV).

Jesus therefore cried with a loud voice: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII); and the priest, raising his voice, pronounces: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” [Col. 0897B–C]

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the Lord’s Prayer, in which its dignity and efficacy are discussed
This prayer surpasses other prayers for many reasons: by the authority of its teacher, the brevity of its wording, the sufficiency of its petitions, and the abundance of its mysteries. By the authority of its teacher, because it was uttered by his own mouth. For “the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1). By the brevity of its wording, because it is easily said and spoken; “when you pray,” he says, “do not use many words, as the Gentiles do” (Matt. 6). By the sufficiency of its petitions, because it contains what is necessary for both lives; for godliness [Col. 0897D] “has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4). By the abundance of its mysteries, because it contains immeasurable sacraments: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12).

The Lord knows what we want, but he wishes us to pray aloud in order to stir up devotion; for what breath does to a coal, utterance does to devotion. Hence: “With my mouth I cried to him, and I exalted him beneath my tongue” (Ps. 65). We pray aloud for the instruction of others, so that curtain may draw curtain, and he who hears may say, “Come” (Rev. 22); hence: “Let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5). We do so for the service of the tongue, so that, having sinned with the tongue, we may make satisfaction with the tongue; hence: “As you have presented your members [Col. 0898A] to serve uncleanness unto iniquity, so present them to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6). We do so in order to obtain the thing sought, because what is asked more insistently is obtained more readily; hence: “Ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7). We do so to preserve the thing obtained, because what is requested more often is guarded more carefully; hence: “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Rev. 3).

We pray both to acquire good things and to avoid evils: for temporal, spiritual, and eternal goods; and against past, present, and future evils. Of eternal goods: “May your kingdom come”; of spiritual goods: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”; of temporal goods: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Eternal things are sought as [Col. 0898B] reward, spiritual things as merit, temporal things as sustenance. Of past evils: “Forgive us our debts”; of present evils: “Deliver us from evil”; of future evils: “Lead us not into temptation.” The past is to be mourned, the present overcome, the future guarded against.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the number and order of the petitions

There are seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer, apart from the winning of goodwill. The first three concern the homeland; the final three concern the way. The middle petition belongs to both. The first three follow the order of time but precede in the order of dignity; the final three follow the order of dignity but precede in the order of time. In [Col. 0898C] the prayer the Lord followed the order of dignity, which is artificial, descending from greater matters to lesser. The teachers, in their exposition, follow the order of time, which is natural, condescending from lesser matters to greater, or from temporal things to eternal ones.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the correspondence of the seven petitions and the seven gifts

Here a correspondence is made among the seven petitions, the seven gifts, the seven virtues, and the seven beatitudes, in opposition to the seven capital vices. For gifts are obtained by petitions, virtues by gifts, and beatitudes by virtues.

The seven gifts are these: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear, concerning which the prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon [Col. 0898D] him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

The seven virtues are these: poverty of spirit, meekness, mourning, hunger for righteousness, mercy, purity of heart, and peace. The seven beatitudes are these: the kingdom of heaven, possession of the earth, consolation, fullness, receiving mercy, the vision of God, and divine sonship. Of these the Lord says together: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be consoled. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for [Col. 0899A] righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5).

These are the seven principal vices: vainglory, anger, envy, sloth, avarice, gluttony, and lust. They were signified by the seven peoples holding the promised land of Israel: namely, the Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite (Deut. 7). Thus man is the sick person and God the physician; vices are diseases, petitions are lamentations, gifts are antidotes, virtues are health, and beatitudes are happiness and joys.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the winning of goodwill

[Col. 0899B] “Our Father, who art in heaven.” God is called Father generally, specially, and uniquely. God is Father generally of all through creation; specially of the righteous through adoption; uniquely of Christ through generation. Through creation, as here: “I bend my knees to the Lord, the almighty Father, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3). Through adoption, as here: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11). Through generation, as here: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11).

By saying, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” he dissuades [Col. 0899C] us from two things: from pride, lest we say, “My Father,” making private what is common; and from unworthiness, lest we become unworthy of so great a Father who dwells in heaven. Therefore God is Father of Christ alone by nature, and to him alone it properly belongs to say, “My Father.” He is Father of the faithful by grace, and it belongs to them to say, “Our Father.” The one says: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Mark 14); they say: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.” Hence he himself says: “I go to my Father” (John 16), “and your Father”: mine by nature, yours by grace. He also exhorts us to two things: to preserve the grace of adoption, when he says “Father”; and to the unity of brotherhood, when he says “our.”

Goodwill is won from three persons: the knower, the petitioner, and the assessor. The knower is God, the petitioner is man, and the assessor is the angel. From the person of the knower, when he says “Father”; of the petitioner, when he says “our”; of the assessor, when he says, “Who art in heaven,” [Col. 0899D] that is, in angels or in saints, of whom it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). Hence hope is granted us that he may make us saints, or may make us in heaven—that is, in the secret place of the divine majesty—through which confidence is given of obtaining the hidden gift which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). Thus he gives confidence in obtaining good. He does not say, “Lord,” whom one serves in fear, but “Father,” whom one serves in love, as if to say: You are Father; you will it; because you are in heaven, you are able; therefore you can deliver us from evil.

## CHAPTER XX. On the threefold evil from which we ask to be delivered

[Col. 0900A]

There is a threefold evil from which we ask to be delivered: inborn, added, and inflicted. We contract the first, commit the second, and endure the third. The first is original evil, the second actual evil, the third penal evil. We avoid evil through the spirit of fear; for, as Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclus. 1).

There is, moreover, a threefold fear by which we abstain from evil: servile, initial, and filial. By servile fear we abstain from evil through dread of punishment; by filial fear we abstain from evil through love of righteousness; by initial fear we abstain from evil partly through dread of punishment and partly through love of righteousness. Servile fear belongs to beginners, initial fear to those advancing, filial fear to the perfected.

[Col. 0900B] As if one were to say: Give us the spirit of fear and poverty of spirit, so that through the spirit of fear we may avoid evils, and through poverty of spirit renounce goods; so that, with vices excluded and earthly things despised, we may possess eternal things—namely, the kingdom of heaven—which Lucifer and the first parents lost through vainglory, from which fear, poverty of spirit, and truth draw us back.

There are two goods which we renounce by poverty of spirit: inward and outward goods. Inward goods, by not presuming upon them in our hearts; outward goods, by not setting our hearts upon them, according to the saying: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61). Therefore, when the former are restrained lest we presume, and the latter despised lest we fail, we obtain the kingdom of heaven, according to the saying: [Col. 0900C] “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5), which demons and human beings lost through vainglory. The former by vainly claiming likeness to God, the latter by vainly claiming God’s knowledge. For Lucifer said: “I shall ascend into heaven, and place my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). But to the first parents it was said: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the different temptations into which we ask not to be led

“Lead us not into temptation.” God tempts, man tempts, and the devil tempts. God tempts in order to test; man tempts in order to know; the devil tempts in order to deceive. Of the first it is written: “God tested Abraham” (Gen. 22); of the second it is said: “Test us, I beg you, for ten days” [Col. 0900D] (Dan. 1); of the third it is written: “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” (Acts 5).

Moreover, we are tempted in two ways: inwardly and outwardly. Inwardly through delight, outwardly through suggestion. Yet inward temptation accomplishes little, and outward temptation advances much, provided that one does not consent but resists. For it is written: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10); again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he shall receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1).

Therefore, when we are tempted without consent, we are led into temptation; when we consent, we are brought into temptation, as a fish is led into the net before it is caught. But when it is brought in, it is caught and held; then is fulfilled what the apostle James says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and [Col. 0901A] enticed by his own desire; then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, generates death” (Jas. 1).

Since the same apostle says that God is not a tempter of evils (ibid.), why do we ask that God not lead us into temptation? But God in one sense tempts, and in another sense does not tempt. He tempts in order to test, according to the saying: “Test me, O God, and try my heart” (Ps. 25); he does not tempt in order to deceive, according to the saying: “God tempts no one” (Jas. 1). We therefore ask that God not lead us into temptation—that is, that he not permit us to be led into it—as it is said: “There is no evil in a city which the Lord does not do,” that is, does not permit to happen (Amos 3). For it is written: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10).

[Col. 0901B] As if one were to say: Give us the spirit of piety and meekness of spirit, so that through the spirit of piety we may conquer temptation by exercising ourselves in piety; and through meekness of spirit may conquer anger by not returning evil for evil, so that we may thus possess the land of the living, which we shall obtain through the spirit of piety and meekness. For piety has promise “of the life that now is, and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4); and: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). Hence the Psalmist says: “The meek shall possess the earth and delight in the abundance of peace” (Ps. 26).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the three debts which we ask to be forgiven us

Sins are called debts because they make us debtors to punishment. For here the matter is not money-debts, [Col. 0901C] but debts arising from offenses. There are three debts which we ask to be forgiven us: sin against God, sin against our neighbor, and sin against ourselves. Hence: “We have sinned with our fathers,” against God; “we have acted unjustly,” against our neighbor; “we have committed iniquity,” against ourselves (Ps. 105).

But because we sin against God, we ask him himself to forgive us our debts; because we sin against our neighbors, we ask that he forgive us as we too forgive our debtors. On this condition and with this safeguard our debts are forgiven us: if we forgive our debtors. Otherwise, even debts already forgiven are recalled as debt, according to the saying: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you asked me. Ought you not then also to have had mercy on your fellow-servant, just as I had mercy on [Col. 0901D] you?” And his lord, angry, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt. “So will my heavenly Father do to you if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18).

Therefore, in order to show plainly that there is no fruit from the whole prayer unless we forgive our debtors, the Lord added at the end of all: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your offenses” (Matt. 6). Thus this prayer seems not to benefit those who do not forgive their debtors; indeed, it seems to harm them. For one who asks to be forgiven as he himself forgives his debtors clearly seems, if he does not forgive his own debtors, to ask that he himself not be forgiven.

[Col. 0902A] What, then, ought he forgive in the person who is unwilling either to make satisfaction or to ask pardon? Certainly, a distinction must be made between the perfect and the imperfect. The person who has undertaken the way of perfection ought in every way to pardon even one who does not ask forgiveness. But one who has not yet undertaken the vow of perfection is indeed bound to lay aside rancor from the heart, but is not bound to remit the satisfaction due. Nevertheless, we are all universally bound to love our enemies, to do good to those who hate us, and to pray for those who persecute and slander us (Matt. 5).

For there are faults in which it is itself culpable to relax punishment. And although we are bound to forgive sin against ourselves, we ought nevertheless to punish sin against God and sin against our neighbor. Therefore, whoever is troubled by hatred or envy is burdened [Col. 0902B] more by this prayer than helped by it, unless perhaps he already intends to forgive.

Nevertheless, each person appears to pray not in his own person but in the person of the whole Church. Therefore he does not say, “Forgive me my debts, as I forgive my debtors,” but says, “Forgive us our debts, as we too forgive our debtors.” Some, however, also wish “forgive us . . .” to be understood thus: forgive us our debts in such a way that we too may forgive our debtors—as if to say: Give us the gift and knowledge and mourning and virtue, so that we may recognize and mourn both our own sins and those of others, in order that you may forgive us our debts, and that we may thereby have consolation against envy, which makes a person waste away at another’s good.

For through knowledge and [Col. 0902C] mourning we receive remission in the present, and in the future we shall have consolation, as is written: “Cleanse me from my offense, for I acknowledge my iniquity” (Ps. 50); and: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be consoled” (Matt. 5).

Mourning is divided into the upper and lower watering, which Caleb gave to his daughter Achsah as a dowry (Josh. 15). The lower watering is for our own sins and those of others; hence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). The upper watering is for our sojourn in the present life and desire for the heavenly life; hence: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1). “But woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the five breads which we ask to be given us

[Col. 0902D]

“Our bread . . .” Five breads are necessary for us: four on the way and the fifth in the homeland. They are bodily, spiritual, doctrinal, sacramental, and eternal bread. Bodily bread is for sustenance, spiritual bread for formation, doctrinal bread for instruction, sacramental bread for expiation, eternal bread for enjoyment. Of the first: “Man does not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4); of the second: “Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke 11); of the third: “Come, eat my bread” (Prov. 9); of the fourth: “Whoever eats the bread of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11); of the fifth: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6).

For when a person has been delivered [Col. 0903A] from evil, has conquered temptations, and has had sins forgiven, he needs the spirit of fortitude, lest he fail while awaiting his reward. Therefore he says: “Give us our daily bread,” that is, what is necessary for us every day. Otherwise, what were ours could not be given to us unless it first ceased to be ours.

“Give us this day”: as if to say, Give us the spirit of fortitude, which may strengthen the soul with manifold bread, lest we fail in the present while hungering for righteousness, through which, driving out sloth, we shall in the future be filled with complete righteousness, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5).

Matthew says, “our supersubstantial bread,” which can be understood in two ways: either as one word or as two. As one word: “Give us supersubstantial bread,” that is, Christ, who is supersubstantial—that is, above all substances—who is the bread on the altar. Or thus: “Give us our bread,” that is, Christ, who is the proper food of the faithful; and this beyond bread—that is, beyond substantial bread, bread necessary for sustenance—as if to say: Give us our bread, for mind and body.

[Col. 0903B] Luke says, “our daily bread,” which can be understood of both bodily and sacramental bread, namely of viaticum. The Greek has *epiousion* (ἐπιούσιον), which is translated “supersubstantial.” The Hebrew, however, has *sogolla* [*segullah*?], which is translated “excellent” or “peculiar”; perhaps for this reason Luke, seeing that Matthew had said *sogolla*, which conveys “peculiar,” said “daily.” But the Greek translator of Matthew, seeing that he had said *sogolla*, which conveys “excellent,” says [Col. 0903C] *epiousion*, that is, “supersubstantial.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the will of God which we ask to be done on earth as in heaven

“May your will be done.” The will of God is understood in two ways: God’s eternal good pleasure, and the temporal sign of that good pleasure. God’s good pleasure is always fulfilled; hence: “Who can resist his will?” (Rom. 9); and: “The Lord has done all things whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 113).

There are five signs of good pleasure: command, prohibition, promise, counsel, and operation. Hence: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out [Col. 0903D] in all his wills” (Ps. 110). These are not always fulfilled, but we pray that they may be fulfilled: “May your will be done,” that is, may what you command, counsel, and urge be completed in deed; because willing is insufficient where ability is present.

“As in heaven, so also on earth”: that is, as in angels, so in human beings; or as in the perfect, so also in converts; or as in Christ, so in the Church; or as in the mind, so likewise in the flesh, so that the flesh may not desire against the spirit, according to the saying: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83).

As if to say: Give us the spirit of counsel, so that we may do your will, especially mercy, which destroys avarice, in order that we may obtain mercy, according to the saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall [Col. 0904A] obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). For just as avarice consists in acquiring and retaining, so mercy consists in giving and forgiving.

The fulfillment of this petition and of the other two begins on the way and is consummated in the homeland. There we shall be able to will nothing except what we know God wills. Then we shall love God with all our heart, all our mind, and all our soul (Matt. 22): with the heart, that is, with the understanding, we shall love the Son; wholly, that is, without error. With the mind, that is, with the memory, we shall love the Father; wholly, that is, without forgetfulness. With the soul, that is, with the will, we shall love the Holy Spirit; wholly, that is, without opposition: the Father as power, the Son as wisdom, and the Holy Spirit as kindness.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the kingdom of God which we ask to come

[Col. 0904B]

“May your kingdom come.” The Church militant is called the kingdom of God because it is ruled; the Church triumphant because it reigns. Likewise, both the grace of faith and the glory of sight are called the kingdom of God. Again, the understanding of Scripture and the place of the homeland are called the kingdom of God.

Of the kingdom of the Church militant it is written: “The angels shall go forth as reapers and gather from his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13). Of the kingdom of the Church triumphant it is found: “They shall come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8). Of the kingdom of faith Scripture says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). Of the kingdom of sight the Lord says: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you from the origin of the world” (Matt. 25). Of the kingdom of Scripture we read: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you [Col. 0904C] and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21). Of the kingdom of the homeland it is found: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13).

Christ himself too is called the kingdom of God, according to the saying: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has fully come upon you” (Matt. 14).

“May your kingdom come,” therefore: that is, may kingdom come to kingdom, the militant to the triumphant. “May your kingdom come”: that is, may it come to see you, so that the kingdom of faith may pass into the kingdom of sight; for this is eternal life, “that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17).

As if to say: Give us the spirit of understanding, by which, cleansed in heart, we may understand that you reign in the present through faith, so that in the future [Col. 0904D] we may see you reigning in us through sight (2 Cor. 5). This is opposed to gluttony, concerning which the prophet says: “Wine and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. 4). Then we shall know as we are known, seeing not through a mirror in an enigma; but then face to face we shall see the God of gods in Zion (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the sanctification of the name

“Hallowed be your name.” The Father’s name is sanctified in his children in four ways: two on the way and two in the homeland. On the way, through effecting and perseverance; in the homeland, through consummation and manifestation.

For on the way the Father’s name is sanctified in his children when he works in them the effect of sanctification, or when the sanctification they have received in the [Col. 0905A] Father’s name persists in them. In the homeland, however, the Father’s name is sanctified in his children because it is ratified and confirmed in them, so that they can never be separated from the grace of sonship.

For here the Father’s name in his children is, as it were, movable: Judas was at one time a son and at another was not. Because of this possibility of remaining, the Apostle said: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

And there the Father’s name is sanctified in his children because the children there are such that the Holy Spirit appears in them. Those who are now hidden will then be manifest, according to the saying: “We fools thought their life madness and their end without honor; behold how they are counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints” (Wis. 5).

[Col. 0905B] As if to say: Give us the spirit of wisdom, insofar as it is said to derive from *sapor*, “taste,” that is, eternal delight, so that we may taste how sweet the Lord is (Wis. 12), producing in us peace—that is, the repose of inward motions—so that the flesh may not desire against the spirit (Gal. 5), because “there is no peace in my bones because of sins” (Ps. 37). Thus may your name—that is, the Father in his children—be sanctified, so that they may be separated from the grace of sonship with difficulty in the present, and not at all in the future.

This is plainly opposed to lust. The one troubled by lust does not delight in God—that is, does not have the peace of God; he is not a son of God but is likened to a beast, because, like a beast, he rots in his own dung (Joel 1).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the twofold order

[Col. 0905C]

There are, however, two orders to be noted in the Lord’s Prayer: one in descending, which corresponds with the gifts; and the other in ascending, which corresponds or agrees with the virtues. For the gifts descend from the highest things to the lowest. Hence: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11).

A human being, surrounded by many evils, first [Col. 0906A] asks to be delivered from evil. Since temptation is the life of man upon earth (Job 8), once delivered from evil, he asks not to be led into temptation. And because, while he remains in this life, he is always in some sin—for “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1)—he asks that his debts be forgiven.

When he has been delivered from evil, conquered temptations, and had debts forgiven, because he cannot stand by himself and lest he fail through waiting too long, he asks that daily bread be given to him. Then, when he has been delivered from evils and strengthened in goods, he asks that God’s will be done as in heaven and on earth. Since this cannot be done perfectly in the present life, he immediately asks that the kingdom may come, in which the Father’s name may be sanctified in his children, [Col. 0906B] so that henceforth they may never be able to be separated from sanctification. Amen.

The Hebrew places one of these three at the end: “Amen Salem,” which signifies “truly,” “always,” “peace.” Blessed Gregory judged that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited after the canon over the host.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the silence after the Lord’s Prayer

What follows, said secretly, signifies the Lord’s burial during the intervening Sabbath, when the Lord rested in the tomb. Hence, as Luke testifies: “The women who had prepared spices kept silent on the Sabbath according to the commandment” (Luke 24).

But he who rested in the tomb according to the flesh [Col. 0906C] descended into hell according to the soul, so that, coming upon the strong armed man as one stronger, he might despoil him (Matt. 12). Then, therefore, he bit hell, in order to bring forth his own captives from the pit in which there was no water (Zech. 9): delivering them from past, present, and future evils, and giving them everlasting peace, in which they are always free from sin and secure from disturbance.

This prayer, “Deliver us . . .,” is called the embolism and is an exposition of the final petition of the Lord’s Prayer.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0905]

## CHAPTER I. On the resumption of the paten, which the priest takes and kisses

[Col. 0905D]

After the sorrow of the Passion, one arrives at the joy of the Resurrection, according to the saying: “Weeping shall remain in the evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 29).

The subdeacon and deacon present the paten, which the priest takes and kisses, and with it makes the sign of the cross upon his face. These men signify, both by their number and by their service, those holy women of whom the evangelist Matthew narrates: “At the evening of the Sabbath, when it was beginning to dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb” (Matt. 28). They present the paten, that is, the heart opened wide by the breadth of charity for the service [Col. 0906D] of burial.

Accordingly, it is written: “The women bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus; and very early, on the first day of the week, they come to the monument when the sun had already risen. And they said to one another: Who will roll the stone away for us from the door of the monument?” (Mark 16).

Therefore the priest takes this paten—that is, the heart expanded by the breadth of charity—meaning that Christ accepts it. But because the Crucified One was sought with ardent desire, as the angel said to the women: “I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified” (Matt. 28), his cross is therefore marked with the paten upon the priest’s face. Immediately the priest kisses the paten, showing that Christ at once fulfilled the women’s desire; for he soon met them, saying, “Hail.” “And falling down, they took hold of his feet and worshiped [Col. 0907A] him” (ibid.); without doubt, they kissed his feet.

## CHAPTER II. On the breaking of the host, a particle of which the priest puts into the chalice

Then the priest breaks the host into three parts. Reserving two outside the chalice, with the other he makes the sign of the cross three times over the chalice, from whose mouth the deacon had removed the corporal. Saying in a loud voice, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” he lets the particle of the host fall into the chalice.

The priest breaks the host so that we may know the Lord in the breaking of bread, as those two disciples knew the Lord to whom Jesus appeared that same day of the Resurrection while they were travelling to Emmaus (Luke 24). The mingling of bread and wine signifies [Col. 0907B] the union of flesh and soul, which were joined again in Christ’s Resurrection. For, as stated above, bread refers to the flesh and wine to the soul.

Therefore the sign of the cross is made three times with the host over the chalice, because the power of the Trinity brings the soul of the Crucified One back to the flesh, so that he might not leave his soul in hell nor allow his flesh to see corruption. As he himself says in the Psalm: “I slept and began to sleep, and I rose, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 15, 3). Three crosses are made with the host over the mouth of the chalice because three women sought the Crucified One at the door of the monument. Hence: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke 24).

Thus, in this place, the mouth of the chalice signifies the door of the monument, from which the deacon removes the corporal, signifying that the angel of the Lord rolled away the stone from the door of the monument. This, certainly, must be understood concerning what the priest says when he puts the host into the chalice: “May there be,” he says, “a mingling of the body and blood of the Lord.” This must of course be referred to the species of bread and wine, under which the body and blood are contained.

## CHAPTER III. What the parts made from the sacrifice signify

What these parts signify Pope Sergius determines when he says: “The body of Christ is threefold.” The part offered and put into the chalice shows the body of Christ which has already risen. The part consumed signifies that still walking upon earth. The part remaining on the altar until the end signifies the body lying in the tomb, because until the end [Col. 0907D] of the world the bodies of the saints shall be in the tomb.

This mystery may also be explained otherwise. The body of Christ is the universal Church, namely the head with its members, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Though many, we are one bread and one body” (1 Cor. 10). In this body, from which the whole body consists, there are, as it were, three parts. One part is the head itself, namely Christ, who is both head and a part of the body. The other part consists of those whose bodies rest in tombs and whose souls reign with Christ. These two parts—the head and this other part of the body—are, as it were, together, as it is written: “Wherever the body may be, there the eagles shall be gathered” (Matt. 24).

For this reason two parts are reserved separately upon the altar outside the chalice, as though outside the Passion, which is signified by the chalice. For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6). And the saints who are with him “shall hunger no more, nor thirst, neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 7, 21).

[Col. 0908A] The third part is placed in the chalice, signifying those who still remain in suffering, until, departing from this life, they pass to their head and neither die any more nor suffer in any way.

## CHAPTER IV. On the *Agnus Dei*
Not only through signs, however, but also through words is the joy of the Resurrection made known. For the priest, [Col. 0908B] proclaiming aloud, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” indicates that on the first day of the week Jesus came and stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them, “Peace be with you.” But since Jesus, immediately after greeting the apostles, gave them the power to remit sins—“Whose sins,” he says, “you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20)—therefore the choir cries out to him and asks: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us.” For he has washed us from our sins in his blood.

“Lamb” is said in Greek from ἁγνόν (*hagnon*), meaning “pious”; in Latin from *agnoscendo*, “recognizing,” because amid a great flock it recognizes its mother by her bleating alone. But Christ, upon the altar of the cross, recognized both Father and mother: the Father by obedience, the mother by care. And there, being pious, he offered himself for us. [Col. 0908C] Therefore, in the immolation at the altar, “Lamb of God” is said three times, as though: “O Lamb, who recognized the Father, have mercy on us; O pious one, who redeemed the world, grant us peace.”

Yet according to the ancient custom of the school of singers—which they themselves still preserve, and which is observed in many churches, as at the Lateran, where it is not altered at all—“have mercy upon us” is said uniformly three times, on account of the three kinds of sins for which we ask forgiveness: those of thought, speech, and action—of thought in the heart, of speech in the mouth, and of action in deed. Or this is on account of the three ranks of the faithful in the Church: Noah, Daniel, and Job, whom Ezekiel saw in a vision as to be saved (Ezek. 14). And according to the evangelical parable, there are two in bed, two in the field, and two at the mill; one of them will be taken and the other left (Matt. 24). [Col. 0908D]

Later, as many varied adversities and terrors came upon the Church, it began to cry to the Lord in its tribulation: “Grant us peace.” And, so that its cry might more readily be heard, I deemed that it should be cried out at the very hour of the immolation. Yet this variation does not depart from the custom of the Old Testament, where, after “Spare, O Lord, spare your people” is found twice, the third occurrence varies: “and do not give your inheritance over to reproach” (Joel 2).

Therefore let us say “Have mercy upon us” with respect to the soul; again, “Have mercy upon us” with respect to the flesh; and “Grant us peace” with respect to both: that we may possess spiritual peace of the breast and temporal peace of the body. Pope Sergius decreed [Col. 0909A] that, during communion, the clergy should sing “Lamb of God.”

## CHAPTER V. On the Kiss of Peace

After the Lord greeted the apostles, he again said, “Peace be with you” (John 20), showing that we ought not only to have peace in our mouths, but also peace in our breasts, lest we be among those “who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts” (Ps. 27). Therefore, when he had said this to the apostles, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20).

To signify this, the priest gives a kiss with his mouth to the minister, who, reverently bowing, kisses his breast and extends the paten, so that charity may be understood through the kiss of peace—[Col. 0909B] charity which, as we said above, the paten signifies. Therefore, because the charity of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5), the kiss of peace is passed throughout the Church among all the faithful. For the Apostle also exhorts us (Rom. 16) to greet one another with a holy kiss.

In the primitive Church, those attending the celebration of Masses customarily communicated every day. But as the multitude of faithful increased, it is said that a rule was established that they should communicate only on Sundays. Later, because not even this could be observed, a third ordinance followed: that every Christian should receive the Eucharist at least three times a year. This remedy was found: that the kiss of peace should be given every day as a mystery of unity. Since, through the immolation of the saving Victim, we are reconciled to the Most High by the forgiveness of sins, the Church rightly decreed the kiss of peace when the saving Victim is immolated for sins.

Pope Innocent I, however, assigns another reason. [Note: [Col. 0909D] Innocent I, *To Decentius*, ch. 1.] “You assert,” he says, “that some order the peace to be given to the people before the consecrated mysteries, or that priests exchange it among themselves, whereas, after all those things which I ought not to disclose, the peace must necessarily be proclaimed. Through it, it is made evident that the people have given their assent to everything enacted in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that these things have been concluded by the seal of the peace which brings them to an end.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the Various Kisses Given in Mass

[Col. 0909D] A kiss in Sacred Scripture signifies union, charity, peace, and reverence. Concerning the kiss of union, the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). Concerning the kiss of charity, Isaac says to his son: “Come near to me and give me a kiss, my son” (Gen. 27). Concerning the kiss of peace, the Apostle says in his Epistles: “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (Rom. 16). Concerning the kiss of reverence, the Lord says to Simon: “You did not give me a kiss; but she, since she entered, has not ceased to kiss my feet” (Luke 7).

Therefore, to signify the three unions in Christ, the priest kisses the altar three times: namely, the union of divinity with the soul, of divinity with the flesh, [Col. 0910A] and of flesh with the soul; or the union by which human nature, the holy Church, and the faithful soul are united to Christ. To signify the threefold peace—temporal, spiritual, and eternal—the bishop celebrating solemnly kisses the minister three times; or he kisses the ministers once, the deacon a second time, and the priest a third time.

Also, to indicate the harmony of the two Testaments, the bishop kisses the book twice, because “wheel is within wheel” and the two cherubim look upon one another with faces turned toward the propitiatory [mercy-seat] (Ezek. 1). To signify charity, the priest kisses the paten, which represents a heart open to the height of charity. Hence: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way?” (Luke 29 [apparently an erroneous citation]).

As a sign of reverence, the deacon and subdeacon kiss [Col. 0910B] the feet and hands of the supreme pontiff. The subdeacon kisses the feet after the Epistle has been read; and, before reading the Gospel, the deacon kisses the hand, offering the vessel containing water and the chalice containing wine. The subdeacon likewise offers the paten with the host and the censer with incense; and both, when receiving the Eucharist from the pontiff’s hand, kiss his hand. Nor is it believed devoid of mystery that the supreme pontiff receives a kiss from the minister in seven ways: on the mouth, breast, shoulder, hands, arms, feet, and knees—an explicit mystery, but one to be explained elsewhere.

## CHAPTER VII. Why the Bishop Communicates the Subdeacon and Deacon

[Col. 0910C]

Then the bishop communicates with the ministers, indicating that after the Resurrection Christ ate with his disciples. For, while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem (Acts 1). That he receives one portion and gives the remaining portions to the ministers indicates what Luke the Evangelist recounts: that Jesus, taking bread, ate before his disciples and, taking the leftovers, gave them to them. And because, as the same Evangelist testifies, Jesus took bread, broke it, and handed it to those whose hearts burned within them (Luke 24), the pontiff takes an entire half of the Eucharist upon the paten, breaks it into portions, and gives them to the ministers to eat.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Washing of Hands after Receiving the Eucharist

[Col. 0910D]

After receiving the Eucharistic sacrifice, the priest washes and rinses his hands, lest anything inadvertently remain from contact with the most divine sacrament. This is not because he has contracted anything unclean from contact with the sacrament, but rather so that he may call to mind his own unworthiness—he who has judged himself unworthy to celebrate such great mysteries—according to the Lord’s saying: “When you have done all good things, say: We are useless servants” (Luke 17).

Indeed, it would be unseemly for hands that have handled the incorruptible body to touch a corruptible body until they have been carefully washed. The water of washing [Col. 0911A] ought honorably to be poured into a clean place, so that the sublimity of the sacrament may be honored more reverently.

The priest’s threefold washing, performed at the beginning, middle, and end, signifies the cleansing of thought, speech, and deed; or the purgation of original, mortal, and venial sin; or of that which is done through ignorance, negligence, and deliberate intent, for whose cleansing the saving sacrifice is offered. This washing may also be referred to the washing of baptism, the form of which Christ established after the Resurrection: “Go,” he said, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Matt. 28; Mark 16).

## CHAPTER IX. That the Roman Pontiff Observes Another Custom in Communicating

[Col. 0911B]

So that no deception may arise in receiving Christ’s body and blood, but the reality of reception in both may be clearly apparent, the supreme pontiff does not immediately place the particle of the host in the chalice. Rather, after making the sign of the cross three times, he places it again upon the paten; and after the kiss of peace, ascending to the seat and standing there, in sight of all he receives the larger portion of the offering from the paten which the deacon presents to him. Dividing it in their sight, he takes one particle and puts another into the chalice, which the subdeacon holds before him, and from which he drinks the blood through a reed.

Then he gives one particle with a kiss to the deacon, and another to the subdeacon [Col. 0911C] without a kiss. The deacon kisses the subdeacon, who serves him at the altar with the chalice. Then the subdeacon receives with the blood the particle placed in the chalice.

I have heard from some a reason for this practice—not an allegorical but a historical one—which, since I have never been able to find in an authoritative writing, I judged better left unspoken than rashly asserted. And although a reason cannot be given for everything instituted by our elders, I nevertheless think that profound mysteries lie hidden in these matters.

The Roman pontiff does not communicate where he breaks the bread, but breaks at the altar and communicates at the seat, because Christ broke bread at Emmaus before two disciples, but ate in Jerusalem before the eleven apostles. At Emmaus he is recorded as having broken it [Col. 0911D] (Luke 24), but not as having eaten; in Jerusalem he is not recorded as having broken it, but is recorded as having eaten.

The ministers present the offering and chalice to the pontiff because the disciples offered Christ a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb. The portion of broiled fish signifies the crucified body of the Lord, which was roasted upon the altar of the cross; the honeycomb signifies Christ’s blood, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to the palate of the loving soul.

To indicate the distinction between sacred and non-sacred orders, the deacon and those of higher rank receive a kiss from the bishop when they receive the Eucharist; the acolyte and those of lower orders do not. But the subdeacon, because this rank was once counted among the non-sacred orders but is now counted among the sacred orders, does not receive [Col. 0912A] a kiss from the pontiff upon receiving the body, but receives one from the deacon upon receiving the blood, so that those who are not among the sacred orders may be honored more. Although a mystical reason may also be assigned for this.

## CHAPTER X. On the Post-Communion

The antiphon sung after communion signifies the apostles’ joy at Christ’s Resurrection, according to what is read: that the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord, and in their joy were amazed (John 20). Its responsive singing indicates that the disciples announced the joy of the Resurrection to one another.
