Thus, when the two disciples found the eleven assembled, and those with them, saying, “The Lord has truly risen [Col. 0912B] and has appeared to Simon,” they themselves related what had happened on the way and how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread (Luke 24). Therefore, “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117).

## CHAPTER XI. On the Final Prayer

When the mystery of the altar has been completed, the pontiff proceeds with the ministers to the altar; kissing it, and raising his hands, he performs the final prayer, signifying the blessing which Christ, as he was about to ascend into heaven, is recorded to have spoken over his disciples. For, as Luke recounts, he led them out to Bethany and, lifting up his hands, blessed them. And it came to pass, when he had blessed them, that he withdrew from them and was carried [Col. 0912C] into heaven (Luke 24).

Therefore, after the final greeting which the priest gives to the people, the deacon pronounces aloud: “Go, the dismissal is made,” representing what was said to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven” (Acts 1). The choir, answering with thanksgiving, “Thanks be to God,” imitates the apostles, who worshiped and returned to Jerusalem with great joy and were always in the Temple, praising and blessing God (Luke 24).

This also pertains to the fact that on non-feast days one says, “Let us bless the Lord; Thanks be to God,” and immediately the hymn and psalms called “Bless” and “Praise” are said. It should be noted that after the Resurrection Christ is recorded as having greeted the disciples twice, saying, “Peace be with you,” [Col. 0912D] as a sign of the twofold peace, namely that of time and eternity, which according to the prophet is “peace upon peace” (Isa. 66). Of this the Lord says to the apostles: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14). The priest indicates this twofold peace by a double kiss, when he first kisses the minister and afterward the altar.

## CHAPTER XII. Why It Is Called Mass

*Mass* (*missa*) means both ministry and mystery: that is, the office which is performed and the sacrifice which is offered. The office is divided into the Mass of the catechumens and the Mass of the faithful. The Mass of the catechumens extends from the entrance until after the offertory. It is called *missa* from *emittendo*, “sending out,” because at the time when the priest begins [Col. 0913A] to consecrate the Eucharist, the catechumens are sent outside the church. For after the Gospel had been read, the deacon was accustomed to cry: “If any catechumen is present, let him go out.” Catechumens ought not to be present at the sacred mysteries, which are entrusted only to baptized believers.

Thus it is written of certain persons who bore the type of catechumens and had not yet been reborn: “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them” (John 2). The Mass of the faithful extends from the offertory to the post-communion. It is called *missa* from *dimittendo*, “dismissing,” because then each of the faithful is dismissed to his own home. For it was decreed at the Council of Orléans that when people gather in God’s name to celebrate Masses, they should not leave before the solemnity of Mass is completed. [Note: [Col. 0913D] Canon 22.]

The entire office, however, is called *missa*, [Col. 0913B] as though “a transmission,” because the faithful people, through the ministry of the priest—who performs the office of mediator between God and human beings—transmit prayers, supplications, and vows to the Most High. The sacrifice itself, that is, the victim, is called *missa*, as though “sent”: first sent to us by the Father, that it might be with us; afterward sent by us to the Father, that it might intercede for us with him. First from the Father to us through the Incarnation; afterward from us to the Father through the Passion. And in the sacrament, first from the Father to us through sanctification; afterward from us to the Father through offering. This is the one sufficient and fitting sending, or embassy, for dissolving the enmities and offenses between God and humankind. Thus, when the deacon says, “Go, the dismissal is made,” it is as though he said: “Return to your homes, for the saving Victim has been offered.”

## CHAPTER XIII. Why the Priest Kisses the Pontiff’s Shoulder

[Col. 0913C]

When the prayer is ended, the priest assisting the bishop kisses the altar-table and the pontiff’s right shoulder, showing that he is that pontiff who, according to the Law, must figuratively set apart the right shoulder from the saving or peace offerings (Lev. 6, 8). By the shoulder, indeed, authority is expressed, [Col. 0914A] according to the prophetic saying: “Authority has been placed upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9).

The angelic, prophetic, and legal voice expressed the Savior’s authority. The angel says to the Virgin: “The Lord will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1). The prophet says in the Psalms: “Your throne is for ever and ever; a righteous rod is the rod of your kingdom. Therefore God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Moses says in the Law: “Rejoice together, O heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him” (Deut. 32). To signify this, three persons kiss the pontiff’s shoulder as a token of reverence: the primicerius at the beginning, the deacon in the middle, and the priest at the end.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Final Blessing

[Col. 0914B]

The final blessing which the bishop gives over the people signifies the sending of the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord sent from heaven upon the apostles, as he himself promised them: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you” (Acts 1). This blessing is expressed through the word of the mouth and the sign of the cross, because that mission was revealed through the sound of air and tongues of fire, as it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent rushing wind. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire . . .” (ibid.).

Although the Holy Spirit was specially sent to the apostles, nevertheless, because the works of the Trinity are undivided, the whole Trinity effected that mission. Therefore the bishop gives this blessing in the name of the Trinity, by the authority of the Psalmist saying: “May God, our God, bless us; and may God bless us” (Ps. 66). [Col. 0914C] The authority of the Law set forth the form of blessing, when the Lord said through Moses: “You shall invoke my name upon the children of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless” (Num. 6).

## CONCLUSION OF THE LITTLE BOOK

[Col. 0913]

[Col. 0913D] Let no one, upon hearing this exposition, judge this sacrifice to have been sufficiently expounded. For perhaps, when he has exalted a human work, he may diminish the divine sacrament. For so many and such great mysteries are wrapped up in this office that no one, unless taught by anointing, is sufficient to explain them. “For who knows the order of heaven, and will set forth its reasons upon the earth?” (Job 38). For “the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25).

Indeed, since I was unable with dim eyes to behold the sun in its circuit, I seemed to behold the majesty of so great a mystery as if “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). Not penetrating into the inner chambers of the upper room, but sitting before the doors in the vestibule, I did diligently what I could, not sufficiently what [Col. 0914D] I wished. Especially because, by reason of my office, I am hindered by so many pressing demands and entangled in so many business affairs that, within a short span of time, I have been able to gain neither leisure for reflection nor quiet for dictation. And indeed, least in each respect and divided among individual matters, I could scarcely dictate what I had reflected upon, much less conceive it through reflection.

Therefore I implore not only a kind reader but also desire a free corrector. This is the sole reward for this little work which I expect from people: that they pour forth devout prayers for my sins before the merciful Judge, who perfectly knows with what intention of heart I composed this treatise—whether it may benefit, if not many, at least some, or even myself alone, though only a little. But since I have expounded the canon of the Mass piece by piece, lest anything seem added, omitted, or transposed, and so that a fuller understanding of the exposition itself may be open to readers, I judged that the whole should be appended continuously.

[Col. 0915] When the book is finished, let praise and glory be to Christ.

[Col. 0915]

# ENCOMIUM OF POPE INNOCENT III ON THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY AND HER SON JESUS CHRIST

[Col. 0915B] The Virgin Mother of God is the rod; her son is the flower. I presume to say a few, and only a few, words about the Virgin rod and the Son flower. Wonderful is the flower’s height, and unattainable the rod’s loftiness. This is the straight rod: upright, tall, frail, slender, flexible, leafy, flower-bearing, fruit-bearing. Straight through righteousness; upright through devotion; tall through long-suffering; frail through self-abasement; slender through humility; flexible through gentleness; leafy through most holy conduct; flower-bearing through virginal conception; fruit-bearing through the birth of eternal life.

Straight through faith; upright through hope; tall through charity; frail through modesty; slender through contempt of the world; flexible through compassion for one’s neighbor; leafy through the performance of good works; flower-bearing through the glory of virginity; fruit-bearing through the prerogative of fertility. Wonderful is the prerogative of fertility: that one so great gave birth to one so great, in such a manner. A slender virgin before childbirth and a virgin after childbirth. In what manner? With the angel announcing, the Holy Spirit working, and the power of the Most High overshadowing (Luke 1). To whom did she give birth? To the Holy of holies, the only son of the virgin mother, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, God and Lord of majesty.

O how well and rightly he is called a flower, who springs from the virginal rod, and in whom there is always something to marvel at! [Col. 0916B] For he is slight, tender, and light; gentle and beautiful; fragrant and useful. What is slighter than this flower when it is bound? What more tender when it is crushed? What gentler when it is touched? What lighter when it is carried? What more beautiful when it is seen? What more fragrant when it is adored? What more useful when its effect is considered? (Ps. 64).

The Virgin’s Son and slender flower is slight in indignation, tender in compassion, gentle through meekness, light in dominion, beautiful in moderation, fragrant in promise, useful in reward. Thus he is slight under scourges, tender in mercies, gentle in gifts, light in commandments, beautiful in examples, fragrant in promises, fruitful in rewards.

This flower has become for us medicine; in him drink and food; from him honey and wax. He is medicine in redemption, drink and food in justification, honey and wax in glorification. From this medicine comes the everlasting health of incorruption; from this medicine, the food of the inward refreshment of satiety; from this medicine, the drink of spiritual intoxication and eternal fruitfulness; from his wax, the brightness of supreme radiance; in his honey, the sweetness of perpetual blessedness.

[Col. 0916C] Christ is flower for us in his humanity and fruit in his divinity: flower on earth, fruit in heaven; flower in redemption, fruit in glorification. May he himself deign to grant this to us. Amen.

[Col. 0915]

# THREE MOST EFFECTIVE PRAYERS OF POPE INNOCENT III ON THE LIFE AND PASSION OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

*To those who read them contritely and devoutly, he granted many remissions and indulgences.*

## PRAYER I

[Col. 0915D]

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who for our redemption willed to be born and circumcised; to be rejected by the Jews; to be betrayed by Judas with a kiss; to be seized and bound; to be brought in bonds before Annas, Caiaphas, Herod, and Pilate; to be mocked before them; to be struck with fists, slaps, scourges, and a reed; to have your face veiled and to be spat upon; to be crowned with thorns; to be accused also by false witnesses; [Col. 0916D] to be judged; and, like an innocent lamb, to be led to sacrifice while carrying your cross; to be pierced with nails; to be given gall and vinegar to drink; to be condemned upon the cross to a most shameful death; and to be wounded by a lance: through these most sacred sufferings, free us from all sins and punishments; and through your holy cross lead us miserable sinners to that place to which you led the thief crucified with you when he repented late in the day. You who live, etc.

## PRAYER II

[Col. 0917A]

May all your sufferings aid us, merciful Lord Jesus Christ, and defend us from every pain and sorrow; every danger and misery; every sin and impurity of heart; every scandal and dishonor; the evil diseases of soul and body; sudden and unforeseen death; and every persecution by visible and invisible enemies. For we know that in whatever hour or day we call your Passion to mind, we shall be saved. Therefore, trusting in your boundless mercy, we beseech you, most merciful Savior, through your most benign and most sacred sufferings, protect us with your gracious help and preserve us continually, in your mercy, from every evil. You who live, etc.

## PRAYER III

[Col. 0918A]

Lord, God from God, light from light, who deigned, at the Father’s command, to redeem the human race upon the gibbet of the cross with your own blood: we humbly beseech you not to deal with us according to our sins, but according to your mercy save us, your unworthy servants. Rise also to our aid, and be for us a tower of strength and an unconquerable shield of righteousness against the presence of both bodily and incorporeal enemies. Mercifully free us from every sin and punishment, and graciously defend us from every adversity of body and soul. You who live, etc.

[Col. 0917]

# THREE PRAYERS OF POPE INNOCENT III CONCERNING ALL THE SAINTS, FOR THE DEFENSE AND PEACE OF THE CATHOLIC AND ORTHODOX CHURCH

## PRAYER I

[Col. 0917B]

From all perils of mind and body defend us, we beseech you, O Lord; and through the intercession of the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, together with your blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and blessed N. and all the saints, graciously grant us health and peace, so that, with every adversity and error destroyed, your Church may serve you in secure freedom. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

## PRAYER II

Hear us, our Savior, that through the power of the most sacred Passion of your only-begotten Son you may protect us from all enemies of mind and body, granting grace [Col. 0918B] in the present and glory in the future. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

## PRAYER III

May the most precious blood of your only-begotten Son, poured out and offered to you on the cross, cleanse and fortify us, we beseech you, O Lord; and through the intercession of the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, together with your blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and blessed N. and all the saints, render us cleansed from all perversities and delivered from adversities. Through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0917]

*To it he granted certain great remissions and indulgences.*

[Col. 0917C]

[Col. 0921]

# BOOK OF POPE INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF, ON THE FOURFOLD KIND OF MARRIAGE

*(Trombelli, Little Works of Bede and Claudius of Turin, and likewise of other ancient Fathers, Bologna, 1755, quarto.)*

Here begins the prologue to the book *On the Fourfold Kind of Marriage* [Note: [Col. 0921] Innocent III delivered, at the consecration of a pontiff, a sermon bearing the same title—namely, “On the Four Kinds of Betrothals”—p. 191, vol. 1. But that sermon is brief and scarcely touches the matters which he treats copiously in the work we publish.] by Lord Pope Innocent III, addressed to Benedict, priest.

I rejoice, [Note: [Col. 0921] Is this Benedict the Cardinal of St. Peter in Chains, to whom, together with the Cardinal of the Twelve Apostles, letters of Innocent III are directed (pp. 9 and 18, vol. 2)? Let the reader decide. But why is he called “brother,” when pontiffs customarily call even cardinal-priests “sons”? Must this be attributed to a copyist, who, finding the letter *f.* in an ancient manuscript, interpreted it as *frater* (“brother”) when *filius* (“son”) ought to have been written? Or did Innocent wish to honor with the name of brother a man most approved to him, whom he afterward calls a participant in his difficulties? Let the reader judge this also.] most beloved brother in the Lord, because I understand that you are zealous for the understanding of the sacred Scriptures. For this study befits a priest of the Lord, to whom it has been granted by virtue of his office to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God.

For this reason, in the ancient priesthood—which bore the figure of the new—the *logion* [breastpiece of judgment] adorned the pontiff’s breast among other things; it was square and double. [Note: [Col. 0921] Exod. 28:15–16.] For the priest’s reason, which the breastpiece signifies both by its position and by its name, ought to distinguish among four things: between truth and falsehood, lest it err in what is believed; and between good and evil, lest it err in what is done. It must also distinguish for two parties, namely priest and people, lest, if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit. [Note: [Col. 0921] Matt. 15:14.]

It was therefore square because of the fourfold sense which a priest ought to possess in Scripture. It was also double because of the twofold Testament, which it does not benefit a priest to ignore. It was square because of the New Testament, which is contained in the four Gospels; double because of the Old Testament, which is inscribed upon two tablets. For who can avoid what he does not know? Or who can do what he does not understand? For it is written: “They have not known, nor understood; they walk in darkness.” [Note: [Col. 0921] Ps. 81:5.] “He was unwilling to understand, that he might do good; he devised iniquity upon his bed.” [Note: [Col. 0921] Ps. 35:4–5.] “They have not known my ways, concerning whom I swore in my wrath: if they shall enter into my rest.” [Note: [Col. 0921] Ps. 74:11.] “You have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, that you may not perform priestly office for me.” [Note: [Col. 0921] Hos. 4:6.] “Therefore my people have been led captive into Egypt because they had no knowledge. Their nobles have perished by hunger, and their multitude has dried up with thirst.” [Note: [Col. 0921] Isa. 5:13.] “The sheep failed for lack of food, because there were no sheep in the manger.” [Note: [Col. 0921] Either he follows some ancient translation, or some proverb not at all current in our own times.]

Since, then, the lips of the priest ought to guard knowledge, because the Law is sought from his mouth, you—desiring to be what you are called—meditate continually upon the law of the Lord. And what you are unable to grasp by your own reasoning, you strive to perceive through another’s teaching, preferring to be a disciple of truth rather than a master of error.

For in the breastpiece of judgment which we have mentioned, Urim and Thummim—that is, “manifestation” and “truth”—are recorded to have been placed, because in the priest’s breast there ought to be a manifest knowledge of truth. Therefore, inflamed by zeal for this study, you have often requested with much earnest prayer that I compose for you a concise treatise on the marriages of bridegroom and bride, in which I should set forth the analogies between carnal and spiritual marriages, and especially expound Psalm 44, in which the marriage of bridegroom and bride is discussed with manifold praise.

But I, satisfying not my own desire but yours, offer what you have asked for, knowing that the work does not correspond to its subject, nor the building to its foundation. Yet I have done somehow—not what I wished, but what I could—being hindered by many difficulties, which you yourself have borne with me in great part.

Here ends the prologue.

# The Book on the Fourfold Kind of Marriage Begins

[Col. 0923]

[Col. 0923A] Sacred Scripture teaches us that there are four kinds of marriage, corresponding to the four theological senses: the historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. The first is between a man and his lawful wife; the second between Christ and the holy Church; the third between God and the righteous soul; the fourth between the Word and human nature. Concerning the first marriage, the first-created man, on awaking, prophesied: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” [Gen. 2:24]. Concerning the second, the angel speaks to John in the Apocalypse: “Come, and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb” [Rev. 21:9]. Concerning the third, the Lord says through the prophet Hosea: “I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and compassion” [Hos. 2:19]. [Col. 0923B] Concerning the fourth, the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal” [Song 3:11]. This is as though she said: O daughters of Zion—that is, fragile and fleshly Jews—come forth from the darkness of unbelief and ignorance, and see, not with the eyes of the body but with the eyes of the heart; that is, believe in King Solomon, namely Christ, the true peacemaker, who “made both one” [Eph. 2:14], in the diadem with which his mother crowned him: that is, in that singular grace by which the Virgin Mary conceived him holy, pure, and immaculate, without the stirrings of flesh, without the heat of lust, and without the stain of sin. Thus the angel says to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore [Col. 0923C] the Holy One to be born of you shall be called the Son of God” [Luke 1:35]. On the day of his betrothal, that is, of his Incarnation, when “the Word was made flesh” [John 1:14] and betrothed human nature to himself.

## On the Fourfold Kind of Marriage

In this fourfold kind of marriage we find something equally worthy of wonder and reverence: what is effected in the first, so that two become one flesh, is effected in the second, so that two become one body; in the third, so that two become one spirit; and in the fourth, so that two become one person. For authority testifies concerning the first: “The two shall be one flesh” [Gen. 2:24]; and because of this union Truth added: “Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh” [Mark 10:8]. Concerning the second the Apostle says: “Though the members of the body are many, they are one body” [1 Cor. 12:12]. [Col. 0923D] So too “we are one body in Christ” [Rom. 12:5]; [Col. 0924A] and because of this union the same Apostle adds: “For we have all been baptized into one body” [1 Cor. 6:17; citation as printed]. Concerning the third, the same Apostle says: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit,” and is one spirit with him [1 Cor. 12:13; citation as printed]. Because of this union John the Apostle says: “He who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” [1 John 4:16; citation as printed]. Concerning the fourth, the Catholic faith confesses that, “as a rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ” [Athanasian Creed]. Because of this ineffable union, the Evangelist testifies that “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [John 1:14]. Therefore we may rightly call the first union carnal; the second sacramental; the third spiritual; and the fourth personal: carnal, as we have said, between a man and his lawful wife; sacramental [Col. 0924B] between Christ and the holy Church; spiritual between God and the righteous soul; personal between the Word and human nature.

## On the Cause of the Marriage Between the Word and Human Nature

In order that, once the wall of enmity between God and humankind had been destroyed, the wholeness of peace might be restored, a nuptial covenant between the Word and human nature was made through the mystery of the Incarnation. For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [John 1:14]. Before the Word was made flesh, he dwelt far from us; but when the Word was made flesh, he dwelt among us. Thus elsewhere it is written: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they shall be my people” [2 Cor. 6:16]. But since he could find no equal or like partner either among angels [Col. 0924C] or among human beings, according to what is written, “Who among the clouds shall be compared to the Lord? Or who among the sons of God shall be like God?” [Ps. 88:7], “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man” [Phil. 2:7]. He “was made a little lower than the angels” [Ps. 8:6], when he assumed not merely the form of a servant but also a passible nature.

## On the Betrothal

For he did not take hold of angels, but “the seed of Abraham” [Heb. 2:16], with whom he had long before agreed to contract this marriage, saying: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” [Gen. 22:18]. He does not say “in seeds,” as though in many, but as though in one: “in your seed,” [Gal. 3:16] who is Christ. It is as though he said: From your seed I shall take flesh, [Col. 0924D] through which blessing will be given not to Jews alone but to all nations.

## On the Oath

[Col. 0925A]

He also swore to King David himself that this marriage would be consummated, according to David’s saying: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne’” [Ps. 131:11]. Therefore the angel says to the Virgin: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever” [Luke 1:32]. Isaiah the prophet had likewise foretold: “He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom” [Isa. 9:7].

## On the Family

Since, therefore, he was the son of a king, it was fitting that he should take a wife from royal stock. For he is “King of kings and Lord of lords” [Rev. 19:16]. Concerning his marriage, the Psalmist composed the epithalamium: [Col. 0925B] “My heart has poured forth a good word,” he says; “I speak my works to the king” [Ps. 44].

## On Lineage

And since he was from a father without a mother, it was fitting that he should take a wife from a mother without a father, according to that prophetic saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” [Isa. 11:1]. And again: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” [Isa. 7:14].

## On the Dowry

But because “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” [Ps. 23:1], and because he himself has no need of our goods [Ps. 45:1], a dowry could neither be given to him nor ought to have been given.

## On the Gift

[Col. 0925C] Yet he himself, being boundless, made an extraordinary marriage-gift. “Ask of me,” he says, “and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” [Ps. 2:8]. “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field” [Ps. 8:8].

## On Beauty

But in order that he who is the splendor of glory might betroth to himself one who was glorious and splendid, he both washed and anointed her. He washed her from every stain of sin, so that she might be wholly without wrinkle or blemish, and so that he might receive her free from guilt. For “the Lord ascends upon a light cloud” [Isa. 19:1], that is, he assumed flesh free from sins; and “entered Egypt,” that is, came into the world. And he “anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” [Ps. 44:8], so that he might be [Col. 0925D] “beautiful in form above the children of men,” because of truth, meekness, and righteousness. “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me; therefore he has anointed me and sent me to bring good news to the poor” [Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18].

## On the Time

He chose the time of fullness and the year of favor, in which “God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” [Gal. 4:4]. For “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” [John 1:17].

## On the Paranymph

[Col. 0926A]

In this nuptial transaction the angel Gabriel was the paranymph, or bridal attendant. Sent to the Virgin, he gently greeted her: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” [Luke 1:28]. At once, preparing the virginal bridal chamber, he added: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Luke 1:35]. When it had been prepared by the Virgin’s consent—“Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” [Luke 1:38]—the most holy marriage between the Word and human nature was immediately contracted. For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [John 1:14]. “Blessed is she who believed, because all things were fulfilled for her” [Luke 1:49; citation as printed].

## On the Witnesses

Lest the marriage be wholly clandestine, [Col. 0926B] four persons were present: Father, Mother, Priest, and paranymph. By these, we understand God the Father, the Virgin Mother, the Holy Spirit, and the angel Gabriel. But the Father and the Holy Spirit were present inwardly and invisibly; the Mother and the angel stood by outwardly and visibly.

## Against the Evil One

Few attended this union, and such persons as no one would suspect, so that the mystery of the Incarnation might be hidden from the Devil, lest that envious and malicious one devise something against human salvation. For “through the envy of the Devil, death entered into the world” [Wis. 2:24].

## On the Effect

Nevertheless, every rational spirit was fully present, [Col. 0926C] divine, angelic, and human; for through the mystery of the Incarnation harmony was restored not only between God and humanity but also between angel and humanity, since, according to the Apostle, he “restored the things in heaven and the things on earth” [Eph. 1:10]. For this reason that multitude of the heavenly host sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” [Luke 2:14].

## On the Place

He therefore assigned the Virgin’s bridal chamber as the place for celebrating the marriage, according to the prophetic saying: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he comes forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” [Ps. 18:6].

## On the Ring

[Col. 0926D] In this bridal chamber the Son of God betrothed human nature both with a ring and with a kiss. For if the Holy Spirit is signified by a finger, according to what is written, “This is the finger of God” [Exod. 18:9; citation as printed], and elsewhere, “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” [Luke 11:19–20], then the gift of the Holy Spirit ought rightly to be understood through the ring of the finger.

## On the Earnest Gift

Thus the Word of God gave human nature a ring as an earnest when he filled it without [Col. 0927A] measure with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to the prophetic saying: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” [Isa. 11:2].

## On Adornment

With these virtues he adorned her as with precious necklaces. “He adorned me,” he says, “like a bridegroom with a crown, and ornamented me like a bride with his necklaces” [Isa. 61:10]. For in him, according to the Apostle, “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” [Col. 2:3].

## On the Crown

Of this crown the prophet says in the Psalter: “You crowned him, Lord, with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands” [Ps. 8:6]. This is [Col. 0927B] that magnificence of singularity—or, rather, that singularity of magnificence—of which the Apostle says: “He gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” [Phil. 2:10]. “His name,” says the Prophet, “shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” [Isa. 9:6].

## On the Kiss

He then also gave her a kiss when he joined her to himself personally, as she herself yearningly asks in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Song 1:1]. Certainly two lips are joined in a kiss, because two natures are united in Christ—divinity and humanity—so that he himself is God from God, begotten before the ages, [Ps. 8:6; citation as printed] and man from a human being, born in time.

## On the Giving Away

[Col. 0927C]

Human nature, therefore, which he betrothed in the womb of the Virgin, he led to the Father’s right hand when, according to his assumed humanity, “he ascended into heaven” [Athanasian Creed; Mark 16:19; Apostles’ Creed] and “sits at the right hand of God,” having become so much greater than the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs [Heb. 1:4].

## On the Wedding Feast

Meanwhile he celebrates the wedding feast on high with those from whom he will return for judgment, as he himself says in the Gospel: “And you, be like people awaiting their master when he returns from the wedding feast” [Luke 12:36].

## On the Manner

In this divine marriage there is not a union of two persons [Col. 0927D] in one nature, but a union of two natures in one person. For person did not assume person, but nature assumed nature; nor did nature receive person, but person received nature. A person did indeed assume nature, but into person, not into nature. Such was that assumption that, because of the ineffable union, he is called both bridegroom and bride, as the Prophet himself testifies: “He adorned me like a bridegroom with a crown and ornamented me like a bride with necklaces” [Isa. 61:10]. Since, however, the matter of which we speak is ineffable, John himself was not worthy [Luke 3:16] to loosen the strap of his sandal. Let us not [Col. 0928A] fail by “searching with searching” [Ps. 63:7; literal rendering of the citation], since “the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” [Prov. 25:27]; and, especially lest anyone conceive falsehood as truth from our words, let us treat more plainly and fully of sacramental and spiritual marriage.

## On the Twofold Institution of Marriage

Now sacramental marriage is contracted in likeness to carnal marriage. The sacrament of marriage is said to have had a twofold institution: one before sin and another after sin. Before sin it was instituted for an office, so that nature might be propagated; after sin it was instituted as a remedy, so that sin might be restrained: nature might be propagated in offspring, and sin restrained from fornication. Divine Scripture testifies concerning the first institution, which was made [Col. 0928B] for an office: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” [Gen. 1:28]. Apostolic authority testifies concerning the second institution, which was made as a remedy: “Let each have his own wife because of fornication” [1 Cor. 7:2]—certainly not in order to commit it, but to avoid it. For “fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God” [1 Cor. 6:10]. What we find by nature in carnal marriage, we find by grace in sacramental and spiritual marriage. For Christ joined the holy Church to himself both for the office of propagation, so that she might multiply in children through the sacrament of regeneration, and as a remedy for fornication, so that through religious worship she might be recalled from idols. For before the Church had been sacramentally joined to Christ, [Col. 0928C] she committed adultery everywhere with idols, as the Lord reproached her through the prophet: “You have committed fornication after the nations, among whom you were defiled by their idols” [Ezek. 23:30]. And elsewhere: “Judge your mother, judge her, because she is not my wife and I am not her husband. Let her remove her fornications from before her face and her adulteries from between her breasts” [Hos. 2:2].

## On Spiritual Kinship

But when Christ sacramentally joined the Church to himself, she ceased to commit fornication with idols, as the Lord promises her through the Prophet: “I will betroth you forever . . . and I will betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know that I am the Lord” [Hos. 2:19–20]. “On that day,” [Hos. 2:16–17] “you shall call me, ‘My husband,’ and you shall no longer call me Baalim. And I will remove [Col. 0928D] the names of the Baals from your mouth, and you shall no longer remember their names.”

## On Spiritual Propagation

From that time the Church began everywhere to bear many children. Foreseeing and predicting this, Isaiah the Prophet described it: “Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together; they have come to you. Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise at your side. Then you shall see and abound; your heart shall wonder and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has been turned to you and the strength of the nations has come to you” [Isa. 60:4–5]. [Col. 0929A] For holy mother Church, ever fertile in new offspring, conceives, gives birth, and nourishes. She conceives by catechizing those whom she instructs. She gives birth by baptizing those whom she washes. She nourishes by communicating those whom she refreshes. She regenerates them from water and the Holy Spirit for her husband Christ: those who “were born not of bloods, nor of the will of man” [John 1:13], but “of God” [John 3:6; citation as printed]. For “what is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

## On Spiritual Fornication

For these reasons also a spiritual marriage is contracted between God and the soul: namely, so that the soul may be restrained from vices and may be fruitful in merits. For if, according to the Prophet, idolatry is fornication, and according to the Apostle covetousness is idolatry, it follows that covetousness is fornication. For the Apostle says: [Col. 0929B] “Covetousness is the service of idols” [Col. 3:5]. Again, Samuel’s testimony proves that “to resist is as the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience is as the crime of idolatry” [1 Sam. 15:23]. Whoever, therefore, resists and does not obey the divine commandments commits the sin of divination and the crime of idolatry. As a woman, when she commits bodily adultery, despises her own husband and subjects herself to another, so the soul, when it transgresses mortally, despises the true God and subjects itself to the Devil. For there is no “fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial” [2 Cor. 6:15]. Therefore, as a woman is restrained from adultery by love for her husband, so the soul is restrained from vice by love for God.

## On Spiritual Offspring

[Col. 0929C] When the soul has conceived this love in its heart, it bears perfect children in action, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Your wife is like an abundant vine at the sides of your house; your children like young olive plants around your table” [Ps. 127:3]. It is as though he said: Your wife, that is, the faithful soul, abounds like a vine—that is, it produces abundantly the pleasing fruits of works—“at the sides of your house,” that is, in sincerity of heart and truth: sincerity may shape the intention and truth the end, so that works proceed from a sincere intention toward a true end. The house of God is understood to be the pure heart, as he says elsewhere: “I walked in innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” [Ps. 100:2]. Its two sides are sincerity of intention and truth of end, so that works may be done “not [Col. 0929D] in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [1 Cor. 5:8]. Your children—that is, the good works which you beget from the soul—are like young olive plants: that is, intention is green with the oil of charity. “Around your table,” that is, around the teaching of Sacred Scripture, which elsewhere he calls a table. Hence: “You have prepared a table before me” [Ps. 22:5]. He teaches that the soul should abound like a vine by practicing righteousness, and bear fruit like an olive by practicing mercy. Thus the Samaritan, approaching the wounded man, “pours wine and oil over him” [Luke 10:34]. These are [Col. 0930A] children who bring fruitfulness but do not take away virginity. Indeed, the soul would not preserve virginity unless it produced such children, for barren she who does not give birth is cursed. [Exod. 23:26; Deut. 7:14 readily apply here: “There shall be no barren woman; there shall be no sterile one among you.”] This is well signified in the marriage of Joseph and Mary, because before they “came together, she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit” [Matt. 1:18]. “Before they came together, she was found”: behold virginity in unity. “Having conceived”: behold fruitfulness.

## On Consent of Souls and Intercourse of Bodies

Moreover, there are two things in marriage: consent of souls and intercourse of bodies. One of these signifies charity, which exists in the spirit between God and the righteous soul; the other denotes conformity, which exists in flesh between Christ [Col. 0930B] and the holy Church. Great indeed is the sacrament which is in the flesh, but plainly greater is that which is in the spirit. For “the spirit is what gives life; the flesh profits nothing” [John 6:64].

## On the Bride’s Charity Toward the Bridegroom

The following saying of the bride concerning the bridegroom in the Song applies to spiritual marriage, which is contracted through the charity of the soul between God and the righteous soul: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar and ordered charity within me. Sustain me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” [Song 2:4–5]. Here either the soul or the Church speaks. But the soul says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar,” that is, into the holy Church, which is called a wine-cellar because it contains the grace of the Holy Spirit, the wine that makes glad; of this it is written: [Col. 0930C] “Wine makes glad the heart of man” [Ps. 103:15]. Or the Church says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar,” that is, into Sacred Scripture, which is called a wine-cellar because it contains new wine—that is, evangelical teaching—of which it is written: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” [Luke 6:64; citation as printed]. “And he ordered charity within me,” that is, he taught me the rule of loving.

## On the Order of Charity

The right order of charity is this: a person should love God in the first place; himself in the second; and his neighbor in the third. And in himself he should love more what is greater, namely the soul, and less what is lesser, namely the body. Among neighbors he should love first his parents, then members of his household, and lastly his enemies; and perhaps [Col. 0930D] he ought to prefer the good more in charity. He ought to love God for God’s own sake, and his neighbor for God’s sake. But good in [Note: This passage seems corrupt, but I do not know how to emend it.] God, evil toward God. He then shows, in sequence, how much one has advanced through ordered charity: “Sustain me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” She speaks to the young women and expresses the greatness of charity when she says: “I languish with love”; that is, because of the greatness of charity I am weakened, not in God but in the world; not in spirit but in flesh; not in heavenly things but in earthly things, [Col. 0931A] “desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Phil. 1:23]. For one whom perfect charity has imbued has utterly fallen away from earthly things, according to the saying: “Love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell . . . Many waters,” that is, peoples, “could not extinguish charity” [Song 8:6–7]. Therefore, you young women, “sustain me with flowers,” that is, refresh me with your virtues; “surround me with apples,” that is, uphold me with your works. For by flowers and apples, works and virtues are signified: the soul flowers in virtues and bears fruit in works. The perfect person is greatly refreshed when he sees the imperfect advancing; hence the Apostle said: “You are our glory and joy” [1 Thess. 2:20].

## On the Bridegroom’s Charity Toward the Bride

How great is Christ’s charity for the Church, the Apostle shows when he says: [Col. 0931B] “Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her” [Eph. 5:25]. Therefore, “no one has greater charity than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” [John 15:13]. Thus “God loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” [John 3:16]. “He did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all” [Rom. 8:32].

## On the Conformity of Nature Between Bridegroom and Bride

The saying of Adam applies to sacramental marriage, which is contracted through conformity of nature between Christ and the holy Church: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh . . . Therefore a man shall leave his father and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” [Gen. 2:23–24]. [Col. 0931C] For though Christ “was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing seized as plunder, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man” [Phil. 2:6–7]. Thus the bridegroom may now rightly say of the bride: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [John 1:14].

## How Christ Left Father and Mother and Cleaved to the Church

Therefore, that is, because of his love for the Church, Christ the man—of whom the Psalmist says, “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” [Ps. 86:5]—left his Father; that is, “he [Col. 0931D] emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Phil. 2:7], not by abandoning the divine nature but by assuming human nature, because he appeared not according to divinity but according to humanity. And he left his mother, that is, he abandoned the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh. As its figure, Jesus left [John 11:54] Judea and went into the region near the wilderness, into a city, and remained there with his disciples. And he cleaved to his wife, that is, he joined himself to the Church, so that there might be “one fold and one shepherd” [John 10:16]. Thus the two—namely, [Col. 0932A] the Church and Christ—are one flesh, that is, one nature of flesh. For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.”

## On the Three Goods of Marriage

There are three principal goods of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Fidelity pertains to chastity; offspring to fruitfulness; sacrament to permanence. We find these sacramentally in sacramental marriage.

## On Fidelity

The Church is joined to Christ with such purity of fidelity that the chastity of their marriage is never violated. Hence Solomon, in Proverbs, pursues the praises of the Church, saying: “The heart of her husband trusts in her” [Prov. 31:11]. A husband’s heart trusts in one whom it believes chaste, whom [Col. 0932B] it believes modest, whom it believes honorable; concerning whom it suspects nothing unjust, nothing sinister, nothing hostile. But lest anyone suppose that he is deceived in this faith by the deceit of his wife, let him carefully consider what Truth says concerning this in the Gospel: “I know my sheep, and mine know me” [John 10:14]. “They do not follow a stranger, but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” [John 10:5]. The Church, indeed, which is signified by sheep and their innocence, does not follow another, a stranger, or an adulterer, but her own—that is, her proper—husband, her beloved. She diligently seeks and finds where he feeds and rests at noon, lest, as she says in the Song, she begin “to wander after the flocks of his companions” [Song 1:6]. In order that the Church might preserve inviolate fidelity to Christ, she endured every kind of torment for faith [Col. 0932C] in his name, lest she abandon Christ and cleave to idols. For the saints “experienced mockeries and beatings, moreover also chains and prisons; they were stoned, killed, tested, and died by the slaughter of the sword,” and so forth [Heb. 11:36].

## On Offspring

How earnestly the Church strives to receive offspring from Christ the Doctor of the Church makes plain, among other things, when he says: “My little children, whom I labor to bear again until Christ is formed in you” [Gal. 4:19]. Leah also once, after giving mandrakes, hired Jacob for a reward to enter to her; by him she conceived and bore a child [Gen. 30:16]. Christ likewise expresses through Isaiah his desire to receive offspring, saying: “Shall I, who make others bear, not myself bear?” says the Lord. “Shall I, [Col. 0932D] who grant generation to others, be barren?” [Isa. 66:9]. The Prophet also says in the Psalter: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” [Ps. 112:9]. He calls the same woman both barren and a mother of children: barren first, before she had been joined to Christ; afterwards, a joyful mother of children, according to that prophetic saying: “Praise, barren woman who do not bear; rejoice, you who do not give birth, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” [Isa. 54:1]. [Col. 0933A] “I will multiply your seed like the sand on the seashore” [Gen. 22:17]. Those whom she receives with deepest love she nourishes with utmost devotion, lest what happened to the children of the Synagogue occur to the Church’s children, concerning whom he himself complains through the Prophet: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” [Isa. 1:2]. But the Church instructs those whom she has begotten with saving teachings and forms them in honorable conduct. She feeds them with “the bread of life and understanding” and gives them “the water of saving wisdom” to drink [Sir. 15:3]. “Come,” he says, “eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you. Leave childhood behind and live; walk in the ways of prudence” [Prov. 9:5–6]. She also gives the heavenly bread and saving cup, of which whoever tastes [John 6:52; citation as printed] “shall live forever,” having in itself every delight and every [Col. 0933B] sweetness of taste [Wis. 16:20]. This is “the living bread that came down from heaven” [John 6:51], which the Church has handed over to her children.

## On the Sacrament

The sacrament between Christ and the Church remains inseparable, as the bride says of the bridegroom in the Song: “I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and shall not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house” [Song 3:4]. When Christ said to the Apostles, “Do you also wish to depart?” [John 6:67], Peter answered on behalf of the whole Church: “Lord, you have the words of eternal life; and to whom shall we go?” The saying by which Christ, speaking to the Apostles, promises the Catholic Church is recognized as belonging to this inseparable sacrament: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” [Matt. 28:20]. These matters which have been said [Col. 0933C] concerning the three goods of marriage in relation to sacramental marriage can easily be applied to spiritual marriage.

## On the Firmness of the Marriage Bond

Moreover, fidelity and offspring always adhere in ordered marriage. For sometimes chastity is violated and fruitfulness is impeded. But the sacrament remains so stable that marriage cannot exist without it. The marriage bond always remains between the living, so that even if divorce occurs because of fornication, the firmness of the marriage bond is not dissolved. The Lord testifies to this, saying: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries the dismissed woman commits adultery” [Matt. 19:9]. [Col. 0933D] The Apostle, following the necessary truth, added: “Likewise, he who departs from his wife.” [Note: This sense seems somewhat deficient owing to the copyist. The same defect also occurs at the beginning of the following chapter.] “Likewise,” as one departing from the marriage of Christ and from faith; and likewise a husband if he departs from his wife.

## On Spiritual Marriage
Thus even the apostate who has lost faith [Note: [Col. 0933] Supply *fide* (“faith”); otherwise these words have no sense.] does not lose the sacrament of faith which he received in the washing of regeneration. For it would be restored to one returning to himself, if he departed from what he had received. He who has withdrawn possesses this to the increase of punishment, not to the merit of reward. Therefore, just as a wife is dismissed by her husband through fornication, so, because of apostasy, the soul is separated from Christ.

### On Spiritual Reconciliation

Yet she can be reconciled if she returns and implores her husband’s mercy, as He himself testifies when he says: [Note: [Col. 0933] Zech. 1:2.] “Return to me, and I will return to you.” Otherwise, one who puts his hand to the plough [Note: [Col. 0933] Luke 9:62.] and looks back, together with Lot’s wife [Note: [Col. 0933] Gen. 19:26.], will be changed into a pillar of salt.

### What Prevents or Dissolves Marriage

Although any criminal offense may both prevent the contracting of, and dissolve once contracted, the spiritual marriage which exists between God and the soul—because charity does not permit itself to dwell with vice, whence no one can serve God [Note: [Col. 0933] Matt. 6:24.] and Mammon—yet the sacramental marriage which exists between Christ and the Church [Col. 0934B] is perhaps prevented from being contracted, or hinders what has been contracted, or dissolves it, by unbelief alone.

For one who is baptized deceitfully, like Simon [Note: [Col. 0933] Acts 8:13.], although he receives the sacrament of faith, nevertheless does not receive faith itself; he dissents from Christ and therefore does not contract marriage with him. For who would say that marriage is contracted without consent? But whoever, like Julian the Apostate, although he does not lose the sacrament of faith, nevertheless abandons the faith of the sacrament, withdraws from Christ’s marriage as though by committing fornication. Therefore everyone who does not believe the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word is not believed to belong to the sacramental marriage contracted between Christ and the Church through the mystery of the Incarnation.

### That Sacramental Marriage Is Never Dissolved

[Col. 0934C] Further, when a soul is separated from Christ through apostasy, it does not cease to be a wife; just as a woman separated from her husband because of adultery does not cease to be a wife, even if she is joined to another. For as the bond of marriage endures in the latter, so the sacrament of baptism remains in the former. And just as the former contracted marriage by consent, so the latter did so by faith; yet when consent ceases in the former, the marriage is not dissolved.

### Why, in the Latter Case, Marriage Is Not Dissolved When Faith Ceases

Or perhaps every Christian soul, not only the just but also the apostate, is Christ’s spouse, though adulterous because she does not keep faith with her husband—the faith which she is bound [Col. 0934D] to keep—on account of the debt of the sacrament, which persists even in an apostate. Otherwise, she would not be an adulteress if she herself were not a spouse. Let it be so, if nothing better can be answered.

### Question

Yet the following seems to stand in the way: in the prophet Hosea the Lord declares: [Note: [Col. 0933] Chapter 2:2.] “Judge your mother, judge her: for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband. Let her remove her fornications from before her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts.” Behold: [Col. 0935A] because of fornication and adultery he says that the marriage has been dissolved, so that neither is he husband nor is she wife.

### Solution

Certainly, the spiritual marriage which God contracted with the Synagogue through the charity of the soul was indeed dissolved through idolatry, by which the soul dies because it is separated from God. For as the body lives from the soul, so the soul lives from God. But, taught by the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0935] Rom. 7:2.], we have learned that, when one of the spouses has died, the survivor is released from the law of marriage. Sacramental marriage, however, could not be dissolved, because Christ had not yet contracted it with the Church through conformity of nature: the Word had not yet been incarnate.

### Whether a Baptized Infant Contracts Sacramental Marriage

[Col. 0935B]

But if inquiry is made concerning an infant who does not believe, whether he is betrothed to Christ through the sacrament of faith, perhaps the answer will be that, just as he is baptized in the faith of the Church, so he is betrothed through the faith of the Church. For just as, in an adult, faith in the sacrament can blot out sins without the sacrament of faith, so in an infant the sacrament of faith can remit sin without faith in the sacrament. For what if grace supplies what nature withholds? Although it is true that, in carnal marriage, no one is bound matrimonially by another’s consent.

### Question: Whether Christ Should Be Called a Bigamist

[Col. 0935C]

But since, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0935] 1 Tim. 3:2.], a bishop ought to be the husband of one wife—that is, monogamous—how did Christ, who is the high priest [Note: [Col. 0935] Heb. 9:11.] of good things to come, a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0935] In the same Epistle, 5:6.], after repudiating the Synagogue, take the Church as an additional wife?

Certainly, although Christ abandoned the Synagogue for a time, because, as he himself recalls through the prophet, [Note: [Col. 0935] Ezek. 23:18.] “She uncovered her fornications and disclosed her shame, and he withdrew from her,” nevertheless he later received her again in the first believers. For he is from the Jews alone [Note: [Col. 0935] John 4:22.]; he did not take the Church as an additional wife, but grafted it in like a wild olive into the olive tree, as the Apostle says to it: [Note: [Col. 0935] Rom. 11:17.] “But if some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive, have been grafted [Col. 0935D] among them and made a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree … [lacuna] For partial blindness has come upon Israel [Note: [Col. 0935] vv. 25–26.] until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel might be saved.”

Likewise, after Truth had first said in the Gospel: [Note: [Col. 0935] John 10:15.] “I lay down my life for my sheep,” he immediately added: [Note: [Col. 0935] v. 16.] “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd”: that is, one shepherd, one bridegroom, and one [Col. 0936A] bride—the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0935] Eph. 2:20.] who made [Note: [Col. 0935] ibid., v. 14.] both one. For: [Note: [Col. 0935] Mark 11:9.] “Those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

But according to another kind of marriage, Christ, in the fullness of time, joined the Church to himself—the Church which he had long ago betrothed to himself as the Synagogue. For, so that [Note: [Col. 0935] Gen. 2:25.] “the two might be one flesh,” the Word [Note: [Col. 0935] John 1:14.] “became flesh and dwelt among us,” so that he might say: “This now [Note: [Col. 0935] Gen. 2:23.] is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” According to this kind of marriage, Christ is the sole husband of the sole bride. “One is my dove,” he says [Note: [Col. 0935] Song 6:8.]; he will never repudiate her or bring in another, because he made [Note: [Col. 0935] Ecclus. 17:10 and cf. Acts 20:28.] an everlasting covenant with her in his blood: “I,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0935] Matt. 28:20.] “will be with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.” [Col. 0936B] In that nature in which Christ is the Church’s bridegroom, he was anointed with the oil of gladness [Note: [Col. 0935] Ps. 44:8.] above his companions, so that he might be high priest and priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Therefore Christ, according to that in which he is high priest, is not a bigamist but monogamous.

### Another Question on the Same Subject

Yet one ought not to be troubled because many Churches are described in many authorities of Scripture. For the Apostle Paul says: [Note: [Col. 0935] 2 Cor. 11:28.] “Apart from external things, there is my daily pressure, the care of all the Churches.” And the Apostle John writes to the seven Churches which are in Asia: [Note: [Col. 0935] Rev. 1:11.] “What you see,” he says, “write in a book and send to the seven Churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

[Col. 0936C] But just as there are many members of the body from which one body is formed, so there are many particular Churches from which the one Church consists, which is called Catholic, that is, universal, made alive throughout by the one Spirit of Christ, just as the human body is animated throughout by one soul. Solomon aptly signified this when he said: [Note: [Col. 0935] Prov. 9:1.] “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars.” Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; he built himself a house, that is, the Church, of which the Prophet says: [Note: [Col. 0935] Bar. 3:24.] “O Israel, how great is the house of God!” And he hewed out seven pillars, that is, he distinguished within it seven gifts, or seven orders of saints. [Note: [Col. 0935] Added in the margin: the Virgin Mary, Angels, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors, and Virgins.] For the Lord commended the unity of the Church in the Gospel: [Col. 0936D] [Note: [Col. 0935] Matt. 16:18.] “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church.” And the Prophet says in the Psalter: [Note: [Col. 0935] Ps. 106:32.] “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders.”

### Yet Another Question on the Same Subject

But what further answer shall be given? Since every just soul is betrothed to Christ through faith and joined to him through charity, there are therefore as many brides of Christ as there are just souls. Yet, with respect to the sacrament of the likeness, the first law of marriage made in Paradise and confirmed by Christ in the Gospel, he says: [Col. 0937A] “They shall be,” [Note: [Col. 0937] Matt. 19:5.] not many but two, in one flesh—that is, in one carnal marriage. “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave,” not to wives, but to a wife. But this sacrament is great not between God and the soul, but, as the Apostle says, [Note: [Col. 0937] Eph. 5:32.] “in Christ and in the Church.”

Nevertheless, all just souls are one bride and one virgin because of the unity of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0937] ibid. 4:3.] which they maintain in the bond of peace. “I am jealous for you,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0937] 2 Cor. 11:2.] “with God’s jealousy; for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” He says “you” in the plural and “virgin” in the singular, because all are one virgin in Christ, on account of the one spirit of integrity and the author of virginity. For [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Cor. 12:4, 11.] “there are varieties of gifts … but one Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills.”

### On Lawful Persons

There are certain persons forbidden to contract carnal marriage with one another. Before the Law these were very few; under the Law, more numerous. “For this reason [Note: [Col. 0937] Gen. 2:24.] a man shall leave father and mother”—that is, on account of marital union; neither a daughter shall take her father nor a son his mother. But Christ takes as spouse both mother and daughter and sister, and every person whatsoever who does his Father’s will. “Whoever does [Note: [Col. 0937] Matt. 12:50.] the will of his Father who is in heaven is his brother, sister, [Col. 0937C] and mother.” This bridegroom likewise names the same woman both bride and sister in the Song: [Note: [Col. 0937] Chapter 4:9.] “You have wounded my heart, my sister; my bride, you have wounded my heart.”

Likewise, he both regenerates and betroths the same woman: he regenerates offspring and betroths a wife. Nor does he wait seven years for betrothal, nor twelve years for marriage. What wonder, then, if he takes his daughter in marriage, he who chose his daughter as mother? For the Son begot his mother, and the daughter bore her Begetter. Therefore no one is forbidden to contract spiritual or sacramental marriage. Indeed, persons of every kind are commanded to enter such a union. For there is no distinction, as the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 3:22.] “But the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ is upon all who believe.” “Everyone,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0937] John 6:37.] “who comes to me I will not cast out.” Yet he makes all [Col. 0937D] one, as he himself says to the Father: [Note: [Col. 0937] John 17:22–23.] “The glory which you gave me I have given them, that all may be one, as we also are one. I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, and that the world may know that you sent me.”

### That the Church Gives No Dowry to Christ

But neither the soul gives God, nor the Church Christ, any dowry for contracting its marriage, because he received her freely and without dowry. For it was not [Note: [Col. 0937] Titus 3:5 ff.] [Col. 0938A] “by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out abundantly upon us through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” But if it is by grace, [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 11:6.] it is not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. Therefore it is not [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 9:16.] of one willing or running, but of God who has mercy. No one approaches him unless he first goes before; no one arrives unless he anticipates him. Hence the Prophet says in the Psalter: [Note: [Col. 0937] Ps. 20:4.] “You anticipated him with blessings of sweetness,” and Christ in the Gospel: [Note: [Col. 0937] John 6:44.] “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him.”

For God’s mercy not only precedes but follows. It precedes by inspiring; it follows by helping. It precedes so that one may begin; [Col. 0938B] it follows so that one may complete. Of the preceding mercy he says in the Psalter: [Note: [Col. 0937] Ps. 58:11.] “His mercy will precede me.” Of the following mercy he says elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0937] Ps. 22:6.] “Your mercy will follow me.” Therefore God betrothed the soul to himself, or Christ the Church, not for a dowry but solely by grace. “For who first [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 11:35–36.] gave to him, and shall be repaid? For from him, through him, and in him are all things.” What, then, does a human being possess [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Cor. 4:7.] that he has not received? The charity itself by which the soul is spiritually joined to God is given to it by God, as Paul testifies: [Note: [Col. 0937] Rom. 5:5.] “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

### That Christ Makes a Gift to the Church

This charity forgives the soul’s sins, so that it may join the soul, separated from the Devil, to God. For charity [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Pet. 4:8.] covers a multitude [Col. 0938C] of sins. And the Lord says in the Gospel: [Note: [Col. 0937] Luke 7:47.] “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much.” Having proposed to Simon the Pharisee [Note: [Col. 0937] Luke 7:41 ff.] that two debtors owed one moneylender, one five hundred denarii and the other fifty, and that, since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both: “Who, then, loves more?” Simon rightly replied: “I suppose, the one to whom he forgave more.”

Therefore this is the gift made for marriage: remission of sins. For if charity is the marriage by which God is joined to the soul, and debts are forgiven because of charity, then certainly remission of sins is the gift made for marriage. We say confidently, and he freely declares, that charity is the cause of justification, according to the Gospel and Apostolic testimony which we have adduced: [Col. 0938D] “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much.” And if charity covers a multitude of sins—for darkness flees light—then light surely drives out darkness. For there is no fellowship [Note: [Col. 0937] 2 Cor. 6:15.] of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial.

Christ also promises the Church another gift, which Matthew the Evangelist records in public writing: [Note: [Col. 0937] Chapter 5, v. 3 ff.] “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek,” and so forth.

### On the Mystical Gifts Which the Gentile World Sent in Advance to Christ

[Col. 0939A]

Although the Church gave no dowry to her husband, but received a gift from him, nevertheless through suitable messengers—men, namely, noble and wise—she sent in advance certain mystical gifts of her love and devotion, when the Gentile world dispatched the Magi from the East to Jerusalem, seeking: [Note: [Col. 0939] Matt. 2:1 ff.] “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” For they saw his star in the East; guided by its sign, they went forth and found him; they fell down and worshiped him. And, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Gold for the king; frankincense for the priest; myrrh for the mortal man.

Then the prophecy of the prophets began to be fulfilled: [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 71:10.] “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents.” [Note: [Col. 0939] Isa. 60:6.] “All shall come from [Col. 0939B] Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord.”

### On the Manifold Care Which the Bridegroom Bestowed upon the Bride

Thus Christ betrothed the Church to himself not by merit but by grace; he washed and anointed her, adorned and beautified her. So she is described through the prophet Ezekiel under the figure of the Synagogue: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 16, v. 8 ff.] “I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God, and you became mine. And I washed you with water and cleansed your blood from you; and I anointed you with oil. I clothed you in variegated garments, and [Note: [Col. 0939] This translation differs somewhat from the Vulgate. Should this be attributed to the copyist? Let the reader judge.] shod you with violet-colored leather; I girded you with fine linen and clothed you with delicate garments. I adorned you with ornaments; I put bracelets upon your hands and a necklace around your neck. I put a ring above your mouth, earrings in your ears, and a crown of beauty upon your head. And [Col. 0939C] you were adorned with gold and silver, and clothed in fine linen, embroidered fabric, and many colors; you ate fine flour, honey, and oil; you became exceedingly beautiful and advanced to royalty. Your name went out among the nations because of your beauty, for you were perfect in my splendor which I had put upon you, says the Lord God.”

### On the Washing

Christ therefore washed the Church in order to cleanse her from crimes. He anointed her in order to adorn her with chrism; he decked her in order to distinguish her by virtues. The Apostle says concerning the washing to the Ephesians: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 5, v. 25 ff.] “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, so that he might sanctify her, [Col. 0939D] cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, having no spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind, but that she might be holy and immaculate.”

For baptism washes not merely the body but also the heart: through the outward washing of the body it signifies the inward washing of the heart. Accordingly, the Lord testifies through Ezekiel: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 36:25.] “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements.” And Zechariah: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 13:1.] “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David [Col. 0940A] and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman.” Therefore Truth also says in the Gospel: [Note: [Col. 0939] John 3:5.] “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” But: [Note: [Col. 0939] Mark 16:16.] “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved.”

### On the Ointment

The Bride says to the Bridegroom in the Song: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 1:3.] “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments.” The ointments are the chrismata of the Holy Spirit, compounded from those spices which Isaiah recalls when he says: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 11:2.] “There rests upon him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him.” These are the spices [Note: [Col. 0939] Song, chapter 3:6.] of myrrh and [Col. 0940B] frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.

These ointments give fragrance and richness. They give fragrance outwardly by a joyful reputation; they enrich inwardly by spiritual gladness. Because of the joyful reputation, the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 0939] 2 Cor. 2:14.] “We are Christ’s sweet fragrance in every place”; and: [Note: [Col. 0939] John 12:3.] “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” Because of spiritual gladness, the Psalmist says: [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 22:5.] “You have made my head rich with oil”; and: [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 62:6.] “My soul shall be filled as with marrow and fatness.”

This ointment abounds principally in Christ, to whom the Spirit was given without measure, because [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 44:8.] “he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.” But the ointment [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 132:2–3.] descends from the head to the beard and from the beard descends to the hem of the garment, because [Note: [Col. 0939] John 1:16.] “from his fullness we all have received”: first the Apostles, then the rest. This is the anointing which, according to John, [Note: [Col. 0939] 1 John 2:27.] [Col. 0940C] teaches concerning all things; by it kings and priests are anointed, namely those of whom the Apostle Peter says: [Note: [Col. 0939] 1 Pet. 2:9.] “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood.”

### On Adornment

Solomon speaks of adornment in Proverbs: [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter 31:22.] “She made herself a figured garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing. All [Note: [Col. 0939] Same chapter, v. 21.] her household are clothed in double garments.” The Church’s garments are virtues, by which the Church is protected and adorned, according to that prophetic saying: [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 131:9.] “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness”; and: [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 64:14.] “The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys shall abound with grain.”

Therefore she has as many diversities of clothing as she has varieties of virtues, as is read elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0939] Ps. 44:10.] “The queen stood at your right hand in golden clothing, [Col. 0940D] surrounded with variety.” Hence her household—that is, the faithful dwelling in the house of the Lord—are said to be clothed in double garments, that is, adorned with diverse virtues. But the figured garment is that which is not only woven from virtues but also interwoven with works, so that it is bound together with utmost firmness by variety of pattern. This is virtue at work and virtuous action.

Since there are two kinds of faithful persons in the Church, namely Confessors and Martyrs, it is rightly added: “Fine linen and purple are her clothing.” Purple [Col. 0941A] suits martyrs because of the blood by which it is dyed; fine linen suits confessors because of the whiteness which they obtain through mortification. Accordingly, the priestly ornament was woven [Note: [Col. 0941] Exod. 28:6.] from gold, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, in figured—that is, variegated—work. We have discussed these matters more fully in the little book called *On the Mysteries of the Masses*.

“Let us rejoice,” therefore, [Note: [Col. 0941] Rev. 19:7–8.] “and exult, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself. And it was granted her to cover herself with shining, white fine linen. For fine linen is the justifications of the saints.” She is Sarah more mature, Rebecca wiser, Leah more fruitful, Rachel more pleasing, Anna more devout, Susanna more chaste, Judith more courageous, and Edissa more beautiful. “Many daughters [Note: [Col. 0941] Prov. 31:29.] have gathered riches, but this one has surpassed them all.”

### On the Bride’s Beauty

[Col. 0941B]

Behold with how great a beauty Christ has made the Church lovely, so that he rightly says in the Song: [Note: [Col. 0941] Chapter 4:7.] “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved,” adorned with virtues, “and there is no spot in you,” stripped of crimes. But how is she wholly beautiful and without spot, when there is now a spot in the moon? And when many in the Church are defiled with the filth of vices? For Noah’s ark [Note: [Col. 0941] Gen. 7:8.] contained clean and unclean creatures; Abraham’s household [Note: [Col. 0941] Gal. 4:22 and Gen. 16:15.] had a free woman and a slave woman; Rebekah’s womb [Note: [Col. 0941] Rom. 9:10 ff.] carried one predestined and one reprobate. The fisherman’s net [Note: [Col. 0941] Matt. 13:47.] received good and bad fish; a man’s field [Note: [Col. 0941] Matt. 13:25.] produced wheat and tares; and the king [Note: [Col. 0941] Matt. 22:10.] ordered both good and bad persons to be brought to the wedding.
