Although this is, beyond [Col. 0941C] doubt, most true according to the state of the triumphant Church which she possesses in the homeland, it is also true according to the state of the militant Church which she possesses on the way—but with regard to those who are in the Church not only in number but in merit, not only in name but in divine reality; those who belong not only to sacramental but also to spiritual marriage.

Further, since not even an infant of one day [Note: [Col. 0941] Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint.] is without sin upon earth—for “there is no [Note: [Col. 0941] Eccl. 7:21.] just man on earth who does good and does not sin,” and “if [Note: [Col. 0941] 1 John 1:8.] we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us,” since [Note: [Col. 0941] Jas. 3:2.] “we all offend in many things”—how can it be true that even a just soul is wholly beautiful and has no spot? For it may lack mortal sin, but not entirely venial sin.

[Col. 0941D] Yet venial fault does not stain the beauty of the soul. For just as a drop does not extinguish but kindles the heat of a furnace, so venial offense does not diminish but inflames the fervor of charity. For “the just man shall fall seven times [Note: [Col. 0941] Prov. 24:16. The words “in a day” are nevertheless absent.] in a day and rise stronger.” He falls, I say, not into mortal but into venial sin, from which he rises stronger through the sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0941] Ps. 50:19.] of a contrite spirit.

### On Betrothal

[Col. 0942A]

Thus adorned with these virtues, the Church is betrothed; and, for the complete perfection of betrothal, she is given a ring, embraced, and kissed: with the ring of faith, the embrace of hope, and the kiss of charity. In its figure, the father, running to his returning son, fell upon his neck [Note: [Col. 0941] Luke 15:20 ff.] and kissed him … [lacuna] And the father said to his servants … [lacuna] “Put a ring upon his hand,” and so forth.

### On the Form of Contracting Marriage

The same form of contracting marriage is observed in both cases. When a man and a woman come together to contract marriage, with witnesses present each asks the other whether he or she wishes to take the other; and when the answer has been, “I do,” each immediately says to the other, “And I take you as mine.” So, when a catechumen [Col. 0942B] and priest come together for baptism, with sponsors present, the priest asks whether the catechumen believes in the Trinity; and when he has answered, “I believe,” the priest immediately adds, “And I baptize you in the name of the Trinity.” For sacramental marriage is celebrated in baptism.

This is aptly recalled when, at Epiphany, what is like a nuptial song is sung: [Note: [Col. 0941] Antiphon at the Benedictus on the same feast.] “Today the Church is joined to her heavenly bridegroom, because Christ washed away her crimes in the Jordan; the Magi hasten with gifts to the royal marriage; and the wedding guests rejoice because water has been made wine.” For Christ, through whom sacramental nuptials are contracted by the sacrament of baptism, and to whom the Gentile world was joined by them, was baptized in the Jordan on the same day on which he was worshiped by the Gentiles, after thirty years had elapsed; [Col. 0942C] and, when a year had passed, he consecrated the marriage feast. And as in baptism he gave the waters regenerative power, so at the wedding he exercised their transformative power when he changed water into wine: so that, just as cold liquid was changed into warm, and warm into red, so one who was cold and pale through sin might become warm and red through baptism, reddened by Christ’s blood.

### On the Paranymphs

In the sacramental marriage contracted between Christ and the Church, John was the *paranymphus*, the bridegroom’s friend or attendant, who prepared the way before the face of the Lord, as is written through the prophet Isaiah: [Note: [Col. 0941] Chapter 40:3.] “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

This is he of whom the Father says to the Son through [Col. 0942D] the prophet Malachi: [Note: [Col. 0941] Chapter 3:1.] “Behold, I send my angel”—that is, John, who is called an angel not by the property of his nature but by the dignity of his office, because he proclaimed Christ as present beforehand. “One stronger than I comes after me,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0941] Mark 1:7.] “whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie.” And: [Note: [Col. 0941] John 1:15.] “He who comes after me has been made before me.” Again: [Note: [Col. 0941] ibid. 1:29.] “This is he of whom I told you: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away [Col. 0943A] the sin of the world,” who will prepare the way before you, namely repentance and baptism. “Do repentance,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0943] Matt. 3:2, 11.], “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” And: [Note: [Col. 0943] John 1:26.] “I baptize you with water; but one stands in your midst who will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”

And immediately [Note: [Col. 0943] Matt. 3:1.] after John’s proclamation, “the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, will come to his holy temple”—that is, to the Church, in order to sanctify her by betrothing her; of her the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Cor. 3:17.] “The temple of the Lord is holy, which you are.” It is a *metaplasmus* [a transposition of address]. For he turns his speech to those who desired Christ’s coming, saying: [Note: [Col. 0943] Isa. 16:1.] “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”

Therefore he is the voice of the judging Word, the bridegroom’s attendant, the lamp [Col. 0943B] of the sun; he calls himself the bridegroom’s friend and presents himself as the attendant. “He who has the bride,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0943] John 3:29.] “is the bridegroom; but the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

But in the spiritual marriage celebrated between God and the soul, fear is the attendant which introduces charity. For [Note: [Col. 0943] Ecclus. 1:27.] “the fear of the Lord drives out sin”; and “the beginning of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0943] Ps. 110:10.] is the fear of the Lord.” Of this it is said through the prophet: [Note: [Col. 0943] Isa. 23:18.] “Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation.”

### On Solemn Marriage

Sacramental marriage did not wish to be clandestine, but manifest to all. For: [Note: [Col. 0943] Ps. 18:6.] “He set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom [Col. 0943C] coming forth from his chamber.” “In the sun,” that is, openly; as is said elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0943] Mark 4:21.] “A lamp does not come in order to be placed under a bushel, but upon a lampstand.” For [Note: [Col. 0943] Ps. 97:2.] “the Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness.”

Therefore he said to the Apostles: [Note: [Col. 0943] Matt. 10:17.] “What I say to you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops.” “Going [Note: [Col. 0943] Mark 16:15, 20.] into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature … [lacuna] And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.” Therefore: [Note: [Col. 0943] Ps. 18:4.] “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

Every Christian ought publicly to confess this sacramental marriage. For [Note: [Col. 0943] Rom. 10:10.] “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession [Col. 0943D] is made unto salvation.” Therefore he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven.” And: [Note: [Col. 0943] Matt. 10:32.] “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory, and that of his Father and of the holy angels.”

### On Clandestine Marriage

Spiritual marriage is contracted in secret, because God justifies a person without a human intermediary. “The Spirit [Note: [Col. 0943] Luke 9:26.] [Col. 0944A] breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know whence he comes or where he goes.” And [Note: [Col. 0943] John 3:8.] “no one knows the things that are in a human being except the Spirit of God who made the human being.”

Yet lest this marriage too be contracted without witnesses, those three are present in person [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Cor. 2:11.] who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. The Son testifies when he says: [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 John 5:8.] “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

### On the Bringing Home of the Bride
People commonly first betroth a maiden and afterwards bring home the woman betrothed. Hence, when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0943] John 14:23.] And Joseph, her husband, being righteous and unwilling to bring her home, wished to dismiss her secretly. Thus Christ first betrothed the Church through faith, and will afterwards bring her into sight. When he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father and has abolished every rule and authority . . . when this mortal shall put on immortality and this corruptible shall put on incorruption; when he shall say to those at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”; when he shall say to him who doubled the talent: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord,” then, once strangers have been shut out and enclosed in Gehenna, the bride with the bridegroom, alone with alone, shall rest [Col. 0944C] upon the bed of rest, within the chamber of joy, beneath the shelter of peace, concerning which the Prophet says in the Psalm: “You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your countenance from the disturbance of men.” [Note: [Col. 0943] Matthew 1:18–19.] “They shall come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0943] 30:21.] Then “the saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds.” [Note: [Col. 0943] Matthew 8:11.] For God “shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain any longer, because the former things have passed away. Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth,” says the Lord; “and the former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they rise into mind. But you shall rejoice and exult for ever in the things which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem as exultation and her people as joy. And I shall exult in [Col. 0944D] Jerusalem and rejoice in my people, and there shall no longer be heard in it the sound of weeping or the sound of crying.” [Note: [Col. 0943] Psalm 149:5.] “In their land they shall possess a double portion”: [Note: [Col. 0943] Revelation 21:4; Isaiah 65:17 ff.] for in the land of the living the saints shall receive a twofold robe of glorification, spiritual and bodily: one of the mind, which consists in three things, and the other of the flesh, which consists in four; you will find their properties set out in that sermon which I wrote, *On the Double Crown*. [Note: [Col. 0943] Isaiah 61:7.]

## On the Wedding Feast

[Col. 0945A]

But when the Church enters into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, then, amid the voice of exultation and confession, there shall be the sound of feasting. [Note: [Col. 0945] The sermon which Innocent here cites is the one that occupies the second place among those entitled “On One Martyr,” p. 172, vol. I.] Then she shall celebrate in the palace of heaven the wedding feast of which Truth says to the Apostles: “You shall eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Psalm 41:5.] And the Angel says to John: “Blessed are those called to the wedding supper of the Lamb.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Luke 22:30.] “He shall make them recline, and, passing by, shall minister to them.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Revelation 19:9.] “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Luke 12:37.] And they “shall be inebriated by the abundance of the house of God.” When he gives them drink from the torrent of his delight, they shall always be filled and never grow weary. That fullness shall never incur weariness, because that sweetness shall always awaken [Col. 0945B] desire. Then they shall taste fully how sweet the Lord is, [Note: [Col. 0945] Psalm 35:8.] when God himself shall be all in all: [Note: [Col. 0945] 1 Peter 2:3.] food, drink, fullness, and satisfaction for each; incorporeal sweetness, ineffable pleasantness, inestimable fragrance.

“How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” [Note: [Col. 0945] 1 Corinthians 15:28.] Great indeed is the abundance of sweetness, since one suffices for all, while all do not suffice for one. Yet you do not give it in the present, but reserve it for the future, because you have hidden it for those who fear you. “I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when your glory is manifested.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Psalm 30:20.] For you have said: “To the conqueror I shall give hidden manna.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Psalm 16:15.] “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0945] Revelation 2:17; 1 Corinthians 2:9.] “To the conqueror I shall give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Revelation 2:7.] [Col. 0945C] “To the thirsty I shall give freely from the fountain of living water”; and whoever drinks of it “shall never thirst for ever.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Revelation 21:6.]

## On the Sacramental Feast

Meanwhile, until the bride is brought into the kingdom, lest she fail through waiting, the bridegroom has prepared for her a solemn feast, of such quantity and quality as has not been celebrated since the beginning of time. It is surely that feast which the father provided for his returning son, at which he ordered the fattened calf to be killed. [Note: [Col. 0945] John 4:13.] In this feast spiritual delights abound, which satisfy and nourish the mind beyond all other foods and drinks.

## On the Bread

For heavenly bread is set forth, concerning which it is said: “If anyone eats, he shall live for ever.” [Note: [Col. 0945] Luke 15:23.] This bread is received, not consumed; eaten, not expelled; chewed, [Col. 0945D] yet not incorporated. Rather, when eaten it incorporates, and the eater is incorporated. It is transubstantiated, not transformed; it transforms, but does not transubstantiate. It is eaten daily and does not fail or diminish, because it is transubstantiated daily and neither advances nor increases.

## On the Flesh

Yet under the form of bread the substance of flesh is eaten, according to the saying: “The bread which I shall give [Col. 0946A] is my flesh for the life of the world.” [Note: [Col. 0945] John 6:52.] This is the paschal Lamb, of which we are commanded to eat neither anything raw nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire, devouring the head with the feet and entrails. Whatever remains is to be burned with fire. [Note: [Col. 0945] John 6:52; Exodus 12:9 ff.] It is divided without injury and eaten whole. It lives when eaten, having risen after being slain. When eaten it does not die, because it rose never to die. Whoever eats however much eats the whole, because neither did he who gathered more have more, nor did he who prepared less find less.

## On the Wine

Wine also is offered—such as neither Cyprus produced nor was found in Engaddi—of which the Psalmist says: “Your inebriating cup—how splendid it is!” [Note: [Col. 0945] Exodus 12:9 ff.; Song of Songs 1:13.] It does not make men drunken, but renders them sober; and [Col. 0946B] the more it is drunk, the more it is desired. It produces desire without producing weariness; and therefore whoever drinks more thirsts more, until hope is changed into possession and faith into sight. This is the cup of the New Testament, containing wine in which the robe is washed, and the cloak in the blood of the grape. [Note: [Col. 0945] Psalm 22:5.]

O great and saving feast, in which Christ’s flesh is eaten and Christ’s blood is drunk! Flesh clean, flesh pure, flesh sincere, delightful, lovable, sweet. Blood splendid, blood precious, blood acceptable, sanctifying, life-giving, and cleansing; sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to the soul that loves it. What each person healthfully desires, that tastes sweetly to him. For how could virtues fail to taste sweet in him in whom is the fullness of virtues? If one desires virtue [Col. 0946C] and wisdom, Christ is the power and wisdom of God. [Note: [Col. 0945] Genesis 49:11; 1 Corinthians 1:24.] If one desires truth and life, Christ is the way, truth, and life. Examples will not be lacking to one who runs through each point. For it is written: “You gave them bread from heaven without labour, containing in itself every delight and the sweetness of every flavour.” [Note: [Col. 0945] John 11:6; Wisdom 16:20.] “The bread,” he says, “which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” So great is the bridegroom’s love for the bride that he gives himself to her not only to possess, but truly also to eat. For he who gave himself as the price to redeem us from death gave himself as food to nourish us unto life. “Whoever eats me shall live because of me.” [Note: [Col. 0945] John 6:52, 58.]

Therefore, for the health of the body flesh is eaten under the appearance of bread, and for the health of the spirit blood is drunk under the appearance of wine; each is present under either species. For bread pertains to flesh and wine [Col. 0946D] to soul, because wine produces blood, in which the soul has its seat. Moses indeed testifies that flesh is offered for the body, but blood for the soul. [Note: [Col. 0945] Leviticus 17:11, 13, etc.]

## On the Greatness of the Feast

One day does not suffice for celebrating this feast; one month does not suffice; one year does not suffice. Rather, it began with Christ’s passion and shall continue until the end of the world, so that, because we sin daily through [Col. 0947A] weakness, we may daily be healed from sin by this medicine. “I shall be with you,” he says, “all days, unto the consummation of the age.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Matthew 28:20.] He is always present with us in this feast, indeed under another form, but truly in his own substance.

For, since Christ according to his divine nature exists in things in three ways—in all things by essence, in the righteous alone by grace, and in the assumed man by union—he himself willed, according to his human nature, to exist in things in three ways: locally in heaven, personally in the Word, sacramentally on the altar. For just as according to divinity he is wholly and essentially in all things, so according to humanity he is wholly sacramentally in many places.

## On the Table

[Col. 0947B]

So great is this heavenly feast that not even one place suffices for its celebration; rather, one and the same thing, in no respect variable or different, is celebrated upon every altar-table throughout all regions of the world. This table is adorned with precious cloths, and over it a corporal pall is spread, so that the most holy feast may be celebrated upon a most clean linen cloth. This is the table of which the Prophet says: “You have prepared a table before me,” and of which the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of the table of Christ and of the table of demons.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Matthew 28:20; Psalm 22:5; 1 Corinthians 10:21.]

## On the Ministers

In this excellent feast the orders [Col. 0947C] of ministers are divided. But among all, and before all, are the three chief orders—subdeacons, Levites, and priests—who ought to possess purity of heart and body, according to the prophetic command: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Isaiah 52:11.]

## On the Vessels

The vessels are not wooden, as though cheap; not glass, as though fragile; not bronze, as though rusting; but gold or silver, distinguished by precious stones. In them the ministers perform their service in such ordered fashion that the very ordering of the ministers signifies a wondrous divine sacrament.

## On the Guests

To this universal feast the bridegroom invites all nations: “Come to me,” he says, “all who labour and are burdened, and I shall refresh you.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Matthew 11:28.] “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, [Col. 0947D] “is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0947] Matthew 22:2.] Blessed Gregory expounded this parable so diligently and clearly that it would be not only superfluous but rash to add or alter anything after him. [Col. 0948A]

Therefore he first invited the Jewish people to the feast through the prophets, who foretold this banquet, but they neglected to come. Again he invited the same people to the feast through the apostles, who announced this banquet, but they scorned to come; indeed, they afflicted some of those prophets and apostles with insults and killed them. Therefore, lest the wedding, now prepared, should remain unattended, he invited the Gentile people through various preachers; they believed and came, and the wedding feast was filled with guests reclining at table.

## On the Three Orders

Although there are many orders of guests, because “terrible as an army arrayed in ranks,” [Note: [Col. 0947] Homily 38 on the Gospels; Song of Songs 6:3.] there are nevertheless three principal orders: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, prelates, the continent, and the married. For according to [Col. 0948B] the Gospel parable, two are in the field, two in bed, and two at the mill; one of them shall be taken and the other left. [Note: [Col. 0947] Luke 17:34–35.] Some who enter the wedding feast do not have a wedding garment, [Note: [Col. 0947] Matthew 22:11.] because “whoever eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0947] 1 Corinthians 11:29.] The wedding garment is charity, which covers a multitude of sins. [Note: [Col. 0947] 1 Peter 4:8.] Therefore let a person test himself as to whether he possesses charity, and thus eat of that bread and drink of the cup. [Note: [Col. 0947] In the above-cited epistle of St Paul, chapter 11:28.] Otherwise, with hands and feet bound, he shall be cast into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

## On the Spiritual Feast

But in the spiritual marriage a spiritual feast is celebrated: namely, that which Job’s seven sons held every day with their three sisters. [Note: [Col. 0947] Matthew 22:13; Job 1:4 ff.] [Col. 0948C] For then Job’s seven sons feast with the three sisters when the seven gifts, together with the three virtues, refresh with inward fullness the mind which they affect. Of this the Lord says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I shall enter to him and sup with him, and he with me.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Revelation 3:20.]

The Psalmist invites us to this feast, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Psalm 33:9.] Peter the Apostle says: “Desire milk, that you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.” [Note: [Col. 0947] First Epistle, chapter 2, verse 2.] She had already tasted this sweetness, who said: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk”; and therefore she invites others also to taste: “Eat, friends, and drink, and be inebriated, beloved ones.” [Note: [Col. 0947] Song of Songs 5:1.]

It is tasted upon the table [Col. 0948D] made of shittim wood, standing on four feet, [Note: [Col. 0947] Exodus 25:23.] upon which the loaves of presentation were set before the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0947] Exodus 25:30.] This is the table of Scripture, upon which the Church is fed with the bread of life and the understanding is fed and given drink of the saving water of wisdom.

# Epithalamium in Praise of the Bridegroom and Bride

[Col. 0949]

[Col. 0949A] Singers and psalmists commonly attend wedding feasts, so that they may gladden those reclining at table with instruments and songs. Hence we read that at the feast which the father gave for his returning son, music (*symphonia*) and dancing sounded forth. [Note: [Col. 0949] Ecclesiasticus 15:3.] By *symphonia* we understand stringed instruments; by dancing, songs of voices. Let, then, that excellent lyre-player David come to this wedding feast and sing, in honour of the bridegroom and bride, the epithalamium which his heart poured forth.

## Preface: On the Commendation of the Singer

“My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king.” [Note: [Col. 0949] Luke 15:25; Psalm 44.] He cries out in the person of one knocking at the door, that he may be admitted to the wedding. And as though the doorkeeper [Col. 0949B] replied: “For this reason entrance is not open to you: buffoons and actors are accustomed to be slanderous and adulterating, foolish and arrogant.” “I am not foolish,” he says, “for my heart has poured forth”—that is, it has brought forth a word full of wisdom. “I am not a flatterer, who praises with his mouth but does not praise with his heart, because not only my mouth but my heart has poured forth. I am not arrogant, one who attributes another’s work to himself as though it were his own, because my heart has poured forth. I am not slanderous, one who speaks a harsh and malicious word, because my heart has poured forth a good word, a sweet word, a pleasant word, a delightful word. For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and a good man brings forth new things and old from a good treasure.” [Note: [Col. 0949] These and other related annotations occur in the margin of the manuscript. He is commended from the heart; Matthew 12:34 ff., and chapter 13:52.]

[Col. 0949C] But as though the doorkeeper replied: “Then tell me your good word, so that I may report it to the King.” “It is not fitting,” he says, “that you should reap what you have not sown. Therefore I speak *my* works, not yours, to the King.” [Note: [Col. 0949] Margin: He is commended from his work.] “To the King, not to you, because the labourer is worthy of his wage”—especially since he intends to praise perfectly, that is, with heart, mouth, and work: with heart, because “my heart has poured forth”; with mouth, because it “has poured forth a good word”; with work, because “I speak my works to the king”—namely, the praises of the bridegroom and bride which I have produced by discovering and composing them. “I also speak my works to the King,” that is, I consecrate my songs to Christ.

And as though the doorkeeper mocked him because his speech was confused and sluggish: “It is not confused,” he says, “because my tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.” [Note: [Col. 0949] Luke, chapter 10:7.] As though he said: “Why do you seek proof [Col. 0949D] of him who speaks in me—Christ? My tongue is [Col. 0950A] the pen of a swiftly writing scribe,” that is, the instrument of the Holy Spirit, who inspires swiftly and does not deliberate under human strain, but suddenly breathes wherever he wills; according as elsewhere we read: “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a rushing mighty spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0949] Margin: He is commended from his mouth; 2 Corinthians 13:3; John 3:8; Acts 2:2.]

For as ink from the scribe’s horn is impressed upon parchment through a pen, so the Holy Spirit poured the knowledge of truth from the secret place of divinity, through the prophet’s tongue, into the human heart. He is an excellent writer, who wrote anew on both sides tablets of the Law altogether like the former ones. [Note: [Col. 0949] Exodus 34:1.] Therefore he will write swiftly concerning him who, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, is called: “Hasten, take spoils; seize, make haste to plunder.” [Note: [Col. 0949] Isaiah 8:1.]

Among all the speakers of both kinds, the King orders the lyre-player to be brought in; once introduced, he immediately extols the king’s praises excellently.

## Narrative of the Bridegroom’s Praises

“Fair in form,” he says, “beyond the sons of men.” He proceeds with the praises of both king and queen; but he praises the king first and more highly, as the greater, and the queen afterwards and more moderately, as the lesser. Of the bridegroom he says first: “Fair in form beyond the sons of men.” Of the bride he adds: “The queen stood at your right hand, in clothing embroidered with gold.” He praises the bridegroom in four ways: from form, from power, from judgment, and from adornment. From form, when he says: “Fair in form beyond the sons of men.” From power, when he says: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one.” From judgment, when he adds: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of your kingdom is a righteous sceptre.” From adornment, when he adds: “Myrrh, and liquid myrrh, and cassia are upon your garments.”

[Note: [Col. 0949] Margin: The bridegroom is praised from his form.] Yet he praises him in many ways from his form: comparatively, by preferring him to others—hence, “Fair in form beyond the sons of men”; absolutely, by simply commending him—hence, “In your beauty and your comeliness set forth prosperously,” and so forth. Again, he praises him from form according to each nature: according to humanity, “Fair in form beyond the sons of men”; according to divinity, “In your beauty and your comeliness,” and so forth. Likewise, according to the beauty of the body, “Fair in form beyond the sons of men”; and according to the beauty of the heart, “In your beauty and your comeliness set forth, proceed prosperously, and reign.” As though he said: [Col. 0950D] “O King, although it is written of you in Isaiah, [Note: [Col. 0949] Chapter 53, verse 2.] ‘See him having neither beauty nor comeliness,’ on account of the shame of your despised passion, [Col. 0951A] yet you are fair in form beyond the sons of men on account of the glory of your singular conception. For you alone were conceived of a Virgin without sin, clean from one clean; whereas all others are born corrupt from the corrupt, sinners from sinners. You alone are Son of Man, and not of men; the rest are sons of men, and not of Man. And therefore you are fair in form beyond the sons of men.

“And though you are true man, nevertheless you are truly above all men, because ‘he who comes from heaven is above all.’ [Note: [Col. 0951] John 3:32.] And though you are fair in form beyond the sons of men, because angels desire to look into you, [Note: [Col. 0951] 1 Peter 1:12.] you have truly been made fair because you are free from fault, for ‘he committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.’ [Note: [Col. 0951] 1 Peter 2:22.] Nevertheless, nothing prevents its being understood according to bodily form [Col. 0951B] that he was fairer than other men.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Here Innocent seems to approach the opinion of those who hold that Christ had a beautiful appearance and a comely body.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Margin: The bridegroom is praised from his tongue.] But since many are handsome in form who are not gracious in speech, after praising the bridegroom from form, he immediately commends him from his tongue: “Grace has been poured forth upon your lips.” The word “poured forth” signifies the abundance of grace, according to the saying: “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh”; and: “The charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Acts of the Apostles 2:17; Romans 5:5. Margin: He explains it in various ways.] As though he said: “Your mouth does not abound in wickedness, nor does your tongue devise deceit; rather, grace has been poured forth upon your lips.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Psalm 49:19.]

Upon Moses’ lips vengeance was poured forth: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, burning for burning”; [Note: [Col. 0951] Exodus 21:24.] but upon your lips grace has been poured forth. “If anyone compels [Col. 0951C] you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two. If he takes away your cloak, give him your tunic also. If he strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Matthew 5:39 ff.] For “the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0951] John 1:17.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Margin: He explains “lips.”] “In many portions and in many ways you formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, but in these last times grace has been poured forth upon your lips.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Hebrews 1:1.] Moses said of himself: “Since yesterday and the day before yesterday I have not been eloquent, and I am of a more impeded and slower tongue, ever since you spoke to me.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Exodus 4:10.] And Isaiah: “Woe is me, because I have been silent; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Isaiah 6:5.] And Jeremiah: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Jeremiah 1:6.] But grace has been poured forth [Col. 0951D] upon your lips.

[Note: [Col. 0951] Margin: He explains grace.] Formerly terror was poured forth in your words; hence the Jews, terrified and shaken with fear, stood at a distance and said to Moses: “Speak to us and we shall listen; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Exodus 20:18.] But now grace has been poured forth upon your lips. Hence the servants who had been sent by the chief priests to seize you answered: [Col. 0952A] “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks.” [Note: [Col. 0951] John 7:46.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Margin: He explains “poured forth.”] The envious conceal wisdom so that they may not communicate it to others. But grace has been poured forth upon your lips. For you said: “Everything whatsoever I heard from my Father I have made known to you.” [Note: [Col. 0951] John 13:15.] For what benefit is there in hidden treasure and hidden wisdom? [Note: [Col. 0951] Ecclesiasticus 20:32.] Scripture reproves both the one who hides grain from the people and the one who buries his talent in the ground. [Note: [Col. 0951] Proverbs 11:26; Matthew 25:26.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Margin: He explains grace.] Many sometimes speak wisely, yet are not gladly heard. But grace has been poured forth upon your lips, because your word is pleasing to all and wholly gracious, not only with men but also with God. It follows: “Therefore [Col. 0952B] God has blessed you for ever,” that is, therefore he gave you an eternal blessing—namely a kingdom [Note: [Col. 0951] Luke 1:33.] of which there shall be no end—because through the grace of preaching you merited the glory of resurrection.

But since Christ had been blessed from the beginning, according to what Elizabeth said to the Virgin, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb,” [Note: [Col. 0951] Luke 1:42.] it may be understood thus: “He blessed” means “he showed to be blessed.” The Apostle likewise said: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death upon a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Philippians 2:8–9.] He possessed this name even before death, but what the Son had possessed before death the Father gave him—that is, showed it to have been given after death. As he himself said after the resurrection: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” [Col. 0952C] that is, it is now manifest as though given.

[Note: [Col. 0951] Margin: The bridegroom is praised from his power.] “Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one.” He praises the bridegroom from power, showing him armed in three ways: with sword, arrows, and sceptre. With the sword he strikes those near at hand; with arrows he smites those at a distance; with the sceptre he corrects subjects. Therefore there is no one who can flee his power, as the Prophet says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Psalm 138:7–8.]

Therefore he speaks first of the sword: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one.” He adds concerning the arrows: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you.” [Col. 0952D] He adds concerning the sceptre: “The sceptre of your kingdom is a righteous sceptre.” As though he said: “O most mighty one, whom no one [Note: [Col. 0951] Psalm 78:5.] can resist, since grace has been poured forth upon your lips, gird yourself with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, that by the power of the word you may separate men from the devil; so that, coming as the stronger one, you may overcome the armed strong man and plunder all his goods.” [Note: [Col. 0951] Luke 11:21–22; Matthew 12:29.]

Concerning [Col. 0953A] this sword you say in the Gospel: “I came not to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword. For I came to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother . . . and a man’s enemies [shall be] those of his household.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Matthew 10:34 ff.] But “gird your sword upon your thigh.”

[Note: [Col. 0953] Margin: The thigh is explained in two ways.] I read in Exodus: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbour.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Chapter 32:27.] I read likewise in the Song of Songs: “Sixty strong men of the strongest of Israel surround Solomon’s bed . . . each with his sword upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Chapter 3:7–8.] But I understand the saying concerning them one way and the saying concerning you another way. For they are girded upon the thigh so as to restrain the fault of the flesh; but you are girded upon the thigh so as to show the nature of flesh. For the thigh is the seedbed of human nature or propagation, according to which Abraham said to his servant: “Put your hand beneath my thigh”—not *upon* it, but *beneath* it—because of reverence for you, who according to human nature were [Col. 0953B] to be propagated from that thigh. [Note: [Col. 0953] Genesis 24:2; 22:8.]

Therefore gird yourself upon the thigh, that is, upon humanity, in which you must conquer the devil. [Note: [Col. 0953] John 3:8.] For to gird oneself (*accingi*) is one thing, to tuck up one’s garments (*succingi*) another, and to gird oneself for service (*praecingi*) another. We gird ourselves to fight, according to the saying: “Gird yourselves, and be mighty sons . . . for it is better for us to die in battle than to see the evils of our nation and of the saints.” [Note: [Col. 0953] 1 Maccabees 3:58–59.] We tuck up our garments to go forth, according to the saying: “Simon Peter, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded himself with his tunic and threw himself into the sea.” [Note: [Col. 0953] John 21:7.] We gird ourselves for service, according to the saying: “Then he shall gird himself for service, make them recline, and, passing by, shall minister to them.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Luke 12:37.] Yet one is frequently used for another, as can readily be proved from many authorities of Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Margin: The bridegroom is praised from form according to each nature.] “In your beauty and your comeliness set forth, proceed prosperously, and reign.” Those most beautiful are accustomed to be proud of their beauty, and those most mighty to rage because of their strength. Yet although you are fair in form beyond the sons of men, you are not proud; and therefore, “in your beauty and your comeliness set forth.” Although you are most mighty, girded with a sword upon your thigh, you do not rage; and therefore “proceed prosperously and reign.” [Col. 0953D]

He had praised the bridegroom in three ways, declaring him most beautiful, most eloquent, and most mighty; now he assigns one thing to each: “Set forth, proceed prosperously, and reign.” As though he said: “Because you are fair in form according to humanity, therefore look upon us in your beauty. But because you are fair beyond the sons of men according to divinity, therefore look upon us in your comeliness; so that, looking upon us in your beauty and comeliness, you may look upon us according to both natures”—that [Col. 0954A] is, mercifully behold perishing man, redeeming him through the human nature and glorifying him through the divine.

But in order to accomplish this fittingly, proceed prosperously to the passion—not as one prospered, but as one prospering—so that you may redeem the wretched; and reign through the resurrection, so that you may glorify the redeemed. Or, because grace has been poured forth upon your lips, therefore proceed prosperously in the office of preaching, because you are the tree “planted beside streams of water, which shall give its fruit in its season; and its leaf shall not fall; and everything whatsoever it does shall prosper.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Psalm 1:3.] And therefore, girded with the sword of preaching upon the thigh of humanity, reign: first through faith in the Church militant, then through sight in the Church triumphant, so that “your kingdom may come; your will be done as [Col. 0954B] in heaven and on earth.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Matthew 6:10.]

[Note: [Col. 0953] Margin: The bridegroom is praised for truth, gentleness, and justice.] “Because of truth, gentleness, and justice.” Again he commends the bridegroom in three ways: from the truth of doctrine, the gentleness of patience, and the justice of life; from the truth of doctrine which he preaches, the gentleness of patience which he displays, and the justice of life which he fulfils.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Margin: On the three things necessary to one who reigns.] These three things are especially necessary to one who reigns: that he be truthful in speech, gentle in heart, and just in deed. Therefore reign because of the truth which you preached—whence, “I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.” [Note: [Col. 0953] John 16:7.] Reign because of the gentleness which you displayed—whence, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Matthew 11:29.] Reign because of the justice which you fulfilled—whence, “Thus it is fitting [Col. 0954C] for us to fulfil all justice.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Matthew 3:15.]

You are also called truthful in fulfilling promises—whence, “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0953] John 1:17.] Therefore reign because of truth; for it is written of you: “The Holy of Holies shall be anointed, and vision and prophecy shall be fulfilled, so that iniquity may be destroyed and everlasting justice brought in.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Daniel 9:24.]

You are called gentle in enduring reproaches—whence, “I was like a gentle lamb that is led to sacrifice.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Jeremiah 11:19.] Therefore reign because of gentleness; for you said: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Did not Christ have to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?” [Note: [Col. 0953] Luke 24:25–26.]

You are called just in administering judgments—whence, “The Lord is just and loves justice; his countenance beholds equity.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Psalm 10:8.] Therefore reign because of justice; for it is written of you: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son . . . and has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” [Note: [Col. 0953] John 5:22, 27.]

Most powerful men, forgetful of the human condition, are accustomed to be dreadful, cruel, tyrannical, deceitful, impatient, and unjust. But from you, who are most mighty, all these things are removed. For you are not dreadful, but kindly, because in your beauty and comeliness you press onward [Col. 0955A]. You are not cruel, but merciful, because you proceed prosperously. You are not a tyrant, but a prince, because you reign prosperously. You are not deceitful, but true, because you press onward according to truth. You are not impatient, but gentle, because you proceed according to gentleness. You are not unjust, but righteous, because you reign according to righteousness. And since you are such, your right hand—that is, your power, namely that of which it is said, “Your right hand has wrought strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me”—will lead you wondrously, that is, through miracles, from words to deeds, from death to life, from earth to heaven, from the Jews to the Gentiles, through the course of the whole earth. For it is written of you:

[Note: [Col. 0955] Marginal note: On the abusive exercise of power, which is removed from the Bridegroom.]

“All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.” And those who saw were amazed.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 117:16]: “All were filled with fear, saying: ‘For we have seen wonders today.’” [Col. 0955B] And it was also said to you [Note: [Col. 0955] Luke 2:47]: “Renew signs and change wonders,” because you performed those works [Note: [Col. 0955] Ibid. 5:26] which no one else had ever performed. Therefore your right hand will lead you wondrously.

[Note: [Col. 0955] Ecclesiasticus 36:6.]

“Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you into the hearts of the king’s enemies.” If Holy Scripture is understood by armour, then the arrow ought to be understood as the divine word. For we shoot arrows from the bow when we bring forth words from Holy Scripture. He knew this bow and these arrows who said [Note: [Col. 0955] John 15:24]: “He has bent his bow and made it ready . . . he has made his arrows burning.” Two things are found in an arrow: wood and iron. The wood is straight so that it may fly through the air; the iron is sharp so that it may pierce. Both fittingly belong to the divine word [Col. 0955C]. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0955] Marginal note: The Bridegroom is praised from his armour]: “He sends forth his utterance to the earth; his word runs swiftly.” Likewise [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 7:13 and following]: “The word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two-edged sword.”

He says, then: “Your right hand will truly lead you wondrously, because your arrows are sharp”; that is, your words are penetrating and compunctive. They penetrate so as to introduce love through fear, and they pierce with compunction so as to grant pardon through repentance. Hear an arrow which penetrates and compuncts: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 147:15]. Likewise: “What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss of his soul?” [Note: [Col. 0955] Hebrews 4:12]. Therefore the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” [Note: [Col. 0955] Matthew 3:10.] [Col. 0955D]. For when the beloved speaks, the soul melts, because the divine word softens the human heart through the burning of compunction, so that it may lay aside the hardness of iniquity, and through the fervour of charity, so that it may receive the form of righteousness.

There is, indeed, a twofold use of the arrow: to strike and to set ablaze. By striking it inflicts a wound, and by setting ablaze it introduces flame; for the divine word wounds unto repentance and kindles unto [Col. 0956A] charity. Of the arrows which strike it is said [Note: [Col. 0955] Ibid. 16:26]: “Your arrows are fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand upon me.” Of those which set ablaze we read [Note: [Col. 0955] Chapter 5:6]: “Sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals.” Hear the arrow striking unto repentance: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance” [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 37:3]. Attend to the arrow kindling charity: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 119:4]. She knew this arrow who said: “I am wounded by love” [Note: [Col. 0955] Luke 3:7 and following]. Therefore he wounds peoples with arrows of this sort.

“They will fall beneath you,” that is, they will humble themselves before you. “In the heart,” or “into the hearts,” of the king’s enemies. [Note: [Col. 0955] John 14:23.] The difference of reading produces a difference of interpretation, and according to either reading the construction is arranged in two ways.

For if it is read “in the heart,” the sense is this: Your peoples, struck by arrows, shall fall—that is, shall be humbled—in the heart of the king’s enemies; that is, in their own heart, since they are enemies of the king, that is, enemies of you, who are the great King [Col. 0956B] over all peoples. And enemies shall become friends, so that where they were formerly raised up in pride, there they may now be humbled in devotion: like Paul, who, formerly exalted, was at last humbled, struck in his heart by an arrow sent from heaven, and fell, saying: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” [Note: [Col. 0955] Acts of the Apostles 9:6.]

[Note: [Col. 0955] Marginal note: He expounds it in four ways.]

Or otherwise: “The peoples of the king’s enemies”—that is, many among your enemies, you who are King of kings [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 94:3] and Lord of lords—shall fall beneath you, that is, shall submit themselves to you “in the heart,” that is, from the heart: namely, willingly. For although a person can do other things unwillingly, he cannot believe except willingly: “I will freely sacrifice to you and confess your name, O Lord, because it is good” [Note: [Col. 0955] Acts of the Apostles 9:6].

But if it is read “into the hearts,” the sense is this: “Peoples shall fall beneath you into the hearts,” that is, against the hearts, of the king’s enemies: that is, against the will of your enemies—not only scribes and Pharisees, but also kings and princes. Though these were unwilling and forbade it, the peoples believed. For the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council and said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs” [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Timothy 6:15]. “Behold, the whole world [Col. 0956C] has gone after him” [Note: [Col. 0955] Psalm 93:8]. “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him” [Note: [Col. 0955] John 11:47].

Or otherwise: “Peoples shall fall beneath you,” that is, submit themselves to you, because “your sharp arrows are fixed into the hearts of the king’s enemies,” that is, they have pierced the hearts of your enemies unto repentance [Col. 0956D]. [Note: [Col. 0955] Ibid. 12:19.] The good fall and the evil fall; but the good fall on their faces, whereas the evil fall backward. Of the good it is written [Note: [Col. 0955] Ibid. 11:48]: “They fell upon their faces and worshipped God.” Of the evil it is written [Note: [Col. 0955] Marginal note: On falling]: “They went backward and fell to the ground.” The good fall under Christ and before Christ; the evil fall away from Christ and upon Christ. Of the good who fall it is written: “Peoples shall fall beneath you”; and: “Let us fall down before [Col. 0957A] the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0955] Revelation 5:14]. Of the evil who fall it is written: “A thousand shall fall at your side” [Note: [Col. 0957] John 18:6]; and: “Whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken” [Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 94:6].

[Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 90:7.]

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a straight rod is the rod of your kingdom.” Here he praises the Bridegroom from his judgment, commending him in three ways: from dignity, equity, and purity. From dignity according to office; from equity according to judgment; from purity according to disposition. It is as though he said: Your jurisdiction is not delegated, but ordinary; it is not temporary, but perpetual, because “your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” Your sentence is not crooked, but straight; not inequitable, but just, because “a straight rod is the rod of your kingdom.” Your will is not feigned, but true; not corrupt, but pure, because you have loved righteousness and hated [Col. 0957B] iniquity.

Therefore let no one trust in changeability, because “your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” Let no one presume upon mercy, because “the rod is straight, the rod of your kingdom.” Let no one grow angry at perversity, because you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity. No one can seize your tribunal, because “your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” No one can impugn your judgment, because “a straight rod is the rod of your kingdom.” No one can corrupt your disposition, because you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Matthew 21:44.]

A good judge ought to have steadfastness, lest he be rash; justice, lest he be unjust; prudence, lest he be undiscerning. Therefore you, who are the righteous Judge [Note: [Col. 0957] Marginal note: The Bridegroom is praised from judgment], strong and long-suffering, are not rash but steadfast, because “your throne, [Col. 0957C] O God, is for ever and ever.” You are not unjust but righteous, because “a straight rod is the rod of your kingdom.” You are not undiscerning but provident, because you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.

The throne is judicial authority, concerning which Truth says [Note: [Col. 0957] Marginal note: On the things necessary for a good Judge]: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0957] Matthew 19:28]. This throne is for ever and ever, because what it establishes is not changed, and what it decrees is not annulled. By the rod of the kingdom, which is called a sceptre, royal power is understood. It is called a rod of direction because it directs the crooked, governs the righteous, and crushes the wicked, according to the saying [Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 7:12]: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and break them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.”

[Col. 0957D] “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” A sentence is judged unjust in three ways: from the disposition, from the procedure, and from the cause. From the disposition, if it is pronounced contrary to sincerity of mind; from the cause, if it is pronounced contrary to the truth of the matter; from the procedure, if it is pronounced contrary to legal formality. In these three ways the sentence was unjust by which the two elders condemned Susanna [Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 2:9].

But your sentence is not unjust from disposition, because it is not pronounced from malice but from charity, because you have loved. It is not unjust in procedure, because it is not pronounced [Col. 0958A] unjustly but lawfully, since you have loved righteousness. It is not unjust in cause, because it is not pronounced contrary to desert but according to what is due, since you have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.

God loves righteousness in three ways: because he creates it, approves it, and rewards it. Conversely, he hates iniquity in three ways: because he forbids it, destroys it, and punishes it. There are, indeed, two precepts of the natural law: one is for loving righteousness, taught in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0957] Marginal note: On a just sentence]: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them.” The other is for hating iniquity, found in Tobit: “What you would hate to have done to you by another, do not do to another” [Note: [Col. 0957] Daniel 13:41].

When, however, we hate an unjust person, we ought to hate not humanity but iniquity, as the Church instructs us. When we love an unjust person, we ought to love not iniquity but humanity; for whoever [Col. 0958B] loves iniquity hates his own soul [Note: [Col. 0957] Matthew 7:12].

[Note: [Col. 0957] Chapter 4:16.]

“Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” Not because you loved righteousness and hated iniquity, but in order that you might love righteousness and hate iniquity. For Christ was not anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions because he loved righteousness and hated iniquity; rather, he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions in order that he might love righteousness and hate iniquity.

Thus it is shown who anointed: God; whom he anointed: you; with what he anointed: the oil of gladness; how greatly he anointed: above your companions; and for what purpose he anointed: that you might love righteousness and hate iniquity. In these words the Trinity of persons is expressed: for the Father is the anointer, the Son the anointed, and the Holy Spirit the anointing. From this anointing the Son received his name, because in Hebrew he is called Messiah, in Greek Christ, and in Latin Anointed.

Concerning him the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” [Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 10:6], because Christ is called from *chrism*, which is made principally from oil; “poured out,” because the other faithful are called anointed from the anointing, that is, Christians from Christ. Literally, by “the oil of gladness” is understood the priestly and royal anointing which gladdens those anointed. Therefore God anointed you both king and priest, that you might be King of kings [Col. 0958C] and Lord of lords, and that you might be a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0957] Chapter 1:2].

[Note: [Col. 0957] Marginal note: On Anointing.]

He anointed you with the oil of gladness, that is, with the fullness of grace, which gladdens and delights the mind, as the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” [Note: [Col. 0957] 1 Timothy 6:15]. Or “oil of gladness” means the Holy Spirit, who is the gladness of Father and Son, the love and mutual affection of both; concerning whom elsewhere it is written: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 109:4]. He knew this oil who said: “The yoke has decayed because of the oil” [Note: [Col. 0957] 2 Corinthians 1:12]; and he who foretold: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone” [Note: [Col. 0957] Psalm 45:5]. What this oil is Peter explains in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus of Nazareth,” he says, “whom God anointed [Col. 0959A] with the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0957] Isaiah 10:27]. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the oil of gladness with which Jesus of Nazareth was anointed above his companions.

Christ’s companions are all the faithful, who, according to the Apostle, are heirs of God and fellow-heirs of Christ [Note: [Col. 0959] Deuteronomy 32:13], sharers in the promise, that is, in the eternal inheritance [Note: [Col. 0959] Chapter 10:38]. But Christ received the fullness of anointing, because the Spirit was given to him without measure, and in him the fullness of divinity dwells bodily [Note: [Col. 0959] Romans 8:17]. The rest, however, receive a portion of that fullness, since “the ointment descended from the head to the beard, and from the beard descended to the hem of the garment,” because “from his fullness we have all received” [Note: [Col. 0959] Ephesians 3:6]: first the Apostles, then the rest [Note: [Col. 0959] Colossians 2:9]. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.

Let the Jew, the heretic, and the pagan blush, who with perverse heart falsely maintain [Col. 0959B] that Christ is not God, when David, greatest among the prophets, openly declares Christ to be God: “God, your God, has anointed you”; God the Father has anointed you, God the Son. This is sufficiently clear in the Greek, in which the vocative is distinguished from the nominative. Therefore, in the preceding verse, without changing person, he called him God: “Your throne,” he says, “O God, is for ever and ever.” Isaiah agrees: “His name,” he says, “shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” [Note: [Col. 0959] Psalm 132:2]. And Jeremiah: “This is our God, and no other shall be counted beside him . . . . After these things he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” [Note: [Col. 0959] John 1:16].

God therefore anointed God: namely, God made man [Col. 0959C] for the sake of man, God. For God is the Father of the Son according to divinity; but the Father is the God of the Son according to humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0959] Chapter 9, verse 6.]

“Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses.” He praises the Bridegroom from the adornment of things and persons. From the adornment of things in two ways, namely garments and houses: hence, “Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses.” Likewise, from the adornment of persons in two ways, namely household and bride: hence, “Daughters of kings delighted you in your honour. The queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment.” In the garments he commends fragrance as against foulness; in the houses brightness as against filth; in the household honour as against buffoonery; in the bride beauty as against ugliness [Col. 0959D].

He first says concerning the fragrance of the garments: “Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia from your garments.” He adds concerning the brightness of the houses: “From ivory houses.” He then states concerning the honour of the household: “Daughters of kings delighted you in your honour.” He concludes concerning the bride’s beauty: “The queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment.”

Myrrh, a bitter spice which drives away worms and preserves from decay, signifies mortification of the flesh, which excludes the worms of fleshly desires and guards against the fullness of spiritual vices. Stacte, called *aromaca* [Col. 0960A] [Note: [Col. 0959] Baruch 3:36 and 38; perhaps *aromatica* should be read], which relieves swellings and restrains inflations, signifies humility, which drives out swelling of heart and empties the inflation of mind. Cassia, called *fistula*, growing in moisture and cleansing from heat, signifies faith, which grows in the water of baptism and cleanses from the heat of sin.

The garments of Christ are all the faithful, to whom the Apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” [Note: [Col. 0959] Marginal note: The Bridegroom is praised from his garments]. And of them the Psalmist says: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends to the hem of the garment” [Note: [Col. 0959] Psalm 132:2]. From these garments breathe forth the three virtues that give fragrance, of which the Apostle says: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God in every place” [Note: [Col. 0959] Galatians 3:27]. This is that fragrance of garments which Isaac perceived when he blessed and said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed.”

These three spices distinguish the three orders of faithful persons in the Church: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, prelates, continent persons, and married persons. For stacte, that is humility, ought to belong to prelates, according to the saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” [Note: [Col. 0959] 2 Corinthians 2:15]; and: “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as the servant” [Note: [Col. 0959] Genesis 27:27], because “whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0959] Ecclesiasticus 3:20]. Myrrh, that is, mortification of the flesh, belongs to continent persons, according to the saying: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, and concupiscence” [Note: [Col. 0959] Luke 22:26]. And, “If you mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live” [Note: [Col. 0959] Matthew 23:12 and Luke 14:11, and elsewhere]. For “the flesh lusts against the spirit [Col. 0960C], and the spirit against the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0959] Colossians 3:5].

Cassia, that is faith, befits married persons, according to the saying: “The heart of her husband trusts in her” [Note: [Col. 0959] Romans 8:13]. For there are also three goods of marriage: faith, offspring, and sacrament. Faith, so that, on account of the lawful use of a wife, they may in no way defile themselves with another man or woman.

It is as though he said: O King, you alone received the fullness of anointing, because you were anointed with the oil of gladness above your companions; but the rest received a portion of the fullness, because myrrh, stacte, and cassia—that is, mortification of the flesh, humility, and faith—breathe forth from your garments, that is, from your faithful. They breathe not falsely but truly, because they breathe from ivory houses, that is, from pure hearts. For ivory is cold and shining: because it is cold, it signifies chastity; because it shines, it signifies purity [Col. 0960D]. Therefore an ivory house is a clean and pure heart, concerning which the Prophet says: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” [Note: [Col. 0959] Proverbs 31:11].

But because the feathers of the ostrich resemble the feathers of the heron, lest Satan’s angel transform himself into an angel of light [Note: [Col. 0959] Psalm 100:2], when he had said that myrrh, stacte, and cassia breathe forth from your garments, he added “from ivory houses,” so that those virtues might be understood as not feigned but true: that is, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0959] Job 39:18]. Or, according to another reading: “from ivory steps” [Col. 0961A], that is, from pure works, by which, as by certain steps, one ascends from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion [Note: [Col. 0961] 2 Corinthians 11:14]. These steps are differences of merits, concerning which elsewhere it is written: “God shall be known in her steps, when he receives her” [Note: [Col. 0961] 1 Timothy 1:5; Psalm 83:8].

[Note: [Col. 0961] Psalm 47:4.]

“From these”—the fragrances of the virtues—“daughters of kings delighted you,” offering incense worthy as an odour of sweetness to the Most High. [Note: [Col. 0961] In the Vulgate the reading is: “houses.”]

It is as though he said: You have a delightful household, because “they delighted you”; a noble household, because they are “daughters of kings”; an honourable household, because “they delighted you in your honour.” Such a household, then, befits so great a king.

“Daughters of kings” may be understood as daughters either of carnal or of spiritual kings. Of carnal kings: as certain virgin queens, who, scorning earthly kingdoms, delighted the heavenly King with the fragrance of virtues. Of spiritual kings: as all apostolic men, who are called daughters of kings not because of the frailty of their sex, but because of the conjugal affection which they conceive from Christ [Col. 0961B].

The added words, “in your honour,” can be understood in two ways. Either they are joined with the verb: “they delighted you in your honour,” as seeking not their own honour but yours, bearing the mortification of the cross in their own body for the honour of your name [Note: [Col. 0961] Marginal note: The Bridegroom is praised from his household].

Or they are joined with the noun: “daughters of kings in your honour”; that is, those whom the Apostles begot not in their own honour but in yours, because they are called neither Petrines from Peter nor Paulines from Paul, but Christians from Christ. This was provided for by the ancient law, which decreed: “If his brother should die without offspring, his brother, or another near kinsman, shall take his wife, in order to raise up offspring not for himself but for his brother; and the child born shall bear the name of the dead man” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ecclesiasticus 45:20].

This applies spiritually to Christ, who according to the Apostle [Col. 0961C] is “the firstborn among many brethren” [Note: [Col. 0961] 2 Corinthians 4:10], concerning whom he himself says in the Psalm: “I will declare your name to my brethren” [Note: [Col. 0961] Deuteronomy 25:5]. Likewise in the Gospel: “Go and tell my brethren,” because he died without offspring: for while hanging on the Cross he conceived scarcely one thief. “I am alone,” he says, “until I pass over” [Note: [Col. 0961] Psalm 21:23]. And: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people unbelieving and contradicting me” [Note: [Col. 0961] John 20:17].

But the brother who takes his wife raises up offspring for him: that is, the apostolic order, which undertook to govern Christ’s bride, namely the holy Church. It is not the bridegroom but the bridegroom’s friend, according to the saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the bridegroom’s friend stands and rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice” [Note: [Col. 0961] Psalm 140:10]. Through its preaching a multitude of Gentiles entered the faith; and it bears the name of the dead, because the convert to the faith receives the name of the crucified one, so that they are called Christians from Christ [Col. 0961D].

[Note: [Col. 0961] Isaiah 65:2 and Romans 10:21.]

“The queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment, surrounded with variety.” Two things are commended in the bride: dignity and adornment. In dignity, position and place, because “the queen stood at your right hand.” In adornment, preciousness and variety, because she stood “in a gilded garment, surrounded with variety” [Col. 0962A].

Therefore the queen—that is, the Church, because under you she rules and reigns—stood, not bent by fear but made upright by love, because perfect charity casts fear out [Note: [Col. 0961] John 3:29]; at your right hand, not at the left as the goats, but at the right as the lambs [Note: [Col. 0961] Marginal note: The Bridegroom is praised from the Bride]: that is, among spiritual and eternal things—among these by reality, among those by sight. “In a gilded garment,” that is, in good works informed by charity, concerning which elsewhere it is written: “Let your garments be white at all times,” that is, let your works be clean [Note: [Col. 0961] 1 John 4:18]. For gold signifies charity, because as gold surpasses all metals, so charity excels all virtues [Col. 0962B], according to the saying: “The greatest of these is charity” [Note: [Col. 0961] Matthew 25:33].

By a gilded rather than golden garment, therefore, are understood works—not charity itself, but works informed by charity—since, according to the Apostle, faith works through love [Note: [Col. 0961] Ecclesiastes 9:8]. The queen, I say, is “surrounded,” that is, adorned, with a variety of virtues: not merely with works but with virtues; diverse but not opposed, various but not divergent. For all virtues support one another, so that none can be possessed without the others; if one string of virtues is lacking, the spiritual harmony is discordant. Hence the curtains of the Tabernacle and the priestly garments were woven from four precious colours, not only with embroidered work but with *polymitum*, that is, variegated work [Note: [Col. 0961] 1 Corinthians 13:13; Galatians 5:6].

[Col. 0962C] “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father’s house” [Note: [Col. 0961] Exodus 26:1]. At this wedding feast the five senses are spiritually refreshed. Sight, in what is said: “Attend and see.” Hearing, in what is said: “Incline your ear and hear.” Smell, in what is said: “Myrrh, stacte, and cassia.” Taste, in what is said: “My heart has uttered a good word.” Touch, in what is said: “The reed of a scribe writing swiftly.”

Therefore, as the Prophet is about to praise the Queen, he first gives an exhortation, admonishing her to understanding when he says, “Hear, daughter, and see”; to obedience when he adds, “Incline your ear”; and to steadfastness when he continues, “Forget your people and your father’s house.” The order is fitting, and the fitness well ordered: first, that she may understand truth; then obey truth; finally persevere in truth [Col. 0962D]. Thus, that she may believe, let her understand; that she may act, let her obey; that she may be perfected, let her persevere. For “without faith it is impossible to please God” [Note: [Col. 0961] Ibid. 28:6]. But “faith without works is dead.” And “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0961] Hebrews 11:6].

[Note: [Col. 0961] Marginal note: Exhortation to the Bride.]

The Prophet, as one of the Fathers, addresses the Bride newly led in, as though she were grieving and sighing for the house she had left and the people she had forsaken. It is as if he said: [Col. 0963A] “Hear, daughter, the choirs of singers; see the celebrations of those singing psalms, to which incline your ear so that you may put aside grief. And forget your people, whom you have left, because you shall find a better people. For all the rich among the people shall entreat your countenance. And forget your people and your father’s house, from which you came out, because you shall enter a better house: for you shall be brought into the king’s temple.”

If you do this, “the King shall desire your beauty, because he is your Lord God.” You therefore, daughter—that is, Church, whom I conceived by catechizing and bore by baptizing—hear the prophecies and see them fulfilled; or hear the Gospel and see God: in the present through faith, in the future through sight. And incline your ear, so that you may both hear visibly and obey willingly. And thus forget your people, that is, idolatries [Col. 0963B], and your father’s house, namely the manner of life of the Devil. It is as if he said: Forget Babylon, because you have come to Jerusalem; forget Zebulun, because you have received Jesus. Thus it had been commanded to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I shall show you” [Note: [Col. 0961] Hebrews 11:6], that you may abandon those to whom the Lord said: “You are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0963] James 2:26].

[Note: [Col. 0963] Matthew 10:22.]

“And the king shall desire your beauty, because he is your Lord God. And the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts.” Above he admonished her whom he was to praise; now he praises her whom he has admonished. Just as he had praised the Bridegroom in four ways, so he praises the Bride fourfold: from beauty and glory, from maidens [Col. 0963C] and sons. From beauty when he says: “The king shall desire your comeliness.” From glory when he adds: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” From maidens when he states: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her.” From sons when he concludes: “Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers.”

It is as though he said: Forget your people and your father’s house, because the king—that is, Christ—has desired your beauty, that is, has accepted the beauty of virtues which he made in you without you. I say, the King, not such as your former father, the devil, but your Lord God: God, because he is to be revered; yours, because he is to be loved. God, that is, Creator; Lord, that is, Redeemer; your God, because he redeemed you with his own blood—he who by creating gave you nature, and by redeeming bestowed grace.

So great and such a one is he that the daughters of Tyre shall worship [Col. 0963D] him with gifts: that is, with rites, vows, and alms. Tyre is interpreted “narrowness”; its daughters are the Gentiles, hemmed in by the narrow straits of sins. Hence the Canaanite woman, who came out from those borders, bearing the type of the Gentile Church, came and worshipped [Note: [Col. 0963] Genesis 12:1].

Because you have so great and such a husband, therefore all the rich among the people—that is, the wise and noble of this age, princes and philosophers—will entreat your countenance, that is, your kindness, for themselves, because now converted they venerate the Church. Or “the rich among the people” are understood as the Jews, who formerly [Col. 0964A] possessed the Temple and priesthood, the riches of law and prophecy. For just as, before the Saviour’s coming, whoever from Tyre—that is, from the Gentile people—wished to become proselytes entreated Israel to introduce them through themselves into the Temple, so after the Saviour’s coming, whoever from Israel—that is, from the Jewish people—wish to become Christians will entreat the Church to receive them to baptism, so that they may find in the Church the salvation which they had lost in Judaea. By “countenance” kindness is signified, according to the saying: “May he make his face shine upon us, and have mercy upon us” [Note: [Col. 0963] John 8:44].

[The supplied source ends here.]

[Note: [Col. 0963] Margin: The Bride is praised for her beauty.] “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; clothed round about in golden fringes, she is arrayed in diversity.”

The one whom he had foretold as queen he calls the king’s daughter; Christ regenerates her whom he espouses. [Col. 0964B] He therefore praises the Bride for her glory, which he commends in two ways: by her inward adornment and by her outward adornment. The inward adornment is the brightness of conscience. The outward adornment is the splendour of teaching. Concerning the inward adornment he first says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” that is, in conscience, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: [Note: [Col. 0963] Matt. 15:22 and 25.] “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.” Hence: “Let him who glories [Note: [Col. 0963] Ps. 66:2.] glory in the Lord.” Certainly, those who shine outwardly and are foul within are like [Note: [Col. 0963] Margin: He praises the Bride for glory.] whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but within are full of dead men’s bones and every kind of uncleanness.

Concerning the outward adornment he adds: “In golden fringes,” that is, they are adorned with illustrious teachings. These are the golden bells [Col. 0964C] which hung [Note: [Col. 0963] 2 Cor. 1:12.] from the violet-blue tunic. For by gold wisdom is signified, because, just as gold excels all metals, so wisdom surpasses all gifts. “The spirit of wisdom and understanding,” he says, “shall rest upon him,” etc. Therefore he says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold”; but “all her glory,” that is, the glory of the king’s daughter, “is within,” that is, in conscience. For it is not [Note: [Col. 0963] Matt. 23:27.] he who is openly a Jew, nor that which is openly circumcision in the flesh; but he who is a Jew in secret, and circumcision is of the heart, in spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from men but from God.

Her adornment, however, is not only inward, in conscience, but also outward, in teaching.
