For “in golden fringes,” that is, in exceedingly bright teachings which shine with the light of wisdom, [Col. 0964D] she is “arrayed round about,” that is, adorned on every side with a diversity of tongues, according to that saying: [Note: [Col. 0963] Exod. 28:33.] “They spoke in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.” For they are greatly adorned by the gold of wisdom and the silver of eloquence. Hence the Bridegroom says to the Bride in the Song of Songs: [Note: [Col. 0963] Isa. 11:2.] “We will make for you chains of gold, inlaid with silver.” By gold wisdom is signified; by silver, eloquence.

For of wisdom it is written: [Note: [Col. 0963] Rom. 2:28 ff.] “You shall make a table of shittim wood . . . and you shall overlay it with the purest gold.” Of eloquence, however, we read: [Note: [Col. 0963] Acts 2:4.] “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, [Col. 0965A] silver tried by fire.” Aptly, therefore, by the chains of gold are signified the flowers of wisdom with which the neck and breast of the Church—that is, the preachers and teachers of the Church—are adorned. “Studded,” that is, distinguished and varied with silver, namely eloquence, so that, according to the diversity of subject or person, the style and character of speech may vary. Thus he says: [Note: [Col. 0965] Ch. 1:10.] “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” “Among you [Note: [Col. 0965] Exod. 25:23 ff.] I judged that I knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” And again: [Note: [Col. 0965] Ps. 11:7.] “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal persons. As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.”

But if by the Church’s garment individual believers are understood, according to what is said to her by the Lord through the Prophet: [Note: [Col. 0965] 1 Cor. 2:6.] “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with [Col. 0965B] an ornament,” then by the fringe, which is the outermost part of a garment, the last believers ought to be understood—those who will be at the end of the age. Thus the sense is: the queen will be surrounded by a diversity of virtues “in golden fringes,” that is, in the final saints, who will be golden—that is, perfect—like gold [Note: [Col. 0965] Same chapter, v. 2.] which is tried by fire.

[Note: [Col. 0965] In the same Epistle, ch. 3, v. 1 ff.] “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be presented to you. They shall be presented in gladness and exultation; they shall be brought into the temple of the king.”

When a girl is led from her father’s house to the house of her bridegroom, she is accustomed to grieve for the relatives and acquaintances whom she leaves behind. Therefore she is told: “Forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty.” When the bride approaches, all are accustomed to rise [Col. 0965C] and bow humbly; therefore it is said: “The daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts; all the rich among the people shall entreat your countenance.” A bride is accustomed to proceed adorned in precious garments and varied clothing; therefore it is said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; clothed round about in golden fringes, she is arrayed in diversity.” She is accustomed to bring with her bridesmaids—not strangers, but relatives; therefore it is said: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her, her companions.” They are accustomed to be conducted festively with hymns and songs; therefore it is said: “They shall be brought to you in gladness and exultation.” They are accustomed to be brought into a temple for the consecration of the marriage; therefore it is said: “They shall be brought into the temple of the king.”

Although there is one universal Church, of which it is said: [Note: [Col. 0965] Isa. 49:18.] “My dove is one, [Col. 0965D] my perfect one,” nevertheless there are many different classes of believers, concerning whom it is added: [Note: [Col. 0965] 1 Pet. 1:7.] “The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her.” Therefore after that queen, who is the mother of all—that is, after the primitive Church—virgins shall be brought and companions presented, because virgins more easily deserve entrance to the king’s inner chamber than widows, and those who are continent more easily than married persons. For, as the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 0965] Margin: The Bride is praised by the young women.] “He who is without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord and how he may please God. But he who has a wife [Col. 0966A] is concerned with the things of the world.”

Virgins, therefore, who are chaste both in heart and in body, shall be brought to the king, namely Christ: in the present by faith, and in the future by sight. And her companions—that is, married women or widows—shall be presented to you, King Christ, in the place next after them, so that you may give to these the golden crown and to those the lesser crown. For the fruit of the former is [Note: [Col. 0965] Song 6:8.] a hundredfold, of the latter sixtyfold or thirtyfold. Yet both shall be presented in gladness of heart and exultation of body, because of the double robe.

But since [Note: [Col. 0965] Ibid.] not all virgins are prudent, and some are foolish, while the prudent alone entered the wedding feast and the door was shut, it is rightly added: “They shall be brought into the temple of the king,” that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, into the triumphant Church, when the kingdom shall come, [Col. 0966B] of which the Psalmist says: [Note: [Col. 0965] 1 Cor. 7:32 ff.] “In his temple all shall speak glory.” Into that temple, therefore, only prudent virgins shall be brought; for as the shepherd [Note: [Col. 0965] Matt. 13:8.] separates lambs from kids, he shall bring the lambs into glory and hand the kids over to punishment. But into the temple of the militant Church both prudent and foolish virgins are brought, because now grain is mixed with chaff and tares with wheat.

[Note: [Col. 0965] Matt. 25, vv. 3 and 10.] “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth.”

The Bride is praised for her sons; and her sons are commended for their greatness, because they have been born in place of fathers; for their strength, because sons have been born; [Note: [Col. 0965] Ps. 28:9.] for their loftiness, because “you shall appoint them princes”; for their breadth, because they are “over all the earth”; [Col. 0966C] for their gratitude, because they shall remember your name, O Lord; and for their duration, because this shall be “in every generation and offspring.”

Now fathers may be understood not only according to the flesh but also according to faith, as Truth itself testifies when it says: [Note: [Col. 0965] Matt. 25:32 ff.] “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.” The fathers of the Church according to the flesh were idolaters, in whose place Christians have been born. The fathers according to faith were formerly the Prophets, in whose place the Apostles were finally born. In place of the Apostles bishops are born daily, whom the Church appoints princes over all the earth.

Although it may be understood differently: “Sons have been born in place of fathers”; the sons whom you beget, you establish as fathers for yourself when you make disciples into teachers. Yet it was not the Bride but the Bridegroom who appointed the Apostles princes over the earth. After [Col. 0966D] the Resurrection he breathed upon them and said: [Note: [Col. 0965] Margin: The Bride is praised for her sons.] “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained. Go [Note: [Col. 0965] Here something seems to be missing, unless it is interpreted thus: Sons were born like their fathers (strong men), kings.] into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned.”

But what is said—“You shall appoint them princes over all the earth”—may be referred to both: to the Bride, of whom it was said before, “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you”; and to the Bridegroom, concerning whom it is added, “They shall remember [Col. 0967A] your name, O Lord.” Of these princes it is read elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0967] John 8:39.] “The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham.” “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their rule has been greatly strengthened.” [Note: [Col. 0967] John 20:22 ff.]

[Note: [Col. 0967] Mark 16:15 ff.] This rule, moreover, does not confer lordship but grants ministry, in accordance with what the Lord says to the Apostles: [Note: [Col. 0967] Ps. 46:10.] “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not to be so; rather, let the greater among you be as the younger, and the leader as one who serves.” And Peter, the teacher of the Apostles, says: [Note: [Col. 0967] Ps. 138:17.] “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock.”

“They shall remember your name, O Lord, in every generation and offspring.” As though he said: they shall not be ungrateful for the benefit received, because they shall remember your name, [Col. 0967B] O Lord, not merely somewhere, but everywhere; because in every generation and offspring they shall not forget the office entrusted to them. Therefore the peoples shall confess you, not only once but always, because it shall be for ever and ever.

Formerly God was known [Note: [Col. 0967] Margin: On spiritual rule.] in Judaea, and his name was great in Israel; but the Apostles and apostolic men shall remember your name, O Lord, in every generation: in the generation of the Jews and among the offspring of the Gentiles; for [Col. 0968A] “their sound has gone out into all [Note: [Col. 0967] Luke 22:25 ff.] the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Or “in every generation and offspring” means through all successors, as they preach your great and glorious name, which has been invoked over them.

The Apostle Peter explained this name to the rulers and elders of the Jews: “Let it be known,” he said, [Note: [Col. 0967] 1 Pet. 5:3. This refers to those words of Luke 22:32: ‘And when you have at last turned, strengthen your brethren.’ Moreover, Innocent here most clearly declares Peter to be the teacher of the Apostles.] “to all of you that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth . . . this man stands before you whole . . . For no other name has been given under heaven to men in which we must be saved.”

“Therefore the peoples shall confess you for ever and ever.” As though he said: because the princes shall remember your name, O Lord, in every generation and offspring, therefore the Christian peoples, imitating their rulers, shall confess you—that is, praise you. For [Col. 0968B] what is done by superiors is readily drawn by inferiors into imitation. “For ever and ever,” that is, through all time and through eternity itself. Yet “for ever” is placed first on account of its dignity, and “age” is placed after it on account of its dignity. [Note: [Col. 0967] Ps. 75:2.] Or one expression explains the other: “for ever and ever,” that is, in the future which follows the present. Blessed, therefore, are [Note: [Col. 0967] Ps. 18:5.] those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you.

[Col. 0967] Here ends the book *On the Fourfold Character of the Nuptials of the Lord*, by Pope Innocent III.

## APPENDIX OF DOUBTFUL WORKS

[Col. 0967]

## COMMENTARY ON THE SEVEN PENITENTIAL PSALMS

(*Works of Innocent III*, Cologne edition, 1575, folio, p. 208.) (G)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0967C] Lest, amid the manifold occupations and pressing anxieties which I suffer beyond my strength, not only from the burden of government but also from the evil of the times, I should be, as it were, wholly swallowed up by the deep, I gladly steal a few little hours for myself in which I may recall and bring back the spirit to itself, lest it be altogether divided from and alienated from itself, and may meditate on something in the law of the Lord—which, by the inspiration of him whose [Col. 0968C] Spirit blows where it wills (John 3), may further this very end—so that I may not always be handed over to others and never restored to myself.

For even the only-begotten Word of the Father did not so descend from the Father as not to remain with the Father, as he himself testifies: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (ibid.). Nor do rivers so flow out from the sea that they do not return to the sea. For, according to Solomon’s saying, [Col. 0969A] “to the place from which rivers go forth, they return” (Eccles. 1).

But because, just as one who touches pitch is defiled by it (Ecclus. 13), so from the occupations and anxieties of this age a grave fault is often contracted, which certainly ought to be expiated through serious repentance, I recently turned my eyes to the Psalmist, who has treated the power of repentance more fully and perfectly, especially in the seven penitential Psalms, inspired by the sevenfold gift. Thus, entering the sanctuary with him, I may understand the last things, if perhaps the key of David, who shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts (Isa. 22; Rev. 3), may deign to open them; so that, investigating human misery and divine mercy in them with humbled spirit and contrite heart, I may flee from the torrent [Col. 0969B] of human headlong ruin to the fountain of divine propitiation. And may I, under the teaching of him who teaches man knowledge (Isa. 28), be able both to understand and to expound them in such a way as ought and can contribute to the glory of his name, to the salvation of my soul, and also to the benefit not only of the reader but of the hearer—although I do not fail to know that, according to the saying of the Wise Man, wisdom ought to be written in a time of leisure, and that one diminished in activity acquires it (Ecclus. 38). Yet in this poor little meal—or rather, poor little supper—I have resolved to serve not the sweetness of wisdom but the bitterness of repentance.

Although there are many penitential Psalms, nevertheless, by reason of mystery only seven have been selected from the many and are called penitential by a special designation; just as, although many wrote [Col. 0969C] gospels, only four out of the many have been received by the grace of the sacrament and are specially called Evangelists.

For the number seven is sacred because of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Isaiah enumerates when he says: “Resting upon him shall be the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). Hence: “Wisdom has built herself a house and hewn out seven columns” (Prov. 9). Thus we read that there were seven lamps on one lampstand (Exod. 25), seven eyes in one stone (Zech. 3), and likewise seven oxen seen coming up from one river, and seven ears of grain sprouting on [Col. 0969D] one stalk (Gen. 41); seven seals likewise in one book (Rev. 5), and seven baskets filled with fragments (Matt. 15), and seven trumpets, whose use was in the jubilee (Josh. 6). Job had seven sons, who held feasts with their sisters on successive days (Job 1); and the Apostles chose seven men full of the Holy Spirit as deacons (Acts 6).

John too, writing to seven Churches, declares that he saw in the midst of seven golden lampstands one like the Son of Man, clothed in a long robe, holding seven stars in his right hand, which are the angels of the seven Churches (Rev. 1); and in the midst of the throne a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth (Rev. 5).

[Col. 0970A] The Lord’s Prayer likewise contains seven petitions: three pertaining to the future life, three pertaining to the present life, and the middle one pertaining to both (Matt. 6). Similarly, seven beatitudes are distinguished in the Lord’s sermon (Matt. 5). For the eighth beatitude returns to the beginning, just as the eighth day returns to the beginning. Moreover, the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh month, and the seventh year were sacred [variant: festal] under the Law, especially the solemnity of Pentecost, which followed after the seventh set of seven days; and after the seventh set of seven years came the observance of the jubilee.

For seven is the special number of universality, rest, perfection, and sanctification, because all time unfolds and repeats itself in seven days. Hence the Lord says: [Col. 0970B] “I do not say to you seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18), that is, always; and: “On the seventh day the Lord rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2)—the very day on which Christ rested in the tomb.

And the complete human being is perfected from the parts of seven: by three with respect to the soul, because of the soul’s three natural powers; and by four with respect to the body, because of the four elements of the body. This number, first among units, contains in itself the first perfect number, produced by the sum of its parts; and, multiplied only by the other of its parts, it generates from itself the first perfect number among tens. Thus it contains first in itself simple perfection, and alone generates from itself double perfection, as has been said, general [variant: numerical] perfection. Concerning the sanctification of this number the Law commands: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20).

Hence God cast seven nations out of the land of promise (Deut. 7), and expelled seven demons from Mary (Mark 16), signifying the casting out of vices and expulsion of sins by which the soul is sanctified when sevenfold grace is infused. For the number seven signifies not only the seven principal gifts of the Holy Spirit but also the three theological and four principal virtues; the two coins of the innkeeper (Luke 10); the five bodily senses; one baptism; and six works of mercy, all of which together effect perfect sanctification.

This number, therefore, [Col. 0970D] is composed not only of four and three, but also of five and two, and likewise of six and one, so that the human being, made perfect in soul and body, having doubled the two and five talents, may by the exercise of mercy pass from labour to rest, according to what Truth says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her” (ibid.). The Psalmist himself longed for this, saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26).

Hence the calculation of seven reaches twenty-eight, because sevenfold grace, with the coin doubled in the double robe which shall be given to those who labour in the vineyard, leads to the eighth day [Col. 0971A] of blessed resurrection, in which God shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15), the fruit, reward, and prize of each person. The eighth day of the Lord’s resurrection prefigured this. Hence it is not unfittingly written: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. 11), leaving aside, since it does not bear upon this matter, what is said through the Prophet: “We shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight princes” (Mic. 5). And according to Ezekiel’s vision, the ascent to the outer court had seven steps, and the ascent to the inner court had eight steps (Ezek. 40). Deep and fruitful, marvellous and magnificent, therefore, are the mysteries of seven, which are commended not only by theologians but also by philosophers.

But for the commendation of the seven penitential [Col. 0971B] Psalms these matters suffice; some of them are touched upon in the exposition of the Psalms themselves. Add this: the penitential Psalms are comprised in the number seven so that we may erase by repentance under the same number the sins which we commit by transgression under that number.

For there are seven principal vices from which all sins arise: namely, vain glory, anger, envy, sloth, avarice, gluttony, and lust. They are signified by the seven peoples whom God drove from the land of promise: namely, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite (Deut. 7); and also by the seven more wicked spirits whom the unclean spirit brought so that they might enter to dwell in the house swept clean and decorated (Luke 11). Thus, just as the stains [Col. 0971C] of crimes are contracted during the seven-day week of this age, so they are washed away by repentance through these seven Psalms, which are to be recited continually before the Lord with a contrite and humbled spirit.

Of these seven Psalms, four are alike and three unlike in their beginnings, in respect of figures and words. They are arranged in such a way that one of the unlike Psalms always stands between two alike ones, and one of the alike Psalms is placed between two unlike ones. The alike ones are the first, third, fifth, and seventh; the unlike ones are the second, fourth, and sixth.

Of the four alike Psalms, the first two are wholly alike to each other; likewise the last two, in respect of figures and words, [Col. 0971D] because they agree in one complete sentence. But the first two and the last two are partly alike in the matters mentioned, because they agree only in the first word. Yet in the first pair the penitent asks that wrath be turned away, while in the last pair he asks that prayer be heard.

Of the three unlike Psalms, two are wholly unlike each other: namely, the first, which speaks of the blessedness of grace, and the last, which speaks from the depth of misery. The middle one, however, differs from all the rest in figures and words, but agrees with all in purpose and sense, because it speaks of guilt to be removed and mercy to be bestowed—the purposes for which all penitential Psalms have been composed and established. Therefore, just as it occupies the middle place among them all, so it is also in meaning.

That [Col. 0972A] one of the unlike Psalms is placed between two alike ones, and one of the alike ones is placed between two unlike ones, plainly signifies this: since penitential Psalms belong only to those on the way, nothing on the way is so perfect that some imperfection does not intervene; nor is anything so evil that some good does not occur within it. Thus neither presumption is granted to the perfect nor despair to the wicked. This is especially fitting and necessary for the penitent: that he may neither presume too much upon mercy by hoping nor despair too much of justice by fearing, but may be ground between the upper and lower millstone of the spirit [variant: spiritually].

Now among all kinds of prayer, after the Lord’s Prayer psalmody holds the first place. If anyone investigates the individual Psalms carefully, he will find in them a perfect form of praying by which the grace of divine propitiation may be merited. Therefore I must first set before the mind certain circumstances of prayer, so that, [Col. 0972B] being prepared beforehand, the soul may more easily attain the power of prayer in the Psalms themselves.

It should be noted, therefore, that Christ prays; angels pray; demons pray; human beings pray; the good pray; the wicked pray; the living pray; the dead pray; they pray for themselves and for others. Yet among these there is a great and manifold difference.

For whether Christ prays for himself or for others, he is always heard in all things. He prayed for himself on the cross: “Father,” he said, “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 18); and immediately he was heard, because, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit. He prayed [Col. 0972C] for others: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid.); and he was heard for all for whom he prayed, as elsewhere he says: “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me. But I knew that you always hear me” (John 11).

He prayed for himself and was heard; hence the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2). He prayed for others and likewise was heard. For when he had said to the Father: “Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are one” (John 17), he immediately added: “And the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one as we are” (ibid.). Behold, the same one prays and the same one hears. [Col. 0972D] He prays as man; he hears as God.

Thus it must rightly be understood of the Holy Spirit that the Apostle says: “The Spirit himself makes petition for you with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8), because he causes us to make petition. Indeed, we have as advocate with the Father Jesus Christ, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2); according to the Apostle, he always intercedes for us with the Father (Rom. 8), living always to intercede for us (Heb. 7). For, as the same Apostle says, “in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who could save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5).

Did he not pray that the cup might pass from him when he said: “Abba, Father, if it is possible, take this cup from [Col. 0973A] me” (Mark 14)? Yet, even if he said this not according to the will of prayer but according to the will of sensibility, it can nevertheless be understood that he was heard in this: the cup passed from him to others, as he had said to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am to drink?” They say to him, “We can.” He says to them: “Indeed, you shall drink my cup” (Matt. 20), etc.

Or rather, as he prayed, so he was heard. For he prayed not simply but conditionally, saying: “Father, if you will, take this cup from me” (Luke 22). “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). For he desired that, if it could be done, that hour might pass; hence he added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.); “not my will but yours be done.” And thus he obtained what he prayed for.

[Col. 0973B] Likewise angels pray, and are always heard by God; but for others they offer the aid of prayers, while for themselves they render thanksgivings. An angel prayed, saying: “Lord God of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry? This is now the seventieth year.” And the Lord answered the angel good words, consoling words: “I shall return,” he said, “to Jerusalem in mercy; my house shall be built in it, says the Lord of hosts, and a measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem” (Zech. 1).

The angels themselves also offer the prayers of the faithful to God, as the angel Raphael said to Tobias: “When you prayed with tears, I offered your prayer to the Lord” (Tob. 12). And in the Apocalypse: “An angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer in [Col. 0973C] his hand; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer it from the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the presence of God. And the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints ascended from the hand of the angel before God” (Rev. 8).

Angels are said to offer the prayers of the faithful to God in order to show that he regards them favourably; or in order that, concerning them, they may discover the divine good pleasure, which they sometimes make known to human beings. Hence the angel says to Cornelius: “Your prayers and your alms have risen in remembrance before God” (Acts 10). But for themselves they render thanksgiving, as it is written: “There was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2). And elsewhere: “Now have come salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, and they overcame him through the blood of the Lamb; therefore rejoice, O heavens, [Col. 0973D] and you who dwell in them” (Rev. 12).

Demons pray indeed for themselves, not for others but against others; and sometimes they are heard and sometimes not heard. They are heard, as in: “They begged him to permit them to enter the swine, and he permitted them. Therefore the demons came out from the man and entered the swine” (Luke 8; Matt. 8; Mark 5). They are not heard, as there: “Be silent, unclean spirit, and come out of him”—although he had first cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Leave us alone! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? [Col. 0974A] I know that you are the Holy One of God” (Mark 1; Luke 4).

They also pray against others, and sometimes are heard, as there: “Put forth your hand and touch his flesh and his bone, and then you will see that he will bless you to your face.” Therefore the Lord said to Satan: “Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life” (Job 2). At times they pray against others and are not heard, as there: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he may sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at last turned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

Moreover, the good who have died are heard when they pray, both for themselves and for others. Hence in the Apocalypse: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those slain for the word of God, and they cried out in a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, [Col. 0974B] holy and living, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” And they were told to rest a little while longer, until their fellow servants and brothers who were to be slain, as they also had been, should be completed (Rev. 6).

Likewise, in the Second Book of Maccabees: “This is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel. This is he who prays much for the people and for the whole holy city: Jeremiah, the prophet of God.” He saw him extending his right hand and giving Judas a golden sword, saying: “Receive the holy sword, a gift from God, by which you shall overthrow the adversaries of my people Israel” (2 Macc. 15).

What, then, is meant by what is written: “Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people” (Jer. 15)? But this is said hypothetically—that is, even if they stood—just as it is said elsewhere: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can those from there cross over to us” (Luke 16), that is, even if they wished, they could not.

[Col. 0974C] The wicked who have already died do pray, but are not heard, neither for themselves nor for others. Hence the rich man who died and was buried in hell cried out, saying: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.” And he said to him: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, whereas you are tormented.”

Again he said: “I beg you, therefore, Father, [Col. 0974D] to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torments.” And Abraham said to him: “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them” (Luke 16).

Moreover, good people living pray for themselves, pray for others, and pray against others; and sometimes they are heard and sometimes they are not. Peter prayed for himself when, beginning to sink, he cried out, saying: “Lord, save me,” and he deserved to be heard; for Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him, saying: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14).

Paul too prayed three times that the Lord might remove from him the thorn of the flesh, and the Lord said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12). At times [Col. 0975A] they likewise pray against others and for others, and are heard by God. Hence James says: “Elijah was a man subject to suffering like ourselves, and in prayer he prayed that it might not rain upon the earth; and it did not rain for three years and six months. Again he prayed, and heaven gave rain and the earth gave its fruit” (James 5; 3 Kings 17 and 18).

At other times they pray for others and are not heard. Hence it was said to Jeremiah (chs. 7, 11, and 14): “Do not pray for this people.” Therefore he himself said: “When I cry out and plead, he has shut out my prayer” (Lam. 3). And to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (1 Kings 16). At times they also pray against others and are not heard, as James and John said: “Lord, do you wish us to command fire [Col. 0975B] to come down from heaven and consume them?” And, turning, he rebuked them, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are” (Luke 9).

Likewise, evil persons while living are sometimes heard on their own behalf, as was the Pharisee who asked Jesus to eat with him; and Jesus entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table (Luke 7). So too the prodigal son was heard, when he said: “Father, give me the portion of the estate that falls to me,” and he divided his property among them (Luke 15). For the saying of the man born blind in the Gospel, “We know that God does not hear sinners” (John 9), is rejected by all as false. Such persons are also sometimes heard on behalf of others, as the elders of the Jews, who asked Jesus for the centurion’s servant, saying: “He is worthy that you should grant him this; for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us” [Col. 0975C]. Jesus, moreover, went with them. And those who had been sent, returning home, found the servant who had been ill restored to health (Luke 7). Finally, evil persons sometimes pray for themselves and are not heard by God, as Antiochus, of whom it is written: “That wicked man prayed to the Lord, from whom he would not obtain mercy” (2 Maccabees 9), not only in this life but also in the life to come. Hence the foolish virgins, when the door had been shut, cried: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” He answered them: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25). At times likewise evil persons praying for others are not heard, as the Lord says to certain wicked priests: “I will curse your blessings” (Malachi 2), that is, I shall not hear the prayers which you pour forth to bless the people, but shall instead curse them—that is, I shall utterly reject them as though cursed; hence: “They cried to the Lord” (Jonah 1), etc.

Moreover, sometimes the Lord hastens and hears at the beginning; sometimes he delays and hears in the middle; sometimes he postpones and hears at the end. He heard Daniel at the beginning of his prayers: “While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, Gabriel, the man flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice, and spoke to me: From the beginning of your prayers the word went forth” (Daniel 9). And elsewhere: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: ‘Here I am.’” But for a time the Lord delayed to hear certain faithful persons crying: “Come, Lord, and do not delay; forgive the sins of your people Israel.” To them the prophet replied: “If he delays, wait for him” [Col. 0976A], “for he will come and will not be late” (Habakkuk 2). Sometimes he even defers hearing until the end, as was said above: “Wait until the number of your brethren is complete” (Revelation 6). For unless the Lord sometimes deferred hearing until the end, the Psalmist would not say: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end?” (Psalm 12). And again: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us unto the end” (Psalm 43).

Prayer ought to be faithful, humble, pious, devout, attentive, brief, constant, and discerning; and prayer of this kind undoubtedly deserves to be heard. That prayer ought to be faithful is shown by Truth himself, who says: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive” (Matthew 21); for “without faith it is impossible” [Col. 0976B] “to please God” (Hebrews 12); and “the righteous lives by faith” (Romans 1). Hence the apostle James says: “If any lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, and it shall be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (James 1).

That it ought to be humble, the Wise Man declares: “The prayer of one humbling himself pierces the heavens; and until it draws near, it will not be comforted, and it will not depart until the Most High looks upon it” (Ecclesiasticus 35). Hence that publican who went up to the Temple to pray, standing at a distance, would not lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner”; according to the judgment of Truth, he went down to his house justified. “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18).

[Col. 0976C] That it ought to be pious, so as to ask for those things which pertain to the salvation of the soul, the Lord says: “Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full; for whatever you ask the Father in my name”—that is, in the name of Christ Jesus, namely in the name of the Savior, that is, what pertains to salvation—“will indeed be done for you” (John 16), if you ask for yourselves as you ought to ask; it will be done, I say, either in the present life or in the future.

That it ought to be devout, so as to give forth a sweet fragrance like incense, the Psalmist shows: “Let my prayer,” he says, “be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140). This incense is offered as a worthy odor of sweetness, concerning which elsewhere it is written: [Col. 0976D] “The smoke of the incense from the prayers of the saints rose up before the Lord” (Revelation 8). Care must therefore be taken lest “dead flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Ecclesiastes 10), that is, lest intrusive thoughts take away prayer’s devotion.

That it ought to be attentive, so that it proceeds not so much from the mouth as from the heart, Scripture says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Psalm 36). “My prayer is to the God of my life,” he says, “within me” (Psalm 41). Such was the prayer of Jehoshaphat, who, as is read in Chronicles, devoted his whole self to entreating the Lord (2 Chronicles 20). Hence Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, and no voice at all was heard, as she poured out her soul before the Lord (1 Samuel 1). For it is written: [Col. 0977A] “Before prayer, prepare your soul” (Ecclesiasticus 18). Yet it is fitting that the utterance of the mouth should accompany devotion of heart; for what breath does to a coal, utterance does to devotion.

That it ought to be brief, the Lord says: “When praying, do not speak much, like the Gentiles; for they think that they are heard because of their many words” (Matthew 6). Therefore he immediately taught his disciples a short prayer, saying: “Thus shall you pray: Our Father, who art in heaven” (ibid.). Hence elsewhere it is written: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Ecclesiasticus 7), since “sin is not lacking in much speaking” (Proverbs 10). What, then, is meant by what is read—that the Lord himself, when in agony, prayed more at length? (Luke 22). And: “He spent the whole night” [Col. 0977B] “in the prayer of God” (Luke 6). But “many words” is not understood to be useless when prayer is devout; rather, many words are understood when prayer becomes wearisome through an unprofitable prolixity of speech.

That it ought to be constant, Paul says: “Pray without ceasing, brethren” (1 Thessalonians 5). In accordance with this, Truth says: “One ought always to pray and never to grow weary” (Luke 18). For, as James says, “the persevering supplication of a righteous man has great power” (James 5); indeed, “the prayer of the righteous enriches the altar” (Ecclesiasticus 35). Thus unceasing prayer was made by the Church to God for Peter, and he was freed from prison (Acts 12). Therefore the Lord commanded: “Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened” [Col. 0977C] “to you” (Luke 11). Hence the man who persisted in knocking obtained from his friend as many loaves as he needed, because of his importunity (ibid.); and the widow who troubled the unjust judge deserved through him to be delivered from her adversary (Luke 8). For prayer’s persistence has such power that it wrests from God what he had expressly denied, as is said in the Book of Judges: “I will no longer deliver you. Go and call upon the gods whom you have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of distress.” And the children of Israel said to God: “We have sinned; repay us according to whatever pleases you, only deliver us now.” He was grieved at their miseries and, by the hand of Jephthah, delivered them from the hands of the children of Ammon (Judges 10). [Col. 0977D] Hence also, although the Lord answered the Canaanite woman: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs,” nevertheless, because she did not cease to cry after him and his disciples, saying: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table,” she deserved to hear: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you wish” (Matthew 15).

That it ought to be discerning, Christ himself testifies when he says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matthew 6). Hence he taught the faithful thus, saying: “May your kingdom come. May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread.” He showed that one must ask discerningly: eternal things indeed [Col. 0978A] as reward—hence, “May your kingdom come”; spiritual things for merit—hence, “May your will be done”; temporal things for sustenance—hence, “Give us this day our daily bread.” One must likewise ask discerningly to be delivered from evils past, present, and future: of the past it is said, “Forgive us our debts”; of the present, “Deliver us from evil”; of the future, “And lead us not into temptation” (ibid.).

One who prays in this manner sometimes obtains from the Lord not only what he asks, but something else besides, and more abundantly. Thus Zechariah, when he had entered the Temple of the Lord while all the multitude of the people prayed outside at the hour of incense, heard from the angel: “Do not fear, Zechariah; behold, your prayer has been heard, and Elizabeth your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John” [Col. 0978B] (Luke 1). Hezekiah too, when he had fallen ill and heard the prophet Isaiah saying, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and shall not live,” turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord with great weeping. Immediately through the same prophet he heard: “Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I have healed you, and I shall add fifteen years to your days; I shall deliver you from the hand of the king of the Assyrians and protect this city.” A wonderful sign was also wrought: at his request, the sun returned ten degrees on the dial (Isaiah 38), just as, at Joshua’s request, the sun stood in the middle of heaven for the space of one day (Joshua 10). [Col. 0978C] So too Solomon heard from the Lord: “Because you have asked for this thing, and have not asked for riches, nor many days, nor the lives of your enemies, but have asked for wisdom to exercise judgment, behold, I have done according to your words and given you a wise and understanding heart, so that none before you has been like you, nor shall any arise after you. But I have also given you those things which you did not ask for, namely riches and glory, so that among all kings in all former days none has been like you” (2 Chronicles 1).

Prayers are sometimes unworthy because of the person, sometimes because of the cause, sometimes because of the intention, sometimes because of the manner, sometimes because of the order, and sometimes because of the end. Prayers are unworthy because of the person, [Col. 0978D] as the Lord says through Isaiah: “When you multiply prayer, I shall not hear; for your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 2). And this is so not only because of the person who prays, but also because of the person for whom prayer is made. Accordingly the Lord commanded Jeremiah: “Do not pray for this people” (Jeremiah 7). Prayers are unworthy because of the cause, as the apostle James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, namely that you may spend it upon your lusts. Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?” (Isaiah 4). Of such prayer it is said: “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108). Prayers are unworthy because of intention, such as [Col. 0979A] that of the man who said to the Lord: “Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said: “Man, who made me judge and divider over you?” And he said to them: “See to it, and beware of all covetousness” (Luke 2). Prayers are unworthy because of their manner, such as that of Simon Peter, who, when he heard that Christ must suffer and be killed, thinking unwisely and carnally said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” Hence he deserved to hear: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not savor the things that are of God” (Matthew 6). Likewise Elijah, when he asked for his own life that he might die, asked unworthily in respect of manner, because he wished to die too hastily before his time; hence he deserved not to be heard (3 Kings 19). Prayers are unworthy because of their order, such as those of the sons [Col. 0979B] of Zebedee, who, through their mother sent before them, asked for reward before merit and a crown before the contest. For when she said, “Command that these my two sons may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom,” Jesus answered them: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” They said to him: “We can.” He said to them: “You shall indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right or my left is not mine to give you, but belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matthew 20), because, as the Apostle says, “No one shall be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Timothy 2). Those prayers are unworthy because of their end which the Lord reproves when he says: “When you pray, do not pray like hypocrites, who love the foremost places in synagogues and stand praying at the corners of streets, that they may be seen [Col. 0979C] by men. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6).

Finally, there are, above all others, three things that prevent prayer from passing through to God: namely, the frying pan, the wall, and the cloud. That is, the lust of the flesh, namely lustfulness, in which the flesh is fried as in a pan; the lust of the eyes, namely avarice, in which wealth is piled up as stones in a wall; and the pride of life, namely boastfulness, which is carried about by winds like a cloud without water. Of these the apostle John says: “Whatever is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes” [Col. 0979D] “and the pride of life” (1 John 2). Of such a frying pan it is written: “And you, son of man, take for yourself an iron frying pan, and set it between yourself and the city, and set your face firmly against it” (Ezekiel 4). Of this wall it is said: “In you I shall be delivered from temptation, and in my God I shall pass over a wall” (Psalm 17). And of this cloud it is written: “You have set a cloud before yourself, lest my prayer pass through” (Lamentations 3). Or rather, the iron frying pan is hardness of mind; the earthen wall, the defense of iniquity; and the dark cloud, the mind’s obscurity. These undoubtedly do not permit prayer to reach the ears of the Lord.

Moreover, one prays with the heart, one prays with the mouth, one prays with deeds. Of prayer of the heart the Apostle says: “I shall pray with the spirit, [Col. 0980A] and I shall pray also with the mind; I shall sing with the spirit, and I shall sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14). Of prayer of the mouth the Psalmist says: “To him I cried with my mouth, and I extolled him beneath my tongue” (Psalm 65). Of prayer in deed the Wise Man declares: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it itself will pray for you” (Ecclesiasticus 29), because one who never ceases from doing good never ceases from praying.

Again, some pray lying down, some sitting, and some standing. David prayed lying down when he entreated the Lord for the little child and went apart and lay upon the earth (2 Samuel 12). Hezekiah likewise, lying in bed, turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord (Isaiah 38), who said to him: “I have heard your prayer and seen your tears; behold, I have healed you” (Exodus 17). Moses, however, prayed sitting [Col. 0980B] upon the stone which Aaron and Hur placed beneath him, when Joshua overcame Amalek. Elijah likewise, when he sat beneath a juniper tree, prayed to the Lord and asked for his life that he might die (3 Kings 10). But the publican, standing at a distance, prayed and did not dare lift his eyes to heaven (Luke 18). Judith also, standing before Holofernes’ bed, prayed to the Lord to strengthen her (Judith 13). Again, some pray with eyes and hands raised to heaven; some with knees and head bent down to the earth; some with body bowed; and some wholly prostrate. Christ prayed with eyes raised to heaven when he raised Lazarus. And when he said: “Father, glorify your Son” (John 11). Moses prayed with hands outspread when Joshua overcame Amalek (Exodus 17). [Col. 0980C] Hence the prophet says: “Let us raise our hearts with our hands to the Lord in heaven” (Lamentations 3). The Apostle prayed with bent knees, saying: “I bend my knees to God, and to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Ephesians 3). And Elijah, upon the summit of Carmel, bent down to the earth and put his face between his knees, praying the Lord to give rain upon the face of the earth; and great rain came (3 Kings 18). Elisha bowed down and prayed when he bent himself over the child and prayed to the Lord, and the child’s flesh grew warm (4 Kings 4). Elijah also stretched himself over the child and measured himself upon him, saying: “O Lord my God, I pray, let the soul of this child return into his body”; and the Lord heard Elijah’s voice (3 Kings 17). [Col. 0980D] The twenty-four elders prayed prostrate, falling before the Lamb, each holding golden lyres and bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5). And all the angels stood about the throne, the twenty-four elders, and the living creatures; and they fell before the throne upon their faces and worshiped God (Revelation 7). In those who pray lying down is signified an affection of humility, to which the remembrance of the human condition especially invites. Hence he said: “Remember, I beseech you, that you made me like clay and will reduce me to dust” (Job 10). In those who pray sitting is signified the repose of contemplation. Of this it is written that, when the Lord had given David rest from all his enemies, he entered and [Col. 0981A] sat before the Lord and said: “Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me so far? You revealed to the ear of your servant, saying: ‘I will build you a house’; therefore your servant found his heart to pray this prayer to you” (2 Samuel 7). For although in devout prayer a person speaks to God, nonetheless in it and from it he likewise tastes the sweetness of contemplation, while the devout worshiper beholds God as though present. In those who pray standing is signified the desire for the heavenly homeland, toward which the hope of the promise from above chiefly draws one; for this reason he said: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’ Our feet stood in your courts, O Jerusalem” (Psalm 21). Finally, those who pray with bent knees [Col. 0981B] but hands extended and eyes raised follow her who says in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you. We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

Moreover, following the examples of the ancients, one ought to pray three or seven times a day. For Daniel, entering his house and opening the windows of his upper chamber toward Jerusalem, three times a day bent his knees and prayed, confessing before the Lord his God, as he had been accustomed to do before (Daniel 6). Hence the Psalmist says: “At evening, morning, and noon I shall recount and declare, and he will hear my voice” (Psalm 54). He likewise said of himself: “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you for the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118). The Church still observes this number in the canonical hours: three times a day because of faith in the undivided Trinity, [Col. 0981C] and seven times through day and night because of the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, who illumines and enlightens those praying in faith by the gifts of grace. But according to the testimonies of Scripture, one ought to pray three times during the night: at its beginning, middle, and end. Of the beginning the prophet says: “Arise, give praise in the night at the beginning of your watches; pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord your God” (Lamentations 2). Of the middle the Psalmist says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Psalm 118). Of the end the prophet says: “Rise early; great is your faith” (Lamentations 3). And the Psalmist says: “In the morning my prayer shall come before you” (Psalm 87). Thus the faithful soul may remain awake through the night in prayer against the temptations of the princes of darkness, [Col. 0982A] according to the Lord’s command: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26). At every hour of prayer dawn is invoked, of which the Psalmist said: “O God, my God, from the dawn I keep watch for you” (Psalm 62). And the Wise Man declares: “The righteous will give his heart to watching at dawn, to the Lord who made him, and will pray in the presence of the Most High” (Ecclesiasticus 30). At this hour Jacob, who had wrestled with the angel all night, deserved to be blessed (Genesis 32).

Although a faithful person may pray in every place, it is nevertheless more fitting to pray in the Temple, on high, and in secret. For concerning the Temple the Lord says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matthew 21). And Solomon says: “When he comes, therefore, and prays in this place, you will hear [Col. 0982B] in heaven, O Lord, in the firmament of your dwelling-place, and will do all things for which he calls upon you” (3 Kings 8). Jesus customarily went up on high to pray; of him it is written that “he went up alone upon the mountain to pray” (Matthew 14). Therefore he commends a hidden place for prayer: “But you,” he says, “when you pray, enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (John 4). For when Christ was asked by the Samaritan woman about the place of worship, he answered: “Woman, believe me: the hour is coming when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but true worshipers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (Psalm LXLV). Thus he rejected both the error of the Samaritans, who said that there was no [Col. 0982C] place of worship except Gerizim, and that of the Jews, who maintained that there was no place for praying to God except Jerusalem. Yet God is specially to be worshiped in the Temple, according to the saying: “Worship the Lord in his holy court” (Psalm 45). One should likewise worship especially toward the east, as is written: “It is fitting to worship at the rising of the light” (Wisdom 16), so that, as we worship the Lord, the true light of righteousness may rise for us, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). For the angels of God attend the faithful worshiping in sacred basilicas, in order to offer their devout prayers to God, according to the saying: “In the presence of angels I shall sing psalms to you, O my God; I shall worship toward your holy Temple and give thanks to your name” (Psalm 137).

## [PSALM I]

[Col. 0981]

The title of the first penitential Psalm is as follows: “Unto the end: a Psalm of David for the eighth.”—Explanation of this title.

[Col. 0981D] Since all time runs its course through the repetition of seven days, by “the eighth” is understood the last day, namely that of resurrection and judgment, prefigured by the eighth day of circumcision. It is also reckoned the eighth for another reason: namely, that after the seven ages of this world there will follow an eighth age of those at rest, concurrent with the sixth age of those engaged in warfare, which began at the first coming and will endure until the last. The day of judgment is also signified by the eighth because it will follow after the two lives signified by the number seven. For as a human being has two parts, the exterior, namely the body, and the interior, namely the spirit, so there are two lives: one bodily, by which the body lives; and another spiritual, by which the soul lives from God. These two lives are signified by the number seven because of their two respective parts: the number four, which refers to the body, because of the four elements—earth, fire, air, and water—of which [Col. 0983A] the body itself is composed; and the number three, which refers to the spirit, because of its three faculties—the rational, irascible, and concupiscible—in which the spirit itself subsists. Likewise, in the human body there are four humors ordered according to the four seasons of the year, and in the spirit there are three properties through which it is likened to the undivided Trinity. Therefore after these two lives, as an eighth after the number seven, the day of judgment will follow, on which the just Judge will render to each according to merits. Hence the fearful, penitent sinner cries and prays: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury” (Psalm 6).

[Col. 0984A] The meaning of the title, therefore, is this: This Psalm, directing us unto the end—that is, Christ, who is the perfection of the faithful, in the present age indeed unto righteousness and in the future age unto the crown—is attributed to David, that is, to the person repenting of his sins, in whose person David speaks in this Psalm. It is, I say, a Psalm composed “for the eighth,” that is, in fear of the judgment which will be held in the eighth, the resurrection. In this Psalm there is a supplicatory confession, because guilt is acknowledged in it and pardon requested. Although such a confession brings a sentence of condemnation before secular judges, before God it merits a sentence of absolution.

## ELUCIDATION OF THE FIRST PENITENTIAL PSALM

[Col. 0983]

[Col. 0983B] “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger [your fury], nor chastise me in your fury [your anger]” (Psalm 6).

According to the translation used by the Roman Church, this Psalm contains nine verses, through which the penitent ascends step by step to the nine orders of angels; for there is greater joy among God’s angels over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance (Luke 15). Yet the number of ten verses, which it is known to have according to another translation, also fits the argument well, because the person who fell through offense rises through repentance, so that through him the tenth order may be restored. This Psalm also fittingly has three groups of three, because repentance ought to have three parts: contrition in the heart, [Col. 0983C] confession in the mouth, and satisfaction in deed; and each of these is subdivided into three. For in contrition the penitent ought to have fear because of punishment, sorrow because of guilt, and love because of grace. In confession, he ought to express truth concerning the deed, its number, and its manner. In satisfaction, he ought to direct prayer toward God, almsgiving toward his neighbor, and fasting toward himself. There are also nine verses in this Psalm because of the nine kinds of sins over which the penitent ought to grieve: namely, original, mortal, and venial sin. These are the serpent, the woman, and the man. The serpent—that is, concupiscence—suggests originally; the woman—that is, delight—eats venially; the man—that is, reason—consents mortally. Likewise there is sin of thought, [Col. 0983D] speech, and deed: thought in the heart, speech in the mouth, action in habitual practice. This is death in the house, death in the gate, death in the tomb. Again, there is sin of frailty, simplicity, and malice: of frailty through incapacity, of simplicity through ignorance, and of malice through envy. This is sin against the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In the first group of three, the penitent fears and prays; in the middle group, he groans and weeps; in the final group, he rejoices and desires. He fears and prays for the removal of a twofold punishment, [Col. 0984B] the healing of a twofold wound, and the taking away of a twofold delay: for eternal and temporal punishment, as he shows in the first verse, saying: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury.” As if he said more plainly: Do not rebuke me in anger by condemning me in the future, nor chastise me in fury by punishing me in the present. For bodily and spiritual affliction, as he shows in the second verse, saying: “Heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled, and my soul is exceedingly troubled.” As if he said more plainly: Heal me of bodily sickness, because my bones are troubled; of spiritual sickness, because my soul is exceedingly troubled. For delay in removing misery and conferring glory, as he shows in the third verse, saying: “And you, O Lord—how long? Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for your mercy’s sake.” As if he said more plainly: And you, O Lord, how long do you delay healing? As though to say: do not delay, but deliver my soul from present misery. Likewise: “Turn, O Lord,” as though to say: do not delay, but save me in future glory.

You have heard how the penitent, in the first group of three, fears and prays; hear how, in the second group of three, he groans and weeps. “I have labored,” he says, “in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch.” He groans and weeps because of the mind’s forgetfulness and the suppression of praise: because of the forgetfulness of mind which belongs to the reprobate in death, and because of the suppression of praise which belongs to the condemned in hell. Of these he first speaks in the fourth verse, saying: “For in death there is none who remembers you; but in hell who shall confess to you?” As if he said more plainly: Therefore I have labored in my groaning, because in death—that is, in mortal sin—there is none who remembers you, that is, who remembers your law, which he scorns by transgressing it. And therefore every night I shall wash my bed, because in hell—that is, in the abyss of despair—who shall confess to you? As though to say: absolutely no one, [Col. 0985A] because he distrusts your mercy. Or, in death—that is, in the condition of a sinner already dead—there is none who remembers you unto salvation. But in hell—that is, in the place of Gehenna’s punishment—who shall confess to you? As though to say: none unto praise. He likewise groans and weeps because his judgment for discerning is troubled and his practice in making offerings has grown old; concerning these he adds in the sixth verse: “My eye is troubled because of anger; I have grown old among all my enemies.” As if he said more plainly: My eye, namely the understanding, is troubled—that is, darkened—because of anger, which hinders reason. And I have grown old through long practice of sinning among all my enemies, that is, the vices and sins which are hostile to me.

You have heard how the penitent, in the second group of three, [Col. 0985B] groans and weeps; hear how, in the third, he rejoices and desires. He rejoices that he has been heard in three things, namely in tears, prayers, and supplications: in tears, for punishment to be removed; in prayers, for guilt to be blotted out; in supplications, for grace to be conferred. Of tears heard he first says: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” Of supplications received he adds: “The Lord has heard my entreaty.” Of prayers accepted he then says: “The Lord has received my prayer.” He desires for his enemies, out of charity, the sorrow of compunction, the blush and shame of confession, and the labor of satisfaction. The sorrow of compunction, when he said: “Let them be troubled”; the shame of confession, when he says: “Let them blush”; the labor of satisfaction, where he says: “Let them be turned back,” and this very swiftly, [Col. 0985C] so that they may be immediately delivered.

The penitent makes six petitions in this Psalm: two out of fear of punishment, namely present and future, of which he says: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury.” Again, two because of the pain of guilt, namely bodily and spiritual, of which he adds: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for all my bones are troubled. And my soul is exceedingly troubled; but you, O Lord—how long?” Again, two because of love of grace, namely grace that delivers and grace that saves, of which he continues: “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for your mercy’s sake.” In these are marked three fears: servile, initial, and filial. To each petition he gives its own reason: “Do not,” he says, “rebuke me in your anger, because in death there is none who remembers you. Nor chastise me in fury, because in hell who shall confess to you?” Again: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, because I have labored in my groaning. Heal me, O Lord, because every night I shall wash my bed, and with my tears I shall water my couch.” Likewise: “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul, because my eye is troubled because of anger. Save me for your mercy’s sake, because I have grown old among all my enemies.” Yet I do not despair miserably, but hope in mercy, saying: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” And the penitent shows that he has been heard in these petitions. [Col. 0986A] First, because the Lord the Father has heard the voice of my weeping. Second, because the Lord the Son has heard my entreaty. Third, because the Lord the Holy Spirit has received my prayer. Therefore let all my enemies blush and be exceedingly troubled; let them be turned back and blush very swiftly.

In order that the penitent may more readily obtain what he implores, he fittingly seeks favour. First, from the person of the judge, through his power, where he says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and through his mercy, where he says: “Save me for the sake of your mercy.” Second, from the matter itself: because he has weakness in the flesh, of which he says, “My bones are troubled”; and weakness in the mind, of which he says, “My soul is greatly troubled” [Col. 0986B]. Third, from the suitability of the time, whence he says: “For in death there is none who remembers you”; and from the suitability of the place, where he adds: “But in hell who will confess you?” Fourth, from his own person: because of inward devotion, when he says: “I have laboured in my groaning”; because of the mortification of the flesh, when he adds: “Every night I shall wash my bed, and water my couch with my tears”; because of the disturbance of the heart, whence he adds: “My eye is troubled because of anger”; because of separation from evildoers: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity”; and because of love for enemies: “Let all my enemies be troubled; let them turn back and be greatly ashamed very swiftly.”

Likewise, the psalm begins with fear, since “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Ecclesiasticus 1] [Col. 0986C]. But it ends in charity, since “the end of the commandment is charity” [1 Timothy 1]. For out of fear the penitent asks the Lord at the beginning not to rebuke him in anger or correct him in fury. But out of charity, at the end, he desires for his enemies that they should be ashamed, troubled, and converted. This is the end of every perfection, as is read in another psalm [Psalm 118], namely charity, “a commandment exceedingly broad,” because it extends even to enemies, according to the Lord’s command: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” [Matthew 5]. Rightly, therefore, fear begins and charity completes, because “perfect charity casts out fear” [1 John 4] [Col. 0986D]. Thus it begins in fear and ends in love; it begins in sorrow and ends in joy. Therefore he says:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

As if he said: You are my God, my judge, my physician, my guide, my defender, my saviour. Because you are my God, I fear you, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” Because you are my judge, I entreat you: “Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled and my soul is greatly troubled.” Because you are my guide, I desire to follow you, saying: “Turn, Lord.” Because you are my defender, I ask help from you, saying: “Deliver my soul.” Because you are my saviour, I seek salvation [Col. 0987A], saying: “Save me for the sake of your mercy.” You therefore, Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.

Tell me, sinner, you who desire forgiveness: on what grounds do you presume to profess that anger and fury exist in God himself, saying, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury”? For a person who hears himself called irascible, indeed even furious, is ordinarily provoked not to mercy but to anger, not to kindness but to fury; since this seems to tend not to glory but to insult, not to praise but to reproach. At least you might have said: “Do not rebuke me in anger, nor correct me in fury,” without adding, for stronger expression, “your,” that is, “in your anger” or “in your fury”; for perhaps [Col. 0987B] the understanding would shudder less and the hearing bear it more readily, if you said it without that addition. For who that is truly faithful could now bear calmly and hear patiently anger and fury ascribed to his Lord, especially when he knows him to be most gentle and most kind?

Moreover, since elsewhere you ask of him, “Hear me in your truth, in your righteousness” [Psalm 142], and here say, “Do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury,” you plainly seem to suggest that his anger exceeds righteousness and his fury surpasses truth. It is impious to think this of him who judges the world in righteousness and peoples in equity [Psalm 97]. And since Scripture testifies of him: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquillity” [Wisdom 12] [Col. 0987C], who are you to dare say to him, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury”?

“Why,” he says, “do you weary me with objections and press me with questions, when my fear of punishment is so great, my grief for guilt so great, that amid the straits of fear and sorrow, as though bewildered in mind, I can scarcely answer? For ‘out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’ [Luke 6]; and thus those things proceed from the mouth which are carried in the heart. Hence my words are full of fear and sorrow. Yet I ask you not to rebuke the sinner or correct the penitent because he speaks such words of God, when God himself speaks such words of himself through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: ‘Behold,’ he says to the land of Israel, ‘I shall soon pour out my anger upon you and fulfil my fury in you’ [Ezekiel 7].”

Why then should a human being hesitate to say of God what God himself says of himself, when he has learned from God what to say concerning him? Yet in speaking of the Creator, man borrows these words from creatures, because he has no suitable words by which to speak of God according to God’s own proper nature; and therefore he begs borrowed words, so that he may speak of him by a certain likeness [Col. 0987D]. For among creatures anger is a fury of the mind breaking forth from inward things into outward, when someone, because of an injury done, desires to carry out a vengeance already conceived. Fury, however, is the vehement agitation of one who is indignant, when he longs to pour out all his anger against another.

Sometimes one term is taken for the other, as here in one translation: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” In another it is said: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” [Col. 0988A]. For in Greek *furor* is the same as *ira*, “anger”; hence both expressions are found in Scripture, “the anger of fury” and “the fury of anger.”

But in speaking of fury and anger in God, I do not signify some affection of disturbance in him, in whom these terms can signify nothing but the divine essence; rather, I signify the effect of vehement disturbance in the human being upon whom such things are deservedly exercised because of his sins. Therefore the penitent says: Lord, who can do all things and whom nothing at all resists, do not rebuke me in your anger—that is, do not judge and convict me after the manner of an angry person who strives, because of an injury done, to inflict vengeance already conceived. Nor correct me in your fury—that is, do not punish [Col. 0988B] and scourge me in the manner of one enraged, who, stirred by vehement indignation, seeks to pour out all his anger. For if you wished to deal with me according to what my deeds deserve, I could certainly not stand before the face of your anger, nor endure the onset of your fury, since my sins, crimes, offences, and transgressions are so many and so great, so excessive and grave. Ungrateful as I am, I have deserved both anger and fury; nor would punishment be sufficient or vengeance proportionate even if fire descending from heaven consumed me wholly, or the earth opened its mouth and swallowed me alive.

Yet I will, desire, wish, and ask that in the present life you rebuke and correct me in a spirit of gentleness, because a father corrects the son whom he loves, and you rebuke and chasten the one whom you love [Revelation 3] [Col. 0988C]; so that in the future, Lord—who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna—you may not rebuke me in your anger, as regards the sentence of condemnation, nor correct me in fury, as regards the Gehenna of perdition: that is, you may not rebuke me at the judgment and correct me in hell.

But lest anyone understand this of the judgment unto salvation, I add: “in your anger,” because that same one will be judge and advocate, accuser and witness, and against the reprobate he will allege: “I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not receive me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me” [Matthew 25]. Then the wicked will answer him: “Lord, when did we see you hungry, thirsty [Col. 0988D], a stranger, naked, sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?” Then he will answer them: “Amen I say to you: insofar as you did not do it to one of my least ones, neither did you do it to me” [ibid.].

“And do not correct me,” that is, do not punish me in hell. But lest anyone understand a light and passing punishment, I add: “in your fury,” that is, in the unquenchable and eternal fire of which he will thunder terribly: “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” [ibid.]. Truly that day is a day of anger, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of storm and darkness, a day of fury and terror [Zephaniah 1]. If on that day the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear? [1 Peter 4]. Since, therefore, it is exceedingly dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God [Hebrews 10] [Col. 0989A], I cry out, trembling and grieving: “Lord, do not correct me in your fury, nor rebuke me in your anger.” Surely, if you rebuked me at judgment with complete tranquillity, I could not be delivered; for if I presented myself as innocent, you would prove me crooked. How much less, then, could I be delivered if you rebuked me in your anger? Therefore, “do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” [Psalm 142].

Indeed, the Father is angry, the Lord is angry, and the judge is angry. A father is angry with a son in order to correct and amend him; a master is angry with a servant in order to punish and scourge him; a judge is angry with an accused person in order to reject and condemn him. I ask that the first anger be applied, that the second be softened, and that the third be wholly [Col. 0989B] turned away. Of the first it is written: “He was angry and had mercy on us” [Psalm 59]. God’s anger is grave in this way: not to be angry at all. Thus he says: “My zeal has departed from you; I shall no longer be angry with you” [Ezekiel 16]. Of the second it is written: “You have softened all your anger; you have turned away from the anger of your indignation” [Psalm 84]. For when you have been angry, you will remember mercy. Of the third it is written: “A fire has been kindled by your anger, and it shall burn even to the lowest hell” [Psalm 88]. Therefore turn your anger away from us, so that you may not be angry with us for ever.

There is also a threefold anger of man: natural, venial, and criminal. Of the first it is said: “Be angry, and do not sin” [Psalm 4]. Have this anger if you desire the anger of a pious father [alternative reading: *piam*, “pious,” modifying *iram*, “anger”] to be applied to you. Of the second it is written: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” [Ephesians 4] [Col. 0989C]. Moderate this anger if you desire the just anger of the Lord toward you to be softened. Of the third it is written: “The anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” [James 1]. Entirely avoid this anger if you desire the severe anger of the judge to be wholly turned away from you. For “everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” [Matthew 5]. “Their anger,” he says, “is according to the likeness of a serpent, and their fury is like that of an incurable asp” [Psalm 57]. Wholly shun this anger and this fury if you desire to escape the Lord’s fury and anger. Say, therefore:

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for all my bones are troubled.

“And my soul is greatly troubled; but you, Lord—how long?”
