[Col. 0989D] Match each thing to its corresponding thing. Do not rebuke me in anger, but have mercy on me, because I am weak in body, whence all my bones are troubled. Do not correct me in your fury, but heal me, because I am weak in mind, whence my soul is greatly troubled. Great indeed is bodily weakness, because all my bones are troubled; but greater is the weakness of the mind, because my soul is greatly troubled. The former is a punishment, of which the Apostle says: “Use a little wine because of your frequent infirmities” [1 Timothy 5]. The latter is guilt, of which the Psalmist says: “My enemies who trouble me” [Psalm 41], “they themselves were weakened and fell” [Psalm 26].

Therefore, “have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak”—not as the one who said: “When I am weak, then I am strong” [2 Corinthians 12] [Col. 0990A], because “the weak have been girded with strength”; nor as she who said: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” [Song of Songs 2], because such weakness is undoubtedly salutary. Nor am I weak as those of whom it is said: “They shall be weakened and perish from before your face” [Psalm 9], because “they were weakened, and there was none to help”; nor am I weak as those of whom it is written: “God gave them over to passions of dishonour” [Romans 1], to do things unfitting, because such weakness is undoubtedly deadly. But I confess myself to be among those of whom it is said: “Their weaknesses were multiplied; afterwards they hastened” [Psalm 15]; and among those of whom it is written: “Their conscience, being weak, is defiled” [Col. 0990B].

Behold, I hasten, crying: “Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled.” Certainly not your bones, for it is written: “You shall not break a bone of it,” or, “you shall not break his bone” [Exodus 12]. For you have the bone of divinity, concerning which you say: “My bone has clung to my flesh” [Psalm 101]. You also have the bone of humanity, concerning which the Church says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” [Genesis 2]. But neither do I speak of those bones concerning which you say in the Psalm: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones have been scattered” [Psalm 21]; and the Church says in Lamentations: “From on high he sent fire into my bones” [Lamentations 1]. Nor do I speak of bones that trouble more than they are troubled: “His bones,” it says, “are like pipes of bronze” [Job 40], and “rottenness is in his bones” [Proverbs 12]. “His bones [Col. 0990C] are full of fat and marrow; his bones are moistened.” But I speak of my bones, because “my bones are troubled,” that is, the virtues and powers of my soul.

Those bones are troubled by outward vices, according to the saying: “The Lord scattered the bones of those who please men; they were confounded, because God despised them” [Psalm 52]. But these are troubled by vices, according to the saying: “My bones have dried up because of the heat” [Job 30], or “they have been crushed as in a frying-pan.” Therefore heal and guard all my bones, so that not one of them may be broken, and let your fear be the watering of my bones.

Thus spiritual languor is guilt, while bodily languor is punishment; yet bodily languor frequently follows from guilt, as Truth said to the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years: “Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” [John 5] [Col. 0990D]. And the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore among you many are weak and sickly, and many sleep” [1 Corinthians 11]. It is therefore the most healthful counsel that one who needs bodily healing should first seek and receive the medicine of spiritual things, so that, when the cause has ceased, the effect may also cease.

Yet bodily infirmity, though it often arises from sin, does not always arise from sin. The Apostle proves this when he says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn for my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. Because of this I asked the Lord three times that he might remove it from me; and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness’” [2 Corinthians 12; John 11] [Col. 0991A]. Behold, the Apostle was made weak for the preservation of his humility.

Truth also says in the Gospel: “This infirmity is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” And when he was asked by his disciples: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” he replied: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, that he should be born blind, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” [John 9]. Behold, Lazarus was ill, and the blind man was ill, for the display of divine power. Job also, it is written, was made ill for the testing of his patience; sitting on a dungheap, he scraped his sores with a potsherd [Job 2]. Likewise Tobias [chapter 2], upon whose eyes warm droppings from a swallow’s nest fell, became blind [Col. 0991B]. The Lord permitted this infirmity to happen to him so that an example of his patience, as also of holy Job’s, might be given to posterity.

Sometimes, moreover, someone is made ill out of compassion for neighbours. Thus the Apostle said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” [2 Corinthians 11]. The Saviour himself was wounded for our sins and crushed for our crimes; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we are healed, and the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity. For these and many other reasons, bodily infirmity is sometimes inflicted without the desert of sin, although more often because of sin.

Therefore heal me, Lord, as a merciful and wise [Col. 0991C] physician: for I am the sick person and you are the physician; I have infirmity, you have health; I am weak through guilt—heal me through grace, because all my bones are troubled and my soul is greatly troubled. A troubled soul troubles the body, as Solomon testifies: “A sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” [Proverbs 17]. Hence elsewhere he says: “Because of the sound of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh” [Psalm 101]. Indeed, “my bones have been crushed as in a frying-pan,” because “by the things through which a person sins, by those he is also tormented” [Psalm 11].

For as long as the thorn of reason pricks the spirit because of sin, and the worm of conscience bites the mind because of offence, not only is the soul scorched and tormented, but the body too is afflicted and disturbed. Therefore [Col. 0991D] it is good for a person to cease from sin, not only for the sake of eternal rest, which he awaits in the age to come, but also for the sake of temporal repose, which he experiences in the present age; because, according to the Apostle, godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come.

This may also be understood otherwise: by “bones” may be understood the powers of the mind, insofar as they concern the spirit, which is strong and ready; and by “soul,” sensuality, insofar as it concerns the flesh, which is frail and weak. Accordingly the Lord says: “The spirit indeed is ready, but the flesh is weak” [Matthew 26]. Although spirit is soul, nevertheless spirit and soul are sometimes distinguished, so that “spirit” means the higher part, that is, the mind, and “soul” the lower part, that is, sensuality, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” [Hebrews 4] [Col. 0992A].

The penitent therefore says: Heal me, Lord, from the guilt of sin; and you certainly ought to heal me, because my bones—that is, the powers of my soul—are troubled. The rational power, which distinguishes between good and evil; the irascible power, which rejects evil; and the concupiscible power, which seeks good—all are troubled toward salutary repentance.

The rational power is troubled when it does not discern subtly between good and evil. The irascible power is troubled when it does not strongly reject evil. The concupiscible power is troubled when it does not delightfully seek the good. Therefore my bones are troubled; that is, the sensuality of the soul is greatly troubled [Col. 0992B], because a great offence demands grave repentance, so that I who sinned while carnally delighted may repent while spiritually troubled, and thus by another road return to my own country.

There is disturbance of fear and agitation, of which it is written: “When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him” [Matthew 2]. There is disturbance of fury and confusion, of which it is said: “They were troubled like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” [Psalm 106]. There is disturbance of toil and occupation, of which the Lord says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” [Luke 10]. There is disturbance of grief and compunction, of which the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My soul was troubled because of the chariots of Amminadab” [Song of Songs 6] [Col. 0992C]. There is disturbance of sorrow and compassion, of which it is written that Jesus troubled himself and wept [John 3]. There is disturbance of astonishment and wonder: “Mary was troubled at the angel’s saying and considered what manner of greeting this might be” [Luke 1].

There are many other kinds of disturbance, but all are reduced to four: misery, guilt, punishment, and grace. The penitent treats of these in this psalm: “My bones,” he says, “are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled. My eye is troubled because of anger; all my enemies are troubled.”

“Turn, Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy.”

Soul is understood in many ways in a human being: the person himself [Col. 0992D], present life, the spirit of reason, the animating spirit, the intention of the mind, and the sensuality of the flesh. Of the first: “The male whose foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people” [Genesis 17]. Of the second: “I do not make my life more precious than myself” [Acts 20]. Of the third: “The soul that sins shall itself die” [Ezekiel 18]. Of the fourth: “The life of the flesh is in the blood” [Leviticus 7]. Of the fifth: “I carry my soul in my hands” [Psalm 118]. Of the sixth: “My eye, my soul, and my belly are troubled in anger” [Psalm 30].

Therefore deliver my soul, that is, my spirit or myself; and hasten to deliver me. For my soul is troubled unto repentance. You therefore, Lord, who are merciful and kind, turn to me, and I shall turn to you [Col. 0993A]. Although it is said through the prophet, “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” [Zechariah 1], nevertheless unless you turn to me, I cannot turn to you; and unless you come before me, I cannot come to you. But since you are always ready for perfect conversion, as the prophet testifies, “we shall find him prepared as the dawn” [Hosea 6], I say more confidently: “Turn, Lord”—that is, make me turn perfectly from error to truth, from vices to virtues.

Further, just as God turns himself away from someone in three ways—first, when he withdraws spiritual grace, whence elsewhere he says: “Do not turn your face away from me” [Psalm 26]; second, when he imposes temporal punishment, whence: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” [Psalm 29] [Col. 0993B]; third, when he inflicts eternal vengeance, whence it is said: “Turn your anger away from us, and do not be angry with us for ever” [Psalm 84]—so he turns himself toward someone in three ways. First, when he pours spiritual grace into him, as in this place: “Turn, Lord, and deliver my soul”; second, when he remits temporal punishment, whence: “Turn, Lord, a little while, and be entreated concerning your servants” [Psalm 80]; third, when he grants eternal salvation, whence: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” [Zechariah 1]. As if he said: Turn to me by abandoning wickedness, and I shall turn to you by granting salvation.

Therefore, without any difficulty or delay whatsoever, deliver my soul from present misery and save me in eternal glory, for the sake of [Col. 0993C] your mercy. In that mercy alone I hope, not in my own merit, in which I have no confidence; and so I do not plead my merit, which demands punishment, but implore your mercy, which bestows grace.

Behold, this sinner grieved greatly for his guilt, whence he said: “My soul is greatly troubled.” He asked pardon, whence he cried: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak.” Yet he had not received the grace of justification, whence he said: “And you, Lord—how long? Turn and deliver my soul.” But you will say: What more is required for a penitent to be converted than that he should grieve greatly over what he has committed, resolving faithfully to confess it and wholly to abstain from committing it? For it is written: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, I will remember none of his sins” [Ezekiel 12]. And again: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the iniquity of my heart” [Psalm 31].

But if this is so, since a person knows when he repents in this way, he knows when he is converted, and therefore when he is justified. Yet he cannot be justified unless charity has first been infused into him, according to Truth’s saying: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” [Luke 7] [Col. 0993D]. For “charity covers a multitude of sins” [1 Peter 4]. Therefore he knows when charity is infused into him—yet true is what the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” [1 Corinthians 4]. For “who understands his offences?” Hence David prays: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” [Psalm 18]. Job says: “Even if I were simple, my soul itself would not know it” [Job 9]. Solomon also says: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean, and I am pure from sin’?” [Proverbs 10]. As if to say: No one, unless perhaps it has been revealed to him.

For among unbelievers there are some who grieve greatly over sins committed and resolve, with the intention of confessing, to abstain from committing them; yet they are not justified, because they have some offence of which they are unaware—namely, that of which the Lord says: “He who does not believe is already judged” [John 3]. Likewise, perhaps some great sin is hidden from a Christian; because he does not repent of it, justification is delayed. Or perhaps he grieves less than [Col. 0994B] he ought to grieve; or perhaps there is another cause known to God but unknown to us.

For who would dare to impose a fixed measure upon grace and say: “If the sinner grieves so much, or in such a manner, his sin is forgiven; but if not, it is not forgiven”? The sinner’s justification would then not be gratuitous but owed. Rather, by God’s most just dispensation it comes about that, just as requested pardon is sometimes deferred, so pardon that has been granted is sometimes not known. For it is more expedient that a justified person should doubt whether he is righteous than that an unrighteous person should believe himself justified.

Healing is sometimes delayed lest the sick person suppose that he has been healed not by the physician’s power but by the strength of nature or the mildness of the illness, and thus think lightly of the physician and make little of the disease. Therefore, so that he may distrust his own strength, recognize the greatness of his infirmity, and implore the healer’s help, healing is deferred until he repeatedly cries and says: “Heal my soul, Lord, for I have sinned against you” [Col. 0994C]. For this sick person had not yet cried so perfectly that it could be said to him: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: ‘Here I am.’”

Moreover, because of the difficulty of healing, infirmity is guarded against more carefully; for what is easily healed is not much guarded against. Therefore the healing of illness is delayed so that health may be guarded more diligently. But it must not be deferred until after death.

“For in death there is none who remembers you; but in hell who will confess you?”

There is a threefold death: bodily, spiritual, and Gehenna’s death. Of the first it is written: “The body is dead because of sin” [Romans 8]; hence: “What man is there who shall live and not see death?” [Psalm 88]. As if to say: No living person fails eventually to incur bodily death. Of the second it is said: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead” [1 Timothy 5]. And: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” [1 John 5]; as if to say: There is a certain mortal sin for which one should not pray, because it is forgiven neither in this age nor in the future. Of the third it is written: “He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death” [Revelation 2]. And: “Like sheep they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” [Psalm 48]. That is: just as a sheep does not pluck grass but grazes, so that grass continually grows again for feeding, so Gehenna’s death [Col. 0995A] does not consume a human being but afflicts him, so that he always lives for death.

There is also a death of grace, of which the Apostle says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” [Colossians 3]. And Solomon says: “Love is strong as death, and jealousy hard as hell. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters cannot extinguish charity” [Song of Songs 8]. Christ himself calls himself, through the prophet, the death of death: “O death,” he says, “I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” [Hosea 13].

The death of nature separates body from soul; the death of guilt separates soul from God; the death of Gehenna separates soul and body from glory; the death of grace separates the body from the world. In the first death there is often no one who remembers God unto salvation; in the second there is scarcely anyone; in the third, no one; in the fourth, a person always remembers God [Col. 0995B].

For at the moment of bodily death there is sometimes such bitterness of pain and such distress of suffering that the dying person is deprived of memory to such an extent that he can remember nothing at all. Although one must despair of no one while he remains alive, it is nevertheless not safe to postpone repentance until the final moment of death. A person repents safely when he is still able to sin. Therefore, whoever wishes to be freed from danger should abandon what is uncertain and retain what is certain.

Likewise, concerning spiritual death it must be understood that in death there is none who remembers you, because such is the obstinacy of crime that the sinner, despairing of pardon, scarcely ever remembers God unto repentance, having cast him away from himself in contempt through pride. By a just judgment the sinner is punished with such a penalty that, dying, he forgets himself, because while living he forgot God.

But concerning Gehenna’s death it can and should be understood that in death there is no one who remembers God, because in Gehenna there is no remembrance unto salvation, but rather unto torment. For the damned will curse the Most High and blaspheme the Exalted One, complaining that he is malicious because he created them for punishment and is never inclined to pardon; they will wish him not to exist at all, he through whom they complain that they exist so unhappily [Col. 0995C]. Therefore it fittingly follows: “But in hell who will confess you?”

In Holy Scripture, “hell” sometimes means the misery of the present life: “The perils of hell found me” [Psalm 114]. Sometimes it means the depth of vices: “They went down alive into hell” [Numbers 16]. Sometimes it means the very one who draws others to destruction: “The sorrows of hell surrounded me” [Psalm 17]. Sometimes it means a chasm in the earth: “The earth was split under their feet, and they went down alive into hell” [Numbers 16]. Sometimes it means the place of punishments: “Hell beneath was troubled at the meeting of your coming” [Isaiah 14]. It has two parts, lower and upper; hence it is said: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell” [Psalm 85]. The upper part was called the limbo of hell, or Abraham’s bosom, of which Job says: “May my soul descend into hell” [Job 17]. The lower part [Col. 0996A] is called Tartarus or Gehenna, of which the Lord says: “But the rich man died and was buried in hell” [Luke 6]. In this hell, indeed, no one confesses the Lord.

Hell is also the devil himself: “Hell has enlarged its soul without any limit” [Isaiah 5]. For if, according to the Apocalypse of John, people blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it became exceedingly great [Revelation 16], how much more will people blaspheme God in hell because of the torment of fire, which will indeed be more violent than can even be imagined? Rightly therefore the prophet said: “Neither will hell confess you, nor will death praise you” [Isaiah 38]. “The dead shall not praise you, Lord” [Psalm 113; Ecclesiasticus 17]. For from a dead man, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes.

There are two kinds of confession in Scripture: one of sins, the other of praises. Of the latter it is said: “Confess the Lord upon the harp, and sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery” [Psalm 32]. Of the former: “Confess your sins to one another” [James 5] [Col. 0996B]. Therefore, although in hell there is no confession of praises, there is confession of sins; but it is wholly fruitless and useless, as the Wise Man declares: “Groaning because of the distress of spirit, they will say within themselves, repenting: ‘We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us. What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow’” [Wisdom 5]. “Such things,” he says, “said in hell those who sinned.” Therefore they will confess unto punishment, but they will not turn unto pardon. For it is just that those who would not when they could should not be able when they will.

For this reason the rich man who was tormented in the flame said to Abraham: “I ask you, father, send Lazarus to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they also come into this place of torments.” When Abraham answered him, “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them,” he added: “No, father Abraham; but if someone rose from the dead, they would believe” [Luke 16] [Col. 0996C]. He too was doing penance in hell; but because he knew it was useless, he asked that this be announced to his brothers, so that they might do fruitful penance in this age. Therefore this penitent speaks not of the future but of the past:

“I have laboured in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears.”

The righteous person labours in heart, labours in speech, labours in deed. Of the first: “I have laboured in my groaning”; of the second: “I have laboured crying out; my throat has become hoarse, while I hope in my God” (Ps. 68); of the third: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall go well with you” (Ps. 127). God, however, is said to labour through patience, in that he waits for repentance; hence: “They have become burdensome to me; I have laboured in bearing them” (Isa. 1). But the devil labours through deceit, in order to draw people into wickedness; hence: “Under his tongue are toil and pain” (Ps. 10). [Col. 0997A] Moreover, there is the labour of earthly pilgrimage, of which we read: “Man is born for labour, and the bird for flight” (Job 5); the labour of human transgression, of which it is said: “They are not in the labour of men, nor shall they be scourged with men” (Ps. 72); and the labour of everlasting damnation, of which it is written: “He shall labour forever and yet live on to the end.”

He would not have said, “I have laboured in my groaning,” of groaning that is rare and slight, but of that which is prolonged and continual (Ps. 48). For one does not labour in groaning who immediately laughs; nor, certainly, does one groan penitently who does not persevere in repentance but rather mocks it, passing from groaning to laughter. But he laboured in groaning who said: “All day long I went about sorrowful; I roared because of the groaning of my heart, and my pain is [Col. 0997B] ever before me” (Ps. 37). Certainly the dove has groaning in place of song. And you, penitent soul, if you wish to be a dove, so as to be free from the gall of sin, let groaning take the place of song for you, and sorrow the place of laughter.

Furthermore, two things are necessary for the penitent: inward groaning and outward weeping. Therefore, after saying, “I have laboured in my groaning,” he immediately added: “I shall wash,” that is, drench, “my material bed through each night, and with my tears I shall water my couch”—not merely inward tears, but outward ones also. Certainly one must not weep once only, but often; therefore he says: “I shall wash my bed through each night.” Nor must one weep a little, but abundantly; therefore he adds: “With my tears I shall water my couch.” For where there is watering, there is an abundance of moisture. [Col. 0997C]

He does not say “on nights,” but “through nights”; nor “through some,” but “through each,” in order to show that his weeping is continuous and prolonged, reproving the hardness of those who can scarcely, or only rarely, be softened to tears. For he has a stony breast, a heart of stone, and an iron spirit, who, over himself—not so much in his body, which is to die, as perhaps in his mind, already dead—produces no groans, sends forth no sighs, and sheds no tears. Let him know, then, that he is culpably hard and harshly guilty who mourns the bodily death of his friend but does not weep for the spiritual death of his own soul.

Consider, penitent, the tears of that sinful woman who, standing behind at the feet of the Lord Jesus, watered his feet with tears and wiped them with the hair of [Col. 0997D] her head; and do likewise, if you wish to hear with her: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7). Although one must weep not only at night but also by day, he nevertheless says “through nights,” and not “through days,” because a person ordinarily weeps more abundantly and frequently at night, when alone in private, than by day, when among many people in public. At night he also rests, removed from tumult, whereas by day he labours amid noise.

Night also signifies sin, which darkens the mind and obscures it with the gloom of sins. By bed is understood conscience, in which the spirit sleeps when it rests from the disturbance of vices. He therefore says: “I shall wash my bed,” that is, “I shall cleanse [al. inundate] my conscience, through each [Col. 0998A] night,” that is, through each sin. For each individual sin the penitent ought to offer individual sacrifices, that, according to the divine law, he may offer a sacrifice worthy for sin: namely that of which it is said, “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50), in which all the inward parts of the victim are washed.

Of such nights we read: “Those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk are drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5). Job says (ch. 3): “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night—the night in which it was said: ‘A man is conceived.’” Of this bed it is said: “If I say, ‘My little bed shall comfort me, and I shall be relieved, speaking with myself on my couch,’ you terrify me through dreams and shake me with horror through visions” (Job 7).

“Bed” is also used of a human being in many other ways: the leisure of contemplation—“Two shall be in one bed: one shall be taken, and the other left” (Luke 17); worldly prosperity—“On my little bed, through the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3); bodily sickness—“May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain” (Ps. 4); pleasure of the flesh—“You luxuriate on ivory beds” (Amos 6); the torpor of negligence—“I shall cast her upon a bed, and everyone who commits fornication with her” (Rev. 2); the teaching of heretics—“I have woven my bed with cords” (Prov. 7); and the depth of hell—“In darkness I have spread my little bed” (Job 17). Here, however, bed is understood as the secrecy of conscience or as fleshly pleasure.

Certainly, just as there are seven days—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which spiritual life is perfected in the brightness of virtues—so there are seven [Col. 0998C] nights: the seven principal vices, by which carnal life is conducted in the darkness of vices. The former are signified by the seven lamps in the candlestick of the tabernacle (Exod. 25), and by the seven eyes in the one stone (Zech. 3). The latter are signified by the seven nations expelled from the land of promise (Deut. 7), and by the seven more wicked spirits whom the unclean spirit took to himself (Matt. 12; Luke 11).

Therefore, “I shall wash my bed through each night.” There is a threefold washing: in water, in tears, and in blood. Of the first we read: “Christ put water into a basin and washed the disciples’ feet” (John 13), because unless one has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, one cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 3). Of the second it is said: “I shall wash [Col. 0998D] my bed through each night.” And elsewhere: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall wash the blood of Jerusalem in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” (Isa. 4). Of the third it is written in the Apocalypse: “These are those who have come out of great tribulation; and they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7). And again: “Who washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1).

The first and the last are of little value without the middle, because neither baptism nor martyrdom avails for salvation without repentance, since sin is not forgiven to one who does not repent—original sin alone excepted, which is forgiven to infants in baptism without repentance. For as, in regeneration, guilt is forgiven and passes away without consent, until it is wholly forgiven. But because he had not said with what he would wash the bed, [Col. 0999A] he specifies it by adding: “With tears I shall water my couch.”

There are tears of one who grieves and repents; tears of one who sympathizes and loves; tears of one who contemplates and exults; and tears of one who curses and despairs. Of the first we read: “Hezekiah wept with great weeping,” and it was said to him: “I have heard your prayer and seen your tears; and behold, I have healed you” (4 Kings 20; Isa. 38). The woman also who was a sinner in the city began to water the Lord’s feet with tears and to wipe them with the hair of her head, and it was said to her: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7).

Of the second kind of tears we read that, when Jesus saw Mary weeping and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he groaned and troubled himself, and wept. Therefore the Jews said: “See how he loved him” (John 11). Joseph also, when he had embraced the neck of Benjamin [Col. 0999B] his brother, wept, while Benjamin likewise wept upon his neck (Gen. 45).

Of the third kind of tears the Prophet says: “My tears were my bread day and night, when I shall enter into the place of the tabernacle, I shall go on to the house of God” (Ps. 41). Tobias also kissed his son with his wife, and both began to weep for joy (Tob. 11). Of the fourth the Lord says: “Cast him into the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22). And elsewhere: “All the kings of the earth, who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury, shall weep and mourn over her” (Rev. 18).

Moreover, God shall wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away [Col. 0999C] (Rev. 21). Therefore, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125).

But those “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2), who take up tambourine and lyre and rejoice at the sound of the instrument, yet in a moment descend to hell (Job 21)—their laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and grief shall seize the end of their joy (Prov. 14). Therefore, “With my tears I shall water my couch,” because tears wash conscience from the filth of sins; and the more bitter they are to the penitent, the sweeter they are to the one granting pardon. Of such tears it is elsewhere written that Peter, going out, “wept bitterly” (Matt. 26). Likewise: “The angels of peace”—that is, priests praying for peace—“wept bitterly” (Isa. 33), according to the saying: “Between the vestibule and the altar, the priests and ministers of the Lord wept” (Joel 2). For “the lips of the priest preserve knowledge,” since he is “the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). Hannah also wept abundantly with a bitter heart (1 Kings 1).

Therefore, with inward tears—that is, with the bitterness of repentance—“I shall water my couch,” namely sensuality, so that it may become fertile, though formerly dry; so that, once watered, it may produce worthy fruits of repentance, whereas, when parched, it brought forth thorns and thistles. Of this couch it is elsewhere said: “You have turned his whole bed in his sickness” (Ps. 40).

From his saying, “I shall wash my bed through each night,” it is clearly inferred that [Col. 1000A] it is not enough for a person to confess generally that he has committed many sins. He must descend to particulars, so that he may be contrite for each one, especially those which he can recall through diligent examination. Moreover, a distinction can be made between bed and couch: by bed, in which the body rests with delight, bodily pleasure is denoted; by couch, upon which a heap of coverings is piled, the heap of sins is understood. Thus through the tears of repentance the multitude of sins and the pleasure of sinning may be washed away and destroyed.

He says “through each night,” rather than “through each day,” to suggest that he experiences days and nights in alternation. For one who is now suffused with the light of truth and now darkened by the gloom of iniquity is changed, as it were, by alternating dispositions between days and nights: as though he endures night if he serves the law of sin in the [Col. 1000B] flesh, but beholds day if he serves the law of God in the mind (Rom. 7). Therefore, as though what he had said about the past—“I have laboured in my groaning”—were insufficient, he immediately adds something concerning the future, in order to show the penitent’s progress, as he advances from groaning to tears, and from tears to confession:

> My eye has been troubled by anger; I have grown old among all my enemies.

Assign each thing to its counterpart: “I shall wash my bed through each night,” because “I have grown old among all my enemies.” “With my tears I shall water my couch,” because “my eye has been troubled by anger.” It should be noted that there is a sin of sudden onset, which is quickly abandoned, and a sin of habit, which is practiced for a longer time. [Col. 1000C] The penitent grieves that he has sinned in both ways: through sudden onset, and therefore says, “My eye has been troubled by anger.” For anger is called a brief madness, according to the saying: “Let not the sun set upon your anger” (Eph. 4). He grieves also over sin through habit, and therefore adds: “I have grown old among all my enemies,” for old age results from duration.

“My eye,” namely understanding, reason, or intention, “has been troubled by anger,” or by fury—which is the same thing—because “the anger of man does not work the justice of God” (Jas. 1); and:

> Anger prevents the mind from being able to discern the truth.  
> (Horace.)

Of these eyes we read: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118). “The eyes [Col. 1000D] of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2). And: “If your eye is single, your whole body shall be full of light” (Matt. 6). Such eyes are sometimes troubled by one’s own anger, and at other times are troubled by divine fury. For while the sinner is prevented by his own anger from contemplating the sun of justice, he incurs, by divine fury and indeed by just judgment, inward darkness in the present—that is, blindness of mind—being given over to a reprobate sense. In the future he shall incur outer darkness, because “the wicked shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of God”; for God “dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6), outside of which the wicked person shall in the future be wholly, utterly separated from God. Thus that darkness is called outer darkness because it places people altogether outside the light.

Yet I have not sinned only sometimes [Col. 1001A] through sudden onset; I have also often sinned through habit, because I have grown old through long practice among all my enemies. Certainly, while the soul is a pilgrim from the Lord in this world, it suffers many great enemies, of whom it is written: “Her enemies have become the head” (Lam. 1). For the world and flesh, demon and human being, are enemies to it. The world with its elements: “The whole world shall fight against the senseless” (Wis. 5). The flesh with its senses: “Death has entered through the windows” (Jer. 9). “The eye despoils the soul” (Lam. 3). The demon with his vices: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. 6). Human beings [Col. 1001B] with beasts: “When men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123). “They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth” (Ps. 78).

The enemies, then, are demons and human beings, vices and sins, the world and flesh. Of them we read: “Our enemies have mocked us” (Ps. 79). “Let my enemies be confounded and ashamed” (Ps. 34). “You have given me the back of my enemies.” “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them” (Ps. 17). Moreover, just as the devil is the enemy of virtues, concerning whom it is said, “An enemy, a man, sowed weeds over the seed” (Matt. 13), so God is the enemy of vices, who says of himself: “I shall be an enemy to your enemies” (Exod. 23). [Col. 1001C] Truly, therefore, “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7).

The penitent thus says: “I have grown old,” that is, I have sinned through long habit, “among all my enemies,” who persecute me on every side and draw me toward evil; I have become foul and useless, like an old garment, which is fit neither for use nor ornament. Oh, how grave is the oldness of sin, how grave the sin of oldness, through which fault is almost turned into nature, and nature almost passes into fault. There is oldness of body, oldness of sensuality, oldness of reason, oldness of habit, oldness of ignorance, oldness of guilt, oldness of law, oldness of life, oldness of time, and oldness of eternity.

Of oldness of body we read: “All shall grow old like a garment” (Ps. 101); of oldness of sensuality [Col. 1001D]: “Our old man was crucified with him” (Rom. 6); of oldness of reason: “Because I kept silent, all my bones grew old” (Ps. 31); of oldness of habit: “Put off the old man with his deeds” (Eph. 4); of oldness of ignorance: “The old error has passed away” (Isa. 26); of oldness of life: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Luke 5); of oldness of guilt: “Grow old in days of evil” (Dan. 13); of oldness of law: “Not in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the spirit” (Rom. 7); of oldness of time: “You shall eat the very oldest of old stores” (Lev. 26); and of oldness of eternity: “The Ancient of Days sat, and the books were opened” (Rev. 20).

Although this sinner has grown old [Col. 1002A] among his enemies, he does not despair. Rather, rebuked and heard by the Lord, he says to them:

> Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.

As though he said: I am separated from you—if not yet in place, yet already in resolve; if not yet in body, yet already in heart. For in this world we neither can nor ought altogether to separate ourselves bodily from evil people, except only from those who, deservedly because of their sins, have been cut off from the Church by a sentence of excommunication. With these, according to the Apostle’s word, we ought not even to eat; otherwise, as that same Apostle says, we would have to leave this world (1 Cor. 5). For the Lord also commanded: “Do not uproot the weeds, lest you uproot the wheat with them. [Col. 1002B] Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13).

Meanwhile, before the threshing floor is winnowed, because grain is mixed with chaff and weeds with wheat, the good must remain with the evil. Thus Lot lived in Sodom and Job was in the land of Hus. The bridegroom likewise says to the bride in the Song: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song 2). Therefore Christ himself ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 5).

Yet although the righteous ought not bodily to separate themselves from the ungodly in this world with respect to ordinary association, they ought, when it can be done without scandal, to separate themselves from others with respect to intimate cohabitation; for habits are formed by companionship, and “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15).

[Col. 1002C]

> And a grape pressed close to another grape takes on its dark stain from it.

Therefore it is said: “With the holy you shall be holy, and with the innocent you shall be innocent” (Ps. 17). Elsewhere we read: “With men who work iniquity I shall not communicate, nor with their chosen ones” (Ps. 140). Again: “I have chosen to be cast down in the house of my God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83). Therefore they shall always be wholly separated spiritually, and sometimes also bodily.

The penitent, justified by God, thus says: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

> The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has accepted [al. received] my prayer.

[Col. 1002D] He had prayed for three things in the first ternary: namely, for punishment to be removed, for the wound to be healed, and for delay to be taken away. Rejoicing that he has been heard by the Lord concerning these three things, he says: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping; the Lord has accepted my prayer.” There is weeping in the heart, weeping in the mouth, and weeping in deed: in the heart with sorrow, in the mouth with crying out, in deed with labour.

Of the first we read that, when Hannah was bitter in soul and wept abundantly, she prayed to the Lord; she spoke in her heart, and her voice was not heard at all (1 Kings 1). Of the second we read: “A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and wailing: Rachel weeping for her children; she would not be comforted” (Matt. 2). Of the third we read: “The woman who was a sinner in the city, standing behind at the feet of the Lord Jesus, began to water his feet with tears and wipe them with the hair of her head” (Luke [Col. 1003A] 7).

Some people weep often from excessive joy; of such it is read that Tobias, having taken the boy by the hand, ran to meet his son and, receiving him, kissed him with his wife, and both began to weep for joy (Tob. 11). Likewise Joseph, seeing his father Jacob, threw himself upon his neck and wept amid embraces; and his father said to him: “Now I shall die happily, because I have seen your face” (Gen. 46).

Moreover, from excessive joy as well as excessive sorrow, some are sometimes unable to keep their voices from weeping. Thus we read that Joseph could no longer restrain himself, and raised his voice in weeping, so that the Egyptians and all Pharaoh’s household heard it; and he made himself known to his brothers (Gen. 45). David, ascending into the upper chamber of the gate, wept and cried out in a loud voice: “My son Absalom, [Col. 1003B] Absalom my son! Who would grant that I might die for you?” (2 Kings 16).

Previously, then, the penitent, exceedingly sad, said: “With my tears I shall water my couch.” But now, exceedingly joyful, he declares: “The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has accepted my prayer.” Therefore, because the Lord, mercifully accepting his repentance, has heard him, he desires his enemies to repent after his example in a twofold way, saying:

> Let all my enemies be ashamed and exceedingly troubled; let them turn [al. be converted and be ashamed] backward, and be greatly ashamed very swiftly.

Let them be troubled in heart through the pain of contrition; ashamed in speech through the shame of confession; turned backward in deed through the labour of satisfaction. He repeats again, “Let them be ashamed,” because in [Col. 1003C] remembering their crimes one must be ashamed inwardly before God, and in confessing sins one must be ashamed outwardly before a human being. For the shame of the confessor is no small punishment for the penitent, and the shame of confession is no small part of satisfaction. Oh, with how much blushes one confesses before another what one does not even consider within oneself without great shame.

But one ought to be more ashamed, before God who sees all things, to commit shameful abominations than before a human being who hears of certain shameful deeds already committed, to disclose them—although you disclose them to that person not as to a human being, but as to God. Let them therefore be ashamed of their sins unto repentance. For although there is a kind of shame that is evil, of which the Lord says: “Whoever is ashamed of me [Col. 1003D] and my words before men, of him shall the Son of Man be ashamed before the angels of God” (Luke 9), and: “Then you shall begin with shame to take the last place” (Luke 14), nevertheless this shame is good, of which the Apostle says: “What fruit, therefore, did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6).

And the Prophet reproves her who would not be ashamed of sins: “You have acquired the forehead [Col. 1004A] of a harlot; you did not know how to be ashamed” (Jer. 3). Elisha also said to Joram, king of Israel: “As the Lord of hosts lives, in whose presence I stand, if I did not reverence the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would neither attend to you nor look upon you” (4 Kings 3). For, as the Wise Man testifies, there is shame that brings glory and shame that brings disgrace (Ecclus. 4). Hence elsewhere it is read: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23).

He desires that they be troubled, according to the other reading, “exceedingly,” so that the disturbance may be not only great but forceful—*vae adimens*, “taking away woe,” that is, averting eternal damnation. For unless the penitent’s disturbance is of such a kind and extent as suffices to avert eternal punishment, it undoubtedly bruises, but does not break; [Col. 1004B] it inflicts punishment but does not bestow pardon. For two correlative things are involved here: the debt of hellish punishment must be remitted, and the bond of criminal guilt loosed.

He also desires that they “turn backward,” so that, just as they fell from virtues into vices by performing evil deeds, so they may return from vices to virtues by performing good merits. For the whole punishment is not always forgiven whenever the whole guilt is forgiven. By saying “very swiftly,” moreover, he shows that confession is not to be delayed at all, because a sin not washed away through repentance soon draws another after it by its own weight; indeed, to delay is itself to sin. “You do not know,” says the Lord, “the day or the hour” (Matt. 25). “But woe to those who are pregnant [Col. 1004C] and nursing in those days” (Luke 21). Pregnant women are those who conceal sin conceived in the heart; nursing women are those who foster in deed the sin brought forth. Woe—that is, damnation—shall be theirs in those days.

This can also be understood as spoken not with the desire of one wishing, but in the spirit of prophecy. As though he said: The Lord has heard me, but all my enemies shall be ashamed and troubled—that is, they shall be troubled and ashamed, not indeed in the present, where the wicked mock the good, but in the future, where the wicked, ashamed of themselves, shall say concerning the good: “These are those whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. We fools accounted their life madness and their end without honour. Behold how they are counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints” (Wis. 5). Seeing this, they shall be troubled with dreadful fear and shall be amazed at the suddenness of salvation. They shall be ashamed very swiftly, because “when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, and calamity shall rush upon them unexpectedly” (1 Thess. 5).

But here the end of the Psalm returns to its beginning, because what he asks to be removed from himself at the beginning, he foretells as inflicted upon the reprobate at the end.

## [PSALM II.]

[Col. 1003]

The title of the second penitential Psalm is this: “The understanding of David.”—An explanation of this title.

[Col. 1003D] This title requires no explanation other than the Psalm itself, because in the exposition of the Psalm the title will be expounded, to which the Psalm alludes not only in sense but also in wording, especially where it says: “I will give you understanding [Col. 1005A] and instruct you. Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding.” Its principal subject, however, is the grace and mercy of God. Thus the Apostle, writing to the Romans (ch. 4), takes from it an argument for grace against those who glory in good works and boast of merits, saying that blessedness belongs to the person to whom God credits righteousness, as the Prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.”

It therefore begins with the blessedness of the way and ends with the blessedness of the homeland. It begins with grace and concludes in glory. Thus, while at the beginning of the Psalm it is said, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,” at the end it concludes: “And glory, all you upright in heart.” It is also worth considering that, of these seven Psalms, there are two [Col. 1005B] each of which receives a special title from a weekday, namely the first and third; likewise two each of which has its own title from its contents, namely the second and fifth; again, two each of which bears a distinctive title from history, namely the fourth and seventh. Finally, the sixth alone is read to have a title in common with the other Songs of Ascents.

But since David confesses that he understands beyond the aged (Ps. 118), it certainly appears that this Psalm, which is inscribed “the understanding of David,” contains a profound understanding: namely that of which Truth says, “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6), that is, a spiritual rather than a carnal understanding. For just as the spirit [Col. 1005C] gives life to the flesh, so understanding gives life to the letter, which lies dead without spiritual understanding. Indeed, the Apostle says more: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3).

For David sets forth apparently contrary and conflicting propositions in this Psalm, so that he may kill the carnal and give life to the spiritual understanding. He says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.” If they are forgiven, how are they covered? Or if covered, how forgiven? Again: “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old, while I cried all day long.” If he is silent, how does he cry? Or if he cries, how is he silent? Christ likewise sets forth such sayings in the Gospel: [Col. 1006A] “Whoever loves his soul shall lose it, and whoever hates his soul in this world shall preserve it unto eternal life” (John 12); again: “My teaching is not mine” (John 7); and: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John 9). Thus he draws one away from carnal understanding and attracts one to spiritual understanding, which he received from him who also “gives the cock understanding, the prudence of understanding from of old” (Job 38).

This Psalm has thirteen verses according to our translation, which are referred to the mystery of the Trinity and the Decalogue of the Law, expressing faith and works necessary for blessedness. For “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2), and “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). But according to another translation [Col. 1006B] it has fourteen verses, signifying the Law and the Gospel by reason of the ten commandments of the Law and the four Gospels, so that it may be shown that the understanding possessed by David—that is, by the penitents—in this Psalm both accords with the Gospel and agrees with the Law.

This Psalm is fourfold in structure. In the first part, the penitent first commends in God mercy and grace: grace, by which God freely dissolves the bond of guilt; and mercy, by which he mercifully remits the debt of punishment. He shows what follows from this, namely blessedness. Hence he begins: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven”; and: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.” Second, he reproves in himself negligence and pride: negligence, by which he long kept silent about his sins [Col. 1006C] to evil effect; and pride, by which he long cried out about his merits to evil effect. He shows what followed from this, namely oldness, and adds: “Because I kept silent, all my bones grew old, while I cried all day long.” Third, he intensifies the vengeance upon himself, because the hand of the Lord has grown heavy upon him; and his misery, because he was turned into affliction. He shows what follows from this, namely suffering, because the thorn is fixed in him. Hence it is further added: “For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; I was turned in my misery, while the thorn is fixed.”

Thus, commending grace and mercy, he begins:

## Exposition of Psalm 31, which is second in the order of the penitential Psalms

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005D] “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31).

Of blessedness, one kind belongs to the way and another to the homeland. Of the former we read: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118); of the latter it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 38). The blessedness of the way consists in faith; the blessedness of the homeland consists in sight. The former consists in hope; the latter in possession.

Of the former it is prefaced: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, [Col. 1006D] and whose sins are covered.” Of the latter it is added: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit.” Therefore, in speaking of the former, which belongs to the present way, he uses the present tense: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.” But in speaking of the latter, which shall belong to the future life, he uses the future tense: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.”

There is, moreover, divine blessedness, which is supreme and eternal, and worldly blessedness, which is false and fleeting. The former belongs, as the Apostle says, to the one “blessed and mighty” being, “who alone possesses immortality” (1 Tim. 6). [Col. 1007A] The latter belongs to the person who abounds in temporal goods, of whom the Prophet says: “They called blessed the people to whom these things belong” (Ps. 143); but “those who call you blessed deceive you.”

Some sins are original, which are contracted; others are actual, which are committed. Of original sins he says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven”; and of actual sins he adds: “Whose sins are covered.” Further, he distinguishes actual faults into sins of thought, speech, and action. Of sins of thought he first says: “Whose sins are covered”; of sins of action he adds: “Blessed is the man [Col. 1007B] to whom the Lord will not impute sin”; and to sins of speech he attaches: “And in whose mouth there is no deceit.”

The passage may also be distinguished differently, so that the three kinds of sin are understood: original, venial, and mortal. Of original sins he says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven”; of venial sins he adds: “And whose sins are covered”; of mortal sins he adds: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.” He says that original sins are forgiven, venial sins covered, and mortal sins not imputed to the blessed man, thus subtly and wisely marking the distinction among them.

For original sin is also called *iniquitas* (“inequity”), so that the word *iniquitas* denotes the privation of equity. Equity is that the son should not bear the iniquity of the father, nor [Col. 1007C] the father that of the son, but that the soul which sins should itself die (Ezek. 18). Yet children do not commit original sin, but contract it from their parents, and nevertheless are damned for it, so that they may say: “Our fathers ate a sour grape, and the teeth of the children were set on edge” (Jer. 31). Since original sin is punished contrary to such equity, it is plausibly called *iniquitas*, although its punishment is just for another reason.

Original sin is intense in a person when it exists in that person both with respect to guilt and with respect to act: guilt referring to the stain, and act to the tinder. But in one who has been baptized, the stain is cleansed while the tinder remains; for guilt passes away while the act remains. It is therefore forgiven after [Col. 1007D] baptism, whereas before baptism it was intense. For although it is not destroyed with respect to the tinder, it is nevertheless destroyed with respect to the stain, so that through it a person is no longer bound to guilt, but is exercised for struggle.

Venial sin is found not only alongside vices, but is committed even alongside virtues; for a person endowed with virtues often commits venial sin. But when a person is stripped of virtues, then he is made naked, because virtues are the garments of the soul; and on one who is naked a stain is seen which is covered when he is clothed. Therefore, when someone is clothed with charity, which is the wedding garment, venial sin exists beneath it as though covered, so that it is, as it were, harmless; because [Col. 1008A] what a drop of water does in a furnace, a venial offense does in charity; just as a slight stench is not perceived amid a sweet fragrance.

Therefore those are blessed with the blessedness of the way whose iniquities have been forgiven, whose original faults have been mitigated or weakened in baptism, so that they do not rule in this mortal body. For although they have not been destroyed with respect to the tinder of sin, because of the act which remains, nevertheless they have now been destroyed with respect to the stain, because the liability has passed away. Likewise, those are blessed with the blessedness of the way whose venial sins are covered—that is, veiled by the covering of charity—because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV), namely venial sins. Their multitude is so great that even those who are perfect in this life cannot be wholly without them; but they are covered by charity, [Col. 1008B] so that those formed by the beauty of charity are not shown ugly through them.

This may especially be understood of sins of thought, which, not proceeding into action, are covered in the heart by the shade of grace. Or, without distinction, “forgiven iniquities” may be understood as “covered sins,” which in baptism are covered just as the Egyptians were covered in the Red Sea—which was a figure of baptism. The Egyptians, pursuing the Hebrews, signified sins pursuing virtues; and these two are mutually opposed. For just as the Red Sea covered and destroyed the Egyptians, so the water of baptism covers and destroys original guilt.

Covered sins may also be understood differently: since what is covered is not seen, those sins are covered from God which are not seen by him. For God’s seeing sins is the same as punishing them, as is said elsewhere: [Col. 1008C] “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. L). But God did not choose to regard the sins which he chose to cover; and what is not regarded by God—that is, what is not seen—is not punished by him, since for him to see sins is the same as to punish them. Hence he adds consequently: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.”

Or “iniquities” are those things which precede faith and baptism, while “sins” are those which follow faith and baptism. The former, like a debt freely remitted, are remitted without any satisfaction, because baptism remits both guilt and punishment. The latter are diligently covered through the pursuit of satisfaction, lest they be revealed at the judgment, in which “the hidden things of hearts” [Col. 1008D] will become manifest (1 Cor. IV), and the things hidden in darkness will be disclosed: so that what is covered here may be uncovered there, and what is uncovered here may be covered there. For if you cover, God uncovers; and if you uncover, God covers.

Or iniquity, sin, and deceit may be distinguishedly referred to the offense which a person commits against God, the fault which he commits against himself, and the injury which he commits against his neighbor, according to what is said elsewhere: “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity” (Ps. CV). Therefore:

> Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute [variant: *has not imputed*] sin,  
> and in whose mouth [variant: spirit] there is no deceit.

Mortal sin is sometimes forgiven both with respect to guilt and with respect to punishment; at other times it is forgiven with respect to guilt, but not wholly [Col. 1009A] with respect to punishment. Now punishment is twofold: temporal and eternal. Whenever mortal guilt is forgiven, eternal punishment is also forgiven; but sometimes mortal guilt is forgiven while temporal punishment is not forgiven—for example, if contrition is not so great that it suffices for the removal of both. Thus temporal satisfaction is frequently imposed upon the penitent.

For although Nathan said to David, “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Kings XII), he had nevertheless foretold: “You have slain Uriah the Hittite with the sword and taken his wife as your wife; therefore the sword shall not depart from your house for ever” (ibid.). Since to impute is also to hold someone liable to punishment, sin is not imputed when one is not held for punishment—that is, when it is forgiven in such a manner that punishment is entirely remitted. This will surely occur when “this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality” (1 Cor. XV); for then God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there will no longer be mourning, crying, or any pain, because former things have passed away (Apoc. XXI).

Or, in the past tense: that man is blessed to whom the Lord has not imputed sin—that is, who has guarded himself against criminal sin, which the Lord imputes for eternal punishment. Therefore he has not imputed sin to him, because he forgave his iniquities and covered his sins. But because one to whom sin will not be imputed in the future is not always blessed in the present—for he may now have mortal sin which will eventually be forgiven through repentance—he consequently adds: “And there is no deceit in his mouth.” As though he said more plainly: That man is blessed, if not yet by sight, nevertheless by faith, to whom the Lord will at last not impute sin unto punishment, and in whose mouth there is now no deceit—that is, no excuse concerning sins. For he now, as a penitent, truthfully confesses his sin in order to obtain pardon, so that he does not excuse himself but accuses himself. Such was Nathanael, of whom the Lord said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John I); and that humble tax collector who said to the Lord: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII).

For deceit is in the mouth of one who proclaims himself righteous when he is unrighteous. He makes himself free from this deceit who does not excuse his own transgression, but, as one truly penitent, truthfully confesses [Col. 1009D] his own sin. Another translation has, “there is no deceit in his spirit,” that is, in his heart. For there is deceit in the heart, deceit in the mouth, and deceit in deed. Of the first it is said: “All day they devised deceits” (Ps. XXXVII); of the second: “He spoke peaceful words deceitfully” (1 Macc. I); of the third: “Usury and deceit have not departed from her streets” (Ps. LIV). Yet all proceed from the heart; thus, to remove them all, he says that there is no deceit in his spirit.

Yet deceit is sometimes taken in a good sense, according to the Apostle’s words: “Being crafty, I caught you by deceit” (2 Cor. XII). That deceit is of fraud; this, however, is of prudence. Likewise there is evil feigning, of which it is said: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from what is feigned” (Wis. I); and good feigning, of which it is said: “Jesus [Col. 1010A] pretended to be going farther” (Luke XXIV). There is also evil simulation, of which Solomon says: “One who dissembles with his mouth deceives his friend” (Prov. II); and good simulation, by which David pretended to be mad before Achish, king of Gath (1 Kings XI). The Lord too overlooks human sins for the sake of repentance.

Therefore it is not enough for a person to refrain from sin so that God may not impute it to him for punishment, unless he does this with purity so as to obtain eternal glory. For even the hypocrite turns away from evil for empty glory; yet he is not blessed, but altogether unhappy, because there is deceit in his spirit—that is, the fraud of pretense. Therefore blessed is, or will be, the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin, and in whose mouth or spirit there is no deceit. But:

> [Col. 1010B] Because I kept silence, all my bones grew old [variant: *he does not have, all*],  
> while I cried out all day long.

It is a striking statement: that the same person both kept silence and cried out all day. But he kept silence about his crimes, which he could rightly have cried out; and he cried out about his merits, which he could rightly have kept silent. He kept silence about his crimes in order to conceal them, and cried out about his merits in order to boast of them. He was silent about what would have profited him, and cried out about what would have harmed him. Thus he both kept silence badly and cried out badly; and so the penitent inserts: “Because I kept silence, all my bones grew old, while I cried out all day.”

He speaks by comparison with a person who conceals a wound from a physician. It becomes chronic for this reason: because it is not treated; and it is not treated because it is concealed. For just as pus collected beneath the skin increases swelling and pain until, brought out through an opening, the swelling and pain are relieved, so the rottenness of sin, gathered in the hiding-place of the heart, inflates and disturbs the soul until it is expelled through confession, and the distress of inflation and disturbance is wholly alleviated. Certainly from this not only is the spirit made cheerful, but the body also rejoices, so that it feels itself relieved after having previously been weighed down by a great burden.

Although one must generally keep silent from every harmful word, one must not keep silent from confession of sin, as is said here: “Because I kept silence, my bones grew old”; nor from the praise of God, as is read elsewhere: “If people were silent, the stones would cry out” (Luke XIX); nor even from rebuke of iniquity, as the prophet says: “Woe is me, because I kept silent, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa. VI). [Col. 1009C] Nor from preaching the truth, as the same prophet testifies: “For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest” (Isa. LXII)—unless perhaps those who hear are dogs or swine, of whom Truth says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII). Hence the Psalmist said: “I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was dumb and humbled, and I kept silence even from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII). Therefore Solomon says: “There is a time for keeping silence and a time for speaking” (Eccl. III).

Certainly that Pharisee kept silence while crying out, who, having gone up to the Temple to pray, suppressed his sins and expressed his merits: “I give you thanks, Lord,” he said, “because I am not like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.” But the tax collector, standing at a distance, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII). Behold, the tax collector was silent about his merits and cried out about his sins. Therefore, as the Lord testifies, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other (ibid.).

I also kept silence with my mouth by concealing my offense, while I cried out in deed by repeatedly committing sin. For the cry of sin rises up when the ungodly person repeatedly commits what he has done, according to the Lord’s words: “The cry of Sodom rises before me” (Gen. XVIII). In vain does anyone strive to conceal what he does not cease to repeat. Yet some glory when they have done evil and exult in most wicked matters (Prov. II), proclaiming their sin like Sodom.

There are many kinds of cries, both good and evil, which are read in the divine Scriptures; but all are referred to three: cries of heart, mouth, and deed. Of the cry of the heart the Psalmist says: “I cried to you when my heart was in anguish” (Ps. LX). And the Apostle: “In which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII). Of the cry of the mouth the Psalmist says: “I cried to him with my mouth, and rejoiced beneath my tongue” (Ps. LXV). And the prophet: “Cry out; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. LVIII). Of the cry of deed the Lord says: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry that has come to me” (Gen. XVIII). And elsewhere: “Your brother’s blood cries out to me [Col. 1009D] from the earth” (Gen. IV).

What resulted from both silence and crying out, he adds and says: “All my bones grew old while I cried out all day.” The bones are the soul, namely its inner powers. For just as the outward person—that is, the body—fails in strength when it grows old, so every strength of the inward person—that is, the soul, which the bones signify (because just as bones are beneath the flesh and support it, so the soul is beneath the body and governs it)—fails through the old age of sin. But because affliction gives understanding, he adds:

> Because your hand was heavy upon me day and night,  
> I was turned in my misery while the thorn is driven in.

[Col. 1010A] Day and night are understood in many ways in Scripture: as light and darkness, whence: “God called the light day, and the darkness night” (Gen. I); prosperity and adversity, whence: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they will not cease to praise the name of the Lord” (Isa. LXII); truth and ignorance, whence: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII); prudence and simplicity, whence: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII); justice and iniquity, whence: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world; but if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because light is not in him” (John XI). Nights and days are understood in many other ways as well, of which it would take too long to provide examples one by one.

But in this place day and night may mean brightness and darkness, so that the sense is this: “Because your hand”—that is, your correction—“was heavy upon me day and night,” that is, openly and secretly; “it grievously afflicted me,” after the manner of a wise physician whose hand, when necessity requires, burns and cuts in order to cure and heal. Therefore, in this misery—that is, this severe affliction—I turned to you, my physician, while the thorn of fear and reason is driven into the mind, so that the pricked conscience may hasten toward salvation. For the higher part of reason, called *synderesis*, always pricks and stimulates—that is, opposes and murmurs against sin—while “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V), although in this conflict reason often yields to sensuality.

Yet the thorn may be understood as guilt, which pricks, wounds, and makes bloody. It pricks in thought, wounds in consent, and makes bloody in action; for blood is brought outward when guilt, signified by blood according to the words, “Blood touched blood” (Hos. IV), proceeds to an outward act. Thus the sense is: “Because your hand”—that is, your vengeance—“was heavy upon me day and night,” that is, continually; “it grievously afflicted and struck me; I was turned in misery,” that is, I was made miserable, unhappy, and wretched, “while the thorn is driven in,” that is, while guilt is brought as far as consent and action. For then the thorn is driven in when it inflicts a wound.

Or, according to another reading: “While [Col. 1010B] the thorn is driven in,” that is, while pride is humbled. Pride raises the heart in the spirit just as a thorn raises the body in the back; its breaking humbles not unto destruction, but raises unto salvation.

There are, then, thorns which prick and thorns which fortify, and these are good. There are also thorns which choke and thorns which destroy, and these are evil. The thorns which prick are fear of God and worldly adversity. Of the former it is said: “I was turned in my misery while the thorn is driven in”; of the latter we read: “Behold, I will hedge up your ways with thorns” (Hos. II). The thorns which fortify are the diligence of care and the example of virtue. Of the former it is said: “Hedge your possession with thorns”; of the latter we read: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclus. XXVIII). The thorns which choke are worldly occupations and unlawful impulses. Of the former we read: “The thorns sprang up together and choked it” (Luke VIII); of the latter it is said: “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Gen. III). The thorns which destroy are mortal sins and heretical perversities. Of the former it is said: “Thorns and thistles spring up in the hands of a drunkard” (Prov. XXVI); of the latter we read: “Do they gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles?” (Matt. VII). Therefore the ways of the righteous are without stumbling-block, but “the path of the wicked is like a hedge of thorns” (Prov. XV); and: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song II).

Certainly many things show the penitent to be burdened: the strength of the burdener, when he says, “Your hand”; the greatness of the burden, when he adds, “was heavy upon me”; the constancy of the burdening, when he adds, “day and night”; the weakness of the burdened person, when he says, “I was turned in misery”; and the sharp point of the heaviness, when he adds, “while the thorn is driven in.” Now the hand of the Lord performs various offices toward us. At times it creates: “Your hands made me and formed me” (Job X); at times it threatens: “Still your hand is stretched out” (Isa. V); at times it strikes: “The hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX); at times it protects: “He protected me under the shadow of his hand” (Isa. XLIX); at times it bestows: “You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” (Ps. CXLIV). It follows:

> [Col. 1010C] I made my offense known to you,  
> and I did not cover [variant: *hide*] my injustice.

In this second part he commends his confession, showing it to be perfect, cautious, humble, discerning, devout, and effective. Perfect, because he confesses offenses (*delicta*) and confesses sins: “I made my offense known to you.” Cautious, because he confesses not by accidental chance but by firm purpose: “I said, I will confess my injustice to the Lord.” Humble, because he does not glorify himself by excusing sin, but humbles himself by accusing himself: “I will confess against myself.” Discerning, because he does not recount another’s offense but declares his own guilt: “I will declare my injustice.” Devout, because he does not declare it indifferently to just any person, but reverently declares it to God himself: “I will declare it to the Lord.” Effective, because he did not declare it in vain but to great profit: “And you forgave the iniquity of my heart.” Therefore: “I made my offense known to you, and I did not cover my injustice.”

Here [Col. 1013C] is written *diapsalma* [a psalmic pause]. For having first treated of grace, through which iniquities are forgiven and sins covered so that they are not imputed for punishment; secondly, of guilt, through which sins are passed over in silence and merits cried out, whereby the bones grow old; and thirdly, of punishment, according to which the hand of the Lord becomes heavy and the thorn is driven in, whereby the sinner is turned in misery—he now, as though dividing and distinguishing, explains the grounds of each, prudently beginning from the [Col. 1010D] middle in order to connect the extremes more fittingly.

As though he had said more plainly: “Because I kept silence, my bones grew old while I cried out all day. Therefore I made my offense known to you and did not cover my injustice; but I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart. And because those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered are blessed; and because blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit: therefore every saint will pray to you for this in an opportune time. Yet in a flood of many waters they will not draw near to you. And because your hand was heavy upon me day and night, I was turned in my misery while the thorn was driven in. Therefore you are my refuge from the pressure which surrounded me, my exultation; deliver me from those surrounding me: because you spare and heal, you kill and make alive, you lead down to hell and bring back” (1 Kings II). Therefore: “I made my offense known to you, and I did not cover my injustice.”

There is a covering of nature, a covering of Scripture, a covering of grace, a covering of repentance, a covering of conscience, a covering of guilt, and a covering of Gehenna. Of the first: “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (Matt. VI); and: “You will change them as a covering, and they shall be changed” (Ps. CI).
