Of the second: “The Gospel is covered among those who perish” (1 Cor. IV); and: “Curtains were made to cover the tabernacle of God, of hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, in embroidered work” (Exod. XX). Of the third: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV); and: “You have covered their sins” (Ps. LXXXIV). Of the fourth: “I covered my soul in fasting” (Ps. LXVIII); and: “Let those who seek evils against me be covered with confusion and shame” (Ps. LXX). Of the fifth: “A vessel which has no cover is unclean” (Num. XIX). Of the sixth: “They are covered in their iniquity and ungodliness” (Ps. LXXII). Of the seventh: “I shall go and not return to a land dark and covered with the gloom of death” (Job X).

There is besides a covering of corruption, of which we read: “Worms shall cover them” (Job XXI); a covering of confusion, of which it is said: “Let them be covered with their confusion as with a double garment” (Ps. CVIII); a covering of death, of which it is written: “The shadow of death has covered us” [Col. 1011A] (Ps. XLII); and a covering of adornment, of which it is said to Lucifer: “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. XXVIII). From these, a similar and proper distinction may be drawn in regard to what was said above about covered sins.

A distinction is made between an offense (*delictum*) and sin (*peccatum*): an offense consists in omitting, sin in committing. For an offense is failing to do what ought to be done, and sin is doing what ought not to be done. Negligence belongs to offense, because it omits what ought to be done; injustice belongs to sin, because it commits what ought not to be done. Therefore, because this penitent had offended by keeping silence and sinned by crying out, he now says: “I made my offense known to you,” because he offended by keeping silence; “and I did not cover my injustices,” because I sinned by crying out—openly showing that the penitent must confess offenses and sins alike, since sometimes an offense is more serious than a sin. Thus in Leviticus (ch. VII) it is distinctly commanded that sacrifice be offered for an offense and for a sin.

But you will say: Since God knows all things, even before they happen, as foreknowing all and aware of each thing, why does this penitent say to God, “I made my offense known to you,” as though it had first been hidden from God and afterward, through his confession, had become known to God? It must therefore be understood that sometimes one who knows makes something known to one who knows; sometimes one who does not know, to one who does not know; sometimes one who does not know, to one who knows; and sometimes one who knows, to one who does not know. For when two people know something but one discloses his conscience concerning it to the other, then one who knows makes it known to one who knows. But when two people are ignorant of the same thing, yet the one who does not understand says it to the one who immediately understands it on hearing it, then one who does not know makes it known to one who does not know. The other two cases may be understood from these two.

Therefore the penitent is said to make his sin or offense known to God when, through confession, he opens his conscience about it to God, so that what he formerly wished concealed he now strives to confess [variant: *to reveal*]. Therefore, lest anyone wrongly understand his statement that he had made his offense known to God as though God had not known it until the penitent himself revealed it, he adds by way of clarification: “I did not cover my injustices, but said: ‘I will confess’”—showing that making an offense known to God is the same thing as not concealing injustice but rather confessing it. Thus he says: “I did not cover my injustices, but rather uncovered them so that you might cover them; I disclosed them so that you might conceal them; I acknowledged them so that you might forgive them.” And therefore:

> [Col. 1015B] I said: I will declare [variant: *confess*] my injustice against myself to the Lord,  
> and you forgave the iniquity of my heart [variant: *my sin*].

There is the confession of a sinner, the confession of one who praises, and the confession of one who affirms. Of the first James says: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. V). Of the second the Lord says: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. II). Of the third John says: “He confessed and did not deny, and confessed: ‘I am not the Christ’” (John I). In each of these ways some confess well and some badly.

David confessed well: when he said, “I have sinned,” he immediately heard: “And the Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Kings XII). Judas confessed badly: when he said, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood,” he immediately went away and hanged himself with a noose (Matt. XXVII). Likewise, those confess well who say: “We will confess to you, O God, we will confess, and call upon your name” (Ps. LXXIV). Those confess badly of whom it is said: “They will confess to you when you do them good; but if they are not satisfied, they will murmur” (Ps. XLVIII). Again, those confess well of whom it is said: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Luke XII). But those confess badly of whom it is said: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Tit. I).

These things are necessary for a sinner, if one truly penitent is to be justified by the Lord: namely, that he turn and withdraw from evil—“I was turned in my misery while the thorn was driven in”—because through the evil of punishment I withdrew from the evil of guilt; that he be pierced and grieve over what he has committed—“the thorn is driven in”—because conscience is pricked through repentance; that he recognize and confess offenses in his heart—“I made my offense known to you, and I did not cover my injustice”; that he resolve to declare his sin with his mouth—“I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord”; and thus forgiveness of sins is present—“You forgave the ungodliness of my heart.”

He does not say in the past tense, “I declared,” and in the future, “You will forgive”; rather, conversely, he says in the future, “I will declare,” and in the past, “You forgave,” in order to show plainly that sin is forgiven by God through compunction of heart before it is declared by a person through confession of the mouth. Hence it is clear that this must not be understood of the inward confession made to God in the heart, without which sin is never forgiven, but of outward confession made by the mouth to a person, namely a priest, which very often follows forgiveness of sin.

But perhaps you object: Why, then, is it necessary to confess sin if it has already been wholly forgiven? Certainly, lest it return through contempt, because it is commanded and may not be passed over: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. V). It is also commanded in Leviticus that a man whose skin displays a variegated color come to a priest and show himself to him (Lev. XIII). This indicates that confession of sin, signified by leprosy, must be made to a priest. The same thing is suggested by the command that a calf be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle and slain before the Lord (Lev. IV). After guilt has also been forgiven, satisfaction is necessary; and no small part of it is the shame of embarrassment which the sinner endures in confession.

I said in my heart: “I will confess with my mouth.” “I said” is in the past tense because speaking in the heart precedes forgiveness of sin. Therefore I said, not as one improvident and careless, or by accidental chance, but as one provident and diligent, with deliberate purpose—that is, I considered, decided, and resolved this: “I will confess.” But against whom? Against myself. To whom? To the Lord, before his vicar, namely the priest. What? My injustices, committed by myself. Why? Because you alone can forgive sins, and you forgave the iniquity of my heart. For although some iniquity is committed through an act of the body, it is principally committed through the affection of the heart, according to Truth’s words: “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are what defile a person” (Matt. XV). Therefore he calls mortal sin the ungodliness of the heart.

Moreover, some certainly confess sin, yet not against themselves, because they cast it back upon a neighbor, the devil, or God, like the first parents. Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.” Eve too replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Gen. III). Others ascribe it to fate, event, or nature, like certain heretics who falsely maintain that there are two natures in a person: one good according to the spirit, which they say is from the good God, author of light; the other evil according to the flesh [variant: *body*], which they say is evil and from the evil god, prince of darkness. Or like others who falsely say that all lower things occur from the disposition of the stars, which they call constellation; while others, altogether foolish, assert that everything happens by chance. Yet all agree together in vanity, because they destroy freedom of choice, although for falling into ruin a person is sufficient to himself: he alone can cast himself down; but, once broken by the fall, he cannot rise alone through himself and needs the help of another.

Therefore let him say: “I am the one who sinned; I am the one who acted foolishly. But you, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you”—even when I consented to one who urged me, whom I ought to have resisted. Hence this penitent rightly says: “I will declare my injustices to the Lord.” As if he said: Not another’s, but my own; for although they are sometimes suggested by another, they are nevertheless always done with one’s own consent.

Yet beware prudently lest you confess your own sins in such a way as to reveal another’s. Perhaps, in confessing adultery, you might betray the woman with whom you committed that adultery; for you must confess not another’s injustices but your own. But you will say: What if the sinner cannot express the circumstances of the fault without identifying the person—for example, if a son has committed detestable incest with his mother? He must then do what he can to express his own guilt while suppressing another’s offense. But he must not so suppress another’s offense that he fails to express his own guilt, especially before a suitable priest, namely one who is discerning and honorable, who can be of help and cannot do harm.

Therefore, sinner, however burdened you may be by crimes, do not hesitate or fear to confess them to the Lord, as though, having confessed, you must be condemned in judgment for being convicted; for it is otherwise in divine judgment than in human judgment. Whoever accuses himself before God, God excuses him; whoever excuses himself before God, God accuses him. In human judgment, when the accused confesses a sin, the judge is informed; but in divine judgment, when the accused confesses sin, God forgets it. For “at whatever hour the sinner turns back and groans, I will remember none of his iniquities any longer,” says the Lord (Ezek. XVIII). In that judgment, when the accused confesses sin, he is condemned; but in this judgment, when the accused confesses sin, he is absolved. Therefore he says: “I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart.”

Therefore declare your iniquities so that you may be justified (Isa. XLIII), because “the righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII); and: “Whoever conceals his crimes shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. XXVIII). So David, when he said: “I have sinned,” immediately heard from Nathan the prophet: “The Lord has taken away your sin from you” (2 Kings XII). Hence another rightly cried to the Lord: “I will confess to you, Lord, because you were angry with me; your wrath has turned away, and you have comforted me” (Isa. XII).

But not every confession is of this kind. There is the confession of one despairing wretchedly, like Judas, who said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood,” but went away and hanged himself with a noose (Matt. XXVI). Cain also said to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve pardon for”; and he went wandering and fugitive over the earth (Gen. IV). There is the confession of one deceitfully pretending, like Saul, when he said to Samuel: “I have sinned, because I have transgressed the words of the Lord, fearing the people; but now, I pray, bear my sin.” Samuel said to Saul: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you” (1 Kings XV). And there is the confession of those lamenting to no purpose, like those who will say such things in hell: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us. What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow, and we were consumed in our wickedness, because the hope of the ungodly is like down which the wind scatters in a storm” (Wis. V). But the humble and true confession is salutary—the kind of which he immediately adds:

> [Col. 1018B] For this every saint shall pray to you in an opportune time.  
> Yet in a flood of many waters they shall not draw near to him.

In this third part he commends the forgiveness of sins, through which the ungodly person is justified and the unjust person sanctified. He distinguishes between the Lord who sanctifies and the servant who has been sanctified; between the cause of sanctifying and the time of sanctification, when he says: “For this every saint shall pray to you in an opportune time.” For it is sufficiently clear who prays: every saint, namely the sanctified servant; to whom he prays: to you, namely the sanctifying Lord; why he prays: for this, that is, for the remission of ungodliness, which is the cause of sanctification; and when he prays: in an opportune time, that is, in the present life, which affords the opportunity for sanctification.

Accordingly, a twofold benefit of holiness is added: one in the future, because “in a flood of many waters they shall not come near him,” that is, the holy man; and the other in the present, because the holy man says to the Lord, “You are my refuge from the distress that has surrounded me.” As though he said: In the future you will deliver [him] from anguish, and in the present you will protect the holy man from oppression. Therefore for this—that is, for remission of sin, or for the removal of ungodliness—every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time, because no one is so holy in the present life as to be wholly without sin. For “if we say that we have no sin,” [Col. 1018D] “we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Therefore anyone in this life, however holy, needs remission of sin; and hence every holy person will pray to you for this at an opportune time—that is, while there is an opportune time for sins to be remitted, namely, the present life. For this reason it is said elsewhere: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55); for “the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144). “While you are still speaking,” he says, “I will say: Behold, I am here” (Isa. 52). For in the other life he prays fruitlessly who does not pray profitably in this life, like that rich man buried in hell who cried: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and [Col. 1019A] cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.” Abraham said to him: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented” (Luke 16). “And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you.” Likewise the foolish virgins cried, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us”; to whom the Lord replied: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

But although every holy person prays to you for this at an opportune time, those who are in a flood of many waters—that is, in the flow of fleshly pleasures, concerning which it is written, “Stolen waters are sweeter than others” (Prov. 9)—or in the confusion of diverse sects, of which it is said, “He who lets out waters is the beginning of strife” (Prov. 17), shall not come near [Col. 1019B] to him, that is, to God—namely, to you, with a change of person—as is read elsewhere: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3). For such persons are unworthy to approach the Lord. Or the waters themselves shall not come near him, that is, the holy man, because “many waters cannot quench love” (Song 8), just as the waters did not come near Noah in the flood (Gen. 7); for at the judgment the holy man will at last be free from punishments and distresses. As though he said: Although in this age the holy man is not without every fault, and therefore prays for this, that is, for remission of ungodliness, yet in a flood of many waters they shall not come near him; for then utter confusion will not hold him. Alas, how many are drowned, [Col. 1019C] plunged down, and submerged in these floods! Therefore one must cry out with the Prophet: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground; I have come into the depths of the sea, and the tempest has submerged me” (Ps. 68).

Now “flood” is not understood only in an evil sense, according to the words, “I will destroy all flesh with the waters of a flood” (Gen. 6), which must be understood of mortal sin or the final judgment; but also in a good sense, according to the words, “The Lord dwells in the flood” (Ps. 28), which must be understood of the sacrament of human regeneration or of the depth of the divine ordering. For water is understood in many ways in the divine Scriptures: there is water of nature, doctrine, wisdom, grace, [Col. 1019D] fault, punishment, and misery. Of the water of nature it is read: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1), and: “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148). Of the water of doctrine it is said: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17); but there is water of perverse doctrine, concerning which it is read: “He who lets out waters is the beginning of strife” (Prov. 17). And there is water of sound doctrine, of which it is said: “Divide your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5); nevertheless, perverse waters can be healed, according to the words: “I have healed these waters, and there shall be no more death or barrenness in them” (4 Kings 2). Of the water of wisdom it is read: “The water of saving wisdom shall give him drink” (Ecclus. 15), said in contrast with worldly wisdom, concerning which the command is given: “You shall not eat anything of it raw, nor boiled in water, [Col. 1020A] but roasted only with fire” (Exod. 12). Of the water of grace the Lord says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). Of the water of fault Jacob said to Reuben: “You have been poured out like water; you shall not increase” (Gen. 49). Of the water of punishment it is said: “We have passed through fire and water, and you have led us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65). Of the water of misery it is read: “Waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68). And these miseries or distresses are not only temporal and passing, but also unending and perpetual, concerning which it is read: “They were submerged like lead in mighty waters” (Exod. 15); and: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job 24). Moreover, the Holy Spirit himself is called water, whence: [Col. 1020B] “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7). Spiritual understanding: “Fill the jars with water” (John 2). Baptism: “And blood and water flowed from Christ’s side” (John 19). The people: “Many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 19); and: “All melt away like waters that do not return” (2 Sam. 14). It follows:

> You are my refuge from the distress [otherwise: *my refuge from tribulation*] that has surrounded me;  
> my exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.

Sometimes oppressors press upon a person, and oppressions obstruct him; sometimes oppressors do not press upon him, but oppressions obstruct him; and sometimes oppressions do not obstruct him, but oppressors press upon him. [Col. 1020C] For those who are weak, even if oppressors do not press upon them, oppressions nevertheless obstruct them, because they easily succumb to adversities. For those who are strong, even if oppressors press upon them, oppressions nevertheless do not obstruct them, because they resist adversities stoutly. But for those who are of middling strength, when oppressors press upon them, oppressions obstruct them. Therefore, because it is difficult to be in the fire and not burn, the holy man prays to be delivered not only from oppressions but also from oppressors, when he says: “You are my refuge from the distress that has surrounded me; my exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.” As though he said: Deliver me from my oppressions, because you are my refuge from the distress which has surrounded me; but also redeem me from those surrounding me—that is, deliver me from my oppressors [Col. 1020D].

Certainly, the four principal virtues surround the mountain of the holy man: justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude. For he has justice in front, prudence behind, temperance at the right, and fortitude at the left. The places accord well with the virtues: for what is in front is certain; what is behind is doubtful; what is at the right is prosperous; and what is at the left is adverse. In matters that are certain, justice must be exercised; in doubtful matters, prudence must be employed; in prosperity, temperance is needed; and in adversity, fortitude is necessary. Therefore, when iniquity bears down upon justice, oppression presses from the front; when folly bears down upon prudence, oppression presses from behind; when excess bears down upon temperance, [Col. 1021A] oppression presses from the right; and when faint-heartedness bears down upon fortitude, oppression presses from the left. But when diverse oppressions assail all these virtues at once, then they surround the mind on every side. Therefore the holy man prays to be redeemed from those surrounding him, that is, to be freed from the oppressions which threaten from every direction.

The penitent offers this one petition alone in this psalm, weighty and fruitful, containing within itself the implied meaning of many petitions. He leaves it rather to be understood than judges it necessary to distinguish it, so that it may be referred to the understanding of which he states beforehand in the title: “The Understanding of David.” Yet some fail and become sad amid oppressions, while others make progress and rejoice, like the apostles, of whom it is said: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were accounted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” [Col. 1021B] (Acts 5). Hence the Apostle James says: “Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into diverse temptations” (James 1); and Paul says: “Rejoicing in hope, not failing in tribulations” (Rom. 12). Therefore, that the holy man may show that he has not failed but has made progress amid oppressions, he inserts and says: “My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me”; that is, you, O God, in whom and concerning whom I exult amid oppressions, redeem me from those surrounding me.

“Redemption” is sometimes used broadly for deliverance effected even by gift alone. Hence: “He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy and gathered them from the regions” (Ps. 106). And again: “He delivered them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of their enemies.” Sometimes it is used properly for deliverance effected by a price being given. Hence: “We were redeemed, not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb” (1 Pet. 1); and elsewhere: “You have redeemed us, Lord, in your blood” (Rev. 5). Sometimes redemption also means the Redeemer himself, as the Apostle says that Christ was made for us wisdom and redemption (1 Cor. 1). And the Psalmist says: “The Lord sent redemption to his people” (Ps. 110).

The price of redemption was given to the king, that he might free the captive from the tyranny of his jailer. It was given to the Lord, that he might free man from the devil’s power, the slavery of sin, and the punishments of hell. Hence: “I redeemed them, and they themselves spoke lies against me” (Hos. 7). “He himself shall redeem [Col. 1021D] Israel from all his iniquities” (Ps. 129). “Awaiting also the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8). “We await,” he says, “the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3); he who has delivered us from the gates of death and from the hand of hell. Therefore redeem me from those surrounding me—from the devil, sin, and hell—because you are my refuge from oppression. O pious, O merciful, O good God: I must flee from you to you—from you when angry to you when appeased; from you offended to you propitious; from you as judge to you as father. For if I wished to flee, I could not escape; if I wished to hide, I could not be protected, since there is no one who can deliver from your hand. “For where shall I go from your Spirit, or where [Col. 1022A] shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138). Therefore you, and no other, are my highest and supreme refuge from the oppression that has surrounded me—that is, from the tribulation which unsettles me on every side. “Upon you I was cast from the womb, from my mother’s belly; you are my protector; in you is my song always.” If you are present, nothing will harm; if you are absent, nothing will help. It follows:

> I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall walk;  
> I will fix my eyes upon you.

In this final part he commends understanding, which is the second among the gifts, and concerning which the title is inscribed: “The Understanding of David.” Two talents are necessary for a human being: understanding and action. Discipline is necessary for understanding, while [Col. 1022B] perseverance is necessary for action. These four things are noted in this first verse: understanding, when it says, “I will give you understanding”; discipline, when it adds, “I will instruct you”; action, when it continues, “in this way in which you shall walk”; perseverance, when it concludes, “I will fix my eyes upon you.” Further, concerning the first talent, two things are fitting: the teachableness of the pupil and the teaching of the master. Of the former it says beforehand: “I will give you understanding,” so that you may be teachable in learning. Of the latter it adds: “I will instruct you,” so that teachableness may advance toward learning. Likewise, for the second talent, two things are necessary to one walking in the way of good work: the left foot of fear, so that through fear of punishment he may turn away from evil; and the right foot of love, so that through love of justice he may strive toward good. But because a man’s ways are not in himself, and the steps of a man are directed by the Lord [Col. 1022C] so that he may persevere in good to the end (Jer. 10), the Lord promises help and says: “In this way in which you shall walk,” turning the foot of fear away from evil and stretching the foot of love toward good, “I will fix my eyes upon you”—namely, the eye of correction, so that through scourges I may call you back from evil, and the eye of consolation, so that through benefits I may draw you toward good. Of these eyes it is said elsewhere: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33). For by these eyes all things are naked and open, because “his eyes are like a flame of fire” (Rev. 1). Yet he is said to have not merely two eyes, but seven, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.

There are two things that impede discipline: pride [Col. 1022D] and stupidity. The proud, because of arrogance, refuse to learn; and the stupid, because of imprudence, cannot learn. The proud man is denoted by a horse, the stupid by a mule, from which he dissuades them when he says: “Do not become like the horse and mule, which have no understanding.” He then shows how such persons must be restrained and chastised, adding: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle.” “Many are the scourges of the sinner.” Therefore the horse—that is, the proud person—must be bridled, lest through arrogance he run too far; and the mule—that is, the stupid person—must be scourged, lest through imprudence he wander too far and thus not come near you to know, venerate, and worship you. One must fear, but not despair; for although “many are the scourges of the sinner,” [Col. 1023A] as he says beforehand, “Constrain with bridle and bit the jaws of those who do not come near you,” nevertheless mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord. Hence he also adds: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart.” For many indeed are the scourges of the sinner, because they not only punish outwardly in the body but also torment inwardly in the heart. For “by the things through which a man sins, by those same things he is tormented” (Wis. 11). But mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord, granting strength in the present and salvation in the future. Therefore, “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous,” on account of the robe of the body; “and glory, all you upright in heart,” on account of the robe of the soul; for you shall receive double things from the hand of the Lord (Isa. 40). Therefore rejoice in body and exult in heart, according to the words: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” [Col. 1023B] (Ps. 83).

The holy man had prayed to be delivered from those surrounding him; and God, hearing his prayer, immediately answered the one praying: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall walk; I will fix my eyes upon you.” Against those surrounding him who besiege the roads in order to seize and destroy travelers, he promises a twofold aid: instruction and support, so that by instruction they may avoid the errors of the roads and by support repel the assaults of enemies. To instruction belongs what is said beforehand: “I will give you understanding,” so that you may know that all good things proceed from grace; “and I will instruct you,” lest perhaps you wander by ascribing them to your own merits [Col. 1023C], but may ascribe wholly to divine grace whatever good you recognize that you possess, and not to your own merits. Certainly, one who thinks and believes otherwise is foolish and goes astray; and such error impedes the right understanding by which one comes to true blessedness. “I will instruct you” through the anointing of the Spirit, which teaches concerning all things: the Spirit of truth, who teaches all truth (John 16), teacher of teachers and master of masters. To support belongs what is added: “In this way in which you shall walk,” that is, in the course of the present life, “I will fix my eyes upon you,” that is, I will give you firm protection and guardianship. For we are accustomed to look carefully at that which we earnestly wish to guard. Therefore, because you lift your eyes to me, I too will fix my eyes upon you. Having received understanding and been instructed by God, the penitent now turns to the proud and stupid, who boast of their merits and defend their sins:

> Do not become like the horse or mule, which have no understanding.

The horse is understood both in a good sense and in an evil sense. The good horse is the body of Christ; hence: “A white horse, and he who sat upon it was called faithful and true” (Rev. 19). The horse is an angel or any holy person; hence: “The armies that are in heaven followed him upon white horses” (ibid.). The horse is a preacher; hence: “Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with neighing?” (Job 39). The horse is a righteous man; hence: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord will grant victory” [Col. 1024A] (Prov. 21). The evil horse is a lustful man; hence: “Their emission is like the emission of horses” (Ezek. 23). The horse is an imprudent man; hence: “I will take horses from your midst” (Mic. 5). The horse is the proud man; hence: “These in chariots and those on horses, but we shall be exalted in the name of our God” (Ps. 19). The horse is the arrogant man; hence: “The horse is deceitful for salvation; in the abundance of his strength he shall not be saved” (Ps. 32). The horse is soft and weak; hence: “Those who mounted horses slept” (Ps. 65). And: “Biting the horse’s hoofs, so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. 49). Further, there are red, black, and pale horses, which Ezekiel, Zechariah, and John saw: tyrants, heretics, and hypocrites. Therefore, do not become like the horse and mule. [Col. 1024B] He does not say “like the ox,” because it is sufficiently humble, nor “like the dog,” because it is exceedingly sagacious, but “like the horse,” which signifies the proud because it walks stiff-necked with its neck stretched out, and the mule, which signifies the stupid because it is improvident and defective.

But in Tobit (ch. 6), the horse and mule signify the lustful, Raphael bearing witness: “Those,” he says, “who enter marriage in such a way as to exclude God from their mind and devote themselves to their own lust, like the horse and mule which have no understanding—the demon has power over them.” Or by the mule, which is begotten but does not beget, is signified the ungrateful person, who receives grace but does not return it. Such proud and arrogant persons stretch out their neck against God, attributing to merits what should be attributed to grace; they are as stupid and senseless as those saying: “Our lips are our own; who is our lord?” (Ps. [Col. 1024C] 11). Therefore they have no understanding humbly to know the truth, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). Or by the horse is understood one who carries the devil as rider, and by the mule one who bears the burden of sin; and such persons have no understanding because they do not wish to understand in order to do good, but meditate iniquity in their beds. But you, O God:

> Constrain with bit and bridle their jaws,  
> those who do not come near you.

Because the bit (*chamus*) is that part of the bridle which is put into a horse’s mouth, and every part is smaller than its whole, the greater and lesser restraint may fittingly be signified by bit and bridle. By these the jaws of such persons—that is, pride and stupidity—are constrained, lest they glory in their merits. For by greater and lesser afflictions the mouths which proclaim merits and keep silent about sins must be beaten down and restrained: the mouths, that is, of those who do not come near you through humble confession, but withdraw from you through proud boasting. And because the more the horse and mule are fattened, the more gravely they become insolent, their fodder must sometimes be restricted to restrain their wantonness. Therefore he says: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle”; and the scourge must be applied. Hence he says: “Many are the scourges of sinners.” For jaws and mandibles are named from chewing, [Col. 1025A] and certainly cannot chew when constrained with bridle and bit. So arrogant and ungrateful people commonly grow proud and insolent because of the soundness of their bodies and abundance of possessions; but to restrain their wickedness they must sometimes be checked by the bridle of illness and the bit of poverty, so that vexation may give them understanding. Hence it may soundly be understood thus: “Do not become like the horse and mule,” that is, do not be proud and insolent as arrogant and ungrateful people are, who have no understanding. But you, O God, who know how to apply a remedy to each evil, constrain their jaws—that is, restrain the arrogance of the proud—with bridle and bit, that is, through loss of possessions and harm to persons. Behold, those who do not understand are compared to horse and [Col. 1025B] mule, as is said elsewhere: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48). But because those who cannot be restrained by a bridle ought to be corrected by a scourge, he adds and says:

> Many are the scourges of the sinner,  
> but mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord.

There is the scourge of correction, concerning which it is read: “A father corrects the son whom he loves” (Prov. 3). “But he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). There is the scourge of detraction, concerning which it is said: “You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and shall not fear calamity when it comes” (Job 5). The scourge of affliction, concerning which it is written: “I was scourged all the day” (Ps. 72). [Col. 1025C] And the scourge of condemnation, concerning which it is read: “Evil shall not come near you, and the scourge shall not approach your tent” (Ps. 90). Therefore the righteous are scourged, and the unrighteous too; for “many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. 35). But the latter are scourged so that, if they repent, they may be corrected; if they do not repent, they may be condemned. The former, however, are afflicted so that they may be cleansed from evil and proved in good; for what the scourge does to grain and fire to gold, tribulation does likewise to the righteous man.

“Many” are said to be the scourges of sinners because they are scourged outwardly in the flesh and inwardly in the mind; scourged in the present life and scourged in the future life; scourged on account of fault and scourged on account of punishment; scourged by God and scourged by man; scourged by the world and scourged [Col. 1025D] by the devil. Nor could anyone enumerate individually the scourges of sinners. Nor is it surprising if, once the bridle has been applied to an unbroken animal, the scourge is added. Would that it may thus be tamed completely! For it must be feared lest, by resisting too much, it be left untamed and so wander along the broad way that leads to death (Matt. 7). But mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord—not in the world, in grace and not in merit—that is, it will be present in all things for salvation: in every place and every time, in every cause and every undertaking, in certainties and doubts, in prosperity and adversity, in body and heart, in the present and the future. But “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 7). Therefore:

> [Col. 1026A] Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous;  
> glory, all you upright in heart.

Among those who hope—the righteous and upright—three ranks are indicated: beginners, those making progress, and those who have attained. Mercy is given to the first: “Mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord”; joy to the second: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous”; but glory to the third: “Glory, all you upright in heart.” The righteous rejoice, and the unrighteous also rejoice, but the righteous rejoice in the Lord while the unrighteous rejoice in the world. The unrighteous exult in carnal and worldly things; the righteous in virtues, the unrighteous in vices. Of the former it is read: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their dwellings” (Ps. 49); of the latter it is said: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” [Col. 1026B] (Prov. 2). Yet the joy of the righteous is blessed and perpetual, according to the words: “Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full”; and: “No one shall take your joy from you” (John 16). But the joy of the unrighteous is unhappy and momentary. Thus it is said: “They take up the tambourine and harp and rejoice at the sound of the organ; they spend their days in good things and in a moment descend to hell” (Job 21). The man who said, “My harp has been turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of weepers” (Job 30), knew this; for sorrow occupies the end of joy (Prov. 34). Therefore one must rejoice in those things which pertain to merit or reward, grace or glory, virtue or salvation. Such were the things in which those rejoiced to whom Christ said: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 1). And the prophet said: “But I will glory in the Lord and rejoice in God my Jesus” (Hab. 3). On account of these two joys—one possessed from merits, the other from rewards—the Psalmist doubles the expression when he says: “Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you righteous.” The Apostle also repeats this, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4). Nor must the righteous merely rejoice; they must also glory. Hence it adds: “And glory, all you upright in heart.” You, namely, who can say with the Apostle: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). Therefore let each person prove his own work, [Col. 1026D] and then he shall have glory in himself and not in another. For the hypocrite seeks glory in another and not in himself, and his glory is like “the flower of hay” (1 Pet. 1), which flourishes today and is cast into the oven tomorrow (Matt. 6). Thus every hope of the hypocrite shall perish, because he hunts false glory among human beings and does not seek true glory with God. For that is upright which is not twisted by any crookedness, but is directed toward God with pure intention.

Behold, having treated punishments and faults at the beginning, he concludes with glory and exultation at the end—a pattern he observes in this, as in the other penitential psalms.

## [PSALM III]

[Col. 1027]

The title of the third penitential psalm is as follows: “A Psalm of David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath.” — Explanation of this title.

[Col. 1027A] From certain passages of Scripture it is manifestly understood that *Sabbath* means both “seventh” and “rest”; hence it is fittingly written that God rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished (Gen. 1). There are, however, three Sabbaths, outward and higher: namely, temporal, spiritual, and eternal. Of the first it is read in the Gospel: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed” (John 5). Of the second the Apostle says: “A sabbatism remains for the people of God” (Heb. 4). Of the third it is written through the prophet: “There shall be Sabbath after Sabbath” (Isa. 66). The first Sabbath is a sacrament and not the reality. The last, however, is the reality and not a sacrament. The middle one is both reality and sacrament. For the first signifies and is not signified; the last is signified [Col. 1027B] and does not signify; the middle is both signified and signifies.

Therefore in this psalm the penitent treats of the remembrance of the middle and final Sabbath, that is, the spiritual and eternal Sabbath, recalling the rest of both: the one he had lost, and the other which he had forfeited through sin. Hence he said: “There is no health in my flesh because of the face of your wrath; there is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins” (Ps. 37). For he incurs affliction of mind and body from sin, since the worm of conscience gnawed his mind inwardly, while the sting of suffering pricked his body outwardly. Hence he treats in turn of faults and punishments, amplifying his misery in many ways. These things compelled him frequently to recall in his mind, lamenting, both the Sabbath lost through sin and the Sabbath of eternity forfeited [Col. 1027C]. For as water is sweet after thirst and shade pleasant after heat, so rest is delightful after labor—especially tranquility of mind, which the righteous person possesses even amid bodily distresses. Of it the Lord said to the apostles: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace—[Col. 1028A] not as the world gives do I give it to you” (John 14). This is indeed a peculiar fountain in which no stranger shares. The penitent pants for it after sin all the more ardently insofar as he himself, when righteous, had tasted it more sweetly.

This psalm, according to the translation observed by the Roman Church, has three sets of seven verses—that is, twenty-one verses—which are not unreasonably referred to the three Sabbaths mentioned above. For Sabbath signifies not only the seventh day, but also a week of days and any day of the week. The seventh day: “Remember to sanctify the day of the Sabbath” (Exod. 20). A week of days: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke 18). Any day: “Very early, on one of the Sabbaths” (Mark 16). [Col. 1028B] Seven days pertain to the temporal Sabbath; seven virtues to the spiritual Sabbath; and seven endowments to the eternal Sabbath: three of the glorified soul—knowledge, love, and delight—and four of the glorified body: brightness, subtlety, agility, and impassibility. Each day of the week has its proper praises in the titles of psalms drawn from the Sabbath, except the third, whose reason I have explained elsewhere as best I could. Here Sabbath is used for rest, according to the words: “It is a Sabbath of rest, and the rest of the Sabbath is sanctified to the Lord.” In the temporal Sabbath the Jew rests; in the spiritual Sabbath the righteous person rests; and in the eternal Sabbath the blessed person rests: the first from the accomplishment of work, the second from committing sin, and the third from the deficiency of corruption [Col. 1028C]. Therefore, through the repentance which he shows that he has for faults, and the patience which he shows that he has in punishments, he sets himself before others as an example, that they may imitate him as another Job, violently afflicted and grievously tormented.

### Elucidation of the Third Penitential Psalm

[Col. 1027]

[Col. 1027D] “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger [otherwise: *in your fury*], nor correct me in your fury [otherwise: *in your anger*]” (Ps. 37).

This psalm has four parts. In the first, the penitent directs his prayer to God, asking to be delivered from the punishments of hell when he says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger” [Col. 1028D]; and also from the punishment of purgatory when he adds: “Nor correct me in your fury.” Having offered this prayer, he first describes the punishments he endures; secondly, the sins he committed; thirdly, the miseries he has incurred. As though he said: I am the one who endures many and great punishments: namely, the wound of a blow, [Col. 1029A] the weight of oppression, affliction of the flesh, and vexation of the mind. The wound of a blow, because “your arrows have been fixed in me.” The weight of oppression, because “you have strengthened your hand over me.” Affliction of the flesh, because “there is no health in my flesh because of the presence of your wrath.” Vexation of the mind, because “there is no peace in my bones because of the presence of my sins.” Nor is this surprising, because I am the one who committed great and grievous, foul and foolish sins. Great, because “my iniquities have passed over my head”; grievous, because “like a heavy burden they have weighed me down”; foul, because “my scars have putrefied”; foolish, because “they have become worse because of my folly.” Therefore I am the one who has incurred continual and prolonged, bodily and spiritual miseries. Continual, because “all day long I went about sorrowful” [Col. 1029B]; prolonged, because “I have been afflicted with miseries and disturbed unto the end”; spiritual, because “my soul has been filled with delusions”; bodily, because “there is no health in my flesh.”

Thus, having prefaced his words with prayer, he cried to the Lord, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.” Some will pass through fire and be saved; others will pass into fire and be condemned. Those who pass through the fire of purgatory will be saved; of them the Apostle says (1 Cor. 3) that they “will be saved, yet so as through fire.” For “the fire will test what sort of work each person has done.” Those who pass into the fire of hell will be condemned; to them the Lord will say: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). [Col. 1029C] For “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66). From each fire the penitent asks to be delivered when he says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

As though he said: Lord, Father and God of my life, do not rebuke me in your anger—that is, do not convict me in the strict judgment in which you will appear angry to the reprobate, when you say to those standing at the left: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink. Inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these least ones of mine, neither did you do it to me” (ibid.). Behold, the reproach of sinners. “Go therefore, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” Behold, the judge’s wrath. And do not merely rebuke me in your anger, [Col. 1029D] but neither correct me in your fury—that is, do not punish me in the fire of purgatory, in which the vehemence of the blaze will be so great that you will seem, as it were, to rage even against the elect, since the least punishment in purgatory is reckoned greater than any punishment whatever in this world. But who can endure that thunderclap of wrath or that lightning-flash of fury? Avoid sin if you wish to escape punishment.

Or the penitent prays that God may inflict punishment not angrily for vengeance, but mercifully for correction, so that the meaning is: Lord, rebuke me, but not in anger; correct me, but not in fury. As though he said: Do not rebuke me in anger, but rebuke me in mercy, because it is written: “God rebukes and chastises those whom he loves” (Heb. 12). Nor correct me in fury, but in gentleness; because [Col. 1030A] “a father corrects the son whom he loves” (Prov. 1). Thus let punishment proceed from mercy toward correction, not from wrath toward vengeance. Indeed, the evils which I suffer in the present ought to suffice, lest I suffer in the future.

“For your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand over me.”

Therefore the blows that I suffer are many, great, and deep: many, because there are “arrows,” not only one but several; great, because the blows are not those of a human being but of God; deep, because “they have been fixed in me,” not outwardly in the skin but inwardly in the heart. The oppressions too are unbearable, because “you have strengthened,” as if with great force, “over me,” as if from a high place, “your hand,” as if strong and mighty.

[Col. 1030B] The arrows of the Lord are divine threats, which are fixed in the sinner’s mind through fear of strict judgment. Thus it is said elsewhere: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118). Hence blessed Job also says: “The arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit, and the terrors of the Lord wage war against me” (Job 6). Therefore “your arrows,” that is, your threats concerning eternal punishments, have been fixed in me like sharp arrows that reach to the inner parts of the heart; and so, struck by fear, I am compelled to cry: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” When such arrows are fixed in a person, they do not kill but give life; they do not lead down to hell but bring one back, because through fear of punishment they restrain the hands from committing sin.

Or the arrows of the Lord are punishments [Col. 1030C] inflicted by God, as is said: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh, and I will fill my arrows upon them” (Deut. 32). “This is the arrow of the Lord’s salvation, and the arrow of salvation against Syria.” These are not the arrows of heretics, of whom it is read: “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10). Nor are they the arrows of the Jews, of whom it is said: “The arrows of little children became their wounds” (Ps. 63). Nor again are they the arrow of the devil, concerning which it is written: “From the arrow flying by day, from the noonday demon” (Ps. 90).

The arrows of the Lord are also divine words, of which one reads elsewhere: “Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44). Again: “Your arrows passed through; [Col. 1030D] the sound of your thunder was in the wheel” (Ps. 76). And again: “Send out your arrows, and you will throw them into confusion” (Ps. 143). Christ and his saints send forth these arrows; they too are called arrows, as it is written: “He made me like a chosen arrow” (Isa. 49); and: “As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of the outcast” (Ps. 126). Therefore “your arrows,” that is, punishments inflicted by you, have been fixed in me; and you have also strengthened your hand over me.

“Hand” is used in seven ways in Holy Scripture. The divine hand is the Son, as in: “I will lift up my hand to heaven”; and: “Send forth your hand from on high” (Ps. 143). It signifies power, as in: “Through the strength of your hand I have failed” (Ps. 38); and: “In your hand are all the ends of the earth” (Ps. 94). It signifies grace, as in: “When you open [Col. 1031A] your hand, all things shall be filled with abundance” (Ps. 103); and: “You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” (Ps. 144). It signifies help, as in: “When the righteous man falls, he will not be dashed down, because the Lord supports him with his hand” (Ps. 36); and: “My times are in your hands” (Ps. 39). It signifies protection, as in: “He protected me beneath the shadow of his hand” (Isa. 49). It signifies operation, as in: “Your hands, O Lord, made me and fashioned me wholly round about” (Job 10); and: “The heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 103).

But here the Lord’s hand is understood as divine vengeance, as in: “Remove your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me” (Job 15); and: “His hand is still stretched out” (Isa. 5). This hand was made firm against Adam, who through the fault he committed incurred the punishment he deserved, [Col. 1031B] as the Lord had threatened him: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2). It has also been strengthened over us, who contract from him both guilt and punishment until the end of life—would that it might not endure without end after that end. He indeed was the origin of miseries; we are their offspring. Thus the penitent says: O God, you have strengthened—that is, heavily aggravated—over me your hand, that is, your vengeance in countless punishments and infinite miseries, which disturb me so greatly that, because of overwhelming pain, I am compelled to cry: “Nor correct me in your fury.” You have strengthened your hand over me so greatly that:

“There is no health in my flesh because of the presence [or: face] of your wrath; and there is no peace in my bones because of the presence of my sins.” [Col. 1031C]

The face of God the Father is the Son, as in: “We have walked in the light of your face” (Ps. 88); and: “May he make his face shine upon us” (Ps. 66). It signifies knowledge, as in: “I have sought your face; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26). It signifies propitiation, as in: “Let my judgment come forth from your face” (Ps. 16). It signifies indignation, as in: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33). It signifies reason, as in: “The light of your face, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4). It signifies kindness, as in: “All the rich of the people shall entreat your face” (Ps. 44). Thus “face” or “countenance” here is taken for the recognition by which each person is known in the face. Anger too is perceived in the countenance, and sin is often denoted by the face, according to the saying:

> Alas, how difficult it is not to betray one’s crime by one’s face.  
> *(Ovid)*

[Col. 1031D] “Flesh” too is understood in many ways in Scripture. For flesh means a human being, as in: “The Word was made flesh” (Luke 24); and: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3). It means a part of the human being, as in: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24). It means animal nature, as in: “One flesh is that of birds, another of fish, and another of beasts” (1 Cor. 15); and: “God gives food to all flesh” (Ps. 135). It means human frailty, as in: “My spirit shall not remain in man, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6); and: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40). It means sensuality, as in: “The spirit desires against the flesh, [Col. 1032A] and the flesh against the spirit” (Gal. 5). It means corruptibility, as in: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (2 Cor. 5). It means a life of pleasure, as in: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). It means legal observance, as in: “Those who wish to please you in the flesh compel you to be circumcised” (Gal. 6). It means earthly consideration, as in: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. 16). It means literal understanding, as in: “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). It means conjugal intercourse, as in: “The two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2). It means woman herself, as in: “They were born not of bloods, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1). It means blood relationship, as in: “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5). It means sin, [Col. 1032B] as in: “When evildoers approach me to devour my flesh” (Ps. 26); and punishment, as in: “Be satisfied with my flesh” (Job 19).

“There is no health,” I say, “in my flesh,” because through sin it has been made subject to the necessity of death; for what can easily be harmed is not sufficiently sound. This is “because of the presence of your wrath,” that is, because of contemplation of your indignation, which through fear of future judgment not only disturbs the mind but afflicts the flesh. And not merely the flesh, which is fragile, but even the bones, which are thought strong; because “there is no peace in my bones,” that is, in the powers of my mind. This is “because of the presence,” that is, because of the recollection, “of my sins,” which disturb the bones: for “a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. 17). “For who has resisted him and had peace?” (Job 9). “The wicked have no joy,” says the Lord (Isa. [Col. 1032C] 48), because “by the things through which a man sins, by those same things he is tortured” (Wis. 2).

But “the righteous is confident like a lion” (Prov. 28), concerning whom it is written: “The lion, strongest of beasts, fears no encounter with anyone” (Prov. 30). The righteous person also remains always undisturbed whatever may occur, because he is neither cast down by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity. He keeps watch joyfully, sleeps peacefully, sits in peace, and rests securely; because all things fear the person who fears God. Having obtained a great reward for his righteousness in the present, he will obtain the greatest in the future.

There is the peace of sinners, the peace of the righteous, and the peace of the blessed. Of the first: “I did not come to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10); and: “I was jealous when I saw the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72). Of the second: [Col. 1032D] “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14); and: “Great peace belongs to those who love your name” (Ps. 118). Of the third: “In peace, in the selfsame state, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4); and: “May the peace of God which surpasses all understanding guard your hearts and minds” (Phil. 4). Moreover, there is a peace common to good and bad alike, of which one reads: “May the good word of the Lord be peace to me, and truth in our days.” Christ himself is also called “our peace,” he “who made both one,” making peace “in one new man”: peace to those who are near and peace to those who are far off (Eph. 2).

Now some have peace neither from sin nor with sin, and these are the best. Conversely, some have peace with sin but not from sin, and these are evil. Others have peace [Col. 1033A] both with sin and from sin, and these are the worst. For those who have been so “given over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1) and “sold under sin” (Rom. 7) that they voluntarily give themselves over to sin and take no concern over sin—such people assuredly have peace with sin, in which they delight sweetly, and peace from sin, by which they are not in the least reproved. Of such persons it is written: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst deeds” (Prov. 2), because “when the wicked man has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). For just as, according to the Apostle, “those who by nature do the things of the law are a law unto themselves” (Rom. 2), so those who freely do the things of sin are sin unto themselves—that is, the cause of sin—so that anything whatever may be permitted to them, while what is permitted does not please them.

Submerged in the depths of iniquity and utterly swallowed up by sin, thinking nothing of punishment and taking no concern over guilt, they have become like “the horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31), going after their own desires. If they are at times scourged so that they may turn back, they do not feel the wounds or heed the blows, as it is written: “They struck me, and I did not hurt; they dragged me, and I did not feel” (Prov. 23). This happens especially when “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who performs wicked deeds is blessed.” Such persons have made a covenant with death, either by faithlessness in not believing or by malice in despairing, stinking in the tomb like a man four days dead (John 2).

But those who commit sin and delight in it, yet are reproved [Col. 1033C] and assailed by it, have peace indeed with sin but not from sin: they delight in guilt, yet are reproved by conscience. Such persons are assailed but do not resist, because they feel the impulses and consent to them, being drawn away and enticed by desire (Jas. 1). They do not dash their little ones against the rock (Ps. 136), but cherish them in their desire, lying and sleeping in the pleasure and foulness of sin, like beasts that rot in their own dung, to whom stench gives off fragrance and bitterness grows sweet.

Conversely, some endure temptations and resist them, resisting the assaults; these have peace neither with sin nor from sin, because they wrestle with it so that sin may not rule in their mortal body. The struggle is indeed hard, but the battle useful; for though it has punishment, it will also have a crown. And the more difficult the conflict, the more glorious the triumph. But those who have conquered temptations, so that not only do they not consent to them but do not even feel them any longer, except perhaps very slight ones which do not disturb the peace of the soul—these assuredly have peace from sin but not with sin, so that they can say with the Apostle: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). For those sinners can truly glory in peace in the Lord whom neither criminal guilt bites nor a seared conscience reproves, because, even if they have perhaps committed grave sins, they have nevertheless entirely washed them away through the worthy fruits of repentance. [Col. 1034A] Therefore, when the Spirit himself now bears witness to their spirits that they are children of God, then they have peace from sin but not with sin, having become true peacemakers, “who shall be called children of God” (Rom. 6): fearful indeed concerning their own affairs, but secure concerning those of others.

It is clear, then, that not to have peace with sin is always good, and to have peace with sin is always evil. Yet to have peace from sin is sometimes good and sometimes evil. Therefore do not have peace with sin; do not form friendship with the serpent, lest through persuasion it infect and kill you with poison. For the poison of sin is deadlier than that of a serpent. The latter kills the body; the former destroys the soul, without which the body does not live. But if, enticed by the body’s concupiscence, [Col. 1034B] you sometimes have peace with sin, take care at least not to have peace from it. For if you have peace both with sin and from sin, you will be reckoned among the living dead. He next shows what is the cause why there is no health in human flesh because of the presence of God’s wrath, nor peace in the bones because of the presence of sins.

“Because my iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down.”

“The head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11); hence: “The head of my beloved is like the finest gold” (Song 5). He is “the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1). The head of the soul is the mind, as in: “You have made my head fat with oil” (Ps. 22). [Col. 1034C] The head of a thing is its beginning, as in: “At the head of the book it is written of me” (Ps. 39). The head of a province is its metropolis, as in: “The head of Syria is Damascus” (Isa. 7). The head of a people is its ruler, as in: “You will appoint me head of the nations” (Ps. 17). The head of the wicked is the devil, as in: “You struck the head from the house of the impious; you laid bare its foundations even to the neck” (Hab. 3); and: “You broke the heads of the dragons; you gave them as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. 73). The head of an evil deed is the devil’s suggestion, as in: “He shall suck the head of the asp, and the viper’s tongue shall kill him” (Job 20); and: “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3). The head of vices is pride, as in: “If he raises his head to the clouds, like dung [Col. 1034D] he shall perish in the end” (Job 20).

Therefore, by the head of the inner person—the soul—is understood the mind or reason. Of this Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head,” that is, faith and understanding are in the mind of the wise. For bodily eyes are also in the head of a foolish man. Upon this head one sort of iniquity is placed: the iniquity committed with fear of God and without an intention of repenting is placed beneath reason, because in it the sinner respects the judgment of reason. But the iniquity committed without fear of God and without an intention of repenting is placed over the mind, because in it the sinner despises the judgment of reason. Both weigh it down, but the former as a moderate burden, the latter as a heavy burden that sinks one into the depths.

And this is what he says: “My iniquities,” which [Col. 1035A] I committed without fear and without the intention of repenting, “have placed themselves over,” that is, have set themselves over my head. Or, according to another reading, “have passed over my head,” that is, they have depressed and despised the reason of my soul. For this reason they “have weighed me down,” not as a moderate burden but as a heavy one that sinks me into the depths of vices. According to the prophet, iniquity is described as sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5), because it does not permit the mind which it presses down to be raised to heaven, but compels it to sink into hell.

Or: “My iniquities have placed over,” that is, in pride they have placed my head—my mind—in pride; they have raised it up in pride. And therefore, because “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14), “they have weighed heavily upon me”: that is, with the mass of punishments they have grievously pressed me down. As though he said: I exalted myself in the spirit of pride, because “my iniquities have passed over my head”; and God humbled me under the weight of punishment, because “like a heavy burden they have weighed me down.”

There is the burden of Christ, the burden of the world, and the burden of the devil: the first is of grace, the second of punishment, the third of sin. Of the first: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11); of the second: “The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amos saw” (Isa. 13); of the third: “Do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day” (Isa. 17). Though it is written: “Each person shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6), the Apostle nevertheless exhorts: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ” (ibid.).

Not only have my iniquities passed over my head, but also:

“My scars have putrefied and become worse [another reading: have become corrupt] because of my folly.” [Col. 1035C]

Something is said to putrefy in many ways: in respect of material, as in the girdle which Jeremiah hid in the Euphrates “putrefied” (Jer. 13); in respect of punishment, as in the Philistines, whose protruding bowels putrefied (1 Sam. 5); in respect of sin, as in: “The beasts have putrefied in their dung” (Joel 1); and in respect of grace, as in: “The yoke has putrefied because of God” (Isa. 10).

A scar is the site of a wound already healed; but here the container is put for its contents, so that by scars in the flesh are meant wounds which, after having been healed, recur—and the later wounds are far worse than the former. So scars in the mind are sins which, after having been forgiven, are repeated, and these are far more serious than the earlier ones. He says, therefore: “My scars,” that is, the sins forgiven me through baptism or repentance, “have putrefied,” that is, they have turned into rottenness because they were repeated so as to incur guilt, which is the rottenness of the mind. Alas, if anyone saw how foul, stinking, and putrid the sinful soul is, it would certainly be more leprous than a leprous body. And “they have become worse,” that is, have become worse through the vice of ingratitude, “because of the presence of my folly,” that is, because of my folly, which appears like a manifest face. For what folly is more evident than for a penitent person [Col. 1036A] to return to sin, “like a dog to its vomit” (2 Pet. 2)? The food the dog eats is unclean, but the vomit to which it returns is far more unclean.

Or: “My scars have putrefied,” corrupting others who have been corrupted by the example of my crime as though by the stench of rottenness; and they have made worse me, who by frequenting sin have become worse, “because of the presence of my folly,” that is, because of the fault of negligence which makes my folly manifest, since I have not employed the powers received in baptism. For what is more foolish than the sinner who both knows the crime and commits it, knowingly hurling himself into death? Certainly, if a brute animal sees a pit, it turns aside from it lest it fall in; and if it happens to encounter some difficulty somewhere, it cannot be brought back there without difficulty. But a human being is always enticed by what is unlawful [Col. 1036B] and continually delights in transgressions.

Therefore, penitent person, beware of repeating sin, lest, because of the vice of ingratitude, the debt already forgiven be demanded of you. “Behold,” he says, “you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5). Take care also not to sin in secret—and still more not to sin openly—for secret sin harms only its perpetrator, while manifest sin harms both the perpetrator and the imitator.

Or: “My scars,” that is, my sins which I repeated after repentance, “have putrefied in me through defect [another reading: effect],” because they have caused me to putrefy—that is, to wither amid the filth of vices—like irrational beasts which, according to the prophet’s testimony, “putrefied in their dung” (Joel 1), and like those whose protruding bowels putrefied (1 Sam. 5). Thus they “have become worse because of the presence of my folly,” that is, because of my folly they have made me worse.

Scars are accustomed to putrefy for two reasons: either because wounds are not perfectly treated or because harmful things are not fully avoided. The person who cuts off sinful acts but does not kill sinful thoughts does not perfectly heal the wounds of sins, since rubbing over the thought easily brings one back to the habit of action. Likewise, the person who does not diligently flee occasions for sinning does not fully avoid the harmful things of vices. Therefore flee a suspect person, a suitable place, a fitting time, and whatever is an occasion for committing sin; for just as it is difficult to be in fire and not [Col. 1036D] burn, so it is difficult to have an opportunity to sin and not sin. It follows:

“I have been afflicted with miseries [another reading: I have been made wretched] and disturbed unto the end; all day long I went about sorrowful.”

Who can recount all the miseries named by this word, when the whole life of a human being is misery? For “a human being born of woman, living a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14). Life is brief, but the miseries with which he is said to be filled are many, so that nothing in him is left empty of misery. Yet by three terms he indicates three kinds of miseries—namely fears, pains, and labours—to which all miseries are referred. As though he said: I have been afflicted through labour, disturbed through fear, and made sorrowful [Col. 1037A] through pain. My miseries are long, because “I have been disturbed unto the end”; they are constant, because “all day long I went about sorrowful”; they are spiritual, because “my soul has been filled with delusions”; and bodily, because “there is no health in my flesh.”

“End” signifies Christ, as in: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10), who says of himself: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1), and of whom it is written: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” It signifies charity, as in: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith” (1 Tim. 1); and: “I have seen an end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118). It signifies fulfilment, as in: “The things written concerning me have their fulfilment” (Luke 22). [Col. 1037B] It signifies extremity, as in: “In the time of the end the vision shall be fulfilled” (Dan. 8). It signifies blessedness, as in: “Death shall be destroyed last; then comes the end” (1 Cor. 15). It signifies perseverance, as in: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end” (John 11); for “the one who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). It signifies a limit, as in: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end and the number of my days” (Ps. 38). It signifies consummation, as in: “The end comes; the end comes upon the four regions of the earth” (Ezek. 7). It signifies damnation, as in: “He shall labour forever and yet live unto the end” (Ps. 48); and: “Their end is death” (Phil. 3).

Therefore, “I have been disturbed unto the end,” that is, until the limit of life—speaking of the future as though it were past—because I am certain that miseries will by no means end before death. For this reason the Apostle cried out: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). “Great travail has been created for all human beings, and a heavy yoke upon all the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40). Would that death were the limit of miseries, lest after death their accumulation increase! For after death miseries in hell will be incomparably greater than those in the world before death: because there will be “a worm that does not die, and a fire that is not extinguished” (Isa. 66). There people “will seek death and not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them” (Rev. 9).

And therefore [Col. 1037D] “all day long I went about sorrowful” into the chamber of my heart, so as to be sad and mournful in secret because of the delay of the Sabbath, on which I desired to pour out my soul before the Lord. This accords with his own saying: “When you pray, enter into your chamber; and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6). Nor did I do this once only, but often; nor superficially, but constantly: because “all day long I went about sorrowful,” until I should finally depart from this life and arrive at that one in which, in the true Sabbath, there will be rest without end. Let those take note who think it sufficient to grieve over sin together and once, returning immediately after groaning to joy and after weeping to laughter, when, on the contrary, to repent is to endure punishment. Therefore “all day long I went about sorrowful.”

[Col. 1038A] “For my soul has been filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh.”

The delusions which a human being suffers in this life are innumerable: surrounded by perverse persuasions, he believes falsehoods instead of truths, does evil instead of good, and abandons heavenly things for earthly ones. For the sake of transient, vain, and frivolous things, he is turned away from divine service, withdrawn from a devout intention, recalled from a holy purpose; and then they begin to mock him, saying: “This man began to build and could not finish” (Luke 14). The world allures, the flesh deceives, and the devil deludes. The world allures through worldly flatteries, the flesh deceives through sensual enticements, and the devil deludes through spiritual deceits. For these are the three deceitful sophists who have surrounded and seduced the miserable soul with their wiles. The world proposes, the flesh assumes, the devil concludes. The world proposes worldly blandishments; the flesh assumes unlawful desires; the devil concludes with everlasting torments. Thus the soul is allured in order that it may be crushed; it is deceived in order that it may be deluded.

A shameful delusion occurs when the devil, ceasing his delusion for a while, deludes all the more, as it is written: “They mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1). For demons mock anyone’s Sabbaths when they withdraw for a time from tempting him, so that, when they perceive that he has carelessly rested from sin, they may bring him back to sinning more shamefully; and so one who had thought himself to have kept a Sabbath is mocked by demons. Therefore the same God-fearing and righteous man prays elsewhere and says: “My God, [Col. 1038C] I trust in you; I shall not be put to shame, nor let my enemies mock me” (Ps. 14). “For all who wait for you shall not be confounded.”

The soul is deluded in many ways, particularly by obscene affections and importunate thoughts.
