When these rush in shamelessly, the soul is scarcely allowed to pray and is rarely permitted to contemplate, while images of bodies arise, carrying and drawing the mind from this to that and from one thing to another. For it is written: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccles. 10), because shameless thoughts destroy devotion in prayer.

What shall I say of those delusions through which the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light (1 Cor. 11), and, by feigning virtues, introduces impiety under the appearance of piety? Certainly no one can express how great [Col. 1038D] is the multitude and magnitude of the delusions suffered by the soul in this world. Hence the penitent says: “My soul has been filled with delusions.” Behold, he declares that the soul is not merely sprinkled, but filled with delusions, in order to show the multitude and magnitude of the delusions. Because of them too there is no health in my flesh, which is defiled by its delusions, especially when it incurs nocturnal emissions in dreams. Do not regard this kind of delusion as slight, for a real effect proceeds from a false cause: though the dream-image is false, the pollution of the flesh is real. Thus Leviticus commands that the man defiled by a nocturnal emission go outside the camp and not return until, before evening, he has washed with water; after sunset he may return into [Col. 1039A] the camp (Lev. 15). “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but one who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6).

Thus, according to another reading, it is said: “My loins have been filled with delusions,” or “with disgrace.” For in the loins is the incentive of lust, according to the saying: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 14); hence the command: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). For there is great delusion and grave disgrace in the pleasure of lust: ardour and wantonness precede it; stench and filth accompany it; pain and repentance follow it. It follows:

“I have been bent over and humbled utterly [another reading: I have been afflicted and humbled exceedingly]; I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”

[Col. 1039B] In the first part he first recalled punishments inflicted by God and then punishments brought upon himself. Concerning the former he says: “Your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand over me”; concerning the latter he adds: “My iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down.” But in this second part he first recalls punishments inflicted by himself and then punishments inflicted by others. Of the former he says: “I have been bent over and humbled utterly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart. My heart has been disturbed within me; my strength has failed me; and the light of my eyes is not with me.” Of the latter he adds: “My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me, and my nearest ones stood afar off. Those seeking my life used violence; those seeking evils for me spoke vanities and devised deceits all day long.” He thereby shows how much he has profited from both. For from the former he has advanced toward the desire for the homeland; therefore he continues and says: “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and like a mute man not opening his mouth. And I became like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.”

Acting, therefore, of the punishments that he suffers, he confesses that he endures from himself a bending of the body and a humbling of the mind; hence: “I am bowed down and humbled altogether.” He suffers the roaring of the mouth and the groaning of the heart; hence: “I roared because of the groaning of my heart.” He suffers weariness of living and a desire to die; hence: “Before thee is all my desire, and my groaning is not hidden from thee” [Col. 1039D]. And at once he assigns the causes of the foregoing. “My heart,” he says, “is troubled within me; my strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes is not with me.” As though he said more plainly: I said that I roared because of the groaning of my heart; and no wonder, because my heart is troubled within me. I said that I am bowed down and humbled altogether; and no wonder, because my strength has forsaken me. I said that all my desire is before thee; and no wonder, because the light of my eyes is not with me. Therefore, because thou, who art the light of my eyes, art not with me, I desire to be before thee, that I may be with thee; and this not falsely, but truly, because my groaning is not hidden from thee. Affliction often gives understanding, because lashes sometimes chastise [Col. 1040A] one whom benefits do not amend. Therefore he says: “I am bowed down and humbled altogether,” that is, in respect of both parts of man: the outward, in the bending of the body; and the inward, in the humbling of the mind. Therefore, through the groaning of a heart inwardly lamenting the multitude, greatness, and foulness of its sins, I roared outwardly with a mournful, plaintive, and confused cry, like a lion roaring for food: because, suffering hunger for good works, I roared with longing for heavenly food, sighing with my whole mind toward the Sabbath of eternity.

Moreover, these words may be referred to the virtue of repentance, so that the penitent says: “I am bowed down in body and humbled in mind,” prostrate in prayer and confession; nor humbled merely, but also “altogether” [Col. 1040B], expressing every circumstance in full, so that I who, in committing sin, raised a proud neck against God may, in confessing sin, bow a submissive mind before God. Further, “I roared because of the groaning of my heart,” wailing with loud cries and groaning with deep sighs; “because before thee is all my desire”: no part of my desire is before thee and another behind thee, so that I express one of my sins in confession and suppress another by concealment, condemn one by accusing it and defend another by excusing it. Rather, all my desire is before thee, because with my final desire I lay open my entire conscience before thee. You may infer this clearly from the fact that “my groaning [Col. 1040C] is not hidden from thee,” before whose eyes all things are naked and exposed.

In Scripture, bending is understood both in a good sense and in a bad. There is a bending of embracing, whence: “Elisha bent himself over the child, and he revived” (4 Kings 4); of adoration, whence: “Joseph’s brothers, bowed down, worshipped him” (Gen. 42); of humiliation, whence: “The loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men humbled” (Isa. 5); of subjection, whence: “May the sons of thy mother bow down before thee” (Gen. 27); likewise, there is a bending of covetousness, whence: “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51); of iniquity, whence: “They prepared a snare for my feet and bowed down my soul” (Ps. 56); of obscenity, whence: “Let thy wife be another man’s harlot, and let others bend over her” [Col. 1040D] (Job 31); and of distress, whence: “The wife of Phinehas bent herself down and gave birth, for sudden pains came upon her” (1 Kings 4).

“Lord, before thee is all my desire, and my groaning is not hidden from thee.”

Behold, he has both the upper and the lower irrigation: the upper, namely the mind’s desire for the goods of the homeland; and the lower, namely the heart’s groaning for the evils of the world. As though he said more plainly: “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccl. 1). Therefore I now desire nothing in this world; rather, all my desire is before thee, that I may stand before thee in the homeland, where there is true rest, full security, supreme sweetness, perfect joy, and everlasting blessedness; where, in the highest good, whatever good is sought [Col. 1041A] is found. Therefore my groaning over the innumerable miseries of this life—which is altogether warfare upon earth—is not hidden from thee: not only because it is known to thee, who beholdest all things and art ignorant of nothing, but also because it is pleasing to thee, who art said in a special sense not to know what thou disapprovest, and to know what thou approvest. Hence: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25); and: “The Lord knows those who are his.” For those things are hidden from God that are unworthy of the divine gaze; hence Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord after sinning (Gen. 3), because whoever does evil undoubtedly hates the light (John 3). And therefore:

“My heart is troubled within me; my strength has forsaken me [another reading: and my power abandons me], and the light [Col. 1041B] of my eyes [another reading: it itself] is not with me.”

He shows that he has incurred anxiety of heart, saying: “My heart is troubled within me,” because of the bitterness of pain; and weakness of body, adding: “My strength has forsaken me,” because of the scantiness of fasts; and dimness of sight, saying: “The light of my eyes is not with me,” because of the abundance of tears. Thus he now brings forth fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. 3). At times a person’s heart is troubled within himself, when, through the pain of compunction, the spirit is saddened and afflicted for itself, according to the words: “I shall recount to thee all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38). At times it is troubled in another, when, through the spirit of compassion, it is afflicted and saddened for another, according to the words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). He says, then: “My heart is troubled within me,” because there is in myself that for which I should grieve over myself, because my strength has forsaken me. For it is written that the righteous exchange their strength, while they lay aside bodily strength and assume spiritual strength; on which account the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12). “And the light of my eyes is not with me,” but rather against me, because “death entered through the windows” (Jer. 9), and “the eye has despoiled the soul” (Lam. 3). Hence those eyes themselves, now pierced by compunction from God, flow with tears, so that their light, as though failing, is not with me.

[Col. 1041D] “My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me, and my neighbours [another reading: who were near me] stood afar off.”

Thus far the penitent has pursued the punishments which he suffers inwardly, namely from God and from himself; now he pursues the punishments which he suffers outwardly, from friends and enemies. For concerning the punishments inflicted by God he had said earlier: “Thine arrows are fixed in me, and thou hast confirmed thy hand upon me”; concerning the punishments inflicted by himself he added: “My iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down.” But now he speaks of punishments he suffers from friends: “My friends and neighbours stood afar off.” Concerning punishments which he suffers from enemies he adds: “My enemies live and have grown strong against me, [Col. 1042A] and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.”

Indeed, when a sinner turns to God through repentance, he encounters more grievous temptations, according to what is written: “My son, when thou drawest near to the service of God, prepare thy soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). Therefore, when he turns to repentance, behold: at the devil’s instigation, friends, relatives, and neighbours rise against him. Hence he says: “My friends and my neighbours drew near,” not, to be sure, for me, to offer me consolation, but “against me,” to inflict harm. Nor merely in passing, but urgently: for they not only approached, but also “stood against me,” namely in order to oppose me. And those who were near me, that is, my neighbours, “stood afar off” [Col. 1042B], denying me every counsel and aid conducive to salvation. The former approached in order to inflict loss; the latter withdrew lest they provide consolation; so that I might be wholly exposed to evils and receive no help at all from the good.

“And they used violence, who sought my soul; and those who sought evils for me spoke vanities and meditated deceits all day long.”

Speaking of the punishments which he confesses he endures from others, he shows them separately: not from enemies, but from friends; not from foreigners, but from kindred; not from strangers, but from neighbours. Because he is unworthy and angered, he endures persecution from these as well as from others. “And they,” he says, “persecute me in many ways: in deed, violently and hatefully, because ‘those who sought my soul used violence’; by mouth, maliciously and deliberately, because ‘those who seek evils for me spoke vanities’; and in heart, incessantly and deceitfully, because ‘they meditated deceits all day long.’ Alas, those who are today accounted friends ought rather to be regarded as enemies: they love the body but hate the soul. Such are these men who, seeing this person turn to God, strive violently to hinder him, seeking his soul not to save it but to destroy it. While they endeavour to draw him back from God’s way and seek temporal goods, they procure spiritual evils, speaking vanity deceitfully when they suggest vain and wicked things to him.

“But I, as one deaf, did not hear; and as one dumb who did not open [another reading: not opening] his mouth.”

[Col. 1042D] There is a good deafness and an evil deafness. Good deafness is to close the ear to wicked counsels and malicious suggestions; hence: “Who made man’s mouth, or fashioned the dumb and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I?” (Exod. 4). “Go, tell John: the deaf hear” (Matt. 2). For those obey God who are deaf to the devil. Evil deafness is to close the ear to sound counsels and divine commands; hence: “Deaf and dumb spirit, go out of him” (Mark 9); and: “Like the deaf asp which stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of the enchanter who charms skilfully” (Ps. 57). Someone is rendered mute at times through prudence; hence: “I became mute and was humbled, and kept silence even from good things” (Ps. 38). At times through patience; hence: “Like a lamb before its shearer, he shall become mute” [Col. 1043A] (Isa. 53). Conversely, someone is rendered mute at times through fear; hence: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56). At times through a seared conscience; hence: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?” But he became mute (Matt. 22). Here, however, dumb and deaf are understood in a good sense. It is indeed a great virtue not to return evil for evil; but it is sometimes a greater one not to return reviling for reviling (1 Pet. 3), since this can far more easily be returned than the former. Yet more perfect patience is neither to take offence nor to offend in word. Therefore, not by repetition but by definition, he adds:

“And I became like a person who does not hear, and who has no rebukes [another reading: reproofs] in his mouth.”

[Col. 1043B] As though he said more plainly: I was not truly deaf and dumb; rather, though I could hear and speak, I became like one who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth, because I did not return reviling for reviling (ibid.). Concerning such rebukes it is written: “Even unto night my reins rebuked me” (Ps. 15). There are also good rebukes, of which it is said: “Rebuke the beasts of the forest” (Ps. 67); and: “Argue, exhort, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4). There are others, of which Scripture says: “May God rebuke Satan in thee” (Zech. 3); and: “He rebuked the Red Sea” (Ps. 15). These words may also be understood in the person of the Head, as though they were Christ’s words, though uttered only with a changed voice: “My friends,” not true friends [Col. 1043C] but false ones, such as those who said in testing him: “Master, we know that thou art truthful and teachest the way of God in truth, and dost not care for anyone. Tell us, therefore: is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22). “And my neighbours,” namely those related according to the flesh, such as those who said: “Depart hence and go into Judaea, that thy disciples may see the works that thou doest.” For even his brothers did not believe in him (John 7). Both these and the others drew near against me, saying before Pilate: “Crucify him, crucify him” (John 19), and stood before Herod persistently accusing me. And those near me, namely the disciples who had lived with me, stood afar off, fleeing through fear of death. For Peter followed afar off (Matt. 26). And those who sought my soul, not to imitate me [Col. 1043D] but to destroy me, used violence by seizing, binding, striking, and spitting upon me. And those who sought evils for me, since they found no crimes, spoke vanities by fabricating false testimony, like those who said: “We heard him say: I will destroy this temple made with hands, and within three days build another not made with hands” (Mark 15); and their testimony was not consistent. And they meditated deceits all day long, that is, frauds, as when they bribed the guards with money to say: “While we slept, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. 28). “But I, as one deaf, did not hear,” because I gave no answer, as though I heard nothing; “and as one dumb, who did not open his mouth,” that what is written might be fulfilled: “Like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” [Col. 1044A] (Isa. 53). “And I became like a person who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth.” Thus, when one of the attendants of Annas struck Jesus, saying, “Is this how thou answerest the high priest?”, Jesus replied, not by rebuking him but by giving a reason: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why dost thou strike me?” (John 18).

“Because I have hoped in thee, O Lord; thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God.”

The third part, in which he says that amid adversities he hopes—a great consolation for the oppressed. For while they hope amid tribulations, they do not fail, believing that they will be delivered by the Lord. The penitent commends in himself the gift of hope, saying: “Because I have hoped in thee, O Lord”; the vow of prayer: “Because thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God”; the judgment of discernment: “Because I said: lest my enemies ever exult over me”; the merit of patience: “Because, while my feet were moved, they spoke great things against me”; the purpose of satisfaction: “Because I am ready for scourges”; the feeling of contrition: “Because my pain is ever before me”; the utterance of confession: “Because I declare my iniquity”; and the diligence of examination: “Because I shall consider my sin.” Yet amid all these things persecutors do not fail me: lively and ready, because “my enemies live”; strong and firm, because “they have grown strong against me”; numerous and diverse [Col. 1044C], because “they have multiplied”; cruel and impious, because “they hate me unjustly”; ungrateful and slanderous, because “those who returned evils to me for goods slandered me.” He also adds the reason why they behave so toward him: “Because,” he says, “I have followed righteousness”; or, according to another reading, “because I was following goodness.” For the unjust persecute the righteous because of righteousness, and evil persons persecute the good because of goodness: as Cain persecuted Abel (Gen. 4), Ishmael Isaac (Gen. 21), Esau Jacob (Gen. 27), Saul David, and the Jewish people the Lord Christ. Therefore he says: “Because I have hoped in thee, O Lord, thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God.” Whoever hopes believes and loves; for unless he believed, he would not hope, and unless he hoped, he certainly would not love. For hope does not confound, that is, it does not permit the person who hopes to be confounded [Col. 1044D]. As is said elsewhere: “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me not be confounded for ever” (Ps. 30). Therefore one who believes and loves rightly hopes to be heard by the Lord. But whoever does not hope does not ask in faith, and therefore does not deserve to be heard, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 2). Therefore he says: O Lord, who changest sorrowful things into joyful and turnest adversities into prosperities: because I have hoped in thee as one ought to hope, I therefore said—not so much with my mouth as with my heart—that thou wilt hear me, that is, hear me unto the desired outcome: Lord God, my creator, redeemer, and saviour; who by creating bestowed nature, by redeeming gave grace, and by saving will confer glory. For then thou wilt most certainly be mine, when thou canst no longer be not mine [Col. 1045A]. I said indeed that thou wilt hear me, and not without reason.

“Because I said: Let not my enemies ever exult over me [another reading: rejoice over me], and, while my feet are moved, they spoke great things against me.”

Above he had not explained what he asked; but now he explains it: because I said this, I asked this, “Let not my enemies ever exult over me,” that is, let me not do that on account of which my enemies may be able to exult over me. As is said elsewhere: “My God, in thee I trust; let me not be ashamed, and let not my enemies mock me; for all who wait for thee shall not be confounded.”

Among the other reasons for which a righteous person guards himself against sin, this is not the least: lest an unrighteous person rejoice and exult over him [Col. 1045B]. For it belongs to enemies to rejoice and exult in the misfortunes of those whom they hate. Therefore I said: “Let not my enemies exult over me,” because, when my feet—that is, my acts—were at some time moved through human weakness, they, according to their wicked custom, spoke against me, namely vehemently insulting words. Thus the impious person rejoices and exults when he sees the righteous shaken, according to the words: “Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved” (Ps. 12). But on the contrary, the godly person is saddened and grieves with the unrighteous when he sees him disturbed, as the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. [Col. 1045C] 2). For the sins of neighbours are a griddle [*frixorium*, perhaps “a scorching affliction”] to the righteous.

A person’s foot is affection, action, and support. Each is twofold, namely right and left. Of the feet of affection it is said: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5); and: “He who has washed does not need except to wash his feet.” Of the right foot: “My foot stood in the straight way; in the churches I will bless thee, O Lord” (John 13). Of the left: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, nor the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 25). Of the feet of action it is said: “He made my feet like those of harts” (Ps. 17); and: “He will preserve the feet of his saints” (Prov. 3). Of right feet: “Their feet are straight” (1 Isa. 69) [citation as printed]. Of left feet: “Their feet run to evil” (Ezek. 1). Of the right foot of support blessed Job says: “I was an eye to the blind [Col. 1045D] and a foot to the lame” (Job 29). Of the left foot of support Truth says: “If thy foot causes thee to stumble, cut it off and cast it from thee” (Matt. 18).

This may also be understood otherwise: although he said, “Let not my enemies rejoice over me,” he may nevertheless not have been heard in this, because, he says, “while my feet were moved, they spoke great things against me” (Ps. 35). God sometimes permits this to happen not without reason: namely, that the righteous person may be moved and fall, because “the righteous man falls seven times in a day and rises stronger” (Prov. 24). For he rises more humble, more cautious, more merciful, like Peter, who, because he answered heedlessly and presumptuously when he said, “Lord, even if I must die with thee, I will not deny thee” (Matt. 26), was permitted to fall, that he might recognize his own presumption, imprudence, and weakness, and learn in himself how he ought to have mercy upon others. Therefore, after the resurrection, when he was questioned by the Lord, “Simon son of John, dost thou love me more than these?”, he answered humbly and cautiously: “Lord, thou knowest that I love thee” (John 21), leaving undecided whether he loved more than the others, and holding certain that he loved him. He who had denied the Lord three times through fear also confessed him three times through love, so that a threefold confession might answer the threefold denial, and his tongue might serve love no less than fear. Thus it became love’s office to feed the Lord’s flock, as it had been fear’s judgment to deny the Lord of the flock. Nor only because I hoped, I said, “Thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God,” but also:

“Because I am ready for scourges, and my pain is always before me [another reading: in my sight].”

He recalls the three things necessary in true repentance: the pain of compunction in the heart, the utterance of confession by the mouth, and the scourge of satisfaction in deed, indicating each by its circumstances. Of the first he says: “My pain is always before me”; of the second: “I declare my iniquity”; of the third: “I am ready for scourges.” For the pain of compunction ought not to be superficial but continual, not light but grave, because to repent is to hold fast to punishment. Hence he joins the words and says: “My pain,” emphatically—that is, that over which I grieve, namely the cause of pain—is always before me, before my face, not behind my back, so that I may always see what I ought to grieve over; and I am ready, prompt and prepared, to receive and endure scourges in satisfaction for sin: not merely to practise fasting, prayer, and almsgiving, but also to undergo bodily discipline through labours, vigils, and other mortifications of the flesh. The penitent knows that the Father scourges every son whom he loves (Prov. 1), and therefore freely offers himself to receive scourges, which, if borne with equanimity, do not kill but give life; do not lead down to hell but bring back; indeed correct, but correct so as to heal; strike, yet in such a manner as to cure. Nor only for the reasons just stated wilt thou hear me, O Lord my God, but also:

[Col. 1046D] “Because I declare [another reading: I shall declare] my iniquity, and consider [another reading: I shall consider] my sin.”

“I declare my iniquity,” that is, I announce it thoughtfully, I confess it discerningly; or, in the future tense, “I shall declare,” that is, I shall confess faithfully. Therefore “I shall consider my sin,” so that by prudent investigation I may find every circumstance of iniquity whatever, which I may be able to confess without any suppression, excuse, or diminution. In this passage those are reproved who, sorrowing for a moment, thoughtlessly confess their sins, unwilling to undergo any but a light penance. But if they carefully considered that, through the remedy of repentance, eternal punishment is exchanged for temporal punishment, they would count nothing difficult which they could endure in any measure for such [Col. 1047A] an exchange. Therefore let the penitent willingly take up the burden of satisfaction imposed upon him, even if it seems difficult, and begin earnestly to bear it. If it perhaps exceeds his strength, let him have recourse to the priest, who, employing discerning moderation, should endeavour to temper it. But because what the scourge does to grain and the furnace to gold, persecution does to the righteous man and adversity to the God-fearing person, he adds:

“My enemies live, and have grown strong against me, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.”

The good always die to the world, because they mortify themselves, as the Apostle says: “I die daily for your glory, brethren” (1 Cor. 12). But the evil live in the world, because they enjoy the prosperity of the world with desire, saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15); not eating in order to live, but living in order to eat. God permits them to live for the testing of the good; and therefore, he says, “they have grown strong against me,” to overcome me by strength, and “they have multiplied against me,” to conquer me by number—those who hate me unjustly, although I have loved them perfectly. Hence:

“Those who returned evils to me for goods slandered me, because I followed righteousness [another reading: I was following goodness].”

There is a fourfold recompense: goods are rendered for goods (Josh. 7), evils for evils, goods for evils, and evils for goods. The Israelites rendered goods for goods to Rahab; Samson evils for evils to the Philistines (Judg. 16); Joseph goods for evils to his brothers; the Jews evils for goods [Col. 1047C] to Christ (Gen. 45; Matt. 27). Everyone is bound to render goods for goods, because of the Lord’s command: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them” (Luke 6). No one is bound to render evils for evils except a judge, because of the precept in the Law: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exod. 21). But to all others it is said: “Do not render evil for evil, nor reviling for reviling” (1 Pet. 3). Every person at least who is perfect is bound to render goods for evils, because the Lord commands: “Do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5). But no one whatever is bound to render evils for goods. Hence, after the Lord had said in the Psalm: “They set evils against me for goods, and hatred for my love,” he immediately added: “Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand” (Ps. 108). From these four distinctions arise four further negative ones: not to render good for good, and this is evil; not to render evil for evil, and this is good; not to render good for evil, and this is evil at least for the perfect; and not to render evil for goods, and this is good for all.

God, insofar as he is Father, renders both goods for goods and goods for evils, according to what is written: “The heavenly Father [Col. 1048A] causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5). But insofar as he is judge, he renders not only goods for the good, but also evils for evils, because he renders to each according to his works (Matt. 6). Hence he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32). Lucifer, however, insofar as he is Satan, renders not only evils for evils but also evils for goods, because he returns hatred for love to his Creator, as is written of him and his members: “The pride of those who hate thee rises ever against thee” (Ps. 73).

Moreover, both goods and evils are in part temporal and in part everlasting. They stand in such relation that, for temporal goods, both temporal and everlasting goods are rendered, according to the words: “Whoever leaves father or mother, house or field for my sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” [Col. 1048B] (Matt. 19). Likewise, for temporal evils both temporal and everlasting evils are rendered, because sinners “are clothed, as with a double garment, in their own confusion” (Pss. 34, 108). Of temporal matters it was said: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exod. 28). But of everlasting matters it will be said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; therefore, depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

Likewise, for everlasting goods both everlasting and temporal goods are rendered. For God will glorify the elect perpetually, and the elect will glorify the Lord perpetually, according to what is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in thy house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise thee” (Ps. 83). But concerning temporal goods it is written that labourers work in the vineyard for a denarius, giving temporal things for eternal ones; as also the man of whom it is written that, having found one precious pearl, he gave all he possessed and purchased it (Matt. 13). Likewise, for everlasting evils both temporal and everlasting evils are rendered. For the Lord will condemn the reprobate perpetually, and they will hate him perpetually, as was said: “The pride of those who hate thee rises ever” (Ps. 73). Hence it is also written: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66), hatred and punishment accompanying each other in hell. For everlasting punishments, moreover, the obstinate will blaspheme God in the present life, since, if—as it is written—people blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it became exceedingly great (Rev. 16), they will blaspheme him much more vehemently when they hear that the punishment of Gehenna is to be inflicted upon them eternally by the Lord himself, thereby rendering him such recompense as they can.

For temporal evils, both temporal and everlasting goods are rendered. For Christ bestowed both grace in the present and glory in the future upon those who crucified him, for whom he prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). But for temporal goods which people misuse, at least by occasion, though perhaps not by cause, not only temporal evils but also everlasting ones will be repaid [Col. 1049A]. For goods of this kind aggravate mortal guilt and the punishment of Gehenna. Therefore the Lord says: “Woe to you, lawyers, who took away the key of knowledge: you yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11). As though he said: From this there will be woe to you, that is, eternal damnation: that you bore the key of knowledge, which is good in itself, in an evil manner.

These things, however, have been said more in disputation than as assertions. Therefore, because the subject is sufficiently disputable, authority should not prejudice reason. For how will human beings hate and blaspheme God in the future if, as it is written, they will say within themselves, repenting and groaning in distress of spirit: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone for us. We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked difficult paths; but the way of the Lord we have not known. What has pride profited us? Or what has the boasting of riches brought us? Those things have passed away like a shadow and like a messenger running ahead; and like a ship which passes through the heaving water, after it has passed no trace can be found, nor the path of its keel amid the waves; or like a bird flying through the air, of whose course no sign is found, but only the sound of wings beating the light wind; and, cutting the air by the force of its course, it flew through with wings set in motion, and afterwards no sign of its course is found,” and so forth; “but we have been consumed in our wickedness” (Wis. 5). If, then, they will repent of hatred and blasphemy, just as they are said to repent of boasting and wickedness, how then will they hate and blaspheme the Most High?

Yet because of the bitterness of punishment they will repent of the past evil whereby they deserved to incur such punishment. They will not, however, repent only of the evil then present, by which they will hate God more vehemently because of the bitterness of punishment, when they expect no remedy from him. That God renders everlasting evils for temporal evils ought not to be imputed to him as injustice, because, although they are temporal as regards the act which passes away, they are nevertheless everlasting as regards the guilt which remains and the hatred which endures. Therefore God justly punishes the reprobate eternally, because he finds them eternal enemies; and he himself justly decreed to punish them in his own eternal punishment, since they presumed unjustly to offend him [Col. 1049D].

Although all slanderers are hateful to God (Rom. 1), those who slander anyone precisely because he has followed righteousness [Col. 1050A] and follows goodness seem to persecute the grace of the Holy Spirit in him, and thus in a certain manner to sin against the Holy Spirit. Those who prefer free choice to grace know this: that, according to the Prophet, righteousness does not follow a person, but the person follows righteousness; for the grace of God goes before, so that good action may follow.

“Do not forsake me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me. Attend to my help, O Lord, God of my salvation.”

The final part, in which the penitent implores divine aid, lest he fail among so many and such great persecutors, asking not only not to be abandoned but also to be helped. For God forsakes a human being and departs from him in two ways: when he withdraws protection, abandoning [Col. 1050B] him to punishment; hence he says, “Do not forsake me, O Lord my God”; and when he withdraws grace, abandoning him in guilt; hence he adds, “Do not depart from me.” In the first manner the Father forsook the Son on the cross, whence he cried: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Ps. 21). Thus God at times forsakes one by whom he is in no way forsaken. For Job, abandoned to punishment, did not abandon innocence. In the second manner the Lord forsakes the sinner, as is written of Saul, who feared David because the Lord was with David and had departed from Saul (1 Kings 18). Thus the Lord forsakes only those who forsake him. Of them it is written: “They have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters” (Jer. 17).

But God forsakes some for a time: “For a little while I have forsaken thee.” Others he forsakes forever: “My zeal has departed from thee” (Isa. 54). Therefore, do not forsake me, who, abandoned by all, am left to thee alone; lest I fail amid persecutions and persecutors so many and so great; and lest, after pardon has been granted me, I offend thee. For as relapse is more grievous after recovery, so offence is more grievous after pardon. But if thou forsakest me for an hour, do not nevertheless depart from me forever; rather, attend to my help, to deliver and protect me, O Lord God, giver and preserver of my salvation, so that thou who helpest me in the present may also save me forever. A joyful conclusion, after the manner of the other penitential [Col. 1050D] Psalms, which always end in joy.

[PSALM IV.]

[Col. 1049]

### Elucidation of the Fourth Penitential Psalm

The title of this psalm is as follows: “For the end. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” — Explanation of the same title.

[Col. 1049D] This title is clear from the well-known history in the Second Book of Kings (chapter XII). But it should be carefully noted that this psalm is fiftieth in the order of the Psalms and contains twenty verses. Twenty is an abundant number, and, when its parts are added together, it makes two tens, which signify the twofold transgression: because eleven exceeds the Decalogue of the Law but does not attain the apostolic number of twelve. David composed this psalm particularly on account of the twofold transgression [Col. 1051A] which he committed, namely adultery and homicide.

Moreover, five are the additive parts of twenty. One, which refers to the first and to unity, signifies original sin. Two signifies the two kinds of actual sins, distinguished into venial and mortal sins. Four signifies the four ways of sinning: through frailty or incapacity; simplicity or ignorance; security or negligence; and malice or envy [otherwise: distinction]. Five signifies the five bodily senses through which one sins: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Ten signifies the ten transgressions of the Decalogue which, as has been said, a person commits by sinning.

[Col. 1051B] Since, moreover, the jubilee was the fiftieth year in the Law (Leviticus XXV), in which debts were forgiven and alienated possessions restored, this psalm, foremost among the penitential psalms [Col. 1052A] and placed in their midst, fittingly occupies the fiftieth place among the psalms: for through penitential humility, or humble repentance, of which this psalm principally treats, sins that have been committed are forgiven and lost goods are restored.

Through him God gave the Jews the law of Scripture on the fiftieth day (Exodus XX), and on the fiftieth day gave the apostles the law of grace (Acts II)—not as that law was written on tablets of stone, but in human hearts by the finger of God (II Corinthians III). Fifty is produced by adding together the parts of forty, because through penitential satisfaction, signified by forty, the special number of satisfaction, the grace of the Holy Spirit at work brings full forgiveness of sins. Hence this psalm is used in the Church more often than the others, and by its power very many are converted to repentance.

### Exposition of the Fourth Penitential Psalm, Which Is Fiftieth in the Order of the Psalms

[Col. 1051]

[Col. 1051B] “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

This psalm is divided into five parts, suitably distinguished in their respective places. In the first part, therefore, the penitent magnifies his own fault and implores divine mercy, which he asks to be shown to him in three ways: namely, that the iniquity of the heart may be blotted out—hence, “Blot out my iniquity”; that he may be washed from the injustice of the mouth—hence, “Wash me from my injustice”; and that he may be cleansed from the fault of deed—hence, “Cleanse me from my sin.” Therefore: Have mercy on me, O God, because you can have mercy and have the means by which to show mercy.

Indeed, you can show mercy, since your mercy is great; hence: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” And you have the means to show mercy, since your acts of compassion are many (Psalm CVIII); hence: “According to the multitude of your acts of compassion, blot out my iniquity.” You ought also to show mercy, because I confess my sin by acknowledging it and detest it by assailing it; hence: “I know [Col. 1051D] my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.” And you know upon whom you should have mercy, because I sinned while you were present and seeing; hence: “Against you I have sinned, and I have done evil before you.”

Since the righteous person is the accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech, this penitent, desiring to be justified, magnifies his faults at the outset, showing that his sins are great, many, foul-smelling, and ugly; that he sinned not only once but often, and not in one manner only. It is as though he said: “My sins are great, O God; therefore have mercy on me according to your great mercy. My sins are many, O God; therefore according to the multitude of your acts of compassion blot out my iniquity. My sins are foul-smelling and ugly; therefore wash me and cleanse me. [Col. 1052B] I sinned not merely once but often; therefore wash me still more. Nor did I sin in only one fashion, but in many; therefore cleanse me, not only from injustice, which consists in committing what is wrong, but also from transgression, which consists in omitting what ought to be done.”

David committed not only adultery and homicide, [Col. 1052C] but added deceit and contempt as well: through Uriah himself, whose wife he had known (II Kings II), he sent the letter ordering Uriah’s death; and he disdained to confess his sins until he was rebuked by Nathan the prophet. On account of these four distinct sins, he prays distinctly in four ways. For the crime of adultery he says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,” because adultery is a great disgrace, which I committed from the misery of human frailty. For the crime of homicide he adds: “And according to the multitude of your acts of compassion blot out my iniquity,” because through my unjust command not only Uriah but many others were wickedly killed.

Again, on account of [Col. 1052D] the crime of treachery and deceit, he adds: “Wash me still more from my injustice,” since I committed a greater injustice when, by means of an innocent and righteous man, I deceitfully and treacherously sent the letter concerning his own death. And for the crime of negligence and contempt he concludes: “And cleanse me from my transgression,” because I grievously offended in delaying and scorning to confess my sins.

He does not say, “Have mercy on David,” but “Have mercy on me.” It is as though he said more plainly: “Elsewhere I was accustomed to state my proper name, when I believed that I possessed grace, saying, ‘Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness’ (Psalm CXXXI). But here I fear to state my proper name, since I know that I have lost grace, lest God, on hearing the infamous name of the sinner, be provoked more to vengeance than to [Col. 1053A] pardon.”

Therefore: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” Have mercy on me, O God, because it is proper to you to have mercy, since for you to have mercy is nothing other than to be. For your mercy fills the earth (Psalm XXXII), and your acts of compassion are over all your works (Psalm CXLIV). Therefore have mercy on me, dealing with me according to mercy [otherwise: not according to vengeance, but according to mercy], not according to justice; and not merely according to a small mercy, but entirely according to great mercy. Hence: “Have mercy on me according to your great mercy,” which is immeasurable and infinite. For great misery needs great mercy, and much wickedness requires much pity.

Certainly, my crimes are so great, many, and shameful [Col. 1053B] that I would despair because of their greatness, multitude, and shamefulness, unless I knew that your mercy is incomparably, incomprehensibly, and ineffably great. Therefore, despairing of my own misery but hoping in your mercy, I cry out confidently and say: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,” which indeed is so great that it brought down from heaven God himself, the only-begotten, and clothed him in a body, so that in it he might suffer and die to remove human misery and grant the forgiveness of sins.

O delightful saying, sweet utterance, pleasant word: necessary for the sinner, useful for the miserable, fitting for the penitent; to be pondered not once but often with bitterness, [Col. 1053C] spoken with grief, repeated with tears [otherwise: lamentations]; with the whole heart, the whole mind, and the whole soul (Matthew XXII), with every affection, every inward part, every marrow; with sighs, sobs, and tears: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” Have mercy, Lord, on me who am miserable. Lord, have mercy on miserable me, according to your great mercy.

“And according to the multitude of your acts of compassion, blot out my iniquity.”

He wisely distinguishes by referring to the greatness of mercy and to the multitude of acts of compassion, because God’s mercy is one in nature, but his acts of compassion are many in effect. Therefore elsewhere he says: “Remember your acts of compassion, O Lord, [Col. 1053D] and your mercy”—that is, those acts of compassion—“which are from eternity” (Psalm XXIV). Elsewhere, however, “mercies” are used effectively for acts of compassion, as in: “The mercies of the Lord are many, because we have not been consumed” (Lamentations III).

Therefore, “according to the multitude of your acts of compassion,” that is, according to the manifold effects of your mercy, “blot out my iniquity,” which, by reason of its excessive multitude, seems to exceed the number of the sand of the sea. For who can comprehend the number of sins, transgressions, and negligences? No one at all. Blot out my iniquity, therefore, so that, just as writing is erased from parchment with a razor, leaving no trace of it, so by your mercy fault may be blotted from my soul, leaving in it no [Col. 1054A] liability to punishment.

Blot out my iniquity, I pray, lest I be among those of whom it is said: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Psalm LXVIII); and again: “You have blotted out their names for ever and ever” (Psalm IX). Since one who confesses voluntarily is treated more gently, this penitent neither conceals nor minimizes his fault, but reveals, magnifies, and condemns it, saying:

“Wash me still more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my transgression [otherwise: sin].”

“Still more,” that is, wash me more and more from my injustice, which I practiced more and more by adding sins to sins. “How cheaply you have become, repeating your ways” (Jeremiah II). “And cleanse me from my transgression,” because it makes my soul exceedingly ugly and [Col. 1054B] foul-smelling. Therefore wash me from ugliness and cleanse me from stench.

But since fault is forgiven not separately in parts but entirely at once in true repentance—for God does not halve forgiveness, he who healed the whole person on the Sabbath—why does this penitent ask to be washed still more from injustice, as though it had not been wholly forgiven in repentance? The fault which has just recently been forgiven, although wholly washed away through repentance, nevertheless still seems foul and unclean to the penitent, who does not yet possess the security and serenity of conscience. Therefore he asks to be washed [otherwise: delivered] from this stench, though he has already been cleansed from the ugliness of liability, so that his conscience, secure concerning forgiveness, may become serene.

Yet he also asks to be cleansed still more from the sin that has been purged with respect to guilt, with respect to punishment: because not whenever the whole guilt is forgiven [Col. 1054C] is the whole punishment also forgiven. Or “still more” means “in addition, wash me.” It is as though he said: “Blot out my iniquity, which I committed against God; and in addition wash me from my injustice, which I committed against my neighbor; and further cleanse me from my iniquity, which I committed against myself; for I have sinned against God, against my neighbor, and against myself.”

But although this penitent sinned grievously, he nevertheless more easily obtains pardon who recognizes himself than one who is unaware of having erred; one who grieves deeply rather than lightly over his sin; and one who sinned secretly rather than openly. Therefore, after saying, “Wash me still more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my transgression,” in order to show that pardon should be granted him more readily, [Col. 1054D] he adds:

“For I acknowledge [otherwise: know] my iniquity, and my transgression [otherwise: sin] is always before [otherwise: against] me.”

Thus he asserts that he does not fail to know but acknowledges his fault: “For I know my iniquity.” He says that he grieves over his fault not lightly but gravely, because “my sin is always before me.” Nor does he say that he sinned openly but secretly: “Against you alone I have sinned.” Explaining what it means to have sinned against him alone, he adds: “And I have done evil before you,” namely, with you alone seeing.

For David, wishing to conceal his sin, summoned Uriah so that he might enter in to his wife Bathsheba, whom David himself had made pregnant, in order that the conception might seem to have been received from Uriah [Col. 1055A] (II Kings). Nor did he wish to confess that sin until he was rebuked for it by Nathan the prophet.

Or rather, because some sin through ignorance, others through negligence, and others deliberately, this penitent, in order to show that he sinned grievously, removes from himself the first and second, lighter modes of sinning and ascribes to himself the third, which is more serious. Thus he says: “Against you alone I have sinned”—not through ignorance, because “I acknowledge my iniquity”; nor through negligence, because “my sin is always before me”; but deliberately, because “I have done evil before you.”

It is as though he said: “Have mercy on me; wash and cleanse me, for I acknowledge my iniquity, since I am not among those who do not understand their crimes, nor even wish to understand them, in order that they may more freely delight in [Col. 1055B] their desires. And my sin is always before me, because I am not among those who sometimes reflect on their sins and immediately forget them, as if casting them behind their backs (Isaiah XXXVIII), and do not hold them before their faces because they neglect and postpone them. David himself did not hold his sin before his face, but had cast it, as it were, behind his back, when he pronounced judgment upon the rich man who took the poor man’s sheep, forgetting himself in that judgment.”

Thus he says that his sin is always before him because at suitable and fitting times he reflects on it, as elsewhere it is said: “One ought always to pray and never fail” (Luke XVIII). He reflects upon it, I say, in order to grieve and so to erase it, not in order to revive [otherwise: rub up afresh] [Col. 1055C] or repeat it. Therefore the reading that more properly expresses the meaning is: “My sin is always against me,” so that I may pursue it as an enemy rather than embrace it as a friend.

“Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

David therefore magnifies his fault both from the dignity of the person who committed the sin and from the exaltedness of the person against whom he committed it: namely, a king sinned against God. He notes the first when he says, “Against you alone I have sinned,” and the second when he adds, “And I have done evil before you,” and thereby have despised you more greatly.

It is as though he said more plainly: “My sin is left for you alone to punish, because I have no other superior who can punish me, since I myself am king. Yet I sinned all the more on that account, because the greater the eminence, the graver the fall. For the powerful shall suffer powerful torments (Wisdom VI), and ‘a harsh judgment shall be made for those who rule’ [Col. 1055D] (ibid.).”

Certainly, it is one thing to sin against someone, and another to sin to someone. One sins against someone when one commits an offense against that person; one sins to someone when one is subject to that person’s punishment. Thus a king sins to God alone; others, however, sin both to God and to the king.

What then? Cannot prelates of churches, especially the supreme pontiff, punish secular princes if, after admonition, they refuse to make satisfaction for what they have committed, as though they sinned only to God and not to a human being? For the king’s heart is in God’s hand, and he will turn it wherever he wills (Proverbs XXI). They certainly can, because since Jesus of Nazareth was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Psalm XLIV) and was made a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm CIX), kingship does not disdain to be subject to priesthood.

This is also clear because the priest’s anointing remained upon the head, whereas the king’s anointing descended from the head to the shoulder. Therefore, although kingship was formerly priestly, as Moses says in the Law (Exodus XVI), now priesthood is royal, as Peter says in his Epistle. And he who says to blessed Peter, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew XVI), by saying “whatever” excepted nothing, in order manifestly to show that by the authority entrusted to him he can bind kings as well as others. They are subject to him in this matter because of God, and in this matter he is set over them in God’s stead. Therefore, when a prince thus sins against the pontiff, he nevertheless sins against God alone [Col. 1056B; variant: “against God himself”].

“And I have done before you the evil of adultery or even homicide which I committed against my neighbor”: namely, while you saw and were present, because you behold all things and are present everywhere. Since, then, an offense committed before a judge is inexcusable, undoubtedly we cannot excuse our offenses, all of which we commit before God.

Why, then, does he say particularly of this evil that he did it before God? If it is answered that this is said because he sinned in secret, where God alone sees, and not openly, where human beings see as well, that circumstance does not aggravate the sin [Col. 1056C] but lessens it, because to sin openly is more serious than to sin secretly.

But “the evil before you” means the evil which you always retain in memory and which greatly displeases you. I knowingly committed this evil—namely, the first and second sins prohibited in the second table: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Deuteronomy V). Hence in what follows he says: “Turn your face from my sins.” There is an evil which God patiently overlooks, and that evil in a sense does not seem to exist before him; and there is an evil which God utterly detests, and that evil seems to exist before him in every way. Therefore, magnifying the sin which God detests in every way, he says here: “I have done evil before you,” just as elsewhere it is said: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke [Col. 1056D] XV).

“That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

It might have been thought that, because of so grave and great a sin—which David had committed both against God and against his neighbor—God would revoke the promise he had made him concerning Christ, who was to be born from his seed: “The Lord has sworn truth to David, and he will not disappoint him: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” (Psalm CXXXI). Therefore, in order to remove this idea—that such a promise ought not be revoked—he said first: “Have mercy on me; wash and cleanse me,” so that, once sin has been forgiven, you may be justified—that is, be found righteous and true in your words concerning the promise of Christ which you made me—and thus prevail over those who say that you have revoked such a promise, showing them to be liars [Col. 1057A] when you are judged by them as not intending to do what you promised in this way.

That judge is therefore greatly to be feared, from whose wisdom nothing can be hidden and against whose justice no one can stand. Such is God. Hence this penitent says: “O God, I cannot hide from your wisdom, because I have done evil before you. I cannot corrupt your justice, because you are justified in your words. I cannot resist your power, because you prevail when you are judged”—that is, when you judge.

For this reason it is written: “Do not seek to be a judge” (Ecclesiastes VII), unless by your strength you can break through iniquities. Who, then, would not fear that judge who is always so wise that all things are naked and open to his eyes; always so just that he renders to each according to his works (Matthew X); and always so powerful that nothing resists his will? “For who has resisted him and had peace?” (Job IX). Rightly, therefore, this penitent does not call for judgment but appeals for mercy: “Have mercy on me, O God, because I have done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

“That you may be justified,” that is, that you may appear righteous and true in your words, in which you said: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezekiel XVIII). “And prevail,” that is, convict the adversaries of truth, when you are judged—that is, accused by them as though you were not just because you are supremely merciful, easily forgiving a grave sin—as you easily forgave David. For when, after hearing Nathan, he said only, “I have sinned,” Nathan immediately answered: “And the Lord has taken away your sin” (II Kings XII).

[Col. 1057C] A glorious victory: when God blots out and destroys everything which the disobedient and rebellious servant had done against him, and recalls and brings back to himself the servant, deceived and occupied by the most wicked enemy, merely by forgiving his errors.

But if the speech is directed to Christ, it may suitably be understood thus: “Against you alone I have sinned, O Christ, because you alone among human beings can punish justly, since you have no sin whatever. Thus you alone are a just punisher, since there is in you nothing that ought to be punished, as you said to the scribes and Pharisees concerning the woman caught in adultery: ‘Let him who is without sin among you first cast a stone at her’” (John VIII).

For you alone among human beings are such a one, Isaiah the prophet testifying that you committed no sin, nor was deceit found in your mouth (Isaiah LIII). Every other human being, however, is a liar (Psalm CXV), so that you may be justified in your words—that is, so that all your words may be righteous and true. For who else does not offend in speech? “And you may prevail,” that is, surpass all human beings in justice, when you are judged—that is, when you are compared with them in judgment—because “no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII).

Christ’s justice is so great that he does not refuse to be judged with a human being: “Judge,” he says, “between me and my vineyard” (Micah VI). And, setting forth his case as though before a judge, he says: “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I troubled you? Answer me.” Thus he prevails when he is judged together with [Col. 1058A] a human being, in whose sight not even the stars are clean, and in whose angels he finds perversity.

Moreover, according to another reading, there is no conjunction here, but simply: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you.” Immediately, without any conjunction, there follows: “You may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” Thus the penitent, according to the earlier sense, beseeching God who was to be incarnate, says: “May you be justified”—that is, become righteous for me, so as to redeem me through justice, certainly not mine but yours. “For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (John II).

“May you be justified,” I say, “in your words,” that is, according to the words which you spoke through the Law and the prophets: namely, that by your punishment you would redeem humanity from its fault, as you testify through the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your sting, O hell” (Hosea XIII). “For the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his wound we have been healed.” And may you conquer death when you are judged to death—the death of guilt through the death of punishment. May you conquer justly when you are judged unjustly by Pilate and the Jews.

“Behold, for I was conceived in iniquities, and in transgressions [otherwise: sins] my mother bore [otherwise: conceived] me.”

This penitent still further magnifies his fault, showing that he not only committed actual fault but also contracted original fault. Concerning actual fault he had said before: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil [Col. 1058C] before you.” Concerning original fault he adds: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in transgressions my mother bore me.”

There is a twofold conception: one of seeds, the other of natures. Parents commit actual fault in the first, while offspring contract original fault in the second. Therefore he says: “Behold, I was conceived in the iniquities which my parents committed in the conception of my seed, and in transgressions my mother bore me,” transgressions which I myself contracted in the conception of my nature.

Far be it altogether that this should be used as an occasion for saying that David was conceived in adultery, since his father Jesse begot him by his lawful wife. But even if it is said that marital intercourse is sometimes excused from all criminal guilt on account of the goods of marriage, nevertheless, because sin is more often committed in that intercourse, he says that he was conceived in his parents’ iniquities because of what more commonly occurs.

But if, as is truer, it is said that marital intercourse performed in due order is excused from mortal sin but not from venial sin by the goods of marriage, then “iniquities” here is broadly used for even venial sins, in accordance with what the apostle John says in his Epistle: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity” (I John III).

It follows: “And in transgressions, or sins, my mother bore—or conceived—me.” He says “in transgressions,” or “sins,” in the plural because of the three original corruptions by which the three natural powers of the soul are originally corrupted. Who does not know that even marital intercourse is never performed wholly without the itch of the flesh and without [Col. 1059A] the heat and stench of concupiscence, by which the seeds conceived are defiled and corrupted? Hence elsewhere we read: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” (Job XIV).

Therefore, from defiled and corrupted seeds is conceived a body that is likewise corrupt and defiled; when the soul is finally infused into it, it is corrupted and defiled—not from an integrity or purity which it had, but from the integrity or purity which it would have had if it had not been joined to a defiled and corrupted body. For it is infused in being created, and created in being infused.

Just as liquid poured into a corrupted vessel is corrupted, and something touching what is polluted is polluted by that contact itself, so the soul is corrupted and defiled by bodily contagion. The soul has three natural powers: the rational power, to discern good from evil; the irascible power, to reject evil; and the concupiscible power, to seek good. These three powers are originally corrupted; and, once corrupted, the soul contracts three opposite defects: ignorance, making it difficult to discern good from evil; irascibility, making it easy to reject good; and concupiscence, making it easy to seek evil.

For in carnal intercourse the vision of reason is put to sleep, the itch of lust is aroused, and the appetite for pleasure is satisfied; from these the three defects are originally contracted. Such corruptions or defects are here called transgressions or sins, in which he declares that his mother conceived or bore him.

Must it therefore be said that the soul simultaneously contracts three original sins: difficulty or slowness in discerning good from evil, which belongs to ignorance; readiness or inclination to reject good, which belongs to irascibility; and inclination or readiness to seek evil, which belongs to concupiscence? This does not seem absurd to some. Yet it may plausibly be said that there is one original sin in the soul, although it is less properly called sin, and that it contains two things: the stain and the tinder [*fomes*].

The stain is the defilement of the body by which the soul is unclean, and on account of which it is unworthy of the divine vision; or rather, it is deserving of the deprivation of the divine vision, as we read: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V). From this ugliness or impurity the soul of an infant is cleansed through water and Spirit in baptism. Adults, however, are cleansed not only through the baptism of regeneration in water, but also through the baptism of compunction in tears or of suffering in blood, so that, baptismal grace remaining, it is no longer unworthy of the vision but rather worthy of the divine vision.

The tinder [*fomes*], however, is a weakness or infirmity of nature: namely, a certain passive quality or deprivation, from which the first movements toward sinning or concupiscence proceed. Such a quality or deprivation remains even after baptism. Therefore it is said that original sin passes away in liability, with respect to the stain, and remains in act, with respect to the tinder, from which acts or movements of sin arise. Conversely, actual sin is customarily said to pass away in act [Col. 1060A] and remain in liability.

This quality and deprivation are understood to concern the concupiscible power, corrupted and defiled in the manner described, because concupiscence produces the itch around the gateway of human propagation through which the original cause of sin is poured forth. Let it suffice to have said this here; for though the matter is very disputable, it is still more lamentable, because the shoot of our origin is corrupted from its very root. Hence the Apostle said that “we are by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians II). And David himself was speaking of this when he said: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me”; in this place these words simply and plainly mean defilement and an inclination to sin.

“I say, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” [Col. 1060B] Nor is this surprising. For behold, speaking in the person of humanity in general: “I was conceived in iniquities; I too have sinned against you alone and done evil before you.” Nor is this surprising, because “my mother bore me in transgressions.”

Although above a distinction was made between iniquities and transgressions, iniquities may nevertheless be taken for transgressions, so that both iniquities and transgressions refer to the offspring, who is corrupted and defiled in his conception: in the conception of seeds with regard to the body, and in the conception of natures with regard to the soul.

Observe, O penitent, and consider how David confesses all sins and all the circumstances of sins, so that you too may endeavor to confess every kind and circumstance of sins: according as you have sinned more gravely in place, time, number, and person; [Col. 1060C] according to age, knowledge, rank, and order; whether easily, frequently, openly, or perseveringly. For these and any other such circumstances magnify sin. Therefore they should not be suppressed in that judgment in which God excuses the one who accuses himself before God, while God accuses the one who excuses himself before God.

“Behold, for you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

The second part, in which the penitent recounts the gifts of God already given and commends those yet to be given. Among those already given he recalls the true confession of sins, when he says: “For behold, you have loved truth”; and the full knowledge of hidden things [Col. 1060D], when he adds: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” For he who reveals his own sins to God, God makes known to him his own hidden things.

Among the gifts yet to be given, however, he commends future cleansing through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood, when he says: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed”; and future purification through the washing of the water of baptism, when he adds: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” Again, among the gifts yet to be given he commends joy at the remission of sins and gladness at the promise of rewards, and thus “the humbled bones shall rejoice.”

Moreover, some do not know, some neglect, some excuse, and some minimize their faults; and because such people are worthy not of pardon but of vengeance, the penitent removes these things from himself. “I do not fail to know,” he says, “but acknowledge [Col. 1061A] my sin: ‘For I acknowledge my iniquity.’ Nor do I neglect my sin, but oppose it: ‘For my transgression is ever against me.’ Nor do I defend it, but accuse it: ‘Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you.’ Nor do I minimize my sin, but aggravate it: ‘For I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins.’”

And as though God were asking him, “Why do you confess your sins so carefully?” he replies: “Because behold, it is evident that you have loved the truth of a confession without deceit, so that the sinner may confess every circumstance of his sins.” For that confession is not true but deceitful which states the deed while concealing its manner, and reveals one sin to one person and another to another. Therefore [Col. 1061B] one must beware lest shame at confession impede the purity of confession.

This may also be understood otherwise, as though God were asking him: “Why do you punish your sin so distinctly, so that you have said: ‘My sin is ever before me’?” He replies: “That in punishing sin I may conform to your truth; for you have loved truth, so that you may be both a true punisher and a true pardoner,” according to the saying: “The Lord loves mercy and truth” (Ps. 83). For God preserves mercy in truth and truth in mercy: he both forgives justly and punishes mercifully. It is truth that sin is punished; it is mercy that the sinner is delivered.

Or he assigns each statement to its corresponding point. For he had said: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” No wonder, since behold, you have loved truth [Col. 1061C], not duplicity or falsehood, but simplicity and purity also. For he is justified in his words who loves truth.

Again he had said: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins”; the first of these was uncertain, the second hidden. And as though God were asking him, “Why do you affirm what is uncertain and hidden?” he replies: “Because you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

Certainly, it was uncertain whether the parents had committed any iniquities in their conception. For marital intercourse is sometimes excused from blame, as when spouses come together properly for the begetting of offspring; but sometimes it is not excused from fault, as when spouses mingle improperly for the satisfaction of lust. [Col. 1061D] Likewise, it was hidden on what ground the soul is held liable for a sin which it committed neither by will nor act, since it is written that “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son; but the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18). “This proverb shall no longer be used in Israel,” says the Lord: “The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (ibid.).

But God revealed to him, through the Spirit of wisdom, both that uncertainty and this hidden matter. Therefore he did not rashly say: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins”; for, he says, “you have made known to me, through the spirit of prophecy, the uncertain matters concerning my parents’ iniquities committed in my conception, and the hidden matters concerning my own sins contracted in my conception.” Therefore I cannot be excused by ignorance, “because you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” For “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12).

But David here gives the reason why God the Father ought to be justified in his words concerning the incarnation of Christ which had been foretold: namely, because he loves truth and therefore ought not to render void what has proceeded from his lips. “For,” he says, “you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom,” namely, the coming of your Only-Begotten, who is your wisdom, whose coming was uncertain to some and hidden from others.

Finally, these words may be referred not only to what precedes, but also to what follows. As though he were plainly saying: “You have made known to me the uncertain [Col. 1062B] and hidden things of your wisdom,” since:

> You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed;  
> you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.

“You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with the hyssop of humility, and I shall be cleansed from stain. You shall wash me when through you I have been cleansed from vices, and I shall be made white when through you I have been adorned with virtues. You shall wash me by pardon, and I shall be made white by grace—indeed, whiter than snow, because the whiteness of snow is not increased but diminished. But the whiteness of grace is not diminished but increased, because charity either always advances or declines; hence it may be lost, but cannot be diminished.

“Because, however, being white is one thing and being made white another, snow—which is naturally white in itself—may signify virtue, naturally [Col. 1062C] good in itself, concerning which it is said: ‘They shall be made white as snow in Zalmon’ (Ps. 67). Whitening may signify the action proceeding from virtue. Thus the meaning is: ‘I shall be made white beyond snow,’ that is, beyond the virtue which is white inwardly, I shall be made white outwardly by good work, so that the edifice of good work may be raised upon the foundation of virtue.

“And thus the order of justification is first indicated when it is said: ‘You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed’; and afterwards the progress of those justified [variant: *the perfection of justification*] is shown when it is added: ‘You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.’

“For hyssop is a lowly but medicinal herb. It fixes its root in a rock and is effective for cleansing the lungs. It signifies humility, which fixes its root in the humble Christ and cleanses the swelling of the lungs—that is, drives away the swelling [Col. 1062D] of the mind. Therefore, when this humility comes, so that the sinner humbles himself to true repentance, he is immediately sprinkled with the dew of grace and cleansed from the stain of guilt. For unless grace is infused, guilt is beyond doubt not driven out, just as darkness is not dispelled unless light comes upon it and drives the darkness itself away.

“Truth teaches this when he says: ‘Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much’ (Luke 7). Therefore you, Lord, shall sprinkle me with hyssop—that is, through the virtue of humility you shall pour upon me the dew of grace—and I shall be cleansed from the filth of vices. Nor will the cleansing be ineffectual, for you shall wash me from sins, and beyond snow—that is, beyond the brightness of virtue—I shall also be made white by good works.”

In this alone hope is given to the sinner: that through repentance he may return not merely to his former purity, but to a far greater purity. This confidence is very useful, lest some despair creep in, which is more grievous than all sins.

Certainly three states of persons are marked here: of beginners, those making progress, and those who have arrived; or of converts, the righteous, and the perfect. The state of beginners or converts is marked where it is first said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” The state of those making progress or of the righteous is marked where it is secondly added: “You shall wash me.” The state of those who have arrived or of the perfect is marked thirdly where it is inferred: “I shall be made whiter than snow.” By these words progress according to these states is sufficiently expressly indicated, because to be sprinkled [Col. 1063B] is less than to be washed, and to be washed less than to be made white.

This will indeed be fully accomplished when “this mortal puts on immortality and this corruptible puts on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15), because “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” and then Christ’s garments shall be white as snow (Matt. 13).
