But because by Christ’s blood and the water of baptism the soul is perfectly cleansed not only from guilt but also from punishment, David, speaking in the person of the believer in general and directing his understanding to these cleansings, says not only: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom,” but also: “You shall sprinkle me with Christ’s blood, and you shall wash me with the water of baptism; and thus I shall be cleansed and made white even beyond snow”—that is, more than I can express. Not, indeed, beyond that snow concerning which it is said, “She shall not fear the cold of snow for her household” (Prov. 31), nor beyond that concerning which it is said, “He who fears frost, snow shall fall upon him” (Job 6); but rather beyond that of which we read: “If I shall have washed myself as it were with waters of snow,” etc. (Job 9). And also beyond that of which we read: “If your sins are as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” (Isa. 1). For among material things nothing whiter than snow can be found.

This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ, from whose side blood and water flowed. And when he says, “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop,” he alludes to the old law, according to which the sprinkler was made from hyssop for a mystical reason, as the Apostle also says: “After Moses had read every commandment of the law to all the people, he took the blood of goats and calves, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which God commanded unto you.’ He likewise sprinkled with blood both the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry. And according to the law almost all things are cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission” (Heb. 9).

For hyssop, as was stated above, signifies humility, inasmuch as Christ “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2), on which he shed his blood. With that blood the faithful are sprinkled through the virtue of humility and cleansed from iniquity—namely, those who observe the pattern of his humility. [Col. 1064A]

Observe, then, discerning reader, plurality in the redeemed, humility in the Redeemer, and usefulness in redemption. Plurality in the redeemed is indicated by the words, “You shall sprinkle.” For what is sprinkled is scattered about in many places. Hence Truth says: “This is the blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26). Humility in the Redeemer is indicated by the addition, “with hyssop,” a medicinal and lowly herb, because Christ by his superabundant humility grants healing medicine to his faithful; hence he said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). Usefulness in redemption is indicated by what follows: “I shall be cleansed”; for, as the apostle John says, “the blood of Jesus, the Son of God, cleanses [Col. 1064B] us from every sin” (1 John 1).

Three things belong to the effect of baptism: remission of guilt, release from punishment, and infusion of grace. The first is marked when it is said, “You shall wash me”; the second when it is added, “I shall be made white”; the third when “beyond snow” is joined. “I will pour out upon you clean water,” says the Lord through the prophet, “and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36). “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13).

Therefore, when you hear, “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed,” understand in the sprinkling of Christ’s blood faith in the Passion. But when you hear, “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow,” recognize in the washing of water the sacrament of baptism.

Now faith benefits adults without the sacrament where an exigency of necessity, rather than contempt for religion, excludes the sacrament; but the sacrament of baptism is of no avail to adults without faith, according to what Truth says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16). Why then is more attributed here to the sacrament than to faith? For to be sprinkled is less than to be washed, and to be cleansed less than to be made white, especially beyond snow.

It must therefore be understood that faith in Christ, which justifies the ungodly, truly cleanses from guilt, but not always from every punishment. The true sacrament of baptism, if received worthily, wholly frees from guilt and punishment alike. Hence the Lord calls it the sacrament of regeneration when he says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3), because through this sacrament a person is regenerated in grace and freed alike from guilt and punishment, since he had been born under the wrath of guilt and at the same time subject to punishment.

Rightly, therefore: “You shall wash me through the sacrament of baptism, and beyond the snow of grace which cleanses from guilt I shall be made white, also by the power of the sacrament, from every punishment, except only that which the necessity of the first corruption brings with it.” Deservedly, therefore:

> You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing,  
> and the humbled bones shall rejoice.

There is a twofold hearing: external, concerning which the Apostle says: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Rom. 10); and internal, concerning which the Prophet says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84). This may be understood of either: “You shall give joy to my hearing,” concerning the remission of sins, because the Lord says, “It is not for the ungodly to rejoice.” And: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Ps. 37). “And gladness,” concerning the promise of rewards, according to what Truth says: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5).

But it is better understood of the inward hearing, concerning which the prophet said: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 35). To him who said: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified” (Hab. 3), you shall also give joy of heart and gladness of body, according to the saying: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). [Col. 1065B]

The heart rejoices when it believes itself cleansed from spiritual foulness; the body is glad when it feels itself cleansed from bodily stench. Thus with a twofold gladness the humbled bones shall rejoice—not so much the bones of the body as those of the mind: namely, the powers of the soul, which formerly were humbled—that is, cast down and bent over—by sin, but now are humbled—that is, inclined to hear and obey. For one who hears humbly and obeys reverently is indeed the friend of the bridegroom, “who stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

Oh, how few are those who rejoice in spiritual and eternal things, compared with those who delight in carnal and earthly things! But mourning occupies the end of their joy, because “they rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 14). The joy of the former, therefore, is blessed and everlasting, as it is said: “Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full”; and: “No one shall take your joy from you” (John 14). But the joy of the latter is unhappy and momentary, as we read: “They take up the tambourine and lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the organ; they spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend into hell” (Job 21).

But you, O God, shall give joy and gladness to my hearing—that is, to my understanding—not false and passing joy concerning carnal and earthly things; rather [variant: *although*] my humbled bones shall rejoice in true and spiritual gladness. That is, my inward parts, like hidden bones, formerly lifted up by pride [Col. 1065D], are now inclined to [variant: *through*] obedience. For as long as the soul raises itself in pride, it cannot rejoice in true exultation; but when it puts down pride and assumes humility, then it delights in true joy in the Lord.

> Turn your face away from my sins,  
> and blot out all my iniquities.

The fourth part, in which the penitent, having taken up confidence, asks that punishments be turned away from him when he says: “Turn your face away from my sins”; and that faults be blotted out when he adds: “Blot out all my iniquities.” Again, he asks that purity be created in him when he says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God”; and that uprightness of spirit be renewed when he adds: “Renew a right spirit within me.” He also asks that the presence of divine contemplation not be excluded from him [Col. 1066A], when he says: “Do not cast me away from your presence”; and that the grace of spiritual sanctification not be taken from him, when he says: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

Again, he asks that the gladness arising from Christ’s promise be restored to him when he says first: “Restore to me the gladness of your salvation”; and that strength through the confirmation of the Holy Spirit be granted to him when he adds: “Strengthen me with a ruling spirit.” Behold how prudent, modest, and careful he was in his requests, since he asks for things that are permitted, fitting, and useful—just, honourable, and necessary—so that you too may learn to ask for such things. Otherwise, if perhaps you ask for unjust things, “your prayer may become sin” (Ps. 108); if you ask for dishonourable things, you may not receive because you ask wrongly (John 4); and if you ask for useless things, you may be told: “You do not know what you ask” [Col. 1066B] (Matt. 20).

But just as this penitent had accused the person of the defendant in many ways, so he commends the person of the judge in many ways, that he may more readily obtain pardon. As though he said: “You are a just examiner; hence: ‘You have loved truth.’ You are a discerning teacher; hence: ‘You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom.’ You are a holy expiator; hence: ‘You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow.’ You are a generous promiser; hence: ‘You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones shall rejoice.’ You are a gracious pardoner; hence: ‘Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.’ You are an omnipotent Creator; hence: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God.’ You are a wondrous renewer; hence: ‘Renew a right spirit within me.’ [Col. 1066C] You are an irrevocable giver; hence: ‘Do not cast me away from your presence.’ You are a useful restorer; hence: ‘Restore to me the gladness of your salvation.’ You are an eminent confirmer; hence: ‘Strengthen me with a ruling spirit.’”

He therefore says: “Because you are such and so great, turn your face—not from me, but from my sins—lest you take notice of me on account of my sins, because I could not stand before the face of your wrath. Turn, I say, your face away from my sins, because I turn my attention to my sin before my own face. Therefore turn your face away from them, lest you punish justly, because I turn them before my own face, that I may repent worthily.”

For if a person attends to guilt, God turns away punishment; for he is the watchful rod, who says to Jeremiah: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” “I see,” he says, “a watchful rod” [Col. 1066D] (Jer. 1). The watchful rod is God, who watches over his people in order to punish when they sleep instead of repenting, and conversely. If the latter watches in order to repent, the former sleeps instead of punishing. For “he who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps” (Ps. 120). Yet he does not sleep from punishment unless this person sleeps in guilt.

Therefore he adds: “And blot out from your knowledge all my iniquities. Do not remember my sins, nor take vengeance for my sins, Lord my God; for you have said: ‘At whatever hour the sinner turns and groans, I shall not remember any of his iniquities’” (Ezek. 18).

Above he had said in the singular, “Blot out my iniquity”; but here he says universally, “Blot out all [Col. 1067A] my iniquities.” For, having gained confidence, he now presumes more than before, securely asking that not merely one iniquity but all without exception be blotted out, since he does not have only one iniquity but many. Hence he does not say in the singular, “Blot out one iniquity,” but universally: “Blot out all my iniquities,” because “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3).

> Create in me a clean heart, O God,  
> and renew a right spirit within me.

Since to create is to make something out of nothing, and to renew is to reform something to its former state, why does he speak differently when he says: “Create a clean heart,” and “Renew a right spirit”? For if he asks that God create purity of heart in him, by the same reasoning he ought to ask that God create uprightness [Col. 1067B] of spirit in him, since he lost both through sin. And if it is said that he had lost the heart itself, because of what is written: “Ephraim is like a deceived dove, having no heart” (Hos. 7), perhaps by the same reasoning it should be said that he had lost the spirit itself, because of what is written: “When the queen of Sheba saw Solomon’s wisdom, there was no spirit left in her” (3 Kgs. 10); and also because in a certain psalm he says concerning the spirit: “My spirit has failed” (Ps. 142).

For that person is said to lose his heart who acts faithlessly against God; hence the prophet: “Return to the heart, you transgressors” (Isa. 46). And he abandons his heart who is alienated from God; hence the Psalmist himself: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps. 39).

Yet it may rightly be understood that, in comparison with the condition of reforming grace which his heart possesses after it has been cleansed of guilt, the condition of his corrupted nature which his heart possessed before it was cleansed was as though nothing. [Col. 1067C] Thus James says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be some firstfruits of his creation” (Jas. 1); and Paul: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away” (1 Cor. 5). Here *create* may properly be used for *re-create*, according to what is written: “The people that shall be created shall praise the Lord” (Ps. 101). For that people rightly praises who is created through grace.

Therefore this penitent asks that a clean heart be created in him: namely, that God may create in him clean affections of heart, chaste thoughts and wills, lest he again turn aside to uncleanness, as David himself did. For from the heart proceed affections, whether good or evil. Of good affections it is written: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4). Of evil affections it is said: “From the heart come evil thoughts, thefts, adulteries, murders, false testimonies, perjuries, and similar things, which defile a person” (Matt. 15).

He therefore asks that a right spirit be renewed in him: that is, that the Holy Spirit be restored afresh to him. This Spirit is called right because he makes people upright. In his own nature he is wholly unchangeable; therefore, with respect to his effect, David asks that he be renewed in him, lest he again turn aside to iniquity, as David himself, who had caused an unjust murder to be committed.

Nevertheless, either term may suitably be said of either: the heart may be created and renewed clean and right, and the spirit may be renewed and created right and clean. But the words are varied merely for the flower of expression; or rather, because David had fallen from purity of heart through the foulness of adultery, but had turned away from uprightness of spirit through the perversity of homicide. Since he had not wholly lost the judgment of reason but had utterly lost the virtue of chastity, he discreetly and rightly asks that grace be given him so that purity of heart may be created in him and nature reformed so that uprightness of spirit may be renewed. For this reason he distinguishes: “Create a clean heart, and renew a right spirit.”

He asks that a clean heart be created, on account of clean affections for loving; and that a right [heart] be created, on account of clean affections for loving; and a right spirit renewed, on account of right understandings for discerning, so that he may have zeal according to knowledge—sincere in loving and discerning in judgment. What he adds, “within me,” refers to both of the foregoing, so that both a clean heart may be created and a right spirit renewed within him, in order that his inward parts may be re-created and renewed in him together with the heart and spirit. [Col. 1068B]

For such is the familiarity between flesh and soul joined together in a human being that each is, now for this and now for that, urged on by the other’s particular enticements. Although it is written that “the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5)—which is indeed true regarding sensuality and reason—it is nevertheless written that “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9), and: “A sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. 17). For “death enters through the windows” (Jer. 9), and “the eye plunders the soul” (Lam. 3); hence: “Keep the bars of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom” (Mic. 7).

David therefore says: “Renew a right spirit within me,” from which adultery proceeds, because the loins are the seat of pleasure. Thus it is written of the devil, who is the inciter of pleasure, that “his strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). It follows:

> Do not cast me away from your presence,  
> and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.

[Col. 1068D] As though he said: “Turn your face away from my sins, but do not cast me away from your presence. Do not reject me from your sight; do not remove me from your grace; do not estrange me from your mercy; do not exclude me from your knowledge; do not drive me away from your contemplation. For when you turn away your face, all things shall be troubled” (Ps. 103). And: “Where shall I go from your spirit, or where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 138). Why, then, do you hide your face? “Show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). “Make your face shine upon us, and have mercy on us” (Ps. 66).

Oh, how dangerous it is to be cast away from God’s presence! Certainly he is light, he is salvation; and one cast away from his presence shall surely, as a reprobate, be cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth [Col. 1069A] (Matt. 13), where there is “the worm that does not die and the fire that is not extinguished” (Isa. 66). “Take away the ungodly, lest he see the glory of God.” Thus Lucifer was cast down—the great dragon, the ancient serpent (Rev. 12). Thus also those shall be cast out to whom it is said at the end: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

Therefore, do not turn your face away from me, because if you turn it away, “I shall become like those who descend into the pit” (Ps. 152). And do not take your Holy Spirit from me, without whom I can do nothing good, for he is the giver of all graces. This penitent already had the Holy Spirit, without whose gift he could not so humble himself. Or surely David was asking that the spirit of prophecy not be taken from him, which he judged more precious than all other things.

But take greater care that you do not withdraw yourself from the Holy Spirit than that the Holy Spirit withdraw himself from you. Is it not naturally prior to commit a fault than to lose grace, since the gift of grace is lost through the desert of fault? The sun’s radiance does not withdraw itself from a person; nor is it in the sun, which always shines, that it should not be seen by a person; rather, it is in the person, who sometimes closes his eyes so that he himself does not then see the sun.

But you will say: “How could I lose the Holy Spirit unless I had first been abandoned by him? For no one loses what he does not have.” But the Holy Spirit is lost or taken away not so much when one ceases to have him as when one begins not to have him. Thus he is lost when he is no longer had by a person, although just before he had been had by that person; for “there is no fellowship of light with darkness” (2 Cor. 6), and light flees when darkness comes. [Col. 1069C]

Therefore, if you desire that the Holy Spirit not be taken away from you, beware not only of unclean deeds but also of indecent thoughts, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from what is feigned, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1). It follows:

> Restore to me the gladness of your salvation,  
> and strengthen me with a ruling spirit.

Oh, with how much delight does a devout mind rejoice, with how much gladness does a faithful soul exult, when it recalls and considers the benefits of the Redeemer, who came “to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19); who came not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (John 12); who came so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but have eternal life (John 3); who “washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1); because he “died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4).

“Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our pains. He was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53). “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8).

He had experienced this gladness of salvation who said: “I will glory in the Lord and rejoice in God my Jesus” (Hab. 3). But when a person, by grievously offending, makes himself ungrateful for so great a grace and unworthy of so great a good, he loses this gladness of salvation. Yet when he has turned back and groaned, he asks that it be restored to him after sin has been forgiven.

Therefore he says: “Most merciful Father, most gentle Father, sweetest Father, restore to me the gladness of your salvation and of my Savior, who is altogether salvation, because he was delivered by you; and my Savior, because he was given for me. Hence: ‘Help us, O God, our salvation,’ etc. [Col. 1070A] (Ps. 78).”

But David had lost the gladness of this salvation when, in committing adultery and murder, he feared that he had rendered himself unworthy of the promise concerning Christ which had been made to him. Therefore he said: “When you, God, have forgiven me my sin, restore to me the gladness of your salvation. And lest I admit that thing again, strengthen me in your good pleasure, so that I may not return to my vomit, may not look back, and may never be turned into a statue of tasteless salt.”

And lest such confirmation be capable of being weakened, “strengthen me with a ruling spirit,” as by supreme authority which no one can resist. It is also called a ruling spirit because, together with you and with your salvation, it is one universal principle, one Creator of all things.

By saying “spirit” three times, some discern here the Trinity in God, who is spirit and not body. They call the right Spirit the Son; by the Spirit under his own name they understand the Holy Spirit; and they take the ruling Spirit as the Father, because the Catholic faith confesses the Father himself as the principle without a principle. Yet the discerning reader may understand the indivisible Trinity in these words otherwise. When you hear, “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” understand God the Father as Creator. When you hear, “Restore to me the gladness of your salvation,” take God the Son as Savior. And when you hear, “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me,” recognize God as sanctifier, although to create, save, and sanctify belongs to all collectively and individually, since they are one. For “there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5).

Yet one of the three is here specifically called the right, holy, and ruling Spirit, because he, by the appropriated name, makes people upright, renders them holy, and establishes them as rulers; just as he is called the Spirit of wisdom [Col. 1070D], the Spirit of understanding, and the Spirit of strength (Isa. 11), and is called by other names according to the differences of graces.

> I shall teach the wicked your ways,  
> and the ungodly shall turn to you.

The fourth part, in which it is plainly shown how greatly this man has advanced through humble repentance and devout prayer: for from a transgressor he became a preacher, as Paul from a persecutor became an apostle (Acts 19), and Matthew from a tax collector became an evangelist (Matt. 9). Hence the Psalms of David, the Epistles of Paul, and the Gospel of Matthew are used in the Church more frequently than other Scriptures, so that sinners may learn from their example not to despair because of guilt but to hope in grace, when they understand that God granted them [Col. 1071A] not only pardon for such great crimes but also the grace of spiritual gifts.

For he had chiefly asked two things: remission of crimes and the infusion of spiritual gifts. And as though God were asking him why he requested deliverance from so many and such great sins and the gift of so many and such great benefits—“What fruit, then, will come from this?”—he replies: “Certainly great fruit, because it will benefit others: ‘I shall teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you.’ It will benefit my salvation: ‘My tongue shall exult in your justice.’ It will redound to your praise: ‘My mouth shall proclaim your praise.’ And that I may be able worthily to fulfil this, first ‘deliver me from bloodguiltiness,’ and afterwards ‘you shall open my lips’; because:”

“Shameful is it for a teacher when guilt rebukes the man himself.” [Col. 1071B] (CATO.) He therefore shows whom he teaches: “I will teach,” he says, “the wicked.” What he teaches: “I will teach your ways.” And to what end he teaches: “and the ungodly will be converted to you.” He also shows what sort of man he ought to be who teaches, when he prays: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God”; and how he ought to teach, when he says: “My tongue shall exult in your righteousness.” My teaching, therefore, is not idle, since “I will teach the wicked your ways”; nor fruitless, since “the ungodly will be converted to you”; nor sorrowful, since “my tongue shall exult in your righteousness.” It is indeed lawful, fitting, and advantageous to teach in this way. It is lawful because “I will teach your ways”; fitting because “my tongue shall exult in your righteousness”; advantageous because “the ungodly will be converted to you.”

Therefore I desire to teach others: hence, “I will teach the wicked your ways.” I desire to be delivered from my sins: hence, “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God.” I desire to praise you, because “my tongue shall exult in your righteousness.” I desire to offer you an acceptable sacrifice, because “a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.” I desire to build the walls of your city: therefore, “Deal graciously, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” And thus my good desire will be fulfilled. “For then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and whole burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.”

Therefore I shall teach not merely by word but by example; for when I am spared, hope is given to others, lest the wicked despair because of their wickedness. And therefore, “I will teach the wicked your ways,” namely mercy and truth, because “all your ways are mercy and truth” (Ps. 118 [119]). For I shall teach mercy because you forgave the sinner; and I shall teach truth because you did not withdraw your promises. Thus the ungodly—who are called wicked beforehand—stirred by me alike through word and example, will be converted to you, so that you may both forgive their sins and grant the promises to them also.

Therefore I will teach the wicked your ways, and my teaching will not be fruitless, because the ungodly will be converted to you, and thus will also return to themselves. For when a sinner is estranged from God, he is also removed from himself. So we read of the prodigal son: after he had gone into a far country and squandered all his goods, “returning to himself,” he said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance, while I perish here with hunger!” [Col. 1072A]

Yet certainly a sinner cannot turn to God unless God turns to him. Hence, while he was still far away, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, ran to him, fell upon his neck, and kissed him (Luke 15). Let sinners, therefore, however far away they may be, not lose confidence in their confession, but be secure in his promise, who says: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Ezek. 18). As though he said: Turn to me by repenting, and I will turn to you by pardoning. For the sinner cannot come to God unless God first comes to the sinner, in accordance with the saying: “Your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22 [23]). For fear introduces love: fear is from God, but fear is not with God. Love is both from God and with God, because it is written: “There is no fear in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4). Moreover, “he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (ibid.).

But that I may worthily say:

> Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue shall exult in your righteousness.

He plainly shows that a teacher is unworthy when he has in himself what he reproves in another; and it is said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4). “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7). “You who preach that one ought not commit adultery—do you commit adultery? And you who preach that one ought not steal—do you steal?” (Rom. 2.) For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous ordinances and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49 [50].)

Therefore deliver me now from blood-guiltiness, that is, from mortal sins, concerning which it is written: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4); so that in the future you may deliver me from blood-guiltiness, that is, from infernal punishments, concerning which it is said: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood” (Deut. 32). For the negligence of a teacher is commonly denoted in Scripture by the name of blood, as the Lord says through the prophet: “If you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man, I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3). And the Apostle says: “My hands are clean from the blood of all of you. For I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God” [Col. 1072D] (Acts 20).

Thus this penitent man, about to teach the Lord’s ways, rightly asks to be delivered from those blood-guiltinesses by which he was stained through the unjust killing not only of Uriah but also of others—such blood-guiltinesses as are meant where it is said: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. 54 [55]). Therefore: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God,” author or giver of my salvation—salvation now in hope and hereafter in reality—for you alone can grant salvation. Elsewhere you say of yourself: “I am the salvation of the people.” For “salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3), who saves those hoping in him (Dan. 13).

And thus “my tongue shall exult,” that is, it shall joyfully proclaim, “your righteousness.” For a teacher ought not to be sluggish, but eager in teaching, so that he may set forth the word of God cheerfully, as it is read elsewhere: “I exulted under my tongue” (Ps. 65 [66]). [Col. 1073A] Such eagerness he ought not only to possess in his heart, but also to display in his body, so that by the motion of his mouth and the bearing of his body he may draw his hearers. The more useful he is to them, the more fruitful he is to himself. Therefore my tongue shall exult—that is, with exultation of heart it shall proclaim—your righteousness, namely your commandments, which are righteous. Hence: “I will meditate upon your statutes; I will not forget your words” (Ps. 118 [119]).

To express the ardour of intention and the affection of the mind, together with the eagerness of heart and body which a teacher ought to have in setting forth the word of God, he mentions here all the instruments of speech, namely mouth, tongue, and lips, so that nothing in him may be found empty of instruction of his neighbour and praise of God. [Col. 1073B] The mouth pronounces, the tongue forms, and the lips arrange words. Therefore “my tongue shall exult in your righteousness,” yet not by its own power, but by yours; for you:

> O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.

“For it is not you who speak,” says the Lord, “but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). “Do you seek,” says the Apostle, “proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13.) And another says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84 [85]). For the mouth of one whose lips the Lord does not open, but who speaks from himself, attributing wisdom and eloquence to himself rather than to God—as those did who said: “Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” [Col. 1073C] (Ps. 11 [12])—does not humbly proclaim God’s praise, but boastfully exalts its own praise. Such a person either scarcely or never edifies his hearers, because he seeks not their salvation but his own glory.

A preacher, therefore, according to the Apostle’s teaching, must not rely on persuasive words of human wisdom; rather, his speech must be in the manifestation of spirit and power, so that through the power of his speech he may show that Spirit who speaks in him (1 Cor. 2). This he will rightly do if he asks wisdom from God, “who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach” (Jas. 1), and thus speaks “as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4). When those utterances have worked the force of their power in the hearts of hearers, they will certainly show that Spirit who invisibly spoke through the preacher’s mouth. He is the one who says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80 [81]). You open it as an obedient minister, and I fill it as an instructing master.

Therefore, O Lord, you will open my lips, which were previously closed because of sins; and thus the bodily mouth will bring forth the secret things of the mind, because it will proclaim your praise, namely the works of creation and re-creation [alternative reading: “the works of the Creator and of creation”], which declare you praiseworthy above all things. Note also that we ought in charity to love three things: God, ourselves, and our neighbour. The Lord says: “You shall love your God with all your heart”: behold the first; “and as yourself”: behold the second; “you shall love your neighbour”: behold the third (Deut. 4; Matt. 22).

Love of neighbour pertains to the saying: “I will teach [Col. 1074A] the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will be converted to you.” Love of self pertains to what follows: “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God of my salvation.” Love of God pertains to what is added: “My mouth shall proclaim your praise.” This is the sacrifice of praise concerning which you said: “The sacrifice of praise will honour me; and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49 [50]). Therefore, “offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High” (ibid.).

> For if you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; in whole burnt offerings you will not delight.

Above, David had prayed that the spirit of prophecy might not be taken from him; and now he is shown to have been heard, because he prophesies of the abolition of legal sacrifices. “For if you had desired sacrifice,” he says, “I would surely have given it.” The penitent had promised that, for expiation of sin, he would offer a sacrifice of praise, saying: “O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” And as though someone asked him: Why do you not offer the sacrifice of the Law? He answers: Because legal sacrifices and carnal whole burnt offerings are no longer pleasing or acceptable to God. For if you, O God, had wished to receive a legal sacrifice from me, I would surely have given it, obedient to your will; but you will not delight in carnal whole burnt offerings, especially after the one true sacrifice has been instituted.

Between whole burnt offerings and sacrifices there was this difference in the old Law: whole burnt offerings were burned completely, being so called from *holo*, “whole,” and *cauma*, “burning”; sacrifices, however, were not burned whole, but due portions of them were reserved for the offering priests. [Col. 1074C] Further, there is this difference between those old sacrifices and this new one: they only signified and did not justify; this one both signifies and justifies. For those were made from irrational animals, namely birds and cattle. “For it is impossible,” as the Apostle says, “for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls or goats” (Heb. 10). This sacrifice alone is not merely non-rational but rational: namely, the true man, himself both priest and sacrifice, physician and medicine. Of him the same Apostle says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5); and he himself says: “He who eats me shall live because of me” (John 6).

This sacrifice certainly bears signification in hope, which signifies, but provides justification in reality, which justifies; for it is itself both sacrament and thing, yet the thing of one reality and the sacrament of another. Those were figure; this is truth. Those were shadow; this is light. For when truth came, the figure ceased; and the shadow vanished when the light shone, as Truth itself had said through this same Psalmist: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me. Whole burnt offerings also for sin you did not require; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39 [40]).

Whether sacrifices were meritorious works is not without reason doubted, since the Lord says of them through the prophet: “I gave them ordinances that were not good and statutes by which they should not live” (Ezek. 20). For this reason the Apostle also says [Col. 1075A] that that Law “brought no one to perfection” (Heb. 7). Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices; but your whole burnt offerings are always before me. I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49 [50].) And through the prophet Isaiah the Lord says: “He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man; he who slaughters cattle is as one who breaks a dog’s neck. He who offers an oblation is as one who offers swine’s blood. He who offers incense in remembrance is as one who blesses an idol” (Isa. 66). Again through the same prophet: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? says the Lord. I am full; I have not desired the whole burnt offerings of rams and fat of fatlings, nor the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands?” (Isa. 1.)

Thus sacrifices of this kind were not pleasing or acceptable to God, since they were instituted not in order to merit eternal reward, but to tame and restrain a rebellious and stiff-necked people, lest, occupied with these sacrifices, they should sink into idolatry, and so that their transgression of them might be severely punished. Therefore the apostle Peter says: “Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15.) Hence their performance seems not to have merited eternal glory.

Yet since, in addition to the aforesaid reasons, they were also instituted for signification, and whatever was commanded for whatever reason was from God himself, those who performed them from the root of charity and the power of obedience appeared beyond doubt to deserve reward. For in this way transgression deserved punishment and observance deserved reward. Let it be said, then, if one pleases, that those commands were good in themselves, but were not good for those who performed them unworthily. The Lord reproves such persons through the prophet: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes from you”; and: “When you multiply prayer, I will not hear; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1). Just as the Apostle says of the new and true sacrifice that whoever eats unworthily “eats judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

All the testimonies set forth above must accordingly be referred to this sense. Or they refer to the time of grace, when, after the true sacrifice had been instituted, those sacrifices were no longer to be performed as a duty. Thus the Apostle says above: “Victims and offerings and whole burnt offerings for sin you did not desire, nor were they pleasing to you, which are offered according to the Law. Then I said: Behold, I come to do your will, O God. He takes away the first in order to establish what follows; by this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ” (Ps. 36 [37]; Heb. 10).

Thus, wherever one reads that those sacrificial works were not meritorious, the general statement must be understood with an exception for a few. For almost all performed those works not from love but from fear, not as free persons but as slaves: fearing punishment but not loving righteousness. Yet the few who reverenced in their signification the mystery and fulfilled them from charity for the sake of obedience not only avoided temporal punishment but also merited eternal life. But the sacrifice that has always pleased God—after the Law, before the Law, and even during the Law—he shows when he adds:

> A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you do not despise [alternative reading: *despecies*, a variant form of *despicies*, “you will not despise”].

Here six kinds of sacrifices and six kinds of sacrificers may be denoted: the sacrifice of praise and of the Law; the sacrifice of repentance and of righteousness; the sacrifice of perfection and of preaching. Of the first it is said: “My mouth shall proclaim your praise”; of the second: “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; in whole burnt offerings you will not delight”; of the third: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise”; of the fourth it is said: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness”; of the fifth: “You will accept offerings and whole burnt offerings”; of the sixth: “Then they will place calves upon your altar.” The first is the sacrifice of those who confess, and the second of the Hebrews; the third is the sacrifice of penitents, and the fourth of the righteous; the fifth is the sacrifice of contemplatives, and the sixth of teachers, as will be shown more fully in the course of the exposition.

The three things necessary to true repentance may also suitably be understood here: compunction of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. Thus being troubled is referred to satisfaction, contrition to compunction, and humiliation to confession. For the spirit is troubled—that is, troubled together with the body—when it endures the pain of compunction; it is humbled when it endures the shame of confession. Thus the spirit is troubled in punishment for wanton action; the heart is broken in punishment for wicked action; and the mouth is humbled in punishment for proud speech. God does not despise but accepts such a sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart. Therefore the sacrifice pleasing to God is not a goat or bull, but a troubled spirit. Hence you, O God, will not despise a contrite and humbled heart, but will rather accept it.

> Deal graciously, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.

The fifth part: having first rejected the Synagogue along with its carnal sacrifices, David prays for the Church to be built, in which spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God may be offered. He designates this Church by three names, calling it Zion, Jerusalem, and altar, because of the three orders in the Church: regular, lay, and clerical. Elsewhere these are denoted by Noah, Daniel, and Job, whom the prophet saw as being saved; and in the Gospel there are said to be two in the field, two at the mill, and two in bed (Matt. 24).

The regular life is contemplative and spiritual; those who lead such a life dwell below in the city of Jerusalem. The clerical life is, as it were, mixed and common; those who lead it minister in the middle at the altar, because it is partly secular, insofar as it possesses worldly things, and partly likewise spiritual, insofar as it ministers divine things. Thus the Temple itself, where the altar was, stood in the middle between Mount Zion, which rose above, and the city of Jerusalem, which lay below. Therefore, O Lord, deal graciously with Zion—that is, with the Church, which now beholds through faith and at last will contemplate by sight—for “now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

Zion, which is interpreted “watchtower” or “watching,” deal graciously with, I say, in your good will—that is, according to the good pleasure of your will—or in your Holy Spirit, who is your good will. For in the holy and undivided Trinity, mind is appropriated to the Father, reason to the Son, and will to the Holy Spirit. “That the walls of Jerusalem may be built”: namely, the saints who fortify Jerusalem, that is, the Church, concerning whom it is written: “All your walls are precious stones” (Isa. 16). And elsewhere: “Upon your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen” (Isa. 62). But Christ also is the wall of walls, of whom it is written: “Zion, the city of our strength: a saviour will be set in it as a wall” (Isa. 26).

The first and chief foundation of these walls, the foundation as it were of foundations, is Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid, besides which no other can be laid: Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3). The second and secondary foundations are the apostles, of whom the same Apostle says: “You have been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2); and elsewhere: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86 [87]). The stones are all the faithful, of whom it is written: “I will lay precious stones throughout the world” (Isa. 54). These are the stones which iron did not touch, from which the Lord commanded an altar to be built for himself. Christ too is the stone of stones, which, according to the prophet, was cut from the mountain without hands. Of him the Psalmist himself says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117 [118]).

The cement by which spiritual stones are joined is the glue of charity, denoted by the bitumen with which the various boards of Noah’s ark were joined and with which the ark itself was coated within and without. Of this the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” [Col. 1077D] (Rom. 5). Christ too is charity, as it were the glue, of whom the apostle John says: “God is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

Therefore deal graciously with Zion—that is, with the order of prelates, who are set in the watchtower, as is said to the prophet: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3)—so that through them the walls of Jerusalem may be built, that is, so that the body of faithful persons may be ordered in the Church. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” This is the Church, which, although it does not now see outward peace, nevertheless sees inward peace, of which the Lord says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you. I do not give to you as the world gives” (John 14). And at last it will see the higher peace, concerning which the Lord says through the Psalmist: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4).

> Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and whole burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.

This “then” may refer either to the state of earthly Jerusalem, that is, the Church militant, to which it is said: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, because your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 60); or to the state of heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church triumphant, of which it is said: “That Jerusalem which is above is our mother” (Gal. 4).

Therefore then, namely when the walls of Jerusalem have been built—that is, when the Church of the Gentiles has been gathered and ordered—you, O God, will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, that is, the spiritual sacrifice which the righteous will offer to you in her. For although every virtue offers its own sacrifice, because it presents its own sacred deed, nevertheless the work of every virtue generally is called a sacrifice of righteousness because righteousness is a common virtue; hence all virtuous persons are called righteous.

Further, there are the carnal whole burnt offerings of the Jews, in which the Lord does not delight, as was said above: “You will not delight in whole burnt offerings.” And there are the spiritual whole burnt offerings of Christians, which God accepts, of which it is said here: “You will accept offerings and whole burnt offerings,” that is, those who offer themselves to you as a whole burnt offering: namely perfect men, who set themselves entirely on fire with the fire of charity in love for you, leaving all things for your sake and cleaving wholly to you alone, devoting themselves only to your contemplation. A distinction may, however, be drawn between offerings and whole burnt offerings, so that offerings denote the perfect and whole burnt offerings the most perfect.

Then also those to whom the ordering of the Church belongs—that is, the greater prelates—will place calves: not the sort which the newly calved cows had left shut up at home while they went in one path to Beth-shemesh (1 Sam. 6), nor such as God commanded to be offered for the sin of the priest and of the multitude. They will place, I say, calves—that is, preachers innocent in conduct and resounding with lowing—of whom it is said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18 [19]). Upon the altar—that is, upon the Church—by appointing them rulers and teachers of the Church, as is written: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim the Gospel to Zion” [Col. 1078D] (Isa. 40).

They are like the calf which is one of the four living creatures that, according to Ezekiel’s vision, signify the chief preachers, namely the four Evangelists (Ezek. 1). Of such, now grown, it is written: “The oxen were ploughing, and the asses were feeding beside them” (Job 1); and concerning them the prophet says: “You shall leap like calves of the herd” (Mal. 4). Concerning this altar the Lord commanded: “If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it from hewn stones” (Exod. 20). For one who gathers a multitude of the faithful to God ought prudently to take care not to assemble it from persons divided by heresy or schism, but united by faith and charity.

Or calves may mean martyrs, and the altar, faith, concerning which the Lord commands: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (ibid.). This is faith in the incarnation and death of Christ, which he himself assumed according to earthly substance. Therefore they will place calves—that is, martyrs, who were slain for faith in the incarnation and death of Christ—upon this altar of faith, because faith is the foundation of martyrdom. Of faith the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11).

Such persons imitate the fattened calf that was killed for the return of the prodigal son (Luke 15), concerning whom Truth says: “My bulls and my fattened animals have been killed” (Matt. 22); and concerning whom the Psalmist himself also says: “The Lord will break the cedars, and crush them like a calf of Lebanon” (Ps. 28 [29]). But what is meant by the saying of the apostle John in Revelation: “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those killed for the word of God and for the testimony which they held” (Rev. 6)? This altar is one thing and that altar another: upon that altar the martyrs suffered on their journey; beneath this one they rest in their homeland.

But if this is taken not of the state which is on the journey, but of the state which is in the homeland, it may indeed be understood thus: Then—that is, in the age to come—you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, that is, of most righteous praise; for then the saints, freed by you from every corruption of souls and bodies and clothed in two robes, namely the robe of glorification in the body and the robe of glorification in the mind, will praise you most righteously. Then you will also accept offerings and whole burnt offerings, that is, the greater and lesser elect, because “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15), all set ablaze in you by the fire of charity. For then the elect will love you with all their heart, with all their mind, and with all their soul (Matt. 22): that is, with understanding without error, memory without forgetfulness, and will without opposition, because they will will absolutely nothing except what they know you will.

Then the angels, the reapers, will place calves—that is, saints without any yoke of sin—upon your altar, that is, upon the triumphant Church, which is the highest altar after the undivided Trinity. Concerning it, it is written: “You shall not go up to my altar by steps” (Exod. 29). For we must not establish degrees within the undivided Trinity, saying that the Father is greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit least, as the impious Arian asserts. But one ascends by steps to the altar of the triumphant Church, that is, by differences of merits; concerning these it is written: “God shall be known in her steps when he receives her” (Ps. 47 [48]).

These will place upon the altar of the heart, of which the Lord says: “Fire shall always burn upon my altar” (Lev. 6), calves of the lips—that is, the most perfect praises of God. For “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83 [84]).

Behold, this psalm begins with guilt and misery and ends in glory and joy, because from the misery of sinners one ascends through true repentance to the glory of the blessed.

## [PSALM V.]

[Col. 1079]

### Elucidation of the fifth penitential psalm

The title of this psalm is as follows: “A prayer of the poor man when he was afflicted and poured out his prayer in the presence of the Lord.” Explanation of the same title.

[Col. 1079C] By the poor man in the title is denoted the humble penitent, who is distressed because of his miseries and pours out his prayers before the Lord. Poverty is good, evil, and intermediate. Good poverty is that of humility; evil poverty that of covetousness; intermediate poverty that of necessity. The first makes the poor of Christ, the second the poor of Zabul (the Devil), the third the poor of the world. Of the first it is said: “The poor and needy shall praise your name” (Ps. 73 [74]); and: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Of the second: “You do not know that you are poor and miserable” (Rev. 3); and: “We have become exceedingly poor” (Ps. 78 [79]). Of the third: “Even a poor man is hateful to his friend” (Prov. 14); and: “You will always have the poor with you, but me you will not always have” (Matt. 26).

Christ himself too, though he is true God and true man, is at once rich and poor. He said of himself: “I am poor and sorrowful” (Ps. 68 [69]). For “foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8; Luke 9). Hence: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” (Ps. 40 [41]), because he who was rich became poor for us, so that he might make us poor people rich in himself. For he took our poverty and gave us his riches. Since he descended to earth to transact business, as God, with human beings, he could not trade with them otherwise than by receiving their wares and rendering his own to them. Thus he gave the rich wares which he possessed and received the poor wares which he found. He gave divine powers and received human defects; he assumed servitude and bestowed freedom; and, to summarize much briefly, he received death and gave life; he bestowed glory and received misery.

[Col. 1080D] Therefore the humble penitent, pursuing such a transaction in this psalm, first sets forth human misery and then expounds divine glory.

### Explanation of Psalm 101 [102] in the order of the Psalms, but fifth in the order of the penitential psalms

[Col. 1079]

[Col. 1079D] “O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come [alternative reading: “reach”] to you.”

[Col. 1080D] This psalm is fifth in the order of the penitential psalms. It contains twenty-five [alternatively, twenty-nine] [Col. 1081A] verses, to be divided into five groups of five; and at its beginning it sets forth in sequence five petitions, so that the mystery of the number five may be commended throughout. Ezekiel (ch. 10) expressly commends it in his description of the Temple, saying that the vestibule of the Temple all around was twenty-five cubits in length and five in breadth. Certainly, because five multiplied by itself always returns into itself, it signifies eternity, which remains within itself and always endures unchanged. This psalm mentions it in five places. First: “But thou, O Lord, endurest for ever, and thy memorial unto generation and generation”; second: “Do not call me back in the midst of my days; thy years are unto age upon age”; third: “They shall perish, but thou shalt endure”; fourth: “But thou, [Col. 1081B] O Lord, art the same, and thy years shall not fail”; fifth: “The children of thy servants shall dwell there” [alternatively, “with thee”], that is, in thy years. Hence it is added: “And their seed shall be directed for ever and ever.” Therefore, to signify this, the psalm contains twenty-five [alternatively, twenty-nine] verses, a number obtained by multiplying five by itself and bringing it back into itself.

In the first group of five, the penitent sets forth the form of prayer and the reason for being heard. Concerning the form of prayer he begins: “Lord, hear my prayer”; concerning the reason for being heard he adds: “For my days have failed like smoke.” He repeats the form of prayer five times without any intervening matter. First: “Hear my prayer”; second: [Col. 1081C] “Let my cry come unto thee”; third: “Turn not thy face away from me”; fourth: “Incline thine ear unto me”; fifth: “Hear me speedily.” By repeating one and the same thing so often, he plainly shows with what urgency of supplication and what affection of devotion we ought to pray to God.

Yet he also suggests that at times someone prays so faintly that his prayer cannot be heard. Sometimes, however, he cries loudly, but his cry is not allowed to reach the ruler. At other times the cry reaches the ruler, but he turns his ear away from the petitions. Sometimes again he inclines his ears when occasion requires, but delays too long in hearing the petitioner. Therefore, to remove these five impediments, this penitent repeats his prayer so often, [Col. 1081D] saying: “Lord, Creator and Restorer, hear my prayer, which is not small or feeble but at once clear and clamorous. Therefore let my cry reach thee; and when it has reached thee, do not turn thy face away from me, but, when thou hast inclined thine ear, incline it at the fitting time. And therefore, on whatever day I am troubled, incline thine ear to me; and when the fitting time comes, do not long delay to hear me. Therefore, on whatever day I call upon thee, hear me speedily.”

Here the penitent shows that his prayers are worthy, devout, welcome, necessary and humble, timely and effectual. Therefore, because they are worthy: “Hear my prayer.” Because they are devout: “Let my cry come unto thee.” Because they are welcome: “Turn not thy face away from me.” Again, because they are necessary and humble: [Col. 1082A] “On whatever day I am troubled, incline thine ear unto me.” And because they are timely and effectual: “On whatever day I call upon thee, hear me speedily.”

He says, therefore: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come unto thee.” This cry must be understood not so much as an exertion of the voice as a devotion of the heart. Thus Susanna cried out, who, weeping, looked up to heaven; for her heart had confidence in the Lord, and therefore the Lord heard her voice (Dan. 13). Therefore let my cry come unto thee—not like the cry of the Sodomites, which provoked thee to anger (Gen. 18), but like the cry of the Ninevites, which inclined thee to pardon (Jonah 3).

Moreover, there are three things that prevent a cry from reaching the ears of the Most High so as to be heard by him: namely, a griddle, a wall, and [Col. 1082B] a cloud. Of the griddle it is written: “And thou, son of man, take for thyself an iron griddle, and place it between thee and the city, and set thy face firmly toward it” (Ezek. 4). Of the wall it is said: “In thee I shall be delivered from temptation, and in my God I shall pass over a wall” (Ps. 17). Of the cloud it is written: “Thou hast placed a cloud before thee, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. 3). Since these matters have been explained, they need not be repeated here. It follows:

“Turn not thy face away from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline thine ear unto me.

“On whatever day I call upon thee, hear me speedily.”

Turn away indeed the face of severity and punishment, but show the face of kindness and propitiation. Of the former it is written: “I shall not be hidden from thy face—from the face of thy wrath” (Job 13). Adam with his wife wished to hide himself from this face in the midst of Paradise; but assuredly he could not, because of what is written: “Whither shall I go from thy spirit, and whither shall I flee from thy face?” (Ps. 138). Of the latter it is said: “Why dost thou hide thy face? Show us thy face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). In accordance with this Jacob says: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32). “Face to face” is a leading from the bodily to the spiritual, as is said elsewhere: “Because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed” (John 20).

Therefore, “turn not thy face away from me,” but “turn thy face away from my sins” (Ps. 50), because thou dost not hate nature but guilt. “For thou hatest none of the things which thou hast made, O Lord” (Wis. 11). But because [Col. 1082D] I am often troubled, both in body and in mind, by devil and by man, by the world and by the flesh, therefore, on whatever day I am troubled, incline—thou who art exalted—to me who am lowly, thine ear, that is, the hearing of kindness. “On whatever day I call upon thee, hear me speedily,” that thy promise may be fulfilled: “While thou art still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here” (Gen. 46).

“For my days have failed like smoke, and my bones have been shattered as in a frying-pan” [alternatively, “have dried up like a firebrand”].

He sets forth the miseries that he suffers in himself: namely, the brevity of life, whence, “My days have failed like smoke”; the anguish of his soul, whence, “My bones have been shattered as in a frying-pan”; the dryness of his heart, whence, “I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up”; and the weakness [Col. 1083A] of his body, whence, “I forgot to eat my bread.” Thus, “at the sound of my groaning my bones clung to my flesh”; and I have become thin like a pelican in the wilderness, like a night-raven in its dwelling-place, and like a solitary sparrow on a building—birds that, literally speaking, are exceedingly lean. Therefore thou oughtest to hear me speedily, because “my days have failed like smoke.”

There is smoke of breathing, whence: “Who is this that goes up like a little rod of smoke, from perfumes of myrrh and frankincense?” (Song 3). Of prayer, whence: “The smoke of the perfumes rose in the presence of the Lord from the hand of the angel” (Rev. 8). Of compunction, whence: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143). Of contemplation, whence: “The house was filled with smoke” (Isa. 6); and: “The people saw the mountain smoking” (Exod. 20). Again, there is smoke of failing, whence: [Col. 1083B] “As smoke fails, let them fail” (Ps. 36). Of warning, whence: “There are three things that drive a man from his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife.” Of pride, whence: “The light of the wicked is like a storm; his day is like smoke that is scattered” (Wis. 5). Of pretence, whence: “A smoking wood he shall not extinguish” (Isa. 42). Of corruption, whence: “From the smoke of the pit came locusts” (Rev. 9). Of damnation, whence: “Their smoke rises from generation to generation, and it shall be desolate for ever and ever” (Rev. 19).

Therefore my days have failed like smoke: that is, my life quickly passes away, as smoke quickly vanishes. In accordance with what is written: “What is our life? A vapour appearing for a little while” (Jas. 4). And elsewhere it is said: “My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut down by the weaver” (Job 7). Or, because the smoke of pride [Col. 1083C] by which Adam was disobedient to his Creator was the cause for which man was made subject to the necessity of dying, “my days have failed like smoke”: that is, after the likeness of the smoke that introduced this failure. For life declines by decreasing, just as smoke fails by rising.

Morally, the days of the person whose manner of life is empty of the fruit of good work fail. And “my bones have been shattered as in a frying-pan”: that is, the powers of my soul have been crushed by distress, as though in a frying-pan, just as flesh is burned in a pan; according to what is elsewhere written: “My bones dried up because of the heat” (Job 30). For when the soul is oppressed and afflicted, its powers contract and dry up, especially through remembrance of sin and fear of judgment; [Col. 1083D] for then a man is fried when he fears that he will burn.

Morally, “my bones,” that is, my inner parts, “have been shattered”: that is, they have been afflicted through compassion for neighbours, as the Apostle said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11 [the citation is printed “II Cor. II”]). For the stumbling of one’s neighbours is the frying-pan of the righteous. But wishing to show whence the failure of his days and the frying of his bones had come upon him, he adds:

“I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up, because I forgot to eat my bread.”

Almost everything about me speaks of misery: failure, frying, striking, dryness, forgetfulness, groaning, and thinness. These are indicated when it is said: “My bones clung to my flesh,” because my flesh, thinned and dried [Col. 1084A] through emaciation, seems almost to have passed into bone. Hence this poor man is rightly distressed and says: “I was struck by the sentence of death in Adam, when the Lord said: ‘On whatever day thou eatest, thou shalt die by death’” (Gen. 2). From him the material has been propagated to his descendants.

“I was struck like grass,” that is, after the likeness of grass, which before it is struck is green and flowering; but when struck, it falls and dries up. Thus man, before he sinned, stood upright and innocent; but when he sinned, he fell, wretched and unhappy. Or, I was struck by the serpent’s poison, that is, by the devil’s suggestion, when he promised: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). I was struck, I say, like grass, because I truly am grass: that is, frail and mortal. For “all flesh is grass, and all [Col. 1084B] its glory is as the flower of grass” (1 Pet. 1), which is green today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace (Matt. 6). Thus a man now lives and shortly afterward is plunged into hell.

For there is the frailty of the flesh, whence: “All flesh is grass”; and: “Truly the people are grass” (Isa. 40). There is the greenness of the mind, whence: “They shall flourish like the grass of the earth” (Ps. 71); and: “He brings forth grass on the mountains” (Ps. 146). There is the vanity of the heart, whence: “The inward parts of a fool are like the wheel of a cart” (Sirach 33), which carries hay and is always creaking. There is the carnal man, whence: “He shall eat grass like an ox” (Job 40). There is also Christ’s very humanity, whence: “Bringing forth grass for cattle and herb for the service of men” (Ps. 103), because Christ, like grass, was laid in a manger.

“And my heart dried up,” because through the barrenness of sin it lost its greenness, [Col. 1084C] that is, its virtue. For by sinning man was stripped of gratuitous gifts, wounded in his natural powers, and so left half-alive. Assign each thing to its corresponding thing: because “I was struck like grass,” “my days failed like smoke”; and because “my heart dried up,” “my bones dried up like a firebrand.” And this arose because “I forgot to eat my bread.”

For man ate the food forbidden him, and neglected to eat—that is, to keep—the bread given him by God, namely the word spoken to him by God. “Of the tree,” he says, “of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat” (Gen. 2). “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4).

Bread is understood in many ways in Scripture. It is Christ himself according to his divinity, whence: [Col. 1084D] “Man shall eat the bread of angels” (Ps. 77); and: “Thou gavest them bread from heaven, having in itself every delight and the sweetness of every flavour” (Wis. 16). It is the same Christ according to his humanity, whence: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6); and his flesh, whence: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid.). It is eternal blessedness, whence: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14). It is heavenly desire, whence: “I did not eat desirable bread” (Dan. 10). It is the universal Church, whence: “We are one bread and one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 10). It is a good work, whence: “We shall eat our bread” (Isa. 4); and: “You shall eat unleavened breads with wild lettuces” (Exod. 12). It is Holy Scripture, whence: “The little ones asked for bread, [Col. 1085A] and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4); and: “In the sweat of thy face thou shalt eat thy bread” (Gen. 3). It is the word of God, whence: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4); and: “He shall feed him with the bread of life” (Sirach 15). It is true repentance, whence: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126); and: “My tears became my bread by day and by night” (Ps. 41). It is sincere charity, whence: “If he asks for bread, will he give him a stone?” (Matt. 7). It is strength of mind, whence: “Bread strengthens the heart of man” (Ps. 103); and: “He broke all the support of bread” (Ps. 104). It is the gift of the Holy Spirit, whence: “I shall satisfy her poor with breads” (Ps. 131).

Furthermore, bread is the teaching of heretics, whence: “The bread of falsehood is sweet to a man” [Col. 1085B] (Prov. 20); and: “When he begins to seek bread, he knows that a day of darkness is prepared in his hand” (Job 15). It is the life of hypocrites, whence: “Ephraim has become a bread baked under ashes, which is not turned” (Hos. 7). It is the delight of sin, whence: “Hidden bread is sweeter” (Prov. 9); and: “Come, eat hidden breads” (ibid.). It is worldly pleasure, whence: “Their bread shall be turned into the gall of asps” (Job 20).

“At the sound of my groaning my bone clung to my flesh.”

Therefore I was struck like grass, and my heart dried up, because I forgot to eat my bread: that is, because I did not firmly retain in my memory, nor keep, God’s word. Hence, “at the sound of my groaning”—that is, at the devil’s suggestion, who is my groaning, [Col. 1085C] that is, the reason why I groan—“my bone clung to my flesh”: that is, reason consented to sensuality, when the man yielded to his wife. “The woman,” he says, “whom thou gavest me, gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3).

Or, because I did not keep God’s word, “at the sound of my groaning my bones clung to my flesh,” because “a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. 17). In Christ, however, bone clung to flesh when divinity was united to humanity, because “the Word was made flesh” (John 1). In the Church it clung to flesh when the strong bear the weak, according to the Apostle’s saying: “We who are strong ought to bear the infirmity of the weak” (Rom. 14). It follows:

“I have become like the pelican of the wilderness; I have become [Col. 1085D] like a night-raven in its dwelling-place.

“I watched, and I became like a solitary sparrow on a building” [alternatively, “a solitary one on a roof”].

Here the Psalmist distinguishes three birds: the pelican, the night-raven, and the sparrow; and the wilderness, the dwelling-place, and the building or roof. The pelican is a lean bird remaining in the wilderness. The night-raven rests by day and keeps watch by night, dwelling in walls and uttering a mournful cry. The sparrow is lustful and cunning, but becomes chaste when it remains alone on a building. By these three birds three kinds of penitents are denoted. For some wholly leave the world in order to perform repentance; others still remain in the world; while others partly leave the world and partly remain in the world.

The one who, in order to perform repentance, passes from the world into solitude, and there grows thin through vigils, fasts, other mortifications of the body, and contritions of the heart—having, as it were, skin in place of flesh—is surely like a pelican remaining in the wilderness. The one, however, who, groaning and weeping, withdraws himself from worldly conduct and, abstaining from pleasures, avoids the snares of temptation—as though attending to the night—unquestionably strives to keep watch like a night-raven in its dwelling-place. But the one who abandons the works of lust and embraces the celibacy of chastity has indeed become like a sparrow: no longer lustful but solitary, that is, chaste; freed from disgraceful passion; remaining on the building or roof of which the Lord says: “He who is on the roof, let him not come down to take anything from the house” (Matt. 24), [Col. 1086B] “that every building, being constructed, may grow into a holy temple in the Lord” (Eph. 2).

Thus the general penitent says: “I have become like a pelican in the wilderness,” with respect to the first kind of penitents; “and like a night-raven,” with respect to the second; “and like a solitary sparrow on a building,” with respect to the third.

This can also be explained otherwise: first, that he expresses the sin which he committed unworthily and the repentance which he performed worthily, after the likeness of the first man, Adam; then the temptations he suffered from the devil and the persecutions he endured from men, after the likeness of the second man, Christ. Thus the sense is: “I was struck by the devil’s suggestion like grass,” that is, like Adam, who truly was grass, because in the morning of creation [Col. 1086C] he flourished in virtues, but in the evening of transgression fell into misery. “And my heart dried up” in the barrenness of sin, “because I forgot to eat my bread,” that is, to observe the Lord’s command, like Adam, who neglected to keep God’s precept, saying to him: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. 3).

But when I recognized my sin, I repented, because “at the sound of my groaning my bones clung to my flesh.” Thus there was in my heart a groan of compunction, from which came a voice of confession in my mouth, and then the affliction of satisfaction in my deed, because I undertook a strict fast; whence: “My bones clung to my flesh.” After the fast I was tempted by the devil, as Christ was, in three vices: in the wilderness concerning [Col. 1086D] gluttony; on the mountain concerning avarice; and in the Temple concerning boasting or pride.

For Christ was like a pelican in the wilderness when he fasted in the desert forty days and forty nights, and afterward was hungry (Matt. 4). For the pelican, remaining in the wilderness, is worn down by excessive leanness. He was likewise like a night-raven in its dwelling-place, when the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world on the mountain’s brow. For the night-raven has an exceptionally clear sight, and therefore sees clearly even in the night. He also was like a solitary sparrow on a building, or one alone on a roof: alone from his Father, alone from his mother; from the Father without a mother, from the mother without a father; solitary in the womb, solitary in the tomb. And, as he himself testifies: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John [Col. 1087A] 3).

Nor did I suffer temptations from the devil only, like Christ, but also from men, just as he endured them from the Jews; for “all day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.” Although the word “I watched” is placed in the middle, it pertains not only to the middle but also to the first and last clauses, so that it should be said: “I became like a pelican in the wilderness. I watched, and I became like a solitary sparrow on a building,” because everyone in every place is bound to keep watch against demons, the world, and the flesh. Therefore let not the hermit be secure in the wilderness, nor the monk secure in the cloister, for Adam was tempted in Paradise and Jesus in the wilderness.

Certainly, God watches, the angel watches, man watches, and the Devil watches. God watches through mercy [Col. 1087B] and justice, in order to pardon and punish; whence: “When thou comest to the Lord, he will immediately awaken toward thee” (Job 8). Again: “The Lord watched over the evil and brought it upon us” (Dan. 9). For this reason he himself is called a wakeful rod (Jer. 1). The angel watches through diligence and caution, to guard and help; whence: “A watcher and a holy one came down from heaven” (Dan. 4); and: “The decree is in the judgment of the watchers” (ibid.).
