Man watches through circumspection, whence: “There were shepherds in that region keeping watch and keeping the watches of the night over their flock” (Luke 2); through instruction, whence: “Write to the angel of the church of Sardis: Be watchful and strengthen the things that were about to die” (Rev. 3); through preaching, [Col. 1087C] whence: “Watch in all things, labour, do the work of an evangelist” (2 Tim. 4); through prayer, whence: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26); through contemplation, whence: “I sleep, and my heart watches” (Song 5); through attentiveness, whence: “Blessed is he who watches at the doors of wisdom and keeps watch at the posts of my tabernacle” (Prov. 8).

But the Devil watches in order to harm and deceive. Hence Peter warns, saying: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5). He watches also when he makes men watch in wickedness, whence: “They do not sleep unless they have done evil, and sleep is taken from them unless they have caused someone to fall” (Prov. 4). Wickedness itself is also said to watch [Col. 1087D] when someone watches in it, whence: “The yoke of their iniquities kept watch” (Lam. 1).

Therefore: “Awake, ye righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15). “Watch, because you do not know at what hour the Lord may come: in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning; lest, coming suddenly, he find you asleep” (Mark 13). For blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching (Luke 12). “For watchfulness in honourable things will wear away the flesh, and concern for it will take away sleep” (Sirach 31). The Lord commanded the doorkeeper to watch, adding: “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch” (Mark 13).

The sparrow, too, bears a manifold figure in Scripture. For the sparrow is called Christ, whence: “I became like a solitary sparrow on a roof.” Hence the cleansed leper offered two living sparrows, one of which was sacrificed [Col. 1088A] as an offering and the other released into the field, because Christ’s humanity was sacrificed for cleansing the leprosy of the human race, while his divinity was released free in the Passion. The sparrow is also called human perception, whence: “Are not five sparrows sold for an as?” (Matt. 10). It is the reason of the heart, whence: “The sparrow finds itself a house, and the turtledove a nest” (Ps. 83). It is also called the righteous man, whence: “Our soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 123); and: “There the sparrows shall make nests” (Ps. 103). It is also called the carnal man, whence: “You are worth more than many sparrows” (Luke 12); and the proud heretic, whence: “Move to the mountain like a sparrow” (Ps. 10).

“All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.”

[Col. 1088B] In the first group of five the penitent expounded the inward miseries that he suffers in himself; in this second group of five he expounds the outward miseries that he feels himself to suffer from others. For he suffers continual mockery and secret conspiracies from true enemies and false friends, whence: “All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.” He suffers this because “I ate my bread in weeping and mixed my drink with weeping.”

For when the devil sees a sinner turn to repentance, he stirs up mockers, who put him to shame by reproaching him, and introduces conspirators, who overthrow him by plotting against him—namely, those whom he does not easily detect, false flatterers; or even those who praised him while he enjoyed worldly life with them—in order to recall him from the pursuit of repentance through open injuries and hidden snares. See how greatly the devil grieves at a sinner’s repentance, and how hard he labours to call him back to sin. Therefore, “those who praised me swore against me.”

“Because I ate ashes like bread, and tempered [alternatively, mixed] my drink with weeping.”

He notes in the penitent the vileness of his food when he says, “I ate ashes like bread,” and the harshness of his drink when he adds, “I mixed my drink with weeping.” There is ash of the Lord’s Passion, whence: “Make pans to receive the ashes” (Exod. 27). This is the ash of the red heifer, of which the Apostle says: “If the blood of goats [Col. 1088D] and bulls and the ash of a heifer, sprinkled upon those who are defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh” (Heb. 9). There is the ash of penitential sanctification, whence: “I repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42); and: “I covered my flesh with ashes” (Job 16). There is the ash of human lowliness, whence: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18); and: “In the house of ashes sprinkle yourselves with ashes” (Jer. 25). And there is the ash of final corruption, whence: “Man shall return to ashes” (Job 34); and: “Thou art ashes, and unto ashes thou shalt return” (Gen. 3).

Drink, too, is understood in many ways in Scripture. There is the drink of the Eucharist, whence: “My heart and my flesh exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). Of understanding, whence: “He gave him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Sirach 15). Of teaching, whence: [Col. 1089A] “Waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains; all the beasts of the field shall drink of them” (Ps. 103). Of glory, whence: “Thou shalt give them drink from the torrent of thy delight” (Ps. 35). Of compunction, whence: “Thou hast given us to drink the wine of compunction” (Ps. 59). Of affliction, whence: “Thou wilt give us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 76). Of manifestation, whence: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68). Of deception, whence: “Woe to him who gives his friend drink, mixing in gall!” (Hab. 2).

Therefore I ate ashes like bread: that is, ashes with bread, or bread with ashes—namely, vile and despised bread, as though ash-covered bread or ash-bread. “And I mixed my drink with weeping,” because there was such an abundance of tears that I poured them into my drink. Otherwise: ash is what remains of wood consumed by fire. But wood consumed by fire is sin forgiven through charity, according to the saying: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7). Sin itself is also sometimes pleasantly revived in memory; and this revival, which remains from sin, is its ash, and itself a sin. [Col. 1089B] Therefore I ate this ash—that is, consumed it through repentance—like bread, which is consumed when eaten.

Or understand sin by bread, since an act of sin delights: whence, “Hidden bread is sweeter” (Prov. 9). For light sins must be consumed through true repentance; and I mixed my drink—that is, the cup of bitterness and sorrow—with weeping. Elsewhere it is said of this: “Thou hast given us to drink the wine of compunction” (Ps. 59), that is, with an abundance of tears, in accordance with what is written: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93). For the bitterness of sorrows is greatly tempered by the sweetness of tears: the more bitter they are in their cause, the sweeter they are in their end.

Or: my enemies reproached me all day long, but I rejoiced because I ate ashes like bread; for I was refreshed by reproach as by praise, according to what is elsewhere written: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). This especially advances the penitent’s merit. And I mixed my drink—that is, temporal gladness, [Col. 1089D] of which it is written, “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Sirach 40)—with weeping, mindful of what is written: “In the day of good things do not be forgetful of evil things” (Sirach 11); and: “Sorrow occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). But as though he were asked, “Whence comes this great weeping to thee?” he replies:

“From before the face of thy wrath and indignation, because, raising me up, thou hast dashed me down.”

It has been shown above how wrath or indignation should be understood of God; therefore it need not be repeated. But it should be carefully noted that almost every word indicates misery and pain: reproach, enmity, conspiracy, ashes, weeping, wrath, indignation, dashing down, shadow, decline, and dryness, so that the anguish of this poor man may be plainly recognized.

[Col. 1090A] He shows the source of the weeping which he mixed with his drink: “From before the face,” he says, “of thy wrath and indignation”—that is, from the manifest punishment which thou, being angry, didst inflict from the beginning upon Adam. Born from his offspring, we are, as it were, by nature children of wrath (Eph. 2). This is evident because, having raised me up in glory and honour by creating me in thine image and likeness and setting me over the birds of heaven, the fish of the sea, and the beasts of the earth, thou didst dash me down when, in that first parent, thou didst cast me out of Paradise and thrust me into the misery of this exile (Gen. 1, 3), a misery which I cannot sufficiently lament. Therefore, because I turned away from the true sun, rightly:

“My days have declined like a shadow, and I have dried up like grass.”

For just as a shadow, when it declines and passes, leaves no trace [Col. 1090B] of itself, so my days declined and passed away useless and empty, leaving no fruit of good work. Having lost the greenness of grace, I dried up like grass, cut down by the sickle of sin.

There is a shadow of the Incarnation, whence: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1). Of protection, whence: “Under the shadow of his hand he protected me” (Isa. 49). Of refreshment, whence: “I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song 2). Of dissolution, whence: “The shadow of death covered us” (Ps. 43). Of forgetfulness, whence: “Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure him” (Job 3). Of light, whence: “His shadow covered the mountains” (Ps. 79). Of ignorance, whence: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. 87). Of sin, whence: “He sleeps under the shadow and in the secrecy of the chamber” (Job 40). Of misery, whence: [Col. 1090C] “Like a flower he comes forth and is crushed, and flees like a shadow” (Job 14). Of Gehenna, whence: “A land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death is and there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10). Therefore I am like a shadow and like grass:

“But thou, O Lord, endurest for ever, and thy memorial unto age upon age” [alternatively, “unto generation and generation”].

After the penitent has enumerated his miseries, he turns to proclaiming God’s glory, that he may more readily obtain grace and mercy from him. He commends him from his nature, which is eternal: “For thou, O Lord, endurest for ever”; and from his fame, which is perpetual: “And thy memorial unto age upon age”; [Col. 1090D] from his mercy, which is abundant: “For thou, arising, shalt have mercy on Zion”; from his wisdom, which is provident: “For the time has come to have mercy on her”; from his household, which is kindly: “For thy servants have taken pleasure in her stones”; and likewise from that household, which is pious: “For they shall have mercy upon her earth”; from his reverence, which is great: “For the nations shall fear thy name, O Lord”; from his glory, which is great: “And all the kings of the earth shall fear thy glory”; from his power, which is renowned: “For the Lord shall build Zion”; and from his supreme honour: “For he shall be seen in his majesty.” Who, then, would not fear so great a Redeemer, or love such a one?

Therefore, continuing his commendation, the penitent says: “But thou, O Lord, endurest for ever,” because thou lackest beginning and end, since thou art [Col. 1091A] α and ω, the beginning and the end (Rev. 1), through whom we receive nature and attain glory. “And thy memorial unto age upon age.” For although by his own condition man is like grass and shadow, yet if he remembers thee in order to obey thee in all things and to love thee above all things, he shall be with thee unto the age upon age to come, which will follow upon the present age; because what is denied to him by his own nature is granted by thy grace.

“And thy memorial,” that is, the one who remembers thee, shall not pass away like a shadow, but shall be unto age upon age: that is, he shall remain for ever, adorned with the glory of the resurrection, because thou who art eternal wilt preserve what is temporal. Or, “thy memorial” is the memorable promise concerning thee, by which thou rememberest us; or thy remembrance, by which thou art mindful of us, shall be in the present generation [Col. 1091B] and unto the generation to come, because godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4). Hence:

“Thou, arising, O Lord [Note: [Col. 1091D] The alternative reading does not have ‘O Lord.’], shalt have mercy upon Zion, for the time to have mercy upon her has come” [alternatively, “for her time of mercy, for the time has come”].

How great the power and efficacy of true and humble repentance are is clearly proved also according to the spirit of prophecy. For behold, in this third group of five, prophesying concerning Christ and the Church, he says among other things: “For the time to have mercy has come”; and according to another translation he repeats: “For the time has come.” This repetition signifies confirmation, in accordance with Joseph’s words to Pharaoh: “That you saw a dream a second time, concerning the same matter, is an indication of its certainty” (Gen. 41). Or this repetition expresses desire, according to what is said elsewhere: “Have mercy upon me, O God, have mercy upon me” (Ps. 56).

Because all the Lord’s ways are mercy and truth (Ps. 24), and the Psalmist himself testifies, “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100), it is clear that mercy and judgment came together; but the former was manifest, the latter hidden. Therefore he says twice, “the time has come,” “the time has come.” For, as Solomon testifies, “There is a time for every thing under heaven” (Eccl. 3).

But in the first instance he sets forth and expresses mercy, saying, “the time for showing mercy has come,” because mercy is manifest; in the second he neither expresses nor states justice, [Col. 1091D] but says simply, “Because the time has come,” because justice was hidden. This is the time of fullness of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4).

But you will say: “Was there not always a time for showing mercy?” Or: “Why did God delay so long to show mercy?” Perhaps someone might answer that Christ, mediator of God and human beings, coming into the world, as he appeared in the middle of places, so wished to appear in the middle of times, in order that, having delayed from the beginning of the world until the first advent for as long as he would delay before the second advent until the end of the world, he might be mediator in all things and through [Col. 1092A] all things.

The Psalmist shows that he appeared in the middle of places when he says: “God our king before the ages worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73). The Wise Man seems to indicate that he appeared in the middle of times, saying thus: “While all things held deep silence, and night in its course had completed half its journey, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). For it is fitting that the mediator should always occupy the middle. Hence the prophet says: “In the midst of two living creatures you shall be known; when the time comes you shall reveal yourself” (Ezek. 1). And his parents found him in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them (Luke 2). The Jews likewise crucified with him two thieves, one on either side, but Jesus in the middle (John 19). But John saw, in the midst of [Col. 1092B] seven golden lampstands, one like a son of man, clothed in a long robe (Rev. 1). Again he saw, in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain (Rev. 5).

Hence he says of himself: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matt. 18); and again: “I am in your midst as one who serves” (Luke 22). And after the resurrection Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them: “Peace be with you” (Luke 24).

But you will say that this cannot stand because of what the Apostle Paul says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10); and the Apostle John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2). Yet, since the Lord says, “These things must happen first, but the end is not immediately [Col. 1092C] yet” (Luke 21), and the Apostle warns the Thessalonians not to be alarmed as though the day of the Lord were at hand (2 Thess. 2), without doubt “the end of the age” or “the last hour” is understood as the final age. The advocate of this opinion would say that it will last as long as the other ages lasted, after the pattern of the ages of human life, of which the last sometimes endures longer than the rest.

For the first age of a human being is infancy, lasting until seven years; the second, childhood, lasting until fourteen; the third, adolescence, lasting until twenty-five; the fourth, youth, until fifty; the fifth, old age, until eighty—for “if men are strong, eighty years; and most of them are labor and sorrow” (Ps. 89); the sixth, decrepitude, which lasts until the end of life, however long the person may live. [Col. 1092D] So too there are six ages of the world: the first, from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian deportation; the fifth, from the Babylonian deportation to Christ; the sixth, from Christ to the end of the age, however long it may endure.

If, therefore, a man’s final age were assumed to have lasted as long as the others, he would be found to have lived one hundred and sixty years. If these are divided into six equal parts, each will contain twenty-six whole years and eight months, but sixteen [half-months], lest one depart from the number six. Together these two numbers make forty-two, the number of [Col. 1093A] encampments of the children of Israel in the wilderness. And such a mystery would indeed suit the human race passing through the wilderness of this age.

But I neither wish nor ought to assert such an opinion, because the Lord says: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). Likewise: “Of that day no one knows, neither angel nor Son” (Matt. 24)—namely, the adopted son, or even the only-begotten Son according to his human nature. Or certainly, he does not know it for us, because he has not made us know it, since it is more expedient for us to be ignorant of these things than to know them.

What most strongly contradicts this assertion is that, speaking of the day of judgment in the parable of the ten virgins, the Lord concludes: “Watch therefore, because you do not know the day nor the hour” (Matt. [Col. 1093B] 23). And elsewhere: “When you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come” (Luke 12). For, as the Apostle says, “the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. For when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. 5).

But the reason for this delay is that which the Wise Man indicates in the foregoing words: “While,” he says, “all things held deep silence, and night in its course had completed half its journey, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). Although this is explained differently by different people, it may suitably be understood that the first silence was under the law of nature, the second under the law of Scripture, and the third under the law of grace.

For God the Creator implanted a natural law in human minds [Col. 1093C] from the very beginning of creation, containing a twofold command: one affirmative, which the Gospel teaches for the rendering of benefits: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7); the other negative, which is read in Tobit for the avoidance of injuries: “What you hate to have done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4).

But this law fell silent at the beginning when Cain killed Abel (Gen. 4), doing to another what he would not have wished done to himself. Thus the first silence lasted until Moses, through whom God “raised up a testimony in Jacob and set a commandment in Israel” (Ps. 77), giving through him the Decalogue of the law written on two tablets: one containing love of God, the other love of neighbor; “on these two hang the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22).

But this law fell silent at the beginning when the people [Col. 1093D] worshipped the molten calf (Exod. 23), contrary to the first commandment of the law, worshipping foreign gods. Thus the second silence lasted until Christ, who came in mercy and bestowed the law of grace, writing it in human hearts with the finger of God. But this law will fall silent at the end, when the son of perdition is revealed, who “will exalt himself above everything that is called or worshipped as God” (2 Thess. 2). And perhaps it is already silent, because “iniquity has abounded and the love of many has grown cold” (Matt. 15:44 [probably Matt. 24:12]). “There is none who does good, no, not even one” (Ps. 13).

In the first law God granted human beings the ability; in the second, knowledge; in the third, the will. In the first he granted power through nature; in the second, knowledge through Scripture; in the third, [Col. 1094A] will through grace. Therefore God first gave the natural law, by which he might convict the transgressor, lest perhaps he offer the excuse, saying, “I fell because I was unable to stand.” But the excuse is removed, because through the good of nature he was able to stand in good, but did not will to do so.

He also first gave the written law, by which he might convict the presumptuous person, lest perhaps he offer the excuse, saying, “I fell because I did not know how to stand.” But the excuse is removed, because through the instruction of Scripture he was able to turn away from evil, but did not will to do so. Therefore, after both laws, at the fitting time—namely, when the night of guilt had completed half its journey—the almighty Word came, that is, “the Word was made flesh” (John 1), and bestowed the law of grace, so that what a person could do by nature and knew [Col. 1094B] through Scripture, he might fulfill through grace.

Elisha likewise first sent his staff to raise the son of the Shunammite woman; when the boy did not rise by means of it, Elisha himself came, bent himself down, fitted himself to the boy, and thus the dead child rose (4 Kings 4).

“You, therefore, rising up, will have mercy on Zion.” As though he said more plainly: “You who seemed to sleep for so long by delaying, now at last, rising up, will have mercy on Zion.” For this reason the ancient faithful cried: “Rise up, O Lord, help us, and deliver us for your name’s sake” (Ps. 46). “Rise up, why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us forever” (Ps. 43), because the time has come to show mercy to her.

There were two peoples, Jewish and Gentile; at his advent the Lord willed to show mercy to both, [Col. 1094C] that he might join two different walls in one cornerstone. He first showed mercy to the Jews; hence he begins: “You, rising up, will have mercy on Zion,” that is, Judea, whose metropolis was Zion. Afterwards he showed mercy to the Gentiles; hence he adds: “And the nations will fear your name, O Lord.” This was fittingly signified in the shepherds, who, being Jews, first came from nearby at the angel’s voice (Luke 2); and in the Magi, who, being Gentiles, later came from afar at the sign of the star (Matt. 2).

Yet both came to him who is our peace, who made both one, making peace in one man—peace for those near and peace for those far away (Eph. 2). And perhaps because of these two peoples to whom he showed mercy when he came, he first says, “Because the time [Col. 1094D] has come to show mercy to the Jews,” and afterward says, “Because the time has come to show mercy to the Gentiles.” Truly you will have mercy on Zion:

> For her stones have pleased your servants,  
> and they will have pity on her earth.

This stone is Christ himself. Hence: “The stone rejected by the builders has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117). He is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (1 Pet. 2), a stone cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. 2). The angelic order is a stone: “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. 38). The holy Church is a stone: “Taking a stone, they put it under him” (Lam. 3). Again, every saint is a stone: “I will strew precious stones throughout the world” (Isa. 54); and, “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every [Col. 1095A] street” (Lam. 4). The Gentile people are a stone: “A stone melted by heat is turned into bronze” (Job 28); and, “God is able from these stones to raise children to Abraham” (1 Cor. 3). The hardened Jew is a stone: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11).

Again, a stone is spiritual virtue: “The foundations of the city adorned with every precious stone” (Rev. 21); and, “Another builds with gold, silver, and precious stones” (1 Kings 17). A stone is sacred Scripture, that is, the divine law: “David chose five very smooth stones from the torrent and put them in the shepherd’s bag.” A stone is the literal sense: “There was a cave, and a stone had been laid upon it” (John 11); and, “Coming near, he rolled the stone from the entrance of the tomb” (Matt. 28).

Moreover, a stone is the devil: “His heart will be hardened [Col. 1095B] like a stone and tightened like a blacksmith’s anvil” (Job 41). A wicked man is a stone: “An angel took up a stone like a millstone and threw it into the sea” (Rev. 18). The weight of sin is a stone: “They sank into the depth like a stone” (Exod. 15).

But the stones of Zion in this place are understood as the prophets, strong and steadfast in faith; and Christ’s servants are understood as the apostles, of whom he himself said: “A servant is not greater than his lord” (John 13). Therefore “her stones,” that is, the prophets, pleased “your servants,” that is, the apostles, because, on the testimony of the prophets, the apostles preached the Gospel to the Jews through prophetic authorities, preaching the Gospel where prophecy had been founded. For the apostles began preaching [Col. 1095C] where the prophets had begun prophesying: “For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

Or the stones of Zion are the Jews themselves: formerly hard, but afterwards softened by the apostles’ preaching, as we read that on the very day of Pentecost, having heard the words spoken by Peter, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). Therefore those who received his word were baptized, and on that day about three thousand souls were added. Truly, then, you, rising up, will have mercy on Zion, because her stones—that is, the first Jews converted to faith—pleased your servants, that is, the apostles, who converted them to faith by preaching and baptizing.

“And they will have pity on her earth.” If [Col. 1095D] the stones mean those who are strong and steadfast, the earth must mean those who are weak and infirm, whether in body or mind. The apostles had pity on these, recalling some of them through admonitions and teachings from error to truth and from vices to virtues: such were those who, at the apostles’ preaching, sold their possessions and placed the price at their feet; “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul,” and no one among them lacked anything, because distribution was made to each according to need (Acts 4).

The apostles had pity on others through signs and miracles, healing them of diverse ailments and curing unclean spirits: such as those of whom we read that a multitude from the neighboring cities ran together to Jerusalem, so that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow [Col. 1096A] them and they might be healed of their infirmities (Acts 5). Thus her stones pleased your servants, and they will have pity on her earth. Yet not only Zion—that is, the Jews—will obtain mercy, but:

> And the nations will fear your name, O Lord,  
> and all the kings of the earth your glory.

All will indeed fear: altogether, not only lesser persons, such as the nations, but greater persons, such as kings, according to what is elsewhere said: “All the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. 71). They will fear, not with worldly fear, of which it is said: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13); nor with servile fear, of which we read: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4); but with initial fear, of which it is said: [Col. 1096B] “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Eccl. 1), or rather filial fear, of which we read: “The holy fear of the Lord remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 18).

With this fear, which is devotion and reverence, the nations—that is, the Gentile people converted to faith—will fear your name, O Lord: not a terrible name, but a lovable one. It is that name of which we read: “You shall call his name Jesus,” which means Savior; “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). For this is the holy and glorious name invoked over us; “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which they must be saved” (Acts 4). Of it the prophet said: “But I will glory in the Lord and rejoice in God [Col. 1096C] my Jesus” (Hab. 3).

And for this reason all kings of the earth will fear your glory: whether that holy and glorious name which shall be invoked over them, or the divine nature in which you are glorified equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of whom the two Seraphim cried one to the other: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts. The whole earth is full of your glory” (Isa. 6). These things will happen because:

> The Lord will build Zion,  
> and will appear in his majesty [or: in his glory].

Zion was formerly understood literally as Judea, but now spiritually as the Church. For it is understood in three ways: historically, as Jerusalem: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2); allegorically, [Col. 1096D] as the Church: “Deal graciously, in your good will, with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50); and tropologically, as the soul: “I will give salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. 46).

For Zion means “contemplation” or “watchtower”: that is, the universal Church or the faithful soul, which now contemplates God through faith and will at last behold him in direct vision. For “now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face”; we shall see not through a mirror but face to face, knowing as we are known (1 Cor. 13).

This Zion, then—that is, the Church—the Lord built from Jews and Gentiles whom he converted to faith. And when it has been wholly built, after the fullness of the Gentiles enters into faith and thus all Israel [Col. 1097A] is saved (Rom. 11), he who was formerly seen as humble and despised, according to the saying, “We saw him having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53), will then, when judgment comes, appear in his majesty, glorious and exalted. As he himself testifies: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 25); and “all flesh shall see him” (Luke 3), and those who pierced him (Rev. 1), etc. Thus, therefore:

> He looked upon the prayer of the poor [or: humble],  
> and did not despise their petition.

Long ago the ancient faithful, who were poor in spirit, cried out with great longing and prayed that Christ might come and build Zion—that is, gather the Church [Col. 1097B]—saying to the Father: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). He looked upon these prayers of the poor when he descended from heaven to gather into one the scattered children of God. In doing this he did not despise their petition, but mercifully heard it.

> Let these things be written for another generation,  
> and the people that will be created shall praise the Lord.

Not only the matters already stated, but also those to be stated in this fourth group of five, should be faithfully written down and solemnly praised as mighty works of God. They are to be written, that they may be firmly committed to memory: “Let these things be written for another generation.” They are to be praised, [Col. 1097C] that thanks may humbly be rendered to God: “And the people that will be created shall praise the Lord.”

He next explains why the Lord will be praised by the people that will be created: because, although exalted in nature—“He looked down from his holy height”—he became humble by grace—“The Lord looked from heaven to earth.” How fittingly loftiness and humility meet in him: lofty in humility and humble in loftiness; God-man and man-God.

He now gives the reasons why the Lord looked from heaven to earth: “that he might hear the groaning of those in fetters”—behold the disposition of condescension; “and might release the children of the slain”—behold the disposition of compassion; “that the name of the Lord might be proclaimed in Zion”—behold the preaching of truth; “and his praise in Jerusalem”—behold the glorification of majesty; “when the peoples are gathered together into one”—behold the bond of peace; “and kings, that they may serve the Lord”—behold the service of obedience.

[Col. 1097D] There are indeed two generations: one of the wicked, of which it is said, “A wicked and adulterous generation” (Matt. 12); the other of the good, of which it is written, “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord” (Ps. 23), and “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 3). Therefore these things which have been stated—namely, the deformation brought about through Adam and the reformation to be accomplished through Christ—are to be written, to be committed to memory, for the other generation, that is, the generation of the good, who desire to understand them; not for the generation of the wicked, who disdain to consider them.

Likewise, there is one generation of Jews, which came first, and another of Christians, which followed. Therefore let these things be written, lest [Col. 1098A] they be consigned to oblivion, for the use of the other generation—that is, the Christian people—to whom they will be more beneficial; because by the things foretold in the prophetic Spirit, Christians will be more firmly established in the faith which they understand to be commended by prophetic testimonies.

Thus the people that will be created—that is, the Christian people, recreated through the grace of redemption so as to be a new creation, as the Apostle says, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. 6); and, “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5)—that people, I say, will praise the Lord in heart, mouth, and deed: by loving, confessing, and obeying, so that life, speech, and conscience may unite in perfect praise.

[Col. 1098B] For in creation the human being was made in the image of God (Gen. 1), but in re-creation God was made in the image and likeness of the human being. The former is certainly of greater dignity, but the latter of greater condescension.

Or the Prophet prays that these things may be written by God’s finger in the hearts of others, so that the people who will be created may immediately praise God for such great benefits. For Scripture is higher and lower, inward and outward. Higher Scripture is divine predestination, called the book of life or Scripture of truth: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68); “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10); “I will not blot their names from the book of life” (Rev. 3); and, [Col. 1098C] “I will declare to you what is written in the Scriptures of truth” (Dan. 10).

Lower Scripture is the stain of sin: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth”; and, “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jer. 17). Inward Scripture is spiritual anointing: “You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God” (2 Cor. 3); and, “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?” (Matt. 22). Outward Scripture is literal writing: “All the wise men having entered were unable to read the writing or make its interpretation known to the king” (Dan. 5); and, “He interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24).

God writes the higher and the lower Scripture: “Either forgive them this offense, or blot me out of your book which you have written” [Col. 1098D] (Exod. 32); and, “You write bitter things against me” (Job 13). Likewise: “He gave Moses two stone tablets of testimony, written by the finger of God” (Exod. 34); and, “Those who by nature do what the law requires have the law of God written in their hearts” (Rom. 2).

A human being writes the outward Scripture: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph of Nazareth, whom Moses wrote of in the law and the prophets” (John 1). And Moses wrote a song to the Lord. But the devil, or also a wicked person, writes the lower Scripture: false prophets wrote and prophesied, though the Lord had not sent them.

Therefore the supreme scribe is the Holy Spirit, of whom we read: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44). The middle scribe is he of whom it is said: “Every scribe instructed in [Col. 1099A] the kingdom of heaven is like a householder,” etc. (Matt. 13). The lowest scribe is an evil prelate, of whom it is said: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23).

Or let these things, written in the generation of the Jews through the law and the prophets, be written in the generation of the Gentiles through translations and interpretations. This occurred in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, who had the Jewish library translated into the language of the Greeks by the seventy interpreters. More especially, let them be written in human hearts by God’s finger.

> For he looked down from his holy height;  
> the Lord looked from heaven to earth.

[Col. 1099B] Christ is the Holy of holies, exalted among the saints, who is the Holy One of God the Father, as he himself says in the Psalm: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Acts 2). And in the Gospel it is said to him: “I know that you are the Holy One of God” (Mark 1). From this exalted Holy One, the Lord the Father looked down—that is, provided for the human race—by sending him into the world, that he might redeem humankind by his precious blood.

Or Christ himself looked down from his exalted holy place—that is, from the sublimity of his divine nature, which is not merely holy but holiness itself, because there is nothing in it that is not holy. Hence he adds by way of explanation: “The Lord looked from heaven”—that is, from divine nature—“to earth,” that is, upon human misery, in order to free miserable human beings. For “heaven” and “earth” are sometimes understood in this manner in the divine [Col. 1099C] Scriptures, as will be shown below.

He states why Christ looked down from heaven to earth, adding:

> That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters,  
> and release the children of the slain.

There are bonds of the body: “The saints endured mockeries and scourging, and moreover bonds and prisons” (Heb. 2). Of poverty: “If they are in chains and bound with cords of poverty, you will declare their works to them” (Job 36). Of peace: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4). Of love: “Have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. 3). Of wisdom: “Her bonds are a binding of health” (Ecclus. 6). Of the law: [Col. 1099D] “Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Ps. 29). Of teaching: “You have broken my bonds, and said, ‘I will not serve’” (Ps. 115). Of fear: “You have raised bonds even to the neck.”

Furthermore, there are bonds of sins: “You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 105). Of darkness: “The wicked are persuaded that they can rule the holy nation with bonds of darkness” (Wis. 17). Of torments: “[God] has reserved under dark bonds for the judgment of the great day the angels who did not keep their own principality but abandoned their dwelling.”

Christ came spiritually into the world in order to free the dead from hell and release the living from sins. This is what he says: “The Lord looked from heaven [Col. 1100A] to earth, that he might hear the groaning of the bound,” that is, hear effectively the groaning prayers of those held in hell, as though bound or shackled by the bonds of darkness. Descending to hell during the three days of his death, Christ freed them. Then, having loosed the pains of hell, “in the blood of his covenant he brought forth his bound ones from the pit in which there was no water,” leading our captivity captive by his own power.

And he looked from heaven to earth in order to release from sins “the children of the slain,” that is, of the first parents, who were both killers and killed, because they transmitted to their children the cause of killing and death, namely original sin. For, as the Apostle says, through one human being—that is, Adam and Eve, who were two in one flesh—death passed also into all [Col. 1100B] human beings (Rom. 5). They themselves were killed because of disobedience, incurring death of body and soul, as had been foretold to them: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die” (Gen. 2). Therefore he looked down in order to release from sins the children of the slain—that is, the human race, carnally propagated from the first parents, who were both killers and killed.

Or by “the bound” and “the shackled” he means the saints, who are bound, as it were, with certain bonds and fetters by the fear of God. The Wise Man testifies concerning them: “Hear, my son, and receive my saying; do not reject my counsel. Put your foot into her fetters and your neck into her collar; and her fetters shall be for you a protection of strength, and her collars a robe of glory” [Col. 1100C] (Ecclus. 6). But the Lord looked from heaven to earth so that he might hear the groaning of such shackled persons, who groaned and prayed that Christ might come for the redemption of the human race, release us from the bonds of crimes, and restore the children of the slain: that is, the imitators of those who were killed and put to death for truth, such as many prophets in the Old Testament and all martyrs in the New, whose children are those who follow their faith.

The Lord also looked from heaven to earth when, in divine mercy, he looked upon human misery, that he might effectively hear the groaning of the shackled: those entangled in mortal sins, who, recognizing their misery, cried to the Lord with groaning that they might be freed through his grace. And that he might [Col. 1100D] release the children of the shackled—that is, the imitators of those killed by the devil’s deceit—freeing them from their ancestral errors. For the Lord does this daily when he calls back to salvation through repentance both those who commit their own sins and those who follow the sins of others.

He next adds the purpose for which he might hear and groan:

> That they may proclaim in Zion the name of the Lord,  
> and his praise in Jerusalem.

The name of God is understood in many ways in Scripture. One is essential, commonly signifying the essence, such as *Heloi*, *Adonai*, God, Lord, and the like. Another is personal, specially naming a person, such as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, [Col. 1101A] Christ, Jesus, and similar names.

A name sometimes signifies power: “The works which I do in the name of my Father, they bear witness of me” (John 5). Sometimes knowledge: “Father, I have made known your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world” (John 17). Sometimes invocation: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Sometimes honor: “In your name I will lift up my hands” (Ps. 62). Sometimes reputation: “Through you the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. 2). Sometimes immutability: “If the children of Israel say, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” The Lord said: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). Sometimes worship: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, [Col. 1101B] and the God of Jacob has sent me to you; this is my name forever” (Exod. 6). Sometimes secrecy: “I did not make known to them my name *Adonay*” (ibid.). Sometimes justice: “This is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness” (Jer. 23).

There is also the tetragrammaton name of the Lord, I, e, v, e [YHWH], which is called ineffable and signifies in an eminent manner the mystery of Trinity and unity, as he has indicated elsewhere. The names of the Son are likewise diverse. For he is called Jesus: “You shall call his name Jesus,” which means Savior, “for he will save his people from their sins.” He is called Christ: “Joseph begot the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ,” which is explained as “anointed” (Matt. 11), because [Col. 1101C] “God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44); hence, “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 6). He is called Emmanuel, which means “God with us.” He is called the Rising One: “Behold, a man—the Rising One is his name” (Zech. 6), because “the Rising One from on high has visited us” (Luke 1).

Isaiah enumerates many of his names together, saying: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). He is the name of the Lord of whom the prophet says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar” (Isa. 30), to whom “a name above every name” has been given, so that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Phil. 2). Rightly, therefore, the Psalmist exclaimed: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. [Col. 1101D] 8).

Therefore the Lord heard and released them in order that through them it might be proclaimed in Zion—that is, the Church—that his name [variant: any name] is to be glorified, blessed, and praised; and that through them his praise might also be proclaimed for the magnificent works performed for human salvation in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church of the saints, who will therefore praise God.

Why, then, is “name” joined with Zion and “praise” with Jerusalem, except because those who watch (*speculatores*) understand the power of the divine name, and those who see peace raise up the proclamation of praise? For Zion is called “contemplation,” and Jerusalem “vision of peace.”

Jerusalem is understood in four ways, according to the four theological senses: historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. For there is a Jerusalem above and below, inward and outward. The higher is in the homeland; the lower is on the way; the inward is in the soul; the outward is in Palestine. Of the higher it is written: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same” (Ps. 121). To the lower it is said: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 60). Of the inward it is written: “I will give salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. 46). To the outward it is said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (Matt. [Col. 1102A] 22).

> When the peoples are gathered together into one,  
> and kings, that they may serve the Lord.

Not only did he do the things mentioned above, so that the name of the Lord might be proclaimed in Zion [Col. 1102B] and his praise in Jerusalem, but also when peoples are gathered into one: Jewish and Gentile into one worship and one faith, so that there may be one fold and one shepherd (John 10); for there is one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4). And likewise when the kingdoms of the world are gathered together, that they may serve the Lord—namely him of whom it is said: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4), that is, to him alone you shall render the service of worship, which in Greek is called *latria*. For this is he who has written on his garment and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19); to serve whom is to reign.

“He answered him in the way of his strength: Make known [al. declare] to me the fewness of my days. And do not call me back in the middle of my days; your years are from generation to generation.”

Here the Church commends the resolve of singular persecution: “He answered him in the way of his strength”; longing for the heavenly homeland: “Make known to me the fewness of my days”; the beginning of final perseverance: “Do not call me back in the middle of my days”; the reward of eternal blessedness: “Your years are for ever and ever” (Ps. 101). For the Church, stirred by the benefits previously mentioned and kindled with love of eternity, answered the Lord in her perfect and vigorous children, not in the weak and imperfect. (For she has flesh and bones, concerning which he had previously said: “My bones adhered to my flesh.”) With ardent desire she asks and implores [Col. 1102D] that he indicate to her whether, after a few days, she is to reach the homeland of heavenly blessedness. She desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1).

For this is the difference between the perfect and the imperfect: the perfect have death in desire and life in patience; the imperfect, however, have death in patience and life in desire. Therefore Jerusalem—that is, the Church—answered him, that is, the Lord, not so much with voice as with heart, nor so much with word as with desire. She answered, I say, “in the way of his strength,” that is, in those who have already undertaken the way of strength and perfection, not in those who still walk by the way of weakness and imperfection.

She answered this indeed: “Declare to me the fewness of my days,” that is, indicate to me [Col. 1103A] whether I must remain only a few days in this exile of pilgrimage, because I long to come to your kingdom. Hence I continually pray, “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6). But lest anyone should suppose that, because of the fewness of days which she desires before the end of the age, the Church is to come to an end, he adds and says: “Do not call me back in the middle of my days,” that is, before the end of the age—for the middle is what stands between two extremes—when you have promised your faithful that you will be with them all days until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28).

For I do not desire the fewness of days in order to cease to exist before the end of the age, but in order that the end of the age may draw near. Therefore I ask that the day of the age be revealed to me not as certain but as near, lest I violate that evangelical saying [Col. 1103B]: “Of that day and hour no one knows, neither angel nor Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. 24); for the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night. And although I desire the days of this age to be shortened, I nevertheless desire to be with you in the years of eternity, since “your years are for ever and ever” (Ps. 101). They never fail, because they have neither beginning nor end.

This is your eternity, which, though one and the same, is designated in the plural by “years,” just as elsewhere it is designated in the plural by “days,” when the prophet says of Christ: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5). For he remains unchangeable through all years and every day, having nothing past or future.

This can also be understood otherwise. Since he had foretold that Zion would be built and that the Lord would be seen in majesty, the Church, signified by Zion and desiring to see the Lord’s majesty, answered him with desire and affection “in the way of his strength,” namely the Lord’s strength, not Zion’s, so that the possessive pronoun is referred not to Zion but to the Lord. She answered, therefore, not “in the way of her strength,” that is, not by the merit of her own work, lest she presume upon her own strength; but “in the way of his strength,” that is, in faith in Christ—not now passible and mortal, but immortal and impassible—that is, in faith in his resurrection, through which his power is preeminently displayed. For this is the way by which one comes to life. And in this way of strength the Church answered, because she longs for the glory of the resurrection.

But what did she answer? This, namely: [Col. 1103D] “Declare to me the scantiness of my days,” not the day of death, which it is expedient to be ignorant of. For this reason the Lord says: “You do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. 25), so that one may always be willing to live here as though one must always die. For if anyone foreknew the day of death, he would indulge greatly in the enticements of the flesh and the pleasures of the world, presuming upon final repentance.

Nor is this contrary to what is said elsewhere: “Make known to me, Lord, my end and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me” (Ps. 38). For, if it is correctly expounded, it does not pertain to this meaning. But, he says, “Indicate to me the scantiness of my days,” so that I may know not when, but how soon, the number of my days will end, since I desire the exile of my pilgrimage [Col. 1104A] soon to be brought to an end.

“And therefore do not call me back in the middle of my days,” so that as much of life may remain to me as has passed; for that is properly the middle which is equally distant from both extremes. Or: because I desire few days, in order to arrive more quickly at the years of eternity, do not call me back—that is, do not allow me to be called back—to the middle of my days, that is, to that life which adolescents or young men are accustomed to pursue in carnal desires, and which would hinder ascent to the heavenly homeland; for adolescence and youth are middle ages between infancy and old age and senility.

Or again: those days are ours in which we live well and merit eternal life; but those in which we perform the works of the devil are not ours, but rather another’s. Although [Col. 1104B] the Church desires the fewness of temporal days, she nevertheless does not wish to be called back in the middle of her spiritual days, lest these be diminished. And this is what she says: “Do not call me back in the middle of my days,” that is, do not diminish for me the spiritual days which are truly and properly mine, lest, with merit diminished, the reward too be diminished. But the years of everlasting life, which are truly yours, because after the resurrection only the saints will live unto life—on account of which the Apostle says that you will be all in all (1 Cor. 15)—are mine for ever and ever, so that I may remain with you always in eternal happiness.

Or understand the Lord to answer, as though saying more plainly: “You ask me not to call you back in the middle of your days, and I answer you that your years will be for ever [Col. 1104C] and ever.” Truly, Lord, your years are for ever and ever, since you are eternal, preceding every nature, because:

“In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.”

See how, with respect to the works of creation, authority is commended in God: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth.” Sublimity: “The heavens are the works of your hands.” Stability: “They themselves shall perish, but you remain.” Power: “As a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed.” Eternity: “You are the same, and your years shall not fail.” Generosity and kindness: “The children of your servants shall dwell there, and their seed shall be guided for ever and ever.”

Do not be surprised if, when the prophet speaks of the works of God, he sometimes directs [Col. 1104D] his speech to one person and sometimes to another, since the works of the Trinity are undivided. Three things, moreover, were created together: angel, world, and time. And in the creation of the world heaven and earth were created together—the first and lowest among the four elements—and with them likewise the two middle elements, namely air and water, confused and mingled together, because the water was vaporous and the air dense; but afterwards they were separated and divided.

Now Moses had said that in the beginning God created heaven and earth, etc. (Gen. 1). Therefore, lest anyone attending to the order of the words should suppose that he created heaven first and earth afterwards, David in this place names earth before heaven, in order that it may be shown that heaven and earth were created together; but what could be made together could not be spoken together.

The word “beginning” or “principle” is read in Scripture in many senses. God the Father is called principle: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). God the Son: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you.” God the Holy Spirit, because the three are one principle: “With you is principality on the day of your strength” (Ps. 109). The beginning of time: “Before he made anything, I was ordained from the beginning” (Prov. 8). The beginning of dignity: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). The beginning of virtue: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110); and the beginning of vices: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). The outset of any matter is also called a beginning: “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea” (Hos. 1).

When, therefore, it is said: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth,” it may be understood either of the beginning of times, because the earth was created together with time; or of the beginning of things, that is, of the Son, who is the beginning of all things, through whom and in whom God the Father founded the earth. For both are read concerning him: “All things were made through him” (John 1), and “You made all things in wisdom, O Lord” (Ezek. 28). In the one, authority is signified when the Father is said to have made all things through the Son, since the Son received this very thing from the Father. In the other, consubstantiality is denoted when the Father is said to have made all things in the Son, because the Son is consubstantial with the Father; for which reason he says elsewhere: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10).

Yet, to mark the distinction of the three persons in one substance, the Apostle says [Col. 1105C] that all things are from him, through him, and in him (Rom. 11). Therefore, “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth,” that is, you placed it in the lowest position; for among the parts of a building the foundation is lowest [al. “in every level building, lowest”], and in a spherical body that which is in the middle is lowest.

Although the distinction between the heavens and the earth is set forth at excessive length in Scripture, nevertheless, because it is most necessary for understanding this passage, it must here be stated in a concise summary. “Earth,” therefore, means the structure of the world: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), that is, angelic and worldly nature. It means the fourth element: “God called the dry land earth” (ibid.). Any region: “At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened” (Isa. 9). It means the habitable zone: “Our king, God, before the ages worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73). Human nature: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5). Our flesh: “He digs the earth with his hoof” (Job 39). The lower air: “The great dragon, the ancient serpent, was cast down to earth” (Rev. 12), that is, into this dark air. The holy Church: “You have blessed, Lord, your earth” (Ps. 84). The faithless synagogue: “I saw a strong angel descending from heaven, and he placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth” (Rev. 10). The Gentile people: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance [Col. 1106A] and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2). The faithful person: “Earth, do not cover the blood of the righteous” (Job 16). The active man: “He summoned heaven above and earth, that he might judge his people” (Ps. 49). The hearer’s mind: “The earth drinking the rain that comes upon it produces excellent grass” (Heb. 6). A good work: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of earth, abundance of grain, wine, and oil” (Gen. 27). Holy Scripture: “He who works his earth shall be filled with bread” (Prov. 12). Christ’s flesh: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked.” The heavenly homeland: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). The Virgin Mary: “Our earth shall give her fruit” (Ps. 84). Secular conduct: “Our belly has cleaved to the earth.” [Col. 1106B] Carnal pleasure: “It shall not be found in the land of those living delightfully” (Job 28). Earthly understanding: “Silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11). Sin: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3). The mind of the reprobate: “The earth bringing forth thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse” (Heb. 6). Hell: “Before I go to the dark land and one covered with the gloom of death” (Job 10).

Although God the Father created good earth in the beginning, that is, in the Son, he himself created earth, according to the first four senses, in the beginning of time, together with time. “And the heavens are the works of your hands.”

There is a divine heaven: “I came down from heaven” [Col. 1106C] (John 6), that is, from the secret place of divine majesty, having become visible; and: “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven” (John 3). There is the empyrean heaven: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). The starry heaven: “Let great lights be made in the firmament of heaven” (ibid.). And the airy heaven: “The birds of heaven ate it” (Luke 8).

Again, angels are heaven: “Who begot the frost from heaven?” (Job 38). Holy preachers: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). The faithful soul: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66). Holy Scripture: “The heaven shall be folded up like a book” (Rev. 6). Spiritual life: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Moreover, the devil and his angels, who according to the Apostle are spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. [Col. 1106D] 6): “Fire fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and servants it touched” (Job 1). This is he who, lifted up in pride, said of himself: “I shall ascend into heaven; I shall set my throne toward the North; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). And the proud imitate him, who set their mouth in heaven when their tongue passes over the earth.

All these heavens, except the last, which are evil, were made by the first heaven, which is not a thing made but the Maker. Therefore it is said to him: “The works of your hands,” that is, of your power. Though this power is one, it is designated in the plural as “hands” because of its diverse effects: it creates, orders, sustains, and governs. So it is said elsewhere: “Your hands, Lord, made me and formed me” (Job 10), etc.

“They themselves shall perish, but you remain [al. remainest], and all shall grow old like [al. as] a garment. And like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed.”

On this matter the divine Scriptures seem to offer testimonies not merely diverse but contrary. For the Psalmist testifies that the heavens shall perish and all shall grow old like a garment. The Apostle Peter agrees with this, saying: “The day of the Lord shall come as a thief, in which the heavens shall pass away with a great rushing sound” (2 Pet. 3). He also testifies concerning heaven and earth that “the heavens which now are, and the earth, are by the same word stored up, kept for fire unto the day of judgment” (ibid.). Truth himself also says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but [Col. 1107B] my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21).

Yet the same Psalmist seems to have said the contrary. Having prefaced the psalm with: “Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (ibid.), he immediately adds: “He established them for ever and for ever and ever” (ibid.). And Solomon says: “The earth stands for ever” (Eccl. 1). He says the same concerning heaven and earth: “We know, Lord, that you made for yourself a perpetual house, heaven and earth and sea”; although the Apocalypse says that the sea shall be no more (Rev. 21).

Lest, therefore, the sacred Scriptures seem to contradict themselves, let it be said that heaven and earth will truly pass away (Matt. 24) with respect to quality and form, but will remain with respect to substance and nature. [Col. 1107C] Concerning the airy heavens, it is indeed plain that they and the earth will undoubtedly be purified by fire and changed into a better form, as Peter says, that “the heavens, being on fire, shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the heat of fire” (2 Pet. 3). This is clearly indicated here where it says: “Like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed.”

But concerning the higher heavens, with the stars and other lights, it is not wholly certain whether they too will be changed in some measure, since the stench and foulness arising from human evil deeds has not reached them; although apostate angels sinned in them and were cast out of heaven. For “he found perversity in his angels” (Job 4). Indeed, the Apostle John testifies in the Apocalypse that he who sat upon the throne said: “Behold, I make all things new”; and John saw a new heaven [Col. 1107D] and a new earth. For the first heaven departed, and the first earth (Rev. 21). And Isaiah: “Behold, I create a new heaven and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered” (Isa. 65).

But in the Apocalypse of John it is read that the city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminates it and its lamp is the Lamb (Rev. 21). Likewise Isaiah: “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and your God your glory” (Isa. 60). Yet elsewhere he says that the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord shall bind up [Col. 1108A] the wound of his people and heal the stroke of their wound (Isa. 30).

The Apostle gave wholesome counsel: “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. 12); and another says: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search out things greater than yourself” (Ecclus. 3), “for those who search with searching have failed” (Ps. 63). For what preceded the beginning of the world and what follows its end are hidden from us; the middle things, however, are manifest. This is excellently signified by the two Seraphim, who with two wings covered the Lord’s face, with two covered his feet, and with two flew (Isa. 6).

Certainly it may be understood that when it says, “They shall perish,” the word indicates not an actuality but a capacity: for what was made from nothing could by nature return to nothing. Yet they shall be preserved perpetually by a certain grace; since it is written even of angels that those who serve are not stable (Job 4), which must certainly be referred to their nature.

Or let it be understood of the righteous, who, though called heavens because their citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3), shall nevertheless all perish according to the body, which is the garment of the soul. Therefore it is rightly said that all shall grow old like a garment, that is, they shall fail with respect to the body, because what grows old and ages is near destruction.

“And like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed.” A covering is frequently and variously changed in the world, because a human being born of woman, living for a short time, never remains in the same state (Job 14). Who can explain all the changes of mortal humanity? Therefore it is enough here to explain two. You, then, shall change them—that is, the righteous, who are called heavens—in the dissolution of death; and they shall at last be changed in the glory of resurrection.

But the material heavens are also rightly compared to a covering, because they cover the things placed beneath them; hence they are called *caeli*, “heavens,” from *celare*, “to cover.” Therefore the heavens shall perish.

“But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.”

Because you are wholly invariable and immutable, having in yourself nothing except yourself; nor is there in you one thing having and another thing had, nor one thing possessed and another possessing—although in one who possesses there is no accident of possession, nor is the possessor himself an accident possessed by something—since in you what is is altogether the same as to be. For “to be” is not other than what you are, but altogether the same. “And your years shall not fail.” This has been explained above [Col. 1108D], but he repeats it in order to add:

“The children of your servants shall dwell [al. shall inhabit] there, and their seed shall be guided for ever.”

The Lord is generous and kind, sharing his glory with his servants. There, therefore—that is, in your years—the children of your servants shall dwell, that is, they shall remain perpetually: the imitators of the apostles, who were above called your servants. And not only they, or their children, but their seed—that is, all who imitate their faith and works—shall be guided for ever and ever, that is, shall be led onward into the glory of eternity. A joyful conclusion, promising the delights of eternal happiness.

## [PSALM VI.]

[Col. 1109]

An elucidation of the sixth penitential psalm. The title of this psalm is: “A Song of Ascents.” — Explanation of the same title.

[Col. 1109A] This psalm is the eleventh among the Songs of Ascents and the sixth among the penitential psalms. By the number six perfection is signified, because six is a perfect number, being composed by the sum of its parts. Hence on the sixth day God completed heaven and earth and all their adornment (Gen. 2). And when, in the fullness of time, the sixth age had come, on the sixth day, at the sixth hour, he redeemed the human race; and he uttered six final words on the cross.

But transgression is signified by the number eleven, because eleven exceeds the ten of the Law and does not reach the apostolic twelve. Hence there were also eleven haircloth curtains, or goats’-hair coverings, in the tabernacle of the Lord; there are eleven psalms of Asaph; and the apostles, after Judas the traitor was removed, remained at this number, though they returned to twelve when Matthias was appointed. By these things we are given to understand that, however perfect anyone may be, he is nevertheless not without every sin. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1), because “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3), Solomon testifying: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean, and I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. 20). Since no one in this mortal life is so perfect that repentance for sin is not necessary to him, this is fittingly signified here by eleven joined to six.

Explanation of Psalm 129 in the order of the Psalms, and of the sixth in the order of the penitential psalms

[Col. 1109]

[Col. 1109B] “Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice.”

This psalm contains eight verses, admonishing and teaching us that we ought so to pass through the seven days of this age that we may merit happily to arrive at the eighth day of resurrection, on which God will circumcise the elect from every corruption, and then wholly redeem Israel from all its iniquities.

The penitent shows in this psalm from where he cried: “Out of the depths,” not one only but many. To whom? “To you, O Lord,” who alone have power to deliver. What? Namely this: “Hear my prayer.” With what disposition? Certainly humble and devout: “Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.” With what necessity? Great indeed and manifold: “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” With what confidence? At once full and secure: “For with you is propitiation, and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.” How? By hoping and waiting: “My soul has waited on his word; my soul has hoped in the Lord.” Until when? “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord,” namely in prosperity and adversity. For what reason? Because you are God both willing and able to deliver: “For with the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” Finally, to what end? Surely a welcome and saving one: “For he himself shall redeem Israel from all its iniquities.”

Therefore: “Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my prayer.” There is a depth of divine wisdom, of which it is said: “Lord, your thoughts are exceedingly deep” [Col. 1109D] (Ps. 91). A depth of Holy Scripture, of which we read: “He reveals deep things out of darkness” (Job 12). And a depth of human conscience, concerning which [Col. 1110B] it is written: “The heart of man is deep and inscrutable” (Jer. 17). Likewise, there is a depth of damnable guilt: “When the wicked man comes into the depths of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18). A depth of worldly misery: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep” (Ps. 68). And a depth of hellish Gehenna: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God in the depth of hell” (Isa. 7).

From all these depths some cry out and deserve to be heard, except only the last, from which one who cries is in no way heard, because in hell there is no redemption. Thus, when that rich man who had been buried in hell cried, “Father Abraham, have mercy on me” (Luke 16), etc., the Apostle cried out in wonder from the first depth: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11). He himself was caught up even to the third heaven, where he heard secret words which it is not permitted for a man to speak (2 Cor. 12).

From the second depth David cried in prayer: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law”; and the Lord unveiled his ear, because he understood above the elders (Ps. 118). From the third depth Daniel cried to the Lord in prayer, informing his companions of the matter of the kingdom so that they might seek mercy from the face of the God of heaven concerning the king’s mystery, lest they perish with the other wise men of Babylon (Dan. 2). And indeed he deserved to be heard, because then the mystery was revealed to him by a vision in the night.

From the fourth depth the publican cried with groaning: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” and he went down to his house justified (Luke 18). From the fifth depth Peter cried while shipwrecked: “Lord, save me”; and Jesus immediately stretched out his hand, caught hold of him, and said, “Man of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14).

But beneath these depths some lie so submerged that they do not cry at all. Of them it is said: “They went down into the deep like a stone” (Matt. 18). Such was he who said: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 4). For those are submerged too deeply who, overwhelmed with sins and weighed down by iniquities, neither cry themselves nor wish to hear others crying; indeed, they mock even those who urge them to cry.

But this penitent, knowing that the Lord brings back from Bashan (Ps. 67) and sends forth his ice like morsels (Ps. 147), cries to him who heard Jonah crying in the belly of the whale (Matt. 12). He cries not so much with voice as with heart, strongly and urgently, after the example of him who merited illumination by his loud and persistent cry. When the crowds rebuked him from every side to make him silent, he cried out all the more: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me”; and by his cry he made Jesus stand still, and so, crying, obtained what he desired (Luke 18). For he cried from the depths, that is, from the innermost bowels and hidden marrow, from which a cry goes forth to heaven and rises to God’s ears.

The penitent here cries not from one depth only but from many: namely, from the depth of perversity and from the depth of adversity, or from the depth of guilt and the depth of misery, in which he feels himself to lie submerged. He does not say, “I cry,” as though he were beginning to cry now, but says, “I cried,” as though he had been crying for a long time already, because one ought always to pray and not grow weary (ibid.). “I cried,” I say, “to you, O Lord,” who, since you are almighty, are able to deliver. Therefore I cried confidently, namely this: “Lord, hear my prayer,” because, though I am unworthy to be heard on account of my excessive offenses and countless negligences, you are nevertheless worthy to hear because of your boundless goodness and infinite mercy. Therefore:

“Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant [al. to the voice of my supplication].”

There is an ear of the Godhead, an ear of the human being, and an ear of the demon. Each, moreover, is understood in many ways in Scripture. The ear of the Godhead is that by which God opens himself to mercy, and this is the ear of mercy, of which it is said: “Incline, O Lord, your ear and hear me” (Ps. 85); hence: “The Lord heard and had mercy on me” (Ps. 29). There is also the ear which he opens to vengeance, and this is the ear of justice, of which we read: “The ear of heaven judges all things” (Matt. 16); hence: “The Lord heard and rejected, and utterly brought Israel to nothing” (Ps. 77).

One human ear is bodily: “Neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2), etc. Another is spiritual: “The hearing ear pronounced me blessed, and the seeing eye bore witness to me” (Job 29).

[Col. 1112A] This is twofold: the ear of understanding, of which it is said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 2); and the ear of obedience, of which we read: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17).
