The ear of the demon is likewise twofold: one which it stops against good, whence: “That rage is according to the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp which stops its ears” (Ps. 57); and another which it inclines toward evil, whence: “The sound of terror is always in his ears, and when there is peace, he always suspects ambushes” (Job 15).

But although the ear of God is one, because it has many effects the penitent here speaks in the plural: “Let your ears be attentive,” that is, let the hearing of your mercy—one for forgiving guilt [Col. 1112B] and another for remitting punishment—be attentive to the prayer of your servant. That is, let your mercy attend to me, so that you may forgive both guilt and punishment, because I am your servant and the son of your handmaid (Ps. 115): a servant by condition, redemption, and profession.

But that I may be your servant in reverence, devotion, and love, free me from the slavery of sin, concerning which we read: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. 6); for by whom one is overcome, by him one is made a servant. Of such servants it is written: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you asked me; ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. 18). Hence: “Make the side of a wicked servant bleed” (Ecclus. 42). “Fodder and a rod and a burden for an ass; bread and discipline and work for a servant” (Ecclus. 33).

Make me a servant of righteousness, that I may be among those of whom it is written: “You are my servant; in you I shall be glorified” (Isa. 49); and: “God shall be comforted in his servants” (Ps. 134). “Serve the Lord in fear and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2). I hope, moreover, that you are willing and will deign to do this, because though you are Lord of all, you became a servant for me, as the Apostle Paul says of you: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2). And God the Father says through Isaiah: “Behold my servant; I shall uphold him” (Isa. 42).

There is, therefore, good servitude—that of humility—of which the Lord says: “Whoever is greatest among you shall be servant of all” (Mark 10); bad servitude—that of iniquity—of which Truth says: “Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8); and indifferent servitude—that of necessity—of which the Apostle says: “Were you called while a servant? Do not be concerned; but if you can become free, make use of it rather” (1 Cor. 7). Likewise elsewhere: “Servants, be subject in all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the perverse” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore, “let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.”

“If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?”

There is a twofold observing: one for considering and investigating; another for obeying [Col. 1113A] and complying. Of the former we read: “You observed all my paths and considered the tracks of my feet” (Job 13), etc.; and: “The Pharisees watched the Lord” (Luke 6), in order to catch him in speech (Matt. 22). Of the latter it is said: “Fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole duty of man” (Eccl. 12); and: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Prov. 7).

If, therefore, you, Lord, observe—that is, preserve for eternal punishment—the iniquities of anyone, Lord, who will endure you as judge? He does not say, “I shall not endure,” but “Who shall endure?” As though he said: Almost no one, because nearly every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. Hence: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4). How much less shall I be able to endure, who am filled with iniquities? “For my iniquities have passed over my head and, like a heavy burden, have weighed me down” (Ps. 37). From these depths, therefore, I cried, asking to be heard, so that you, Lord, might not observe my iniquities. And indeed I trust that I shall be heard.

“For with you is propitiation, and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.”

The propitiator and the propitiation, the physician and the medicine, the priest and the sacrifice, are one and the same: namely, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, the Word who was in the beginning with God (John 1). Of him the apostle John says: “We have an advocate with God the Father, Jesus Christ, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2). Therefore with you, [Col. 1113C] almighty Father, is our propitiation, ever living to make intercession for us (Heb. 7). Nor do I doubt that he obtains what he asks, since, as the Apostle says, “he is heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5), just as he himself says to the Father: “But I knew that you always hear me” (John 11). For he both asks and hears: he asks as man and hears as God, because “the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Thus the Trinity of persons may be marked out in this way, so that it may faithfully and rightly be said: with you, Father, is propitiation—the Son. “And because of your law,” namely the Holy Spirit, who is the saving law, written not on tablets of stone but in human hearts (2 Cor. 3), because “the love of God [Col. 1113D] has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). Because of this law, I say—your love, your kindness, your anointing, which teaches concerning all things—I have waited, that is, I have awaited you, Lord: that through this same Spirit you may forgive me my sins. Thus I, who a little earlier was saying that, if you observed iniquities, I could not endure, now say that “because of your law I have waited for you, Lord.”

This Spirit, indeed, is the law of grace, which was given from heaven to the apostles on the fiftieth day amid sound and fire (Acts 2), just as formerly the law of the letter was given to the Jews on the fiftieth day amid lightning and thunder from Mount Sinai (Exod. 19). Scripture speaks of many kinds of law: the law of grace, the law of righteousness, the law of clemency, the law of nature, the law of Scripture, and the law of sin.

[Col. 1114A] Of the first: “The law of the Lord is spotless, irreproachable, converting souls” (Ps. 18). For “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Of the second: “For this reason he established a law for sinners in the way” (Ps. 24). And: “Israel did not attain the law of righteousness” (Rom. 9). Of the third: “A law of clemency is on his lips” (Prov. 31). Of the fourth: “When the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what the law requires, they are a law unto themselves” (Rom. 2). Of the fifth: “The law entered in, so that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5). Of the sixth: “I perceive another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin” (Rom. 7). Therefore I am always awaiting your propitiation because of the law of your clemency. Otherwise, because of the multitude, magnitude, and foulness [Col. 1114B] of my iniquities, I would have utterly despaired.

Yet let no one at all despair, because with you is propitiation—that is, there is a propitiator. He is distinct from you in person, but one with you in essence: consubstantial and co-omnipotent, coequal and coeternal, with the Paraclete Spirit who proceeds from both. And therefore:

> My soul has waited in his word; my soul has hoped in the Lord.

He whom it had called “propitiation” it now calls “word,” because, in order to become propitiation for us, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). This man was one of those who, with intense longing for the Redeemer, awaited his coming, saying: “Come, Lord” (Rev. 22), but do not delay; remit the sins [Col. 1114C] of your people Israel. “Lord God of hosts, restore us; show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come down” (Isa. 64). “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Ps. 69). “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Ps. 84). “Remember us, Lord, in the favour shown to your people, and visit us with your salvation” (Ps. 105). “Send forth the Lamb, Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). With longing for him burned the one who says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” (Song 1).

Thus the aged Simeon, righteous and devout, awaiting [Col. 1114D] the redemption of Israel, when he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before seeing the Lord’s Christ, came into the temple in the Spirit. Receiving him into his arms, he blessed God and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace,” etc. (Luke 2). Hence Christ himself said to the apostles: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it,” etc. (Luke 10).

“My soul has waited in your word,” namely, in that word which you spoke through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33); and which your Word says in the Gospel: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9); and: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Matt. 18). Therefore my soul has hoped [Col. 1115A] in the Lord, in that very Word of whom it is written through the prophet that “the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67). It has hoped, I say, not in itself, not in a human being, not in the world, but only in the Lord, who alone can save and does not abandon those who hope in him. Therefore:

> From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.

There is a morning of time, a morning of the age, a morning of human life, a morning of the day, a morning of salvation, a morning of the sinner, a morning of glory, a morning of prosperity, and a morning of sin.

The morning of time is the beginning of creation, concerning which it is said to Lucifer: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14). The morning of the age is its first era, concerning which we read: “He went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20). The morning of human life is childhood, [Col. 1115B] concerning which Truth says: “Watch, because you do not know when the Lord will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning” (Mark 13). The morning of the day is dawn, concerning which we read: “Very early on the first day of the week” (Mark 16). The morning of salvation is the incarnation of the Redeemer, concerning which it is said: “In the evening you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory” (Exod. 16). The morning of the sinner is the infusion of grace, concerning which the prophet says: “In their affliction they will rise early to me” (Hos. 6). The morning of glory is the resurrection, concerning which the Psalmist says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see, for you are not a God who wills iniquity” (Ps. 5). The morning of prosperity is temporal good fortune, concerning which it is said: “Woe to the land whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. 10). The morning of sin is a wicked suggestion, concerning which it is said: “As the morning [Col. 1115C] spread over the mountains” (Joel 2).

Therefore, “from the morning watch until night,” that is, from the infusion of grace until the end of life, of which it is written: “Night comes, when no one can work” (John 9). Or, from the hour of the incarnation until the time of judgment, of which it is said: “At midnight a cry was raised” (Matt. 25). Or again, from a state of prosperity to the onset of adversity, concerning which we read: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120). Let Israel, that is, the faithful person, hope in the Lord.

It may also be understood thus: “From the morning watch until night,” that is, from the righteous person to the sinner, may all without exception hope in the Lord. For from the moment grace is poured into a person, he must persevere in good, so that he may rightly hope in God until life’s end; for “the one who perseveres [Col. 1115D] to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10; 24). Hence under the law both the head and the tail of the sacrifice had to be offered (Lev. 7). Since the time of Christ’s incarnation, a sure hope has been given to the Christian people, that they may trust in the glorification of the resurrection—especially since the Lord rose from death.

But from morning until night, that is, in prosperity and adversity, the faithful person ought to hope in the Lord, so that by trusting in him he may neither be lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity. From that very morning onward a watch without sleep is always necessary, lest a devout intention be corrupted by the serpent’s cunning. Therefore it is said elsewhere: “He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126). For the enemies are demons, who oppose the human being; the gate is the beginning of a wicked suggestion, through which demons strive to enter the mind. Thus the person is not put to shame who, by resisting and protesting, speaks with his enemies at the gate, so that at the very beginning of wicked suggestion he may cast out and drive away the demons; and, lest they become his enemies at the head, he may dash the little ones against the rock (Ps. 137).

[Col. 1116A] Therefore the morning watch or guard is not to be despised. The Psalmist says: “In the morning I put to death all the sinners of the land” (Ps. 100). For in the morning watch the Lord looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians and drowned it in the Red Sea (Exod. 14). Therefore, from the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord; and it may rightly hope.

> For with the Lord is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption.

[Col. 1116B] He calls the same one “mercy” whom he had earlier called “propitiation”: that is, Christ, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “God sent forth his mercy and his truth.” The Redeemer himself is elsewhere called “redemption”; hence Paul says: “He became for us wisdom and redemption” (1 Cor. 1), and the Psalmist: “The Lord sent redemption to his people” (Ps. 110). He calls him “mercy,” therefore, to show why he is above all a merciful propitiator: namely, because with him is abundant redemption, that is, the sprinkling of his blood, poured forth abundantly from five parts, sufficient for the full redemption of all.

For since he is true God, and therefore all nations are reckoned as nothing before him (Isa. 40), one was sufficient for all—indeed, entirely more than sufficient. Thus it does not say that redemption with him is necessary, but that it is abundant. For we have been redeemed not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of an immaculate lamb (1 Pet. 1), as is said elsewhere: “You redeemed us, Lord, by your blood” (Rev. 5). For redemption properly means liberation accomplished by a price paid. A human being could sell himself into the devil’s slavery, but could not redeem himself from the devil’s slavery; therefore the Lord’s abundant mercy was necessary for his redemption.

Indeed, by sinning, a human being withdrew and took away from God a servant whom he handed over and subjected to the devil. Thus peace between them could not reasonably be made unless the damage he had inflicted were [Col. 1116D] repaired. But the human being had nothing with which he could worthily compensate God for the damage: for if something from an irrational creature were rendered, it would be less than the rational substance. Yet he could not worthily restore a human being, because he had taken away one who was righteous and innocent, while finding no one but a sinner.

Therefore, seeing that man could not by his own strength escape the yoke of condemnation, God anticipated him by mercy alone, so that he might afterward also free him through justice. Accordingly, in order that God might be appeased by man, God freely gave to man what man owed God as a debt. He gave a man to a man, whom a man might restore for a man, who, in order that the compensation might be worthy, would not merely equal the former but exceed him. Indeed, he had to be [Col. 1117A] greater, so that one might be deemed sufficient for all. Therefore “the Word became flesh” (John 1), so that God-man might be given to human beings, as Isaiah foretold: “A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us” (Isa. 9). In utterly pure flesh, entirely free from sin, by undergoing an undeserved penalty, he paid to God the Father the price of human redemption, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2). Thus he took upon himself the punishment for all, so that through himself he might give glory to all, Isaiah bearing witness when he says: “He was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised for our crimes,” etc. (Isa. 53).

Or rather, with the Lord the Son is mercy, since he deigned to experience our miseries, as the Apostle says: “We do not [Col. 1117B] have a high priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every respect in the likeness of us, without sin” (Heb. 4). For in that wherein he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted. Thus it is rightly added:

> And he himself shall redeem Israel from all its iniquities.

[Col. 1118A] A servant had offended the king and was therefore delivered to a tyrant, who held him in prison and cruelly afflicted him. Since he could not free himself, a merciful mediator came forward who, paying the penalty for the fault, made satisfaction to the king for the servant. Thus, when the cause ceased, the effect ceased. The servant was consequently freed from the debt of guilt, the tyrant’s yoke, and the prison-house.

The servant is humanity; the king, God; the mediator, Christ; the offence, disobedience; the tyrant, the devil; and the prison, hell. Christ paid to God the Father the penalty of death for human guilt; thus, the price having been paid, humankind was redeemed from sin, the devil, and hell. This, then, is he who redeemed Israel from all its iniquities. Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God”; hence spiritual Israel, not carnal Israel, must here be understood, because “it is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). Therefore Christ redeemed by his passion from every fault those persons, and in the end he will redeem them from every punishment, when God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall be no more mourning, etc. (Rev. 21). A pleasing conclusion: from a sad beginning comes a joyful end.

[PSALM VII.]

[Col. 1117]

Explanation of the seventh penitential psalm. The title of this psalm is as follows: “A psalm of David, when his son Absalom persecuted him.”—Explanation of the same title.

[Col. 1117C] The history touched upon by the title is known from the second book of Kings (Wis. 17) [citation as printed]; yet the psalm does not treat of that history, but only of its meaning. For just as Absalom persecuted David, his father, so an unlawful impulse disturbs and persecutes the mind from which it is born and proceeds. Therefore the penitent says: “The enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground.” Thus a reprobate [Col. 1118C] son persecutes his father and an iniquitous offspring its parent, just as, conversely, a good affection restores the spirit and a devout thought the mind. This psalm has [fourteen] thirteen verses, signifying that the mind must be freed from this persecution through observance of the Decalogue and faith in the undivided Trinity; or through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the six works of piety.

Explanation of Psalm one hundred and forty-two in the order of the psalms, and last in the order of the penitential psalms.

[Col. 1117]

[Col. 1117D]

> Lord, hear my prayer; with your ears receive my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness.

This psalm is divided into four parts. The first sets forth the form and cause of the petition. It distinguishes the form of petition into prayer and supplication, which it asks to be heard in truth and righteousness: “Lord, hear my prayer; with your ears receive my supplication,” etc. In distinguishing the cause of the petition, it shows that it is not fitting for the Lord to enter into judgment with his servant, nor advantageous for the servant to enter into judgment with the Lord: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant,” etc.

Thus the penitent says: “Lord, hear [Col. 1118D] my prayer; with your ears receive my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness.” Hear my prayer, which I lay before you, not in my own justifications but in your mercies. With your ears receive my supplication, which I pour out before you, trusting not in my own hearing but in your will and truth; hoping not in my merits but in your righteousness. Therefore, in your truth, hear me in your righteousness.

He repeats the same thing in different words when he says, “Hear my prayer,” and adds, “Receive my supplication,” thereby expressing desire through this repetition and confirming what has been said. A distinction may be made between prayer and supplication: prayer is that which is offered with entreaty, as: “Hear, we beseech you, O Lord, the prayers of your suppliants” [Note: [Col. 1119D] *Officium ecclesiasticum*, ecclesiastical office]. Supplication, however, is that which is uttered with adjuration, as: “By your cross and passion, deliver us, Lord” [Note: [Col. 1120D] *Litaniae sanctorum*, Litany of the Saints].

With your ears, then—that is, with the hearing of kindness and piety, which, though one, has diverse effects, since it remits both punishment and guilt—receive my supplication, not in my truth but in yours; likewise, in your righteousness, not in mine.

For there is truth of essence: “God is true, and every human being a liar” (Rom. 3); and “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5). Truth of teaching: “We know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22). Of Scripture: “It is written in the Scripture of truth” (Dan. 10). Of censure: “He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in his truth” (Ps. 95). [Col. 1119B] Of promise: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Of commandment: “All your commandments are truth” (Ps. 118). Of testimony: “For this I came into the world, that I might bear witness to the truth” (John 18). Of sacrament: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). Of heart: “One must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4). Of speech: “Speak truth, each one with his neighbour” (Eph. 4). Of deed: “I found some of your children walking in truth” (2 John).

Christ is true in all these ways; hence he is called, by antonomasia, Truth itself. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life,” etc. (John 14). Therefore hear me in [Col. 1119C] your truth, so that you may appear true, because you promised: “At whatever hour the sinner turns and groans, I will remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 33). And hear me in your righteousness, so that you may appear just, because you decreed: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (ibid.). Let truth therefore correspond to the promise, and righteousness to the decree, so that you may be found just and true. Certainly it is just that, as you are angry with the perverse, so you have mercy on the converted.

Or, because according to the Gospel saying true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4), you, Lord Father, hear me in your truth, that is, in your Son, in whom and through whom you accomplish all things. Therefore in him, whom we have with you as propitiator and mediator, [Col. 1119D] hear me in your righteousness—divine righteousness, namely, not human. For according to human righteousness, when the guilty person confesses a sin, he is convicted by the judge and condemned; according to divine righteousness, one absolved by the Lord is not condemned, as it is written: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Ecclus. 4); and: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Ps. 31). A human being judges according to the evils the perverse person has committed; God, however, according to the evils the converted person has abandoned. Let it therefore be: “In your truth, hear me in your righteousness.”

> And do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord, because no living person shall be justified in your sight.

[Col. 1120A] There is the judgment of authority, by which the whole Trinity judges, as we read: “Judge, Lord, those who wrong me” (Ps. 34); “He shall judge the poor of this people” (Ps. 71); and “I judge in my spirit.” There is the judgment of manifestation: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5), because the Son alone shall appear in judgment; and by appropriation judgment seems to belong more to wisdom than to power or kindness. There is the judgment of discernment: “For judgment I came into this world” (John 9); and “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Ps. 42). Of examination: “If the equity of judgment is sought, no one dares speak testimony on my behalf” (Job 9). Therefore the Psalmist cried: “Do not enter into judgment with [Col. 1120B] your servant, because no living person shall be justified in your sight.” Of correction: “It is time for judgment to begin with the house of God” (1 Pet. 4); “When we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected” (1 Cor. 11). Of blinding: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). Of salvation: “He shall not condemn him when he is judged” (Ps. 36). Of condemnation: “God shall judge the sexually immoral and adulterers” (Heb. 12 [as printed]). Of comparison: “The queen of the South shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom” (Luke 11 [citation printed as Luke 2]). Of presumption: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14). Of suspicion: “But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you, or by a human day,” etc. (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore do not examine [Col. 1120C] my merits in judgment, because if you choose to judge me according to what my merits deserve, I shall without doubt be unable to be justified. My merits are evil, deserving not grace but punishment, not pardon but vengeance. For “if you observe iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129). Absolutely no one. Therefore, Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant—with me, namely, who am certainly your servant. For it is not fitting for the Lord to enter into judgment with his servant, especially one immeasurable with one most lowly, over whom he can wholly fulfil his good pleasure without judgment. Nor is it advantageous for the servant that you, Lord of all, should enter into judgment with him, because in your sight—that is, before you, who behold [Col. 1120D] all things, since to your eyes all things are naked and open—no living person in this mortal flesh shall be justified.

For in this present life there is no one who is not bound by the chains of sins. Hence: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and truth is not in us” (1 John 1); for “we all stumble in many things” (Jas. 3). Solomon bears witness: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean, and I am pure from sin?’ Not even an infant of one day is without sin upon the earth.” But that person enters into judgment with the Lord who, establishing his own righteousness, is not subject to divine righteousness; concerning him the prophet says: “Why do you desire to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord” (Jer. 2).

But I [Col. 1121A] do not wish to contend with you in judgment, because I do not establish my own righteousness but condemn my unrighteousness, knowing that no living person shall be justified in your sight. Therefore it is dreadful for every living person to plead a criminal cause before you: since, being most powerful, no one can escape your hands; being most wise, nothing can be hidden from your eyes; and being most just, no one can corrupt your mind. Before you conscience is accuser, the mind is defendant, reason is advocate, memory is witness; and you are judge—just, powerful, and wise; indeed, justice, power, and wisdom—rendering to each according to his works.

But someone will say: Are there not in this mortal life some righteous persons who, although not wholly free from venial sins, have nevertheless been freed from criminal sins? Could such persons be condemned by a just judgment, since it is true that no living person shall be justified in God’s sight? One might perhaps reply that, just as there is a good death, so there is also a bad life. Of the former it is said: “Love is strong as death, and jealousy hard as hell. Many waters cannot quench love” (Song 8); and: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3). Of the latter we read: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while living” (1 Tim. 5); and of the prodigal son, who went into a far country and squandered all his substance by living extravagantly (Luke 15).

Those, then, who live for themselves and not for Christ, for flesh and not for spirit, for the world and not for God, certainly cannot be justified in the sight of God unless they first die to themselves, so that they may live to Christ; die to flesh, so that they may live to spirit; and die to the world, so that they may live to God. The present penitent knew that he had lived in this manner. Therefore he asked that the Lord not enter into judgment with him, because in his sight no person living such a life and in such a way shall be justified.

Moreover, since no one is justified except by the gift of grace, it is clear that no one is justified by the merit of life. For the infusion of grace is properly called justification, and God would grant it to no one if he judged that person according to the strict requirement of merits. Or it may be understood of comparative judgment, so that the sense is: “In your sight,” that is, in comparison with you, no living being—whether angel or human—shall be justified, that is, appear righteous. Thus no particular substantive term is added, in order that it may be understood of every living being, because in his sight not even the stars are clean. Hence blessed Job says: “Truly I know that a human being shall not be justified when compared with God” (Job 15 [citation as printed]); and: “If I show myself innocent, he will prove me perverse” (Job 9). For all creaturely purity is unclean when compared with the Creator’s purity. Therefore the same holy Job says: “If I were washed as with waters of snow, and my hands shone as though most clean, yet you would plunge me into filth, and my garments would abhor me” (ibid.). For as a star does not shine beside the sun, and silver becomes worthless beside gold, so—indeed, incomparably more so—no living being shall be justified in the sight of God.

[Col. 1122A] Therefore hear my prayer, that you may free me from those who persecute me (Ps. 141).

> For the enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground.

In the literal sense, he seems to suggest that he fought with an enemy but was put to flight by him. “For the enemy,” he says, “has persecuted my soul”; cast down upon the ground, because “he has humbled my life to the ground”; shut up in prison, because “he has placed me in darkness,” not in a spacious and bright place, but in one dark and cramped, like the tomb of the dead. Hence he adds: “like those dead of old.” Therefore, because of the confinement of the prison, my spirit was distressed within me; and because of its darkness, my heart was troubled within me—especially [Col. 1122B] by remembering former happiness. For “I remembered the days of old,” in which I was accustomed to flourish; hence, “I meditated on all your works,” in which I recall that I prospered; “and I meditated upon the works of your hands,” by which I desire to prosper.

And rightly so, because I suffer such misery in that prison that, through the dryness of thirst, “I stretched out my hands to you,” since my soul sighs for you “like land without water.” Unless you free me immediately, I shall soon breathe out my soul; therefore “hear me speedily,” because my spirit has now almost failed. Therefore do not turn your face from me, because if you turn away, I shall be like those descending into the pit, as though submerged in the depths. Do not delay deliverance beyond the day, but “make me hear your mercy in the morning,” because I hoped not in myself but in you, Lord. And when you have led me from prison, “make known to me the way in which I should walk,” because I lifted up my soul not to another but to you. And lest I be seized again by my enemies, “rescue me from my enemies,” because I have fled to you as to a secure stronghold. Therefore teach me to do your will, that I may offend against it in nothing and thereby lose your protection, because you—not another—are my God and protector.

I hope, then, that “your good spirit will lead me into the right way,” lest I wander from the straight path, and so may quickly come to you. And because of your name, Lord, which I have invoked for my help, you shall make me live, as one already nearly dead through the excessive misery [Col. 1122D] that I endure. And you shall do this not in my righteousness but in your equity. Thus you shall bring my soul out of the tribulation which I suffer; and in your mercy, not because of my merits, you shall destroy all my enemies, like wanderers and fugitives upon the earth. And you shall destroy all who afflict my soul, certainly for this reason: because I am your servant. And you, Lord, avenge and defend your servants.

Thus he says: “The enemy has persecuted my soul.” This is the second part, in which he recounts both what he suffers and what he does. He suffers persecution in the soul: “The enemy has persecuted my soul.” Humiliation in life: “He has humbled my life to the ground.” Darkness in prison: “He has placed me in darkness like those dead of old.” [Col. 1123A] Distress in spirit: “My spirit was distressed within me.” And disturbance in heart: “My heart was troubled within me.”

But he performs remembrance of former days, when he himself flourished: “I remembered the days of old”; of divine works, by which God created the world: “I meditated on all your works”; and of the Lord’s deeds, by which Christ redeemed the world: “I meditated upon the works of your hands.” He also stretches out his hands in prayer: “I stretched out my hands to you”; and kindles his spirit to longing: “My soul is to you as land without water.”

Thus the enemy has persecuted my soul—not only one enemy, but many: demon and human being, world and flesh, vice and sin. Therefore elsewhere he says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6); and: “Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied” (Ps. 24). And by persecuting me he has greatly prevailed against me, because “he has humbled my life to the ground,” that is, amid earthly pleasures, so that I might eat earth like the serpent cursed by God (Gen. 3). For as one who beholds heavenly things is raised to heaven, so one who desires earth is humbled to earth. But one who digs a talent into the earth deserved to be rejected by the Lord (Matt. 25). For this is the aim of the enemy’s persecution: to cast the soul down from the hope of heavenly things to desire for earthly things.

Christ is life, who says of himself: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11 [citation printed as John 2]). There is life of nature: “He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2). Of teaching: “The Lord fed him with the bread of life and understanding” (Ecclus. 15). Of grace: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). Of glory: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). There are also many human modes of life, such as active, contemplative, regular, secular, and the like; hence we read: “Your mercy is better than lives” (Ps. 62). There is furthermore the life of sin: “He went into a far country and squandered all his substance by living extravagantly” (Luke 15); of misery: “A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14); of punishment: “I praised the dead more than the living” (Eccles. 4); [Col. 1123D] and of Gehenna: “He shall labour forever and still live to the end” (Ps. 48).

> He has placed me in darkness like those dead of old; and my spirit has been distressed within me [variant: over me]; my heart has been troubled within me.

Apply each point to its corresponding phrase. “My spirit,” he says, “was distressed within me,” because my enemy, so far as lay in his power, humbled my life to the ground. “And my heart was troubled within me,” because he placed me in darkness, that is, in the shadows of vices that darken and obscure the mind, just as the Apostle says of sinners: “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1).

“He placed me in darkness,” he says, [Col. 1124A] “like those dead of old,” that is, like secular persons dead in sins: living in body as regards the world, but dead in soul as regards the Lord. Recognizing his danger, therefore, “my spirit was distressed within me,” seized by intense fear. “And my heart was troubled within me,” pierced by intense grief. Yet it was not only within me but also against me that “my spirit was distressed within me and my heart troubled,” because I am the cause of this distress and disturbance. I acted culpably; therefore disturbance of heart and distress of spirit came upon me. I do not transfer the blame to another, but accuse myself, that I may deserve more readily to obtain pardon. But lest I fall into despair and instead find consolation:

> [Col. 1124B] I remembered the days of old, and [variant: “and” absent] meditated on all your works; and [variant: “and” absent] I meditated [variant: “I shall meditate”] upon the works of your hands.

It is a great consolation amid the straits of tribulation to remember the Lord’s mercies. Therefore I remembered the days of old, in which God long ago bestowed upon the ancient Fathers many remedies of consolation. “And I meditated on all your works,” which concern creation and nature, so that “all” extends not to individual species but to the kinds of individual things. “And I shall meditate upon the works of your hands,” which concern redemption and grace, which your hands themselves properly performed. From all these things I conceive hope of deliverance while placed amid diverse tribulations. And therefore:

> I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is to you like land without water.

Confidently, therefore, I have stretched out my hands to you, O Lord, because you graciously stretched out yours for me, extended upon the gibbet of the cross. And I have stretched out my hands in the form of a cross, glorying with the Apostle in your cross, O Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 6), which became for me the cause of salvation. I have also stretched out my hands—that is, I have enlarged my affections and works, which had previously been in some manner constricted, while I hoped less for deliverance. The “hand” of man has many meanings: that of activity, whence: “My hands dripped with myrrh” (Song 5); and: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, [Col. 1124D] you are blessed” (Ps. 127). That of prayer, whence: “Lifting up pure hands in prayer” (1 Tim. 2). And when Moses raised his hands in prayer, Israel prevailed (Exod. 17). That of contemplation, whence: “The hands of a man were under their wings” (Ezek. 1); and: “The lizard supports itself with its hands, and dwells in the houses of kings” (Prov. 30). That of healing, whence: “They shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall be well” (Mark 16); and: “He gave her his hand and raised her up” (Acts 9). That of praise, whence: “All nations, clap your hands” (Ps. 46); and: “The rivers shall clap their hands together” (Ps. 97).

I have therefore stretched out my hands to heaven in prayer, because my soul is to you as land without water: lacking the moisture of virtues, it produces no shoot of a good work, and therefore desires rain, that, watered, it may germinate. [Col. 1125A] But lest it utterly wither and become barren:

> Quickly hear me, O Lord; my spirit has failed.  
> Do not turn your face away from me, lest I become like those going down into the pit.

The third part, in which he expresses what he asks and sets forth the grounds for his request. First, he asks that the divine face not be turned away from him, whence: “Do not turn your face away from me.” And he adds the reason: because, if you turned it away, “I shall be like those going down into the pit.” Secondly, he asks that divine mercy be present to him, whence: “Cause me to hear your mercy in the morning”; and he gives the reason: “For I have hoped in you, O Lord.” Thirdly, he asks that the way in which he should walk be made known to him, whence: “Make known to me the way in which I should walk”; and at once [Col. 1125B] gives the reason: “For I have lifted up my soul to you.” Fourthly, he asks to be delivered from his enemies, whence: “Deliver me from my enemies”; and he shows the reason, because “to you, O Lord, I have fled.” Fifthly, he asks to be taught to do the divine will, whence: “Teach me to do your will”; and immediately expresses the reason: “For you are my God.”

Truly, therefore, O Lord, my soul is like land without water: for my spirit has failed—not as to the life of nature, but of grace, which I lost through sin. Or: “Hear me, O Lord, for my spirit has failed,” that is, I have become poor in spirit, pride failing and humility advancing. Therefore do not turn your face—that is, your kindness—away from me; rather, restore to the humble what you took away from the proud. For, [Col. 1125C] if you turn away your face, I shall be like those going down into the pit, that is, into the depth of sin, of which it is elsewhere said: “When the wicked man has come into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18), because, without hope of pardon, he gives himself licence to sin, loosening the reins of iniquities. Or: “I shall be like those going down into the pit,” that is, one of the reprobate descending into hell. For there is a pit of guilt, whence: “You saved me from those going down into the pit” (Ps. 29); of misery, whence: “He drew me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of the dregs” (Ps. 39); and of Gehenna, whence: “I have been reckoned among those going down into the pit” (Ps. 87). Therefore, do not turn your face away from me.

> Cause me to hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you, O Lord [variant: lacks “O Lord”].

[Col. 1125D] “In the morning,” that is, at the rising of light, namely in the infusion of grace: cause me to hear your mercy—that is, cause me to hear, namely to understand, that mercy which makes the light of truth and charity flash forth in the soul. Or, in the morning of the resurrection, after the end of the age, cause me to hear your mercy, namely that word full of your mercy: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matt. 25). For I have hoped in you, O Lord, that you may grant me both grace in the present and glory in the future. But so that I may be able to arrive there by a straight path:

> Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you.

God indeed did this when he kindled the prophetic word, to which, as Peter says, we ought to give heed [Col. 1126A] as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns (2 Pet. 1). For he shows the way of truth, that is, the Catholic faith, through which we must walk by good works in order to arrive at life. But one who goes by another way, as does a Jew, a heretic, or a pagan, certainly does not proceed to life but goes to death.

He also who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14), made the path known; he made himself known as the way by which we approach life itself, when he set forth the light of the Godhead in the vessel of humanity, so that through the form of a servant we may proceed to the form of God, to the most merciful light, the Word which was in the beginning with God (John 1). Therefore make known to me this way in which I should walk. And certainly you ought to do so, because I have lifted up my soul to you; I have not bent it down toward [Col. 1126B] the world, but have brought a vessel to the fountain, that you may fill it with water springing up into eternal life (John 4).

Let no one, then, presume upon his own intellect, thinking his own knowledge sufficient for knowing the way by which he may tend toward his fatherland: for a man’s ways are not in himself, but a man’s steps are directed by the Lord (Ps. 36). “There is a way which seems right to a man, but its latter end leads to destruction” (Prov. 14). Therefore make known to me the way in which I should walk, because I have lifted up my soul to you, O Lord. For I did not keep it in myself as though it were sufficient, but lifted it up to you as insufficient, that I might ask from you understanding for knowing the way in which I should walk. Hence I raised it from earthly things to heavenly things; for “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). But upon that very way of salvation:

> Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord; to you I have fled. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.

Many enemies beset the way in order to make travellers stray: visible and invisible, spiritual and bodily. Deliver me from all these enemies, lest they obstruct my way, because I have fled to you, who are the refuge of those hoping in you, O Lord. For no one can escape you; hence anyone ought to flee to you, since you do not cast out those who come to you, but permit them to enter. And lest I withdraw from you again, teach me through your Holy Spirit, who is the anointing that teaches concerning all things [Col. 1126D] (1 John 2), to do your will—that is, to fulfil your commandments.

For the will of God which is God himself, and is called his good pleasure, is not done, but does all things whatsoever it wills to be done, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abyss (Ps. 134). It is indeed one, but it has many signs, of which he speaks in the plural: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110). Among these are counsel and commandment, concerning which he says: “Teach me to do your will,” that I may do what you counsel and command to be done. I have fled to you because you are my God. For I would flee to another if I had been made by another; but because you are my God, my creator, I flee to you. Therefore teach me to do your will, because you are my master and teacher.

> [Col. 1127A] Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way; for your name’s sake, O Lord, you will make me alive in your righteousness.

The fourth part, in which he commends the divine benefits bestowed upon him: because God will be his guide (Num. 10), whence: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way”; his giver of life, whence: “You will make me alive in your righteousness”; his deliverer, because “you will bring my soul out of tribulation”; and his avenger, because “you will destroy all my enemies.” He who formerly conceived the hope of deliverance now possesses certainty, and therefore confidently says: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way.”

“Spirit” may mean the divine Spirit, of whom it is said: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4). More particularly, it means the third person in the Trinity, whence: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5). It means an angelic spirit, whence: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103); and: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for ministry?” (Heb. 1). It means the human spirit, whence: “In his hand is the soul of every living thing, and the spirit of all human flesh” (Job 12). It means a demonic spirit, whence: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6). And it means the animal spirit, whence it is said: “Who knows whether the spirit of Adam’s sons ascends upward and the spirit of beasts descends downward?” [Col. 1127C] (Ecclus. 3).

Likewise, it means the spirit of grace, whence: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (Rom. 8); and: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfil the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5). The spirit of prophecy, whence: “The spirits of prophets were subject to them” (1 Cor. 14). The spirit of wisdom, whence: “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6). The spirit of Scripture, whence: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Also the spirit of power, whence: “Where the impulse—that is, the power—of the spirit was, there they went” (Ezek. 1), whether toward saving good or damning evil. And of this the Apostle says: “The Lord Jesus shall kill him with the spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2). The spirit of will, whence: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6). The spirit of indignation, [Col. 1127D] whence: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6). And the spirit of contemplation, whence: “The spirit lifted me between heaven and earth and brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God” (Ezek. 8). The spirit of virtues, whence: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him,” etc. (Isa. 2). The spirit of vices, whence: “I saw three unclean spirits like frogs go out of the mouth of the dragon, the mouth of the beast, and the mouth of the false prophet” (Rev. 16); and: “Behold, two women coming forth, and spirit in their wings” (Zech. 5). These are the spirits of pride, vain glory (*xenodoxia*), and the like. The spirit of infirmities, whence: “Behold a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years” (Luke 13). And the spirit of storms, whence: “A stormy blast [Col. 1128A] is the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10).

But “your good Spirit will lead me into the right way.” This is he who makes known to me the way in which I should walk and teaches me to do your will (Ps. 142), because he himself will lead me into the right way. Good indeed in himself, because he is goodness itself; and good in us, because he makes us good. O how good, how merciful, how kind, how sweet, how delightful, and how pleasant is your Spirit, O Lord, to those who love you with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith! (1 Tim. 1). He will lead me into the right way, that is, into the way of your commandments (Ps. 118), by which one goes rightly to the fatherland.

The good Spirit of God may also here be understood as a good angel, given for guardianship. He indeed will lead me into the right way. For my evil spirit led me into a crooked way, but your good Spirit will lead me into the right way—not because of my merit, but for your name’s sake, that you may fulfil the meaning of your name, which is Jesus, that is, Saviour. For I killed myself through guilt, but you will justify me through grace. Yet that grace will not be without justice, because you will make me alive in righteousness—not mine, indeed, but yours, as was shown above. Or: “You will make me alive in your righteousness, for your name’s sake,” so that, being named from this, you may be gloriously praised, as it is elsewhere said: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113).

> You will bring my soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy you will destroy my enemies.

[Col. 1128C] As long as the soul remains enclosed in this mortal body, it is afflicted by many distresses; but when it is brought out of that prison, it is delivered from the tribulation of this world, lest it incur a more grievous tribulation. For this reason the Psalmist elsewhere said: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141). And the Apostle Paul: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). This therefore takes place when, pardon for sins having been granted, God commands the soul to leave the body, as though released from prison. And in your mercy, as regards me who did not deserve it, you will destroy all my enemies, so that they may no longer be able to harm me. This is undoubtedly true concerning spiritual enemies, that is, demons, that you will destroy them all; and also concerning bodily enemies—all those who have persevered as enemies until their death.

But the words said at the end of the preceding verse and at the end of the following one should be noted. For there it is said, “You will make me alive in your righteousness,” and here, “In your mercy you will destroy my enemies.” Yet it would seem rather that mercy pertains to justification and righteousness to destruction. But each pertains to both, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). For this reason the Psalmist sang to him of mercy and judgment (Ps. 110).

But because some of my enemies are predestined to eternal life and some are reprobated to eternal death, concerning the predestined I say, in my earnest desire, that “in your mercy,” that is, through the effect of [Col. 1129A] your mercy, “you will destroy all my enemies,” that is, all their enmities, so that enemies may become friends, according to what is elsewhere said: “Turn the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. 12). But concerning the reprobate I say in a prophetic spirit:

> And you will destroy all who afflict my soul, because I am your servant.

You will destroy in the Gehenna of eternal fire all such as afflict my soul with an obstinate heart, because I am your servant—that is, in punishment for the sin by which they wickedly persecute me, your servant. Or: you will destroy those who afflict my soul precisely because I am your servant, that is, because I serve you. It is also a grave sin to persecute someone because he serves God. A jubilant conclusion, in which, by divine inspiration, he predicts the deliverance of his soul and the destruction of his enemies.

Because in human works nothing is wholly perfect, I kindly ask the reader of this work that, if he finds anything worthy in it, he may ascribe it wholly to divine grace. But whatever he recognizes in it as less worthy, let him attribute it to human imperfection, humbly praying that he himself may intercede suppliantly for me with the most merciful Father and the most just Judge, that he may grant me full pardon of sins through the power of true and fruitful repentance, which I have, in some fashion, described in this exposition of the penitential Psalms, to the praise and glory of the name of Jesus Christ; who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1129] End of the Commentaries of Lord Innocent on the Seven Penitential Psalms.

[Col. 1129]

# RULE OF THE ORDER OF THE HOLY SPIRIT OF SAXIA, APPARENTLY FOUNDED BY INNOCENT III

(Brockie, *Codex Regularum*, vol. V, p. 495.)

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION

[Col. 1129B] Among the principal duties of Christian charity, service in hospitals, care for the sick, and aid for the necessities of other miserable persons are considered no small religious task. Hence in every age God has raised up men endowed with such mercy that very many have not thought it beneath them to render so holy a ministry to their neighbours. Among the several religious orders established in the twelfth century and the following one, some were called Hospitallers, specially appointed to observe this pious office; such was the institution of the present sacred order, which still possesses under its direction the very extensive hospital of the entire Catholic Church. Its miraculous origin is related by the Most Reverend Ascanius Tamburini, formerly Abbot General of Vallombrosa, in *De jure abbatum*, vol. II, disputation 24, question 4, p. 314, although others give a different origin.

But before other authors, let us hear the oft-cited Tamburini speak thus concerning the origin of this order:

[Col. 1129C] “The Order, or Congregation, of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, so called in apostolic letters and under the Rule of St Augustine, had a truly wondrous beginning from Innocent III, Supreme Pontiff. While he was praying, a voice from heaven said to him: ‘Innocent, go fishing in the river Tiber.’ Having communicated the matter to the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, he went to the Tiber; and, having cast out nets, on the first occasion he drew out eighty-seven, and on the second three hundred and forty, aborted infants, suffocated by impious mothers and thrown into the Tiber. A remedy divinely revealed was not lacking to the most merciful pontiff. Gathering together very many pious men, he placed them in charge of caring for the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, which he built at Rome about the year 1201. [Col. 1130B] Their duty is to receive and care for pilgrims and the sick, and to nourish boys and infants. They are called Brothers of the Holy Spirit from the certainly magnificent foundation built under the guardianship and patronage of the Holy Spirit. It is called ‘in Saxia’ either because the foundation stands beneath the rock or castle of Nero, or because Saxons, a people of Germany, once lived there.”

Meanwhile, there are some who wish the origin of this order to be much more ancient, asserting that it arose from St Lazarus, brother of the most holy virgins Martha and Mary; having landed near Marseilles in Gaul, he is said to have founded there a military order and an outstanding hospice in honour of the Holy Spirit. More will be said below concerning this fabulous beginning, since fierce disputes arose among the members of this sacred order—especially Italians and Frenchmen—in support of such trifles. Other writers likewise vainly wish to derive the beginning of the order from a certain St Cyriacus, or Judas Quiriacus, as Trithemius writes in the first part of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, fol. 527. Their opinion too must be altogether rejected, since it rests upon no foundation of truth. For in the first centuries of the Church we never find that any definite Order of Hospitallers was founded; and that St Cyriacus was neither Bishop of Jerusalem at the time when the Holy Cross was found, nor could he have occupied that see under Julian the Apostate, as the most learned Bollandist associates show at greater length in vol. I of the May *Acta*, under the fourth day of that month, furnishing it with learned notes; they call him Judas Quiriacus.

Nor are writers lacking who do not deny the origin of this order to Pope Innocent III, but maintain that it was not instituted under the protection and invocation of the Holy Spirit until the most pious Count Guy of Montpellier was made first master of the Roman arch-hospital. It is indeed admitted by all that this Count of Montpellier, a little before Innocent III, founded a notable hospital in his own city and instituted it under the invocation and protection of the Holy Spirit. Later, however, he was summoned to Rome by the Supreme Pontiff and made first master of the Roman arch-hospital, and governed both hospices under the invocation of the Holy Spirit, as will become clearer from what follows.

Accordingly, we must acknowledge both Pope Innocent III and Count Guy as founders of this sacred order, but in different respects: that Supreme Pontiff was the author of the arch-hospital, under whose jurisdiction all the others depended; whereas the most pious count founded the first hospice, which was nevertheless to be subject to the other. For it matters little [Col. 1131B] whether, from the beginning, the members of this sacred order served the sick and served God under one name or the other, since only a few years intervened between the erection of the two hospitals. Indeed, in a solemn bull issued in 1204 and addressed to the same Guy as master of both hospices, that most pious pontiff expressly says that this Roman arch-hospital was erected by himself in the place called St Mary in Saxia, as appears in the bull itself, published in the *Bullarium Romanum*, vol. I, p. 58, which it is also pleasing to present here.

### Bull of Pope Innocent III confirming the foundation of the Roman arch-hospital and its union with the Hospital of Montpellier

**INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GUY, master of the hospitals of St Mary in Saxia and of the Holy Spirit at Montpellier, and to his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.**

“Among the works of piety,” etc. See Book VII of the *Regesta*, col. 377, vol. II.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of John, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1204, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent III.

This Roman hospice, therefore, at the time of its foundation was called the Hospital of St Mary in Saxia, and perhaps derived its name from the Saxon English themselves, since it was erected in the same place where the most pious Ina, king of the East Saxons in England, had caused a church to be built in 715 in honour of St Mary, Virgin Mother of God. For this most pious king, later coming to Rome about the year 718 to visit the holy places, built there an eminent hospice and endowed it with very ample revenues for receiving his East Saxons who visited the holy places. Likewise, following Ina’s pious example, Offa, king of the Middle Saxons or Mercians, enriched a hospital there with royal gifts, though it was afterwards utterly reduced to ruin. For in 817 it was consumed by flames so great that they could be extinguished only by a miracle: after the most pious Pope Paschal I, accompanied in procession by clergy and people with a miraculous image of the Virgin Mother of God, came to the place, the fire was extinguished. And although it was reduced to ashes in 847 and again restored through the piety of Pope Leo IV and the generosity of the kings of England, yet in the eleventh and twelfth centuries we find that the part of Rome in which it stood was so devastated by the factions of Guelphs and Ghibellines that, when Pope Innocent III ascended St Peter’s chair in 1198, scarcely the memory of that Hospital of the East Saxons survived. Therefore the most pious Pope Innocent III ought rightly to be called its true restorer and founder, though the place seems to have taken its designation from its ancient Saxon inhabitants, since even today it is called *de Sassia* or “in Saxia.”

But as to the miraculous beginning: although that Supreme Pontiff, in his aforementioned bull, makes no mention of it, as was said above, yet his successors Nicholas IV and Sixtus IV expressly treat of it in their bulls. Moreover, in the most costly hospital itself there is an ancient painted panel representing the entire wonderful story. All this may indeed indicate a sufficiently pious tradition. However this may be, we find a certain trace of this miraculous origin in the very letters of the most pious Pope Innocent III, published by the eminent Baluze. In Letter 112, he grants indulgences to those who take prostitutes as lawful wives, since such frequent infanticides are accustomed to be committed through such brothels. The letter reads as follows:

[Col. 1132B] “To all Christ’s faithful to whom these letters shall come. Among the works of charity proposed to us for imitation on the authority of Sacred Scripture, as Gospel authority testifies, it is not the least to call back one who has gone astray from the path of error; and especially to invite women living voluptuously and indiscriminately admitting anyone to sexual intercourse, to live chastely in the fellowship of lawful marriage. Taking this into account, by the authority of these presents we decree that for all who remove public women from a brothel and marry them, what they do may avail for the remission of sins. Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.”

Since some say that the heavenly revelation was made immediately after the election of Pope Innocent III, it may very well be inferred that he issued this decree concerning marriages with prostitutes and at the same time founded this hospital to receive and nourish such abandoned infants, so that the crime of infanticide might thereafter cease.

[Col. 1132C] Since, therefore, this most celebrated hospice was completed in 1201, and thus before the granting of the aforementioned bull of confirmation, Guy, founder of the Hospital of Montpellier, had been made its master; and eventually it began to be called the Hospital of the Holy Spirit. From this, the true origin of the Regular Canons of the Order of the Holy Spirit must be derived, taking its designation from both hospitals.

For the claims put forward by some concerning a certain military Order of the Holy Spirit, supposedly founded in the earliest years of Christianity by St Lazarus and his most holy sisters Martha and Mary, as we said above, are mere nonsense and empty old wives’ tales. The frequently cited Hippolyte Hélyot, in his *History of Religious Orders*, vol. II, ch. 30, learnedly refutes that fabulous military order, supported only by certain invented legends. For the Knights of the Holy Spirit can bring forward no other authority for their fabulous antiquity than a certain reading taken from some breviary printed about 1553, in which these words were read in the lessons for St Martha: “While Magdalene devoted herself wholly to devotion and contemplation, and Lazarus gave himself more to military service, prudent Martha vigorously managed the affairs both of her sister and her brother, and diligently ministered to servants and soldiers.” I do not wish here to overturn the whole story of St Lazarus and his most holy sisters, since learned Catholic men have sufficiently purged it of fabulous falsehoods; and the very words of this reading provide a very weak argument for establishing the antiquity of such a military order.

Meanwhile, leaving these old wives’ tales, let us proceed to more certain arguments that may indicate the true origin and ancient state of this order. Among Italians the order is called that of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, and among the French, that of the Holy Spirit of Montpellier. First, it is certain [Col. 1133A] that the first author of this order, still flourishing under the protection and guardianship of the Holy Spirit, was the aforementioned Guy. At the end of the twelfth century, at Montpellier, he had founded a very extensive hospice for supporting the sick and poor; summoned to Rome by Pope Innocent III, he took charge of the new hospital erected by that Supreme Pontiff at St Mary in Saxia. Afterwards it began to be called the Hospital of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, after the aforesaid pontiff wished to unite the two into one.

Further, it cannot be denied that from its beginning this beneficial institution was composed of more laymen than ecclesiastics. The Hospitallers of Montpellier had received no sacred orders; and Pope Innocent III decreed in the bull cited above that there should be only four clerics in the Roman arch-hospital, observing the rule of that hospital exactly and administering the sacraments to the sick independently of the master and other brothers of the order, while subject only to the Supreme Pontiff, as the words of the bull declare.

And this is the true and genuine origin of the sacred Order of Canons of the Holy Spirit of Saxia. Although it was governed more by laymen than clerics, the most pious pontiff appears to have prescribed to its members the Augustinian Rule as a common norm of regular life, adding certain constitutions, which we also append here. From these constitutions it is clear that the present Rule was strictly observed by all the brothers, who were bound by it not only diligently to nourish and educate abandoned infants but also to receive all sick and infirm persons who arrived and to serve them in every best possible way.

Although that most pious pontiff united these two arch-hospitals, the Roman and the Montpellier institution, under one master and subjected the latter to the former, he nevertheless wished a certain separation of goods to be maintained. Thus he decreed that all alms [Col. 1133C] collected in Italy, Sicily, England, and Hungary should belong to the Roman institution, as should the very ample revenues situated in Rome and its vicinity; the remaining alms collected in France, Spain, and other parts of Europe were to go to the hospice of Montpellier.

After Pope Honorius III wished to dissolve this union and granted the French their own master general, this sacred order then began in some manner to be dispersed. For although from its earliest institution it consisted of laymen and clerics, the laymen, always retaining the temporal jurisdiction of the hospitallers, eventually behaved not as regular masters but wished to live as secular preceptors and perpetual commendatory holders, converting the patrimony of the poor to their own uses and rendering no obedience to the master general. From these arose the Knights of the Holy Spirit, although they belonged to no military order and were never called, like the members of other military orders, to undertake holy wars, as all historians acknowledge and as is entirely evident from what has already been said concerning their fabulous origin from St Lazarus.

I do not wish here to recount the fierce quarrels formerly conducted between the clerics of this order and those spurious knights, since the frequently cited Hippolyte Hélyot treats them sufficiently fully and readers may consult him. For we do not intend to present the complete history of this sacred order, but only to bring forward matters conducive to a better knowledge of the following constitutions, which seem to have been made not for the French but for the Italians. Nor do we speak here of the most celebrated equestrian Order of the Holy Spirit still flourishing in France, founded by King Henry III, which never had dealings with the Hospitallers of Montpellier and is not customarily numbered among religious orders.

But let us return to the sacred Order of the Holy Spirit in Saxia, which extended widely not only among Italians and Sicilians but was also dispersed through England, Germany, Hungary, and Poland. At last, under the pontificate of Nicholas IV, the Hospitallers of Montpellier wished again to enter into union with the Italians, making a certain submission to the Roman master general, in recognition of which they promised annually to pay him three gold florins, as we learn from a bull of that pontiff issued in 1292.

There are, however, some writers who maintain that Pope Gregory XI, elected in 1370, restored the Hospitallers of Montpellier to the former liberty granted them by Honorius III. Other authors reject that bull as spurious, especially Launier, historian of this order and superior of the Roman arch-hospital, because it is addressed to Berengar Gioni, general of the arch-hospital of the militia of the Holy Spirit, who died first in 1486 or the following year; he would therefore have had to extend his generalate for more than a hundred years, an assertion that would be most ridiculous.

Meanwhile, from these and the other documents adduced, it is altogether clear [Col. 1134B] that this sacred Order of the Holy Spirit in Saxia remained filled with clerics and laymen for at least some centuries and was not properly a religious order, since those laymen, to whom the clerics were subject, were bound by no solemn religious vows. Hence arose so many abuses and dissipations of alms, as every master of a hospice lived as a secular commendatory holder and converted the patrimony of the poor to his own uses, as said above.

Thus not before the year 1458 did this sacred order assume the true character of a religious order, when Pope Pius II, elected in that year, suppressed all those commendatory masters and united those spurious commendams to his new military Order of Bethlehem, as his bull attests, published by the eminent Leibniz in his *Codex juris gentium*. From that time this sacred order truly began to exist as a religious order, freed from all lay masters or superiors and governed only by religious men. Thus Pope Sixtus IV commanded in a solemn bull of 1476:

[Col. 1134C] “Establishing and likewise decreeing that the hospitals, preceptories, dependencies, and places of the said order may not and cannot be conferred in title or commendam upon any person whatsoever, of whatever dignity, estate, rank, or condition, except upon brothers of our said hospital and persons expressly professing the order itself; yet such persons shall hold them only at the will of the said preceptor then in office and shall be recalled to the cloister whenever expedient.”

From this authentic bull, also reproduced in the *Bullarium Magnum Romanum*, vol. I, p. 406, we learn that certain Transalpine commanders or masters, especially in France, did not obey the commands of the supreme pontiffs Pius II and Paul II, but turned such hospitals to their own uses, denied the obedience due to the Roman master-general, and conducted themselves not as religious men but rather as secular commendatory holders [Col. 1134D]. Accordingly it sharply rebukes them in these words, depriving them of all ownership of property: “Since therefore, as we have learned with displeasure, certain brothers of that hospital, holding commanderies, hospitals, dependencies, and pious places dependent upon the hospital itself in Saxia, led on by blind ambition and covetousness and not content with their limits, have with their own rashness presumed to call themselves general commanders of the said order, especially beyond the mountains, etc.” Thus all the commendatory knights of this order were suppressed, and by apostolic authority all the remaining commanders and hospitalers everywhere were subjected to the Roman master-general, as is there prescribed: “Indeed, all and each of the commanders, hospitalers, and religious of the said order—whom we will to be fully subject in law to the said commander of our hospital in Saxia—are bound and ought to render to him, as to their superior, due obedience and reverence; and, saving the authority of this See, to obey him in all things [Col. 1135A] as their sole commander.”

From the promulgation of this papal bull, therefore, even among the French, all commanders and hospitalers of the Holy Spirit lived under the jurisdiction of the Roman master-general and, through the three solemn vows, became true religious, until the beginning of the seventeenth century. For in 1619 the supreme pontiff Paul V granted the French a vicar-general, though in some manner dependent upon the Roman general of the order; and Pope Gregory XV ordained that such a vicar and general visitor should make the three solemn religious vows and put on the habit of the order. Thus it was not until 1625 that the supreme pontiff Urban VIII, at the request of King Louis XIII, made the master-general of the hospital of Montpellier and the other commanders and hospitalers scattered throughout the kingdoms of France and Navarre free from the jurisdiction of the Roman master-general.

From this arose [Col. 1135B] the whole relaxation of regular discipline, and in those regions secular and commendatory commanders and masters began again to flourish, attempting everywhere to introduce a spurious military order. And although the more zealous and devout commanders strongly resisted such usurpations, they achieved nothing until the year 1700, when the magnanimous king of France, Louis XIV, declared that this Order of the Holy Spirit in Saxia ought to be regarded as a true regular order, and that those secular and commendatory commanders should be suppressed. But at last, owing to the frequent importunities of certain great courtiers, a master-general of this order throughout France was appointed from among the foremost nobility of the kingdom. Under his direction all religious and lay brothers are to live and to observe hospitality duly in all the hospitals; for which reason he is called Master of the Order of the Holy Spirit of Montpellier.

Meanwhile, the remaining hospitals of this sacred order [Col. 1135C], established in other regions outside Italy and Sicily, remained under the jurisdiction of the Roman arch-hospital, whose residents duly observe the rule prescribed by Pope Innocent III. A notable example is afforded by the hospital at Memmingen, situated in the imperial city of the same name. Although it depends upon a Lutheran magistracy with regard to temporal jurisdiction, the religious hospitalers nevertheless retain the public exercise of the Catholic religion. They are free in their own church, bells being rung, solemnly to celebrate divine worship by day and night, administer the sacraments, carry the most holy Eucharist in Catholic rite, with a little bell and a light, to the sick lying even in the houses of Lutherans, publicly bury the dead, and perform with due reverence all other ceremonies customary among orthodox Christians.

There was formerly also, in the same circle of Swabia, at the imperial city of Wimpfen, an eminent hospital [Col. 1135D] of this order. At the time of the change of religion it was reduced to utter ruin; but about the middle of the seventeenth century the religious of Memmingen laboured to restore it. Though they could never recover its very extensive revenues, they are accustomed nevertheless to maintain some religious at their own expense. For these two hospitals situated in Germany, the commander of the hospital at Memmingen was accustomed annually to pay seven Byzantine gold pieces, in acknowledgment of the subjection due to the Roman arch-hospital, as is learned from the ancient records of the city of Memmingen.

Nor can it be doubted that the other exceedingly wealthy hospitals scattered through the various provinces of the Catholic world did the same. Many that remain in Spain, Belgium, Hungary, and Poland still today annually acknowledge their due payment to this Roman arch-hospital, as the supreme master-general of all hospitalers of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, this Roman arch-hospital [Col. 1136A] extends so widely, is equipped with magnificent buildings, and is endowed with such ample revenues, that it seems to resemble a great castle, containing several palaces separated by various intervals of space, in which dwell various classes of persons of both sexes.

In one palace live more than a hundred nurses who suckle abandoned infants; for such children, legitimate as well as illegitimate, are received there lest they perish from hunger.
