In another live about five hundred older boys, who are instructed by devout commanders in Christian doctrine and in various other arts and sciences. In a third palace live an equal number of girls, instructed by nuns of the same order in every kind of virtue, as in a regular monastery. Finally, in a fourth palace there are two very long halls, each furnished with a thousand beds: one contains sick men, the other [Col. 1136B] sick women, etc. But besides all these and many other splendid buildings provided for abandoned infants, sick persons, and arriving pilgrims, there is there a magnificent monastery inhabited by religious men who, devoted day and night to the divine praises, live the regular life under the Rule of St Augustine and the following constitutions. The master-general of the whole order also customarily resides there. At this arch-hospital more than two hundred thousand Roman scudi are spent annually for the use of the sick, calculated as an average over two years.

But let us return to the constitutions to be set forth below, which in 1564 at Rome were published by the Most Reverend Lord Bernardinus Cyrillus of L’Aquila, commander and master-general of the entire order; and he calls them the Rule of the Sacred Order of the Holy Spirit in Saxia. Since these constitutions agree entirely with the bull of the supreme pontiff Innocent III, [Col. 1136C] there can be no doubt that that most devout pontiff, in founding this order, prescribed the same statutes for religious of both sexes, although he also gave them the Augustinian Rule, shared with other hospitalers, as the norm of life. Yet anyone who even lightly surveys these constitutions can readily perceive that not all the statutes presented here had been customary from the beginning of the order, but that in the course of time many of them were added.

For since it is altogether certain that from its original foundation this sacred order was governed rather by secular than by religious persons, upon the suppression of those secular commanders or masters it was altogether necessary to establish certain new statutes common to all religious of both sexes. Meanwhile, these present constitutions are most salutary for the administration and government of hospitals. All persons of both sexes are bound, besides the three solemn religious vows, to undertake special care of the sick [Col. 1136D] and abandoned infants. Hence they enjoy very many privileges, are exempt from the jurisdiction of all ordinaries, and are granted all the privileges of other sacred orders. As for these religious calling themselves Regular Canons, this arose only from the time when they began to lead a true regular life according to the Rule of St Augustine, and after the congregation of Regular Canons of the Holy Spirit dispersed through France and Lorraine was joined to it.

They never customarily wear canonical dress; their habit is altogether the same as that of secular clerics, except that, for distinction, they must wear over their black garment a white cross sewn upon the breast, doubly cross-barred, of which the first bar is smaller, as the above-cited Tamburini relates. There now follows the text of the Rule itself, as it was communicated to us in manuscript.

# RULE OF THE ORDER OF THE HOLY SPIRIT IN SAXIA

[Col. 1137]

[Col. 1137A] Bernardinus Cyrillus of L’Aquila, commander and master-general of the Order of the Holy Spirit, to the brothers of the Order of the Holy Spirit in Saxia established wherever they may be.

Dearest brothers, we set before you anew the Rule of our order and the institutions of our Fathers of old, to the observance of which we exhort you with every duty and affection within our power: that through them Almighty God may direct us in his way; and that, by the gift of his Holy Spirit and by your prayers, whatever is weak in our order may be strengthened by heavenly aid, what is sick may be healed, what is broken may be bound up, what is cast down may be restored, and what is lost may be sought through the devout affection of charity [Col. 1138A]. May the power of that same Holy Spirit console the faint-hearted among us; may it rebuke those, if any, who are unruly; and may it guard and protect with its right hand those who are cast down and languishing, and our houses. May he further deign, by his gift and by your prayers, to grant compassion and mercy to me also—who am bound to render an account for you all and for myself. May each of you be well in the Lord, and in his fear observe his commandments and these regular precepts.

At Rome, in the sacred hospital church of the Holy Spirit, 1 April 1564.

# FOUNDATION OF THE SAME SACRED ORDER OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 1137]

[Col. 1137B] A reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 25.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When the Son [of Man] shall come,” etc., as far as: “But the righteous [shall go] into eternal life.”

Stephen, by divine mercy priest of the title of St Mary across the Tiber, and Rainerius, deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, cardinals, to their beloved sons, the master and chapter of the house of the Holy Spirit in the city of Rome, and all the rectors, brothers, and sisters dwelling in other houses under its order and mastership: greeting in the Lord.

This is the Rule which, by command and authority of the Apostolic See, we enjoin you to observe; it was given by the supreme pontiff, Lord Pope Innocent III, and confirmed by all the cardinals of the most holy Church [Col. 1137C]. It begins as follows:

## CHAPTER I.—May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us.

In the name of the Lord and of the undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. We command and enjoin all brothers and sisters, both present and future, of the whole Order of the Holy Spirit, to live in obedience, chastity, and without private property, devoting themselves principally to the care and service of the poor.

## CHAPTER II.—On the promise of novices.

I, N., offer and give myself to God, to blessed Mary, to the Holy Spirit, and to our lords the sick, that on all the days of my life I may be their servant. I promise, with God’s help, to preserve chastity; to live without private property; to render obedience to you, N., and your successors; and faithfully to safeguard the goods of the poor themselves. So help me God and these holy Gospels.

And let the person offer himself or herself at the altar with a book, etc.

## CHAPTER III.—On receiving novices.

Through the promise which you have made to God, to blessed [Col. 1138B] Mary, to the Holy Spirit, and to our lords the sick, we receive you and the soul of your father and mother into the Masses, matins, fasts, prayers, almsgivings, and all good works which are done and shall be done in the house of the Holy Spirit: that God may grant you such a share as each one of us hopes to have. And the house of the Holy Spirit promises you bread and water and will give you humble clothing.

When this has been completed, if it seems good to the commander or master and the chapter, the commander, master, or prior shall take a cloak, show the person the cross, and place it around his or her neck, saying: “By this sign of the cross may every evil flee from you, and may Christ lead you to the eternal kingdom. Amen.”

[Col. 1138C] When these words have been spoken, they shall prostrate themselves on the ground and make prayers to the Lord for him or her; and the prior, master, or some priest shall begin the Psalm, namely: “May God have mercy,” with the *Glory be to the Father*; then he says: *Lord, have mercy. Our Father.*

V. And lead us not into temptation.  
R. But deliver us from evil.  
V. Save your servant, O Lord.  
R. My God, who trusts in you.  
V. Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary.  
R. And defend him from Zion.  
V. Be to him, O Lord, a tower of strength.  
R. Against the face of the enemy.  
V. O Lord, hear my prayer.  
[Col. 1138D] R. And let my cry come unto you.  
V. The Lord be with you.  
R. And with your spirit.

Let us pray.

Protect, O Lord, your servant (or handmaid), and multiply in him or her the gifts of your grace: that he or she may be guarded from all offences and not be deprived of temporal [Col. 1139A] helps, but may rejoice in everlasting spiritual ordinances. Through Christ.

O God, whose special property is always to have mercy and to spare: receive our supplication; and let the compassion of your mercy absolve your servant, whom the chain of sins binds. Through Christ.

O God, who gave your Holy Spirit to your apostles, grant to your servant the fulfilment of his or her devout petition: that to one to whom you have given faith, you may also grant peace. Through our Lord.

## CHAPTER IV.—How our fellowship is to be granted to those who seek it.

When anyone asks for the fellowship of the brothers and wishes to commend himself or herself to their prayers, let the person prostrate himself or herself upon the ground in chapter. Then the prior or priest shall begin these psalms: “I lifted up my eyes”; “Out of the depths”; “Behold, how good”; *Lord, have mercy. Our Father.*

V. And lead us not into temptation.  
R. But deliver us from evil.  
V. Save your servant.  
R. My God, who trusts in you.  
V. Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary.  
R. And defend him from Zion.  
V. Show us, O Lord, your mercy.  
R. And give us your salvation.  
V. O Lord, hear my prayer.  
R. And let my cry come unto you.  
V. The Lord be with you.  
R. And with your spirit.

Let us pray.

[Col. 1139C] O God, who are the fountain of all mercy, the hope and comforter of those who mourn, the life and salvation of those who cry to you: hear the prayers of your people and of those who commend themselves to our prayers, that the right hand of your power may protect and defend him or her; so that, being able to serve you alone, O Lord, with a secure mind, and freed from every vexation of temptations, he or she may deserve in the tranquil safety of peace continually to render thanks to your mercy. Through the Lord.

Another prayer.

O God, who are the glory of the righteous and the mercy of sinners: we have laid before you our humble prayer, that you may graciously receive your servant N. and bestow upon him or her the guardianship of your mercy, so that he or she may serve you with the whole mind and stand under your protection. And [Col. 1139D] when their last day comes, may he or she receive the fellowship of the saints, with whom he or she may possess glory beyond telling without end. Through Christ.

Another prayer.

We beseech you, O Lord, that through the intercession of the blessed Virgin Mary with all your saints, you may grant your servant N. forgiveness of sins, bring his or her work to a good end, grant him or her your mercy and grace, fill him or her with faith, hope, and charity, raise the mind to heavenly desires, defend him or her from every adversity, and bring him or her to good perseverance. Through the Lord.

After this the fellowship sought shall be granted to the person with book and stole, the prior or priest saying:

[Col. 1140A] “We grant you (or you all) our fellowship, through participation in our prayers and the benefit of our alms.” And *Thanks be to God* is said.

Afterwards let the person be kissed by the brothers, and enrolled in the book of confraternity; and also let that which he or she has promised to give in each year be written down. When the person has died, let him or her be entered in the calendar.

## CHAPTER V.—When someone is offered in childhood through parental devotion.

O Lord God almighty, who are incomprehensible and immeasurable, and who have deigned to choose your creature by a holy calling, grant this servant, or child, an honourable life, diligent conduct, and acceptable prayer, that he or she may be made worthy of the fellowship of the saints. Through you, who are blessed [Col. 1140B] for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER VI.—What the brothers ought to request as their due, and no more.

Let no one presume to call anything his own. Thus it was said of Christ’s first disciples: “They had all things in common” (Acts 4). Let the steward of the house faithfully provide for all according to the need of each, as it is also written: “It was distributed to each according as anyone had need” (ibid.). Let the brothers request as their due no more than bread and water; and let their clothing be humble, because they are the poor of the Lord, whose servants we confess ourselves to be: they go naked and filthy, and it is shameful for a servant to be proud while his lord is humble.

## CHAPTER VII.—What and by whom things are to be carried to table.

[Col. 1140C] Let no one except the cellarer carry food or drink to the table or from the table, unless by permission of the master. Likewise, if possible, let all approach table together and, after the verse, rise and depart together.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The table verse, if clerics are not present, is to be performed thus.

“Bless.” The clerics respond: “Bless.” *Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Our Father.* This is to be said silently. But if the steward of the house or the one holding his place is present, let him say:

R. And lead us not into temptation.

Let the others respond:

R. But deliver us from evil.

Let him add: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 1140D] And thus let them sit at table. Afterwards let all say: Amen.

Then, rising from table, let them say: “Have mercy upon me, O God.”

After this let be added: *Glory be to the Father*, etc.; *As it was*. Then: *Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Our Father.*

V. And lead us not into temptation.  
R. But deliver us from evil.

Let the one who said the blessing say, the others responding: “But deliver us from evil.”

Let “Let us bless the Lord” be added, and let all respond: “Thanks be to God.”

Those who do not know “Have mercy upon me, O God” shall say the *Our Father* five times.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the reader at table.

[Col. 1141A]

For a week one cleric shall read, and one lay brother shall serve; in their absence the master shall have others supply their places.

## CHAPTER X.—That they are not to eat except twice a day.

We forbid brothers and sisters to eat except twice a day, apart from those who are sick and infirm. The determination of infirmity, however, shall rest with the judgment and oversight of the master, who is to act discreetly in the fear of God, doing nothing from favour or personal partiality or—God forbid—from envy.

## CHAPTER XI.—On fasting.

From the first Sunday after the feast of All Saints until the Nativity of the Lord, let them fast as in Lent. On every Wednesday and Friday, moreover, from the feast of the Holy Cross until the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, let them fast as in Lent. Whoever refuses shall go without wine on the following day; and if he does so a second time, let him fast on Wednesday and Friday on bread and water.

## CHAPTER XII.—On eating meat.

[Col. 1141B] Let them eat meat only three times a week: namely, Tuesday, Thursday, and Sunday, unless there is illness or unless it is the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. Whoever acts contrary to this shall fast for three days on bread and water.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On receiving the sick and ministering to them.

When the sick arrive or are brought to the house of the Holy Spirit, let them be received in this manner: [Col. 1141C] first, let them confess their sins to a priest and receive communion devoutly; afterward, let them be carried or led to bed. There, as lords, they shall be charitably refreshed every day according to the means of the house, before the brothers go to dine. On Sundays, while priests, clerics, brothers, and sisters proceed in procession through the house of the Holy Spirit, let only the Mass, or the Epistle and Gospel, be said. At the hour of the poor’s dinner and the hour of supper, let the bell be rung; at its sound, the brothers not occupied in their duties shall immediately come and serve devoutly.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the decorum of the brothers and their service of the sick.

[Col. 1141D] It is further ordained that their bearing in church be dignified and their conduct suitable: namely, that clerics in white vestments assist the priest at the altar; that a deacon or subdeacon perform this office, and, if need be, another cleric also; and that there always be light in the church, by day and night. When visiting the sick, the priest shall go in white vestments, devoutly carrying the body of the Lord; and a deacon, or at least an acolyte, shall go before him, carrying a lantern with a lighted candle and a sponge with holy water.

## CHAPTER XV.—How brothers ought to travel and reside.

In cities, villages, or castles in which they have houses of their own, let them eat nothing at all outside those houses, unless the local superior detains them [Col. 1142A] or invites them. Whoever presumes to do this shall fast for three continuous days on bread and water, and for fourteen days shall eat on the ground without table or tablecloth.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On those who go anywhere.

If one of ours has need to go somewhere, let him go with those whom the master orders him to accompany. On the journey, let him take care that there be nothing in all his behaviour to offend anyone’s sight or to be unworthy of his holiness. Sitting at table, let him strive to keep silence as far as possible.

## CHAPTER XVII.—That no one is to go alone.

No one shall go on foot through the city alone, nor take as companion anyone except one assigned to him by the master or by the person who, in the master’s absence, acts in his place. [Col. 1142B] Let the master, or the one acting in his place, provide suitable companionship. Whoever presumes to go without command or without companionship, as stated above, shall on the first occasion sit on the ground; on the second, do penance for two days; on the third, for seven days, fasting on Wednesday and Friday on bread and water.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On procession in the hospital.

In the hospital, for processions during the Lent of St Martin and the greater Lent, clerics, laymen, and sisters shall assemble. When Compline has been said, the brothers shall go silently to their dormitory and the sisters to theirs, where no outsider may be admitted for sleeping. They shall never sleep naked, but clothed in linen or woollen shirts or any other garments, each sleeping alone [Col. 1142C]. Silence shall likewise be observed there until morning. Whoever breaks it shall lose that day’s wine; if he does not amend, he shall otherwise be punished according to the judgment of the commander.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On silence in church.

Likewise, silence shall be kept in church, so that the divine office cannot be impeded. If something must be said from necessity, it shall be said in a brother’s ear. Whoever breaks silence shall lose wine.

## CHAPTER XX.—On preserving charity.

Let them strive to have charity toward all people. Let them maintain peace and concord among themselves, and wholly cast away from themselves avarice, envy, pride, hatred, anger, detraction, murmuring, and malice.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the general chapter of the brothers.

[Col. 1142D]

At the Ember seasons of the year, on the first days of the Ember fasts, the commander of the house shall hold a general chapter with his brothers and faithfully deliberate concerning the business of the house. If he has not done so then, he shall diligently do it within eight days, as soon as he can.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On the master’s community.

The commander shall carefully ensure that the community of brothers, the praiseworthy custom of the house, and the precepts of the Rule are observed in every respect.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the common table of the brothers.

The commander shall always eat at the common table of the brothers [Col. 1143A], unless he remains away because of guests or for another honourable or necessary reason.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the election of the master.

His election shall be held within a month after the death of the previous master, by the common counsel of the brothers. He shall be elected not according to the rank of his family, but according to the merit of his life and the teaching of wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On silence at table.

At table, as the Apostle says (2 Thessalonians 3), let the brothers eat their bread in silence and listen to the reading without disturbance, so that not only the throat may receive food but the ears also may hunger for the word of God. If it is necessary to speak, let a brother say it quietly in the ear of one of the servants. The greater master, however, if he wishes, may speak publicly to all out of necessity [Col. 1143B], but let him do so with discretion and restraint. After Compline they shall not drink, and in their beds they shall keep silence, as has been written above.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the correction of clerics.

The correction of clerics and of other special persons shall not belong to a lay commander, but to the cardinals to whom the house itself has been entrusted by the lord pope. Those cardinals may, for such time as they wish, delegate their authority to a cleric of that house.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the office and precedence of clerics.

The aforesaid clerics shall observe the custom of the Roman Curia in the day and night offices; and in the refectory they shall sit first, together in one part, before the lay brothers [Col. 1143C], precedence among them being observed according to sacred orders.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the status of clerics.

If it should happen that any of the clerical brothers is sent to some daughter house, or that those clerics delegate their offices, this must be so ordered that, in accordance with the tenor of the privilege of Pope Innocent III, there shall always be at least four clerics in that hospital professed under the Rule of the same hospital. They shall freely administer all spiritual matters, making special intercession for us, our predecessors and successors, and the brothers both living and dead.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the correction of clerics.

[Col. 1143D] If clerics commit offences for which lay brothers would sit on the ground in the refectory without a tablecloth, then, in honour of the clerical order, they shall not sit on the ground, lest through such a quasi-public penance they become in some way disreputable in the eyes of grave and worthy persons. Instead of that punishment, on every day on which they ought thus to do penance, they shall be deprived of one dish and sit in the last place, not merely after the clerics but after their lay brothers.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On the chapter.

At least once a week the master, or the one holding his place, shall hold chapter with the brothers. The master shall hold chapter with the sisters in the presence of a priest-brother and two other brothers.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On the penalties of fornicators.

[Col. 1144A]

If any brother or sister is caught in fornication, we will that he or she be confined in prison and remain there for one year, all occasion for escape removed, and that his or her manner of life be as follows: on Friday he or she shall fast on bread and water, and throughout the entire year shall not presume to eat meat or drink wine. After the year, if the person is found to be chastened and adorned with good morals, he or she shall return to the community with the other brothers according to the judgment of the presiding officer. This shall be done on the first occasion. If caught a second time, it shall be done for two years, as stated above. If, perhaps—God avert it!—the person is again caught in such an offence, he or she shall remain there without remedy for the whole of life.

On the Friday within the octave of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 1144B], the person may drink wine; likewise, if necessary, during the octave of Easter. If the feast of All Saints falls on a Friday, and its vigil is observed on Thursday with bread and water, the person may use seasoned foods on the feast itself. The commander, with the counsel of the chapter, may on occasion mitigate the penalty if necessary.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On brothers who quarrel and strike one another.

If a brother quarrels with another brother and there is an outcry heard by the commander, let his penalty be as follows: for seven days he shall fast, on Wednesday and Friday on bread and water, eating on the ground without table or hand-towel. If he strikes another, he shall eat [Col. 1144C] on the ground for forty days; if he sheds blood, he shall leave the habit. But if he leaves the house without the will of his commander, to whom he was entrusted, and afterward returns, he shall eat on the ground for forty days, fasting on Wednesday and Friday on bread and water. For as long a time as he was outside, he shall remain in an external place.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On the arrangement of the hours.

When the brothers rise for matins and are in church, they shall hear matins and the Hours of the Blessed Mary standing upright or kneeling, unless illness prevents it. At the matins of the day and at the Hours, while the psalms are said, the lessons read, and the responsories sung, the brothers shall sit; but at the *Glory be to the Father*, out of reverence for the Trinity, they shall rise [Col. 1144D] and bow their heads toward the altar. Brothers who are not ordained and are not in church shall say twelve *Our Fathers* for the matins of the Blessed Mary, and the same for the matins of the day; for each of the other Hours of the Blessed Mary, seven *Our Fathers*, and the same for those of the day; for vespers, nine; and for the dead, likewise nine. All counted together, there are 133 *Our Fathers*.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On brothers who are unwell.

If a brother who is unwell, after being reproved and admonished twice or three times by other brothers, refuses, at the devil’s prompting, to amend himself, let him be sent to us on foot with a letter containing his offence. Nevertheless, he shall be given limited provisions so that he may come to us, and we shall correct him.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—On brothers living with private property.

[Col. 1145A]

If any brother at his death possesses private property and, while alive, has not disclosed it to his master or priest for the benefit of the house, no divine office shall be performed for him. Rather, as though excommunicated, he shall be buried with that property outside the cemetery. If, while alive and well, he possesses private property, and it is discovered, and he has concealed it from his master but is afterwards found to have it, that money shall be tied around his neck and he shall be led through the hospital of the Holy Spirit, or through the other houses where he has stayed.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—On proprietors.

Every year at the chapter of Pentecost, possessors of private property shall be excommunicated; and, after receiving absolution, they shall restore [Col. 1145B] the money and do penance for seven days, fasting on Wednesday and Friday on bread and water. If they are found a second time, their penalty shall be doubled. If, a third time—God forbid!—they incur the same offence, they shall do penance for forty days, separated from all fellowship with the brothers.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On the office to be performed for deceased brothers and sisters.

Since this is very necessary, we firmly prescribe and command that for all brothers and sisters entering upon the way of all flesh, in every obedience in which they die in a house of the Holy Spirit, Masses for the soul of that brother or sister shall be celebrated for thirty days. The priests [Col. 1145C] who are in the house of the Holy Spirit shall render five Masses for that brother or sister. The remaining clerics shall say two psalters; lay brothers who know seven psalms shall say them seven times; if they do not know them, they shall say 200 *Our Fathers*.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On judgment in chapter.

Concerning all complaints, judgment shall be made in chapter and discernment exercised according to the love of God and right judgment. We command all these things, as we said above, on behalf of Almighty God, blessed Mary ever-virgin, the Holy Spirit, and our lords the sick, that they be observed in every respect with the utmost diligence.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—On clothing the poor.

[Col. 1145D] In winter, from the feast of All Saints until the Lord’s Nativity, poor persons shall be clothed in woollen garments; and in summer, from Pentecost until the feast of St John, at least forty shall be clothed from the old garments of the brothers and also of the sick. The master, with the counsel of two brothers, shall always bestow this alms upon those in need, according to the charity of God and not from particular favour or affection.

## CHAPTER XL.—On seeking out the poor.

On one day of every week, sick poor people shall be sought through the lanes and streets, brought to the house of the Holy Spirit, and cared for with the greatest diligence.

## CHAPTER XLI.—On nourishing orphans and pregnant women.

[Col. 1146A]

Abandoned orphan children shall be nourished as far as the resources of the house permit; and poor pregnant women shall be gladly received and ministered to charitably.

## CHAPTER XLII.—On service to the poor.

On Tuesday the sisters shall wash the heads of the sick in the hospital; on Thursday, their feet. They shall also wash their linen whenever they are instructed to do so.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On receiving the poor.

Common poor persons who wish to lodge in the House of the Holy Spirit shall willingly be received, according to the means of the house, and treated charitably.

CAP. XLIV.—On receiving religious persons.

If any religious person comes to lodge in the same [Col. 1146B] house, or in our houses, he shall be received kindly as a servant of God, and charitable provision shall be made for him.

CAP. XLV.—On the lodging of great persons.

If, however, the person is of high rank, special lodging shall be prepared for him, and he shall be served reverently according to the means of the house.

CAP. XLVI.—On receiving sinful women.

Sinful women who wish, for the preservation of chastity, to reside in the House of the Holy Spirit during Holy Week until after the octave of Easter shall be admitted without objection.

CAP. XLVII.—On carrying letters.

No one shall carry letters unless he has first heard them read; and if, when the letters have been read, he learns that they contain anything [Col. 1146C] from which some harm might arise, no one shall carry them; for Uriah carried the letters of his own death (II Kings 11).

CAP. XLVIII.—On deposits.

No one shall receive a deposit without the knowledge of the master and some of the brethren, except the hospitaler, who may keep only the deposits of pilgrims and outsiders.

CAP. XLIX.—That no one may build a church.

No one shall cause a church or house to be built without the command of the master and chapter. If anyone acts contrary to this, he shall do penance for forty days and shall fast on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. L.—On avoiding insults.

[Col. 1146D] No one shall dare call any brother a traitor, a renegade, foul-mouthed, a liar, or the son of a prostitute. Whoever falls into these faults shall not go unpunished, but shall be severely punished for seven days, and shall fast on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. LI.—On supporting lepers.

We ordain that if any of our brethren or sisters falls into the disease of leprosy, provision shall be made for him or her in the House of the Holy Spirit, as for one of the other brethren, in some part of the house.

CAP. LII.—On receiving gifts.

If any of our members conceals something bestowed upon him, he shall be punished and judged to be a proprietor. And if a brother or sister receives *eulogiae*—blessed gifts—or a small present [Col. 1147A] from his or her parents or friends, he or she shall not dare retain them without the permission and consent of the preceptor. If anyone acts otherwise, that person shall lose the *eulogiae* and do penance for four days, fasting on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. LIII.—That no one may sell or buy clothes.

We firmly and strictly command that no one presume to sell or buy clothes without the consent of the master, or of whoever holds his place: so that, just as you are fed from one cellar, so you may be clothed from one wardrobe. The garment shall be humble, as is written, and purchased by the master or chamberlain. If it is otherwise done, the master shall take it, and the offender shall undergo a penalty of seven days, fasting on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. LIV.—If any brother falls into heresy.

[Col. 1147B]

If any brother, which God forbid, falls into heresy, or knowingly has participation and familiarity with heretics, and this comes to the knowledge of the master or brethren, it shall be reported to the lord pope or to his visitor. But if anyone lays so grave an accusation against a brother and is unable to prove it, he shall suffer the penalty that the other would have suffered. If, however, anyone is suspected because of familiarity with heretics, he shall be warned before the chapter and commanded on behalf of the chapter to avoid their association. If, after the chapter’s command, he refuses to avoid it, he shall do penance in prison, separated from the others.

CAP. LV.—How brethren are to correct brethren.

[Col. 1147C]

If there are two, three, or more brethren, and one of them behaves wickedly and badly in his manner of life, another brother must not defame him either to the people or to the preceptor. Rather, he shall first correct him privately; and if he refuses correction, he shall bring two or three others with him to correct him. If he reforms, the brother ought to rejoice at this. If he refuses to reform, then he shall secretly write his fault to his master; and whatever the master directs concerning him shall be done.

CAP. LVI.—How a brother ought to accuse a brother.

A brother ought not accuse another brother [Col. 1147D] unless he can prove the matter well. If he alleges crimes against him and fails in proof, he shall bear the same penalty that he himself would have suffered.

CAP. LVII.—How the brethren ought to wear the banner of the cross.

Brethren of all obediences, who now or hereafter offer themselves to God and to the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, shall wear the sign of the cross on their capes and mantles: on capes, before the breast; on mantles, on the left side. Through that banner, and through works and obedience, may God preserve us and defend us from the power of the devil in this world and in the world to come, in soul and body; and likewise all our benefactors.

CAP. LVIII.—On the rites for deceased brethren and pilgrims.

[Col. 1148A]

We also command that all bodies of the dead, and of other Christians who die after the hour of all Vespers, shall have burial deferred until the next day. In the hospital where they died, they shall not lie without a light in their biers; it is prescribed that they be carried to the church before Prime.

CAP. LIX.—On children’s cradles.

For the use of children of foreign women who are born in the houses of the Holy Spirit, small cradles shall be made, so that they may lie separately and alone, lest any harm should befall the children.

CAP. LX.—That the master shall have no private property.

The master likewise shall have no private property. If, at his death, he is found to possess anything without the knowledge of the clerical brother of the hospital, to whom the cardinal has entrusted his authority, and of the chamberlain and two other brethren, no office, as prescribed, shall be performed by the brethren for him; rather, like an excommunicate, he shall be buried outside the cemetery.

CAP. LXI.—On discretion concerning old men and boys.

Old men and boys shall remain under the discretion of the preceptor.

CAP. LXII.—On the governors of daughter houses.

All governors of the daughter houses founded by the House of the Holy Spirit of Rome shall receive their office or habit in that house from the master and chapter. Nor shall they presume to receive any man or woman without the command of the master [Col. 1148C]; if they do so, they shall lose the habit, be judged excommunicate, and be held guilty of perjury, etc.

CAP. LXIII.—That no married person shall be received.

If any man or woman is lawfully joined in marriage, he or she shall in no way be received into the order to take the habit; for it is written: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19).

CAP. LXIV.—On the election of the master.

After a master has been elected, if he should be found culpable, he shall be admonished by the brethren up to three times. If, which God forbid, he does not turn from wickedness and change his way, he shall be reported to the lord pope, not to the cardinal visitor whom the lord pope has appointed; and he shall be corrected by the due penalty and also deposed [Col. 1148D], if that is just and his fault requires it; and another worthy person shall be substituted in his place.

CAP. LXV.—On the chamberlains of the house.

The house shall never be without a chamberlain, who shall have full authority to administer and provide for the necessities of the brethren, sisters, and poor. Yet, with the counsel of the master and chapter, he shall render an account on every Kalends. If he fails to do so then, he shall not postpone doing so beyond eight days. If he does not do so, provided that the master and brethren have required it of him, he shall fast on bread and water on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday until he has done it; and, if he persists in obstinacy, he shall otherwise be punished according to the judgment of the master and brethren. If any members of the chapter refuse to hear the account [Col. 1149A], the master shall hear it with those remaining. If it is delayed through the master’s negligence or malice, the master himself shall be subject to the same penalty, namely, he shall fast on bread and water on Friday. Clerical brethren may, if they wish, be present, so that, if they see something poorly done, they may admonish their brethren concerning it. If these neglect to amend themselves, they shall appeal to the lord pope or to the cardinal appointed for them.

CAP. LXVI.—On the revenue and expenses of the house.

We also will that all income and revenues of the house be placed in one chest, which shall have three keys: one held by the master, another by the chapter, and another by the chamberlain. The revenues received shall first come to the knowledge of the master, chapter, and chamberlain, and then [Col. 1149B] be placed in the chest. The chamberlain shall take from this chest the expenses of the house which he must incur; and the seal of the chapter shall be kept in the same chest.

CAP. LXVIII.—On the infirmary of the brethren.

We will that there be one house for sick brethren and one brother as infirmarian, who shall exercise care, concern, and diligence toward them. He shall also have as many servants as are necessary and suitable for him; and at the Ascension of the Lord he shall receive from the chamberlain twenty pounds of revenues. If more is necessary for those expenses, it shall be given to him by the chamberlain without anyone’s objection, until the following year; and whatever he requests for the sick shall be supplied from the cellar. The infirmarian shall render an account three times [Col. 1149C] a year.

CAP. LXVIII.—On the contumacy of daughter houses.

If any House of the Holy Spirit rises in rebellion against the command of the Rule, it shall be severely punished by the master with the counsel of the chapter. If it refuses obedience, it shall be reported to the Roman Church, and, by its command, the help of secular power shall also be sought.

CAP. LXIX.—On the oaths of the brethren.

We ordain that no brother whatsoever shall swear an oath except for necessary business of the house. Then a layman shall take the oath with the consent of the preceptor; but a cleric, by command of the cardinal appointed as their protector, or of the person to whom that cardinal has entrusted [Col. 1149D] his authority, and also with the knowledge of the preceptor.

CAP. LXX.—How brethren are to be received.

When anyone seeks fellowship in the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, the preceptor shall take counsel with the brethren whether they wish to receive him. If they receive him, he shall come before all the brethren in chapter, and the preceptor shall ask him whether he desires fellowship in the house, whether he can endure religious life, whether he will keep chastity, maintain obedience, and live without private property. He shall consider these matters in his heart before making profession. For previously, when he was under his own authority, he did what he wished; but when he is in religion, he will be under the power of another. If he says, “With God’s help I shall endure religious life [Col. 1150A], voluntarily fulfill the commands of the house, and, as long as I live, be a servant to the lords who are sick,” the preceptor shall again ask him whether he has a wife, has sworn an oath, has made a promise to any religious order, or has a debt. If he denies all these things, he may be received. But if he says that he has a wife, has sworn an oath, belonged to another religious order, made a promise, or incurred a debt, he shall not be received unless he has letters from his bishop or monastery and has paid the debt.

CAP. LXXI.—On receiving someone for probation.

No one shall be granted entrance into our order unless he has been tested for the space of one year. Then the Rule and constitutions shall be read to him in order, and he shall be told: “Behold [Col. 1150B] the law under which you wish to serve.” If he promises to observe the Rule and constitutions of the house, and everything commanded him, and humbly requests the habit, the habit shall be granted him. He shall always serve in the house in his own office, by the will of the preceptor or of the person acting in his place. If he refuses to do this, he shall be dismissed as proud and disobedient. For one cannot seem to have made himself a servant of the poor who disdains to do for the poor what he did in the world to acquire his own necessities.

CAP. LXXII.—That none of us may enter another order.

No one shall dare lightly to change our order, unless he goes to a stricter way of life, and he shall do this with letters from his chapter. Whoever acts otherwise shall know himself to be under sentence of excommunication.

CAP. LXXIII.—That no one may refuse prescribed penalties.

If any brother, lifted up in pride, refuses to observe an appointed penalty, the penalty shall be doubled for him. If he does not complete it, he shall be admonished before the chapter. If he does not comply with the chapter’s command, his cross shall be taken away and shall not be restored without the chapter’s consent. If, after his cross has been taken away, he is unwilling to observe the obediences imposed upon him, he shall, according to the form of the privilege, be punished as a disturber of the house; and fourteen days shall be added to his penalty, during which he shall fast on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. LXXIV.—On obedience.

In virtue of obedience, we command our brethren and sisters not only to render good obedience [Col. 1150D] to the master, but we command that, in good things, the brethren obey one another, knowing that by this obedience they shall go to Christ.

CAP. LXXV.—The form of the oath which the master shall take.

I, N., master of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, swear and promise that I shall administer the affairs of that hospital in good faith, for the honour of God and the benefit of that house; for the support of the poor and sick, for whom, with God’s help, I myself shall have care and diligence, and shall cause it to be exercised by others. I shall not divert the alms and revenues of the same hospital to uses other than those for which they are principally assigned, namely, the support of poor and sick guests and of the household. Of these I shall fraudulently transfer or send nothing [Col. 1151A] to another house or to any other person. I shall in no way dissipate, nor alienate under any title, the possessions and documents of that hospital without consulting the Roman pontiff, to whom I shall be wholly obedient and faithful. So help me God and these holy Gospels.

CAP. LXXVI.—On retaining or marrying off girls.

To all abandoned girls of the House of the Holy Spirit who desire to remain in service to the poor, to live in obedience, chastity, and without private property, and who promise chiefly to devote themselves to care for the poor, the house’s bread and water shall be granted. The others, however, shall be joined in marriage.

CAP. LXXVII.—On intercession for brethren.

[Col. 1151B]

We will that, if any brother has incurred the penalties contained in these same institutions and has paid them, and if it happens that some great person is present there or religious persons arrive who make petitions to the master and chapter that they may deign to pardon that suffering brother through the intervention of their prayers, the master and chapter ought willingly and generously to hear them.

CAP. LXXVIII.—That all shall sleep in the common dormitory.

We will that no brother, sister, or oblate shall have a private room for sleeping, but that all sleep in the common dormitory. In it the chamberlain shall have a chest beside the bed [Col. 1151C], containing the expenses of the house; for we believe that the house’s treasure, placed in the common dormitory, is kept more safely by all than when entrusted to individual custody in a private room.

CAP. LXXIX.—That those who have the habit shall preside.

We will that if a brother of the house who holds a *baliva* is stationed with an oblate, that brother shall preside over the oblate who does not have the habit.

CAP. LXXX.—That women shall not wash brethren’s heads.

Women shall not wash the brethren’s heads or feet, make their beds, or remove their shoes. Likewise, brethren shall not do these things for women; but men shall serve men and women women, except in case of illness and then with the master’s permission and command.

CAP. LXXXI.—On a brother striking a servant.

If a brother strikes a servant of the house, or if the preceptor sees it or hears an outcry about it, he shall do penance for a week. If he draws blood, except from the nose, he shall do penance for forty days. If the servant dies from that blow, the brother shall lose the habit, go to the lord pope, and receive penance from him. Afterwards, if he brings letters of the lord pope with him and seeks mercy, he shall be readmitted, without prejudice to the justice of the house, after doing penance for forty days.

CAP. LXXXII.—On a servant quarrelling against a brother.

If a servant quarrels against a brother and that brother makes an outcry to the preceptor, the servant shall make satisfaction through the palace court [Col. 1152A]. But if he calls the brother a thief, fornicator, or evildoer, and cannot prove this through the brethren, he shall be beaten through the palace and cloister, led while being beaten as far as the gate, expelled from the house, and paid the wages of his service.

CAP. LXXXIII.—On servants who commit theft.

If servants steal or sell any property of the hospital, or a whole loaf of bread, and this can certainly be proved, the things they stole shall be tied around their necks; they shall be beaten through the palace as far as the gate; carrying the bread in their hands, they shall be expelled from the house; and afterwards the agreed payment for which they served shall be rendered to them.

CAP. LXXXIV.—On sending a brother to another house.

[Col. 1152B]

We ordain that if a brother of the House of the Holy Spirit of the City is sent to reside in any daughter house, he shall be honourably received there and shall rank first after the person who presides in that house, unless he is sent to that church because of an offence or fault.

CAP. LXXXV.—On servants quarrelling.

If servants quarrel among themselves and an outcry comes to the preceptor and brethren, the guilty persons who committed the offences shall be severely beaten with straps or rods before everyone throughout the hospital. But if they offend one another with insulting words or bloody blows [Col. 1152C], or strike one another with swords, stones, or knives, those found guilty through witnesses shall receive this penalty: they shall be led naked through the cloister and hospital to the gate and most harshly whipped with straps; they shall be expelled from the house, and their wages withheld.

CAP. LXXXVI.—On receiving brethren.

We will that the habit be given to no one, and that no one be received there as an oblate or on probation, except in the general chapter—unless necessity requires otherwise, namely that someone be received there apart from the general chapter; and then this shall be done with the approval of the lord cardinal.

CAP. LXXXVII.—On collecting alms.

For collecting alms, faithful and respectable persons [Col. 1152D] shall be sent, who live soberly and preserve themselves chastely and honourably, lest the religious order thereby be demeaned and people’s devotion diminished.

CAP. LXXXVIII.—That no outsider may be retained in the house.

We ordain that food shall not be furnished to anyone in the house or outside it for more than eight days, without the will and consent of the preceptor and chapter. At Matins, moreover, all shall rise when the other religious persons of the City have risen.

CAP. LXXXIX.—On the visitor of the house.

Since this House of the Holy Spirit is endowed from the goods of the Roman Church, we decree that a cardinal shall always be sought from the lord pope to be visitor and protector of that house.

CAP. XC.—On those who become proud because of their good works.

[Col. 1153A]

If anyone, perhaps elated because of the good which God has done through him in the House of the Holy Spirit, refuses to observe the common life of the brethren and leads a separate life, as though he had performed sufficiently well and, because his merits demand it, it befitted him to have special precedence in table, refectory, dormitory, and every other matter, he shall be severely punished, with seven days added in which he shall sit on the ground, without a napkin, on bread and water. For we believe such a person to be hypocritical and ostentatious, and to have done the good he did not for the salvation of his soul but for a kind of empty glory, or as one serving only for a time and contemplating rest in due time, following the manner of him of whom the Gospel says: “My soul, you have many [Col. 1153B] goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, and drink” (Luke 12).

CAP. XCI.—On those who go elsewhere than where the preceptor sends them.

This vice must especially be cut out by the roots from our order: no one shall presume to go from place to place without the master’s command. If anyone does so, he shall be punished according to the master’s judgment. Nor shall anyone presume to report outside whatever he has seen or heard in chapter, because this brings very great destruction. Whoever presumes to do so shall do penance for seven days and fast on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. XCII.—That no one say anything dishonourable about the house.

[Col. 1153C] No one shall presume to disclose to anyone outside the house anything dishonourable about the house or a brother, except to the lord pope, his brethren, or the visitor. If anything against him is discovered, he shall lose the habit; but if he does it further, he shall be severely punished with the master’s counsel.

CAP. XCIII.—On electing the master’s vicar.

If the master of our order needs to go anywhere, he shall himself summon the assembly and state where he is going. One of the brethren shall be chosen by the master and chapter to govern the house until his return. The person chosen shall not be excessively gluttonous, proud, turbulent, abusive, sluggish, or wasteful; rather, fearing God, he shall guard his soul and remember the apostolic saying: “He who administers well acquires a good rank for himself” [Col. 1153D] (I Tim. 3). He shall care with every diligence for the sick, infants, guests, and poor, knowing without doubt that he will render account for all these on the Day of Judgment. If any of these persons, puffed up by some pride, is found blameworthy, after correction once, twice, and a third time, if he refuses to reform, he shall be deposed and another worthy person shall succeed in his place.

CAP. XCIV.—That no one abandon the habit.

If anyone abandons the habit of his own will without the chapter’s counsel, he shall not be received back without a fixed penalty and discipline: namely, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Or if he breaks a fast before its time, withdraws from the common table without the preceptor’s permission [Col. 1154A], or drinks to drunkenness, he shall do penance for seven days and be on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays. Afterwards he shall be rebuked by the preceptor; and if he chooses to persist in drunkenness and refuses amendment, he shall be sent to a house where wine is not abundant, so that he may not become drunk.

CAP. XCV.—On the *balivae* of the house.

We will that all *balivae* of the house be distributed by the will of the preceptor, and established or removed by the whole chapter. If any brother or sister tries to act contrary to its counsel, or rises from table in indignation, he or she shall do penance for fourteen days.

CAP. XCVI.—On threats and dispensations.

No brother shall cause threats to be made against another, nor procure petitions to be offered for himself in order that he may obtain or retain a *baliva*, or that any indulgence be granted him contrary to the regular institutions. Whoever acts against these provisions shall be expelled from all fellowship of the brethren.

CAP. XCVII.—That sisters are subject to the same Rule.

Whatever is established in the Rule is to be understood as applying to brethren and sisters, so that they may be subject to the same Rule. For it would seem quite unworthy if the reception or correction of brethren and sisters in the House of the Holy Spirit were conducted in two ways. Therefore it has been ordained that, as we live under one Rule, so we ought to be subject to the same judgments of the Rule.

CAP. XCVIII.—On those who, without the preceptor’s command, associate with an excommunicate or disobedient person.

If any brother or sister presumes, without the command of the preceptor [Col. 1154C] or of the person acting in his place, to associate with excommunicated or disobedient brethren or sisters, speak with such a person, or send them a message, he or she shall suffer a similar penalty or punishment of excommunication.

CAP. XCIX.—On a disobedient brother.

If the preceptor commands a brother to undertake some house of the Holy Spirit or some business of the house, and he refuses, he shall be subject to a seven-day penalty. If he refuses a second time, he shall likewise be subject to it. But if the preceptor commands him under obedience and that brother refuses to obey, he shall lose the habit and whatever *baliva* he holds. If he commands him under obedience a fourth time, he shall be deprived and put in prison, eating bread and water. If, however [Col. 1154D], he asks mercy, his habit shall be restored and he shall be sent to another house.

CAP. C.—On a brother lying in a town.

If a brother presumes to lie in a town because of bodily levity, fear of the master, or in any other way, when a house is nearby and he refuses to lie in it, he shall lose the habit. If he leaves the house and later returns and asks mercy, he shall be received; and he shall remain in a foreign place for as long as he was outside. When that period has ended, the master and brethren shall restore the habit to him; and, if they judge it expedient, he shall do penance for forty days and fast on bread and water on Wednesdays and Fridays.

CAP. CI.—On a deceitful brother.

[Col. 1155A]

If a brother entrusts money, a bag, or his saddlebags in a town, and the master inquires concerning money or other goods, and he says that he entrusted his clothes in the town, he shall do penance for forty days. But if he denies that he entrusted his money and saddlebags in the town, and the saddlebags are afterward found, he shall be condemned as guilty of theft, subject nevertheless to the master’s disposition.

CAP. CII.—On a fleeing brother.

If a brother receives money in the house or hospital, or anything else, flees to secular life, and squanders that money by living luxuriously or otherwise, and later comes to amendment, he shall be placed under the judgment of the master and brethren as to whether he is to be received. [Col. 1155B] If they receive him, they must restore his habit and he shall do penance for forty days.

CAP. CIII.—On a proud and irreligious brother.

If a brother lends property of the hospital or house to counts, barons, or any secular persons, stands surety, or pledges hospital property for any secular person, he shall lose the habit and be expelled from the house. If the brother has only recently been received, he shall be put under oath by the master upon the habit as to whether he heard this command from the brethren. If he says that he did not hear it, he shall do penance for forty days.

CAP. CIV.—On brethren quarrelling after Compline.

If brethren quarrel after Compline or exchange idle words with one another in the dormitory, they must first be rebuked. If on the second occasion they refuse to cease, they shall be punished by a seven-day penalty. If on the third occasion they dispute with wicked speech, namely by supporting kings and princes, they shall be punished for forty days. Such jealousies commonly generate destruction; therefore, as a ruin of the house, they must be avoided by the brethren. Hence the Apostle: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. 15).

CAP. CV.—On the chapter at Pentecost.

When the brethren come to chapter, the house in which it is to be held shall be cleaned. The brethren shall assemble there, and the prior of the church, with a procession of clerics, the deacon vested and the subdeacon, shall come to the chapter and begin: “Come, Creator Spirit.” Kneeling three times with the brethren, and at the third repetition of the verse “Come [Col. 1155D] Creator,” the entire hymn shall be sung. When it is finished, the deacon shall read the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes [Col. 1156A] in the seat of his majesty.” After the Gospel has been read, the procession shall return to the church while the brethren remain in chapter. Then the prior, another brother, or someone else shall give an address. After the address, the master shall set before the brethren the institutions and Rule of the Holy Spirit. He shall then require the alms for living and dead persons that they have brought with them; next, he shall command the brethren that each render up his *baliva*. When this has been done, he shall demand their private property from the brethren. Afterwards he shall inquire from the brethren concerning the condition of the houses and *balivae*: whether they have animals, debts, or provisions, and whether all is prosperous. Thus he will be able to know who has treated the house, office, or *baliva* entrusted to him more poorly or more well. If the master wishes to make a complaint against any brother [Col. 1156B], or any brother against a brother, the brethren shall hear the complaint and likewise the response. After hearing the complaints, the brethren shall render a just judgment according to the complaint; and the accused person who has been proved guilty through witnesses shall satisfy the justice of the house according to the tenor of the Rule. After these matters have been spoken, the master, with certain brethren, shall choose a hospitaler, a prior in the church, a chamberlain in the house, and a treasurer, either from those previously holding office or from others able faithfully to fulfill the commands and business of the house. Once these have been chosen, they shall return to the chapter; the master and chapter shall speak, and the master shall assign them *balivae*, giving the kiss of peace. Likewise, discreet preceptors shall be appointed in the other houses. Again, if the master asks the brethren’s counsel concerning some deed or business of the house [Col. 1156C], the brethren shall give counsel as well as they can; but all decisions (*esgardi*) and elections shall be committed to the master’s judgment and discretion.

When the chapter has ended, the prior of the church shall say prayers with collects for peace, for the lord pope, for kings, for the brethren, for our benefactors, etc. When the prayers have been said, the brethren, kissing the master and giving one another the kiss of peace, shall quickly return to their *balivae*. They shall guard well the animals and goods of the house, both within and without; they shall have the vineyards dug, the lands cultivated and sown, for he who fails in sowing will not rejoice in harvest. If they labour diligently, they shall have sufficient necessities. May the Lord himself grant this to all [Col. 1156D] brethren and sisters, he who lives and reigns through all things, etc.

B. Cyril, general preceptor, to the brethren of the same order.

[Col. 1155D]

Most beloved brethren, you have seen the Rule of life handed down to us by the Fathers of old. None of us professed it by entreaty, secretly, or under compulsion. For of our own accord we offered ourselves and gave ourselves over to the Holy Spirit of God, to the blessed Virgin, and to the lords who are sick, that we might be their servants forever. By a free act, with no one compelling us, we have promised chastity, poverty, obedience, and humble patience under oath and by solemn vow. We were bound to observe these not only by the Rule itself and the institutions of the ancient Fathers, but also by observance of God’s commandments and the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, even before making our profession; and now we are bound still more and more. For our God himself did and taught all these things, so that we might be instructed by his action.

[Col. 1157A] The chastity which we have promised, with God’s help, to preserve, the Son of God himself commanded and taught us to preserve. He chose for himself a chaste and virgin mother; he himself remained a virgin and wished to be called the Bridegroom of virgins. He was pleased to be baptized only by a virgin and to entrust his mother only to a virgin. The Lamb was seen upon Mount Zion, and the voice of harpists was heard before the throne of God; nor could any sing the song except those redeemed from the earth, those who had not been defiled with women, who followed the Lamb wherever he went (Rev. 14). These and similar things are set forth by the Lord for those who preserve chastity.

Our Lord himself also embraced poverty. For when he is born, he is laid in a manger; while he lives, he has nowhere [Col. 1157B] to lay his head; when he dies, he is nailed naked to the cross. He has nothing from which to pay the tax; weary from the journey, he asks a woman to give him water. He took poor persons as his companions; to the poor he promises blessedness. Therefore, brethren, let us pursue poverty with a willing heart, for the poor man has been left to the Lord, and he will be a helper to us who are orphaned.

By preserving humility, the Lord himself also showed us that it must be preserved. He is born at Nazareth, a humble village of Galilee, from a humble mother, whose humility the Lord had regarded. He loved the humble, associated with the humble, and taught humility. “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble” (Matt. 11). To display this in deeds, when going to Jerusalem he mounted not [Col. 1157C] a horse but an ass; he washed the disciples’ feet, and, in an act of humility, died with bowed head. Let us therefore imitate his teachings, because he receives the prayer of the humble (Ps. 101), looks upon the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar (Ps. 137); and the supplication of the humble has always pleased him, so that he may hear us in the time of tribulation.

He taught patience and gentleness when he patiently endured injuries from the Jews in word and deed. At one time they called him a Samaritan, at another one possessed by a demon; now they said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, now that he was a blasphemer, now that he ate with sinners, and they assailed him with other verbal insults. Moreover, in their deeds they drove him out of the city and took up stones to throw at him; when seized and bound, they called him a seducer; the rulers mocked him; one of the attendants struck him on the face; at one time they displayed him clothed in white, at another in purple; they scourged him; they preferred the robber Barabbas to him; finally, they condemned him to a most shameful death. Yet for this reason he did not depart from patience and gentleness: he called his betrayer friend, prayed for his persecutors, and, when reviled, did not revile in return; when suffering, he did not threaten (1 Pet. II). Therefore, imitating the example of our Lord himself, let us not repay evil among ourselves for evil, nor cursing for cursing, but overcome evil with good. And, when injured, let us have recourse to the Lord, who performs mercy [Col. 1158A] and judgment for all who suffer injustice (Ps. CXLV); and let us forgive our brethren, so that the Lord may forgive us.

Moreover, the Lord himself commands that obedience be rendered to superiors, as he rendered it to his Father and to his parents: “He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them” (Luke II). He said that his food was to do the will of him who had sent him (John IV), and that he sought not his own will but the Father’s (Matt. XII); and, humbling himself, he became obedient (Phil. II): “Not my will,” he says, “but yours be done” (Luke XXII). We ought consequently to learn that, after we have offered ourselves to God by a solemn vow, willing and unwilling no longer remain with us, but with those who preside over us. And let us beware lest through disobedience we fall under that sentence: “Because I called and you refused, I stretched out my hand and there was none who looked; I also will laugh at your destruction, and will mock when that which you feared comes upon you” (Prov. I). [Col. 1158B]

Poverty, patience, obedience, gentleness, and things like these are the fruits of our warfare, which the servants of Christ attained. “We hunger and thirst,” Paul said, “and are naked, and are beaten with fists, and are unsettled, and we labor, working with our hands; we are cursed and bless, we suffer persecution and endure it; we are blasphemed and entreat; we have become as the refuse of the world” (1 Cor. IV). Therefore we must run with patience toward [Col. 1158C] the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame.

Therefore, brethren, as we know, without anyone compelling us, we promised all these things to God by solemn vow and put our hand to the plough. If any one of us should wish to look back, he will not be fit for the kingdom of God. We must by no means suppose that, because we have vowed chastity and obedience and undertaken other regular vows, we can attain the blessed life, unless they are joined to the virtues of God’s commandments. The end indeed of these commandments is charity, the chief foundation of our order and religious life. Therefore let all our works be done in it; let us be strengthened in it and grow in it. It is an excellent mother: it cherishes the weak, trains the advanced, reproves [Col. 1158D] the restless, kindly supplies different things to different persons, and loves all as children. For when it reproves, it is gentle; when it caresses, it is guileless. It is piously severe, soothes without pain, is patiently angry, humbly indignant, bears adversity, moderates prosperity, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. If we embrace it, brethren, it will nourish concord among us and preserve unity; and, gathered together in the Holy Spirit, the God of peace and consolation will be with us—may he be blessed for ever. Amen.

There now follows the Rule of our holy father Augustine, which they likewise profess, namely:

“Before all things, dearest brethren, let God be loved,” etc.

# ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## POPE INNOCENT III

### SUPPLEMENT TO THE REGESTA. YEAR 1198

I. — To the provost, dean, and canons of the Cathedral Church of Strasbourg. — He confirms to them the prebend resigned by F., provost of St Thomas. 9

II. — To Matthew, abbot of St Nicholas of the Meadows of Ribemont, diocese of Laon. — They are received under the protection of St Peter, and the properties belonging to them are enumerated. 10

III. — To the … bishop of Soissons and the abbot of St German of the Meadows, Paris. — That they may protect and defend the abbot and convent of St Denis against the bishop of Auxerre and others, both ecclesiastical and lay. 15

[Col. 1190]

IV. — To Florentinus, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of the Field of Blessed Mary. — He confirms their possessions and privileges. 16

V. — To the abbot and brethren of Cluny. — Confirmation concerning the court of Mercurius. 19

VI. — To the master and brethren of the House of God at Provins. — He confirms to them possession of a prebend in the church of St Quiriacus. 20

VII. — To Ranulf, abbot of the monastery of Aurillac, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life, in perpetuity. — He confirms their goods and possessions. 20

VIII. — To Robert, abbot of St German at Paris, and his brethren. — He receives them under protection and confirms to them their goods and possessions. 26

IX. — To the abbot of Prémontré; H., archdeacon, [Col. 1191] and Master R., canon of Laon. — He entrusts to them for judgment the case pending between the abbot and monks of St Nicholas of Ribemont and W., deacon, concerning the church of Villers-le-Sec. 31

X. — To the abbot and convent of the monastery at Gengenbach, diocese of Strasbourg. — Confirmation of privileges. 36

XI. — To the king of the Danes. — That he may arm himself against the tyranny of Swabia. 36

XII. — To Peter, bishop of Arousa. — He confirms the first six prebends of the church of Arousa. 37

XIII. — To the abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, diocese of Modena. — He grants him authority to absolve certain excommunicated persons. 38

### YEAR 1199

XIV. — To the patriarch of Jerusalem. — That the prior and canons of the Holy Sepulchre may have free authority to arrange the houses and priories of their obediences. 39

XV. — To Abbot E., the provost, and Canon C. of St Emmeram at Regensburg. — That they may protect the parish priest’s rights at Riekofen against the monastery of Wolderbach. 39

XVI. — To Gerbodon, abbot, and the convent of St Wulmar, diocese of Boulogne. — He confirms the judgment issued in their favour by the bishop of Thérouanne and the co-judges in the case between them and the abbot of Cluny concerning liberty to elect abbots. 40

XVII. — To Gerbodon, abbot of St Wulmar, and his brethren, present and future. — He receives them under the protection of St Peter, and the properties belonging to them are enumerated. 41

XVIII. — To John, abbot of St Bertin, and his brethren, present and future, in perpetuity. — Concerning confirmation of privileges. 46

XIX. — To Elias, abbot, and the brethren of St Mary of Régnier. — Confirmation of privileges. 47

XX. — To the abbot and convent of St German of the Meadows. — He confirms to them the possessions which the noblewoman Philippa had granted to their monastery. 51

XXI. — To the abbot and convent of the monastery of Hautmont. — He confirms to them possession of the chapel of Grantreing. 52

XXII. — To John, abbot of St Geneviève at Paris. — He grants him the use of the mitre. 52

XXIII. — To the dean and chapter of St Mary and St Theobald at Metz. — They are received under the protection of St Peter; the church of Holy Cross and the chapel of St Ferrucius are specifically confirmed to them. 53

XXIV. — He confirms one prebend in the church of St Stephen at Meaux to the lepers of St Lazarus at Meaux. 53

XXV. — To all Christ’s faithful established in Saxony and Westphalia. — That they may arm themselves manfully for the Christian faith. 54

XXVI. — To Odo, bishop of Paris, and his successors. — Concerning confirmation of goods and privileges. 55

XXVII. — To the abbot and convent of St Maximin at Micy. — Possession of the church of St Mary of Bourg is confirmed to them. 57

### YEAR 1200

XXVIII. — To the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem. — They are not to presume henceforth to celebrate in lands placed under an ecclesiastical interdict. 57

XXIX. — To N. — That he may cause the sentence of interdict pronounced against Philip, king of France, to be observed inviolably. 58

XXX. — To the chapter of Langres. — Concerning provisional maintenance for the bishop of Langres upon his resignation of the bishopric. 58

XXXI. — To R., abbot, and the convent of St Michael. — He confirms certain possessions to them. 58

XXXII. — To Thiemo, bishop of Bamberg. — Concerning the canonization of St Cunegund. 59

XXXIII. — To the parish priests and all the clergy of the diocese of Castello. — That the name of John, patriarch of Grado, together with that of the doge of Venice, may be pronounced in the blessing of the candle, according to the ancient custom and the dignity of the patriarch of Grado. 60

XXXIII *bis*. — To the abbot and convent of Dervent. — Confirmation of churches and rights in the diocese of Troyes. 61

XXXIII *ter*. — To the same persons. — Privilege concerning Gigny and the churches in the diocese of Châlons. 61

XXXIV. — To all archbishops, bishops, and abbots. — That they may protect and defend the privileges granted to the abbot and convent of Fountains. 62

XXXV. — To the people of St Denis. — That, while the land of Philip [Col. 1192], king of the Franks, lies under interdict, they may celebrate divine offices “with suppressed voice and closed doors.” 63

XXXVI. — To the convent of St German of the Meadows. — He permits them, during the interdict, to have two or three of their number read the canonical hours together. 64

XXXVII. — To archbishops and bishops established throughout the kingdom of England. — He grants various privileges. 64

XXXVIII. — To the noblewoman Gela. — He confirms the foundation of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Sparmalia at Honkeuliet. 65

XXXIX. — To the dean and chapter of Rheims. — That the canons of Rheims may adhere to a common table. 66

XXXIX *bis*. — To the archbishops of Armagh and Tuam; all bishops, abbots, priors, and canons professing the Order of Arrouaise in Ireland. — That, in accordance with the statutes of the Order of Arrouaise, they shall not neglect to send at least one or two of their members to the annual chapter at that place. 67

XL. — The form in which the lord pope gives counsel concerning the celebration of a divorce. 68

### YEAR 1201

XLI. — To the canons of Holy Trinity, London. — He receives them and their possessions under his protection. 69

XLII. — To Thaddeus, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Ferrara, diocese of Theano. — He confirms their privileges. 70

XLIII. — To the brethren of St Remigius at Rheims. — Confirmation concerning the fishery of Courmonsteruel, twenty pounds of wax, and twenty measures of wine remitted to them by the archbishop. 74

XLIV. — To the … bishop of Strasbourg. — That he may support Otto, emperor-elect. 74

XLV. — To the archbishop of Sens. — On behalf of Clarembald, chancellor of the church of Meaux. 75

XLVI. — To Odo, bishop of Paris, and the abbot of Lagny, against the clerics of Résbac. 76

XLVII. — To Peter, archbishop of Sens, and the abbot of St Columba. — Concerning the establishment of rural deans in the church of Meaux. 77

XLVIII. — To Raymond, abbot of Nonantola. — He confirms his election. 78

XLIX. — To the dean and archdeacon of Amiens. — That they may cause the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the burgesses of St Omer, for their unjust retention of a certain watercourse and certain marshes rightfully belonging to the church of St Bertin, to be observed inviolably until fitting satisfaction has been made. 80

L. — To the abbots of St Peter, St Mary, and Tembach. — That they may cause the judgment pronounced in favour of the monks of Cella Vilmari to be observed. 81

LI. — To Andrew, archbishop of Lund. — He confirms the privileges of his church. 82

LII. — To Andrew, archbishop of Acerenza. — He confirms the privileges of the church of Acerenza. 84

LIII. — To Odo, bishop of Paris. — He settles the long-disputed lawsuit between Odo himself and the abbot of St Geneviève at Paris over possession of parochial right in the parish of Mont, defining the rights of each party. 86

LIV. — He confirms privileges to the chapel belonging to the household of William of Montpellier. 90

### YEAR 1202

LV. — To all archbishops, bishops, and others established throughout France. — On behalf of the monastery of Fountains. 90

LVI. — To the abbot and canons of St Geneviève at Paris. — By apostolic authority he confirms the agreement made between their church and that of St Victor concerning the water of Brevée. 92

LVII. — To Walter, bishop of Luni. — He confirms his agreements and exchanges with the canons of Luni, and all rights and possessions of the church of Luni. 92

LVIII. — To the abbot and convent of St Bertin. — That no one may dare, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce against them, their churches, or the chaplains serving in them, a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication. 94

LIX. — To the abbots of Blangy and Alciacus and the prior of Hesdin. — That, under threat of ecclesiastical censures, they may forbid the canons of St Omer to celebrate divine offices in the presence of the burgesses of St Omer, who have been excommunicated because of injuries inflicted on the abbot and convent of St Bertin. 94

LX. — To William, archbishop of Rheims [Col. 1193], cardinal of St Sabina; A. S. L., abbot of St Remigius; and the dean of Rheims. — That they may cause the sentence of excommunication justly pronounced against the burgesses of St Omer, on account of certain marshes belonging to the monks of St Bertin which were taken away, to be published and observed. 95

LXI. — To the archbishop of Rouen and his suffragans. — That they may defend the abbey of La Lucerne against wrongdoers and assist it in its distress. 96

### YEAR 1203

LXII. — To the chapter of Arousa. — He confirms the establishment of prebends. 96
