LXV. — To the abbot of St Columba, M., archdeacon of Sens, and the master of the schools of Orléans. — Concerning the procurations and visitations of the bishop of Paris. 100

LXVI. — To the venerable brother, bishop of Rodez, and beloved sons Hippolytus of Montsalvy and the prior of St Antoninus, diocese of Rodez: greeting and apostolic blessing. — That they may determine the controversy between the chapters of St Cecilia and St Saviour of Albi concerning the church of St Marciana. 101

LXVII. — To the bishop of Rodez, the provost of Montsalvy, and the prior of St Antoninus, diocese of Rodez. — Against the canons of Blessed Saviour of Albi. 101

LXVII *bis*. — Letter of Pelagius, cardinal of the title of St Cecilia, to William, bishop of Albi. — On the same subject. 102

LXVIII. — To the abbot and convent of St Denis at Paris. — That they may restrain the rashness of the clerics of the town of St Denis, notwithstanding an appeal lodged by those clerics. 102

LXIX. — He confirms the foundation of the collegiate church of Mirabello. 103

## Profession of Faith of the Editor

I therefore submit this completed Course of Patrology, with the utter humility of a prostrate spirit, to the judgment of the Holy See. If anything which I may have published—carried away by excessive haste, deceived by weakness of knowledge, or distracted by the immense quantity of thousands of difficult matters—has, certainly unknowingly and not deliberately, for a time injured holy doctrine, holy morality, or holy discipline, then let all that heterodox material quickly be anathema without mercy.

Whatever Pius IX, reigning happily to his greatest glory and to the highest good of the Church, approves in my works, I eagerly approve; whatever he condemns as insufficiently sound in expression, I condemn. For my knowledge vanishes before the knowledge of my Lord, my Teacher, my Judge, as a little lamp before the noonday sun. For I, as a Catholic in every respect, profess that the holy Roman Church—whose supreme Pontiff alone is its visible and immediate head under Christ, the invisible head—is the mother and mistress of all Churches, the centre of unity, the source of all jurisdiction, the interpreter of all truth, the norm of all justice, the judge of every controversy, and the infallible and unfailing guardian of holy doctrine. From these titles with which the Church is endowed, she acquires her dignity and authority; but upon me there immediately fall an equal number of duties.

For if she is mother of those Churches which are themselves fertile, childbearing sheep, how much more is she mother of me, the weakest among lambs, able to create nothing of myself and by my own strength! Indeed, she is more truly mother to me than all other mothers. Those who needed a mother to be born into the light can, when strengthened by passing years, abundantly provide for their own needs; but I can neither be born without her nor live without her. For she is the vine bringing forth and nourishing her bud; the instant my life departs from her life, I perish—I have perished. Since she is my mother, I must, like a little child, bear her name always on my lips, her good always in my mind, and her love always in my heart: rejoicing in her joys and grieving in her griefs.

If she is mistress of all Churches, how much more is she mistress of the humblest priest! I must therefore make myself obedient to her commands and impulses, knowing through her knowledge alone and wise through her wisdom alone.

If she is the centre of unity, I must seek that centre nowhere else; and therefore I must reject absolutely everything that separates itself from her and adhere to everything that adheres to her. Outside her, that is, all either rend unity as schismatics, or deny some truth as heretics, or spread the poison of some error.

If she is the source of all jurisdiction, I cannot commission myself. I must be united with her, nor can I suppose that any true authority has been entrusted to me except that which she has conferred mediately or immediately.

If she is the interpreter of all truth, I must submit all my thoughts to her; and therefore believe and embrace as true whatever she has pronounced true, but regard as false and abominate whatever she has rejected or marked as false.

If she is the norm of all justice, I must subject all my actions to her, approving as good whatever she has declared good and rejecting as evil whatever she has pronounced evil.

If she is the judge of every controversy, I must lay all my difficulties at her feet and acknowledge every matter as clear, certain, and determined as soon as she has spoken. Rome has spoken; the case is closed.

If she is the infallible guardian of the deposit of divine faith and morals, I must believe that every judgment of approval which she has issued is just, and every decree of doctrinal condemnation which she has made wholly deserved. Moreover, I must listen to her alone, since she alone can restrain the torments of a doubting mind, disperse the clouds of an erring intellect, and steady the unstable motions of my understanding—if I believe everything which she teaches must be believed, because then I shall believe everything that is true. She alone can also pour peace into my heart, removing from it every possibility of remorse and sting, if I do everything which she prescribes as to be done, because then I shall do everything that is good.

If she is unfailing, she does not belong among those things which, over these latter nineteen centuries, have undergone the alternations of life and death. On the contrary, it must be firmly fixed in our minds that everything which lives outside the Church is liable to death, however greatly it may promise duration and long life by an outward appearance of health.

O holy Roman Church! As Christ established you and endowed you with titles and prerogatives, so I profess you necessary in religion, so that, unless you existed by divine institution, human beings would have had to create you in order to govern and order the world of spirits. One must cling to you from the depths of one’s heart; and because you exist, thanks must be rendered to God for ever.

O holy Roman Church! I now eagerly desire to celebrate in print every oracle that you have issued since Christ, and I hope that the whole world may fully learn with how great wisdom, learning, providence, and holiness you have excelled in every age.

O holy Roman Church! If I should ever dare to injure you by any word, let my tongue cleave to my throat, since it would be matricidal; and if my right hand should dare to set down anything against you, let it wither and be consigned to oblivion, since it would be matricidal.

O holy Roman Church! Whenever I hear good news concerning you—for example, that a people sitting in the shadow of death has come to your light; that a notorious sinner has returned to grace with you; or that some impious writer, now your friend, assists you with the very weapons by which he formerly attacked you—then my heart is enlarged and overflows with joy. Conversely, if anyone persecutes you with calumnies or criminal acts, if anyone abandons you, I am afflicted with immense sorrow; yet I pursue you with so much greater reverence and more filial love as fiercer injuries assail you or more grievous betrayals strike you. I cling to you by a closer bond as your authority is more insolently despised, because to the sublimity of spurned dignity is added the glory of great misfortune and the sacred crown of noble sufferings. I cover your wounds with kisses and water them with tears; and from them I hope that, as once from the blood of martyrs, you may emerge more eminent in patience and glory. What are persecutions, betrayals, calumnies, and apostasies to you but mists before the sun? For a little while they seem to obscure its brightness, but the untouched and inviolable star comes forth from them like a bridegroom from his chamber. In you the majesty of old age is joined to youthful strength; for, after the example of your Founder, you shine ever ancient and ever new in form.

O holy Roman Church! I have disclosed what I think of you; my inmost being lies open to you. I shall rejoice, and it will suffice me, if—even though from myself I am neither learned nor wise—I have been prompted in my actions by a pure cause and a pure end: namely, the glory of God and of the immaculate Virgin, your good, and the honour of the Catholic clergy.

And so may God, the Best and Greatest, help me; may the immaculate Virgin Mary protect me; may the Church inspire me by her gaze; and may the clergy desire that I tirelessly cultivate, ever more successfully, all the other branches of sacred learning, after the manner of biblical and theological studies.

[Col. 1212]

L’Abbé Migne.

[Col. 0007]

## Epilogue to the Excellent Catholic Reader and Conclusion of the Whole Latin Patrology

With this volume, which completes the number of two hundred and seventeen volumes, we bring the *Patrologia Latina* to its end, continually assisted by the help of almighty God.

This *Patrologia Latina*, beginning from the apostolic age, extends to the death of Innocent III, that is, to the year 1216.

We had first intended to append various indexes at the end of this final volume; but since, besides those tables which we had ready for the press, quite a number of other indexes, devised by us for the greater convenience of readers, subsequently came crowding in, we resolved to set them all apart together in two special volumes. These indexes will present and fully explain not only writings, but also authors, arranged alphabetically, chronologically, statistically, synthetically, analytically, analogically, logically, and so forth.

From that series of tables, whose number will exceed one hundred, with subjects and topics displayed under every possible aspect, there will be opened wide for every reader an exceedingly easy and sure approach to the study and investigation of the Holy Fathers—not only for Doctors and men who devote themselves day and night to the study of sacred literature, but also for anyone entangled in the greatest occupations; indeed, even for the unlearned, the inexperienced, the untaught, or even the ignorant, and finally for one buried in sloth.

Yet the great and solemn title placed at the head of each of our volumes, and likewise of the various prospectuses by which new works were announced, promised only two indexes: namely, an analytical index and a scriptural index, or Index of Holy Scripture, embracing all the verses explained by the individual Fathers.

But being able to create and produce greater things, we shall produce and create greater things. For, while we labour, that work is a duty owed by us to the Catholic clergy; and when at last our labour is finished, it will be a source of the greatest happiness.

This being so, excellent reader, we have at last brought to completion this immense, arduous, all-embracing mass of books—this monument more enduring than bronze, whose completion no one dared to believe possible—and, relying upon the greatest confidence and hope, have brought forth into the light and throughout the Christian world, within a few—that is, nine—years, this army, not to say nation, of sacred writers and authors: the greatest of all that typography, throughout the whole world, has issued from its beginning down to the present day. But enough of this.

We now undertake the *Patrologia Graeca*. Let no one doubt that it will be shorter than the Latin *Patrologia*, and that it will be rapidly prepared, completed, and perfected. He who has accomplished greater things will certainly accomplish lesser ones. For, with the past works plainly and openly set before the eyes of all, the whole clergy of the Catholic world devoted to sacred learning will await the future with good and assured hope; for from accomplishment there will follow the capacity to accomplish.
